Here, on the other hand, are the same images, but each referred to itself; no doubt influencing one another, but in such a way that the effect always remains proportionate to the cause: this is what I call the universe. How is it to be explained that these two systems coexist, and that the same images are relatively invariable in the universe, infinitely variable in perception?

The problem at issue between realism and idealism, perhaps even between materialism and spiritualism, is thus posed, in our view, in the following terms: Whence comes it that the same images can enter simultaneously into two different systems, one in which each image varies for itself and in the well-defined measure in which it undergoes the real action of the surrounding images, the other in which all vary for one alone, and in the variable measure in which they reflect the possible action of this privileged image? Every image is internal to certain images and external to others; but of the totality of images one cannot say either that it is internal to us or that it is external to us, since interiority and exteriority are only relations between images.

To ask whether the universe exists only in our thought or outside it is therefore to state the problem in insoluble terms, assuming that they are intelligible; it is to condemn oneself to a sterile discussion, in which the terms thought, existence, universe, will necessarily be taken on either side in quite different senses. In order to settle the debate, one must first find common ground on which the struggle may be engaged, and since, for both sides, we grasp things only in the form of images, it is in terms of images, and of images alone, that we must pose the problem.

Now, no philosophical doctrine disputes that the same images can enter simultaneously into two distinct systems, one belonging to science, and in which each image, being referred only to itself, retains an absolute value, the other being the world of consciousness, in which all images are regulated by a central image, our body, whose variations they follow. The question posed between realism and idealism then becomes very clear: what relations do these two systems of images maintain with one another? And it is easy to see that subjective idealism consists in deriving the first system from the second, materialist realism in deriving the second from the first.

The realist begins, in fact, with the universe, that is to say, with a set of images governed in their mutual relations by immutable laws, in which effects remain proportionate to their causes, and whose characteristic is to have no centre, all images unfolding on a single plane that is prolonged indefinitely. But he is indeed compelled to acknowledge that, in addition to this system, there are perceptions, that is to say, systems in which these same images are referred to one alone among them, are arranged around it on different planes, and are transfigured in their totality by slight modifications
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 16

of this central image. It is from this perception that the idealist begins, and in the system of images he gives himself there is a privileged image, his body, by which the other images are regulated. But as soon as he wishes to connect the present with the past and foresee the future, he is indeed obliged to abandon this central position, to replace all the images on the same plane, to suppose that they no longer vary for him but for themselves, and to treat them as if they formed part of a system in which each change gives the exact measure of its cause. Only on this condition does the science of the universe become possible; and since this science exists, since it succeeds in foreseeing the future, the hypothesis on which it is founded is not an arbitrary hypothesis.

The first system alone is given to present experience; but we believe in the second merely because we affirm the continuity of past, present, and future. Thus, in idealism as in realism, one posits one of the two systems, and seeks to deduce the other from it.

But, in this deduction, neither realism nor idealism can succeed, because neither of the two systems of images is implied in the other, and each is sufficient unto itself. If you give yourself the system of images that has no centre, and in which each element possesses its absolute magnitude and value, I do not see why this system should add to itself a second, in which each image takes on an indeterminate value, subject to all the vicissitudes of a central image. In order to generate perception, one will therefore have to invoke some deus ex machina such as the materialist hypothesis of consciousness as epiphenomenon.

Among all the images with absolute changes that one will first have posited, one will choose the one we call our brain, and will confer upon the internal states of this image the singular privilege of being doubled, no one knows how, by the reproduction, this time relative and variable, of all the others.

It is true that one will then pretend to attach no importance to this representation, to see in it a phosphorescence left behind by cerebral vibrations: as if cerebral substance, cerebral vibrations, set within the images composing this representation, could be of a nature other than theirs! Every realism will therefore make perception an accident, and consequently a mystery. But conversely, if you give yourself a system of unstable images arranged around a privileged centre and profoundly modified by imperceptible displacements of this centre, you first exclude the order of nature, that order indifferent to the point at which one places oneself and to the term from which one begins.

You will be able to restore this order only by invoking in your turn a deus ex machina, by supposing, through an arbitrary hypothesis, I know not what pre-established harmony between things and the mind, or at least, to speak like Kant, between sensibility and understanding. Science will then become an accident, and its success a mystery.—You can therefore deduce neither the first system of images from the second, nor the second from the first, and these two opposed doctrines, realism and idealism, when they are finally replaced on the same ground, come, in opposite directions, up against the same obstacle.

If we now dig beneath the two doctrines, we should dis-cover in them a common postulate, which we shall formulate thus—the perception has a wholly speculative interest; it is pure knowledge. The whole discussion concerns the rank that must be assigned to this knowledge with respect to scientific knowledge. Some give themselves the order required by science, and see in perception only a confused and provisional science. Others posit
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 17
perception first, raise it to the absolute, and regard science as a symbolic expression of the real. But for both alike, to perceive means above all to know.

Now, it is this postulate that we dispute. It is contradicted by an examination, even the most superficial, of the structure of the nervous system throughout the animal series. And it cannot be accepted without profoundly obscuring the threefold problem of matter, consciousness, and their relation.

Do we in fact follow, step by step, the progress of external perception from the monera to the higher vertebrates? We find that, in the state of a simple protoplasmic mass, living matter is already irritable and contractile, that it undergoes the influence of external stimuli, that it responds to them by mechanical, physical, and chemical reactions. As one rises in the series of organisms, one sees physiological work become divided. Nerve cells appear, become differentiated, tend to group themselves into a system. At the same time, the animal reacts to external excitation by more varied movements.

But even when the shock received is not immediately prolonged into a completed movement, it seems simply to await the opportunity for it, and the same impression which conveys to the organism the modifications of its environment determines it, or prepares it, to adapt itself to them. In the higher vertebrates, the distinction undoubtedly becomes radical between pure automatism, which is located especially in the spinal cord, and voluntary activity, which requires the intervention of the brain. One might imagine that the impression received, instead of still unfolding into movements, becomes spiritualized into knowledge. But it suffices to compare the structure of the brain with that of the spinal cord to be convinced that there is only a difference of complication, and not a difference of nature, between the functions of the brain and the reflex activity of the medullary system. What happens, in fact, in reflex action?

The centripetal movement communicated by excitation is immediately reflected, through the intermediary of the nerve cells of the spinal cord, into a centrifugal movement determining a muscular contraction. In what, on the other hand, does the function of the cerebral system consist?

The peripheral shock, instead of propagating itself directly to the motor cell of the spinal cord and impressing upon the muscle a necessary contraction, first rises to the encephalon, then descends again to the same motor cells of the spinal cord which intervened in the reflex movement. What, then, has it gained by this detour, and what has it gone to seek in the so-called sensory cells of the cerebral cortex? I do not understand, I shall never understand, that it draws from them the miraculous power to transform itself into a representation of things, and moreover I hold this hypothesis to be useless, as will presently be seen.

But what I see very clearly is that these cells of the various so-called sensory regions of the cortex, cells interposed between the terminal arborizations of the centripetal fibres and the motor cells of the Rolandic zone, enable the received shock to reach, at will, this or that motor mechanism of the spinal cord and thus to choose its effect. The more these interposed cells multiply, the more they emit amoeboid prolongations capable, doubtless, of approaching one another in various ways, the more numerous and varied also will be the paths capable of opening before one and the same shock coming from the periphery, and the more, consequently, there will be systems of movements among which one and the same excitation will leave a choice.
The brain, therefore, must in our view be nothing other than a kind of central telephone exchange: its role is to “put through the communication,” or to make it wait. It adds
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 18

nothing to what it receives; but since all the perceptive organs send their final prolongations to it, and since all the motor mechanisms of the spinal cord and the medulla have their appointed representatives there, it truly constitutes a centre, where peripheral excitation is brought into relation with this or that motor mechanism, chosen and no longer imposed. On the other hand, since an enormous multitude of motor paths may open in this substance, all together, to one and the same shock coming from the periphery, this shock has the capacity to divide itself there indefinitely and, consequently, to lose itself in innumerable, merely nascent motor reactions.

Thus the role of the brain is sometimes to conduct the movement received to a chosen organ of reaction, sometimes to open to this movement the totality of motor paths so that it may trace there all the possible reactions with which it is pregnant, and so that it may analyse itself by dispersing itself. In other words, the brain seems to us to be an instrument of analysis in relation to the movement received and an instrument of selection in relation to the movement executed. But in either case, its role is limited to transmitting and dividing movement. And, no more in the higher centres of the cortex than in the spinal cord, do the nervous elements work with a view to knowledge: they merely sketch out all at once a plurality of possible actions, or organize one of them.

That is to say that the nervous system has nothing of an apparatus intended to manufacture or even to prepare representations. Its function is to receive excitations, to set up motor apparatuses, and to present the greatest possible number of these apparatuses to a given excitation. The more it develops, the more numerous and more distant become the points in space which it brings into relation with ever more complex motor mechanisms: thus grows the latitude it leaves to our action, and therein precisely consists its increasing perfection. But if the nervous system is constructed, from one end to the other of the animal series, with a view to action that is less and less necessary, must one not think that perception, whose progress is regulated by its own, is also wholly oriented toward action, not toward pure knowledge?

And then, must not the increasing richness of this perception itself simply symbolize the increasing share of indetermination left to the choice of the living being in its conduct in relation to things? Let us therefore take this indetermination as the true principle. Once this indetermination has been posited, let us seek whether one might not deduce from it the possibility and even the necessity of conscious perception.

In other words, let us posit this system of interdependent and closely connected images which is called the material world, and imagine here and there in this system centres of real action represented by living matter: I say that around each of these centres images must be arranged which are subordinate to its position and variable with it; I say consequently that conscious perception must occur, and that, moreover, it is possible to understand how this perception arises.

Let us first observe that a rigorous law connects the extent of conscious perception with the intensity of action at the disposal of the living being. If our hypothesis is well founded, this perception appears at the precise moment when a shock received by matter is not prolonged into a necessary reaction. In the case of a rudimentary organism, it will indeed require immediate contact with the object of interest for the shock to occur, and then the reaction can scarcely be delayed. Thus, in the lower species, touch is at once passive and active; it serves to recognize a prey and to seize it, to
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 19

feel danger and to make an effort to avoid it. The varied prolongations of protozoa, the ambulacra of echinoderms, are organs of movement as well as of tactile perception; the stinging apparatus of coelenterates is an instrument of perception at the same time as a means of defence. In a word, the more immediate the reaction must be, the more perception must resemble a simple contact, and the complete process of perception and reaction then scarcely differs from mechanical impulse followed by a necessary movement. But as the reaction becomes more uncertain, as it leaves more room for hesitation, so too increases the distance at which the action of the object that interests it makes itself felt upon the animal.

Through sight, through hearing, it enters into relation with an ever greater number of things; it undergoes influences from increasingly distant objects; and whether these objects promise it an advantage or threaten it with danger, promises and threats defer their fulfilment. The share of independence at the disposal of a living being, or, as we shall say, the zone of indetermination surrounding its activity, thus makes it possible to assess a priori the number and remoteness of the things with which it is in relation. Whatever this relation may be, whatever therefore the intimate nature of perception may be, one may affirm that the amplitude of perception measures exactly the indetermination of the consequent action, and consequently state this law: perception commands space in the exact proportion in which action commands time.

But why does this relation of the organism to objects more or less distant take the particular form of a conscious perception? We have examined what happens in the organized body; we have seen movements transmitted or inhibited, metamorphosed into completed actions or scattered into nascent actions. These movements seemed to us to concern action, and action alone; they remain absolutely foreign to the process of representation. We then considered action itself and the indetermination surrounding it, an indetermination implied in the structure of the nervous system, and for the sake of which this system appears to have been constructed far more than for the sake of representation.

From this indetermination, accepted as a fact, we were able to conclude the necessity of a perception, that is to say, of a variable relation between the living being and the more or less distant influences of the objects that interest it. Whence comes it that this perception is consciousness, and why does everything happen as if this consciousness were born of the internal movements of cerebral substance?

To answer this question, we shall first greatly simplify the conditions under which conscious perception is accomplished. In fact, there is no perception that is not impregnated with memories. With the immediate and present data of our senses we mingle thousands upon thousands of details from our past experience. Most often, these memories displace our real perceptions, from which we then retain only a few indications, simple “signs” intended to recall old images to us. The convenience and rapidity of perception are at this price; but from this also arise illusions of every kind. Nothing prevents us from substituting for this perception, wholly penetrated by our past, the perception that an adult and formed consciousness would have, but one enclosed in the present and absorbed, to the exclusion of every other task, in the task of moulding itself upon the external object.
Will it be said that we are making an arbitrary hypothesis, and that this ideal perception, obtained by the elimination of individual accidents, no longer corresponds at all to reality? But we hope
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 20

precisely to show that individual accidents are grafted onto this impersonal perception, that this perception lies at the very basis of our knowledge of things, and that it is through having misunderstood it, through not having distinguished it from what memory adds to it or subtracts from it, that perception as a whole has been made into a kind of inner and subjective vision, differing from memory only by its greater intensity. Such, then, will be our first hypothesis. But it naturally entails another. However brief a perception may be supposed to be, it always occupies a certain duration, and consequently requires an effort of memory, which prolongs a plurality of moments one into another.

Indeed, as we shall try to show, the “subjectivity” of sensible qualities consists above all in a kind of contraction of the real, effected by our memory. In short, memory in these two forms—insofar as it covers a ground of immediate perception with a layer of memories and insofar also as it contracts a multiplicity of moments—constitutes the principal contribution of individual consciousness to perception, the subjective side of our knowledge of things; and, by neglecting this contribution in order to make our idea clearer, we shall advance much further than is fitting along the path upon which we have embarked. We shall merely have to retrace our steps afterwards, and to correct, above all by reintegrating memory, whatever may be excessive in our conclusions.

What follows, then, must be regarded only as a schematic exposition, and we ask that, provisionally, perception be understood to mean not my concrete and complex perception, the one swollen by my memories and always offering a certain thickness of duration, but pure perception, a perception which exists in law rather than in fact, the perception that a being situated where I am, living as I live, but absorbed in the present, and capable, by the elimination of memory in all its forms, of obtaining from matter a vision at once immediate and instantaneous, would have. Let us therefore place ourselves in this hypothesis, and ask how conscious perception is to be explained.

To deduce consciousness would be a very bold undertaking, but it is not really necessary here, because in positing the material world one has given oneself a set of images, and moreover it is impossible to give oneself anything else. No theory of matter escapes this necessity. Reduce matter to atoms in motion: these atoms, even though stripped of physical qualities, are nevertheless determined only in relation to a possible vision and contact, the former without illumination and the latter without materiality.

Condense the atom into centres of force, dissolve it into vortices evolving in a continuous fluid: this fluid, these movements, these centres are themselves determined only in relation to a powerless touch, an ineffective impulse, a colourless light; they are still images. It is true that an image may be without being perceived; it may be present without being represented; and the distance between these two terms, presence and representation, seems precisely to measure the interval between matter itself and the conscious perception we have of it. But let us examine these things more closely and see precisely what this difference consists in.

If there were more in the second term than in the first, if, in passing from presence to representation, it were necessary to add something, the distance would be uncrossable, and the passage from matter to perception would remain shrouded in an impenetrable mystery. It would not be the same if one could pass from the first term to the second by way of diminution, and if the representation of an image were less
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 21

than its mere presence; for then it would suffice that present images be compelled to relinquish something of themselves for their mere presence to convert them into representations. Now, here is the image that I call a material object; I have its representation. Whence comes it that it does not appear to be in itself what it is for me? It is because, being bound up with the totality of the other images, it continues itself in those that follow it as it prolonged those that precede it. To transform its pure and simple existence into representation, it would suffice suddenly to suppress what follows it, what precedes it, and also what fills it, retaining only its outer crust, its superficial film.

What distinguishes it, a present image, an objective reality, from a represented image, is the necessity under which it lies of acting, through each of its points, upon all the points of the other images, of transmitting the totality of what it receives, of opposing to every action an equal and contrary reaction, of being, finally, only a path along which the modifications that propagate themselves throughout the immensity of the universe pass in every direction. I would convert it into representation if I could isolate it, if above all I could isolate its envelope. Representation is indeed there, but always virtual, neutralized, at the moment when it would pass into actuality, by the obligation to continue itself and lose itself in something else.

What is needed to obtain this conversion is not to illuminate the object, but on the contrary to obscure certain aspects of it, to diminish it by the greater part of itself, so that the residue, instead of remaining set into its surroundings like a thing, detaches itself from them like a picture. Now, if living beings constitute in the universe

“centres of indetermination,” and if the degree of this indetermination is measured by the number and the elevation of their functions, one can understand that their mere presence may amount to the suppression of all the parts of objects in which their functions have no interest. They will allow themselves, as it were, to be traversed by those among external actions that are indifferent to them; the others, isolated, will become “perceptions” by their very isolation. Everything will then take place for us as though we reflected upon surfaces the light emanating from them, light which, always propagating itself, would never have been revealed. The images surrounding us will seem to turn toward our body—but this time illuminated—the face that interests it; they will detach from their substance what we have arrested in passing, what we are capable of influencing.

Indifferent to one another by reason of the radical mechanism binding them, they reciprocally present to one another all their faces at once, which amounts to saying that they act and react upon one another through all their elementary parts, and that none of them, consequently, is consciously perceived or perceives. But if, on the contrary, they encounter somewhere a certain spontaneity of reaction, their action is diminished by so much, and this diminution of their action is precisely the representation we have of them. Our representation of things would thus arise, in short, from their coming to be reflected against our freedom.

When a ray of light passes from one medium into another, it generally traverses it by changing direction. But the respective densities of the two media may be such that, for a certain angle of incidence, refraction is no longer possible. Then total reflection occurs. A virtual image of the luminous point is formed, which in some way symbolizes the impossibility for the light rays to pursue their path. Perception is a phenomenon of the same kind. What is given is the totality of images of the material world together with the totality of their internal elements. But if
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 22

you suppose centres of genuine activity, that is to say spontaneous activity, the rays that reach them and that would concern this activity, instead of traversing them, will seem to return and trace the contours of the object sending them forth. There will be nothing positive there, nothing added to the image, nothing new. Objects will merely relinquish something of their real action in order thus to figure their virtual action, that is to say, fundamentally, the possible influence of the living being upon them. Perception closely resembles those phenomena of reflection that arise from impeded refraction; it is like a mirage effect.

This amounts to saying that, for images, there is a mere difference of degree, and not of nature, between being and being consciously perceived. The reality of matter consists in the totality of its elements and of their actions of every kind. Our representation of matter is the measure of our possible action upon bodies; it results from the elimination of what does not concern our needs and, more generally, our functions. In one sense, one could say that the perception of any unconscious material point, in its instantaneousness, is infinitely vaster and more complete than ours, since this point receives and transmits the actions of all the points of the material world, whereas our consciousness reaches only certain parts of it from certain sides. Consciousness—in the case of external perception—consists precisely in this choice.
But in this necessary poverty of our conscious perception there is something positive, and something that already heralds mind: it is, in the etymological sense of the word, discernment.

The whole difficulty of the problem occupying us arises from the fact that perception is represented as a photographic view of things, taken from a determinate point with a special apparatus such as the organ of perception, and subsequently developed in cerebral substance by some process, I know not what, of chemical and psychical elaboration. But how can one fail to see that the photograph, if there is a photograph, is already taken, already printed, within things themselves and for all points in space? No metaphysics, indeed no physics, can evade this conclusion.

Compose the universe of atoms: in each of them are felt, in quality and quantity, varying according to distance, the actions exerted by all the atoms of matter. Of centres of force? The lines of force emitted in every direction by all the centres direct upon each centre the influences of the entire material world. Of monads, finally? Each monad, as Leibniz held, is the mirror of the universe. Thus everyone agrees on this point. Only, if one considers any place whatever in the universe, one may say that the action of the whole of matter passes there without resistance and without loss, and that the photograph of the whole is translucent there: behind the plate there is lacking a black screen against which the image would stand out.
Our “zones of indetermination” would, in a sense, play the role of a screen.
They add nothing to what is; they merely cause real action to pass through and virtual action to remain.

This is not a hypothesis. We confine ourselves to formulating the data without which no theory of perception can dispense. No psychologist, indeed, will undertake the study of external perception without positing at least the possibility of a material world, that is to say, fundamentally, the virtual perception of all things. Within this merely possible material mass one will isolate
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 23

the particular object that I call my body, and within this body the perceptive centres: one will show me the disturbance arriving from any point whatever in space, propagating itself along the nerves, reaching the centres. But here a dramatic turn takes place. This material world that surrounded the body, this body that shelters the brain, this brain in which centres were distinguished, are abruptly dismissed; and, as under a magic wand, the representation of what had first been posited is made to arise, in the manner of something absolutely new.

This representation is pushed outside space, so that it may have nothing further in common with the matter from which one started: as for matter itself, one would like to dispense with it, yet cannot, because its phenomena present among themselves an order so rigorous, so indifferent to the point one chooses as origin, that this regularity and this indifference truly constitute an independent existence. One must then resign oneself to retaining matter's phantom. At least it will be stripped of all the qualities that give life.

In an amorphous space, figures that move will be cut out; or else (which comes to approximately the same thing), one will imagine relations of magnitude composing themselves with one another, functions evolving by developing their content: from then on, representation, laden with the spoils of matter, will unfold freely in an unextended consciousness. But it is not enough to cut; one must sew.

These qualities which you have detached from their material support, it will now be necessary to explain how they are to rejoin it. Every attribute from which you diminish matter widens the interval between representation and its object. If you make this matter unextended, how will it receive extension? If you reduce it to homogeneous movement, whence, then, will quality arise? Above all, how are we to imagine a relation between the thing and the image, between matter and thought, since each of these two terms possesses, by definition, only what the other lacks? Thus difficulties will arise beneath your feet, and every effort you make to dispel one of them can only resolve it into many others. What, then, do we ask of you?

Simply to renounce your stroke of the magic wand, and to continue along the path upon which you first entered. You had shown us external images reaching the organs of sense, modifying the nerves, propagating their influence into the brain. Go to the end. Movement will pass through cerebral substance, not without having remained there, and will then unfold into voluntary action. There you have the whole mechanism of perception. As for perception itself, as image, you need not retrace its genesis, since you posited it at the outset and since, moreover, you could not but posit it: in giving yourselves the brain, in giving yourselves the slightest particle of matter, did you not give yourselves the totality of images?

What you therefore have to explain is not how perception arises, but how it is limited, since it would, in principle, be the image of the whole, and is, in fact, reduced to what interests you. But if it is distinguished precisely from the pure and simple image in that its parts are ordered in relation to a variable centre, its limitation is easily understood: indefinite in principle, it is restricted, in fact, to delineating the share of indetermination left to the movements of that special image which you call your body. And consequently, conversely, the indetermination of the movements of the body, such as it results from the structure of the brain's grey substance, gives the exact measure of the extent of your perception.

We must not therefore be surprised if everything takes place as though your perception resulted from the inner movements of the brain and emerged, in some way, from the cortical centres. It cannot come from them, for the brain is
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 24

an image like the others, enveloped in the mass of the other images, and it would be absurd for the container to emerge from the contained. But since the structure of the brain gives the detailed plan of the movements from among which you have a choice, since, on the other hand, the portion of external images which seems to turn back upon itself in order to constitute perception delineates precisely all the points of the universe upon which these movements would have a hold, conscious perception and cerebral modification correspond rigorously. The reciprocal dependence of these two terms thus arises simply from the fact that both are functions of a third, which is the indetermination of willing.

Let there be, for example, a luminous point P whose rays act upon the different points a, b, c, of the retina. At this point P science locates vibrations of a certain amplitude and a certain duration. At this same point P consciousness perceives light. In the course of this study, we propose to show that both are right, and that there is no essential difference between this light and these movements, provided that movement is restored to the unity, indivisibility, and qualitative heterogeneity which an abstract mechanics denies it, provided also that sensible qualities are seen as so many contractions effected by our memory: science and consciousness would coincide in the instantaneous. Let us confine ourselves for the moment to saying, without probing too deeply here into the meaning of the words, that point P sends luminous vibrations to the retina.
What will happen? If the visual image of point P were not given, there would be reason to seek how it is formed, and one would very quickly find oneself confronted with an insoluble problem.

But however one goes about it, one cannot help positing it first: the sole question, then, is to know why and how this image is selected to form part of my perception, while an infinity of other images remain excluded from it. Now, I see that the vibrations transmitted from point P to the various retinal corpuscles are conducted to the subcortical and cortical optic centres, often also to other centres, and that these centres sometimes transmit them to motor mechanisms, sometimes provisionally arrest them. The nervous elements involved are therefore indeed what gives the received vibration its efficacy; they symbolize the indetermination of willing; upon their integrity this indetermination depends; and consequently every lesion of these elements, by diminishing our possible action, will diminish perception by as much.

In other words, if there exist in the material world points where the vibrations received are not mechanically transmitted, if there are, as we were saying, zones of indetermination, these zones must precisely be found along the path of what is called the sensorimotor process; and from then on everything must take place as though the rays P a, P b, P c were perceived along this path and subsequently projected at P. Moreover, if this indetermination is something that escapes experimentation and calculation, the same is not true of the nervous elements upon which the impression is received and transmitted. It is therefore with these elements that physiologists and psychologists must concern themselves; upon them will be regulated, and through them will be explained, every detail of external perception.

One may say, if one wishes, that excitation, after travelling along these elements, after reaching the centre, is there converted into a conscious image which is subsequently externalized at point P. But in expressing oneself thus, one merely complies with the requirements of scientific method; one does not at all describe the real process. In fact, there is no unextended image that would be formed in consciousness and then projected at P.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 25

The truth is that point P, the rays it emits, the retina, and the nervous elements involved form a single interdependent whole; that the luminous point P is part of this whole; and that it is indeed at P, and not elsewhere, that the image of P is formed and perceived.

In thus representing things to ourselves, we merely return to the naïve conviction of common sense. We all began by believing that we entered into the object itself, that we perceived it in it, and not in ourselves. If the psychologist disdains an idea so simple, so close to reality, it is because the intracerebral process, that minute part of perception, seems to him to be the equivalent of the entire perception. Suppress the perceived object while retaining this internal process; it seems to him that the image of the object remains.

And his belief is easily explained: there are many states, such as hallucination and dream, in which images arise that imitate external perception in every respect. Since, in such a case, the object has disappeared while the brain remains, it is concluded from this that the cerebral phenomenon suffices for the production of the image. But one must not forget that, in all psychological states of this kind, memory plays the leading role. Now, we shall try to show later that, once perception is admitted as we understand it, memory must arise, and that this memory, no more than perception itself, has its real and complete condition in a cerebral state. Without yet undertaking the examination of these two points, let us confine ourselves to presenting a very simple observation, which is moreover not new.

Many congenitally blind persons have their visual centres intact: yet they live and die without ever having formed a visual image. Such an image can therefore appear only if the external object has played a role at least once: consequently, at least the first time, it must have actually entered into representation. Now, for the moment we ask for nothing else, for it is pure perception that we are treating here, and not perception complicated by memory. Reject, then, the contribution of memory; consider perception in its raw state; you are indeed compelled to recognize that there is never an image without an object. But as soon as you add to the intracerebral processes the external object which is their cause, I see very well how the image of this object is given with it and in it; I do not at all see how it would arise from cerebral movement.

When a lesion of the nerves or of the centres interrupts the course of the nervous vibration, perception is diminished by as much. Should one be surprised by this? The role of the nervous system is to make use of this vibration, to convert it into practical movements, actually or virtually carried out. If, for one reason or another, excitation no longer passes through, it would be strange if the corresponding perception still took place, since this perception would then place our body in relation with points in space that would no longer directly invite it to make a choice.

Sever an animal's optic nerve; the vibration issuing from the luminous point is no longer transmitted to the brain and thence to the motor nerves; the thread which linked the external object to the animal's motor mechanisms, including the optic nerve, is broken: visual perception has therefore become powerless, and it is precisely in this powerlessness that unconsciousness consists. That matter may be perceived without the aid of a nervous system, without sense organs, is not theoretically inconceivable; but it is practically impossible, because a perception of this kind would serve no purpose. It would suit a phantom, not a living being, that is-
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 26

to say, an acting being. The living body is represented as an empire within an empire, the nervous system as a separate being, whose function would be first to elaborate perceptions, then to create movements. The truth is that my nervous system, interposed between the objects that set my body vibrating and those which I might influence, plays the role of a simple conductor, which transmits, distributes, or inhibits movement. This conductor consists of an enormous multitude of threads stretched from the periphery to the centre and from the centre to the periphery. As many as there are threads going from the periphery towards the centre, so many are there points in space capable of soliciting my will and of posing, so to speak, an elementary question to my motor activity: each question posed is precisely what is called a perception.

Thus perception is diminished by one of its elements each time one of the so-called sensory threads is cut, because then some part of the external object becomes powerless to solicit activity; and likewise each time a stable habit has been acquired, because then the ready-made response makes the question useless. What disappears in one case as in the other is the apparent reflection of the vibration upon itself, the return of light to the image from which it departs, or rather that dissociation, that discernment, by which perception is detached from the image. One may therefore say that the detail of perception is moulded exactly upon that of the so-called sensory nerves, but that perception, as a whole, has its true raison d'être in the body's tendency to move.

What generally creates an illusion on this point is the apparent indifference of our movements to the excitation that occasions them. It seems that the movement of my body to reach and modify an object remains the same, whether I have been apprised of its existence by hearing, or whether it has been revealed to me by sight or touch. My motor activity then becomes an entity apart, a kind of reservoir from which movement emerges at will, always the same for the same action, whatever the kind of image that has solicited its production.

But the truth is that the character of outwardly identical movements is inwardly modified according as they reply to a visual, tactile, or auditory impression. I perceive a multitude of objects in space; each one of them, as a visual form, solicits my activity. I suddenly lose sight. No doubt I still have at my disposal the same quantity and the same quality of movements in space; but these movements can no longer be coordinated with visual impressions; henceforth they will have to follow tactile impressions, for example, and a new arrangement will doubtless take shape in the brain; the protoplasmic extensions of the motor nervous elements in the cortex will be related, this time, to a much smaller number of those nervous elements called sensory.

My activity is indeed truly diminished, in the sense that, if I can produce the same movements, objects provide me with fewer occasions for them. And consequently, the abrupt interruption of optical conduction has had the essential, profound effect of suppressing an entire part of the solicitations of my activity: now this solicitation, as we have seen, is perception itself. Here we touch with our finger upon the error of those who make perception arise from sensory stimulation properly so called, and not from a kind of question put to our motor activity. They detach this motor activity from the perceptual process, and, as it seems to survive the abolition of perception, they conclude that perception is localized in the nerve elements called sensory. But the truth is that it is no more in the centres
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 27
sensory than in the motor centres; it measures the complexity of their relations, and exists where it appears.

Psychologists who have studied childhood know well that our representation begins by being impersonal. It is little by little, and by dint of inductions, that it adopts our body as its centre and becomes our representation. The mechanism of this operation is, moreover, easy to understand. As

my body moves through space, all the other images vary; this one, on the contrary, remains invariable. I must therefore indeed make it a centre, to which I shall relate all the other images. My belief in an external world does not come, cannot come, from my projecting outside myself unextended sensations: how would these sensations acquire extension, and from where could I derive the notion of exteriority? But if it is granted, as experience attests, that the totality of images is given first, I see very well how my body ends up occupying a privileged position in this totality. And I also understand how there then arises the notion of the interior and the exterior, which at the outset is only the distinction between my body and other bodies.

Indeed, begin with my body, as is ordinarily done; you will never make me understand how impressions received at the surface of my body, and which concern only that body, will constitute themselves for me as independent objects and form an external world.

Give me, on the contrary, images in general; my body will necessarily end up standing out among them as a distinct thing, since they change incessantly and it remains invariable. The distinction between the interior and the exterior will thus be reduced to that between the part and the whole. There is first the totality of images; there are, in this totality, “centres of action”

against which the interesting images seem to be reflected; thus perceptions arise and actions are prepared. My body is that which stands out at the centre of these perceptions; my person is the being to which these actions must be related. Things become clearer if one thus proceeds from the periphery of representation to the centre, as the child does, as immediate experience and common sense invite us to do. Everything, on the contrary, becomes obscured, and problems multiply, if one claims, with the theoreticians, to proceed from the centre to the periphery. Whence then comes this idea of an external world artificially constructed, piece by piece, out of unextended sensations, of which one understands neither how they could come to form an extended surface nor how they could then be projected outside our body?

Why is it desired, contrary to all appearance, that I should proceed from my conscious self to my body, then from my body to other bodies, whereas in fact I place myself from the outset in the material world in general, in order progressively to delimit this centre of action that will be called my body and thus distinguish it from all the others? There are, in this belief in the initially unextended character of our external perception, so many illusions combined; one would find, in this idea that we project outside ourselves purely internal states, so many misunderstandings, so many lame answers to ill-posed questions, that we could not claim to shed light upon it all at once.

We hope that light will gradually be shed, as we show more clearly, behind these illusions, the metaphysical confusion of undivided extension and homogeneous space, the psychological confusion of “pure perception” and memory. But they are also connected with real facts, which we can point out even now in order to correct their interpretation.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 28

The first of these facts is that our senses need education. Neither sight nor touch immediately succeeds in locating its impressions. A series of comparisons and inductions is necessary, by means of which we gradually coordinate our impressions with one another. From this one leaps to the idea of sensations essentially unextended, which would constitute extension by juxtaposing themselves. But who does not see that, in the very hypothesis in which we have placed ourselves, our senses will likewise need education—not, doubtless, in order to agree with things, but in order to agree among themselves? Here, amid all the images, is a certain image which I call my body and whose virtual action is expressed by an apparent reflection, upon themselves, of the surrounding images.
As many kinds of possible action as there are for my body, so many different systems of reflection there will be for other bodies, and each of these systems will correspond to one of my senses.

My body therefore behaves like an image that reflected others by analysing them from the point of view of the various actions to be exerted upon them. And consequently, each of the qualities perceived by my different senses in the same object symbolizes a certain direction of my activity, a certain need. Now, will all these perceptions of one body by my various senses, when united, give the complete image of that body? No, doubtless, since they have been gathered from the totality. To perceive all the influences from all the points of all bodies would be to descend to the state of a material object.

To perceive consciously means to choose, and consciousness consists above all in this practical discernment. The diverse perceptions of the same object supplied by my various senses will not therefore, by being united, reconstitute the complete image of the object; they will remain separated from one another by intervals which measure, in a way, so many gaps in my needs: it is to fill these intervals that an education of the senses is necessary.

The purpose of this education is to harmonize my senses with one another, to restore between their data a continuity that has been broken by the very discontinuity of my body's needs, and finally to reconstruct approximately the whole of the material object. Thus, in our hypothesis, the necessity of an education of the senses will be explained. Let us compare this explanation with the preceding one. In the first, unextended sensations of sight will combine with unextended sensations of touch and of the other senses in order to give, by their synthesis, the idea of a material object. But first, one does not see how these sensations will acquire extension, nor above all how, once extension has been acquired in principle, the actual preference of one such sensation for one point in space will be explained.

And then one may ask by what happy accord, by virtue of what pre-established harmony, these sensations of different kinds will coordinate together to form a stable object, henceforth solidified, common to my experience and to that of all human beings, subject, in relation to other objects, to those inflexible rules called the laws of nature.

In the second, on the contrary, the “data of our different senses” are qualities of things, perceived first in them rather than in us: is it surprising that they join together, when abstraction alone has separated them?—In the first hypothesis, the material object is nothing of all that we perceive: on one side one will place the conscious principle with sensible qualities, on the other a matter of which nothing can be said, and which is defined by negations because it has first been stripped of everything that reveals it. In the second, an ever more thorough knowledge of matter is possible. Far from subtracting from it anything perceived, we must, on the contrary, bring all sensible qualities closer together, rediscover their kinship, restore between them the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 29

continuity that our needs have broken. Our perception of matter is then no longer relative or subjective, at least in principle and apart from, as we shall shortly see, affection and above all memory; it is simply split up by the multiplicity of our needs.—In the first hypothesis, spirit is as unknowable as matter, for it is attributed the indefinable capacity to evoke sensations, one does not know whence, and to project them, one does not know why, into a space where they will form bodies. In the second, the role of consciousness is clearly defined: consciousness means possible action; and the forms acquired by spirit, those which veil its essence from us, will have to be set aside in the light of this second principle.
Thus, in our hypothesis, one glimpses the possibility of distinguishing spirit more clearly from matter, and of bringing them together.
But let us set aside this first point, and come to the second.

The second fact alleged would consist in what was for a long time called “the specific energy of the nerves.” It is known that the excitation of the optic nerve by an external shock or by an electric current will produce a visual sensation, that this same electric current, applied to the auditory or glossopharyngeal nerve, will make one perceive a taste or hear a sound. From these very particular facts one passes to the two very general laws that different causes, acting upon the same nerve, excite the same sensation, and that the same cause, acting upon different nerves, provokes different sensations. And from these laws themselves one infers that our sensations are simply signals, that the role of each sense is to translate into its own language homogeneous and mechanical movements occurring in space.

Hence, finally, the idea of splitting our perception into two distinct parts, henceforth incapable of rejoining one another: on one side homogeneous movements in space, on the other unextended sensations in consciousness. It does not belong to us to enter into the examination of the physiological problems raised by the interpretation of the two laws: however these laws are understood, whether specific energy is attributed to the nerves or referred to the centres, one encounters insurmountable difficulties. But the laws themselves appear increasingly problematic. Lotze had already suspected their falsity. In order to believe in them, he awaited “that sound waves should give the eye the sensation of light, or that luminous vibrations should make the ear hear a sound 1.”

The truth is that all the alleged facts seem reducible to a single type: the single stimulus capable of producing different sensations, the multiple stimuli capable of engendering one and the same sensation, are either the electric current or a mechanical cause capable of bringing about in the organ a modification of electrical equilibrium. Now, one may ask whether electrical excitation might not include diverse components, corresponding objectively to sensations of different kinds, and whether the role of each sense would not simply be to extract from the whole the component that concerns it: then indeed it would be the same excitations that gave the same sensations, and diverse excitations that provoked different sensations.

To speak more precisely, it is difficult to admit that the electrification of the tongue, for example, does not occasion chemical modifications; now, it is these modifications that we call, in all cases, tastes. On the other hand, if the physicist has been able to identify light with an electro-magnetic disturbance, 1
LOTZE. Metaphysics, p. 528 ff.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the relation of the body to the mind. (1939) 30

one may conversely say that what he here calls an electro-magnetic disturbance is light, so that it would indeed be light that the optic nerve objectively perceived in electrification. For no sense did the doctrine of specific energy seem more solidly established than for hearing; nowhere, too, has the real existence of the perceived thing become more probable. We do not dwell on these facts, because their exposition and thorough discussion will be found in a recent work 1. Let us merely observe that the sensations of which we speak here are not images perceived by us outside our body, but rather affections localized in our body itself.

Now it follows from the nature and destination of our body, as we shall see, that each of its so-called sensitive elements has its own real action, which must be of the same kind as its virtual action, upon the external objects that it ordinarily perceives, so that one would thus understand why each of the sensory nerves appears to vibrate according to a determinate mode of sensation. But, in order to elucidate this point, it is fitting to investigate more deeply the nature of affection. We are thereby led to the third and final argument that we wished to examine.
This third argument is drawn from the fact that one passes, by imperceptible degrees, from the representative state, which occupies space, to the affective state, which appears unextended.

From this is concluded the natural and necessary inextension of every sensation, extension being added to sensation, and the process of perception consisting in an exteriorization of internal states. The psychologist does indeed start from his body, and since the impressions received at the periphery of this body seem to him sufficient for the reconstruction of the whole material universe, it is to his body that he first reduces the universe. But this first position is untenable; his body has and can have neither more nor less reality than all other bodies. It is therefore necessary to go further, to follow through the application of the principle, and, after having shrunk the universe to the surface of the living body, to contract this body itself into a centre that will ultimately be supposed unextended.

Then, from this centre, one will make inextensive sensations proceed, which will swell, so to speak, increase into extension, and will end by giving first our extended body, then all other material objects. But this strange supposition would be impossible, if there were not precisely between images and ideas, the latter inextended and the former extended, a series of intermediate states, more or less confusedly localized, which are affective states.

Our understanding, yielding to its habitual illusion, posits this dilemma: that a thing is extended or is not; and since the affective state vaguely partakes of extension, is imperfectly localized, it concludes that this state is absolutely inextensive. But then the successive degrees of extension, and extension itself, will be explained by I know not what acquired property of inextensive states; the history of perception will become that of internal and inextensive states extending themselves and projecting themselves outward. Does one wish to put this argument in another form? There is scarcely any perception that cannot, through an increase in the action of its object upon our body, become affection and, more particularly, pain. Thus, one passes imperceptibly from the contact of the pin to the prick.

Conversely, diminishing pain gradually coincides with the perception of its cause and exteriorizes itself, so to speak, into representation. Thus there does indeed seem to be a difference of degree, and not of nature, between affection and perception. Now the former is intimately connected with 1
SCHWARZ, Das Wahrnehmungsproblem, Leipzig, 1892, p. 313 ff.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the relation of the body to the mind. (1939) 31

my personal existence: for what, indeed, would a pain detached from the subject who feels it be? It must therefore, it seems, be the same with the latter, and external perception must be constituted by the projection into space of affection that has become harmless. Realists and idealists agree in reasoning in this way. The latter see nothing else in the material universe than a synthesis of subjective and inextensive states; the former add that there is, behind this synthesis, an independent reality corresponding to it; but both alike conclude, from the gradual transition from affection to representation, that the representation of the material universe is relative, subjective, and, so to speak, that it has come out of us, instead of our having first disengaged ourselves from it.

Before criticizing this questionable interpretation of an exact fact, let us show that it does not succeed in explaining, that it does not even manage to clarify, either the nature of pain or that of perception. That affective states essentially connected with my person, and which would vanish if I disappeared, should come, by the sole effect of a diminution of intensity, to acquire extension, to take a determinate place in space, to constitute a stable experience, always in agreement with itself and with the experience of other men, is something that it will be difficult to make us understand. Whatever one does, one will be led to restore to sensations, in one form or another, first extension, then the independence one had wished to dispense with. But, on the other hand, affection will scarcely be clearer, on this hypothesis, than representation.

For if one does not see how affections, by diminishing in intensity, become representations, neither does one understand how the same phenomenon, which was first given as perception, becomes affection through an increase in intensity. There is in pain something positive and active, which is poorly explained by saying, with certain philosophers, that it consists in a confused representation. But that is not yet the principal difficulty. That the gradual increase of the stimulus ends by transforming perception into pain is indisputable; it remains no less true that the transformation takes shape from a precise moment onward: why this moment rather than another? and what is the special reason that makes a phenomenon of which I was at first only the indifferent spectator suddenly acquire for me a vital interest?

Thus, in this hypothesis, I grasp neither why, at such a determinate moment, a diminution of intensity in the phenomenon confers upon it a right to extension and to an apparent independence, nor how an increase of intensity creates, at one moment rather than another, this new property, the source of positive action, called pain.

Let us now return to our hypothesis, and show how affection must, at a determinate moment, arise from the image. We shall also understand how one passes from a perception that occupies extension to an affection believed to be inextensive. But a few preliminary remarks on the real meaning of pain are indispensable.

When a foreign body touches one of the amoeba's prolongations, that prolongation retracts; each part of the protoplasmic mass is therefore equally capable of receiving the excitation and reacting against it; perception and movement here merge into a single property, which is contractility. But as the organism becomes more complex, labour is divided, functions become differentiated, and the anatomical elements thus constituted
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the relation of the body to the mind. (1939) 32

alienate their independence. In an organism such as ours, the so-called sensitive fibres are exclusively charged with transmitting excitations to a central region from which the disturbance will spread to motor elements. It thus seems that they have renounced individual action in order to contribute, as advanced sentinels, to the movements of the body as a whole. But they remain no less exposed, separately, to the same causes of destruction that threaten the organism as a whole: and whereas this organism has the faculty of moving in order to escape danger or repair its losses, the sensitive element retains the relative immobility to which the division of labour condemns it. Thus pain arises, which is nothing else, according to us, than an effort of the injured element to put things back in place, -

a kind of motor tendency in a sensitive nerve. Every pain must therefore consist in an effort, and in a powerless effort. Every pain is a local effort, and it is this very isolation of the effort that causes its powerlessness, because the organism, by reason of the solidarity of its parts, is no longer suited except to effects of the whole. It is also because the effort is local that pain is absolutely disproportionate to the danger incurred by the living being: the danger may be mortal and the pain slight; the pain may be unbearable (like that of a toothache) and the peril insignificant. There is therefore, there must be, a precise moment at which pain intervenes: it is when the affected portion of the organism, instead of receiving the excitation, repels it.
And it is not merely a difference of degree that separates perception from affection, but a difference of nature.

This granted, we have considered the living Body as a kind of centre from which is reflected back upon the surrounding objects the action that these objects exert upon it: external perception consists in this reflection. But this centre is not a mathematical point: it is a body, exposed, like all bodies in nature, to the action of external causes that threaten to disintegrate it. We have just seen that it resists the influence of these causes. It does not merely reflect the action from without; it struggles, and thus absorbs - something of this action. There would be the source of affection. One could therefore say, metaphorically, that if perception measures the reflective power of the body, affection measures its absorptive power.

But this is only a metaphor. We must look at things more closely, and clearly understand that the necessity of affection follows from the very existence of perception. Perception, understood as we understand it, measures our possible action upon things and thereby, conversely, the possible action of things upon us. The greater the body's power of acting (symbolized by a higher degree of complexity in the nervous system), the wider the field that perception embraces. The distance separating our body from a perceived object therefore truly measures the greater or lesser imminence of a danger, the more or less proximate fulfillment of a promise. And consequently, our perception of an object distinct from our body, separated from our body by an interval, never expresses anything but a virtual action.

But the more the distance between this object and our body decreases, the more, in other words, the danger becomes urgent or the promise immediate, the more virtual action tends to be transformed into real action. Now pass to the limit, suppose that the distance becomes nil, that is, that the object to be perceived coincides with our body, that is finally, that our own body is the object to be perceived. Then it is no longer a virtual action, but a real action that this perception
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 33

of a quite special kind will express: affection consists in this very thing. Our sensations are therefore to our perceptions what the real action of our body is to its possible or virtual action. Its virtual action concerns other objects and is outlined in those objects; its real action concerns itself and is consequently outlined within it. Thus everything will finally take place as if, by a genuine return of real and virtual actions to their points of application or origin, external images were reflected by our body in the space surrounding it, and real actions were arrested by it within its substance. And this is why its surface, the common limit of exterior and interior, is the only portion of extension that is both perceived and felt.

This always amounts to saying that my perception is outside my body, and my affection, on the contrary, within my body. Just as external objects are perceived by me where they are, in themselves and not in me, so my affective states are experienced where they occur, that is, at a determinate point of my body. Consider this system of images called the material world. My body is one of them. Around this image is arranged representation, that is, its eventual influence upon the others. Within it affection occurs, that is, its present effort upon itself. Such is indeed, fundamentally, the distinction that each of us naturally, spontaneously establishes between an image and a sensation. When we say that the image exists outside us, we mean by this that it is external to our body.

When we speak of sensation as an inner state, we mean that it arises in our body. And this is why we affirm that the totality of perceived images subsists even if our body vanishes, whereas we cannot suppress our body without making our sensations vanish.

By this we glimpse the necessity of a first cor. rection to our theory of pure perception. We have reasoned as though our perception were a part of images detached just as it is from their substance, as though, expressing the virtual action of the object upon our body or of our body upon the object, it were limited to isolating from the total object the aspect of it that interests us.

But it must be taken into account that our body is not a mathematical point in space, that its virtual actions become complicated and are im-pregnated with real actions, or, in other words, that there is no perception without affection. Affection is therefore what we mingle, from the interior of our body, with the image of external bodies; it is what must first be extracted from perception in order to recover the purity of the image. But the psychologist who closes his eyes to the difference in nature, to the difference in function between perception and sensation,—the latter involving a real action and the former an action merely possible,—can no longer find between them anything but a difference of degree.

Taking advantage of the fact that sensation (because of the confused effort it involves) is only vaguely localized, he immediately declares it inextensive, and hence makes sensation in general the simple element with which we obtain external images by way of composition. The truth is that affection is not the raw material of which perception is made; it is rather the impurity mingled with it. Here we grasp, at its origin, the error that leads the psychologist to consider sensation in turn as inextensive and perception as an aggregate of sensations. This error is strengthened along the way, as we shall see, by arguments that it borrows from a false conception of the role of space and of
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 34
the nature of extension. But it also has in its favor misinterpreted facts, which should now be examined.

First, it seems that the localization of an affective sensation at a place in the body requires a genuine education. Some time passes before the child succeeds in touching with his finger the precise point on the skin where he has been pricked. The fact is indisputable, but all that can be concluded from it is that groping is necessary in order to coordinate the painful impressions of the skin, which has received the prick, with those of muscular sense, which guides the movements of the arm and hand. Our internal affections, like our external perceptions, are distributed into different kinds. These kinds, like those of perception, are discontinuous, separated by intervals which education fills. It does not at all follow from this that there is not, for each kind of affection, an immediate localization of a certain kind, a local colour proper to it.

Let us go further: if affection does not have this local colour immediately, it will never have it. For all that education can do will be to associate with the present affective sensation the idea of a certain possible perception of sight and touch, so that a determinate affection evokes the image of a visual or tactile perception, likewise determinate. There must therefore indeed be, in this affection itself, something that distinguishes it from the other affections of the same kind and permits it to be connected with such-and-such a possible datum of sight or touch rather than with any other. But does this not amount to saying that affection possesses, from the outset, a certain extensive determination?

Erroneous localizations are also adduced, the illusion of amputees (which, moreover, ought to be submitted to a new examination). But what can be concluded from this, except that education persists once acquired, and that the data of memory, more useful in practical life, displace those of immediate consciousness? With a view to action, it is indispensable for us to translate our affective experience into possible data of sight, touch, and muscular sense. Once this translation has been established, the original pales, but it could never have been made if the original had not first been posited, and if affective sensation had not, from the outset, been localized by its own force and in its own way.

But the psychologist has very great difficulty in accepting this idea of common sense. Just as, it seems to him, perception could not be in perceived things unless things perceived, so a sensation could not be in the nerve unless the nerve felt: now the nerve obviously does not feel. One will therefore take sensation at the point where common sense localizes it, extract it from there, bring it nearer to the brain, upon which it appears to depend even more than upon the nerve; and one would thus logically end by placing it in the brain.

But one soon realizes that if it is not at the point where it appears to occur, it cannot be elsewhere either; that if it is not in the nerve, neither will it be in the brain; for, in order to explain its projection from the center to the periphery, a certain force is necessary, which must be attributed to a more or less active consciousness. It will therefore be necessary to go further, and after making sensations converge upon the cerebral center, to drive them at once out of the brain and out of space. We shall then represent sensations as absolutely inextensive, and, on the other hand, an empty space indifferent to the sensations that will come to be projected into it; then we shall exhaust ourselves in
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 35

efforts of every kind to make us understand how inextensive sensations acquire extension, and choose, in order to localize themselves there, such points of space in preference to all others. But this doctrine is not only incapable of showing us clearly how the unextended becomes extended; it also renders affection, extension, and representation inexplicable.

It will have to posit affective states as so many absolutes, and one cannot see why they appear or disappear at such-and-such moments in consciousness. The passage from affection to representation will remain enveloped in a mystery equally impenetrable, because, we repeat, one will never find in inner states, simple and inextensive, a reason why they should adopt, in preference, one or another determinate order in space. And finally representation itself will have to be posited as an absolute: neither its origin nor its destination can be seen.

Things become clear, on the contrary, if one starts from representation itself, that is, from the totality of perceived images. My perception, in its pure state and isolated from my memory, does not proceed from my body to other bodies: it is first in the whole of bodies, then little by little becomes limited, and adopts my body as its center. And it is brought there precisely by the experience of the twofold faculty that this body possesses of performing actions and undergoing affections, in a word by the experience of the sensorimotor power of a certain image, privileged among all images.

On the one hand, indeed, this image always occupies the center of representation, so that the other images are ranged around it in the very order in which they might undergo its action; on the other hand, I perceive its interior, its inside, through sensations that I call affective, instead of knowing only, as with other images, its superficial film. There is therefore, in the whole of images, a favored image, perceived in its depths and no longer merely at its surface, the seat of affection at the same time as the source of action: it is this particular image that I adopt as the center of my universe and as the physical basis of my personality.

But before going further and establishing a precise relation between the person and the images in which it is installed, let us briefly summarize, by contrasting it with the analyses of usual psychology, the theory of “pure perception” that we have just sketched.

To simplify the exposition, we shall return to the sense of sight that we had chosen as an example. One ordinarily posits elementary sensations, corresponding to the impressions received by the cones and rods of the retina. It is with these sensations that one will reconstruct visual perception. But first, there is not one retina, there are two. It will therefore be necessary to explain how two sensations, supposed distinct, merge into a single perception, corresponding to what we call a point in space.

Let us suppose this question resolved. The sensations in question are inextensive. How do they receive extension? Whether one sees in extension a framework all ready to receive sensations or an effect of the mere simultaneity of sensations which coexist in consciousness without merging together, in either case one will introduce with extension something new, which one will not account for, and the process by which sensation
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Mind. (1939) 36
joins extension, the choice by each elementary sensation of a determinate point in space, will remain unexplained.

Let us pass over this difficulty. Here is visual extension constituted. How does it in turn join tactile extension? Everything that my sight observes in space, my touch verifies. Will it be said that objects are constituted precisely by the cooperation of sight and touch, and that the agreement of the two senses in perception is explained by the fact that the perceived object is their common work?
