recognition. But let us hasten to say that it is most often accompanied by something else.

While, indeed, motor mechanisms are being set up under the influence of perceptions increasingly analyzed by the body, our earlier psychological life is there: it survives itself—we shall try to prove it—with every detail of its events localized in time. Continually inhibited by the practical and useful consciousness of the present moment, that is to say by the sensorimotor equilibrium of a nervous system stretched between perception and action, this memory merely waits for a fissure to arise between the present impression and the concomitant movement, in order to let its images pass through it.

Ordinarily, in order to go back along the course of our past and discover the known, localized, personal memory-image that would relate to the present, an effort is necessary, by which we disengage ourselves from the action toward which our perception inclines us: it would propel us toward the future; we must retreat into the past. In this sense, movement would rather drive the image away. Yet, in a certain respect, it helps to prepare it. For if the whole of our past images remains present to us, the representation analogous to the present perception must still be chosen from among all possible representations.

The movements performed, or merely beginning, prepare this selection, or at least delimit the field of images from which we shall go and gather. By virtue of the constitution of our nervous system, we are beings in whom present impressions are prolonged into appropriate movements: if old images can likewise be prolonged into these movements, they take advantage of the opportunity to slip into the present perception and have themselves adopted by it. They then appear, in fact, to our consciousness, whereas they would seem, in principle, bound to remain covered over by the present state. One might therefore say that the movements which bring about mechanical recognition on one side prevent, and on the other favor, recognition by images.

In principle, the present displaces the past. But on the other hand, precisely because the suppression of old images is due to their inhibition by the present attitude, those whose form could fit within this attitude will encounter a lesser obstacle than the others; and if, consequently, any one of them can cross the obstacle, it is the image resembling the present perception that will cross it.

If our analysis is correct, disorders of recognition will affect two profoundly different forms, and two kinds of psychic blindness will be found. Sometimes, indeed, it will be the old images that can no longer be evoked; sometimes it will only be the link between perception and the usual concomitant movements that is broken, perception bringing about diffuse movements as though it were new. Do the facts verify this hypothesis?

There can be no dispute on the first point. The apparent abolition of visual memories in psychic blindness is a fact so common that for a time it was used to define this affection. We shall have to ask to what extent and in what sense memories can really vanish. What interests us for the moment is that cases occur in which recognition no longer takes place, without visual memory being practically abolished. Is it then indeed, as we maintain, a simple disturbance of motor habits, or at least an interruption
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 58

of the link that unites them to sensory perceptions? As no observer has posed a question of this kind, we should be greatly at a loss to answer it if we had not noted here and there, in their descriptions, certain facts that seem significant to us.

The first of these facts is the loss of the sense of orientation. All authors who have dealt with psychic blindness have been struck by this particularity. Lissauer's patient had completely lost the ability to find his way about his house 1. Fr. Müller insists on the fact that, whereas blind persons learn very quickly to find their way again, a subject afflicted with psychic blindness cannot, even after months of practice, orient himself in his own room 2. But is the ability to orient oneself anything other than the ability to coordinate the movements of the body with visual impressions, and mechanically to prolong perceptions into useful reactions?

There is a second fact, still more characteristic. We mean the way in which these patients draw. Two ways of drawing may be conceived. The first would consist in fixing a certain number of points on paper, by trial and error, and connecting them with one another, checking at every moment whether the image resembles the object. This is what would be called drawing “by points.”
But the method we ordinarily use is quite different. We draw
“in one continuous stroke,” after having looked at the model or thought of it.

How can such a faculty be explained, if not by the habit of immediately disentangling the organization of the most usual outlines, that is to say by a motor tendency to figure their schema all in one stroke? But if it is precisely habits or correspondences of this kind that dissolve in certain forms of psychic blindness, the patient may still perhaps trace elements of line, which he will join together as best he can; he will no longer know how to draw in one continuous stroke, because he will no longer have in his hand the movement of the outlines. Now this is precisely what experience verifies.

Lissauer's observation is already instructive in this respect 3. His patient had the greatest difficulty in drawing simple objects, and if he wished to draw them from memory, he traced detached portions of them, taken here and there, which he could not succeed in joining to one another. But cases of complete psychic blindness are rare. Much more numerous are cases of verbal blindness, that is to say, a loss of visual recognition limited to the characters of the alphabet. Now it is a fact of common observation that, in such cases, the patient is incapable of grasping what might be called the movement of letters when he tries to copy them. He begins to draw them at any point whatever, checking at every moment whether he remains in agreement with the model. And this is all the more remarkable because he has often kept intact the ability to write from dictation or spontaneously.

What is abolished here, then, is indeed the habit of disentangling the articulations of the perceived object, that is to say of completing its visual perception by a motor tendency to draw its schema. From this one may conclude, as we had announced, that this is indeed the primordial condition of recognition.

But we must now pass from automatic recognition, which is effected chiefly through movements, to that which requires the regular intervention of memory-images. The first is recognition by distraction: the second, as we shall see, is attentive recognition.

It too begins with movements. But whereas, in automatic recognition, our movements prolong our perception in order to draw useful effects from it and thus take us away from the perceived object, here, on the contrary, they bring us back to the object in order to emphasize its outlines. Hence the preponderant, no longer accessory, role played in it by memory-images. Suppose, indeed, that movements renounce their practical end, and that motor activity, instead of continuing perception by useful reactions, turns back in order to draw its salient features: then the images analogous to the present perception, images whose form these movements will already have sketched, will come regularly, and no longer accidentally, to fit themselves into this mould, though indeed they must abandon many of their details in order to facilitate their entry.
III.—Gradual passage from memories to movements. Recogni-

tion and attention. — We here touch upon the essential point of the debate. In cases where recognition is attentive, that is to say where memory-images regularly rejoin present perception, is it perception that mechanically determines the appearance of memories, or are memories the ones that spontaneously go forth to meet perception?

The nature of the relations established between the brain and memory will depend on the answer given to this question. In every perception, indeed, there is a vibration transmitted by the nerves to the perceptive centres. If the propagation of this movement to other cortical centres had the real effect of causing images to arise there, one might maintain, at a pinch, that memory is merely a function of the brain. But if we were to establish that here, as elsewhere, movement can produce only movement, that the role of the perceptive vibration is simply to impress upon the body a certain attitude into which memories come to insert themselves, then, all the effect of material vibrations being exhausted in this work of motor adaptation, one would have to seek the memory elsewhere.

In the first hypothesis, the disorders of memory occasioned by a cerebral lesion would arise from the fact that memories occupied the damaged region and were destroyed along with it. In the second, on the contrary, these lesions would affect our nascent or possible action, but our action alone. At times they would prevent the body, in the presence of an object, from assuming the attitude appropriate to the recollection of the image; at times they would sever this memory's ties with present reality, that is to say, by suppressing the final phase of the realization of the memory, by suppressing the phase of action, they would thereby also prevent the memory from becoming actualized.
But in neither case would a cerebral lesion truly destroy memories.
This second hypothesis will be ours. But, before seeking its verification, let us briefly state how we conceive the relations
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 60

in general between perception, attention, and memory. In order to show how a memory might, degree by degree, come to insert itself into an attitude or a movement, we shall have to anticipate somewhat the conclusions of our next chapter.

What is attention? On the one hand, attention has the essential effect of making perception more intense and of bringing out its details: considered in its matter, it would thus be reduced to a certain enlargement of the intellectual state 1.

But, on the other hand, consciousness observes an irreducible difference in form between this increase in intensity and that which is due to a greater force of external excitation: indeed, it seems to come from within, and to testify to a certain attitude adopted by the intelligence. But here precisely obscurity begins, for the idea of an intellectual attitude is not a clear idea.
One will speak of a “concentration of the mind 2,” or again of an

“apperceptive 3” effort to bring perception under the gaze of distinct intelligence. Some, materializing this idea, will suppose a particular tension of cerebral energy 4, or even a central expenditure of energy added to the excitation received 5. But either one merely translates in this way the psychologically observed fact into a physiological language which seems to us still less clear, or one always returns to a metaphor.

Degree by degree, one will be led to define attention by a general adaptation of the body rather than of the mind, and to see in this attitude of consciousness, above all, the consciousness of an attitude. Such is the position taken by Th. Ribot in the debate 6, and although attacked 7, it seems to have retained all its force, provided, however, we believe, that one sees in the movements described by Th. Ribot only the negative condition of the phenomenon. If

we suppose, indeed, that the concomitant movements of voluntary attention were chiefly movements of arrest, it would still remain to explain the work of the mind corresponding to them, that is, the mysterious operation by which the same organ, perceiving the same object in the same surroundings, discovers in it an increasing number of things. But one can go further, and maintain that the phenomena of inhibition are only a preparation for the effective movements of voluntary attention. Let us suppose, indeed, as we have already intimated, that attention implies a backward movement of the mind which renounces pursuing the useful effect of present perception: there will first be an inhibition of movement, an arresting action. But upon this general attitude there will soon be grafted more subtle movements, some of which 1

have been observed and described 1, and whose role is to retrace the contours of the perceived object. With these movements begins the positive, and no longer merely negative, work of attention. It is continued by memories.

If external perception, indeed, provokes on our part movements that trace its broad outlines, our memory directs upon the perception received the old images that resemble it and whose sketch our movements have already traced. It thus creates anew the present perception, or rather it doubles this perception by sending back to it either its own image or some memory-image of the same kind. If the retained or recollected image does not succeed in covering all the details of the perceived image, an appeal is made to the deeper and more distant regions of memory, until other known details come to be projected upon those that are unknown. And the operation may continue indefinitely, memory strengthening and enriching perception, which, in its turn, increasingly developed, draws to itself an increasing number of complementary memories.

Let us no longer think, then, of a mind that would dispose of I know not what fixed quantity of light, now diffusing it all around, now con-centrating it upon a single point. Image for image, we should prefer to compare the elementary work of attention to that of the telegraph operator who, on receiving an important dispatch, retransmits it word for word to its place of origin in order to verify its accuracy.

But in order to send back a dispatch, one must know how to operate the apparatus. And likewise, in order to reflect upon a perception the image we have received of it, we must be able to reproduce it, that is, to reconstruct it by an effort of synthesis. It has been said that attention was a faculty of analysis, and rightly so; but it has not been sufficiently explained how an analysis of this kind is possible, nor by what process we succeed in discovering in a perception what did not at first manifest itself there. The truth is that this analysis is effected by a series of trials of synthesis, or, what amounts to the same thing, by so many hypotheses: our memory successively chooses various analogous images which it launches in the direction of the new perception. But this choice does not take place at random.

What suggests the hypotheses, what from afar presides over the selection, are the movements of imitation by which perception is continued, and which will serve as a common framework for perception and remembered images.

But then, the mechanism of distinct perception must be conceived otherwise than is ordinarily done. Perception does not consist solely in impressions gathered or even elaborated by the mind. At most this is so for those perceptions dissipated as soon as received, those which we scatter into useful actions. But every attentive perception truly presupposes, in the etymological sense of the word, a reflection, that is to say, the external projection of an actively created image, identical with or similar to the object, and which comes to mould itself upon its contours. If, after fixing our gaze upon an object, we suddenly turn our eyes away from it, we obtain an after-image of it: must we not suppose that this image was already being produced while we were looking at it?

The recent discovery of centrifugal perceptive fibres would incline us to think that things regularly take place in this way, and that alongside the afferent process which carries the impression to the centre, there is another, 1

inverse, which brings the image back to the periphery. It is true that here images photographed upon the object itself are concerned, and memories immediately consecutive to the perception of which they are but the echo. But behind these images identical with the object, there are others, stored in memory, which merely resemble it, and finally others which have with it only a more or less distant kinship. They all move toward the perception, and, nourished by its substance, acquire sufficient force and life to externalize themselves with it. The experiments of Münsterberg 1, of Külpe 2, leave no doubt on this last point: every memory-image capable of interpreting our present perception slips into it so thoroughly that we no longer know how to distinguish what is perception from what is memory.

But nothing is more interesting in this respect than the ingenious experiments of Goldscheider and Müller on the mechanism of reading 3. Against Grashey, who had maintained in a famous work 4 that we read words letter by letter, these experimenters established that ordinary reading is a veritable work of divination, our mind picking out here and there a few characteristic features and filling in the whole interval with memory-images which, projected onto the paper, take the place of the actually printed characters and give us the illusion of them.

Thus, we continually create or reconstruct. Our distinct perception is truly comparable to a closed circle, in which the perception-image directed toward the mind and the memory-image cast into space would run one after the other.

Let us insist on this last point. Attentive perception is readily represented as a series of processes proceeding along a single thread, the object exciting sensations, the sensations causing ideas to arise before them, each idea successively setting in motion more remote points of the intellectual mass. There would thus be a movement in a straight line, by which the mind would move farther and farther away from the object, never to return to it. We maintain, on the contrary, that reflective perception is a circuit, in which all the elements, including the perceived object itself, are held in a state of mutual tension as in an electric circuit, so that no disturbance originating in the object can stop on the way in the depths of the mind: it must always return to the object itself. This must not be seen as a mere question of words.

Two radically different conceptions of intellectual work are at issue. According to the first, things take place mechanically, and through an entirely accidental series of successive additions. At each moment of an attentive perception, for example, new elements, emanating from a deeper region of the mind, might join the old elements without creating a general disturbance, without requiring a transformation of the system. In the second, on the contrary, an act of attention implies such solidarity between the mind and its object, it is such a well-closed circuit, that one cannot pass to states of higher concentration without creating from whole cloth as many new circuits which envelop the first, and which 1

have in common only the object perceived. Of these different circles of memory, which we shall study in detail later, the narrowest, A, is nearest to immediate perception. It contains only the object O itself together with the after-image which comes back to cover it. Behind it, the increasingly wider circles B, C, D correspond to increasing efforts of intellectual expansion. It is the whole of memory, as we shall see, that enters into each of these circuits, since memory is always present; but this memory, which its elasticity permits to be indefinitely expanded, reflects upon the object an increasing number of suggested things—now details of the object itself, now concomitant details capable of helping to elucidate it.

Thus, after having reconstituted the perceived object as an independent whole, we reconstitute with it the increasingly remote conditions with which it forms a system. Let us call B', C', D' these causes of increasing depth, situated behind the object, and virtually given with the object itself. It can be seen that the progress of attention has the effect of creating anew not only the perceived object, but the increasingly vast systems to which it can be connected; so that, as the circles B, C, D represent a higher expansion of memory, their reflection reaches in B', C', D' deeper layers of reality.

## Figure 1

The same psychological life would thus be repeated an indefinite number of times, at the successive levels of memory, and the same act of the mind could be played out at many different heights. In the effort of attention, the mind always gives itself wholly, but simplifies or complicates itself according to the level it chooses for carrying out its evolutions. It is ordinarily present perception that determines the orientation of our mind; but according to the degree of tension our mind adopts, according to the height at which it places itself, this perception develops in us a greater or lesser number of memory-images.

Finally, in other words, personal memories, exactly localized, and whose series would trace the course of our past existence, together constitute the last and widest envelope of our memory. Essentially fugitive-
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 64

tive, they materialize only by chance, whether an accidentally precise determination of our bodily attitude attracts them, or the very indeterminacy of this attitude leaves free play to the caprice of their manifestation. But this outermost envelope contracts and is repeated in inner and concentric circles which, being narrower, bear the same diminished memories, increasingly remote from their personal and original form, increasingly capable, in their banality, of being applied to present perception and of determining it in the manner of a species encompassing the individual. A moment comes when the memory thus reduced fits so well into present perception that one could not say where perception ends and memory begins.
At that precise moment, memory, instead of making its representations appear and disappear capriciously, adjusts itself to the detail of bodily movements.

But as these memories draw nearer to movement and thereby to external perception, the operation of memory acquires a higher practical importance. Past images, reproduced as they are with all their details and even their affective coloration, are the images of reverie or dream; what we call acting is precisely bringing about the contraction, or rather the increasing sharpening, of this memory, until it presents only the cutting edge of its blade to the experience into which it will penetrate. Fundamentally, it is because the motor element of memory has not here been disentangled that what is automatic in the evocation of memories has sometimes been misconceived, sometimes exaggerated.

In our view, an appeal is made to our activity at the precise moment when our perception has automatically broken down into movements of imitation: we are then supplied with a sketch, the detail and colour of which we recreate by projecting into it memories more or less remote. But this is not how things are ordinarily viewed. Sometimes the mind is granted an absolute autonomy; it is credited with the power to work upon present or absent objects as it pleases; and one then no longer understands the profound disturbances of attention and memory that may follow the slightest perturbation of the sensorimotor equilibrium.

At other times, on the contrary, imaginative processes are made into so many mechanical effects of present perception; it is held that, through a necessary and uniform progression, the object gives rise to sensations, and the sensations to the ideas that attach themselves to them: then, since there is no reason why the phenomenon, mechanical at the outset, should change its nature along the way, one arrives at the hypothesis of a brain in which intellectual states might be deposited, slumber, and awaken. In either case, the true function of the body is misconceived; and since it has not been seen wherein the intervention of a mechanism is necessary, neither is it known, once appeal has been made to it, where it must be stopped.

But the time has come to leave these generalities behind. We must inquire whether our hypothesis is confirmed or refuted by the known facts of cerebral localization. The disorders of imaginative memory corresponding to localized lesions of the cortex are always diseases of recognition, whether of visual or auditory recognition in general (psychic blindness and deafness), or of the recognition of words (word blindness, word deafness, etc.). These, then, are the disorders that we must examine.
But if our hypothesis is well founded, these disorders of recognition will not arise at all from the fact that memories occupied the injured region. They
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 65

must be due to two causes: sometimes to the fact that our body can no longer automatically assume, in the presence of stimulation coming from without, the precise attitude through which a selection among our memories would be effected; sometimes to the fact that memories no longer find in the body a point of application, a means of prolonging themselves into action. In the first case, the lesion will affect the mechanisms that continue the received excitation in automatically executed movement: attention can no longer be fixed by the object. In the second, the lesion will involve those particular centres of the cortex that prepare voluntary movements by furnishing them with the necessary sensory antecedent, and which are called, rightly or wrongly, imaginative centres: attention can no longer be fixed by the subject.
But, in either case, it is present movements that will be impaired, or future movements that will cease to be prepared: there will have been no destruction of memories.

Now pathology confirms this prediction. It reveals to us the existence of two absolutely distinct kinds of psychic blindness and deafness, of word blindness and word deafness. In the first, visual or auditory memories are still evoked, but can no longer be applied to the corresponding perceptions. In the second, the evocation of memories is itself prevented. Does the lesion indeed affect, as we were saying, the sensorimotor mechanisms of automatic attention in the first case, the imaginative mechanisms of voluntary attention in the other? To verify our hypothesis, we must confine ourselves to a precise example.

Certainly, we could show that visual recognition of things in general, and of words in particular, implies first a semi-automatic motor process, then an active projection of memories that insert themselves into the corresponding attitudes. But we prefer to attend to the impressions of Poule, and more particularly to the hearing of articulated language, because this example is the most comprehensive of all. To hear speech, indeed, is first to recognize its sound, then to recover its meaning, and finally to carry its interpretation more or less far: in short, it is to pass through all the degrees of attention and to exercise several successive powers of memory. Moreover, there are no disorders more frequent or better studied than those of the auditory memory of words.

Finally, the abolition of acoustic verbal images does not occur without serious injury to certain definite convolutions of the cortex: we shall therefore be provided with an indisputable example of localization, concerning which we may ask whether the brain is really capable of storing memories. We must therefore show in auditory recognition of words: 1º a sensorimotor automatic process; 2º an active and, so to speak, eccentric projection of memory-images.

1º I listen to two persons conversing in an unknown language. Is that enough for me to hear them? The vibrations that reach me are the same as those that strike their ears. Yet I perceive only a confused noise in which all sounds resemble one another. I distinguish nothing and could repeat nothing. In this same mass of sound, on the contrary, the two interlocutors disentangle con-sonants, vowels, and syllables that scarcely resemble one another, and finally distinct words. Between them and me, where is the difference?
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 66

The question is how knowledge of a language, which is only memory, can modify the materiality of a present perception, and presently make some hear what others, under the same physical conditions, do not hear. It is indeed supposed that the auditory memories of words, accumulated in memory, here answer the call of sound impressions and come to reinforce their effect. But if the conversation I hear is for me only a noise, one may suppose the sound reinforced as much as one likes: the noise, for being louder, will be no clearer. In order for the memory of the word to allow itself to be evoked by the word heard, the ear must at least hear the word.

How will perceived sounds speak to memory, how will they choose, from the store of auditory images, those that must be laid upon them, if they have not already been separated, distinguished, and finally perceived as syllables and as words?

This difficulty does not appear to have struck the theorists of sensory aphasia sufficiently. In word deafness, indeed, the patient finds himself with respect to his own language in the same situation in which we ourselves find ourselves when we hear an unknown language spoken. He has generally retained intact the sense of hearing, but understands nothing of the words he hears pronounced, and often does not even succeed in distinguishing them. It is believed that this state has been sufficiently explained by saying that the auditory memories of words are destroyed in the cortex, or that a lesion, sometimes transcortical, sometimes subcortical, prevents the auditory memory from evoking the idea, or perception from rejoining memory.

But, at least in the last case, the psychological question remains intact: what is the conscious process that the lesion has abolished, and through what intermediary is the discernment of words and syllables generally effected, given first to the ear as a continuity of sound?

The difficulty would be insurmountable if we really had to deal only with auditory impressions on one side and auditory memories on the other. It would not be the same if auditory impressions organized nascent movements, capable of scanning the sentence listened to and marking its principal articulations. These automatic movements of inner accompaniment, at first confused and poorly coordinated, would then emerge more and more clearly as they were repeated; they would end by tracing a simplified figure, in which the person listening would recover, in their broad lines and principal directions, the very movements of the person speaking. Thus there would unfold in our consciousness, in the form of nascent muscular sensations, what we shall call the motor schema of the speech heard.

To train one's ear to the elements of a new language would then consist neither in modifying the raw sound nor in adding a memory to it; it would be to coordinate the motor tendencies of the muscles of the voice with the impressions of the ear, it would be to perfect the motor accompaniment.

To learn a physical exercise, we begin by imitating the movement as a whole, as our eyes show it to us from without, as we believed we saw it performed. Our perception of it was confused: confused will be the movement that attempts to repeat it. But whereas our visual perception was that of a continuous whole, the movement by which we seek to reconstruct its image is composed of a multitude of muscular contractions and tensions; and our consciousness of it itself comprises multiple sensations, arising from the varied play of the joints.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 67

The confused movement which imitates the image is therefore already its virtual decomposition; it bears within itself, so to speak, what is needed to analyze itself. The progress that will arise from repetition and practice will consist simply in bringing out what was at first enveloped, in giving each of the elementary movements that autonomy which ensures precision, while preserving for it, with the others, the solidarity without which it would become useless. It is right to say that habit is acquired through the repetition of effort; but what use would repeated effort be, if it always reproduced the same thing? The true effect of repetition is first to decompose, then to recompose, and thus to speak to the intelligence of the body.

With each new attempt, it develops movements that were enveloped; each time it calls the attention of the body to a new detail that had passed unnoticed; it causes it to divide and to classify; it underscores for it what is essential; one by one, within the total movement, it rediscovers the lines that mark its inner structure. In this sense, a movement is learned as soon as the body has understood it.

Thus, a motor accompaniment of the speech heard would break up the continuity of this mass of sound. It remains to be known what this accompaniment consists in. Is it speech itself, reproduced inwardly? But then the child would know how to repeat all the words that his ear distinguishes; and we ourselves would only have to understand a foreign language in order to pronounce it with the right accent. Things are far from happening so simply.

I may grasp a melody, follow its design, even fix it in my memory, and not know how to sing it. I readily discern peculiarities of inflection and intonation in an Englishman speaking German—I therefore correct him inwardly;—it does not follow from this that I would give the German sentence the correct inflection and intonation if I were speaking. Clinical facts, moreover, here confirm everyday observation. One can still follow and understand speech when one has become incapable of speaking. Motor aphasia does not entail verbal deafness.

This is because the schema by means of which we scan the speech heard marks only its salient contours. It is to speech itself what a sketch is to the finished painting. Indeed, to understand a difficult movement is one thing, to be able to execute it another. In order to understand it, it is enough to realize what is essential in it, just enough to distinguish it from other possible movements. But in order to know how to execute it, one must moreover have made one's body understand it. Now, the logic of the body admits no ellipses. It requires that all the constituent parts of the movement demanded be shown one by one, then recomposed together. A complete analysis becomes necessary here, one that neglects no detail, and a present synthesis, in which nothing is abbreviated. The imaginative schema, composed of a few nascent muscular sensations, was only an outline.
The muscular sensations really and completely experienced give it colour and life.

It remains to be known how an accompaniment of this kind could occur, and whether it always does in fact occur. It is known that the effective pronunciation of a word requires the simultaneous intervention of the tongue and lips for articulation, of the larynx for phonation, and finally of the thoracic muscles for the production of the expiratory current of air. To each syllable pronounced there therefore corresponds the coming into play of a set of mechanisms, all set up in the spinal and bulbar centres. These mechanisms are connected to the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 68

higher centres of the cortex by the cylinder-axial processes of the pyramidal cells of the psycho-motor zone; it is along these paths that the impulse of the will travels. Thus, according as we wish to articulate one sound or another, we transmit the order to act to one or another of these motor mechanisms. But if the ready-made mechanisms corresponding to the various possible movements of articulation and phonation are related to the causes, whatever they may be, that set them in motion in voluntary speech, there are facts which place beyond doubt the communication of these same mechanisms with the auditory perception of words. Among the numerous varieties of aphasia described by clinicians, two are first known (Lichtheim's 4th and 6th forms), which appear to imply a relation of this kind.

Thus, in a case observed by Lichtheim himself, the subject, following a fall, had lost the memory of the articulation of words and consequently the faculty of speaking spontaneously; yet he repeated with the greatest correctness what was said to him 1. On the other hand, in cases where spontaneous speech is intact, but where verbal deafness is absolute, the patient no longer understanding anything that is said to him, the faculty of repeating another's speech can still be entirely preserved 2. Shall it be said, with Bastian, that these phenomena simply testify to a sluggishness of the articulatory or auditory memory of words, the acoustic impressions doing no more than awaken this memory from its torpor 3?

This hypothesis, to which we shall moreover give a place, does not seem to us to account for the very curious phenomena of echolalia long noted by Romberg 4, by Voisin 5, by Winslow 6, and which Kussmaul has called, no doubt with some exaggeration, acoustic reflexes 7. Here the subject repeats mechanically, and perhaps unconsciously, the words heard, as if auditory sensations converted themselves into articulatory movements. Starting from this, some have supposed a special mechanism that would connect an acoustic centre of words with an articulatory centre of speech 8.

The truth appears to lie between these two hypotheses: in these various phenomena there is more than absolutely mechanical actions, but less than an appeal to voluntary memory; they testify to a tendency of auditory verbal impressions to prolong themselves into movements of articulation, a tendency that surely does not escape the habitual control of our will, that perhaps even implies a rudimentary discernment, and that is expressed, in the normal state, by an inward repetition of the salient features of the speech heard. Now, our motor schema is nothing else.

By examining this hypothesis more deeply, one might perhaps find in it the psychological explanation we were seeking just now for certain forms of verbal deafness. A few cases of verbal deafness with the integral survival of acoustic memories are known. The patient has kept intact both the auditory memory of words and the sense of hearing; yet he recognizes none of the words he hears pronounced 1. It is supposed here that there is a subcortical lesion which would prevent acoustic impressions from going to find the auditory verbal images in the centres of the cortex where they would be deposited. But first, the very question is whether the brain can store images; and next, the mere observation of a lesion in the conducting pathways of perception would not dispense us from seeking the psychological interpretation of the phenomenon.

By hypothesis, indeed, auditory memories can be recalled to consciousness; by hypothesis also, auditory impressions reach consciousness: there must therefore be, in consciousness itself, a gap, a break in continuity, something, finally, that opposes the conjunction of perception and memory. Now, the fact will be clarified if one observes that raw auditory perception is truly that of a sonic continuity, and that the sensorimotor connections established by habit must have the role, in the normal state, of decomposing it: a lesion of these conscious mechanisms, by preventing the decomposition from taking place, would abruptly halt the upsurge of memories that tend to set themselves upon the corresponding perceptions. It is therefore the “motor schema” that the lesion could affect.

Let us review the cases, rather rare moreover, of verbal deafness with preservation of acoustic memories: we shall note, we believe, certain characteristic details in this respect. Adler points out as a remarkable fact in verbal deafness that patients no longer react to noises, even intense ones, whereas hearing has retained in them its greatest acuity 2. In other words, sound no longer finds its motor echo in them. A patient of Charcot's, suffering from temporary verbal deafness, relates that he could hear the chime of his clock clearly, but that he would not have been able to count the strokes sounded 3. He therefore probably could not separate and distinguish them. Another patient will declare that he perceives the words of conversation, but as a confused noise 4.

Finally, the subject who has lost the understanding of speech heard recovers it if the word is repeated to him several times and especially if it is pronounced while being scanned, syllable by syllable 5. Is not this latter fact, observed in several absolutely clear cases of verbal deafness with preservation of acoustic memories, particularly significant?

Stricker's error 1 was to believe in an integral inner repetition of speech heard. His thesis would already be refuted by the simple fact that not a single case is known of motor aphasia having entailed verbal deafness.

But all the facts converge to demonstrate the existence of a motor tendency to disarticulate sounds, to establish their schema. This automatic tendency does not, moreover—as we said above—exist without a certain rudimentary intellectual work: otherwise, how could we identify together, and consequently follow by means of the same schema, similar words pronounced at different pitches with different voice timbres? These inner movements of repetition and recognition are like a prelude to voluntary attention. They mark the boundary between will and automatism.

Through them are prepared and decided, as we have led one to anticipate, the characteristic phenomena of intellectual recognition. But what is this complete recognition, having attained full consciousness of itself?

2° We come to the second part of this study: from movements we pass to memories. Attentive recognition, we said, is a veritable circuit, in which the external object delivers to us increasingly deep parts of itself as our memory, symmetrically situated, adopts a higher tension in order to project its memories toward it. In the particular case that concerns us, the object is an interlocutor whose ideas unfold in his consciousness into auditory representations, then materialize in spoken words. Thus, if we are right, the hearer must at once place himself among corresponding ideas, and develop them into auditory representations which will cover the raw sounds perceived while themselves fitting into the motor schema. To follow a calculation is to do it again for oneself.

To understand another's speech would likewise consist in intelligently reconstituting, that is to say, starting from ideas, the continuity of sounds perceived by the ear. And more generally, to attend, to recognize intelligently, to interpret, would merge into one and the same operation by which the mind, having fixed its level, having chosen within itself, in relation to raw perceptions, the symmetrical point of their more or less proximate cause, would allow to flow toward them the memories that will cover them.

Let us hasten to say it: this is not ordinarily how things are envisaged. Our associationist habits are there, by virtue of which we represent sounds to ourselves as evoking auditory memories by contiguity, and auditory memories as evoking ideas. Then there are cerebral lesions, which seem to entail the disappearance of memories: more particularly, in the case that concerns us, one may invoke the lesions characteristic of cortical verbal deafness. Thus psychological observation and clinical facts seem to agree.

There would be, for example in the form of physico-chemical modifications of the cells, auditory representations dormant in the cortex: a shock coming from outside awakens them, and by an intra-cerebral process, perhaps by transcortical movements that seek out the complementary representations, they evoke ideas.

Let one nevertheless reflect on the strange consequences of a hypothesis of this kind. The auditory image of a word is not an object whose contours are definitively fixed, for the same word, pronounced by different voices or by the same voice at different pitches, produces different sounds. There will therefore be as many auditory memories of a word as there are pitches of sound and voice timbres. Will all these images be piled up in the brain, or, if the brain chooses, which one will it prefer? Yet let us admit that it has its reasons for choosing one: how will this same word, pronounced by a new person, join a memory from which it differs? Let us note indeed that this memory is, by hypothesis, an inert and passive thing, consequently incapable of grasping an internal similarity beneath external differences.

We are spoken of the auditory image of the word as though it were an entity or a genus: this genus unquestionably exists for an active memory that schematizes the resemblance of complex sounds; but for a brain which records, and can record, only the materiality of perceived sounds, there will be a thousand and a thousand distinct images of the same word. Pronounced by a new voice, it will constitute a new image which will be added purely and simply to the others.
But here is something no less troubling. A word has individuality for us only from the day our teachers taught us to abstract it. It is not words that we first learn to pronounce, but sentences.

A word always anastomoses with those accompanying it, and according to the gait and movement of the sentence of which it forms an integral part, it takes on different aspects: thus each note of a melodic theme vaguely reflects the whole theme. Let us therefore admit that there are model auditory memories, represented by certain intra-cerebral arrangements, and awaiting sound impressions as they pass: these impressions will pass without being recognized. For where is the common measure, where is the point of contact between the dry, inert, isolated image and the living reality of the word organizing itself with the sentence? I understand very well this beginning of automatic recognition which would consist, as we have seen above, in marking the principal articulations of this sentence, and thus adopting its movement.

But unless one supposes that all men have identical voices pronouncing the same stereotyped sentences in the same tone, I do not see how the words heard could join their images in the cerebral cortex.

Now, if there really are memories deposited in the cells of the cortex, one will observe, in sensory aphasia for example, the irreparable loss of certain determinate words, the complete preservation of the others.

In fact, this is not how things happen. Sometimes it is the totality of memories that disappears, the faculty of mental hearing being purely and simply abolished; sometimes one witnesses a general weakening of this function; but it is ordinarily the function that is diminished, and not the number of memories. It seems that the patient no longer has the strength to recapture his acoustic memories, that he circles around the verbal image without managing to settle upon it. Often, in order to make him recover a word, it is enough to set him on the track, to indicate the first syllable to him 1, or simply to 1

We have reviewed a large number of these facts, and it seemed to us that they could be divided into two absolutely distinct categories. In the first, the loss of memories is generally sudden; in the second it is progressive. In the first, the memories detached from memory are random, arbitrarily and even capriciously chosen: they may be certain words, certain numbers, or even, often, all the words of a learned language. In the second, the words follow, in disappearing, a methodical and grammatical order, the very one indicated by Ribot's law: proper names first vanish, then common nouns, finally verbs 3.
These are the external differences.

Here now, it seems to us, is the internal difference. In amnesias of the first kind, which are almost all consequent upon a violent shock, we would be inclined to believe that the apparently abolished memories are really present, and not only present, but active. To take an example often borrowed from Winslow 4, that of the subject who had forgotten the letter F, and the letter F only, we ask ourselves whether one can abstract from a determinate letter wherever one encounters it, consequently detach it from the spoken or written words of which it forms part, unless one has first implicitly recognized it. In another case cited by the same author 5, the subject had forgotten languages that he had learned and also poems that he had written. Having returned to composing, he remade approximately the same verses.

Moreover, in such a case one often witnesses an integral restoration of the disappeared memories. Without wishing to pronounce too categorically on a question of this kind, we cannot help finding an analogy between these phenomena and the divisions of personality described by M. Pierre Janet 6: one of them bears a striking resemblance to those “negative hallucinations” and “suggestions with a point of reference” induced by hypnotists 7.

Then verbs, whose essence is to express imitable actions, are precisely the words that a bodily effort will enable us to recapture when the function of language is about to escape us: on the contrary, proper names, being, of all words, the most remote from those impersonal actions that our body can sketch out, are those that a weakening of the function would affect first.

In neither case do we find memories localized in determinate cells of cerebral substance, and which destruction of these cells would abolish.

But let us question our consciousness. Let us ask it what happens when we listen to another's speech with the idea of understanding it. Do we wait passively for impressions to go and seek their images? Do we not rather feel that we place ourselves in a certain disposition, variable with the interlocutor, variable with the language he speaks, with the kind of ideas he expresses and above all with the general movement of his sentence, as though we began by setting the tone of our intellectual work? The motor schema, marking its intonations, following, turn by turn, the curve of his thought, shows our thought the way. It is the empty receptacle, determining by its form the form toward which the fluid mass that rushes into it tends.

But one will hesitate to understand the mechanism of interpretation in this way, because of the invincible tendency that leads us, on every occasion, to think things rather than progressions. We have said that we start from the idea, and develop it into auditory memory-images, capable of inserting themselves into the motor schema in order to cover the sounds heard. There is here a continuous progression by which the nebulosity of the idea condenses into distinct auditory images, which, still fluid, are finally to solidify in their coalescence with materially perceived sounds. At no moment can one say precisely that the idea or the memory-image ends, that the memory-image or sensation begins.

And indeed, where is the line of demarcation between the confusion of sounds perceived en masse and the clarity that remembered auditory images add to it, between the discontinuity of these remembered images themselves and the continuity of the original idea which they dissociate and refract into 1

But scientific thought, analyzing this uninterrupted series of changes and yielding to an irresistible need for symbolic representation, arrests and solidifies into completed things the principal phases of this evolution. It erects the raw sounds heard into separate and complete words, then the remembered auditory images into entities independent of the idea which they develop: these three terms, raw perception, auditory image, and idea, will thus form distinct wholes, each of which will suffice unto itself.

And whereas, if one had adhered to pure experience, it would necessarily have been necessary to begin with the idea, since auditory memories owe their cohesion to it and raw sounds in turn are completed only by memories, one sees no objection, once the raw sound has arbitrarily been completed and the memories likewise arbitrarily joined together, to reversing the natural order of things, to affirming that we proceed from perception to memories and from memories to the idea. Yet, in one form or another, at one time or another, the broken continuity of the three terms will have to be restored. It will therefore be supposed that these three terms, lodged in distinct portions of the medulla and cortex, maintain communications with one another, perceptions awakening auditory memories, and memories in turn ideas.

Just as the principal phases of development have been solidified into independent terms, development itself is now materialized in lines of communication or movements of impulse. But one will not thus have inverted the true order with impunity and, as a necessary consequence, introduced into each term of the series elements that are realized only after it. Nor will one with impunity have frozen into distinct and independent terms the continuity of an undivided progress. This mode of representation may perhaps suffice so long as it is strictly confined to the facts that served to invent it: but each new fact will compel one to complicate the figure, to interpose new stations along the movement, without these juxtaposed stations ever succeeding in reconstituting the movement itself.

But how could it have been otherwise? To hear certain theorists of sensory aphasia, one would think that they had never closely considered the structure of a sentence. They reason as though a sentence were composed of names that evoke images of things. What becomes of those various parts of speech whose very role is to establish among images relations and nuances of every kind? Will it be said that each of these words itself expresses and evokes a material image, doubtless more confused, but determinate? Let one then consider the multitude of different relations that the same word can express according to the position it occupies and the terms it joins! Will you allege that these are refinements of an already highly perfected language, and that a language is possible with concrete names intended to call forth images of things?

I readily grant it; but the more primitive and devoid of terms expressing relations the language you speak to me is, the more room you will have to make for the activity of my mind, since you force it to restore the relations that you do not express: that is to say, you will abandon more and more the hypothesis according to which each image would go and fetch its idea. In truth, this is never anything but a question of degree: refined or crude, a language implies far more things than it can express. Essentially discontinuous, since it proceeds by juxtaposed words, speech does no more than mark out, at intervals, the principal stages of the movement of thought.

This is why I shall understand your speech if I begin from a thought analogous to yours, in order to follow its windings with the help of verbal images intended, like so many signposts, to show me the way from time to time. It is therefore in vain that memory-images and ideas are treated as ready-made things, to which problematic centres are then assigned as their dwelling-place. One may disguise the hypothesis in language borrowed from anatomy and physiology, but it is nothing other than the associationist conception of mental life; it has in its favour only the constant tendency of discursive intelligence to cut up every process into phases and then to solidify these phases into things; and, since it was born, a priori, of a kind of metaphysical prejudice, it has neither the advantage of following the movement of consciousness nor that of simplifying the explanation of the facts. But we must pursue this illusion to the precise point at which it results in a manifest contradiction.

Ideas, we said, pure memories, called forth from the depths of memory, develop into memory-images increasingly capable of being inserted into the motor schema. In proportion as these memories take the form of a more complete, more concrete, and more conscious representation, they tend more and more to merge with the perception which attracts them or whose framework they adopt. Therefore there is not, there cannot be in the brain a region where memories become fixed and accumulate. The alleged destruction of memories by cerebral lesions is merely an interruption of the continuous process by which memory becomes actualized.

And consequently, if one insists at all costs on localizing auditory memories of words, for example, at a determined point in the brain, one will be led, for reasons of equal value, either to distinguish this imaginative centre from the perceptive centre, or to confuse the two centres together. Now, this is precisely what experience verifies.

Let us note, indeed, the singular contradiction into which this theory is led by psychological analysis on the one hand, and by pathological facts on the other. On the one hand, it would seem, if perception, once accomplished, remains in the brain in the state of a stored memory, it can only be as an acquired disposition of the very elements upon which perception has made an impression: how, at what precise moment, could it go in search of others? And it is indeed at this natural solution that Bain 1 and Ribot 2 stop. But on the other hand pathology is there, warning us that the totality of memories of a certain kind may escape us while the corresponding faculty of perception remains intact. Psychic blindness does not prevent seeing, any more than psychic deafness prevents hearing.

More particularly, with regard to the loss of auditory memories of words—the only one that concerns us—there are numerous facts showing it to be regularly associated with a destructive lesion of the first and second left temporo-sphenoidal convolutions 3, without a single case being known in which this lesion has brought about deafness properly so called: it has even been experimentally produced in the monkey without causing in it anything other than psychic deafness, that is to say 1

But this hypothesis will then have against it the most elementary psychological observation; for we see that a memory, as it becomes clearer and more intense, tends to become perception, without there being a precise moment when a radical transformation takes place and when one can consequently say that it passes from imaginative elements to sensory elements. Thus these two contrary hypotheses, the first identifying the elements of perception with the elements of memory, the second distinguishing them, are of such a nature that each refers back to the other, without our being able to remain with either of them.

How could it be otherwise? Here again distinct perception and the memory-image are envisaged in a static state, as things of which the former would already be complete without the latter, instead of considering the dynamic process by which one becomes the other.

On the one hand, indeed, complete perception is defined and distinguished only by its coalescence with a memory-image which we project ahead of it. Attention is at this price, and without attention there is only a passive juxtaposition of sensations accompanied by a mechanical reaction. But on the other hand, as we shall show further on, the memory-image itself, reduced to the state of pure memory, would remain ineffective. Virtual, this memory can become actual only through the perception which attracts it. Powerless, it borrows its life and force from the present sensation in which it materializes. Does this not amount to saying that distinct perception is brought about by two currents of contrary senses, one of which, centripetal, comes from the external object, and the other, centrifugal, has as its starting-point what we call “pure memory”?

The first current, by itself, would give only a passive perception with the mechanical reactions that accompany it. The second, left to itself, tends to give an actualized memory, increasingly actual in proportion as the current becomes more marked. United, these two currents form, at the point where they meet, distinct and recognized perception.

This is what inner observation tells us. But we have no right to stop there. Certainly, there is great danger in venturing, without sufficient light, amid the obscure questions of cerebral localization. But we have said that the separation of complete perception and the memory-image brings clinical observation into conflict with psychological analysis, and that there results from this, for the doctrine of the localization of memories, a grave antinomy. We are bound to seek what becomes of the known facts when one ceases to regard the brain as the repository of memories 2.

The theory we are outlining here moreover resembles, in one respect, that of Wundt.

Let us at once indicate the common point and the essential difference. With Wundt, we consider that distinct perception implies a centrifugal action, and we are thereby led to suppose with him (though in a somewhat different sense) that the so-called imaginative centres are rather centres for grouping sensory impressions. But whereas, according to Wundt, centrifugal action consists in an “apperceptive stimulation” whose nature can be defined only in a general way and which seems to correspond to what is ordinarily called the fixation of attention, we maintain that this centrifugal action assumes in each case a distinct form, that of the very “object
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Spirit. (1939) 78

Let us admit for a moment, in order to simplify the exposition, that excitations coming from without give rise, whether in the cerebral cortex or in other centres, to elementary sensations. We still have here only elementary sensations. Yet, in fact, each perception encompasses a considerable number of these sensations, all coexisting and arranged in a determinate order. Whence comes this order, and what ensures this coexistence? In the case of a present material object, the answer is beyond doubt: order and coexistence come from a sense organ, impressed by an external object. This organ is constructed precisely so as to allow a plurality of simultaneous excitations to impress it in a certain manner and in a certain order, by distributing themselves all at once over selected parts of its surface.

It is therefore an immense keyboard, upon which the external object executes all at once its chord of a thousand notes, thereby provoking, in a determinate order and in a single moment, an enormous multitude of elementary sensations corresponding to all the points involved in the sensory centre.

Now remove the external object, or the sense organ, or both: the same elementary sensations may be excited, for the same strings are there, ready to resonate in the same way; but where is the keyboard that will make it possible to strike a thousand and a thousand of them at once and unite so many simple notes in the same chord? In our view, the “region of images,” if it exists, can only be a keyboard of this kind. Certainly, there would be nothing inconceivable in a purely psychic cause directly setting all the relevant strings in motion.

But in the case of mental hearing—the only one that concerns us—the localization of the function appears certain, since a determinate lesion of the temporal lobe abolishes it; and moreover we have set forth the reasons why we could neither admit nor even conceive residues of images deposited in a region of cerebral substance. Thus only one hypothesis remains plausible: namely, that this region occupies, in relation to the very centre of hearing, the symmetrical place of the sense organ, which here is the ear: it would be a mental ear.

But then the contradiction noted disappears. On the one hand, we understand that the remembered auditory image sets the same nervous elements in motion as the original perception, and that recollection thus gradually transforms itself into perception. And we understand also, on the other hand, that the faculty of recalling complex sounds, such as words, may involve other parts of nervous substance than the faculty of perceiving them: this is why real hearing survives, in psychic deafness, mental hearing. The strings are still there, and under the influence of external sounds they still vibrate; it is the inner keyboard that is lacking.

“virtual” which tends, degree by degree, to actualize itself. Hence an important difference in the conception of the role of the centres. Wundt is led to posit: 1º a general organ of apperception, occupying the frontal lobe; 2º particular centres which, doubtless incapable of storing Images, nevertheless retain tendencies or dispositions to reproduce them. We maintain, on the contrary, that nothing of an image can remain in cerebral substance, and that neither can there exist a centre of apperception, but that there are simply, in this substance, organs of virtual perception, influenced by the intention of recollection, just as there are at the periphery organs of real perception, influenced by the action of the object. See Physiological Psychology, vol. I, pp. 242–252.)
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 79

Finally, in other words, the centres in which elementary sensations arise can be activated, as it were, from two different sides, from the front and from behind. From the front they receive the impressions of the sense organs and consequently of a real object; from behind they undergo, through intermediary after intermediary, the influence of a virtual object. The image-centres, if they exist, can only be the organs symmetrical to the sense organs in relation to these sensory centres. They are no more repositories of pure recollections, that is, of virtual objects, than the sense organs are repositories of real objects.

Let us add that this is an infinitely abridged translation of what may take place in reality. The various sensory aphasias sufficiently prove that the evocation of an auditory image is not a simple act. Between the intention, which would be what we call pure recollection, and the auditory memory-image properly so called, there are most often interposed intermediate recollections, which must first realize themselves as memory-images in centres more or less remote. It is then by successive degrees that the idea comes to take body in this particular image which is the verbal image. Thus, mental hearing may be subordinated to the integrity of the various centres and of the pathways leading to them. But these complications change nothing in the fundamental state of affairs.

Whatever the number and nature of the intervening terms, we do not go from perception to idea, but from idea to perception, and the characteristic process of recognition is not centripetal, but centrifugal.

It would remain to be known, indeed, how excitations emanating from within can give rise, through their action upon the cerebral cortex or upon other centres, to sensations. And it is quite evident that this is only a convenient way of speaking. Pure recollection, as it actualizes itself, tends to provoke in the body all the corresponding sensations. But these virtual sensations themselves, in order to become real, must tend to make the body act, to impart to it the movements and attitudes of which they are the habitual antecedent. The disturbances of the so-called sensory centres—disturbances which ordinarily precede movements executed or sketched by the body, and whose normal role is indeed to prepare them by beginning them—are therefore less the real cause of sensation than the mark of its power and the condition of its efficacy.

The progress by which the virtual image realizes itself is nothing other than the series of stages through which this image comes to obtain useful actions from the body. The excitation of the so-called sensory centres is the last of these stages; it is the prelude to a motor reaction, the beginning of an action in space. In other words, the virtual image evolves toward virtual sensation, and virtual sensation toward real movement: this movement, in realizing itself, realizes at the same time the sensation of which it would be the natural prolongation and the image that has sought to become embodied with the sensation. We shall examine these virtual states more deeply and, by penetrating further into the inner mechanism of psychic and psychophysical actions, show by what continuous progress the past tends to regain its lost influence by actualizing itself.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 80
Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind (1939)
