## index_split_005

Le processus de localisation d'un souvenir dans le passé, par exemple, ne consiste pas du tout, comme on l'a dit, à plonger dans la masse de nos souvenirs comme dans un sac, pour en retirer des souvenirs de plus en plus rapprochés entre lesquels prendra place le souvenir à localiser. Par quelle heureuse chance mettrions-nous justement la main sur un nombre croissant de souvenirs intercalaires ? Le travail de localisation consiste en réalité dans un effort croissant d'expansion, par lequel la mémoire, toujours présente tout entière à elle-même, étend ses souvenirs sur une surface de plus en plus large
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 102

et finit par distinguer ainsi, dans un amas jusque-là confus, le souvenir qui ne retrouvait pas sa place. Ici encore, d'ailleurs, la pathologie de la mémoire nous fournirait des renseignements instructifs. Dans l'amnésie rétrograde, les souvenirs qui disparaissent de la conscience sont vraisemblablement conservés sur les plans extrêmes de la mémoire, et le sujet pourra les y retrouver par un effort exceptionnel, comme celui qu'il accomplit dans l'état d'hypnotisme.

Mais, sur les plans inférieurs, ces souvenirs attendaient, en quelque sorte, l'image dominante à laquelle ils pussent s'adosser. Tel choc brusque, telle émotion violente, sera l'événement décisif auquel ils s'attacheront : et si cet événement, en raison de son caractère soudain, se détache du reste de notre histoire, ils le suivront dans l'oubli. On conçoit donc que l'oubli consécutif à un choc, physique ou moral, comprenne les événements immédiatement antérieurs, - phénomène bien difficile à expliquer dans toutes les autres conceptions de la mémoire. Remarquons-le en passant : si l'on refuse d'attribuer quelque attente de ce genre aux souvenirs récents, et même relativement éloignés, le travail normal de la mémoire deviendra inintelligible. Car tout événement dont le souvenir s'est imprimé dans la mémoire, si simple qu'on le suppose, a occupé un certain temps.

Les perceptions qui ont rempli la première période de cet intervalle, et qui forment maintenant avec les perceptions consécutives un souvenir indivisé, étaient donc véritablement « en l'air » tant que la partie décisive de l'événement n'était pas encore produite. Entre la disparition d'un souvenir avec ses divers détails préliminaires et l'abolition, par l'amnésie rétrograde, d'un nombre plus ou moins grand de souvenirs antérieure, à un événement donné, il y a donc une simple différence de degré, et non pas de nature.

De ces diverses considérations sur la vie mentale inférieure découlerait une certaine conception de l'équilibre intellectuel. Cet équilibre ne sera évidemment faussé que par la perturbation des éléments qui lui servent de matière. Il ne saurait être question ici d'aborder les problèmes de pathologie mentale : nous ne pouvons cependant les éluder entièrement, puisque nous cherchons à déterminer la relation exacte du corps à l'esprit.

Nous avons supposé que l'esprit parcourait sans cesse l'intervalle compris entre ses deux limites extrêmes, le plan de l'action et le plan du rêve. S'agit-il d'une décision à prendre ? Ramassant, organisant la totalité de son expérience dans ce que nous appelons son caractère, il la fera converger vers des actions où vous trouverez, avec le passé qui leur sert de matière, la forme imprévue que la personnalité leur imprime ; mais l'action ne sera réalisable que si elle vient s'encadrer dans la situation actuelle, c'est-à-dire dans cet ensemble de circonstances qui naît d'une certaine position déterminée du corps dans le temps et dans l'espace. S'agit-il d'un travail intellectuel, d'une conception à former, d'une idée plus ou moins générale à extraire de la multiplicité des souvenirs ?

Une grande marge est laissée à la fantaisie d'une part, au discernement logique de l'autre : mais l'idée, pour être viable, devra toucher à la réalité présente par quelque côté, c'est-à-dire pouvoir, de degré en degré et par des diminutions ou contractions progressives d'elle-même, être plus ou moins jouée par le corps en même temps que représentée par l'esprit. Notre corps, avec les sensations qu'il reçoit d'un côté et les mouvements qu'il est capable
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 103

d'exécuter de l'autre, est donc bien ce qui fixe notre esprit, ce qui lui donne le lest et l'équilibre. L'activité de l'esprit déborde infiniment la masse des souvenirs accumulés, comme cette masse de souvenirs déborde infiniment elle-même les sensations et les mouvements de l'heure présente ; mais ces sensations et ces mouvements conditionnent ce qu'on pourrait appeler l'attention à la vie, et c'est pourquoi tout dépend de leur cohésion dans le travail normal de l'esprit, comme dans une pyramide qui se tiendrait debout sur sa pointe.

Qu'on jette d'ailleurs un coup d'œil sur la fine structure du système nerveux, telle que l'ont révélée des découvertes récentes. On croira apercevoir partout des conducteurs, nulle part des centres. Des fils placés bout à bout et dont les extrémités se rapprochent sans doute quand le courant passe, voilà tout ce qu'on voit. Et voilà peut-être tout ce qu'il y a, s'il est vrai que le corps ne soit qu'un lieu de rendez-vous entre les excitations reçues et les mouvements accomplis, ainsi que nous l'avons supposé dans tout le cours de notre travail.

Mais ces fils qui reçoivent du milieu extérieur des ébranlements ou des excitations et qui les lui renvoient sous forme de réactions appropriées, ces fils si savamment tendus de la périphérie à la périphérie, assurent justement par la solidité de leurs connexions et la précision de leurs entre-croisements l'équilibre sensori-moteur du corps, c'est-à-dire son adaptation à la situation présente.
Relâchez cette tension ou rompez cet équilibre : tout se passera comme si l'attention se détachait de la vie. Le rêve et l'aliénation ne paraissent guère être autre chose.

Nous parlions tout à l'heure de la récente hypothèse qui attribue le sommeil à une interruption de la solidarité entre neurones. Même si l'on n'accepte pas cette hypothèse (confirmée pourtant par de curieuses expériences), il faudra bien supposer pendant le sommeil profond une interruption au moins fonctionnelle de la relation établie dans le système nerveux entre l'excitation et la réaction motrice. De sorte que le rêve serait toujours l'état d'un esprit dont l'attention n'est pas fixée par l'équilibre sensori-moteur du corps. Et il paraît de plus en plus probable que cette détente du système nerveux est due à l'intoxi-cation de ses éléments par les produits non éliminés de leur activité normale à l'état de veille. Or, le rêve imite de tout point l'aliénation.

Non seulement tous les symptômes psychologiques de la folie se retrouvent dans le rêve, - au point que la comparaison de ces deux états est devenue banale, - mais l'aliénation paraît bien avoir également son origine dans un épuisement cérébral, lequel serait causé, comme la fatigue normale, par l'accumulation de certains poisons spécifiques dans les éléments du système nerveux 1. On sait que l'aliénation est souvent Consécutive aux maladies infectieuses, et que d'ailleurs on peut reproduire expérimentalement avec des toxiques tous les phénomènes de la folie 2. N'est-il pas vraisemblable, dès lors, que la rupture de l'équilibre mental dans l'aliénation tient tout simplement à une perturbation des relations sensori-motrices établies dans l'organisme ?

Cette perturbation suffirait à créer une espèce de vertige psychique, et à faire ainsi que la mémoire et l'attention perdent contact avec la réalité. Qu'on lise les descriptions données par certains fous de leur maladie naissante : on verra qu'ils éprouvent souvent un senti-1
Cette idée a été développée récemment par divers auteurs. On en trouvera l'exposé très systématique dans le travail de COWLES, The mechanism of insanity (American Journal of Insanity, 1890-91).

2

Voir surtout MOREAU DE TOURS, Du hachisch, Paris , 1845.
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 104

ment d'étrangeté ou, comme ils disent, de « non-réalité », comme si les choses perçues perdaient pour eux de leur relief et de leur solidité 1. Si nos analyses sont exactes, le sentiment concret que nous avons de la réalité présente consisterait en effet dans la conscience que nous prenons des mouvements effectifs par lesquels notre organisme répond naturellement aux excitations ; - de sorte que là où les relations se détendent ou se gâtent entre sensations et mouvements, le sens du réel s'affaiblit ou disparaît 2.

Il y aurait d'ailleurs ici une foule de distinctions à faire, non seulement entre les diverses formes de l'aliénation, mais encore entre l'aliénation proprement dite et ces scissions de la personnalité qu'une psychologie récente en a si curieusement rapprochées 3. Dans ces maladies de la personnalité, il semble que des groupes de souvenirs se détachent de la mémoire centrale et renoncent à leur solidarité avec les autres. Mais il est rare qu'on n'observe pas aussi des scissions concomitantes de la sensibilité et de la motricité 4. Nous ne pouvons nous empêcher de voir dans ces derniers phénomènes le véritable substrat matériel des premiers.

S'il est vrai que notre vie intellectuelle repose tout entière sur sa pointe, c'est-à-dire sur les fonctions sensori-motrices par lesquelles elle s'insère dans la réalité présente, l'équilibre intellectuel sera diversement troublé selon que ces fonctions seront lésées d'une manière ou d'une autre. Or, à côté des lésions qui affectent la vitalité générale des fonctions sensori-motrices, affaiblissant ou abolissant ce que nous avons appelé le sens du réel, il en est d'autres qui se traduisent par une diminution mécanique, et non plus dynamique, de ces fonctions, comme si certaines connexions sensori-motrices se séparaient purement et simplement des autres. Si notre hypothèse est fondée, la mémoire sera très diversement atteinte dans les deux cas.

Dans le premier, aucun souvenir ne sera distrait, mais tous les souvenirs seront moins lestés, moins solidement orientés vers le réel, d'où une rupture véritable de l'équilibre mental. Dans le second, l'équilibre ne sera pas rompu, mais il perdra de sa complexité. Les souvenirs conserveront leur aspect normal, mais renonceront en partie à leur solidarité, parce que leur base sensori-motrice, au lieu d'être pour ainsi dire chimiquement altérée, sera mécaniquement diminuée. Pas plus dans un cas que dans l'autre, d'ailleurs, les souvenirs ne seront directement atteints ou lésés.

L'idée que le corps conserve des souvenirs sous forme de dispositifs cérébraux, que les pertes et les diminutions de la mémoire consistent dans la destruction plus ou moins complète de ces mécanismes, l'exaltation de la mémoire et l'hallucination au contraire dans une exagération de leur activité, n'est donc confirmée ni par le raisonnement ni par les faits. La vérité est qu'il y a un cas, un seul, où l'observation semblerait d'abord suggérer cette vue : nous voulons parler de l'aphasie, ou plus généralement des troubles de la reconnaissance auditive ou visuelle. C'est le seul cas où l'on puisse assigner à la maladie un siège constant dans une circonvolution déterminée du cerveau ; mais c'est précisément aussi le cas où l'on n'assiste pas à l'arrachement 1
BALL , Leçons sur les maladies mentales, Paris, 1890, p. 608 et suiv. - Cf. une bien curieuse analyse : Visions, a personal narrative ( Journal of mental science , (1896, p.

2

Voir plus haut, p. 152.

3

Pierre JANET, Les accidents mentaux , Paris, 1894, p. 292 et suiv.

4

Pierre JANET, L'automatisme psychologique, Paris, 1889, p. 95 et suiv.
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 105

mécanique et tout de suite définitif de tels et tels souvenirs, mais plutôt à l'affaiblissement graduel et fonctionnel de l'ensemble de la mémoire intéressée. Et nous avons expliqué comment la lésion cérébrale pouvait occasionner cet affaiblissement, sans qu'il faille supposer en aucune manière une provision de souvenirs accumulée dans le cerveau. Ce qui est réellement atteint, ce sont les régions sensorielles et motrices correspondant à ce genre de perception, et surtout les annexes qui permettent de les actionner intérieurement, de sorte que le souvenir, ne trouvant plus à quoi se prendre, finit par devenir pratiquement impuissant : or, en psychologie, impuissance signifie inconscience.

Dans tous les autres cas, la lésion observée ou supposée, jamais nettement localisée, agit par la perturbation qu'elle apporte à l'ensemble des connexions sensori-motrices, soit qu'elle altère cette masse soit qu'elle la fragmente : d'où une rupture ou une simplification de l'équilibre intellectuel, et, par ricochet, le désordre ou la disjonction des souvenirs. La doctrine qui fait de la mémoire une fonction immédiate du cerveau, doctrine qui soulève des difficultés théoriques insolubles, doctrine dont la complication défie toute imagination et dont les résultats sont incompatibles avec les données de l'observation intérieure, ne peut donc même pas compter sur l'appui de la pathologie cérébrale.

Tous les faits et toutes les analogies sont en faveur d'une théorie qui ne verrait dans le cerveau qu'un intermédiaire entre les sensations et les mouvements, qui ferait de cet ensemble de sensations et de mouvements la pointe extrême de la vie mentale, pointe sans cesse insérée dans le tissu des événements, et qui, attribuant ainsi au corps l'unique fonction d'orienter la mémoire vers le réel et de la relier au présent, considérerait cette mémoire même comme absolument indépendante de la matière. En ce sens le cerveau contribue à rappeler le souvenir utile, mais plus encore à écarter provisoirement tous les autres. Nous ne voyons pas comment la mémoire se logerait dans la matière ; mais nous comprenons bien, - selon le mot profond d'un philosophe contemporain, - que « la matérialité mette en nous l'oubli 1 ».

1

RAVAISON, La philosophie en France au XIXe siècle, 3e éd., p. 176.
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 106
Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit (1939)

## Chapter III On the survival of images. Memory and mind
Chapter III
On the survival of images.
Memory and mind
Back to the table of contents

Let us briefly summarize what precedes. We have distinguished three terms, pure memory, memory-image, and perception, none of which, moreover, actually occurs in isolation. Perception is never a simple contact of the mind with the present object; it is thoroughly permeated by the memory-images which complete it by interpreting it. The memory-image, in turn, partakes of the

“pure memory” which it begins to materialize, and of the perception in which it tends to become incarnate: considered from this latter point of view, it would be defined as a nascent perception. Finally, pure memory, doubtless independent in principle, normally manifests itself only in the coloured and living image which reveals it. By symbolizing these three terms by the consecutive segments AB, BC, CD of one and the same straight line AD, one may say that our thought describes this line in a continuous movement that goes from A to D, and that it is impossible to say precisely where one of the terms ends and the other begins.

Moreover, this is what consciousness readily observes whenever it follows, in order to analyse memory, the very movement of memory at work. Is it a matter of recovering a memory, of evoking a period in our history? We are conscious of an act sui generis by which we
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 81

detach ourselves from the present in order first to place ourselves again in the past in general, then in a certain region of the past: a groping labour, analogous to the focusing of a photographic apparatus. But our memory still remains in a virtual state; we merely thus prepare ourselves to receive it by adopting the appropriate attitude. Little by little it appears like a nebulosity condensing; from virtual it passes into the actual state; and as its contours are traced and its surface is coloured, it tends to imitate perception. But it remains attached to the past by its deep roots, and if, once realized, it did not retain the effect of its original virtuality, if it were not, at the same time as a present state, something that stands out from the present, we should never recognize it as a memory.

The constant error of associationism is to substitute for this continuity of becoming, which is living reality, a discontinuous multiplicity of inert and juxtaposed elements. Precisely because each of the elements thus constituted contains, by reason of its origin, something of what precedes it and also of what follows it, it should assume in our eyes the form of a mixed and, as it were, impure state. But, on the other hand, the principle of associationism requires that every psychological state should be a kind of atom, a simple element.

Hence the necessity of sacrificing, in each of the phases that have been distinguished, the unstable to the stable, that is to say, the beginning to the end. Is it a matter of perception? Only the agglomerated sensations that colour it will be seen in it; the recollected images which form its obscure nucleus will be overlooked.

Is it in turn a matter of the recollected image? It will be taken as ready-made, realized in the state of a faint perception, and eyes will be closed to the pure memory which this image has progressively developed. In the competition thus instituted by associationism between the stable and the unstable, perception will therefore always displace the memory-image, and the memory-image pure memory. This is why pure memory disappears altogether. Associationism, cutting the whole progress AD in two by a line MO, sees in the portion OD only the sensations that terminate it and that constitute, for it, the whole of perception; —and, on the other hand, it likewise reduces the portion AO to the realized image in which pure memory culminates as it unfolds. Psychological life is then wholly reduced to these two elements, sensation and image.

And since, on the one hand, pure memory, which made it an original state, has been drowned in the image; since, on the other hand, the image has been brought still closer to perception by putting into perception in advance something of the image itself; there will no longer be found between these two states anything but a difference of degree or intensity. Hence the distinction between strong states and weak states, the former of which would be raised by us to perceptions of the present, the latter,—for no one knows why,—to representations of the past. But the truth is that we shall never reach the past unless we place ourselves in it at once. Essentially virtual, the past can be grasped by us as past only if we follow and adopt the movement by which it unfolds into a present image, emerging from darkness into broad daylight.
It is vain to seek its trace in something actual and already realized: one might as well seek darkness beneath light.

There precisely lies the error of associationism: situated in the actual, it exhausts itself in vain efforts to discover, in a realized and present state, the mark of its past origin, to distinguish memory from perception, and to erect into a difference of nature what it has condemned in advance to be only a difference of magnitude.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 82

To imagine is not to remember. Doubtless, as a memory becomes actualized, it tends to live in an image; but the converse is not true, and the pure and simple image will refer me back to the past only if it is indeed in the past that I have gone to seek it, thus following the continuous progress that brought it from darkness to light. This is what psychologists too often forget when they conclude, from the fact that a recollected sensation becomes more actual when one dwells upon it more, that the memory of the sensation was that nascent sensation. The fact they adduce is doubtless exact.

The greater the effort I make to recall a past pain, the more I tend actually to experience it. But this is readily understood, since the progress of memory consists precisely, as we were saying, in materializing itself. The question is whether the memory of the pain was truly pain at the outset. Because the hypnotized subject ends by feeling hot when he is insistently told that he is hot, it does not follow that the words of the suggestion are already hot. Nor should one conclude, from the fact that the memory of a sensation is prolonged into that sensation itself, that the memory was a nascent sensation: perhaps indeed this memory plays, with respect to the sensation that is about to arise, precisely the role of the magnetizer who gives the suggestion.

The reasoning we are criticizing, presented in this form, is therefore already without probative value; it is not yet vicious, because it benefits from the incontestable truth that memory is transformed as it becomes actualized. But absurdity becomes manifest when one reasons by following the inverse course,—which should nevertheless be equally legitimate in the hypothesis one adopts,—that is to say, when one makes the intensity of sensation decrease instead of making the intensity of pure memory increase. It should then happen, indeed, if the two states differed simply in degree, that at a certain moment sensation should be metamorphosed into memory. If the memory of a great pain, for example, is only a faint pain, conversely an intense pain which I experience will end, as it diminishes, by becoming a great recollected pain.

Now there comes a moment, without doubt, when it is impossible for me to say whether what I feel is a faint sensation that I experience or a faint sensation that I imagine (and this is natural, since the memory-image already partakes of sensation), but this faint state will never appear to me as the memory of a strong state. Memory is therefore something quite different.

But the illusion that consists in establishing between memory and perception only a difference of degree is more than a simple consequence of associationism, more than an accident in the history of philosophy. It has deep roots. It rests, in the final analysis, on a false idea of the nature and object of external perception. One wishes to see in perception only instruction addressed to a pure mind, and of an entirely speculative interest. Then, since memory itself is, in essence, knowledge of this kind, since it no longer has an object, one can find between perception and memory only a difference of degree, perception displacing memory and thus constituting our present, simply by virtue of the law of the stronger. But there is far more between past and present than a difference of degree.

My present is what interests me, what lives for me, and, to put it all in a word, what provokes me to action, whereas my past is essentially powerless. Let us dwell on this point. By opposing it to present perception, we shall already better understand the nature of what we call “pure memory.”
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Mind. (1939) 83

Indeed, one would vainly seek to characterize the memory of a past state unless one began by defining the concrete mark, accepted by consciousness, of present reality. What is, for me, the present moment? The nature of time is to flow; time already elapsed is the past, and we call present the instant at which it flows. But there can be no question here of a mathematical instant. To be sure, there is an ideal present, purely conceived, an indivisible limit that would separate the past from the future. But the real, concrete, lived present, that of which I speak when I speak of my present perception, necessarily occupies a duration. Where, then, is this duration situated? Is it on this side, or beyond, the mathematical point that I determine ideally when I think of the present instant?

It is all too evident that it is both on this side and beyond at once, and that what I call “my present” encroaches at once upon my past and upon my future. Upon my past first, for “the moment when I speak is already far from me”; upon my future next, for this moment leans toward the future, it is toward the future that I tend, and if I could fix this indivisible present, this infinitesimal element of the curve of time, it is the direction of the future that it would show. Thus the psychological state that I call “my present” must be at once a perception of the immediate past and a determination of the immediate future. Now the immediate past, insofar as it is perceived, is, as we shall see, sensation, since every sensation translates a very long succession of elementary vibrations; and the immediate future, insofar as it is being determined, is action or movement.

My present is therefore at once sensation and movement; and since my present forms an undivided whole, this movement must be connected with this sensation, prolong it into action. Hence I conclude that my present consists in a combined system of sensations and movements. My present is, in essence, sensorimotor.

This is to say that my present consists in the consciousness I have of my body. Extended in space, my body experiences sensations and at the same time executes movements. Since sensations and movements are localized at determinate points of this extension, there can be, at a given moment, only one system of movements and sensations. This is why my present appears to me to be something absolutely determinate, and sharply distinct from my past. Placed between the matter that acts upon it and the matter upon which it acts, my body is a centre of action, the place where the impressions received intelligently choose their path in order to be transformed into accomplished movements; it therefore indeed represents the current state of my becoming, that which, in my duration, is in the process of being formed.

More generally, in this continuity of becoming which is reality itself, the present moment is constituted by the quasi-instantaneous section that our perception makes in the mass in the course of flowing, and this section is precisely what we call the material world: our body occupies its centre; it is, of this material world, that which we directly feel flowing; the actuality of our present consists in its current state. Since matter, insofar as it is extended in space, must be defined, according to us, as a present that ceaselessly begins again, conversely our present is the very materiality of our existence, that is to say, a set of sensations and movements, nothing else.

And this set is determinate, unique for each moment of duration, precisely because sensations and movements occupy places in space and there cannot be, in the same place, several things at once. — How is it that one has been able to disregard a truth so simple, so evident, and which is, after all, only the idea of common sense?
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Mind. (1939) 84
The reason is precisely that one persists in finding only a difference of degree, and not of nature, between current sensations and pure memory.

The difference, in our view, is radical. My current sensations are what occupies determinate portions of the surface of my body; pure memory, on the contrary, concerns no part of my body. Doubtless it will engender sensations by becoming materialized; but at that precise moment it will cease to be memory in order to pass into the state of a present thing, actually lived; and I shall restore to it its character as memory only by referring back to the operation through which I evoked it, virtual, from the depths of my past. It is precisely because I shall have made it active that it will have become actual, that is to say, sensation capable of provoking movements. On the contrary, most psychologists see in pure memory only a weaker perception, a set of nascent sensations.

Having thus effaced beforehand every difference of nature between sensation and memory, they are led by the logic of their hypothesis to materialize memory and to idealize sensation. Is it a matter of memory? They perceive it only in the form of an image, that is to say, already embodied in nascent sensations. Having thus transferred to it the essential part of sensation, and unwilling to see, in the ideality of this memory, something distinct, something sharply distinct from sensation itself, they are obliged, when they return to pure sensation, to leave it the ideality that they had thus implicitly conferred upon nascent sensation. If the past, indeed, which by hypothesis no longer acts, can subsist in the state of weak sensation, then there are powerless sensations.
If pure memory, which by hypothesis concerns no determinate part of the body, is a nascent sensation, then sensation is not essentially localized at a point of the body.

Hence the illusion that consists in seeing sensation as a floating and unextended state, which would acquire extension and become consolidated in the body only accidentally: an illusion which deeply vitiates, as we have seen, the theory of external perception, and raises a good number of the questions pending among the various metaphysics of matter. One must accept it: sensation is, in essence, extensive and localized; it is a source of movement; — pure memory, being unextended and powerless, participates in sensation in no way.

What I call my present is my attitude with respect to the immediate future; it is my imminent action. My present is therefore indeed sensorimotor. Of my past, only that becomes image, and consequently at least nascent sensation, which can collaborate in this action, insert itself into this attitude, in a word, make itself useful; but as soon as it becomes image, the past leaves the state of pure memory and merges with a certain part of my present. Memory actualized in an image thus differs profoundly from that pure memory.

The image is a present state, and can participate in the past only through the memory from which it has emerged. Memory, on the contrary, powerless so long as it remains useless, remains pure of every admixture with sensation, without attachment to the present, and consequently unextended.
This radical powerlessness of pure memory will help us precisely to understand how it is preserved in a latent state. Without yet entering into the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Mind. (1939) 85

heart of the question, let us confine ourselves to observing that our reluctance to conceive unconscious psychological states arises chiefly from the fact that we take consciousness to be the essential property of psychological states, so that a psychological state could not, it seems, cease to be conscious without ceasing to exist. But if consciousness is only the characteristic mark of the present, that is to say, of what is currently lived, that is to say finally, of what is acting, then that which does not act may cease to belong to consciousness without necessarily ceasing to exist in some manner.

In other words, in the psychological domain, consciousness would not be synonymous with existence but only with real action or immediate efficacy, and the extension of this term thus being limited, one would have less difficulty representing an unconscious psychological state, that is to say, in short, a powerless one. Whatever idea one may form of consciousness in itself, such as it would appear if it were exercised without hindrance, one cannot deny that, in a being that performs bodily functions, consciousness has above all the role of presiding over action and illuminating a choice. It therefore casts its light upon the immediate antecedents of the decision and upon all those past memories which can organize themselves usefully with them; the rest remains in shadow.

But here we find again, in a new form, the ever-renewing illusion that we have been pursuing since the beginning of this work. It is held that consciousness, even when joined to bodily functions, is a faculty accidentally practical, essentially directed toward speculation. Then, since one does not see what interest it would have in letting the knowledge it possesses escape, devoted as it would be to pure knowledge, one does not understand that it renounces illuminating what is not wholly lost to it. It would follow that only that belongs to it by right which it possesses in fact, and that, in the domain of consciousness, all that is real is actual.

But restore to consciousness its true role: there will be no more reason to say that the past, once perceived, is effaced, than there is to suppose that material objects cease to exist when I cease to perceive them.

Let us insist on this last point, for here is the centre of the difficulties and the source of the equivocations surrounding the problem of the unconscious. The idea of an unconscious representation is clear, despite a widespread prejudice; one may even say that we make constant use of it and that there is no conception more familiar to common sense. Everyone admits, indeed, that the images currently present to our perception are not the whole of matter. But on the other hand, what can an unperceived material object, an unimagined image, be, if not a kind of unconscious mental state? Beyond the walls of your room, which you perceive at this moment, there are the neighbouring rooms, then the rest of the house, finally the street and the city in which you live.

Whatever the theory of matter to which you subscribe: realist or idealist, when you speak of the city, the street, the other rooms of the house, you obviously think of so many perceptions absent from your consciousness and yet given outside it. They are not created as your consciousness receives them; they therefore already were in some manner, and since, by hypothesis, your consciousness did not apprehend them, how could they exist in themselves except in the unconscious state? Whence comes it, then, that an existence outside consciousness appears clear to us when objects are concerned, obscure when we speak of the subject? Our perceptions, actual and virtual, extend along two lines, one horizontal AB, which contains all simultaneous objects in space, the other vertical CI, upon
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Mind. (1939) 86

along which our successive memories, distributed over time, are arranged. Point I, the intersection of the two lines, is the only one currently given to our consciousness. How does it come about that we do not hesitate to posit the reality of the entire line AB, although it remains unnoticed, whereas, on the contrary, of line CI the present I, currently perceived, is the only point that seems to us truly to exist? At the basis of this radical distinction between the temporal and spatial series there are so many confused or poorly sketched ideas, so many hypotheses devoid of all speculative value, that we could not exhaust its analysis all at once.

To unmask the illusion completely, one would have to go back to its origin and follow through all its turns the double movement by which we come to posit objective realities unrelated to consciousness and states of consciousness without objective reality, space then seeming indefinitely to preserve the things juxtaposed within it, while time would destroy, as it goes, the states that succeed one another within it. One part of this work was done in our first chapter, when we dealt with objectivity in general; another will be done in the final pages of this book, when we speak of the idea of matter.
Let us confine ourselves here to indicating a few essential points.

First, the objects arranged along this line AB represent to our eyes what we are about to perceive, whereas line CI contains only what has already been perceived. Now, the past no longer interests us; it has exhausted its possible action, or will regain an influence only by borrowing the vitality of present perception. On the contrary, the immediate future consists in imminent action, in energy not yet expended. The unperceived part of the material universe, pregnant with promises and threats, thus has for us a reality which the periods of our past existence that are presently unperceived cannot and should not have. But this distinction, wholly relative to practical utility and the material needs of life, assumes in our mind the increasingly distinct form of a metaphysical distinction.

We have in fact shown that the objects situated around us represent, to varying degrees, an action that we can perform upon things or that we shall have to undergo from them. The due date of this possible action is marked precisely by the greater or lesser remoteness of the corresponding object, so that distance in space measures the nearness of a threat or a promise in time. Thus space provides us all at once with the schema of our near future; and since this future must unfold indefinitely, the space that symbolizes it has the property of remaining, in its immobility, indefinitely open. Hence the immediate horizon given to our perception necessarily seems to us surrounded by a wider circle, existing though unperceived, this circle itself implying another that surrounds it, and so on indefinitely.
It is therefore of the essence of our present perception, insofar as it is extended, always to be only a content
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 87

in relation to a vaster, even indefinite, experience that contains it: and this experience, absent from our consciousness since it exceeds the perceived horizon, nevertheless appears to be currently given. But whereas we feel ourselves dependent upon these material objects which we thus erect into present realities, our memories, as past, are so many dead weights that we drag along with us and of which we prefer to pretend ourselves rid. The same instinct by virtue of which we open space indefinitely before us causes us to close time behind us as it elapses. And whereas reality, as extension, seems to us to exceed our perception infinitely, on the contrary, in our inner life, only that which begins with the present moment seems real to us; the rest is practically abolished.

Then, when a memory reappears in consciousness, it has the effect upon us of a ghost whose mysterious appearance would have to be explained by special causes. In reality, the adherence of this memory to our present state is altogether comparable to that of unperceived objects to the objects we perceive, and the unconscious plays in both cases a role of the same kind.

But we experience great difficulty in representing things to ourselves in this way, because we have acquired the habit of emphasizing the differences, and, on the contrary, effacing the resemblances, between the series of objects simultaneously arranged in space and that of states successively developed in time. In the former, the terms condition one another in a wholly determinate manner, so that the appearance of each new term could have been foreseen. Thus I know, when I leave my room, which rooms I am going to pass through. On the contrary, my memories present themselves in an apparently capricious order. The order of representations is therefore necessary in one case, contingent in the other; and it is this necessity that I hypostatize, as it were, when I speak of the existence of objects outside all consciousness.

If I see no difficulty in supposing the totality of objects that I do not perceive to be given, it is because the rigorously determined order of these objects lends them the appearance of a chain, of which my present perception would be but one link: this link then communicates its actuality to the rest of the chain. — But, on looking more closely, one would see that our memories form a chain of the same kind, and that our character, always present in all our decisions, is indeed the present synthesis of all our past states. In this condensed form, our previous psychological life exists even more for us than the external world, of which we never perceive more than a very small part, whereas, on the contrary, we make use of the totality of our lived experience.

It is true that we possess it in this way only in abbreviated form, and that our former perceptions, considered as distinct individualities, give us the impression either of having wholly disappeared or of reappearing only at their own fancy. But this appearance of complete destruction or capricious resurrection arises simply from the fact that present consciousness accepts at every moment what is useful and temporarily rejects what is superfluous. Ever directed toward action, it can materialize from our former perceptions only those which organize themselves with present perception in order to contribute to the final decision.

If, in order for my will to manifest itself at a given point in space, my consciousness must pass one by one through those intermediaries or obstacles whose totality constitutes what is called distance in space, it is, on the other hand, useful to it, in order to illuminate this action, to leap over the interval of time that separates the present situation from an
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 88

analogous earlier situation; and since it transports itself there in a single leap, the entire intermediate part of the past escapes its grasp. The same reasons that cause our perceptions to arrange themselves in rigorous continuity in space thus cause our memories to be illuminated discontinuously in time. With respect to unperceived objects in space and unconscious memories in time, we are not dealing with two radically different forms of existence; but the requirements of action are inverse in one case from what they are in the other.

But here we touch upon the capital problem of existence, a problem which we can only touch upon lightly, lest we be led, from question to question, to the very heart of metaphysics. Let us simply say that with regard to the things of experience,—the only ones that concern us here,—existence appears to imply two conditions taken together: 1º presentation to consciousness, 2º the logical or causal connection of what is thus presented with what precedes and what follows. For us, the reality of a psychological state or of a material object consists in this double fact: that our consciousness perceives them and that they form part of a temporal or spatial series in which the terms determine one another. But these two conditions admit of degrees, and it is conceivable that, though both necessary, they may be unequally fulfilled.

Thus, in the case of present internal states, the connection is less close, and the determination of the present by the past, leaving a wide place for contingency, does not have the character of a mathematical derivation;—on the other hand, presentation to consciousness is perfect, a present psychological state delivering to us the totality of its content in the very act by which we apprehend it. On the contrary, if external objects are in question, it is the connection that is perfect, since these objects obey necessary laws; but then the other condition, presentation to consciousness, is never more than partially fulfilled, for the material object, precisely by reason of the multiplicity of unperceived elements that connect it to all the other objects, seems to us to contain within itself and to conceal behind itself infinitely more than what it allows us to see.

— We should therefore say that existence, in the empirical sense of the word, always implies both conscious apprehension and regular connection, but in different degrees. But our understanding, whose function is to establish sharp distinctions, does not understand things in this way. Rather than admitting the presence, in all cases, of the two elements mixed in diverse proportions, it prefers to dissociate these two elements, and thus to attribute to external objects on the one hand, to internal states on the other, two radically different modes of existence, each characterized by the exclusive presence of the condition that should simply be declared preponderant.

Then the existence of psychological states will consist entirely in their apprehension by consciousness, and that of external phenomena likewise entirely in the rigorous order of their concomitance and succession. Hence the impossibility of allowing materially existing but unperceived objects the slightest participation in consciousness, and non-conscious internal states the slightest participation in existence. We showed, at the beginning of this book, the consequences of the first illusion: it results in falsifying our representation of matter. The second, complementary to the first, vitiates our conception of mind by spreading an artificial obscurity over the idea of the unconscious.
Our entire past psychological life conditions our present state without determining it in a necessary manner; it is also wholly revealed in our character, although none of the past states
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 89
manifests itself explicitly in character. Taken together, these two conditions assure each of the past psychological states a real, though unconscious, existence.

But we are so accustomed to reversing, to the greater advantage of practice, the real order of things, we are subjected to such a degree to the obsession of images drawn from space, that we cannot refrain from asking where memory is preserved. We conceive that physico-chemical phenomena take place in the brain, that the brain is in the body, the body in the air that bathes it, etc.; but the past, once accomplished, if it is preserved, where is it? To place it, in the state of a molecular modification, in cerebral substance, seems simple and clear, because we then have a reservoir currently given, which it would suffice to open in order to cause the latent images to flow into consciousness. But if the brain cannot serve such a use, in what storehouse shall we lodge the accumulated images?

One forgets that the relation of container to content borrows its apparent clarity and universality from the necessity under which we are always to open space before us, always to close duration behind us. Because one has shown that one thing is in another, one has not thereby in the least elucidated the phenomenon of its preservation. More than that: let us admit for a moment that the past survives itself in the form of memory stored in the brain. It will then be necessary for the brain, in order to preserve memory, at the very least to preserve itself.

But this brain, as an image extended in space, occupies only the present moment; together with all the rest of the material universe, it constitutes a constantly renewed cross-section of universal becoming. Either, then, you will have to suppose that this universe perishes and is reborn, by a veritable miracle, at every moment of duration, or you will have to transfer to it the continuity of existence that you refuse to consciousness, and make of its past a reality that survives itself and is prolonged in its present: you will therefore have gained nothing by storing memory in matter, and you will instead find yourself obliged to extend to the totality of the states of the material world that independent and integral survival of the past which you refused to psychological states.

This survival of the past in itself therefore imposes itself in one form or another, and the difficulty we experience in conceiving it comes simply from our attributing to the series of memories, in time, that necessity of containing and being contained which is true only of the ensemble of bodies instantaneously perceived in space. The fundamental illusion consists in transferring to duration itself, as it flows, the form of the instantaneous cross-sections which we make in it.

But how could the past, which, by hypothesis, has ceased to be, preserve itself by itself? Is there not here a genuine contradiction?—We reply that the question is precisely whether the past has ceased to exist, or whether it has merely ceased to be useful. You arbitrarily define the present as that which is, whereas the present is simply that which is being made. Nothing is less than the present moment, if by that you mean that indivisible limit which separates the past from the future. When we think of this present as yet to be, it is not yet; and when we think of it as existing, it is already past. But if, on the contrary, you consider the concrete present actually lived by consciousness, one may say that this present consists in large part of the immediate past.
In the fraction of a second lasting the shortest possible perception of light, trillions of vibrations have taken
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 90

place, the first of which is separated from the last by an enormously divided interval. Your perception, however instantaneous it may be, thus consists of an incalculable multitude of remembered elements, and, in truth, all perception is already memory. Practically, we perceive only the past, pure present being the elusive progress of the past gnawing at the future.

Consciousness therefore sheds its light, at every moment, upon that immediate part of the past which, leaning over the future, works to realize it and to join it to itself. Solely concerned with thus determining an indeterminate future, it may cast a little of its light upon those of our states further back in the past which would usefully organize themselves with our present state, that is to say, with our immediate past; the rest remains obscure. It is in this illuminated part of our history that we remain situated, by virtue of the fundamental law of life, which is a law of action: hence the difficulty we experience in conceiving memories that would preserve themselves in the shadows.

Our reluctance to admit the integral survival of the past thus stems from the very orientation of our psychological life, a veritable unfolding of states in which we have an interest in looking at what is unfolding, and not at what has entirely unfolded.

Thus, by a long detour, we return to our starting point. There are, we said, two memories profoundly distinct from one another: one, fixed in the organism, is nothing other than the ensemble of intelligently constructed mechanisms that ensure a suitable reply to the various possible solicitations. It enables us to adapt ourselves to the present situation, and causes the actions undergone by us to prolong themselves of their own accord in reactions sometimes accomplished, sometimes merely nascent, but always more or less appropriate. Habit rather than memory, it enacts our past experience, but does not evoke its image. The other is true memory.

Coextensive with consciousness, it retains and arranges in succession all our states as they occur, leaving each fact its place and consequently marking its date, moving quite genuinely in the definitive past, and not, like the first, in a present that begins anew unceasingly.

But while profoundly distinguishing these two forms of memory, we had not shown their connection. Above the body, with its mechanisms symbolizing the accumulated effort of past actions, memory which imagines and repeats hovered, suspended in the void. But if we never perceive anything other than our immediate past, if our consciousness of the present is already memory, the two terms which we had at first separated will become intimately joined together. Viewed from this new standpoint, indeed, our body is nothing other than the invariably reborn part of our representation, the ever-present part, or rather that which has just at every moment passed.

Itself an image, this body cannot store images, since it is part of the images; and this is why the undertaking of wishing to localize past, or even present, perceptions in the brain is chimerical: they are not in it; it is in them. But this quite particular image, which persists amid the others and which I call my body, constitutes at each instant, as we said, a transverse cross-section of universal becoming. It is therefore the place of passage of movements received and returned, the link between the things that act upon me and the things upon which I act, the seat, in a word, of sensori-motor phenomena. If I represent by a cone SAB the totality of the memories accumulated in my memory, the base AB, resting in the past, remains motionless, while the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 91
apex S, which at every moment represents my present, constantly advances, and constantly also touches the mobile plane P of my present representation of the universe.

At S the image of the body is concentrated; and, forming part of the plane P, this image confines itself to receiving and returning the actions emanating from all the images of which the plane is composed.

The memory of the body, constituted by the ensemble of sensori-motor systems organized by habit, is therefore a quasi-instantaneous memory upon which the true memory of the past serves as a base. Since they do not constitute two separate things, since the first is, as we said, only the mobile point inserted by the second into the moving plane of experience, it is natural that these two functions should lend one another mutual support. On the one hand, indeed, the memory of the past presents to sensori-motor mechanisms all the memories capable of guiding them in their task and directing the motor reaction in the direction suggested by the lessons of experience: this is precisely what associations by contiguity and by similarity consist in.

But on the other hand sensori-motor apparatuses furnish powerless, that is to say unconscious, memories with the means of taking on a body, of materializing themselves, finally of becoming present. For a memory to reappear in consciousness, it must indeed descend from the heights of pure memory to the precise point where action is accomplished. In other words, it is from the present that the call proceeds to which memory responds, and it is from the sensori-motor elements of present action that memory borrows the warmth which gives it life.

Is it not by the solidity of this agreement, by the precision with which these two complementary memories fit into one another, that we recognize “well-balanced” minds, that is to say, fundamentally, men perfectly adapted to life? What characterizes the man of action is the promptness with which he calls to the aid of a given situation all the memories relating to it; but it is also the insurmountable barrier encountered in him, as they present themselves at the threshold of consciousness, by useless or indifferent memories. To live in the wholly pure present, to respond to an excitation by an immediate reaction that prolongs it, is characteristic of an inferior animal: the man who proceeds thus is an impulsive person.

But he is scarcely better adapted to action who lives in the past for the pleasure of living there, and in whom memories emerge into the light of consciousness without profit for the present situation: he is no longer impulsive, but a dreamer. Between these two extremes lies the fortunate disposition of a memory docile enough to follow precisely the contours of the present situation, but energetic enough to resist every other call. Common sense, or practical sense, is probably nothing else.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 92

The extraordinary development of spontaneous memory in most children is due precisely to the fact that they have not yet made their memory solidaristic with their conduct. They ordinarily follow the impression of the moment, and, since action does not bend in them to the indications of memory, conversely their memories are not limited to the necessities of action. They seem to retain more easily only because they remember with less discernment. The apparent diminution of memory, as intelligence develops, is therefore due to the increasing organization of memories with acts. Conscious memory thus loses in extent what it gains in penetrating force: at first it had the facility of dream-memory, but that was because it was quite genuinely dreaming.

Moreover, this same exaggeration of spontaneous memory is observed in men whose intellectual development scarcely surpasses that of childhood. A missionary, after preaching a long sermon to savages in Africa, saw one of them repeat it word for word, with the same gestures, from beginning to end 1.

But if our past remains almost wholly hidden from us because it is inhibited by the necessities of present action, it will recover the strength to cross the threshold of consciousness in all cases where we cease to take an interest in effective action in order to place ourselves, in a manner of speaking, once more in the life of dreams. Sleep, natural or artificial, produces precisely a detachment of this kind. We were recently shown in sleep an interruption of contact between the ner. vous elements, sensory and motor 2. Even if one does not linger over this ingenious hypothesis, it is impossible not to see in sleep a relaxation, at least functional, of the tension of the nervous system, always ready during waking to prolong the received excitation in an appropriate reaction. Now it is a fact of commonplace observation that the “exaltation”

of memory occurs in certain dreams and in certain somnambulistic states. Memories believed to have been abolished then reappear with striking exactitude; we relive in all their details entirely forgotten scenes of childhood; we speak languages which we did not even remember having learned. But nothing is more instructive in this regard than what occurs in certain cases of sudden suffocation, among the drowned and the hanged. The subject, restored to life, declares that he saw pass before him, in a short time, all the forgotten events of his history, with their most minute circumstances and in the very order in which they had occurred 3.

A human being who dreamed his existence instead of living it would thus doubtless keep before his gaze, at every moment, the infinite multitude of details of his past history. And he who, on the contrary, repudiated this memory together with all that it engenders would incessantly play out his existence instead of truly representing it to himself: a conscious automaton, he would follow the incline of useful habits¹
