which prolong excitation into an appropriate reaction. The former would never emerge from the particular, and even from the individual. Leaving to each image its date in time and its place in space, he would see how it differs from the others and not how it resembles them. The latter, always borne along by habit, would, on the contrary, discern in a situation only the aspect by which it practically resembles previous situations. No doubt incapable of thinking the universal, since the general idea supposes the at least virtual representation of a multitude of remembered images, he would nevertheless move within the universal, habit being to action what generality is to thought.

But these two extreme states, one of an entirely contemplative memory that apprehends only the singular in its vision, the other of an entirely motor memory that stamps the mark of generality upon its action, are isolated and fully manifested only in exceptional cases. In normal life, they intimately penetrate one another, thus each relinquishing something of its original purity. The first is expressed by the recollection of differences, the second by the perception of resemblances; at the confluence of the two currents appears the general idea.
The question here is not to settle wholesale the question of general ideas.

Among these ideas there are some whose sole origin is not perceptions and which relate only very remotely to material objects. We shall leave them aside, in order to consider only the general ideas founded upon what we call the perception of resemblances. We wish to follow pure memory, integral memory, in the continuous effort it makes to insert itself into motor habit. In this way we shall make the role and nature of this memory better known; but in this way also we shall perhaps clarify, by considering them under a quite particular aspect, the two equally obscure notions of resemblance and generality.

By pressing as closely as possible upon the psychological difficulties raised around the problem of general ideas, we shall arrive, we believe, at enclosing them within this circle: in order to generalize, one must first abstract, but in order to abstract usefully, one must already know how to generalize. It is around this circle that nominalism and conceptualism gravitate, consciously or unconsciously, each of the two doctrines having principally in its favor the inadequacy of the other. The nominalists, indeed, retaining from the general idea only its extension, see in it simply an open and indefinite series of individual objects. For them, therefore, the unity of the idea can consist only in the identity of the symbol by which we designate indifferently all these distinct objects.

If they are to be believed, we begin by perceiving a thing, then add a word to it: this word, reinforced by the faculty or habit of extending to an indefinite number of other things, then sets itself up as a general idea. But in order for the word thus to extend and nevertheless be limited to the objects it designates, these objects must still present to us resemblances which, by bringing them closer to one another, distinguish them from all the objects to which the word does not apply. Generalization therefore does not seem to proceed without the abstract consideration of common qualities, and, step by step, nominalism will be led to define the general idea by its comprehension, and no longer merely by its extension, as it wished
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 94

at first. Conceptualism starts from this comprehension. According to it, intelligence resolves the superficial unity of the individual into diverse qualities, each of which, isolated from the individual that limited it, thereby becomes representative of a genus. Instead of considering each genus as comprising, in act, a multiplicity of objects, it is now desired, on the contrary, that each object should contain, in potency, and as so many qualities that it would hold captive, a multiplicity of genera.

But the question is precisely whether individual qualities, even isolated by an effort of abstraction, do not remain individual as they were at first, and whether, in order to erect them into genera, a new operation of the mind is not necessary, by which it first imposes a name upon each quality, then collects under this name a multiplicity of individual objects. The whiteness of a lily is not the whiteness of a cloth of snow; even isolated from the snow and the lily, they remain lily-whiteness and snow-whiteness. They renounce their individuality only if we take account of their resemblance in order to give them a common name: then applying this name to an indefinite number of similar objects, we send back to the quality, by a kind of rebound, the generality that the word has gone to seek in its application to things.

But in reasoning thus, do we not return to the point of view of extension that we had abandoned at first? We are therefore indeed turning in a circle, nominalism leading us to conceptualism, and conceptualism bringing us back to nominalism. Generalization can be accomplished only through an extraction of common qualities; but in order to appear common, qualities must already have undergone a work of generalization.

Now, by probing these two opposing theories more deeply, one would discover in them a common postulate: both suppose that we start from the perception of individual objects. The first composes the genus through an enumeration; the second disengages it through an analysis; but it is upon individuals, considered as so many realities given to immediate intuition, that analysis and enumeration bear. Such is the postulate. Despite its apparent obviousness, it is neither plausible nor in conformity with the facts.

A priori, indeed, it certainly seems that the clear distinction of individual objects is a luxury of perception, just as the clear representation of general ideas is a refinement of intelligence. The perfect conception of genera is doubtless proper to human thought; it requires an effort of reflection, by which we efface from a representation the particularities of time and place. But reflection upon these particularities, reflection without which the individuality of objects would escape us, presupposes a faculty of noticing differences, and thereby a memory of images, which is certainly the privilege of man and of the higher animals.

It therefore seems that we begin neither with the perception of the individual nor with the conception of the genus, but with an intermediate knowledge, with a confused feeling of a striking quality or of resemblance: this feeling, equally distant from fully conceived generality and from clearly perceived individuality, engenders both by way of dissociation. Reflective analysis purifies it into a general idea; discriminating memory solidifies it into perception of the individual.

But this will appear clearly if we return to the wholly utilitarian origins of our perception of things. What interests us in a given situation, what we must first grasp in it, is the aspect by which it
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 95

can respond to a tendency or a need: now, need goes straight to resemblance or quality, and has no use for individual differences. The perception of animals must ordinarily be limited to this discernment of the useful.

It is grass in general that attracts the herbivore: the color and odor of grass, felt and undergone as forces (we do not go so far as to say: thought as qualities or genera), are the sole immediate data of its external perception. Upon this ground of generality or resemblance its memory may bring out the contrasts from which differentiations will arise; it will then distinguish one landscape from another landscape, one field from another field; but that is, we repeat, the superfluous in perception and not the necessary. Will it be said that we have merely pushed back the problem, that we have simply relegated to the unconscious the operation by which resemblances are disengaged and genera constituted?

But we relegate nothing to the unconscious, for the very simple reason that, in our view, it is not an effort of a psychological nature that here disengages resemblance: this resemblance acts objectively as a force, and provokes identical reactions by virtue of the wholly physical law that requires the same overall effects to follow the same profound causes. Because hydrochloric acid always acts in the same way upon calcium carbonate—whether it be marble or chalk—will it be said that the acid disentangles among species the characteristic traits of a genus? Now, there is no essential difference between the operation by which this acid draws its base from the salt and the act of the plant that invariably extracts from the most diverse soils the same elements that are to serve it as nourishment.

Now take a further step; imagine a rudimentary consciousness such as that of the amoeba stirring in a drop of water: the little animal will sense the resemblance, and not the difference, among the various organic substances that it can assimilate. In short, from mineral to plant, from plant to the simplest conscious beings, from animal to man, one follows the progress of the operation by which things and beings seize, in their surroundings, what attracts them, what practically interests them, without their needing to abstract, simply because the rest of the surroundings has no hold on them: this identity of reaction to superficially different actions is the germ that human consciousness develops into general ideas.

Let us reflect, indeed, on the purpose of our nervous system, such as it appears to result from its structure. We see very diverse perceptive apparatuses, all connected, through the intermediary of the centres, to the same motor apparatuses. Sensation is unstable; it may take on the most varied shades; on the other hand, the motor mechanism, once set up, will function invariably in the same manner. We may therefore suppose perceptions as different as possible in their superficial details: if they are continued by the same motor reactions, if the organism can extract from them the same useful effects, if they impress upon the body the same attitude, something common will emerge from them, and the general idea will thus have been felt, undergone, before being represented. - Thus we are finally freed from the circle in which we at first seemed enclosed.

In order to generalize, we said, one must abstract resemblances, but in order usefully to bring out resemblance, one must already know how to generalize. The truth is that there is no circle, because the resemblance from which the mind starts, when it first abstracts, is not the resemblance at which the mind arrives when it consciously generalizes. The one from which it starts is a felt, lived resemblance, or, if you will, one automatically enacted. The one to which it returns is an intelligently perceived or thought resemblance. And it is
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 96

precisely in the course of this progress that, through the double effort of understanding and memory, the perception of individuals and the conception of genera are constructed,—memory grafting distinctions onto spontaneously abstracted resemblances, understanding drawing from the habit of resemblances the clear idea of generality. This idea of generality was originally only our consciousness of an identity of attitude amid a diversity of situations; it was habit itself, rising from the sphere of movements to that of thought. But from genera thus mechanically sketched by habit, we have passed, through an effort of reflection carried out upon this very operation, to the general idea of the genus; and once this idea had been constituted, we constructed, this time voluntarily, an unlimited number of general notions.

It is not necessary here to follow intelligence in the detail of this construction. Let us confine ourselves to saying that understanding, imitating the work of nature, has also set up motor apparatuses, this time artificial ones, in order to make them correspond, in limited number, to an unlimited multitude of individual objects: the totality of these mechanisms is articulated speech.

Moreover, it is far from the case that these two divergent operations of the mind, one by which it discerns individuals, the other by which it constructs genera, require the same effort and progress with equal rapidity. The first, requiring only the intervention of memory, is accomplished from the beginning of our experience; the second continues indefinitely without ever being completed. The first results in constituting stable images which, in their turn, are stored in memory; the second forms unstable and evanescent representations. Let us dwell on this last point. Here we touch upon an essential phenomenon of mental life.

The essence of the general idea, indeed, is to move incessantly between the sphere of action and that of pure memory. Let us return, indeed, to the diagram that we have already drawn. At S is the present perception I have of my body, that is to say, of a certain sensorimotor equilibrium. Upon the surface of the base A B will be arranged, if one wishes, my memories in their totality. In the cone thus determined, the general idea will continually oscillate between the apex S and the base A B. At S it would take the very distinct form of a bodily attitude or of a word uttered; at A B it would assume the no less distinct aspect of the thousand individual images against which its fragile unity would be shattered.

And this is why a psychology that confines itself to what is ready-made, that knows only things and ignores progress, will perceive in this movement only the extremities between which it oscillates; it will make the general idea coincide now with the action that enacts it or the word that expresses it, now with the multiple images, indefinite in number, which are its equivalent in memory. But the truth is that the general idea escapes us as soon as we claim to fix it at either of these two extremities. It consists in the double current that goes from one to the other,—always ready either to crystallize into words uttered, or to evaporate into memories.

This amounts to saying that, between the sensorimotor mechanisms represented by point S and the totality of memories arranged in A B, there is room, as we suggested in the preceding chapter, for thousands upon thousands of repetitions of our psychological life, represented by as many sections A'B', AB', etc., of the same cone. We tend to disperse ourselves in A B as we detach ourselves ever more from our sensory and motor state in order to live the life of
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 97

dream; we tend to concentrate ourselves in S as we attach ourselves more firmly to present reality, responding by motor reactions to sensory excitations. In fact, the normal self never fixes itself in one of these extreme positions; it moves between them, successively adopts the positions represented by the intermediate sections, or, in other words, gives its representations just enough of the image and just enough of the idea for them to be able usefully to contribute to present action.

From this conception of lower mental life, the laws of the association of ideas may be deduced. But before examining this point more deeply, let us show the inadequacy of the current theories of association.

That every idea arising in the mind has a relation of resemblance or contiguity with the preceding mental state is incontestable; but an assertion of this kind tells us nothing about the mechanism of association, and indeed, truthfully, teaches us absolutely nothing. One would seek in vain, indeed, for two ideas that did not have between them some feature of resemblance or did not touch each other on some side. Is it a matter of resemblance? However deep the differences that separate two images may be, one will always find, by going back high enough, a common genus to which they belong, and consequently a resemblance serving them as a connecting link.

Does one consider contiguity? A perception A, as we said above, evokes by “contiguity” an old image B only if it first recalls to us an image A' which resembles it, for it is a memory A', and not perception A, that truly touches B in memory. However distant from one another the two terms A and B may be supposed to be, a relation of contiguity can always be established between them if the intermediary term A' maintains with A a sufficiently remote resemblance. This amounts to saying that between any two ideas whatsoever, chosen at random, there is always resemblance and always, if one wishes, contiguity, so that in discovering a relation of contiguity or resemblance between two successive representations, one does not at all explain why one evokes the other.

The real question is to know how the selection is made among an infinity of memories all of which resemble the present perception in some respect, and why only one of them,—this one rather than that one,—
emerges into the light of consciousness. But to this question associationism
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 98

cannot reply, because it has erected ideas and images into independent entities, floating, in the manner of Epicurus' atoms, in an inner space, approaching one another, clinging to one another when chance brings them into one another's sphere of attraction. And by examining the doctrine more deeply on this point, one would see that its fault has been to intellectualize ideas too much, to attribute to them an entirely speculative role, to have believed that they exist for themselves and not for us, to have failed to recognize the relation they bear to the activity of willing.

If memories wander about, indifferent, in an inert and amorphous consciousness, there is no reason why present perception should attract one of them rather than another: I can therefore only observe the encounter, once it has occurred, and speak of resemblance or contiguity,—which amounts, fundamentally, to vaguely acknowledging that states of consciousness have affinities with one another.

But associationism can furnish no explanation of this affinity itself, which takes the double form of contiguity and resemblance. The general tendency to associate remains as obscure, in this doctrine, as the particular forms of association. Having erected individual memory-images into ready-made things, given as such in the course of our mental life, associationism is reduced to supposing mysterious attractions between these objects, of which one could not even say in advance, as of physical attraction, by what phenomena they will manifest themselves. Why, indeed, would an image which, by hypothesis, suffices unto itself, aim to aggregate to itself others, whether similar or given in contiguity with it? But the truth is that this independent image is an artificial and late product of the mind.
In fact, we perceive resemblances before the individuals that resemble one another, and, in an aggregate of contiguous parts, the whole before the parts.

We go from resemblance to resembling objects, embroidering upon resemblance, this common canvas, the variety of individual differences. And we also go from the whole to the parts, through a work of decomposition whose law will be seen later, and which consists in breaking up, for the greater convenience of practical life, the continuity of the real. Association is therefore not the primitive fact; it is through dissociation that we begin, and the tendency of every memory to aggregate others to itself is explained by a natural return of the mind to the undivided unity of perception.

But here we discover the radical defect of associationism. Given a present perception which forms in turn, with various memories, several successive associations, there are two ways, we said, of conceiving the mechanism of this association. One may suppose that perception remains identical with itself, a veritable psychological atom to which others aggregate themselves as the latter pass by it.

Such is the point of view of associationism. But there is a second, and it is precisely this one that we indicated in our theory of recognition. We supposed that our entire personality, with the totality of our memories, entered, undivided, into our present perception.

Then, if this perception successively evokes different memories, it is not by a mechanical addition of ever more numerous elements that it would attract, motionless, around itself; it is by an expansion of our whole consciousness, which, then spreading out over a vaster surface, can carry further the detailed inventory of its wealth. Thus, a nebular cluster, seen through increasingly powerful telescopes, resolves itself into an increasing number of stars. In the first hypothesis (which has little in its favour beyond its apparent
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 99

simplicity and its analogy with a misconceived atomism), each memory constitutes an independent and fixed being, of which one can say neither why it aims to aggregate others to itself, nor how it chooses, in order to associate them with itself by virtue of contiguity or resemblance, among a thousand memories that would have equal claims. One must suppose that ideas collide with one another by chance, or that mysterious forces are exerted between them; and one still has against oneself the testimony of consciousness, which never shows us psychological facts floating in an independent state. In the second, one confines oneself to noting the solidarity of psychological facts, always given together to immediate consciousness as an undivided whole which reflection alone breaks up into distinct fragments.

What must then be explained is no longer the cohesion of internal states, but the double movement of contraction and expansion by which consciousness narrows or broadens the development of its content.

But this movement follows, as we shall see, from the fundamental necessities of life; and it is also easy to see why the “associations” that we appear to form along this movement exhaust all the successive degrees of contiguity and resemblance.

Let us suppose, indeed, for a moment, that our psychological life is reduced to sensory-motor functions alone. In other words, let us place ourselves, in the schematic figure that we have drawn (page 181), at that point S which would correspond to the greatest possible simplification of our mental life.

In this state, every perception prolongs itself of its own accord in appropriate reactions, for analogous prior perceptions have set up motor apparatuses more or less complex which await, in order to come into play, only the repetition of the same summons. Now there is, in this mechanism, an association by resemblance, since the present perception acts by virtue of its similarity to past perceptions, and there is also here an association by contiguity, since the movements consequent upon those old perceptions are reproduced, and can even bring in their train an indefinite number of actions coordinated with the first. Thus we grasp here, at their very source and almost merged together—not thoughts, doubtless, but enacted and lived—association by resemblance and association by contiguity.

These are not contingent forms of our psychological life. They represent the two complementary aspects of one and the same fundamental tendency: the tendency of every organism to extract from a given situation what is useful in it, and to store up the eventual reaction, in the form of a motor habit, in order to make it serve situations of the same kind.

Let us now transport ourselves, in a single leap, to the other extremity of our mental life. Let us pass, according to our method, from psychological existence merely “enacted” to that which would be exclusively “dreamed.” Let us place ourselves, in other words, on that base AB of memory (page 181) where all the events of our past life are delineated in their smallest details.

A consciousness which, detached from action, thus held beneath its gaze the totality of its past, would have no reason to fix upon one part of that past rather than upon another. In one sense, all its memories would differ from its present perception, for, if they are taken with the multiplicity of their details, two memories are never identically the same thing. But, in another sense, any memory whatsoever could be brought near to the present situation: it would suffice to neglect, in this perception and in this memory, enough details for resemblance alone to appear. Moreover, once the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 100

memory was connected with perception, a multitude of events contiguous to the memory would thereby be connected with perception—a multitude indefinite, which would be limited only at the point where one chose to stop it. The necessities of life are no longer there to regulate the effect of resemblance and consequently of contiguity; and since, fundamentally, everything resembles everything else, it follows that everything can be associated. A moment ago, present perception was prolonged into determined movements; now it dissolves into an infinity of equally possible memories. In AB association would therefore provoke an arbitrary choice, as in S it would produce a fated procedure.

But these are only two extreme limits at which the psychologist must place himself in turn for the convenience of study, and which, in fact, are never attained. There is not, at least in man, a purely sensory-motor state, any more than there is in him an imaginative life without a substratum of vague activity. Our normal psychological life oscillates, we said, between these two extremes. On the one hand, the sensory-motor state S directs memory, of which it is, fundamentally, only the present and active extremity; and on the other hand, this memory itself, with the totality of our past, exerts a forward thrust in order to insert into present action the greatest possible part of itself. From this double effort there result, at every moment, an indefinite multitude of possible states of memory, states represented by the sections A'B', A''B'', etc., of our schema.
These are, we said, so many repetitions of our entire past life.

But each of these sections is more or less extensive, according as it approaches more closely the base or the summit; and moreover, each of these complete representations of our past brings to the light of consciousness only what can be framed within the sensory-motor state, what, consequently, resembles present perception from the point of view of the action to be performed. In other words, integral memory answers the summons of a present state by two simultaneous movements: one of translation, by which it moves as a whole toward the experience and thus contracts itself more or less, without dividing itself, in view of action; the other of rotation upon itself, by which it orients itself toward the situation of the moment in order to present to it its most useful face. To these various degrees of contraction correspond the varied forms of association by resemblance.

Everything therefore takes place as though our memories were repeated an indefinite number of times in these thousand and thousand possible reductions of our past life. They take on a more commonplace form when memory contracts more closely, a more personal form when it expands, and thus enter into an unlimited multitude of different “systematizations.” A word in a foreign language, pronounced in my ear, may make me think of that language in general or of a voice that once pronounced it in a certain manner. These two associations by resemblance are not due to the accidental arrival of two different representations which chance would have brought in turn into the sphere of attraction of present perception.

They correspond to two diverse mental dispositions, to two distinct degrees of tension of memory, here closer to the pure image, there more disposed to immediate response, that is to say, to action. To classify these systems, to seek the law that respectively binds them to the various “tones” of our mental life, to show how each of these tones is itself determined by the necessities of the moment and also by the variable degree of our personal effort, would be a difficult undertaking: all this psychology still remains to be done, and for the moment we do not even wish
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 101

to attempt it. But each of us clearly feels that these laws exist, and that there are stable relations of this kind. We know, for example, when we read a psychological novel, that certain associations of ideas described to us are true, that they could have been lived; others jar upon us or fail to give us the impression of reality, because we feel in them the effect of a mechanical juxtaposition between different levels of the mind, as though the author had not known how to remain on the plane of mental life that he had chosen. Memory therefore does indeed have its successive and distinct degrees of tension or vitality, difficult to define, doubtless, but which the painter of the soul cannot confuse with one another with impunity. Pathology moreover confirms here—on crude examples, it is true—a truth of which we all have an instinct.

In the “systematized amnesias” of hysterics, for example, the memories that appear to be abolished are really present; but they are all doubtless connected with a certain determined tone of intellectual vitality in which the subject can no longer place himself.

If there are thus different planes, indefinite in number, for association by resemblance, the same is true of association by contiguity. In the extreme plane which represents the base of memory, there is no memory that is not linked, by contiguity, to the totality of the events that precede it and also of those that follow it. Whereas at the point where our action is concentrated in space, contiguity brings back, in the form of movement, only the reaction immediately consequent upon a similar prior perception. In fact, every association by contiguity implies a position of the mind intermediate between these two extreme limits.

If one supposes here again a multitude of possible repetitions of the totality of our memories, each of these copies of our past life will cut itself up, in its own way, into determined slices, and the mode of division will not be the same if one passes from one copy to another, because each of them is precisely characterized by the nature of the dominant memories against which the other memories lean as against points of support. The closer one comes to action, for example, the more contiguity tends to partake of resemblance and thus to distinguish itself from a simple relation of chronological succession: thus one could not say of the words of a foreign language, when they evoke one another in memory, whether they associate by resemblance or by contiguity.

On the contrary, the more we detach ourselves from real or possible action, the more association by contiguity tends purely and simply to reproduce the consecutive images of our past life. It is impossible to enter here into an in-depth study of these various systems. It will suffice to point out that these systems are not formed of memories juxtaposed like so many atoms. There are always a few dominant memories, true bright points around which the others form a vague nebulosity. These bright points multiply as our memory expands.

## index_split_005

The process of locating a memory in the past, for example, does not at all consist, as has been said, in plunging into the mass of our memories as into a bag, in order to draw out memories that are increasingly close together, among which the memory to be located will take its place. By what happy chance would we lay our hands precisely upon an increasing number of interposed memories? The work of localization consists in reality in an increasing effort of expansion, by which memory, always wholly present to itself, spreads its memories over an ever wider surface
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 102

and thus ends by distinguishing, in a hitherto confused heap, the memory that could not find its place again. Here too, moreover, the pathology of memory would provide us with instructive information. In retrograde amnesia, the memories that disappear from consciousness are plausibly preserved on the extreme planes of memory, and the subject may recover them there through an exceptional effort, such as that which he makes in the hypnotic state.

But, on the lower planes, these memories were waiting, in a sense, for the dominant image against which they might lean. Some sudden shock, some violent emotion, will be the decisive event to which they will attach themselves: and if this event, by reason of its sudden character, stands out from the rest of our history, they will follow it into oblivion. Thus one can understand how the oblivion consequent upon a physical or moral shock may include the events immediately preceding it—a phenomenon very difficult to explain in all other conceptions of memory. Let us note in passing: if one refuses to attribute some expectation of this kind to recent, and even relatively remote, memories, the normal work of memory will become unintelligible. For every event whose memory has been impressed upon memory, however simple it may be supposed to be, occupied a certain time.

The perceptions that filled the first period of this interval, and which now form with the subsequent perceptions an undivided memory, were therefore truly « in the air » so long as the decisive part of the event had not yet occurred. Between the disappearance of a memory with its various preliminary details and the abolition, by retrograde amnesia, of a greater or lesser number of memories prior to a given event, there is therefore a mere difference of degree, and not of nature.

From these various considerations concerning lower mental life there would follow a certain conception of intellectual equilibrium. This equilibrium will obviously be distorted only by a disturbance of the elements that serve as its material. There can be no question here of approaching the problems of mental pathology: we nevertheless cannot entirely evade them, since we are seeking to determine the exact relation of the body to the mind.

We have supposed that the mind constantly traversed the interval between its two extreme limits, the plane of action and the plane of dream. Is a decision to be made? Gathering together and organizing the totality of its experience in what we call its character, it will make this experience converge toward actions in which you will find, along with the past that serves as their material, the unforeseen form which personality impresses upon them; but action will be realizable only if it comes to fit within the present situation, that is to say, within that set of circumstances arising from a certain determinate position of the body in time and space. Is it a matter of intellectual work, of forming a conception, of extracting an idea more or less general from the multiplicity of memories?

A wide margin is left, on the one hand, to fancy, and, on the other, to logical discernment: but the idea, in order to be viable, must touch present reality on some side, that is to say, it must be capable, by degrees and through progressive diminutions or contractions of itself, of being more or less acted out by the body at the same time as it is represented by the mind. Our body, with the sensations it receives on the one hand and the movements it is capable
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 103

of executing on the other, is thus indeed what fixes our mind, what gives it ballast and equilibrium. The activity of the mind infinitely exceeds the mass of accumulated memories, just as this mass of memories itself infinitely exceeds the sensations and movements of the present moment; but these sensations and movements condition what might be called attention to life, and this is why everything depends upon their cohesion in the normal work of the mind, as in a pyramid standing upright on its point.

Moreover, let one cast a glance at the fine structure of the nervous system, as recent discoveries have revealed it. One will believe oneself to discern conductors everywhere, centres nowhere. Wires placed end to end, whose extremities no doubt draw close together when the current passes: that is all one sees. And perhaps that is all there is, if it be true that the body is but a meeting-place between received excitations and accomplished movements, as we have supposed throughout the course of our work.

But these wires, which receive shocks or excitations from the external environment and send them back to it in the form of appropriate reactions, these wires so skilfully stretched from periphery to periphery, ensure precisely, through the solidity of their connections and the precision of their intercrossings, the sensori-motor equilibrium of the body, that is to say, its adaptation to the present situation.
Relax this tension or break this equilibrium: everything will happen as though attention were detaching itself from life. Dream and alienation appear to be scarcely anything else.

We were speaking just now of the recent hypothesis that attributes sleep to an interruption of solidarity among neurons. Even if one does not accept this hypothesis (yet confirmed by curious experiments), one must at least suppose, during deep sleep, a functional interruption of the relation established in the nervous system between excitation and motor reaction. Thus dream would always be the state of a mind whose attention is not fixed by the sensori-motor equilibrium of the body. And it appears increasingly probable that this relaxation of the nervous system is due to the intoxi-cation of its elements by the products of their activity that are not eliminated in the waking state. Now, dream imitates alienation in every respect.

Not only are all the psychological symptoms of madness found again in dream—to the point that the comparison of these two states has become commonplace—but alienation itself also seems to have its origin in a cerebral exhaustion, which would be caused, like normal fatigue, by the accumulation of certain specific poisons in the elements of the nervous system 1. It is known that alienation is often Consecutive to infectious diseases, and that, moreover, all the phenomena of madness can be experimentally reproduced with toxic substances 2. Is it not plausible, then, that the rupture of mental equilibrium in alienation is due simply to a disturbance of the sensori-motor relations established in the organism?

This disturbance would suffice to create a kind of psychic vertigo, and thus to cause memory and attention to lose contact with reality. Let one read the descriptions given by certain madmen of their incipient illness: one will see that they often experience a feel-1
This idea has recently been developed by various authors. A very systematic exposition of it will be found in the work of COWLES, The mechanism of insanity (American Journal of Insanity, 1890-91).

2

See especially MOREAU DE TOURS, Du hachisch, Paris, 1845.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 104

ing of strangeness or, as they say, of « non-reality », as though perceived things lost for them some of their relief and solidity 1. If our analyses are correct, the concrete feeling we have of present reality would in fact consist in the consciousness we acquire of the actual movements by which our organism naturally responds to excitations;—so that where the relations between sensations and movements relax or deteriorate, the sense of the real weakens or disappears 2.

Moreover, there would here be a host of distinctions to make, not only among the various forms of alienation, but also between alienation properly so called and those divisions of personality to which a recent psychology has so curiously assimilated it 3. In these diseases of personality, it seems that groups of memories detach themselves from central memory and renounce their solidarity with the others. But it is rare not also to observe concomitant divisions of sensibility and motricity 4. We cannot help seeing in these latter phenomena the true material substratum of the former.

If it be true that our intellectual life rests wholly upon its point, that is to say, upon the sensori-motor functions by which it is inserted into present reality, intellectual equilibrium will be differently disturbed according as these functions are impaired in one way or another. Now, alongside the lesions that affect the general vitality of the sensori-motor functions, weakening or abolishing what we have called the sense of the real, there are others that manifest themselves in a mechanical, and no longer dynamic, diminution of these functions, as though certain sensori-motor connections simply separated themselves from the others. If our hypothesis is well founded, memory will be affected very differently in the two cases.

In the first, no memory will be diverted, but all memories will be less encumbered, less firmly oriented toward reality, whence a genuine break in mental equilibrium. In the second, equilibrium will not be broken, but it will lose some of its complexity. Memories will retain their normal aspect, but will partly relinquish their solidarity, because their sensorimotor basis, instead of being, so to speak, chemically altered, will be mechanically diminished. In neither case, moreover, will memories be directly affected or impaired.

The idea that the body preserves memories in the form of cerebral arrangements, that losses and diminutions of memory consist in the more or less complete destruction of these mechanisms, and that the exaltation of memory and hallucination, on the contrary, consist in an exaggeration of their activity, is therefore confirmed neither by reasoning nor by facts. There is, indeed, one case, and one alone, where observation might at first seem to suggest this view: we mean aphasia, or more generally disorders of auditory or visual recognition. It is the only case in which one can assign the disease a constant seat in a determined convolution of the brain; but it is precisely also the case in which one does not witness the mechanical and immediately definitive tearing away of such and such memories, but rather the gradual and functional weakening of the whole of the memory concerned. And we have explained how the cerebral lesion could bring about this weakening, without there being any need whatsoever to suppose a store of memories accumulated in the brain. What is really affected are the sensory and motor regions corresponding to this kind of perception, and above all the appendages that make it possible to activate them inwardly, so that the memory, no longer finding anything to which it can attach itself, ends by becoming practically powerless: now, in psychology, powerlessness means unconsciousness.

mechanical and immediately definitive tearing away of such and such memories, but rather the gradual and functional weakening of the whole of the memory concerned. And we have explained how the cerebral lesion could bring about this weakening, without there being any need whatsoever to suppose a store of memories accumulated in the brain. What is really affected are the sensory and motor regions corresponding to this kind of perception, and above all the appendages that make it possible to activate them inwardly, so that the memory, no longer finding anything to which it can attach itself, ends by becoming practically powerless: now, in psychology, powerlessness means unconsciousness.

In all other cases, the lesion observed or supposed, never clearly localized, acts through the disturbance it brings to the whole of the sensorimotor connections, whether it alters this mass or fragments it: whence a break or a simplification of intellectual equilibrium, and, by repercussion, the disorder or disjunction of memories. The doctrine that makes memory an immediate function of the brain—a doctrine that raises insoluble theoretical difficulties, a doctrine whose complexity defies all imagination and whose results are incompatible with the data of inner observation—cannot therefore even count on the support of cerebral pathology.

All the facts and all the analogies favour a theory that would see in the brain only an intermediary between sensations and movements, that would make this aggregate of sensations and movements the extreme point of mental life, a point constantly inserted into the tissue of events, and that, thus attributing to the body the sole function of orienting memory toward reality and connecting it with the present, would consider this memory itself as absolutely independent of matter. In this sense the brain contributes to recalling the useful memory, but even more to provisionally setting aside all the others. We do not see how memory could lodge in matter; but we understand well—according to the profound saying of a contemporary philosopher—that “materiality places forgetfulness within us 1”.
