lequel le mouvement réel se pose ; c'est le mouvement réel, au contraire, qui le dépose au-dessous de lui. Mais notre imagination, préoccupée avant tout de la commodité de l'expression et des exigences de la vie matérielle, aime mieux renverser l'ordre naturel des termes. Habituée à chercher son point d'appui dans un monde d'images toutes construites, immobiles, dont la fixité apparente reflète surtout l'invariabilité de nos besoins inférieurs, elle ne peut s'empêcher de croire le repos antérieur à la mobilité, de le prendre pour point de repère, de s'installer en lui, et de ne plus voir enfin dans le mouvement qu'une variation de distance, l'espace précédant le mouvement.

Alors, dans un espace homogène et indéfiniment divisible elle dessinera une trajectoire et fixera des positions : appliquant ensuite le mouvement contre la trajectoire, elle le voudra divisible comme cette ligne et, comme elle, dépourvu de qualité. Faut-il s'étonner si notre entendement, s'exerçant désormais sur cette idée qui représente justement l'inversion du réel, n'y découvre que des contradictions ? Ayant assimilé les mouvements à l'espace, on trouve ces mouvements homogènes comme l'espace ; et comme on ne veut plus voir entre eux que des différences calculables de direction et de vitesse, toute relation est abolie entre le mouvement et la qualité. Il ne reste plus alors qu'à parquer le mouvement dans l'espace, les qualités dans la conscience, et à établir entre ces deux séries parallèles, incapables par hypothèse de se rejoindre jamais, une mystérieuse correspondance.

Rejetée dans la conscience, la qualité sensible devient impuissante à reconquérir l'étendue. Relégué dans l'espace, et dans l'espace abstrait, où il n'y a jamais qu'un instant unique et où tout recommence toujours, le mouvement renonce à cette solidarité du présent et du passé qui est son essence même. Et comme ces deux aspects de la perception, qualité et mouvement, s'enveloppent d'une égale obscurité, le phénomène de la perception, où une conscience enfermée en elle-même et étrangère à l'espace traduirait ce qui a lieu dans l'espace, devient un mystère. -

Écartons au contraire toute idée préconçue d'interprétation ou de mesure, plaçons-nous face à face avec la réalité immédiate : nous ne trouvons plus une distance infranchissable, plus de différence essentielle, pas même de distinction véritable entre la perception et la chose perçue, entre la qualité et le mouvement.

Nous revenons ainsi, par un long détour, aux conclusions que nous avions dégagées dans le premier chapitre de ce livre. Notre perception, disions-nous, est originairement dans les choses plutôt que dans l'esprit, hors de nous plutôt qu'en nous. Les perceptions des divers genres marquent autant de directions vraies de la réalité. Mais cette perception qui coïncide avec son objet, ajoutions-nous, existe en droit plutôt qu'en fait : elle aurait lieu dans l'instantané. Dans la perception concrète la mémoire intervient, et la subjectivité des qualités sensibles tient justement à ce que notre conscience, qui commence par n'être que mémoire, prolonge les uns dans les autres, pour les contracter dans une intuition unique, une pluralité de moments.

Conscience et matière, âme et corps entraient ainsi en contact dans la perception. Mais cette idée restait obscure par un certain côté, parce que notre perception, et par conséquent aussi notre conscience, semblaient alors participer de la divisibilité qu'on attribue à la matière. Si nous répugnons naturellement, dans l'hypothèse dualiste, à accepter la coïncidence partielle de l'objet perçu et du sujet qui perçoit, c'est parce que nous avons conscience de l'unité indivisée de notre perception, au lieu que l'objet nous paraît être, par essence,
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 130

indéfiniment divisible. De là l'hypothèse d'une conscience avec des sensations inextensives, placée en face d'une multiplicité étendue. Mais si la divisibilité de la matière est tout entière relative à notre action sur elle, c'est-à-dire à notre faculté d'en modifier l'aspect, Si elle appartient, non à la matière même, mais à l'espace que nous tendons au-dessous de cette matière pour la faire tomber sous nos prises, alors la difficulté s'évanouit. La matière étendue, envisagée dans son ensemble, est comme une conscience où tout s'équilibre, se compense et se neutralise ; elle offre véritablement l’indivisibilité de notre perception; de sorte qu'inversement nous pouvons, sans scrupule, attribuer à la perception quelque chose de l'étendue de la matière.

Ces deux termes, perception et matière, marchent ainsi l'un vers l'autre à mesure que nous nous dépouillons davantage de ce qu'on pourrait appeler les préjugés de l'action : la sensation reconquiert l'extension, l'étendue concrète reprend sa continuité et son indivisibilité naturelles. Et l'espace homogène, qui se dressait entre les deux termes comme une barrière insurmontable, n'a plus d'autre réalité que celle d'un schème ou d'un symbole. Il intéresse les démarches d'un être qui agit sur la matière, mais non pas le travail d'un esprit qui spécule sur son essence.
Par là même s'éclaircit, dans une certaine mesure, la question vers laquelle toutes nos recherches convergent, celle de l'union de l'âme et du corps.

L'obscurité de ce problème, dans l'hypothèse dualiste, vient de ce que l'on considère la matière comme essentiellement divisible et tout état d'âme comme rigoureusement inextensif, de sorte que l'on commence par couper la communication entre les deux termes. Et en approfondissant ce double postulat, on y découvre, en ce qui concerne la matière, une confusion de l'étendue concrète et indivisible avec l'espace divisible qui la sous-tend, comme aussi, en ce qui concerne l'esprit, l'idée illusoire qu'il n'y a pas de degrés, pas de transition possible, entre l'étendu et l'inétendu.

Mais si ces deux postulats recèlent une erreur commune, s'il y a passage graduel de l'idée à l'image et de l'image à la sensation, si, à mesure qu'il évolue ainsi vers l'actualité, c'est-à-dire vers l'action, l'état d'âme se rapproche davantage de l'extension, si enfin cette extension, une fois atteinte, reste indivisée et par là ne jure en aucune manière avec l'unité de l'âme, on comprend que l'esprit puisse se poser sur la matière dans l'acte de la perception pure, s'unir à elle par conséquent, et néanmoins qu'il s'en distingue radicalement. Il s'en distingue en ce qu'il est, même alors, mémoire, c'est-à-dire synthèse du passé et du présent en vue de l'avenir, en ce qu'il contracte les moments de cette matière pour s'en servir et pour se manifester par des actions qui sont la raison d'être de son union avec le corps.
Nous avions donc raison de dire, au début de ce livre, que la distinction du corps et de l'esprit ne doit pas s'établir en fonction de l'espace, mais du temps.

Le tort du dualisme vulgaire est de se placer au point de vue de l'espace, de mettre d'un côté la matière avec ses modifications dans l'espace, de l'autre des sensations inextensives dans la conscience. De là l'impossibilité de comprendre comment l'esprit agit sur le corps ou le corps sur l'esprit. De là les hypothèses qui ne sont et ne peuvent être que des constatations déguisées du fait, - l'idée d'un parallélisme ou celle d'une harmonie préétablie. Mais de là aussi l'impossibilité de constituer soit une psychologie de la mémoire, soit une métaphysique de la matière. Nous avons essayé d'établir que cette psychologie et cette métaphysique sont solidaires, et que les difficultés s'atténuent dans un dualisme qui, partant de la perception pure où le sujet et l'objet coïncident,
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 131
pousse le développement de ces deux termes dans leurs durées respectives, -

la matière, à mesure qu'on en continue plus loin l'analyse, tendant de plus en plus à n'être qu'une succession de moments infiniment rapides qui se déduisent les uns des autres et par là s'équivalent; l'esprit étant déjà mémoire dans la perception, et s'affirmant de plus en plus comme un prolongement du passé dans le présent, un progrès , une évolution véritable.

Mais la relation du corps à l'esprit en devient-elle plus claire ? À une distinction spatiale nous substituons une distinction temporelle : les deux termes en sont-ils plus capables de s'unir ? Il faut remarquer que la première distinction ne comporte pas de degrés : la matière est dans l'espace, l'esprit est hors de l'espace ; il n'y a pas de transition possible entre eux. Au contraire, si le rôle le plus humble de l'esprit est de lier les moments successifs de la durée des choses, si c'est dans cette opération qu'il prend contact avec la matière et par elle aussi qu'il s'en distingue d'abord, on conçoit une infinité de degrés entre la matière et l'esprit pleinement développé, l'esprit capable d'action non seulement indéterminée, mais raisonnable et réfléchie.

Chacun de ces degrés successifs, qui mesure une intensité croissante de vie, répond à une plus haute tension de durée et se traduit au dehors par un plus grand développement du système sensori-moteur. Considère-t-on alors ce système nerveux ? Sa complexité croissante paraîtra laisser une latitude de plus en plus grande à l'activité de l'être vivant, la faculté d'attendre avant de réagir, et de mettre l'excitation reçue en rapport avec une variété de plus en plus riche de mécanismes moteurs.

Mais ce n'est là que le dehors, et l'organisation plus complexe du système nerveux, qui semble assurer une plus grande indépendance à l'être vivant vis-à-vis de la matière, ne fait que symboliser matériellement cette indépendance même, c'est-à-dire la force intérieure qui permet à l’être de se dégager du rythme d'écoulement des choses, de retenir de mieux en mieux le passé pour influencer de plus en plus profondément l'avenir, c'est-à-dire enfin, au sens spécial que nous donnons à ce mot, sa mémoire. Ainsi, entre la matière brute et l'esprit le plus capable de réflexion il y a toutes les intensités possibles de la mémoire, ou, ce qui revient au même, tous les degrés de la liberté.

Dans la première hypothèse, celle qui exprime la distinction de l'esprit et du corps en termes d'espace, corps et esprit sont comme deux voies ferrées qui se couperaient à angle droit; dans la seconde, les rails se raccordent selon une courbe, de sorte qu'on passe insensiblement d'une voie sur l'autre.

Mais y a-t-il là autre chose qu'une image ? Et la distinction ne reste-t-elle pas tranchée, l'opposition irréductible, entre la matière proprement dite et le plus humble degré de liberté ou de mémoire ? Oui sans doute, la distinction subsiste, mais l'union devient possible, puisqu'elle serait donnée, sous la forme radicale de la coïncidence partielle, dans la perception pure. Les difficultés du dualisme vulgaire ne viennent pas de ce que les deux termes se distinguent, mais de ce qu'on ne voit pas comment l'un des deux se greffe sur l'autre. Or, nous l'avons montré, la perception pure, qui serait le plus bas degré de l'esprit,

- l'esprit sans la mémoire, - ferait véritablement partie de la matière telle que nous l'entendons. Allons plus loin : la mémoire n'intervient pas comme une fonction dont la matière n'aurait aucun pressentiment et qu'elle n'imiterait pas déjà à sa manière. Si la matière ne se souvient pas du passé, c'est parce qu'elle répète le passé sans cesse, parce que, soumise à la nécessité, elle déroule une série de moments dont chacun équivaut au précédent et peut s'en déduire : ainsi, son passé est véritablement donné dans son présent. Mais un être qui
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 132

évolue plus ou moins librement crée à chaque moment quelque chose de nouveau : c'est donc en vain qu'on chercherait à lire son passé dans son présent si le passé ne se déposait pas en lui à l'état de souvenir. Ainsi, pour reprendre une métaphore qui a déjà paru plusieurs fois dans ce livre, il faut, pour des raisons semblables, que le passé soit joué par la matière, imaginé par l'esprit.
Henri Bergson, Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit. (1939) 133
Matière et mémoire. Essai sur la relation du corps à l’esprit (1939)

translations.title: Chapter IV On the Delimitation and Fixation of Images. Perception and Matter Soul and Body

paragraphs.text: Chapter IV
On the delimitation
and fixation of images.
Perception and matter
Soul and body.
Return to the table of contents

A general conclusion follows from the first three chapters of this book: namely, that the body, always directed toward action, has as its essential function that of limiting, in view of action, the life of the mind. In relation to representations, it is an instrument of selection, and of selection only. It can neither generate nor occasion an intellectual state. Is perception at issue? By the place it occupies at every instant in the universe, our body marks out those parts and aspects of matter over which we might have a hold: our perception, which precisely measures our virtual action upon things, is thus limited to the objects that presently influence our organs and prepare our movements.

Is memory considered? The role of the body is not to store memories, but simply to choose, in order to bring it to distinct consciousness through the real efficacy it confers upon it, the useful memory, that which will complete and clarify the present situation in view of final action. It is true that this second selection is much less rigorous than the first, because our past experience is an individual and no longer a common experience, because we always have many different memories capable of fitting
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 107

equally well with one and the same present situation, and because nature cannot have here, as in the case of perception, an inflexible rule for delimiting our representations. A certain margin is therefore necessarily left this time to fancy; and if animals scarcely profit from it, captive as they are to material need, it seems that, on the contrary, the human mind constantly presses with the totality of its memory against the door that the body will half-open for it: hence the play of fancy and the work of imagination,—so many liberties that the mind takes with nature. It is nonetheless true that the orientation of our consciousness toward action appears to be the fundamental law of our psychological life.

Strictly speaking, we might stop there, for it was in order to define the role of the body in the life of the mind that we had ,undertaken this work. But on the one hand we have raised along the :way a metaphysical problem that we cannot ,bring ourselves to leave pending, and on the other hand our researches, (although chiefly psychological, have enabled us to glimpse À various times, if not a means of solving the problem, at least one side from which to approach it.

This problem is none other than that of the union of soul and body. It presents itself to us in an acute form, because we profoundly distinguish matter from mind. And we cannot hold it to be insoluble, because we define mind and matter by positive characteristics, not by negations. Pure perception would indeed place us in matter, and it is truly into mind itself that we would already penetrate with memory. On the other hand, the same psychological observation that revealed to us the distinction between matter and mind makes us witness their union.
Thus either our analyses are tainted by an original vice, or they must help us out of the difficulties they raise.

The obscurity of the problem, in all doctrines, is due to the double antithesis that our understanding establishes between the extended and the unextended on the one hand, quality and quantity on the other. It is indisputable that mind is first opposed to matter as a pure unity to an essentially divisible multiplicity, and that moreover our perceptions consist of heterogeneous qualities whereas the perceived universe seems bound to be resolved into homogeneous and calculable changes. Thus there would be inextension and quality on one side, extension and quantity on the other. We have repudiated materialism, which claims to derive the first term from the second; but we no more accept idealism, which would have the second be merely a construction of the first.

Against materialism, we maintain that perception infinitely exceeds the cerebral state; but against idealism, we have tried to establish that matter overflows on every side the representation we have of it, a representation that the mind has, so to speak, gathered from it through an intelligent choice. Of these two opposed doctrines, one attributes to the body and the other to the mind a gift of genuine creation, the first holding that our brain generates representation and the second that our understanding draws the plan of nature. And against both doctrines we invoke the same testimony, that of consciousness, which shows us in our body an image like the others, and in our understanding a certain faculty of dissociating, distinguishing, and logically opposing, but not of creating or constructing.
Thus, voluntary prisoners of psychological analysis and consequently of common sense, it seems that after having exacerbated the conflicts
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 108
that vulgar dualism raises, we have formed all the exits that metaphysics could open to us.

But precisely because we have pushed dualism to the extreme, our analysis has perhaps dissociated its contradictory elements. The theory of pure perception on one side, and of pure memory on the other, would then prepare the way for an approximation between the unextended and the extended, between quality and quantity.

Is pure perception considered? By making the cerebral state the beginning of an action and not the condition of a perception, we cast the perceived images of things outside the image of our body; we thus restored perception to the things themselves. But then, since our perception forms part of things, things partake of the nature of our perception. Material extension is no longer, can no longer be, that multiple extension of which the geometer speaks; it resembles rather the undivided extension of our representation. That is to say that the analysis of pure perception has enabled us to glimpse, in the idea of extension, a possible approximation between the extended and the unextended.
But our conception of pure memory should lead, by a parallel path, to mitigating the second opposition, that of quality and quantity.

Indeed, we have radically separated the pure memory from the cerebral state that prolongs it and renders it efficacious. Memory is therefore in no degree an emanation of matter; quite the contrary, matter, as we apprehend it in a concrete perception that always occupies a certain duration, derives in large part from memory. Now, where exactly lies the difference between the heterogeneous qualities that succeed one another in our concrete perception and the homogeneous changes that science places behind these perceptions in space? The former are discontinuous and cannot be deduced from one another; the latter, on the contrary, lend themselves to calculation. But for them to lend themselves to it, there is no need to make them pure quantities: that would be tantamount to reducing them to nothing.

It suffices that their heterogeneity be, as it were, diluted enough to become, from our point of view, practically negligible. Now, if every concrete perception, however brief it may be supposed, is already the synthesis, by memory, of an infinity of “pure perceptions” that succeed one another, should we not think that the heterogeneity of sensible qualities is due to their contraction in our memory, and the relative homogeneity of objective changes to their natural relaxation? And might not the interval from quantity to quality then be diminished by considerations of tension, just as the distance from the extended to the unextended is diminished by considerations of extension?

Before embarking upon this path, let us formulate the general principle of the method we should like to apply. We have already made use of it in an earlier work, and even, implicitly, in the present work.

What is ordinarily called a fact is not reality as it would appear to an immediate intuition, but an adaptation of the real to the interests of practice and to the requirements of social life. Pure intuition, external or internal, is that of an undivided continuity. We divide it into juxtaposed elements, which correspond, here to distinct words, there to independent objects. But precisely because we have thus broken the unity of our
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 109

original intuition, we feel obliged to establish between the disjoined terms a link, which can no longer be anything but external and superadded. For the living unity, which arose from inner continuity, we substitute the factitious unity of an empty framework, inert like the terms that it keeps united. Empiricism and dogmatism agree, fundamentally, in setting out from phenomena thus reconstructed, and differ only in that dogmatism attaches itself more to this form, empiricism to this matter. Empiricism, indeed, vaguely sensing what is artificial in the relations that unite the terms with one another, confines itself to the terms and neglects the relations.

Its error is not to value experience too highly, but, on the contrary, to substitute for true experience, that which arises from the immediate contact of the mind with its object, an disarticulated and consequently doubtless denatured experience, arranged in any case for the greater facility of action and language. Precisely because this fragmentation of the real has been effected with a view to the requirements of practical life, it has not followed the inner lines of the structure of things: this is why empiricism cannot satisfy the mind on any of the great problems, and even, when it arrives at full consciousness of its principle, refrains from posing them. — Dogmatism discovers and brings out the difficulties to which empiricism closes its eyes; but, in truth, it seeks their solution along the path that empiricism has marked out.

It too accepts these detached, discontinuous phenomena with which empiricism is content, and merely strives to make of them a synthesis which, not having been given in an intuition, will necessarily always have an arbitrary form. In other words, if metaphysics is only a construction, there are several equally plausible metaphysics, which consequently refute one another, and the last word will remain with a critical philosophy, which holds all knowledge to be relative and the ground of things inaccessible to the mind. Such is indeed the regular course of philosophical thought: we set out from what we believe to be experience, we try various possible arrangements among the fragments that apparently compose it, and, in the face of the acknowledged fragility of all our constructions, we end by renouncing construction.

— But there would be one final undertaking to attempt. It would be to seek experience at its source, or rather above that decisive turning-point where, bending in the direction of our utility, it properly becomes human experience. The impotence of speculative reason, as Kant demonstrated it, is perhaps, fundamentally, only the impotence of an intelligence enslaved to certain necessities of bodily life and exercised upon a matter that had to be disorganized for the satis-faction of our needs. Our knowledge of things would then no longer be relative to the fundamental structure of our mind, but only to its superficial and acquired habits, to the contingent form it derives from our bodily functions and our lower needs. The relativity of knowledge would therefore not be definitive.
By undoing what these needs have done, we would restore intuition to its original purity and would regain contact with the real.

This method presents, in application, considerable and ever-recurring difficulties, because it requires, for the solution of each new problem, an entirely new effort. To renounce certain habits of thought and even of perception is already difficult: yet that is only the negative part of the work to be done; and when one has done it, when one has placed oneself at what we called the turning-point of experience, when one has taken advantage of the dawning light which, illuminating the passage from the immediate to the useful, begins
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 110

the dawn of our human experience, it remains to reconstruct, from the infinitely small elements which we thus perceive of the real curve, the form of the curve itself which extends in darkness behind them. In this sense, the task of the philosopher, as we understand it, closely resembles that of the mathematician who determines a function by starting from the differential. The ultimate procedure of philosophical inquiry is a genuine work of integration.

We formerly attempted the application of this method to the problem of consciousness, and it seemed to us that the utilitarian work of the mind, as regards the perception of our inner life, consisted in a kind of refraction of pure duration through space, a refraction that enables us to separate our psychological states, to bring them into an increasingly impersonal form, to impose names upon them, and finally to make them enter into the current of social life.

Empiricism and dogmatism take inner states under this discontinuous form, the former confining itself to the states themselves in order to see in the self only a succession of juxtaposed facts, the latter understanding the necessity of a link, but no longer able to find this link except in a form or in a force,—an external form into which the aggregate would be inserted, an indeterminate and, as it were, physical force that would ensure the cohesion of the elements. Hence the two opposing points of view on the question of freedom: for determinism, the act is the resultant of a mechanical composition of the elements among themselves; for its adversaries, if they were rigorously in agreement with their principle, the free decision would have to be an arbitrary fiat, a genuine creation ex nihilo. — We thought that there would be a third course to adopt.

It would be to replace ourselves in pure duration, whose flow is continuous, and where one passes, by imperceptible gradations, from one state to another: continuity genuinely lived, but artificially decomposed for the greater convenience of ordinary knowledge. Then we believed we saw action issue from its antecedents through an evolution sui generis, such that one finds again in this action the antecedents that explain it, and yet it adds to them something absolutely new, being in advance of them as the fruit is of the flower. Freedom is in no way thereby reduced, as has been said, to sensible spontaneity. At most, this would be so in the animal, whose psychological life is chiefly affective. But in man, a thinking being, the free act may be called a synthesis of feelings and ideas, and the evolution leading to it a reasonable evolution.

The artifice of this method consists simply, in sum, in distinguishing the point of view of ordinary or useful knowledge from that of true knowledge. The duration in which we watch ourselves acting, and in which it is useful that we should watch ourselves, is a duration whose elements dissociate and are juxtaposed; but the duration in which we act is a duration in which our states merge into one another, and it is there that we must make an effort to replace ourselves in thought in the exceptional and unique case where we speculate upon the intimate nature of action, that is to say, in the theory of freedom.
Is a method of this kind applicable to the problem of matter?

The question is whether, in that “diversity of phenomena” of which Kant spoke, the confused mass with an extensive tendency could be grasped on this side of the homogeneous space upon which it is applied and through the intermediary of which we subdivide it,—just as our inner life can detach itself from indefinite and empty time in order to become pure duration again. Certainly, the undertaking
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 111

would be chimerical if it sought to free itself from the fundamental conditions of external perception. But the question is whether certain conditions, which we ordinarily take to be fundamental, might not concern the use to be made of things, the practical advantage to be drawn from them, far more than the pure knowledge that we can have of them. More particularly, as regards concrete, continuous, diversified, and at the same time organized extension, one may dispute that it is bound up with the amorphous and inert space which underlies it, a space which we divide indefinitely, in which we cut out figures arbitrarily, and in which movement itself, as we said elsewhere, can appear only as a multiplicity of instantaneous positions, since nothing there could ensure the cohesion of past and present.

Thus one could, to a certain extent, free oneself from space without leaving extension, and there would indeed be here a return to the immediate, since we genuinely perceive extension, whereas we only conceive space in the manner of a schema. Will this method be reproached for arbitrarily attributing a privileged value to immediate knowledge? But what reasons would we have to doubt a knowledge—the very idea of doubting it, would it ever come to us without the difficulties and contradictions that reflection points out, without the problems that philosophy poses?

And would not immediate knowledge then find in itself its justification and its proof, if one could establish that these difficulties, these contradictions, these problems arise chiefly from the symbolic representation that covers it over, a representation which has become for us reality itself, and whose thickness only an intense, exceptional effort can succeed in piercing?

Let us at once choose, among the results to which the application of this method may lead, those which concern our inquiry. We shall moreover confine ourselves to indications; there can be no question here of constructing a theory of matter.
I. — Every movement, insofar as it is a passage from one state of rest to another, is
absolutely indivisible.
This is not a hypothesis, but a fact, generally covered over by a hypothesis.

Here, for example, is my hand placed at point A. I move it to point B, traversing the interval in a single stroke. In this movement there are, at once, an image that strikes my sight and an act grasped by my muscular consciousness. My consciousness gives me the inner sensation of a simple fact, for at A there was rest, at B there is rest again, and between A and B there occurs an indivisible, or at least undivided, act, a passage from rest to rest, which is movement itself. But my sight perceives movement in the form of a line AB that is traversed, and this line, like all space, is indefinitely divisible. Thus it seems at first that I may, as I please, regard this movement as multiple or as indivisible, according as I consider it in space or in time, as an image taking shape outside myself or as an act that I myself perform.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 112
Nevertheless, setting aside every preconceived idea, I soon realize that I have no choice, that my sight itself apprehends the movement from A to B

as an indivisible whole, and that if it divides anything, it is the line supposed to have been traversed and not the movement that traverses it. It is indeed true that my hand does not go from A to B without passing through the intermediate positions, and that these intermediate points resemble stages, as numerous as one might wish, arranged all along the route; but between the divisions thus marked and stages properly so called there is this capital difference: at a stage one stops, whereas here the moving body passes. Now passage is a movement, and stopping an immobility. Stopping interrupts movement; passage is one with movement itself.

When I see the moving body pass through a point, I no doubt conceive that it can stop there; and even when it does not stop there, I am inclined to regard its passage as an infinitely short rest, because I need at least the time to think about it; but it is my imagination alone that rests here, and the role of the moving body is, on the contrary, to move. As every point in space necessarily appears to me fixed, I find it very difficult not to attribute to the moving body itself the immobility of the point with which I make it coincide for a moment; it then seems to me, when I reconstruct the total movement, that the moving body halted for an infinitely short time at every point of its trajectory. But one must not confuse the data of the senses, which perceive movement, with the artifices of the mind that recomposes it.

The senses, left to themselves, present to us real movement, between two real stoppages, as a solid and undivided whole. Division is the work of imagination, whose very function is to fix the moving images of our ordinary experience, like the instantaneous flash of lightning that illuminates, during the night, a storm scene.

Here we grasp, in its very principle, the illusion that accompanies and covers over the perception of real movement. Movement visibly consists in passing from one point to another, and consequently in traversing space. Now the space traversed is divisible to infinity, and since movement applies itself, so to speak, along the line it traverses, it appears bound up with that line and divisible like it. Has it not itself drawn that line? Has it not traversed, one after another, its successive and juxtaposed points? Yes, certainly, but these points have reality only in a traced line, that is to say, an immobile one; and by the very fact that you represent movement successively at these different points, you necessarily stop it there; your successive positions are, fundamentally, only imaginary stoppages.

You substitute the trajectory for the journey, and because the journey is underlain by the trajectory, you believe that it coincides with it. But how could a progress coincide with a thing, a movement with an immobility?

What facilitates the illusion here is that we distinguish moments in the course of duration, as positions along the path of the moving body. Assuming that movement from one point to another forms an undivided whole, this movement nonetheless fills a determinate time, and it suffices to isolate from this duration an indivisible instant for the moving body to occupy, at that precise moment, a certain position, which thus stands out from all the others. The indivisibility of movement therefore implies the impossibility of the instant, and a very summary analysis of the idea of duration will indeed show us, at once, why we attribute instants to duration, and how it cannot have them.
Let there be a simple movement, such as the journey of my hand when it moves
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 113

from A to B. This journey is given to my consciousness as an undivided whole. It lasts, no doubt; but its duration, which moreover coincides with the inner aspect it takes on for my consciousness, is compact and undivided like it. Now, while it presents itself, insofar as it is movement, as a simple fact, it describes in space a trajectory that I may consider, in order to simplify matters, as a geometrical line; and the extremities of this line, as abstract limits, are no longer lines but indivisible points. Now, if the line described by the moving body measures for me the duration of its movement, how could the point at which the line ends not symbolize an extremity of this duration? And if this point is an indivisible of length, how could one not terminate the duration of the journey by an indivisible of duration?

The total line representing the total duration, the parts of this line must correspond, it seems, to parts of duration, and the points of the line to moments of time. Indivisibles of duration, or moments of time, thus arise from a need for symmetry; one arrives at them naturally as soon as one asks space for an integral representation of duration. But that is precisely the error. If the line AB symbolizes the elapsed duration of the movement accomplished from A to B, it cannot in any way, being immobile, represent movement being accomplished, duration elapsing; and from the fact that this line is divisible into parts, and that it terminates in points, one must conclude neither that the corresponding duration is composed of separate parts nor that it is bounded by instants.
The arguments of Zeno of Elea have no other origin than this illusion.

All of them consist in making time and movement coincide with the line that underlies them, in attributing to them the same subdivisions, and finally in treating them as it is treated. Zeno was encouraged in this confusion by common sense, which ordinarily transfers to movement the properties of its trajectory, and also by language, which always translates movement and duration into space. But common sense and language are here within their rights, and even, in a certain way, do their duty, for, always considering becoming as a usable thing, they need concern themselves no more with the inner organization of movement than the worker with the molecular structure of his tools.

In holding movement to be divisible like its trajectory, common sense simply expresses the two facts that alone matter in practical life: 1º that every movement describes a space; 2º that at each point of this space the moving body could stop. But the philosopher who reasons about the intimate nature of movement is bound to restore to it the mobility that is its essence, and this is what Zeno does not do. By the first argument (the Dichotomy), the moving body is supposed to be at rest, so as thereafter to consider only stages, indefinite in number, on the line it must traverse: you would seek in vain, we are told, how it could succeed in crossing the interval. But this merely proves that it is impossible to construct movement a priori out of immobilities, which has never been in doubt for anyone.

The sole question is whether, movement being posited as a fact, there is a kind of retrospective absurdity in an infinite number of points having been traversed. But we see in this nothing but what is very natural, since movement is an undivided fact or a succession of undivided facts, whereas the trajectory is indefinitely divisible. In the second argument (Achilles), movement is granted, indeed it is attributed to two moving bodies, but, always through the same error, these movements are required to coincide with their trajectory and to be, like it, arbitrarily decomposable. Then, instead
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 114

of recognizing that the tortoise takes tortoise steps and Achilles Achilles steps, so that after a certain number of these indivisible acts or leaps Achilles will have passed the tortoise, one believes oneself entitled to disarticulate the movement of Achilles as one pleases and the movement of the tortoise as one pleases: one thus amuses oneself by reconstructing the two movements according to an arbitrary law of formation, incompatible with the fundamental conditions of mobility. The same sophism appears even more clearly in the third argument (the Arrow), which consists in concluding, from the fact that one can fix points on the trajectory of a projectile, that one has the right to distinguish indivisible moments in the duration of the journey.

But perhaps the most instructive of Zeno's arguments is the fourth (the Stadium), which, we believe, has been quite unjustly neglected, and whose absurdity is manifest only because in it one sees displayed in all its frankness the postulate concealed in the other three 1. Without entering here into a discussion that would not be in its place, let us confine ourselves to observing that immediately perceived movement is a very clear fact, and that the difficulties or contradictions pointed out by the Eleatic school concern much less movement itself than an artificial and unviable reorganization of movement by the mind. Let us moreover draw the conclusion from all that precedes:
II.— There are real movements.

The mathematician, expressing more precisely an idea of common sense, defines position by distance from reference points or axes, and movement by variation of distance. Thus he knows of movement only changes of length; and since the absolute values of the variable distance between a point and an axis, for example, express equally well the displacement of the axis in relation to the point as that of the point in relation to the axis, he will indifferently attribute to the same point rest or 1

Let us briefly recall this argument. Let there be a moving body that moves at a certain speed and passes simultaneously before two bodies, one of which is immobile and the other moving to meet it at the same speed as its own. At the same time as it traverses a certain length of the first body, it naturally crosses a double length of the second. From this Zeno concludes “that a duration is double itself.” — Childish reasoning, it is said, since Zeno does not take account of the fact that the speed is double in one case what it is in the other. — Granted, but how, pray, could he notice it?

That, in the same time, a moving body should traverse different lengths of two bodies, one of which is at rest and the other in movement, is clear to one who makes duration a kind of absolute and places it either in consciousness or in something participating in consciousness. While a determinate portion of this conscious or absolute duration elapses, indeed, the same moving body will traverse, along the two bodies, two spaces one double the other, without one being able to conclude from this that a duration is double itself, since duration remains something independent of both spaces. But Zeno's fault, throughout his argumentation, is precisely to leave true duration aside in order to consider only its objective trace in space.

How, then, would the two traces left by the same moving body not deserve equal consideration, as measures of duration? And how would they not represent the same duration, even if they were twice one another? In concluding from this that a duration “is double itself,” Zeno remained within the logic of his hypothesis, and his fourth argument is worth exactly as much as the other three.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of Body to Spirit. (1939) 115

mobility. If, then, movement is reduced to a change of distance, the same object becomes mobile or immobile according to the reference points to which it is related, and there is no absolute movement.

But things already change in aspect when one passes from mathematics to physics, and from the abstract study of movement to the consideration of the concrete changes that take place in the universe. If we are free to attribute rest or movement to any material point taken in isolation, it remains no less true that the aspect of the material universe changes, that the internal configuration of every real system varies, and that we no longer have a choice here between mobility and rest: movement, whatever its intimate nature, becomes an incontestable reality. Let us admit that one cannot say which parts of the whole are moving; there is nonetheless movement in the whole. Thus one should not be surprised if the same thinkers who regard every particular movement as relative treat the totality of movements as an absolute.

The contradiction has been noted in Descartes, who, after having given the thesis of relativity its most radical form by affirming that all movement is “reciprocal” 1, formulates the laws of movement as if movement were an absolute 2. Leibniz, and others after him, pointed out this contradiction 3: it simply arises from the fact that Descartes treats movement as a physicist after having defined it as a geometer.

All movement is relative for the geometer: this means only, in our view, that there is no mathematical symbol capable of expressing that it is the moving body that moves rather than the axes or the points to which it is related.

And this is quite natural, since these symbols, always intended for measurements, can express only distances. But that there is a real movement, no one can seriously contest: otherwise, nothing would change in the universe, and above all one does not see what the consciousness we have of our own movements would mean. In his controversy with Descartes, Morus playfully alluded to this latter point: “When I am sitting quietly, and another man, having gone a thousand paces away, is red with fatigue, it is indeed he who is moving and I who am resting 4.”

But if there is absolute movement, can one persist in seeing in movement only a change of place? It would then be necessary to make diversity of place into an absolute difference, and to distinguish absolute positions in an absolute space. Newton went that far 5, followed moreover by Euler 6 and by others.

But can this be imagined or even conceived? One place would be distinguished absolutely from another place only by its quality, or by its relation to the whole of space: so that space would become, under this hypothesis, either composed of heterogeneous parts or finite. But to a finite space we would give another space as a boundary, and beneath heterogeneous parts of space we would imagine a homogeneous space as their support: in both cases, we would necessarily return to homogeneous and indefinite space.1

We can therefore refrain neither from holding every place to be relative, nor from believing in an absolute movement.

Will it then be said that real movement is distinguished from relative movement in that it has a real cause, in that it emanates from a force? But one would have to agree on the meaning of this latter word. In the natural sciences, force is only a function of mass and velocity; it is measured by acceleration; it is known and evaluated only through the movements that it is supposed to produce in space. Bound up with these movements, it shares their relativity. Thus the physicists who seek the principle of absolute movement in force thus defined are led back, by the logic of their system, to the hypothesis of an absolute space which they had initially wished to avoid 1.

It will therefore be necessary to fall back on the metaphysical sense of the word, and to ground the movement perceived in space upon profound causes, analogous to those that our consciousness believes it grasps in the feeling of effort. But is the feeling of effort really that of a profound cause? And have decisive analyses not shown that there is nothing else in this feeling but the consciousness of movements already effected or begun at the periphery of the body? It is therefore in vain that we would seek to ground the reality of movement on a cause distinct from it: analysis always brings us back to movement itself.

But why seek elsewhere? So long as you set movement against the line it traverses, the same point appears to you in turn, according to the origin to which you relate it, at rest or in movement. It is no longer the same if you extract from movement the mobility that is its essence.

When my eyes give me the sensation of a movement, this sensation is a reality, and something actually takes place, whether an object moves before my eyes or my eyes move before the object. All the more am I assured of the reality of movement when I produce it after having willed to produce it, and muscular sense brings me the consciousness of it.

That is to say that I touch the reality of movement when it appears to me, inwardly, as a change of state or quality. But then, how could it not be the same when I perceive changes of quality in things? Sound differs absolutely from silence, just as one sound differs from another sound. Between light and darkness, between colours, between shades, the difference is absolute. The passage from one to the other is likewise an absolutely real phenomenon. Thus I hold the two ends of the chain, the muscular sensations within me, the sensible qualities of matter outside me, and no more in one case than in the other do I grasp movement, if there is movement, as a simple relation: it is an absolute. -

Between these two ends come to be placed the movements of external bodies properly so called. How is one to distinguish here an apparent movement from a real movement? Of what externally perceived object can one say that it moves, and of what other that it remains motionless? To pose such a question is to admit that the discontinuity established by common sense between objects independent of one another, each having its individuality, comparable to kinds of persons, is a well-founded distinction. Under the contrary hypothesis, indeed, it would no longer be a matter of knowing how changes of position occur in such determined parts of matter, but 1
Newton in particular.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 117
how, in the whole, a change of aspect takes place, a change whose nature, moreover, would still remain for us to determine. Let us therefore formulate our third proposition at once:
III. - Any division of matter into independent bodies with contours
absolutely determined is an artificial division.

A body, that is to say an independent material object, first presents itself to us as a system of qualities, in which resistance and colour,—data of sight and touch,—occupy the centre and hold suspended, as it were, all the others. On the other hand, the data of sight and touch are those which extend most manifestly in space, and the essential character of space is continuity.

There are intervals of silence between sounds, for hearing is not always occupied; between odours, between tastes, one finds gaps, as though smell and taste functioned only accidentally: on the contrary, as soon as we open our eyes, our entire visual field becomes coloured, and since solids are necessarily contiguous with one another, our touch must follow the surface or the edges of objects without ever encountering a genuine interruption. How do we divide the continuity originally perceived in material extension into so many bodies, each of which would have its substance and its individuality? No doubt this continuity changes aspect from one moment to the next: but why do we not purely and simply observe that the whole has changed, as though one had turned a kaleidoscope?

Why, finally, do we seek, in the mobility of the whole, tracks followed by moving bodies? A moving continuity is given to us, in which everything changes and remains at once: whence comes it that we dissociate these two terms, permanence and change, in order to represent permanence by bodies and change by homogeneous movements in space? This is not a datum of immediate intuition; but neither is it a requirement of science, for science, on the contrary, proposes to recover the natural articulations of a universe that we have artificially cut up. What is more, by demonstrating ever more clearly the reciprocal action of all material points upon one another, science returns, in spite of appearances, as we shall see, to the idea of universal continuity.

Science and consciousness are, fundamentally, in agreement, provided that consciousness is considered in its most immediate data and science in its most remote aspirations. Whence then comes the irresistible tendency to constitute a discontinuous material universe, with bodies having sharply defined edges, which change place,) that is to say, their relation to one another?

Alongside consciousness and science, there is life. Beneath the principles of speculation, so carefully analysed by philosophers, there are those tendencies whose study has been neglected and which are explained simply by the necessity under which we are to live, that is to say, in reality, to act. Already the power conferred upon individual consciousnesses to manifest themselves through acts requires the formation of distinct material zones respectively corresponding to living bodies: in this sense, my own body, and, by analogy with it, the other
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 118

living bodies, are those that I am best justified in distinguishing within the continuity of the universe. But once this body has been constituted and distinguished, the needs it experiences lead it to distinguish and constitute others.

In the humblest of living beings, nutrition requires a search, then a contact, finally a series of efforts converging toward a centre: this centre will become precisely the independent object that must serve as food. Whatever the nature of matter may be, one may say that life will already establish in it a first discontinuity, expressing the duality of need and that which must serve to satisfy it. But the need to feed oneself is not the only one. Others are organized around it, all having as their object the preservation of the individual or of the species: now, each of them leads us to distinguish, alongside our own body, bodies independent of it that we must seek out or flee. Our needs are therefore so many beams of light which, directed upon the continuity of sensible qualities, trace distinct bodies there.

They can be satisfied only on condition that they carve out a body for themselves in this continuity, then delimit within it other bodies with which that body will enter into relation as with persons. Establishing these quite particular relations between portions thus cut out of sensible reality is precisely what we call living.

But if this first subdivision of the real corresponds much less to immediate intuition than to the fundamental needs of life, how could a closer knowledge of things be obtained by carrying the division still further? In this way one prolongs the vital movement; one turns one's back on true knowledge. This is why the crude operation of decomposing the body into parts of the same nature as itself leads us to an impasse, since we soon feel ourselves incapable of conceiving either why this division would stop or how it would continue to infinity. It represents, in fact, an ordinary form of useful action, inappropriately transferred into the domain of pure knowledge.

One will therefore never explain the simple properties of matter by particles, whatever they may be: at most one will follow, down to corpuscles, artificial like the body itself, the actions and reactions of this body with respect to all the others. This is precisely the object of chemistry. It studies bodies less than matter; one therefore understands why it stops at an atom, still endowed with the general properties of matter. But the materiality of the atom dissolves more and more under the physicist's gaze. We have no reason, for example, to represent the atom as solid rather than liquid or gaseous, nor to imagine the reciprocal action of atoms through impacts rather than in any other way. Why do we think of a solid atom, and why of impacts?

Because solids, being the bodies upon which we most manifestly have a hold, are those that interest us most in our relations with the external world, and because contact is the only means that we appear to possess for making our body act upon other bodies. But very simple experiments show that there is never real contact between two bodies that push one another 1; and moreover solidity is far from being an absolutely distinct state of matter 2. Solidity and impact therefore derive their 1

apparent clarity from the habits and necessities of practical life;—images of this kind shed no light on the depths of things.

If, moreover, there is one truth that science has placed beyond all dispute, it is that of a reciprocal action of all parts of matter upon one another. Between the supposed molecules of bodies attractive and repulsive forces are exerted. The influence of gravitation extends across interplanetary spaces. Something therefore exists between atoms. It will be said that this is no longer matter, but force. One will imagine threads stretched between atoms, which will be made thinner and thinner, until they have been rendered invisible and even, it is believed, immaterial. But what use could this crude image be? The preservation of life doubtless requires that we distinguish, in our daily experience, inert things and actions exerted by these things in space.

Since it is useful for us to fix the seat of the thing at the precise point where we could touch it, its tangible contours become for us its real limit, and we then see in its action an I-know-not-what that detaches itself from it and differs from it. But since a theory of matter proposes precisely to recover reality beneath these usual images, all relative to our needs, it must first abstract from these images. And, in fact, we see force and matter draw nearer and come together as the physicist probes their effects more deeply.

We see force becoming materialized, the atom becoming idealized, these two terms converging toward a common limit, and the universe thus recovering its continuity. We shall still speak of atoms; the atom will even retain its individuality for our mind, which isolates it; but the solidity and inertia of the atom will dissolve either into movements or into lines of force, whose reciprocal solidarity will restore universal continuity. This conclusion was necessarily to be reached, though starting from quite different points, by the two nineteenth-century physicists who penetrated furthest into the constitution of matter, Thomson and Faraday. For Faraday, the atom is a “centre of forces”.

By this he means that the individuality of the atom consists in the mathematical point where the indefinite lines of force that radiate through space and truly constitute it intersect: each atom thus occupies, to use his expressions,

“the whole space to which gravitation extends,” and “all atoms interpenetrate one another 1.” Thomson, placing himself in an entirely different order of ideas, supposes a perfect, continuous, homogeneous, and incompressible fluid, which would fill space: what we call an atom would be a ring of invariable form whirling in this continuity, and would owe its properties to its form, its existence and consequently its individuality to its movement 2. But in both hypotheses, we see the discontinuity that our perception had established at the surface vanish as we approach the ultimate elements of matter. Psychological analysis had already revealed to us that this discontinuity is relative to our needs: every philosophy of nature ends by finding it incompatible with the general properties of matter.
