On the one hand, there is a multiple matter, composed of parts more or less independent, diffused in space, and on the other a mind that can have no point of contact with it, unless it be, as the materialists would have it, its unintelligible epiphenomenon. Does one prefer to consider Kantian realism?

Between the thing in itself, that is to say the real, and the sensible diversity with which we construct our knowledge, one finds no conceivable relation, no common measure. Now, on probing these two extreme forms of realism, one sees them converge upon the same point: both set up homogeneous space as a barrier between intelligence and things. Naïve realism makes this space a real medium in which things would be suspended; Kantian realism sees in it an ideal medium in which the multiplicity of sensations is coordinated; but for the one as for the other this medium is given first, as the necessary condition of what comes to be placed within it.

And on probing this common hypothesis in turn, one finds that it consists in attributing to homogeneous space a disinterested role, whether it renders material reality the service of supporting it, or whether it
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 137

has the function, still wholly speculative, of providing sensations with the means of coordinating themselves with one another. Thus the obscurity of realism, like that of idealism, comes from its directing our conscious perception, and the conditions of our conscious perception, toward pure knowledge, not toward action. — But let us now suppose that this homogeneous space is not logically prior, but posterior to material things and to the pure knowledge we can have of them; let us suppose that extension precedes space; let us suppose that homogeneous space concerns our action, and our action alone, being like an infinitely divided net that we spread beneath material continuity in order to master it, in order to decompose it in the direction of our activities and our needs.

Then we gain not only the advantage of rejoining science, which shows us each thing exerting its influence upon all the others, consequently occupying in a certain sense the totality of extension (although we perceive of this thing only its centre and set its limits at the point where our body would cease to have a hold upon it). We gain not only, in metaphysics, the advantage of resolving or mitigating the contradictions raised by divisibility in space, contradictions which always arise, as we have shown, from the failure to dissociate the two points of view of action and knowledge. Above all, we gain the advantage of bringing down the insurmountable barrier that realism erected between extended things and the perception we have of them.

Whereas, indeed, one placed on the one hand a multiple and divided external reality, and on the other sensations foreign to extension and having no possible contact with it, we perceive that concrete extension is not really divided, any more than immediate perception is truly unextended. Having started from realism, we return to the same point to which idealism had led us; we replace perception in things. And we see realism and idealism very nearly coincide, as we remove the postulate, accepted without discussion by both, which served them as their common limit.

In summary, if we suppose an extended continuity, and, within this continuity itself, the centre of real action that is represented by our body, this activity will seem to illuminate with its light all the parts of matter upon which at each moment it would have a hold. The same needs, the same power of acting that have cut out our body from matter will delimit distinct bodies in the environment surrounding us. Everything will take place as though we allowed the real action of external things to pass through, in order to stop and retain their virtual action: this virtual action of things upon our body and of our body upon things is perception itself.

But since the shocks that our body receives from surrounding bodies continually determine, in its substance, nascent reactions, and since these internal movements of cerebral substance thus give at every moment the outline of our possible action upon things, the cerebral state corresponds exactly to perception. It is neither its cause, nor its effect, nor, in any sense, its duplicate: it simply continues it, perception being our virtual action and the cerebral state our action begun.
IV. — But this theory of “pure perception” had to be both qualified and completed on two points. This pure perception, indeed, which
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 138

would be like a fragment detached as such from reality, would belong to a being that would mingle with the perception of other bodies neither that of its own body, that is to say its affections, nor with its intuition of the present moment that of other moments, that is to say its memories. In other words, for the convenience of study, we have first treated the living body as a mathematical point in space and conscious perception as a mathematical instant in time. It was necessary to restore to the body its extension and to perception its duration. In this way we reintegrated into consciousness its two subjective elements, affectivity and memory.

What is an affection? Our perception, we said, outlines the possible action of our body upon other bodies. But our body, being extended, is capable of acting upon itself as well as upon others. Something of our body will therefore enter into our perception. Nevertheless, when it is a question of surrounding bodies, they are, by hypothesis, separated from ours by a more or less considerable space, which measures in time the remoteness of their promises or their threats: this is why our perception of these bodies outlines only possible actions. On the contrary, the more the distance between these bodies and ours decreases, the more possible action tends to be transformed into real action, action becoming all the more urgent as the distance is less considerable.

And when this distance becomes nil, that is to say when the body to be perceived is our own body, it is a real, and no longer virtual, action that perception outlines. Such is precisely the nature of pain, the present effort of the injured part to set things right again, a local, isolated effort, and thereby condemned to failure in an organism no longer capable except of overall effects. Pain is where it occurs, as the object is in the place where it is perceived. Between the affection felt and the image perceived, there is this difference: the affection is in our body, the image outside our body. And this is why the surface of our body, the common boundary of this body and other bodies, is given to us both in the form of sensations and in the form of an image.

The subjectivity of affective sensation consists in this interiority; the objectivity of images in general, in this exteriority. But here we rediscover the ever-recurrent error that we have pursued throughout the whole course of our work. It is desired that sensation and perception should exist for themselves; a wholly speculative role is attributed to them; and since those real and virtual actions with which they form a whole, and which would serve to distinguish them, have been neglected, one can no longer find between them anything but a difference of degree. Then, taking advantage of the fact that affective sensation is only vaguely localized (because of the confusion of the effort it envelops), one immediately declares it wholly unextended; and one makes of these diminished affections, or unextended sensations, the materials with which we would construct images in space.

By this means one condemns oneself to explain neither whence come the elements of consciousness, or sensations, which one posits as so many absolutes, nor how, being unextended, these sensations rejoin space in order to coordinate themselves therein, nor why they adopt one order there rather than another, nor finally by what means they succeed in constituting there a stable experience common to all men. On the contrary, it is from this experience, the necessary theatre of our activity, that one must begin. Thus it is pure perception, that is to say the image, that must first be given. And sensations, far from being the materials with which the image is made, will then appear, on the contrary, as
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 139
the impurity that mingles with it, being what we project of our body into all the others.

V. — But so long as we remain at sensation and pure perception, one can scarcely say that we are dealing with mind. Doubtless, against the theory of consciousness as epiphenomenon, we establish that no cerebral state is the equivalent of a perception. Doubtless, the selection of perceptions from among images in general is the effect of a discernment that already announces mind. Doubtless, finally, the material universe itself, defined as the totality of images, is a kind of consciousness, a consciousness in which everything compensates and neutralizes everything else, a consciousness whose every eventual part, balancing one another through reactions always equal to actions, mutually prevent one another from standing out.

But in order to touch the reality of mind, one must place oneself at the point where an individual consciousness, prolonging and preserving the past in a present enriched by it, thus withdraws itself from the very law of necessity, which requires that the past continually succeed itself in a present that merely repeats it in another form, and that everything always flows away. In passing from pure perception to memory, we definitively left matter for mind.

VI. — The theory of memory, which forms the centre of our work, had to be at once the theoretical consequence and the experimental verification of our theory of pure perception. That the cerebral states accompanying perception are neither its cause nor its duplicate, that perception maintains with its physiological concomitant the relation of virtual action to action begun, is what we could not establish by facts, since in our hypothesis everything will take place as though perception resulted from the cerebral state. In pure perception, indeed, the perceived object is a present object, a body that modifies ours.

Its image is therefore actually given, and from that point onward the facts allow us indifferently to say (at the cost of understanding ourselves very unequally) that cerebral modifications outline the nascent reactions of our body or that they create the conscious duplicate of the present image. But it is quite otherwise with memory, for recollection is the representation of an absent object. Here the two hypotheses will yield opposite consequences. If, in the case of a present object, a state of our body were already sufficient to create the representation of the object, then, a fortiori, this state will still suffice in the case of the same absent object. In this theory, then, recollection must arise from the attenuated repetition of the cerebral phenomenon that occasioned the first perception, and consist simply in a weakened perception.

Hence this double thesis: memory is only a function of the brain, and there is only a difference of intensity between perception and recollection. — On the contrary, if the cerebral state did not in any way generate our perception of the present object but merely continued it, it may still prolong and bring to fruition the recollection that we evoke of it, but not bring it into being. And since, moreover, our perception of the present object was something of that object itself, our representation of the absent object will be a phenomenon of an entirely different order from perception, since between presence and absence there is no degree, no
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 140

middle. Hence this double thesis, the reverse of the preceding one: Memory is something other than a function of the brain, and there is not a difference of degree, but of nature, between perception and recollection. - The opposition between the two theories then takes on an acute form, and experience can this time decide between them.

We shall not return here to the details of the verification we attempted. Let us simply recall its essential points. All the factual arguments that may be invoked in favour of a probable accumulation of recollections in the cortical substance are drawn from localized diseases of memory.

But if recollections were really deposited in the brain, distinct forgettings would correspond to characteristic lesions of the brain. Now, in the amnesias in which an entire period of our past existence, for example, is suddenly and radically torn from memory, no precise cerebral lesion is observed; and conversely, in the disorders of memory in which cerebral localization is clear and certain, that is to say, in the various aphasias and in diseases of visual or auditory recognition, it is not such and such determinate recollections that are as though torn from the place where they would reside; it is the faculty of recall that is more or less diminished in its vitality, as if the subject had more or less difficulty in bringing his recollections into contact with the present situation.

It is therefore the mechanism of this contact that would have to be studied, in order to see whether the role of the brain might not be to ensure its functioning, rather than to imprison the recollections themselves in its cells. We were thus led to follow, through all its evolutions, the progressive movement by which past and present come into contact with one another, that is to say, recognition. And we found, indeed, that the recognition of a present object could take place in two absolutely different ways, but that, in neither case, did the brain behave like a reservoir of images.

At times, indeed, through an entirely passive recognition, acted rather than thought, the body makes an automatic movement correspond to a renewed perception: everything is then explained by the motor apparatuses that habit has set up in the body, and disorders of memory may result from the destruction of these mechanisms.

At other times, on the contrary, recognition takes place actively, through memory-images that advance to meet present perception; but then these recollections, at the moment of settling upon perception, must find a way of setting in motion in the brain the same apparatuses that perception ordinarily brings into play in order to act: otherwise, condemned beforehand to impotence, they will have no tendency to actualize themselves. And this is why, in all cases where a lesion of the brain affects a certain category of recollections, the recollections affected do not resemble one another, for example, in being from the same period, or in having a logical kinship with one another, but simply in all being auditory, or all visual, or all motor.

What appears to be damaged, therefore, are the various sensory and motor regions or, still more often, the appendages that make it possible to set them in motion from within the cortex itself, rather than the recollections themselves. We went further, and, through an attentive study of the recognition of words as well as of the phenomena of sensory aphasia, we attempted to establish that recognition did not take place at all through a mechanical awakening of recollections slumbering in the brain. On the contrary, it implies a more or less high tension of consciousness, which seeks in pure memory the
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 141
pure recollections, in order progressively to materialize them in contact with present perception.
But what is this pure memory, and what are these pure recollections? In answering this question, we completed the demonstration of our thesis.
We had just established its first point, namely that memory is something other than a function of the brain. It remained for us to show, through the analysis of the
“pure recollection,” that there is not between recollection and perception a simple difference of degree, but a radical difference of nature.

VII. - Let us immediately point out the metaphysical, and no longer merely psychological, significance of this last problem. The following is doubtless a thesis of pure psychology: recollection is a weakened perception. But let there be no mistake about it: if recollection is only a weaker perception, conversely perception will be something like a more intense recollection. Now, the germ of English idealism lies here. This idealism consists in seeing only a difference of degree, and not of nature, between the reality of the perceived object and the ideality of the conceived object. And the idea that we construct matter out of our inner states, that perception is only a true hallucination, likewise comes from there. It is this idea that we have never ceased to combat when we have dealt with matter.
Thus either our conception of matter is false, or recollection differs radically from perception.

We have thus transposed a metaphysical problem so as to make it coincide with a problem of psychology, which pure and simple observation can decide. How does it decide it? If the recollection of a perception were only that weakened perception, it would happen to us, for example, to take the perception of a faint sound for the recollection of an intense noise. Now, such confusion never occurs.

But one can go further, and prove, again by observation, that consciousness of a recollection never begins by being a weaker actual state that we would seek to relegate to the past after becoming conscious of its weakness: moreover, how, if we did not already have the representation of a previously lived past, could we relegate to it the least intense psychological states, when it would be so simple to juxtapose them with the strong states as a more confused present experience with a clearer present experience? The truth is that memory does not at all consist in a regression from the present to the past, but on the contrary in a progress from the past to the present. It is in the past that we place ourselves at once.

We start from a “virtual state,” which we gradually lead, through a series of different planes of consciousness, to the point where it materializes in a present perception, that is to say, to the point where it becomes a present and acting state, that is to say finally, to that extreme plane of our consciousness where our body is outlined. Pure recollection consists in this virtual state.

Why is the testimony of consciousness disregarded here? Why is recollection made into a weaker perception, of which one can say neither why we relegate it to the past, nor how we recover its date, nor by what right it reappears at one moment rather than another? Always because the practical destination of our present psychological states is forgotten
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Spirit. (1939) 142

current. Perception is made into a disinterested operation of the mind, a mere contemplation. Then, since pure recollection can evidently only be something of this kind (since it does not correspond to a present and pressing reality), recollection and perception become states of the same nature, between which one can find only a difference of intensity.

But the truth is that our present must not be defined by what is more intense: it is what acts upon us and what makes us act; it is sensory and it is motor; - our present is above all the state of our body. Our past, on the contrary, is what no longer acts, but could act, what will act by inserting itself into a present sensation from which it will borrow its vitality. It is true that at the moment when recollection thus actualizes itself by acting, it ceases to be recollection, it becomes perception again.

One then understands why recollection could not result from a cerebral state. The cerebral state continues the recollection; it gives it a hold on the present through the materiality it confers upon it; but pure recollection is a spiritual manifestation. With memory we are indeed truly in the domain of spirit.

VIII. - We did not have to explore this domain. Placed at the confluence of spirit and matter, desirous above all of seeing them flow into one another, we were to retain from the spontaneity of intelligence only its point of junction with a bodily mechanism. Thus we were able to witness the phenomenon of the association of ideas, and the birth of the simplest general ideas.

What is the capital error of associationism? It is to have placed all memories on the same plane, to have failed to recognize the more or less considerable distance separating them from the present bodily state, that is to say, from action.

Thus it has been unable to explain either how memory adheres to the perception that evokes it, or why association occurs through resemblance or contiguity rather than in any other way, or finally by what caprice this determinate memory is selected among the thousand memories that resemblance or contiguity would equally well attach to present perception. This is to say that associationism has blurred and confused all the different planes of consciousness, obstinately refusing to see in a less complete memory anything but a less complex memory, whereas it is in reality a less dreamed memory, that is to say, closer to action and thereby more commonplace, more capable of being shaped, -
like a ready-made garment, - to the novelty of the present situation.

The adversaries of associationism have, moreover, followed it onto this ground. They reproach it with explaining the higher operations of the mind by associations, but not with failing to recognize the true nature of association itself. Yet therein lies the original vice of associationism.

Between the plane of action, - the plane on which our body has contracted its past into motor habits, - and the plane of pure memory, where our mind preserves in all its details the picture of our life gone by, we believed we discerned, on the contrary, a thousand and a thousand different planes of consciousness, a thousand complete yet diverse repetitions of the totality of our lived experience.
To complete a memory with more personal details does not at all consist
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 143

in mechanically juxtaposing memories to that memory, but in transporting oneself onto a more extensive plane of consciousness, in moving away from action in the direction of dream. Nor does localizing a memory consist in mechanically inserting it among other memories, but in describing, through an increasing expansion of memory in its entirety, a circle wide enough for this detail of the past to appear within it. These planes are not, moreover, given as ready-made things, superimposed upon one another. Rather, they exist virtually, with that existence proper to things of the mind. Intelligence, moving at every moment along the interval that separates them, finds them again, or rather creates them anew unceasingly: its life consists in this very movement.

We then understand why the laws of association are resemblance and contiguity rather than other laws, and why memory chooses, among similar or contiguous memories, certain images rather than other images, and finally how the first general notions are formed through the combined work of body and mind. The interest of a living being is to grasp in a present situation what resembles a prior situation, then to bring near it what preceded it and above all what followed it, in order to profit from its past experience. Of all the associations one might imagine, associations by resemblance and by contiguity are thus at first the only ones that have a vital utility.

But in order to understand the mechanism of these associations and above all the apparently capricious selection that they make among memories, one must place oneself in turn on these two extreme planes which we have called the plane of action and the plane of dream. In the first, there appear only motor habits, of which one may say that they are associations played or lived rather than represented: here resemblance and contiguity are fused together, for analogous external situations, by being repeated, have ended by binding together certain movements of our body, and thenceforth the same automatic reaction in which we shall unfold these contiguous movements will also extract from the situation occasioning them its resemblance to prior situations.

But as one passes from movements to images, and from poorer images to richer images, resemblance and contiguity dissociate: they end by opposing one another on that other extreme plane where no action any longer adheres to images. The choice of one resemblance among many resemblances, of one contiguity among other contiguities, therefore does not occur by chance: it depends on the ever-variable degree of tension of memory, which, according as it inclines more to insert itself into present action or to detach itself from it, transposes itself entirely into one tone or another.

And it is also this double movement of memory between its two extreme limits that outlines, as we have shown, the first general notions: motor habit rising toward similar images in order to extract their similarities from them, similar images descending toward motor habit in order to merge, for example, in the automatic pronunciation of the word that unites them. The nascent generality of the idea thus already consists in a certain activity of the mind, in a movement between action and representation. And this is why it will always be easy for a certain philosophy, as we said, to locate the general idea at one of the two extremities, to make it crystallize into words or evaporate into memories, whereas it consists in reality in the movement of the mind that goes from one extremity to the other.
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 144

IX. - In thus representing elementary mental activity to ourselves, in making our body this time, together with all that surrounds it, the final plane of our memory, the extreme image, the moving point that our past at every moment thrusts into our future, we confirmed and clarified what we had said of the role of the body, while at the same time preparing the way for a rapprochement between body and mind.

After studying in turn, indeed, pure perception and pure memory, it remained for us to bring them together. If pure memory is already mind, and if pure perception would still be something of matter, we had to, by placing ourselves at the point of junction between pure perception and pure memory, cast some light upon the reciprocal action of mind and matter. In fact, “pure” perception, that is to say instantaneous perception, is only an ideal, a limit. Every perception occupies a certain thickness of duration, prolongs the past into the present, and thereby partakes of memory. By then taking perception in its concrete form, as a synthesis of pure memory and pure perception, that is to say of mind and matter, we narrowed the problem of the union of soul and body within its strictest limits.
Such is the effort that we attempted above all in the last part of our work.

The opposition of the two principles, in dualism in general, is resolved into the threefold opposition of the unextended to the extended, of quality to quantity, and of freedom to necessity. If our conception of the role of the body, if our analyses of pure perception and pure memory, are to clarify in some respect the correlation of body and mind, this can only be on condition that these three oppositions be removed or attenuated. Let us therefore examine them in turn, presenting here in a more metaphysical form the conclusions that we wished to derive from psychology alone.

1º If one imagines, on the one hand, an extension really divided into corpuscles, for example, and on the other a consciousness with sensations in themselves unextended that would come to be projected into space, one will obviously find nothing in common between this matter and this consciousness, between body and mind. But this opposition of perception and matter is the artificial work of an understanding that decomposes and recomposes according to its habits or its laws: it is not given in immediate intuition. What is given is not unextended sensations: how could they join space, choose a place there, and finally coordinate themselves there in order to construct a universal experience?

Nor is what is real an extension divided into independent parts: how, moreover, having thus no possible relation with our consciousness, could it unfold a series of changes whose order and relations would correspond exactly to the order and relations of our representations? What is given, what is real, is something intermediate between divided extension and pure unextendedness; it is what we have called the extensive. Extension is the most apparent quality of perception. It is by consolidating it and subdividing it by means of an abstract space, stretched by us beneath it for the needs of action, that we constitute multiple and indefinitely divisible extension. It is by subtilizing it
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 145

on the contrary, by making it dissolve in turn into affective sensations and evaporate into counterfeits of pure ideas, that we obtain those unextended sensations with which we then vainly seek to reconstitute images. And the two opposite directions in which we pursue this double work open themselves to us quite naturally, for it follows from the very necessities of action that extension is cut up for us into absolutely independent objects (whence an indication for subdividing extension), and that one passes by imperceptible degrees from affection to perception (whence a tendency to suppose perception increasingly unextended). But our understanding, whose role is precisely to establish logical distinctions and consequently sharp oppositions, launches itself alternately upon the two paths, and in each of them goes to the end.

Thus, at one extremity, it sets up an indefinitely divisible extension, at the other absolutely unextended sensations. And it thus creates the opposition that it subsequently gives itself the spectacle of.

2º Much less artificial is the opposition of quality to quantity, that is to say of consciousness to movement: but this second opposition is radical only if one begins by accepting the first. Suppose indeed that the qualities of things are reduced to unextended sensations affecting a consciousness, so that these qualities represent only, as so many symbols, homogeneous and calculable changes taking place in space; you will have to imagine an incomprehensible correspondence between these sensations and these changes. Renounce, on the contrary, establishing a priori between them this factitious contrariety: you will see all the barriers that seemed to separate them fall one by one. First, it is not true that consciousness, folded back upon itself, witnesses an inner procession of unextended perceptions.

It is therefore within perceived things themselves that you will relocate pure perception, and you will thus remove a first obstacle. You do indeed encounter a second: the homogeneous and calculable changes upon which science operates appear to belong to multiple and independent elements, such as atoms, of which they would be merely the accident; this multiplicity will interpose itself between perception and its object. But if the division of extension is purely relative to our possible action upon it, the idea of independent corpuscles is a fortiori schematic and provisional; science itself, moreover, authorizes us to set it aside. There is a second barrier fallen. One final interval remains to be crossed: that which lies between the heterogeneity of qualities and the apparent homogeneity of movements in extension.

But precisely because we have eliminated the elements, atoms or others, which would be the seat of these movements, there can no longer be any question here of movement that is the accident of a mobile body, of the abstract movement studied by mechanics and which is, fundamentally, only the common measure of concrete movements. How could this abstract movement, which becomes immobility when one changes one's point of reference, ground real changes, that is to say, changes that are felt? How, composed of a series of instantaneous positions, could it fill a duration whose parts prolong and continue themselves into one another?

One hypothesis alone therefore remains possible: that concrete movement, capable, like consciousness, of prolonging its past into its present, capable, by repeating itself, of generating sensible qualities, is already something of consciousness, already something of sensation. It would be this same sensation diluted, distributed over an infinitely greater number of moments, this same sensation vibrating, as we
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 146

were saying, within its chrysalis. Then one final point would remain to be elucidated: how does the contraction occur, no doubt no longer of homogeneous movements into distinct qualities, but of less heterogeneous changes into more heterogeneous changes? But our analysis of concrete perception answers this question: this perception, a living synthesis of pure perception and pure memory, necessarily condenses, in its apparent simplicity, an enormous multiplicity of moments. Between sensible qualities envisaged in our representation, and these same qualities treated as calculable changes, there is therefore only a difference in the rhythm of duration, a difference in inner tension. Thus, through the idea of tension we have sought to remove the opposition of quality to quantity, just as through the idea of extension we have sought to remove that of the unextended to the extended.

Extension and tension admit of multiple, but always determinate, degrees. The function of the understanding is to detach from these two kinds, extension and tension, their empty container, that is to say homogeneous space and pure quantity; thereby to substitute for flexible realities, which admit of degrees, rigid abstractions, born of the needs of action, which can only be accepted or rejected; and thus to set before reflective thought dilemmas neither alternative of which is accepted by things.

3º But if one thus envisages the relations of the extended to the unextended, of quality to quantity, one will have less difficulty in understanding the third and final opposition, that of freedom to necessity. Absolute necessity would be represented by a perfect equivalence of the successive moments of duration to one another. Is this the case with the duration of the material universe?

Could each of its moments be mathematically deduced from the preceding one? Throughout this work, for the convenience of the study, we have assumed that this was indeed so; and such is in fact the distance between the rhythm of our duration and that of the flow of things that the contingency of the course of nature, so profoundly studied by recent philosophy, must practically amount for us to necessity. Let us therefore retain our hypothesis, though it would nevertheless need to be qualified. Even then, freedom will not be in nature like an empire within an empire. We said that this nature could be considered as a neutralized and consequently latent consciousness, a consciousness whose possible manifestations would hold one another mutually in check and cancel one another out at the precise moment when they seek to appear.

The first gleams cast upon it by an individual consciousness therefore do not illuminate it with an unexpected light: this consciousness has merely removed an obstacle, extracted a virtual part from the real whole, finally chosen and disengaged what interested it; and if, through this intelligent selection, it indeed bears witness that it derives its form from mind, it is from nature that it draws its matter.

At the same time, moreover, as we witness the emergence of this consciousness, we see living bodies take shape, capable, in their simplest form, of spontaneous and unforeseeable movements. The progress of living matter consists in a differentiation of functions that brings about first the formation, then the gradual complication, of a nervous system capable of channeling excitations and organizing actions: the more the higher centers develop, the more numerous will become the motor pathways among which one and the same excitation will offer action a choice. An ever greater latitude left to movement in space: this indeed is what one sees. What one does not see is the growing and concomitant tension of consciousness in time. Not only, through its memory of experiences
Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory. Essay on the Relation of the Body to the Mind. (1939) 147

already remote, does this consciousness retain the past better and better in order to organize it with the present in a richer and newer decision, but, living a more intense life, contracting, through its memory of immediate experience, an increasing number of external moments into its present duration, it becomes more capable of creating acts whose internal indetermination, having to be distributed over a multiplicity, as great as one pleases, of moments of matter, will all the more easily pass through the meshes of necessity. Thus, whether one envisages it in time or in space, freedom always appears to sink deep roots into necessity and to organize itself intimately with it. Mind borrows from matter the perceptions from which it draws its nourishment, and returns them to matter in the form of movement, upon which it has impressed its freedom.
End of the text.

Man kann sich des Eindrucks nicht erwehren, daß
die Menschen gemeinhin mit falschen Maßstäben messen,
Macht, Erfolg und Reichtum für sich anstreben und bei
anderen bewundern, die wahren Werte des Lebens
aber unterschätzen. Und doch ist man bei jedem solchen
allgemeinen Urteil in Gefahr, an die Buntheit der
Menschenwelt und ihres seelischen Lebens zu vergessen.
Es gibt einzelne Männer, denen sich die Verehrung
ihrer Zeitgenossen nicht versagt, obwohl ihre Größe
auf Eigenschaften und Leistungen ruht, die den Zielen
und Idealen der Menge durchaus fremd sind. Man wird
leicht annehmen wollen, daß es doch nur eine Minder-
zahl ist, welche diese großen Männer anerkennt, wäh-
rend die große Mehrheit nichts von ihnen wissen will.
Aber es dürfte nicht so einfach zugehen, dank den
Unstimmigkeiten zwischen dem Denken und dem Han-
deln der Menschen und der Vielstimmigkeit ihrer
Wunschregungen.

6 Das ozeanische Gefühl,

Schrift zugeschickt, welche die Religion als Illusion be-
handelt, und er antwortete, er wäre mit meinem Urteil
über die Religion ganz einverstanden, bedauerte aber,
daß ich die eigentliche Quelle der Religiosität nicht ge-
würdigt hätte. Diese sei ein besonderes Gefühl, das
ihn selbst nie zu verlassen pflege, das er von vielen
anderen bestätigt gefunden und bei Millionen Menschen
voraussetzen dürfe. Ein Gefühl, das er die Empfindung
der „Ewigkeit“ nennen möchte, ein Gefühl wie von
etwas Unbegrenztem, Schrankenlosem, gleichsam „Ozea-
nischem*. Dies Gefühl sei eine rein subjektive Tatsache,
kein Glaubenssatz ; keine Zusicherung persönlicher Fort-
dauer knüpfe sich daran, aber es sei die Quelle der
religiösen Energie, die von den verschiedenen Kirchen
und Religionssystemen gefaßt, in bestimmte Kanäle ge-
leitet und gewiß auch aufgezehrt werde. Nur auf Grund
dieses ozeanischen Gefühls dürfe man sich religiös
heißen, auch wenn man jeden Glauben und jede Ilu-
sion ablehne.

Diese Äußerung meines verehrten Freundes, der selbst
einmal den Zauber der Illusion poetisch gewürdigt hat,
brachte mir nicht geringe Schwierigkeiten. Ich selbst
kann dies „ozeanische* Gefühl nicht in mir entdecken.
Es ist nicht bequem, Gefühle wissenschaftlich zu be-
arbeiten. Man kann versuchen, ihre physiologischen
Anzeichen zu beschreiben. Wo dies nicht angeht, —
ich fürchte, auch das ozeanische Gefühl wird sich einer

One cannot escape the impression that

admire them in others, but underestimate the true values

There are individual men to whom the veneration

rests upon qualities and achievements that are wholly foreign

readily want to assume that it is nevertheless only a minor-
ity that recognizes these great men, whereas
the great majority wants to know nothing of them.
But matters are probably not so simple, thanks to the

and the many-voiced character of their

I have nothing to offer that would decisively influence the solution of this
problem. The idea
that man should receive knowledge of his connection
with the environment through an immediate feeling directed to this end from the outset, sounds so strange, fits so poorly into the fabric of our
¹ D. Chr. Grabbe: Hannibal: “Yes, we shall not fall out of the world. We are in it once and for all.”
[Source scan 11 · printed page 8](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n11/mode/1up)
8 The feeling of the ego

psychology, that a psychoanalytic, i.e. genetic,
derivation of such a feeling may be attempted.
Then the following train of thought becomes available to us: Normally, nothing is more certain to us than
the feeling of our self, of our own ego. This
ego appears to us independent, unitary, sharply set off
from everything else. That this appearance is a deception,
that the ego rather continues inwardly, without a sharp
boundary, into an unconscious mental entity
which we designate as the id, to which it serves, as it were, as a façade,
has first been taught us by psychoanalytic research,
which still owes us much information about the relation
of the ego to the id. But outwardly at least,
the ego seems to maintain clear and sharp boundary
lines. Only in one state, an extraordinary one indeed,
which, however, cannot be condemned as pathological, is it otherwise.

At the height
of being in love, the boundary between ego
and object threatens to become blurred. Contrary to all the testimony
of the senses, the person in love maintains that I
and thou are one and is prepared to behave
as though it were so. What can be temporarily abolished by a
physiological function must naturally also be capable of being disturbed by pathological processes.
Pathology acquaints us with a great number
of states in which the delimitation
of the ego against the external world becomes uncertain, or the
[Source scan 12 · printed page 9](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n12/mode/1up)
Development of the feeling of the ego 9

boundaries are actually drawn incorrectly; cases in
which parts of one’s own body, indeed, portions of one’s
own mental life, perceptions, thoughts, feelings, appear to us as alien
and as not belonging to the ego; others in which one attributes to the external world
what has evidently arisen in the ego and should be acknowledged
by it. Thus the feeling of the ego too
is subject to disturbances, and the ego-boundaries are
not constant.

A further consideration tells us: This feeling of the ego in the
adult cannot have been so from the beginning. It must
have undergone a development which, understandably, cannot be demonstrated, but can be
constructed with considerable probability.¹ The
infant does not yet separate its ego from an external
world as the source of the sensations streaming in upon it.
It learns to do so gradually in response to various
stimuli. It must make the strongest impression
upon it that some of the sources of excitation, in which
it will later recognize its bodily organs, can at all times
send it sensations, while others temporarily withdraw from it—
among them the most desired: the mother's breast—and can only be fetched back by a scream
calling for help. Thus there first presents itself to the

¹ See the numerous works on ego-development and the feeling of the ego
by Ferenczi, Stages in the Development of the Sense of Reality (1913),
through to the contributions of P. Federn, 1926, 27, and later.
[Source scan 13 · printed page 10](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n13/mode/1up)
10 Pleasure-ego and reality-ego

The ego is first confronted with an “object,” as something that is situated “outside” and is only forced into appearance by a special action. A further incentive for the detachment of the ego from the mass of sensations, that is, for the recognition of an “outside,” of an external world, is provided by the frequent, manifold, unavoidable sensations of pain and unpleasure, which the unreservedly ruling pleasure principle bids one to abolish and avoid. There arises the tendency to detach from the ego everything that can become a source of such unpleasure, to cast it outside, to form a pure pleasure-ego, confronting which stands an alien, threatening outside. The boundaries of this primitive pleasure-ego cannot escape correction by experience.

Some things which one would not wish to relinquish as pleasure-giving are nevertheless not ego, are object, and some torment which one wishes to expel nevertheless proves inseparable from the ego, to be of internal origin. One learns a procedure by which, through intentional direction of sensory activity and appropriate muscular action, one can distinguish what is internal—belonging to the ego—from what is external—originating in an external world—and thus takes the first step toward the establishment of the reality principle, which is to govern further development. This distinction naturally serves the practical purpose of defending oneself against the unpleasurable sensations that are felt and those that are threatening
[Source scan 14 · printed page 11](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n14/mode/1up)

a an BT 1 er Sr a a a a ee
Survival of the primary feeling of the ego 11

oneself against. That the ego, in warding off certain unpleasure-excitations from its interior, employs no other methods than those of which it avails itself against unpleasure from without, then becomes the point of departure for significant pathological disturbances.

Thus the ego detaches itself from the external world in this manner. More correctly stated: originally the ego contains everything; later it separates an external world from itself. Our present feeling of the ego is thus only a shrunken remnant of a far more comprehensive, indeed—an all-embracing feeling, which corresponded to a more intimate connection of the ego with the environment. If we may assume that this primary feeling of the ego has been preserved in the mental life of many human beings—to a greater or lesser extent—then it would stand alongside the more narrowly and sharply delimited feeling of the ego of maturity as a kind of counterpart, and the ideational contents appropriate to it would be precisely those of boundlessness and connectedness with the All, the same ones with which my friend elucidates the “oceanic”*“ feeling.
But do we have a right to assume the survival of the original alongside the later, which has become of it?

Undoubtedly; such an occurrence is strange neither in the mental sphere nor in other fields. With regard to the animal series, we adhere to the assumption that the most highly developed species have arisen from the lowest
[Source scan 15 · printed page 12](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n15/mode/1up)
12 The preservation of the primitive in the psyche

ones. Yet we still find all simple forms of life among the living today. The genus of the great saurian reptiles has become extinct and made room for the mammals, but a genuine representative of this genus, the crocodile, still lives with us. The analogy may be too remote; it also suffers from the circumstance that the surviving lower species are for the most part not the actual ancestors of those of today, more highly developed. The intermediate links have as a rule died out and are known only through reconstruction. In the mental sphere, on the other hand, the preservation of the primitive alongside the transformed thing that has arisen from it is so frequent that it is superfluous to prove it by examples. For the most part this occurrence is the consequence of a splitting of development.
One quantitative portion of an attitude, of an instinctual impulse, has remained unchanged; another has undergone further development.

Here we touch upon the more general problem of preservation in the psychical, which has scarcely yet received treatment, but is so attractive and significant that we may devote some attention to it for a while even on an insufficient occasion. Since we have overcome the error that the forgetting familiar to us means a destruction of the memory-trace, thus an annihilation, we are inclined toward the opposite assumption that in mental life nothing that
[Source scan 16 · printed page 13](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n16/mode/1up)
The preservation of the past in a city 15

has once been formed can perish, that everything is somehow preserved and can under suitable circumstances, e.g. through a regression reaching so far back, be brought to light again. Let us try to make clear to ourselves by means of a comparison from another field what this assumption contains. Let us take, for example, the development of the Eternal City as an illustration.¹ Historians inform us that the oldest Rome was the Roma quadrata, an enclosed settlement on the Palatine. Then followed the phase of the Septimontium, a union of the settlements on the individual hills; thereafter the city bounded by the Servian Wall; and still later, after all the transformations of the republican and early imperial periods, the city enclosed by Emperor Aurelianus with his walls.

We do not wish to pursue the transformations of the city further and shall ask what a visitor, whom we imagine equipped with the most complete historical and topographical knowledge, might still find in present-day Rome of these early stages. He will see the Aurelian Wall almost unchanged, apart from a few breaches. At individual points, he may find stretches of the Servian rampart brought to light by excavation. If he knows enough—more than
1) According to The Cambridge Ancient History, vol. VII. 1928. “The founding of Rome” by Hugh Last.
[Source scan 17 · printed page 14](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n17/mode/1up)
14 The city of Rome as an example

present-day archaeology—he can perhaps draw the entire course of this wall and the outline of the Roma quadrata into the cityscape. Of the buildings which once filled these old frames he finds nothing, or scant remains, for they no longer exist. The utmost that the best knowledge of Rome in the Republic can do for him would be that he knows how to indicate the places where the temples and public buildings of that time had stood. What now occupies these places are ruins, but not of them themselves, rather of their renewals from later times after fires and destructions. It scarcely requires special mention that all these remains of old Rome appear as insertions amid the confusion of a great city from the last centuries since the Renaissance.

Some ancient things are certainly still buried in the soil of the city or beneath its modern buildings. This is the kind of preservation of the past that confronts us in historical cities such as Rome.

Now let us make the fantastic assumption that Rome is not a human habitation, but a psychical being of similarly long and rich a past. One in which, therefore, nothing that had once come about has perished, in which, alongside the last phase of development, all earlier ones still continue to exist. For Rome, this would thus mean,
[Source scan 18 · printed page 15](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n18/mode/1up)
Fantastic consequences of an assumption 15

that on the Palatine the imperial palaces and the Septi-
zonium of Septimius Severus still rose to their former height,
that the Castel Sant’Angelo still bore upon its battlements
the beautiful statues with which it was adorned until
the Gothic siege, etc. But more still: on the site of the Palazzo
Caffarelli there would stand again, without any need to demolish
this building, the temple of Capitoline Jupiter, and indeed
this not only in its last form, as the Romans of the imperial
period saw it, but also in its earliest, when it still displayed
Etruscan forms and was adorned with terracotta antefixes.
Where the Coliseum now stands, we could also admire Nero’s
vanished Domus aurea; on the Piazza della Rotonda we should find not only the present Pantheon, as
“it was left to us by Hadrian, but on

the same ground also the original structure of
M. Agrippa; indeed, the same soil would bear the church of Maria
sopra Minerva and the ancient temple over which it
is built. And perhaps it would require only a change
in the direction of the gaze or in the observer’s position
to bring forth the one or the other view.

It obviously makes no sense to spin out this fantasy further;
it leads to the unimaginable, indeed, to the ab-
surd. If we wish to represent historical succession spatially,
it can occur only through a side-by-side
[Source scan 19 · printed page 16](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n19/mode/1up)
16 Objections and

existence in space; the same space does not admit
two different fillings. Our attempt appears to be an
idle plaything; it has only one justification:
it shows us how far we are from being able to master
the peculiarities of mental life by means of an intuitive representation.

We should still take a position on one objection.
It asks us why we chose precisely the past of a city
to compare it with the mental past. The assumption
that everything past is preserved applies to mental life
only on condition that the organ of the psyche has remained
intact, that its tissue has not suffered through
“trauma” or inflammation. Yet destructive influences
which could be equated with these causes of illness are not
absent from the history of any city, even if it has had
a less eventful past than Rome, even if, like London,
it has scarcely ever been visited by an enemy. The most
peaceful development of a city includes demolitions and
replacements of buildings, and for that reason the city is
from the outset unsuitable for such a comparison with a
mental organism.

We evade this objection, and, renouncing an impressive contrast effect,
turn to an object of comparison that is at any rate more closely related, such as
[Source scan 20 · printed page 17](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n20/mode/1up)
other comparisons 17

the animal or human body is. But here too we find
the same thing. The earlier phases of development are no longer
preserved in any sense; they have been absorbed into
the later ones, to which they supplied the material.
The embryo cannot be detected in the adult; the thymus gland,
which the child possessed, is after puberty replaced by connective
tissue, but itself is no longer present; in the tubular
bones of the mature man I can indeed draw in
the outline of the child’s bone, but it itself has passed away,
as it lengthened and thickened until it attained its final form. It
remains the case that such a preservation of all preliminary stages
beside the final configuration is possible only in the mental sphere,
and that we are not in a position to make this phenomenon
intuitive. ’
Perhaps we go too far in this assumption.

Perhaps we should content ourselves with asserting that
the past can be preserved in mental life, that it need not
necessarily be destroyed. It
is after all possible that in the psychic realm too, some old things—
in the normal case or exceptionally—are so far effaced or consumed
that they can no longer be restored and reanimated by
any process, or that preservation in general is bound to certain
favourable conditions. It is possible, but
we know nothing about it. We may only hold fast to the fact

2

[Source scan 21 · printed page 18](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n21/mode/1up)
18 Doubts concerning the role of the oceanic feeling

that the preservation of the past in mental
life is more the rule than a strange exception.

If we are thus quite ready to acknowledge that
many people have an “oceanic” feeling, and are inclined
to trace it back to an early phase of the feeling of the ego,
the further question arises: what claim does this feeling have
to be regarded as the source of religious
needs?

This claim does not appear compelling to me. A
feeling can surely be a source of energy only if it is itself
the expression of a strong need. As regards religious needs, the derivation
from infantile helplessness and the longing for the father
awakened by it seems inescapable to me, especially since
this feeling does not simply continue from childhood,
but is permanently maintained by fear of the overwhelming power
of fate. I should not know how to name a need from childhood
as strong as that for paternal
protection. Thus the role of the oceanic feeling, which might seek
something like the restoration of unrestricted narcissism,
is pushed out of the foreground. One can trace the origin of the religious
attitude in clear outline as far as the feeling of infantile
helplessness.

There
may be something else behind it, but for the present this is concealed
by the mist.
I can imagine that the oceanic feeling
[Source scan 22 · printed page 19](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n22/mode/1up)
Other connections 19

has subsequently entered into relations with religion.
This being-one with the All, which belongs to it as
ideational content, does indeed strike us as a first attempt
at religious consolation, as another way of
denial of the danger which the ego recognizes as threatening from the external
world. I repeat the confession
that it is very burdensome for me to work with these scarcely
apprehensible magnitudes. Another friend of mine,
whom an unquenchable thirst for knowledge has driven to the
most unusual experiments and finally
made into an omniscient man, assured me that in
Yogic practices, by turning away from the external
world, by fixing attention upon bodily
functions, by special modes of breathing,
one can actually awaken new sensations and general feelings
within oneself, which he wishes to regard as regressions to
primordial, long-overlaid states of mental life.

He sees in them a, so to speak, physio-
logical foundation for many wisdoms of mysticism.
Relations to certain obscure modifications of
mental life, such as trance and ecstasy, would be close at hand here.
Yet I feel impelled, for once, to cry out as well in the words
of Schiller’s ‘Diver’:
“Let him rejoice who breathes in the rosy light.”

sources.title: Chapter II
sources.text:
[Source scan 23 · printed page 20](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n23/mode/1up)

I

In meiner Schrift „Die Zukunft einer Illusion“ han-
delte es sich weit weniger um die tiefsten Quellen des
religiösen Gefühls, als vielmehr um das, was der ge-
meine Mann unter seiner Religion versteht, um das
System von Lehren und Verheißungen, das ihm einer-
seits die Rätsel dieser Welt mit beneidenswerter Voll-
ständigkeit aufklärt, anderseits ihm zusichert, daß eine

sorgsame Vorsehung über sein Leben wachen und
_ etwaige Versagungen in einer jenseitigen Existenz gut-
machen wird. Diese Vorsehung kann der gemeine Mann
sich nicht anders als in der Person eines großartig er-
höhten Vaters vorstellen. Nur ein solcher kann die
Bedürfnisse des Menschenkindes kennen, durch seine
Bitten erweicht, durch die Zeichen seiner Reue be-
schwichtigt werden. Das Ganze ist so offenkundig in-
fantil, so wirklichkeitsfremd, daß es einer menschen-
freundlichen Gesinnung schmerzlich wird zu denken,
die große Mehrheit der Sterblichen werde sich niemals
über diese Auffassung des Lebens erheben können.
Noch beschämender wirkt es zu erfahren, ein wie

[Source scan 24 · printed page 21](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n24/mode/1up)

Die Religion des gemeinen Mannes 21

großer Anteil der heute Lebenden, die es einsehen
müssen, daß diese Religion nicht zu halten ist, doch
Stück für Stück von ihr in kläglichen Rückzugsgefechten
zu verteidigen sucht. Man möchte sich in die Reihen
der Gläubigen mengen, um den Philosophen, die den
Gott der Religion zu retten glauben, indem sie ıhn
durch ein unpersönliches, schattenhaft abstraktes Prinzip
ersetzen, die‘ Mahnung vorzuhalten: Du sollst den
Namen des Herrn nicht zum Eitlen anrufen! Wenn
einige der größten Geister vergangener Zeiten das
Gleiche getan haben, so darf man sich hierin nicht auf
sie berufen. Man weiß, warum sie so mußten.

Wir kehren zum gemeinen Mann und zu seiner
Religion zurück, der einzigen, die diesen Namen tragen
sollte. Da tritt uns zunächst die bekannte Äußerung
eines unserer großen Dichter und Weisen entgegen,
die sich über das Verhältnis der Religion zur Kunst
und Wissenschaft ausspricht. Sie lautet:

„Wer Wissenschaft und Kunst besitzt,
hat auch Religion ;

Wer jene beiden nicht besitzt,

der habe Religion !“ '

Dieser Spruch bringt einerseits die Religion in einen
Gegensatz zu den beiden Höchstleistungen des Menschen,
anderseits behauptet er, daß sie einander in ihrem

ı) Goethe in den „Zahmen Xenien“ IX (Gedichte aus dem
Nachlaß).

[Source scan 25 · printed page 22](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n25/mode/1up)

22 Schwierigkeiten des Lebens und Linderungen

Lebenswert vertreten oder ersetzen können. Wenn wir
auch dem gemeinen Mann die Religion bestreiten
wollen, haben wir offenbar die Autorität des Dichters
nicht auf unserer Seite. Wir versuchen einen besonderen
Weg, um uns der Würdigung seines Satzes zu nähern.
Das Leben, wie es uns auferlegt ist, ist zu schwer für
uns, es bringt uns zuviel Schmerzen, Enttäuschungen,
unlösbare Aufgaben. Um es zu ertragen, können wir
Linderungsmittel nicht entbehren. (Es geht nicht ohne
Hilfskonstruktionen, hat uns Theodor Fontane ge-
sagt.) Solcher Mittel gibt es vielleicht dreierlei : mächtige
Ablenkungen, die uns unser Elend gering schätzen
lassen, Ersatzbefriedigungen, die es verringern, Rausch-
stoffe, die uns für dasselbe unempfindlich machen. Irgend-
etwas dieser Art ist unerläßlich.‘ Auf die Ablenkungen
zielt Voltaire, wenner seinen „Gandide“ in den Rat
ausklingen läßt, seinen Garten zu bearbeiten ; solch eine
Ablenkung ist auch die wissenschaftliche Tätigkeit. Die
Ersatzbefriedigungen, wie die Kunst sie bietet, sind
gegen die Realität Illusionen, darum nicht minder psy-
chisch wirksam dank der Rolle, die die Phantasie im
Seelenleben behauptet hat. Die Rauschmittel beeinflussen
unser Körperliches, ändern seinen Chemismus. Es ist
nicht einfach, die Stellung der Religion innerhalb dieser
Reihe anzugeben. Wir werden weiter ausholen müssen.



ı) Auf erniedrigtem Niveau sagt Wilhelm Busch in der
„Frommen Helene“ dasselbe: „Wer Sorgen hat, hat auch Likör.“

[Source scan 26 · printed page 23](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n26/mode/1up)

Der Zweck des Lebens 28

Die Frage nach dem Zweck des menschlichen Lebens
ist ungezählte Male gestellt worden; sie hat noch nie
eine befriedigende Antwort gefunden, läßt eine solche
vielleicht überhaupt nicht zu. Manche Fragesteller haben
hinzugefügt: wenn sich ergeben sollte, daß das Leben
keinen Zweck hat, dann würde es jeden Wert für sie
verlieren. Aber diese Drohung ändert nichts. Es scheint
vielmehr, daß man ein Recht dazu hat, die Frage ab-
zulehnen. Ihre Voraussetzung scheint jene menschliche
Überhebung, von der wir soviel andere Äußerungen
bereits kennen. Von einem Zweck des Lebens der Tiere
wird nicht gesprochen, wenn deren Bestimmung nicht
etwa darin besteht, dem Menschen zu dienen. Allein
auch das ist nicht haltbar, denn mit vielen Tieren weiß
der Mensch nichts anzufangen — außer, daß er sie
beschreibt, klassifiziert, studiert — und ungezählte Tier-
arten haben sich auch dieser Verwendung entzogen,
indem sıe lebten und ausstarben, ehe der Mensch sie
gesehen hatte. Es ist wiederum nur die Religion, die
die Frage nach einem Zweck des Lebens zu beant-
worten weiß. Man wird kaum irren, zu entscheiden,
daß die Idee eines Lebenszweckes mit dem religiösen
System steht und fällt.

Wir wenden uns darum der anspruchsloseren Frage
zu, was die Menschen selbst durch ihr Verhalten als
Zweck und Absicht ihres Lebens erkennen lassen,
was sie vom Leben fordern, in ıhm erreichen wollen.

[Source scan 27 · printed page 24](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n27/mode/1up)

24 Das Streben nach dem Glück

Die Antwort darauf ist kaum zu verfehlen ; sie streben
nach dem Glück, sie wollen glücklich werden und so

bleiben. Dies Streben hat zwei Seiten, ein positives
' und ein negatives Ziel, es will einerseits die Abwesen-
heit von Schmerz und Unlust, anderseits das Erleben
starker Lustgefühle. Im engeren Wortsinne wird „Glück“
nur auf das letztere bezogen. Entsprechend dieser
Zweiteilung der Ziele entfaltet sich die "Tätigkeit der
Menschen nach zwei Richtungen, je nachdem sie das
eine oder das andere dieser Ziele — vorwiegend oder
selbst ausschließlich — zu verwirklichen sucht.

Es ist, wie man merkt, einfach das Programm des
Lustprinzips, das den Lebenszweck setzt. Dies Prinzip
beherrscht die Leistung des seelischen Apparates vom
Anfang an; an seiner Zweckdienlichkeit kann kein
Zweifel sein, und doch ist sein Programm im Hader
mit der ganzen Welt, mit dem Makrokosmos eben-
sowohl wie mit dem Mikrokosmos. Es ist überhaupt
nicht durchführbar, alle Einrichtungen des Alls wider-
streben ihm; man möchte sagen, die Absicht, daß der
Mensch „glücklich“ sei, ist im Plan der „Schöpfung“
nicht enthalten. Was man im strengsten Sinne Glück
heißt, entspringt der eher plötzlichen Befriedigung hoch
aufgestauter Bedürfnisse und ist seiner Natur nach nur
als episodisches Phänomen möglich. Jede Fortdauer
einer vom Lustprinzip ersehnten Situation ergibt nur
ein Gefühl von lauem Behagen; wir sind so ein-

[Source scan 28 · printed page 25](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n28/mode/1up)

Die Quellen des Leidens 25

gerichtet, daß wir nur den Kontrast intensiv genießen
können, den Zustand nur sehr wenig.‘ Somit sind un-
sere Glücksmöglichkeiten schon durch unsere Konsti-
tution beschränkt. Weit weniger Schwierigkeiten hat es,
Unglück zu erfahren. Von drei Seiten droht das
Leiden, vom eigenen Körper her, der zu Verfall und
Auflösung bestimmt sogar Schmerz und Angst als
Warnungssignale nicht entbehren kann, von der Außen-
welt, die mit übermächtigen, unerbittlichen, zerstören-
den Kräften gegen uns wüten kann, und endlich aus
den Beziehungen zu anderen Menschen. Das Leiden,
das aus dieser Quelle stammt, empfinden wir vielleicht
schmerzlicher als jedes andere; wir sind geneigt, es als
eine gewissermaßen überflüssige Zutat anzusehen, ob-
wohl es nicht weniger schicksalmäßig unabwendbar
sein dürfte als das Leiden anderer Herkunft.

Kein Wunder, wenn unter dem Druck dieser Leidens-
möglichkeiten die Menschen ihren Glücksanspruch zu
ermäßigen pflegen, wie ja auch das Lustprinzip selbst
sich unter dem Einfluß der Außenwelt zum bescheide-
neren Realitätsprinzip umbildete, wenn man sich bereits
glücklich preist, dem Unglück entgangen zu sein, das
Leiden überstanden zu haben, wenn ganz allgemein
die Aufgabe der Leidvermeidung die der Lustgewin-

ı) Goethe mahnt sogar: „Nichts ist schwerer zu ertragen
als eine Reihe von schönen Tagen“. Das mag immerhin eine
Übertreibung sein.

[Source scan 29 · printed page 26](https://archive.org/details/DasUnbehagenInDerKultur/page/n29/mode/1up)

26 Verschiedene Methoden der Lebensweisheit

nung in den Hintergrund drängt. Die Überlegung lehrt,
daß man die Lösung dieser Aufgabe auf sehr ver-
schiedenen Wegen versuchen kann; alle diese Wege
sind von den einzelnen Schulen der Lebensweisheit
empfohlen und von den Menschen begangen worden.
Uneingeschränkte Befriedigung aller Bedürfnisse drängt
sich als die verlockendste Art der Lebensführung vor,
aber das heißt den Genuß vor die Vorsicht setzen
und straft sich nach kurzem Betrieb. Die anderen
Methoden, bei denen die Vermeidung von Unlust die
vorwiegende Absicht ist, scheiden sich je nach der
Unlustquelle, der sie die größere Aufmerksamkeit zu-
wenden. Es gibt da extreme und gemäßigte Verfahren,
einseitige und solche, die zugleich an mehreren Stellen
angreifen. Gewollte Vereinsamung, Fernhaltung von
den anderen ist der nächstliegende Schutz gegen das
Leid, das einem aus menschlichen Beziehungen er-
wachsen kann. Man versteht: das Glück, das man auf
diesem Weg erreichen kann, ist das der Ruhe. Gegen
die gefürchtete Außenwelt kann man sich nicht anders
als durch irgendeine Art der Abwendung verteidigen,
wenn man diese Aufgabe für sich allein lösen will. Es
gibt freilich einen anderen und besseren Weg, indem

The question of the purpose of human life has been asked countless times; it has never yet received a satisfactory answer, perhaps indeed admits of none at all. Some questioners have added: if it should turn out that life has no purpose, then it would lose all value for them. But this threat changes nothing. Rather, it seems that one has a right to reject the question. Its premise seems to be that human presumption of which we have already become acquainted with so many other manifestations. No one speaks of a purpose in the life of animals, unless their destiny consists perhaps in serving man.

But even this is untenable, for with many animals man knows nothing to do—except to describe, classify, study them—and countless animal species have also escaped this use, in that they lived and died out before man had seen them. The service rendered by intoxicants in the struggle for
