FINIS PARTIS PRIMÆ

With these things I have sufficiently explained what I promised in the first place. But in order now to show that Nature has set before itself no end, and that all final causes are nothing but human fictions, there is no need of much. For I believe that this is already sufficiently established, both from the foundations and causes from which I showed that this prejudice derived its origin, and from Proposition 16 and the Corollaries of Proposition 32, and moreover from all those things by which I showed that all things in Nature proceed by a certain eternal necessity and with the highest perfection. Yet I shall add this further, namely, that this doctrine concerning an end utterly overturns Nature. For it regards as an effect that which is in reality a cause, and conversely. Next, it makes that which is prior by nature posterior. And finally, it renders that which is highest and most perfect most imperfect.

For (omitting the first two, because they are self-evident), as is clear from Propositions 21, 22, and 23, that effect is most perfect which is produced immediately by God; and the more intermediate causes something requires in order to be produced, the more imperfect it is. But if the things which were produced immediately by God had been made for the sake of attaining God's end, then necessarily the last things, for the sake of which the earlier things were made, would be the most excellent of all. Next, this doctrine takes away God's perfection: for, if God acts for the sake of an end, He necessarily desires something which He lacks.

And although Theologians and Metaphysicians distinguish between an end of need and an end of assimilation, they nevertheless admit that God has done all things for His own sake, and not for the sake of things to be created; for before creation they can assign nothing besides God for the sake of which God might act; and therefore they are necessarily compelled to confess that God lacked those things for which He wished to prepare means, and desired them, as is clear of itself. Nor should it here be passed over that the adherents of this doctrine, who wished to display their ingenuity in assigning the ends of things, have introduced, to prove this doctrine of theirs, a new manner of arguing: namely, reducing not to the impossible, but to ignorance; which shows that there was no other means of arguing for this doctrine. For if, for example, a stone falls from some height upon someone's head and kills him, they will demonstrate in this way that the stone fell in order to kill the man.

For unless it fell to that end, God so willing it, how could so many circumstances (for often many concur at once) have concurred by chance? Perhaps you will answer that this happened because the wind was blowing and because the man was making his way there. But they will press on: why was the wind blowing at that time? Why was the man making his way there at that same time? If you answer again that the wind then arose because the sea had begun to be agitated on the preceding day, when the weather was still calm, and that the man had been invited by a friend, they will press on again, since there is no end to asking: but why was the sea agitated? Why was the man invited for that time? And so they will not cease asking for causes of causes until you take refuge in the will of God, that is, the asylum of ignorance.

Likewise, when they see the structure of the human body, they are astonished, and from the fact that they are ignorant of the causes of so great an art, they conclude that it is fashioned not by mechanical art but by divine or supernatural art, and so constituted that one part does not injure another. And hence it comes about that one who seeks the true causes of miracles, and who endeavors to understand natural things as a learned person, rather than to admire them as a fool, is everywhere regarded and proclaimed as a heretic and impious man by those whom the common people worship as interpreters of Nature and of the Gods. For they know that, once ignorance is removed, astonishment—that is, the sole means they possess of arguing and maintaining their authority—is removed. But I leave these matters and proceed to what I resolved to treat here in the third place.

After men had persuaded themselves that all things which happen happen for their sake, they had to judge as chief in each thing that which was most useful to themselves, and to esteem most excellent all those things by which they were most beneficially affected. Hence they had to form these notions by which to explain the natures of things: namely, Good, Evil, Order, Confusion, Hot, Cold, Beauty, and Ugliness. And because they consider themselves free, there arose from this the notions Praise and Blame, Sin and Merit; but I shall treat of these below, after I have dealt with human nature, whereas I shall briefly explain the former here. Namely, they called Good everything that conduces to health and to the worship of God, and Evil that which is contrary to these.

And because those who do not understand the nature of things affirm nothing about things, but merely imagine things and take imagination for intellect, they therefore firmly believe that there is Order in things, being ignorant of things and of their own nature. For when things are so disposed that, when they are represented to us through the senses, we can easily imagine them and consequently easily remember them, we call them well ordered; but if the contrary, badly ordered, or confused.

And because those things are more pleasing to us than others which we can easily imagine, men therefore prefer order to confusion, as though order were something in Nature apart from a relation to our imagination; and they say that God created all things in order, and thus, unbeknownst to themselves, attribute imagination to God—unless perhaps they wish that God, providing for human imagination, had disposed all things in such a way that men could most easily imagine them. Nor will it perhaps give them pause that infinitely many things are found which far surpass our imagination, and very many which confuse it because of its weakness. But enough on this matter.

The remaining notions, then, are likewise nothing but modes of imagining by which the imagination is variously affected, and yet they are regarded by the ignorant as chief attributes of things, because, as we have already said, they believe that all things have been made for their sake; and they call the nature of some thing good or bad, sound or putrid and corrupt, according as they are affected by it. For example, if the motion which the nerves receive from objects represented through the eyes conduces to health, the objects which cause it are called beautiful; but those which excite the contrary motion, ugly. Those which move sensation through the nostrils they call fragrant or fetid; those through the tongue, sweet or bitter, savory or insipid, etc. Those through touch, hard or soft, rough or smooth, etc. And finally, those which move the ears are said to produce noise, sound, or harmony; the last of which has so maddened men that they have believed even God to delight in harmony.

Nor are there lacking Philosophers who have persuaded themselves that the celestial motions compose harmony. All these things sufficiently show that everyone has judged things according to the disposition of his brain, or rather has taken affections of the imagination for things. Hence it is not surprising (to note this also in passing) that among men there have arisen as many controversies as we experience, from which Skepticism has finally arisen. For although human bodies agree in many respects, they nevertheless differ in very many; and therefore what seems good to one seems evil to another; what seems ordered to one, confused to another; what is pleasing to one, displeasing to another; and so with the rest, which I pass over here, both because it is not the business of this place to treat of these matters expressly, and because everyone has sufficiently experienced this.

For everyone has on his lips: As many heads, so many opinions; Each abounds in his own judgment; the differences of brains are no less than those of palates. These sayings sufficiently show that men judge things according to the disposition of their brain, and imagine things rather than understand them. For if they understood things, then, as Mathematics bears witness, all things would, if they did not attract them, at least convince them.

We see, therefore, that all the notions by which the common people are accustomed to explain Nature are merely modes of imagining, and indicate the constitution not of any thing but only of the imagination; and because they have names as if they were beings existing outside the imagination, I call them beings not of reason but of imagination; and accordingly all arguments brought against us from similar notions can easily be repelled. For many are accustomed to argue thus: If all things have followed from the necessity of God's most perfect nature, whence then are there so many imperfections in Nature? Namely, the corruption of things even to foulness, the ugliness of things that provokes nausea, confusion, evil, sin, etc. But, as I have just said, they are easily refuted.

For the perfection of things is to be estimated from their nature and power alone; nor are things therefore more or less perfect because they delight or offend human sense, because they conduce to human nature or are repugnant to it. To those who ask why God did not create all men so that they might be governed by the guidance of reason alone, I reply nothing other than that He did not lack material for creating all things, from the highest to the lowest degree of perfection; or, to speak more properly, that the laws of Nature itself were ample enough to suffice for producing everything that can be conceived by some infinite intellect, as I demonstrated in Proposition 16. These are the prejudices that I undertook to note here. If any of this sort still remain, they can be corrected by anyone with moderate reflection.
END OF PART ONE
