sources.text:
Cum maxime unusquisque homo suum sibi utile quærit, tum maxime homines sunt sibi invicem utiles. Nam quo magis unusquisque suum utile quærit, et se conservare conatur, eo magis virtute præditus est (per Prop. 20 hujus), sive, quod idem est (per Defin. 8 hujus), eo majore potentia præditus est ad agendum ex suæ naturæ legibus, hoc est (per Prop. 3 p. III) ad vivendum ex ductu Rationis. At homines tum maxime natura conveniunt, cum ex ductu Rationis vivunt (per Prop. præced.) ; ergo (per præc. Coroll.) tum maxime homines erunt sibi invicem utiles, cum maxime unusquisque suum utile sibi quærit. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Quæ modo ostendimus, ipsa etiam experientia quotidie tot tamque luculentis testimoniis testatur, ut omnibus fere in ore sit : hominem homini Deum esse. Fit tamen raro, ut homines ex ductu Rationis vivant ; sed cum iis ita comparatum est, ut plerumque invidi, atque invicem molesti sint. At nihilominus vitam solitariam vix transigere queunt, ita ut plerisque illa definitio, quod homo sit animal sociale, valde arriserit ; et revera res ita se habet, ut ex hominum communi societate multo plura commoda oriantur, quam damna. Rideant igitur, quantum velint, res humanas Satyrici, easque detestentur Theologi, et laudent, quantum possunt, Melancholici vitam incultam et agrestem, homines contemnant, et admirentur bruta ; experientur tamen, homines mutuo auxilio ea, quibus indigent, multo facilius sibi parare, et non nisi junctis viribus pericula, quæ ubique imminent, vitare posse ; ut jam taceam, quod multo præstabilius sit, et cognitione nostra magis dignum, hominum, quam brutorum facta contemplari. Sed de his alias prolixius.

PROPOSITIO XXXVI

Summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, omnibus commune est, eoque omnes æque gaudere possunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Ex virtute agere est ex ductu Rationis agere (per Prop. 24 hujus) et quicquid ex Ratione conamur agere, est intelligere (per Prop. 26 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 28 hujus) summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, est Deum cognoscere, hoc est (per Prop. 47 p. II et ejusdem Schol.) bonum, quod omnibus hominibus commune est, et ab omnibus hominibus, quatenus ejusdem sunt naturæ, possideri æque potest. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Si quis autem roget, quid si summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, non esset omnibus commune ? an non inde, ut supra (vide Prop. 34 hujus), sequeretur, quod homines, qui ex ductu Rationis vivunt, hoc est (per Prop. 35 hujus) homines, quatenus natura conveniunt, essent invicem contrarii ? Is hoc sibi responsum habeat, non ex accidenti, sed ex ipsa natura Rationis oriri, ut hominis summum bonum omnibus sit commune, nimirum quia ex ipsa humana essentia, quatenus Ratione definitur, deducitur ; et quia homo nec esse nec concipi posset, si potestatem non haberet gaudendi hoc summo bono. Pertinet namque (per Prop. 47 p. II) ad Mentis humanæ essentiam, adæquatam habere cognitionem æternæ et infinitæ essentiæ Dei.

PROPOSITIO XXXVII

Bonum, quod unusquisque, qui sectatur virtutem, sibi appetit, reliquis hominibus etiam cupiet, et eo magis, quo majorem Dei habuerit cognitionem.

DEMONSTRATIO

Homines quatenus ex ductu Rationis vivunt, sunt homini utilissimi (per Coroll. 1 Prop. 35 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 19 hujus) ex ductu Rationis conabimur necessario efficere, ut homines ex ductu Rationis vivant. At bonum, quod unusquisque, qui ex Rationis dictamine vivit, hoc est (per Prop. 24 hujus) qui virtutem sectatur, sibi appetit, est intelligere (per Prop. 26 hujus) ; ergo bonum, quod unusquisque, qui virtutem sectatur, sibi appetit, reliquis hominibus etiam cupiet. Deinde Cupiditas, quatenus ad Mentem refertur, est ipsa Mentis essentia (per 1 Affect. Defin.) ; Mentis autem essentia in cognitione consistit (per Prop. 11 p. II), quæ Dei cognitionem involvit (per Prop. 47 p. II), et sine qua (per Prop. 15 p. I), nec esse nec concipi potest ; adeoque quo Mentis essentia majorem Dei cognitionem involvit, eo Cupiditas, qua is, qui virtutem sectatur, bonum, quod sibi appetit, alteri cupit, etiam major erit. Q. E. D.

ALITER

Bonum, quod homo sibi appetit et amat, constantius amabit, si viderit, alios idem amare (per Prop. 31 p. III) ; atque adeo (per Coroll. ejusdem Prop.) conabitur, ut reliqui idem ament ; et quia hoc bonum (per Prop. præced.) omnibus commune est, eoque omnes gaudere possunt, conabitur ergo (per eandem rationem), ut omnes eodem gaudeant, et (per Prop. 37 p. III) eo magis, quo hoc bono magis fruetur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM I

Qui ex solo affectu conatur, ut reliqui ament, quod ipse amat, et ut reliqui ex suo ingenio vivant, solo impetu agit, et ideo odiosus est, præcipue iis, quibus alia placent, quique propterea etiam student, et eodem impetu conantur, ut reliqui contra ex ipsorum ingenio vivant. Deinde quoniam summum, quod homines ex affectu appetunt, bonum sæpe tale est, ut unus tantum ejus possit esse compos, hinc fit, ut qui amant, mente sibi non constent, et dum laudes rei, quam amant, narrare gaudent, timeant credi. At qui reliquos conatur Ratione ducere, non impetu, sed humaniter et benigne agit, et sibi mente maxime constat. Porro quicquid cupimus et agimus, cujus causa sumus, quatenus Dei habemus ideam, sive quatenus Deum cognoscimus, ad Religionem refero. Cupiditatem autem bene faciendi, quæ ex eo ingeneratur, quod ex Rationis ductu vivimus, Pietatem voco. Cupiditatem deinde, qua homo, qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, tenetur, ut reliquos sibi amicitia jungat, Honestatem voco et id honestum, quod homines, qui ex ductu Rationis vivunt, laudant et id contra turpe, quod conciliandæ amicitiæ repugnat. Differentia deinde inter veram virtutem et impotentiam facile ex supra dictis percipitur ; nempe quod vera virtus nihil aliud sit, quam ex solo Rationis ductu vivere ; atque adeo impotentia in hoc solo consistit, quod homo a rebus, quæ extra ipsum sunt, duci se patiatur, et ab iis ad ea agendum determinetur, quæ rerum externarum communis constitutio, non autem ea, quæ ipsa ipsius natura, in se sola considerata, postulat. Atque hæc illa sunt, quæ in Scholio Propositionis 18 hujus Partis demonstrare promisi, ex quibus apparet, legem illam de non mactandis brutis magis vana superstitione et muliebri misericordia, quam sana Ratione fundatam esse. Docet quidem ratio nostrum utile quærendi necessitudinem cum hominibus jungere ; sed non cum brutis, aut rebus, quarum natura a natura humana est diversa ; sed idem jus, quod illa in nos habent, nos in ea habere. Imo quia uniuscujusque jus virtute seu potentia uniuscujusque definitur, longe majus homines in bruta, quam hæc in homines jus habent. Nec tamen nego bruta sentire ; sed nego, quod propterea non liceat nostræ utilitati consulere, et iisdem ad libitum uti, eademque tractare prout nobis magis convenit ; quandoquidem nobiscum natura non conveniunt, et eorum affectus ab affectibus humanis sunt natura diversi (vide Schol. Prop. 57 p. III). Superest ut explicem quid justum, quid injustum, quid peccatum, et quid denique meritum sit. Præter hæc civitatis etiam quænam sint fundamenta ostendam. Sed de his vide seq. Scholium.

SCHOLIUM II

In appendice Partis primæ explicare promisi, quid laus et vituperium, quid meritum et peccatum, quid justum et injustum sit. Laudem et vituperium quod attinet, in Scholio Propositionis 29 partis III explicui ; de reliquis autem hic jam erit dicendi locus. Sed prius pauca de statu hominis naturali et civili dicenda sunt.

Existit unusquisque summo Naturæ jure, et consequenter summo Naturæ jure unusquisque ea agit, quæ ex suæ naturæ necessitate sequuntur ; atque adeo summo Naturæ jure unusquisque judicat, quid bonum, quid malum sit, suæque utilitati ex suo ingenio consulit (vide Prop. 19 et 20 hujus), seseque vindicat (vide Coroll. 2 Prop. 40 p. III), et id, quod amat, conservare, et id, quod odio habet, destruere conatur (vide Prop. 28 p. III). Quod si homines ex ductu Rationis viverent, potiretur unusquisque (per Coroll. 1 Prop. 35 hujus) hoc suo jure absque ullo alterius damno. Sed quia affectibus sunt obnoxii (per Coroll. Prop. 4 hujus), qui potentiam seu virtutem humanam longe superant (per Prop. 6 hujus) ideo sæpe diversi trahuntur (per Prop. 33 hujus), atque sibi invicem sunt contrarii (per Prop. 34 hujus), mutuo dum auxilio indigent (per Schol. Prop. 35 hujus). Ut igitur homines concorditer vivere et sibi auxilio esse possint, necesse est, ut jure suo naturali cedant, et se invicem securos reddant, se nihil acturos, quod possit in alterius damnum cedere. Qua autem ratione hoc fieri possit, ut scilicet homines, qui affectibus necessario sunt obnoxii (per Coroll. Prop. 4 hujus), atque inconstantes et varii (per Prop. 33 hujus), possint se invicem securos reddere, et fidem invicem habere, patet ex Propositione 7 hujus partis et Propositione 39 partis III. Nempe quod nullus affectus coerceri potest, nisi affectu fortiore et contrario affectui coercendo, et quod unusquisque ab inferendo damno abstinet timore majoris damni. Hac igitur lege Societas firmari poterit, si modo ipsa sibi vindicet jus, quod unusquisque habet, sese vindicandi, et de bono et malo judicandi ; quæque adeo potestatem habeat communem vivendi rationem præscribendi, legesque ferendi, easque non Ratione, quæ affectus coercere nequit (per Schol. Prop. 17 hujus), sed minis firmandi. Hæc autem Societas, legibus et potestate sese conservandi firmata, Civitas appellatur, et qui ipsius jure defenduntur, Cives ; ex quibus facile intelligimus, nihil in statu naturali dari, quod ex omnium consensu bonum aut malum sit ; quandoquidem unusquisque, qui, in statu est naturali, suæ tantummodo utilitati consulit, et ex suo ingenio, et quatenus suæ utilitatis tantum habet rationem, quid bonum quidve malum sit, decernit, et nemini, nisi sibi soli, obtemperare lege ulla tenetur. Atque adeo in statu naturali peccatum concipi nequit ; at quidem in statu Civili, ubi et communi consensu decernitur, quid bonum quidve malum sit, et unusquisque Civitati obtemperare tenetur. Est itaque peccatum nihil aliud quam inobedientia, quæ propterea solo Civitatis jure punitur, et contra obedientia Civi meritum ducitur, quia eo ipso dignus judicatur, qui Civitatis commodis gaudeat. Deinde in statu naturali nemo ex communi consensu alicujus rei est Dominus, nec in Natura aliquid datur, quod possit dici hujus hominis esse, et non illius ; sed omnia omnium sunt ; ac proinde in statu naturali nulla potest concipi voluntas unicuique suum tribuendi, aut alicui id, quod ejus sit, eripiendi ; hoc est, in statu naturali nihil fit, quod justum aut injustum possit dici ; at quidem in statu civili, ubi ex communi consensu decernitur, quid hujus, quidve illius sit. Ex quibus apparet, justum et injustum, peccatum et meritum, notiones esse extrinsecas ; non autem attributa, quæ Mentis naturam explicent. Sed de his satis.

PROPOSITIO XXXVIII

Id, quod Corpus humanum ita disponit, ut pluribus modis possit affici, vel quod idem aptum reddit ad corpora externa pluribus modis afficiendum, homini est utile ; et eo utilius, quo Corpus ab eo aptius redditur, ut pluribus modis afficiatur, aliaque corpora afficiat ; et contra id noxium est, quod Corpus ad hæc minus aptum reddit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Quo corpus ad hæc aptius redditur, eo Mens aptior ad percipiendum redditur (per Prop. 14 p. II) ; adeoque id, quod Corpus hac ratione disponit, aptumque ad hæc reddit, est necessario bonum seu utile (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus), et eo utilius, quo Corpus ad hæc aptius potest reddere ; et contra (per eandem Prop. 14 p. II inversam, et Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) noxium, si corpus ad hæc minus aptum reddat. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XXXIX

Quæ efficiunt, ut motus et quietis ratio, quam Corporis humani partes ad invicem habent, conservetur, bona sunt ; et ea contra mala, quæ efficiunt, ut Corporis humani partes aliam ad invicem motus et quietis habeant rationem.

DEMONSTRATIO

Corpus humanum indiget, ut conservetur, plurimis aliis corporibus (per Postul. 4 p. II). At id, quod formam humani Corporis constituit, in hoc consistit, quod ejus partes motus suos certa quadam Ratione sibi invicem communicent (per Defin. ante Lem. 4, quam vide post Prop. 13 p. II). Ergo quæ efficiunt, ut motus et quietis ratio, quam Corporis humani partes ad invicem habent, conservetur, eadem humani Corporis formam conservant, et consequenter efficiunt (per Post. 3 et 6 p. II), ut Corpus humanum multis modis affici, et ut idem corpora externa multis modis afficere possit, adeoque (per Prop. præced.) bona sunt. Deinde, quæ efficiunt, ut Corporis humani partes aliam motus et quietis rationem obtineant, eadem (per eandem Defin. p. II), efficiunt, ut corpus humanum aliam formam induat, hoc est (ut per se notum, et in fine præfationis hujus partis monuimus), ut Corpus humanum destruatur, et consequenter ut omnino ineptum reddatur, ne possit pluribus modis affici, ac proinde (per Prop. præc.) mala sunt. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Quantum hæc Menti obesse vel prodesse possunt, in Quinta Parte explicabitur. Sed hic notandum, quod Corpus tum mortem obire intelligam, quando ejus partes ita disponuntur, ut aliam motus et quietis rationem ad invicem obtineant. Nam negare non audeo, Corpus humanum, retenta sanguinis circulatione, et aliis, propter quæ Corpus vivere existimatur, posse nihilominus in aliam naturam a sua prorsus diversam mutari. Nam nulla ratio me cogit, ut statuam Corpus non mori, nisi mutetur in cadaver ; quin ipsa experientia aliud suadere videtur. Fit namque aliquando, ut homo tales patiatur mutationes, ut non facile eundem illum esse dixerim ; ut de quodam Hispano Poeta narrare audivi, qui morbo correptus fuerat, et quamvis ex eo convaluerit, mansit tamen præteritæ suæ vitæ tam oblitus, ut Fabulas et Tragœdias, quas fecerat, suas non crediderit esse ; et sane pro infante adulto haberi potuisset, si vernaculæ etiam linguæ fuisset oblitus. Et si hoc incredibile videtur quid de infantibus dicemus ? Quorum naturam homo provectæ ætatis a sua tam diversam esse credit, ut persuaderi non posset, se unquam infantem fuisse, nisi ex aliis de se conjecturam faceret. Sed ne superstitiosis materiam suppeditem movendi novas quæstiones, malo hæc in medio relinquere.

PROPOSITIO XL

Quæ ad hominum communem Societatem conducunt, sive quæ efficiunt, ut homines concorditer vivant, utilia sunt, et illa contra mala, quæ discordiam in Civitatem inducunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Nam quæ efficiunt, ut homines concorditer vivant, simul efficiunt, ut ex ductu Rationis vivant (per Prop. 35 hujus), atque adeo (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) bona sunt, et (per eandem rationem) illa contra mala sunt, quæ discordias concitant. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLI

Lætitia directe mala non est, sed bona ; Tristitia autem contra directe est mala.

DEMONSTRATIO

Lætitia (per Prop. 11 p. III cum ejusdem Schol.) est affectus, quo corporis agendi potentia augetur vel juvatur ; Tristitia autem contra est affectus, quo corporis agendi potentia minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) Lætitia directe bona est, etc. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLII

Hilaritas excessum habere nequit, sed semper bona est ; et contra Melancholia semper mala.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hilaritas (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) est Lætitia, quæ quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit, quod Corporis omnes partes pariter sint affectæ ; hoc est (per Prop. 11 p. III) quod Corporis agendi potentia augetur vel juvatur, ita ut omnes ejus partes eandem ad invicem motus et quietis rationem obtineant ; atque adeo (per Prop. 39 hujus) Hilaritas semper est bona, nec excessum habere potest. At Melancholia (cujus etiam Defin. vide in eodem Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) est Tristitia, quæ quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit, quod Corporis agendi potentia absolute minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) semper est mala. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIII

Titillatio excessum habere potest, et mala esse ; Dolor autem eatenus potest esse bonus, quatenus Titillatio seu Lætitia est mala.

DEMONSTRATIO

Titillatio est Lætitia, quæ, quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit quod una vel aliquot ejus partes præ reliquis afficiuntur (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) ; cujus affectus potentia tanta esse potest, ut reliquas Corporis actiones superet (per Prop. 6 hujus), eique pertinaciter adhæreat, atque adeo impediat quo minus Corpus aptum sit, ut plurimis aliis modis afficiatur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) mala esse potest. Deinde Dolor, qui contra Tristitia est, in se solo consideratus, non potest esse bonus (per Prop. 41 hujus). Verum quia ejus vis et incrementum definitur potentia causæ externæ cum nostra comparata (per Prop. 5 hujus) possumus ergo hujus affectus infinitos virium concipere gradus et modos (per Prop. 3 hujus) ; atque adeo eundem talem concipere qui Titillationem possit coercere, ut excessum non habeat, et eatenus (per primam partem Prop. hujus) efficere, ne Corpus minus aptum reddatur ; ac proinde eatenus erit bonus. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIV

Amor et cupiditas excessum habere possunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Amor est Lætitia (per Defin. 6 Affect.) concomitante idea causæ externæ ; Titillatio igitur (per Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) concomitante idea causæ externæ Amor est ; atque adeo Amor (per Prop. præced.) excessum habere potest. Deinde Cupiditas eo est major, quo affectus, ex quo oritur major est (per Prop. 37 p. III). Quare ut affectus (per Prop. 6 hujus) reliquas hominis actiones superare potest ; sic etiam Cupiditas, quæ ex eodem affectu oritur, reliquas Cupiditates superare, ac proinde eundem excessum habere poterit, quem in præcedenti Propositione Titillationem habere ostendimus. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hilaritas, quam bonam esse dixi, concipitur facilius quam observatur. Nam affectus, quibus quotidie conflictamur, referuntur plerumque ad aliquam Corporis partem, quæ præ reliquis afficitur ; ac proinde affectus ut plurimum excessum habent, et Mentem in sola unius objecti contemplatione ita detinent, ut de aliis cogitare nequeat ; et quamvis homines pluribus affectibus obnoxii sint, atque adeo rari reperiantur, qui semper uno eodemque affectu conflictentur, non desunt tamen, quibus unus idemque affectus pertinaciter adhæreat. Videmus enim homines aliquando ab uno objecto ita affici, ut quamvis præsens non sit, ipsum tamen coram habere credant ; quod quando homini non dormienti accidit, eundem delirare dicimus vel insanire ; nec minus insanire creduntur, qui Amore ardent, quique noctes atque dies solam amasiam vel meretricem somniant, quia risum movere solent. At cum avarus de nulla alia re, quam de lucro vel de nummis cogitet, et ambitiosus de gloria, etc., hi non creduntur delirare, quia molesti solent esse, et Odio digni æstimantur. Sed revera Avaritia, Ambitio, Libido, etc. delirii species sunt, quamvis inter morbos non numerentur.

PROPOSITIO XLV

Odium nunquam potest esse bonum.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hominem, quem odimus, destruere conamur (per Prop. 39 p. III), hoc est (per Prop. 37 hujus) aliquid conamur, quod malum est ; Ergo, etc. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Nota, me hic et in seqq. per Odium illud tantum intelligere, quod est erga homines.

COROLLARIUM I

Invidia, Irrisio, Contemptus, Ira, Vindicta, et reliqui affectus, qui ad Odium referuntur vel ex eodem oriuntur, mali sunt ; quod etiam ex Prop. 39 p. III et Prop. 37 hujus patet.

COROLLARIUM II

Quicquid ex eo, quod odio affecti sumus, appetimus, turpe et in Civitate injustum est. Quod etiam patet ex Prop. 39 p. III et ex Defin. turpis et injusti, quas vide in Scholiis Prop. 37 hujus.

SCHOLIUM

Inter Irrisionem (quam in I Coroll. malam esse dixi) et risum magnam agnosco differentiam. Nam risus, ut et jocus, mera est Lætitia ; adeoque, modo excessum non habeat, per se bonus est (per Prop. 41 hujus). Nihil profecto nisi torva et tristis superstitio delectari prohibet. Nam qui magis decet famem et sitim extinguere, quam melancholiam expellere ? Mea hæc est ratio, et sic animum induxi meum. Nullum numen, nec alius, nisi invidus, mea impotentia et incommodo delectatur, nec nobis lacrimas, singultus, metum, et alia hujusmodi, quæ animi impotentis sunt signa, virtuti ducit ; sed contra, quo majore Lætitia afficimur, eo ad majorem perfectionem transimus, hoc est, eo nos magis de natura divina participare necesse est. Rebus itaque uti, et iis, quantum fieri potest, delectari (non quidem ad nauseam usque, nam hoc delectari non est), viri est sapientis. Viri, inquam, sapientis est, moderato et suavi cibo et potu se reficere et recreare, ut et odoribus, plantarum virentium amœnitate, ornatu, musica, ludis exercitatoriis, theatris, et aliis hujusmodi, quibus unusquisque absque ullo alterius damno uti potest. Corpus namque humanum ex plurimis diversæ naturæ partibus componitur, quæ continuo novo alimento indigent et vario, ut totum Corpus ad omnia, quæ ex ipsius natura sequi possunt, æque aptum sit, et consequenter ut Mens etiam æque apta sit ad plura simul intelligendum. Hoc itaque vivendi institutum et cum nostris principiis et cum communi praxi optime convenit ; quare si quæ alia, hæc vivendi ratio optima est, et omnibus modis commendanda ; nec opus est de his clarius neque prolixius agere.

PROPOSITIO XLVI

Qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, quantum potest conatur, alterius in ipsum Odium, Iram, Contemptum, etc., Amore contra, sive Generositate compensare.

DEMONSTRATIO

Omnes Odii affectus mali sunt (per Coroll. 1 præc. Prop.) ; adeoque, qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, quantum potest conabitur efficere, ne Odii affectibus conflictetur (per Prop. 19 hujus), et consequenter (per Prop. 37 hujus) conabitur, ne etiam alius eosdem patiatur affectus. At Odium Odio reciproco augetur, et Amore contra extingui potest (per Prop. 43 p. III), ita ut Odium in Amorem transeat (per Prop. 44 p. III) ; Ergo qui ex ductu Rationis vivit ; alterius Odium, etc. Amore contra compensare conabitur, hoc est Generositate (cujus Defin. vide in Schol. Prop. 59 p. III). Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Qui injurias reciproco Odio vindicare vult, misere profecto vivit. At qui contra studet Odium Amore expugnare, ille sane lætus et secure pugnat, æque facile pluribus ac uni homini resistit, et fortunæ auxilio quam minime indiget. Quos vero vincit, ii læti cedunt, non quidem ex defectu, sed ex incremento virium ; quæ omnia adeo clare ex solis Amoris et Intellectus definitionibus sequuntur, ut opus non sit eadem sigillatim demonstrare.

PROPOSITIO XLVII

Spei et Metus affectus non possunt esse per se boni.

DEMONSTRATIO

Spei et Metus affectus sine Tristitia non dantur. Nam Metus est (per 13 Affect. Defin.) Tristitia, et Spes (vide Explicationem 12 et 13 Affect. Defin.) non datur sine Metu ; ac proinde (per Prop. 41 hujus) hi affectus non possunt esse per se boni, sed tantum quatenus Lætitiæ excessum coercere possunt (per Prop. 43 hujus). Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Huc accedit, quod hi affectus cognitionis defectum et Mentis impotentiam indicant ; et hac de causa etiam Securitas, Desperatio, Gaudium et Conscientiæ morsus animi impotentis sunt signa. Nam, quamvis Securitas et Gaudium affectus sint Lætitiæ, Tristitiam tamen eosdem præcessisse supponunt, nempe Spem et Metum. Quo itaque magis ex ductu Rationis vivere conamur, eo magis Spe minus pendere, et Metu nosmet liberare, et fortunæ quantum possumus, imperare conamur, nostrasque actiones certo Rationis consilio dirigere.

PROPOSITIO XLVIII

Affectus Existimationis et Despectus semper mali sunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Hi enim affectus (per 21 et 22 Affect. Defin.) rationi repugnant ; adeoque (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) mali sunt. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO XLIX

Existimatio facile hominem, qui existimatur, superbum reddit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Si videmus aliquem de nobis plus justo præ amore sentire, facile gloriabimur (per Schol. Prop. 41 p. III), sive Lætitia afficiemur (per 30 Affect. Defin.) ; et id boni, quod de nobis prædicari audimus, facile credemus (per Prop. 25 p. III) ; atque adeo de nobis præ amore nostri plus justo sentiemus, hoc est (per Defin. 28 Affect.) facile superbiemus. Q. E. D.

PROPOSITIO L

paragraphs.text: Cum maxime unusquisque homo suum sibi utile quærit, tum maxime homines sunt sibi invicem utiles. Nam quo magis unusquisque suum utile quærit, et se conservare conatur, eo magis virtute præditus est (per Prop. 20 hujus), sive, quod idem est (per Defin. 8 hujus), eo majore potentia præditus est ad agendum ex suæ naturæ legibus, hoc est (per Prop. 3 p. III) ad vivendum ex ductu Rationis. At homines tum maxime natura conveniunt, cum ex ductu Rationis vivunt (per Prop. præced.) ; ergo (per præc. Coroll.) tum maxime homines erunt sibi invicem utiles, cum maxime unusquisque suum utile sibi quærit. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Quæ modo ostendimus, ipsa etiam experientia quotidie tot tamque luculentis testimoniis testatur, ut omnibus fere in ore sit : hominem homini Deum esse. Fit tamen raro, ut homines ex ductu Rationis vivant ; sed cum iis ita comparatum est, ut plerumque invidi, atque invicem molesti sint. At nihilominus vitam solitariam vix transigere queunt, ita ut plerisque illa definitio, quod homo sit animal sociale, valde arriserit ; et revera res ita se habet, ut ex hominum communi societate multo plura commoda oriantur, quam damna.

Rideant igitur, quantum velint, res humanas Satyrici, easque detestentur Theologi, et laudent, quantum possunt, Melancholici vitam incultam et agrestem, homines contemnant, et admirentur bruta ; experientur tamen, homines mutuo auxilio ea, quibus indigent, multo facilius sibi parare, et non nisi junctis viribus pericula, quæ ubique imminent, vitare posse ; ut jam taceam, quod multo præstabilius sit, et cognitione nostra magis dignum, hominum, quam brutorum facta contemplari. Sed de his alias prolixius.
PROPOSITIO XXXVI
Summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, omnibus commune est, eoque omnes æque gaudere possunt.
DEMONSTRATIO

Ex virtute agere est ex ductu Rationis agere (per Prop. 24 hujus) et quicquid ex Ratione conamur agere, est intelligere (per Prop. 26 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 28 hujus) summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, est Deum cognoscere, hoc est (per Prop. 47 p. II et ejusdem Schol.) bonum, quod omnibus hominibus commune est, et ab omnibus hominibus, quatenus ejusdem sunt naturæ, possideri æque potest. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Si quis autem roget, quid si summum bonum eorum, qui virtutem sectantur, non esset omnibus commune ? an non inde, ut supra (vide Prop. 34 hujus), sequeretur, quod homines, qui ex ductu Rationis vivunt, hoc est (per Prop. 35 hujus) homines, quatenus natura conveniunt, essent invicem contrarii ? Is hoc sibi responsum habeat, non ex accidenti, sed ex ipsa natura Rationis oriri, ut hominis summum bonum omnibus sit commune, nimirum quia ex ipsa humana essentia, quatenus Ratione definitur, deducitur ; et quia homo nec esse nec concipi posset, si potestatem non haberet gaudendi hoc summo bono. Pertinet namque (per Prop. 47 p. II) ad Mentis humanæ essentiam, adæquatam habere cognitionem æternæ et infinitæ essentiæ Dei.
PROPOSITIO XXXVII
Bonum, quod unusquisque, qui sectatur virtutem, sibi appetit, reliquis hominibus etiam cupiet, et eo magis, quo majorem Dei habuerit cognitionem.
DEMONSTRATIO

Homines quatenus ex ductu Rationis vivunt, sunt homini utilissimi (per Coroll. 1 Prop. 35 hujus) ; atque adeo (per Prop. 19 hujus) ex ductu Rationis conabimur necessario efficere, ut homines ex ductu Rationis vivant. At bonum, quod unusquisque, qui ex Rationis dictamine vivit, hoc est (per Prop. 24 hujus) qui virtutem sectatur, sibi appetit, est intelligere (per Prop. 26 hujus) ; ergo bonum, quod unusquisque, qui virtutem sectatur, sibi appetit, reliquis hominibus etiam cupiet. Deinde Cupiditas, quatenus ad Mentem refertur, est ipsa Mentis essentia (per 1 Affect. Defin.) ; Mentis autem essentia in cognitione consistit (per Prop. 11 p. II), quæ Dei cognitionem involvit (per Prop. 47 p. II), et sine qua (per Prop. 15 p.

I), nec esse nec concipi potest ; adeoque quo Mentis essentia majorem Dei cognitionem involvit, eo Cupiditas, qua is, qui virtutem sectatur, bonum, quod sibi appetit, alteri cupit, etiam major erit. Q. E. D.
ALITER

Bonum, quod homo sibi appetit et amat, constantius amabit, si viderit, alios idem amare (per Prop. 31 p. III) ; atque adeo (per Coroll. ejusdem Prop.) conabitur, ut reliqui idem ament ; et quia hoc bonum (per Prop. præced.) omnibus commune est, eoque omnes gaudere possunt, conabitur ergo (per eandem rationem), ut omnes eodem gaudeant, et (per Prop. 37 p. III) eo magis, quo hoc bono magis fruetur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM I

Qui ex solo affectu conatur, ut reliqui ament, quod ipse amat, et ut reliqui ex suo ingenio vivant, solo impetu agit, et ideo odiosus est, præcipue iis, quibus alia placent, quique propterea etiam student, et eodem impetu conantur, ut reliqui contra ex ipsorum ingenio vivant. Deinde quoniam summum, quod homines ex affectu appetunt, bonum sæpe tale est, ut unus tantum ejus possit esse compos, hinc fit, ut qui amant, mente sibi non constent, et dum laudes rei, quam amant, narrare gaudent, timeant credi. At qui reliquos conatur Ratione ducere, non impetu, sed humaniter et benigne agit, et sibi mente maxime constat. Porro quicquid cupimus et agimus, cujus causa sumus, quatenus Dei habemus ideam, sive quatenus Deum cognoscimus, ad Religionem refero. Cupiditatem autem bene faciendi, quæ ex eo ingeneratur, quod ex Rationis ductu vivimus, Pietatem voco.

Cupiditatem deinde, qua homo, qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, tenetur, ut reliquos sibi amicitia jungat, Honestatem voco et id honestum, quod homines, qui ex ductu Rationis vivunt, laudant et id contra turpe, quod conciliandæ amicitiæ repugnat. Differentia deinde inter veram virtutem et impotentiam facile ex supra dictis percipitur ; nempe quod vera virtus nihil aliud sit, quam ex solo Rationis ductu vivere ; atque adeo impotentia in hoc solo consistit, quod homo a rebus, quæ extra ipsum sunt, duci se patiatur, et ab iis ad ea agendum determinetur, quæ rerum externarum communis constitutio, non autem ea, quæ ipsa ipsius natura, in se sola considerata, postulat. Atque hæc illa sunt, quæ in Scholio Propositionis 18 hujus Partis demonstrare promisi, ex quibus apparet, legem illam de non mactandis brutis magis vana superstitione et muliebri misericordia, quam sana Ratione fundatam esse.

Docet quidem ratio nostrum utile quærendi necessitudinem cum hominibus jungere ; sed non cum brutis, aut rebus, quarum natura a natura humana est diversa ; sed idem jus, quod illa in nos habent, nos in ea habere. Imo quia uniuscujusque jus virtute seu potentia uniuscujusque definitur, longe majus homines in bruta, quam hæc in homines jus habent. Nec tamen nego bruta sentire ; sed nego, quod propterea non liceat nostræ utilitati consulere, et iisdem ad libitum uti, eademque tractare prout nobis magis convenit ; quandoquidem nobiscum natura non conveniunt, et eorum affectus ab affectibus humanis sunt natura diversi (vide Schol. Prop. 57 p. III). Superest ut explicem quid justum, quid injustum, quid peccatum, et quid denique meritum sit. Præter hæc civitatis etiam quænam sint fundamenta ostendam. Sed de his vide seq. Scholium.
SCHOLIUM II

In appendice Partis primæ explicare promisi, quid laus et vituperium, quid meritum et peccatum, quid justum et injustum sit. Laudem et vituperium quod attinet, in Scholio Propositionis 29 partis III explicui ; de reliquis autem hic jam erit dicendi locus. Sed prius pauca de statu hominis naturali et civili dicenda sunt.

Existit unusquisque summo Naturæ jure, et consequenter summo Naturæ jure unusquisque ea agit, quæ ex suæ naturæ necessitate sequuntur ; atque adeo summo Naturæ jure unusquisque judicat, quid bonum, quid malum sit, suæque utilitati ex suo ingenio consulit (vide Prop. 19 et 20 hujus), seseque vindicat (vide Coroll. 2 Prop. 40 p. III), et id, quod amat, conservare, et id, quod odio habet, destruere conatur (vide Prop. 28 p. III). Quod si homines ex ductu Rationis viverent, potiretur unusquisque (per Coroll. 1 Prop. 35 hujus) hoc suo jure absque ullo alterius damno. Sed quia affectibus sunt obnoxii (per Coroll. Prop. 4 hujus), qui potentiam seu virtutem humanam longe superant (per Prop. 6 hujus) ideo sæpe diversi trahuntur (per Prop. 33 hujus), atque sibi invicem sunt contrarii (per Prop. 34 hujus), mutuo dum auxilio indigent (per Schol. Prop. 35 hujus).

Ut igitur homines concorditer vivere et sibi auxilio esse possint, necesse est, ut jure suo naturali cedant, et se invicem securos reddant, se nihil acturos, quod possit in alterius damnum cedere. Qua autem ratione hoc fieri possit, ut scilicet homines, qui affectibus necessario sunt obnoxii (per Coroll. Prop. 4 hujus), atque inconstantes et varii (per Prop. 33 hujus), possint se invicem securos reddere, et fidem invicem habere, patet ex Propositione 7 hujus partis et Propositione 39 partis III. Nempe quod nullus affectus coerceri potest, nisi affectu fortiore et contrario affectui coercendo, et quod unusquisque ab inferendo damno abstinet timore majoris damni.

Hac igitur lege Societas firmari poterit, si modo ipsa sibi vindicet jus, quod unusquisque habet, sese vindicandi, et de bono et malo judicandi ; quæque adeo potestatem habeat communem vivendi rationem præscribendi, legesque ferendi, easque non Ratione, quæ affectus coercere nequit (per Schol. Prop. 17 hujus), sed minis firmandi. Hæc autem Societas, legibus et potestate sese conservandi firmata, Civitas appellatur, et qui ipsius jure defenduntur, Cives ; ex quibus facile intelligimus, nihil in statu naturali dari, quod ex omnium consensu bonum aut malum sit ; quandoquidem unusquisque, qui, in statu est naturali, suæ tantummodo utilitati consulit, et ex suo ingenio, et quatenus suæ utilitatis tantum habet rationem, quid bonum quidve malum sit, decernit, et nemini, nisi sibi soli, obtemperare lege ulla tenetur.

Atque adeo in statu naturali peccatum concipi nequit ; at quidem in statu Civili, ubi et communi consensu decernitur, quid bonum quidve malum sit, et unusquisque Civitati obtemperare tenetur. Est itaque peccatum nihil aliud quam inobedientia, quæ propterea solo Civitatis jure punitur, et contra obedientia Civi meritum ducitur, quia eo ipso dignus judicatur, qui Civitatis commodis gaudeat. Deinde in statu naturali nemo ex communi consensu alicujus rei est Dominus, nec in Natura aliquid datur, quod possit dici hujus hominis esse, et non illius ; sed omnia omnium sunt ; ac proinde in statu naturali nulla potest concipi voluntas unicuique suum tribuendi, aut alicui id, quod ejus sit, eripiendi ; hoc est, in statu naturali nihil fit, quod justum aut injustum possit dici ; at quidem in statu civili, ubi ex communi consensu decernitur, quid hujus, quidve illius sit.
Ex quibus apparet, justum et injustum, peccatum et meritum, notiones esse extrinsecas ; non autem attributa, quæ Mentis naturam explicent. Sed de his satis.
PROPOSITIO XXXVIII

Id, quod Corpus humanum ita disponit, ut pluribus modis possit affici, vel quod idem aptum reddit ad corpora externa pluribus modis afficiendum, homini est utile ; et eo utilius, quo Corpus ab eo aptius redditur, ut pluribus modis afficiatur, aliaque corpora afficiat ; et contra id noxium est, quod Corpus ad hæc minus aptum reddit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Quo corpus ad hæc aptius redditur, eo Mens aptior ad percipiendum redditur (per Prop. 14 p. II) ; adeoque id, quod Corpus hac ratione disponit, aptumque ad hæc reddit, est necessario bonum seu utile (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus), et eo utilius, quo Corpus ad hæc aptius potest reddere ; et contra (per eandem Prop. 14 p. II inversam, et Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) noxium, si corpus ad hæc minus aptum reddat. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XXXIX

Quæ efficiunt, ut motus et quietis ratio, quam Corporis humani partes ad invicem habent, conservetur, bona sunt ; et ea contra mala, quæ efficiunt, ut Corporis humani partes aliam ad invicem motus et quietis habeant rationem.
DEMONSTRATIO

Corpus humanum indiget, ut conservetur, plurimis aliis corporibus (per Postul. 4 p. II). At id, quod formam humani Corporis constituit, in hoc consistit, quod ejus partes motus suos certa quadam Ratione sibi invicem communicent (per Defin. ante Lem. 4, quam vide post Prop. 13 p. II). Ergo quæ efficiunt, ut motus et quietis ratio, quam Corporis humani partes ad invicem habent, conservetur, eadem humani Corporis formam conservant, et consequenter efficiunt (per Post. 3 et 6 p. II), ut Corpus humanum multis modis affici, et ut idem corpora externa multis modis afficere possit, adeoque (per Prop. præced.) bona sunt. Deinde, quæ efficiunt, ut Corporis humani partes aliam motus et quietis rationem obtineant, eadem (per eandem Defin. p.

II), efficiunt, ut corpus humanum aliam formam induat, hoc est (ut per se notum, et in fine præfationis hujus partis monuimus), ut Corpus humanum destruatur, et consequenter ut omnino ineptum reddatur, ne possit pluribus modis affici, ac proinde (per Prop. præc.) mala sunt. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Quantum hæc Menti obesse vel prodesse possunt, in Quinta Parte explicabitur. Sed hic notandum, quod Corpus tum mortem obire intelligam, quando ejus partes ita disponuntur, ut aliam motus et quietis rationem ad invicem obtineant. Nam negare non audeo, Corpus humanum, retenta sanguinis circulatione, et aliis, propter quæ Corpus vivere existimatur, posse nihilominus in aliam naturam a sua prorsus diversam mutari. Nam nulla ratio me cogit, ut statuam Corpus non mori, nisi mutetur in cadaver ; quin ipsa experientia aliud suadere videtur.

Fit namque aliquando, ut homo tales patiatur mutationes, ut non facile eundem illum esse dixerim ; ut de quodam Hispano Poeta narrare audivi, qui morbo correptus fuerat, et quamvis ex eo convaluerit, mansit tamen præteritæ suæ vitæ tam oblitus, ut Fabulas et Tragœdias, quas fecerat, suas non crediderit esse ; et sane pro infante adulto haberi potuisset, si vernaculæ etiam linguæ fuisset oblitus. Et si hoc incredibile videtur quid de infantibus dicemus ? Quorum naturam homo provectæ ætatis a sua tam diversam esse credit, ut persuaderi non posset, se unquam infantem fuisse, nisi ex aliis de se conjecturam faceret. Sed ne superstitiosis materiam suppeditem movendi novas quæstiones, malo hæc in medio relinquere.
PROPOSITIO XL
Quæ ad hominum communem Societatem conducunt, sive quæ efficiunt, ut homines concorditer vivant, utilia sunt, et illa contra mala, quæ discordiam in Civitatem inducunt.
DEMONSTRATIO

Nam quæ efficiunt, ut homines concorditer vivant, simul efficiunt, ut ex ductu Rationis vivant (per Prop. 35 hujus), atque adeo (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) bona sunt, et (per eandem rationem) illa contra mala sunt, quæ discordias concitant. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLI
Lætitia directe mala non est, sed bona ; Tristitia autem contra directe est mala.
DEMONSTRATIO

Lætitia (per Prop. 11 p. III cum ejusdem Schol.) est affectus, quo corporis agendi potentia augetur vel juvatur ; Tristitia autem contra est affectus, quo corporis agendi potentia minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) Lætitia directe bona est, etc. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLII
Hilaritas excessum habere nequit, sed semper bona est ; et contra Melancholia semper mala.
DEMONSTRATIO

Hilaritas (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) est Lætitia, quæ quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit, quod Corporis omnes partes pariter sint affectæ ; hoc est (per Prop. 11 p. III) quod Corporis agendi potentia augetur vel juvatur, ita ut omnes ejus partes eandem ad invicem motus et quietis rationem obtineant ; atque adeo (per Prop. 39 hujus) Hilaritas semper est bona, nec excessum habere potest. At Melancholia (cujus etiam Defin. vide in eodem Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) est Tristitia, quæ quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit, quod Corporis agendi potentia absolute minuitur vel coercetur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) semper est mala. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIII
Titillatio excessum habere potest, et mala esse ; Dolor autem eatenus potest esse bonus, quatenus Titillatio seu Lætitia est mala.
DEMONSTRATIO

Titillatio est Lætitia, quæ, quatenus ad Corpus refertur, in hoc consistit quod una vel aliquot ejus partes præ reliquis afficiuntur (vide ejus Defin. in Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) ; cujus affectus potentia tanta esse potest, ut reliquas Corporis actiones superet (per Prop. 6 hujus), eique pertinaciter adhæreat, atque adeo impediat quo minus Corpus aptum sit, ut plurimis aliis modis afficiatur ; adeoque (per Prop. 38 hujus) mala esse potest. Deinde Dolor, qui contra Tristitia est, in se solo consideratus, non potest esse bonus (per Prop. 41 hujus). Verum quia ejus vis et incrementum definitur potentia causæ externæ cum nostra comparata (per Prop. 5 hujus) possumus ergo hujus affectus infinitos virium concipere gradus et modos (per Prop. 3 hujus) ; atque adeo eundem talem concipere qui Titillationem possit coercere, ut excessum non habeat, et eatenus (per primam partem Prop.
hujus) efficere, ne Corpus minus aptum reddatur ; ac proinde eatenus erit bonus. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIV
Amor et cupiditas excessum habere possunt.
DEMONSTRATIO

Amor est Lætitia (per Defin. 6 Affect.) concomitante idea causæ externæ ; Titillatio igitur (per Schol. Prop. 11 p. III) concomitante idea causæ externæ Amor est ; atque adeo Amor (per Prop. præced.) excessum habere potest. Deinde Cupiditas eo est major, quo affectus, ex quo oritur major est (per Prop. 37 p. III). Quare ut affectus (per Prop. 6 hujus) reliquas hominis actiones superare potest ; sic etiam Cupiditas, quæ ex eodem affectu oritur, reliquas Cupiditates superare, ac proinde eundem excessum habere poterit, quem in præcedenti Propositione Titillationem habere ostendimus. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hilaritas, quam bonam esse dixi, concipitur facilius quam observatur. Nam affectus, quibus quotidie conflictamur, referuntur plerumque ad aliquam Corporis partem, quæ præ reliquis afficitur ; ac proinde affectus ut plurimum excessum habent, et Mentem in sola unius objecti contemplatione ita detinent, ut de aliis cogitare nequeat ; et quamvis homines pluribus affectibus obnoxii sint, atque adeo rari reperiantur, qui semper uno eodemque affectu conflictentur, non desunt tamen, quibus unus idemque affectus pertinaciter adhæreat. Videmus enim homines aliquando ab uno objecto ita affici, ut quamvis præsens non sit, ipsum tamen coram habere credant ; quod quando homini non dormienti accidit, eundem delirare dicimus vel insanire ; nec minus insanire creduntur, qui Amore ardent, quique noctes atque dies solam amasiam vel meretricem somniant, quia risum movere solent.

At cum avarus de nulla alia re, quam de lucro vel de nummis cogitet, et ambitiosus de gloria, etc., hi non creduntur delirare, quia molesti solent esse, et Odio digni æstimantur. Sed revera Avaritia, Ambitio, Libido, etc. delirii species sunt, quamvis inter morbos non numerentur.
PROPOSITIO XLV
Odium nunquam potest esse bonum.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hominem, quem odimus, destruere conamur (per Prop. 39 p. III), hoc est (per Prop. 37 hujus) aliquid conamur, quod malum est ; Ergo, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
Nota, me hic et in seqq. per Odium illud tantum intelligere, quod est erga homines.
COROLLARIUM I
Invidia, Irrisio, Contemptus, Ira, Vindicta, et reliqui affectus, qui ad Odium referuntur vel ex eodem oriuntur, mali sunt ; quod etiam ex Prop. 39 p. III et Prop. 37 hujus patet.
COROLLARIUM II
Quicquid ex eo, quod odio affecti sumus, appetimus, turpe et in Civitate injustum est. Quod etiam patet ex Prop. 39 p. III et ex Defin. turpis et injusti, quas vide in Scholiis Prop. 37 hujus.
SCHOLIUM

Inter Irrisionem (quam in I Coroll. malam esse dixi) et risum magnam agnosco differentiam. Nam risus, ut et jocus, mera est Lætitia ; adeoque, modo excessum non habeat, per se bonus est (per Prop. 41 hujus). Nihil profecto nisi torva et tristis superstitio delectari prohibet. Nam qui magis decet famem et sitim extinguere, quam melancholiam expellere ? Mea hæc est ratio, et sic animum induxi meum. Nullum numen, nec alius, nisi invidus, mea impotentia et incommodo delectatur, nec nobis lacrimas, singultus, metum, et alia hujusmodi, quæ animi impotentis sunt signa, virtuti ducit ; sed contra, quo majore Lætitia afficimur, eo ad majorem perfectionem transimus, hoc est, eo nos magis de natura divina participare necesse est. Rebus itaque uti, et iis, quantum fieri potest, delectari (non quidem ad nauseam usque, nam hoc delectari non est), viri est sapientis.

Viri, inquam, sapientis est, moderato et suavi cibo et potu se reficere et recreare, ut et odoribus, plantarum virentium amœnitate, ornatu, musica, ludis exercitatoriis, theatris, et aliis hujusmodi, quibus unusquisque absque ullo alterius damno uti potest. Corpus namque humanum ex plurimis diversæ naturæ partibus componitur, quæ continuo novo alimento indigent et vario, ut totum Corpus ad omnia, quæ ex ipsius natura sequi possunt, æque aptum sit, et consequenter ut Mens etiam æque apta sit ad plura simul intelligendum. Hoc itaque vivendi institutum et cum nostris principiis et cum communi praxi optime convenit ; quare si quæ alia, hæc vivendi ratio optima est, et omnibus modis commendanda ; nec opus est de his clarius neque prolixius agere.
PROPOSITIO XLVI
Qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, quantum potest conatur, alterius in ipsum Odium, Iram, Contemptum, etc., Amore contra, sive Generositate compensare.
DEMONSTRATIO

Omnes Odii affectus mali sunt (per Coroll. 1 præc. Prop.) ; adeoque, qui ex ductu Rationis vivit, quantum potest conabitur efficere, ne Odii affectibus conflictetur (per Prop. 19 hujus), et consequenter (per Prop. 37 hujus) conabitur, ne etiam alius eosdem patiatur affectus. At Odium Odio reciproco augetur, et Amore contra extingui potest (per Prop. 43 p. III), ita ut Odium in Amorem transeat (per Prop. 44 p. III) ; Ergo qui ex ductu Rationis vivit ; alterius Odium, etc. Amore contra compensare conabitur, hoc est Generositate (cujus Defin. vide in Schol. Prop. 59 p. III). Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Qui injurias reciproco Odio vindicare vult, misere profecto vivit. At qui contra studet Odium Amore expugnare, ille sane lætus et secure pugnat, æque facile pluribus ac uni homini resistit, et fortunæ auxilio quam minime indiget. Quos vero vincit, ii læti cedunt, non quidem ex defectu, sed ex incremento virium ; quæ omnia adeo clare ex solis Amoris et Intellectus definitionibus sequuntur, ut opus non sit eadem sigillatim demonstrare.
PROPOSITIO XLVII
Spei et Metus affectus non possunt esse per se boni.
DEMONSTRATIO

Spei et Metus affectus sine Tristitia non dantur. Nam Metus est (per 13 Affect. Defin.) Tristitia, et Spes (vide Explicationem 12 et 13 Affect. Defin.) non datur sine Metu ; ac proinde (per Prop. 41 hujus) hi affectus non possunt esse per se boni, sed tantum quatenus Lætitiæ excessum coercere possunt (per Prop. 43 hujus). Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Huc accedit, quod hi affectus cognitionis defectum et Mentis impotentiam indicant ; et hac de causa etiam Securitas, Desperatio, Gaudium et Conscientiæ morsus animi impotentis sunt signa. Nam, quamvis Securitas et Gaudium affectus sint Lætitiæ, Tristitiam tamen eosdem præcessisse supponunt, nempe Spem et Metum. Quo itaque magis ex ductu Rationis vivere conamur, eo magis Spe minus pendere, et Metu nosmet liberare, et fortunæ quantum possumus, imperare conamur, nostrasque actiones certo Rationis consilio dirigere.
PROPOSITIO XLVIII
Affectus Existimationis et Despectus semper mali sunt.
DEMONSTRATIO
Hi enim affectus (per 21 et 22 Affect. Defin.) rationi repugnant ; adeoque (per Prop. 26 et 27 hujus) mali sunt. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO XLIX
Existimatio facile hominem, qui existimatur, superbum reddit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Si videmus aliquem de nobis plus justo præ amore sentire, facile gloriabimur (per Schol. Prop. 41 p. III), sive Lætitia afficiemur (per 30 Affect. Defin.) ; et id boni, quod de nobis prædicari audimus, facile credemus (per Prop. 25 p. III) ; atque adeo de nobis præ amore nostri plus justo sentiemus, hoc est (per Defin. 28 Affect.) facile superbiemus. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITIO L

translations.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 3

paragraphs.text: To the greatest extent that each man seeks what is useful to himself, to that same extent men are most useful to one another. For the more each one seeks what is useful to himself, and strives to preserve himself, the more he is endowed with virtue (by Prop. 20 of this Part), or—which is the same thing (by Def. 8 of this Part)—the greater is the power with which he is endowed for acting according to the laws of his own nature, that is (by Prop. 3, Part III), for living according to the guidance of Reason. But men agree in nature most of all when they live according to the guidance of Reason (by the preceding Prop.); therefore (by the preceding Coroll.) men will be most useful to one another when each one most of all seeks what is useful to himself. Q.E.D.
SCHOLIUM

What we have just shown is also attested by daily experience itself through so many and such striking testimonies that it is almost on everyone's lips: man is a god to man. Yet it rarely happens that men live according to the guidance of Reason; rather, they are so constituted that for the most part they are envious and mutually troublesome. Nevertheless, they can scarcely pass their lives in solitude, so that the definition that man is a social animal has greatly pleased most people; and indeed the matter stands so that many more advantages arise from men's common society than disadvantages.

Therefore let Satirists laugh at human affairs as much as they please, and let Theologians detest them, and let Melancholics praise, as much as they can, the uncultivated and rustic life; let them despise men and admire brutes: they will nevertheless find by experience that men can much more easily procure for themselves by mutual assistance the things they need, and that only by joining forces can they avoid the dangers that everywhere threaten them; not to mention that it is far more excellent, and more worthy of our knowledge, to contemplate the deeds of men than those of brutes. But on these matters elsewhere, more at length.
PROPOSITION XXXVI
The highest good of those who pursue virtue is common to all, and all can equally enjoy it.
DEMONSTRATION

To act from virtue is to act according to the guidance of Reason (by Prop. 24 of this Part), and whatever we strive to do from Reason is to understand (by Prop. 26 of this Part); and therefore (by Prop. 28 of this Part) the highest good of those who pursue virtue is to know God, that is (by Prop. 47, Part II, and its Schol.) a good that is common to all men and can be possessed equally by all men, insofar as they are of the same nature. Q.E.D.
SCHOLIUM

But if anyone should ask: what if the highest good of those who pursue virtue were not common to all? would it not then follow, as above (see Prop. 34 of this Part), that men who live according to the guidance of Reason, that is (by Prop. 35 of this Part), men insofar as they agree in nature, would be contrary to one another? Let him have this answer: that it arises not accidentally, but from the very nature of Reason, that man's highest good is common to all, namely because it is deduced from human essence itself, insofar as it is defined by Reason; and because man could neither be nor be conceived if he did not have the power of enjoying this highest good. For it pertains (by Prop. 47, Part II) to the essence of the human Mind to have an adequate knowledge of the eternal and infinite essence of God.
PROPOSITION XXXVII
The good which everyone who pursues virtue seeks for himself, he will also desire for other men, and the more so as he has a greater knowledge of God.
DEMONSTRATION

Men, insofar as they live according to the guidance of Reason, are most useful to man (by Coroll. 1, Prop. 35 of this Part); and therefore (by Prop. 19 of this Part) from the guidance of Reason we shall necessarily strive to bring it about that men live according to the guidance of Reason. But the good which everyone who lives according to the dictate of Reason, that is (by Prop. 24 of this Part), who pursues virtue, seeks for himself, is to understand (by Prop. 26 of this Part); therefore the good which everyone who pursues virtue seeks for himself, he will also desire for other men. Next, Desire, insofar as it is referred to the Mind, is the very essence of the Mind (by Def. 1 of the Affects); but the essence of the Mind consists in knowledge (by Prop. 11, Part II), which involves the knowledge of God (by Prop. 47, Part II), and without which (by Prop. 15, Part

I), it can neither be nor be conceived; and therefore, the more the essence of the Mind involves a greater knowledge of God, the greater also will be the Desire by which he who pursues virtue desires for another the good which he seeks for himself. Q.E.D.
OTHERWISE

The good which a man seeks and loves for himself, he will love more constantly if he sees that others love the same thing (by Prop. 31, Part III); and therefore (by the Coroll. of the same Prop.) he will strive that others love the same thing; and because this good (by the preceding Prop.) is common to all, and all can enjoy it, therefore (by the same reasoning) he will strive that all enjoy it, and (by Prop. 37, Part III) the more so as he enjoys this good more. Q.E.D.
SCHOLIUM I

He who from affect alone strives that others love what he himself loves, and that others live according to his own disposition, acts by impulse alone, and is therefore hateful, especially to those who are pleased by other things, and who for that reason also endeavor, and strive with the same impulse, that others, on the contrary, live according to their disposition. Further, since the highest good which men seek from affect is often such that only one can possess it, it follows that those who love are not constant in mind, and while they delight in recounting the praises of the thing they love, they fear being believed. But he who strives to lead others by Reason acts not by impulse, but humanely and kindly, and is most constant in mind. Moreover, whatever we desire and do, of which we are the cause insofar as we have the idea of God, or insofar as we know God, I refer to Religion. But the Desire of doing good which is engendered from our living according to the guidance of Reason, I call Piety.

Further, the Desire by which a man who lives according to the guidance of Reason is bound to join others to himself in friendship, I call Honesty; and I call honorable that which men who live according to the guidance of Reason praise, and, on the contrary, base that which is opposed to forming friendship. Further, the difference between true virtue and powerlessness is easily perceived from what has been said above; namely, that true virtue is nothing other than to live according to the guidance of Reason alone; and therefore powerlessness consists in this alone: that a man allows himself to be led by things that are outside him, and to be determined by them to do those things which the common constitution of external things, but not that which his own nature, considered in itself alone, demands. And these are the things which I promised to demonstrate in the Scholium of Proposition 18 of this Part, from which it is apparent that the law concerning not slaughtering brutes is founded more on empty superstition and womanish compassion than on sound Reason.

Reason indeed teaches that the necessity of seeking our own advantage joins us with men, but not with brutes or with things whose nature is different from human nature; rather, we have the same right over them that they have over us. Indeed, since the right of each is defined by the virtue, or power, of each, men have far greater right over brutes than these have over men. Yet I do not deny that brutes feel; but I deny that for that reason it is not permitted us to consult our own advantage, to use them at our pleasure, and to treat them as is most suitable for us; since they do not agree with us in nature, and their affects differ in nature from human affects (see Schol. Prop. 57, Part III). It remains for me to explain what is just, what unjust, what sin, and finally what merit is. Besides these, I shall also show what the foundations of the state are. But on these matters see the following Scholium.
SCHOLIUM II

In the Appendix to Part I I promised to explain what praise and blame are, what merit and sin, what just and unjust, are. As regards praise and blame, I explained them in the Scholium of Proposition 29, Part III; but there will now be occasion to speak here concerning the rest. But first, a few things must be said concerning man's natural and civil state.

Each thing exists by the supreme right of Nature, and consequently by the supreme right of Nature each does those things which follow from the necessity of its nature; and therefore by the supreme right of Nature each judges what is good and what is bad, and, according to its own disposition, provides for its own advantage (see Props. 19 and 20 of this Part), vindicates itself (see Coroll. 2, Prop. 40, Part III), and strives to preserve what it loves and to destroy what it hates (see Prop. 28, Part III). If men lived according to the guidance of Reason, each would possess (by Coroll. 1, Prop. 35 of this Part) this right of his without any harm to another. But because they are subject to affects (by the Coroll. of Prop. 4 of this Part), which far surpass human power, or virtue (by Prop. 6 of this Part), they are therefore often drawn in different directions (by Prop. 33 of this Part), and are contrary to one another (by Prop. 34 of this Part), while they need one another's mutual assistance (by the Schol. of Prop. 35 of this Part).

Therefore, in order that human beings may be able to live harmoniously and be of assistance to one another, it is necessary that they yield their natural right and render one another secure that they will do nothing which may turn to another's harm. Now by what means this can be brought about—namely, that human beings, who are necessarily subject to affects (by the Corollary of Proposition 4 of this Part), and inconstant and variable (by Proposition 33 of this Part), may render one another secure and have mutual trust—is evident from Proposition 7 of this Part and Proposition 39 of Part III. Namely, that no affect can be restrained except by an affect stronger than and contrary to the affect to be restrained, and that everyone abstains from inflicting harm through fear of a greater harm.

Therefore, by this law a Society can be established, provided that it claims for itself the right which each person has of avenging himself and of judging concerning good and evil; and consequently, provided that it has the power to prescribe a common rule of life and to enact laws, and to uphold them not by Reason, which cannot restrain the affects (by the Scholium of Proposition 17 of this Part), but by threats. Such a Society, established by laws and by the power of preserving itself, is called a State, and those who are defended by its right, Citizens; from which we readily understand that in the state of nature nothing is given which, by the consent of all, is good or evil; since each person who is in the state of nature consults only his own advantage, and, according to his own disposition and insofar as he takes account only of his own advantage, determines what is good and what evil, and is bound by no law to obey anyone except himself alone.

And thus in the state of nature sin cannot be conceived; but it can indeed be conceived in the civil state, where by common consent it is determined what is good and what evil, and everyone is bound to obey the State. Sin, therefore, is nothing but disobedience, which is consequently punished by the right of the State alone; and, conversely, obedience is counted as merit in a Citizen, because by that very fact he is judged worthy to enjoy the advantages of the State. Further, in the state of nature no one is, by common consent, the owner of anything, nor is anything given in Nature that can be said to belong to this person and not to that; but all things belong to all. Consequently, in the state of nature no will can be conceived of rendering to each his own, or of taking from anyone what is his; that is, in the state of nature nothing takes place that can be called just or unjust; but it can indeed be so called in the civil state, where by common consent it is determined what belongs to this person and what to that.
From these things it is apparent that just and unjust, sin and merit, are extrinsic notions, and not attributes which explain the nature of the Mind. But enough on these matters.
PROPOSITION XXXVIII

That which so disposes the human Body that it can be affected in many ways, or which renders the same fit to affect external bodies in many ways, is useful to a human being; and it is the more useful insofar as the Body is rendered by it more fit to be affected in many ways and to affect other bodies; and, conversely, that is harmful which renders the Body less fit for these things.
DEMONSTRATION

Insofar as the body is rendered more fit for these things, the Mind is rendered more fit for perceiving (by Proposition 14, Part II); and therefore that which disposes the Body in this manner and renders it fit for these things is necessarily good or useful (by Propositions 26 and 27 of this Part), and is the more useful insofar as it can render the Body more fit for these things; and, conversely (by the same Proposition 14 of Part II taken inversely, and by Propositions 26 and 27 of this Part), it is harmful if it renders the body less fit for these things. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XXXIX

Those things which bring about the preservation of the ratio of motion and rest which the parts of the human Body have to one another are good; and, conversely, those are evil which bring it about that the parts of the human Body have another ratio of motion and rest to one another.
DEMONSTRATION

The human Body requires, in order to be preserved, very many other bodies (by Postulate 4, Part II). But that which constitutes the form of the human Body consists in this: that its parts communicate their motions to one another according to a certain fixed ratio (by the Definition before Lemma 4, which see after Proposition 13, Part II). Therefore, those things which bring about the preservation of the ratio of motion and rest which the parts of the human Body have to one another likewise preserve the form of the human Body, and consequently bring it about (by Postulates 3 and 6, Part II) that the human Body can be affected in many ways, and that it can affect external bodies in many ways; and thus (by the preceding Proposition) they are good. Next, those things which bring it about that the parts of the human Body acquire another ratio of motion and rest likewise (by the same Definition, Part

II) bring it about that the human Body assumes another form; that is (as is self-evident, and as we noted at the end of the Preface of this Part), that the human Body is destroyed and consequently rendered wholly unfit to be affected in many ways; and therefore (by the preceding Proposition) they are evil. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

How much these things can harm or benefit the Mind will be explained in Part V. But here it should be noted that I understand the Body to undergo death when its parts are so disposed that they acquire another ratio of motion and rest to one another. For I do not dare deny that the human Body, while retaining the circulation of the blood and other things on account of which the Body is thought to live, may nevertheless be changed into another nature altogether different from its own. For no reason compels me to maintain that the Body does not die unless it is changed into a corpse; indeed, experience itself seems to suggest otherwise.

For it sometimes happens that a man undergoes such changes that I would not readily say that he is the same man; as I have heard related of a certain Spanish poet, who had been seized by an illness and, although he recovered from it, nevertheless remained so forgetful of his past life that he did not believe the Fables and Tragedies which he had composed to be his own; and he could surely have been taken for an adult infant, had he also forgotten his native language. And if this seems incredible, what shall we say of infants? A man of advanced age believes their nature to be so different from his own that he could not be persuaded that he had ever been an infant, unless he formed a conjecture about himself from others. But lest I furnish the superstitious with material for stirring up new questions, I prefer to leave these matters undecided.
PROPOSITION XL

Those things which conduce to the common Society of human beings, or which bring it about that human beings live harmoniously, are useful; and, conversely, those things are evil which introduce discord into the State.
DEMONSTRATION

For those things which bring it about that human beings live harmoniously also bring it about that they live under the guidance of Reason (by Proposition 35 of this Part), and therefore (by Propositions 26 and 27 of this Part) are good; and (by the same reasoning), conversely, those things are evil which provoke discords. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLI
Joy is not directly evil, but good; Sadness, on the other hand, is directly evil.
DEMONSTRATION

Joy (by Proposition 11, Part III, together with its Scholium) is an affect by which the body's power of acting is increased or assisted; Sadness, on the other hand, is an affect by which the body's power of acting is diminished or restrained; and therefore (by Proposition 38 of this Part) Joy is directly good, etc. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLII
Cheerfulness cannot have excess, but is always good; and, on the contrary, Melancholy is always evil.
DEMONSTRATION

Cheerfulness (see its Definition in the Scholium to Prop. 11, Part III) is Joy which, insofar as it is referred to the Body, consists in this, that all the parts of the Body are equally affected; that is (by Prop. 11, Part III), that the Body's power of acting is increased or aided, so that all its parts maintain the same ratio of motion and rest to one another; and therefore (by Prop. 39 of this Part) Cheerfulness is always good, nor can it have excess. But Melancholy (the Definition of which also see in the same Scholium to Prop. 11, Part III) is Sadness which, insofar as it is referred to the Body, consists in this, that the Body's power of acting is absolutely diminished or restrained; and therefore (by Prop. 38 of this Part) is always evil. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIII
Titillation can have excess, and be evil; but Pain can be good insofar as Titillation, or Joy, is evil.
DEMONSTRATION

Titillation is Joy which, insofar as it is referred to the Body, consists in this, that one or several of its parts are affected more than the rest (see its Definition in the Scholium to Prop. 11, Part III); and the power of this affect can be so great that it surpasses the other actions of the Body (by Prop. 6 of this Part), adheres to it obstinately, and thus prevents the Body from being apt to be affected in many other ways; and therefore (by Prop. 38 of this Part) it can be evil. Next, Pain, which is, on the contrary, Sadness, considered in itself alone, cannot be good (by Prop. 41 of this Part). But since its force and increase are defined by the power of an external cause compared with our own (by Prop. 5 of this Part), we can therefore conceive infinite degrees and modes of forces of this affect (by Prop. 3 of this Part); and consequently conceive one such as can restrain Titillation, so that it does not have excess, and insofar (by the first part of the Proposition
of this Part) bring it about that the Body is not rendered less apt; and consequently, insofar, it will be good. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIV
Love and desire can have excess.
DEMONSTRATION

Love is Joy (by Def. 6 of the Affects) accompanied by the idea of an external cause; therefore Titillation (by the Scholium to Prop. 11, Part III) accompanied by the idea of an external cause is Love; and consequently Love (by the preceding Prop.) can have excess. Next, Desire is greater to the extent that the affect from which it arises is greater (by Prop. 37, Part III). Wherefore, as an affect (by Prop. 6 of this Part) can surpass a man's other actions, so also the Desire which arises from the same affect can surpass the other Desires, and consequently can have the same excess which we showed Titillation to have in the preceding Proposition. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Cheerfulness, which I have said to be good, is conceived more easily than it is observed. For the affects with which we struggle daily are for the most part referred to some part of the Body which is affected more than the rest; and consequently the affects for the most part have excess, and so hold the Mind in the contemplation of one object alone that it cannot think of others; and although men are subject to several affects, and consequently few are found who are always struggling with one and the same affect, nevertheless there are not lacking those to whom one and the same affect obstinately clings. For we sometimes see men so affected by one object that, although it is not present, they nevertheless believe that they have it before them; and when this happens to a man who is not asleep, we say that he is delirious or insane; nor are those believed to be less insane who burn with Love and dream night and day only of a beloved woman or a harlot, because they are wont to provoke laughter.

But when the avaricious man thinks of nothing other than gain or money, and the ambitious man of glory, etc., these are not believed to be delirious, because they are wont to be troublesome and are judged worthy of Hatred. But in truth Avarice, Ambition, Lust, etc., are species of delirium, although they are not numbered among diseases.
PROPOSITION XLV
Hatred can never be good.
DEMONSTRATION
We strive to destroy the man whom we hate (by Prop. 39, Part III), that is (by Prop. 37 of this Part), we strive for something which is evil; Therefore, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM
Note that here and in what follows, by Hatred I understand only that which is toward men.
COROLLARY I
Envy, Derision, Contempt, Anger, Vengeance, and the remaining affects which are referred to Hatred or arise from it, are evil; as is also evident from Prop. 39, Part III and Prop. 37 of this Part.
COROLLARY II

Whatever we desire from the fact that we are affected by hatred is base and unjust in the State. This is also clear from Prop. 39 p. III and from the Definitions of the base and the unjust, which see in the Scholiums of Prop. 37 of this Part.
SCHOLIUM

Between Mockery (which in Coroll. I I said to be bad) and laughter I recognize a great difference. For laughter, as also jesting, is mere Joy; and therefore, provided that it has no excess, it is good in itself (by Prop. 41 of this Part). Indeed, nothing except a grim and sad superstition forbids one to take delight. For why is it more fitting to assuage hunger and thirst than to dispel melancholy? This is my rule, and thus have I persuaded myself. No deity, nor anyone else unless envious, takes delight in my weakness and discomfort, nor reckons as virtue in us tears, sobs, fear, and other things of this kind, which are signs of a powerless mind; but, on the contrary, the greater the Joy by which we are affected, the greater the perfection to which we pass, that is, the more we must participate in the divine nature. Therefore, to use things and to take delight in them, so far as possible (not indeed to the point of nausea, for that is not taking delight), is the part of a wise man.

It is the part, I say, of a wise man to restore and refresh himself with moderate and pleasant food and drink, as also with scents, the charm of green plants, adornment, music, exercise-games, theatres, and other things of this kind, which each person can use without any injury to another. For the human Body is composed of very many parts of diverse natures, which continually require new and varied nourishment, so that the whole Body may be equally fitted for all the things that can follow from its nature, and consequently so that the Mind also may be equally fitted to understand many things at once. This manner of life therefore agrees best both with our principles and with common practice; wherefore, if any manner of life is best, this is so, and is to be recommended in every way; nor is there need to treat these matters more clearly or at greater length.
PROPOSITION XLVI
He who lives according to the guidance of Reason strives, as far as he can, to requite another's Hatred, Anger, Contempt, etc., toward him with Love in return, or Generosity.
DEMONSTRATION

All affects of Hatred are bad (by Coroll. 1 of the preceding Prop.); and therefore he who lives according to the guidance of Reason will, as far as he can, strive to bring it about that he is not assailed by affects of Hatred (by Prop. 19 of this Part), and consequently (by Prop. 37 of this Part) will strive that another also not suffer the same affects. But Hatred is increased by reciprocal Hatred, and can, on the contrary, be extinguished by Love (by Prop. 43 p. III), so that Hatred passes into Love (by Prop. 44 p. III); Therefore, he who lives according to the guidance of Reason will strive to requite another's Hatred, etc., with Love in return, that is, with Generosity (for the Defin. of which see the Schol. of Prop. 59 p. III). Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

He who wishes to avenge injuries by reciprocal Hatred surely lives miserably. But he who, on the contrary, strives to overcome Hatred with Love, certainly fights joyfully and securely, resists many men as easily as one, and has the least possible need of the aid of fortune. Moreover, those whom he conquers yield joyfully, indeed not from a defect but from an increase of strength; all of which follows so clearly from the definitions of Love and Intellect alone that there is no need to demonstrate them severally.
PROPOSITION XLVII
The affects of Hope and Fear cannot be good in themselves.
DEMONSTRATION

The affects of Hope and Fear are not given without Sadness. For Fear is (by Defin. 13 of the Affects) Sadness, and Hope (see the Explanation of Defins. 12 and 13 of the Affects) is not given without Fear; and therefore (by Prop. 41 of this Part) these affects cannot be good in themselves, but only insofar as they can restrain an excess of Joy (by Prop. 43 of this Part). Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

To this must be added that these affects indicate a defect of knowledge and a powerlessness of Mind; and for this reason also Security, Despair, Gladness, and Remorse of Conscience are signs of a powerless mind. For although Security and Gladness are affects of Joy, they nevertheless suppose that Sadness has preceded them, namely, Hope and Fear. Therefore, the more we strive to live according to the guidance of Reason, the more we strive to depend less on Hope, to free ourselves from Fear, to command fortune as far as we can, and to direct our actions by the sure counsel of Reason.
PROPOSITION XLVIII
The affects of Esteem and Contempt are always bad.
DEMONSTRATION
For these affects (by Defins. 21 and 22 of the Affects) are contrary to reason; and therefore (by Props. 26 and 27 of this Part) they are bad. Q. E. D.
PROPOSITION XLIX
Esteem easily renders proud the man who is esteemed.
DEMONSTRATION

If we see that someone has, out of love, an opinion of us beyond what is just, we shall easily glory (by the Scholium to Prop. 41, Part III), or be affected with Joy (by Def. 30 of the Affects); and we shall easily believe the good which we hear proclaimed of us (by Prop. 25, Part III); and thus, out of self-love, we shall have an opinion of ourselves beyond what is just, that is (by Def. 28 of the Affects), we shall easily become proud. Q.E.D.
PROPOSITION L
