sources.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 5
sources.text:
Illum liberum esse dixi, qui sola ducitur Ratione ; qui itaque liber nascitur, et liber manet, non nisi adæquatas ideas habet ; ac proinde mali conceptum habet nullum (per Coroll. Prop. 64 hujus), et consequenter (nam bonum et malum correlata sunt) neque boni. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hujus Propositionis hypothesin falsam esse, nec posse concipi, nisi quatenus ad solam naturam humanam, seu potius ad Deum attendimus, non quatenus infinitus, sed quatenus tantummodo causa est, cur homo existat, patet ex 4 Propositione hujus Partis. Atque hoc, et alia quæ jam demonstravimus, videntur a Mose significari in illa primi hominis historia. In ea enim nulla alia Dei potentia concipitur, quam illa, qua hominem creavit, hoc est potentia, qua hominis solummodo utilitati consuluit ; atque eatenus narratur, quod Deus homini libero prohibuerit, ne de arbore cognitionis boni et mali comederet, et quod, simulac de ea comederet, statim mortem metueret potius quam vivere cuperet. Deinde, quod inventa ab homine uxore, quæ cum sua natura prorsus conveniebat, cognovit nihil posse in Natura dari, quod ipsi posset illa esse utilius ; sed quod, postquam bruta sibi similia esse credidit, statim eorum affectus imitari inceperit (vide Prop. 27 p. III), et libertatem suam amittere ; quam Patriarchæ postea recuperaverunt, ducti Spiritu Christi, hoc est Dei idea, a qua sola pendet, ut homo liber sit, et ut bonum, quod sibi cupit, reliquis hominibus cupiat, ut supra (per Prop. 37 hujus) demonstravimus.

PROPOSITIO LXIX

Hominis liberi virtus æque magna cernitur in declinandis quam in superandis periculis.

DEMONSTRATIO

Affectus coerceri nec tolli potest, nisi affectu contrario, et fortiore affectu coercendo (per Prop. 7 hujus). At cœca Audacia et Metus affectus sunt, qui æque magni possunt concipi (per Prop. 5 et 3 hujus) : Ergo æque magna animi virtus, seu fortitudo (hujus Definitionem vide in Schol. Prop. 59 p. III) requiritur ad Audaciam quam ad Metum coercendum ; hoc est (per Defin. 40 et 41 Affect.), homo liber eadem animi virtute pericula declinat, qua eadem superare tentat. Q. E. D.

COROLLARIUM

Homini igitur libero æque magnæ Animositati fuga in tempore, ac pugna ducitur : sive homo liber eadem Animositate, seu animi præsentia, qua certamen, fugam eligit.

SCHOLIUM

Quid Animositas sit, vel quid per ipsam intelligam, in Scholio Prop. 59 p. III explicui. Per periculum autem id omne intelligo, quod potest esse causa alicujus mali, nempe Tristitiæ, Odii, Discordiæ etc.

PROPOSITIO LXX

Homo liber, qui inter ignaros vivit, eorum, quantum potest, beneficia declinare studet.

DEMONSTRATIO

Unusquisque ex suo ingenio judicat, quid bonum sit (vide Schol. Prop. 39 p. III) ; ignarus igitur, qui in aliquem beneficium contulit, id ex suo ingenio æstimabit, et si minoris ab eo, cui datum est, æstimari videt, contristabitur (per Prop. 42 p. III). At homo liber reliquos homines amicitia sibi jungere (per Prop. 37 hujus), nec paria hominibus beneficia ex eorum affectu referre, sed se et reliquos libero Rationis judicio ducere, et ea tantum agere studet, quæ ipse prima esse novit : Ergo homo liber, ne ignaris odio sit, et ne eorum appetitui, sed soli Rationi obsequatur, eorum beneficia, quantum potest, declinare conabitur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Dico quantum potest. Nam quamvis homines ignari sint, sunt tamen homines, qui in necessitatibus humanum auxilium, quo nullum præstabilius est, adferre queunt ; atque adeo sæpe fit, ut necesse sit ab iisdem beneficium accipere, et consequenter iisdem contra ex eorum ingenio congratulari ; ad quod accedit, quod etiam in declinandis beneficiis cautio esse debet, ne videamur eosdem contemnere, vel præ Avaritia remunerationem timere, atque ita dum eorum Odium fugimus, eo ipso in eorum offensionem incurramus. Quare in declinandis beneficiis ratio utilis et honesti habenda est.

PROPOSITIO LXXI

Soli homines liberi erga invicem gratissimi sunt.

DEMONSTRATIO

Soli homines liberi sibi invicem utilissimi sunt, et maxima amicitiæ necessitudine invicem junguntur (per Prop. 35 hujus, et 1 ejus Coroll.) parique amoris studio sibi invicem benefacere conantur (per Prop. 37 hujus) ; adeoque (per 34 Affect. Defin.) soli homines liberi erga se invicem gratissimi sunt. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Gratia, quam homines qui cœca Cupiditate ducuntur, invicem habent, mercatura seu aucupium potius, quam gratia plerumque est. Porro ingratitudo affectus non est. Est tamen ingratitudo turpis, quia plerumque hominem nimio Odio, Ira, vel Superbia, vel Avaritia, etc., affectum esse indicat. Nam qui præ stultitia dona compensare nescit, ingratus non est, et multo minus ille, qui donis non movetur meretricis, ut ipsius libidini inserviat, nec furis, ut ipsius furta celet, vel alterius similis. Nam hic contra animum habere constantem ostendit, qui scilicet se nullis donis ad suam vel communem perniciem patitur corrumpi.

PROPOSITIO LXXII

Homo liber nunquam dolo malo, sed semper cum fide agit.

DEMONSTRATIO

Si liber homo quicquam dolo malo, quatenus liber est, ageret, id ex dictamine Rationis ageret (nam eatenus tantum liber a nobis appellatur) : atque adeo dolo malo agere virtus esset (per Prop. 24 hujus), et consequenter (per eandem Prop.) unicuique ad suum esse conservandum consultius esset, dolo malo agere ; hoc est (ut per se notum), hominibus consultius esset, verbis solummodo convenire, re autem invicem esse contrarios, quod (per Coroll. Prop. 31 hujus) est absurdum. Ergo homo liber etc. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Si jam quæratur, quid si homo se perfidia a præsenti mortis periculo posset liberare, an non ratio suum esse conservandi omnino suadet, ut perfidus sit ? Respondebitur eodem modo, quod si Ratio id suadeat, suadet ergo id omnibus hominibus, atque adeo Ratio omnino suadet hominibus, ne nisi dolo malo paciscantur, vires conjungere et jura habere communia, hoc est, ne revera jura habeant communia, quod est absurdum.

PROPOSITIO LXXIII

Homo, qui Ratione ducitur, magis in Civitate, ubi ex communi decreto vivit, quam in solitudine, ubi sibi soli obtemperat, liber est.

DEMONSTRATIO

Homo, qui Ratione ducitur, non ducitur Metu ad obtemperandum (per Prop. 63 hujus) sed, quatenus suum esse ex Rationis dictamine conservare conatur, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 66 hujus) quatenus libere vivere conatur, communis vitæ et utilitatis rationem tenere (per Prop. 37 hujus), et consequenter (ut in Schol. 2 Prop. 37 hujus ostendimus) ex communi Civitatis decreto vivere cupit. Cupit ergo homo, qui Ratione ducitur, ut liberius vivat, communia Civitatis jura tenere. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hæc et similia, quæ de vera hominis libertate ostendimus, ad Fortitudinem, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 59 p. III) ad Animositatem et Generositatem referuntur. Nec operæ pretium duco, omnes Fortitudinis proprietates hic separatim demonstrare, et multo minus, quod vir fortis neminem odio habeat, nemini irascatur, invideat, indignetur, neminem despiciat, minimeque superbiat. Nam hæc, et omnia, quæ ad veram vitam et Religionem spectant, facile ex Propositione 37 et 46 hujus Partis convincuntur ; nempe quod Odium Amore contra vincendum sit, et quod unusquisque, qui Ratione ducitur, bonum, quod sibi appetit, reliquis etiam ut sit, cupiat. Ad quod accedit id, quod in Scholio Propositionis 50 hujus Partis, et aliis in locis notavimus : quod scilicet vir fortis hoc apprime consideret, nempe quod omnia ex necessitate divinæ naturæ sequantur, ac proinde quicquid molestum et malum esse cogitat, et quicquid præterea impium, horrendum, injustum, et turpe videtur, ex eo oritur, quod res ipsas perturbate, mutilate, et confuse concipit ; et hac de causa apprime conatur res, ut in se sunt, concipere, et veræ cognitionis impedimenta amovere, ut sunt Odium, Ira, Invidia, Irrisio, Superbia, et reliqua hujusmodi, quæ in præcedentibus notavimus ; atque adeo, quantum potest, conatur ut diximus, bene agere et lætari. Quousque autem humana virtus ad hæc consequenda se extendat, et quid possit, in sequenti Parte demonstrabo.

APPENDIX

Quæ in hac Parte de recta vivendi Ratione tradidi, non sunt ita disposita ut uno aspectu videri possint, sed disperse a me demonstrata sunt, prout scilicet unum ex alio facilius deducere potuerim. Eadem igitur hic recolligere et ad summa capita redigere proposui.

CAPUT I

Omnes nostri conatus, seu Cupiditates, ex necessitate nostræ naturæ ita sequuntur, ut vel per ipsam solam, tanquam per proximam suam causam, possint intelligi, vel quatenus Naturæ sumus pars, quæ per se absque aliis individuis non potest adæquate concipi.

CAPUT II

Cupiditates, quæ ex nostra natura ita sequuntur, ut per ipsam solam possit intelligi, sunt illæ, quæ ad Mentem referuntur, quatenus hæc ideis adæquatis constare concipitur ; reliquæ vero Cupiditates ad Mentem non referuntur, nisi quatenus res inadæquate concipit, et earum vis et incrementum non humana, sed rerum, quæ extra nos sunt, potentia definiri debet ; et ideo illæ recte actiones, hæ autem passiones vocantur ; illæ namque nostram potentiam semper indicant, et hæ contra nostram impotentiam et mutilatam cognitionem.

CAPUT III

Nostræ actiones, hoc est Cupiditates illæ, quæ hominis potentia seu Ratione definiuntur, semper bonæ sunt, reliquæ autem tam bonæ quam malæ possunt esse.

CAPUT IV

In vita itaque apprime utile est, intellectum seu Rationem, quantum possumus, perficere, et in hoc uno summa hominis felicitas seu beatitudo consistit ; quippe beatitudo nihil aliud est, quam ipsa animi acquiescentia, quæ ex Dei intuitiva cognitione oritur : at intellectum perficere nihil etiam aliud est, quam Deum, Deique attributa et actiones, quæ ex ipsius naturæ necessitate consequuntur, intelligere. Quare hominis, qui Ratione ducitur, finis ultimus, hoc est summa Cupiditas, qua reliquas omnes moderari studet, est illa, qua fertur ad se, resque omnes, quæ sub ipsius intelligentiam cadere possunt, adæquate concipiendum.

CAPUT V

Nulla igitur vita rationalis est sine intelligentia ; et res eatenus tantum bonæ sunt, quatenus hominem juvant, ut Mentis vita fruatur, quæ intelligentia definitur. Quæ autem contra impediunt, quo minus homo Rationem perficere et rationali vita frui possit, eas solummodo malas esse dicimus.

CAPUT VI

Sed quia omnia illa, quorum homo efficiens est causa, necessario bona sunt, nihil ergo mali homini evenire potest, nisi a causis externis ; nempe quatenus pars est totius Naturæ, cujus legibus humana natura obtemperare, et cui infinitis modis pœne sese accommodare cogitur.

CAPUT VII

Nec fieri potest, ut homo non sit Naturæ pars, et communem ejus ordinem non sequatur ; sed si inter talia individua versetur, quæ cum ipsius hominis natura conveniunt, eo ipso hominis agendi potentia juvabitur et fovebitur. At si contra inter talia sit, quæ cum ipsius natura minime conveniunt, vix absque magna ipsius mutatione iisdem sese accommodare poterit.

CAPUT VIII

Quicquid in rerum Natura datur, quod judicamus malum esse, sive posse impedire, quo minus existere et vita rationali frui queamus, id a nobis removere ea via, quæ securior videtur, licet ; et quicquid contra datur, quod judicamus bonum sive utile esse ad nostrum esse conservandum, et vita rationali fruendum, id ad nostrum usum capere, et eo quocunque modo uti nobis licet ; et absolute id unicuique summo Naturæ jure facere licet, quod ad ipsius utilitatem conferre judicat.

CAPUT IX

Nihil magis cum natura alicujus rei convenire potest, quam reliqua ejusdem speciei individua ; adeoque (per Caput VII) nihil homini ad suum esse conservandum, et vita rationali fruendum utilius datur quam homo, qui Ratione ducitur. Deinde, quia inter res singulares nihil novimus, quod homine, qui Ratione ducitur, sit præstantius, nulla ergo re magis potest unusquisque ostendere, quantum arte et ingenio valeat, quam in hominibus ita educandis, ut tandem ex proprio Rationis imperio vivant.

CAPUT X

Quatenus homines Invidia aut aliquo Odii affectu in se invicem feruntur, eatenus invicem contrarii sunt, et consequenter eo magis timendi, quo plus possunt quam reliqua Naturæ individua.

CAPUT XI

Animi tamen non armis sed Amore et Generositate vincuntur.

CAPUT XII

Hominibus apprime utile est consuetudines jungere, seseque iis vinculis astringere, quibus aptius de se omnibus unum efficiant, et absolute ea agere, quæ firmandis amicitiis inserviunt.

CAPUT XIII

Sed ad hæc ars et vigilantia requiritur. Sunt enim homines varii (nam rari sunt, qui ex Rationis præscripto vivunt), et tamen plerumque invidi, et magis ad vindictam quam ad Misericordiam proclives. Unumquemque igitur ex ipsius ingenio ferre et sese continere, ne eorum affectus imitetur, singularis animi potentiæ opus est. At qui contra homines carpere, et vitia potius exprobrare quam virtutes docere, et hominum animos non firmare sed frangere norunt, ii et sibi et reliquis molesti sunt ; unde multi, præ nimia scilicet animi impatientia, falsoque religionis studio, inter bruta potius quam inter homines vivere maluerunt ; ut pueri vel adolescentes, qui parentum jurgia æquo animo ferre nequeunt, militatum confugiunt, et incommoda belli et imperium tyrannidis præ domesticis commodis et paternis admonitionibus eligunt, et quidvis oneris sibi imponi patiuntur, dummodo parentes ulciscantur.

CAPUT XIV

Quamvis igitur homines omnia plerumque ex sua libidine moderentur, ex eorum tamen communi societate multo plura commoda quam damna sequuntur. Quare satius est, eorum injurias æquo animo ferre, et studium iis adhibere, quæ concordiæ et amicitiæ conciliandæ inserviunt.

CAPUT XV

Quæ concordiam gignunt sunt illa, quæ ad justitiam, æquitatem, et honestatem referuntur. Nam homines præter id, quod injustum et iniquum est, etiam ægre ferunt, quod turpe habetur, sive quod aliquis receptos civitatis mores aspernatur. Amori autem conciliando illa apprime necessaria sunt, quæ ad Religionem et Pietatem spectant. De quibus vide Schol. 1 et 2 Prop. 37 et Schol. Prop. 46 et Schol. Prop. 73 p. IV.

CAPUT XVI

Solet præterea concordia ex Metu plerumque gigni, sed sine fide. Adde, quod Metus ex animi impotentia oritur, et propterea ad Rationis usum non pertinet ; ut nec Commiseratio, quamvis Pietatis speciem præ se ferre videatur.

CAPUT XVII

Vincuntur præterea homines etiam largitate, præcipue ii qui non habent, unde comparare possint illa, quæ ad vitam sustentandam necessaria sunt. Attamen unicuique indigenti auxilium ferre, vires et utilitatem viri privati longe superat. Divitiæ namque viri privati longe impares sunt ad id suppeditandum. Unius præterea viri facultas limitatior est, quam ut omnes sibi possit amicitia jungere ; quare pauperum cura integræ societati incumbit, et ad communem tantum utilitatem spectat.

CAPUT XVIII

In beneficiis accipiendis et gratia referenda alia prorsus debet esse cura, de qua vide Schol. Prop. 70 et Schol. Prop. 71 p. IV.

CAPUT XIX

Amor præterea meretricius, hoc est generandi libido, quæ ex forma oritur, et absolute omnis Amor, qui aliam causam præter animi libertatem agnoscit, facile in Odium transit ; nisi, quod pejus est, species delirii sit, atque tum magis discordia quam concordia fovetur. Vid. Schol. Prop. 31 p. III.

CAPUT XX

Ad matrimonium quod attinet, certum est, ipsum cum Ratione convenire, si Cupiditas miscendi corpora non ex sola forma, sed etiam ex Amore liberos procreandi et sapienter educandi ingeneretur ; et præterea si utriusque, viri scilicet et fœminæ, Amor non solam formam, sed animi præcipue libertatem pro causa habeat.

CAPUT XXI

Gignit præterea adulatio concordiam ; sed fœdo servitutis crimine, vel perfidia ; nulli quippe magis adulatione capiuntur quam superbi, qui primi esse volunt, nec sunt.

CAPUT XXII

Abjectioni falsa pietatis et religionis species inest. Et quamvis Abjectio Superbiæ sit contraria, est tamen abjectus superbo proximus. Vide Schol. Prop. 57 p. IV.

CAPUT XXIII

Confert præterea concordiæ Pudor in iis tantum, quæ celari non possunt. Deinde, quia ipse Pudor species est Tristitiæ, ad Rationis usum non spectat.

CAPUT XXIV

Cæteri Tristitiæ erga homines affectus directe justitiæ, æquitati, honestati, pietati, et religioni opponuntur ; et, quamvis Indignatio æquitatis speciem præ se ferre videatur, ibi tamen sine lege vivitur, ubi unicuique de factis alterius judicium ferre, et suum vel alterius jus vindicare licet.

CAPUT XXV

Modestia, hoc est Cupiditas hominibus placendi, quæ ex Ratione determinatur, ad Pietatem (ut in Schol. 1 Prop. 37 p. IV diximus) refertur. Sed si ex affectu oriatur, Ambitio est sive Cupiditas, qua homines falsa Pietatis imagine plerumque discordias et seditiones concitant. Nam qui reliquos consilio aut re juvare cupit, ut simul summo fruantur bono, is apprime studebit eorum sibi Amorem conciliare ; non autem eos in admirationem traducere, ut disciplina ex ipso habeat vocabulum, nec ullas absolute Invidiæ causas dare. In communibus deinde colloquiis cavebit hominum vitia referre, et de humana impotentia non nisi parce loqui curabit : at largiter de humana virtute seu potentia, et qua via possit perfici ; ut sic homines, non ex Metu aut aversione, sed solo Lætitiæ affectu moti ex Rationis præscripto, quantum in se est, conentur vivere.

CAPUT XXVI

Præter homines nihil singulare in Natura novimus, cujus Mente gaudere, et quod nobis amicitia aut aliquo consuetudinis genere jungere possumus ; adeoque quicquid in rerum Natura extra homines datur, id nostræ utilitatis ratio conservare, destruere, vel quocunque modo ad nostrum usum adaptare nos docet.

CAPUT XXVII

Utilitas, quam ex rebus, quæ extra nos sunt, capimus, est, præter experientiam et cognitionem, quam acquirimus ex eo, quod easdem observamus, et ex his formis in alias mutamus, præcipua corporis conservatio ; et hac Ratione res illæ imprimis utiles sunt, quæ Corpus ita alere et nutrire possunt, ut ejus omnes partes officio suo recte fungi queant. Nam quo Corpus aptius est, ut pluribus modis possit affici, et corpora externa pluribus modis afficere, eo Mens ad cogitandum est aptior (vide Prop. 38 et 39 p. IV). At hujus notæ perpauca in Natura esse videntur ; quare ad Corpus, ut requiritur, nutriendum, necesse est, multis naturæ diversæ alimentis uti. Quippe humanum Corpus ex plurimis diversæ naturæ partibus componitur, quæ continuo alimento indigent, et vario, ut totum Corpus ad omnia, quæ ex ipsius natura sequi possunt, æque aptum sit, et consequenter ut Mens etiam æque apta sit ad plura concipiendum.

CAPUT XXVIII

Ad hæc autem comparandum vix uniuscujusque vires sufficerent, nisi homines operas mutuas traderent. Verum omnium rerum compendium pecunia attulit, unde factum, ut ejus imago Mentem vulgi maxime occupare soleat ; quia vix ullam Lætitiæ speciem imaginari possunt, nisi concomitante nummorum idea tanquam causa.

CAPUT XXIX

Sed hoc vitium eorum tantum est, qui non ex indigentia, nec propter necessitates nummos quærunt, sed quia lucri artes didicerunt, quibus se magnifice efferunt. Cæterum Corpus ex consuetudine pascunt, sed parce, quia tantum de suis bonis se perdere credunt, quantum sui Corporis conservationi impendunt. At qui verum nummorum usum norunt, et divitiarum modum ex sola indigentia moderantur, paucis contenti vivunt.

CAPUT XXX

Cum igitur res illæ sint bonæ, quæ Corporis partes juvant, ut suo officio fungantur, et Lætitia in eo consistat, quod hominis potentia, quatenus Mente et Corpore constat, juvatur vel augetur ; sunt ergo illa omnia, quæ Lætitiam afferunt, bona. Attamen, quoniam contra non eum in finem res agunt, ut nos Lætitia afficiant, nec earum agendi potentia ex nostra utilitate temperatur, et denique quoniam Lætitia plerumque ad unam Corporis partem potissimum refertur ; habent ergo plerumque Lætitiæ affectus (nisi Ratio et vigilantia adsit), et consequenter Cupiditates etiam, quæ ex iisdem generantur, excessum ; ad quod accedit, quod ex affectu id primum habeamus, quod in præsentia suave est, nec futura æquali animi affectu æstimare possumus. Vide Schol. Prop. 44 et Schol. Prop. 60 p. IV.

CAPUT XXXI

At superstitio id contra videtur statuere bonum esse, quod Tristitiam, et id contra malum quod Lætitiam affert. Sed, ut jam diximus (vide Schol. Prop. 45 p. IV), nemo, nisi invidus, mea impotentia et incommodo delectatur. Nam quo majore Lætitia afficimur, eo ad majorem perfectionem transimus, et consequenter eo magis de natura divina participamus ; nec Lætitia unquam mala esse potest, quam nostræ utilitatis vera ratio moderatur. At qui contra Metu ducitur, et bonum, ut malum vitet, agit, is Ratione non ducitur.

CAPUT XXXII

Sed humana potentia admodum limitata est, et a potentia causarum externarum infinite superatur ; atque adeo potestatem absolutam non habemus, res, quæ extra nos sunt, ad nostrum usum aptandi. Attamen ea, quæ nobis eveniunt contra id, quod nostræ utilitatis ratio postulat, æquo animo feremus, si conscii simus, nos functos nostro officio fuisse, et potentiam, quam habemus, non potuisse se eo usque extendere, ut eadem vitare possemus ; nosque partem totius Naturæ esse, cujus ordinem sequimur. Quod si clare et distincte intelligamus, pars illa nostri, quæ intelligentia definitur, hoc est pars melior nostri, in eo plane acquiescet, et in ea acquiescentia perseverare conabitur. Nam, quatenus intelligimus, nihil appetere nisi id, quod necessarium est, nec absolute, nisi in veris, acquiescere possumus ; adeoque quatenus hæc recte intelligimus, eatenus conatus melioris partis nostri cum ordine totius Naturæ convenit.

FINIS QUARTÆ PARTIS

paragraphs.text: Illum liberum esse dixi, qui sola ducitur Ratione ; qui itaque liber nascitur, et liber manet, non nisi adæquatas ideas habet ; ac proinde mali conceptum habet nullum (per Coroll. Prop. 64 hujus), et consequenter (nam bonum et malum correlata sunt) neque boni. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hujus Propositionis hypothesin falsam esse, nec posse concipi, nisi quatenus ad solam naturam humanam, seu potius ad Deum attendimus, non quatenus infinitus, sed quatenus tantummodo causa est, cur homo existat, patet ex 4 Propositione hujus Partis. Atque hoc, et alia quæ jam demonstravimus, videntur a Mose significari in illa primi hominis historia. In ea enim nulla alia Dei potentia concipitur, quam illa, qua hominem creavit, hoc est potentia, qua hominis solummodo utilitati consuluit ; atque eatenus narratur, quod Deus homini libero prohibuerit, ne de arbore cognitionis boni et mali comederet, et quod, simulac de ea comederet, statim mortem metueret potius quam vivere cuperet.

Deinde, quod inventa ab homine uxore, quæ cum sua natura prorsus conveniebat, cognovit nihil posse in Natura dari, quod ipsi posset illa esse utilius ; sed quod, postquam bruta sibi similia esse credidit, statim eorum affectus imitari inceperit (vide Prop. 27 p. III), et libertatem suam amittere ; quam Patriarchæ postea recuperaverunt, ducti Spiritu Christi, hoc est Dei idea, a qua sola pendet, ut homo liber sit, et ut bonum, quod sibi cupit, reliquis hominibus cupiat, ut supra (per Prop. 37 hujus) demonstravimus.
PROPOSITIO LXIX
Hominis liberi virtus æque magna cernitur in declinandis quam in superandis periculis.
DEMONSTRATIO

Affectus coerceri nec tolli potest, nisi affectu contrario, et fortiore affectu coercendo (per Prop. 7 hujus). At cœca Audacia et Metus affectus sunt, qui æque magni possunt concipi (per Prop. 5 et 3 hujus) : Ergo æque magna animi virtus, seu fortitudo (hujus Definitionem vide in Schol. Prop. 59 p. III) requiritur ad Audaciam quam ad Metum coercendum ; hoc est (per Defin. 40 et 41 Affect.), homo liber eadem animi virtute pericula declinat, qua eadem superare tentat. Q. E. D.
COROLLARIUM
Homini igitur libero æque magnæ Animositati fuga in tempore, ac pugna ducitur : sive homo liber eadem Animositate, seu animi præsentia, qua certamen, fugam eligit.
SCHOLIUM

Quid Animositas sit, vel quid per ipsam intelligam, in Scholio Prop. 59 p. III explicui. Per periculum autem id omne intelligo, quod potest esse causa alicujus mali, nempe Tristitiæ, Odii, Discordiæ etc.
PROPOSITIO LXX
Homo liber, qui inter ignaros vivit, eorum, quantum potest, beneficia declinare studet.
DEMONSTRATIO

Unusquisque ex suo ingenio judicat, quid bonum sit (vide Schol. Prop. 39 p. III) ; ignarus igitur, qui in aliquem beneficium contulit, id ex suo ingenio æstimabit, et si minoris ab eo, cui datum est, æstimari videt, contristabitur (per Prop. 42 p. III). At homo liber reliquos homines amicitia sibi jungere (per Prop. 37 hujus), nec paria hominibus beneficia ex eorum affectu referre, sed se et reliquos libero Rationis judicio ducere, et ea tantum agere studet, quæ ipse prima esse novit : Ergo homo liber, ne ignaris odio sit, et ne eorum appetitui, sed soli Rationi obsequatur, eorum beneficia, quantum potest, declinare conabitur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Dico quantum potest. Nam quamvis homines ignari sint, sunt tamen homines, qui in necessitatibus humanum auxilium, quo nullum præstabilius est, adferre queunt ; atque adeo sæpe fit, ut necesse sit ab iisdem beneficium accipere, et consequenter iisdem contra ex eorum ingenio congratulari ; ad quod accedit, quod etiam in declinandis beneficiis cautio esse debet, ne videamur eosdem contemnere, vel præ Avaritia remunerationem timere, atque ita dum eorum Odium fugimus, eo ipso in eorum offensionem incurramus. Quare in declinandis beneficiis ratio utilis et honesti habenda est.
PROPOSITIO LXXI
Soli homines liberi erga invicem gratissimi sunt.
DEMONSTRATIO

Soli homines liberi sibi invicem utilissimi sunt, et maxima amicitiæ necessitudine invicem junguntur (per Prop. 35 hujus, et 1 ejus Coroll.) parique amoris studio sibi invicem benefacere conantur (per Prop. 37 hujus) ; adeoque (per 34 Affect. Defin.) soli homines liberi erga se invicem gratissimi sunt. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Gratia, quam homines qui cœca Cupiditate ducuntur, invicem habent, mercatura seu aucupium potius, quam gratia plerumque est. Porro ingratitudo affectus non est. Est tamen ingratitudo turpis, quia plerumque hominem nimio Odio, Ira, vel Superbia, vel Avaritia, etc., affectum esse indicat. Nam qui præ stultitia dona compensare nescit, ingratus non est, et multo minus ille, qui donis non movetur meretricis, ut ipsius libidini inserviat, nec furis, ut ipsius furta celet, vel alterius similis. Nam hic contra animum habere constantem ostendit, qui scilicet se nullis donis ad suam vel communem perniciem patitur corrumpi.
PROPOSITIO LXXII
Homo liber nunquam dolo malo, sed semper cum fide agit.
DEMONSTRATIO

Si liber homo quicquam dolo malo, quatenus liber est, ageret, id ex dictamine Rationis ageret (nam eatenus tantum liber a nobis appellatur) : atque adeo dolo malo agere virtus esset (per Prop. 24 hujus), et consequenter (per eandem Prop.) unicuique ad suum esse conservandum consultius esset, dolo malo agere ; hoc est (ut per se notum), hominibus consultius esset, verbis solummodo convenire, re autem invicem esse contrarios, quod (per Coroll. Prop. 31 hujus) est absurdum. Ergo homo liber etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Si jam quæratur, quid si homo se perfidia a præsenti mortis periculo posset liberare, an non ratio suum esse conservandi omnino suadet, ut perfidus sit ? Respondebitur eodem modo, quod si Ratio id suadeat, suadet ergo id omnibus hominibus, atque adeo Ratio omnino suadet hominibus, ne nisi dolo malo paciscantur, vires conjungere et jura habere communia, hoc est, ne revera jura habeant communia, quod est absurdum.
PROPOSITIO LXXIII
Homo, qui Ratione ducitur, magis in Civitate, ubi ex communi decreto vivit, quam in solitudine, ubi sibi soli obtemperat, liber est.
DEMONSTRATIO

Homo, qui Ratione ducitur, non ducitur Metu ad obtemperandum (per Prop. 63 hujus) sed, quatenus suum esse ex Rationis dictamine conservare conatur, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 66 hujus) quatenus libere vivere conatur, communis vitæ et utilitatis rationem tenere (per Prop. 37 hujus), et consequenter (ut in Schol. 2 Prop. 37 hujus ostendimus) ex communi Civitatis decreto vivere cupit. Cupit ergo homo, qui Ratione ducitur, ut liberius vivat, communia Civitatis jura tenere. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hæc et similia, quæ de vera hominis libertate ostendimus, ad Fortitudinem, hoc est (per Schol. Prop. 59 p. III) ad Animositatem et Generositatem referuntur. Nec operæ pretium duco, omnes Fortitudinis proprietates hic separatim demonstrare, et multo minus, quod vir fortis neminem odio habeat, nemini irascatur, invideat, indignetur, neminem despiciat, minimeque superbiat. Nam hæc, et omnia, quæ ad veram vitam et Religionem spectant, facile ex Propositione 37 et 46 hujus Partis convincuntur ; nempe quod Odium Amore contra vincendum sit, et quod unusquisque, qui Ratione ducitur, bonum, quod sibi appetit, reliquis etiam ut sit, cupiat.

Ad quod accedit id, quod in Scholio Propositionis 50 hujus Partis, et aliis in locis notavimus : quod scilicet vir fortis hoc apprime consideret, nempe quod omnia ex necessitate divinæ naturæ sequantur, ac proinde quicquid molestum et malum esse cogitat, et quicquid præterea impium, horrendum, injustum, et turpe videtur, ex eo oritur, quod res ipsas perturbate, mutilate, et confuse concipit ; et hac de causa apprime conatur res, ut in se sunt, concipere, et veræ cognitionis impedimenta amovere, ut sunt Odium, Ira, Invidia, Irrisio, Superbia, et reliqua hujusmodi, quæ in præcedentibus notavimus ; atque adeo, quantum potest, conatur ut diximus, bene agere et lætari. Quousque autem humana virtus ad hæc consequenda se extendat, et quid possit, in sequenti Parte demonstrabo.
APPENDIX

Quæ in hac Parte de recta vivendi Ratione tradidi, non sunt ita disposita ut uno aspectu videri possint, sed disperse a me demonstrata sunt, prout scilicet unum ex alio facilius deducere potuerim. Eadem igitur hic recolligere et ad summa capita redigere proposui.
CAPUT I

Omnes nostri conatus, seu Cupiditates, ex necessitate nostræ naturæ ita sequuntur, ut vel per ipsam solam, tanquam per proximam suam causam, possint intelligi, vel quatenus Naturæ sumus pars, quæ per se absque aliis individuis non potest adæquate concipi.
CAPUT II

Cupiditates, quæ ex nostra natura ita sequuntur, ut per ipsam solam possit intelligi, sunt illæ, quæ ad Mentem referuntur, quatenus hæc ideis adæquatis constare concipitur ; reliquæ vero Cupiditates ad Mentem non referuntur, nisi quatenus res inadæquate concipit, et earum vis et incrementum non humana, sed rerum, quæ extra nos sunt, potentia definiri debet ; et ideo illæ recte actiones, hæ autem passiones vocantur ; illæ namque nostram potentiam semper indicant, et hæ contra nostram impotentiam et mutilatam cognitionem.
CAPUT III
Nostræ actiones, hoc est Cupiditates illæ, quæ hominis potentia seu Ratione definiuntur, semper bonæ sunt, reliquæ autem tam bonæ quam malæ possunt esse.
CAPUT IV

In vita itaque apprime utile est, intellectum seu Rationem, quantum possumus, perficere, et in hoc uno summa hominis felicitas seu beatitudo consistit ; quippe beatitudo nihil aliud est, quam ipsa animi acquiescentia, quæ ex Dei intuitiva cognitione oritur : at intellectum perficere nihil etiam aliud est, quam Deum, Deique attributa et actiones, quæ ex ipsius naturæ necessitate consequuntur, intelligere. Quare hominis, qui Ratione ducitur, finis ultimus, hoc est summa Cupiditas, qua reliquas omnes moderari studet, est illa, qua fertur ad se, resque omnes, quæ sub ipsius intelligentiam cadere possunt, adæquate concipiendum.
CAPUT V

Nulla igitur vita rationalis est sine intelligentia ; et res eatenus tantum bonæ sunt, quatenus hominem juvant, ut Mentis vita fruatur, quæ intelligentia definitur. Quæ autem contra impediunt, quo minus homo Rationem perficere et rationali vita frui possit, eas solummodo malas esse dicimus.
CAPUT VI

Sed quia omnia illa, quorum homo efficiens est causa, necessario bona sunt, nihil ergo mali homini evenire potest, nisi a causis externis ; nempe quatenus pars est totius Naturæ, cujus legibus humana natura obtemperare, et cui infinitis modis pœne sese accommodare cogitur.
CAPUT VII

Nec fieri potest, ut homo non sit Naturæ pars, et communem ejus ordinem non sequatur ; sed si inter talia individua versetur, quæ cum ipsius hominis natura conveniunt, eo ipso hominis agendi potentia juvabitur et fovebitur. At si contra inter talia sit, quæ cum ipsius natura minime conveniunt, vix absque magna ipsius mutatione iisdem sese accommodare poterit.
CAPUT VIII

Quicquid in rerum Natura datur, quod judicamus malum esse, sive posse impedire, quo minus existere et vita rationali frui queamus, id a nobis removere ea via, quæ securior videtur, licet ; et quicquid contra datur, quod judicamus bonum sive utile esse ad nostrum esse conservandum, et vita rationali fruendum, id ad nostrum usum capere, et eo quocunque modo uti nobis licet ; et absolute id unicuique summo Naturæ jure facere licet, quod ad ipsius utilitatem conferre judicat.
CAPUT IX

Nihil magis cum natura alicujus rei convenire potest, quam reliqua ejusdem speciei individua ; adeoque (per Caput VII) nihil homini ad suum esse conservandum, et vita rationali fruendum utilius datur quam homo, qui Ratione ducitur. Deinde, quia inter res singulares nihil novimus, quod homine, qui Ratione ducitur, sit præstantius, nulla ergo re magis potest unusquisque ostendere, quantum arte et ingenio valeat, quam in hominibus ita educandis, ut tandem ex proprio Rationis imperio vivant.
CAPUT X
Quatenus homines Invidia aut aliquo Odii affectu in se invicem feruntur, eatenus invicem contrarii sunt, et consequenter eo magis timendi, quo plus possunt quam reliqua Naturæ individua.
CAPUT XI
Animi tamen non armis sed Amore et Generositate vincuntur.
CAPUT XII
Hominibus apprime utile est consuetudines jungere, seseque iis vinculis astringere, quibus aptius de se omnibus unum efficiant, et absolute ea agere, quæ firmandis amicitiis inserviunt.
CAPUT XIII

Sed ad hæc ars et vigilantia requiritur. Sunt enim homines varii (nam rari sunt, qui ex Rationis præscripto vivunt), et tamen plerumque invidi, et magis ad vindictam quam ad Misericordiam proclives. Unumquemque igitur ex ipsius ingenio ferre et sese continere, ne eorum affectus imitetur, singularis animi potentiæ opus est. At qui contra homines carpere, et vitia potius exprobrare quam virtutes docere, et hominum animos non firmare sed frangere norunt, ii et sibi et reliquis molesti sunt ; unde multi, præ nimia scilicet animi impatientia, falsoque religionis studio, inter bruta potius quam inter homines vivere maluerunt ; ut pueri vel adolescentes, qui parentum jurgia æquo animo ferre nequeunt, militatum confugiunt, et incommoda belli et imperium tyrannidis præ domesticis commodis et paternis admonitionibus eligunt, et quidvis oneris sibi imponi patiuntur, dummodo parentes ulciscantur.
CAPUT XIV

Quamvis igitur homines omnia plerumque ex sua libidine moderentur, ex eorum tamen communi societate multo plura commoda quam damna sequuntur. Quare satius est, eorum injurias æquo animo ferre, et studium iis adhibere, quæ concordiæ et amicitiæ conciliandæ inserviunt.
CAPUT XV

Quæ concordiam gignunt sunt illa, quæ ad justitiam, æquitatem, et honestatem referuntur. Nam homines præter id, quod injustum et iniquum est, etiam ægre ferunt, quod turpe habetur, sive quod aliquis receptos civitatis mores aspernatur. Amori autem conciliando illa apprime necessaria sunt, quæ ad Religionem et Pietatem spectant. De quibus vide Schol. 1 et 2 Prop. 37 et Schol. Prop. 46 et Schol. Prop. 73 p. IV.
CAPUT XVI

Solet præterea concordia ex Metu plerumque gigni, sed sine fide. Adde, quod Metus ex animi impotentia oritur, et propterea ad Rationis usum non pertinet ; ut nec Commiseratio, quamvis Pietatis speciem præ se ferre videatur.
CAPUT XVII

Vincuntur præterea homines etiam largitate, præcipue ii qui non habent, unde comparare possint illa, quæ ad vitam sustentandam necessaria sunt. Attamen unicuique indigenti auxilium ferre, vires et utilitatem viri privati longe superat. Divitiæ namque viri privati longe impares sunt ad id suppeditandum. Unius præterea viri facultas limitatior est, quam ut omnes sibi possit amicitia jungere ; quare pauperum cura integræ societati incumbit, et ad communem tantum utilitatem spectat.
CAPUT XVIII
In beneficiis accipiendis et gratia referenda alia prorsus debet esse cura, de qua vide Schol. Prop. 70 et Schol. Prop. 71 p. IV.
CAPUT XIX

Amor præterea meretricius, hoc est generandi libido, quæ ex forma oritur, et absolute omnis Amor, qui aliam causam præter animi libertatem agnoscit, facile in Odium transit ; nisi, quod pejus est, species delirii sit, atque tum magis discordia quam concordia fovetur. Vid. Schol. Prop. 31 p. III.
CAPUT XX

Ad matrimonium quod attinet, certum est, ipsum cum Ratione convenire, si Cupiditas miscendi corpora non ex sola forma, sed etiam ex Amore liberos procreandi et sapienter educandi ingeneretur ; et præterea si utriusque, viri scilicet et fœminæ, Amor non solam formam, sed animi præcipue libertatem pro causa habeat.
CAPUT XXI
Gignit præterea adulatio concordiam ; sed fœdo servitutis crimine, vel perfidia ; nulli quippe magis adulatione capiuntur quam superbi, qui primi esse volunt, nec sunt.
CAPUT XXII
Abjectioni falsa pietatis et religionis species inest. Et quamvis Abjectio Superbiæ sit contraria, est tamen abjectus superbo proximus. Vide Schol. Prop. 57 p. IV.
CAPUT XXIII
Confert præterea concordiæ Pudor in iis tantum, quæ celari non possunt. Deinde, quia ipse Pudor species est Tristitiæ, ad Rationis usum non spectat.
CAPUT XXIV

Cæteri Tristitiæ erga homines affectus directe justitiæ, æquitati, honestati, pietati, et religioni opponuntur ; et, quamvis Indignatio æquitatis speciem præ se ferre videatur, ibi tamen sine lege vivitur, ubi unicuique de factis alterius judicium ferre, et suum vel alterius jus vindicare licet.
CAPUT XXV

Modestia, hoc est Cupiditas hominibus placendi, quæ ex Ratione determinatur, ad Pietatem (ut in Schol. 1 Prop. 37 p. IV diximus) refertur. Sed si ex affectu oriatur, Ambitio est sive Cupiditas, qua homines falsa Pietatis imagine plerumque discordias et seditiones concitant. Nam qui reliquos consilio aut re juvare cupit, ut simul summo fruantur bono, is apprime studebit eorum sibi Amorem conciliare ; non autem eos in admirationem traducere, ut disciplina ex ipso habeat vocabulum, nec ullas absolute Invidiæ causas dare. In communibus deinde colloquiis cavebit hominum vitia referre, et de humana impotentia non nisi parce loqui curabit : at largiter de humana virtute seu potentia, et qua via possit perfici ; ut sic homines, non ex Metu aut aversione, sed solo Lætitiæ affectu moti ex Rationis præscripto, quantum in se est, conentur vivere.
CAPUT XXVI

Præter homines nihil singulare in Natura novimus, cujus Mente gaudere, et quod nobis amicitia aut aliquo consuetudinis genere jungere possumus ; adeoque quicquid in rerum Natura extra homines datur, id nostræ utilitatis ratio conservare, destruere, vel quocunque modo ad nostrum usum adaptare nos docet.
CAPUT XXVII

Utilitas, quam ex rebus, quæ extra nos sunt, capimus, est, præter experientiam et cognitionem, quam acquirimus ex eo, quod easdem observamus, et ex his formis in alias mutamus, præcipua corporis conservatio ; et hac Ratione res illæ imprimis utiles sunt, quæ Corpus ita alere et nutrire possunt, ut ejus omnes partes officio suo recte fungi queant. Nam quo Corpus aptius est, ut pluribus modis possit affici, et corpora externa pluribus modis afficere, eo Mens ad cogitandum est aptior (vide Prop. 38 et 39 p. IV). At hujus notæ perpauca in Natura esse videntur ; quare ad Corpus, ut requiritur, nutriendum, necesse est, multis naturæ diversæ alimentis uti.

Quippe humanum Corpus ex plurimis diversæ naturæ partibus componitur, quæ continuo alimento indigent, et vario, ut totum Corpus ad omnia, quæ ex ipsius natura sequi possunt, æque aptum sit, et consequenter ut Mens etiam æque apta sit ad plura concipiendum.
CAPUT XXVIII

Ad hæc autem comparandum vix uniuscujusque vires sufficerent, nisi homines operas mutuas traderent. Verum omnium rerum compendium pecunia attulit, unde factum, ut ejus imago Mentem vulgi maxime occupare soleat ; quia vix ullam Lætitiæ speciem imaginari possunt, nisi concomitante nummorum idea tanquam causa.
CAPUT XXIX

Sed hoc vitium eorum tantum est, qui non ex indigentia, nec propter necessitates nummos quærunt, sed quia lucri artes didicerunt, quibus se magnifice efferunt. Cæterum Corpus ex consuetudine pascunt, sed parce, quia tantum de suis bonis se perdere credunt, quantum sui Corporis conservationi impendunt. At qui verum nummorum usum norunt, et divitiarum modum ex sola indigentia moderantur, paucis contenti vivunt.
CAPUT XXX

Cum igitur res illæ sint bonæ, quæ Corporis partes juvant, ut suo officio fungantur, et Lætitia in eo consistat, quod hominis potentia, quatenus Mente et Corpore constat, juvatur vel augetur ; sunt ergo illa omnia, quæ Lætitiam afferunt, bona. Attamen, quoniam contra non eum in finem res agunt, ut nos Lætitia afficiant, nec earum agendi potentia ex nostra utilitate temperatur, et denique quoniam Lætitia plerumque ad unam Corporis partem potissimum refertur ; habent ergo plerumque Lætitiæ affectus (nisi Ratio et vigilantia adsit), et consequenter Cupiditates etiam, quæ ex iisdem generantur, excessum ; ad quod accedit, quod ex affectu id primum habeamus, quod in præsentia suave est, nec futura æquali animi affectu æstimare possumus. Vide Schol. Prop. 44 et Schol. Prop. 60 p. IV.
CAPUT XXXI

At superstitio id contra videtur statuere bonum esse, quod Tristitiam, et id contra malum quod Lætitiam affert. Sed, ut jam diximus (vide Schol. Prop. 45 p. IV), nemo, nisi invidus, mea impotentia et incommodo delectatur. Nam quo majore Lætitia afficimur, eo ad majorem perfectionem transimus, et consequenter eo magis de natura divina participamus ; nec Lætitia unquam mala esse potest, quam nostræ utilitatis vera ratio moderatur. At qui contra Metu ducitur, et bonum, ut malum vitet, agit, is Ratione non ducitur.
CAPUT XXXII

Sed humana potentia admodum limitata est, et a potentia causarum externarum infinite superatur ; atque adeo potestatem absolutam non habemus, res, quæ extra nos sunt, ad nostrum usum aptandi. Attamen ea, quæ nobis eveniunt contra id, quod nostræ utilitatis ratio postulat, æquo animo feremus, si conscii simus, nos functos nostro officio fuisse, et potentiam, quam habemus, non potuisse se eo usque extendere, ut eadem vitare possemus ; nosque partem totius Naturæ esse, cujus ordinem sequimur. Quod si clare et distincte intelligamus, pars illa nostri, quæ intelligentia definitur, hoc est pars melior nostri, in eo plane acquiescet, et in ea acquiescentia perseverare conabitur.

Nam, quatenus intelligimus, nihil appetere nisi id, quod necessarium est, nec absolute, nisi in veris, acquiescere possumus ; adeoque quatenus hæc recte intelligimus, eatenus conatus melioris partis nostri cum ordine totius Naturæ convenit.
FINIS QUARTÆ PARTIS

translations.title: Part Four - On Human Bondage, or the Powers of the Affects · passage 5

paragraphs.text: I said that he is free who is led by Reason alone; who therefore is born free and remains free, has none but adequate ideas; and consequently has no concept of evil (by the Corollary of Proposition 64 of this Part), and consequently (for good and evil are correlates) neither of good. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

That the hypothesis of this Proposition is false, and cannot be conceived except insofar as we attend to human nature alone, or rather to God, not insofar as he is infinite, but insofar only as he is the cause why man exists, is evident from Proposition 4 of this Part. And this, together with the other things which we have now demonstrated, seems to be signified by Moses in that history of the first man. For in it no other power of God is conceived than that by which he created man, that is, the power by which he provided only for man's advantage; and accordingly it is narrated that God forbade free man to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and that, as soon as he ate of it, he would immediately fear death rather than desire to live.

Then, that when he had found a wife who agreed altogether with his nature, he knew that nothing could be given in Nature which could be more useful to him than she; but that, after he believed the brutes to be like himself, he immediately began to imitate their affects (see Proposition 27, Part III), and to lose his freedom; which the Patriarchs afterward recovered, led by the Spirit of Christ, that is, by the idea of God, upon which alone it depends that man be free, and that he desire for the other men the good which he desires for himself, as we demonstrated above (by Proposition 37 of this Part).
PROPOSITION LXIX
The virtue of a free man is seen to be equally great in avoiding as in overcoming dangers.
DEMONSTRATION

An affect can neither be restrained nor removed except by a contrary affect, and by one stronger than the affect to be restrained (by Proposition 7 of this Part). But blind Daring and Fear are affects which can be conceived as equally great (by Propositions 5 and 3 of this Part): Therefore equally great strength of mind, or fortitude (for its definition see the Scholium to Proposition 59, Part III), is required to restrain Daring as to restrain Fear; that is (by Definitions 40 and 41 of the Affects), a free man avoids dangers by the same virtue of mind by which he attempts to overcome them. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY

Therefore, to a free man, timely flight is ascribed to as great a strength of mind as fighting; or, a free man chooses flight with the same strength of mind, or presence of mind, with which he chooses combat.
SCHOLIUM

What strength of mind is, or what I understand by it, I explained in the Scholium to Proposition 59, Part III. But by danger I understand everything which can be the cause of some evil, namely Sadness, Hatred, Discord, etc.
PROPOSITION LXX
A free man, who lives among the ignorant, endeavors, as far as he can, to avoid their benefits.
DEMONSTRATION

Everyone judges from his own disposition what is good (see the Scholium to Proposition 39, Part III); therefore an ignorant man who has conferred a benefit on someone will appraise it according to his own disposition, and if he sees it valued less highly by him to whom it was given, he will be saddened (by Proposition 42, Part III). But a free man endeavors to join other men to himself in friendship (by Proposition 37 of this Part), and not to return equal benefits to men from their affect, but to guide himself and the others by the free judgment of Reason, and to do only those things which he himself knows to be primary: Therefore, lest he be hateful to the ignorant, and lest he comply with their appetite rather than with Reason alone, a free man will endeavor, as far as he can, to avoid their benefits. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

I say, as far as he can. For although men are ignorant, they are nevertheless men who, in necessities, can bring human aid, than which none is more excellent; and so it often happens that it is necessary to accept a benefit from them, and consequently in return to congratulate them according to their disposition. To this must be added that caution is necessary even in avoiding benefits, lest we seem to despise them, or to fear recompense through Avarice, and thus, while we flee their Hatred, incur their offense precisely thereby. Therefore, in avoiding benefits, account must be taken of what is useful and honorable.
PROPOSITION LXXI
Only free men are most grateful toward one another.
DEMONSTRATION

Only free men are most useful to one another, and are joined to one another by the greatest bond of friendship (by Proposition 35 of this Part and its first Corollary), and endeavor with equal zeal of love to do good to one another (by Proposition 37 of this Part); and therefore (by Definition 34 of the Affects), only free men are most grateful toward one another. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

The gratitude which men led by blind Desire have for one another is for the most part rather commerce or bird-catching than gratitude. Further, ingratitude is not an affect. Yet ingratitude is shameful, because it for the most part indicates that a man is affected by excessive Hatred, Anger, or Pride, or Avarice, etc. For one who, through stupidity, does not know how to repay gifts is not ungrateful; still less is one who is not moved by the gifts of a prostitute to serve her lust, nor by those of a thief to conceal his thefts, or of another like person. For such a one shows, on the contrary, that he has a steadfast mind, namely, one who suffers himself to be corrupted by no gifts to his own or the common ruin.
PROPOSITION LXXII
A free man never acts with malicious deceit, but always in good faith.
DEMONSTRATION

If a free man were to act in any way with malicious deceit, insofar as he is free, he would act so from the dictate of Reason (for only to that extent do we call him free): and therefore to act with malicious deceit would be a virtue (by Prop. 24 of this Part), and consequently (by the same Prop.) it would be more advantageous for everyone, for the preservation of his own being, to act with malicious deceit; that is (as is self-evident), it would be more advantageous for men to agree only in words, while in fact being mutually opposed, which (by Coroll. to Prop. 31 of this Part) is absurd. Therefore a free man, etc. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

If it is now asked what if a man could free himself from a present danger of death by perfidy: does not reason, in preserving his being, wholly advise him to be perfidious? The answer will be the same: if Reason advises this, then it advises it to all men, and therefore Reason altogether advises men not to make agreements, unite their forces, and possess common rights except with malicious deceit; that is, that they should not in reality possess common rights, which is absurd.
PROPOSITION LXXIII
A man who is guided by Reason is freer in a State, where he lives according to a common decree, than in solitude, where he obeys himself alone.
DEMONSTRATION

A man who is guided by Reason is not led by Fear to obey (by Prop. 63 of this Part); but insofar as he strives to preserve his being according to the dictate of Reason, that is (by the Schol. to Prop. 66 of this Part), insofar as he strives to live freely, he strives to observe the principle of common life and utility (by Prop. 37 of this Part), and consequently (as we have shown in Schol. 2 to Prop. 37 of this Part) he desires to live according to the common decree of the State. Therefore, in order to live more freely, a man who is guided by Reason desires to observe the common rights of the State. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

These things, and others like them, which we have demonstrated concerning the true freedom of man, are referred to Fortitude, that is (by the Schol. to Prop. 59, Part III), to Courage and Generosity. Nor do I think it worthwhile to demonstrate here separately all the properties of Fortitude, and much less that a courageous man hates no one, is angry with no one, envies no one, is indignant with no one, despises no one, and is least of all proud. For these things, and all things which pertain to true life and Religion, are readily established from Propositions 37 and 46 of this Part; namely, that Hatred is to be overcome by Love, and that everyone who is guided by Reason desires that the good which he seeks for himself should also be for others.

To this must be added what we have noted in the Scholium to Proposition 50 of this Part, and elsewhere: namely, that a courageous man considers especially this, that all things follow from the necessity of the divine nature, and consequently that whatever he judges to be troublesome and evil, and whatever besides appears impious, horrible, unjust, and base, arises from the fact that he conceives things themselves in a disturbed, mutilated, and confused manner; and for this reason he especially strives to conceive things as they are in themselves, and to remove the impediments to true knowledge, such as Hatred, Anger, Envy, Mockery, Pride, and the other things of this kind which we have noted above; and consequently, as far as he can, he strives, as we have said, to act well and to rejoice. But how far human virtue extends toward attaining these things, and what it can accomplish, I shall demonstrate in the following Part.
APPENDIX

The things which I have set forth in this Part concerning the right way of living are not so arranged that they can be seen at a single glance, but have been demonstrated by me in a scattered manner, according as I could more easily deduce one thing from another. I have therefore resolved here to collect the same things and reduce them to their principal heads.
CHAPTER I

All our strivings, or Desires, follow from the necessity of our nature in such a way that they can be understood either through that nature alone, as through their proximate cause, or insofar as we are a part of Nature which cannot be adequately conceived through itself without other individuals.
CHAPTER II

The Desires which follow from our nature in such a way that it can be understood through itself alone are those which are referred to the Mind insofar as it is conceived to consist of adequate ideas; but the remaining Desires are not referred to the Mind except insofar as it conceives things inadequately, and their force and increase must be defined not by human power but by the power of things which are outside us; and therefore the former are rightly called actions, but the latter passions; for the former always indicate our power, whereas the latter, on the contrary, indicate our impotence and mutilated knowledge.
CHAPTER III
Our actions, that is, those Desires which are defined by the power or Reason of man, are always good; but the rest can be as much good as evil.
CHAPTER IV

Therefore, in life it is above all useful to perfect the intellect or Reason as much as we can, and in this alone consists the highest happiness or blessedness of man; indeed, blessedness is nothing other than the very contentment of mind which arises from the intuitive knowledge of God: while to perfect the intellect is likewise nothing other than to understand God, and the attributes and actions of God which follow from the necessity of his nature. Wherefore the ultimate end of the man who is guided by Reason, that is, the highest Desire by which he strives to moderate all the others, is that by which he is borne toward conceiving adequately himself and all things that can fall under his intelligence.
CHAPTER V

Therefore no rational life exists without understanding; and things are good only insofar as they help a human being to enjoy the life of the Mind, which is defined by understanding. But those things which, on the contrary, prevent a human being from perfecting Reason and enjoying a rational life, we say are evil only.
CHAPTER VI

But since all those things of which a human being is the efficient cause are necessarily good, therefore no evil can happen to a human being except from external causes; namely, insofar as he is a part of the whole of Nature, whose laws human nature is bound to obey, and to which it is compelled to accommodate itself in almost infinitely many ways.
CHAPTER VII

Nor can it happen that a human being is not a part of Nature and does not follow its common order; but if he lives among such individuals as agree with the nature of the human being himself, by that very fact the human being's power of acting will be aided and fostered. But if, on the contrary, he is among such things as agree least with his own nature, he will scarcely be able to accommodate himself to them without a great change in himself.
CHAPTER VIII

Whatever is given in the Nature of things that we judge to be evil, or able to prevent us from existing and enjoying a rational life, we are permitted to remove from ourselves by the way that seems safer; and whatever, on the contrary, is given that we judge to be good or useful for preserving our being and enjoying a rational life, we are permitted to take for our use and to use in whatever way; and absolutely everyone is permitted, by the highest right of Nature, to do that which he judges to contribute to his own advantage.
CHAPTER IX

Nothing can agree more with the nature of any thing than the other individuals of the same species; and therefore (by Chapter VII) nothing more useful is given to a human being, for preserving his being and enjoying a rational life, than a human being who is guided by Reason. Further, since among singular things we know nothing more excellent than a human being guided by Reason, no one can therefore show more fully how much he can accomplish by skill and ingenuity than by so educating human beings that they may at last live according to Reason's own command.
CHAPTER X

Insofar as human beings are borne against one another by Envy or by some affect of Hate, they are contrary to one another, and consequently are to be feared all the more because they can do more than the other individuals of Nature.
CHAPTER XI
Minds, however, are conquered not by arms but by Love and Generosity.
CHAPTER XII

It is especially useful for human beings to join their practices together and to bind themselves by such bonds as may more fittingly make them all into one, and absolutely to do those things which serve to strengthen friendships.
CHAPTER XIII

But for these things skill and vigilance are required. For human beings are various (since those who live according to the prescription of Reason are rare), and yet are for the most part envious and more inclined to vengeance than to Compassion. Therefore, to bear with each one according to his own disposition, and to restrain oneself from imitating their affects, is the work of singular strength of mind. But those, on the contrary, who know how to censure human beings and to reproach vices rather than teach virtues, and not to strengthen but to break human beings' minds, are troublesome both to themselves and to others. Hence many, namely through excessive impatience of mind and false zeal for religion, have preferred to live among beasts rather than among human beings; just as boys or youths who cannot bear their parents' scoldings with equanimity flee to military service, and choose the hardships of war and the rule of tyranny in preference to domestic advantages and paternal admonitions, and suffer any burden to be imposed upon them, provided only that they may avenge themselves upon their parents.
CHAPTER XIV

Although, therefore, human beings for the most part govern all things according to their own desire, nevertheless far more advantages than disadvantages follow from their common society. Therefore it is preferable to bear their injuries with equanimity and to apply one's effort to those things which serve to establish concord and friendship.
CHAPTER XV

Those things which produce concord are those which pertain to justice, equity, and honesty. For human beings, besides what is unjust and unfair, also take ill what is held to be shameful, or when someone rejects the accepted customs of the state. But for conciliating Love, those things are especially necessary which concern Religion and Piety. On these, see Schol. 1 and 2 of Prop. 37, and Schol. of Prop. 46, and Schol. of Prop. 73, pt. IV.
CHAPTER XVI

Moreover, concord is usually for the most part produced from Fear, but without trust. Add that Fear arises from impotence of mind, and therefore does not pertain to the use of Reason; nor does Compassion, although it seems to present the appearance of Piety.
CHAPTER XVII

Moreover, men are also won over by generosity, especially those who do not have the means to procure the things necessary for sustaining life. Nevertheless, to bring aid to every needy person far surpasses the powers and advantage of a private individual. For the wealth of a private individual is far too unequal to supplying this. Moreover, the means of one man are too limited for him to be able to unite all to himself by friendship; therefore the care of the poor rests upon society as a whole, and concerns only the common advantage.
CHAPTER XVIII
In receiving benefits and returning gratitude there ought to be an altogether different concern, concerning which see Schol. Prop. 70 and Schol. Prop. 71, p. IV.
CHAPTER XIX

Moreover, meretricious love, that is, the lust of begetting which arises from beauty, and absolutely every Love which acknowledges a cause other than freedom of mind, easily passes into Hatred; unless, what is worse, it be a kind of madness, and then discord rather than concord is fostered. See Schol. Prop. 31, p. III.
CHAPTER XX

As regards marriage, it is certain that it agrees with Reason if the desire to unite bodies is generated not from beauty alone, but also from Love of begetting and wisely educating children; and moreover, if the Love of each, namely of the man and of the woman, has for its cause not beauty alone, but especially freedom of mind.
CHAPTER XXI
Moreover, flattery produces concord, but by the foul crime of servitude or treachery; for no one is more readily caught by flattery than the proud, who wish to be first, and are not.
CHAPTER XXII

A false appearance of piety and religion is inherent in Abjectness. And although Abjectness is contrary to Pride, the abject person is nevertheless close to the proud person. See Schol. Prop. 57, p. IV.
CHAPTER XXIII
Moreover, Shame contributes to concord only in matters that cannot be concealed. Then, because Shame itself is a species of Sadness, it does not pertain to the use of Reason.
CHAPTER XXIV

The other affects of Sadness toward men are directly opposed to justice, equity, uprightness, piety, and religion; and although Indignation seems to bear before itself an appearance of equity, nevertheless there one lives without law where each is permitted to pass judgment upon the deeds of another, and to vindicate his own right or another's.
CHAPTER XXV

Modesty, that is, the Desire to please men which is determined by Reason, is referred to Piety (as we said in Schol. 1, Prop. 37, p. IV). But if it arises from an affect, it is Ambition, or the Desire by which men for the most part stir up discords and seditions under a false image of Piety. For he who desires to assist the rest by counsel or deed, so that they may together enjoy the highest good, will strive especially to win their Love for himself; not, however, to lead them into admiration, so that a doctrine may take its name from him, nor absolutely to furnish any causes of Envy. Then, in ordinary conversation, he will beware of recounting men's vices, and will take care to speak only sparingly of human impotence; but he will speak abundantly of human virtue or power, and by what way it can be perfected; so that men, moved not by Fear or aversion, but by the affect of Joy alone, may, insofar as lies in them, endeavor to live according to the precept of Reason.
CHAPTER XXVI

Besides men, we know of no singular thing in Nature whose Mind we may enjoy, and which we can join to ourselves by friendship or by some kind of association; and therefore the principle of our advantage teaches us to preserve, destroy, or adapt in whatever way to our use whatever is given in the nature of things outside men.
CHAPTER XXVII

The advantage which we derive from things outside us is, besides the experience and knowledge that we acquire by observing them and changing them from one form into another, principally the preservation of the body; and by this reasoning those things are especially useful which can so feed and nourish the Body that all its parts may rightly perform their function. For the more apt the Body is to be affected in many ways and to affect external bodies in many ways, the more apt the Mind is for thinking (see Props. 38 and 39, p. IV). But very few things in Nature seem to be of this kind; therefore, to nourish the Body as is required, it is necessary to use many foods of diverse nature.

For the human Body is composed of very many parts of diverse nature, which continually require varied nourishment, so that the whole Body may be equally apt for all things that can follow from its nature, and consequently so that the Mind too may be equally apt for conceiving many things.
CHAPTER XXVIII

But for procuring these things, the powers of each individual would scarcely suffice, unless men exchanged services with one another. Yet money has provided a compendium of all things, whence it has come about that its image is wont especially to occupy the mind of the common people; because they can scarcely imagine any kind of Joy unless accompanied by the idea of coins as its cause.
CHAPTER XXIX

But this fault belongs only to those who seek money not from need, nor for necessities, but because they have learned the arts of gain, by which they proudly exalt themselves. The rest nourish the Body according to custom, but sparingly, because they believe that they lose from their own goods as much as they expend on the preservation of their Body. But those who know the true use of money, and regulate the measure of wealth from need alone, live content with little.
CHAPTER XXX

Since, therefore, those things are good which assist the parts of the Body to perform their office, and Joy consists in this, that the power of man, insofar as he consists of Mind and Body, is assisted or increased; therefore all those things which bring Joy are good. Nevertheless, since things do not, on the other hand, act to the end of affecting us with Joy, nor is their power of acting regulated by our advantage, and finally since Joy is for the most part chiefly referred to one part of the Body; therefore the affects of Joy (unless Reason and vigilance are present), and consequently also the Desires which are generated from them, for the most part have excess; to which is added that from affect we hold first that which is pleasant in the present, nor can we estimate future things with an equal affect of mind. See Schol. Prop. 44 and Schol. Prop. 60, Part IV.
CHAPTER XXXI

But superstition appears, on the contrary, to establish that as good which brings Sadness, and, on the contrary, that as evil which brings Joy. But, as we have already said (see Schol. Prop. 45, Part IV), no one, unless envious, delights in my impotence and inconvenience. For the greater the Joy by which we are affected, the greater the perfection to which we pass, and consequently the more we participate in the divine nature; nor can Joy ever be evil when it is regulated by the true account of our advantage. But he who, on the contrary, is led by Fear, and acts rightly in order to avoid evil, is not led by Reason.
CHAPTER XXXII

But human power is exceedingly limited, and is infinitely surpassed by the power of external causes; and therefore we do not have absolute power to adapt things which are outside us to our use. Nevertheless, we shall bear with equanimity those things which happen to us contrary to what the account of our advantage requires, if we are conscious that we have performed our duty, and that the power which we have could not extend itself so far that we might have avoided them; and that we are a part of the whole of Nature, whose order we follow. If we understand this clearly and distinctly, that part of ourselves which is defined by understanding, that is, the better part of ourselves, will be wholly content in this, and will endeavor to persevere in that contentment.

For insofar as we understand, we desire nothing except what is necessary, nor can we be absolutely content except in true things; and therefore, insofar as we rightly understand these things, to that extent the striving of the better part of ourselves agrees with the order of the whole of Nature.
END OF THE FOURTH PART
