sources.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or Human Freedom · passage 3
sources.text:
Quia corpora humana ad plurima apta sunt, non dubium est, quin ejus naturæ possint esse, ut ad Mentes referantur, quæ magnam sui et Dei habeant cognitionem, et quarum maxima seu præcipua pars est æterna, atque adeo ut mortem vix timeant. Sed ut hæc clarius intelligantur, animadvertendum hic est, quod nos in continua vivimus variatione, et prout in melius sive in pejus mutamur, eo felices aut infelices dicimur. Qui enim ex infante vel puero in cadaver transiit, infelix dicitur, et contra id felicitati tribuitur, quod totum vitæ spatium Mente sana in Corpore sano percurrere potuerimus. Et revera qui Corpus habet, ut infans vel puer, ad paucissima aptum, et maxime pendens a causis externis, Mentem habet, quæ in se sola considerata nihil fere sui nec Dei nec rerum sit conscia ; et contra, qui corpus habet ad plurima aptum, Mentem habet, quæ in se sola considerata multum sui et Dei et rerum sit conscia ; In hac vita igitur apprime conamur, ut Corpus infantiæ in aliud, quantum ejus natura patitur, eique conducit, mutetur quod ad plurima aptum sit, quodque ad Mentem referatur, quæ sui et Dei et rerum plurimum sit conscia ; atque ita ut id omne, quod ad ipsius memoriam vel imaginationem refertur, in respectu ad intellectum vix alicujus sit momenti, ut in Schol. Prop. præced. jam dixi.

PROPOSITIO XL

Quo unaquæque res plus perfectionis habet, eo magis agit et minus patitur et contra, quo magis agit, eo perfectior est.

DEMONSTRATIO

Quo unaquæque res perfectior est, eo plus habet realitatis (per Defin. 6 p. II), et consequenter (per Prop. 3 p. III cum ejus Schol.) eo magis agit et minus patitur ; quæ quidem demonstratio inverso ordine eodem modo procedit, ex quo sequitur, ut res contra eo sit perfectior, quo magis agit. Q. E. D.

COROLLARIUM

Hinc sequitur, partem Mentis, quæ remanet, quantacunque ea sit, perfectiorem esse reliqua. Nam pars Mentis æterna (per Prop. 23 et 29 hujus) est intellectus, per quem solum nos agere dicimur (per Prop. 3 p. III) ; illa autem, quam perire ostendimus, est ipsa imaginatio (per Prop. 21 hujus), per quam solam dicimur pati (per Prop. 3 p. III et gen. Affect. Defin.) ; atque adeo (per Prop. præced.) illa, quantacunque ea sit, hac est perfectior. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Hæc sunt, quæ de Mente, quatenus sine relatione ad Corporis existentiam consideratur, ostendere constitueram : ex quibus, et simul ex Prop. 21 p. I et aliis, apparet, quod Mens nostra, quatenus intelligit æternus cogitandi modus sit, qui alio æterno cogitandi modo determinatur, et hic iterum ab alio, et sic in infinitum ; ita ut omnes simul Dei æternum et infinitum intellectum constituant.

PROPOSITIO XLI

Quamvis nesciremus, Mentem nostram æternam esse, Pietatem tamen, et Religionem, et absolute omnia, quæ ad Animositatem et Generositatem referri ostendimus in quarta Parte, prima haberemus.

DEMONSTRATIO

Primum et unicum virtutis seu recte vivendi Rationis fundamentum (per Coroll. Prop. 22 et per Prop. 24 p. IV) est suum utile quærere. Ad illa autem determinandum, quæ Ratio utilia esse dictat, nullam rationem habuimus Mentis æternitatis, quam demum in hac quinta Parte novimus. Quamvis igitur tum temporis ignoraverimus, Mentem esse æternam, illa tamen, quæ ad Animositatem et Generositatem referri ostendimus, prima habuimus ; atque adeo, quamvis etiam nunc hoc ipsum ignoraremus, eadem tamen Rationis præscripta prima haberemus. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

Communis vulgi persuasio alia videtur esse. Nam plerique videntur credere, se eatenus liberos esse, quatenus libidini parere licet, et eatenus de suo jure cedere, quatenus ex legis divinæ præscripto vivere tenentur. Pietatem igitur et Religionem, et absolute omnia, quæ ad animi Fortitudinem referuntur, onera esse credunt, quæ post mortem deponere, et pretium servitutis, nempe Pietatis et Religionis, accipere sperant ; nec hac Spe sola, sed etiam et præcipue Metu ne diris scilicet suppliciis post mortem puniantur, inducuntur, ut ex legis divinæ præscripto, quantum eorum fert tenuitas et impotens animus, vivant. Et nisi hæc Spes et Metus hominibus inessent, at contra si crederent, Mentes cum Corpore interire, nec restare miseris, Pietatis onere confectis, vivere longius ; ad ingenium redirent, et ex libidine omnia moderari, et fortunæ potius quam sibi parere vellent. Quæ mihi non minus absurda videntur, quam si quis, propterea quod non credit, se posse bonis alimentis Corpus in æternum nutrire, venenis potius et lethiferis se exsaturare vellet ; vel, quia videt Mentem non esse æternam seu immortalem, ideo amens mavult esse et sine Ratione vivere : quæ adeo absurda sunt, ut vix recenseri mereantur.

PROPOSITIO XLII

Beatitudo non est virtutis præmium, sed ipsa virtus ; nec eadem gaudemus, quia libidines coercemus, sed contra, quia eadem gaudemus, ideo libidines coercere possumus.

DEMONSTRATIO

Beatitudo in Amore erga Deum consistit (per Prop. 36 hujus, et ejus Schol.), qui quidem Amor ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur (per Coroll. Prop. 32 hujus) ; atque adeo hic Amor (per Prop. 59 et 3 p. III) ad Mentem, quatenus agit, referri debet ; ac proinde (per Defin. 8 p. IV) ipsa virtus est ; Quod erat primum. Deinde quo Mens hoc Amore divino seu beatitudine magis gaudet, eo plus intelligit (per Prop. 32 hujus), hoc est (per Coroll. Prop. 3 hujus), eo majorem in affectus habet potentiam, et (per Prop. 38 hujus) eo minus ab affectibus qui mali sunt, patitur ; atque adeo ex eo, quod Mens hoc Amore divino seu Beatitudine gaudet, potestatem habet libidines coercendi. Et quia humana potentia ad coercendos affectus in solo intellectu consistit, ergo nemo beatitudine gaudet, quia affectus coercuit, sed contra potestas libidines coercendi ex ipsa beatitudine oritur. Q. E. D.

SCHOLIUM

His omnia, quæ de Mentis in affectus potentia, quæque de Mentis Libertate ostendere volueram, absolvi. Ex quibus apparet, quantum Sapiens polleat, potiorque sit ignaro, qui sola libidine agitur. Ignarus enim, præterquam quod a causis externis multis modis agitatur, nec unquam vera animi acquiescentia potitur, vivit præterea sui et Dei et rerum quasi inscius, et simulac pati desinit, simul etiam esse desinit. Cum contra sapiens, quatenus ut talis consideratur, vix animo movetur, sed sui et Dei et rerum æterna quadam necessitate conscius, nunquam esse desinit, sed semper vera animi acquiescentia potitur. Si jam via, quam ad hæc ducere ostendi, perardua videatur, inveniri tamen potest. Et sane arduum debet esse, quod adeo raro reperitur. Qui enim posset fieri, si salus in promptu esset, et sine magno labore reperiri posset, ut ab omnibus fere negligeretur ? Sed omnia præclara tam difficilia quam rara sunt.

FINIS

paragraphs.text: Quia corpora humana ad plurima apta sunt, non dubium est, quin ejus naturæ possint esse, ut ad Mentes referantur, quæ magnam sui et Dei habeant cognitionem, et quarum maxima seu præcipua pars est æterna, atque adeo ut mortem vix timeant. Sed ut hæc clarius intelligantur, animadvertendum hic est, quod nos in continua vivimus variatione, et prout in melius sive in pejus mutamur, eo felices aut infelices dicimur. Qui enim ex infante vel puero in cadaver transiit, infelix dicitur, et contra id felicitati tribuitur, quod totum vitæ spatium Mente sana in Corpore sano percurrere potuerimus.

Et revera qui Corpus habet, ut infans vel puer, ad paucissima aptum, et maxime pendens a causis externis, Mentem habet, quæ in se sola considerata nihil fere sui nec Dei nec rerum sit conscia ; et contra, qui corpus habet ad plurima aptum, Mentem habet, quæ in se sola considerata multum sui et Dei et rerum sit conscia ; In hac vita igitur apprime conamur, ut Corpus infantiæ in aliud, quantum ejus natura patitur, eique conducit, mutetur quod ad plurima aptum sit, quodque ad Mentem referatur, quæ sui et Dei et rerum plurimum sit conscia ; atque ita ut id omne, quod ad ipsius memoriam vel imaginationem refertur, in respectu ad intellectum vix alicujus sit momenti, ut in Schol. Prop. præced. jam dixi.
PROPOSITIO XL
Quo unaquæque res plus perfectionis habet, eo magis agit et minus patitur et contra, quo magis agit, eo perfectior est.
DEMONSTRATIO

Quo unaquæque res perfectior est, eo plus habet realitatis (per Defin. 6 p. II), et consequenter (per Prop. 3 p. III cum ejus Schol.) eo magis agit et minus patitur ; quæ quidem demonstratio inverso ordine eodem modo procedit, ex quo sequitur, ut res contra eo sit perfectior, quo magis agit. Q. E. D.
COROLLARIUM

Hinc sequitur, partem Mentis, quæ remanet, quantacunque ea sit, perfectiorem esse reliqua. Nam pars Mentis æterna (per Prop. 23 et 29 hujus) est intellectus, per quem solum nos agere dicimur (per Prop. 3 p. III) ; illa autem, quam perire ostendimus, est ipsa imaginatio (per Prop. 21 hujus), per quam solam dicimur pati (per Prop. 3 p. III et gen. Affect. Defin.) ; atque adeo (per Prop. præced.) illa, quantacunque ea sit, hac est perfectior. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Hæc sunt, quæ de Mente, quatenus sine relatione ad Corporis existentiam consideratur, ostendere constitueram : ex quibus, et simul ex Prop. 21 p. I et aliis, apparet, quod Mens nostra, quatenus intelligit æternus cogitandi modus sit, qui alio æterno cogitandi modo determinatur, et hic iterum ab alio, et sic in infinitum ; ita ut omnes simul Dei æternum et infinitum intellectum constituant.
PROPOSITIO XLI
Quamvis nesciremus, Mentem nostram æternam esse, Pietatem tamen, et Religionem, et absolute omnia, quæ ad Animositatem et Generositatem referri ostendimus in quarta Parte, prima haberemus.
DEMONSTRATIO

Primum et unicum virtutis seu recte vivendi Rationis fundamentum (per Coroll. Prop. 22 et per Prop. 24 p. IV) est suum utile quærere. Ad illa autem determinandum, quæ Ratio utilia esse dictat, nullam rationem habuimus Mentis æternitatis, quam demum in hac quinta Parte novimus. Quamvis igitur tum temporis ignoraverimus, Mentem esse æternam, illa tamen, quæ ad Animositatem et Generositatem referri ostendimus, prima habuimus ; atque adeo, quamvis etiam nunc hoc ipsum ignoraremus, eadem tamen Rationis præscripta prima haberemus. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

Communis vulgi persuasio alia videtur esse. Nam plerique videntur credere, se eatenus liberos esse, quatenus libidini parere licet, et eatenus de suo jure cedere, quatenus ex legis divinæ præscripto vivere tenentur. Pietatem igitur et Religionem, et absolute omnia, quæ ad animi Fortitudinem referuntur, onera esse credunt, quæ post mortem deponere, et pretium servitutis, nempe Pietatis et Religionis, accipere sperant ; nec hac Spe sola, sed etiam et præcipue Metu ne diris scilicet suppliciis post mortem puniantur, inducuntur, ut ex legis divinæ præscripto, quantum eorum fert tenuitas et impotens animus, vivant. Et nisi hæc Spes et Metus hominibus inessent, at contra si crederent, Mentes cum Corpore interire, nec restare miseris, Pietatis onere confectis, vivere longius ; ad ingenium redirent, et ex libidine omnia moderari, et fortunæ potius quam sibi parere vellent.

Quæ mihi non minus absurda videntur, quam si quis, propterea quod non credit, se posse bonis alimentis Corpus in æternum nutrire, venenis potius et lethiferis se exsaturare vellet ; vel, quia videt Mentem non esse æternam seu immortalem, ideo amens mavult esse et sine Ratione vivere : quæ adeo absurda sunt, ut vix recenseri mereantur.
PROPOSITIO XLII
Beatitudo non est virtutis præmium, sed ipsa virtus ; nec eadem gaudemus, quia libidines coercemus, sed contra, quia eadem gaudemus, ideo libidines coercere possumus.
DEMONSTRATIO

Beatitudo in Amore erga Deum consistit (per Prop. 36 hujus, et ejus Schol.), qui quidem Amor ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur (per Coroll. Prop. 32 hujus) ; atque adeo hic Amor (per Prop. 59 et 3 p. III) ad Mentem, quatenus agit, referri debet ; ac proinde (per Defin. 8 p. IV) ipsa virtus est ; Quod erat primum. Prop. 3 hujus), eo majorem in affectus habet potentiam, et (per Prop. 38 hujus) eo minus ab affectibus qui mali sunt, patitur ; atque adeo ex eo, quod Mens hoc Amore divino seu Beatitudine gaudet, potestatem habet libidines coercendi. Et quia humana potentia ad coercendos affectus in solo intellectu consistit, ergo nemo beatitudine gaudet, quia affectus coercuit, sed contra potestas libidines coercendi ex ipsa beatitudine oritur. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

His omnia, quæ de Mentis in affectus potentia, quæque de Mentis Libertate ostendere volueram, absolvi. Ex quibus apparet, quantum Sapiens polleat, potiorque sit ignaro, qui sola libidine agitur. Ignarus enim, præterquam quod a causis externis multis modis agitatur, nec unquam vera animi acquiescentia potitur, vivit præterea sui et Dei et rerum quasi inscius, et simulac pati desinit, simul etiam esse desinit. Cum contra sapiens, quatenus ut talis consideratur, vix animo movetur, sed sui et Dei et rerum æterna quadam necessitate conscius, nunquam esse desinit, sed semper vera animi acquiescentia potitur. Si jam via, quam ad hæc ducere ostendi, perardua videatur, inveniri tamen potest. Et sane arduum debet esse, quod adeo raro reperitur. Qui enim posset fieri, si salus in promptu esset, et sine magno labore reperiri posset, ut ab omnibus fere negligeretur ?
Sed omnia præclara tam difficilia quam rara sunt.
FINIS

translations.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or Human Freedom · passage 3

paragraphs.text: Because human bodies are capable of very many things, there is no doubt that they can be of such a nature as to be related to Minds which have a great knowledge of themselves and of God, and whose greatest or principal part is eternal, and therefore that they scarcely fear death. But in order that these things may be understood more clearly, it must here be observed that we live in continual variation, and, according as we are changed for the better or for the worse, are called happy or unhappy. For one who has passed from being an infant or a boy into a corpse is called unhappy; and, on the contrary, it is attributed to happiness that we have been able to traverse the whole span of life with a sound Mind in a sound Body.

And indeed, one who has a Body, as an infant or a boy does, capable of very few things and dependent in the highest degree upon external causes, has a Mind which, considered in itself alone, is scarcely conscious of itself, or of God, or of things; and conversely, one who has a Body capable of very many things has a Mind which, considered in itself alone, is greatly conscious of itself, of God, and of things. In this life, therefore, we especially strive that the Body of infancy may be changed into another which, as far as its nature permits and as is conducive to it, is capable of very many things and is related to a Mind that is very greatly conscious of itself, of God, and of things; and thus that all that pertains to its memory or imagination may be of scarcely any moment in comparison with the intellect, as I have already said in the Schol. of the preceding Prop.
PROPOSITION XL
The more perfection each thing has, the more it acts and the less it suffers; and conversely, the more it acts, the more perfect it is.
DEMONSTRATION

The more perfect each thing is, the more reality it has (by Defin. 6 p. II), and consequently (by Prop. 3 p. III with its Schol.) the more it acts and the less it suffers; and this demonstration proceeds in the same way in reverse order, from which it follows that, conversely, a thing is more perfect the more it acts. Q. E. D.
COROLLARY

From this it follows that the part of the Mind which remains, however great it may be, is more perfect than the rest. For the eternal part of the Mind (by Prop. 23 and 29 of this Part) is the intellect, through which alone we are said to act (by Prop. 3 p. III); but that which we have shown to perish is imagination itself (by Prop. 21 of this Part), through which alone we are said to suffer (by Prop. 3 p. III and the general Defin. of the Affects); and therefore (by the preceding Prop.), however great it may be, that part is more perfect than this. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

These are the things which I had resolved to demonstrate concerning the Mind, insofar as it is considered without relation to the existence of the Body; from which, and at the same time from Prop. 21 p. I and other things, it appears that our Mind, insofar as it understands, is an eternal mode of thinking, which is determined by another eternal mode of thinking, and this again by another, and so on to infinity; so that all together constitute the eternal and infinite intellect of God.
PROPOSITION XLI

Although we did not know that our Mind is eternal, we should nevertheless hold Piety and Religion, and absolutely all things which we have shown to be related to Strength of Mind and Generosity in Part Four, as primary.
DEMONSTRATION

The first and sole foundation of virtue, or of the rule of right living (by Coroll. Prop. 22 and by Prop. 24 p. IV), is to seek one's own advantage. But for determining those things which Reason dictates to be useful, we had no account of the eternity of the Mind, which we have only come to know in this fifth Part. Therefore, although at that time we were ignorant that the Mind is eternal, we nevertheless held as primary those things which we have shown to be related to Strength of Mind and Generosity; and therefore, even if we were now ignorant of this very thing, we should nevertheless hold the same precepts of Reason as primary. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

The common persuasion of the multitude seems to be otherwise. For most seem to believe that they are free insofar as they are permitted to obey lust, and that they surrender their right insofar as they are bound to live according to the prescription of the divine law. They therefore believe that Piety and Religion, and absolutely all things which are referred to Strength of Mind, are burdens which they hope to lay aside after death and to receive the price of their servitude, namely, of Piety and Religion. And they are induced to live according to the prescription of the divine law, as far as their poverty and feeble mind allow, not by this Hope alone, but also, and especially, by Fear—namely, lest they be punished after death by dreadful penalties. And if this Hope and Fear were not present in human beings, but, on the contrary, they believed that Minds perish with the Body, and that no longer life remains for the wretched, exhausted by the burden of Piety, they would return to their natural disposition and would wish to govern everything according to lust and to obey fortune rather than themselves.

These things seem to me no less absurd than if someone, because he does not believe that he can nourish his Body eternally with good food, should prefer instead to gorge himself with poisons and deadly things; or because he sees that the Mind is not eternal or immortal, should therefore prefer to be mad and to live without Reason. These are so absurd that they scarcely deserve to be mentioned.
PROPOSITION XLII
Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself; nor do we enjoy it because we restrain lusts, but, on the contrary, because we enjoy it, we are able to restrain lusts.
DEMONSTRATION

Blessedness consists in Love toward God (by Prop. 36 of this Part, and its Schol.), which Love indeed arises from the third kind of knowledge (by Coroll. Prop. 32 of this Part); and therefore this Love (by Prop. 59 and 3 p. III) must be referred to the Mind insofar as it acts, and consequently (by Defin. 8 p. IV) is virtue itself. This was the first point. Next, the more the Mind enjoys this divine Love, or blessedness, the more it understands (by Prop. 32 of this Part), that is (by Coroll. Prop. 3 of this Part), the greater power it has over the affects, and (by Prop. 38 of this Part) the less it suffers from affects which are evil; and therefore, from the fact that the Mind enjoys this divine Love, or Blessedness, it has the power to restrain lusts. And because human power to restrain the affects consists in the intellect alone, therefore no one enjoys blessedness because he has restrained the affects; but, on the contrary, the power to restrain lusts arises from blessedness itself. Q. E. D.
SCHOLIUM

With these things I have completed all that I wished to show concerning the power of the Mind over the affects, and concerning the Freedom of the Mind. From them it appears how much the wise person can do, and how much more powerful he is than the ignorant person, who is driven by lust alone. For the ignorant person, besides being agitated in many ways by external causes and never possessing true tranquillity of mind, furthermore lives as though unconscious of himself, of God, and of things, and, as soon as he ceases to suffer, at the same time ceases to be. By contrast, the wise person, insofar as he is considered as such, is scarcely disturbed in mind, but, conscious of himself, of God, and of things by a certain eternal necessity, never ceases to be, and always possesses true tranquillity of mind. If now the way which I have shown to lead to these things seems very arduous, it can nevertheless be found. And indeed, that which is found so rarely must be arduous. For how could it come about, if salvation were at hand and could be found without great labor, that it should be neglected by almost everyone?
But all excellent things are as difficult as they are rare.
THE END
