items.text: Textus quaerit utrum substantia, cuius essentia existentiam involvit, necessario existat et utrum omne ens ad talem substantiam referatur.
Quaestio de Deo transfertur in quaestionem de differentiis inter id quod in se et per se concipitur et id quod in alio atque per aliud concipitur.
Argumentatio axiomatica-deductiva distinctionem substantiæ et modi convertit in exclusionem pluralitatis substantiarum eiusdem attributi et causalitatis externæ substantiæ.
Ex improductibilitate substantiæ deducitur eius causalitas sui, necessaria existentia et infinitas.
Deus definitur ut substantia absolute infinita; ex natura substantiæ eius existentia necessaria, unitas et indivisibilitas inferuntur.
Clausura argumenti negat substantiam extra Deum et omne ens, quatenus substantia vel modus est, in Deo collocat.
Omnia quæ sunt vel in se vel in alio sunt.
Substantia est id quod in se est et per se concipitur.
Modus est substantiae affectio quae in alio est et per aliud concipitur.
Res finita in suo genere terminatur ab alia re eiusdem naturæ.
Attributum est id quod intellectus de substantia percipit tamquam eius essentiam constituens.
Ex causa determinata effectus necessario sequitur, et sine causa determinata effectus sequi non potest.
Cognitio effectus a cognitione causæ dependet eandemque involvit.
Res quae nihil commune habent per se invicem intelligi non possunt.
Idea vera cum suo ideato convenire debet.
Cuius res non existens concipi potest, eius essentia existentiam non involvit.
Causa sui est id cuius essentia existentiam involvit et cuius natura non potest concipi nisi existens.
Deus est substantia infinitis attributis constans, quorum unumquodque aeternam et infinitam essentiam exprimit.
Aeternitas est existentia quae ex sola rei aeternae definitione necessario sequitur nec per durationem vel tempus explicatur.
Substantia neque in alio est neque per conceptum alterius rei concipitur; modus contra neutram independentiam habet.
Finitudo non per rem alterius naturæ, sed solum per terminum eiusdem naturæ definitur.
Infinitum absolute non est infinitum tantum in suo genere, quia nullum attributum essentiam exprimens ab eo negari potest.
Distinctio realis attributorum non sufficit ad pluralitatem substantiarum inferendam.
Substantia non est effectus causæ externæ neque res quae ab alia substantia produci possit.
Substantia, quatenus substantia est, non est divisibilis nec ex partibus substantiam retinentibus componitur.
Natura divina non est cum affectibus humanis aut cura humana confundenda.
Substantia natura suis affectionibus prior est.
Substantiae diversa attributa habentes nihil inter se commune habent.
Res quae nihil commune habent una alterius causa esse non potest.
Distinctio rerum extra intellectum solum ex diversitate attributorum substantiarum vel ex diversitate affectionum procedit.
Duae aut plures substantiae eiusdem naturae sive attributi dari non possunt.
Una substantia ab alia substantia produci non potest.
Substantia ab alio produci non potest.
Substantia, quia ab alio produci non potest, causa sui est; ideo eius essentia existentiam involvit.
Omnis substantia necessario infinita est, quia finiri deberet ab alia substantia eiusdem naturae.
Quo plus realitatis sive esse res habet, eo plura attributa ipsi competunt.
Unumquodque attributum unius substantiae per se concipi debet.
Plura attributa per se concepta unam eandemque substantiam exprimere possunt nec pluralitatem substantiarum necessario efficiunt.
Deus, ut substantia infinitis attributis constans, necessario existit.
Substantia absolute infinita indivisibilis est.
Praeter Deum nulla substantia dari neque concipi potest.
Quicquid est in Deo est, et nihil sine Deo esse neque concipi potest.
Explicatio substantiæ non procedit per seriem productionum externarum, sed per identitatem essentiae et existentiae.
Infinitas substantiæ non est quantitas indefinita, sed exclusio omnis termini homogeneae naturae et omnis negationis essentialis.
Multiplicitas attributorum non dividit substantiam, sed maiorem realitatem eiusdem substantiae exprimit.
Unitas Dei non significat exclusionem rerum, sed exclusionem omnis substantiae exterioris; res singulares ut modi intra naturam divinam ordinantur.
Extensio et cogitatio non constituunt ordines substantiales autonomos, sed attributa Dei vel affectiones attributorum Dei sunt.
Existentia aeterna substantiae non est duratio interminabilis, sed necessitas ex sola definitione rei orta.
Falsum esse debet exemplar secundum quod omne ens, etiam substantia, ab externa causa producitur.
Falsum esse debet exemplar secundum quod existentia substantiæ contingens est et ab essentia eius separabilis.
Falsum esse debet principium quod attributa per se concepta tot substantias distinctas necessario constituunt.
Falsum esse debet principium quod definitio naturae certum numerum individuorum ex se exprimat vel explicet.
Idea clara et vera substantiae cum dubio de eius existentia componi non potest.
Possibilitas ontologica vel conceptualis alicuius substantiae extra Deum praecluditur.
Possibilitas causae internae vel externae quae existentiam Dei tollat praecluditur.
Negatio essentialis non potest ad constitutionem entis absolute infiniti pertinere.
Possibilitas quod existentia aeterna per tempus, etiam sine principio et fine, explicetur praecluditur.
In-se / in-alio → substantia / modus → dependentia conceptus modalis a substantia.
Attributum / affectio → unica forma distinctionis rerum → exclusio pluralitatis substantiarum eiusdem attributi.
Nulla communitas inter substantias diversarum naturarum → nulla causalitas mutua → nulla productio substantiae a substantia.
Nulla productio externa → causa sui → essentia involvens existentiam → substantia necessario infinita.
Substantia absolute infinita → Deus necessario existens et indivisibilis → nulla substantia extra Deum → modi omnes in Deo.
Causa sui + substantia + attributum + modus → partitio entis in id quod in se est et id quod in alio est.
Partitio entis → distinctio per attributa vel affectiones → impossibilitas pluralitatis substantiarum eiusdem attributi.
Unitas eiusdem naturae + absentia communitatis → improductibilitas substantiæ.
Improductibilitas → causa sui → existentia necessaria → infinitas substantiæ.
Infinitas absoluta + attributa infinita → Deus necessario existens.
Necessitas et infinitas Dei → indivisibilitas → exclusio omnis substantiae exterioris.
Exclusio substantiae exterioris + dependentia modorum → quicquid est in Deo est et sine Deo nec est nec concipitur.
Res non iam ut individua aequaliter primaria disponuntur, sed ut substantia per se existens et modi ab ea conceptualiter dependentes.
Pluralitas numerica substantiarum non est species generalis entium, sed quaestio limitata per attributum et per causam externam individuorum.
Deus non collocatur iuxta res ut substantia una inter plures, sed ut unica substantia extra quam nulla substantia dari aut concipi potest.
Cogitatio et extensio reclassificantur ut attributa Dei vel affectiones attributorum Dei, non ut substantiae sibi invicem externae.
Aeternitas reclassificatur ab ordine durationis ad ordinem necessitatis essentialis.
Surface — Deus necessario existit, nulla substantia praeter Deum datur, et quicquid est in Deo est.
Structural — Relatio substantiae ad modum est relatio independentiae ontologico-conceptualis ad dependentiam, cui attribuuntur causae, distinctiones et ordines entium.

Metastrategic — Dubium de Deo vel de substantiae existentia reclassificatur ut confusio inter substantiam et modificationem, inter causam externam et causam sui, aut inter pluralitatem attributorum et pluralitatem substantiarum.
Ontological/Temporal — Esse substantiae est necessarium, infinitum et aeternum; eius existentia non ex tempore, duratione aut eventu productivo intelligitur.
Axiomata de in-se, in-alio, conceptione per se, causalitate et finitudine sufficiunt ad seriem ab unitate substantiæ ad causalitatem sui, existentiam necessariam et infinitatem reconstruendam.
Validitas clausurae finalis maxime pendet ab exhaustione ontologica: praeter substantias et earum modos nihil dari ponitur.
Transitus a non-productione substantiæ per substantiam ad non-productionem substantiæ ab omni alio modorum causalitatem non plene explicat.

Cohaerentia inter distinctionem realem attributorum et unitatem numericam unius substantiae in scholiis asseritur per simultaneam attributorum existentiam, sed nexus positivus ulterius non demonstratur.
Demonstratio necessariae existentiae Dei requirit ut definitio entis absolute infiniti iam substantiam existentiae-capacem et omni attributo essentiali comprehensivam determinet.

Restitutio motum textus servat, si catena improductibilitas → causa sui → existentia → infinitas → unicitas → immanentia retinetur, dum demonstrationes alternativa et defensio indivisibilitatis tamquam clausurae confirmatoriae agnoscuntur.
The text asks whether substance, whose essence involves existence, necessarily exists and whether every being is referred to such a substance.
The question of God is transferred into the question of the differences between that which is conceived in itself and through itself and that which is conceived in another and through another.
The axiomatic-deductive argument converts the distinction between substance and mode into the exclusion of a plurality of substances of the same attribute and of the external causality of substance.
From the unproducibility of substance are deduced its self-causality, necessary existence, and infinity.
God is defined as absolutely infinite substance; from the nature of substance are inferred its necessary existence, unity, and indivisibility.
The closure of the argument denies substance outside God and places every being, insofar as it is substance or mode, in God.
Everything that is, is either in itself or in another.
Substance is that which is in itself and is conceived through itself.
A mode is an affection of substance which is in another and is conceived through another.
A thing finite in its kind is limited by another thing of the same nature.
An attribute is that which the intellect perceives of substance as constituting its essence.
From a determinate cause an effect necessarily follows, and without a determinate cause an effect cannot follow.
Knowledge of the effect depends on and involves knowledge of the cause.
Things which have nothing in common cannot be understood through one another.
A true idea must agree with its ideate.
If a non-existing thing can be conceived, its essence does not involve existence.
The cause of itself is that whose essence involves existence and whose nature cannot be conceived except as existing.
God is a substance consisting of infinite attributes, each of which expresses eternal and infinite essence.
Eternity is existence which necessarily follows from the definition alone of an eternal thing and is not explained through duration or time.
Substance is neither in another nor conceived through the concept of another thing; a mode, by contrast, possesses neither independence.
Finitude is defined not through a thing of another nature, but only through a limit of the same nature.
The absolutely infinite is not infinite merely in its kind, because no attribute expressing essence can be denied of it.
The real distinction of attributes is not sufficient for inferring a plurality of substances.
Substance is not the effect of an external cause, nor a thing that can be produced by another substance.
Substance, insofar as it is substance, is not divisible, nor is it composed of parts retaining the nature of substance.
Divine nature is not to be confused with human affections or human concern.
By nature, substance is prior to its affections.
Substances having different attributes have nothing in common with one another.
Things which have nothing in common cannot be causes of one another.
The distinction of things outside the intellect proceeds solely from the diversity of the attributes of substances or from the diversity of affections.
Two or more substances of the same nature or attribute cannot be given.
One substance cannot be produced by another substance.
Substance cannot be produced by another.
Substance, because it cannot be produced by another, is the cause of itself; therefore its essence involves existence.
Every substance is necessarily infinite, because it would have to be limited by another substance of the same nature.
The more reality or being a thing has, the more attributes belong to it.
Each attribute of one substance must be conceived through itself.
Several attributes conceived through themselves can express one and the same substance and do not necessarily produce a plurality of substances.
God, as a substance consisting of infinite attributes, necessarily exists.
Absolutely infinite substance is indivisible.
Apart from God, no substance can be given or conceived.
Whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God.
The explanation of substance does not proceed through a series of external productions, but through the identity of essence and existence.
The infinity of substance is not indefinite quantity, but the exclusion of every limit of homogeneous nature and of every essential negation.
The multiplicity of attributes does not divide substance, but expresses the greater reality of the same substance.
The unity of God does not signify the exclusion of things, but the exclusion of every external substance; singular things are ordered as modes within divine nature.
Extension and thought do not constitute autonomous substantial orders, but are attributes of God or affections of the attributes of God.
The eternal existence of substance is not interminable duration, but necessity arising from the definition of the thing alone.
The model according to which every being, including substance, is produced by an external cause must be false.
The model according to which the existence of substance is contingent and separable from its essence must be false.
The principle that attributes conceived through themselves necessarily constitute so many distinct substances must be false.
The principle that the definition of a nature expresses or explains from itself a determinate number of individuals must be false.
A clear and true idea of substance cannot be reconciled with doubt concerning its existence.
The ontological or conceptual possibility of any substance outside God is precluded.
The possibility of an internal or external cause that removes the existence of God is precluded.
Essential negation cannot belong to the constitution of an absolutely infinite being.
The possibility that eternal existence be explained through time, even without beginning and end, is precluded.
In-itself / in-another → substance / mode → dependence of the modal concept on substance.
Attribute / affection → sole form of the distinction of things → exclusion of a plurality of substances of the same attribute.
No community between substances of different natures → no mutual causality → no production of substance by substance.
No external production → cause of itself → essence involving existence → necessarily infinite substance.
Absolutely infinite substance → necessarily existing and indivisible God → no substance outside God → all modes in God.
Cause of itself + substance + attribute + mode → partition of being into that which is in itself and that which is in another.
Partition of being → distinction through attributes or affections → impossibility of a plurality of substances of the same attribute.
Unity of the same nature + absence of community → unproducibility of substance.
Unproducibility → cause of itself → necessary existence → infinity of substance.
Absolute infinity + infinite attributes → necessarily existing God.
Necessity and infinity of God → indivisibility → exclusion of every external substance.
Exclusion of external substance + dependence of modes → whatever is, is in God, and without God neither is nor is conceived.
Things are no longer arranged as equally primary individuals, but as self-existing substance and modes conceptually dependent upon it.
The numerical plurality of substances is not a general species of beings, but a question limited by attribute and by the external cause of individuals.
God is not placed alongside things as one substance among many, but as the sole substance outside which no substance can be given or conceived.
Thought and extension are reclassified as attributes of God or affections of the attributes of God, not as substances external to one another.
Eternity is reclassified from the order of duration to the order of essential necessity.
Surface — God necessarily exists, no substance apart from God is given, and whatever is, is in God.
Structural — The relation of substance to mode is a relation of ontological-conceptual independence to dependence, to which causes, distinctions, and orders of beings are attributed.

Metastrategic — Doubt concerning God or the existence of substance is reclassified as confusion between substance and modification, between external cause and cause of itself, or between plurality of attributes and plurality of substances.
Ontological/Temporal — The being of substance is necessary, infinite, and eternal; its existence is not understood from time, duration, or a productive event.

The axioms concerning in-itself, in-another, conception through itself, causality, and finitude suffice to reconstruct the sequence from the unity of substance to self-causality, necessary existence, and infinity.
The validity of the final closure depends chiefly on ontological exhaustiveness: apart from substances and their modes, nothing is posited as given.
The transition from the non-production of substance by substance to the non-production of substance by anything else does not fully explain the causality of modes.

The coherence between the real distinction of attributes and the numerical unity of one substance is asserted in the scholia through the simultaneous existence of attributes, but the positive nexus is not further demonstrated.

The demonstration of the necessary existence of God requires that the definition of an absolutely infinite being already determine a substance capable of existence and comprehensive of every essential attribute.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if the chain unproducibility → cause of itself → existence → infinity → uniqueness → immanence is retained, while alternative demonstrations and the defense of indivisibility are recognized as confirmatory closures.
Textus polemico-diagnostice examinat utrum extensio divinae naturae repugnet et utrum Dei causalitas libero arbitrio contingenti indigeat.
Argumenta contra extensionem ex falsa praesuppositione nascuntur, quod substantia corporea ex partibus finitis, mensurabilibus et realiter distinctis componatur.
Distinctio imaginationis et intellectus quantitatem ab objecto abstracto ad substantiam extensam transfert, unde extensio infinita, unica et indivisibilis intelligitur.
Definitio divinae naturae ut absolute infinitae necessitatem productionis convertit in principium: infinita infinitis modis necessario sequuntur.
Causalitas divina constituitur ut immanens, necessaria et libera ex propria natura; res particulares ut modi dependentiae causalis infinitae ordinantur.
Deus est substantia absolute infinita, necessario existens, praeter quam nulla substantia datur neque concipi potest.
Ex data rei definitione proprietates ex ipsius essentia necessario sequuntur.
Attributum est id quod essentiam substantiae exprimit; attributa Dei essentiam infinitam in suo genere exprimunt.
Extensio, quatenus substantiae attributum est, infinita, unica et indivisibilis concipitur; corpus est quantitas figura determinata terminata.
Quantitas imaginatione concepta finita, divisibilis et ex partibus composita apparet; eadem intellectu ut substantia concepta infinita, unica et indivisibilis est.
Omnia in Deo sunt et per Deum concipiuntur; res particulares sunt affectiones attributorum Dei.
Extra Deum nulla res datur quae Deum ad agendum determinare, cogere vel pati facere possit.
Ex data causa effectus necessario sequitur; non-sequentia effectus ex causa data contradictoria est.
Causa libera ex sola suae naturae necessitate existit et agit.
Essentia rei a Deo productae neque existentiam neque durationem involvit.
Deus est causa efficiens tam essentiae quam existentiae rerum, atque causa earum perseverantiae in existendo.
Omne singulare finitum et determinate existens ad existendum et operandum ab alia causa finita et determinata exigitur, et sic in infinitum.
Res a Deo ad operandum determinata se ipsam indeterminatam reddere non potest.
Deus non est corpus figura determinata terminatum neque persona humana passionibus obnoxia; negatio corporis finiti non est negatio extensionis attributivae.
Substantia extensa non est res a Deo creata vel extra Deum posita, sed attributum divinae substantiae.
Infinitas extensionis non est quantitas mensurabilis, ex partibus finitis conflata, multiplicabilis aut realiter divisibilis.
Libertas divina non est indifferentia inter producere et non producere, nec potestas effectum a causa data separandi.
Deus non agit ex impulsu externo, ex defectu interno, aut ex voluntate decreto contingenti constituta.
Deus non est causa transiens quae effectus extra se relinquit.
Res finita non est causa sui, nec principium sui actus, nec principium suae perseverantiae.
Argumenta quae extensionem a Deo removent solum ostendunt quantitatem infinitam non esse mensurabilem nec ex partibus finitis conflari posse.
Deus eiusque attributa sunt aeterna; divina existentia et divina essentia unum idemque sunt, atque attributa immutabilia sunt.
Ex necessitate naturae divinae infinita infinitis modis sequuntur, id est omnia quae sub intellectum infinitum cadere possunt.
Deus est causa efficiens rerum, causa per se et causa absolute prima, quae ex solis suae naturae legibus agit.
Deus est causa omnium rerum immanens, quia effectus in Deo sunt et nulla substantia extra Deum subsistit.
Modi particulares dependent a Deo non tantum ut incipiant existere, sed etiam quoad essentiam et continuationem existentiae.
Omnis modus necessario infinitus vel immediate ex absoluta natura attributi divini sequitur vel mediante modificatione quae ipsa necessaria et infinita est.
Ordo rerum finitarum est ordo determinationum finitarum in infinitum, in quo nulla res finita se ipsam ad agendum instituit aut a determinatione recepta liberat.
Si intellectus aut voluntas ad divinam essentiam pertinerent, a facultatibus humanis non specie graduve, sed essentia et existentia differrent.
Creatio transiens substituitur dependentia immanenti: res non extra Deum producuntur, sed Dei attributa certo et determinato modo exprimunt.
Systema duplicem ordinem causalitatis constituit: modi infiniti ex natura absoluta attributorum oriuntur, res finitae per seriem causarum finitarum determinantur.
Omnipotentia non est potentia possibilitates non actu productas reservans, sed actualitas aeterna inexhaustibilis naturae necessario productivae.
Paradoxa infiniti non afficiunt esse infinitum, sed oriuntur cum schema imaginationis, mensurae et compositionis ad substantiam transfertur.
Falsum esse debet exemplar ontologicum quo plures substantiae independentes, partes reales vel vacuum inter res subsistant.
Falsa esse debet possibilitas qua effectus divinus ab essentia divina separari possit, vel qua Deus id quod intelligit producere non possit.
Falsa esse debet assumptio quod finita individua propriam existentiam, durationem vel autonomam originem in se contineant.
Omne “extra Deum” excluditur simul ut locus substantiae, causa, conditio intelligibilitatis et terminus causalitatis.
Omne intervallum inter potentiam divinam et actualitatem divinam excluditur; divina potentia non potest esse capacitas otiosa aut futuribilis.
Quantitas imaginata → partes finitae et mensura → paradoxa infiniti → falsa exclusio extensionis a natura divina.
Substantia extensa intellecta → unitas et indivisibilitas → extensio ut attributum divinum, non ut corpus finitum.
Definitio essentiae → proprietates necessariae → attributa absolute infinita → infinita infinitis modis sequuntur.
Omnia in Deo + nulla causa extra Deum → actio ex propriis legibus → causa libera, per se et immanens.
Essentia divina existentiam involvens / essentia modi existentiam non involvens → Deus causa essentiae et existentiae modorum → dependentia perseverans.
Modus necessarius infinitus → attributum absolute consideratum vel modificatio infinita; res finita → causa finita determinans → regressus infinitus.
Corpus figuratum et passibile → falsa identificatio extensionis cum corpore finito → exclusio apparens extensionis divinae.
Divisio, mensura et multiplicatio infiniti → diagnosis imaginationis → restitutio substantiae extensae indivisibilis.
Natura divina absolute infinita → consequentia necessaria proprietatum → productio infinita infinitis modis.
Nulla exterior determinatio → actio ex natura → libertas ut necessitas sui → recusatio voluntatis indifferentis.
Omnia in Deo → causalitas immanens → modi ut affectiones attributorum → dependentia essentiae et existentiae.
Modus infinitus necessarius / res finita determinata → duplex architectura causalitatis → series finita causarum in infinitum.
Oppositio “Deus aut corpus aut incorporeus” dissolvitur per distinctionem inter corpus determinatum et extensionem ut attributum substantiae.
Infinitum non amplius classificatur per numerum, mensuram vel aggregationem partium, sed per naturam substantiae et attributi.
Libertas et necessitas desinunt esse oppositae, quia libertas divina definitur per actionem ex sola necessitate naturae.
Relatio Dei ad res redescribitur ab exteriori fabricatione ad immanentem causalitatem essentiae, existentiae et perseverantiae.
Tempus et causalitas differunt secundum gradum entis: attributa et modi infiniti aeternitatem exprimunt, res finitae ordinem determinationum finitarum.
Surface — Textus refutat argumenta quae extensionem divinae naturae indignam faciunt et definit Deum causam omnium rerum.
Structural — Argumentatio opponit imaginationem intellectui, substantiam modis, causalitatem immanentem causalitati transeunti, et determinationem necessitatemque indifferentiae.
Metastrategic — Adversariorum reductio ad absurdum retorquetur: absurdum non sequitur ex infinito, sed ex praemissis adversariorum de partibus, mensura et compositione.
Ontological/Temporal — Deus est existentia et essentia aeterna idem; res finitae essentiam ab existentia distinguunt et per seriem causarum ad utramque dependent.
Axiomata de substantia unica, attributis, distinctione imaginationis et intellectus, causalitate necessaria et dependentia modorum sufficiunt ad motum principalem restituendum.
Commissura firmissima est transitus ab errore mensurae ad indivisibilitatem substantiae, quia argumenta adversaria eodem supposito compositionali dissolvuntur.

Tensio manet inter Deum ut determinantem omne agens et rem finitam ut immediate ab alia causa finita determinatam; immanentia hanc compatibilitatem postulat, sed relatio mediationis hic non plene formalizatur.
Distinctio modorum infinitarum et rerum finitarum ordinem systematis servat, sed nexus exactus inter productionem aeternam et seriem finitam causalem compendiose tantum datur.
Refutatio extensionis pendet ex negatione vacui et ex propositionibus prioribus de substantia, quae in hoc fonte invocantur potius quam denuo demonstrantur.
De intellectu et voluntate divina conditionalis demonstratio aequivocationem cum facultatibus humanis stabilit, sed plena exclusio earum a natura divina ad demonstrationem posteriorem differtur.
Propositio de regressu causarum finitarum structuraliter necessaria est, sed demonstratio eius in fonte dato post titulum “DEMONSTRATIO” non continuatur.
The text examines, polemically and diagnostically, whether extension is incompatible with the divine nature and whether God's causality requires a contingent free will.
Arguments against extension arise from the false presupposition that corporeal substance is composed of finite, measurable, and really distinct parts.
The distinction between imagination and intellect transfers quantity from the abstract object to extended substance, whence extension is understood as infinite, one, and indivisible.
The definition of the divine nature as absolutely infinite converts the necessity of production into a principle: infinitely many things follow necessarily in infinitely many modes.
Divine causality is constituted as immanent, necessary, and free from its own nature; particular things are ordered as modes of infinite causal dependence.
God is an absolutely infinite substance, necessarily existing, besides which no substance is given or can be conceived.
From a given definition of a thing, properties necessarily follow from its very essence.
An attribute is that which expresses the essence of substance; God's attributes express infinite essence in their own kind.
Extension, insofar as it is an attribute of substance, is conceived as infinite, one, and indivisible; body is quantity determined and bounded by figure.
Quantity conceived by imagination appears finite, divisible, and composed of parts; the same quantity, conceived by intellect as substance, is infinite, one, and indivisible.
All things are in God and are conceived through God; particular things are affections of God's attributes.
Outside God no thing is given that can determine God to act, compel Him, or make Him suffer.
From a given cause an effect necessarily follows; the non-following of an effect from a given cause is contradictory.
A free cause exists and acts from the necessity of its nature alone.
The essence of a thing produced by God involves neither existence nor duration.
God is the efficient cause both of the essence and of the existence of things, and the cause of their persevering in existence.
Every singular thing that is finite and exists in a determinate manner is required to exist and act by another finite and determinate cause, and so on to infinity.
A thing determined by God to act cannot render itself undetermined.
God is not a body bounded by determinate figure, nor a human person subject to passions; the negation of finite body is not the negation of attributive extension.
Extended substance is not a thing created by God or posited outside God, but an attribute of divine substance.
The infinity of extension is not measurable quantity, compounded of finite parts, multipliable, or really divisible.
Divine freedom is not indifference between producing and not producing, nor the power to separate an effect from a given cause.
God does not act from an external impulse, an internal deficiency, or a will constituted by a contingent decree.
God is not a transitive cause that leaves effects outside Himself.
A finite thing is not the cause of itself, nor the principle of its own action, nor the principle of its own perseverance.
Arguments that remove extension from God show only that infinite quantity is not measurable and cannot be compounded of finite parts.
God and His attributes are eternal; divine existence and divine essence are one and the same, and the attributes are immutable.
From the necessity of the divine nature infinitely many things follow in infinitely many modes, that is, all things that can fall under infinite intellect.
God is the efficient cause of things, the cause through itself, and the absolutely first cause, which acts from the laws of its nature alone.
God is the immanent cause of all things, because effects are in God and no substance subsists outside God.
Particular modes depend on God not only in order to begin to exist, but also with respect to essence and the continuation of existence.
Every necessarily infinite mode follows either immediately from the absolute nature of a divine attribute or through a modification that is itself necessary and infinite.
The order of finite things is an order of finite determinations to infinity, in which no finite thing establishes itself to act or frees itself from a received determination.
If intellect or will belonged to the divine essence, they would differ from human faculties not in species or degree, but in essence and existence.
Transitive creation is replaced by immanent dependence: things are not produced outside God, but express God's attributes in a certain and determinate manner.
The system constitutes a twofold order of causality: infinite modes arise from the absolute nature of attributes, while finite things are determined through a series of finite causes.
Omnipotence is not a power reserving possibilities not actually produced, but the inexhaustible eternal actuality of a necessarily productive nature.
The paradoxes of the infinite do not affect infinite being, but arise when the schema of imagination, measure, and composition is transferred to substance.
The ontological model according to which several independent substances, real parts, or a void between things subsist must be false.
The possibility whereby a divine effect could be separated from the divine essence, or whereby God could not produce what He understands, must be false.
The assumption that finite individuals contain within themselves their own existence, duration, or autonomous origin must be false.
Every “outside God” is excluded at once as a place of substance, cause, condition of intelligibility, and terminus of causality.
Every interval between divine power and divine actuality is excluded; divine power cannot be an idle or futurible capacity.
Imagined quantity → finite parts and measure → paradoxes of the infinite → false exclusion of extension from the divine nature.
Understood extended substance → unity and indivisibility → extension as a divine attribute, not as a finite body.
Definition of essence → necessary properties → absolutely infinite attributes → infinitely many things follow in infinitely many modes.
All things in God + no cause outside God → action from its own laws → free, through-itself, and immanent cause.
Divine essence involving existence / essence of a mode not involving existence → God as cause of the essence and existence of modes → persevering dependence.
Necessary infinite mode → attribute considered absolutely or infinite modification; finite thing → determining finite cause → infinite regress.
Figured and passible body → false identification of extension with finite body → apparent exclusion of divine extension.
Division, measure, and multiplication of the infinite → diagnosis of imagination → restoration of indivisible extended substance.
Absolutely infinite divine nature → necessary consequence of properties → infinite production in infinitely many modes.
No external determination → action from nature → freedom as necessity of itself → rejection of indifferent will.
All things in God → immanent causality → modes as affections of attributes → dependence of essence and existence.
Necessary infinite mode / determinate finite thing → twofold architecture of causality → finite series of causes to infinity.
The opposition “God either body or incorporeal” is dissolved through the distinction between determinate body and extension as an attribute of substance.
The infinite is no longer classified through number, measure, or aggregation of parts, but through the nature of substance and attribute.
Freedom and necessity cease to be opposites, because divine freedom is defined through action from the necessity of nature alone.
God's relation to things is redescribed from external fabrication to immanent causality of essence, existence, and perseverance.
Time and causality differ according to the grade of being: attributes and infinite modes express eternity, finite things the order of finite determinations.
Surface — The text refutes arguments that render extension unworthy of the divine nature and defines God as the cause of all things.
Structural — The argumentation opposes imagination to intellect, substance to modes, immanent causality to transitive causality, and determination and necessity to indifference.
Metastrategic — The adversaries' reductio ad absurdum is turned back: the absurdity does not follow from the infinite, but from the adversaries' premises concerning parts, measure, and composition.
Ontological/Temporal — God is eternal existence and essence, one and the same; finite things distinguish essence from existence and depend on a series of causes for both.
The axioms concerning one substance, attributes, the distinction between imagination and intellect, necessary causality, and the dependence of modes suffice to reconstruct the principal movement.
The strongest joint is the transition from the error of measure to the indivisibility of substance, because the adversaries' arguments are dissolved by the same compositional presupposition.

A tension remains between God as determining every agent and the finite thing as immediately determined by another finite cause; immanence requires this compatibility, but the relation of mediation is not fully formalized here.
The distinction between infinite modes and finite things preserves the order of the system, but the exact nexus between eternal production and the finite causal series is given only summarily.
The refutation of extension depends on the negation of the void and on prior propositions concerning substance, which are invoked in this source rather than demonstrated anew.

The conditional demonstration concerning divine intellect and will establishes their equivocation with human faculties, but their full exclusion from the divine nature is deferred to a later demonstration.
The proposition concerning the regress of finite causes is structurally necessary, but its demonstration in the given source does not continue after the title “DEMONSTRATIO”.
Textus quaerit qua ratione res finitae et determinatae intra Deum causentur, et quomodo ex hac causalitate contingentia, liberum arbitrium et ordo rerum alternativus excludantur.
Demonstratio a discrimine incipit inter effectum infinitum atque aeternum, qui ex natura absoluta attributi sequitur, et modum finitum, qui media modificatione finita causari debet.
Series causarum finitarum in infinitum producit thesim universalem: omnia ad existendum et operandum ex necessitate divinae naturae determinantur.
Necessitas ontologica per distinctionem Naturae Naturantis et Naturae Naturatae ordinatur, ut Deus causalis et modi causati non confundantur.
Intellectus, voluntas et ceterae affectiones mentales ad Naturam Naturatam rediguntur; ideo voluntas non est principium liberum nec divinum arbitrium.
Unicitas ordinis rerum ex identitate essentiae, potentiae et causalitatis divinae deducitur; possibilitas alterius ordinis in contradictionem cum natura divina incidit.
Appendix transit ab ontologia necessitatis ad genealogiam finalismi, explicans quomodo ignorantia causarum et conscientia appetitus naturam ad fines humanos ordinatam fingant.
Omne quod determinatum est ad existendum et operandum, a Deo determinatur.
Quod ex absoluta natura alicuius attributi divini sequitur, infinitum et aeternum est.
Modus finitus et determinatam existentiam habens non sequitur ex Deo vel attributo quatenus modificatione aeterna et infinita affectum consideratur.
Modus finitus ex Deo vel attributo sequi debet quatenus modificatione finita et determinate existente modificatum est.
Quaevis causa finita et determinata ab alia causa finita et determinata causatur, et haec concatenatio in infinitum procedit.
Praeter substantiam et modos nihil datur, et modi sunt affectiones attributorum Dei.
Omnia in Deo sunt et ab eo ita dependent ut sine eo nec esse nec concipi possint.
Deus necessario existit, et modi divinae naturae necessario sequuntur atque a Deo causantur tam quatenus existunt quam quatenus agunt.
Natura Naturans est Deus quatenus attributa essentiam aeternam et infinitam exprimentia causa libera consideratur; Natura Naturata est complexus modorum necessario sequentium.
Idea vera cum suo ideato convenire debet, et in Natura nulla substantia praeter Deum nec affectiones praeter affectiones in Deo datas reperiuntur.
Intellectus actu, sive finitus sive infinitus, et ceterae affectiones cogitandi sunt modi, non absoluta cogitatio.
Voluntas, sive finita sive infinita concipiatur, causam requirit a qua ad existendum et operandum determinetur.
Res alio modo aut alio ordine produci non possunt, quia alter ordo aliam naturam divinam et consequenter plures deos posceret.
Necessitas ex essentia rei vel causa efficiente sequitur; impossibilitas ex contradictione essentiali vel absentia causae externae; contingentia et possibilitas ex cognitionis defectu oriuntur.
Potentia Dei est ipsa essentia Dei, et quicquid in divina potestate concipitur necessario est.
Omne existens divinam potentiam certo modo exprimit, atque ex natura cuiusque existentis aliquis effectus sequi debet.
Ignorantia causarum, cum conscientia appetitus coniuncta, homines disponit ut se liberos et res naturales media ad fines humanos ordinata existiment.
Mathesis essentias et proprietates figurarum, non fines, considerat atque normam veritatis a finalismo distinctam exhibet.
Modus finitus non est effectus immediatus naturae absolutae attributi nec modificationis aeternae et infinitae.
Nulla res finita est substantia independens aut ens extra affectiones divinas constitutum.
Modus a Deo determinatus se ipsum nec determinare nec indeterminatum reddere potest.
Deus non est causa remota rerum, quia nullus effectus a Deo causaliter et conceptualiter seiungitur.
Intellectus potentia non assumitur ut facultas distincta ab intellectione actuali.
Intellectus, voluntas, cupiditas et amor ad Naturam Naturantem non referuntur.
Voluntas non est causa libera, sed causa necessaria vel coacta.
Ordo rerum alternus nec natura rerum altera possibilis est.
Contingentia et possibilitas non sunt determinationes ontologicae rerum.
Deus non agit ex arbitrio voluntatis, nec Natura ex fine humano vel bono externo gubernatur.
Omnis res finita ad existendum et operandum per seriem causarum finitarum in infinitum determinatur.
Deus est causa absolute proxima rerum ab ipso immediate productarum, sed non causa remota, quia effectus divini sine Deo nec esse nec concipi possunt.
Determinatio divina complectitur non solum existentiam modorum, sed etiam certum eorum agendi modum.
Natura Naturans designat principium causale infinitum, Natura Naturata ordinem modalem ab eo necessario dependentem.
Intellectus actu finitus aut infinitus nihil comprehendit praeter attributa Dei et affectiones eorum.
Voluntas, etiam si infinita ponatur, non potest libertatem causaliter originariam possidere.
Voluntas et intellectus eodem ontologico ordine collocantur quo motus, quies et cetera naturalia.
Contingens et possibile sunt nomina epistemica rei cuius ordo causarum ignoratur, non modi reales ipsius rei.
Quicquid in potestate Dei concipitur necessario est, quia divina potentia ab essentia divina non distinguitur.
Nullum ens est causaliter otiosum, quia omne existens determinatam expressionem potentiae divinae et fontem effectus constituit.
Ordo rerum actualis non est electio inter ordines aeque possibiles, sed expressio unica naturae divinae.
Interpretatio finalis Naturae ex projectione appetituum humanorum in res ignoratis causis oritur, et in superstitionem de rectoribus Naturae convertitur.
Mathesis facultatem cognoscendi ostendit quae veritatem per essentias et proprietates, non per usus et fines, quaerit.
Systema causalitatem immanentem et clausam constituit: omnis causa, omnis effectus et omnis intelligibilitas intra Deum atque modos Dei manent.
Libertas divina a facultate eligendi inter possibilia ad necessitatem qua Deus ex propria essentia agit transfertur.
Necessitas rerum est ontologica, dum contingentia nomen est limitationis humanae cognitionis; ignorantia igitur non indicat indeterminationem rei.
Actus mentales privilegio causali privantur, quia intellectus et voluntas non sunt principia supra naturam, sed affectiones naturae productae.
Perfectionis affirmatio non designat ordinem a Deo praeoptatum, sed necessitatem qua natura divina se sine defectu et sine alternativa exprimit.
Finalismus non est explicatio causalis rivalis, sed effectus secundarius condicionis humanae quae fines proprios pro structura Naturae sumit.
Nulla causa finita prima aut seipsam originans admittitur, quia omne finitum in regressu causarum finitarum continetur.
Separatio realis inter Creatorem transcendentem et ordinem creatum negatur, quia res omnes in Deo sunt et sine eo nec esse nec concipi possunt.
Subiectum voluntarium autonomum tacite excluditur, quia omnis volitio ab alia causa determinatur.
Mundus possibilis alternativus excluditur, quia alter rerum ordo aliam naturam divinam postularet.
Ens pure passivum vel causaliter sterile excluditur, quia ex quocumque existente aliquis effectus sequi debet.
Finis, bonum et utilitas humana ut principia explicativa Naturae excluduntur, quia ex ignorantia causarum et projectione appetitus oriuntur.
Possibilitas Dei deliberantis ante ordinem rerum, inter plures ordines eligentis, systemati praecluditur.
Nulla norma veritatis, causalitatis vel bonitatis extra Deum statui potest, quia extra substantiam divinam et eius modos nihil datur.
Natura ut apparatus ad usum hominis praeparatus admitti non potest, quia talis imago finem humanum in structuram rerum transfert.
Contingentia ontica ut residuum inexplicabile vel ruptura ordinis causalis praecluditur.
Natura absoluta attributi → effectus infinitus et aeternus; modus finitus → exclusio productionis immediatae ex absoluto.
Exclusio originis absolutae modorum finitorum → mediatio per modificationem finitam → regressus causarum finitarum in infinitum.
Regressus modalium causarum + inexistentia rerum extra Deum → dependentia universalis → necessitas existendi et agendi.
Necessitas universalis → distinctio Naturae Naturantis et Naturae Naturatae → relocatio intellectus, voluntatis et affectuum inter modos.
Voluntas ut modus causatus + exclusio ordinis alterius → recusatio liberi arbitrii et decreti divini indifferentis.
Essentia divina = potentia divina → possibile in divina potestate = necessarium → omne existens = expressio activa potentiae.
Ignorantia causarum + conscientia appetitus + interpretatio utilitatis → opinio libertatis → finalismus → rectores Naturae, superstitio et iudicia anthropomorphica.
Motus demonstrativus procedit a determinatione finita ad mediationem modalem finitam, deinde ad regressum causarum et necessitatem universalem.
Necessitas universalis → Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → intellectus et voluntas ut modi → recusatio libertatis voluntariae.
Unicitas naturae divinae → exclusio ordinis alterius → identitas potentiae et essentiae → necessitas omnium possibilium.
Causalitas necessaria Naturae → genealogia ignorantiae humanae → constitutio finalismi → indicatio cognitionis mathematicae non-finalis.
Res singularis finita reclassificatur ut nodus in serie infinita determinationum modalium, non ut ens causaliter sui iuris.
Contingens et possibile transferuntur ex ontologia rerum ad epistemologiam cognitionis defectivae.
Intellectus, voluntas et affectus ex ordine principiorum regentium ad ordinem modorum naturalium causatorum transferuntur.
Dei causalitas describitur ut immanens et proxima, non ut actio remota artificis extra effectus suos posita.
Oppositio inter necessitatem et perfectionem dissolvitur, quia perfectio iam non designat optionem optimam sed expressionem necessariam naturae divinae.
Explicatio finalis rerum naturalium reclassificatur ut projectio anthropologica orta ex ignorantia causarum, non ut descriptio ordinis Naturae.
Surface — Textus affirmat nullum contingens dari, voluntatem non liberam esse, res aliter produci non potuisse, potentiam Dei eius essentiam esse, et omne existens effectum producere.
Structural — Ordinem rerum constituit catena infinita modorum finitorum, intra substantiam divinam causaliter et conceptualiter comprehensa.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio vocabula libertatis, possibilitatis, perfectionis et finalitatis ex eorum usu theologico-voluntaristico in analysin necessitatis et ignorantiae transfert.
Ontological/Temporal — Aeternitas divina nullum ante vel post decretorum admittit, dum temporalis apparentia mutationis ad seriem modorum determinatorum refertur.
Axiomata de effectu absoluto infinito, mediatione finita et regressu causarum sufficiunt ad restitutionem thesis de necessitate universali.
Fortissimum systematis cardo est nexus inter immanentiam divinam, determinationem modalem et negationem contingentiae onticae.
Distinctio Naturae Naturantis et Naturae Naturatae necessaria est ne Deus ut voluntas inter modos numerata aut modi ut substantiae independentes concipiantur.
Identificatio potentiae cum essentia Dei stabilit transitum a causalitate divina ad necessitatem omnium quae in illa potestate concipiuntur.
Commissura fragilis manet in vocabulo libertatis: Deus causa libera dicitur, voluntas autem necessaria vel coacta; distinctio pendet a definitione libertatis quae hic tantum praesupponitur.
Transitus a necessitate ordinis ad affirmationem summae perfectionis requirit notionem perfectionis quae non per electionem, bonum externum aut comparationem graduum definiatur.
Appendix genealogiam finalismi satis constituit per ignorantiam causarum et appetitum consciam, sed derivationem singulorum iudiciorum de bono, malo, merito et ordine in hoc loco adhuc promittit.
Restitutio motum textus servat, quia a causalitate finiti ad necessitatem totalem, ab hac ad demotionem voluntatis, et denique ad criticam finalismi procedit.
The text asks by what means finite and determinate things are caused within God, and how contingency, free will, and an alternative order of things are excluded by this causality.

The demonstration begins from the distinction between an infinite and eternal effect, which follows from the absolute nature of an attribute, and a finite mode, which must be caused through a finite modification.
The series of finite causes extending to infinity yields the universal thesis: all things are determined to exist and to act from the necessity of the divine nature.
Ontological necessity is ordered through the distinction between Natura Naturans and Natura Naturata, so that causal God and caused modes are not confused.
Intellect, will, and the other mental affections are reduced to Natura Naturata; therefore, the will is not a free principle or divine arbitrium.
The uniqueness of the order of things is deduced from the identity of divine essence, power, and causality; the possibility of another order falls into contradiction with the divine nature.
The appendix moves from the ontology of necessity to a genealogy of finalism, explaining how ignorance of causes and consciousness of appetite imagine nature as ordered toward human ends.
Everything that is determined to exist and to act is determined by God.
Whatever follows from the absolute nature of some divine attribute is infinite and eternal.
A finite mode having determinate existence does not follow from God or an attribute insofar as it is considered as affected by an eternal and infinite modification.
A finite mode must follow from God or an attribute insofar as it is modified by a finite and determinately existing modification.
Every finite and determinate cause is caused by another finite and determinate cause, and this concatenation proceeds to infinity.
Apart from substance and modes, nothing is given, and modes are affections of the attributes of God.
All things are in God and so depend upon him that without him they can neither be nor be conceived.
God necessarily exists, and the modes of the divine nature necessarily follow and are caused by God, both insofar as they exist and insofar as they act.
Natura Naturans is God considered as a free cause insofar as the attributes expressing eternal and infinite essence are considered; Natura Naturata is the complex of necessarily following modes.
A true idea must agree with its ideate, and in Nature no substance besides God nor affections besides the affections given in God are found.
Actual intellect, whether finite or infinite, and the other affections of thinking are modes, not absolute thought.
Will, whether conceived as finite or infinite, requires a cause by which it is determined to exist and to act.
Things cannot be produced in another way or in another order, because another order would require another divine nature and consequently several gods.

Necessity follows from the essence of a thing or from an efficient cause; impossibility, from an essential contradiction or the absence of an external cause; contingency and possibility, from a defect of knowledge.
The power of God is the very essence of God, and whatever is conceived to be in divine power necessarily is.
Everything existing expresses divine power in a determinate manner, and some effect must follow from the nature of each existing thing.
Ignorance of causes, joined with consciousness of appetite, disposes people to consider themselves free and natural things as means ordered to human ends.
Mathematics considers the essences and properties of figures, not ends, and presents a norm of truth distinct from finalism.
A finite mode is not an immediate effect of the absolute nature of an attribute or of an eternal and infinite modification.
No finite thing is an independent substance or a being constituted outside divine affections.
A mode determined by God can neither determine itself nor render itself undetermined.
God is not a remote cause of things, because no effect is causally and conceptually separated from God.
Potential intellect is not assumed as a faculty distinct from actual intellection.
Intellect, will, desire, and love are not referred to Natura Naturans.
Will is not a free cause, but a necessary or compelled cause.
Neither an alternative order of things nor another nature of things is possible.
Contingency and possibility are not ontological determinations of things.
God does not act from the arbitrium of will, nor is Nature governed by a human end or external good.
Every finite thing is determined to exist and to act through an infinite series of finite causes.
God is the absolutely proximate cause of things immediately produced by him, but not a remote cause, because divine effects can neither be nor be conceived without God.
Divine determination encompasses not only the existence of modes, but also their determinate manner of acting.
Natura Naturans designates the infinite causal principle; Natura Naturata, the modal order necessarily dependent upon it.
Actual intellect, finite or infinite, comprehends nothing except the attributes of God and their affections.
Will, even if posited as infinite, cannot possess causally original freedom.
Will and intellect are situated in the same ontological order as motion, rest, and other natural things.
Contingent and possible are epistemic names for a thing whose order of causes is unknown, not real modes of the thing itself.
Whatever is conceived to be in the power of God necessarily is, because divine power is not distinguished from divine essence.
No being is causally idle, because every existing thing constitutes a determinate expression of divine power and a source of an effect.
The actual order of things is not a choice among equally possible orders, but the unique expression of the divine nature.
The final interpretation of Nature arises from the projection of human appetites onto things whose causes are unknown, and is transformed into superstition concerning rulers of Nature.
Mathematics displays a faculty of knowing that seeks truth through essences and properties, not through uses and ends.
The system establishes immanent and closed causality: every cause, every effect, and every intelligibility remain within God and the modes of God.
Divine freedom is transferred from the faculty of choosing among possibilities to the necessity by which God acts from his own essence.
The necessity of things is ontological, whereas contingency is a name for the limitation of human knowledge; ignorance therefore does not indicate the indeterminacy of a thing.
Mental acts are deprived of causal privilege, because intellect and will are not principles above nature, but produced affections of nature.
The affirmation of perfection does not designate an order preferred beforehand by God, but the necessity by which the divine nature expresses itself without defect and without alternative.
Finalism is not a rival causal explanation, but a secondary effect of the human condition that takes its own ends for the structure of Nature.
No first or self-originating finite cause is admitted, because every finite thing is contained within the regress of finite causes.
A real separation between a transcendent Creator and the created order is denied, because all things are in God and without him can neither be nor be conceived.
An autonomous voluntary subject is tacitly excluded, because every volition is determined by another cause.
An alternative possible world is excluded, because another order of things would require another divine nature.
A purely passive or causally sterile being is excluded, because some effect must follow from whatever exists.
End, good, and human utility are excluded as explanatory principles of Nature, because they arise from ignorance of causes and the projection of appetite.
The possibility of a God deliberating before the order of things and choosing among several orders is foreclosed to the system.
No norm of truth, causality, or goodness can be established outside God, because apart from divine substance and its modes nothing is given.
Nature cannot be admitted as an apparatus prepared for human use, because such an image transfers a human end into the structure of things.
Ontic contingency as an inexplicable remainder or rupture of the causal order is foreclosed.
Absolute nature of an attribute → infinite and eternal effect; finite mode → exclusion of immediate production from the absolute.
Exclusion of the absolute origin of finite modes → mediation through a finite modification → regress of finite causes to infinity.
Regress of modal causes + nonexistence of things outside God → universal dependence → necessity of existing and acting.
Universal necessity → distinction between Natura Naturans and Natura Naturata → relocation of intellect, will, and affects among the modes.
Will as a caused mode + exclusion of another order → rejection of free will and of an indifferent divine decree.
Divine essence = divine power → possible in divine power = necessary → every existing thing = active expression of power.
Ignorance of causes + consciousness of appetite + interpretation of utility → opinion of freedom → finalism → rulers of Nature, superstition, and anthropomorphic judgments.
The demonstrative movement proceeds from finite determination to finite modal mediation, then to the regress of causes and universal necessity.
Universal necessity → Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → intellect and will as modes → rejection of voluntary freedom.
Uniqueness of the divine nature → exclusion of another order → identity of power and essence → necessity of all possibilities.
Necessary causality of Nature → genealogy of human ignorance → constitution of finalism → indication of non-final mathematical knowledge.
The finite singular thing is reclassified as a node in an infinite series of modal determinations, not as a causally self-governing being.
Contingent and possible are transferred from the ontology of things to the epistemology of defective knowledge.
Intellect, will, and affects are transferred from the order of governing principles to the order of caused natural modes.
God's causality is described as immanent and proximate, not as the remote action of an artificer positioned outside his effects.
The opposition between necessity and perfection is dissolved, because perfection no longer designates the best option but the necessary expression of the divine nature.
The final explanation of natural things is reclassified as an anthropological projection arising from ignorance of causes, not as a description of the order of Nature.

Surface — The text affirms that nothing contingent is given, that will is not free, that things could not have been produced otherwise, that the power of God is his essence, and that every existing thing produces an effect.
Structural — The order of things is constituted by an infinite chain of finite modes, causally and conceptually comprehended within divine substance.
Metastrategic — The argument transfers the terms freedom, possibility, perfection, and finality from their theological-voluntarist use into an analysis of necessity and ignorance.
Ontological/Temporal — Divine eternity admits no before or after of decrees, whereas the temporal appearance of change is referred to the series of determinate modes.
The axioms concerning the infinite absolute effect, finite mediation, and regress of causes suffice for reconstructing the thesis of universal necessity.
The strongest hinge of the system is the nexus between divine immanence, modal determination, and the denial of ontic contingency.
The distinction between Natura Naturans and Natura Naturata is necessary lest God be conceived as a will numbered among modes, or modes as independent substances.
The identification of power with the essence of God establishes the transition from divine causality to the necessity of all that is conceived in that power.
A fragile juncture remains in the term freedom: God is called a free cause, while will is necessary or compelled; the distinction depends on a definition of freedom that is here only presupposed.
The transition from the necessity of order to the affirmation of highest perfection requires a notion of perfection not defined through choice, external good, or comparison of degrees.

The appendix sufficiently establishes the genealogy of finalism through ignorance of causes and conscious appetite, but still promises here the derivation of individual judgments concerning good, evil, merit, and order.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text, because it proceeds from the causality of the finite to total necessity, from this to the demotion of will, and finally to the critique of finalism.
Textus quaerit quo fundamento doctrina finium naturalium et vocabula vulgaria, quibus Natura imperfecta appellatur, sustineri possint.
Textus statuit Naturam nullo fine agere, sed omnia ex necessitate aeterna et perfectione naturae divinae consequi.
Argumentatio polemico-diagnostica finem transformat ex causa explicante in effectum imaginationis humanae, utilitatem propriam quaerentis.
Causalitas finalis dissolvitur, quia ordinem causalem invertit, Deum indigentem facit, et regressum interrogationum in ignorantiam concludit.
Notiones boni, mali, ordinis, confusionis, pulchritudinis et deformitatis reducuntur ad affectiones imaginativas corporum humanorum.
Perfectionis aestimatio ab effectu in sensus humanos ad naturam et potentiam singularium rerum restituitur.
Omnia naturae ex necessitate aeterna naturae divinae consequuntur.
Natura nullum finem sibi praefigit.
Causa efficiens natura prior est effectu quem producit.
Effectus a Deo immediate productus perfectior est effectu qui pluribus causis intermediis indiget.
Agens qui propter finem agit id appetit quo caret.
Deus nullo bono, obiecto vel perfectione extra se indiget.
Ignorantia causarum efficientium non constituit probationem causae finalis.
Homines res bonas vel malas iudicant prout res eorum valetudini, usui vel affectionibus conducunt aut repugnant.
Imaginatio rerum dispositiones secundum facilitatem repraesentandi et recordandi ordinat.
Dispositiones imaginativae diversorum corporum et cerebrorum inter homines discrepant.
Perfectio rei ex sola eius natura et potentia aestimanda est.
Leges Naturae ad omnia producenda quae ab intellectu infinito concipi possunt sufficiunt.
Natura non est agens deliberans quod media ad finem externum disponit.
Deus non agit ad obtinendum quod nondum possidet.
Causa finalis non est principium explicativum aequale causae efficienti.
Concursus circumstantiarum ignotus non est casus qui voluntatem divinam postulat.
Admiratio corporis humani non demonstrat structuram eius esse supernaturalem vel non-mechanicam.
Ordo non est attributum Naturae extra relationem ad facilitatem humanae imaginationis.
Bonum, malum, pulchritudo et deformitas non indicant naturas intrinsecas rerum.
Imperfectio rerum non sequitur ex eo quod res sensum humanum offendunt aut utilitati humanae repugnant.
Vocabula imaginationis non sunt entia realia quae argumentis contra necessitatem Naturae adhiberi possunt.
Doctrina finium invertit relationem causae et effectus, cum effectum postulatum tamquam rationem causae antecedentis tractet.
Si res immediate productae media ad finem divinum essent, effectus ultimi praeponerentur causis prioribus contra gradum perfectionis causaliter constitutum.
Teleologia perfectionem divinam tollit, quia Deum desiderio carentis subicit.
Regressus a causa ignota ad voluntatem Dei explicandi munus non perficit, sed ignorantiam nomine causae occultat.
Notiones aestimativae et sensibiles indicant constitutionem imaginationis iudicantis, non naturam obiecti iudicati.
Dissensio iudiciorum humanorum sequitur ex varietate dispositionum imaginativarum, non necessario ex varietate naturarum rerum.
Quaestio de malis et imperfectionibus Naturae solvenda est per naturam et potentiam rerum, non per comparationem cum commodo humano.
Systema teleologicum simul producit theologicam imminutam perfectionem Dei et epistemologiam imminutam cognitionem causarum efficientium.
Humanus anthropocentrismus transformat affectiones locales corporis in iudicia universalia de constitutione Naturae.
Sublata causalitate finali, Natura apparet ut campus productionis necessariae cuius varietas perfectionum non requirit normam externam.
Stupor conservat auctoritatem interpretum tantum dum causae verae occultae manent; cognitio causarum medium illius auctoritatis evacuat.
Falsum esse debet quod utilitas humana sit mensura ontologica perfectionis rerum.
Falsum esse debet quod ignorantia causalitatis licentiam praebeat ad causam transcendentem affirmandam.
Falsum esse debet quod cognitio Naturae ex admiratione vel horrore sensibiliter constituto oriatur.
Falsum esse debet quod Deus sit artifex qui finem praeconceptum per instrumenta ordinat.
Falsum esse debet quod vocabula valoris et ordinis, quia nomina habent, res sive proprietates rerum significent.
Systema excludit omnem normam extrinsecam ex qua Natura deficiens, prava vel incompleta iudicari possit.
Systema excludit mundum factum propter hominem, quia haec possibilitas necessitatem productionis naturalis in privilegium imaginarium convertit.
Systema excludit transitum legitimam ab experientia subiectiva ad structuram metaphysicam rerum sine cognitione causarum.
Necessitas naturae divinae → productio rerum sine fine praestituto.
Productio sine fine → exclusio Dei indigentis et exclusio inversionis causae-effectus.
Ignorantia causarum efficientium + inquisitio finis → voluntas divina ut asylum ignorantiae.
Utilitas humana + imaginatio affecta → vocabula aestimativa, ordinativa et moralia tamquam modi imaginandi.
Reductio vocabulorum ad imaginationem + mensura perfectionis ex natura et potentia → dissolutio objectionis ex malo, deformitate et corruptione.
Leges Naturae amplissimae → varietas graduum perfectionis sine defectu materiae, finis vel ordinis transcendentis.
Praeiudicium finis naturalis → detectio originis humanae et utilitariae.
Finis suppositus → inversio causalitatis + imminutio perfectionis divinae.
Circumstantiae ignotae → regressus interrogationum → voluntas Dei ut nomen ignorantiae.
Utilitas et affectio corporis → bonum/malum, ordo/confusio, pulchritudo/deformitas.
Varietas imaginandi → controversia et scepticismus → distinctio imaginationis ab intellectu.
Distinctio imaginationis ab intellectu → perfectio ex natura et potentia → defensio necessitatis Naturae.
Causa finalis reclassificatur ab elemento Naturae ad figmentum humanum ex ignorantia et utilitate ortum.
Deus reclassificatur ab artifice finem quaerente ad naturam infinitam cuius productio ex necessitate sequitur.
Malum, deformitas, confusio et corruptio reclassificantur ab imperfectionibus ontologicis ad relationes imaginativas vel utilitarias.
Ordo reclassificatur ab architectura obiectiva rerum ad modum quo res imaginationi facile repraesentantur et memoriae traduntur.
Scepticismus reclassificatur ab effectu necessario cognitionis ad effectum iudiciorum fundatorum in dispositionibus imaginativis discrepantibus.
Surface — Textus negat Naturam propter finem agere et negat imperfectiones vulgo nominatas contra perfectionem Naturae valere.
Structural — Praeiudicium teleologicum generatur per concatenationem ignorantiae causarum, quaestus utilitatis et imaginationis corpore affectae.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio adversaria a quaestione “cur hoc factum est?” ad quaestionem de causis efficientibus et de conditionibus iudicii transfertur.
Ontological/Temporal — Natura constituitur ut ordo necessarius in quo prioritas causalis et gradus perfectionis non a finibus futuris, sed a potentia producente dependent.
Axiomata de necessitate Naturae, exclusionis finis et prioritate causae efficientis sufficiunt ad nucleum critique teleologiae restituendum.
Axiomata de utilitate, imaginatione et varietate corporum sufficiunt ad generationem notionum aestimativarum et controversiarum explicandam.

Nexus inter doctrinam metaphysicam necessitatis et doctrinam psychologicam imaginationis manet validus, sed transitum a dispositione corporali ad formas historicas auctoritatis tantum breviter determinat.
Firmissimum systematis punctum est reductio causae finalis ad contradictionem causalitatis inversae, indigentiae divinae et ignorantiae explicativae.

Commissura fragilis manet in reductione ordinis, pulchritudinis et valoris ad imaginationem, quia textus distinctionem inter relationem imaginativam et structuram obiectivam singulorum casuum non plene formalizat.
Restitutio motum textus servat, si necessitas Naturae, critica teleologiae, genealogia notionum vulgarium et mensura perfectionis ex natura rei in eadem catena tenentur.
The text asks on what foundation the doctrine of natural ends and the common terms by which Nature is called imperfect can be sustained.
The text establishes that Nature acts for no end, but that all things follow from the eternal necessity and perfection of the divine nature.
The polemical-diagnostic argument transforms end from an explaining cause into an effect of the human imagination seeking its own advantage.
Final causality is dissolved because it inverts the causal order, makes God needy, and concludes a regress of questions in ignorance.
The notions of good, evil, order, confusion, beauty, and deformity are reduced to imaginative affections of human bodies.
The assessment of perfection is restored from its effect upon human senses to the nature and power of singular things.
All things in nature follow from the eternal necessity of the divine nature.
Nature sets before itself no end.
An efficient cause is by nature prior to the effect that it produces.
An effect immediately produced by God is more perfect than an effect that requires several intermediate causes.
An agent that acts for an end desires that which it lacks.
God needs no good, object, or perfection outside himself.
Ignorance of efficient causes does not constitute proof of a final cause.
Human beings judge things good or evil insofar as things conduce or are opposed to their health, use, or affections.
Imagination orders the dispositions of things according to ease of representing and remembering them.
The imaginative dispositions of different bodies and brains differ among human beings.
The perfection of a thing is to be assessed from its nature and power alone.
The laws of Nature suffice to produce all things that can be conceived by an infinite intellect.
Nature is not a deliberating agent that disposes means toward an external end.
God does not act in order to obtain what he does not yet possess.
A final cause is not an explanatory principle equal to an efficient cause.
An unknown concurrence of circumstances is not chance that requires a divine will.
Wonder at the human body does not demonstrate that its structure is supernatural or non-mechanical.
Order is not an attribute of Nature apart from its relation to the ease of human imagination.
Good, evil, beauty, and deformity do not indicate intrinsic natures of things.
The imperfection of things does not follow from the fact that things offend human sense or conflict with human utility.
The terms of imagination are not real entities that can be employed as arguments against the necessity of Nature.
The doctrine of ends inverts the relation of cause and effect, insofar as it treats the postulated effect as the reason for the antecedent cause.
If immediately produced things were means to a divine end, the final effects would be preferred to prior causes, contrary to the causally established degree of perfection.
Teleology removes divine perfection because it subjects God to the desire of one who lacks.
The regress from an unknown cause to the will of God does not fulfill the explanatory function, but conceals ignorance under the name of cause.
Evaluative and sensible notions indicate the constitution of the judging imagination, not the nature of the judged object.
The disagreement of human judgments follows from the variety of imaginative dispositions, not necessarily from the variety of the natures of things.
The question of the evils and imperfections of Nature must be resolved through the nature and power of things, not through comparison with human convenience.
The teleological system simultaneously produces a theological diminution of God's perfection and an epistemological diminution of knowledge of efficient causes.
Human anthropocentrism transforms local affections of the body into universal judgments about the constitution of Nature.
With final causality removed, Nature appears as a field of necessary production whose variety of perfections requires no external norm.
Wonder preserves the authority of interpreters only so long as true causes remain hidden; knowledge of causes voids the means of that authority.
It must be false that human utility is the ontological measure of the perfection of things.
It must be false that ignorance of causality grants license to affirm a transcendent cause.
It must be false that knowledge of Nature arises from sensibly constituted admiration or horror.
It must be false that God is an artisan who orders a preconceived end through instruments.
It must be false that terms of value and order, because they have names, signify things or properties of things.
The system excludes every extrinsic norm by which Nature could be judged deficient, depraved, or incomplete.
The system excludes a world made for humankind, because this possibility converts the necessity of natural production into an imaginary privilege.
The system excludes a legitimate transition from subjective experience to the metaphysical structure of things without knowledge of causes.
Necessity of the divine nature → production of things without a pre-established end.
Production without an end → exclusion of a needy God and exclusion of the inversion of cause and effect.
Ignorance of efficient causes + inquiry into end → divine will as an asylum of ignorance.
Human utility + affected imagination → evaluative, ordering, and moral terms as modes of imagining.
Reduction of terms to imagination + measure of perfection from nature and power → dissolution of the objection from evil, deformity, and corruption.
Most extensive laws of Nature → variety of degrees of perfection without defect of matter, end, or transcendent order.
Prejudice of natural end → detection of its human and utilitarian origin.
Supposed end → inversion of causality + diminution of divine perfection.
Unknown circumstances → regress of questions → will of God as the name of ignorance.
Utility and affection of the body → good/evil, order/confusion, beauty/deformity.
Variety of imagining → controversy and skepticism → distinction of imagination from intellect.
Distinction of imagination from intellect → perfection from nature and power → defense of the necessity of Nature.
Final cause is reclassified from an element of Nature to a human fiction arising from ignorance and utility.
God is reclassified from an artisan seeking an end to infinite nature whose production follows from necessity.
Evil, deformity, confusion, and corruption are reclassified from ontological imperfections to imaginative or utilitarian relations.
Order is reclassified from an objective architecture of things to the mode in which things are easily represented to imagination and committed to memory.
Skepticism is reclassified from a necessary effect of knowledge to an effect of judgments founded on discrepant imaginative dispositions.
Surface — The text denies that Nature acts for an end and denies that commonly named imperfections count against Nature's perfection.
Structural — Teleological prejudice is generated through the concatenation of ignorance of causes, pursuit of utility, and bodily affected imagination.
Metastrategic — The adversarial argument is shifted from the question “why was this made?” to the question of efficient causes and of the conditions of judgment.
Ontological/Temporal — Nature is constituted as a necessary order in which causal priority and degrees of perfection depend not on future ends, but on productive power.
The axioms concerning the necessity of Nature, the exclusion of end, and the priority of the efficient cause suffice to reconstruct the core of the critique of teleology.
The axioms concerning utility, imagination, and the variety of bodies suffice to explain the generation of evaluative notions and controversies.

The connection between the metaphysical doctrine of necessity and the psychological doctrine of imagination remains valid, but determines only briefly the transition from bodily disposition to historical forms of authority.
The strongest point of the system is the reduction of final cause to the contradiction of inverted causality, divine need, and explanatory ignorance.

A fragile joint remains in the reduction of order, beauty, and value to imagination, because the text does not fully formalize the distinction between imaginative relation and the objective structure of individual cases.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if the necessity of Nature, the critique of teleology, the genealogy of common notions, and the measure of perfection from the nature of the thing are held in the same chain.
