items.text: Textus potentiam Mentis adversus affectus et libertatem quaerit, distinguens id quod tempori et Corpori adstrictum est ab eo quod Mentis essentiae aeternum manet.
Argumentatio demonstrativa et reconstructiva affectuum remedia ex gradu cognitionis derivat, non ex voluntaria affectuum repressione.
Idea Dei adaequata primum amorem divinum ab odio, tristitia, invidia et zelotypia segregat.
Potentia Mentis dein ad proportionem idearum adaequatarum et inadaequatarum reducitur atque per ordinationem affectuum explicatur.
Imaginatio, memoria et passiones ad durationem Corporis referuntur; essentia Corporis in Deo concepta ad aeternitatem Mentis refertur.
Cognitio tertii generis ex aeternitate Mentis procedens summam laetitiam et Amorem Dei intellectualem producit.
Amor intellectualis ut pars amoris infiniti Dei libertatem, beatitudinem, imminutam mortis metum et maiorem Mentis partem aeternam constituit.
Contemplatio Dei ex idea in nobis adaequata est actio Mentis cui tristitia non concomitatur.
Deus, qui a finito amatur, ex humana cupiditate in naturam mutabilem vel non-divinam transire non potest.
Amor rationalis erga Deum est summum bonum omnibus commune et per imaginationem gaudii communis augetur.
Vis affectus ex comparatione causae externae cum nostra, potentia Mentis ex sola cognitione, passio autem ex cognitionis privatione definitur.
Mens cognitione affectus a confusa cogitatione causae externae separat eosque secundum ordinem intellectus ordinare et concatenare potest.
Affectus ad res intellectas, proprietates communes vel Deum relati, pluribus causis fulti, affectus ex cognitione confusa ortos superant.
Imaginatio, memoria, conceptio rerum sub duratione et passiones ad actualem Corporis existentiam pertinent.
In Deo necessario datur idea essentiae cuiusque Corporis humani, quae ad essentiam Mentis humanae pertinet et aeterna est.
Tertium cognitionis genus procedit ab idea adaequata attributorum Dei ad cognitionem adaequatam essentiarum rerum singularium.
Cupiditas res tertio cognitionis genere cognoscendi ex primo cognitionis genere oriri non potest, sed ex secundo oritur.
Mens, quatenus aeternam Corporis essentiam concipit, Dei cognitionem habet et causa formalis cognitionis tertii generis est.
Ex cognitione tertii generis oritur summa Mentis laetitia cum idea Dei tamquam causae.
Amor Dei intellectualis, qui ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur, est aeternus.
Amor intellectualis Mentis erga Deum pars est amoris infiniti quo Deus se ipsum amat.
Nihil in Natura datur quod Amori Dei intellectuali contrarium sit aut eum tollere possit.
Quo Mens plura secundo et tertio cognitionis genere intelligit, eo minus ab affectibus malis patitur et eo minus mortem timet.
Corpus plurimis actionibus aptum Mentem disponit ad affectiones secundum intellectum ordinandas et ad maiorem Mentis partem aeternam constituendam.
Tristitia cum idea Dei consistere non potest; ideo Deus odio haberi nequit et Amor erga Deum in odium verti nequit.
Amor Dei non includit conatum ut Deus amantem contra amet, quia talis cupiditas Deum non-Deum esse vellet.
Amor Dei rationalis nec invidia nec zelotypia inquinatur, quia summum bonum commune non per participationem minuitur.
Cognitio clara et distincta passiones non necessario omnes absolute tollit; eas tamen minimam Mentis partem efficit.
Mens sine Corpore nihil imaginari, rerum praeteritarum recordari aut passionibus obnoxia esse potest.
Aeternitas per durationem explicari neque ad tempus referri potest.
Cognitio mutilata et confusa primi generis cupiditatem cognitionis tertii generis gignere non potest.
Nullus Amor praeter Amorem intellectualem aeternus est.
Nullum verum contrarium Amori intellectuali dari potest, quia eius destructio veritatem in falsitatem converteret.
Idea Dei adaequata Deum ab obiecto tristitiae et odii in obiectum actionis et amoris convertit.
Qui Deum amat, non potest desiderare ut Deus ipsum reciproce amet, quia amor iste mutationem divinae naturae postularet.
Communicatio Amoris Dei non est imminutio boni sed causa incrementi amoris; plures homines eodem bono fruentes amorem unius augent.
Magnitudo affectus non per se indicat potentiam Mentis, quia affectuum conflictus a viribus externis, Mentis actio autem ab ideis adaequatis aestimatur.
Animi aegritudines ex nimio amore rerum mutabilium et incompossibilium oriuntur; cognitio causalis affectus reordinat, et Amor in rem immutabilem atque vere possidendam transfert.
Cum Corpore desinunt imaginatio, memoria et passiones; manet tamen id Mentis quod per aeternam ideam essentiae Corporis in Deo concipitur.
Actualitas bifariam concipitur: vel sub certo tempore et loco, vel in Deo ex necessitate divinae naturae; sola secunda conceptio res sub specie aeternitatis exhibet.
Quo Mens aptior est cognitioni tertii generis, eo magis res eodem cognitionis genere cognoscere cupit; progressio eius ab adequate cognito procedit, non ex confusione.
Cognitio rerum singularium tertio genere Mentem efficacius afficit quam cognitio universalis secundi generis, quia ex ipsa singulari essentia dependentia a Deo concipitur.
Cognitio tertii generis summam laetitiam producit, quae cum idea Dei causae Amorem Dei intellectualem constituit atque aeternitatem eius sequitur.
Amor intellectualis Mentis erga Deum et Amor Dei erga homines idem Amor sunt, quatenus infinitus amor divinus per essentiam Mentis humanae explicatur.
Amor intellectualis, quia ex veritate aeterna necessario sequitur, non ab affectu contrario destrui potest; amoribus imaginativis et corporalibus sola temporalitas competit.
Incrementum cognitionis adaequatae et aptitudo Corporis ad plura agendum minuunt passiones malas, mortis metum et proportionem Mentis pereuntem.
Libertas non est exemptio a causalitate neque vacuitas affectuum, sed stabilis praevalentia actionum cognitivae originis super passiones ex ideis inadaequatis ortas.
Aeternitas Mentis non est proprietas indivisa totius personae empiricae, sed proportio eius quod Mentem ad essentiam aeternam referentem constituit.
Summum bonum rationaliter intellectum structuram non-rivalem habet: communicatio eius non divisionem inducit, sed causam sui incrementi.
Cognitio intuitiva rerum singularium non est applicatio secundaria universalis cognitionis, sed locus in quo dependentia divina affective efficax fit.
Corpus non est simplex impedimentum aeternitatis, sed condicio strategica qua Mens ad ordinationem affectionum et ad maiorem partem aeternam disponitur.
Falsum esse debet libertatem consistere in imperio voluntatis quod omnes affectus omnino exstinguat; systema libertatem in mutatione proportionis inter actionem et passionem ponit.
Falsum esse debet aeternitatem esse continuationem memoriae, imaginationis aut narrationis personalis post mortem; haec omnia ad durationem Corporis pertinent.
Falsum esse debet Deum esse alterum externum, cuius amor reciproce petitur aut cui tristitia passive imputatur; Deus intelligitur causa immanens, non obiectum mutuae negotiationis affectivae.
Falsum esse debet omnes cognitionis gradus aequaliter ad cognitionem intuitivam ducere; primum genus est structuraliter sterile respectu cupiditatis tertii generis.
Falsum esse debet beatitudinem esse bonum scarce distributum, cuius participatio alterius felicitatem minuere possit.
Praecluditur subiectum finitum extra Deum subsistens, quod Deum tamquam obiectum extrinsecum amet; Amor intellectualis est determinatio amoris divini ipsius.
Praecluditur mensura temporalis qua aeternitas, salus aut beatitudo aestimari possint; principium, duratio et recordatio ad ordinem aeternum non transferuntur.
Praecluditur possibilitas ut veritas aeterna actionis intellectualis per vim oppositam naturalem annihiletur; destructio amoris intellectualis falsitatem veri postularet.
Idea inadaequata + imaginatio Corporis sub duratione + amor rei mutabilis → passio, anxietas, conflictus et vulnerabilitas affectiva.
Cognitio causae + separatio ab externo confuse imaginato + ordinatio affectionum → imminutio passionis et praevalentia actionis Mentis.
Actualitas Corporis temporalis / essentia Corporis in Deo aeterna → distinctio memoriae pereuntis et partis Mentis aeternae.
Mens quatenus aeterna → cognitio Dei → cognitio tertii generis → summa laetitia → Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus.
Amor intellectualis ut pars amoris Dei + absentia contrarii → beatitudo stabilis, imminutio mortis metus et libertas affectiva.
Aptitudo Corporis ad plura agendum → ordinatio plurium affectionum → relatio earum ad ideam Dei → maior pars Mentis aeterna.
Idea Dei adaequata → actio sine tristitia → impossibilitas odii et conversionis Amoris Dei in odium.
Summum bonum commune → imminutio invidiae et zelotypiae → Amor Dei per participationem aliorum auctus.
Potentia ut cognitio → remedia per cognitionem causalem et ordinationem affectuum → imminutio passionum, non absoluta earum abolitio.
Corpus durans → imaginatio et memoria temporales; essentia Corporis in Deo → pars Mentis aeterna.
Mens aeterna → tertium cognitionis genus → summa laetitia → Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus.
Amor intellectualis ut amor divinus partialiter explicatus → nulla destructio contraria → beatitudo, libertas et imminutio mortis metus.
Affectus a scala intensitatis psychologicae ad proportionem inter causas externas, cognitionem adaequatam et cognitionis privationem reclassificantur.
Actualitas dividitur in actualitatem temporalem imaginabilem et actualitatem aeternam in Deo conceptam.
Amor Dei ab amore reciproco, possessivo et rivalitario ad laetitiam intellectualem causae divinae refertur.
Genera cognitionis in structuram asymmetricam disponuntur: primum genus tertium non generat, secundum transitum aperit, tertium essentias singulares intuetur.
Corpus ab altero aeternitatis ad instrumentum dispositionis Mentis reclassificatur.
Surface — Deus odio haberi nequit, Amor Dei intellectualis aeternus est, et Mens quatenus Corpus actu durat imaginatur atque recordatur.
Structural — Potentia Mentis ex cognitione, passio ex ideis inadaequatis, et remedia ex causali affectuum reordinatione oriuntur.
Metastrategic — Libertatis quaestio a dominio voluntario affectuum ad productionem actionum intellectualium et ad mutationem proportionis Mentis reconstituitur.
Ontological/Temporal — Duratio pertinet ad existentiam actualem Corporis, aeternitas ad essentiam eius in Deo conceptam, et Amor intellectualis ad ordinem aeternum huius essentiae.
Systema extractum argumentationem restituit, si definitiones externae idearum adaequatarum, passionis, conatus et generum cognitionis iam concessae sunt.
Catena firmissima est nexus inter ideam Dei adaequatam, actionem Mentis, cognitionem tertii generis, laetitiam et Amorem intellectualem aeternum.
Compressio relinquit indeterminatum quomodo notiones adaequationis, inadaequationis et causae formalis intra hunc locum sola constitui possint, quia textus eas ex Partibus prioribus accipit.
Commissura fragilis manet inter absentiam memoriae ante Corpus et assertionem quod nos aeternos sentimus ac experimur; transitio a demonstratione ad experientiam hic non independenter mechanizatur.

Tensio temporalis manet inter Amorem intellectualem sine principio et narrationem qua Mens paulatim aptior ad cognitionem tertii generis fit; textus hanc tensionem per fictionem expositionis temporalis administrat, non removet.

Commissura inter aptitudinem Corporis et maiorem partem Mentis aeternam pendet a longa catena ordinationis affectionum, relationis ad Deum et amoris crescentis, cuius nexus non hic separatim demonstratur.
Restitutio motum textus servat: remedia affectuum → distinctio durationis et aeternitatis → cognitio intuitiva → Amor Dei intellectualis → libertas et imminutio mortis metus.

translations.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or on Human Freedom · passage 2

items.text: The text investigates the power of the Mind over the affects and freedom, distinguishing what is bound to time and the Body from what remains eternal to the essence of the Mind.
Demonstrative and reconstructive argument derives remedies for the affects from the degree of knowledge, not from voluntary repression of the affects.
An adequate idea of God first separates divine love from hatred, sadness, envy, and jealousy.
The power of the Mind is then reduced to the proportion of adequate and inadequate ideas and explained through the ordering of the affects.
Imagination, memory, and passions are referred to the duration of the Body; the essence of the Body conceived in God is referred to the eternity of the Mind.
Knowledge of the third kind, proceeding from the eternity of the Mind, produces the highest joy and the intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love, as a part of God's infinite love, constitutes freedom, blessedness, diminished fear of death, and the greater eternal part of the Mind.
Contemplation of God from an adequate idea in us is an action of the Mind not accompanied by sadness.
God, who is loved by a finite being, cannot, through human desire, pass into a mutable or non-divine nature.
Rational love toward God is the highest good common to all and is increased through the imagination of common joy.
The force of an affect is defined by comparison of the external cause with our own, the power of the Mind by knowledge alone, and passion by the privation of knowledge.
By knowledge the Mind separates an affect from the confused thought of an external cause and can order and connect affects according to the order of the intellect.
Affects referred to things understood, common properties, or God, supported by several causes, overcome affects arising from confused knowledge.
Imagination, memory, the conception of things under duration, and passions pertain to the actual existence of the Body.
In God there is necessarily given an idea of the essence of each human Body, which pertains to the essence of the human Mind and is eternal.
The third kind of knowledge proceeds from an adequate idea of God's attributes to the adequate knowledge of the essences of singular things.
The desire to know things by the third kind of knowledge cannot arise from the first kind of knowledge, but arises from the second.
The Mind, insofar as it conceives the eternal essence of the Body, has knowledge of God and is the formal cause of knowledge of the third kind.
From knowledge of the third kind arises the Mind's highest joy, together with the idea of God as cause.
The intellectual Love of God, which arises from the third kind of knowledge, is eternal.
The intellectual Love of the Mind toward God is a part of the infinite love by which God loves himself.
Nothing is given in Nature that is contrary to the intellectual Love of God or can remove it.
The more the Mind understands by the second and third kinds of knowledge, the less it suffers from evil affects and the less it fears death.
A Body suited to very many actions disposes the Mind to order affections according to the intellect and to constitute a greater eternal part of the Mind.
Sadness cannot coexist with the idea of God; therefore God cannot be hated, and Love toward God cannot be turned into hatred.
Love of God does not include the striving that God should love the lover in return, because such desire would will God to be non-God.
Rational Love of God is polluted by neither envy nor jealousy, because the common highest good is not diminished through participation.
Clear and distinct knowledge does not necessarily abolish all passions absolutely; nevertheless, it makes them the smallest part of the Mind.
Without the Body the Mind can imagine nothing, recall past things, or be subject to passions.
Eternity can neither be explained through duration nor referred to time.
Mutilated and confused knowledge of the first kind cannot generate the desire for knowledge of the third kind.
No Love other than intellectual Love is eternal.
No truth contrary to intellectual Love can be given, because its destruction would convert truth into falsehood.
An adequate idea of God transforms God from an object of sadness and hatred into an object of action and love.
One who loves God cannot desire that God love him in return, because that love would require a change in divine nature.
The sharing of Love of God is not a diminution of good but a cause of the increase of love; more people enjoying the same good increase the love of one.

The magnitude of an affect does not in itself indicate the power of the Mind, because the conflict of affects is assessed from external forces, whereas the action of the Mind is assessed from adequate ideas.
Ailments of the mind arise from excessive love of mutable and incompatible things; causal knowledge reorders affects and transfers Love to an immutable thing that can truly be possessed.
With the Body, imagination, memory, and passions cease; yet there remains that of the Mind which is conceived through the eternal idea of the essence of the Body in God.
Actuality is conceived in two ways: either under a determinate time and place, or in God from the necessity of divine nature; only the second conception presents things under the aspect of eternity.
The more suited the Mind is to knowledge of the third kind, the more it desires to know things by the same kind of knowledge; its progress proceeds from what is adequately known, not from confusion.

Knowledge of singular things by the third kind affects the Mind more efficaciously than universal knowledge of the second kind, because from the singular essence itself dependence on God is conceived.
Knowledge of the third kind produces the highest joy, which, together with the idea of God as cause, constitutes the intellectual Love of God and entails its eternity.
The intellectual Love of the Mind toward God and God's Love toward human beings are the same Love, insofar as infinite divine love is explained through the essence of the human Mind.
Intellectual Love, because it necessarily follows from eternal truth, cannot be destroyed by a contrary affect; imaginative and bodily loves belong to temporality alone.
The increase of adequate knowledge and the aptitude of the Body for doing more things diminish evil passions, fear of death, and the perishing proportion of the Mind.
Freedom is neither exemption from causality nor emptiness of affects, but the stable predominance of actions of cognitive origin over passions arising from inadequate ideas.
The eternity of the Mind is not an undivided property of the entire empirical person, but the proportion of that which constitutes the Mind as referring to eternal essence.
The highest good, rationally understood, has a non-rivalrous structure: its sharing does not introduce division but the cause of its own increase.
Intuitive knowledge of singular things is not a secondary application of universal knowledge, but the locus in which divine dependence becomes affectively efficacious.
The Body is not a mere impediment to eternity, but a strategic condition by which the Mind is disposed to the ordering of affections and to a greater eternal part.
It must be false that freedom consists in a command of the will that wholly extinguishes all affects; the system places freedom in a change of proportion between action and passion.
It must be false that eternity is a continuation of memory, imagination, or personal narrative after death; all these pertain to the duration of the Body.

It must be false that God is an external other, whose love is reciprocally sought or to whom sadness is passively imputed; God is understood as immanent cause, not as an object of mutual affective negotiation.
It must be false that all degrees of knowledge equally lead to intuitive knowledge; the first kind is structurally sterile with respect to the desire of the third kind.
It must be false that blessedness is a scarce-distributed good, participation in which could diminish another's happiness.
A finite subject subsisting outside God, which loves God as an extrinsic object, is precluded; intellectual Love is a determination of divine love itself.
A temporal measure by which eternity, salvation, or blessedness could be assessed is precluded; beginning, duration, and recollection are not transferred to the eternal order.
The possibility that the eternal truth of intellectual action be annihilated by an opposed natural force is precluded; the destruction of intellectual Love would require the falsehood of truth.
Inadequate idea + imagination of the Body under duration + love of a mutable thing → passion, anxiety, conflict, and affective vulnerability.
Knowledge of the cause + separation from the externally and confusedly imagined + ordering of affections → diminution of passion and predominance of the Mind's action.
Temporal actuality of the Body / eternal essence of the Body in God → distinction between perishing memory and the eternal part of the Mind.
Mind insofar as eternal → knowledge of God → knowledge of the third kind → highest joy → eternal intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love as part of God's love + absence of a contrary → stable blessedness, diminution of fear of death, and affective freedom.
Aptitude of the Body for doing more things → ordering of more affections → their relation to the idea of God → greater eternal part of the Mind.
Adequate idea of God → action without sadness → impossibility of hatred and of the conversion of Love of God into hatred.
Common highest good → diminution of envy and jealousy → Love of God increased through the participation of others.
Power as knowledge → remedies through causal knowledge and ordering of affects → diminution of passions, not their absolute abolition.
Durable Body → temporal imagination and memory; essence of the Body in God → eternal part of the Mind.
Eternal Mind → third kind of knowledge → highest joy → eternal intellectual Love of God.
Intellectual Love as partially explained divine love → no contrary destruction → blessedness, freedom, and diminution of fear of death.
Affects are reclassified from a scale of psychological intensity to a proportion among external causes, adequate knowledge, and privation of knowledge.
Actuality is divided into imaginable temporal actuality and eternal actuality conceived in God.
Love of God is referred away from reciprocal, possessive, and rivalrous love to intellectual joy in the divine cause.
The kinds of knowledge are arranged in an asymmetric structure: the first kind does not generate the third, the second opens the transition, and the third intuits singular essences.
The Body is reclassified from the other of eternity to an instrument for disposing the Mind.
Surface — God cannot be hated, intellectual Love of God is eternal, and the Mind, insofar as the Body actually endures, imagines and remembers.
Structural — The power of the Mind arises from knowledge, passion from inadequate ideas, and remedies from the causal reordering of affects.
Metastrategic — The question of freedom is reconstituted from voluntary mastery of affects to the production of intellectual actions and to a change in the proportion of the Mind.
Ontological/Temporal — Duration pertains to the actual existence of the Body, eternity to its essence conceived in God, and intellectual Love to the eternal order of this essence.
The extracted system restores the argumentation if the external definitions of adequate ideas, passion, conatus, and the kinds of knowledge have already been granted.
The firmest chain is the connection among the adequate idea of God, the action of the Mind, knowledge of the third kind, joy, and eternal intellectual Love.
The compression leaves indeterminate how the notions of adequacy, inadequacy, and formal cause can be constituted solely within this passage, because the text receives them from the prior Parts.

A fragile joint remains between the absence of memory before the Body and the assertion that we feel and experience ourselves to be eternal; the transition from demonstration to experience is not independently mechanized here.

A temporal tension remains between intellectual Love without beginning and the narrative by which the Mind gradually becomes more suited to knowledge of the third kind; the text manages this tension through the fiction of temporal exposition, rather than removing it.

The joint between the aptitude of the Body and the greater eternal part of the Mind depends upon a long chain of ordering affections, relation to God, and increasing love, whose connection is not separately demonstrated here.

The restoration preserves the movement of the text: remedies for affects → distinction of duration and eternity → intuitive knowledge → intellectual Love of God → freedom and diminution of fear of death.

items.text: Textus variationem corporis et mentis constituit ut condicionem ex qua felicitas, infelicitas et ordinatio vitae intelligendae sunt.
Capacitas corporis ad plura agendum cum ampliore mentis conscientia sui, Dei et rerum conectitur, ita ut transformatio corporis ad intellectum dirigatur.
Perfectio ex gradu agendi et imminutis passionibus definitur; hinc intellectus aeternus imaginatione pereunte perfectior demonstratur.
Fundamentum virtutis ab cognitione immortalitatis removetur et in rationali quaesitione proprii utilis collocatur.
Beatitudo non consequens disciplinae affectuum, sed amor intellectualis Dei, virtus ipsa et fons potestatis affectus coercendi constituitur.
Textus oppositionem inter ignarum externis causis et libidine actum atque sapientem ex necessitate aeterna intelligentem concludit.
Res eo perfectior est quo magis agit et quo minus patitur; perfectio, realitas et potentia agendi eundem gradum exprimunt.
Intellectus est pars mentis aeterna, imaginatio autem pars quae perire dicitur.
Mens per intellectum agit et per imaginationem patitur.
Unicum fundamentum virtutis seu recte vivendi est proprium utile ratione quaerere.
Praecepta rationis de pietate, religione, animositate et generositate ex cognitione aeternitatis mentis non dependent.
Beatitudo consistit in amore erga Deum qui ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur.
Amor intellectualis Dei, quatenus ad mentem agentem refertur, ipsa virtus est.
Quo mens beatitudine magis gaudet, eo plus intelligit, maiorem in affectus potentiam habet et minus ab affectibus malis patitur.
Corpus ad plura aptum menti respondet quae amplius sui, Dei et rerum conscia est; vita igitur ad hanc aptitudinem, quantum natura fert, ordinari potest.
Mens, quatenus intelligit, est modus cogitandi aeternus ab aliis modis aeternis in infinitum determinatus.
Virtus non definitur per spem praemii post mortem nec per metum supplicii post mortem.
Pietas, religio, animositas et generositas non sunt onera servilia quae solum compensatione ultramortali tolerari possint.
Beatitudo non est praemium virtutis neque effectus posterior coercitionis libidinum.
Libertas non est licentia libidini parendi neque imminutio iuris ex sola observantia legis externa recepta.
Pars mentis imaginativa non est locus eius perfectionis quae post corporis existentiam considerari potest.
Sapientia non consistit in evadenda necessitate, sed in eius aeternae cognitionis forma.
Pars mentis quae manet perfectior est reliqua, quia per intellectum agit, dum imaginatio peritura passionum sedes manet.
Ratio pietatem et fortitudinem exigere potest etiam sub ignorantia aeternitatis mentis, quia earum norma est utile rationale, non destinatio post mortem.
Coercitio libidinum non producit beatitudinem; beatitudo, intellectum augens, ipsam coercendi potentiam producit.
Vita rationalis non requirit oppugnationem affectuum ut finem primarium, sed incrementum intellectus ex quo imminutio passionum sequitur.
Institutio vitae tendit ad corpus aptius et mentem magis consciam, ut memoria et imaginatio respectu intellectus minorem vim obtineant.
Stabilitas animi sapientis oritur ex intellectione necessitatis, dum ignorantia externarum causarum et libidinum imperio mentem fluctuantem relinquit.
Ordo ethicus a ratione mercedis differtur ad immanentiam: virtus suum effectum constitutivum, beatitudinem, intra ipsum exercitium habet.
Ordo liberationis est epistemicus et affectivus simul: cognitio non affectibus extrinsece additur, sed potentiam activam qua affectus ordinantur efficit.
Discrimen sapientis et ignari non in possessione futuri praemii, sed in diverso modo praesentis existentiae consistit: alter agit et intelligit, alter patitur et quasi inscius vivit.
Corpus non est mera sarcina mortalitatis, sed condicio practica qua mens ad ampliorem conscientiam et ad intellectus praevalentiam disponi potest.
Identitas mentis perfectioris non cum memoria, imaginatione aut historia singulari corporis coincidit.
Bonum vivere non pendet ex promissione compensationis quae vitam praesentem post mortem iustificet.
Affectuum dominium non est actus voluntatis nudae, quia humana potentia ad eos coercendos in solo intellectu ponitur.
Externae causae, quatenus mentem passive determinant, veram animi acquiescentiam producere non possunt.
Necessitas causalis non destruit libertatem sapientis, sed arbitrium indeterminatum tamquam condicionem libertatis excludit.
Textus excludit oeconomiam moralem in qua virtus sine promisso praemio aut comminatione poenae caret ratione exercendi.
Textus excludit conceptionem libertatis ut exemptio a causatione, quia mens intelligens in serie infinita modorum aeternorum determinatur.
Textus excludit mortem corporis ut principium absolutum quo omnis esse mentis, omnis veritas vitae et omnis ratio virtutis aboleri debeant.
Variatio corporis → diversus gradus aptitudinis → diversus gradus conscientiae mentis → directio practica ad corpus aptius et intellectum praevalentem.
Perfectio-realitas → maior actio et minor passio → intellectus ut pars activa → eius perfectio prae imaginatione peritura.
Utile rationale → praecepta virtutis → independentia a doctrina immortalitatis → exclusio spei et metus ut fundamentorum moralium.
Cognitio tertii generis → amor Dei → beatitudo-virtus → augmentum intellectus → imminutio passionum et potentia coercendi libidines.
Intellectus necessitatis aeternae → imminutio agitationis → vera animi acquiescentia → figura sapientis contra ignorantem.

Variatio corporis et mentis → aptitudo ad intelligendum → distinctio intellectus et imaginationis → perfectio ut actio → virtus sine praemio ultramortali → beatitudo ut virtus → libertas sapientis sub necessitate.
Spes-metúsque vulgares → falsa ratio pietatis → separatio virtutis ab eschatologia → amor intellectualis Dei → imminutio passionum → animi acquiescentia.
Perfectio a qualitate morali externa ad rationem activitatis et passionis reclassificatur.
Pietas et religio a regimine praemii-poenae ad normam rationis et proprii utilis transferuntur.
Beatitudo a termino posteriore disciplinae ad causam immanentem virtutis et potentiae affectivae transfertur.
Libertas a licentia libidinis et ab exemptionis causalitate imagine ad stabilitatem intellectus sub necessitate aeterna reordinatur.
Corpus a mero correlato mortalitatis ad condicionem mutabilem progressionis intellectualis reclassificatur.
Surface — Textus declarat partem mentis aeternam perfectiorem esse, virtutem ex immortalitate non pendere, et beatitudinem ipsam virtutem esse.
Structural — Intellectus, imaginatio, actio, passio, aptitudo corporis et causae externae constituunt mechanismum quo diversae formae vitae producuntur.
Metastrategic — Argumentatio mutat modum affectus regendi: non metus aut imminutio voluntaria, sed cognitio et beatitudo sunt principium transformationis.
Ontological/Temporal — Mens intelligens in ordine aeterno modorum cogitandi ponitur, dum imaginatio, memoria et corporis existentia ad ordinem transitorium referuntur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restitutionem catenae principalis: perfectio → actio → intellectus → beatitudo → virtus → imminutio passionum.
Nexus inter aptitudinem corporis et ampliorem conscientiam mentis affirmatur, sed mechanismus eius intra hunc locum non plene explicatur.
Independentia virtutis ab immortalitate cohaeret cum fundamento utilitatis rationalis, quamvis textus simul cognitionem aeternitatis ad summam sapientis formam pertinere servet.
Structura firmissima est ubi beatitudo causaliter, non remunerative, explicatur ut principium potentiae in affectus.
Commissura fragilis manet inter partem mentis aeternam et singularitatem vitae imaginativae, quia quantitas et modus transitus inter has rationes hic non determinantur.
Restitutio motum textus servat, quia a conditionibus corporis et mentis ad fundamentum virtutis, deinde ad causam immanentem libertatis procedit.

translations.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect or on Human Freedom · passage 3

items.text: The text establishes the variation of body and mind as the condition from which happiness, unhappiness, and the ordering of life are to be understood.
The body's capacity for doing more is connected with the mind's broader consciousness of itself, God, and things, so that the transformation of the body is directed toward the intellect.
Perfection is defined by the degree of acting and by diminished passions; hence the eternal intellect is shown to be more perfect than perishing imagination.
The foundation of virtue is removed from the knowledge of immortality and placed in the rational pursuit of one's own advantage.
Blessedness is constituted not as a consequence of the discipline of the affects, but as the intellectual love of God, virtue itself, and the source of the power to restrain the affects.
The text concludes with the opposition between the ignorant person, driven by external causes and desire, and the wise person, who understands from eternal necessity.
A thing is more perfect insofar as it acts more and suffers less; perfection, reality, and power of acting express the same degree.
The intellect is the eternal part of the mind, whereas imagination is the part said to perish.
The mind acts through the intellect and suffers through imagination.
The sole foundation of virtue, or of living rightly, is rationally to seek one's own advantage.
The precepts of reason concerning piety, religion, courage, and generosity do not depend on knowledge of the eternity of the mind.
Blessedness consists in love toward God arising from the third kind of knowledge.
The intellectual love of God, insofar as it is referred to the acting mind, is virtue itself.
The more the mind enjoys blessedness, the more it understands, the greater power it has over the affects, and the less it suffers from evil affects.
A body capable of more corresponds to a mind more conscious of itself, God, and things; therefore life can, insofar as nature permits, be ordered toward this capacity.
The mind, insofar as it understands, is an eternal mode of thinking determined to infinity by other eternal modes.
Virtue is not defined by hope of reward after death or by fear of punishment after death.
Piety, religion, courage, and generosity are not servile burdens that could be endured only by post-mortem compensation.
Blessedness is neither the reward of virtue nor a subsequent effect of restraining desires.
Freedom is neither the license to obey desire nor the diminution of right accepted merely through observance of external law.
The imaginative part of the mind is not the locus of that perfection which can be considered after the body's existence.
Wisdom does not consist in escaping necessity, but in its form of eternal knowledge.
The part of the mind that remains is more perfect than the rest, because it acts through the intellect, whereas perishing imagination remains the seat of passions.
Reason can require piety and fortitude even under ignorance of the eternity of the mind, because their norm is rational advantage, not a destiny after death.
The restraint of desires does not produce blessedness; blessedness, by increasing the intellect, produces the very power of restraint.
Rational life does not require the combating of the affects as its primary end, but the increase of the intellect from which the diminution of passions follows.
The ordering of life tends toward a more capable body and a more conscious mind, so that memory and imagination acquire less force in relation to the intellect.
The wise person's steadiness of mind arises from understanding necessity, whereas ignorance of external causes and the rule of desires leaves the mind wavering.
The ethical order is shifted from the logic of reward to immanence: virtue has its constitutive effect, blessedness, within its own exercise.
The order of liberation is simultaneously epistemic and affective: knowledge is not added extrinsically to the affects, but produces the active power by which the affects are ordered.

The difference between the wise and the ignorant consists not in possession of a future reward, but in a different mode of present existence: the one acts and understands, the other suffers and lives as if unaware.
The body is not a mere burden of mortality, but the practical condition through which the mind can be disposed toward broader consciousness and the predominance of the intellect.
The identity of the more perfect mind does not coincide with memory, imagination, or the singular history of the body.
Living well does not depend on the promise of compensation that would justify present life after death.
Mastery of the affects is not an act of bare will, because the human power to restrain them is located in the intellect alone.
External causes, insofar as they determine the mind passively, cannot produce true peace of mind.
Causal necessity does not destroy the freedom of the wise person, but excludes indeterminate choice as a condition of freedom.
The text excludes a moral economy in which virtue lacks reason to be practiced without a promised reward or a threat of punishment.
The text excludes a conception of freedom as exemption from causation, because the understanding mind is determined in an infinite series of eternal modes.
The text excludes the death of the body as an absolute principle by which all being of the mind, all truth of life, and all ground of virtue must be abolished.
Variation of the body → different degree of capacity → different degree of consciousness of the mind → practical direction toward a more capable body and a predominant intellect.
Perfection-reality → greater action and lesser passion → intellect as the active part → its perfection over perishing imagination.
Rational advantage → precepts of virtue → independence from the doctrine of immortality → exclusion of hope and fear as moral foundations.
Knowledge of the third kind → love of God → blessedness-virtue → increase of the intellect → diminution of passions and power to restrain desires.
Understanding of eternal necessity → diminution of agitation → true peace of mind → figure of the wise person against the ignorant person.

Variation of body and mind → capacity for understanding → distinction of intellect and imagination → perfection as action → virtue without post-mortem reward → blessedness as virtue → freedom of the wise under necessity.
Common hope and fear → false ground of piety → separation of virtue from eschatology → intellectual love of God → diminution of passions → peace of mind.
Perfection is reclassified from an external moral quality to the ratio of activity and passion.
Piety and religion are transferred from the regime of reward and punishment to the norm of reason and one's own advantage.
Blessedness is transferred from the subsequent terminus of discipline to the immanent cause of virtue and affective power.
Freedom is reordered from the image of the license of desire and causal exemption to the stability of the intellect under eternal necessity.
The body is reclassified from a mere correlate of mortality to a mutable condition of intellectual advancement.
Surface — The text declares that the eternal part of the mind is more perfect, that virtue does not depend on immortality, and that blessedness is virtue itself.
Structural — Intellect, imagination, action, passion, bodily capacity, and external causes constitute the mechanism through which different forms of life are produced.
Metastrategic — The argument changes the mode of governing the affects: not fear or voluntary diminution, but knowledge and blessedness are the principle of transformation.
Ontological/Temporal — The understanding mind is placed in the eternal order of modes of thinking, whereas imagination, memory, and bodily existence are referred to the transitory order.
The axioms suffice for the reconstruction of the principal chain: perfection → action → intellect → blessedness → virtue → diminution of passions.
The connection between bodily capacity and the mind's broader consciousness is affirmed, but its mechanism is not fully explained within this passage.

The independence of virtue from immortality coheres with the foundation of rational advantage, although the text simultaneously preserves knowledge of eternity as pertaining to the highest form of the wise person.
The strongest structure is where blessedness is explained causally, not remuneratively, as the principle of power over the affects.
A fragile juncture remains between the eternal part of the mind and the singularity of imaginative life, because the quantity and mode of transition between these aspects are not determined here.
The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text, because it proceeds from the conditions of body and mind to the foundation of virtue, then to the immanent cause of freedom.

identity.title: Part Five - On the Power of the Intellect, or Human Freedom · passage 3
identity.original_title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 3

units.original_title: Pars quinta - De potentia intellectus seu de libertate humana · passage 3

items.text: Quaestio centralis est quomodo substantia necessario existens simul principium immanens omnium modorum fiat, sine exteriori causa, arbitrio contingenti aut ordine rerum alternativo.
Thesis globalis affirmat unicam substantiam divinam, cuius essentia existentiam et potentiam involvit, omnia entia intra se continere atque necessario determinare.
Argumentatio geometrica distinctiones ontologicas in exclusiones convertit, exclusiones in causalitatem necessariam, causalitatem autem in diagnosin errorum imaginationis et appetitus.
Motus a substantiae improductibilitate ad causalitatem sui procedit, deinde infinitatem staticam in productivitatem infinitam naturae divinae transformat.
Productivitas infinita per modos infinitos et concatenationes finitas distribuitur, donec necessitas ontologica in criticam contingentiae, voluntatis liberae et finalismi terminetur.
Motus est cumulativus et spiralis: omnis exclusio exterioritatis redit ut ulterior clausura causalis, modalis, epistemica vel teleologica.
Systema a constitutione entis ad unicitatem ordinis progreditur, tum ordinem ipsum contra interpretationes voluntaristicas et finales tuetur.
Clausura producta est immanens et actualistica: neque extra Deum, neque praeter ordinem actualem, neque intra contingentiam onticam spatium residuum relinquitur.
[Persistent] Omne ens aut substantia est aut modus; tertium genus ontologicum quo dependentia immanens effugiatur non datur.
[Persistent] Deus est unica substantia absolute infinita, causa sui, cuius essentia ab existentia separari non potest.
[Mutating] Attributa essentiam substantiae exprimunt sine eius divisione; multiplicitas eorum fit principium differentiationis internae, non pluralitatis substantialis.
[Persistent] Modi sunt affectiones substantiae quae in Deo sunt, per Deum concipiuntur atque ab eo quoad essentiam, existentiam et operationem dependent.
[Persistent] Ex causa determinata effectus necessario sequitur; causalitas vera nullam indifferentiam inter causam datam et effectum admittit.
[Mutating] Infinitas a negatione termini homogenei transit ad plenitudinem productivam qua infinita infinitis modis necessario consequuntur.
[Mutating] Libertas non est electio inter possibilia, sed actio ex sola necessitate propriae naturae sine determinatione externa.
[Emergent] Causalitas divina est immanens: effectus non extra causam constituuntur, sed intra eandem naturam ut expressiones attributorum permanent.
[Emergent] Productio modalis duplicem ordinem format: modi infiniti ex absoluta natura attributorum sequuntur, modi finiti per modificationes finitas mediantur.
[Terminal] Omnis res finita ad existendum et operandum ab alia causa finita determinatur, nullo primo termino finito admisso.
[Terminal] Potentia divina est ipsa essentia divina; ideo ordo actualis non est electus ex ordine possibilitatum non actualium.
[Terminal] Intellectus et voluntas, etiam infinite concepta, sunt modi determinati, non facultates originariae supra naturam positae.
[Emergent] Necessitas pertinet ad res et causas; contingentia, possibilitas et finalitas oriuntur ex cognitione causali defectiva.
[Attractor] Intelligibilitas ad essentias, proprietates et causas convergit, dum imaginatio mensurans et appetitus conscius falsa exemplaria ontologica producunt.
Substantia identitatem ontologicam retinet, sed a termino independentiae ad principium causaliter activum totius naturae promovetur.
Infinitas functionem mutat: primum terminum et negationem excludit, deinde productionem effectuum infinitis modis affirmat.
Attributum ab indice essentiae ad canalem productivum transit, per quem modi infiniti et finiti ordinate consequuntur.
Formula qua omnia in Deo sunt amplificatur ab inexistentia ontologica ad clausuram causalitatis, conceptionis et determinationis.
Libertas inversionem patitur: indifferentia repudiata est, dum necessitas sui ipsius nomen libertatis recipit.
Intellectus primum imaginationi opponitur ut modus rectae conceptionis, deinde ipse inter modos Naturae Naturatae reponitur.
Aeternitas ab infinita duratione separata manet, sed eius oppositum nunc non tempus externum, verum series interna determinationum finitarum est.
Contingentia ex categoria rei expellitur et ad statum epistemicum cognitionis incompletae transfertur.
Anthropomorphismus a simplici confusione naturae divinae cum affectibus humanis ad genealogiam finalismi et superstitionis extenditur.
Demonstrationes locales contra pluralitatem substantiarum hoc gradu absorbentur in propositionem latiorem nullam exterioritatem substantialem vel causalem dari.
Refutatio compositionis extensionis manet casus localis, sed distinctio imaginationis et intellectus fit mechanismus generalis ad pseudo-contradictiones ontologicas detegendas.
Distinctio modorum infinitarum et finitarum est architectura inferior mediationis; hoc gradu ea coniungit productivitatem aeternam cum determinatione singularium.
Distinctio Naturae Naturantis et Naturae Naturatae non est altera divisio substantiae, sed instrumentum praesentis gradus quo causalitas et dependentia sine transcendentia distinguuntur.
Difficultas localis transitus a non-productione substantiae ad causalitatem sui superatur structuraliter per clausuram immanentem, non per introductionem causae ulterioris.
Quaestiones locales de intellectu et voluntate divina cedunt propositioni globali qua omnis facultas mentalis inter modos causatos collocatur.
Genealogia finalismi, quamvis appendicis forma procedat, praesentem structuram claudit ostendendo quomodo contrarium causalitatis necessariae ab ipsa condicione cognitiva humana generetur.
Nulla substantia, causa aut condicio intelligibilitatis extra Deum admittitur.
Substantia infinita nec ex partibus realibus componitur nec per vacuum, mensuram aut divisionem imaginationis explicatur.
Deus non est artifex transiens cuius effectus extra ipsum consistant.
Actio divina nec ex decreto contingenti nec ex deliberatione inter ordines possibiles oritur.
Res finita neque causa sui neque subiectum voluntarium causaliter autonomum est.
Contingentia ontica et finis humanus tamquam principia Naturae simul excluduntur.
Systema requirit ut falsa sit separabilitas essentiae substantiae ab eius existentia; aliter necessitas Dei et tota dependentia modalis corruerent.
Falsa esse debet potentia divina quae possibilitates inexercitas reservet, quia hiatus inter essentiam, potentiam et actualitatem ordinem necessarium solveret.
Nulla prima causa finita admitti potest; eius admissio concatenationem modalem interrumperet et finitum in substantiam latentem converteret.
Facultas mentalis extra ordinem naturalem posita falsa esse debet, quia privilegium causale intellectus aut voluntatis clausuram immanentem frangeret.
Utilitas, bonum et finis humanus normam veritatis naturae praebere non possunt; cognitio debet per essentias, proprietates et causas procedere.
Absentia ordinans est ipsum “extra”: systema nullum locum ontologicum, causalem vel epistemicum extra immanentiam concedere potest.
Possibilitas indisponibilis est mundus vere alternativus; alter ordo non variatio huius naturae, sed contradictoria substitutio alterius naturae divinae esset.
Nulla norma transcendens veritatis, causalitatis aut bonitatis super naturam stat, ex qua ordo actualis iudicari vel eligi possit.
Ruptura causalis ontica praecluditur; quod ut casus, possibilitas aut contingentia apparet defectum cognitionis, non hiatum realitatis, indicat.
Unicitas substantiae cum productivitate infinita coniuncta creationem ut eventum externum tollit et eam in expressionem aeternam naturae convertit.
Series causarum finitarum non est pons inter Deum et mundum, sed articulatio interna causalitatis immanentis.
Infinitas et omnipotentia convergunt in actualitatem exhaustivam: potentia divina neque mensuratur neque ut copia effectuum nondum productorum reservatur.
Cum libertas per necessitatem propriae naturae definiatur et voluntas inter modos causatos reponatur, libertas originaria soli causae immanenti convenit, non facultati eligenti.
Multiplicitas attributorum cum extensione divina coniuncta materiam ab ordine substantiae independentis removet et in differentiationem internam unius naturae reclassificat.
Asymmetria inter substantiam, cuius essentia existentiam involvit, et modos, quorum essentia eam non involvit, perseverantiam modalem in causalitatem continuam convertit.
Exclusio ordinis alterius et translatio contingentiae ad cognitionem efficiunt ut possibilitas sit relatio ad ignorantiam causae, non status incompletus rei.
Mensura partium et proiectio finium sunt formae eiusdem erroris: structurae modales imaginationis aut appetitus in naturam substantiae transferuntur.
Realitas praesentis systematis est actualismus immanens: possibilitas realis potentiam divinam non excedit, et potentia divina ab essentia actuali non separatur.
Tempus non continet naturam divinam nec decretum ante productionem; aeternitas est necessitas essentiae, dum successio pertinet ad ordinem modorum finitorum.
Subiectum finitum fit nodus causalis intra seriem determinationum, non centrum transcendentale unde actus incipiant.
Ignorantia non constituit indeterminationem rei, sed machinam quae necessitatem in contingentiam et causalitatem in finalitatem apparentem transformat.
Agere non significat seriem causarum absolute incipere, sed potentiam naturae sub certa determinatione exprimere et effectus ulteriores producere.
Methodus congrua huic ontologiae non quaerit cui fini res serviat, sed ex qua essentia, proprietate et concatenatione causarum necessario sequatur.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: Partitio entis in substantiam et modos dependentiam conceptualem instituit; dependentia conceptualis causalitatem immanentem requirit; causalitas immanens partitionem initialem claudit.
Exclusio substantiae exterioris causam externam tollit; causalitas sine exterioritate ordinem alternativum excludit; exclusio alternativae iterum unicitatem substantiae confirmat.
Attributa per se concepta differentiam augent sine substantiam dividendo; eadem differentia productivitatem infinitam unius naturae amplificat.
Quaelibet causa finita ad aliam causam finitam remittit, unde regressus non defectum explicationis sed formam recursionis modalis efficit.
Imaginatio partes et fines fingit, ex fictionibus contradictiones vel utilitates elicit, deinde easdem fictiones pro structura naturae accipit.
Ignorantia causarum opinionem libertatis parit; opinio libertatis finalismum generat; finalismus causas occultans ignorantiam initialem reproduci facit.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Exhaustio entis in substantiam aut modum → independentia substantiae / dependentia modi → impossibilitas tertii ordinis ontologici.
Distinctio per attributa aut affectiones → exclusio pluralitatis substantiarum eiusdem naturae → unica substantia absolute infinita.
Nulla productio substantiae ab alio → causa sui → essentia involvens existentiam → necessitas et aeternitas.
Attributa essentiam exprimunt → natura infinita est interne differentiata → infinita infinitis modis necessario sequuntur.
Causalitas immanens → modi infiniti ex absoluto / modi finiti per finitum → determinatio universalis intra Deum.
Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → intellectus et voluntas inter modos → exclusio arbitrii originarii → unicitas ordinis actualis.
Ignorantia causarum + conscientia appetitus → libertas imaginaria → finalismus → correctio per cognitionem essentiarum et causarum.

sections.original_name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Partitio in-se / in-alio → substantia / modus → dependentia conceptualis → exclusio substantiae exterioris.
Improductibilitas substantiae → causa sui → existentia necessaria → infinitas → productivitas infinita.
Productivitas infinita → causalitas immanens → modi infiniti et finiti → concatenatio determinationum singularium.
Determinatio universalis → Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → demotio voluntatis → exclusio ordinis alternativi.
Clausura ontologica → contingentia epistemica → genealogia finalismi → restitutio cognitionis per causas et essentias.
Oppositio inter Deum et mundum corruit: Deus non est ens iuxta alia, iarum autem ordo est expressio modalis causalitatis divinae.
Oppositio inter substantiam materialem et substantiam spiritualem dissolvitur, quia extensio et cogitatio ad attributa unius substantiae referuntur.
Oppositio inter libertatem et necessitatem reordinatur: indifferentia libertati detrahitur, actio ex propria natura libertatem constituit.
Oppositio inter possibile et actuale ex ontologia ad epistemologiam transfertur; ordo actualis non est unus inter plures ordines aeque reales.
Explicatio per fines reclassificatur ut effectus ignorantiae, dum explicatio per causas, essentias et proprietates norma methodologica fit.
Agens singulare reclassificatur a principio sui iuris ad nodum activum sed determinatum intra seriem causalitatis immanentis.
Gradus superficiei affirmat Deum necessario existere, omnia in Deo esse, nihil contingens dari, voluntatem non esse liberam et naturam non agere propter fines.
Gradus structuralis constituit campum unius substantiae interne per attributa et modos differentiatae, cuius causalitas per modos infinitos et concatenationes finitas distribuitur.
Gradus metastrategicus vocabula libertatis, possibilitatis, perfectionis et finalitatis ex theologia voluntaristica in analysin necessitatis, determinationis et ignorantiae transfert.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis distinguit aeternam necessitatem substantiae a successione interna modorum, nullo decreto temporali ante naturam posito.
Gradus methodologicus et performativus negationes axiomatice cumulat, objectiones ad falsa schemata imaginationis reducit et finalismum genealogice producendo dissolvit.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Attributa per se concipiuntur et realiter distinguuntur, sed nexus positivus quo eadem attributa unam substantiam numericam constituant potius asseritur quam plene derivatur.
Deus omnes modos determinat, sed res finita immediate ab alia causa finita determinatur; relatio exacta inter causalitatem divinam et mediationem finitam manet compressa.
Productio aeterna modorum infinitarum et series causarum finitarum cohaerere debent, sed transitus inter hos ordines non plene formalizatur.
Deus liber dicitur quia ex necessitate sua agit, voluntas autem necessaria vel coacta; differentia pendet ex distinctione inter necessitatem internam et determinationem ab alio.
Transitus ab ordine necessario ad eius summam perfectionem notionem perfectionis postulat quae neque electione neque bono externo neque comparatione possibilitatum nitatur.
Infinitas mutatur a pura exclusione termini in principium productionis inexhaustae.
Libertas mutatur ab indifferentia voluntatis in necessitatem activam propriae naturae.
Possibilitas et contingentia mutantur a statibus rerum in indices cognitionis causalis incompletae.
Intellectus et voluntas mutantur a facultatibus divinis vel humanis privilegiatis in modos Naturae Naturatae.
Causalitas mutatur ab imagine creationis transeuntis in dependentiam immanentem quae effectus intra causam retinet.

sections.original_name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Realitas implicite est machina sui causalis, infinite differentiata et immanens, cuius effectus non ab ea exeunt sed eius potentiam exprimunt.
Res singularis est nodus temporalis determinationum, simul effectus causarum antecedentium et fons effectuum ulteriorum.
Subiectum est modus conscius appetitus sed ignarus causarum, ideo pronus libertatem et fines fingere, non principium extra naturam.
Tempus est series modalium determinationum intra aeternitatem quae ipsa neque duratione neque successione explicatur.
Navigatio possibilis non est fuga ex causalitate, sed transitus ab imaginatione finium ad cognitionem essentiarum, proprietatum et causarum.
Axiomata de substantia, modo, causa necessaria, attributis et mediatione finita sufficiunt ad motum praesentis gregis ab unitate substantiae ad necessitatem universalem restituendum.
Structura firmissima est nexus inter immanentiam, determinationem modalem et negationem contingentiae onticae.
Minus determinata manet mediatio inter productionem aeternam, modos infinitos et seriem causarum finitarum, praesertim ubi demonstratio regressus in fonte truncatur.
Unitas substantiae sub pluralitate attributorum ad restitutionem necessaria est, sed eius coordinatio positiva ultra exclusiones pluralitatis adhuc resistit compressioni axiomaticae.

Restitutio verum motum servat si seriem improductibilitas → causa sui → productivitas infinita → immanentia → determinatio → critica finalismi retinet; probationes scholasticae singulae non sunt totius structurae substitutae.
The central question is how a necessarily existing substance can at once become the immanent principle of all modes, without an external cause, contingent will, or alternative order of things.
The global thesis affirms a single divine substance, whose essence involves existence and power, to contain all beings within itself and determine them necessarily.
The geometrical argumentation converts ontological distinctions into exclusions, exclusions into necessary causality, and causality into a diagnosis of the errors of imagination and appetite.
The movement proceeds from the unproducibility of substance to self-causation, then transforms static infinity into the infinite productivity of divine nature.
Infinite productivity is distributed through infinite modes and finite concatenations, until ontological necessity culminates in a critique of contingency, free will, and finalism.
The movement is cumulative and spiral: every exclusion of exteriority returns as a further causal, modal, epistemic, or teleological closure.
The system advances from the constitution of being to the uniqueness of order, then defends order itself against voluntaristic and final interpretations.
The produced closure is immanent and actualist: no residual space is left either outside God, beyond the actual order, or within ontic contingency.
[Persistent] Every being is either substance or mode; no third ontological kind by which immanent dependence may be escaped is given.
[Persistent] God is the single absolutely infinite substance, cause of itself, whose essence cannot be separated from existence.
[Mutating] Attributes express the essence of substance without dividing it; their multiplicity becomes a principle of internal differentiation, not of substantial plurality.
[Persistent] Modes are affections of substance which are in God, are conceived through God, and depend on him with respect to essence, existence, and operation.
[Persistent] From a determinate cause an effect necessarily follows; true causality admits no indifference between a given cause and an effect.
[Mutating] Infinity passes from the negation of a homogeneous limit to the productive fullness by which infinitely many things follow in infinitely many modes.
[Mutating] Freedom is not a choice among possibilities, but action from the sole necessity of one's own nature without external determination.
[Emergent] Divine causality is immanent: effects are not constituted outside the cause, but remain within the same nature as expressions of attributes.
[Emergent] Modal production forms a double order: infinite modes follow from the absolute nature of attributes, while finite modes are mediated through finite modifications.
[Terminal] Every finite thing is determined to exist and operate by another finite cause, with no first finite term admitted.
[Terminal] Divine power is divine essence itself; therefore the actual order is not chosen from an order of non-actual possibilities.
[Terminal] Intellect and will, even when conceived as infinite, are determinate modes, not original faculties set above nature.
[Emergent] Necessity pertains to things and causes; contingency, possibility, and finality arise from defective causal knowledge.
[Attractor] Intelligibility converges upon essences, properties, and causes, while measuring imagination and conscious appetite produce false ontological models.
Substance retains ontological identity, but is advanced from a term of independence to a causally active principle of the whole of nature.
Infinity changes function: first it excludes limit and negation, then it affirms the production of effects in infinitely many modes.
Attribute passes from an index of essence to a productive channel through which infinite and finite modes follow in order.
The formula by which all things are in God is expanded from ontological inherence to the closure of causality, conception, and determination.
Freedom undergoes an inversion: indifference is repudiated, while self-necessity receives the name of freedom.
Intellect is first opposed to imagination as the mode of correct conception, then is itself placed among the modes of Natura Naturata.
Eternity remains separated from infinite duration, but its opposite is now not external time, but the internal series of finite determinations.
Contingency is expelled from the category of the thing and transferred to the epistemic state of incomplete knowledge.
Anthropomorphism is extended from a simple confusion of divine nature with human affects to a genealogy of finalism and superstition.
Local demonstrations against a plurality of substances are at this level absorbed into the broader proposition that no substantial or causal exteriority is given.
The refutation of the composition of extension remains a local case, but the distinction between imagination and intellect becomes a general mechanism for detecting pseudo-ontological contradictions.
The distinction between infinite and finite modes is a lower architecture of mediation; at this level it joins eternal productivity with the determination of singular things.

The distinction of Natura Naturans and Natura Naturata is not a second division of substance, but an instrument of the present level by which causality and dependence are distinguished without transcendence.
The local difficulty of the transition from the non-production of substance to self-causation is overcome structurally through immanent closure, not through the introduction of a further cause.
Local questions concerning divine intellect and will yield to the global proposition by which every mental faculty is placed among caused modes.

The genealogy of finalism, although it proceeds in the form of an appendix, closes the present structure by showing how the contrary of necessary causality is generated by the very human cognitive condition.
No substance, cause, or condition of intelligibility outside God is admitted.
Infinite substance is neither composed of real parts nor explained through the void, measure, or division of imagination.
God is not a transitive craftsman whose effects subsist outside himself.
Divine action arises neither from a contingent decree nor from deliberation among possible orders.
A finite thing is neither cause of itself nor a voluntarily causally autonomous subject.
Ontic contingency and human end are simultaneously excluded as principles of Nature.
The system requires the separability of the essence of substance from its existence to be false; otherwise the necessity of God and all modal dependence would collapse.
A divine power that reserves unexercised possibilities must be false, because a gap between essence, power, and actuality would dissolve necessary order.
No first finite cause can be admitted; its admission would interrupt the modal concatenation and convert the finite into a latent substance.
A mental faculty placed outside the natural order must be false, because the causal privilege of intellect or will would break immanent closure.
Human utility, good, and end cannot furnish a norm of the truth of nature; knowledge must proceed through essences, properties, and causes.
The ordering absence is “outside” itself: the system cannot concede any ontological, causal, or epistemic place outside immanence.
The unavailable possibility is a genuinely alternative world; another order would not be a variation of this nature, but the contradictory substitution of another divine nature.
No transcendent norm of truth, causality, or goodness stands above nature, from which the actual order might be judged or chosen.
An ontic causal rupture is precluded; what appears as chance, possibility, or contingency indicates a defect of knowledge, not a gap in reality.
The uniqueness of substance conjoined with infinite productivity abolishes creation as an external event and converts it into the eternal expression of nature.
The series of finite causes is not a bridge between God and the world, but an internal articulation of immanent causality.
Infinity and omnipotence converge in exhaustive actuality: divine power is neither measured nor reserved as a store of effects not yet produced.
When freedom is defined through the necessity of one's own nature and will is placed among caused modes, original freedom belongs only to the immanent cause, not to a choosing faculty.
The multiplicity of attributes conjoined with divine extension removes matter from the order of independent substance and reclassifies it as an internal differentiation of one nature.
The asymmetry between substance, whose essence involves existence, and modes, whose essence does not involve it, converts modal persistence into continuous causality.
The exclusion of another order and the translation of contingency into knowledge make possibility a relation to ignorance of a cause, not an incomplete state of a thing.
The measure of parts and the projection of ends are forms of the same error: modal structures of imagination or appetite are transferred into the nature of substance.
The reality of the present system is immanent actualism: real possibility does not exceed divine power, and divine power is not separated from actual essence.
Time contains neither divine nature nor a decree before production; eternity is the necessity of essence, while succession belongs to the order of finite modes.
The finite subject becomes a causal node within the series of determinations, not a transcendental center from which acts begin.
Ignorance does not constitute the indetermination of a thing, but the mechanism that transforms necessity into contingency and causality into apparent finality.
To act does not mean to begin a series of causes absolutely, but to express the power of nature under a certain determination and to produce further effects.
The method suited to this ontology does not ask for what end a thing serves, but from what essence, property, and concatenation of causes it necessarily follows.

sections.name: Recursive Loops, Escalation Paths, and Conceptual Attractors

items.text: The partition of being into substance and modes establishes conceptual dependence; conceptual dependence requires immanent causality; immanent causality closes the initial partition.

The exclusion of external substance removes an external cause; causality without exteriority excludes an alternative order; the exclusion of the alternative again confirms the uniqueness of substance.
Attributes conceived through themselves increase difference without dividing substance; this same difference amplifies the infinite productivity of one nature.
Every finite cause refers to another finite cause, whereby regress produces not a defect of explanation but a form of modal recursion.
Imagination invents parts and ends, derives contradictions or utilities from the fictions, and then takes these same fictions for the structure of nature.
Ignorance of causes produces the opinion of freedom; the opinion of freedom generates finalism; finalism, by concealing causes, causes the initial ignorance to be reproduced.

sections.name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Exhaustion of being into substance or mode → independence of substance / dependence of mode → impossibility of a third ontological order.
Distinction through attributes or affections → exclusion of a plurality of substances of the same nature → one absolutely infinite substance.
No production of substance by another → cause of itself → essence involving existence → necessity and eternity.
Attributes express essence → infinite nature is internally differentiated → infinitely many things necessarily follow in infinitely many modes.
Immanent causality → infinite modes from the absolute / finite modes through the finite → universal determination within God.
Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → intellect and will among modes → exclusion of original free will → uniqueness of the actual order.
Ignorance of causes + consciousness of appetite → imaginary freedom → finalism → correction through knowledge of essences and causes.

sections.original_name: Formal Generative Schema of the Whole Book

items.text: Partition into-in-itself / in-another → substance / mode → conceptual dependence → exclusion of external substance.
Unproducibility of substance → cause of itself → necessary existence → infinity → infinite productivity.
Infinite productivity → immanent causality → infinite and finite modes → concatenation of singular determinations.
Universal determination → Natura Naturans / Natura Naturata → demotion of will → exclusion of an alternative order.
Ontological closure → epistemic contingency → genealogy of finalism → restoration of knowledge through causes and essences.
The opposition between God and world collapses: God is not a being alongside others, but their order is a modal expression of divine causality.
The opposition between material substance and spiritual substance is dissolved, because extension and thought are referred to the attributes of one substance.
The opposition between freedom and necessity is reordered: indifference is removed from freedom, while action from one's own nature constitutes freedom.
The opposition between possible and actual is transferred from ontology to epistemology; the actual order is not one among several equally real orders.
Explanation through ends is reclassified as an effect of ignorance, while explanation through causes, essences, and properties becomes the methodological norm.
The singular agent is reclassified from a self-governing principle to an active yet determined node within the series of immanent causality.
The surface level affirms that God necessarily exists, that all things are in God, that nothing contingent is given, that will is not free, and that nature does not act for ends.
The structural level constitutes the field of one substance internally differentiated through attributes and modes, whose causality is distributed through infinite modes and finite concatenations.
The metastrategic level transfers the terms freedom, possibility, perfection, and finality from voluntaristic theology into an analysis of necessity, determination, and ignorance.
The ontological and temporal level distinguishes the eternal necessity of substance from the internal succession of modes, with no temporal decree posited before nature.
The methodological and performative level accumulates negations axiomatically, reduces objections to false schemas of imagination, and dissolves finalism by genealogically producing it.

sections.name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Attributes are conceived through themselves and are really distinct, but the positive nexus by which the same attributes constitute one numerical substance is asserted rather than fully derived.
God determines all modes, but a finite thing is immediately determined by another finite cause; the exact relation between divine causality and finite mediation remains compressed.
The eternal production of infinite modes and the series of finite causes must cohere, but the transition between these orders is not fully formalized.
God is called free because he acts from his own necessity, whereas will is necessary or compelled; the difference depends on the distinction between internal necessity and determination by another.
The transition from necessary order to its highest perfection requires a notion of perfection resting neither on choice, nor on external good, nor on comparison of possibilities.
Infinity changes from the pure exclusion of limit into a principle of inexhaustible production.
Freedom changes from indifference of will into the active necessity of one's own nature.
Possibility and contingency change from states of things into indices of incomplete causal knowledge.
Intellect and will change from privileged divine or human faculties into modes of Natura Naturata.
Causality changes from the image of transitive creation into immanent dependence that retains effects within the cause.

sections.original_name: Internal Tensions, Mutation Points, and Fault Lines

items.text: Reality is implicitly a self-causal, infinitely differentiated, and immanent machine, whose effects do not depart from it but express its power.
The singular thing is a temporal node of determinations, at once the effect of antecedent causes and the source of further effects.
The subject is a mode conscious of appetite but ignorant of causes, and therefore prone to invent freedom and ends, not a principle outside nature.
Time is a series of modal determinations within eternity, which itself is explained neither by duration nor by succession.
Possible navigation is not an escape from causality, but a transition from the imagination of ends to knowledge of essences, properties, and causes.
Axioms concerning substance, mode, necessary cause, attributes, and finite mediation suffice to reconstruct the movement of the present whole from the unity of substance to universal necessity.
The firmest structure is the nexus between immanence, modal determination, and the negation of ontic contingency.
Less determined remains the mediation between eternal production, infinite modes, and the series of finite causes, especially where the demonstration of regress is truncated in the source.
The unity of substance beneath the plurality of attributes is necessary for reconstruction, but its positive coordination beyond the exclusions of plurality still resists axiomatic compression.

Reconstruction preserves the true movement if it retains the sequence unproducibility → cause of itself → infinite productivity → immanence → determination → critique of finalism; individual scholastic proofs are not substitutes for the whole structure.
