But one who is at a loss and wonders thinks himself ignorant (which is why the lover of myth is in a way a philosopher, for myth is composed of wonders). Hence, if they philosophized in order to escape ignorance, it is clear that they pursued knowing for the sake of knowing and not for the sake of any use. And the actual occurrence bears witness to this: for it was when nearly all the necessities, and things for ease and recreation, were already available that this kind of understanding began to be sought.

It is clear, then, that we seek it for no other need, but that, just as we say a human being is free who is for his own sake and not for another's, so we seek this science as alone free among the sciences; for it alone is for its own sake. Hence its possession might justly be thought not human; for in many ways human nature is enslaved, so that, according to Simonides,
only a god might possess this prerogative,
and it is unworthy of a man not to seek the science in accordance with himself. If what the poets say has any truth, and the divine is by nature envious, it is likely that this would occur especially in this case, and that all who excel would be unfortunate. But it is neither possible for the divine to be envious—rather, according to the proverb, poets tell many lies—nor should any science be thought more honorable than this one. For it is the most divine and most honorable; and it alone could be such in two ways. For that science which a god would most possess is divine among the sciences, as is also any science concerned with divine things.

This science alone has obtained both of these characteristics. For god is thought to be among the causes of all things and to be a certain principle, and god alone, or most of all, would possess such a science. All the others, then, are more necessary than this, but none is better.—Yet in a way its acquisition must end for us in the opposite of the inquiries from which we began. For, as we said, all begin from wondering whether something is so, as with the self-moving things among marvels, or with the turnings of the sun, or the incommensurability of the diagonal (for it seems marvelous to all who have not yet contemplated the cause if something is not measured by the least unit). But one must end in the opposite and the better, according to the proverb, as also in these cases when they have learned; for a geometrician would not wonder at anything so much as if the diagonal became commensurable. What, then, is the nature of the science sought, and what is the aim which the inquiry and the whole method must attain, has been stated.

Since it is clear that we must acquire knowledge of the original causes (for we say that we know each thing when we suppose that we know its first cause), and causes are spoken of in four ways: one cause, we say, is the substance and the what-it-was-to-be (for the why is reduced ultimately to the account, and the first why is cause and principle); another is the matter and the underlying subject; a third is that from which the principle of motion comes; and a fourth is the cause opposed to this, that for the sake of which and the good (for this is the end of every coming-to-be and motion). Although we have considered these sufficiently in the works on nature, nevertheless let us also take up for examination those who before us came to investigate beings and philosophized about truth.

For it is clear that they too speak of certain principles and causes. Our survey of them, then, will be of some service to the present method: for either we shall discover some other kind of cause, or we shall have more confidence in those now spoken of.—Of those who first philosophized, most supposed that the principles of all things were only those in the form of matter. For that from which all beings are, and from which they first come to be, and into which they are finally destroyed, while the substance remains but its attributes change—this, they say, is the element and this the principle of beings. And therefore they suppose that nothing comes to be or is destroyed, since such a nature is always preserved; just as we do not say that Socrates simply comes to be when he becomes beautiful or musical, nor is destroyed when he loses these states, because the underlying subject, Socrates himself, remains. So too with none of the other things; for there must always be some nature, either one or more than one, from which the other things come to be, while that nature is preserved.

Yet not all state the same number and form of such a principle. Thales, the founder of this kind of philosophy, says that it is water (which is why he also declared that the earth rests upon water), perhaps taking this supposition from seeing that the nourishment of all things is moist, and that heat itself comes to be from this and lives by this (and that from which something comes to be is the principle of all things)—taking this supposition, then, both for this reason and because the seeds of all things have a moist nature, water being the principle of the nature of moist things. There are some who think that even the very ancient persons, who long before the present generation and first theologized, held this view about nature. For they made Ocean and Tethys the parents of generation, and water, called by them Styx, the oath of the gods. For the most ancient is most honorable, and an oath is the most honorable thing.

Whether, then, this opinion about nature happens to be ancient and old is perhaps unclear; but Thales is said to have declared himself in this way concerning the first cause (for no one would deem Hippo worthy of being placed among these because of the poverty of his thought). Anaximenes and Diogenes posit air as prior to water and as the most fundamental principle of simple bodies; Hippasus of Metapontum and Heraclitus of Ephesus posit fire; Empedocles posits the four, adding earth as a fourth to those mentioned (for these always remain and do not come to be, except in quantity and scarcity, being combined and separated into one and from one); while Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, earlier than Empedocles in age but later in his works, says that the principles are infinite. For he says that nearly all homoeomerous things, such as water or fire, come to be and perish in this way, by combination and separation only; otherwise they neither come to be nor perish, but remain eternal.—From these, then,

one might suppose that the only cause is the one spoken of in the form of matter. But as they proceeded in this way, the matter itself made a road for them and compelled them to seek further. For even if every coming-to-be and perishing is, as much as possible, from some one thing or even from several things, why does this happen, and what is the cause? Surely the underlying subject itself does not make itself change. I mean, for example, neither wood nor bronze is the cause of either's changing; nor does the wood make a bed, nor the bronze a statue, but something else is the cause of the change. To seek this is to seek the other principle, as we would say, that from which comes the principle of motion.

Those, then, who from the beginning wholly embraced this method and said that the underlying subject is one did not make any difficulty for themselves; indeed, some of those who say it is one, as though defeated by this inquiry, say that the one is unmoved and that the whole of nature is unmoved not only with respect to coming-to-be and perishing (for this is ancient and all agreed on it), but also with respect to every other change. And this is peculiar to them.

Of those who say that the all is one, no one succeeded in discerning a cause of this kind, except perhaps Parmenides—and he only insofar as he posits not merely one cause but, in a way, two. But for those who make them more numerous, it is more possible to speak of it, for example for those who make them hot and cold, or fire and earth; for they employ fire as having a nature capable of causing motion, and water and earth and such things as having the contrary nature.—But after these, and after principles of this kind, since these were insufficient to generate the nature of beings, they were again, as we said, compelled by truth itself to seek the next principle. For perhaps neither fire nor earth nor any other such thing is likely to be the cause of some beings being, and others coming to be, well and beautifully; nor is it likely that those men thought so. Nor again was it fitting to entrust so great a matter to spontaneity and chance.

Someone who said that intellect is present—as in animals—also in nature, and that it is the cause of the world and of all order, appeared like a sober man beside those who had spoken at random before him. We know that Anaxagoras manifestly touched upon these arguments, though Hermotimus of Clazomenae has a prior claim to have said it. Those, then, who held this view posited at once the good as a cause, as a principle of beings, and also that kind of cause from which motion belongs to beings;

One might suppose that Hesiod was the first to seek such a thing, or anyone else who posited love or desire among beings as a principle, as Parmenides also did. For he too, in constructing the generation of the all,
“First of all, he devised Love of all the gods.”
Parmenides Fr. 13 (Diels), but Hesiod:
“First of all Chaos came to be, but then thereafter”
“broad-bosomed Earth [Gap in source]”
“and Love, who stands out among all the immortals,”

Hes. Th. 116–20, as though there must be present among beings some cause which will move and bring things together. How, then, these men should be apportioned with regard to who was first, may be decided later. But since contraries to goods also appeared to be present in nature, and not only order and the beautiful but also disorder and the ugly, and since evils were more numerous than goods and base things than beautiful ones, someone else introduced Love and Strife, each the cause of each of these respectively.

For if one were to follow and grasp Empedocles' thought, rather than what he stammers in speaking, one would find that Love is the cause of goods and Strife of evils. Thus, if someone were to say that in a way Empedocles both says, and is the first to say, that the bad and the good are principles, he would perhaps speak correctly, if indeed the Good itself is the cause of all goods.—These men, then, as we say, appear to have touched upon two of the causes which we distinguished in the writings on nature, namely matter and that from which motion comes; though dimly and not at all clearly, but as untrained men do in battles. For they too, moving about, often strike fine blows, but neither do those do so from knowledge nor do these seem to know what they are saying; for they appear to make almost no use of these principles, except to a small extent.

For Anaxagoras employs intellect as a device for world-making, and whenever he is at a loss through what cause something is necessarily so, then he drags it in; but in other matters he assigns every cause of what comes to be rather than intellect. And Empedocles uses these causes more than he does, yet neither sufficiently nor does he find in them what is consistent. At any rate, in many places with him Love separates, while Strife combines.

For whenever the all is divided into the elements by Strife, then fire is combined into one, and likewise each of the other elements; but whenever they again come together into the one under Love, the parts must again be separated out from each.—Empedocles, then, beyond his predecessors, was the first to introduce a division of the cause, making the principle of motion not one but different and contrary ones; further, he was the first to say that the elements spoken of as in the form of matter are four (though in fact he does not employ four, but as though there were only two: fire by itself, and the opposed things as one nature—earth, air, and water; one might infer this by considering his verses).—He, then, as we say, stated the principles in this way and in this number. But Leucippus and his associate Democritus say that the full and the void are elements, calling the one being and the other non-being; of these, the full and solid is being, while the void is non-being (whence they also say that being is no more

than non-being, because body is no more than the void), and they take these as causes of beings in the manner of matter. And just as those who make the underlying substance one generate the other things by its affections, positing the rare and the dense as principles of the affections, so these too say that the differences are causes of the other things. They say that these are three: shape, arrangement, and position. For they say that being differs only by rhythm, contact, and turning; and of these rhythm is shape, contact arrangement, and turning position. For A differs from N in shape, AN from NA in arrangement, and Z from H in position. But concerning motion—whence or how it will belong to beings—these too, like the others, carelessly let the matter go. Thus far, then, it seems that the earlier thinkers investigated the two causes of which we speak.

Among these, and before them, the so-called Pythagoreans, having first taken up mathematics and advanced it, and having been brought up in it, supposed its principles to be the principles of all beings. Since numbers are by nature first among these things, and since in numbers they seemed to discern many likenesses to beings and things that come to be, more than in fire and earth and water—because one such affection of numbers was justice, another soul and intellect, another opportunity, and similarly, so to speak, each of the other things; and further, since they saw in numbers the affections and ratios of harmonies—since, then, all other things seemed to have their whole nature assimilated to numbers, while numbers were first in the whole of nature, they supposed the elements of numbers to be the elements of all beings, and the whole heaven to be harmony and number. And whatever correspondences they had in numbers and harmonies with the affections and parts of heaven and with the whole ordering of things, these

they collected and fitted together. And if anything was lacking anywhere, they sought to supply it, so that their whole account might be connected. I mean, for example, since the decad seems to be perfect and to comprise the whole nature of numbers, they say that the bodies moving in heaven are ten; but since only nine are visible, for this reason they make the counter-earth the tenth. We have distinguished these matters more precisely elsewhere. But the reason we are reviewing them is this: that we may learn from these men also what principles they posit and how they fall under the causes stated.

These too, then, evidently suppose number to be a principle, both as matter for beings and as their affections and states; and the elements of number are the even and the odd, of which the one is limited and the other unlimited; while the one is composed of both of these (for it is both even and odd), and number is from the one; and, as has been said, the whole heaven is numbers.—But others among these same people say that the principles are the ten spoken of in pairs of opposites: 
limit  unlimited,
odd  even,
one  plurality,
right  left,
male  female,
at rest  moving,
straight  curved,
light  darkness,
good  bad,
square  oblong.
Alcmaeon of Croton seems to have held the same view; and either he received this account from them or they from him. For Alcmaeon also declared things in a manner similar to these. He says that the many human things are two, speaking of contrarieties not determined as these are, but of whatever ones occur, such as

white and black, sweet and bitter, good and bad, great and small. This man, then, threw out his remarks about the remaining opposites without determination; but the Pythagoreans declared both how many and which the oppositions are. From both of these, then, one can gather this much: that contraries are principles of beings; from the latter, how many they are and what they are. But how they can be brought under the stated causes has not been clearly articulated by them; yet they seem to arrange the elements as in the form of matter. For they say that substance is composed and fashioned from these as things present within it.—From these considerations it is sufficient to discern the thought of the ancients who speak of more than one element of nature. But there are some who have declared concerning the all as though its nature were one, though not all in the same way, either in correctness or in accordance with nature.

For the account concerning them does not at all fit the present inquiry into causes (for they do not, like some natural philosophers, posit being as one and yet generate all things from the one as from matter; rather, these men speak in another way. For the former add motion, since they generate the all, whereas these say that it is motionless). Yet it is relevant to the present inquiry to this extent. For Parmenides seems to touch upon the one according to account, Melissus upon the one according to matter (and hence the former says that it is limited, the latter unlimited). Xenophanes, however, who first unified among these—for Parmenides is said to have been his pupil—made nothing clear, nor does he seem to touch either of these two natures; rather, looking to the whole heaven, he says that the one is god.

These men, then, as we said, must be set aside for the present inquiry—two of them altogether, as being somewhat too rustic, Xenophanes and Melissus. But Parmenides seems in some respect to speak with greater insight. For, judging that beside being non-being is nothing, he thinks that necessarily being is one, and nothing else (concerning which we have spoken more clearly in the writings on nature). But, compelled to follow the appearances, and supposing that the one is one according to account but many according to perception, he again posits two causes and two principles, hot and cold, calling them fire and earth; and of these he assigns the hot to being, and the other to non-being.—From what has been said, then, and from the wise men who have already taken their seats with our argument, we have received these things: from the first, that the principle is bodily (for water and fire and such things are bodies), and that some posit one bodily principle and others several, though both posit these as in the form of matter;

and from certain others, that they posit both this cause and, in addition to it, that from which motion comes—one such cause according to some, two according to others. Up to the Italians, then, and apart from them, the others have spoken of these matters more confusedly; except that, as we said, they happen to have employed two causes, and of these they make one, some one and others two: the cause from which motion comes. The Pythagoreans too have spoken of two principles in the same manner; but they added something which is peculiar to them: they did not think that the limited and the unlimited were certain other natures, such as fire or earth or some other such thing, but that the unlimited itself and the one itself were the substance of those things of which they are predicated; hence they held number to be the substance of all things. They declared themselves thus about these matters; and they began to speak and define concerning what something is, but their treatment was exceedingly simple.

For they defined superficially, and whatever thing first had the stated definition, this they thought to be the substance of the thing—as if someone thought that double and two were the same because doubleness first belongs to two. But perhaps being double and being two are not the same; otherwise the one will be many, which also happened to them. Such, then, is what may be gathered from the earlier thinkers and the others.

After the philosophies mentioned, Plato's inquiry arose, in many respects following these, but also possessing things peculiar to itself beyond the philosophy of the Italians. For in his youth he first became acquainted with Cratylus and the Heraclitean opinions, that all sensible things are always flowing and that there is no knowledge concerning them; and he retained these views later as well. But since Socrates was occupied with ethical matters and not at all with the whole of nature, while in these matters he was seeking the universal and was the first to fix his thought upon definitions, Plato, accepting this, supposed that this concerned other things and not sensibles. For it was impossible, he thought, for the common definition to be of any sensible thing, since they are always changing. Such beings, then, he called Ideas; and he said that all sensibles are named apart from these and in accordance with these. For the many are homonymous with the Forms by participation.

He changed only the name of participation. For the Pythagoreans say that beings exist by imitation of numbers, whereas Plato says by participation, changing the name. But what the participation or imitation of Forms might be, they left open to common inquiry. Further, besides sensible things and the Forms, he says that the mathematical objects of things are intermediate, differing from sensibles in being eternal and motionless, and from Forms in that there are many things alike, whereas each Form itself is one alone. And since Forms are causes for the other things, he thought that their elements were elements of all beings. As matter, the great and the small are principles; as substance, the one. For numbers are from those, through participation in the one.

Now, that the one is substance, and is not called one while being some other thing, he said similarly to the Pythagoreans; likewise, that numbers are causes of the substance of other things. But making a dyad, instead of the unlimited as one, and making the unlimited out of the great and the small—this is peculiar to him. Further, he places numbers apart from sensibles, whereas they say that the things themselves are numbers and do not posit mathematical objects as intermediate between these. Thus, his making the one and numbers separate from things, unlike the Pythagoreans, and his introduction of the Forms arose from inquiry in accounts (for the earlier thinkers did not participate in dialectic); while making the other nature a dyad arose because numbers, apart from the first, are naturally generated from it as from some mould. Yet the contrary happens; for this is not reasonable.

For those who proceed from matter make many things, whereas the form generates only once; yet from one matter one table appears to come to be, while he who imposes the form, though being one, makes many. The male also stands similarly in relation to the female: the female is filled by one intercourse, whereas the male fills many; and yet these are imitations of those principles. Plato, then, thus distinguished concerning the matters under inquiry. But it is clear from what has been said that he employed only two causes, that of what-it-is and that according to matter (for the Forms are causes of what-it-is for other things, and the One for the Forms), and [said] what the underlying matter is, according to which the Forms are predicated in the case of sensibles and the One among the Forms: that it is the dyad, the Great and the Small. Further, he assigned to the elements, respectively, the cause of well and ill, as we say that certain of the earlier philosophers also sought to do, such as Empedocles and Anaxagoras.

Briefly, then, and in outline, we have reviewed who they are and in what manner they happen to have spoken concerning principles and truth. Yet we gain at least this much from them: that none of those who speak concerning principle and cause has said anything outside the [causes] distinguished by us in the writings on nature, but all appear, though obscurely, somehow to touch upon these.

For some speak of the principle as matter, whether they posit one [such principle] or more, and whether they posit it as body or as incorporeal (for example, Plato in speaking of the Great and the Small; the Italians, of the Unlimited; Empedocles, of fire and earth and water and air; Anaxagoras, of the infinity of homoeomeries; all these, then, have laid hold of this kind of cause; as have also all those who [posit] air or fire or water, or something denser than fire but finer than air—for some have said the first element to be of this sort). These, then, have touched upon this cause alone; but certain others [have touched upon] that whence the principle of motion comes (for example, all who make friendship and strife, or intellect, or love, a principle). But no one has clearly rendered the what-it-was-to-be and the substance, though those who posit the Forms speak of it most of all (for they do not suppose the Forms to be matter for sensibles, nor the One for the Forms, nor [suppose] the principle of motion to arise from these—for they say

that they are rather causes of immobility and of being at rest—but the Forms provide the what-it-was-to-be for each of the other things, and the One for the Forms). As for that for the sake of which actions and changes and motions [occur], they in a way call it a cause, but they do not call it so in this way, nor in the way in which it naturally is [a cause].

For those who speak of intellect or friendship posit these causes as good, but not as that for the sake of which something among beings either is or comes to be; rather, they say that motions proceed from them. Similarly too, those who say that the One or Being is such a nature say that it is a cause of substance, but not that it is for the sake of this that things either are or come to be. Thus it happens to them, in a way, both to say and not to say that the good is a cause; for they do not say it simply, but incidentally. That the causes have been correctly distinguished, both how many and what sorts they are, all these men too seem to bear witness for us, since they are unable to touch upon any other cause. And, in addition to these, it is clear that the principles must be sought either all in this way or in some such manner. But how each of these has spoken concerning them, and what is the situation regarding the principles, let us next go through the possible difficulties concerning them.

All, then, who posit both that the whole is one and some one nature as matter, and posit this as bodily and as having magnitude, plainly err in many ways. For they posit elements only of bodies, not of incorporeals, though there are incorporeals also. And while undertaking to state the causes concerning coming-to-be and passing-away, and while theorizing about all things concerning nature, they eliminate the cause of motion. Further, [they err] by positing neither substance nor what-it-is as the cause of anything; and, besides these things, by readily declaring any one whatsoever of the simple bodies, except earth, to be a principle, without considering how they come to be from one another—I mean fire and water and earth and air. For some come to be from one another by combination, others by separation; and this makes the greatest difference with respect to being prior and posterior.

For, on the one hand, that from which things first come to be by combination would seem to be most elemental of all; and such would be the most fine-parted and thinnest of bodies. Hence those who posit fire as a principle would speak most consistently according to this account. And each of the others too agrees that the element of bodies is of this sort; at any rate, none of those who say that [all is] one thought fit to make earth an element, evidently because of its large parts, whereas each of the other three elements has found some advocate: some say that it is fire, others water, others air. And yet why do they not also speak of earth, as most human beings do? For they say that all things are earth; and Hesiod too says that earth came to be first among bodies—so ancient and popular has this supposition happened to be. According to this account, then, neither if someone says any one of these except fire, nor if someone posits it as denser than air but finer than water, would he speak correctly. But if what is posterior in

generation is prior by nature, and what has been concocted and combined is posterior in generation, the opposite of these [claims] would hold: water would be prior to air, and earth to water. Let this, then, have been said concerning those who posit one cause of the sort we have mentioned. But the same [objections apply] also if someone posits more of these, as Empedocles says that matter consists of four bodies. For to him it is necessary that some consequences be the same and others peculiar. For we observe them coming to be from one another, since fire and earth do not always remain the same body (and concerning these things it has been spoken in the writings on nature); and concerning the cause of things in motion, whether one or two should be posited, one must not think that he has spoken altogether either correctly or reasonably. In general, those who speak in this way must eliminate alteration; for there will not be cold from hot, nor hot from cold. For what would the contraries undergo, and what one nature would there be that became fire and water—which he does not assert.

If one were to suppose that Anaxagoras says there are two elements, one would most especially suppose this in accordance with an argument which he himself did not articulate, but which he would necessarily have followed if others had led him [to it]. For it is absurd in other ways too to say that all things were mixed at the beginning: both because it follows that the unmixed must pre-exist, and because one random thing is not naturally fitted to mix with another random thing; and besides, because affections and accidents would be separable from substances (for mixing and separation belong to the same things). Nevertheless, if someone followed him by articulating jointly what he wishes to say, he might perhaps appear to speak more originally. For when nothing was separated off, plainly nothing true could be said of that substance; I mean, for example, that it was neither white nor black nor gray nor any other colour, but was necessarily colourless—for it would otherwise have had some one of these colours. Likewise, by this same argument, it was tasteless, and none of the other similar things; for it could not be either a something-qualified or a quantity or a what.

For some of the forms spoken of in part would belong to it; but this is impossible if all things are mixed, for they would already have been separated off. Yet he says that all things are mixed except intellect, and that intellect alone is unmixed and pure. From these [claims], then, it follows for him to say that the principles are both the One (for this is simple and unmixed) and the Other, such as we posit the indefinite before it has been determined and participated in some form. Thus he speaks neither correctly nor clearly, though he intends something similar to what those who speak later, and those now apparent [to us], say rather. But these men are at home only in arguments concerning coming-to-be and passing-away and motion (for they investigate principles and causes almost exclusively concerning this kind of substance); whereas those who make their inquiry concerning all beings, and posit that of beings some are sensible and others not sensible, plainly conduct their examination concerning both kinds. Hence one might dwell more upon them, [examining] what they say well or not well

for the inquiry now before us. Those called Pythagoreans, then, employ principles and elements more remote from those of the natural philosophers (the reason being that they took them not from sensibles; for mathematical objects among beings are without motion, except those concerned with astronomy); nevertheless, they discourse and concern themselves wholly with nature. For they generate the heaven, and observe what happens in its parts, affections, and works, and expend their principles and causes upon these, as though agreeing with the other natural philosophers that being is just whatever is sensible and embraced by what is called heaven. But the causes and principles, as we have said, they state to be sufficient for ascending even to the higher regions of beings, and more fitting than for accounts concerning nature.

Yet they say nothing about how motion will arise when only limit and unlimited, odd and even, are posited; or how, without motion and change, coming-to-be and passing-away can occur, or the works of the bodies borne along in heaven. Further, even if one were to grant them that magnitude is composed out of these, or if this were demonstrated, nevertheless how will some bodies be light and others have weight? For from what they posit and say, they speak no more about mathematical bodies than about sensible ones. Hence they have said nothing whatever about fire or earth or any other such bodies, since, I think, they say nothing peculiar about sensibles.

Further, how are we to understand that the affections of number and number are causes of the things that are and come to be in heaven, both from the beginning and now, while there is no number other than this number from which the cosmos has been constituted? For whenever in this part there are, for them, opinion and occasion, and a little higher or lower injustice and judgment or mixture, and they say as proof that each of these is a number, but it happens that already in this place there is a multitude of constituted magnitudes because these affections follow each of the places respectively—is this the same number, the number in heaven, which must be taken to be each of these things, or is it another besides this? Plato says it is another. Yet he too thinks that these things and their causes are numbers, but the former are intelligible causes and the latter sensible.

Let the Pythagoreans, then, be dismissed for the present (for it is sufficient to have touched upon them to this extent). But those who posit the Ideas as causes, first, in seeking to grasp the causes of these beings here, brought in other [beings] equal in number to these, as though someone wishing to count, and thinking he would be unable to do so with fewer things, should make them more numerous and then count them. For the Forms are nearly equal—or not fewer—in number to the things from which, while seeking their causes, they proceeded to the Forms. For corresponding to each thing there is something homonymous, both apart from substances and, among other things, one over many, both in the case of these here and in the case of eternal things. Further, by none of the ways through which we demonstrate that the Forms exist do they appear [to exist]. For from some [arguments] no necessary inference results, while from others Forms result even of things of which we do not think [there are Forms].

For according to the arguments from the sciences, there will be Forms of all things of which there are sciences; and according to the one-over-many, there will be Forms even of negations; and according to thinking of something that has perished, [there will be Forms] of perishables, for there is some phantasm of these. Further, of the more precise arguments, some make Ideas of relatives, though we say that there is no genus of what is by itself; while others state the Third Man.

In general, the arguments concerning the Forms eliminate things which we wish to exist more than the existence of the Ideas. For it follows that the dyad is not first, but number; and that the relative is prior to what is by itself; and all the other things which certain men, following the opinions concerning the Ideas, have held contrary to the principles. Further, according to the supposition by which we say that the Ideas exist, there will be Forms not only of substances but also of many other things (for the conception is one not only concerning substances but also concerning other things, and there are sciences not only of substance but also of other things, and ten thousand other such consequences follow); but according to necessity and the opinions concerning them, if the Forms are participable, there must be Ideas of substances only.

For things do not participate incidentally, but each must participate in that in which it is not predicated of a subject (I mean, for example, if something participates in Double-itself, it also participates in Eternal, but incidentally; for it is incidental to the double to be eternal). Thus the Forms will be substances. But the same things signify substance both here and there; or what will being something apart from these be, the one over many? And if the Ideas and the participants have the same form, there will be something common (for why, in the case of perishable dyads and the many that are eternal, is the dyad one and the same rather than in the case of itself and some particular dyad?). But if they do not have the same form, they will be homonymous, much as if someone called both Callias and a piece of wood “human,” without regarding any community between them. But above all one might be puzzled as to what contribution the Forms make to sensibles, whether to eternal sensibles or to things that come to be and perish. For they are causes neither of motion nor of any change for them.

Nor indeed do they help at all toward knowledge of the other things (for they are not the substance of these things; otherwise they would be in them), nor toward their being, since they are not present in the participants. In that way they might perhaps seem to be causes, as white mixed with white; but this argument is very easily moved, which Anaxagoras first, and Eudoxus later, and certain others, advanced (for it is easy to gather many absurdities against such an opinion). Yet neither do the other things derive from the Forms in any of the customary senses of “from.” And to say that they are paradigms and that the other things participate in them is empty talk and poetic metaphor. For what is it that works while looking to the Ideas? Anything whatever can both be and come to be like [something else] without being likened to that [Idea], so that, whether Socrates exists or does not exist, someone like Socrates could come to be; and similarly, plainly, even if Socrates were eternal.

There will also be several paradigms of the same thing, and hence several Forms; for example, of human being there will be animal and two-footed, and at the same time Human-being-itself. Further, the Forms are paradigms not only of sensibles but also of themselves, as the genus is a genus of Forms; hence the same thing will be paradigm and image.

Again, it would seem impossible for the substance and that of which it is the substance to exist separately; so how could the Ideas, being substances of things, exist separately? In the Phaedo it is stated thus, that the Forms are causes both of being and of coming to be; yet, although the Forms exist, the things which participate in them do not come to be unless there is that which causes motion, and many other things come to be, such as a house and a ring, of which we say that there are no Forms. Hence it is clear that the other things also can both be and come to be through such causes as those now mentioned.—Again, if the Forms are numbers, how will they be causes? Is it because the things that are are other numbers—for example, this number is man, this is Socrates, and this Callias? Why then are the former causes of the latter? For even if the former are eternal and the latter are not, it will make no difference. But if it is because the things here are ratios of numbers, as a concord is, it is clear that there is some one thing of which they are ratios. And if this is something, namely matter, it is evident that the numbers themselves too will be certain ratios of one thing to another.

I mean, for example, if Callias is a ratio in numbers of fire, earth, water, and air, the Idea too will be a number of certain other underlying things; and Man-itself, whether it is some number or not, will nevertheless be a ratio in numbers of certain things, and not a number, nor will anything be a number on account of these things. Again, from many numbers one number comes to be; but how can one Form come to be from Forms? And if it is not from them but from the units in the number, as in ten thousand, how are the units related? For if they are of the same kind, many absurdities will result; and if they are not of the same kind, neither will they themselves be alike to one another nor will all the others be alike to all. For in what will they differ, if they are without affections? These things are neither reasonable nor consonant with thought. Again, it is necessary to construct another kind of number, with which arithmetic is concerned, and all the things called intermediates by some people: from what principles are these, or out of what? Or why will they be intermediate between the things here and the Forms themselves? Again, each of the units in the dyad is from some prior dyad; yet this is impossible.

Again, why is a number, when taken together, one? Again, in addition to what has been said, if the units are different, they ought to speak in the same way as those who posit four or two elements. For each of these too does not call the common thing, such as body, an element, but fire and earth, whether there is some common thing, body, or not. But now the One is spoken of as though it were something homogeneous, like fire or water. If this is so, numbers will not be substances; but it is clear that, if there is some One itself and this is a principle, “one” is said in several ways; for otherwise it is impossible.—But, wishing to reduce substances to principles, we posit lengths from short and long, from a certain small and great, and a plane from broad and narrow, and a solid from deep and shallow.

Yet how will either the plane contain a line, or the solid a line and a plane? For broad and narrow, and deep and shallow, are another genus. Therefore, just as number is not present in them, because much and little are different from these, it is clear that none of the other higher things will be present in the lower. But neither is broad a genus of deep; for body would then be some plane. Again, from what will points be present? Plato indeed disputed against this genus as being a geometrical doctrine, but he called the principle of a line—this he repeatedly posited—indivisible lines.

Yet there must be some limit of these; hence by the same argument by which there is a line, there is also a point.—But, in general, while wisdom seeks the cause concerning the things that are manifest, we have passed this over (for we say nothing concerning the cause from which the principle of change comes); and, thinking that we are stating their substance, we say that there are other substances, but we speak emptily as to how those are the substances of these. For participation, as we said before, is nothing. Nor do the Forms touch at all upon that which we see to be a cause in the sciences, for the sake of which both every intellect and all nature acts—nor upon this cause, which we say is one of the principles; rather, philosophy has become mathematics for the present people, although they say that mathematics must be cultivated for the sake of other things.

Again, one might suppose that the underlying substance, as matter, is rather mathematical, and that it is predicated of substance and matter, and is a difference of them rather than matter—for example, the great and the small—just as the natural philosophers also say of rare and dense, asserting that these are the primary differences of the underlying subject. For these are a kind of excess and deficiency. And concerning motion: if these will be motion, it is clear that the Forms will be moved; but if not, whence did motion come? For the whole inquiry concerning nature is abolished. And what seems easy, namely to show that all things are one, does not come about; for by the exposition all things do not become one, but some one thing itself, if one grants everything; and not even this, unless one grants that the universal is a genus; but in some cases this is impossible.

Nor is there any account of the lengths, planes, and solids after the numbers: neither how they are or will be, nor what power they possess. For these can be neither Forms (for they are not numbers), nor the intermediates (for those are mathematical), nor perishable things; rather, this appears again to be a fourth different genus. In general, to seek the elements of beings without having distinguished them, though they are spoken of in many ways, is impossible; especially when one seeks in this manner the elements of which they consist. For from what elements acting, being acted upon, or straightness consist, it is surely not possible to discover; but, if at all, it is possible only in the case of substances. Hence it is not true either to seek or to think one has the elements of all beings. And how could anyone even learn the elements of all things? For clearly one cannot previously possess any knowledge of them.

For just as one who is learning geometry can know other things beforehand, but has no previous knowledge of the things of which the science is concerned and which he is about to learn, so too in the case of the other sciences; hence, if there is a science of all things, such as some assert, this person would have no prior knowledge at all. Yet every learning is through things previously known, either all or some, both learning by demonstration and learning by definitions (for the things from which a definition is composed must be previously known and familiar); and likewise learning by induction. But indeed, even if it should happen to be innate, it is strange that we are unaware that we possess the most authoritative of the sciences. Again, how will one know from what things it consists, and how will this be clear? For this too presents a difficulty. One might dispute about it as about certain syllables: some say that “za” consists of s, d, and a, while others say that it is another sound and none of the familiar ones.

Again, how could anyone know things of which there is perception without possessing the perception? Yet this ought to be possible, if indeed all things have the same elements from which they consist, just as compound sounds consist of their proper elements.

That all seem to seek the causes stated in the Physics, and that we could name no cause apart from these, is clear also from what has been said before; but they have stated these obscurely, and in one way all have been stated before, but in another way not at all. For first philosophy seems to stammer concerning all things, since it is young and at its beginning. For Empedocles too says that bone exists by its ratio; and this is the what-it-was-to-be and the substance of the thing. But it is equally necessary that flesh and each of the other things should be their ratio, or else not one of them should be. For it is because of this that flesh and bone and each of the other things will be, and not because of the matter which he speaks of—fire, earth, water, and air. But if another had said these things, he would necessarily have agreed; yet he has not stated them clearly.

What concerns these matters has been made clear before; but let us return again to the difficulties that one might raise concerning these same things. For perhaps from them we may obtain some resource for the difficulties that follow.

sources.text:
ἡ περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας θεωρία τῇ μὲν χαλεπὴ τῇ δὲ ῥᾳδία. σημεῖον δὲ τὸ μήτʼ ἀξίως μηδένα δύνασθαι θιγεῖν αὐτῆς μήτε πάντας ἀποτυγχάνειν,  ἀλλʼ ἕκαστον λέγειν τι περὶ τῆς φύσεως, καὶ καθʼ ἕνα μὲν ἢ μηθὲν ἢ μικρὸν ἐπιβάλλειν αὐτῇ, ἐκ πάντων δὲ συναθροιζομένων γίγνεσθαί τι μέγεθος· ὥστʼ εἴπερ ἔοικεν ἔχειν καθάπερ τυγχάνομεν παροιμιαζόμενοι, τίς ἂν θύρας ἁμάρτοι; ταύτῃ μὲν ἂν εἴη ῥᾳδία, τὸ δʼ ὅλον τι ἔχειν καὶ μέρος μὴ δύνασθαι δηλοῖ τὸ χαλεπὸν αὐτῆς. ἴσως δὲ καὶ τῆς χαλεπότητος οὔσης κατὰ δύο τρόπους, οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασιν ἀλλʼ ἐν ἡμῖν τὸ αἴτιον αὐτῆς· ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος ἔχει τὸ μεθʼ ἡμέραν, οὕτω καὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας ψυχῆς ὁ νοῦς πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων. οὐ μόνον δὲ χάριν ἔχειν δίκαιον τούτοις ὧν ἄν τις κοινώσαιτο ταῖς δόξαις, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἐπιπολαιότερον ἀποφηναμένοις· καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι συνεβάλοντό τι· τὴν γὰρ ἕξιν προήσκησαν ἡμῶν· εἰ μὲν γὰρ Τιμόθεος μὴ ἐγένετο, πολλὴν ἂν μελοποιίαν οὐκ εἴχομεν· εἰ δὲ μὴ Φρῦνις, Τιμόθεος οὐκ ἂν ἐγένετο. τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀποφηναμένων· παρὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐνίων παρειλήφαμέν τινας δόξας, οἱ δὲ τοῦ γενέσθαι τούτους αἴτιοι γεγόνασιν. ὀρθῶς δʼ ἔχει καὶ τὸ καλεῖσθαι τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἐπιστήμην τῆς ἀληθείας. θεωρητικῆς μὲν γὰρ τέλος ἀλήθεια πρακτικῆς δʼ ἔργον· καὶ γὰρ ἂν τὸ πῶς ἔχει σκοπῶσιν, οὐ τὸ ἀΐδιον ἀλλʼ ὃ πρός τι καὶ νῦν θεωροῦσιν οἱ πρακτικοί. οὐκ ἴσμεν δὲ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἄνευ τῆς αἰτίας· ἕκαστον δὲ μάλιστα αὐτὸ τῶν ἄλλων καθʼ ὃ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑπάρχει τὸ συνώνυμον (οἷον τὸ πῦρ θερμότατον· καὶ γὰρ τοῖς ἄλλοις τὸ αἴτιον τοῦτο τῆς θερμότητος)· ὥστε καὶ ἀληθέστατον τὸ τοῖς ὑστέροις αἴτιον τοῦ ἀληθέσιν εἶναι. διὸ τὰς τῶν ἀεὶ ὄντων ἀρχὰς ἀναγκαῖον ἀεὶ εἶναι ἀληθεστάτας (οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀληθεῖς, οὐδʼ ἐκείναις αἴτιόν τί ἐστι τοῦ εἶναι, ἀλλʼ ἐκεῖναι τοῖς ἄλλοις) , ὥσθʼ ἕκαστον ὡς ἔχει τοῦ εἶναι, οὕτω καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας. 



 

 

 ἀλλὰ μὴν ὅτι γʼ ἔστιν ἀρχή τις καὶ οὐκ ἄπειρα τὰ αἴτια τῶν ὄντων οὔτʼ εἰς εὐθυωρίαν οὔτε κατʼ εἶδος, δῆλον. οὔτε γὰρ ὡς ἐξ ὕλης τόδʼ ἐκ τοῦδε δυνατὸν ἰέναι εἰς ἄπειρον (οἷον σάρκα μὲν ἐκ γῆς, γῆν δʼ ἐξ ἀέρος, ἀέρα δʼ ἐκ πυρός, καὶ τοῦτο μὴ ἵστασθαι), οὔτε ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως (οἷον τὸν μὲν ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀέρος κινηθῆναι, τοῦτον δʼ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, τὸν δὲ ἥλιον ὑπὸ τοῦ νείκους, καὶ τούτου μηδὲν εἶναι πέρας)· ὁμοίως δὲ οὐδὲ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα εἰς ἄπειρον οἷόν τε ἰέναι, βάδισιν μὲν ὑγιείας ἕνεκα, ταύτην δʼ εὐδαιμονίας, τὴν δʼ εὐδαιμονίαν ἄλλου, καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ ἄλλο ἄλλου ἕνεκεν εἶναι· καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι δʼ ὡσαύτως. τῶν γὰρ μέσων, ὧν ἐστί τι ἔσχατον καὶ πρότερον, ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι τὸ πρότερον αἴτιον τῶν μετʼ αὐτό. εἰ γὰρ εἰπεῖν ἡμᾶς δέοι τί τῶν τριῶν αἴτιον, τὸ πρῶτον ἐροῦμεν· οὐ γὰρ δὴ τό γʼ ἔσχατον, οὐδενὸς γὰρ τὸ τελευταῖον· ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ τὸ μέσον, ἑνὸς γάρ (οὐθὲν δὲ διαφέρει ἓν ἢ πλείω εἶναι, οὐδʼ ἄπειρα ἢ πεπερασμένα). τῶν δʼ ἀπείρων τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον καὶ ὅλως τοῦ ἀπείρου πάντα τὰ μόρια μέσα ὁμοίως μέχρι τοῦ νῦν· ὥστʼ εἴπερ μηδέν ἐστι πρῶτον, ὅλως αἴτιον οὐδέν ἐστιν.—ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδʼ ἐπὶ τὸ κάτω οἷόν τε εἰς ἄπειρον ἰέναι, τοῦ ἄνω ἔχοντος ἀρχήν, ὥστʼ ἐκ πυρὸς μὲν ὕδωρ, ἐκ δὲ τούτου γῆν, καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ ἄλλο τι γίγνεσθαι γένος. διχῶς γὰρ γίγνεται τόδε ἐκ τοῦδε—μὴ ὡς τόδε λέγεται μετὰ τόδε, οἷον ἐξ Ἰσθμίων Ὀλύμπια, ἀλλʼ ἢ ὡς ἐκ παιδὸς ἀνὴρ μεταβάλλοντος ἢ ὡς ἐξ ὕδατος ἀήρ. ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐκ παιδὸς ἄνδρα γίγνεσθαί φαμεν, ὡς ἐκ τοῦ γιγνομένου τὸ γεγονὸς ἢ ἐκ τοῦ ἐπιτελουμένου τὸ τετελεσμένον (ἀεὶ γάρ ἐστι μεταξύ, ὥσπερ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι γένεσις, οὕτω καὶ τὸ γιγνόμενον τοῦ ὄντος καὶ μὴ ὄντος· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ μανθάνων γιγνόμενος ἐπιστήμων, καὶ τοῦτʼ ἐστὶν ὃ λέγεται, ὅτι γίγνεται ἐκ μανθάνοντος ἐπιστήμων)· τὸ δʼ ὡς ἐξ ἀέρος ὕδωρ, φθειρομένου θατέρου. διὸ ἐκεῖνα μὲν οὐκ ἀνακάμπτει εἰς ἄλληλα,  οὐδὲ γίγνεται ἐξ ἀνδρὸς παῖς (οὐ γὰρ γίγνεται ἐκ τῆς γενέσεως τὸ γιγνόμενον ἀλλʼ ὃ ἔστι μετὰ τὴν γένεσιν· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρα ἐκ τοῦ πρωΐ, ὅτι μετὰ τοῦτο· διὸ οὐδὲ τὸ πρωῒ ἐξ ἡμέρας)· θάτερα δὲ ἀνακάμπτει. ἀμφοτέρως δὲ ἀδύνατον εἰς ἄπειρον ἰέναι· τῶν μὲν γὰρ ὄντων μεταξὺ ἀνάγκη τέλος εἶναι, τὰ δʼ εἰς ἄλληλα ἀνακάμπτει· ἡ γὰρ θατέρου φθορὰ θατέρου ἐστὶ γένεσις.—ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἀδύνατον τὸ πρῶτον ἀΐδιον ὂν φθαρῆναι· ἐπεὶ γὰρ οὐκ ἄπειρος ἡ γένεσις ἐπὶ τὸ ἄνω, ἀνάγκη ἐξ οὗ φθαρέντος πρώτου τι ἐγένετο μὴ ἀΐδιον εἶναι. ἔτι δὲ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα τέλος, τοιοῦτον δὲ ὃ μὴ ἄλλου ἕνεκα ἀλλὰ τἆλλα ἐκείνου, ὥστʼ εἰ μὲν ἔσται τοιοῦτόν τι ἔσχατον, οὐκ ἔσται ἄπειρον, εἰ δὲ μηθὲν τοιοῦτον, οὐκ ἔσται τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα, ἀλλʼ οἱ τὸ ἄπειρον ποιοῦντες λανθάνουσιν ἐξαιροῦντες τὴν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φύσιν (καίτοι οὐθεὶς ἂν ἐγχειρήσειεν οὐδὲν πράττειν μὴ μέλλων ἐπὶ πέρας ἥξειν)· οὐδʼ ἂν εἴη νοῦς ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν· ἕνεκα γάρ τινος ἀεὶ πράττει ὅ γε νοῦν ἔχων, τοῦτο δέ ἐστι πέρας· τὸ γὰρ τέλος πέρας ἐστίν. ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἐνδέχεται ἀνάγεσθαι εἰς ἄλλον ὁρισμὸν πλεονάζοντα τῷ λόγῳ· ἀεί τε γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ ἔμπροσθεν μᾶλλον, ὁ δʼ ὕστερος οὐκ ἔστιν, οὗ δὲ τὸ πρῶτον μὴ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἐχόμενον· ἔτι τὸ ἐπίστασθαι ἀναιροῦσιν οἱ οὕτως λέγοντες, οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε εἰδέναι πρὶν εἰς τὰ ἄτομα ἐλθεῖν· καὶ τὸ γιγνώσκειν οὐκ ἔστιν, τὰ γὰρ οὕτως ἄπειρα πῶς ἐνδέχεται νοεῖν; οὐ γὰρ ὅμοιον ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς, ἣ κατὰ τὰς διαιρέσεις μὲν οὐχ ἵσταται, νοῆσαι δʼ οὐκ ἔστι μὴ στήσαντα (διόπερ οὐκ ἀριθμήσει τὰς τομὰς ὁ τὴν ἄπειρον διεξιών), ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ὅλην οὐ κινουμένῳ νοεῖν ἀνάγκη. καὶ ἀπείρῳ οὐδενὶ ἔστιν εἶναι· εἰ δὲ μή, οὐκ ἄπειρόν γʼ ἐστὶ τὸ ἀπείρῳ εἶναι.—ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ εἰ ἄπειρά γʼ ἦσαν πλήθει τὰ εἴδη τῶν αἰτίων, οὐκ ἂν ἦν οὐδʼ οὕτω τὸ γιγνώσκειν· τότε γὰρ εἰδέναι οἰόμεθα ὅταν τὰ αἴτια γνωρίσωμεν· τὸ δʼ ἄπειρον κατὰ τὴν πρόσθεσιν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν πεπερασμένῳ διεξελθεῖν. 



 

 

αἱ δʼ ἀκροάσεις κατὰ τὰ ἔθη συμβαίνουσιν· ὡς γὰρ εἰώθαμεν οὕτως ἀξιοῦμεν λέγεσθαι,  καὶ τὰ παρὰ ταῦτα οὐχ ὅμοια φαίνεται ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ἀσυνήθειαν ἀγνωστότερα καὶ ξενικώτερα· τὸ γὰρ σύνηθες γνώριμον. ἡλίκην δὲ ἰσχὺν ἔχει τὸ σύνηθες οἱ νόμοι δηλοῦσιν, ἐν οἷς τὰ μυθώδη καὶ παιδαριώδη μεῖζον ἰσχύει τοῦ γινώσκειν περὶ αὐτῶν διὰ τὸ ἔθος. οἱ μὲν οὖν ἐὰν μὴ μαθηματικῶς λέγῃ τις οὐκ ἀποδέχονται τῶν λεγόντων, οἱ δʼ ἂν μὴ παραδειγματικῶς, οἱ δὲ μάρτυρα ἀξιοῦσιν ἐπάγεσθαι ποιητήν. καὶ οἱ μὲν πάντα ἀκριβῶς, τοὺς δὲ λυπεῖ τὸ ἀκριβὲς ἢ διὰ τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι συνείρειν ἢ διὰ τὴν μικρολογίαν· ἔχει γάρ τι τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοιοῦτον, ὥστε, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν συμβολαίων, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν λόγων ἀνελεύθερον εἶναί τισι δοκεῖ. διὸ δεῖ πεπαιδεῦσθαι πῶς ἕκαστα ἀποδεκτέον, ὡς ἄτοπον ἅμα ζητεῖν ἐπιστήμην καὶ τρόπον ἐπιστήμης· ἔστι δʼ οὐδὲ θάτερον ῥᾴδιον λαβεῖν. τὴν δʼ ἀκριβολογίαν τὴν μαθηματικὴν οὐκ ἐν ἅπασιν ἀπαιτητέον, ἀλλʼ ἐν τοῖς μὴ ἔχουσιν ὕλην. διόπερ οὐ φυσικὸς ὁ τρόπος· ἅπασα γὰρ ἴσως ἡ φύσις ἔχει ὕλην. διὸ σκεπτέον πρῶτον τί ἐστιν ἡ φύσις· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ περὶ τίνων ἡ φυσικὴ δῆλον ἔσται .

paragraphs.text: ἡ περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας θεωρία τῇ μὲν χαλεπὴ τῇ δὲ ῥᾳδία. σημεῖον δὲ τὸ μήτʼ ἀξίως μηδένα δύνασθαι θιγεῖν αὐτῆς μήτε πάντας ἀποτυγχάνειν,  ἀλλʼ ἕκαστον λέγειν τι περὶ τῆς φύσεως, καὶ καθʼ ἕνα μὲν ἢ μηθὲν ἢ μικρὸν ἐπιβάλλειν αὐτῇ, ἐκ πάντων δὲ συναθροιζομένων γίγνεσθαί τι μέγεθος· ὥστʼ εἴπερ ἔοικεν ἔχειν καθάπερ τυγχάνομεν παροιμιαζόμενοι, τίς ἂν θύρας ἁμάρτοι; ταύτῃ μὲν ἂν εἴη ῥᾳδία, τὸ δʼ ὅλον τι ἔχειν καὶ μέρος μὴ δύνασθαι δηλοῖ τὸ χαλεπὸν αὐτῆς. ἴσως δὲ καὶ τῆς χαλεπότητος οὔσης κατὰ δύο τρόπους, οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πράγμασιν ἀλλʼ ἐν ἡμῖν τὸ αἴτιον αὐτῆς· ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος ἔχει τὸ μεθʼ ἡμέραν, οὕτω καὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας ψυχῆς ὁ νοῦς πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων.

οὐ μόνον δὲ χάριν ἔχειν δίκαιον τούτοις ὧν ἄν τις κοινώσαιτο ταῖς δόξαις, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἐπιπολαιότερον ἀποφηναμένοις· καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι συνεβάλοντό τι· τὴν γὰρ ἕξιν προήσκησαν ἡμῶν· εἰ μὲν γὰρ Τιμόθεος μὴ ἐγένετο, πολλὴν ἂν μελοποιίαν οὐκ εἴχομεν· εἰ δὲ μὴ Φρῦνις, Τιμόθεος οὐκ ἂν ἐγένετο. τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀποφηναμένων· παρὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐνίων παρειλήφαμέν τινας δόξας, οἱ δὲ τοῦ γενέσθαι τούτους αἴτιοι γεγόνασιν. ὀρθῶς δʼ ἔχει καὶ τὸ καλεῖσθαι τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἐπιστήμην τῆς ἀληθείας. θεωρητικῆς μὲν γὰρ τέλος ἀλήθεια πρακτικῆς δʼ ἔργον· καὶ γὰρ ἂν τὸ πῶς ἔχει σκοπῶσιν, οὐ τὸ ἀΐδιον ἀλλʼ ὃ πρός τι καὶ νῦν θεωροῦσιν οἱ πρακτικοί.

οὐκ ἴσμεν δὲ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἄνευ τῆς αἰτίας· ἕκαστον δὲ μάλιστα αὐτὸ τῶν ἄλλων καθʼ ὃ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑπάρχει τὸ συνώνυμον (οἷον τὸ πῦρ θερμότατον· καὶ γὰρ τοῖς ἄλλοις τὸ αἴτιον τοῦτο τῆς θερμότητος)· ὥστε καὶ ἀληθέστατον τὸ τοῖς ὑστέροις αἴτιον τοῦ ἀληθέσιν εἶναι. διὸ τὰς τῶν ἀεὶ ὄντων ἀρχὰς ἀναγκαῖον ἀεὶ εἶναι ἀληθεστάτας (οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀληθεῖς, οὐδʼ ἐκείναις αἴτιόν τί ἐστι τοῦ εἶναι, ἀλλʼ ἐκεῖναι τοῖς ἄλλοις) , ὥσθʼ ἕκαστον ὡς ἔχει τοῦ εἶναι, οὕτω καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας.

ἀλλὰ μὴν ὅτι γʼ ἔστιν ἀρχή τις καὶ οὐκ ἄπειρα τὰ αἴτια τῶν ὄντων οὔτʼ εἰς εὐθυωρίαν οὔτε κατʼ εἶδος, δῆλον. οὔτε γὰρ ὡς ἐξ ὕλης τόδʼ ἐκ τοῦδε δυνατὸν ἰέναι εἰς ἄπειρον (οἷον σάρκα μὲν ἐκ γῆς, γῆν δʼ ἐξ ἀέρος, ἀέρα δʼ ἐκ πυρός, καὶ τοῦτο μὴ ἵστασθαι), οὔτε ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως (οἷον τὸν μὲν ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀέρος κινηθῆναι, τοῦτον δʼ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, τὸν δὲ ἥλιον ὑπὸ τοῦ νείκους, καὶ τούτου μηδὲν εἶναι πέρας)· ὁμοίως δὲ οὐδὲ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα εἰς ἄπειρον οἷόν τε ἰέναι, βάδισιν μὲν ὑγιείας ἕνεκα, ταύτην δʼ εὐδαιμονίας, τὴν δʼ εὐδαιμονίαν ἄλλου, καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ ἄλλο ἄλλου ἕνεκεν εἶναι· καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι δʼ ὡσαύτως. τῶν γὰρ μέσων, ὧν ἐστί τι ἔσχατον καὶ πρότερον, ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι τὸ πρότερον αἴτιον τῶν μετʼ αὐτό.

εἰ γὰρ εἰπεῖν ἡμᾶς δέοι τί τῶν τριῶν αἴτιον, τὸ πρῶτον ἐροῦμεν· οὐ γὰρ δὴ τό γʼ ἔσχατον, οὐδενὸς γὰρ τὸ τελευταῖον· ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ τὸ μέσον, ἑνὸς γάρ (οὐθὲν δὲ διαφέρει ἓν ἢ πλείω εἶναι, οὐδʼ ἄπειρα ἢ πεπερασμένα). τῶν δʼ ἀπείρων τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον καὶ ὅλως τοῦ ἀπείρου πάντα τὰ μόρια μέσα ὁμοίως μέχρι τοῦ νῦν· ὥστʼ εἴπερ μηδέν ἐστι πρῶτον, ὅλως αἴτιον οὐδέν ἐστιν.—ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδʼ ἐπὶ τὸ κάτω οἷόν τε εἰς ἄπειρον ἰέναι, τοῦ ἄνω ἔχοντος ἀρχήν, ὥστʼ ἐκ πυρὸς μὲν ὕδωρ, ἐκ δὲ τούτου γῆν, καὶ οὕτως ἀεὶ ἄλλο τι γίγνεσθαι γένος. διχῶς γὰρ γίγνεται τόδε ἐκ τοῦδε—μὴ ὡς τόδε λέγεται μετὰ τόδε, οἷον ἐξ Ἰσθμίων Ὀλύμπια, ἀλλʼ ἢ ὡς ἐκ παιδὸς ἀνὴρ μεταβάλλοντος ἢ ὡς ἐξ ὕδατος ἀήρ.

ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐκ παιδὸς ἄνδρα γίγνεσθαί φαμεν, ὡς ἐκ τοῦ γιγνομένου τὸ γεγονὸς ἢ ἐκ τοῦ ἐπιτελουμένου τὸ τετελεσμένον (ἀεὶ γάρ ἐστι μεταξύ, ὥσπερ τοῦ εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι γένεσις, οὕτω καὶ τὸ γιγνόμενον τοῦ ὄντος καὶ μὴ ὄντος· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ μανθάνων γιγνόμενος ἐπιστήμων, καὶ τοῦτʼ ἐστὶν ὃ λέγεται, ὅτι γίγνεται ἐκ μανθάνοντος ἐπιστήμων)· τὸ δʼ ὡς ἐξ ἀέρος ὕδωρ, φθειρομένου θατέρου. διὸ ἐκεῖνα μὲν οὐκ ἀνακάμπτει εἰς ἄλληλα,  οὐδὲ γίγνεται ἐξ ἀνδρὸς παῖς (οὐ γὰρ γίγνεται ἐκ τῆς γενέσεως τὸ γιγνόμενον ἀλλʼ ὃ ἔστι μετὰ τὴν γένεσιν· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρα ἐκ τοῦ πρωΐ, ὅτι μετὰ τοῦτο· διὸ οὐδὲ τὸ πρωῒ ἐξ ἡμέρας)· θάτερα δὲ ἀνακάμπτει.

ἀμφοτέρως δὲ ἀδύνατον εἰς ἄπειρον ἰέναι· τῶν μὲν γὰρ ὄντων μεταξὺ ἀνάγκη τέλος εἶναι, τὰ δʼ εἰς ἄλληλα ἀνακάμπτει· ἡ γὰρ θατέρου φθορὰ θατέρου ἐστὶ γένεσις.—ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἀδύνατον τὸ πρῶτον ἀΐδιον ὂν φθαρῆναι· ἐπεὶ γὰρ οὐκ ἄπειρος ἡ γένεσις ἐπὶ τὸ ἄνω, ἀνάγκη ἐξ οὗ φθαρέντος πρώτου τι ἐγένετο μὴ ἀΐδιον εἶναι. ἔτι δὲ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα τέλος, τοιοῦτον δὲ ὃ μὴ ἄλλου ἕνεκα ἀλλὰ τἆλλα ἐκείνου, ὥστʼ εἰ μὲν ἔσται τοιοῦτόν τι ἔσχατον, οὐκ ἔσται ἄπειρον, εἰ δὲ μηθὲν τοιοῦτον, οὐκ ἔσται τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα, ἀλλʼ οἱ τὸ ἄπειρον ποιοῦντες λανθάνουσιν ἐξαιροῦντες τὴν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φύσιν (καίτοι οὐθεὶς ἂν ἐγχειρήσειεν οὐδὲν πράττειν μὴ μέλλων ἐπὶ πέρας ἥξειν)· οὐδʼ ἂν εἴη νοῦς ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν· ἕνεκα γάρ τινος ἀεὶ πράττει ὅ γε νοῦν ἔχων, τοῦτο δέ ἐστι πέρας· τὸ γὰρ τέλος πέρας ἐστίν.

ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἐνδέχεται ἀνάγεσθαι εἰς ἄλλον ὁρισμὸν πλεονάζοντα τῷ λόγῳ· ἀεί τε γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ ἔμπροσθεν μᾶλλον, ὁ δʼ ὕστερος οὐκ ἔστιν, οὗ δὲ τὸ πρῶτον μὴ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἐχόμενον· ἔτι τὸ ἐπίστασθαι ἀναιροῦσιν οἱ οὕτως λέγοντες, οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε εἰδέναι πρὶν εἰς τὰ ἄτομα ἐλθεῖν· καὶ τὸ γιγνώσκειν οὐκ ἔστιν, τὰ γὰρ οὕτως ἄπειρα πῶς ἐνδέχεται νοεῖν; οὐ γὰρ ὅμοιον ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς, ἣ κατὰ τὰς διαιρέσεις μὲν οὐχ ἵσταται, νοῆσαι δʼ οὐκ ἔστι μὴ στήσαντα (διόπερ οὐκ ἀριθμήσει τὰς τομὰς ὁ τὴν ἄπειρον διεξιών), ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ὅλην οὐ κινουμένῳ νοεῖν ἀνάγκη. καὶ ἀπείρῳ οὐδενὶ ἔστιν εἶναι· εἰ δὲ μή, οὐκ ἄπειρόν γʼ ἐστὶ τὸ ἀπείρῳ εἶναι.—ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ εἰ ἄπειρά γʼ ἦσαν πλήθει τὰ εἴδη τῶν αἰτίων, οὐκ ἂν ἦν οὐδʼ οὕτω τὸ γιγνώσκειν· τότε γὰρ εἰδέναι οἰόμεθα ὅταν τὰ αἴτια γνωρίσωμεν· τὸ δʼ ἄπειρον κατὰ τὴν πρόσθεσιν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν πεπερασμένῳ διεξελθεῖν.

αἱ δʼ ἀκροάσεις κατὰ τὰ ἔθη συμβαίνουσιν· ὡς γὰρ εἰώθαμεν οὕτως ἀξιοῦμεν λέγεσθαι,  καὶ τὰ παρὰ ταῦτα οὐχ ὅμοια φαίνεται ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν ἀσυνήθειαν ἀγνωστότερα καὶ ξενικώτερα· τὸ γὰρ σύνηθες γνώριμον. ἡλίκην δὲ ἰσχὺν ἔχει τὸ σύνηθες οἱ νόμοι δηλοῦσιν, ἐν οἷς τὰ μυθώδη καὶ παιδαριώδη μεῖζον ἰσχύει τοῦ γινώσκειν περὶ αὐτῶν διὰ τὸ ἔθος. οἱ μὲν οὖν ἐὰν μὴ μαθηματικῶς λέγῃ τις οὐκ ἀποδέχονται τῶν λεγόντων, οἱ δʼ ἂν μὴ παραδειγματικῶς, οἱ δὲ μάρτυρα ἀξιοῦσιν ἐπάγεσθαι ποιητήν. καὶ οἱ μὲν πάντα ἀκριβῶς, τοὺς δὲ λυπεῖ τὸ ἀκριβὲς ἢ διὰ τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι συνείρειν ἢ διὰ τὴν μικρολογίαν· ἔχει γάρ τι τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοιοῦτον, ὥστε, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν συμβολαίων, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν λόγων ἀνελεύθερον εἶναί τισι δοκεῖ. διὸ δεῖ πεπαιδεῦσθαι πῶς ἕκαστα ἀποδεκτέον, ὡς ἄτοπον ἅμα ζητεῖν ἐπιστήμην καὶ τρόπον ἐπιστήμης· ἔστι δʼ οὐδὲ θάτερον ῥᾴδιον λαβεῖν.

τὴν δʼ ἀκριβολογίαν τὴν μαθηματικὴν οὐκ ἐν ἅπασιν ἀπαιτητέον, ἀλλʼ ἐν τοῖς μὴ ἔχουσιν ὕλην. διόπερ οὐ φυσικὸς ὁ τρόπος· ἅπασα γὰρ ἴσως ἡ φύσις ἔχει ὕλην. διὸ σκεπτέον πρῶτον τί ἐστιν ἡ φύσις· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ περὶ τίνων ἡ φυσικὴ δῆλον ἔσται .

The inquiry concerning truth is in one respect difficult, in another easy. A sign of this is that no one is able to attain it worthily, nor do all fail, but each says something about nature; and individually they contribute either nothing or little to it, but from all gathered together some magnitude results. Thus, if it is as we happen proverbially to say, “Who could miss a door?”, in this respect it would be easy; but the fact that one can have the whole and not be able to have a part indicates its difficulty. Perhaps, too, since the difficulty is in two ways, its cause lies not in the things but in us: for just as the eyes of bats stand toward the light of day, so too the intellect of our soul stands toward the things which are by nature most evident of all.

It is just to be grateful not only to those whose opinions one might share, but also to those who have made pronouncements more superficially; for these too have contributed something: they have exercised our habit of mind beforehand. For if Timotheus had not existed, we should not have had much music; and if Phrynis had not existed, Timotheus would not have existed. The same is true also of those who have made pronouncements concerning truth: from some we have received certain opinions, while others have been causes of the coming-to-be of these men.

And it is right that philosophy should be called knowledge of truth. For the end of theoretical knowledge is truth, whereas that of practical knowledge is action; for even if practical men investigate how something stands, they contemplate not the eternal but what is relative to something and now.

But we do not know what is true without its cause; and each thing is most of all that by which the synonymous attribute also belongs to the other things (for example, fire is hottest; for it is also the cause of heat in the other things). Thus what is the cause for subsequent things of being true is also most true. Therefore the principles of things that are always are necessarily always most true (for they are not true at one time only, nor is there some cause for them of being, but they are causes for the other things); so that each thing is as it is in respect of being, so also in respect of truth.

But indeed, that there is some principle, and that the causes of beings are not infinite either in a straight succession or in kind, is evident. For it is not possible, as from matter, for this to proceed from this to infinity—for example, flesh from earth, earth from air, air from fire, and for this not to stop—nor is it possible for the source of motion to proceed thus: for example, for man to be moved by air, this by the sun, the sun by Strife, and for there to be no limit to this. Likewise, it is not possible for the final cause to proceed to infinity: walking for the sake of health, health for the sake of happiness, happiness for the sake of something else, and thus always one thing for the sake of another. The same holds also for the what-it-was-to-be. For among intermediates, where there is some last and prior term, the prior must be the cause of what comes after it.

For if we had to say which of three is the cause, we shall say the first. For surely it is not the last, since the last is the cause of nothing; nor indeed is it the middle, for it is the cause of one thing (and it makes no difference whether it is one or many, or infinite or finite). But in infinities of this kind, and in an infinity generally, all the parts are alike intermediate, down to the present point. Therefore, if there is nothing first, there is no cause at all.—But neither is it possible to proceed to infinity downward, if what is above has a principle, so that from fire comes water, and from this earth, and thus some other kind always comes to be. For this comes to be from that in two ways—not in the sense in which this is said to come after that, as the Olympic games after the Isthmian games, but either as a man from a changing child, or as air from water.

Now when we say that a man comes to be from a child, this is as the completed from what is coming to be, or the finished from what is being completed (for there is always something intermediate; and, just as generation is intermediate between being and not-being, so what is coming to be is intermediate between what is and what is not. For the learner is becoming knowledgeable, and this is what is meant by saying that the knowledgeable comes to be from the learner). But water comes from air as one of the two is perishing. Therefore the former do not turn back into one another, nor does a child come to be from a man (for what is coming to be does not come to be from the coming-to-be, but from what is after the coming-to-be; thus day comes from morning because it is after it; therefore morning does not come from day); but the latter do turn back into one another.

But in both ways it is impossible to proceed to infinity. For among things that are intermediate there must be an end, while the things that turn into one another return; for the perishing of one is the coming-to-be of the other.—At the same time, it is impossible for the first thing, being eternal, to perish. For since generation is not infinite upward, that from whose first perishing something came to be must not be eternal. Further, that for the sake of which is an end; and such is that which is not for the sake of another, but the other things are for its sake. Thus, if there will be some such last thing, there will not be an infinity; but if there is nothing such, there will not be that for the sake of which. Yet those who posit the infinite unwittingly abolish the nature of the good (although no one would undertake to do anything if he were not going to arrive at an end); nor would there be intellect among beings, for one who has intellect always acts for the sake of something, and this is a limit; for the end is a limit.

But neither can the what-it-was-to-be be referred back to another definition increasing in account; for the preceding term is always more so, while the subsequent term is not; and where the first is not, neither is what follows. Further, those who speak thus abolish knowledge, for it is not possible to know before reaching the indivisibles; and knowing is impossible, for how can things infinite in this way be thought? For it is not like a line, which does not stop in its divisions, but cannot be thought unless one stops it (which is why one traversing the infinite will not count the cuts); rather, it is necessary to think even the whole without moving through it. And for no infinite thing is there being; if not, then being-infinite is not infinite.—But indeed, even if the kinds of causes were infinite in number, knowing would not exist even so; for we think that we know when we have come to know the causes, whereas what is infinite by addition cannot be gone through in a finite time.

Lectures accord with habits. For as we are accustomed, so we demand things be said; and what is contrary to these habits does not appear similar, but through unfamiliarity appears more unknown and more foreign. For what is customary is familiar. The laws make clear how great the force of what is customary is: in them, mythical and childish matters prevail more than knowledge about them, because of habit. Thus, some do not accept speakers unless they speak mathematically; others, unless they speak by examples; and others demand that a poet be adduced as a witness. Some demand precision in everything, whereas precision distresses others, either because they cannot connect the points or because of pettiness; for precision has something of this character, so that, as in contracts, it seems to some to be ungenerous also in arguments. Therefore one must have been educated in how each kind of thing is to be accepted, since it is absurd to seek at the same time knowledge and the method of knowledge; yet neither of the two is easy to acquire.

Mathematical exactness is not to be demanded in all matters, but in those which do not have matter. Hence this method is not that of natural science; for perhaps all nature has matter. Therefore one must first investigate what nature is; for thus it will also be clear what things natural science concerns.

ἀνάγκη πρὸς τὴν ἐπιζητουμένην ἐπιστήμην ἐπελθεῖν ἡμᾶς πρῶτον περὶ ὧν ἀπορῆσαι δεῖ πρῶτον· ταῦτα δʼ ἐστὶν ὅσα τε περὶ αὐτῶν ἄλλως ὑπειλήφασί τινες, κἂν εἴ τι χωρὶς τούτων τυγχάνει παρεωραμένον. ἔστι δὲ τοῖς εὐπορῆσαι βουλομένοις προὔργου τὸ διαπορῆσαι καλῶς· ἡ γὰρ ὕστερον εὐπορία λύσις τῶν πρότερον ἀπορουμένων ἐστί, λύειν δʼ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀγνοοῦντας τὸν δεσμόν, ἀλλʼ ἡ τῆς διανοίας ἀπορία δηλοῖ τοῦτο περὶ τοῦ πράγματος· ᾗ γὰρ ἀπορεῖ, ταύτῃ παραπλήσιον πέπονθε τοῖς δεδεμένοις· ἀδύνατον γὰρ ἀμφοτέρως προελθεῖν εἰς τὸ πρόσθεν. διὸ δεῖ τὰς δυσχερείας τεθεωρηκέναι πάσας πρότερον, τούτων τε χάριν καὶ διὰ τὸ τοὺς ζητοῦντας ἄνευ τοῦ διαπορῆσαι πρῶτον ὁμοίους εἶναι τοῖς ποῖ δεῖ βαδίζειν ἀγνοοῦσι, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις οὐδʼ εἴ ποτε τὸ ζητούμενον εὕρηκεν ἢ μὴ γιγνώσκειν·  τὸ γὰρ τέλος τούτῳ μὲν οὐ δῆλον τῷ δὲ προηπορηκότι δῆλον. ἔτι δὲ βέλτιον ἀνάγκη ἔχειν πρὸς τὸ κρῖναι τὸν ὥσπερ ἀντιδίκων καὶ τῶν ἀμφισβητούντων λόγων ἀκηκοότα πάντων.—ἔστι δʼ ἀπορία πρώτη μὲν περὶ ὧν ἐν τοῖς πεφροιμιασμένοις διηπορήσαμεν, πότερον μιᾶς ἢ πολλῶν ἐπιστημῶν θεωρῆσαι τὰς αἰτίας· καὶ πότερον τὰς τῆς οὐσίας ἀρχὰς τὰς πρώτας ἐστὶ τῆς ἐπιστήμης ἰδεῖν μόνον ἢ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἐξ ὧν δεικνύουσι πάντες, οἷον πότερον ἐνδέχεται ταὐτὸ καὶ ἓν ἅμα φάναι καὶ ἀποφάναι ἢ οὔ, καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν τοιούτων· εἴ τʼ ἐστι περὶ τὴν οὐσίαν, πότερον μία περὶ πάσας ἢ πλείονές εἰσι, κἂν εἰ πλείονες πότερον ἅπασαι συγγενεῖς ἢ τὰς μὲν σοφίας τὰς δὲ ἄλλο τι λεκτέον αὐτῶν. καὶ τοῦτο δʼ αὐτὸ τῶν ἀναγκαίων ἐστὶ ζητῆσαι, πότερον τὰς αἰσθητὰς οὐσίας εἶναι μόνον φατέον ἢ καὶ παρὰ ταύτας ἄλλας, καὶ πότερον μοναχῶς ἢ πλείονα γένη τῶν οὐσιῶν, οἷον οἱ ποιοῦντες τά τε εἴδη καὶ τὰ μαθηματικὰ μεταξὺ τούτων τε καὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν. περί τε τούτων οὖν, καθάπερ φαμέν, ἐπισκεπτέον, καὶ πότερον περὶ τὰς οὐσίας ἡ θεωρία μόνον ἐστὶν ἢ καὶ περὶ τὰ συμβεβηκότα καθʼ αὑτὰ ταῖς οὐσίαις, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις περὶ ταὐτοῦ καὶ ἑτέρου καὶ ὁμοίου καὶ ἀνομοίου καὶ ἐναντιότητος, καὶ περὶ προτέρου καὶ ὑστέρου καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων τῶν τοιούτων περὶ ὅσων οἱ διαλεκτικοὶ πειρῶνται σκοπεῖν ἐκ τῶν ἐνδόξων μόνων ποιούμενοι τὴν σκέψιν, τίνος ἐστὶ θεωρῆσαι περὶ πάντων· ἔτι δὲ τούτοις αὐτοῖς ὅσα καθʼ αὑτὰ συμβέβηκεν, καὶ μὴ μόνον τί ἐστι τούτων ἕκαστον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἆρα ἓν ἑνὶ ἐναντίον· καὶ πότερον αἱ ἀρχαὶ καὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα τὰ γένη ἐστὶν ἢ εἰς ἃ διαιρεῖται ἐνυπάρχοντα ἕκαστον· καὶ εἰ τὰ γένη, πότερον ὅσα ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀτόμοις λέγεται  τελευταῖα ἢ τὰ πρῶτα, οἷον πότερον ζῷον ἢ ἄνθρωπος ἀρχή τε καὶ μᾶλλον ἔστι παρὰ τὸ καθʼ ἕκαστον. μάλιστα δὲ ζητητέον καὶ πραγματευτέον πότερον ἔστι τι παρὰ τὴν ὕλην αἴτιον καθʼ αὑτὸ ἢ οὔ, καὶ τοῦτο χωριστὸν ἢ οὔ, καὶ πότερον ἓν ἢ πλείω τὸν ἀριθμόν, καὶ πότερον ἔστι τι παρὰ τὸ σύνολον (λέγω δὲ τὸ σύνολον, ὅταν κατηγορηθῇ τι τῆς ὕλης) ἢ οὐθέν, ἢ τῶν μὲν τῶν δʼ οὔ, καὶ ποῖα τοιαῦτα τῶν ὄντων.  ἔτι αἱ ἀρχαὶ πότερον ἀριθμῷ ἢ εἴδει ὡρισμέναι, καὶ αἱ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις καὶ αἱ ἐν τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ; καὶ πότερον τῶν φθαρτῶν καὶ ἀφθάρτων αἱ αὐταὶ ἢ ἕτεραι, καὶ πότερον ἄφθαρτοι πᾶσαι ἢ τῶν φθαρτῶν φθαρταί; ἔτι δὲ τὸ πάντων χαλεπώτατον καὶ πλείστην ἀπορίαν ἔχον, πότερον τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ ὄν, καθάπερ οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι καὶ Πλάτων ἔλεγεν, οὐχ ἕτερόν τί ἐστιν ἀλλʼ οὐσία τῶν ὄντων; ἢ οὔ, ἀλλʼ ἕτερόν τι τὸ ὑποκείμενον, ὥσπερ Ἐμπεδοκλῆς φησὶ φιλίαν ἄλλος δέ τις πῦρ ὁ δὲ ὕδωρ ἢ ἀέρα· καὶ πότερον αἱ ἀρχαὶ καθόλου εἰσὶν ἢ ὡς τὰ καθʼ ἕκαστα τῶν πραγμάτων, καὶ δυνάμει ἢ ἐνεργείᾳ· ἔτι πότερον ἄλλως ἢ κατὰ κίνησιν· καὶ γὰρ ταῦτα ἀπορίαν ἂν παράσχοι πολλήν. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις πότερον οἱ ἀριθμοὶ καὶ τὰ μήκη καὶ τὰ σχήματα καὶ αἱ στιγμαὶ οὐσίαι τινές εἰσιν ἢ οὔ, κἂν εἰ οὐσίαι πότερον κεχωρισμέναι τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἢ ἐνυπάρχουσαι ἐν τούτοις; περὶ γὰρ τούτων ἁπάντων οὐ μόνον χαλεπὸν τὸ εὐπορῆσαι τῆς ἀληθείας ἀλλʼ οὐδὲ τὸ διαπορῆσαι τῷ λόγῳ ῥᾴδιον καλῶς. 



 

 

πρῶτον μὲν οὖν περὶ ὧν πρῶτον εἴπομεν, πότερον μιᾶς ἢ πλειόνων ἐστὶν ἐπιστημῶν θεωρῆσαι πάντα τὰ γένη τῶν αἰτίων. μιᾶς μὲν γὰρ ἐπιστήμης πῶς ἂν εἴη μὴ ἐναντίας οὔσας τὰς ἀρχὰς γνωρίζειν; ἔτι δὲ πολλοῖς τῶν ὄντων οὐχ ὑπάρχουσι πᾶσαι· τίνα γὰρ τρόπον οἷόν τε κινήσεως ἀρχὴν εἶναι τοῖς ἀκινήτοις ἢ τὴν τἀγαθοῦ φύσιν, εἴπερ ἅπαν ὃ ἂν ᾖ ἀγαθὸν καθʼ αὑτὸ καὶ διὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φύσιν τέλος ἐστὶν καὶ οὕτως αἴτιον ὅτι ἐκείνου ἕνεκα καὶ γίγνεται καὶ ἔστι τἆλλα, τὸ δὲ τέλος καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα πράξεώς τινός ἐστι τέλος, αἱ δὲ πράξεις πᾶσαι μετὰ κινήσεως; ὥστʼ ἐν τοῖς ἀκινήτοις οὐκ ἂν ἐνδέχοιτο ταύτην εἶναι τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδʼ εἶναί τι αὐτοαγαθόν. διὸ καὶ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασιν οὐθὲν δείκνυται διὰ ταύτης τῆς αἰτίας, οὐδʼ ἔστιν ἀπόδειξις οὐδεμία διότι βέλτιον ἢ χεῖρον, ἀλλʼ οὐδὲ τὸ παράπαν μέμνηται οὐθεὶς οὐθενὸς τῶν τοιούτων, ὥστε διὰ ταῦτα τῶν σοφιστῶν τινὲς οἷον Ἀρίστιππος προεπηλάκιζεν αὐτάς· ἐν μὲν γὰρ ταῖς ἄλλαις τέχναις, καὶ ταῖς βαναύσοις, οἷον ἐν τεκτονικῇ καὶ σκυτικῇ, διότι βέλτιον ἢ χεῖρον λέγεσθαι πάντα, τὰς δὲ μαθηματικὰς οὐθένα ποιεῖσθαι λόγον περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν.  —ἀλλὰ μὴν εἴ γε πλείους ἐπιστῆμαι τῶν αἰτίων εἰσὶ καὶ ἑτέρα ἑτέρας ἀρχῆς, τίνα τούτων φατέον εἶναι τὴν ζητουμένην, ἢ τίνα μάλιστα τοῦ πράγματος τοῦ ζητουμένου ἐπιστήμονα τῶν ἐχόντων αὐτάς; ἐνδέχεται γὰρ τῷ αὐτῷ πάντας τοὺς τρόπους τοὺς τῶν αἰτίων ὑπάρχειν, οἷον οἰκίας ὅθεν μὲν ἡ κίνησις ἡ τέχνη καὶ ὁ οἰκοδόμος, οὗ δʼ ἕνεκα τὸ ἔργον, ὕλη δὲ γῆ καὶ λίθοι, τὸ δʼ εἶδος ὁ λόγος. ἐκ μὲν οὖν τῶν πάλαι διωρισμένων τίνα χρὴ καλεῖν τῶν ἐπιστημῶν σοφίαν ἔχει λόγον ἑκάστην προσαγορεύειν· ᾗ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχικωτάτη καὶ ἡγεμονικωτάτη καὶ ᾗ ὥσπερ δούλας οὐδʼ ἀντειπεῖν τὰς ἄλλας ἐπιστήμας δίκαιον, ἡ τοῦ τέλους καὶ τἀγαθοῦ τοιαύτη (τούτου γὰρ ἕνεκα τἆλλα), ᾗ δὲ τῶν πρώτων αἰτίων καὶ τοῦ μάλιστα ἐπιστητοῦ διωρίσθη εἶναι, ἡ τῆς οὐσίας ἂν εἴη τοιαύτη· πολλαχῶς γὰρ ἐπισταμένων τὸ αὐτὸ μᾶλλον μὲν εἰδέναι φαμὲν τὸν τῷ εἶναι γνωρίζοντα τί τὸ πρᾶγμα ἢ τῷ μὴ εἶναι, αὐτῶν δὲ τούτων ἕτερον ἑτέρου μᾶλλον, καὶ μάλιστα τὸν τί ἐστιν ἀλλʼ οὐ τὸν πόσον ἢ ποῖον ἢ τί ποιεῖν ἢ πάσχειν πέφυκεν. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις τὸ εἰδέναι ἕκαστον καὶ ὧν ἀποδείξεις εἰσί, τότʼ οἰόμεθα ὑπάρχειν ὅταν εἰδῶμεν τί ἐστιν (οἷον τί ἐστι τὸ τετραγωνίζειν, ὅτι μέσης εὕρεσις· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων), περὶ δὲ τὰς γενέσεις καὶ τὰς πράξεις καὶ περὶ πᾶσαν μεταβολὴν ὅταν εἰδῶμεν τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς κινήσεως· τοῦτο δʼ ἕτερον καὶ ἀντικείμενον τῷ τέλει, ὥστʼ ἄλλης ἂν δόξειεν ἐπιστήμης εἶναι τὸ θεωρῆσαι τῶν αἰτίων τούτων ἕκαστον.—ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀποδεικτικῶν ἀρχῶν, πότερον μιᾶς ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμης ἢ πλειόνων, ἀμφισβητήσιμόν ἐστιν (λέγω δὲ ἀποδεικτικὰς τὰς κοινὰς δόξας ἐξ ὧν ἅπαντες δεικνύουσιν) οἷον ὅτι πᾶν ἀναγκαῖον ἢ φάναι ἢ ἀποφάναι, καὶ ἀδύνατον ἅμα εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι, καὶ ὅσαι ἄλλαι τοιαῦται προτάσεις, πότερον μία τούτων ἐπιστήμη καὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἢ ἑτέρα, κἂν εἰ μὴ μία, ποτέραν χρὴ προσαγορεύειν τὴν ζητουμένην νῦν. μιᾶς μὲν οὖν οὐκ εὔλογον εἶναι· τί γὰρ μᾶλλον γεωμετρίας ἢ ὁποιασοῦν περὶ τούτων ἐστὶν ἴδιον τὸ ἐπαΐειν; εἴπερ οὖν ὁμοίως μὲν ὁποιασοῦν ἐστίν, ἁπασῶν δὲ μὴ ἐνδέχεται,  ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τῶν ἄλλων οὕτως οὐδὲ τῆς γνωριζούσης τὰς οὐσίας ἴδιόν ἐστι τὸ γιγνώσκειν περὶ αὐτῶν. ἅμα δὲ καὶ τίνα τρόπον ἔσται αὐτῶν ἐπιστήμη; τί μὲν γὰρ ἕκαστον τούτων τυγχάνει ὂν καὶ νῦν γνωρίζομεν (χρῶνται γοῦν ὡς γιγνωσκομένοις αὐτοῖς καὶ ἄλλαι τέχναι)· εἰ δὲ ἀποδεικτικὴ περὶ αὐτῶν ἐστί, δεήσει τι γένος εἶναι ὑποκείμενον καὶ τὰ μὲν πάθη τὰ δʼ ἀξιώματʼ αὐτῶν (περὶ πάντων γὰρ ἀδύνατον ἀπόδειξιν εἶναι), ἀνάγκη γὰρ ἔκ τινων εἶναι καὶ περί τι καὶ τινῶν τὴν ἀπόδειξιν· ὥστε συμβαίνει πάντων εἶναι γένος ἕν τι τῶν δεικνυμένων, πᾶσαι γὰρ αἱ ἀποδεικτικαὶ χρῶνται τοῖς ἀξιώμασιν.—ἀλλὰ μὴν εἰ ἑτέρα ἡ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ ἡ περὶ τούτων, ποτέρα κυριωτέρα καὶ προτέρα πέφυκεν αὐτῶν; καθόλου γὰρ μάλιστα καὶ πάντων ἀρχαὶ τὰ ἀξιώματά ἐστιν, εἴ τʼ ἐστὶ μὴ τοῦ φιλοσόφου, τίνος ἔσται περὶ αὐτῶν ἄλλου τὸ θεωρῆσαι τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ ψεῦδος;—ὅλως τε τῶν οὐσιῶν πότερον μία πασῶν ἐστὶν ἢ πλείους ἐπιστῆμαι; εἰ μὲν οὖν μὴ μία, ποίας οὐσίας θετέον τὴν ἐπιστήμην ταύτην; τὸ δὲ μίαν πασῶν οὐκ εὔλογον· καὶ γὰρ ἂν ἀποδεικτικὴ μία περὶ πάντων εἴη τῶν συμβεβηκότων, εἴπερ πᾶσα ἀποδεικτικὴ περί τι ὑποκείμενον θεωρεῖ τὰ καθʼ αὑτὰ συμβεβηκότα ἐκ τῶν κοινῶν δοξῶν. περὶ οὖν τὸ αὐτὸ γένος τὰ συμβεβηκότα καθʼ αὑτὰ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐστὶ θεωρῆσαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν δοξῶν. περί τε γὰρ ὃ μιᾶς καὶ ἐξ ὧν μιᾶς, εἴτε τῆς αὐτῆς εἴτε ἄλλης, ὥστε καὶ τὰ συμβεβηκότα, εἴθʼ αὗται θεωροῦσιν εἴτʼ ἐκ τούτων μία.—ἔτι δὲ πότερον περὶ τὰς οὐσίας μόνον ἡ θεωρία ἐστὶν ἢ καὶ περὶ τὰ συμβεβηκότα ταύταις; λέγω δʼ οἷον, εἰ τὸ στερεὸν οὐσία τίς ἐστι καὶ γραμμαὶ καὶ ἐπίπεδα, πότερον τῆς αὐτῆς ταῦτα γνωρίζειν ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμης καὶ τὰ συμβεβηκότα περὶ ἕκαστον γένος περὶ ὧν αἱ μαθηματικαὶ  δεικνύουσιν, ἢ ἄλλης. εἰ μὲν γὰρ τῆς αὐτῆς, ἀποδεικτική τις ἂν εἴη καὶ ἡ τῆς οὐσίας, οὐ δοκεῖ δὲ τοῦ τί ἐστιν ἀπόδειξις εἶναι· εἰ δʼ ἑτέρας, τίς ἔσται ἡ θεωροῦσα περὶ τὴν οὐσίαν τὰ συμβεβηκότα; τοῦτο γὰρ ἀποδοῦναι παγχάλεπον.—ἔτι δὲ πότερον τὰς αἰσθητὰς οὐσίας μόνας εἶναι φατέον ἢ καὶ παρὰ ταύτας ἄλλας, καὶ πότερον μοναχῶς ἢ πλείω γένη τετύχηκεν ὄντα τῶν οὐσιῶν,  οἷον οἱ λέγοντες τά τε εἴδη καὶ τὰ μεταξύ, περὶ ἃ τὰς μαθηματικὰς εἶναί φασιν ἐπιστήμας; ὡς μὲν οὖν λέγομεν τὰ εἴδη αἴτιά τε καὶ οὐσίας εἶναι καθʼ ἑαυτὰς εἴρηται ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις λόγοις περὶ αὐτῶν· πολλαχῇ δὲ ἐχόντων δυσκολίαν, οὐθενὸς ἧττον ἄτοπον τὸ φάναι μὲν εἶναί τινας φύσεις παρὰ τὰς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, ταύτας δὲ τὰς αὐτὰς φάναι τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς πλὴν ὅτι τὰ μὲν ἀΐδια τὰ δὲ φθαρτά. αὐτὸ γὰρ ἄνθρωπόν φασιν εἶναι καὶ ἵππον καὶ ὑγίειαν, ἄλλο δʼ οὐδέν, παραπλήσιον ποιοῦντες τοῖς θεοὺς μὲν εἶναι φάσκουσιν ἀνθρωποειδεῖς δέ· οὔτε γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐποίουν ἢ ἀνθρώπους ἀϊδίους, οὔθʼ οὗτοι τὰ εἴδη ἄλλʼ ἢ αἰσθητὰ ἀΐδια. ἔτι δὲ εἴ τις παρὰ τὰ εἴδη καὶ τὰ αἰσθητὰ τὰ μεταξὺ θήσεται, πολλὰς ἀπορίας ἕξει· δῆλον γὰρ ὡς ὁμοίως γραμμαί τε παρά τʼ αὐτὰς καὶ τὰς αἰσθητὰς ἔσονται καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν ἄλλων γενῶν· ὥστʼ ἐπείπερ ἡ ἀστρολογία μία τούτων ἐστίν, ἔσται τις καὶ οὐρανὸς παρὰ τὸν αἰσθητὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ ἥλιός τε καὶ σελήνη καὶ τἆλλα ὁμοίως τὰ κατὰ τὸν οὐρανόν. καίτοι πῶς δεῖ πιστεῦσαι τούτοις; οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀκίνητον εὔλογον εἶναι, κινούμενον δὲ καὶ παντελῶς ἀδύνατον· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ ὧν ἡ ὀπτικὴ πραγματεύεται καὶ ἡ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασιν ἁρμονική· καὶ γὰρ ταῦτα ἀδύνατον εἶναι παρὰ τὰ αἰσθητὰ διὰ τὰς αὐτὰς αἰτίας· εἰ γὰρ ἔστιν αἰσθητὰ μεταξὺ καὶ αἰσθήσεις, δῆλον ὅτι καὶ ζῷα ἔσονται μεταξὺ αὐτῶν τε καὶ τῶν φθαρτῶν. ἀπορήσειε δʼ ἄν τις καὶ περὶ ποῖα τῶν ὄντων δεῖ ζητεῖν ταύτας τὰς ἐπιστήμας. εἰ γὰρ τούτῳ διοίσει τῆς γεωδαισίας ἡ γεωμετρία μόνον, ὅτι ἡ μὲν τούτων ἐστὶν ὧν αἰσθανόμεθα ἡ δʼ οὐκ αἰσθητῶν, δῆλον ὅτι καὶ παρʼ ἰατρικὴν ἔσται τις ἐπιστήμη καὶ παρʼ ἑκάστην τῶν ἄλλων μεταξὺ αὐτῆς τε ἰατρικῆς καὶ τῆσδε τῆς ἰατρικῆς· καίτοι πῶς τοῦτο δυνατόν;
