Sakralisierung des Niedrigen → Sichtbarkeit einer Religion, die Bedürftigkeit als Transzendenz organisiert.
Beobachtung des Rituals → Umschlag von religiöser Feier in groteske Diagnose menschlicher Gottesbedürftigkeit.
Lärmende Gemeinschaft → plötzliche Stille → geheime Beobachtung.
Verdecktes Ritual → Entdeckung der Eselanbetung → Umkehrung religiöser Erhabenheit.
Eselhafte Eigenschaften → liturgische Überhöhung → Konstruktion eines affirmativen Gottes.
Wiederholtes „I-A“ → Bestätigung ohne Sprache → Offenlegung mechanischer Frömmigkeit.
Gemeinsame Verehrung → Regression der höheren Menschen → Satire des Bedürfnisses nach widerspruchsloser Transzendenz.
Göttlichkeit wird von geistiger Höhe auf Lasttragen, Duldung, Schweigen und Bedürfnis herab- beziehungsweise umkartiert.
Schweigen erscheint nicht mehr als bloße Sprachlosigkeit, sondern als vermeintliche Quelle von Weisheit und Unfehlbarkeit.
Das Ja wird aus einer sprachlichen Antwort in ein ontologisches Prinzip der Weltbestätigung verwandelt.
Die Grenze zwischen religiösem Ernst und grotesker Nachahmung wird als strukturell instabil sichtbar.
Die höheren Menschen werden nicht als religionslose Kritiker, sondern als Träger eines weiterhin wirksamen Frömmigkeitsbedürfnisses kartiert.
Universalität wird nicht durch Erkenntnis oder Freiheit, sondern durch unterschiedslose Aufnahmefähigkeit definiert.
Surface — Eine Gruppe höherer Menschen betet unter Weihrauch und Litanei einen Esel an.
Structural — Eine religiöse Ordnung erhebt Passivität, Dienstbarkeit, Schweigen und unterschiedslose Duldung zu Tugenden.
Metastrategic — Die Szene verschiebt die Kritik von einzelnen Glaubensinhalten auf die Form eines Bedürfnisses nach einem widerspruchslosen Gott.
Ontological/Temporal — Weltbejahung wird als unbedingtes, immer wiederholtes Ja gesetzt; Veränderung durch Nein, Urteil oder Negation bleibt ausgeschlossen.
Die Axiome reichen aus, um Ritual, Esel, Litanei und „I-A“ als zusammenhängende Erzeugungsstruktur zu rekonstruieren.
Die zentrale Bewegungsform von ausgelassener Gemeinschaft zu regressiver Frömmigkeit bleibt erhalten.
Unterbestimmt bleibt, ob die höheren Menschen den Esel bewusst als Parodie oder unbewusst als Gott verehren.
Nicht vollständig aufgelöst wird die Spannung zwischen echter religiöser Bedürftigkeit und ihrer grotesken Entlarvung.
Die Struktur ist intern kohärent, weil jede Lobpreisung das Prinzip des bedingungslosen Ja weiter verdichtet.
Die stärkste Stelle ist die Kopplung von liturgischer Form und mechanischem Tierlaut.
Die Rekonstruktion hängt an der satirischen Gleichzeitigkeit von Sakralisierung und Entwertung.
The exuberant fellowship of the higher human beings abruptly turns into a religious ceremony.
The object of veneration becomes visible not as a sublime deity, but as a donkey.
A litany transforms bearing burdens, patience, silence, tolerance, and instinctive satisfaction of needs into divine qualities.
The repeated “I-A” functions simultaneously as a liturgical response and as an acoustic emptying of religious meaning.
The scene produces a satire of piety, whose target is not merely the donkey, but the need for a God without contradiction.
The cave of the higher human beings can pass from noise and laughter into complete silence.
Zarathustra occupies the position of an observing outsider in relation to the assembly.
The higher human beings kneel together before a donkey and treat it as God.
The religious act is formalized through incense, prayer, litany, and praise.
The litany ascribes to the donkey the bearing of burdens, the form of a servant, patience, and unconditional saying-yes.
The donkey's silence is interpreted as wisdom, infallibility, or avoidance of error.
The asinine is presented as an inconspicuous, gray, and spirit-concealing order of virtues.
The donkey rejects neither beggars nor kings and is thereby constructed as universally accessible.
The repeated “I-A” replaces the God's verbal response and nevertheless confirms every stanza of the litany.
Bodily neediness and simple pleasure are sacralized as components of divine wisdom.
Donkey worship combines religious sublimity with stupidity, need, and mechanical assent.
Veneration is not grounded in a recognizable transcendent revelation.
The worshipped God utters no conceptually articulated truth.
Religious value is not determined through contradiction, examination, or judgment.
The divine principle does not depend on sublimity, purity, or spiritual superiority.
The litany excludes an active no, a rejection, or a selective decision on the part of God.
The assembled human beings are not organized through enlightened distance or critical self-control.
The scene denies piety an unambiguous separation between seriousness and grotesquerie.
If the donkey's silence counts as wisdom, the absence of statement can appear as protection against error.
If the donkey never says no, assent becomes the primary criterion of its divinity.
If the donkey receives every social figure, religious universality is modeled as indiscriminate tolerance.
If bearing burdens and the form of a servant are praised, subordination is recoded into a virtue of the divine.
If “I-A” accompanies every stanza, the litany is simultaneously confirmed and devalued by a nonverbal form of repetition.
If need and simple pleasure count as wisdom, divinity is bound to bodily immediacy rather than spiritual mediation.
If the higher human beings worship the donkey as God, their religious neediness becomes visible as a relapse into childish and formulaic piety.
The scene produces a model of God whose highest quality is not truth, but contradiction-free confirmation of the existing world.
The religious form transforms passivity, servility, and absence of judgment into apparent metaphysical perfection.
The donkey's mechanical response reveals that the litany produces its meaning independently of a God who understands or speaks.
In donkey worship, the higher human beings seek a form of transcendence that does not surpass their neediness, but confirms it.
The satire is directed at the structural production of holiness from arbitrary qualities suitable precisely because of their lowness.
The system tacitly presupposes that a God without no, judgment, and resistance can count as superior.
It excludes that truth must arise through conceptual speech, examination, or contradiction.
It disqualifies the assumption that divinity requires a distance from the bodily, the needy, and the ridiculous.
It treats critical autonomy as less capable of binding than shared submission to an affirmative symbol.
It excludes a religion whose God does not merely confirm the world, but judges and changes it.
Excluded is the possibility of a transcendence that is not exhausted in the repetition of what is already given.
Absent remains a God who responds, contradicts, distinguishes, or imposes responsibility.
Foreclosed is a community that does not derive its unity from shared regression and shared worship.
Unavailable is a positive determination of the sacred beyond the inversion and intensification of low qualities.
Shared noise → abrupt silence → concealed observation by Zarathustra.
Incense and prayer form → sacred framing of a profane animal.
Donkey as object → transfer of burden, patience, silence, and tolerance into divine predicates.
Litany → ongoing totalization of the unconditional yes.
“I-A” → nonverbal confirmation → simultaneous fulfillment and dismantling of the liturgy.
Sacralization of the low → visibility of a religion that organizes neediness as transcendence.
Observation of the ritual → transformation of religious celebration into a grotesque diagnosis of the human need for God.
Noisy community → sudden silence → secret observation.
Concealed ritual → discovery of donkey worship → inversion of religious sublimity.
Asinine qualities → liturgical elevation → construction of an affirmative God.
Repeated “I-A” → confirmation without language → disclosure of mechanical piety.
Shared worship → regression of the higher human beings → satire of the need for contradiction-free transcendence.
Divinity is remapped downward, or alternatively remapped, from spiritual height onto bearing burdens, tolerance, silence, and need.
Silence no longer appears as mere speechlessness, but as a purported source of wisdom and infallibility.
Yes is transformed from a verbal response into an ontological principle of world-affirmation.
The boundary between religious seriousness and grotesque imitation becomes visible as structurally unstable.
The higher human beings are mapped not as irreligious critics, but as bearers of a still-effective need for piety.
Universality is defined not through knowledge or freedom, but through indiscriminate receptivity.
Surface — A group of higher human beings worships a donkey amid incense and litany.
Structural — A religious order elevates passivity, servility, silence, and indiscriminate tolerance into virtues.
Metastrategic — The scene shifts criticism from individual contents of belief to the form of a need for a God without contradiction.
Ontological/Temporal — World-affirmation is posited as an unconditional, ever-repeated yes; change through no, judgment, or negation remains excluded.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct ritual, donkey, litany, and “I-A” as a coherent generative structure.
The central movement from exuberant community to regressive piety is preserved.
It remains underdetermined whether the higher human beings consciously venerate the donkey as a parody or unconsciously as God.
The tension between genuine religious neediness and its grotesque exposure is not fully resolved.
The structure is internally coherent because every act of praise further condenses the principle of the unconditional yes.
The strongest point is the coupling of liturgical form and mechanical animal sound.
The reconstruction depends on the satirical simultaneity of sacralization and devaluation.
Die Szene problematisiert die Rückkehr religiöser Anbetung in einer als frei verstandenen Zeit.
Zarathustra bestimmt die Eselanbetung als Blasphemie und Dummheit, wird durch sein eigenes I-A jedoch in die Szene hineingezogen.
Der Papst verschiebt die Frage von der Wahrheit der Gottesgestalt auf die Notwendigkeit irgendeiner Gestalt für den Glauben.
Die Stimmen der Gäste verkehren die Gegensätze von Glaube und Unglaube, Freiheit und Pfaffendienst sowie Klugheit und Dummheit.
Die Eselgestalt wird zugleich als Rückfall, als glaubwürdigste Gottesform und als mögliche Gestalt übermäßiger Weisheit lesbar.
Die Bewegung endet nicht mit der Feststellung von Gottes Tod, sondern mit einer unentschiedenen Relation von Wiederbelebung, Tötung und Lachen.
Die Gäste beten einen Esel als Gott an.
Zarathustra beurteilt diese Anbetung als Gotteslästerung und Dummheit.
Zarathustra schreit selbst I-A und springt unter die Anbetenden.
Der Papst setzt die Anbetung Gottes in irgendeiner Gestalt gegen die Anbetung Gottes in gar keiner Gestalt.
Der Papst deutet die Formel „Gott ist ein Geist“ als einen entscheidenden Schritt zum Unglauben.
Der Wanderer und Schatten behauptet, der alte Gott sei durch den hässlichsten Menschen wieder auferweckt worden.
Der kluge Zauberer erkennt seine Gottesverehrung als Dummheit an, ohne dadurch aus ihr herauszutreten.
Der Gewissenhafte des Geistes hält Gott in der Eselgestalt für am glaubwürdigsten und verbindet Langsamkeit sowie Dummheit mit großer zeitlicher Wirksamkeit.
Der Gewissenhafte erklärt, übermäßiger Geist und vollkommene Weisheit könnten in Esel- oder Narrheit umschlagen.
Der hässlichste Mensch erklärt Gottes Lebens- oder Todesstatus für unentscheidbar und erinnert an Zarathustras Lehre, dass man durch Lachen und nicht durch Zorn töte.
Eine Gottesverehrung ohne jede Gestalt wird als religiös unzureichend zurückgewiesen.
Ein rein geistiger Gottesbegriff wird als kein verlässlicher Schutz vor dem Unglauben behandelt.
Die Selbstbezeichnung als freier Geist schließt Götzen- und Pfaffendienst nicht aus.
Klugheit schließt Dummheit und religiösen Rückfall nicht aus.
Geistige Reinlichkeit und Gewissenhaftigkeit verhindern die Zustimmung zur Eselanbetung nicht.
Der Tod eines Gottes wird nicht als endgültig feststehender Zustand anerkannt.
Zarathustra bleibt nicht als äußerer Richter von der dargestellten religiösen Dynamik getrennt.
Zorn wird als notwendige oder höchste Form des Tötens ausgeschlossen.
Im päpstlichen Argument wird die konkrete Gestalt zur Bedingung dafür, dass Gottesverehrung den Unglauben überdauert.
Die Wiederkehr des alten Gottes erscheint als Folge einer erneuten Verkörperung und nicht als Ergebnis einer begrifflichen Widerlegung des Atheismus.
Die religiöse Handlung widerlegt die stabilen Selbstbilder der Beteiligten als freie, kluge oder geistig reine Subjekte.

Die Frage nach Gottes Tod wird in eine unentscheidbare Abfolge von Töten, Wiederbeleben und erneutem Leben überführt.

Lachen fungiert zugleich als Zerstörungsmittel, als Distanzierung vom Zorn und als Verfahren, durch das der Kritiker selbst in die religiöse Szene zurückkehrt.
Das System schließt die Möglichkeit aus, dass ein Gott ohne sinnlich oder symbolisch verfügbare Gestalt dauerhaft verehrt werden kann.
Es schließt eine endgültige Säkularisierung aus, in der der Tod Gottes nicht in Wiederkehr umschlagen kann.
Es schließt ein Subjekt aus, dessen Vernunft, Klugheit oder Geistigkeit es dauerhaft vor Dummheit und Kult schützt.
Es schließt eine reine Trennung zwischen dem religionskritischen Beobachter und dem religiösen Objekt aus.
Es schließt eine eindeutige Zuschreibung der religiösen Wiederkehr an einen einzelnen Urheber aus.
Es schließt eine Tötung aus, deren Wirkung in Zorn, Absicht und endgültigem Abschluss aufgeht.
Unmöglich wird eine endgültige Überwindung der Religion, die weder Gestalt noch Wiederholung noch Rückfall hervorbringt.
Unmöglich wird eine stabile Identität, deren Selbstbeschreibung ihre Handlungen abschließend bestimmt.
Unmöglich wird eine Kritik, die außerhalb der von ihr kritisierten religiösen Affekte und Formen stehen bleibt.
Unmöglich wird die vollständige Entscheidung zwischen Gottes Tod, Gottes Wiederkehr und der bloßen Fortdauer eines Vorurteils.

**Surface** — Die unmittelbare Szene zeigt die Anbetung eines Esels, Zarathustras Empörung und die Verteidigungsreden der Gäste.

The scene problematizes the return of religious worship in an age understood as free.
Zarathustra defines donkey worship as blasphemy and stupidity, yet is drawn into the scene by his own I-A.
The Pope shifts the question from the truth of God's form to the necessity of some form for faith.
The voices of the guests invert the oppositions between faith and unbelief, freedom and priestly service, as well as cleverness and stupidity.
The donkey form becomes readable simultaneously as regression, as the most credible form of God, and as a possible form of excessive wisdom.
The movement ends not with the assertion of God's death, but with an undecided relation of revival, killing, and laughter.
The guests worship a donkey as God.
Zarathustra judges this worship to be blasphemy and stupidity.
Zarathustra himself cries I-A and leaps among the worshippers.
The Pope sets the worship of God in some form against the worship of God in no form at all.
The Pope interprets the formula “God is a spirit” as a decisive step toward unbelief.
The Wanderer and Shadow claims that the old God has been resurrected by the ugliest man.
The clever magician acknowledges his veneration of God as stupidity, without thereby stepping out of it.
The Conscientious One of the Spirit considers God most credible in the donkey form and links slowness and stupidity with great temporal efficacy.
The Conscientious One declares that excessive spirit and perfect wisdom could turn into donkeyhood or folly.
The ugliest man declares God's status as living or dead undecidable and recalls Zarathustra's teaching that one kills through laughter and not through anger.
A veneration of God without any form whatsoever is rejected as religiously insufficient.
A purely spiritual concept of God is treated as no reliable protection against unbelief.
Self-designation as a free spirit does not exclude idolatry and priestly service.
Cleverness does not exclude stupidity and religious regression.
Spiritual cleanliness and conscientiousness do not prevent assent to donkey worship.
The death of a god is not recognized as a definitively established state.
Zarathustra does not remain separated, as an external judge, from the religious dynamic depicted.
Anger is excluded as a necessary or highest form of killing.
In the papal argument, concrete form becomes the condition under which veneration of God outlasts unbelief.
The return of the old God appears as the consequence of a renewed embodiment and not as the result of a conceptual refutation of atheism.
The religious act refutes the stable self-images of the participants as free, clever, or spiritually pure subjects.
The donkey form acquires its credibility precisely through the qualities that are ordinarily supposed to exclude higher spirituality: slowness, stupidity, and folly.
Zarathustra's critique becomes reflexive because his own wisdom is named as a possible origin of the very becoming-donkey that he condemns.
The question of God's death is transferred into an undecidable sequence of killing, reviving, and renewed life.
Laughter is determined as effective destruction without thereby conclusively clarifying the ontological status of what is killed.
The scene generates religious return from the failure of abstract transcendence: where the spiritual God intensifies unbelief, form stabilizes faith.
The categories of free spirit, cleverness, and conscientiousness prove to be not counterpositions to religion, but forms in which religious regression can occur.
Anti-religious critique becomes entangled in its own object: Zarathustra condemns worship, participates physically in it, and is described as a possible donkey.
God's death is transformed from a completed event into a reversible process of initiating killing, return, and renewed destruction.
Laughter functions at once as a means of destruction, as a distancing from anger, and as a procedure through which the critic himself returns to the religious scene.
The system excludes the possibility that a god without a sensuously or symbolically available form can be permanently worshipped.
It excludes a final secularization in which the death of God cannot turn into return.
It excludes a subject whose reason, cleverness, or spirituality permanently protects it from stupidity and cult.
It excludes a pure separation between the observer critical of religion and the religious object.
It excludes an unambiguous attribution of religious return to a single originator.
It excludes a killing whose effect is exhausted in anger, intention, and final completion.
Impossible is a final overcoming of religion that produces neither form, nor repetition, nor regression.
Impossible is a stable identity whose self-description conclusively determines its actions.
Impossible is a critique that remains outside the religious affects and forms it criticizes.
Impossible is the complete decision between God's death, God's return, and the mere persistence of a prejudice.
Abstract concept of God → loss of credibility → primacy of some form over formless worship.
Donkey form → sensuous credibility → renewed worship → assertion of the return of the old God.
Renewed worship → contradiction between action and self-description → dissolution of the oppositions between free spirit, cleverness, conscience, and priestly service.
Zarathustra's accusation → bodily and conceptual self-entanglement → possible becoming-donkey of the critic.
Laughter instead of anger → effective killing without ontological finality → keeping open death, return, and further transformation.

God's form is remapped from a mere object of worship into a condition of the possibility of faith.
The opposition between free spirit and religious service collapses because the free spirit appears as the bearer of service.
Cleverness, conscience, and wisdom are no longer mapped as counterforces to stupidity, but as possible transitional forms into it.
God's death is transformed from a binary state into a temporal loop of killing, return, and renewed killability.
Zarathustra's position shifts from external judge to co-affected component of the religious process.
Laughter is classified from a reaction into an operative force of destruction and reversal.
**Surface** — The immediate scene shows the worship of a donkey, Zarathustra's indignation, and the guests' speeches of defense.
**Structural** — The scene organizes a relation between form and abstraction, action and self-description, as well as wisdom and stupidity.
**Metastrategic** — Critique is neutralized through self-participation and reflexive return; laughter replaces direct confrontation with an indirect form of destruction.
**Ontological/Temporal** — God's being is treated as reversible and temporally unstable; death, return, and form remain intertwined.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from donkey worship to Zarathustra's reflexive entanglement.
It remains underdetermined whether the old God actually lives, lives again, or is fundamentally dead.
It also remains underdetermined whether the ugliest man causes the return or merely supplies its interpretation.
The structure is coherent as a dramatic movement of reversal, not as a contradiction-free doctrine of God.
Its strongest connection lies in the coupling of form, credibility, and return.
Its central unresolved tension consists in the fact that Zarathustra rejects worship while simultaneously embodying its bodily and conceptual conditions.
The reconstruction depends on keeping the different speaker positions separate; a leveling would falsely dissolve the productive contradictions.
The actual movement of argument remains preserved: interruption → defense of form → return → rupture of identity → self-entanglement → ontological openness.

The guests' religious spectacle becomes legible not primarily as an article of faith, but as affective regression and dissimulation.

Die stärkste Verbindung besteht zwischen der kommenden Stunde, der Mutprüfung und der offenen Herrschaftsfrage.

A speaking I experiences time as loss and the world as sleep.
The descent into the depths produces a knowledge that cannot be communicated directly.
The I declares itself dead in advance, while an hour yet to come is announced.
The coming hour transforms intimate midnight knowledge into a test of courage, rule, and capacity to hear.
The question of the lord of the earth is sharpened into the question of the authority permitted to determine the course of the streams.
The discourse ultimately addresses the higher human being, but remains restricted to fine ears and an opened-up midnight language.
Time is experienced as something that has been lost.
Depth is constituted through descent into wells and through midnight as a space of knowledge.
The world is asleep.
The midnight heart bears a thought whose communication is refused.
The death of the speaking I marks a transition, not the conclusion of the discourse.
A coming hour possesses the power to question and to shake.
This hour demands a sufficient heart or, respectively, sufficient courage.
The earth appears as a domain whose rule can be claimed.
Rule over the earth is conceived as directing the course of great and small streams.
The higher human being is a possible addressee of the coming discourse.
The midnight word is not accessible to every ear.
Midnight does not speak directly, but must be heard by an addressee capable of hearing.
The central thought of the midnight heart is not spoken.
The discourse is not intended for the sleeping world.
The coming hour is determined not by an answer, but by repeated questioning.
The lord of the earth has not yet been identified.
The appropriate rule over the streams has not yet been determined.
The discourse is addressed not to arbitrary listeners, but only to “fine ears.”
The higher human being has not yet been shown to be an actually hearing or ruling human being.
The loss of time is transferred into an expectation of the coming hour.
Depth produces not available knowledge, but knowledge whose transmission is bound to a special capacity to hear.
The announced death of the I intensifies the threshold between present speaking and future revelation.
The repeated question of the hour replaces a given order with a test of entitlement to rule.
Rule is determined not as possession, but as the capacity to give direction to natural movements.
The higher human being shifts from the object of address to the possible bearer of an answer not yet fulfilled.
The structure transforms a subjective crisis of time into an ontological-political test of rule over the earth.
Knowledge is organized as a threshold event: it arises in depth, is mediated through death and night, and remains dependent on selective audibility.
Rule appears as a still-open function of a coming decision, not as an already existing order.
The discourse produces its authority through the simultaneous refusal of communication and announcement of a necessary answer.
Truth is not presupposed as a fully present and generally available content.
Time is not presupposed as a continuous, neutral progression, but as loss, threshold, and impending interruption.
Rule is not presupposed as a given legitimacy or institutional possession.
The world is not presupposed as an awake, shared space of understanding.
The higher human being is not presupposed as an already completed subject.
Natural movement is not treated as a merely self-running process withdrawn from every human direction.
Excluded is a world in which truth would be immediately available without threshold, test, or selection.
Excluded is a rule whose right is established independently of courage, answer, and the capacity to give direction.
Excluded is a shared present in which speaker, world, and addressee are already awake and mutually understanding.
The decisive possibility of a legitimate earthly order remains absent; precisely this absence generates the question of the future lord.
Loss of time + sleep of the world → descent into depth → exclusive midnight knowledge.
Exclusive knowledge + refused communication → death-threshold of the I → announced future hour.
Coming hour + repeated question → test of heart and courage → opening of the question of rule.
Question of rule + image of the streams → rule as the giving of direction to natural movement.
Direction-giving rule + selective audibility → invocation of the higher human being as a possible answering authority.
Possible addressee + absent answer → deferred revelation and continued tension between proclamation and concealment.

Loss of time and sleep of the world → descent into depth → incommunicable midnight knowledge → symbolic death → coming questioning hour → test of courage → open question of earth and rule → invocation of the higher human being → selective audibility.
A subjective complaint about lost time is reclassified as a sign of a historical or ontological threshold.
The relation of knowledge and communication is remapped from general communicability to graduated capacity to hear.
The opposition between nature and rule is displaced: streams appear at once as natural movements and as the object of possible directional guidance.
The death of the speaker is reorganized not as an end, but as a transition to the authoritative question.
The higher human being is mapped not as a finished solution, but as an untested recipient and possible executor of the answer.
**Surface** — Complaint, fear, night images, language of death, and direct address constitute the immediate level of expression.
**Structural** — Depth, threshold, question, capacity to hear, and rule organize the conceptual mechanics beneath the imagery.
**Metastrategic** — The discourse controls access and authority by withholding knowledge and compelling the addressee, through a question, to position himself.
**Ontological/Temporal** — Time appears as a discontinuous sequence of loss, death, and coming hour; reality is presupposed as a still-undecided order of earthly movements.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the transition from loss of time and depth to the question of rule and capacity to hear.
What the concealed thought of the midnight heart says in content remains underdetermined.
It likewise remains underdetermined whether the higher human being possesses the demanded answer or is merely invoked as a possible addressee.
The structure is internally coherent insofar as the death of the I is read as a threshold event and not as a final conclusion.
The strongest connection exists between the coming hour, the test of courage, and the open question of rule.
The reconstruction depends on the tension between natural movement and human power to give direction, which is not fully resolved.
The movement of the text is preserved so long as selective audibility is treated not as a mere stylistic device, but as a condition of revelation.

Reife strebt auf das Ende, während Unreife am Leben festhält.
Leiden wird neu bestimmt als Wille zum Weiterleben, zur Reifung und zur Überschreitung des gegenwärtigen Selbst.
Lust widersetzt sich dieser gerichteten Überschreitung, weil sie sich selbst, ihre Dauer und ihre Wiederkehr begehrt.
Das Argument endet in einer unaufgelösten Doppelbewegung: Das Wehe fordert Vergehen, während das Leidende nach Fortdauer und Höherem verlangt.
Der Weinstock wird durch einen gewaltsamen Schnitt bearbeitet.

Das Wehe verbindet Untergang mit Steigerung, indem es Vergehen und Aufstieg in derselben Rede verschränkt.

The poem problematizes the praise of the sufferer in relation to the violence through which it is brought to ripeness.
The cut is determined simultaneously as cruelty, purification, and the condition of completion.
Ripeness strives toward the end, whereas unripeness clings to life.
Suffering is redefined as the will to go on living, to ripen, and to surpass the present self.
Pleasure resists this directed surpassing because it desires itself, its duration, and its recurrence.
The argument ends in an unresolved double movement: woe demands passing away, while the sufferer desires continuance and something higher.
The vine is worked by a violent cut.
The cut produces blood and therefore appears as cruelty.
What is ripe is oriented toward completion and death.
What is unripe wants to live.
Suffering does not merely want to pass away, but to live, ripen, and transform itself.
Suffering is directed toward something more distant, higher, and brighter.
Suffering expresses the will to heirs and children, and thus to continuation beyond its own self.
Pleasure wants neither heirs nor children.
Pleasure wants itself, eternity, and the recurrence of the same.
Woe simultaneously utters the imperative of passing away and the imperative of movement, flight, and ascent.
Ripeness is not mere prolongation of life.
Suffering is not identical with the desire for immediate self-destruction.
Pleasure is not the will to inheritance, progeny, or self-surpassing.
The eternity of pleasure is not directed development toward something higher.
The cut is not merely destruction, but a condition of ripeness.
The praise of the vine does not annul the violence of the vintner's knife.
Woe does not designate exclusively stagnation, downfall, or passivity.
Recognition of the vintner's knife arises from the transformation of injury into ripening.
The will to live can be mediated with the will to pass away when passing away appears as a transition to ripeness.
Suffering receives its direction by surpassing the present self toward something more distant and higher.
Inheritance and children function as forms of a will to life that does not wish to end in the present individual.
Pleasure constitutes an opposing temporal structure: it replaces production and surpassing with self-identity and recurrence.
Woe connects downfall with intensification by intertwining passing away and ascent in the same speech.
The poem organizes life not as the opposite of death, but as opposing forms of continuation: ripening through surpassing and pleasure through repetition.
Violence is structured as an ambiguous productive force: it wounds what is living and at the same time brings it to completion.
The system's highest tension arises between a future-directed, inheriting movement of life and a self-referential pleasure desiring eternal sameness.
The subject of the poem is produced by competing directions of will: it is to pass away, go on living, transform itself, and at the same time return.
The system excludes a life whose sole goal would be mere self-preservation without ripening or surpassing.
It excludes a ripeness that could be attained independently of injury, cut, or passing away.
It excludes a future that would be merely the prolongation of the identical self instead of inheritance, child, or transformation.
It excludes a pleasure that would realize its self through relation, progeny, or directed development.
It excludes a pain that would be only negative, passive, and hostile to life.
Excluded is the possibility of a neutral mediation between life and death; every movement must be determined as ripening, passing away, ascent, or recurrence.
Excluded is an uninjured becoming: completion is conceivable only within an economy of cut, blood, pain, and loss.
Excluded is a future without a decision between self-surpassing and eternal self-identity.
The system's hidden impossibility is a state in which suffering, pleasure, ripeness, and continuance possess the same temporal and volitional direction.

Injury is remapped from a mere harm into a productive condition of ripeness.
Life and death are no longer mapped as simple opposites, but as different modes of development and completion.
Suffering is classified as a directed, future-generating force in contrast to self-referential pleasure.
Progeny becomes visible as an ontological surpassing of the self and not merely as biological continuation.
Eternity is divided into two incompatible forms: repetition of the identical and progression beyond the self.
Woe is mapped as an ambivalent form of movement that simultaneously produces dissolution and intensification.
Surface — A wounded vine, a vintner's knife, ripeness, unripeness, suffering, and pleasure are set against one another in directly apostrophic speech.
Structural — The text orders forms of will according to their relations to violence, ripening, continuation, self-surpassing, and recurrence.
Metastrategic — The opposition between suffering and pleasure shifts the question of life from self-preservation to the choice of its temporal and kinetic form.
Ontological/Temporal — Being appears either as becoming through passing away and surpassing or as the eternal recurrence of the self identical with itself.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movements of cut, ripeness, suffering, pleasure, and woe.
The central distinction between future-directed surpassing and self-identical recurrence remains fully preserved.
It remains underdetermined whether the voices of the vine, suffering, pleasure, and woe are to be read as independent instances or as inner forms of will.
The internal coherence rests on the mediation of life and death through ripening.
The strongest structure is the opposition between inheritance and recurrence as two forms of duration.
The greatest tension lies in the fact that woe simultaneously demands passing away and brings forth movement, ascent, and continuation.
The reconstruction preserves the actual movement of the argument, provided that the concluding turn is read not as a resolution but as a continued intensification of the contradiction.

An ecstatic discourse calls the reliability of its own speaker-position into question through a chain of contradictory designations.
The ordinary oppositions of pleasure and pain, blessing and curse, night and sun are transposed into a reciprocal identity.
The affirmation of a single pleasure is determined as affirmation of the entire occurrence chained together with it.
The wish for the one-time repetition of a moment implies the wish for the return of all things.
The world is thereby constituted as an eternally chained, recurring totality.
The highest affirmation consists in saying even to woe, “perish, but come back!”, because every pleasure demands eternity.
The speaker-position is marked not as an unambiguous identity, but as a threshold between prophecy, dream, intoxication, interpretation, and bell-ringing.
The world can appear perfect.
Midnight and noon can designate the same comprehensive temporal order.
Pain and pleasure are not absolutely separate domains of value.
Curse and blessing can pass into one another.
Night and sun can appear as related or identical figures.
The affirmation of a pleasure entails the affirmation of the woe connected with it.
All things are chained together, threaded together, and in love.
The wish to experience a moment twice includes the wish for the return of the whole.
The world as a whole eternally recurs.
By its innermost claim, pleasure is directed toward eternity.
A wisdom that brings opposites together appears at the same time as folly.
The speaker-instance cannot be fixed to a single epistemic or psychic role.
Pleasure cannot be isolated from pain.
Blessing cannot be determined without curse.
Night is not the simple opposite of the sun.
An affirmed moment cannot be limited to its singularity.
Woe is not admitted as an event that finally passes away.
Wisdom is not separated from folly by a stable boundary.
Whoever affirms a pleasure unconditionally, by virtue of the chaining, simultaneously affirms every woe connected with it.
The selective affirmation of a positive moment is transposed into a total affirmation of the world's interconnectedness.
The wish for a moment's twice-occurring existence presupposes the repetition of all things.
Eternity designates not mere duration, but the repeated return of every individual occurrence.
Complete affirmation of the world demands the affirmation of suffering under the condition of its recurrence.
The value of a pleasure is measured by its capacity to bear along with it the entire recurring world.
Affirmation is transformed from a punctual assent into a test of the capacity for total acceptance of the world.
The temporal order of the argument transforms linear passing-away into cyclical recurrence.
The suspension of the pairs of opposites produces a totalization in which each individual event possesses meaning only as a node of the whole.
The highest form of affirmation of the world is at once an ethical demand, an ontological thesis, and a temporal obligation.
The system cannot rest upon a final separation of positive and negative value.
There can be no valid affirmation that detaches what is affirmed from its painful context.
Time cannot be organized as a one-time, irreversible sequence.
The individual cannot be treated as the sovereign possessor of isolated experiences.
Redemption through the final disappearance of pain is structurally excluded.
A wisdom that merely eliminates contradictions would be inadequate for this system.
Excluded is an outside of the world from which individual events could be evaluated without their recurrence and chaining.
Excluded is the possibility of affirming life selectively and definitively rejecting its negative conditions.
Excluded is a time in which what has occurred can be definitively completed or effaced.
Excluded is a non-tragic form of eternity that preserves pleasure and removes woe.

Dissolution of opposites → chaining of pleasure and woe → exclusion of selective affirmation.
Affirmation of a moment → demand for its repetition → inclusion of all chained things.
Repetition of the whole → eternity as cyclical return → obligation to affirm woe.
Affirmation of pleasure and woe → total love of the world → temporal formula: passing away and returning.

Return of the whole → eternal love of the world, including woe.
Eternal love of the world → final position of total affirmation: woe is to pass away and return.
The opposition of pleasure and pain is remapped into a relational unity.
The individual moment is reclassified from an isolated experience into an index of totality.
Eternity is shifted from timeless duration to the repeated return of every occurrence.
Woe is revalued from a negative value to be eliminated into a necessary component of affirmation of the world.
Wisdom and folly are no longer mapped as exclusive opposites, but as coexisting perspectives.
Surface: A discourse calls upon those addressed to affirm pleasure, woe, and recurrence together.
Structural: The argument binds every value to a network of chains and prevents isolated evaluation.
Metastrategic: Those addressed are pressed from selective assent toward a test of total capacity for affirmation.
Ontological/Temporal: Reality appears as a contradictorily articulated, cyclically recurring totality.

A1 through A6 and A12 explain the rhetorical and conceptual dissolution of stable opposites, but are partially dispensable for the core derivation.

The strongest operation is the derivation of the whole from the affirmation of a single moment.
The weakest point lies in the unelaborated transition from subjective assent to cosmological necessity.
The reconstruction preserves the actual movement from the dissolution of opposites through chaining and repetition to total affirmation of the world.

Ihre Reichweite zeigt sich darin, dass sie Gegensätze zugleich umfasst: Liebe und Hass, Glück und Schmerz, Überfluss und Bedürftigkeit.
Die Selbstbezüglichkeit der Lust erzeugt ihren Willen zu Herzeleid, Hölle, Schmach und Welt.
Die höheren Menschen erscheinen als bevorzugte Träger jenes Leidens, nach dem die ewige Lust verlangt.
Die Argumentbewegung führt von der Entgrenzung der Lust zu ihrer Selbstbejahung als tiefer Ewigkeit.
Lust will die Ewigkeit aller Dinge.
Lust will sich selbst.
Lust ist umfassender als Schmerz, ohne auf Schmerz reduzierbar zu sein.
Lust umfasst widersprüchlich erscheinende Bestimmungen wie Liebe und Hass.
Lust kann zugleich schenken, wegwerfen, bitten und danken.
Überreiche Lust verlangt nach Wehe, Hölle, Hass und Schmach.
Die Welt gehört zu den Gegenständen, nach denen Lust verlangt.
Die ewige Lust verlangt nach dem Leiden der höheren Menschen.
Das Verlangen nach Herzeleid folgt aus dem Willen der Lust zu sich selbst.
Die Ewigkeit der Lust ist eine tiefe, nicht bloß zeitlich verlängerte Ewigkeit.
Lust ist nicht auf angenehme Empfindung begrenzt.
Lust ist nicht der Gegensatz zu Schmerz.
Lust ist nicht durch Bedürfnislosigkeit definiert.
Lust ist nicht auf Liebe oder auf Hass festgelegt.
Lust ist nicht von Welt, Hölle, Schmach oder Missratenem gereinigt.
Ewigkeit ist nicht bloße Dauer eines gegenwärtigen Lustzustands.
Das Leiden der höheren Menschen ist nicht außerhalb des Begehrens der Lust angesiedelt.
Weil Lust alle Dinge in ihre Ewigkeit einbeziehen will, richtet sie sich nicht auf einen einzelnen angenehmen Gegenstand.
Weil Lust sich selbst will, muss sie auch die Zustände wollen, durch die sie sich als umfassende Lust erhält.
Weil Lust Liebe und Hass umfasst, kann ihr Gegenstand nicht durch eine moralische oder affektive Eindeutigkeit bestimmt werden.
Weil Lust überreich ist, widerspricht ihr Betteln nicht ihrem Überfluss.
Weil Lust nach Wehe verlangt, wird Schmerz als Bestandteil ihrer Totalität und nicht als ihr äußerer Gegenpol bestimmt.
Weil die ewige Lust nach dem Leiden der höheren Menschen verlangt, wird deren Missratenheit in den Horizont der Lust integriert.
Lust wird zu einer totalisierenden Bejahungsbewegung, die ihre eigene Negation als Bestandteil ihrer Selbstbejahung einverleibt.
Die Gegensätze Glück und Schmerz verlieren ihre Funktion als voneinander getrennte Endpunkte und werden zu Momenten eines einzigen Begehrens.
Ewigkeit bezeichnet die unabschließbare Rückkehr der Lust zu sich selbst durch die Aufnahme aller Dinge und ihrer Gegensätze.
Das höhere Menschsein wird nicht als Erlösung vom Leiden, sondern als bevorzugte Erscheinungsform der von Lust begehrten Wunde bestimmt.
Das System kann nicht auf einem Modell beruhen, in dem Lust durch Ausschaltung von Schmerz vollendet wird.
Das System kann nicht auf einer linearen Steigerung beruhen, die von Mangel zu endgültiger Befriedigung führt.
Das System schließt eine transzendente Ordnung aus, in der Welt, Leid und Missratenheit überwunden werden müssen.
Das System schließt eine stabile Identität der Lust aus, die von ihren widersprüchlichen Affekten unberührt bleibt.
Das System schließt aus, dass Selbstbejahung mit Selbstschutz oder Schmerzvermeidung gleichgesetzt wird.
Ausgeschlossen wird die Möglichkeit einer Lust, die sich durch Abgrenzung gegen das Nicht-Lustvolle erhält.
Ausgeschlossen wird ein Ende des Begehrens, in dem Lust nicht mehr auf ihre eigene Wiederholung angewiesen wäre.
Ausgeschlossen wird eine Weltordnung, deren Wahrheit erst durch Entfernung des Leidens, des Hasses oder des Missratenen hergestellt werden müsste.
Ausgeschlossen wird eine höhere Existenzform, deren Überlegenheit in der Abwesenheit von Verwundbarkeit bestünde.
Affektive Grundsetzung: Lust will sich selbst.
Totalisierung: Der Selbstwille der Lust erweitert sich zum Willen zur Ewigkeit aller Dinge.
Inklusion der Gegensätze: Liebe, Hass, Glück, Schmerz, Überfluss und Bedürftigkeit werden als kompatible Erscheinungen derselben Lust erzeugt.
Selbstbezügliche Umkehrung: Weil Lust sich selbst will, verlangt sie nach Herzeleid und den Bedingungen ihrer eigenen affektiven Tiefe.
Subjektivierung: Die höheren Menschen werden als Träger des von der Lust gesuchten Leidens eingesetzt.
Temporale Schließung: Die Bewegung endet in der tiefen Ewigkeit einer Lust, die alle Gegenstände und Gegenkräfte in sich zurückführt.

Überfluss und Bedürftigkeit werden als simultane Zustände derselben Lust kartiert.
Die höheren Menschen werden aus der Position möglicher Erlösungsträger in die Position begehrter Leidensgestalten verschoben.
Ewigkeit wird von zeitlicher Verlängerung in selbstbezügliche Totalisierung umgezeichnet.
Surface — Lust verlangt nach Ewigkeit, nach allen Dingen und nach widersprüchlichen Affekten.

Unterbestimmt bleibt, ob die Ewigkeit ontologisch, zyklisch oder ausschließlich affektiv gemeint ist.

Die Struktur ist intern kohärent, sofern Lust nicht als Gegensatz zu Schmerz, sondern als dessen umfassende Bedingung gefasst wird.

Die größte Spannung liegt in der gleichzeitigen Bestimmung der Lust als Überfluss und als bittendes, bedürftiges Verlangen.
Die Rekonstruktion bewahrt die tatsächliche Bewegung, solange die Schlussposition nicht als bloße Steigerung des Glücks, sondern als Totalisierung von Lust und Schmerz verstanden wird.
The central problem consists in determining pleasure not as an isolated feeling of well-being, but as a comprehensive will.
Pleasure is newly determined as the will to the eternity of all things and thus as the will to the totality of its objects.
Its scope is shown in the fact that it simultaneously encompasses opposites: love and hate, happiness and pain, abundance and need.
The self-referentiality of pleasure generates its will to heartache, hell, disgrace, and world.
The higher human beings appear as privileged bearers of that suffering which eternal pleasure demands.
The movement of the argument leads from the unbounding of pleasure to its self-affirmation as deep eternity.
Pleasure wills the eternity of all things.
Pleasure wills itself.
Pleasure is more comprehensive than pain, without being reducible to pain.
Pleasure encompasses apparently contradictory determinations such as love and hate.
Pleasure can simultaneously give, throw away, beg, and give thanks.
Overabundant pleasure demands woe, hell, hate, and disgrace.
The world belongs among the objects that pleasure demands.
Eternal pleasure demands the suffering of the higher human beings.
The demand for heartache follows from the will of pleasure toward itself.
The eternity of pleasure is a deep eternity, not one merely extended in time.
Pleasure is not limited to pleasant sensation.
Pleasure is not the opposite of pain.
Pleasure is not defined by freedom from need.
Pleasure is not fixed upon love or hate.
Pleasure is not purified of world, hell, disgrace, or what has gone wrong.
Eternity is not mere duration of a present state of pleasure.
The suffering of the higher human beings is not situated outside the desire of pleasure.
Because pleasure wills to include all things in its eternity, it is not directed toward a single pleasant object.
Because pleasure wills itself, it must also will the states through which it preserves itself as comprehensive pleasure.
Because pleasure encompasses love and hate, its object cannot be determined by a moral or affective univocity.
Because pleasure is overabundant, its begging does not contradict its abundance.
Because pleasure demands woe, pain is determined as a component of its totality and not as its external counterpole.
Because eternal pleasure demands the suffering of the higher human beings, their failure is integrated into the horizon of pleasure.
Pleasure becomes a totalizing movement of affirmation that incorporates its own negation as a component of its self-affirmation.
The opposites happiness and pain lose their function as endpoints separate from one another and become moments of a single desire.
Eternity denotes the unfinishable return of pleasure to itself through the reception of all things and their opposites.
Higher humanity is determined not as redemption from suffering, but as a privileged form of appearance of the wound desired by pleasure.
The system cannot rest on a model in which pleasure is completed by the elimination of pain.
The system cannot rest on a linear intensification that leads from lack to final satisfaction.
The system excludes a transcendent order in which world, suffering, and failure must be overcome.
The system excludes a stable identity of pleasure that remains untouched by its contradictory affects.
The system excludes equating self-affirmation with self-protection or the avoidance of pain.
Excluded is the possibility of a pleasure that preserves itself through delimitation against what is non-pleasurable.
Excluded is an end of desire in which pleasure would no longer depend on its own repetition.
Excluded is a world order whose truth would first have to be established by the removal of suffering, hate, or what has gone wrong.
Excluded is a higher form of existence whose superiority would consist in the absence of vulnerability.
Affective basic positing: Pleasure wills itself.
Totalization: The self-will of pleasure expands into the will to the eternity of all things.
Inclusion of opposites: Love, hate, happiness, pain, abundance, and need are generated as compatible manifestations of the same pleasure.
Self-referential reversal: Because pleasure wills itself, it demands heartache and the conditions of its own affective depth.
Subjectivation: The higher human beings are installed as bearers of the suffering sought by pleasure.
Temporal closure: The movement ends in the deep eternity of a pleasure that returns all objects and counterforces into itself.
Limited understanding of pleasure → unbounding into the pleasure of all things.
Pleasure of all things → will to the eternity of all things.
Will to eternity → inclusion of pain, hate, disgrace, and world.
Inclusion of the negative → self-referential will of pleasure.
Self-referential will → demand for the suffering of the higher human beings.
Demand for suffering → equation of happiness and pain in deep eternity.
Pleasure is remapped from a positive individual state into a category of totality.
Pain is reclassified from the counterconcept of pleasure into an internal component of its form of movement.
Love and hate become legible no longer as exclusive alternatives, but as coexisting directions of the same will.
Abundance and need are mapped as simultaneous states of the same pleasure.
The higher human beings are shifted from the position of possible bearers of redemption into the position of desired figures of suffering.
Eternity is redrawn from temporal extension into self-referential totalization.
Surface — Pleasure demands eternity, all things, and contradictory affects.
Structural — The text organizes pleasure as a system that takes its counterpoles into its own reproduction.
Metastrategic — The usual opposition of pleasure and suffering is replaced by a shared structure of will.
Ontological/Temporal — Being is determined as a multiplicity to be affirmed, and eternity as the deep return of self-willing pleasure.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from pleasure to eternity and to the inclusion of suffering.
The central dependency between self-will, totalization, and object inclusion is preserved.
It remains underdetermined whether eternity is meant ontologically, cyclically, or exclusively affectively.
It likewise remains underdetermined whether the higher human beings are subjects, symptoms, or metaphorical bearers of pleasure.
The structure is internally coherent insofar as pleasure is conceived not as the opposite of pain, but as its comprehensive condition.
The strongest point of the system lies in the derivation of suffering from the self-will of pleasure.
The greatest tension lies in the simultaneous determination of pleasure as abundance and as begging, needy desire.
The reconstruction preserves the actual movement so long as the concluding position is understood not as a mere intensification of happiness, but as the totalization of pleasure and pain.
Der Text prüft, ob die höheren Menschen den Sinn des vorausgehenden Liedes erkannt haben.
Die Prüfung wird in eine Aufforderung überführt, den Rundgesang selbst zu singen.
Der Rundgesang wird durch „Noch ein Mal“ und „in alle Ewigkeit!“ als Wiederkehr und Ewigkeit bestimmt.
Die Stimme der tiefen Mitternacht enthüllt die Welt als tiefer, als der Tag sie erscheinen lässt.
Innerhalb dieser Tiefe wird Lust gegenüber dem Weh als noch tiefer bestimmt.
Die Bewegung reicht von der Aufforderung zur Wiederholung über die Offenbarung der Welttiefe zur ewigen Bejahung der Lust.
Der Sinn eines Liedes kann durch seine Wiederholung praktisch erwiesen werden.
Die höheren Menschen sind fähig, den geforderten Rundgesang selbst zu singen.
„Noch ein Mal“ bezeichnet nicht bloße Wiederholung, sondern eine auf Ewigkeit gerichtete Wiederkehr.
Die Welt besitzt eine Tiefe, die dem unmittelbaren Bewusstsein verborgen bleibt.
Der Tag bildet keinen ausreichenden Maßstab für die Tiefe der Welt.
Das Weh gehört zur tiefen Struktur der Welt.
Lust ist tiefer als Herzeleid.
Das Weh spricht den Untergang oder das Vergehen aus.
Die Lust verlangt nicht Vergehen, sondern Ewigkeit.
Die tiefste Bestimmung der Lust ist der Wille zur ewigen Wiederkehr.
Der Sinn des Liedes ist nicht durch bloßes Zuhören erfüllt.
Die Welt ist nicht auf das durch den Tag Erschlossene begrenzt.
Die Tiefe der Welt ist nicht mit ihrem Weh erschöpft.
Lust ist nicht dieselbe Größenordnung wie Herzeleid, sondern übertrifft es an Tiefe.
Die letzte Antwort auf die Welt ist nicht die vom Weh ausgesprochene Auflösung.
„Noch ein Mal“ bedeutet nicht einen letzten Durchgang vor dem Ende.
Die höheren Menschen müssen den Sinn des Liedes performativ bestätigen, indem sie es selbst wiederholen.
Der Rundgesang verbindet Wiederholung und Ewigkeit in einer einzigen Formel.
Das Erwachen aus tiefem Traum fungiert als Übergang von verborgener zu ausgesprochener Welterkenntnis.
Das Weh markiert die Welt als leidvolle, aber nicht abschließend bestimmte Realität.
Die größere Tiefe der Lust verschiebt das Gewicht der Welterfahrung vom Leiden zur Bejahung.
Die Ewigkeit wird nicht aus der Abwesenheit von Leid, sondern aus dem Willen der Lust erzeugt.
Die Erkenntnis der ewigen Wiederkehr wird als singbare Handlung und nicht als rein theoretischer Satz konstituiert.
Die tiefste Weltdeutung entsteht durch die Überordnung der Lust über das Vergehenswort des Wehs.
Die Welt erscheint als Struktur, deren stärkster Impuls nicht im Leiden, sondern im Beharren auf Ewigkeit liegt.
Die höheren Menschen werden vom Empfänger einer Lehre zu ihrem ausführenden Medium umgebildet.
Zeit wird von einer linearen Folge in eine wiederkehrende, durch Lust bejahte Dauer umcodiert.
Das sichtbare und wache Bewusstsein besitzt keinen abschließenden Zugang zur Weltstruktur.
Leid kann nicht als tiefster oder letzter Sinn der Welt gelten.
Die Äußerung „Vergeh!“ kann die Welt nicht endgültig bestimmen.
Ewigkeit darf nicht als bloße Fortdauer ohne Wert oder Bejahung verstanden werden.
Erkenntnis bleibt unzureichend, wenn sie nicht in Wiederholung, Gesang und Zustimmung übergeht.
Ausgeschlossen wird eine Welt, deren tiefste Wahrheit im endgültigen Vergehen liegt.
Ausgeschlossen wird eine Zeitordnung, in der Wiederholung nur Rückkehr desselben ohne Ewigkeitssinn wäre.
Ausgeschlossen wird ein Subjekt, das die Wahrheit erkennen kann, ohne von ihr zur eigenen Wiederholung verpflichtet zu werden.
Abwesend bleibt eine Vermittlung, die den Gegensatz zwischen leidvoller Welt und ewiger Lust vollständig erklärt.
Die Kraft des Arguments beruht auf der versperrten Möglichkeit, dass das Weh das letzte Wort behalten könnte.
Ungeprüftes Verständnis → Aufforderung zur eigenen Wiederholung → performative Bestätigung des Liedsinns.
„Noch ein Mal“ → Wiederholung über den Einzelfall hinaus → Bestimmung als Ewigkeit.
Erwachen aus tiefem Traum → Überschreitung des Tagesmaßes → Offenlegung der Welttiefe.
Welttiefe → Weh als Vergehensimpuls → Lust als tiefere Gegenbewegung → Wille zur Ewigkeit.
Tiefste Lust → ewige Wiederkehr → Aufforderung zur singenden Bejahung.
Ungeprüftes Verstehen → performative Aufforderung → Wiederholung als „Noch ein Mal“ → Ewigkeit als Sinn → nächtliches Erwachen → Welttiefe → Überordnung der Lust → Bejahung der ewigen Wiederkehr.
Die Unterscheidung zwischen Verstehen und Singen wird in eine Unterscheidung zwischen passiver Kenntnis und vollzogener Zustimmung überführt.
Der Gegensatz von Wiederholung und Einmaligkeit wird durch die Gleichsetzung von „Noch ein Mal“ und Ewigkeit neu geordnet.

**Surface:** Höhere Menschen sollen den Rundgesang „Noch ein Mal“ singen.

Die Argumentbewegung bleibt erhalten, obwohl die Passage die Spannung zwischen Weltleid und Ewigkeit nicht vermittelt, sondern durch die Vorrangstellung der Lust entscheidet.
The text examines whether the higher human beings have understood the meaning of the preceding song.
The examination is transformed into an exhortation to sing the roundelay themselves.
The roundelay is defined by „Noch ein Mal“ and „in alle Ewigkeit!“ as recurrence and eternity.
The voice of deep midnight reveals the world as deeper than the day lets it appear.
Within this depth, joy is defined as deeper still in relation to woe.
The movement extends from the exhortation to repetition, through the revelation of the world's depth, to the eternal affirmation of joy.
The meaning of a song can be practically demonstrated through its repetition.
The higher human beings are capable of singing the required roundelay themselves.
„Noch ein Mal“ denotes not mere repetition, but a recurrence directed toward eternity.
The world possesses a depth that remains concealed from immediate consciousness.
The day does not provide an adequate measure for the depth of the world.
Woe belongs to the deep structure of the world.
Joy is deeper than heartache.
Woe speaks forth downfall or passing away.
Joy demands not passing away, but eternity.
The deepest determination of joy is the will to eternal recurrence.
The meaning of the song is not fulfilled by mere listening.
The world is not limited to what is disclosed by the day.
The depth of the world is not exhausted by its woe.
Joy is not of the same order of magnitude as heartache, but surpasses it in depth.
The final answer to the world is not the dissolution pronounced by woe.
„Noch ein Mal“ does not mean one final passage before the end.
The higher human beings must confirm the meaning of the song performatively by repeating it themselves.
The roundelay joins repetition and eternity in a single formula.
Awakening from a deep dream functions as a transition from concealed to spoken knowledge of the world.
Woe marks the world as a painful, but not conclusively determined, reality.
The greater depth of joy shifts the weight of world-experience from suffering to affirmation.
Eternity is produced not from the absence of suffering, but from the will of joy.
Knowledge of eternal recurrence is constituted as a singable act and not as a purely theoretical proposition.
The deepest interpretation of the world arises through the subordination of woe's word of passing away to joy.
The world appears as a structure whose strongest impulse lies not in suffering, but in persistence upon eternity.
The higher human beings are transformed from recipients of a teaching into its executing medium.
Time is recoded from a linear sequence into a recurring duration affirmed by joy.
Visible and waking consciousness has no conclusive access to the structure of the world.
Suffering cannot count as the deepest or final meaning of the world.
The utterance „Vergeh!“ cannot determine the world definitively.
Eternity must not be understood as mere continuance without value or affirmation.
Knowledge remains inadequate if it does not pass into repetition, song, and assent.
Excluded is a world whose deepest truth lies in final passing away.
Excluded is a temporal order in which repetition would be merely the return of the same without a sense of eternity.
Excluded is a subject that can recognize the truth without being obliged by it to its own repetition.
Absent remains a mediation that fully explains the opposition between a suffering world and eternal joy.
The force of the argument rests on the blocked possibility that woe might retain the last word.
Unexamined understanding → exhortation to one's own repetition → performative confirmation of the meaning of the song.
„Noch ein Mal“ → repetition beyond the individual case → determination as eternity.
Awakening from a deep dream → transcendence of the measure of day → disclosure of the world's depth.
Depth of the world → woe as impulse toward passing away → joy as deeper counter-movement → will to eternity.
Deepest joy → eternal recurrence → exhortation to singing affirmation.

Unexamined understanding → performative exhortation → repetition as „Noch ein Mal“ → eternity as meaning → nocturnal awakening → depth of the world → subordination to joy → affirmation of eternal recurrence.
The distinction between understanding and singing is transformed into a distinction between passive knowledge and enacted assent.
The opposition between repetition and singularity is reordered through the equation of „Noch ein Mal“ and eternity.
The hierarchy of affects is mapped in such a way that joy appears not as a counterpole alongside suffering, but as its deeper transcendence.
The opposition of day and night becomes an epistemic hierarchy of superficial and deep knowledge of the world.
The human subject is classified from an addressee of revelation into a bearer of its repetition.
**Surface:** Higher human beings are to sing the roundelay „Noch ein Mal“.
**Structural:** World, pain, and joy are interconnected as a graduated order of depth.
**Metastrategic:** Knowledge is transformed through repetition, song, and assent into an attitude of affirmation.
**Ontological/Temporal:** Reality is determined as an eternal, recurring duration whose strongest drive is joy.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from the exhortation to song up to eternal affirmation.
The central dependence on the voice of deep midnight remains preserved as a change of perspective.
It remains underdetermined how the higher human beings actually enact the required assent.
Likewise unresolved remains the relation between the „Vergeh!“ of woe and the drive toward eternity of joy.
The structure is internally coherent insofar as the deeper joy surpasses woe's movement toward passing away.
The strongest point lies in the coupling of affective depth, repetition, and eternity.
The reconstruction hinges on the unsubstantiated positing that the greater depth of joy guarantees its ontological priority.
The argumentative movement remains preserved, although the passage does not mediate the tension between world-suffering and eternity, but decides it through the priority of joy.
Zarathustra sucht die zu seinem Werk und seinem Tag gehörenden Gefährten, erkennt jedoch die höheren Menschen als dafür ungeeignet.
Die Unfähigkeit der höheren Menschen, seine Zeichen zu verstehen und seinem Ruf zu gehorchen, wird als strukturelle Schlafheit bestimmt.
Das Erwachen von Adler, Tauben und Löwe erscheint Zarathustra als Zeichen einer ihm angemessenen Nähe: seiner „Kinder“.
Die Flucht der höheren Menschen vor dem Löwen bestätigt rückwirkend ihre Unvereinbarkeit mit Zarathustras kommender Aufgabe.
Die Erinnerung an den Wahrsager übersetzt ihre Not in die Versuchung zum Mitleiden mit den höheren Menschen.
Die Zurückweisung dieses Mitleidens verschiebt Zarathustras Orientierung von Glück und Rettung auf Werk, Reife und den kommenden großen Mittag.
Zarathustras Handlung ist auf sein Werk gerichtet und nicht auf sein Glück.
Die höheren Menschen verstehen Zarathustras morgendliche Zeichen nicht.
Den höheren Menschen fehlt das hörende und gehorchende Ohr.
Richtige Gefährtschaft verlangt ein Erwachen, das Zarathustras eigenes Erwachen teilt.
Adler, Tauben und Löwe werden als Zarathustra zugehörige und erwachte Tiere anerkannt.
Das Zusammentreffen mit den Tieren gilt Zarathustra als Zeichen der Nähe seiner „Kinder“.
Der Löwe macht die Furcht und Fluchtbereitschaft der höheren Menschen sichtbar.
Die Not der höheren Menschen erzeugt die Versuchung, sie zum Gegenstand des Mitleidens zu machen.
Das Mitleiden mit den höheren Menschen ist Zarathustras „letzte Sünde“.
Diese letzte Sünde hat ihre Zeit gehabt und darf Zarathustras gegenwärtige Bewegung nicht mehr bestimmen.
Zarathustras Reife und Stunde werden durch den Beginn seines Tages und die Anrufung des großen Mittags bestimmt.
Die höheren Menschen sind nicht Zarathustras rechte Gefährten.
Körperliches Erwachen ist nicht identisch mit der Fähigkeit, Zarathustras Zeichen zu verstehen.
Rang oder Höhe des Menschen ist nicht hinreichend für geistige Gefährtschaft.
Zarathustras Weg ist nicht auf das Warten in der Höhle ausgerichtet.
Der Schrei der Not ist nicht der maßgebliche Imperativ für Zarathustras Handeln.
Mitleiden ist nicht die letzte Form von Zarathustras Tugend, sondern die letzte zu überwindende Versuchung.
Glück ist nicht der Endzweck von Zarathustras Bewegung.
Die Bedeutung des Zeichens wird nicht durch die Anerkennung der höheren Menschen bestätigt.
Die höheren Menschen werden von möglichen Empfängern Zarathustras Lehre zu Objekten seiner zurückgewiesenen Versuchung umklassifiziert.
Die Tiere fungieren als positives Gegenmodell zur menschlichen Unempfänglichkeit, weil sie Erwachen, Nähe und Zeichenfähigkeit verkörpern.
Der Löwe ist zugleich Zärtlichkeitszeichen für Zarathustra und Ausschlussmechanismus gegenüber den höheren Menschen.
Die Erinnerung an die Prophezeiung verwandelt die gegenwärtige Szene aus einem bloßen Ereignis in die Wiederkehr einer bereits benannten Prüfung.
Zarathustras Tagesbeginn ist keine astronomische Feststellung, sondern die Vollzugsform seiner Entscheidung gegen Mitleid.
Die Nähe der „Kinder“ legitimiert den Aufbruch, obwohl die rechten Menschen weiterhin fehlen.
Das System ersetzt die Hierarchie „höhere Menschen“ durch ein Selektionskriterium der Resonanz: Zugehörig ist, wer Zeichen empfangen, Erwachen teilen und Zarathustras Bewegung nicht fliehen kann.
Das gefährliche oder furchterregende Ereignis wird als Prüfapparat umcodiert: Was die höheren Menschen vertreibt, bestätigt Zarathustra in seiner Reife.
Die Verweigerung des Mitleidens ist keine Gefühllosigkeit im Allgemeinen, sondern die Abwehr einer Bindung an eine historisch erschöpfte Form menschlicher Notverwaltung.
Zarathustras Zukunft wird durch eine noch nicht anwesende Gemeinschaft der „Kinder“ autorisiert, während die vorhandene Gemeinschaft der höheren Menschen disqualifiziert wird.
Das System setzt voraus, dass bestehende menschliche Exzellenz keine hinreichende Grundlage für die kommende Aufgabe bietet.
Das System schließt aus, dass Leid allein einen verbindlichen Anspruch auf Hilfe oder Selbstunterbrechung erzeugt.
Das System schließt aus, dass Verständigung mit den gegenwärtig Anwesenden die Bedingung legitimer Handlung ist.
Das System setzt voraus, dass symbolische Ereignisse eine höhere Orientierungsfunktion haben können als deliberative menschliche Zustimmung.
Das System schließt aus, dass die Zukunft aus einer graduellen Verbesserung der höheren Menschen hervorgeht.
Die rechte menschliche Gemeinschaft ist im entscheidenden Augenblick abwesend: Die höheren Menschen genügen nicht, die „Kinder“ sind nur als Nähe bezeichnet.
Der große Mittag ist nicht gegenwärtig verfügbar, sondern organisiert die Gegenwart als gerichtete Erwartung und Aufbruch.
Eine allgemein überprüfbare Instanz für die Wahrheit des Zeichens fehlt; seine Geltung entsteht allein innerhalb von Zarathustras Deutung und Entscheidung.
Erwachen Zarathustras → Prüfung der vorhandenen Gefährten → Feststellung ihrer Zeichenunfähigkeit.
Zeichenereignis der Tiere → affektive Gewissheit der Kindernähe → Bestimmung eigener Reife.
Begegnung der höheren Menschen mit dem Löwen → Flucht → sichtbarer Ausschluss aus der kommenden Gemeinschaft.
Erinnerung an Wahrsagung und Not → Identifikation der Versuchung als Mitleid → zeitliche Entwertung dieser Versuchung.
Zurückweisung des Mitleidens → Rückbindung an das Werk → Ausruf des eigenen Morgens und des großen Mittags.
Ungeeignete Gefährten → Zeichenunfähigkeit der höheren Menschen → Erwachen der Tiere.
Erwachen der Tiere → Zeichen der Kindernähe → Reife Zarathustras.
Löwenbegegnung → Flucht der höheren Menschen → Bestätigung ihres Ausschlusses.
Erinnerung an ihre Not → Benennung des Mitleidens als letzte Sünde → Abweisung der Versuchung.
Abweisung des Mitleidens → Vorrang des Werkes → Aufbruch in den kommenden Mittag.
Die Kategorie des „höheren Menschen“ verliert ihren Vorrang und wird von der Kategorie der Zeichenempfänglichkeit überordnet.
Tiere werden nicht als bloße Naturkulisse behandelt, sondern als Träger von Erwachen, Anerkennung, Zärtlichkeit und selektiver Prüfung.
Mitleid wird von einer unmittelbar positiven Reaktion auf Not zu einer geschichtlich überholten Bindungsform umgeordnet.
Die Zeitordnung verschiebt sich von Nacht und Morgen als Chronologie zu Nacht, Morgen, Tag und Mittag als Stufen existenzieller Reife.
Die Zukunft wird nicht als Fortsetzung der gegenwärtigen Gemeinschaft kartiert, sondern als Ankunft einer anderen, erst angekündigten Gemeinschaft.
Surface — Zarathustra verlässt die Höhle, begegnet Adler, Tauben und Löwe, wird von den höheren Menschen getrennt und bricht erneut auf.
Structural — Die Szene selektiert zwischen Zeichenempfänglichkeit und Zeichenunfähigkeit und verteilt Zugehörigkeit entsprechend dieser Differenz.
Metastrategic — Der Text löst Zarathustras Aufgabe aus der Pflicht, bestehende Eliten zu retten, zu überzeugen oder zu bemitleiden.
Ontological/Temporal — Wahrheit und Reife erscheinen als ereignishafte Zeichenordnung, deren Zeit nicht messbar-linear, sondern kairologisch strukturiert ist.
Die Axiome reichen aus, um die Umklassifikation der höheren Menschen, die Funktion der Tiere und die Zurückweisung des Mitleidens zu rekonstruieren.
Unterbestimmt bleibt, wer oder was die „Kinder“ sind und worin ihre tatsächliche Nähe jenseits des Zeichens besteht.
Die Struktur ist kohärent, sofern Zarathustras Deutungshoheit über das Zeichen als interne Geltungsinstanz akzeptiert wird.
Die stärkste Operation liegt in der Verbindung von Löwenangst, Flucht der höheren Menschen und rückwirkender Bestätigung ihres Ausschlusses.
Die stärkste Bruchlinie liegt darin, dass die gewünschten rechten Menschen fehlen, während ihre Nähe dennoch als hinreichende Handlungslegitimation fungiert.
Eine weitere Spannung besteht darin, dass körperliches Erwachen der höheren Menschen ihre fortdauernde geistige Schlafheit nicht aufhebt, sondern erst sichtbar macht.
Die Rekonstruktion bewahrt die Bewegung nur, wenn das Zeichen nicht als objektiver Beweis, sondern als Auslöser einer entscheidenden Selbstdeutung behandelt wird.
Zarathustra seeks the companions belonging to his work and his day, but recognizes the higher human beings as unsuitable for this.
The inability of the higher human beings to understand his signs and obey his call is determined as structural sleepiness.
The awakening of eagle, doves, and lion appears to Zarathustra as a sign of a proximity appropriate to him: that of his “children.”
The flight of the higher human beings from the lion retrospectively confirms their incompatibility with Zarathustra’s coming task.
The recollection of the soothsayer translates their distress into the temptation to suffer-with the higher human beings.
The rejection of this suffering-with shifts Zarathustra’s orientation from happiness and salvation to work, maturity, and the coming great noon.
Zarathustra’s action is directed toward his work and not toward his happiness.
The higher human beings do not understand Zarathustra’s morning signs.
The higher human beings lack the hearing and obedient ear.
Proper companionship requires an awakening that shares Zarathustra’s own awakening.
Eagle, doves, and lion are recognized as animals belonging to Zarathustra and as awakened.
The encounter with the animals counts for Zarathustra as a sign of the proximity of his “children.”
The lion makes the fear and readiness for flight of the higher human beings visible.
The distress of the higher human beings produces the temptation to make them the object of suffering-with.
Suffering-with the higher human beings is Zarathustra’s “last sin.”
This last sin has had its time and may no longer determine Zarathustra’s present movement.
Zarathustra’s maturity and hour are determined by the beginning of his day and the invocation of the great noon.
The higher human beings are not Zarathustra’s proper companions.
Bodily awakening is not identical with the capacity to understand Zarathustra’s signs.
Rank or human elevation is not sufficient for spiritual companionship.
Zarathustra’s path is not oriented toward waiting in the cave.
The cry of distress is not the authoritative imperative for Zarathustra’s action.
Suffering-with is not the final form of Zarathustra’s virtue, but the final temptation to be overcome.
Happiness is not the final end of Zarathustra’s movement.
The meaning of the sign is not confirmed through the recognition of the higher human beings.
The higher human beings are reclassified from possible recipients of Zarathustra’s teaching into objects of his rejected temptation.
The animals function as a positive countermodel to human unreceptivity because they embody awakening, proximity, and capacity for signs.
The lion is at once a sign of tenderness for Zarathustra and a mechanism of exclusion vis-à-vis the higher human beings.
The recollection of the prophecy transforms the present scene from a mere event into the return of an already designated trial.
The beginning of Zarathustra’s day is not an astronomical statement, but the enactment-form of his decision against suffering-with.
The proximity of the “children” legitimates departure, although the proper human beings continue to be absent.

The system replaces the hierarchy of “higher human beings” with a criterion of selection by resonance: belonging is accorded to whoever can receive signs, share awakening, and cannot flee Zarathustra’s movement.
The dangerous or frightening event is recoded as a testing apparatus: what drives away the higher human beings confirms Zarathustra in his maturity.
The refusal of suffering-with is not insensitivity in general, but the defense against a binding to a historically exhausted form of managing human distress.
Zarathustra’s future is authorized by a not-yet-present community of the “children,” while the existing community of the higher human beings is disqualified.
The system presupposes that existing human excellence offers no sufficient basis for the coming task.
The system excludes that suffering alone generates a binding claim to help or self-interruption.
The system excludes that understanding with those presently present is the condition of legitimate action.
The system presupposes that symbolic events can have a higher orienting function than deliberative human assent.
The system excludes that the future emerges from a gradual improvement of the higher human beings.
The proper human community is absent at the decisive moment: the higher human beings do not suffice, the “children” are designated only as proximity.
The great noon is not presently available, but organizes the present as directed expectation and departure.
A universally verifiable instance for the truth of the sign is absent; its validity arises solely within Zarathustra’s interpretation and decision.
Zarathustra’s awakening → testing of the existing companions → determination of their incapacity for signs.
Sign-event of the animals → affective certainty of the children’s proximity → determination of his own maturity.
Encounter of the higher human beings with the lion → flight → visible exclusion from the coming community.
Recollection of soothsaying and distress → identification of the temptation as suffering-with → temporal devaluation of this temptation.
Rejection of suffering-with → return-binding to the work → proclamation of his own morning and of the great noon.
Unsuitable companions → incapacity for signs of the higher human beings → awakening of the animals.
Awakening of the animals → sign of the children’s proximity → Zarathustra’s maturity.
Encounter with the lion → flight of the higher human beings → confirmation of their exclusion.
Recollection of their distress → designation of suffering-with as the last sin → rejection of the temptation.
Rejection of suffering-with → priority of the work → departure into the coming noon.
The category of the “higher human being” loses its priority and is subordinated to the category of receptivity to signs.
Animals are not treated as mere natural scenery, but as bearers of awakening, recognition, tenderness, and selective testing.
Suffering-with is reordered from an immediately positive response to distress into a historically superseded form of binding.
The temporal order shifts from night and morning as chronology to night, morning, day, and noon as stages of existential maturity.
The future is not mapped as a continuation of the present community, but as the arrival of another community, only announced as yet.
Surface — Zarathustra leaves the cave, encounters eagle, doves, and lion, is separated from the higher human beings, and sets out anew.
Structural — The scene selects between receptivity to signs and incapacity for signs and distributes belonging according to this difference.
Metastrategic — The text releases Zarathustra’s task from the duty to save, persuade, or pity existing elites.
Ontological/Temporal — Truth and maturity appear as an event-like order of signs whose time is structured not measurably-linearly, but kairologically.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the reclassification of the higher human beings, the function of the animals, and the rejection of suffering-with.
