> Having begun with the praises of God, he reviews the beginnings of his life up to his fifteenth year. He acknowledges the sins of infancy and childhood; and confesses that at this age he was more inclined toward play and every sort of childish amusement than toward the pursuits of letters.
> I. Stirred up by God himself, he wishes to praise God. Ps. 144, 3; 146, 5. Jas. 4, 6. 1 Pet. 5, 5.

> 1 . Great art thou, O Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise: great is thy power, and of thy wisdom there is no number. And man desires to praise thee, some portion of thy creation; and man, bearing about his mortality, bearing about the testimony of his sin, and the testimony that thou resistest the proud: and yet man desires to praise thee, some portion of thy creation. Thou stirrest him up, that it may delight him to praise thee; because thou hast made us for thyself, and our heart is restless until it rests in thee [6] . Grant me, O Lord, to know and understand whether it is first to invoke thee, or to praise thee; and whether it is first to know thee, or to invoke thee. But who invokes thee without knowing thee? For one who does not know thee may invoke one thing for another. Or rather, art thou invoked that thou mayest be known? Rom. 10, 14. But how shall they invoke him in whom they have not believed? or how shall they believe without a preacher? Ps. 21, 27. Matt. 7, 7. And they who seek him shall praise the Lord.

For those who seek shall find him, and those who find shall praise him. I will seek thee, O Lord, by invoking thee; and I will invoke thee, believing in thee: for thou hast been preached unto us. My faith invokes thee, O Lord, which thou hast given me, which thou hast inspired in me through the humanity of thy Son, through the ministry of thy preacher.
> Page 2
> II. That the God whom he invokes is in him, and that he himself is in God.

> 2. And how shall I invoke my God, my God and my Lord? Since indeed I shall call him into myself [7] when I invoke him. And what place is there in me into which my God may come into me? whither may God come into me, God who made heaven and earth? Is there indeed anything in me, O Lord my God, that can contain thee? Or do heaven and earth, which thou hast made, and in which thou hast made me, contain thee? Or because without thee nothing that is would be, does it follow that whatever is contains thee? Since therefore I too am, why do I ask thee to come into me, who should not be unless thou wert in me? For I am not yet in hell * , and yet even there thou art. For Ps. 138, 8. if I descend into hell, thou art present . Therefore I should not be, O my God, I should not be at all, unless thou wert in me. Or rather, I should not be unless I were in thee, Rom. 11, 36. of whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things? Even so, O Lord, even so. Whither do I invoke thee, when I am in thee? or whence dost thou come into me?
For whither shall I withdraw outside heaven and earth, so that thence my God may come into me, who said: Jer. 23, 24. I fill heaven and earth?
> III. God is thus wholly everywhere, that no thing contains him wholly.

> 3. Do heaven and earth then contain [8] thee, because thou fillest them? Or dost thou fill them, and yet something remains, because they do not contain thee? And whither dost thou pour forth whatever remains of thee after heaven and earth have been filled? Or hast thou no need to be contained anywhere, thou who containest all things; because thou fillest the things which thou fillest by containing them? For the vessels that are full of thee do not make thee stable; because even if they be broken, thou art not poured out. And when Acts 2, 18. thou art poured out upon us , thou dost not lie low, but raisest us up; nor art thou scattered * , but gatherest us together. But thou who * fillest all things, dost thou fill all things with thy whole self? Or, because all things cannot contain thee wholly, do they contain a part of thee, and do all things at once contain that same part? Or do individual things contain individual parts, the greater things greater parts, the lesser things lesser parts? Therefore is some part of thee greater, some lesser? Or art thou wholly everywhere, and no thing contains thee wholly?
> IV. The majesty and perfections of God are inexplicable.

> 4. What then art thou, my God? What, I ask, unless the Lord God? Ps. 17, 32. For who is Lord besides the Lord? or who is God besides our God? Most high, most good, most mighty, most omnipotent, most merciful and most just, most hidden and most present, most beautiful and most strong, stable and incomprehensible; unchangeable, changing all things; never new, Page 3 never old; making all things new, and Job 9, 5. from the old version bringing the proud to old age [9] , Matt. 25, 27. and they know it not : ever acting, ever at rest; gathering, and needing nothing; bearing, and filling, and protecting; creating, and nourishing, and perfecting; seeking, though nothing is lacking to thee. Thou lovest, yet dost not grow warm; thou art jealous, yet secure; thou repentest, yet dost not grieve; thou art angry, yet tranquil; thou changest thy works, yet changest not thy counsel: thou receivest what thou findest, and hast never lost * ; never needy, and thou rejoicest in gains; never covetous, and thou exactest usury.

More is bestowed upon thee than is due to thee, that thou mayest owe; and who has anything that is not thine? Thou renderest debts, owing nothing to anyone; thou forgivest debts, losing nothing. And what have we said * , O my God, my life, my holy sweetness? Or what does anyone say when he speaks of thee? And woe to those who are silent concerning thee; for the talkative are mute.
> V. He asks for the love of God and forgiveness of sins.

> 5. Who will grant me to rest in thee? Who will grant that thou mayest come into my heart and inebriate it, so that I may forget my evils and embrace thee, my one good? What art thou to me? Have mercy, that I may speak. What am I myself to thee, that thou commandest me to love thee, and, unless I do so, art angry with me and threatenest immense miseries? Is it itself a small misery * if I do not love thee? Alas for me! Tell me, by thy mercies, O Lord my God, what thou art to me. Ps. 34. 3. Say to my soul: I am thy salvation . Say it thus, that I may hear. Behold, the ears of my heart are before thee, O Lord; open them, and Ex. 33, 20. say to my soul: I am thy salvation . I will run after this voice and lay hold of thee. Do not hide thy face from me: let me die, lest I die, that I may see it.

> 6. Narrow is the house of my soul into which thou mayest come; let it be enlarged by thee. It is ruinous; repair it. It has things which offend thine eyes; I confess and know it: but who will cleanse it? or to whom other than thee shall I cry, Ps. 18, 13, 14. Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare thy servant from those of others [10] ? Ps. 115, 10. I believe, and therefore I speak ; O Lord, thou knowest. Ps. 31, 5. Have I not declared unto thee against myself my transgressions, O my God: Job 9, 2, 3. and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my heart? I do not contend with thee in judgment, who art truth; and I do not wish to deceive myself, Ps. 26, 12. lest my iniquity lie unto itself . Therefore I do not contend with thee in judgment; because Ps. 129, 3. if thou wilt observe iniquities, O Lord; O Lord, who shall endure ?
> VI. He describes his infancy, and praises God's providence and eternity.

> 7. But nevertheless, permit me to speak before thy mercy, Gen. 18, 27. me, dust and ashes . Yet permit me to speak; for behold, it is thy mercy, not a man who mocks me, to whom I speak. And perhaps thou mockest me; but Jer. 12, 15. when thou hast turned, thou wilt have mercy on me . For what is it that I wish to say, O Lord my God, save that I do not know whence I came hither? Into this, I say, mortal life * , or living death, I know not. And the consolations of thy mercies received me, as I have heard from the parents of my flesh, from whom * and in whom thou didst form me in time; for I do not remember it. Therefore the consolations of human milk received me. Nor did my mother or my nurses fill their breasts for themselves; but through them thou gavest me the nourishment of infancy, according to thy ordinance and thy riches disposed unto the depths of things. Thou didst also grant me not to desire more than thou gavest, and to those who nourished me to desire to give me what thou gavest them.

For by an ordered affection they wished to give me that wherewith they abounded from thee. For my good from them was good to them; though it was not from them * , but through them: for all good things are from thee, O God; 2 Sam. 23, 5. and from my God is all my salvation . This I observed afterward, thou crying out to me through these very things which thou bestowest within and without. For then I knew how to suck, and to rest in pleasures, but to weep at injuries to my flesh; nothing more.

> 8. Afterward I also began to laugh, first in sleep, then when awake. For this was reported to me concerning myself, and I believed it, because we see other infants thus: for I do not remember these things of mine. And behold, little by little I perceived where I was, and wished to show my wishes to those through whom they might be fulfilled, and I could not; because they were within, whereas they were without, nor could they by any sense of theirs enter into my soul. And so I threw about limbs and uttered sounds, signs resembling my wishes, a few that I could, such as I could: for they were not truly like them. And when I was not obeyed, either because I was not understood or lest it be harmful; I was angry with elders who were not subject to me, and with free persons who did not serve me, and by weeping I avenged myself upon them. I learned that infants are such from those whom I could observe, and they showed me, though not knowing it, that I had been such more than my knowing nurses did.

> 9. And behold, my infancy long ago died, and I live. But thou, O Lord, who both always livest and nothing dies in thee, Page 5 because before the beginnings of the ages, and before everything that can even be said to be before, thou art, and art God and Lord of all things which thou hast created: and with thee stand the causes of all unstable things; and the unchangeable origins of all changeable things remain; and the eternal rational principles of all irrational and temporal things live. Tell me, thy suppliant, O God, and merciful to thy wretched one; tell me whether my infancy succeeded some age of mine already dead: or is it that which I passed within my mother's womb? For something concerning that too has been reported to me, and I myself have seen pregnant women. But what was there even before this, O my sweetness, my God? Was I anywhere, or anyone? For I have no one to tell me these things; neither my father nor mother could, nor the experience of others, nor my own memory.
Dost thou mock me for asking these things, and commandest that thou be praised by me and that I confess to thee concerning what I know * ?

> 10. I confess to thee, O Lord of heaven and earth, speaking praise to thee concerning my beginnings and my infancy, which I do not remember; and thou hast given it to man to infer concerning himself from others, and to believe many things concerning himself even on the authority of women. For I was and lived even then, and at the end of infancy I was already seeking signs by which I might make my feelings known to others. Whence is such an animal, unless from thee, O Lord? Or shall anyone be the craftsman of making himself? Or is there any vein drawn from elsewhere, through which being and living may flow into us, other than that Ps. 99, 3. thou makest us , O Lord, to whom being and living are not one thing and another; because to be supremely and to live supremely are the same thing in thee? For thou art most high, and Mal. 3, 6. thou dost not change ; nor does today pass away in thee, and yet it passes away in thee, because all these things are in thee: for they would have no ways of passing away unless thou didst contain them. And because Ps. 101, 28.

thy years do not fail * , thy years are today: and how many days now of ours and of our fathers have passed through thy today, and from it received their measures, and in whatever manner have existed, and still others shall pass and receive, and in whatever manner shall exist! Ibid. But thou art the selfsame ; and all tomorrows and beyond, and all yesterdays and back, thou wilt make today, thou hast made today. What is it to me if anyone does not understand [11] ? Page 6 Let him too rejoice, saying: Ex. 16, 15. What is this ? Let him rejoice even thus; and let him love rather to find thee by not finding, than by finding not to find thee.
> VII. Infancy too is subject to sins.

> 11. Hear me, O God. Woe to the sins of men! And man says this, and you have mercy on him; for you made him, and did not make sin in him. Who * calls to mind the sin of my infancy for me? For no one is clean from sin before you, not even the infant whose life upon earth is but one day. Job 14, 4. from the old version. Who calls it to mind for me? Is it any little child now, in whom I see what I do not remember concerning myself? What, then, was my sin at that time? Was it because I cried, greedily seeking the breast? For if I were now to do so, greedily seeking, not indeed breasts, but food suited to my years, I should most justly be laughed at and rebuked. Therefore I did things then that deserved rebuke; but because I could not understand one rebuking me, neither custom nor reason allowed me to be rebuked. For as we grow, we root out and cast away such things. Nor have I seen anyone who knew, Joh. 5, 2. when cleansing something * , throw away good things.

Or were those things also good for their time: to seek by weeping even what would be given harmfully; to be sharply indignant with people not subject to one—free persons and elders, and those from whom one was begotten, and moreover many wiser persons—not complying with the nod of one's will; by striking, to endeavor to harm as much as one could, because they did not obey commands which it would have been pernicious to obey? Thus the weakness of infant limbs is innocent, but not the mind of infants. I have seen and experienced a jealous little child: he did not yet speak, and he looked pale, with a bitter expression, at his foster-brother. Who does not know this? Mothers and nurses say that they expiate these things by I know not what remedies. Unless, indeed, this too is innocence: not to endure a companion at a fountain of milk flowing copiously and abundantly, though he is most needy of assistance and still sustains life on that one food alone. But these things are gently tolerated, not because they are nonexistent or slight, but because they will perish with the advance of age.
This you may prove, since the very same things cannot be borne with equanimity when they are discovered in someone older.

> 12. Therefore you, Lord my God, who gave life to an infant and a body, which, as we see, you furnished with senses, knit together with limbs, adorned with form, and endowed with every impulse of a living creature for its wholeness and preservation: you command me to praise you in these things and Ps. 91, 2. to confess to you and sing psalms to your name, O Most High: because you are God, almighty and good, even if you had made these things alone, which no one else can make except you, the one from whom is every measure; O most beautiful one, who makes all things beautiful and orders all things by your law. This age, then, O Lord, in which I do not remember * having lived, of which I believed others, and which I inferred that I had passed from other infants—although this is a very trustworthy inference—I am reluctant to count as part of this life of mine which I live in this age. For, so far as the darkness of my forgetfulness is concerned, it is equal to that in which I lived in my mother's womb. And if also * Ps. 50, 7.

I was conceived in iniquity, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb; where, I ask you, my God, where, O Lord, was I your servant innocent, or when? But behold, I pass over that time: and what have I now to do with it, when I recall no traces of it?
> VIII. How the boy learned to speak.

> 13. Was it not by proceeding from infancy that I came hither into boyhood—or rather, did boyhood itself come upon me and succeed infancy? Nor did infancy depart: for where did it go? Yet it was no longer there. For I was no longer an infant unable to speak, but already a speaking boy. And I remember this; and how I learned to speak I noticed afterward. For older people did not teach me, presenting words to me in some fixed order of instruction, as they did letters a little later; but I myself, by the mind which you gave me, my God, when I wished by groans and various sounds and various movements of my limbs to bring forth the feelings of my heart, so that my will might be obeyed, and was unable to express all that I wished to all whom I wished, would make sounds in my memory * ; when they themselves named some object, and, in accordance with that sound, moved their bodies toward something, I observed and retained that they called that object by the sound they uttered when they wished to point it out.

That this was what they wished was made clear by the movement of the body, as though by the natural words of all nations, which are made by the expression of the face and the nodding of the eyes, and the action of the other limbs, and by the sound of the voice indicating the affection of the mind in seeking, possessing, rejecting, or avoiding things. Thus, by degrees, I gathered the words, placed in their positions in various sentences and frequently heard, of what things they were signs; and, my mouth now tamed to these signs, I expressed my own wishes through them. Thus I communicated with those among whom I was the signs for expressing wills, and entered more deeply into the stormy society of human life, dependent upon the authority of my parents and the nod of older people. > IX. Hatred of letters, love of play, and fear of being beaten in boys.

> 14. O God, my God, what miseries and mockeries I experienced there! For as a boy this was set before me as right living: to obey those who admonished me, so that I might flourish in this age and excel in the arts of speech, which serve human honor and false riches. Then I was sent to school to learn letters, in which, poor wretch that I was, I did not know what usefulness there was; and yet, if I was slow in learning, I was beaten. For this was praised by our elders; and many who had lived this life before us had constructed beforehand the toilsome paths through which we were compelled to pass, with multiplied labor and pain for the sons of Adam. Yet we found, O Lord, people praying to you; and from them we learned, sensing you, as much as we could, to be some great being who, even though not appearing to our senses, could hear us and help us.

For as a boy I began to pray to you, my help and my refuge; and in calling upon you I broke the knots of my tongue; and though little, with no little feeling I prayed to you not to be beaten at school. And when you did not hear me—which Ps.21, 3. was not unto folly for me [12]—my beatings, then my great and grievous evil, were laughed at by older people, even by my parents themselves, who wished no evil to befall me.

> 15. Is there anyone, O Lord, of so great a mind, clinging to you with exceedingly great affection? Is there, I say, anyone—for a certain foolishness too does this—is there, then, one who, by devoutly clinging to you, is so greatly affected that he esteems racks and claws and various tortures of this kind, to escape which people supplicate you throughout all lands with great fear, so little that he laughs * at those who most bitterly dread them, just as our parents laughed at the torments by which we boys were afflicted by our teachers? For we did not fear them less, nor did we pray to you less to escape them; and yet we sinned by writing, or reading, or thinking about letters less than was required of us. For we did not lack, O Lord, memory or intelligence, which you willed us to possess sufficiently for that age; but we delighted in playing, and were punished for it by those who certainly did such things themselves.

But the trifles of elders are called business; whereas such things, when they belong to boys, Page 9 are punished by elders: and no one pities the boys, or the elders, or both. Unless, indeed, some good judge of things approves * my having been beaten because, as a boy, I played ball, and was by that play hindered from quickly learning letters, by which as an older man I should play more shamefully; or unless * that very man by whom I was beaten did something else: if he were defeated by a fellow teacher in some petty question, he would be more tormented by anger and envy than I was when I was beaten by my playmate in a contest of ball.
> X. By love of play and spectacles he is drawn away from the study of letters.

> 16. And yet I sinned, O Lord God, ordainer and creator of all natural things, but only ordainer of sins [13]: O Lord my God, I sinned by acting contrary to the commands of my parents and those teachers. For afterward I could have made good use of the letters which my own people wished me to learn, whatever their intention. For I was disobedient not by choosing better things, but through love of play: loving proud victories in contests, and having my ears scratched by false tales so that they might itch more ardently, while the same curiosity flashed forth more and more through my eyes toward the spectacles * and games of adults. Yet those who produce them stand out endowed with such dignity that almost everyone desires this for his little children; whom, nevertheless, they willingly allow to be beaten if they are hindered by such spectacles from the study through which they desire them to attain to producing such things.
Look upon these things mercifully, O Lord, and deliver us who now call upon you; deliver also those who do not yet call upon you, that they may call upon you and you may deliver them.
> XI. Oppressed by illness, he asks for Baptism, which his mother postpones by a settled plan.

> 17. For while still a boy I had heard of the eternal life promised to us through the humility [14] of our Lord God, descending to our pride; and I was already signed with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt [15], from my mother's womb onward, she who Page 10 greatly hoped in you. You saw, O Lord, when I was still a boy, and when one day, under pressure in my stomach * , I suddenly burned with fever and was nearly dying; you saw, my God, since you were already my guardian, with what motion of mind and with what faith I demanded the baptism of your Christ, my God and my Lord, from the piety of my mother and of the mother of us all, your Church. And my mother according to the flesh, troubled because she bore my eternal salvation more dearly in a chaste heart in your faith, would already, in haste, have taken care that I be initiated and washed in the saving Sacraments, confessing you, Lord Jesus, for the remission of sins, had I not immediately recovered.

My cleansing was therefore postponed, as though it were necessary for me still to be defiled if I lived; because, plainly, after that washing the guilt incurred in the filth of sins would be greater and more dangerous. Thus I already believed, as did she and the whole household, except only my father; yet he did not prevail against the right of maternal devotion in me, so as to prevent me from believing in Christ, as he himself did not yet believe. For she was earnestly striving that you should be my father, my God, rather than he; and in this you helped her to overcome her husband, to whom she rendered service as the better person; for in this too she certainly served you, who commanded it.

> 18. I ask you, my God: I would like to know, if you too willed it, for what counsel I was delayed from being baptized then—whether, for my good, the reins of sinning were, as it were, loosened for me, or were not loosened *? Why then even now do we hear on every side concerning one person and another: “Let him be, let him do it *; for he is not yet baptized”? Yet concerning bodily health we do not say: “Let him be more wounded; for he is not yet healed.” How much better, then, would I have been healed quickly, and would it have been brought about through the care of my own people and myself that, once the salvation of my soul had been received, it might be safe under your protection, who had given it? It would indeed have been better. But how many and how great waves of temptations seemed to hang over me after boyhood, she, my mother, already knew; and she wished to entrust to them the earth * from which I might afterward be formed, rather than the image itself already formed.
> XII. He was compelled to study letters, though God used this for good.

> 19. Yet in that very boyhood, concerning which there was less fear for me than concerning adolescence, I did not love letters and hated being driven to them; yet I was driven, and it was done well for me, though I did not act well. For I would not learn unless compelled. But no one acts well unwillingly, even if what he does is good. Nor did those who drove me act well; but it was done well for me by you, my God. For they did not consider to what end I might refer * what they compelled me to learn, except to satisfy the insatiable desires of plentiful poverty and disgraceful glory. Mat. 10, 30. But you, to whom the hairs of our head are numbered, used the error of all those who pressed me to learn for my benefit; but you used my own error—I who did not wish to learn—for my punishment, a punishment which I, a little boy and a great sinner, did not undeservedly suffer. Thus from those not acting well you did good for me; and from my own sinning you justly repaid me.
For you commanded, and so it is, that every disordered mind is its own punishment.
> XIII. The pursuits in which he chiefly took delight.

> 20. But what was the reason why I hated Greek literature, with which I was imbued as a little boy, is not even now sufficiently clear to me. For I had grown to love Latin, not that which the first teachers teach, but that which those called grammarians teach. For those first elements, where one learns to read and write and count, I considered no less burdensome and penal than all Greek. Yet whence was even this, if not from the sin and vanity of life, whereby, Ps. 77, 39. according to the old version, see Sabat. I was flesh *, and a spirit walking and not returning? For certainly those first letters were better, because more certain: by which it was brought about in me—and has been brought about, and I have this—that I may read if I find anything written, and may myself write if I wish anything, than those by which I was compelled to retain the wanderings of some Aeneas, forgetful of my own wanderings; and to weep for Dido dead because she killed herself for love, while meanwhile I most wretchedly endured myself, dying in these things away from thee, O God, my life, with dry eyes.

> 21. For what is more wretched than a wretch not pitying himself, and weeping over the death of Dido, which came about through loving Aeneas, but not weeping over his own death, which came about through not loving thee, O God, light of my heart, and bread of the inward mouth of my soul, and power wedding my mind [16] and the bosom of my thought? I did not love thee, and I fornicated away from thee; and to me, in my fornication, there sounded on every side, “Well done, well done.” For friendship with this world is fornication away from thee [17]; and “Well done, well done” is said, so that a man may be ashamed if he is not such. And I did not weep for these things, but I wept for Dido, “extinguished, and having pursued her last course with the sword [18],” myself pursuing thy last-created things, having forsaken thee, and going, earth *, into earth: and if I were forbidden to read these things, I would grieve because I did not read that over which I would grieve. Such madness is deemed Page 12 more honorable and more fruitful literature than those things by which I learned to read and write.

> 22. But now let my God cry aloud in my soul, and let thy truth say to me: It is not so, it is not so; that former instruction is altogether better. For behold, I am readier to forget the wanderings of Aeneas and all things of that sort than to write and read. But, it may be said, curtains hang at the doorways of the schools of grammarians: yet they signify not so much the dignity of a mystery as a covering for error. Let not those cry out against me whom I no longer fear, while I confess to thee what my soul wills, O my God, and rest in the rebuke of my evil ways, that I may love thy good ways. Let not the sellers or buyers of grammar cry out against me: for if I put to them the question whether it is true that the Poet says Aeneas once came to Carthage, the less learned will answer that they do not know; but the more learned will even deny that it is true.

But if I ask by what letters the name of Aeneas is written, all who have learned these things will give me the correct answer, according to that agreement and convention by which men established these signs among themselves. Likewise, if I ask which of these anyone would forget with the greater detriment to this life—reading and writing, or those poetic fictions—who does not see what he will answer, if he has not utterly forgotten himself? Therefore I sinned as a boy when I set those empty things before these more useful things in love; or rather, when I hated these and loved those. Now, “one and one are two, two and two are four,” was a hateful chant to me; while the sweetest spectacle of vanity was the wooden horse full of armed men, and the burning of Troy, and the shade of Creusa herself [19].
> XIV. He hated Greek letters.

> 23. Why then did I also hate Greek grammar, which sings of such things? For Homer too is skilled in weaving such little fables, and is most sweetly vain; yet he was bitter to me as a boy. I suppose Virgil is likewise to Greek boys when they are forced to learn him as I was forced to learn that poet. Evidently the difficulty—indeed, the difficulty of learning a foreign language—sprinkled, as it were, all the sweetnesses of Greek fabulous narratives with gall. For I knew none of those words, and it was vehemently pressed upon me with savage terrors and punishments that I should know them. For as an infant I too once knew no Latin at all; yet by giving attention I learned it without any fear or torment, amid even the caresses of nurses, Page 13 the jokes of those who smiled upon me, and the merriment of those who played with me.

But I learned those things without the penal burden of persons urging me on, when my own heart urged me to bring forth its conceptions, which I could not * do unless I had learned some words—not from teachers, but from speakers, in whose ears I too gave birth to whatever I felt. From this it sufficiently shines forth that free curiosity has greater power for learning such things than fearful necessity. But thy laws, O God, restrain the overflow of the latter—thy laws, from the rods of teachers even to the trials of martyrs—laws having power to mingle wholesome bitter things, calling us back to thee from the pestilent pleasure through which we departed from thee *.
> XV. Prayer to God.

> 24. Hear, O Lord, my supplication, lest my soul fail beneath thy discipline; nor let me fail in confessing to thee thy mercies, by which thou hast delivered me from all my most evil ways; that thou mayest become sweet [20] to me above all the seductions which I followed; and that I may love thee most mightily and embrace thy hand with all my inmost heart, and that thou mayest deliver me from every temptation unto the end. For behold, thou, O Lord, art my king and my God: let whatever useful thing I learned as a boy serve thee; let what I speak, and write, and read, and count, serve thee. For while I was learning vain things, thou gavest me discipline; and in those vain things thou forgavest me the sins of my delights. For in them I learned many useful words; but words which can also be learned in things not vain: and that is the safe path upon which boys should walk.
> XVI. He censures the manner of educating youth.

> 25. But woe to thee, river of human custom! Who shall resist thee? How long shalt thou not be dried up? How long shalt thou roll the sons of Eve into the great and dreadful sea, which scarcely those who have mounted the wood cross [21]? Did I not read in thee of Jupiter thundering and committing adultery? And surely he could not do these two things; but it was brought about that he should have authority for imitating real adultery, a false thunderbolt playing the pander. But which of the cloak-wearing teachers listens with sober ear to a man crying out from the same dust and saying: “Homer fashioned these things, and transferred human things to the gods; I would rather that he transferred divine things to us [22]”? But it is truer to say that he indeed fashioned these things, but, by attributing divine things to flagitious men, he brought it about that outrages should not be thought outrages *, and that whoever committed them might seem to imitate not ruined men but heavenly gods.

> 26. And yet, O Tartarean river, the children of men are cast into thee, with fees paid that they may learn these things; and a great matter is made of it when this is publicly done in the forum, in sight of laws which decree salaries in addition to fees; and thou dost strike thy rocks and resound, saying: Here words are learned; here eloquence is acquired, most necessary for persuading in matters and setting forth thoughts. As though indeed we would not know such words as golden shower, lap, trickery, temples of heaven, and the other words written in that passage, unless Terence introduced a worthless young man proposing Jupiter to himself as an example for seduction, while he looks at a certain painting drawn upon a wall, where this picture was: “How, they say, Jupiter once sent a golden shower into Danaë’s lap, having made himself a trick to the woman?” And see how he stirs himself up to lust, as though by heavenly instruction:
> But what god (he says)? He who shakes the lofty temples of heaven with sound.
> Would I, a mere little man, not do this? Why, I did it—and willingly [23].

> Not at all through this shamefulness are those words learned more conveniently; but through these words that shamefulness is perpetrated more confidently. I do not accuse the words, as though they were choice and precious vessels; but the wine of error which was poured out to us in them by drunken teachers: and unless we drank, we were beaten, nor was it permitted to appeal to any sober judge. And yet I, O my God, in whose sight my remembrance is now secure, willingly learned these things, and, miserable man, took delight in them; and for this reason I was called a boy of good promise.
> XVII. He continues against the manner of training youth in literary matters.

> 27. Allow me, my God, to say something also about my own talent, thy gift, amid what frenzies it was worn away by me. For there was set before me a task sufficiently disquieting to my soul, with the reward of praise and the fear of disgrace or lashes: namely, that I should speak the words of Juno, angry and grieving because she could not turn the king of the Teucrians away from Italy [24]—words which I had never heard Juno speak. We were compelled to follow, wandering, the tracks of poetic fictions, and to say something in prose such as the Poet had said in verse; and he spoke more commendably in whom, according to the dignity of the portrayed person, an emotion more resembling anger and grief stood out, while the words suitably clothed the thoughts. What was that to me, O thou my true life, my God, that applause was given to me as I recited, beyond many of my contemporaries and fellow-students? Behold, were not all those things smoke and wind? Was there then no other place in which my talent and tongue might be exercised?

Thy praises, O Lord, thy praises through thy Scriptures should have suspended the vine-branch of my heart, and it should not have been snatched away through the empty things of trifles as a shameful prey for flying creatures. For transgressing angels are not sacrificed to in one way only.
> XVIII. That men take care to observe the laws of grammarians, and not those of divine precepts.

> 28. But what wonder is it that I was thus borne into vanities and went forth away from thee, my God, when men were set before me for imitation who, if in recounting certain deeds of theirs not evil in themselves they were reproved for uttering them with a barbarism or solecism, were confounded; but if they copiously and elegantly narrated their lusts in sound and properly connected words, were praised and gloried? Thou seest these things, O Lord, and art silent, long-suffering, and greatly merciful, and true. Wilt thou always be silent? And even now thou dost deliver * from this most monstrous deep a soul seeking thee and thirsting for thy delights, and whose heart says to thee, Ps. 26, 8. “I have sought thy face; thy face, O Lord, will I seek.” For * one goes far from thy face by a dark affection *. For one does not go away from thee, or return to thee, by feet or by distances of places.

Or indeed did that younger son of thine seek horses, or chariots, or ships, or fly away with a visible wing, or make his journey by moving his knee, so that, living in a distant country, he might prodigally waste what thou hadst given him when he set out? Sweet father, because thou hadst given; and sweeter to him returning in need. Luc. 15, 11—32. Therefore in a lustful affection—that is, in darkness—and that is far from thy face.

> 29. See, O Lord God, and patiently, as thou seest, behold how diligently the sons of men observe the conventions of letters and syllables received from earlier speakers, and neglect the eternal covenants of everlasting salvation received from thee; so that one who observes or teaches those old rules concerning sounds, if he should say ominem, contrary to grammatical discipline, without the aspiration of the first syllable, is more displeasing to men than if, contrary to thy precepts, he should hate a man, though he himself is a man. As though he felt any human enemy more ruinously than the hatred itself by which he is provoked against him; or as though anyone devastated another more grievously by persecuting him than he devastates his own heart by being hostile. And certainly there is no more inward knowledge of letters than the written conscience: that one should do to another * what he would not wish to suffer. How hidden thou art, Is. 33, 5. dwelling on high in silence, God alone great, by an untiring law scattering penal blindnesses over unlawful desires!

When a man seeks the reputation of eloquence, standing before a man who is a judge, with a crowd of men surrounding him, while pursuing his enemy with most savage hatred, he takes the most vigilant care not to say, through an error of tongue, Inter hominibus *; but he takes no care, through a frenzy of mind, not to take a man away from among men.
> XIX. The vices of childhood which pass over into later ages.

> 30. As a boy, miserable, I lay at the threshold of these habits; and that school was the wrestling-ground of this arena, where I feared making a barbarism more than I took care, if I did make one, not to envy those who did not. I say and confess these things to you, my God, in matters for which I was praised by those to please whom was then, for me, to live honourably. For I did not see the abyss of depravity into which Ps. 30, 23. I had been cast away from your eyes. For among those things what was more foul than I, when I displeased even such people, by deceiving with innumerable lies both my pedagogue and my teachers and my parents, out of love of play, zeal for watching trifles, and restless desire to imitate theatrical games? I even committed thefts from my parents' store-room and table, either at the command of gluttony, or in order to have something to give to boys who sold me their game, in which they themselves, of course, were equally delighted. In this game too, conquered by the desire for vain * superiority, I often sought fraudulent victories.

But what was it that I was so unwilling to suffer, and so fiercely rebuked if I caught it out, as that which I did to others; and, if caught and rebuked, was more pleased to rage than to yield? Is this childhood innocence? It is not, Lord, it is not: I beseech you, my God. For these very things are those which pass over from pedagogues and teachers, from nuts and balls and sparrows, to prefects and kings, gold, estates, slaves—these very things altogether pass over with the succeeding greater ages, just as greater punishments succeed the rods. Therefore, in the stature of childhood, our King, you approved a sign of humility when you said: Mat. 19, 14. Of such is the kingdom of heaven.
> XX. For the good things bestowed upon him in childhood

> 31. Yet nevertheless, Lord, to you, the most excellent and best creator and ruler of the universe, our God, thanks be given, even if you had willed that I should be only a child. For even then I was, I lived * and felt, and I took care for my safety, a trace Page 17 of the most secret unity from which I was [25] ; He gives thanks to God. I guarded by an inward sense the integrity of my senses, and in the very small thoughts of small things I delighted in truth. I did not wish to be deceived; my memory was strong; I was instructed in speech; I was soothed by friendship; I fled pain, abasement, ignorance. What in such a living creature is not wonderful and praiseworthy? But all these things are gifts of my God; I did not give them to myself: and they are good, and all these things are I. Good, therefore, is he who made me, and he himself is my good; and in him I exult with all the goods by which I was even a boy.

For in this I sinned: that I sought pleasures, sublimities, and truths not in him, but in his creatures—in myself and the rest *; and thus I rushed into pains, confusions, errors. Thanks to you, my sweetness, and my honour, and my confidence, my God: thanks to you for your gifts; but preserve them for me. For thus you will preserve me; and the things which you have given me will be increased and perfected, and I myself shall be with you; because you gave even that I might be.
> Page 18

sources.title: BOOK II.
sources.text:
> Ad ætatem aliam progreditur, primumque adolescentiæ suæ, id est, sextum decimum vitæ annum, quem in paterna domo studiis intermissis consumpserat arbitrio proprio ac libidinibus indulgens, ad mentem revocat cum gravi dolore, in quibus maxime miratur, se furtum quoddam gratis perpetrasse; quod contra, cor humanum non nisi aliqua boni specie in malum trahi.

> I. Adolescentiæ ætatem et vitia recolit.

> 1. Recordari volo transactas fœditates meas, et carnales corruptiones animæ meæ: non quod eas amem; sed ut amem te, Deus meus. Amore amoris tui facio istud, recolens vias meas nequissimas in amaritudine recogitationis meæ, ut tu dulcescas mihi, dulcedo non fallax, dulcedo felix et secura, et colligens * me a dispersione in qua frustatim discissus sum, dum ab uno te aversus in multa evanui [26] . Exarsi enim aliquando satiari inferis * in adolescentia, et silvescere ausus sum variis et umbrosis amoribus; et contabuit species mea; et computrui coram oculis tuis placens mihi, et placere cupiens oculis hominum.

> II. Annum ætatis suæ decimum sextum in ardore libidinoso consumptum.

> 2. Et quid erat quod me delectabat, nisi amare et amari? Sed non tenebatur modus ab animo usque ad animum quatenus est luminosus * limes amicitiæ; sed exhalabantur nebulæ de limosa concupiscentia carnis et scatebra pubertatis, et obnubilabant atque offuscabant cor meum, ut non discerneretur serenitas dilectionis a caligine libidinis. Utrumque in confuso æstuabat, et rapiebat imbecillam ætatem per abrupta cupiditatum, atque mersabat gurgite flagitiorum. Invaluerat super me ira tua, et nesciebam. Obsurdueram * stridore catenæ mortalitatis meæ, pœna superbiæ animæ meæ; et ibam longius a te, et sinebas; et jactabar, et effundebar, et diffluebam, et ebulliebam per fornicationes meas, et tacebas. Page 19 O tardum gaudium meum! Tacebas tunc, et ego ibam porro longe a te in plura et plura sterilia semina dolorum, superba dejectione, et inquieta lassitudine.

> 3. Quis mihi modularetur * ærumnam meam, et novissimarum rerum fugaces pulchritudines in usum verteret, earumque suavitatibus metas præfigeret, ut usque ad conjugale littus exæstuarent fluctus ætatis meæ, si tranquillitas in eis non poterat esse, fine procreandorum liberorum contenta, sicut præscribit lex tua, Domine, qui formas etiam propaginem mortis nostræ * , potens imponere lenem manum ad temperamentum spinarum a paradiso tuo seclusarum? Non enim longe est a nobis omnipotentia tua, etiam cum longe sumus a te. Aut certe sonitum nubium tuarum vigilantius adverterem: 1 Cor. 7, 28. Tribulationem autem carnis habebunt hujusmodi; ego autem vobis parco ; et, ver. 1. Bonum est homini mulierem non tangere ; et, ver. 32, 33. Qui sine uxore est, cogitat ea quæ sunt Dei, quomodo placeat Deo: qui autem matrimonio junctus est, cogitat ea quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori . Mat. 19, 12. Has ergo voces exaudirem vigilantior, et abscisus propter regnum cœlorum, felicior exspectarem amplexus tuos.

> 4. Sed efferbui miser, sequens impetum fluxus mei relicto te; et excessi omnia legitima tua, nec evasi flagella tua: quis enim hoc mortalium? Nam tu semper aderas misericorditer sæviens, et amarissimis aspergens offensionibus omnes illicitas jucunditates meas, ut ita quærerem sine offensione jucundari; et ubi hoc possem, non invenirem quidquam, præter te, Domine, præter te Ps. 93, 20. qui fingis [27] dolorem in præcepto , et percutis ut sanes, et occidis nos ne moriamur abs te. Deut. 32, 39. Ubi eram, et quam longe exsulabam a deliciis domus tuæ, anno illo sexto decimo ætatis carnis meæ, cum accepit in me sceptrum, et totas manus ei dedi, vesania libidinis * , licentiosæ per dedecus humanum, illicitæ autem per leges tuas? Non fuit cura meorum ruentem excipere me matrimonio; sed cura fuit tantum ut discerem sermonem facere quam optimum, et persuadere dictione.

> Page 20

> III. De peregrinatione studiorum causa, et de parentum proposito.

> 5. Et anno quidem illo intermissa erant studia mea, dum mihi reducto a Madauris, in qua vicina urbe jam cœperam litteraturæ atque oratoriæ percipiendæ gratia peregrinari, longinquioris apud Carthaginem peregrinationis sumptus præparabantur, animositate magis quam opibus patris, municipis Thagastensis admodum tenuis. Cui narro hæc? Neque enim tibi, Deus meus; sed apud te narro hæc generi meo, generi humano, quantulacumque ex particula incidere potest in istas meas litteras. Et utquid hoc? Ut videlicet ego et quisquis hæc legit, cogitemus Ps. 129, 1. de quam profundo clamandum sit ad te . Et quid propius auribus tuis, si cor confitens et vita ex fide est? Quis enim non extollebat laudibus tunc hominem patrem meum * , quod ultra vires rei familiaris suæ impenderet filio quidquid etiam longe peregrinanti studiorum causa opus esset? Multorum enim civium longe opulentiorum nullum tale negotium pro liberis erat: cum interea non satageret idem pater qualis crescerem tibi, aut quam castus essem; dummodo essem disertus, vel desertus potius a cultura tua, Deus, qui es unus verus et bonus Dominus agri tui cordis mei.

> 6. Sed ubi sexto illo et decimo anno, interposito otio ex necessitate domestica feriatus ab omni schola, cum parentibus esse cœpi, excesserunt caput meum vepres libidinum; et nulla erat eradicans manus. Quinimo, ubi me ille pater in balneis vidit pubescentem, et inquieta indutum adolescentia, quasi jam ex hoc in nepotes gestiret, gaudens matri indicavit; gaudens vinolentia in qua te iste mundus oblitus est creatorem suum, et creaturam tuam pro te amavit, de vino invisibili perversæ atque inclinatæ * in ima voluntatis suæ. Sed matris in pectore jam inchoaveras templum tuum, et exordium sanctæ habitationis tuæ: nam ille adhuc catechumenus, et hoc recens erat. Itaque illa exsilivit pia trepidatione ac tremore; et quamvis mihi nondum fideli, timuit tamen vias distortas, in quibus ambulant qui Jer. 2, 27. ponunt ad te tergum, et non faciem .

> 7. Hei mihi! et audeo dicere tacuisse te, Deus meus, cum irem abs te longius! Itane tu tacebas tunc mihi? Et cujus erant, nisi tua, verba illa per matrem meam, fidelem tuam, quæ cantasti in aures meas? Nec inde quidquam descendit in cor, ut facerem illud. Volebat enim illa, et secreto memini ut monuerit cum sollicitudine ingenti ne fornicarer, Page 21 maximeque ne adulterarem cujusquam uxorem. Qui mihi monitus muliebres videbantur, quibus obtemperare erubescerem. Illi autem tui erant, et nesciebam; et te tacere putabam, atque illam loqui, per quam mihi tu non tacebas, et in illa contemnebaris a me filio ejus, Ps. 115, 6. filio ancillæ tuæ, servo tuo . Sed nesciebam, et præceps ibam tanta cæcitate, ut inter coætaneos meos puderet me minoris dedecoris, quoniam audiebam eos jactantes flagitia sua, et tanto gloriantes magis, quanto magis turpes essent: et libebat facere non solum libidine facti, verum etiam laudis. Quid dignum est vituperatione nisi vitium? Ego ne vituperarer, vitiosior fiebam; et ubi non suberat quo admisso æquarer perditis, fingebam me fecisse quod non feceram, ne viderer abjectior quo eram innocentior, et ne vilior haberer quo eram castior.

> 8. Ecce cum quibus comitibus iter agebam platearum Babyloniæ, et volutabar in cœno ejus, tanquam in cinnamis et unguentis pretiosis. Et in umbilico ejus, quo tenacius hærerem, calcabat me inimicus invisibilis, et seducebat me, quia ego seductilis eram. Non enim et illa, quæ jam Jer. 51, 6. de medio Babylonis fugerat , sed ibat in cæteris ejus tardior, mater carnis meæ, sicut monuit me pudicitiam, ita curavit quod de me a viro suo audierat, jamque pestilentiosum et in posterum periculosum sentiebat, coercere termino conjugalis affectus, si resecari ad vivum non poterat. Non curavit hoc, quia metus erat ne impediretur spes mea compede uxoria; non spes illa quam in te futuri sæculi habebat mater, sed spes litterarum, quas ut nossem nimis volebat parens uterque: ille, quia de te prope nihil cogitabat, de me autem inania; illa autem, quia non solum nullo detrimento, sed etiam nonnullo adjumento ad te adipiscendum futura existimabat usitata illa studia doctrinæ. Ita enim conjicio, recolens, ut possum, mores parentum meorum. Relaxabantur etiam mihi ad ludendum habenæ, ultra temperamentum severitatis, in dissolutionem affectionum variarum, et in omnibus erat caligo intercludens mihi, Deus meus, serenitatem veritatis tuæ; et Ps. 72, 7. prodibat tanquam ex adipe iniquitas mea .

> IV. Furtum cum sodalibus perpetratum.

> 9. Furtum certe punit lex tua, Domine, et lex scripta in cordibus hominum, quam ne ipsa quidem delet iniquitas. Quis enim fur æquo animo furem patitur? Nec copiosus adactum inopia. Et ego furtum facere volui et feci, nulla Page 22 compulsus egestate nec penuria, sed fastidio justitiæ * , et sagina iniquitatis. Nam id furatus sum quod mihi abundabat, et multo melius: nec ea re volebam frui quam furto appetebam; sed ipso furto et peccato. Arbor erat pirus in vicinia vineæ nostræ pomis onusta, nec forma nec sapore illecebrosis. Ad hanc excutiendam atque asportandam, nequissimi adolescentuli perreximus nocte intempesta, quousque ludum de pestilentiæ more in areis produxeramus; et abstulimus inde onera ingentia, non ad nostras epulas, sed vel projicienda porcis, etiamsi aliquid inde comedimus; dum tamen fieret a nobis quod eo liberet quo non liceret. Ecce cor meum, Deus, ecce cor meum quod miseratus es in imo abyssi. Dicat tibi nunc ecce cor meum quid ibi quærebat, ut essem gratis malus, et malitiæ meæ causa nulla esset nisi malitia. Fœda erat, et amavi eam; amavi perire: amavi defectum meum; non illud ad quod deficiebam, sed defectum meum ipsum amavi: turpis anima et dissiliens a firmamento tuo in exterminium; non dedecore * aliquid, sed dedecus appetens.

> V. Neminem peccare sine causa.

> 10. Etenim species est pulchris corporibus, et auro, et argento, et omnibus; et in contactu carnis congruentia valet plurimum, cæterisque sensibus est sua cuique accommodata modificatio corporum; habet etiam honor temporalis, et imperitandi atque superandi potentia suum decus, unde etiam vindictæ aviditas oritur: et tamen in cuncta hæc adipiscenda non est egrediendum abs te, Domine, neque deviandum a lege tua. Et vita quam hic vivimus habet illecebram suam propter quemdam modum decoris sui, et convenientiam cum his omnibus infimis pulchris. Amicitia quoque hominum charo nodo dulcis est propter unitatem de multis animis. Propter universa hæc atque hujusmodi, peccatum admittitur, dum immoderata in ista inclinatione cum extrema bona sint, meliora et summa deseruntur [28] , tu, Domine Deus noster, et veritas tua, et lex tua. Habent enim et hæc ima delectationes, sed non sicut Deus meus qui fecit omnia; quia Ps. 63, 11. in ipso delectatur justus , et ipse est deliciæ rectorum corde .

> 11. Cum itaque de facinore quæritur qua causa factum sit, credi non solet, nisi cum appetitus adipiscendi alicujus Page 23 illorum bonorum, quæ infima diximus, esse potuisse apparuerit aut metus amittendi. Pulchra sunt enim et decora, quanquam præ bonis superioribus et * beatificis abjecta et jacentia. Homicidium fecit. Cur fecit? Adamavit ejus conjugem aut prædium, aut voluit deprædari unde viveret, aut timuit ab illo tale aliquid amittere, aut læsus ulcisci se exarsit. Num homicidium sine causa faceret, ipso homicidio delectatus? Quis crediderit? Nam et de quo dictum est vecordi et nimis crudeli homine, quod gratuito potius malus atque crudelis erat, prædicta est tamen causa: "Ne per otium, inquit, torpesceret manus aut animus [29] ." Quare id quoque? cur ita? Ut scilicet illa exercitatione scelerum, capta urbe, honores, imperia, divitias assequeretur, et careret metu legum, et difficultate rerum, propter inopiam rei familiaris, et conscientiam scelerum. Nec ipse igitur Catilina amavit facinora sua; sed utique aliud cujus causa illa faciebat.

> VI. Omnia quæ boni specie ad vitia invitant, in solo Deo esse vera et perfecta.

> 12. Quid ego * miser in te amavi, o furtum meum, o facinus illud meum nocturnum sexti decimi anni ætatis meæ? Non enim pulchrum eras, cum furtum esses; aut vero aliquid es, ut loquar ad te? Pulchra erant poma illa quæ furati sumus, quoniam creatura tua erat * , pulcherrime omnium, creator omnium, Deus bone, Deus summum bonum, et bonum verum meum: pulchra erant illa poma; sed non ipsa concupivit anima mea miserabilis. Erat enim mihi meliorum copia; illa autem decerpsi tantum ut furarer. Nam decerpta projeci, epulatus inde solam iniquitatem * , qua lætabar fruens * . Nam et si quid illorum pomorum intravit in os meum, condimentum ibi * facinus erat. Et nunc, Domine Deus meus, quæro quid me in furto delectaverit, et ecce species nulla est: non dico sicut in æquitate atque prudentia; sed neque sicut in mente hominis atque memoria et sensibus et vegetante vita; neque sicut speciosa sunt sidera et decora locis suis et terra et mare plena fetibus, qui succedunt nascendo decedentibus; non saltem ut est quædam defectiva species et umbratica vitiis fallentibus.

> 13. Nam et superbia celsitudinem imitatur; cum tu sis unus super omnia Deus excelsus. Et ambitio quid nisi honores quærit et gloriam; cum tu sis præ cunctis honorandus unus et gloriosus in æternum? Et sævitia potestatum Page 24 timeri vult: quis autem timendus, nisi unus Deus? Cujus potestati eripi aut subtrahi quid potest? quando, aut ubi, aut quo, vel a quo * ? Et blanditiæ lascivientium amari volunt: sed neque blandius est aliquid tua charitate, nec amatur quidquam salubrius, quam illa præ cunctis formosa et luminosa veritas tua. Et curiositas affectare videtur studium scientiæ; cum tu omnia summe noveris. Ignorantia quoque ipsa atque stultitia, simplicitatis et innocentiæ nomine tegitur; quia te simplicius quidquam non reperitur. Quid te autem innocentius, quandoquidem opera sua * malis inimica sunt [30] ? Et ignavia quasi quietem appetit: quæ vero quies certa præter Dominum? Luxuria satietatem atque abundantiam se cupit vocari: tu autem es plenitudo et indeficiens copia incorruptibilis suavitatis. Effusio liberalitatis obtendit umbram: sed bonorum omnium largitor affluentissimus tu es. Avaritia multa possidere vult; et tu possides omnia. Invidentia de excellentia litigat: quid te excellentius? Ira vindictam quærit: te justius quis vindicat? Timor insolita et repentina exhorrescit, rebus quæ amantur adversantia, dum præcavet securitati: Rom. 8, 9. tibi enim quid insolitum? quid repentinum? aut quis a te separat quod diligis? aut ubi, nisi apud te, firma securitas? Tristitia rebus amissis contabescit, quibus se oblectabat cupiditas; quia ita sibi nollet, sicut tibi auferri nihil potest.

> 14. Ita fornicatur anima, cum avertitur abs te, et quærit extra te ea, quæ pura et liquida non invenit, nisi cum redit ad te. Perverse te imitantur omnes qui longe se a te faciunt, et extollunt se adversum te [31] . Sed etiam sic te imitando indicant creatorem te esse omnis naturæ; et ideo non esse quo a te omnimodo recedatur. Quid ergo in illo furto ego dilexi? et in quo Dominum meum vel vitiose atque perverse imitatus sum? An libuit facere contra legem saltem fallacia, quia potentatu non poteram, ut mancam libertatem captivus Page 25 imitarer faciendo impune quod non liceret, tenebrosa omnipotentiæ similitudine? Ecce est ille servus fugiens Dominum suum, et consecutus umbram. O putredo, o monstrum vitæ, et mortis profunditas! Potuitne libere quod non licebat, non ob aliud, nisi quia non licebat?

> VII. Gratias agit Deo pro remissione peccatorum, quodque a multis servatus sit.

> 15. Ps. 115, 4. Quid retribuam Domino , quod recolit hæc memoria mea, et anima mea non metuit inde? Diligam te, Domine, et gratias agam, et confitear nomini tuo, quoniam tanta dimisisti mihi mala et nefaria opera mea. Gratiæ tuæ deputo et misericordiæ tuæ, quod peccata mea tanquam glaciem solvisti. Gratiæ tuæ deputo et quæcumque non feci mala: quid enim non facere potui, qui etiam gratuitum facinus amavi? Et omnia mihi dimissa esse fateor; et quæ mea sponte feci mala, et quæ te duce non feci. Quis est hominum qui suam cogitans infirmitatem, audet viribus suis tribuere castitatem atque innocentiam suam; ut minus amet [32] te, quasi minus ei necessaria fuerit misericordia tua, qua donas peccata conversis ad te? Qui enim vocatus a te secutus est vocem tuam, et vitavit ea quæ me de meipso recordantem et fatentem legit, non me derideat ab eo medico ægrum sanari, a quo sibi præstitum est ut non ægrotaret, vel potius ut minus ægrotaret: et ideo te tantumdem, imo vero amplius diligat; quia per quem me videt tantis peccatorum meorum languoribus exui, per eum se videt tantis peccatorum languoribus non implicari.

> VIII. Amavit in furto consortium simul peccantium.

> 16. Rom. 6, 21. Quem fructum habui miser aliquando in iis quæ nunc recolens erubesco , maxime in illo furto in quo ipsum furtum amavi? Nihil aliud; cum et ipsum esset nihil, et eo ipso ego miserior. Et tamen solus id non fecissem, sic recordor animum tunc meum; solus omnino id non fecissem. Ergo amavi ibi etiam consortium eorum * cum quibus id feci. Non ergo nihil aliud quam furtum amavi; imo vero nihil aliud, quia et illud nihil est. Quid est revera? Quis est qui doceat me, nisi qui illuminat cor meum et discernit umbras ejus? Quid est quod mihi venit in mentem quærere, et discutere, et considerare? Quia si tunc amarem poma illa Page 26 quæ furatus sum, et eis frui cuperem, possem etiam solus, si satis esset committere illam iniquitatem, qua pervenirem ad voluptatem meam; nec confricatione consciorum animorum accenderem pruritum cupiditatis meæ. Sed quoniam in illis pomis voluptas mihi non erat, ea erat in ipso facinore, quam faciebat consortium simul peccantium.

> IX. Contagiosa res sodales mali.

> 17. Quid erat ille affectus animi? Certe enim plane turpis erat nimis; et væ mihi erat qui habebam illum. Sed tamen quid erat? Ps. 18, 13. Delicta quis intelligit? Risus erat, quasi titillato corde, quod fallebamus eos qui hæc a nobis fieri non putabant, et vehementer nolebant. Cur ergo eo me delectabat, quo id non faciebam solus? An quia etiam nemo facile solus ridet? Nemo quidem facile; sed tamen etiam solos et singulos homines, cum alius nemo præsens est, vincit risus aliquando, si aliquid nimie ridiculum, vel sensibus occurrit * , vel animo. At ego illud solus non facerem, non facerem omnino solus. Ecce est coram te, Deus meus, viva recordatio animæ meæ. Solus non facerem furtum illud, in quo me non libebat id quod furabar, sed quia furabar: quod me solum facere prorsus non liberet, nec facerem. O nimis inimica amicitia, seductio mentis investigabilis, ex ludo et joco nocendi aviditas, et alieni damni appetitus; nulla lucri mei, nulla ulciscendi libidine; sed cum dicitur: Eamus, faciamus; et pudet non esse impudentem.

> X. In Deo omne bonum.

> 18. Quis exaperit istam tortuosissimam et implicatissimam nodositatem? Fœda est; nolo in eam intendere, nolo eam videre. Te volo, justitia et innocentia, pulchra et decora honestis luminibus, et insatiabili satietate. Quies est apud te valde, et vita imperturbabilis. Qui intrat in te, Mat. 25, 21. intrat in gaudium Domini sui ; et non timebit, et habebit se optime in optimo. Defluxi abs te ego, et erravi, Deus meus, nimis devius a stabilitate tua in adolescentia, et factus sum mihi regio egestatis.

> Page 27

paragraphs.text: > Ad ætatem aliam progreditur, primumque adolescentiæ suæ, id est, sextum decimum vitæ annum, quem in paterna domo studiis intermissis consumpserat arbitrio proprio ac libidinibus indulgens, ad mentem revocat cum gravi dolore, in quibus maxime miratur, se furtum quoddam gratis perpetrasse; quod contra, cor humanum non nisi aliqua boni specie in malum trahi.
> I. Adolescentiæ ætatem et vitia recolit.

> 1. Recordari volo transactas fœditates meas, et carnales corruptiones animæ meæ: non quod eas amem; sed ut amem te, Deus meus. Amore amoris tui facio istud, recolens vias meas nequissimas in amaritudine recogitationis meæ, ut tu dulcescas mihi, dulcedo non fallax, dulcedo felix et secura, et colligens * me a dispersione in qua frustatim discissus sum, dum ab uno te aversus in multa evanui [26] . Exarsi enim aliquando satiari inferis * in adolescentia, et silvescere ausus sum variis et umbrosis amoribus; et contabuit species mea; et computrui coram oculis tuis placens mihi, et placere cupiens oculis hominum.
> II. Annum ætatis suæ decimum sextum in ardore libidinoso consumptum.

> 2. Et quid erat quod me delectabat, nisi amare et amari? Sed non tenebatur modus ab animo usque ad animum quatenus est luminosus * limes amicitiæ; sed exhalabantur nebulæ de limosa concupiscentia carnis et scatebra pubertatis, et obnubilabant atque offuscabant cor meum, ut non discerneretur serenitas dilectionis a caligine libidinis. Utrumque in confuso æstuabat, et rapiebat imbecillam ætatem per abrupta cupiditatum, atque mersabat gurgite flagitiorum. Invaluerat super me ira tua, et nesciebam. Obsurdueram * stridore catenæ mortalitatis meæ, pœna superbiæ animæ meæ; et ibam longius a te, et sinebas; et jactabar, et effundebar, et diffluebam, et ebulliebam per fornicationes meas, et tacebas. Page 19 O tardum gaudium meum! Tacebas tunc, et ego ibam porro longe a te in plura et plura sterilia semina dolorum, superba dejectione, et inquieta lassitudine.

> 3. Quis mihi modularetur * ærumnam meam, et novissimarum rerum fugaces pulchritudines in usum verteret, earumque suavitatibus metas præfigeret, ut usque ad conjugale littus exæstuarent fluctus ætatis meæ, si tranquillitas in eis non poterat esse, fine procreandorum liberorum contenta, sicut præscribit lex tua, Domine, qui formas etiam propaginem mortis nostræ * , potens imponere lenem manum ad temperamentum spinarum a paradiso tuo seclusarum? Non enim longe est a nobis omnipotentia tua, etiam cum longe sumus a te. Aut certe sonitum nubium tuarum vigilantius adverterem: 1 Cor. 7, 28. Tribulationem autem carnis habebunt hujusmodi; ego autem vobis parco ; et, ver. 1. Bonum est homini mulierem non tangere ; et, ver. 32, 33. Qui sine uxore est, cogitat ea quæ sunt Dei, quomodo placeat Deo: qui autem matrimonio junctus est, cogitat ea quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori . Mat. 19, 12.
Has ergo voces exaudirem vigilantior, et abscisus propter regnum cœlorum, felicior exspectarem amplexus tuos.

> 4. Sed efferbui miser, sequens impetum fluxus mei relicto te; et excessi omnia legitima tua, nec evasi flagella tua: quis enim hoc mortalium? Nam tu semper aderas misericorditer sæviens, et amarissimis aspergens offensionibus omnes illicitas jucunditates meas, ut ita quærerem sine offensione jucundari; et ubi hoc possem, non invenirem quidquam, præter te, Domine, præter te Ps. 93, 20. qui fingis [27] dolorem in præcepto , et percutis ut sanes, et occidis nos ne moriamur abs te. Deut. 32, 39. Ubi eram, et quam longe exsulabam a deliciis domus tuæ, anno illo sexto decimo ætatis carnis meæ, cum accepit in me sceptrum, et totas manus ei dedi, vesania libidinis * , licentiosæ per dedecus humanum, illicitæ autem per leges tuas? Non fuit cura meorum ruentem excipere me matrimonio; sed cura fuit tantum ut discerem sermonem facere quam optimum, et persuadere dictione.
> Page 20
> III. De peregrinatione studiorum causa, et de parentum proposito.

> 5. Et anno quidem illo intermissa erant studia mea, dum mihi reducto a Madauris, in qua vicina urbe jam cœperam litteraturæ atque oratoriæ percipiendæ gratia peregrinari, longinquioris apud Carthaginem peregrinationis sumptus præparabantur, animositate magis quam opibus patris, municipis Thagastensis admodum tenuis. Cui narro hæc? Neque enim tibi, Deus meus; sed apud te narro hæc generi meo, generi humano, quantulacumque ex particula incidere potest in istas meas litteras. Et utquid hoc? Ut videlicet ego et quisquis hæc legit, cogitemus Ps. 129, 1. de quam profundo clamandum sit ad te . Et quid propius auribus tuis, si cor confitens et vita ex fide est? Quis enim non extollebat laudibus tunc hominem patrem meum * , quod ultra vires rei familiaris suæ impenderet filio quidquid etiam longe peregrinanti studiorum causa opus esset?

Multorum enim civium longe opulentiorum nullum tale negotium pro liberis erat: cum interea non satageret idem pater qualis crescerem tibi, aut quam castus essem; dummodo essem disertus, vel desertus potius a cultura tua, Deus, qui es unus verus et bonus Dominus agri tui cordis mei.

> 6. Sed ubi sexto illo et decimo anno, interposito otio ex necessitate domestica feriatus ab omni schola, cum parentibus esse cœpi, excesserunt caput meum vepres libidinum; et nulla erat eradicans manus. Quinimo, ubi me ille pater in balneis vidit pubescentem, et inquieta indutum adolescentia, quasi jam ex hoc in nepotes gestiret, gaudens matri indicavit; gaudens vinolentia in qua te iste mundus oblitus est creatorem suum, et creaturam tuam pro te amavit, de vino invisibili perversæ atque inclinatæ * in ima voluntatis suæ. Sed matris in pectore jam inchoaveras templum tuum, et exordium sanctæ habitationis tuæ: nam ille adhuc catechumenus, et hoc recens erat. Itaque illa exsilivit pia trepidatione ac tremore; et quamvis mihi nondum fideli, timuit tamen vias distortas, in quibus ambulant qui Jer. 2, 27. ponunt ad te tergum, et non faciem .

> 7. Hei mihi! et audeo dicere tacuisse te, Deus meus, cum irem abs te longius! Itane tu tacebas tunc mihi? Et cujus erant, nisi tua, verba illa per matrem meam, fidelem tuam, quæ cantasti in aures meas? Nec inde quidquam descendit in cor, ut facerem illud. Volebat enim illa, et secreto memini ut monuerit cum sollicitudine ingenti ne fornicarer, Page 21 maximeque ne adulterarem cujusquam uxorem. Qui mihi monitus muliebres videbantur, quibus obtemperare erubescerem. Illi autem tui erant, et nesciebam; et te tacere putabam, atque illam loqui, per quam mihi tu non tacebas, et in illa contemnebaris a me filio ejus, Ps. 115, 6. filio ancillæ tuæ, servo tuo .

Sed nesciebam, et præceps ibam tanta cæcitate, ut inter coætaneos meos puderet me minoris dedecoris, quoniam audiebam eos jactantes flagitia sua, et tanto gloriantes magis, quanto magis turpes essent: et libebat facere non solum libidine facti, verum etiam laudis. Quid dignum est vituperatione nisi vitium? Ego ne vituperarer, vitiosior fiebam; et ubi non suberat quo admisso æquarer perditis, fingebam me fecisse quod non feceram, ne viderer abjectior quo eram innocentior, et ne vilior haberer quo eram castior.

> 8. Ecce cum quibus comitibus iter agebam platearum Babyloniæ, et volutabar in cœno ejus, tanquam in cinnamis et unguentis pretiosis. Et in umbilico ejus, quo tenacius hærerem, calcabat me inimicus invisibilis, et seducebat me, quia ego seductilis eram. Non enim et illa, quæ jam Jer. 51, 6. de medio Babylonis fugerat , sed ibat in cæteris ejus tardior, mater carnis meæ, sicut monuit me pudicitiam, ita curavit quod de me a viro suo audierat, jamque pestilentiosum et in posterum periculosum sentiebat, coercere termino conjugalis affectus, si resecari ad vivum non poterat.

Non curavit hoc, quia metus erat ne impediretur spes mea compede uxoria; non spes illa quam in te futuri sæculi habebat mater, sed spes litterarum, quas ut nossem nimis volebat parens uterque: ille, quia de te prope nihil cogitabat, de me autem inania; illa autem, quia non solum nullo detrimento, sed etiam nonnullo adjumento ad te adipiscendum futura existimabat usitata illa studia doctrinæ. Ita enim conjicio, recolens, ut possum, mores parentum meorum. Relaxabantur etiam mihi ad ludendum habenæ, ultra temperamentum severitatis, in dissolutionem affectionum variarum, et in omnibus erat caligo intercludens mihi, Deus meus, serenitatem veritatis tuæ; et Ps. 72, 7. prodibat tanquam ex adipe iniquitas mea .
> IV. Furtum cum sodalibus perpetratum.

> 9. Furtum certe punit lex tua, Domine, et lex scripta in cordibus hominum, quam ne ipsa quidem delet iniquitas. Quis enim fur æquo animo furem patitur? Nec copiosus adactum inopia. Et ego furtum facere volui et feci, nulla Page 22 compulsus egestate nec penuria, sed fastidio justitiæ * , et sagina iniquitatis. Nam id furatus sum quod mihi abundabat, et multo melius: nec ea re volebam frui quam furto appetebam; sed ipso furto et peccato. Arbor erat pirus in vicinia vineæ nostræ pomis onusta, nec forma nec sapore illecebrosis. Ad hanc excutiendam atque asportandam, nequissimi adolescentuli perreximus nocte intempesta, quousque ludum de pestilentiæ more in areis produxeramus; et abstulimus inde onera ingentia, non ad nostras epulas, sed vel projicienda porcis, etiamsi aliquid inde comedimus; dum tamen fieret a nobis quod eo liberet quo non liceret.

Ecce cor meum, Deus, ecce cor meum quod miseratus es in imo abyssi. Dicat tibi nunc ecce cor meum quid ibi quærebat, ut essem gratis malus, et malitiæ meæ causa nulla esset nisi malitia. Fœda erat, et amavi eam; amavi perire: amavi defectum meum; non illud ad quod deficiebam, sed defectum meum ipsum amavi: turpis anima et dissiliens a firmamento tuo in exterminium; non dedecore * aliquid, sed dedecus appetens.
> V. Neminem peccare sine causa.

> 10. Etenim species est pulchris corporibus, et auro, et argento, et omnibus; et in contactu carnis congruentia valet plurimum, cæterisque sensibus est sua cuique accommodata modificatio corporum; habet etiam honor temporalis, et imperitandi atque superandi potentia suum decus, unde etiam vindictæ aviditas oritur: et tamen in cuncta hæc adipiscenda non est egrediendum abs te, Domine, neque deviandum a lege tua. Et vita quam hic vivimus habet illecebram suam propter quemdam modum decoris sui, et convenientiam cum his omnibus infimis pulchris. Amicitia quoque hominum charo nodo dulcis est propter unitatem de multis animis. Propter universa hæc atque hujusmodi, peccatum admittitur, dum immoderata in ista inclinatione cum extrema bona sint, meliora et summa deseruntur [28] , tu, Domine Deus noster, et veritas tua, et lex tua.
Habent enim et hæc ima delectationes, sed non sicut Deus meus qui fecit omnia; quia Ps. 63, 11. in ipso delectatur justus , et ipse est deliciæ rectorum corde .

> 11. Cum itaque de facinore quæritur qua causa factum sit, credi non solet, nisi cum appetitus adipiscendi alicujus Page 23 illorum bonorum, quæ infima diximus, esse potuisse apparuerit aut metus amittendi. Pulchra sunt enim et decora, quanquam præ bonis superioribus et * beatificis abjecta et jacentia. Homicidium fecit. Cur fecit? Adamavit ejus conjugem aut prædium, aut voluit deprædari unde viveret, aut timuit ab illo tale aliquid amittere, aut læsus ulcisci se exarsit. Num homicidium sine causa faceret, ipso homicidio delectatus? Quis crediderit? Nam et de quo dictum est vecordi et nimis crudeli homine, quod gratuito potius malus atque crudelis erat, prædicta est tamen causa: "Ne per otium, inquit, torpesceret manus aut animus [29] ." Quare id quoque? cur ita?

Ut scilicet illa exercitatione scelerum, capta urbe, honores, imperia, divitias assequeretur, et careret metu legum, et difficultate rerum, propter inopiam rei familiaris, et conscientiam scelerum. Nec ipse igitur Catilina amavit facinora sua; sed utique aliud cujus causa illa faciebat.
> VI. Omnia quæ boni specie ad vitia invitant, in solo Deo esse vera et perfecta.

> 12. Quid ego * miser in te amavi, o furtum meum, o facinus illud meum nocturnum sexti decimi anni ætatis meæ? Non enim pulchrum eras, cum furtum esses; aut vero aliquid es, ut loquar ad te? Pulchra erant poma illa quæ furati sumus, quoniam creatura tua erat * , pulcherrime omnium, creator omnium, Deus bone, Deus summum bonum, et bonum verum meum: pulchra erant illa poma; sed non ipsa concupivit anima mea miserabilis. Erat enim mihi meliorum copia; illa autem decerpsi tantum ut furarer. Nam decerpta projeci, epulatus inde solam iniquitatem * , qua lætabar fruens * . Nam et si quid illorum pomorum intravit in os meum, condimentum ibi * facinus erat.

Et nunc, Domine Deus meus, quæro quid me in furto delectaverit, et ecce species nulla est: non dico sicut in æquitate atque prudentia; sed neque sicut in mente hominis atque memoria et sensibus et vegetante vita; neque sicut speciosa sunt sidera et decora locis suis et terra et mare plena fetibus, qui succedunt nascendo decedentibus; non saltem ut est quædam defectiva species et umbratica vitiis fallentibus.

> 13. Nam et superbia celsitudinem imitatur; cum tu sis unus super omnia Deus excelsus. Et ambitio quid nisi honores quærit et gloriam; cum tu sis præ cunctis honorandus unus et gloriosus in æternum? Et sævitia potestatum Page 24 timeri vult: quis autem timendus, nisi unus Deus? Cujus potestati eripi aut subtrahi quid potest? quando, aut ubi, aut quo, vel a quo * ? Et blanditiæ lascivientium amari volunt: sed neque blandius est aliquid tua charitate, nec amatur quidquam salubrius, quam illa præ cunctis formosa et luminosa veritas tua. Et curiositas affectare videtur studium scientiæ; cum tu omnia summe noveris. Ignorantia quoque ipsa atque stultitia, simplicitatis et innocentiæ nomine tegitur; quia te simplicius quidquam non reperitur. Quid te autem innocentius, quandoquidem opera sua * malis inimica sunt [30] ? Et ignavia quasi quietem appetit: quæ vero quies certa præter Dominum?

Luxuria satietatem atque abundantiam se cupit vocari: tu autem es plenitudo et indeficiens copia incorruptibilis suavitatis. Effusio liberalitatis obtendit umbram: sed bonorum omnium largitor affluentissimus tu es. Avaritia multa possidere vult; et tu possides omnia. Invidentia de excellentia litigat: quid te excellentius? Ira vindictam quærit: te justius quis vindicat? Timor insolita et repentina exhorrescit, rebus quæ amantur adversantia, dum præcavet securitati: Rom. 8, 9. tibi enim quid insolitum? quid repentinum? aut quis a te separat quod diligis? aut ubi, nisi apud te, firma securitas? Tristitia rebus amissis contabescit, quibus se oblectabat cupiditas; quia ita sibi nollet, sicut tibi auferri nihil potest.

> 14. Ita fornicatur anima, cum avertitur abs te, et quærit extra te ea, quæ pura et liquida non invenit, nisi cum redit ad te. Perverse te imitantur omnes qui longe se a te faciunt, et extollunt se adversum te [31] . Sed etiam sic te imitando indicant creatorem te esse omnis naturæ; et ideo non esse quo a te omnimodo recedatur. Quid ergo in illo furto ego dilexi? et in quo Dominum meum vel vitiose atque perverse imitatus sum? An libuit facere contra legem saltem fallacia, quia potentatu non poteram, ut mancam libertatem captivus Page 25 imitarer faciendo impune quod non liceret, tenebrosa omnipotentiæ similitudine? Ecce est ille servus fugiens Dominum suum, et consecutus umbram. O putredo, o monstrum vitæ, et mortis profunditas! Potuitne libere quod non licebat, non ob aliud, nisi quia non licebat?
> VII. Gratias agit Deo pro remissione peccatorum, quodque a multis servatus sit.

> 15. Ps. 115, 4. Quid retribuam Domino , quod recolit hæc memoria mea, et anima mea non metuit inde? Diligam te, Domine, et gratias agam, et confitear nomini tuo, quoniam tanta dimisisti mihi mala et nefaria opera mea. Gratiæ tuæ deputo et misericordiæ tuæ, quod peccata mea tanquam glaciem solvisti. Gratiæ tuæ deputo et quæcumque non feci mala: quid enim non facere potui, qui etiam gratuitum facinus amavi? Et omnia mihi dimissa esse fateor; et quæ mea sponte feci mala, et quæ te duce non feci. Quis est hominum qui suam cogitans infirmitatem, audet viribus suis tribuere castitatem atque innocentiam suam; ut minus amet [32] te, quasi minus ei necessaria fuerit misericordia tua, qua donas peccata conversis ad te?

Qui enim vocatus a te secutus est vocem tuam, et vitavit ea quæ me de meipso recordantem et fatentem legit, non me derideat ab eo medico ægrum sanari, a quo sibi præstitum est ut non ægrotaret, vel potius ut minus ægrotaret: et ideo te tantumdem, imo vero amplius diligat; quia per quem me videt tantis peccatorum meorum languoribus exui, per eum se videt tantis peccatorum languoribus non implicari.
> VIII. Amavit in furto consortium simul peccantium.

> 16. Rom. 6, 21. Quem fructum habui miser aliquando in iis quæ nunc recolens erubesco , maxime in illo furto in quo ipsum furtum amavi? Nihil aliud; cum et ipsum esset nihil, et eo ipso ego miserior. Et tamen solus id non fecissem, sic recordor animum tunc meum; solus omnino id non fecissem. Ergo amavi ibi etiam consortium eorum * cum quibus id feci. Non ergo nihil aliud quam furtum amavi; imo vero nihil aliud, quia et illud nihil est. Quid est revera? Quis est qui doceat me, nisi qui illuminat cor meum et discernit umbras ejus? Quid est quod mihi venit in mentem quærere, et discutere, et considerare? Quia si tunc amarem poma illa Page 26 quæ furatus sum, et eis frui cuperem, possem etiam solus, si satis esset committere illam iniquitatem, qua pervenirem ad voluptatem meam; nec confricatione consciorum animorum accenderem pruritum cupiditatis meæ.
Sed quoniam in illis pomis voluptas mihi non erat, ea erat in ipso facinore, quam faciebat consortium simul peccantium.
