> Concerning the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years of that age, spent at Carthage, where, while he was staying for the sake of his studies, he freely gave himself up to spectacles and shameful deeds. By Cicero’s Hortensius he is kindled with love of wisdom. Seeking it proudly, he falls into the heresy of the Manichaeans; while here he briefly assails their errors and absurdities, he discoursed brilliantly concerning shameful deeds and crimes, and concerning true justice. Monica, pouring forth abundant and unceasing tears for her son, is made more certain of his future repentance, by a dream sent from God and by the answer of a certain holy Bishop.
> I. He is taken captive by the love he was hunting.

> 1. I came to Carthage; and all around me there roared a cauldron of shameful loves. I did not yet love, and I loved to love * , and out of a more secret need I hated myself for being less needy. I sought what I might love, loving to love, and I hated safety and a way without snares. For within I was hungry for inner food—yourself, my God—and with that hunger I was not hungry; but I was without desire for incorruptible nourishment: not because I was full of it, but because the emptier I was, the more disgusted I was. And therefore my soul was not well; and, ulcerous, it cast itself forth, miserably eager to be scratched by contact with sensible things. But if they had no soul, they certainly would not be loved. To love and to be loved was sweet to me, especially if I might also enjoy the body of the one loving. Therefore I defiled the vein of friendship with the filth of concupiscence, and beclouded its brightness with the Tartarus of lust * ; and yet, foul and dishonourable though I was, in my excessive vanity I longed to be elegant and urbane.

I rushed also into the love by which I desired to be taken captive. My God, my mercy, with how much gall did you, in your goodness, sprinkle that sweetness for me! For I was loved, and secretly attained the bond of enjoyment; and I was gladly bound with grievous bonds, that I might be scourged with the burning iron rods of jealousy, and suspicions, and fears, and angers, and quarrels.
> II. He loved tragic spectacles.

> 2. Theatrical spectacles carried me away, full of images of my miseries and fuel for my fire. What is it that there a man wishes to suffer pain when he watches mournful and tragic things which he himself would not wish to suffer? Yet, as a spectator, he wishes to suffer pain from them, and that very pain is his pleasure. What is this, Page 28 but miserable madness * ? For each is moved by them all the more the less sound he is from such affections: although, when he himself suffers, it is usually called misery; when he suffers with others, mercy [33] . But what sort of mercy is there, after all, in fictitious and scenic matters? For the hearer is not provoked to give aid, but only invited to grieve; and he favours the actor * of those images more when he grieves more. And if those calamities of men, whether ancient or false, are so enacted that the spectator does not grieve, he departs from there disgusted and finding fault; but if he grieves, he remains attentive and weeps with delight.

> 3. Then are pains also loved * ? Certainly every man wishes to rejoice. Or, although no one likes to be miserable, does he nevertheless like to be merciful, and because this is not without pain, are pains loved for this one reason? And this comes from that vein of friendship. But where does it go? Where does it flow? Why does it run down into the torrent of boiling pitch, the immense heats * of foul lusts, into which it itself is changed and turned by its own inclination, twisted and cast down from heavenly serenity? Let mercy, then, be rejected? By no means. Therefore let pains sometimes be loved. But beware uncleanness, O my soul, under the guardian care of my God, Dan. 3, 52. Vulg. the God of our fathers, praiseworthy and exalted above all for ever ; beware uncleanness. For neither now am I not compassionate; but then in the theatres I rejoiced together with lovers when they enjoyed themselves through shameful acts, although they enacted these only imaginatively * in the play of the spectacle.

But when they lost one another, as though compassionate I was saddened; yet both pleased me. Now, however, I pity more one rejoicing in shameful conduct than one who has, as it were, suffered harshly through the loss of pernicious pleasure and the loss of miserable happiness. This is certainly truer compassion; but pain does not delight in it * . For although one who grieves for the miserable is approved by the office of charity, one who is genuinely compassionate would certainly prefer that there should not be anything over which he might grieve. For if there is malevolent benevolence—which cannot happen—then he too who truly and sincerely pities can wish men to be miserable, in order that he may pity them. Some pain, therefore, is to be approved; none is to be loved. For this is what you do, Lord God, who love souls: you pity far more purely and incorruptibly than we do, because you are wounded by no pain. 2 Cor. 2, 16. And who is sufficient for these things?
> Page 29

> 4. But I then, miserable man, loved to grieve, and sought something over which I might grieve, when, in another’s affliction—false and acted—the performance of the player pleased and drew me all the more vehemently when it wrung tears from me. What wonder, moreover, if, an unhappy beast straying from your flock and impatient of your guardianship, I was defiled by a foul scab? And from this came the loves of pains—not such as penetrated me more deeply; for I did not love to undergo such things as I loved to watch—but such as, when heard and feigned, scratched me as it were upon the surface; yet upon these there followed, like the nails of those scratching, a burning swelling, and corruption, and horrible pus. Such was my life: was it life at all, my God?
> III. In the school of the rhetorician he shrank from the deeds of the Overturners.

> 5. And your faithful mercy hovered over me from afar. Into how great iniquities I descended, following sacrilegious curiosity, so that, abandoning you, it might lead me down to faithless depths and to the deceiving services of demons, to whom I sacrificed my evil deeds; and in all things you scourged me! I even dared, amid the celebration of your solemnities, within the walls of your church, to lust and to transact the business of procuring the fruits of death: for which you struck me with heavy punishments; yet these were nothing compared with my fault, O you my exceeding great mercy, my God, my refuge from fearful harms, amid which I wandered with presumptuous neck, going far away from you, loving my own ways and not yours, loving fugitive freedom.

> 6. Those studies also which were called honourable had their course directed toward the law courts, that I might excel in them—the more praiseworthy, the more fraudulent. So great is the blindness of men who even glory in blindness. And I was now greater in the school of the rhetorician; and I rejoiced proudly and swelled with conceit; although, Lord, you know, far more restrained, and wholly remote from the overturnings practised by the Overturners (for this cruel * and diabolical name was, as it were, a badge of urbanity), among whom I lived with an impudent shame because I was not such as they were. And I was with them, and was sometimes delighted by their friendships, though I always shrank from their deeds—that is, from the overturnings by which they insolently assailed the modesty of strangers, that they might disturb it by gratuitous mockery and thereby feed their malevolent delights. Nothing is more like that act than the acts of demons [34] . What, then, could they more truly be called than Overturners? Page 30
Clearly themselves first overthrown and perverted, while deceitful spirits secretly mocked and seduced them in that very thing by which they love to mock and deceive others.
> IV. Cicero’s Hortensius stirred him to an ardour for philosophy.

> 7. Among these, I, weak in age at that time, was studying books of eloquence, in which I desired to excel, with a damnable and windy end, through the joys of human vanity; and, following the now customary order of learning, I came upon a book by a certain Cicero, whose tongue nearly all admire, though not so his heart. But that book contains his exhortation to philosophy and is called Hortensius. That book indeed changed my affections, changed my prayers to you yourself, Lord, and made my vows and desires different. Suddenly every vain hope became worthless to me, and with an incredible heat of heart I longed for the immortality of wisdom; and I had begun to rise up, that I might return to you. For I did not refer that book to the sharpening of my tongue—which I seemed to be purchasing with my mother’s payment, when I was in my nineteenth year, my father having died two years before—not, therefore, to the sharpening of my tongue did I refer that book; nor was it its manner of speaking, but what it spoke, that had persuaded me.

> 8. How I burned, my God, how I burned to fly back from earthly things to you; and I did not know what you were doing with me! For with you is wisdom. But love of wisdom has the Greek name φιλοσοφίαν, with which those writings kindled me. There are some who deceive through philosophy, colouring and disguising their errors with a great, pleasant, and honourable name; and nearly all who in those times and before them were such are noted and exposed in that book; and there is made manifest that saving admonition of your Spirit through your good and pious servant: Col. 2, 8. 9. See that no one deceive you through philosophy and vain seduction, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily.

And I at that time—you know it, light of my heart—since these apostolic words were not yet known to me, was nevertheless delighted in that exhortation by this alone: that by that discourse I was stirred and kindled and burned to love and seek and Page 31 attain and hold and strongly embrace, not this or that sect, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be; and in so great a flame this alone held me back * , that the name of Christ was not there. For this name, according to your mercy, Lord, the name of my Saviour, your Son, my tender heart had drunk in with my mother’s milk itself, and retained deeply; and whatever had been without this name, however learned, polished, and true, did not wholly carry me away.
> V. He disdained the sacred Scriptures because of the simplicity of their style.

> 9. And so I resolved to direct my mind to the holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were like. And behold, I see a thing not accessible to the proud, nor disclosed to children; lowly in its approach, lofty in its progress, and veiled in mysteries. And I was not such as could enter into it or bend my neck to its steps. For I did not think as I now speak when I gave attention to that Scripture; rather, it appeared to me unworthy of comparison with Tully’s dignity. For my swelling pride recoiled from its manner, and my sharpness did not penetrate its interior. Yet it was such as would grow with little ones; but I disdained to be a little one, and, puffed up with arrogance, seemed great to myself.
> VI. How he was ensnared by the Manichaeans.

> 10 . Thus I fell [35] among men proudly raving, excessively carnal and talkative, in whose mouth were the snares of the devil and birdlime made by the mixture of the syllables of your name, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Paraclete, our Comforter, the Holy Spirit. These names * did not depart [36] from their mouth, except as far as sound * Page 32 and the clatter of the tongue; otherwise their heart was empty of truth. And they said, “Truth,” and “truth”; and they said it much to me, yet 1 Joh. 2, 4. it was nowhere in them ; but they spoke falsehoods, not only concerning you, who are truly Truth, but also concerning these elements of this world, your creation—concerning which I ought to have gone beyond even philosophers who spoke truly, for love of you, my Father supremely good, beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth, how deeply even then did the marrow of my mind sigh for you, when they sounded you to me frequently and in many ways, by voice alone and by many huge books!

And those were the dishes in which, to me hungering for you, there were served up in your place the sun and moon, [37] your beautiful works; but still Page 33 your works, not you, nor even your first works. For your spiritual works are prior to these bodily works, though luminous and heavenly. But I hungered and thirsted not even for those prior things, but for you yourself, you, Truth, in whom Jac. 1, 17. there is no change nor shadow of turning ; and still there were set before me in those dishes splendid phantasms, for which it was already better to love this sun, at least true to these eyes, than those false things through a mind deceived by the eyes. Yet because I thought that you were there, I ate; not greedily [38] indeed, because you did not taste in my mouth as you are; for you were not those empty figments, nor was I nourished by them, but was rather drained.

Food in dreams is very like food when awake, yet those who sleep are not nourished by it; for they are asleep. But those things were not in any way like you, as you have now spoken to me; for they were bodily phantasms, false bodies, more certain than which are these true bodies that we see with fleshly sight, whether heavenly or earthly: we see these together with cattle and birds, and they are more certain than when we imagine them. And again we imagine them more certainly than, from them, we conjecture other things greater and infinite, which are altogether non-existent—the empty things on which I then fed, and was not fed. But you, my love, in whom I fail that I may be strong, are not these bodies which we see, even though they are in heaven; nor are you those which we do not see there, for you created these things, nor do you hold them among your highest creations * . How far, then, are you from those phantasms of mine, phantasms of bodies which are altogether non-existent!

by which the phantasies of bodies are more certain than the bodies that are; and to them bodies are more certain, which yet thou art not: nor art thou the soul, which is the life of bodies. Therefore the life of bodies is better and more certain than bodies. But thou art the life of souls, the life of lives, living by thyself, and thou dost not change, O life of my soul.

For how much better are the little tales of grammarians and poets than those snares! For verse and song and the flying Medea are certainly more useful than the five elements [39] variously disguised, on account of the five caves of darkness, which have no existence whatsoever and kill the believer. For verse and song I may even apply to true food. But though I sang of Medea flying, I did not affirm it; and though I heard it sung, I did not believe it: whereas those things I believed. Woe, woe! By what steps was I led down Prov. 9, 18. into the depths of hell? Indeed, toiling and burning with want of truth, when I sought thee, my God (for to thee I confess, who had mercy on me even when I did not yet confess), when I sought thee not according to the understanding of the mind, by which thou didst will me to excel the beasts, but according to the sense of the flesh.

But thou wast more inward than my inmost self, and higher than my highest [40] . I encountered that * bold woman, lacking prudence, Solomon's enigma, sitting upon a seat at the doors, and saying: Prov. 9, 13-17. Eat hidden bread gladly, and drink stolen sweet water. She seduced me because she found me dwelling outside in the eye of my flesh, and chewing over within myself such things as I had devoured through it *.
> VII. The absurd doctrine of the Manichaeans, to which he gave support.

> 12. For I knew not what truly is; and I was stirred, as though somewhat shrewdly, to support foolish deceivers, when they asked me whence evil came [41] ? and whether God were bounded by bodily form and had hair and nails? and whether those were to be accounted righteous who had many wives at once, and killed men, and sacrificed animals? By these things, being ignorant of realities, I was disturbed; and, withdrawing from the truth, I seemed to myself to be going into it, because I did not know that evil is nothing but the privation of good [42] , even to that which absolutely is not. Whence could I see this, whose sight extended with the eyes as far as body, and with the mind as far as a phantasm? And I did not know that God is spirit, not one who has members in length and breadth, nor one whose being is bulk: for bulk is less in a part than in its whole; and if it be infinite, it is less in some part defined by a certain space than through the infinite; and it is not whole everywhere, as spirit is, as God is.
And what there was in us according to which we are like God and are rightly said in Scripture * to be Gen. 1, 27. after the image of God, I wholly did not know.

> 13. And I did not know true inward justice, judging not by custom, but by the most righteous law * of God Almighty, by which the customs of regions and times should be fashioned according to regions and times; while it itself was everywhere and always the same, not one thing elsewhere and another at another time; according to which Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses, and David, and all those praised by the mouth of God, were righteous: but they are judged unrighteous by the unlearned, 1 Cor. 4, 3.

judging from the human day, and measuring all the customs of the human race by a portion of their own custom, as if someone ignorant, among armour, of what is fitted to which member, should wish the head to be covered by a greave and shod with a helmet, and should complain that they do not fit suitably: or as if, on one day when a suspension of business has been proclaimed from the afternoon hours, someone should be vexed that he is not allowed to offer anything for sale, because it was permitted in the morning: or as if, in one house, he should see something handled by some servant which the one who serves cups is not allowed to do: or something done behind the stables which is forbidden before the table; and should be indignant that, though there is one dwelling and one household, the same thing is not assigned everywhere and to everyone.

Such are those who are indignant when they hear that in that age something was permitted to the righteous which is not permitted to the righteous in this age; and that God commanded one thing to those, another to these, for temporal reasons, although both served the same justice: though in one man, and in one day, and in one house, they see one thing to be suitable for one member, and another to have been permitted some time ago but not permitted after an hour; something allowed or commanded in that corner, which in this is rightly forbidden and punished. Is justice then various and changeable? But the times over which it presides do not proceed alike; for they are times.

But men, whose life upon earth is brief, because by sense they are unable to connect the causes of earlier ages and of other nations which they have not experienced with those which they have experienced; whereas in one body, or day, or house, they can easily see what is fitting for which member, at which moments, in which parts or persons: are offended by those things [43] , and submit to these.

> 14. These things I then did not know, nor did I take heed; and they struck my eyes from every side, and I did not see. And I sang songs, yet I was not permitted to place just any foot anywhere, but differently in one metre and another; and in any one verse, not the same foot in every place. And the art itself by which I sang did not have one thing in one place and another elsewhere, but all things together. And I did not contemplate that justice, which good and holy men serve, as possessing together, far more excellently and sublimely, all that it has commanded * , and as varying in no respect, yet in diverse times not distributing and commanding all things at once, but what is proper to each. And I, blind, reproached the pious fathers; not only using present things as God commanded and inspired, but also foretelling future things as God revealed [44] .
> VIII. Against the Manichaeans he states which shameful acts are always to be abhorred, and which crimes.

> 15. Is it ever or anywhere unjust Mat. 22, 37-39. to love God with one's whole heart, and with one's whole soul, and with one's whole mind, and to love one's neighbour as oneself? Therefore shameful acts which are against nature are everywhere and always to be detested and punished, such as were those of the Sodomites. If all nations committed them, they would be held under the same guilt of crime by the divine law, which did not make men so that they should use one another in that manner. For that very fellowship which ought to exist between us and God is violated when the same nature, of which he is the author, is defiled by the perversity of lust. But shameful acts which are against human customs are to be avoided according to the diversity of customs [45] , so that a compact established among themselves by the custom or law of city or nation may not be violated by the lust of any citizen or foreigner. For every part is unseemly when it does not accord with its whole.

But when God commands something contrary to the custom or compact of any persons, even if it has never been done there, it must be done; and if it has been omitted, it must be restored; and if it was not instituted, it must be instituted. For if it is lawful for a king in the city over which he reigns to command something which neither anyone before him nor he himself had ever commanded, and obedience to him is not contrary to the fellowship of the city—indeed, disobedience is contrary to fellowship (for it is a general compact of human society to obey their kings)—how much more must God, ruler of all his creation, be served without hesitation in those things which he has commanded! For as, among the authorities of human society, the greater authority is set over the lesser for obedience, so God is over all.

> 16 . Likewise, in crimes [46] , where there is a lust to do harm, whether by insult or by injury; and either of these either for the sake of revenge, as enemy against enemy; or for obtaining some extraneous advantage, as a robber against a traveller; or for avoiding evil, as against one who is feared; or through envy, as one more miserable toward one more fortunate; or one who has prospered toward him whom he fears may become his equal, or whose equality grieves him; or through the mere pleasure of another's evil, as spectators of gladiators, or mockers, or deceivers of anyone: these are the heads of iniquity, which sprout from the lust of ruling and of seeing and of feeling [47] , 1 Joh. 2, 16. whether one of these, or two, or all together; and life is lived wickedly against the three-and-seven [48] , Ps. 143, 9. ten-stringed psaltery, thy Decalogue, God most high and most sweet. But what shameful acts are there against thee, who canst not be corrupted? Or what crimes against thee, whom none can harm?

But thou dost punish what men perpetrate against themselves, because even when they sin against thee, they act impiously against their own souls, Ps. 26, 12. and iniquity lies to itself, either by corrupting and perverting its own nature, which thou hast made and ordered, or by using immoderately the things permitted, or by burning Rom. 1. in an unpermitted use, which is against nature; or they are guilty in mind and word, raging against thee, and Act. 9, 5. kicking against the goad; or, with the boundaries of human society broken down, they rejoice in audacious private alliances or divisions, according as something has pleased or offended them. And these things are done when thou, the fountain of life, who art the one and true creator and ruler of the universe, art forsaken; and private pride is loved as a false unity in a part [49] . Therefore by humble piety one returns to thee, and thou cleansest us from evil habit, and art gracious to the sins of those who confess, and Ps. 101, 21.

hearest the groans of those in fetters, and loosest us from the bonds which we have made for ourselves, if we no longer raise against thee the horns of false liberty, Ps. 74, 5, 6. through greed [50] to have more, and through loss to lose the whole; loving what is our own more than thee, the good of all.
> IX. The distinction between sins, and between God's judgment and men's.

> 17. But among shameful acts and crimes and so many iniquities, there are the sins of those making progress, which by those who judge well are both censured according to the rule of perfection and praised in the hope of fruit, like the green blade of grain. And there are certain things similar either to a shameful act or to a crime, and yet they are not sins, because they neither offend thee, the Lord our God, nor the social fellowship: when certain things are procured for a use of life suited to the time, and it is uncertain whether from the lust of possessing; or are punished by an ordered authority with zeal for correction, and it is uncertain whether from the lust of doing harm. Thus many deeds which would seem blameworthy to men have been approved by thy testimony; and many things praised by men are condemned by thy testimony: since often the appearance of the deed is one thing, the mind of the doer another, and the juncture of hidden [51] time another.

But when thou suddenly commandest something unusual and unforeseen, even if thou hast at some time forbidden it, although thou concealest for the time the reason for thy command, and although it be contrary to the compact of some human society, who can doubt that it must be done [52] , when that society of men is just which serves thee? But blessed are those who know that thou hast commanded it. For all things are done by those who serve thee, either to furnish what is needed for the present, or to foretell things to come [53] .
> X. The trifles of the Manichaeans concerning the fruits of the earth.

> 18. Ignorant of these things, I mocked those holy servants and prophets of thine. And what did I accomplish in mocking them [54] , except that I should be mocked by thee, being gradually and little by little led to such trifles that I believed a fig [55] wept when it was plucked, and its mother tree with milky tears? Yet if some holy man ate that fig, plucked, indeed, by another's [56] crime and not his own, he would mingle it with his entrails, and breathe out from it angels—nay rather, particles [57] of God—by groaning in prayer and Page 41 belching [58] : particles which of the most high and true God would have been bound in that fruit, unless they were released by the tooth and belly of the elect [59] saint. And I, wretched man, believed that mercy ought rather to be shown to the fruits of the earth than to the men for whose sake they grew. For if anyone hungry [60] who was not a Manichaean asked for it, the morsel would seem as though condemned to capital punishment if it were given to him.
> XI. The mother's lament and dream concerning her son.

> 19. And Ps. 143, 7. you sent forth your hand from on high , and from this deep darkness Ps. 85, 13. you delivered my soul , when my mother, your faithful one, wept to you for me, more than mothers weep for the bodily funerals of their children. For she saw my death by the faith and spirit which she had from you; and you heard her, O Lord. You heard her, nor did you despise her tears, when, flowing forth, they watered the ground beneath her eyes, in every place of her prayer; you heard her. For whence came that dream by which you consoled her, so that she allowed me to live * and to have the same table with her in the house; which she had begun to refuse, turning away from and detesting the blasphemies of my error?

For she saw herself standing upon a certain wooden rule, and a splendid young man coming toward her, cheerful and smiling upon her, while she was sorrowful and worn out with grief. When he had asked her the causes of her sadness and daily tears—not in order to learn, but, as is his wont, to teach—and she had answered that she was lamenting my perdition, he bade her be at ease, and admonished her to observe and see that where she was, there I also was. When she looked, she saw me standing beside her upon the same rule. Whence was this, unless because your ears were attentive to her heart? O you, good and almighty one, who care for each one of us as though you cared for him alone; and for all, as though for each individually!

> 20. Whence also came this: when she had related that very vision to me, and I tried to draw it toward this meaning, that she herself should rather not despair of becoming what I was; immediately, without any hesitation, she said, “No: for it was not said to me, ‘Where he is, there you are also’; but, ‘Where you are, there he is also.’” I confess to you, O Lord, as far as I recall my recollection—which I have often not kept silent about—that I was moved more by this answer of yours through my watchful mother, who was not disturbed by so near a possibility of false interpretation, and so quickly saw what was to be seen, which I certainly had not Page 43 seen before she spoke, than by the dream itself, by which joy, so long afterward to come to the pious woman, was so long beforehand foretold for the consolation of her then present anxiety.

For nearly nine years followed, during which I wallowed in that mire of the deep and in the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise and being dashed down more heavily; while yet that chaste, devout, and sober widow, such as you love, indeed more cheerful now in hope, but no less diligent in weeping and groaning, did not cease at every hour of her prayers to lament me before you; and Ps. 87, 3. her prayers entered into your sight , and yet you still allowed me to be rolled and entangled in that darkness.
> XII. What answer Augustine’s mother received from a certain bishop concerning his conversion.

> 21. And meanwhile you gave another answer, which I recall. For I pass over many things, because I hasten to those things which more urgently compel me to confess to you, and many things I do not remember. You gave another answer, then, through your priest, a certain bishop, reared in the Church and trained in your Books. When that woman had begged him to deem it worthy to speak with me, and refute my errors, and unteach me evil things and teach me good ones (for he did this if he happened to find any persons suitable for it), he refused, very wisely indeed, as I perceived afterward. For he replied that I was still unteachable, because I was puffed up by the novelty of that heresy, and had already harassed many unlearned persons with certain petty questions [61], as she had informed him. “But leave him there,” he said, “and only pray to the Lord for him: by reading, he himself will discover what that error is and how great its impiety is.”

At the same time he also related that, when he himself was a little boy, he had been given over by his seduced mother to the Manichaeans, and had not only read, but had even written out, nearly all their books; and that it had become apparent to him, without anyone disputing against or refuting him, how that sect ought to be shunned; and so he had fled from it. When he had said these things, and she would not acquiesce but pressed him all the more with entreaties and abundant tears, that he might see me and discuss matters with me, he, now somewhat irritated by weariness, said, “Go away from me; as you live, it * cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.” She often recalled, in her conversations with me, that she had received this as though it had sounded from heaven.
> Page 45

sources.title: BOOK IV.
sources.text:
> Pudet se Manichæorum sectæ addictum fuisse per novennium, atque alios secum in eumdem errorem pertraxisse; tum etiam consuluisse mathematicos: et amicum sibi interea morte præreptum, acerbiori quam æquum esset animi dolore fuisse prosecutum; cujus insignem conversionem memorat, et mortis ejus occasione, de vana et de solida amicitia et quam fluxa sint et caduca terrena omnia, pluribus disserit. Mentionem facit librorum de Pulchro et Apto, a se anno ætatis vigesimo sexto aut vigesimo septimo conscriptorum; necnon quam facili negotio liberalium artium libros atque Aristotelis Categorias, anno ætatis ferme vigesimo, per sese intellexerit.

> I. Quamdiu et quomodo alios seduxerit.

> 1. Per idem tempus annorum novem, ab undevigesimo anno ætatis meæ, usque ad duodetrigesimum, seducebamur et seducebamus, falsi atque fallentes in variis cupiditatibus; et palam per doctrinas quas liberales vocant, occulte autem falso nomine religionis. Hic superbi, ibi superstitiosi, ubique vani. Hac popularis gloriæ sectantes inanitatem, usque ad theatricos plausus, et contentiosa carmina * , et agonem coronarum fenearum, et spectaculorum nugas, et intemperantiam libidinum: illac autem purgari nos ab istis sordibus expetentes, cum eis qui appellarentur electi et sancti, afferremus escas, de quibus nobis in officina [62] aqualiculi sui fabricarent angelos et deos per quos liberaremur [63] ; et sectabar ista atque faciebam cum amicis meis, per me ac mecum deceptis. Irrideant me arrogantes, et nondum salubriter prostrati et Page 46 elisi a te, Deus meus; ego tamen confitear tibi dedecora mea in laude tua. Sine me, obsecro, et da mihi circumire præsenti memoria præteritos circuitus erroris mei, et Ps. 49, 14. immolare tibi hostiam jubilationis . Quid enim sum ego mihi sine te, nisi dux [64] in præceps? Aut quid sum cum mihi bene est, nisi sugens lac tuum, aut fruens Joh. 6, 27. te cibo qui non corrumpitur ? Et quis homo est quilibet homo, cum sit homo? Sed irrideant nos fortes et potentes; nos autem Ps. 73, 21. infirmi et inopes confiteamur tibi .

> II. Rhetoricam docet, concubinam fovet, et aruspicem qui victoriam promittebat, contemnit.

> 2. Docebam in illis annis artem rhetoricam, et victoriosam loquacitatem victus cupiditate vendebam. Malebam tamen, Domine, tu scis, bonos habere discipulos, sicut appellantur boni: et eos sine dolo docebam dolos; non quibus contra caput innocentis agerent, sed aliquando pro capite nocentis. Et, Deus, vidisti de longinquo lapsantem in lubrico, et in multo fumo scintillantem fidem meam, quam exhibebam in illo magisterio Is. 42, 3. Mat. 12, 20. Ps. 4, 3. diligentibus vanitatem, et quærentibus mendacium , socius eorum. In illis annis unam habebam, non eo quod legitimum vocatur, conjugio cognitam, sed quam indagaverat vagus ardor, inops prudentiæ; sed unam tamen, ei quoque servans tori fidem: in qua sane experirer exemplo meo, quid distaret inter conjugalis placiti modum quod fœderatum esset generandi gratia, et pactum libidinosi amoris, ubi proles etiam contra votum nascitur, quamvis jam nata cogat se diligi.

> 3. Recolo etiam, cum mihi theatrici carminis certamen inire placuisset, mandasse mihi nescio quem aruspicem, quid ei dare mercedis vellem ut vincerem; me autem fœda illa sacramenta detestatum et abominatum respondisse, nec si corona illa esset immortaliter aurea, muscam pro victoria mea necari me sinere. Necaturus enim erat ille in sacrificiis suis animantia, et illis honoribus invitaturus mihi suffragatura dæmonia videbatur. Sed hoc quoque malum non ex tua castitate [65] * repudiavi, Deus cordis mei. Non enim amare te Page 47 noveram, qui nisi fulgores corporeos [66] cogitare non noveram. Talibus enim figmentis suspirans anima, nonne fornicatur abs te, et fidit in falsis [67] , et pascit ventos ? Sed videlicet sacrificari pro me nollem dæmonibus, quibus me illa superstitione ipse sacrificabam. Quid est enim aliud, Hos. 12, 1. ventos pascere , quam ipsos pascere; hoc est, errando eis esse voluptati atque derisui?

> III. Ab astrologia, cui deditus erat, per senem medicinæ et rerum peritum revocatur.

> 4. Ideoque illos planos * , quos mathematicos vocant, plane consulere non desistebam, quod quasi nullum eis esset sacrificium, et nullæ preces ad aliquem spiritum ob divinationem dirigerentur: quod tamen christiana et vera pietas consequenter repellit et damnat. Bonum est enim confiteri tibi, Domine, et dicere, Ps. 40, 5. Miserere mei; cura animam meam, quoniam peccavi tibi ; neque ad licentiam peccandi abuti indulgentia tua, sed meminisse dominicæ vocis, Joh. 5, 14. Ecce sanus factus es; jam noli peccare, ne quid tibi deterius contingat . Quam totam illi salubritatem interficere conantur, cum dicunt: De cœlo tibi est inevitabilis causa peccandi; et Venus hoc fecit, aut Saturnus, aut Mars. Scilicet, ut homo sine culpa sit, caro et sanguis et superba putredo; culpandus sit autem cœli ac siderum creator et ordinator. Et quis est hic, nisi Deus noster, suavitas et origo justitiæ, qui Mat. 16, 27. Rom. 2, 6. reddis unicuique secundum opera ejus , et Ps. 50, 19. cor contritum et humiliatum non spernis ?

> inter lucem quod est Deus, et lucem quam fecit Deus, &c. (Aug. c. Faust. xxii. 8.) Alii Deum esse non posse, nisi corpus igneum putaverunt. Alii [Manichæi] candorem lucis immensæ per infinita spatia usquequaque porrectum, ex una tamen parte quasi nigro quodam cuneo fissum, duo adversa regna opinantes, et talia rebus constituentes principia, cum suis phantasmatis fabulati sunt. De verâ relig. §. 96. Sed nec iterum ideo tibi non videatur Deus quod sol, quia sol tamquam rota quædam est, non immensum lucis spatium; et dicas tibi, Ergo Deus infinitæ lucis est et immensæ: ut quasi tendas ipsum solem, et facias illum non habere finem, nec hac nec illac, nec sursum nec deorsum; et tamen lucem tibi immensam proponas Deum: nec hoc est Deus. Aug. Serm. iv. §. 5.]

> Page 48

> 5. Erat eo tempore vir sagax [68] , medicæ artis peritissimus, atque in ea nobilissimus, qui proconsule * manu sua coronam illam agonisticam imposuerat non sano capiti meo, sed non ut medicus. Nam illius morbi tu sanator, qui 1 Pet. 5, 5. Jac. 4, 6. resistis superbis, humilibus autem das gratiam . Numquid tamen etiam per illum senem defuisti mihi, aut destitisti mederi animæ meæ? Quia enim factus ei eram familiarior, et ejus sermonibus (erant enim sine verborum cultu vivacitate sententiarum jucundi et graves) assiduus et fixus inhærebam; ubi cognovit ex colloquio meo libris genethliacorum esse me deditum, benigne ac paterne monuit ut eos abjicerem, neque curam et operam rebus utilibus necessariam, illi vanitati frustra impenderem: dicens ita se illam didicisse, ut ejus professionem primis annis ætatis suæ deferre voluisset, qua vitam degeret; et si Hippocratem intellexisset, et illas utique litteras potuisse intelligere * : et tamen non ob aliam causam se postea, illis relictis, medicinam assecutum, nisi quod eas falsissimas comperisset, et nollet vir gravis decipiendis hominibus victum quærere. "At tu, inquit, quo te in hominibus sustentas * , rhetoricam tenes; hanc autem fallaciam libero studio, non necessitate rei familiaris sectaris; quo magis mihi te oportet de illa credere, qui eam tam perfecte discere elaboravi, quam ex ea sola vivere volui." A quo ego cum quæsissem quæ causa ergo faceret ut multa inde vera pronuntiarentur; respondit ille, ut potuit, vim sortis hoc facere in rerum natura usquequaque diffusam. Si enim de paginis * poetæ cujuspiam longe aliud canentis atque intendentis, cum forte quis consulit, mirabiliter consonus negotio sæpe versus exiret; mirandum non esse dicebat, si ex anima humana, superiore aliquo instinctu, nesciente quid in se fieret, non arte sed sorte sonaret aliquid quod interrogantis rebus factisque concineret.

> 6. Et hoc quidem ab illo vel per illum procurasti mihi. Et quid ipse postea per meipsum quærerem, in memoria mea delineasti. Tunc autem nec ipse, nec charissimus meus Nebridius, adolescens valde bonus et valde castus [69] * , irridens totum illud divinationis genus, persuadere mihi potuerunt ut hæc abjicerem: quoniam me amplius ipsorum auctorum movebat auctoritas; et nullum certum quale quærebam Page 49 documentum adhuc inveneram, quo mihi sine ambiguitate appareret, quæ ab eis consultis vera dicerentur, forte vel sorte, non arte inspectorum siderum dici.

> IV. Morbum et baptismum amici narrat, quem etiam suis erroribus involverat; eoque morte sublato, dolet gravissime. Mirabilis efficacia sacramenti Baptismi.

> 7. In illis annis, quo primum tempore in municipio quo natus sum docere cœperam, comparaveram amicum societate studiorum nimis charum, coævum mihi et conflorentem flore adolescentiæ. Mecum puer creverat, et pariter in scholam ieramus, pariterque luseramus. Sed nondum erat sic amicus, quanquam ne tunc quidem sicuti est vera amicitia; quia non est vera, nisi cum eam tu agglutinas inter inhærentes tibi, Rom. 5, 5. charitate diffusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis . Sed tamen dulcis erat nimis, cocta * fervore parilium studiorum. Nam et a fide vera, quam non germanitus et penitus adolescens tenebat, deflexeram ego eum in superstitiosas fabellas et perniciosas, propter quas plangebat me mater. Mecum jam errabat in animo homo ille, et non poterat anima mea sine illo. Et ecce tu imminens dorso fugitivorum tuorum, Ps. 93, 1. Deus ultionum et fons misericordiarum simul, qui convertis * nos ad te miris modis; ecce abstulisti hominem de hac vita, cum vix explevisset annum in amicitia mea, suavi * mihi super omnes suavitates illius vitæ meæ.

> 8. Ps. 105, 2. Quis laudes tuas enumerat unus, in se uno quas expertus est? Quid tunc fecisti, Deus meus, et quam investigabilis Ps. 35, 7. abyssus judiciorum tuorum ? Cum enim laboraret ille febribus, jacuit diu sine sensu in sudore letali. Et cum desperaretur, baptizatus est nesciens, me non curante, et præsumente id retinere potius animam ejus quod a me acceperat, non quod in nescientis corpore fiebat. Longe autem aliter erat; nam recreatus est et salvus factus. Statimque ut primum cum eo loqui potui (potui autem mox ut ille potuit, quando non discedebam, et nimis pendebamus ex invicem), tentavi apud illum irridere, tanquam et illo irrisuro [70] mecum Baptismum quem Page 50 acceperat mente atque sensu absentissimus, sed tamen jam se accepisse didicerat. At ille ita me exhorruit ut inimicum, admonuitque mirabili et repentina libertate, ut si amicus esse vellem, talia sibi dicere desinerem. Ego autem stupefactus atque turbatus, distuli omnes motus meos, ut convalesceret prius, essetque idoneus viribus valetudinis cum quo agere possem quod vellem. Sed ille abreptus dementiæ meæ, ut apud te servaretur consolationi meæ, post paucos dies, me absente, repetitur febribus et defungitur.

> 9. Quo dolore contenebratum est cor meum; et quidquid aspiciebam, mors erat. Et erat mihi patria supplicium, et paterna domus mira infelicitas; et quidquid cum illo communicaveram, sine illo in cruciatum immanem verterat. Expetebant eum undique oculi mei, et non dabatur mihi; et oderam omnia, quia non haberent eum, nec mihi jam dicere poterant: Ecce veniet, sicut cum viveret, quando absens erat. Factus eram ipse mihi magna quæstio, et interrogabam Ps. 41, 6. animam meam quare tristis esset , et quare conturbaret me valde; et nihil noverat respondere mihi. Et si dicebam, Spera in Deum ; juste non obtemperabat: quia verior erat et melior homo quem charissimum amiserat, quam phantasma [71] in quod sperare jubebatur. Solus fletus erat dulcis mihi et successerat amico meo in deliciis animi mei.

> V. Cur fletus dulcis miseris.

> 10. Et nunc, Domine, jam illa transierunt, et tempore lenitum est vulnus meum. Possumne audire abs te qui veritas es, et admovere aurem cordis mei ori tuo, ut dicas mihi cur fletus dulcis sit miseris? An tu, quamvis ubique adsis, longe abjecisti a te miseriam nostram? Et tu in te manes; nos autem in experimentis volvimur. Et tamen nisi ad aures tuas ploraremus, nihil residui de spe nostra fieret. Unde igitur suavis fructus de amaritudine vitæ carpitur, gemere et flere, et suspirare et conqueri? An hoc ibi * dulce est, quod speramus exaudire te? Recte istud in precibus, quia desiderium perveniendi habent. Numquid in dolore amissæ rei et luctu quo tunc operiebar? Neque enim sperabam reviviscere illum, aut Page 51 hoc petebam lacrymis; sed tantum dolebam et flebam. Miser enim eram, et amiseram gaudium meum. An et fletus res amara est, et præ fastidio rerum quibus prius fruebamur, et tunc dum ab eis abhorremus, delectat?

> VI. Quantus ex amici morte dolor.

> 11. Quid autem ista loquor? Non enim tempus quærendi nunc est, sed confitendi tibi. Miser eram, et miser est omnis animus vinctus amicitia rerum mortalium; et dilaniatur cum eas amittit, et tunc sentit miseriam qua miser est et antequam amittat eas. Sic ego eram illo tempore, et flebam amarissime, et requiescebam in amaritudine. Ita miser eram, et habebam chariorem illo amico meo vitam ipsam miseram [72] . Nam quamvis eam mutare vellem, nollem tamen amittere magis quam illum. Et nescio an vellem vel pro illo, sicut de Oreste et Pylade traditur, si non fingitur, qui vellent pro invicem vel simul mori, quia morte pejus eis erat non simul vivere. Sed in me nescio quis affectus nimis huic contrarius ortus erat; et tædium vivendi erat in me gravissimum, et moriendi metus. Credo quo magis illum amabam, eo magis mortem, quæ mihi eum abstulerat, tanquam atrocissimam inimicam, oderam et timebam; et eam repente consumpturam omnes homines putabam, quia illum potuit. Sic eram omnino, memini. Ecce cor meum, Deus meus: ecce intus vide quia memini, spes mea, qui me mundas a talium affectionum immunditia, dirigens Ps. 24, 15. oculos meos ad te , et evellens de laqueo pedes meos . Mirabar enim cæteros mortales vivere, quia ille, quem quasi non moriturum dilexeram, mortuus erat; et me magis, quia illi alter eram, vivere illo mortuo mirabar. Bene quidam dixit de amico suo: "Dimidium animæ meæ [73] ." Nam ego sensi animam meam et animam illius unam fuisse animam in duobus corporibus [74] : et ideo mihi horrori erat vita, quia nolebam dimidius vivere; et ideo forte mori metuebam, ne totus ille moreretur quem multum amaveram [75] .
