Itaque ubi comperit a præclaro prædicatore atque antistite pietatis præceptum esse ista non fieri, nec ab eis qui sobrie facerent, ne ulla occasio se ingurgitandi daretur ebriosis [130] , et quia illa quasi parentalia superstitioni gentilium essent simillima; abstinuit se libentissime: et pro canistro pleno terrenis fructibus, plenum purgatioribus votis pectus ad memorias martyrum afferre didicerat; ut et quod posset daret egentibus, et sic communicatio [131] Dominici corporis illic celebraretur, cujus passionis imitatione immolati et coronati sunt martyres. Sed tamen videtur mihi, Domine Deus meus, et ita est in conspectu tuo de hac re cor meum, non facile fortasse de hac amputanda consuetudine matrem meam fuisse cessuram, si ab alio prohiberetur, quem non sicut Ambrosium diligebat, quem propter salutem meam maxime diligebat; eam vero ille propter ejus religiosissimam conversationem, qua in bonis operibus tam Rom. 12, 11. fervens spiritu frequentabat ecclesiam: ita ut sæpe erumperet, cum me videret, in ejus prædicationem * , gratulans mihi quod talem matrem haberem; nesciens qualem illa me filium, qui dubitabam de illis omnibus, et inveniri posse viam vitæ minime putabam.
> III. Occupationes et studia Ambrosii.

> 3. Nec jam ingemiscebam orando ut subvenires mihi; sed ad quærendum intentus, et ad disserendum inquietus erat animus meus. Ipsumque Ambrosium felicem quemdam hominem secundum sæculum opinabar, quem sic tantæ potestates honorarent; cælibatus tantum ejus mihi laboriosus videbatur. Quid autem ille spei gereret, et adversus ipsius excellentiæ tentamenta quid luctaminis haberet, quidve solaminis in adversis, et occultum os ejus quod erat in corde ejus, quam sapida gaudia de pane tuo ruminaret [132] ; nec Page 85 conjicere noveram, nec expertus eram: nec ille sciebat æstus meos, nec foveam periculi mei. Non enim quærere ab eo poteram quod volebam, sicut volebam, secludentibus me ab ejus aure atque ore catervis negotiosorum hominum, quorum infirmitatibus serviebat. Cum quibus quando non erat, quod per exiguum temporis erat, aut corpus reficiebat necessariis sustentaculis, aut lectione animum. Sed cum legebat, oculi ducebantur per paginas, et cor intellectum rimabatur, vox autem et lingua quiescebant. Sæpe cum adessemus, non enim vetabatur quisquam ingredi, aut ei venientem nuntiari mos erat; sic eum legentem vidimus tacite, et aliter nunquam: sedentesque in diuturno silentio (quis enim tam intento esse oneri auderet?) discedebamus, et conjectabamus eum parvo ipso tempore, quod reparandæ menti suæ nanciscebatur, feriatum ab strepitu causarum alienarum, nolle in aliud avocari; et cavere fortasse ne auditore suspenso et intento, si qua obscurius posuisset ille quem legeret, etiam exponere necesse esset; aut de aliquibus difficilioribus disceptare quæstionibus, atque huic operi temporibus impensis, minus quam vellet voluminum evolveret: quanquam et causa servandæ vocis, quæ illi facillime obtundebatur, poterat esse justior tacite legendi. Quolibet tamen animo id ageret, bono utique ille vir agebat.

> 4. Sed certe mihi nulla dabatur copia sciscitandi quæ cupiebam de tam sancto oraculo tuo pectore illius, nisi cum aliquid breviter esset audiendum. Æstus autem illi mei otiosum eum valde, cui refunderentur, requirebant, nec unquam inveniebant. Et eum quidem in populo 2 Tim. 2, 15. verbum veritatis recte tractantem omni die dominico audiebam; et magis magisque mihi confirmabatur omnes versutarum calumniarum nodos, quos illi deceptores nostri adversus divinos Libros innectebant, posse dissolvi. Ubi vero etiam comperi ad imaginem tuam hominem a te factum, a spiritualibus filiis tuis quos de matre Catholica per gratiam regenerasti, non sic Page 86 intelligi ut humani corporis forma te terminatum crederent atque cogitarent: quanquam quomodo se haberet spiritualis substantia, ne quidem tenuiter atque in ænigmate suspicabar; tamen gaudens erubui non me tot annos adversus catholicam fidem, sed contra carnalium cogitationum figmenta latrasse. Eo quippe temerarius et impius fueram, quod ea quæ debebam quærendo dicere * accusando dixeram. Tu enim, altissime et proxime, secretissime et præsentissime, cui membra non sunt alia majora et alia minora, sed ubique totus es, et nusquam locorum es; non es utique forma ista corporea: tamen fecisti hominem ad imaginem tuam ; et ecce ipse a capite usque ad pedes in loco est.
> IV. Doctrinam Ecclesiæ Ambrosio concionante intelligit.

> 5. Cum ergo nescirem quomodo hæc subsisteret imago tua, pulsans * proponerem quomodo credendum esset, non insultans opponerem quasi ita creditum esset: tanto igitur acrior cura rodebat intima mea quid certi retinerem, quanto me magis pudebat tam diu illusum et deceptum promissione certorum, puerili errore et animositate, tam multa incerta quasi certa garrisse. Quod enim falso essent, postea mihi claruit. Certum tamen erat quod incerta essent, et a me aliquando pro certis habita fuissent, cum Catholicam tuam cæcis contentionibus accusarem, etsi nondum compertam vera docentem, non tamen ea docentem quæ graviter accusabam. Itaque confundebar, et convertebar: et gaudebam, Deus meus, quod Ecclesia * unica corpus Unici tui, in qua mihi nomen Christi infanti est inditum, non saperet infantiles nugas; neque hoc haberet in doctrina sua sana, quod te creatorem omnium in spatium loci quamvis summum et amplum, tamen undique terminatum membrorum humanorum figura contruderet.

> 6. Gaudebam etiam quod vetera scripta Legis et Prophetarum jam non illo oculo mihi legenda proponerentur, quo antea videbantur absurda, cum arguebam tanquam ita sentientes sanctos tuos; verum autem non ita sentiebant: et tanquam regulam diligentissime commendaret, sæpe in popularibus sermonibus suis dicentem Ambrosium lætus audiebam, 2 Cor. 3, 6. Littera occidit; spiritus autem vivificat : cum ea quæ ad litteram perversitatem docere videbantur, remoto mystico velamento spiritualiter aperiret, non dicens quod me offenderet, quamvis ea diceret, quæ utrum vera essent adhuc ignorarem. Tenebam enim cor meum ab omni assensione, timens præcipitium; et Page 87 suspendio magis necabar. Volebam enim eorum quæ non viderem ita me certum fieri, ut certus essem quod septem et tria decem sint. Neque enim tam insanus eram, ut ne hoc quidem putarem posse comprehendi; sed sicut hoc, ita cætera cupiebam, sive corporalia quæ coram sensibus meis non adessent; sive spiritualia, de quibus cogitare nisi corporaliter nesciebam. Et sanari credendo poteram [133] , ut purgatior acies mentis meæ dirigeretur aliquo modo in veritatem tuam semper manentem, et ex nullo deficientem. Sed sicut evenire assolet ut malum medicum expertus, etiam bono timeat se committere; ita erat valetudo animæ meæ, quæ utique nisi credendo sanari non poterat, et ne falsa crederet, curari recusabat; resistens manibus tuis, qui medicamenta fidei confecisti, et sparsisti super morbos orbis terrarum, et tantam illis auctoritatem tribuisti.
> V. De sacrorum Librorum auctoritate et necessario usu.

> 7. Ex hoc tamen quoque jam præponens doctrinam catholicam, modestius ibi minimeque fallaciter sentiebam juberi ut crederetur quod non demonstrabatur (sive esset quid, sed cui forte non esset, sive nec quid esset [134] ), quam illic temeraria pollicitatione scientiæ credulitatem irrideri; et postea tam multa fabulosissima et absurdissima, quia demonstrari non poterant, credenda imperari [135] . Deinde paulatim tu, Domine, Page 88 manu mitissima et misericordissima pertractans et componens cor meum, consideranti quam innumerabilia crederem quæ non viderem * , neque cum gererentur adfuissem; sicut tam multa in historia gentium [136] , tam multa de locis atque urbibus quæ non videram, tam multa amicis, tam multa medicis, tam multa hominibus aliis atque aliis; quæ nisi crederentur, omnino in hac vita nihil ageremus [137] ; postremo, quam inconcusse fixum Page 89 fide retinerem, de quibus parentibus ortus essem, quod scire non possem, nisi audiendo credidissem: persuasisti mihi, non qui crederent Libris tuis, quos tanta in omnibus fere gentibus auctoritate fundasti [138] ; sed qui non crederent esse culpandos, nec audiendos esse, si qui forte mihi dicerent: Unde scis illos Libros unius veri et veracissimi Dei spiritu esse humano generi ministratos? Idipsum enim maxime credendum erat, quoniam nulla pugnacitas calumniosarum quæstionum, per tam multa quæ legeram inter se confligentium philosophorum, extorquere mihi potuit ut aliquando non crederem, te esse quidquid esses quod ego nescirem; aut administrationem rerum humanarum ad te pertinere.

> 8. Sed id credebam aliquando robustius, aliquando exilius; semper tamen credidi et esse te, et curam nostri gerere; etiamsi ignorabam vel quid sentiendum esset de substantia tua, vel quæ via duceret aut reduceret ad te. Ideoque cum essemus infirmi ad inveniendam liquida ratione veritatem, et ob hoc nobis opus esset auctoritate sanctarum Litterarum; jam credere cœperam nullo modo te fuisse tributurum tam excellentem illi Scripturæ per omnes jam terras auctoritatem, nisi et per ipsam tibi credi, et per ipsam te quæri voluisses. Jam enim absurditatem quæ me in illis Litteris solebat offendere, cum multa ex eis probabiliter exposita audissem, ad sacramentorum altitudinem referebam: eoque mihi illa venerabilior et sacrosancta fide dignior apparebat auctoritas, quo et omnibus ad legendum esset in promptu, et secreti sui dignitatem in intellectu profundiore servaret; verbis apertissimis et humillimo genere loquendi se cunctis præbens, et exercens intentionem eorum, qui non sunt leves corde: ut exciperet omnes populari sinu, et per angusta foramina paucos ad te trajiceret, multo tamen plures, quam si nec tanto apice auctoritatis emineret, nec turbas gremio sanctæ humilitatis hauriret. Cogitabam hæc, et aderas mihi; suspirabam, et audiebas me: fluctuabam, et gubernabas me; ibam per viam sæculi latam, nec deserebas.
> Page 90
> VI. De miseria ambitiosorum, adducto exemplo mendici lætantis]

> 9. Inhiabam honoribus, lucris, conjugio; et tu irridebas. Patiebar in eis cupiditatibus amarissimas difficultates, te propitio tanto magis, quanto minus sinebas mihi dulcescere quod non eras tu. Vide cor meum, Domine, qui voluisti ut hoc recordarer et confiterer tibi. Nunc tibi inhæreat anima mea, quam de visco tam tenaci mortis exuisti. Quam misera erat! et sensum vulneris tu pungebas, ut relictis omnibus converteretur ad te qui es super omnia, et sine quo nulla essent omnia; converteretur, et sanaretur. Quam ergo miser eram, et quomodo egisti ut sentirem miseriam meam, die illo quo cum pararem recitare Imperatori laudes [139] , quibus plura mentirer, et mentienti faveretur ab scientibus, easque curas anhelaret cor meum, et cogitationum tabificarum febribus æstuaret; transiens per quemdam vicum Mediolanensem, animadverti pauperem mendicum, jam credo saturum, jocantem atque lætantem: et ingemui, et locutus sum cum amicis qui mecum erant, multos dolores insaniarum nostrarum; quia omnibus talibus conatibus nostris, qualibus tunc laborabam, sub stimulis cupiditatum trahens infelicitatis meæ sarcinam, et trahendo exaggerans, nihil vellemus aliud nisi ad securam lætitiam pervenire, quo nos mendicus ille jam præcessisset, nunquam fortasse illuc venturos! Quod enim jam ille pauculis et emendicatis nummulis adeptus erat, ad hoc ego tam ærumnosis anfractibus et circuitibus ambiebam, ad lætitiam scilicet temporalis felicitatis. Non enim verum gaudium habebat, sed et ego illis ambitionibus multo falsius quærebam. Et certe ille lætabatur, ego anxius eram; securus ille, ego trepidus. Et si quisquam percontaretur me, utrum mallem exsultare an metuere; responderem, Exsultare. Rursus si interrogaret, utrum me talem mallem qualis ille, an qualis ego tunc essem; meipsum curis timoribusque confectum eligerem: sed perversitate; numquid veritate? Neque enim eo me præponere illi debebam, quo doctior eram, quoniam non inde gaudebam, sed placere inde quærebam hominibus; non ut eos docerem, sed tantum ut placerem. Propterea et tu baculo disciplinæ tuæ Ps. 41, 11. v. Sabat. confringebas ossa mea .

> 10. Recedant ergo ab anima mea qui dicunt ei: Interest unde Page 91 quis gaudeat. Gaudebat mendicus ille vinolentia; tu gaudere cupiebas gloria. Qua gloria, Domine? Quas non est in te. Nam sicut illud verum gaudium non erat, ita nec illa vera gloria; et amplius vertebat mentem meam. Et ille ipsa nocte digesturus erat ebrietatem suam; ego cum mea dormieram et surrexeram, et dormiturus et surrecturus eram; vide quot diebus. Interest vero unde quis gaudeat, scio, et gaudium spei fidelis incomparabiliter distat ab illa vanitate; sed et tunc distabat inter nos. Nimirum quippe ille felicior erat, non tantum quod hilaritate perfundebatur, cum ego curis eviscerarer; verum etiam, quod ille bene optando acquisiverat vinum, ego mentiendo quærebam typhum. Dixi tunc multa in hac sententia charis meis, et sæpe advertebam in his quomodo mihi esset; et inveniebam male mihi esse, et dolebam et conduplicabam ipsum male. Et si quid arrisisset prosperum, tædebat apprehendere, quia pene priusquam teneretur, avolabat.
> VII. Alypium a Circensium insania convertit.

> 11. Congemiscebamus in iis qui simul amice vivebamus, et maxime ac familiarissime cum Alypio et Nebridio ista colloquebar: quorum Alypius ex eodem, quo ego, ortus erat municipio, parentibus primatibus municipalibus, me minor natu. Nam et studuerat apud me, cum in nostro docere cœpi oppido, et postea Carthagini: et diligebat me multum, quod ei bonus et doctus viderer; et ego illum, propter magnam virtutis indolem, quæ in non magna ætate satis eminebat. Gurges tamen morum Carthaginensium, quibus nugatoria fervent spectacula, absorbuerat eum in insaniam Circensium: sed cum in eo miserabiliter volveretur, ego autem rhetoricam ibi professus publica schola uterer, nondum me audiebat ut magistrum, propter quamdam simultatem quæ inter me et patrem ejus erat exorta, et compereram quod circum exitiabiliter amaret, et graviter angebar, quod tantam spem perditurus, vel etiam perdidisse mihi videbatur. Sed monendi eum et aliqua coercitione revocandi nulla erat copia, vel amicitiæ benevolentia, vel jure magisterii. Putabam enim eum de me cum patre sentire; ille vero non sic erat. Itaque postposita in hac re patris voluntate, salutare me cœperat, veniens in auditorium meum, et audire aliquid atque abire.

> 12. Sed enim de memoria mihi lapsum erat agere cum illo, ne vanorum ludorum cæco et præcipiti studio tam bonum Page 92 interimeret ingenium. Verum autem, Domine, tu qui præsides gubernaculis omnium quæ creasti, non eum oblitus eras futurum inter filios tuos antistitem sacramenti tui; et ut aperte tibi tribueretur ejus correctio, per me quidem illam, sed nescientem operatus es. Nam quodam die cum sederem loco solito, et coram me adessent discipuli, venit, salutavit, sedit, atque in ea quæ agebantur animum intendit: et forte lectio in manibus erat, quam dum exponerem, et opportune mihi adhibenda videretur similitudo Circensium, quo illud quod insinuabam et jucundius et planius fieret, cum irrisione mordaci eorum quos illa captivasset insania; tu scis, Deus noster, quod tunc de Alypio ab illa peste sanando non cogitaverim. At ille in se rapuit, meque illud non nisi propter se dixisse credidit. Et quod alius acciperet ad succensendum mihi, accepit honestus adolescens ad succensendum sibi, et ad me ardentius diligendum. Dixeras enim tu jam olim, et innexueras Litteris tuis: Prov. 9, 8. Corripe sapientem, et amabit te . At ego illum jam non corripueram; sed utens tu omnibus, et scientibus et nescientibus, ordine quo nosti, et ille ordo justus est, Is. 6, 6. de corde et lingua mea carbones ardentes operatus es, quibus mentem spei bonæ adureres tabescentem, ac sanares. Taceat laudes tuas qui miserationes tuas non considerat, quæ tibi de medullis meis confitentur. Etenim ille post illa verba proripuit se ex fovea tam alta, qua libenter demergebatur, et cum miserabili voluptate * cæcabatur; et excussit animum forti temperantia, et resiluerunt omnes Circensium sordes ab eo, ampliusque illuc non accessit. Deinde patrem reluctantem evicit, ut me magistro uteretur: cessit ille atque concessit. Et audire me rursus incipiens, illa mecum superstitione involutus est, amans in Manichæis ostentationem [140] continentiæ, quam veram et germanam putabat. Erat autem illa vecors et seductoria, Prov. 6, 26. Sabat. pretiosas animas captans , nondum virtutis Page 93 altitudinem scientes tangere, et superficie decipi faciles, sed tamen adumbratæ simulatæque virtutis.
> VIII. Alypius capitur insania ludorum gladiatoriorum, a quibus antea abhorruerat.

> 13. Non sane relinquens incantatam sibi a parentibus terrenam viam, Romam præcesserat, ut jus disceret; et ibi gladiatorii spectaculi hiatu incredibili et incredibiliter abreptus est. Cum enim aversaretur et detestaretur talia, quidam ejus amici et condiscipuli, cum forte de prandio redeuntibus pervius esset * , recusantem vehementer et resistentem, familiari violentia duxerunt in amphitheatrum, crudelium et funestorum ludorum diebus, hæc dicentem: "Si corpus meum in illum locum trahitis, et ibi constituitis; numquid et animum et oculos meos in illa spectacula potestis intendere? Adero itaque absens, ac sic et vos et illa superabo." Quibus auditis, illi nihilo secius eum adduxerunt secum, idipsum forte explorare cupientes, utrum posset efficere. Quo ubi ventum est, et sedibus quibus potuerunt locati sunt, fervebant omnia immanissimis voluptatibus. Ille clausis foribus oculorum, interdixit animo ne in tanta mala procederet; atque utinam et aures obturavisset! Nam quodam pugnæ casu, cum clamor ingens totius populi vehementer eum pulsasset, curiositate victus, et quasi paratus quidquid illud esset, etiam visum contemnere et vincere, aperuit oculos; et percussus est graviore vulnere in anima, quam ille in corpore, quem cernere concupivit; ceciditque miserabilius quam ille quo cadente factus est clamor qui per ejus aures intravit, et reseravit ejus lumina, ut esset qua feriretur et dejiceretur audax adhuc potius quam fortis animus, et eo infirmior quo de se præsumpserat, qui debuit de te. Ut enim vidit illum sanguinem, immanitatem simul ebibit, et non se avertit, sed fixit aspectum; et hauriebat furias, et nesciebat, et delectabatur scelere certaminis, et cruenta voluptate inebriabatur. Et non erat jam ille qui venerat, sed unus de turba ad quam venerat, et verus eorum socius, a quibus adductus erat. Quid plura? Spectavit, clamavit, exarsit, abstulit inde secum insaniam qua stimularetur redire, non tantum cum illis a quibus prius abstractus est; sed etiam præ illis, et alios trahens. Et inde tamen manu validissima et misericordissima eruisti eum tu, et docuisti non sui habere, sed tui fiduciam; sed longe postea.
> IX. Alypius ut fur apprehenditur

> 14. Verumtamen jam hoc ad medicinam futuram in ejus memoria reponebatur. Nam et illud, quod cum adhuc studeret Page 94 jam me audiens apud Carthaginem, et medio die cogitaret in foro quod recitaturus erat, sicuti exerceri scholastici solent, sivisti eum comprehendi ab æditimis fori tanquam furem. Non arbitror aliam ob causam te permisisse, Deus noster, nisi ut ille vir [141] tantus futurus jam inciperet discere, quam non facile in dignoscendis causis homo ab homine damnandus esset temeraria credulitate. Quippe ante tribunal deambulabat solus cum tabulis ac stilo, cum ecce adolescens quidam ex numero scholasticorum fur verus, securim clanculo apportans, illo non sentiente ingressus est ad cancellos plumbeos qui vico argentario desuper præminent, et præcidere plumbum cœpit. Sono autem securis audito submurmuraverunt argentarii qui subter erant, et miserunt qui apprehenderent quem forte invenissent. Quorum vocibus auditis, relicto instrumento ille discessit, timens ne cum eo teneretur. Alypius autem qui non viderat intrantem, exeuntem sensit, et celeriter vidit abeuntem: et causam scire cupiens ingressus est locum, et inventam securim stans atque admirans considerabat. Cum ecce illi qui missi fuerant, reperiunt eum solum ferentem ferrum cujus sonitu exciti venerant: tenent, attrahunt; congregatis inquilinis fori, tanquam furem manifestum se comprehendisse gloriantur, et inde offerendus judici ducebatur.

> 15. Sed hactenus docendus fuit. Statim enim, Domine, subvenisti innocentiæ cujus testis eras tu solus. Cum enim duceretur vel ad custodiam, vel ad supplicium, fit eis obviam quidam architectus cujus maxima erat cura publicarum fabricarum. Gaudent illi eum potissimum occurrisse, cui solebant in suspicionem venire ablatarum rerum quæ perissent de foro, ut quasi tandem ille cognosceret a quibus hæc fierent. Verum autem viderat homo sæpe Alypium in domo cujusdam senatoris Page 95 ad quem salutandum ventitabat: statimque cognitum manu apprehensa semovit a turbis, et tanti mali causam quærens, quid gestum esset audivit; omnesque tumultuantes qui aderant et minaciter frementes jussit venire secum. Et venerunt ad domum illius adolescentis qui rem commiserat. Puer vero erat ante ostium, et tam parvus erat ut nihil exinde domino suo metuens, facile posset totum indicare: cum eo quippe in foro fuit pedissequus. Quem posteaquam recoluit Alypius, architecto intimavit. At ille securim demonstravit puero, quærens ab eo cujus esset. Qui confestim, Nostra, inquit: deinde interrogatus aperuit cætera. Sic in illam domum translata causa, confusisque turbis quæ de illo triumphare jam cœperant, futurus dispensator [142] verbi tui, et multarum in Ecclesia tua causarum examinator, experientior instructiorque discessit.
> X. De integritate Alypii et adventu Nebridii.

> 16. Hunc ergo Romæ inveneram, et adhæsit mihi fortissimo vinculo, mecumque Mediolanum profectus est, ut nec me deseret, et de jure quod didicerat aliquid ageret, secundum votum magis parentum quam suum. Et ter * jam assederat mirabili continentia cæteris, cum ille magis miraretur eos qui aurum innocentiæ præponerent. Tentata est quoque ejus indoles, non solum illecebra cupiditatis, sed etiam stimulo timoris. Romæ assidebat comiti largitionum Italicianarum * . [143] Erat eo tempore quidam potentissimus senator, cujus et beneficiis obstricti multi et terrori subditi erant. Voluit sibi licere nescio quid ex more potentiæ suæ, quod esset per leges illicitum; restitit Alypius: promissum est præmium; irrisit animo: prætentæ minæ; calcavit: mirantibus omnibus inusitatam animam, quæ hominem tantum, et innumerabilibus præstandi nocendique modis ingenti fama celebratum, vel amicum non optaret, vel non formidaret inimicum. Ipse Page 96 autem judex, cui consiliarius erat, quamvis et ipse fieri nollet, non tamen aperte recusabat: sed in istum causam transferens, ab eo se non permitti asserebat; quia et revera si ipse faceret, iste discederet. Hoc solo autem pene jam illectus erat studio litterario, ut pretiis prætorianis [144] codices sibi conficiendos curaret: sed consulta justitia deliberationem in melius vertit; utiliorem judicans æquitatem qua prohibebatur, quam potestatem qua sinebatur. Parvum est hoc; sed Luc. 16, 10-12. qui in parvo fidelis est, et in magno fidelis est . Nec ullo modo erit inane, quod de tuæ Veritatis ore processit: Si in injusto mammona fideles non fuistis; quod verum est, quis credet vobis? Et si in alieno fideles non fuistis; quod vestrum est, quis dabit vobis? Talis ille tunc inhærebat mihi, mecumque nutabat in consilio, quisnam esset tenendus vitæ modus.

> 17. Nebridius etiam qui relicta patria vicina Carthagini, atque ipsa Carthagine ubi frequentissimus erat, relicto rure paterno optimo, relicta domo et non secutura matre, nullam ob aliam causam Mediolanum venerat, nisi ut mecum viveret in flagrantissimo studio [145] veritatis atque sapientiæ: pariter suspirabat, pariterque fluctuabat, beatæ vitæ inquisitor ardens, et quæstionum difficillimarum scrutator acerrimus. Et erant ora trium egentium, et inopiam suam sibimet invicem anhelantium, et Ps. 144, 15. a te exspectantium, ut dares eis escam in tempore opportuno . Et in omni amaritudine quæ nostros sæculares actus de misericordia tua sequebatur, intuentibus nobis finem cur ea pateremur, occurrebant tenebræ; et aversabamur * gementes, et dicebamus: Quamdiu hæc? Et hoc crebro dicebamus; et dicentes non relinquebamus ea; quia non elucebat certum aliquid quod illis relictis apprehenderemus.
> XI. Anxius Augustinus de instituenda vita deliberat.

> 18. Et ego maxime mirabar, satagens et recolens, quam longum tempus esset ab undevigesimo anno ætatis meæ, quo fervere cœperam studio sapientiæ; disponens, ea inventa, relinquere omnes vanarum cupiditatum spes inanes et insanias mendaces: et ecce jam tricenariam ætatem gerebam, in eodem luto hæsitans aviditate fruendi præsentibus, fugientibus Page 97 et dissipantibus me, dum dico: Cras inveniam; ecce manifestum apparebit, et tenebo: ecce Faustus veniet, et exponet omnia. O magni viri Academici! nihil ad agendam vitam certi comprehendi potest. Imo quæramus diligentius, et non desperemus. Ecce jam non sunt absurda in Libris ecclesiasticis quæ absurda videbantur, et possunt aliter atque honeste intelligi. Figam pedes in eo gradu in quo puer a parentibus eram positus, donec inveniatur perspicua veritas. Sed ubi quæretur? quando quæretur? Non vacat Ambrosio, non vacat legere. Ubi ipsos codices quærimus? unde, aut quando comparamus? a quibus sumimus? Deputentur tempora, distribuantur horæ pro salute animæ. Magna spes oborta est: non docet catholica fides quod putabamus, et vani accusabamus; nefas habent docti ejus credere Deum figura humani corporis terminatum: et dubitamus pulsare quo aperiantur cætera? Antemeridianis horis * discipuli occupant: cæteris quid facimus? cur non id agimus? Sed quando salutamus amicos majores, quorum suffragiis opus habemus? quando præparamus quod emant scholastici? quando reparamus nos ipsos, relaxando animo ab intentione curarum?

> 19. Pereant omnia, et dimittamus hæc vana et inania: conferamus nos ad solam inquisitionem veritatis. Vita * misera est; mors incerta. Si subito obrepit, quomodo hinc exibimus? et ubi nobis discenda sunt quæ hic negleximus, ac * non potius hujus negligentiæ supplicia luenda? Quid, si mors ipsa omnem curam sensu amputabit et finiet? Ergo et hoc quærendum. Sed absit ut ita sit. Non vacat, non est inane quod tam eminens culmen auctoritatis christianæ fidei toto orbe diffunditur [146] . Nunquam tanta et talia pro nobis divinitus agerentur, si morte corporis etiam vita animæ consumeretur. Quid cunctamur igitur relicta spe sæculi, conferre nos totos ad quærendum Deum et vitam beatam? Sed exspecta: jucunda sunt etiam ista; habent non parvam dulcedinem suam: non Page 98 facile ab eis præcidenda est intentio, quia turpe est ad ea rursum redire. Ecce jam quantum est, ut impetretur aliquis honor? et quid amplius in his desiderandum? Suppetit amicorum majorum copia: ut nihil aliud, et multum festinemus, vel præsidatus dari potest; et ducenda uxor cum aliqua pecunia, ne sumptum nostrum gravet [147] ; et ille erit modus cupiditatis. Multi magni viri et imitatione dignissimi, sapientiæ studio cum conjugibus dediti fuerunt.

> 20. Cum hæc dicebam, et alternabant hi venti et impellebant huc atque illuc cor meum, transibant tempora, et tardabam converti ad Dominum, et differebam de die in diem vivere in te, et non differebam quotidie in memetipso mori. Amans beatam vitam, timebam illam in sede sua; et ab ea fugiens, quærebam eam. Putabam enim me miserum fore nimis, si feminæ privarer amplexibus [148] ; et medicinam misericordiæ tuæ ad eamdem infirmitatem sanandam non cogitabam, quia expertus non eram; et propriarum virium credebam esse continentiam, quarum mihi non eram conscius, cum tam stultus essem ut nescirem, sicut scriptum est, neminem posse esse continentem, nisi tu dederis . Utique dares, si gemitu interno pulsarem aures tuas, et fide solida in te jactarem curam meam.
> XII. Contentio inter Alypium et Augustinum de matrimonio et cœlibatu.

> 21. Prohibebat me sane Alypius ab uxore ducenda, cantans * nullo modo nos posse securo otio simul in amore sapientiæ vivere, sicut jam diu desideraremus, si id fecissem. Erat enim ipse in ea re etiam tunc castissimus, ita ut mirum esset; quia vel experientiam concubitus ceperat in ingressu adolescentiæ suæ, sed non hæserat; magisque doluerat et spreverat, et deinde jam continentissime vivebat. Ego autem resistebam illi, exemplis eorum qui conjugati coluissent sapientiam, et promeruissent Deum, et habuissent fideliter ac dilexissent Page 99 amicos. A quorum ego quidem granditate animi longe aberam: et deligatus * morbo carnis mortifera suavitate, trahebam catenam meam, solvi timens, et quasi concusso vulnere repellens verba bene suadentis, tanquam manum solventis. Insuper etiam per me ipsi quoque Alypio loquebatur serpens, et innectebat atque spargebat per linguam meam dulces laqueos in via ejus, quibus illi honesti et expediti pedes implicarentur.

> 22. Cum enim me ille miraretur, quem non parvipenderet, ita hærere visco illius voluptatis, ut me affirmarem, quotiescumque inde inter nos quæreremus, cælibem vitam nullo modo posse degere; atque ita me defenderem, cum illum mirantem viderem, ut dicerem multum interesse inter illud quod ipse raptim et furtim expertus esset, quod pene jam ne meminisset quidem, atque ideo nulla molestia facile contemneret, et delectationes consuetudinis meæ, ad quas si accessisset honestum nomen matrimonii, non eum mirari oportere, cur ego illam vitam nequirem spernere: cœperat et ipse desiderare conjugium, nequaquam victus libidine talis voluptatis, sed curiositatis. Dicebat enim scire se cupere quidnam esset illud, sine quo vita mea quæ illi sic placebat, non mihi vita, sed pœna videretur. Stupebat enim liber ab illo vinculo animus servitutem meam, et stupendo ibat in experiendi cupidinem, venturus in ipsam experientiam, atque inde fortasse lapsurus in eam quam stupebat servitutem; quoniam sponsionem volebat facere cum morte ; et qui amat periculum, incidit in illud . Neutrum enim nostrum, si quod est conjugale decus in officio regendi matrimonii et suscipiendorum liberorum, ducebat, nisi tenuiter. Magna autem ex parte atque vehementer consuetudo satiandæ insatiabilis concupiscentiæ me captum excruciabat: illum autem admiratio capiendum trahebat. Sic eramus, donec tu, Altissime, non deserens humum nostram, miseratus miseros, subvenires miris et occultis modis.
> XIII. Uxor quæritur Augustino.

> 23. Et instabatur impigre ut ducerem uxorem. Jam petebam, jam promittebatur, maxime matre dante operam, quo me jam conjugatum Baptismus salutaris ablueret, quo me in dies gaudebat aptari, et vota sua ac promissa tua in mea fide compleri animadvertebat. Cum sane et rogatu meo et desiderio suo, forti clamore cordis abs te deprecaretur quotidie, Page 100 ut ei per visum ostenderes aliquid de futuro matrimonio meo; nunquam voluisti. Et videbat quædam vana et phantastica, quo cogebat impetus de hac re satagentis humani spiritus; et narrabat mihi, non cum fiducia qua solebat, cum tu demonstrabas ei, sed contemnens ea. Dicebat enim discernere se nescio quo sapore, quem verbis explicare non poterat, quid interesset inter revelantem te, et animam suam somniantem. Instabatur tamen, et puella petebatur, cujus ætas ferme biennio minus quam nubilis erat; et quia ea placebat, exspectabatur.
> XIV. De vita communi agenda dum amicis deliberat.

> 24. Et multi amici agitaveramus animo, et colloquentes ac detestantes turbulentas humanæ vitæ molestias, pene jam firmaveramus remoti a turbis otiose vivere: id otium sic moliti, ut si quid habere possemus, conferremus in medium, unamque rem familiarem conflaremus ex omnibus; ut per amicitiæ sinceritatem non esset aliud hujus et aliud illius; sed quod ex cunctis fieret unum, et universum singulorum esset, et omnia omnium: cum videremur nobis esse posse decem ferme homines in eadem societate, essentque inter nos prædivites, Romanianus [149] maxime communiceps noster, quem tunc graves æstus negotiorum suorum ad comitatum attraxerant, ab ineunte ætate mihi familiarissimus; qui maxime instabat huic rei, et magnam in suadendo habebat auctoritatem, quod ampla res ejus multum cæteris anteibat: et placuerat nobis ut bini annui tanquam magistratus omnia necessaria curarent, cæteris quietis. Sed posteaquam cœpit
> Page 101

> cogitari utrum hoc mulierculæ sinerent, quas et alii nostrum jam habebant, et nos habere volebamus, totum illud placitum quod bene formabamus * , dissiluit in manibus, atque confractum et abjectum est. Inde ad suspiria et gemitus * , et gressus ad sequendas Mat. 7, 13. latas et tritas vias sæculi, quoniam multæ cogitationes erant in corde nostro; Ps. 32, 11. consilium autem tuum manet in æternum . Ex quo consilio deridebas nostra, et tua præparabas, nobis Ps. 144, 15. 16. daturus escam in opportunitate , et aperturus manum atque impleturus animas nostras benedictione .
> XV. In locum discedentis concubinæ alia succedit.

> 25. Interea mea peccata multiplicabantur, et avulsa * a latere meo tanquam impedimento conjugii, cum qua cubare solitus eram, cor ubi adhærebat, concisum et vulneratum mihi erat, et trahebat sanguinem. Et illa in Africam redierat, vovens tibi alium se virum nescituram, relicto apud me naturali ex illa filio meo. At ego infelix nec feminæ imitator, dilationis impatiens, tanquam post biennium accepturus eam quam petebam, quia non amator conjugii sed libidinis servus eram; procuravi aliam, non utique conjugem: quo tanquam sustentaretur et perduceretur vel integer vel auctior morbus animæ meæ, satellitio perdurantis consuetudinis, in regnum uxorium. Nec sanabatur vulnus illud meum quod prioris præcisione factum fuerat; sed post fervorem doloremque acerrimum putrescebat, et quasi frigidius, sed desperatius dolebat [150] .
> XVI. Mortis et judicii metum nunquam deposuit.

> 26. Tibi laus, tibi gloria, fons misericordiarum. Ego fiebam miserior, et tu propinquior. Aderat jam jamque dextera tua ereptura * me de cœno, et ablutura me; et ignorabam. Nec me revocabat a profundiore voluptatum carnalium gurgite, nisi metus mortis et futuri judicii tui, qui per varias quidem opiniones, nunquam tamen recessit de pectore meo. Et disputabam cum amicis meis Alypio et Nebridio de finibus bonorum et malorum, Epicurum accepturum fuisse palmam in animo meo, nisi ego credidissem post mortem restare animæ vitam, et tractus meritorum, quod Epicurus Page 102 credere noluit. Et quærebam, si essemus immortales et in perpetua corporis voluptate sine ullo amissionis terrore viveremus, cur non essemus beati, aut quid aliud quæreremus? Nesciens idipsum ad magnam miseriam pertinere, quod ita demersus et cæcus cogitare non possem lumen honestatis et gratis amplectendæ pulchritudinis, quam non videt oculus carnis, et videtur ex intimo. Nec considerabam miser, ex qua vena mihi manaret, quod ista ipsa, fœda tamen, cum amicis dulciter conferebam; nec esse sine amicis poteram beatus, etiam secundum sensum quem tunc habebam in quantalibet affluentia carnalium voluptatum. Quos utique amicos gratis diligebam, vicissimque ab eis me diligi gratis sentiebam. O tortuosas vias! Væ animæ audaci quæ speravit, si a te recessisset, se aliquid melius habituram! Versa et reversa in tergum, et in latera, et in ventrem; et dura sunt omnia: et tu solus requies [151] . Et ecce ades, et liberas a miserabilibus erroribus, et constituis nos in via tua, et consolaris, et dicis: Currite; ego feram, et ego perducam, et ibi ego feram * .
> Page 103

> The coming of his mother Monica, and her pious devotion toward Ambrose. The character and manner of life of Ambrose. Augustine, being in the thirtieth year of his age, frequents Ambrose’s sermons, and understands more clearly that Catholic doctrine is falsely assailed by the Manichaeans; yet he does not attain the nature and benefits of faith. The character of his friend Alypius. He is drawn in different directions while deliberating concerning the better ordering of his life; struck also by fear of death and judgment, he is from day to day kindled toward conversion of life.
> I. Augustine neither Manichaean nor Catholic.

> 1. My hope from my youth, where wast Thou to me, and whither hadst Thou withdrawn? Or hadst not Thou made me, and distinguished me from the beasts of four feet and the fowls of heaven? Thou hadst made me wiser, and Is. 50, 10. Ps. 34, 6. I walked through darkness and slippery places, and sought Thee outside [128] myself, and found not the God of my heart; and I had come into the depth of the sea, and distrusted and despaired of finding truth. My mother had now come to me, strong in piety, following me by land and sea, secure in Thee amid all dangers. For even amid the perils of the sea she comforted the sailors themselves, by whom inexperienced travellers of the deep, when disturbed, are wont to be comforted; promising them a safe arrival, because Thou hadst promised this to her in a vision. And she found me indeed grievously endangered by despair of discovering truth.

Yet when I told her that I was now indeed no longer a Manichaean, but neither a Catholic Christian, she did not leap for joy as though she had heard something unexpected, since she had already become secure regarding that part of my misery in which she wept to Thee over me as one dead but to be raised again, and Luc. 7, 14. 15. bore me forth upon the bier of her thought, that Thou mightest say to the widow’s son: Young man, I say unto thee, arise; and he might revive and begin to speak, and Thou mightest deliver him to his mother. Therefore her heart did not tremble with any tumultuous exultation when she heard that there had already been accomplished to so great an extent what she daily bewailed before Thee might be accomplished: that I had not yet attained truth, but had already been snatched from falsehood. Nay rather, because she was certain that Thou wouldst give what remained, Thou who hadst promised the whole, she answered me most calmly and with a heart full of confidence that she believed in Christ that, before she departed from this life, she would see me a faithful Catholic. And this indeed she said to me.

But to Thee, fountain of mercies, she offered prayers and tears yet more abundantly *, that Thou mightest hasten Thy help and illumine my darkness; and she ran more eagerly to the Church, and hung upon Ambrose’s * lips, Joh. 4, 14. at the fountain of water springing up into eternal life. Now she loved that man Gal. 4, 14. as an angel of God, because through him she had learned that I had meanwhile been brought to that perilous wavering through which, she confidently presumed, I would pass from sickness to health, with a more severe danger intervening *, as through that crisis which physicians call critical.
> II. Feasts and communion assemblies at the tombs of martyrs.

> 2. Accordingly, when she had brought porridge and bread and wine to the Memorials [129] of the saints, as was customary in Africa, and was forbidden by the doorkeeper, once she learned that the bishop had prohibited this, she embraced the matter so piously and obediently that I myself wondered * how readily she became an accuser rather of her own custom than a disputant against that prohibition. For drunkenness did not besiege her spirit, nor did love of wine spur her to hatred of the truth, as it does most men and women who, sodden as if with a watered drink, are nauseated by the song of sobriety. But when she had brought a basket with the customary food to be tasted beforehand and distributed, she set down no more than one little cup *, tempered to suit her own quite sober palate, from which she might partake as a mark of honour.

And if there were many memorials of the departed which seemed to be honoured in that way, she carried round that same one thing, which she would set down everywhere; and, now not only very well watered but even quite lukewarm *, she shared it with those present in tiny sips, because she sought piety there, not pleasure. Accordingly, when she learned that this had been commanded not to be done by that distinguished preacher and overseer of piety, even by those who did it soberly, lest any occasion for gorging themselves be given to drunkards [130], and because those observances, like funeral rites, were very similar to the superstition of the Gentiles, she most willingly abstained from them. And instead of a basket full of earthly fruits, she had learned to bring to the memorials of the martyrs a heart full of purer prayers; that she might give to the needy what she could, and that thus communion [131] of the Lord’s body might be celebrated there, in imitation of whose Passion the martyrs were sacrificed and crowned.

Yet it seems to me, O Lord my God—and so it is before Thee concerning this matter in my heart—that my mother would perhaps not readily have yielded in abandoning this custom, had she been forbidden by another whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose. Him she loved chiefly for the sake of my salvation; while he loved her because of her most religious way of life, in that, Rom. 12, 11. fervent in spirit in good works, she frequented the church: so that, when he saw me, he would often break forth in praise * of her preaching, congratulating me that I had such a mother; not knowing what a son she had in me, who doubted all those things and thought that the way of life could by no means be found.
> III. The occupations and studies of Ambrose.

> 3. Nor did I yet groan in prayer that Thou mightest come to my aid; but my mind was intent upon inquiry and restless for disputation. And I thought Ambrose himself a certain happy man according to the world, whom such great powers honoured; only his celibacy seemed laborious to me. But what hope he bore, what struggle he had against the temptations of his own eminence, what consolation in adversities, and what savoury joys from Thy bread his hidden mouth—that is, that which was in his heart—chewed over [132], I neither knew how to conjecture nor had experienced; nor did he know my agitations or the pit of my danger. For I could not ask him what I wished, as I wished, because crowds of busy people, to whose weaknesses he ministered, kept me from his ear and mouth.

When he was not with them—which was but for a very little while—he either refreshed his body with necessary sustenance, or his mind with reading. But when he read, his eyes travelled over the pages and his heart searched out the meaning, while his voice and tongue were at rest. Often, when we were present—for no one was forbidden to enter, nor was it customary for an arrival to be announced to him—we saw him reading silently, and never otherwise; and, sitting in prolonged silence (for who would dare to burden one so intent?),

we would depart, and conjectured that in that brief time which he obtained for restoring his mind, free from the noise of other persons’ affairs, he did not wish to be called away to anything else; and perhaps guarded against the possibility that, if the hearer were hanging upon his words and attentive, should the author whom he was reading have stated anything too obscurely, he would also have to explain it, or discuss some rather difficult questions; and that, time being spent on this work, he would turn over fewer volumes than he wished. Although the reason of preserving his voice, which very readily became hoarse, could have been a more just cause for reading silently. Yet whatever his purpose in doing so, that good man certainly acted with a good purpose.

> 4. But assuredly I was given no opportunity to inquire what I desired from the breast of that most holy oracle of Thine, except when something was to be heard briefly. Yet my agitations required that he should have much leisure to which they might be poured out, and never found it. Indeed, every Lord’s day I heard him among the people 2 Tim. 2, 15. rightly handling the word of truth; and it was confirmed to me more and more that all the knots of crafty calumnies which those our deceivers wove against the divine Books could be untied.

But when I had also learned that man, made by Thee in Thine image, was not understood by Thy spiritual sons, whom Thou hast regenerated from the mother Catholic by grace, in such a way that they believed and conceived Thee to be bounded by the form of a human body—although I did not even faintly, or in an enigma, surmise what manner of thing spiritual substance might be—yet, rejoicing, I blushed that for so many years I had barked not against the Catholic faith, but against the fictions of carnal thoughts. For I had been rash and impious in saying by accusation what I ought to have said by inquiry *. For Thou, most high and most near, most secret and most present, who hast not some members greater and others smaller, but art wholly everywhere and nowhere in places, art certainly not that corporeal form; yet Thou hast made man in Thine image; and behold, he himself is in a place from head to foot.
> IV. He understands the doctrine of the Church as Ambrose preaches.

> 5. Therefore, since I did not know how this Thine image subsisted, I should, as one knocking, have proposed how it ought to be believed, not insultingly objected as though it were believed in that manner. Thus, then, the keener did anxiety gnaw at my inward parts as to what certain thing I should hold, the more I was ashamed that, deceived and deluded for so long by the promise of certainties, with childish error and rashness I had babbled of so many uncertainties as though they were certain. For that they were false became clear to me later. Yet it was certain that they were uncertain, and that I had at one time held them as certain when I accused Thy Catholic Church with blind contentions, although I had not yet discovered that it taught truth, yet that it did not teach the things of which I gravely accused it.

Thus I was confounded and converted; and I rejoiced, O my God, that the one Church *, the body of Thy Only One, in which Christ’s name had been put upon me as an infant, did not relish childish trifles; nor did it hold in its sound doctrine that which would force Thee, the creator of all things, into a space of place, however lofty and vast, yet bounded on every side by the shape of human limbs.

> 6. I rejoiced also that the ancient writings of the Law and the Prophets were now set before me to be read not with that eye by which they had formerly seemed absurd, when I reproached Thy holy ones as though they held such views; whereas in truth they did not hold them. And I gladly heard Ambrose, as he most diligently commended, as it were, a rule, often saying in his popular sermons, 2 Cor. 3, 6. The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life: when, removing the mystical veil, he opened spiritually those things which, according to the letter, seemed to teach perversity, saying nothing that offended me, although he said things whose truth I still did not know. For I withheld my heart from every assent, fearing a precipice; and I was more nearly killed by suspension. For I wanted to become as certain of things which I did not see as I was certain that seven and three are ten.

For I was not so mad as to think that not even this could be comprehended; but, as with this, so with other things I desired it, whether bodily things not present to my senses, or spiritual things, of which I knew not how to think except corporeally. And I could be healed by believing [133], so that the purer sight of my mind might in some manner be directed toward Thy truth, which always remains and fails from nothing. But as it commonly happens that one who has experienced a bad physician is afraid to entrust himself even to a good one, so was the condition of my soul, which certainly could not be healed except by believing, and, lest it should believe false things, refused to be cured; resisting Thy hands, which had prepared the medicines of faith and scattered them over the diseases of the world, and had bestowed so great authority upon them.
> V. On the authority and necessary use of the sacred Books.

> 7. Yet from this point onward, preferring Catholic doctrine, I thought it more modestly and by no means deceptively commanded there that what was not demonstrated should be believed (whether there were something, but perhaps not for someone, or whether there were not even anything [134]), than that there, by a rash promise of knowledge, credulity should be ridiculed, and afterward so many utterly fabulous and absurd things, because they could not be demonstrated, should be commanded to be believed [135].

Then, little by little, Thou, O Lord, with a most gentle and most merciful hand, handling and ordering my heart, didst persuade me, as I considered how innumerable were the things I believed which I did not see * and at whose occurrence I had not been present: such as so many things in the history of nations [136], so many concerning places and cities I had not seen, so many things told by friends, so many by physicians, so many by one person and another; things which, unless they were believed, we could do absolutely nothing in this life [137]; finally, how unshakably I held fixed by faith from what parents I had sprung, which I could not know unless I had believed by hearing: Thou didst persuade me that blame lay not upon those who believed Thy Books, which Thou hast established with such great authority among almost all nations [138], but upon those who did not believe; and that those were not to be listened to who might perhaps say to me: Whence knowest thou that those Books were supplied to the human race by the spirit of the one true and most truthful God?

For this very thing was above all to be believed, since no contentiousness of calumnious questions, among so many mutually conflicting philosophers whom I had read, had been able to wrest from me that I should ever not believe that Thou art whatever Thou art, though I knew not what Thou art; or that the administration of human affairs pertains to Thee.

> 8. But I believed this, now more firmly, now more faintly; yet I always believed both that you exist and that you have care for us, although I did not know either what was to be thought concerning your substance, or what way led or led back to you. And therefore, since we were too weak to find the truth by clear reasoning, and for this reason had need of the authority of the holy Scriptures, I had already begun to believe that you would by no means have bestowed upon that Scripture such eminent authority throughout all lands, unless you had willed that through it you should be believed in, and through it sought.

For now I referred to the depth of the mysteries the absurdity which used to offend me in those writings, when I had heard many things from them expounded plausibly; and thus that authority appeared to me the more venerable and more worthy of sacred trust, inasmuch as it was readily available for all to read, while preserving the dignity of its secrecy for a deeper understanding; offering itself to all in the plainest words and the humblest manner of speech, while exercising the attention of those who are not light of heart: so that it might receive all into its popular bosom, and convey a few through narrow openings to you—yet many more than if it neither stood out by so lofty a summit of authority nor drew crowds into its lap by holy humility. I thought these things, and you were present to me; I sighed, and you heard me; I wavered, and you guided me; I went along the broad way of the world, and you did not abandon me.
> Page 90
> VI. On the misery of the ambitious, with the example of a rejoicing beggar adduced]

> 9. I gaped after honours, gain, marriage; and you mocked me. In these desires I endured most bitter difficulties, you being propitious all the more, the less you allowed anything that was not you to become sweet to me. Look upon my heart, Lord, you who willed that I should recall and confess this to you. Now may my soul cleave to you, for you stripped it from that most tenacious birdlime of death. How wretched it was! And you pricked its sense of the wound, that, leaving all things, it might turn to you, who are above all things and without whom all things would be nothing; might turn, and be healed.

How wretched, then, was I; and how did you bring it about that I should feel my wretchedness, on that day when I was preparing to recite praises of the Emperor [139], in which I should utter many lies, and be favoured in my lying by those who knew it, while my heart panted after these concerns and burned with the fevers of wasting thoughts! Passing through a certain street of Milan, I noticed a poor beggar, already, I believe, well fed, jesting and rejoicing; and I groaned, and spoke with the friends who were with me about the many pains of our madnesses. For by all such endeavours of ours—such as those in which I was then toiling, dragging beneath the goads of desires the burden of my unhappiness, and increasing it by dragging it—we wished for nothing else than to attain secure gladness, to which that beggar had already preceded us, though perhaps we should never arrive there!

For what he had already attained with a few begged-for coins, I was striving after by such toilsome windings and turnings: namely, the gladness of temporal happiness. For he did not have true joy; but I too was seeking it much more falsely in those ambitions. And certainly he was glad, while I was anxious; he was secure, I trembled. And if anyone had asked me whether I would rather exult or fear, I should have answered, “Exult.” Again, if he asked whether I would rather be such as he was or such as I then was, I should have chosen myself, worn out with cares and fears—but by perversity; surely not by truth? For I ought not to have preferred myself to him because I was more learned, since I did not rejoice on that account, but sought by it to please men—not that I might teach them, but only that I might please them. Therefore you too, with the rod of your discipline, Ps. 41, 11. v. Sabat. were breaking my bones.

> 10. Let those, then, depart from my soul who say to it: It matters whence Page 91 a man rejoices. That beggar rejoiced in drunkenness; you wished to rejoice in glory. What glory, Lord? One which is not in you. For just as that was not true joy, so neither was this true glory; and it further turned my mind aside. And he was going to digest his drunkenness that very night; I had slept and risen with mine, and was to sleep and rise with it; see for how many days. It does indeed matter whence one rejoices, I know; and the joy of a faithful hope differs incomparably from that vanity. But even then there was a difference between us. For assuredly he was happier, not only because he was suffused with cheerfulness while I was disembowelled by cares, but also because he had acquired wine by wishing well, whereas I sought puffed-up pride by lying.

I said many things to my dear friends at that time to this effect, and I often observed in these matters how it was with me; and I found that I was ill, and grieved, and doubled that very ill. And if anything prosperous smiled upon me, I was weary of grasping it, because almost before it was held, it flew away.
> VII. He turns Alypius from the madness of the Circus.

> 11. We groaned together, we who lived in friendship with one another, and I discussed these matters most especially and intimately with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius was born in the same town as I, of parents who were leading men of the municipality, and was younger than I. For he had also studied under me when I first began to teach in our town, and afterwards at Carthage; and he loved me greatly because I seemed to him good and learned, and I loved him because of his great natural disposition for virtue, which stood out sufficiently in no great age.

Yet the whirlpool of Carthaginian habits, in which frivolous spectacles rage, had swallowed him up into a madness for the Circus. But while he was miserably wallowing in it, and I was employed as a professor of rhetoric there in a public school, he did not yet hear me as his teacher, because of a certain quarrel which had arisen between me and his father. I had learned that he loved the circus ruinously, and I was grievously distressed that so great a promise seemed likely to be lost, or even already lost. Yet I had no opportunity to admonish him and call him back by some restraint, whether through the goodwill of friendship or by the right of a teacher. For I thought that he shared his father’s opinion of me; but he did not. Therefore, setting aside his father’s will in this matter, he began to greet me, coming to my lecture-room, hearing something, and departing.

> 12. But it had slipped from my memory to deal with him, lest he should destroy so good a talent by a blind and headlong devotion to vain games. But you, Lord, who preside over the rudders of all that you have created, had not forgotten that he was to become among your sons a minister of your sacrament; and, so that his correction might openly be ascribed to you, you wrought it indeed through me, though I knew nothing of it. For one day, when I was sitting in my usual place and the students were present before me, he came, greeted me, sat down, and gave his attention to what was being done. And by chance there was in my hands a text which, as I expounded it, seemed to call aptly for an illustration from the Circus, in order that what I was suggesting might become both more pleasant and clearer, with a biting mockery of those whom that madness had captivated. You know, our God, that I had not then thought of healing Alypius from that pest.

But he took it to himself and believed that I had said it only on his account. And what another might have taken as cause to be angry with me, that honourable young man took as cause to be angry with himself and to love me more ardently. For you had long ago said and bound it into your Scriptures: Prov. 9, 8. Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. And yet I had not rebuked him; but you, making use of all, both those who know and those who do not know, in the order which you know—and that order is just—Is. 6, 6. wrought burning coals from my heart and tongue, by which you might burn away and heal a mind wasting in good hope. Let him be silent about your praises who does not consider your mercies, which confess you from my inmost marrow. For after those words, he burst forth from so deep a pit, in which he gladly plunged and was blinded with miserable pleasure; and with strong self-control he shook his mind free, and all the filth of the Circus recoiled from him, nor did he go there any more.

Then he overcame his reluctant father so that he might have me as his teacher; his father yielded and granted it. And beginning again to hear me, he became entangled with me in that superstition, loving in the Manichaeans their display [140] of continence, which he thought true and genuine. But it was mad and deceptive, Prov. 6, 26. Sabat. capturing precious souls, which did not yet know how to touch the height of virtue and were easily deceived by the surface, though it was the surface of a shadowed and feigned virtue.
> VIII. Alypius is seized by the madness of gladiatorial games, which he had previously abhorred.

> 13. Yet he did not abandon the earthly path that had been charmed upon him by his parents, but had gone ahead to Rome to study law; and there he was drawn into a gladiatorial spectacle with an incredible and incredibly avid appetite. For although he shunned and detested such things, some of his friends and fellow students, when they happened to be passing by after dinner, dragged him, vigorously refusing and resisting, into the amphitheatre by familiar violence, on the days of cruel and deadly games, while he said this: “If you drag my body into that place and set it there, can you also direct my mind and my eyes toward those spectacles? I shall therefore be present while absent, and thus shall overcome both you and them.” Having heard this, they nevertheless brought him with them, perhaps wishing to discover precisely whether he could accomplish it. When they arrived there and had seated themselves where they could, everything seethed with most monstrous delights.

He, with the doors of his eyes closed, forbade his mind to proceed into such great evils; and would that he had stopped his ears as well! For by some turn in the combat, when a great cry from the whole people had struck him violently, conquered by curiosity and as though prepared, whatever that might be, even to despise and overcome the sight of it, he opened his eyes; and he was struck with a graver wound in his soul than the man whom he desired to see was in his body. And he fell more miserably than the man whose fall had produced the cry that entered through his ears and opened his eyes, so that there might be something by which his spirit, still rather bold than strong, might be struck and cast down; and it was the weaker for having presumed upon itself, when it ought to have trusted in you. For as soon as he saw that blood, he drank in savagery at the same time, did not turn away, but fixed his gaze; and he drank in frenzy, unaware, and delighted in the crime of the contest, and became intoxicated with bloody pleasure.

And now he was no longer the man who had come, but one of the crowd to which he had come, and a true companion of those by whom he had been brought. What more? He watched, shouted, burned, and carried away with him from there the madness by which he might be spurred to return, not only with those by whom he had first been drawn away, but even before them, drawing others along. Yet from this you tore him away by your most mighty and most merciful hand, and taught him to have confidence not in himself but in you—but much later.
> IX. Alypius is apprehended as a thief

> 14. Nevertheless, this was already being laid up in his memory for his future healing. For you also permitted that incident when, while he was still studying at Carthage and already hearing me, and at midday was thinking in the forum about what he was to recite, as students are accustomed to practise, he should be seized by the attendants of the forum as a thief. I do not think that you permitted it for any other reason, our God, than that this man, [141] destined to be so great, should already begin to learn how a man ought not readily to be condemned by another man in the investigation of cases through rash credulity. For he was walking alone before the tribunal with tablets and stylus, when behold, a certain young man from the number of students, a true thief, secretly bringing an axe, entered, without his noticing it, to the leaden railings which overhang the silversmiths’ street, and began to cut away the lead.

But when the sound of the axe was heard, the silversmiths below murmured together and sent men to seize whomever they might find. Hearing their voices, the fellow left the tool behind and departed, fearing that he might be caught with it. Alypius, however, who had not seen him enter, noticed him coming out and quickly saw him going away; and, desiring to know the reason, he entered the place and, finding the axe, stood looking at it in amazement. And behold, those who had been sent found him alone, carrying the iron at whose sound they had been roused. They held him and dragged him away; gathering the inhabitants of the forum, they boasted that they had seized an obvious thief, and he was being led away from there to be presented to a judge.

> 15. But he needed instruction only so far. For at once, Lord, you came to the aid of an innocence whose sole witness you were. For as he was being led either to custody or to punishment, a certain architect met them, whose chief charge was the public buildings. They were delighted that this very man had met them, to whom they were accustomed to come under suspicion for things stolen that had disappeared from the forum, so that at last, as it were, he might learn by whom these things were done. But the man had often seen Alypius at the house of a certain senator, whom he used to visit in greeting. At once, recognizing him, he took him by the hand and removed him from the crowd; and, asking the cause of so great an evil, he heard what had happened, and ordered all those present who were tumultuously and threateningly raging to come with him. And they came to the house of that young man who had committed the deed.

Now there was a boy before the door, and he was so small that, fearing nothing on that account from his master, he could easily disclose the whole matter; for he had been with him in the forum as an attendant. When Alypius recognized him, he informed the architect. But the latter showed the axe to the boy, asking whose it was. “Ours,” he said at once; then, being questioned, he disclosed the rest. Thus the case having been transferred to that house, and the crowds who had already begun to triumph over him having been put to shame, the future steward [142] of your word and examiner of many cases in your Church departed more experienced and better instructed.
> X. On the integrity of Alypius and the arrival of Nebridius.

> 16. Thus I had found him at Rome, and he clung to me by a most strong bond, and went with me to Milan, both that he might not leave me and that he might do something with the law which he had learned, according to the wish of his parents rather than his own. And already three times * he had sat as an assessor to others with remarkable self-restraint, while he rather wondered at those who preferred gold to innocence. His character was tested, moreover, not only by the enticement of covetousness, but also by the goad of fear. At Rome he was sitting as assessor to the Count of the Italian Largesses * . [143] At that time there was a certain most powerful senator, to whose favors many were indebted and to whose terror they were subject.

He wished to be permitted, I know not what, in accordance with the custom of his power, which was unlawful by the laws; Alypius resisted: a reward was promised; he laughed at it in his mind: threats were held out; he trampled on them: all marveling at an unusual spirit, which neither desired such a man as a friend nor feared him as an enemy—a man celebrated by immense renown for innumerable means of bestowing favors and doing harm. But the judge himself, to whom he was counselor, although he too did not wish it to be done, nevertheless did not openly refuse; but, transferring the cause to this man, he asserted that he was not being permitted by him; because indeed, if he himself did it, this man would withdraw. By this alone he was almost enticed already, through literary zeal, namely, that he should take care to have books copied for himself at praetorian prices [144] : but consulted justice turned his deliberation to the better, judging the equity by which he was forbidden more useful than the power by which he was permitted. This is a small matter; but Luc. 16, 10-12.

he who is faithful in a little thing is also faithful in a great thing . And by no means will that be empty which proceeded from the mouth of thy Truth: If ye have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon; who will entrust to you that which is true? And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another's; who will give you that which is your own? Such was he then, clinging to me and wavering with me in deliberation as to what manner of life ought to be embraced.

> 17. Nebridius also, who, having left his native country near Carthage, and Carthage itself, where he was very well known, having left his excellent paternal estate, having left his house and his mother, who was not to follow him, had come to Milan for no other reason than that he might live with me in a most ardent pursuit [145] of truth and wisdom: together he sighed, and together he fluctuated, an ardent seeker of the blessed life and a most acute investigator of the most difficult questions. And there were the mouths of three needy men, panting to one another for their own want, and Ps. 144, 15. waiting upon thee, that thou mightest give them food in due season . And in all the bitterness which, by thy mercy, followed our worldly affairs, when we considered the end for which we suffered these things, darkness met us; and we turned away * groaning, and said: How long shall these things last? And we said this often; and while saying it, we did not abandon them, because nothing certain shone forth that we might grasp after abandoning those things.
> XI. Anxious Augustine deliberates concerning the ordering of his life.

> 18. And I especially wondered, striving and recalling how long a time it had been since my nineteenth year, when I had begun to burn with the pursuit of wisdom; resolving, once it had been found, to abandon all the empty hopes of vain desires and lying madnesses: and behold, I was now in my thirtieth year, stuck in the same mud through greed of enjoying present things, which were fleeing and scattering me, while I said: Tomorrow I shall find it; behold, it will appear clearly, and I shall hold it: behold, Faustus will come and explain everything. O great men of the Academy! Nothing certain can be comprehended for the conduct of life. Nay, let us seek more diligently, and not despair. Behold, now those things in the ecclesiastical books which seemed absurd are not absurd, and they can be understood otherwise and honorably. I shall set my feet upon that step on which, as a boy, I had been placed by my parents, until perspicuous truth is found. But where shall it be sought? When shall it be sought? Ambrose has no leisure, nor leisure for reading.

Where shall we seek out the books themselves? Whence, or when, shall we procure them? From whom shall we borrow them? Let times be allotted, let hours be distributed for the salvation of the soul. A great hope has arisen: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought, and what we vainly accused; its learned men hold it impious to believe that God is bounded by the figure of a human body: and do we hesitate to knock, that the rest may be opened to us? In the morning hours * the students occupy me: what do we do with the rest? Why do we not do this? But when do we pay our respects to greater friends, whose support we need? When do we prepare what the pupils may buy? When do we restore ourselves, relaxing the mind from the strain of cares?

> 19. Let all things perish, and let us dismiss these vain and empty things: let us devote ourselves to the sole inquiry after truth. Life * is miserable; death uncertain. If it steals upon us suddenly, how shall we depart from here? And where must we learn those things which we have neglected here, and * not rather pay the penalties for this neglect? What if death itself will cut off and end every care with sensation? Therefore this too must be sought. But far be it that this should be so. It is not without leisure, it is not empty, that so lofty a summit of authority of the Christian faith is spread throughout the whole world [146] . Never would such great and such things be done for us by God, if with the death of the body the life of the soul too were consumed. Why then do we delay, abandoning the hope of the world, to devote ourselves wholly to seeking God and the blessed life? But wait: these things too are pleasant; they have no small sweetness of their own: the attention given to them is not easily to be cut off, because it is shameful to return to them again.

Behold now, how much is it to obtain some office? And what more is to be desired in these things? There is an ample supply of greater friends: even if nothing else, and we hasten greatly, a governorship can be given; and a wife is to be taken with some money, so that she may not burden our expenditure [147] ; and that shall be the limit of desire. Many great men, most worthy of imitation, have devoted themselves to the pursuit of wisdom together with their wives.

> 20. While I said these things, and these winds alternated and drove my heart this way and that, time passed, and I delayed turning to the Lord, and from day to day I postponed living in thee, while I did not postpone dying daily in myself. Loving the blessed life, I feared it in its own abode; and fleeing from it, I sought it. For I thought that I should be exceedingly miserable if deprived of a woman's embraces [148] ; and I did not think of the medicine of thy mercy for healing that same infirmity, because I had not experienced it; and I believed continence to be of my own powers, of which I was not conscious, being so foolish that I did not know, as it is written, that no one can be continent unless thou grantest it . Surely thou wouldst grant it, if with inward groaning I knocked upon thine ears and with firm faith cast my care upon thee.
> XII. Dispute between Alypius and Augustine concerning marriage and celibacy.

> 21. Alypius indeed forbade me to take a wife, saying * that in no way could we live together in secure leisure in the love of wisdom, as we had long desired, if I did so. For he himself was even then most chaste in that matter, so that it was wonderful; for he had acquired experience of intercourse at the beginning of his youth, but had not clung to it; rather, he had grieved over it and despised it, and thereafter lived most continently. But I resisted him with the examples of those who, being married, had cultivated wisdom, and had deserved well of God, and had faithfully possessed and loved friends. From whose greatness of spirit I myself was far distant: and bound * by the disease of the flesh with its deadly sweetness, I dragged my chain, fearing to be loosed, and, as though from a shaken wound, repelling the words of one who gave good counsel, as though they were the hand that would loose me.
Moreover, through me the serpent spoke to Alypius himself also, and through my tongue laid and scattered sweet snares in his path, by which his honorable and unencumbered feet might be entangled.

> 22. For when he, who did not think little of me, wondered that I should cling so to the birdlime of that pleasure, so that, whenever we discussed it together, I affirmed that I could in no way lead a celibate life; and when I saw him wondering, defended myself thus, saying that there was a great difference between that which he had experienced hurriedly and secretly, and which he perhaps scarcely even remembered by then, and therefore could easily despise without any trouble, and the delights of my habit; if to these the honorable name of marriage were added, he ought not to wonder why I was unable to despise that life: he too had begun to desire marriage, by no means conquered by lust for such pleasure, but by curiosity. For he said that he wished to know what that was without which my life, which pleased him so much, seemed to me not life but punishment.

For his mind, free from that bond, was amazed at my slavery; and, in being amazed, it passed into a desire of experiencing, about to come to the experience itself and perhaps then to fall into that slavery at which it wondered; since it wished to make a bargain with death ; and he who loves danger shall fall into it . For neither of us was led by whatever is the conjugal dignity in the duty of governing a marriage and receiving children, except slightly. But the habit of satisfying insatiable concupiscence tormented me, held captive, to a great degree and violently; while admiration drew him to be captured. Thus we were, until thou, O Most High, not forsaking our low estate, hadst pity on us miserable men and didst help us by wonderful and hidden ways.
> XIII. A wife is sought for Augustine.

> 23. And efforts were earnestly made that I should take a wife. I was already seeking one, one was already being promised, my mother especially taking pains that, once I was married, saving Baptism might wash me, as she rejoiced to see me being fitted for it day by day, and observed that her vows and thy promises were being fulfilled in my faith. And indeed, both at my request and out of her own desire, she daily begged thee with a strong cry of heart that thou wouldst show her something in a vision concerning my future marriage; but thou never wouldst. And she saw certain vain and phantasmal things, to which the impulse of a human spirit anxiously occupied with this matter compelled her; and she told them to me, not with the confidence she was accustomed to have when thou didst show them to her, but despising them. For she said that by some taste, which she could not explain in words, she discerned the difference between thee revealing and her own soul dreaming. Nevertheless efforts were made, and a girl was sought whose age was about two years less than marriageable; and because she pleased us, she was awaited.
> XIV. While he deliberates with his friends concerning a common life to be led.

> 24. And many friends had pondered in our minds, and, conversing and detesting the turbulent troubles of human life, had almost resolved to live in leisure, withdrawn from the crowds: arranging that leisure in this way, that if we could have anything, we would put it into a common fund and make one estate out of all; so that through the sincerity of friendship this should not be one man's and that another's, but what was made one out of all should be the whole possession of each, and all things should belong to all: since we seemed to ourselves able to be about ten men in the same association, and there were among us very wealthy men, especially Romanianus [149] our fellow citizen, whom at that time the heavy agitations of his affairs had drawn to the imperial court, a man most intimate with me from early youth; he especially urged this plan, and had great authority in recommending it, because his large estate far surpassed that of the others: and it pleased us that two yearly, as though magistrates, should manage all necessities, while the others remained at leisure.
But after it began
> Page 101

> to be considered whether the womenfolk would permit this, whom some of us already had and whom we wished to have, that whole plan which we were framing well * fell apart in our hands, and was broken up and cast aside. Then came sighs and groans * , and steps toward following Mat. 7, 13. the broad and well-trodden ways of the world, because there were many thoughts in our heart; Ps. 32, 11. but thy counsel abides for ever . By this counsel thou didst mock ours and prepare thine own, intending Ps. 144, 15. 16. to give us food in due season , and to open thy hand and fill our souls with blessing .
> XV. Another succeeds the departing concubine.

> 25. Meanwhile my sins were multiplied, and, when she with whom I was accustomed to lie was torn from my side as though an impediment to marriage, my heart, where it clung, was cut and wounded, and it drew blood. And she had returned to Africa, vowing to thee that she would know no other man, leaving with me my natural son by her. But I, unhappy, not even an imitator of the woman, impatient of delay, as though I were to receive after two years her whom I was seeking, because I was not a lover of marriage but a slave of lust, procured another, certainly not a wife: so that the disease of my soul, enduring through the attendant train of habit, might as it were be sustained and brought onward, either whole or increased, into the kingdom of marriage. Nor was that wound of mine healed which had been made by the cutting away of the former woman; but after its most acute heat and pain, it festered, and, as though more coldly, yet more desperately, it hurt [150] .
> XVI. He never laid aside the fear of death and judgment.

> 26. Praise to thee, glory to thee, fountain of mercies. I was becoming more miserable, and thou nearer.
