> He recalls before the eyes of his mind the beginning of his youth, that is, the thirty-first year of his age. He recounts that he was deeply struck by a certain argument of Nebridius, yet was still enveloped in thick darkness, since he could conceive of God only corporeally; he therefore clearly sees that the Manichaeans think impiously, but is altogether unable to embrace the faith of the Church; he is recalled from the errors of the Mathematicians; yet he is miserably tormented by the question, whence is evil? He profits greatly from the books of the Platonists, yet they do not suffice, since he had thought wrongly concerning Christ's incarnation; but when he takes up the Holy Scriptures, and especially the Apostle Paul, all his doubts collapse.
> I. He conceives of God as something corporeal, diffused through infinite spaces.

> 1. By now my evil and wicked adolescence was dead, and I was passing into youth—the greater I was in age, the more shameful in vanity. I could not conceive of any substance except such as is usually seen through these eyes; I did not conceive of thee * , O God, in the form of a human body: ever since I began to hear anything concerning wisdom, I had always shunned this; and I rejoiced that I had found this in the faith of our spiritual mother, thy Catholic Church. But what else I should conceive thee to be did not occur to me; and I tried to conceive thee, a man, and such a man, as the supreme and sole and true God! And with all my inmost being I believed thee incorruptible, inviolable, and unchangeable; for, though ignorant whence and how, I nevertheless plainly saw and was certain that that which can be corrupted is worse than that which cannot; and I unhesitatingly set that which cannot be violated above that which can be violated; and that which suffers no alteration through change to be better than that which can be changed.

My heart cried out violently against all my phantasms, and with this one blow I tried to drive away from the gaze of my mind the hovering throng of impurity; and scarcely had it been dispersed in the blink of an eye when, behold, it was again gathered together and present, and rushed upon my sight and clouded it: so that, although not in the form of a human body, I was nevertheless compelled to conceive something corporeal through spatial extension, whether infused into the world or even diffused outside the world through infinity—this very thing incorruptible and inviolable and unchangeable, which I set above the corruptible and violable and changeable. For whatever I Page 104 deprived of such spaces seemed to me not to exist: indeed, to be absolutely nothing, not even empty space; as if a body were removed from a place and the place remained void of every body, earthly and watery and airy and heavenly, but were still an empty place, as it were a spacious nothing.

> 2. Therefore I, thickened in heart and not even visible to myself [152] , judged that whatever was not extended or diffused or gathered into a mass or swollen through some spatial magnitude, or did not receive or could not receive something of that kind, was absolutely nothing. For through such forms as my eyes are wont to pass, through such images did my heart pass; nor did I see that this very act of attention, by which I formed those images themselves, was not something of that kind—though it would not form them unless it were something great. Thus I also conceived thee, the life of my life, as great, penetrating on every side through infinite spaces the whole mass of the world, and outside it in every direction through the boundless without limit; so that earth might contain thee, heaven might contain thee, all things might contain thee, and these might be bounded in thee, while thou nowhere wert bounded.

But as the body of this air which is above the earth would not obstruct the light of the sun so that it could not pass through it, penetrating it not by breaking or cutting it apart, but by filling it wholly: so I thought that not only the body of heaven and air and sea, but also that of earth, was pervious to thee and, in all its greatest and least parts, penetrable for receiving thy presence, secretly inspiring and administering within and without all things which thou hast created. Thus I supposed, because I could conceive nothing else; for it was false. For in that way a larger part of the earth would contain a larger part of thee, and a smaller part a smaller part; and thus all things would be full of thee, so that the body of an elephant would contain more of thee than that of a sparrow, because it is larger and occupies a larger place; and thus thou wouldst make thy parts present piecemeal to the parts of the world, great parts to great, short parts to short. But thou art not thus. Yet thou hadst not yet illumined my darkness.
> II. The argument by which Nebridius refuted the Manichaeans.

> 3. For this was enough for me, O Lord, against those deceived deceivers, and talkative mutes * , since thy word did not sound forth from them: enough, then, was that which Nebridius had long been accustomed to put forward from the time of Carthage, and by which all of us who had heard it were shaken [153] . What could some nation of darkness, which they are wont to set in opposition from an opposing mass, have done to thee, if thou hadst been unwilling to fight against it * ? For if it were answered that it could have done some harm, thou wouldst be violable and corruptible.

But if it were said that it could have done thee no harm, no cause for fighting would be alleged; and for fighting in such a manner that some portion of thee and member of thee, or offspring from thy very substance, should be mingled with adverse powers and natures not created by thee, and by them so far corrupted and changed for the worse as to be turned from blessedness into misery [154] , and to need aid whereby it could be rescued and cleansed: and that this should be the soul, to which thy Word would bring aid—free to one enslaved, pure to one defiled, whole to one corrupted; but itself also corruptible, because it is of one and the same substance. Therefore, if they should call thee—whatever thou art, that is, thy substance by which thou art—incorruptible, all those things would be false and accursed; but if corruptible, that very statement would already be false and, at its first utterance, abominable.

This, then, was enough against those who were in every way to be vomited forth from the pressure of my breast, because they had no way of escape without a horrible sacrilege of heart and tongue, in thinking and speaking such things concerning thee.
> III. Free choice is the cause of sin.

> 4. But although I still called, and firmly believed our Lord God true, uncontaminable and unchangeable, and in no respect mutable—thou who hast made not only our souls but also our bodies [155] , and not only our souls and bodies, but all souls and all things—I did not have the cause of evil explained * and untangled. Whatever it might be, however, I saw that it must be sought in such a way that by it I should not be compelled to believe the immutable God mutable, lest I myself become that which I was seeking. Therefore I sought it securely, and was certain that what those men said was not true, men whom I fled with my whole soul; for I saw that, in asking whence is evil, they were filled with the evil by which they supposed that thy substance suffered evil rather than that their own did evil [154] .
> Page 106

> 5. And I strove to discern what I heard: that the free choice of the will is the cause why we do evil, and thy right judgment the cause why we suffer [156] ; and I was unable to discern it clearly * . Therefore, when I tried to draw the gaze of my mind up from the deep, I was plunged down again; and when I tried often, I was plunged down again and again. For this raised me into thy light: that I knew myself to have a will just as surely as I knew myself to live. Thus, when I willed or did not will something, I was most certain that none but I willed and did not will; and there I was already beginning to perceive that the cause of my sin lay. But what I did unwillingly, I saw that I suffered rather than did; and I judged that this was not a fault but a punishment, by which, thinking thee just, I quickly confessed that I was not punished unjustly. But again I said: Who made me? Was it not my God, not merely good, but goodness itself? Whence then comes my willing evil and not willing good, so that there might be cause for me justly to pay penalties?

Who placed this in me and implanted in me this nursery of bitterness, when I was made wholly by my most sweet God? If the devil is its author, whence is the devil himself? And if he too by a perverse will was made a devil from a good angel, whence was there in him also an evil will whereby he might become a devil, when he had been made wholly an angel by the best Creator * ? By these thoughts I was again weighed down and suffocated; but I was not dragged down as far as that hell of error, where no one Ps. 6, 6. confesses thee, since thou art rather supposed to suffer evil than man to do evil.
> IV. God must be incorruptible.

> 6. For thus I strove to discover the rest, as I had already discovered that the incorruptible is better than the corruptible; and therefore I confessed thee, whatever thou wert, to be incorruptible. For no soul ever could or will be able to conceive anything better than thee, who art the highest and best good. But since the incorruptible is most truly and certainly set above the corruptible, as I had already set it above it, I could already by thought attain to something better than my God, unless thou wert incorruptible. Therefore, where I saw that the incorruptible must be preferred to the corruptible, there I ought to seek thee, and from there observe where * evil is, that is, whence corruption itself comes, by which thy substance can in no way be violated.

For corruption in absolutely no way violates our God: not by any will, not by any necessity, not by any unforeseen accident; because he is God, and what he wills for himself is good, and he himself is that very good. But to be corrupted is not good. Nor art thou compelled unwillingly to anything, because thy will is not greater than thy power. Yet it would be greater if thou thyself wert greater than thyself: for the will and power of God are God himself. And what can be unforeseen by thee who knowest all things, and no nature exists except because thou knowest it? And why say much as to why the substance which is God is not corruptible, when, if this were so, it would not be God?
> V. Again he asks whence evil is, and what its root is.

> 7. And I sought whence evil is, and I sought badly; and in my very inquiry I did not see evil. And before the sight of my spirit I set the whole creation, whatever we can discern in it: such as earth, sea, air, stars, trees, and other * mortal things; and whatever we do not see in it, such as the firmament of heaven, and besides all the Angels and all its spiritual things; but even these my imagination arranged in places and places, as though they were bodies: and I made thy creation into one great mass, distinguished by kinds of bodies * ; whether those things which were truly bodies, or those which I myself had imagined to be spirits. And I made it great, not as great as it was, which I could not know, but as great as I pleased—yet finite in every direction.

But thee, O Lord, I conceived as surrounding and penetrating it on every side, yet everywhere infinite: as though the sea were everywhere, and only sea, boundless on every side through immensity, and had within itself some sponge, however great yet finite; that sponge would surely be full, in every part of itself, from the boundless sea. Thus I thought thy finite creation full of thee, the infinite one, and said: Behold God, and behold what God has created; and God is good, and far more mighty and excellent than these; yet, being good, he created good things, and behold how he surrounds and fills them. Where then is evil, and whence is it, and by what means did it creep in here? What is its root, and what its seed? Or does it not exist at all? Why then do we fear and avoid what does not exist? Or if we fear in vain, surely fear itself is an evil, by which the heart is needlessly goaded and tortured; and an evil all the graver because there is nothing for us to fear, yet we fear.

Accordingly, either that which we fear is evil, or this is evil, that we fear. Whence, then, is it, since God made all these things, the good God good things? The greater indeed and highest good made lesser goods, yet both creator and created things are all good. Whence is evil? Or was there some evil matter from which he made them * , and did he form and order it, but leave something in it which he would not turn into good? Why this also? Or was he unable to turn and change it wholly, so that no evil might remain, though he is omnipotent? Finally, why did he wish to make something from it rather than, by that same omnipotence, make it so that it did not exist at all? Or could it exist against his will? Or if it was eternal, why did he permit it to be thus for so long through the infinite backward spaces of times, and only so much later pleased him to make something from it?

Or if he suddenly wished to do something, should not the omnipotent one rather have done this: that it should not exist, and that he alone should be the whole, true, highest, and infinite good? Or if it was not good that he, being good, should not also fashion * and create something good, then, after removing and reducing to nothing that matter which was evil, he should himself have established good matter from which to create all things. For he would not be omnipotent if he could not create something good without being assisted by matter which he had not himself created. Such thoughts I turned over in my wretched breast, made pregnant with the most biting anxieties from fear of death and from truth not found; yet the faith of thy Christ, our Lord and Savior, remained firmly fixed in my heart in the Catholic Church—still indeed in many respects unformed, and wandering beyond the norm of doctrine * , but my mind did not abandon it; rather, day by day it drank it in more and more.
> VI. He rejects the divinations of the Mathematicians.

> 8. By now I had also rejected the deceptive divinations of the astrologers and their impious ravings. From this source too may your mercies confess to you from the innermost recesses of my soul, O my God. For you—yes, you alone; for who else calls us back from the death of every error, except the life that knows not how to die, and the wisdom that enlightens needy minds while itself needing no light, by which the world is governed even to the fluttering leaves of trees?

You Page 109 brought this about for my stubbornness, by which I contended against Vindicianus, a sharp-witted old man, and Nebridius, a young man of remarkable soul: the former strongly affirming, the latter, though with some hesitation, nevertheless frequently saying, that that * was not an art of foreseeing the future; that human conjectures often have the force of chance, and that, by saying many things, most of the things to come are said, unbeknownst to those who say them, but are hit upon by their not keeping silent. Therefore you provided me with a friendly man, not indeed an idle consulter of astrologers, nor one well versed in those writings, but, as I said, a curious consulter, who nevertheless knew something which he said he had heard from his father, though he did not know * how much force it had for overthrowing the repute of that art.

This man, then, named Firminus, liberally educated and polished in speech, when he consulted me as one most dear to him concerning certain of his affairs, in which his worldly hope had swelled, as to what seemed to me according to his so-called constellations: I, however, who had now begun to incline toward Nebridius's opinion in this matter, did not indeed refuse to conjecture and say what occurred to me in my uncertainty; but I nonetheless added that I was now almost persuaded that those things were ridiculous and empty. Then he told me that his father had been a most eager student of books of that kind, and had had a friend who pursued these things equally and together with him; that with equal zeal and exchange they fanned the fire of their hearts toward those trifles * , so that, if any dumb animals were born at home, they would observe the moments of their birth also, and note the position of the sky corresponding to them, in order to collect proofs of that quasi-art.

And so he said that he had heard from his father that, when the mother of this same Firminus * was pregnant, a certain maidservant of that paternal friend's was likewise growing large with child; and this could not escape the master, who took care to know, with the most painstaking diligence, even the births of his female dogs. Thus it happened that, while the one counted the days and hours of his wife, and the other those of the slave woman, and the more minute divisions of the hours, with most careful observation, both gave birth at the same time; so that they were compelled to cast the same constellations, down to the same minutes, for each newborn—the one for his son, the other for his little slave. For when the women began to be in labor, both informed each other of what was happening in the house of each, and prepared persons to send to one another as soon as the birth each was bringing forth had been announced; and this, that it might be announced immediately, they easily brought about, as though in their own kingdom.

And so, he said, those sent by either party met one another Page 110 at such equal distances from their respective houses that neither was allowed to note another position of the stars or other portions of the moments. Yet Firminus, born to high standing among his own, ran along the brighter roads of the world, increased in wealth, and was raised to honours; whereas that slave, with the yoke of his condition not relaxed at all, served masters—as was reported by the very man who knew him.

> 9. When I had heard and believed these things—for one such as he had related them—my whole resistance dissolved and collapsed. First I tried to call Firminus himself back from that curiosity, saying that, if I inspected his constellations in order to pronounce truly * , I surely ought to see there parents pre-eminent among their own, a noble family in their native city, free birth, honourable upbringing, and liberal learning. But if that slave had consulted me from the same constellations, since they too were his, so that I might bring forth what was true for him as well, I ought in turn to see there a most lowly family, servile condition, and the rest, far different from the former things and far removed.

But how could it happen that, looking at the same things, I should say different things, if I spoke truly; whereas, if I said the same things, I should speak falsely? From this it is most certainly inferred * that things which are said truly, on considering constellations, are not said by art but by chance; while things said falsely are not due to the incompetence of art but to the falsehood of chance.

> 10. Having gained this opening * , as I turned such matters over with myself, lest any of those same madmen who pursued such a trade—whom I was now eager to assail and refute with ridicule—might resist me by saying that either Firminus or his father had told me falsehoods, I directed my consideration to those who are born twins. Most of these are brought forth one after another in such a way that the very small interval of time, however great a force they may claim it has in the nature of things, nevertheless cannot be grasped by human observation or marked at all in writings which the astrologer is to inspect in order to pronounce truly. And he will not pronounce truly, because, inspecting the same writings, he ought to say the same things of Esau and Jacob; yet the same things did not happen to both. Therefore he would speak falsely; or, if he spoke truly, he would not say the same things, while he would inspect the same things * . Therefore he would speak truth not by art but by chance.

For you, O Lord, most just Governor of the universe, act upon those who consult and those consulted, unaware, by a hidden prompting, so that while each person consults, he may hear Page 111 what he ought to hear according to the hidden deserts of souls, from the abyss of your just judgment; to which let no man say, “What is this?” or “Why this?” Let him not say it, let him not say it; for he is a man.
> VII. He is miserably tormented inquiring whence evil comes.

> 11. Therefore by now you, my helper, had loosed me from those bonds, and I was asking whence evil comes, and there was no way out. But you did not allow me to be carried away by any waves of thought from the faith by which I believed both that you exist, that your substance is unchangeable, that you have care and judgment concerning men, and that in Christ your Son, our Lord, and in the * Holy Scriptures commended by the authority of your Catholic Church, you had established a way of human salvation leading to that life which is to be after this death. With these things preserved and firmly established beyond shaking in my mind, I asked in my distress whence evil comes. What torments were those of my heart in labour! What groans, O my God! And there were your ears, though I did not know it. And when I searched steadfastly in silence, great cries to your mercy were the silent contritions of my soul. You knew what I suffered, and no human being did.

For how much of it was communicated through my tongue into the ears of my closest friends? Did the whole tumult of my soul, for which neither time nor my mouth sufficed, resound to them? Yet all that Ps. 37, 9-11. I roared from the groaning of my heart went into your hearing, and before you was my desire, and the light of my eyes was not with me . For it was within, but I was without. Nor was that in a place; but I fixed my attention upon things contained in places, and there I found no place to rest; nor did these things receive * me so that I might say, “It is enough, and it is well”; nor did they let me return where it would be sufficiently well with me. For I was above these things, but below you; and you are true joy for me when I am subject to you, and you had subjected to me the things you created beneath me. And this was the right ordering [157] , and the middle region of my salvation: that I might remain according to your image and, serving you, rule the body.

But when I rose proudly against you, Job 15, 26. and ran against the Lord with the thick neck of my shield , even these lowest things were set above me, and pressed upon me, and there was nowhere relief and Page 112 breathing-space. They themselves met my sight everywhere in heaps and masses; and when I thought, images of bodies confronted me as I returned, as though it were said: “Where are you going, unworthy and foul one?” And these had grown from my wound, because Ps. 88, 11 you humbled the proud one as wounded ; and by my swelling I was separated from you [158] , and my excessively puffed-up face closed my eyes.
> VIII. How divine mercy came to Augustine's aid.

> 12 . But you, O Lord, remain for ever, and you are not angry with us for ever; for you had pity on earth and ashes, and it pleased you in your sight to reform my deformities. And with inward goads you stirred me, that I might be impatient until you became certain to me through inward sight. My swelling subsided under the hidden hand of your healing, and the troubled and darkened vision of my mind was healed day by day by the sharp eye-salve of my salutary pains.
> IX. In the books of the Platonists he finds the divinity of the eternal Word, not the humility of the incarnate Word.

> 13. And first, wishing to show me how 1 Pet. 5, 5. Jac. 2, 6. you resist the proud but give grace to the humble , and how great was the mercy shown in your pointing out to men the way of humility, because your Word was made flesh and dwelt among men; through a certain man swollen with most monstrous pride, you procured for me certain books of the Platonists [159] translated from Greek into Latin. And there I read, though not in these words, but the very same thing being urged by many and manifold arguments, that Joh. 1, 1-5. in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: this was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made: what was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it .

And that although the soul of man bears witness concerning the light, it is not itself the light [160] ; but the Word, God, is the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world . And that Ver. 9-12. he was in this world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him . But that he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him; whereas to as many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name ; this I did not read there.

> 14. Likewise I read there that the Word, God, Ver. 13. was born not of flesh, not of blood, not of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God [161] . But that Ver. 14. the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us ; this I did not read there. For in those writings I traced out, diversely expressed and in many ways, that the Son is in the form of the Father, not judging equality with God to be robbery , because he is naturally the very same. But that Phil. 2, 6-11. he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross: wherefore God also exalted him from the dead, and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father ; those books do not contain.

For that your only-begotten Son, coeternal with you, remains unchangeably before all times and above all times, and that Joh. 1, 16. souls receive from his fullness in order that they may be blessed, and are renewed by participation in the wisdom abiding in itself in order that they may be wise: this is there. But that Rom. 5, 6. in due time he died for the ungodly ; and Rom. 8, 32. you did not spare your only Son, but delivered him up for us all ; this is not there. Mat. 11, 25. 28. 29. For you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones ; so that those who labour and are burdened might come to him, and he might refresh them, because he is meek and humble of heart , and Ps. 24, 9. 18. guides the meek in judgment and teaches the gentle his ways, seeing our humility and our travail and forgiving all our sins . But those who, lifted up by the buskin as by a loftier learning, do not hear him saying, Mat. 11, 29.

Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls : even if Rom. 1, 21. 22. they know God, they do not glorify him as Lord or give thanks; but they become vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart is darkened; for, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools .

> 15 . And therefore I read there Ver. 23. that even the glory of your incorruption was changed into idols and various images, into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed creatures, and serpents ; namely, Gen. 25, 33. 34. the Egyptian food [162] by which Esau lost his birthright: because the firstborn people honoured the head of a four-footed creature instead of you, Act. 7, 39. turning in heart toward Egypt , and bending your image, their soul, before Ex. 32, 1-6. and Ps. 105, 19. 20. the image of a calf eating hay . I found these things there, and I did not eat them. For it pleased you, O Lord, to take away the reproach of diminution from Jacob, so that Rom. 9, 13. the elder might serve the younger ; and you called the Gentiles into your inheritance. And I had come to you from among the Gentiles, and I fixed my attention on the gold which you willed [163] that your people should take away from Egypt, because it was yours wherever it was. Ex. 3, 22; and 11, 2.

And you said Page 115 to the Athenians through your Apostle that Act. 17, 28. in you we live and move and are; as some also among them have said : and assuredly those books came from there. And I did not attend to the idols of the Egyptians, to whom they ministered with your gold, who Rom. 1, 25. changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator .
> X. Divine things now become more clearly known to Augustine.

> 16. And thence admonished to return to myself, I entered into my inmost self, with you as guide; and I was able to do so, because you had become my helper. I entered, and with whatever eye of my soul I could, I saw above that same eye of my soul, above my mind, an * unchangeable light; not this ordinary light, conspicuous to all flesh [164]; nor was it, as it were, greater by being of the same kind, as though this light should shine much and much more brightly and occupy all things by its magnitude. It was not that, but something else, something altogether different from all these things. Nor was it above my mind as oil is above water, nor as heaven is above earth; but higher, because it itself made me, and I lower, because I was made by it. He who knows truth knows it; and he who knows it knows eternity. Charity knows it. O eternal truth, and true charity, and beloved eternity [165]! You are my God; for you I sigh day and night.

And when I first came to know you, you took me up, that I might see that which I saw, and that I was not yet that which saw. And you struck back the weakness of my sight, shining upon me vehemently, and I trembled with love and horror; and I found myself far from you in a region of dissimilarity [166], as though I heard your voice from on high: I am the food of the grown; grow, and you shall eat me. Nor will you change me into yourself, as the food of your flesh; but you shall be changed into me. And I knew that Ps. 38, 12. for iniquity you have chastened man, and made my soul waste away like a spider; and I said: Is truth perhaps nothing, because it is spread out neither through finite nor through infinite spaces of places? And you cried from afar: Nay indeed, Ex. 3, 14. I am who I am. And I heard as one hears in the heart, and there was altogether no ground for my doubting; and I would more easily doubt that I live than that truth is not, Rom. 1, 20.
which is perceived by the understanding through the things that have been made * .
> XI. How creatures are, and are not.

> 17. And I looked upon the other things beneath you, and saw that they neither altogether are nor altogether are not: they are indeed, because they are from you; but they are not, because they are not that which you are. For that truly is which remains unchangeably [167]. Ps. 72, 28. But for me it is good to cleave to God; for if I shall not remain in him, neither shall I be able to remain in myself. But he, Sap. 7, 27. remaining in himself, renews all things. And Ps. 15, 2. You are my God, because you have no need of my goods.
> XII. All things whatsoever are good.

> 18. And it is manifest to me that the things which are corrupted are good, things which could not be corrupted either if they were supreme goods, or unless they were good: for if they were supreme goods, they would be incorruptible; but if they were no goods at all, there would be nothing in them that could be corrupted. For corruption harms; and unless it diminished good, it would not harm. Therefore either corruption harms nothing—which cannot be—or, what is most certain, all things that are corrupted are deprived of good. But if they are deprived of every good, they will not be at all. For if they shall be, and can no longer be corrupted, they were better, because they will remain incorruptibly. And what could be more monstrous than to say that, having lost every good, they have become better? Therefore, if they are deprived of every good, they will be nothing at all: therefore, as long as they are, they are good: therefore, whatever things are, are good. And that evil which I was seeking, whence it was, is not a substance; for if it were a substance, it would be good.

For it would either be an incorruptible substance, certainly a great good; or it would be a corruptible substance, which could not be corrupted unless it were good. Accordingly I saw, and it was made manifest to me, that you made all things good, and that there are absolutely no substances which you did not make. And because you did not make all things equal, therefore all things are [168]; because individual things are good Page 117 and all things together are very good: because Gen. 1. and Eccli. 39, 21. our God made all things very good.
> XIII. All created things praise God.

> 19. And to you there is utterly no evil, not only to you, but not even to your whole creation; because outside * there is nothing that can break in and corrupt the order which you have imposed upon it. But among its parts, some things, because they do not fit with certain others, are thought evil; yet these same things fit with others [169], and are good, and are good in themselves. And all these things which do not fit mutually with one another fit with the lower part of things, which we call earth, having its own cloudy and windy heaven suited to itself. And far be it from me now to say, Let these things not be *! For even if I perceived these alone, I should indeed desire better things; but even from these alone I ought to praise you, because they show you to be praiseworthy, Ps. 148, 1-12.

from the earth, dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit of tempest, which do your word, mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged fowls; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men with the younger praise your name. And when they praise you also from the heavens, let them praise you, our God, in the heights—all your Angels, all your Powers, sun and moon, all stars and light, heavens of heavens and waters which are above the heavens, let them praise your name: I no longer desired better things, because I considered all things; and, with sounder judgment, I judged all things together better than the higher things alone, although the higher are better than the lower.
> XIV. To a man of sound mind, nothing among God's creatures is displeasing.

> 20. There is no soundness in those to whom anything of your creation is displeasing, just as there was none in me when many things which you made displeased me. And because my soul did not dare that my God should displease it, whatever displeased it, it did not wish to be yours. And from this it had gone into the opinion of two substances, and did not rest, and spoke of alien things. And returning from this, it had made for itself a God through infinite spaces of all places, and had thought him to be you; and it had placed him in its heart, and had again become the temple of its idol, abominable to you. But after you had cherished the head of one who did not know, and had shut Ps. 118, 37. my eyes lest they should see vanity, I rested a little from myself, and my madness was lulled to sleep; and I awoke in you, and saw you as infinite in another way; and this sight was not drawn from the flesh.
> Page 118
> XV. How there is truth and falsity in creatures.

> 21. And I looked upon other things, and saw that they owe it to you that they are, and that all things are bounded in you; but otherwise, not as though in a place, but because you hold all things by the hand of truth; and all things are true insofar as they are; nor is anything falsity, except when that which is not is thought to be. And I saw that each thing is fitting not only in its own place, but also in its own time; and that you, who alone are eternal, did not begin to work after innumerable spaces of times; because all spaces of times, both those which have passed and those which will pass, would neither depart nor come unless you were working and remaining [170].
> XVI. All things are good, though not suited to some.

> 22. And I learned by experience that it is not strange that bread, which is sweet to a healthy palate, is a punishment to one that is not healthy; and that light, which is pleasing to pure eyes, is hateful to diseased ones. And your justice displeases the unjust—not to mention a viper and a little worm, which you created good, suited to the lower parts of your creation; to which the unjust themselves also are suited, the more unlike they are to you; but they are suited to the higher things insofar as they become more like you. And I sought what iniquity was, and found not a substance, but the perversity of a will twisted away from the highest substance, you, O God, casting its inmost parts away into the lowest things * , Eccli. 10, 10. and swelling outward.
> XVII. What things delay one from the knowledge of divine things.

> 23. And I wondered that I now loved you, not a phantom in your stead. Yet I did not stand firm * to enjoy my God, but was snatched up to you by your beauty, and soon was torn away from you by my own weight, and fell headlong into these things with groaning; and this weight was carnal habit. But the memory of you was with me, and I by no means doubted that there was one to whom I ought to cleave, but that I was not yet one who cleaved: Sap. 9, 15. because the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the sense that thinks many things. And I was most certain that Rom. 1, 20. your invisible things, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the understanding through the things that have been made; even your everlasting power and divinity.

For, seeking whence I approved the beauty of bodies, whether heavenly or earthly, and what was at hand for me in judging soundly concerning mutable things and saying, This ought to be so, that not so—for, seeking this, whence I judged when I so judged, I had found the unchangeable and true eternity of truth above my mutable mind. And thus, step by step, from bodies to the soul that senses through the body; and thence to its inner power, to which bodily sense reports external things, as far as beasts are able; and thence again to the reasoning power, to which is referred for judgment that which is received from the bodily senses.

This power, finding itself also mutable in me, raised itself to its own understanding; and withdrew thought from habit, removing itself from the clamorous crowds of phantasms [172], in order that it might find by what light it was sprinkled [173], when it cried out without any doubt that the unchangeable must be preferred to the changeable; whence it might know the unchangeable itself, which, unless it knew it in some way, it would in no way certainly prefer to the changeable. And it came * to that which is, in the flash of a trembling glance. Then indeed I perceived your invisible things by the understanding through the things that have been made; but I was unable * to fix my gaze; and, struck back by my weakness, I returned to familiar things, bearing with me only a loving memory, and, as it were, desiring by smell things which I was not yet able to eat.
> XVIII. Christ alone is the way to salvation.

> 24. And I sought a way of acquiring strength that would be fit to enjoy you; and I did not find it until I embraced 1 Tim. 2, 5. the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, Rom. 9, 5. who is God over all, blessed for ever, calling and saying, Jo. 14, 6. I am the way, and the truth, and the life; and mingling with flesh the food which I was too weak to receive; because Jo. 1, 14. the Word was made flesh, so that your wisdom, through which you created all things, might become milk for our infancy. For I did not yet hold my Lord Jesus, the humble one humbly; nor did I know of what thing his weakness was the teacher.

For your Word, eternal Truth, towering above the higher parts of your creation, raises to itself those subject to it; but among the lower parts it built for itself a humble house from our clay, through which it might bring low from themselves those who were to be made subject, and transfer them to itself, healing their swelling and nourishing love; lest, trusting in themselves, they should proceed farther, but rather should become weak when they saw before their feet a weak divinity through participation in our garment of skin, Gen. 3. 21. [175] and, wearied, should cast themselves down upon it, while it, rising, would lift them up.
> XIX. What he thought concerning Christ's incarnation.

> 25. But I thought otherwise, and I conceived of my Lord Christ only so much as I would of a man of outstanding wisdom, to whom none could be compared; especially because, having been wondrously born of a virgin, he seemed, by divine care on our behalf, to have deserved so great an authority of teaching, as an example of temporal things to be despised for the attaining of immortality. But what mystery the Word made flesh, Jo. 1, 14. contained, I could not even suspect. I had learned only from what was handed down as written concerning him that he ate and drank, slept, walked, rejoiced, was saddened, and conversed; that that flesh did not adhere to your Word except together with a human soul and mind. Everyone knows this who knows the unchangeableness of your Word, which I now knew, as far as I was able; nor did I at all doubt anything about it.

For now to move the limbs of the body by the will, now not to move them; now to be affected by some emotion, now not to be affected; now to utter wise sayings by signs, now to be silent: these are proper to the mutability of soul and mind. If these things had been falsely written concerning him, all things would also be endangered by falsehood, nor would any salvation of faith remain for the human race in those Scriptures. Therefore, since they are written truly, I acknowledged the whole man [176] in Christ: not merely a human body, or a soul without mind with a body *, but the very man. Yet I judged him to be set above the rest, not by the person of Truth, but by some great excellence of human nature and a more perfect participation in wisdom. Alypius, however, thought that Catholics believed God to be clothed in flesh in such a way that, besides God and flesh, there was no soul in Christ; and he did not think that a human mind was proclaimed to be in him.

And because he held as well established that the things committed to memory concerning him could not occur without a living and rational creature, he was slower to be moved toward the Christian faith itself. But later, recognizing this to be the error of the Apollinarian heretics [177], he rejoiced in and was brought into harmony with the Catholic faith. I, however, confess that somewhat later I learned, in the matter that the Word was made flesh, how Catholic truth is distinguished from the falsehood of Photinus [178]. For the refutation of heretics makes conspicuous what your Church thinks and what sound doctrine contains. For there had to be heresies also, so that those who are approved might become manifest among the weak. 1 Cor. 11, 19.
> XX. Through the Platonic books he became more learned, but more puffed up.

> 26. But then, having read those books of the Platonists, after being admonished by them to seek incorporeal truth, I perceived your invisible things, understood through the things that are made; and, repulsed, I felt what I was not permitted to contemplate through the darkness of my soul: being certain that you are, and are infinite, yet not diffused through finite or infinite places; and that you truly are, who would always be the same [179], in no part and by no motion otherwise or otherwise; while all other things are from you—by this one most firm proof, that they are. In these matters I was indeed certain, but far too weak to enjoy you. I plainly talked as though learned; and unless I sought your way in Christ our Savior, I would be not learned but lost. For I had already begun to wish to seem wise, full of my punishment; and I did not weep, but moreover was puffed up with knowledge. 1 Cor. 8, 1. Page 122 Where, indeed, was that 1 Cor. 3, 11.

charity building upon the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus? Or when would those books teach me that? I believe that for this reason you willed that I should fall upon them before I considered your Scriptures: so that how I had been affected by them might be impressed upon my memory; and so that, when afterward I had been softened in your Books and my wounds were handled by your healing fingers, I might discern and distinguish what difference there is between presumption and confession; between those who see where one must go but do not see by what way, and the way [180] leading to the blessed fatherland, not only to be seen but also to be inhabited.

For if I had first been formed by your holy Scriptures and, in familiarity with them, you had grown sweet to me, and afterward I had fallen upon those volumes, perhaps they would have torn me away from the foundation of piety; or, if I had persisted in the wholesome affection which I had imbibed, I might have thought that the same could be conceived from those books if someone had learned them alone.
> XXI. What he found in the sacred Books which was not found in the Platonic ones.

> 27. Therefore I seized most eagerly upon the venerable style of your Spirit, and above all upon the apostle Paul; and those questions perished in which he had at one time seemed to me to contradict himself, and the tenor of his discourse not to agree with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets. And there appeared to me one face of the chaste utterances, and I learned to rejoice with trembling. Ps. 2, 11. And I began *, and I found that whatever truth I had read there was said here together with the commendation of your grace [181]; so that one who sees may not glory as though he had not received, 1 Cor. 4, 7. not only what he sees, but also that he may see—for what has he that he has not received?—and so that he may be admonished not only to see you, who are ever the same, but also be healed so as to hold you; and so that one who cannot see from afar may nevertheless walk by the way by which he may come, and see, and hold; because, although Rom. 7, 22. 23.

the man delights in the law of God according to the inner man, what shall he do with the other law in his members, warring against the law of his mind and leading him captive in the law of sin which is in his members? For you are just, O Lord; but we have sinned, acted unjustly, behaved impiously, Dan. 3, 27-32. and your hand has weighed heavily upon us; and we have justly been delivered over to the ancient sinner, the ruler of death, because he persuaded our will into the likeness of his own will, by which he did not stand in your truth. Joh. 8, 44. What shall miserable man do? Who will deliver him from this body of death, Rom. 7, 24. 25. unless it be your grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom you begot coeternal and created in the beginning of your ways, Prov. 8, 22. in whom the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, Joh. 14, 30. and killed him; and the handwriting that was contrary to us was made void? Col. 2, 14. Those writings do not contain this.

Those pages do not contain the countenance of this piety, the tears of confession, your sacrifice, a troubled spirit, a contrite and humbled heart, Ps. 50, 19. the salvation of the people, the bride-city, Apoc. 21, 2. the pledge of the Holy Spirit, 2 Cor. 5, 5. the cup of our price. No one there sings: Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he himself is my God and my savior; my protector, I shall not be moved any more. Ps. 61, 2. 3. No one there hears him calling: Come to me, all who labor. Mat. 11, 28. 29. 25. They disdain to learn from him because he is meek and humble of heart. For you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones. And it is one thing to see from a wooded summit the fatherland of peace, Deut. 32, 49. and not find the way to it, and vainly endeavor through trackless places, while fugitive deserters beset and lie in ambush all around, with their prince, the lion and dragon; Ps. 90, 13.

and another thing to hold the way leading thither, fortified by the court * of the heavenly Emperor, where those who deserted the heavenly soldiery do not commit robbery; for they avoid it as punishment. These things were wondrously fixed in my inmost parts when I read the least of your Apostles, 1 Cor. 15, 9. [182] and considered your works, and was afraid.
> Page 125

sources.title: BOOK VIII.
sources.text:
> Vitæ ipsius partem attingit celeberrimam, annum ætatis trigesimum secundum, quo nempe cum Simplicianum consuluisset, audita ab eo Victorini conversione, ad imitandum exarsit. Tum vero, iis quæ de Antonio Æygptio monacho et duorum aulicorum conversione a Pontitiano didicit, magis magisque accensus, post vehementem luctam inter carnem et spiritum, codicem Apostoli cœlesti admonitus oraculo inspexit; lectoque qui ipsi primus occurrit versiculo, omnino immutatur, et diruptis cupiditatum vinculis totus ad Deum convertitur.

> I. Studio vitæ melius instituendæ ad Simplicianum ire statuit.

> 1. Deus meus, recorder in gratiarum actione tibi, et confitear misericordias tuas super me. Perfundantur ossa mea dilectione tua * , et dicant: Ps. 34, 10. Domine, quis similis tibi? Dirupisti vincula mea, Ps. 115, 17. sacrificem tibi sacrificium laudis. Quomodo dirupisti ea, narrabo; et dicent omnes qui adorant te, cum audiunt hæc: Benedictus Dominus in cœlo et in terra; magnum et mirabile nomen ejus. Inhæserant præcordiis meis verba tua, et Job 1, 10. undique circumvallabar abs te . De vita tua æterna certus eram: quamvis eam 1 Cor. 13, 12. in ænigmate et quasi per speculum videram ; dubitatio tamen omnis de incorruptibili substantia, quod ab illa esset omnis substantia, ablata mihi erat: nec certior de te, sed stabilior in te esse cupiebam. De mea vero temporali vita nutabant omnia, et Ib. 5, 7. mundandum erat cor a fermento veteri ; et placebat via ipse Salvator, et ire per ejus angustias adhuc pigebat. Et immisisti in mentem meam, visumque est bonum in conspectu meo pergere ad Simplicianum qui mihi bonus apparebat servus tuus, et lucebat in eo gratia tua. Audieram etiam quod a juventute sua devotissime tibi viveret: jam vero tunc senuerat, et longa ætate in tam bono studio sectandæ viæ tuæ, multa expertus, multa edoctus mihi videbatur; et vere sic erat. Unde mihi ut proferret volebam, conferenti secum æstus meos, quis esset aptus modus sic affecto, ut ego eram, ad ambulandum in via tua. Page 126

> 2. Videbam enim plenam Ecclesiam; et alius sic ibat, alius autem sic. Mihi autem displicebat quod agebam in sæculo, et oneri mihi erat valde, non jam inflammantibus cupiditatibus, ut solebant, spe honoris et pecuniæ, ad tolerandam illam servitutem tam gravem. Jam enim me illa non delectabant præ dulcedine tua et Ps. 25, 8. decore domus tuæ quam dilexi ; sed adhuc tenaciter colligabar ex femina: nec me prohibebat Apostolus conjugari, quamvis exhortaretur ad melius, maxime volens omnes homines 1 Cor. 7. sic esse ut ipse erat . Sed ego infirmior eligebam molliorem locum: et propter hoc unum volvebar in cæteris languidus, et tabescens curis marcidis, quod * et in aliis rebus quas nolebam pati, congruere cogebar vitæ conjugali, cui deditus obstringebar. Audieram ex ore Veritatis, esse Mat. 19, 12. spadones qui seipsos absciderunt propter regnum cœlorum ; sed, Qui potest , inquit, capere, capiat . Sap. 13, 1. Vani sunt certe omnes homines quibus non inest Dei scientia; nec de his quæ videntur bona, potuerunt invenire eum qui est. At ego jam non eram in illa vanitate: transcenderam eam; et contestante universa creatura tua [183] , inveneram te creatorem nostrum, et Verbum tuum apud te Deum, tecumque * unum Deum, per quod creasti omnia. Et est aliud genus impiorum, qui cognoscentes Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt . In hoc quoque incideram; et Ps. 17, 36. dextera tua suscepit me , et inde ablatum posuisti ubi convalescerem, quia dixisti homini: Job 28, 28. Ecce pietas est sapientia ; et, Prov. 3, 7. Noli velle videre sapiens ; quoniam Rom. 1. 21, 22. dicentes se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt . Et Mat. 13, 46. inveneram jam bonam margaritam ; et venditis omnibus quæ haberem, emenda erat, et dubitabam.

> II. De Victorino rhetore converso.

> 3. Perrexi ergo ad Simplicianum [184] , patrem in accipienda gratia* tua tunc [185] episcopi Ambrosii*, et quem vere ut patrem Page 127 diligebat. Narravi ei circuitus erroris mei. Ubi autem commemoravi legisse me quosdam libros Platonicorum, quos Victorinus quondam rhetor urbis Romæ, quem Christianum defunctum esse audieram, in Latinam linguam transtulisset; gratulatus est mihi quod non in aliorum philosophorum scripta incidissem, plena fallaciarum et deceptionum Col. 2, 8. secundum elementa hujus mundi : in istis autem, omnibus modis insinuari Deum et ejus Verbum [186] . Deinde, ut me exhortaretur ad humilitatem Christi, Mat. 11, 25. sapientibus absconditam et revelatam parvulis , Victorinum [187] ipsum recordatus est, quem, Romæ cum esset, familiarissime noverat: de quo ille mihi narravit quod non silebo. Habet enim magnam laudem gratiæ tuæ confitendam tibi, quemadmodum ille doctissimus senex, et omnium liberalium doctrinarum peritissimus, quique philosophorum tam multa legerat, et dijudicaverat * ; doctor tot nobilium senatorum, qui etiam ob insigne præclari magisterii, quod cives hujus mundi eximium putant, statuam in Romano foro meruerat et acceperat; usque ad illam ætatem venerator idolorum, sacrorumque sacrilegorum particeps, quibus tunc tota fere Romana nobilitas inflata inspirabat populos jam et omnigenum deum monstra * , et Anubem latratorem, quæ aliquando "Contra Neptunum et Venerem, contraque Minervam" tela tenuerant [188] , et a se victis jam Roma supplicabat [189] ; quæ ista senex Victorinus tot annos ore terricrepo defensitaverat: non erubuerit esse puer Christi tui, et infans fontis tui, subjecto collo ad humilitatis jugum, et edomita fronte ad crucis opprobrium.

> Page 128

> 4. O Domine, Domine, qui Ps. 143, 5. inclinasti cœlos, et descendisti; tetigisti montes, et fumigaverunt : quibus modis te insinuasti illi pectori? Legebat, sicut ait Simplicianus, sanctam Scripturam, omnesque Christianas litteras investigabat studiosissime et perscrutabatur; et dicebat Simpliciano non palam, sed secretius et familiarius: "Noveris me Christianum jam esse." Et respondebat ille: "Non credam, nec deputabo te inter Christianos, nisi in ecclesia Christi videro." Ille autem irridebat dicens: "Ergo parietes faciunt Christianos?" Et hoc sæpe dicebat, jam se esse Christianum; et Simplicianus illud sæpe respondebat, et sæpe ab illo parietum irrisio repetebatur. Amicos enim suos reverebatur offendere superbos dæmonicolas, quorum ex culmine Babylonicæ dignitatis, quasi ex Ps. 28, 5. cedris Libani quas nondum contriverat Dominus, graviter ruituras in se inimicitias arbitrabatur. Mat. 10. 33. Luc. 9, 26. Sed posteaquam legendo et inhiando hausit firmitatem, timuitque negari a Christo coram Angelis sanctis, si eum timeret coram hominibus confiteri, reusque sibi magni criminis apparuit erubescendo de sacramentis humilitatis Verbi tui, et non erubescendo de sacris sacrilegis superborum dæmoniorum, quæ imitator superbus acceperat; depuduit vanitati, et erubuit veritati, subitoque et inopinatus ait Simpliciano, ut ipse narrabat: "Eamus in ecclesiam; Christianus volo fieri." At ille non se capiens lætitia, perrexit cum eo. Ubi autem imbutus est primis instructionum sacramentis, non multo post etiam nomen dedit, ut per Baptismum regeneraretur, mirante Roma, gaudente Ecclesia. Superbi Ps. 111, 10. videbant, et irascebantur; dentibus suis stridebant, et tabescebant : servo autem tuo * Ps. 39, 5. Dominus Deus erat spes ejus , et non respiciebat in vanitates et insanias mendaces .

> 5. Denique, ut ventum est ad horam profitendæ fidei, quæ verbis certis conceptis, retentisque memoriter, de loco eminentiore in conspectu populi fidelis Romæ reddi [190] solet ab eis qui Page 129 accessuri sunt ad gratiam tuam, oblatum esse dicebat Victorino a presbyteris ut secretius redderet, sicut nonnullis qui verecundia trepidaturi videbantur offerri mos erat; illum autem maluisse salutem suam in conspectu sanctæ multitudinis profiteri. Non enim erat salus quam docebat in rhetorica, et tamen eam publice professus erat. Quanto minus ergo vereri debuit mansuetum gregem tuum pronuntians verbum tuum, qui non verebatur in verbis suis turbas insanorum? Itaque ubi ascendit ut redderet, omnes sibimet invicem, quisque ut eum noverant, instrepuerunt nomen ejus strepitu gratulationis. Quis autem ibi non eum noverat? Et sonuit presso sonitu per ora cunctorum collætantium: Victorinus, Victorinus! Cito sonuerunt exsultatione, quia videbant eum; et cito siluerunt intentione, ut audirent eum. Pronuntiavit ille fidem veracem præclara fiducia, et volebant omnes eum rapere intro in cor suum; et rapiebant amando et gaudendo: hæ rapientium manus erant.

> III. Quod Deus et Angeli magis gaudent in peccatorum conversione.

> 6. Deus bone, quid agitur in homine, ut plus gaudeat de salute desperatæ animæ, et de majore periculo liberatæ, quam si spes ei semper affuisset, aut periculum minus fuisset? Etenim tu quoque, misericors Pater, plus gaudes Luc. 15. de uno pœnitente, quam de nonaginta novem justis, quibus non opus est pœnitentia . Et nos cum magna jucunditate audimus, cum audimus quam exsultantibus * pastoris humeris reportetur ovis quæ erraverat; et drachma referatur in thesauros tuos, collætantibus vicinis mulieri quæ invenit: et lacrymas excutit gaudium solemnitatis domus tuæ, cum legitur in domo tua de minore filio tuo, Quoniam mortuus erat, et revixit; perierat, et inventus est. Gaudes quippe in nobis, et in Angelis tuis sancta charitate sanctis. Nam tu semper idem, Page 130 quia quæ non semper nec eodem modo sunt, eodem modo semper nosti omnia.

> 7. Quid ergo agitur in anima, cum amplius delectatur inventis aut redditis rebus quas diligit, quam si eas semper habuisset? Contestantur enim et cætera, et plena sunt omnia testimoniis clamantibus, Ita est. Triumphat victor imperator, et non vicisset, nisi pugnavisset; et quanto majus periculum fuit in prælio, tanto est gaudium majus in triumpho. Jactat tempestas navigantes, minaturque naufragium; omnes futura morte pallescunt: tranquillatur cœlum et mare, et exsultant nimis, quoniam timuerunt nimis. Æger est charus, et vena ejus malum renuntiat; omnes qui eum salvum cupiunt, ægrotant simul animo: fit ei recte, et nondum ambulat pristinis viribus; et fit tale jam gaudium, quale non fuit cum antea salvus et fortis ambularet. Easque ipsas voluptates humanæ vitæ etiam non inopinatis et præter voluntatem irruentibus, sed institutis et voluptariis * molestiis homines acquirunt. Edendi et bibendi voluptas nulla est, nisi præcedat esuriendi et sitiendi molestia. Et ebriosi quædam salsiuscula comedunt, quo fiat molestus ardor, quem dum exstinguit potatio, fit delectatio. Et institutum est ut jam pactæ sponsæ non tradantur statim, ne vilem habeat maritus datam, quam non suspiraverit sponsus dilatam.

> 8. Hoc in turpi et exsecranda lætitia; hoc in ea quæ concessa et licita est; hoc in ipsa sincerissima honestate amicitiæ: hoc in eo qui Luc. 15, 32. mortuus erat, et revixit: perierat, et inventus est . Ubique majus gaudium molestia majori præceditur. Quid est hoc, Domine Deus meus, cum tu æternum tibi tu ipse sis gaudium, et quædam de te circa te semper gaudeant [191] ? Quid est quod hæc rerum pars alternat defectu et profectu, offensionibus et conciliationibus? An is est modus earum; et tantum dedisti eis, cum a summis cœlorum usque ad ima terrarum, ab initio usque in finem sæculorum, ab angelo usque ad vermiculum, a motu primo usque ad extremum, omnia genera bonorum, et omnia justa opera tua, suis quæque sedibus locares, et suis quæque temporibus ageres? Heu mihi, quam excelsus es in excelsis, et quam profundus in profundis! et nusquam recedis, et vix redimus ad te.

> Page 131

> IV. Quare plus lætandum sit in conversione nobilium.

> 9. Age, Domine, fac; excita, et revoca nos; accende, et rape; flagra, dulcesce: jam amemus, et curramus. Nonne multi ex profundiore tartaro cæcitatis quam Victorinus, redeunt ad te, et accedunt, et illuminantur recipientes lumen, quod si qui recipiunt, accipiunt a te Joh. 1, 9. 12. potestatem ut filii tui fiant ? Sed si minus noti sunt populis, minus de illis gaudent etiam qui noverunt eos. Quando enim cum multis gaudetur, et in singulis uberius est gaudium, quia fervefaciunt se, et inflammantur ex alterutro. Deinde, quod multis noti, multis sunt auctoritati ad salutem, et multis præeunt secuturis. Ideoque multum de illis et qui eos præcesserunt lætantur, quia non de solis lætantur. Absit enim ut in tabernaculo tuo præ pauperibus accipiantur personæ divitum, aut præ ignobilibus nobiles: quando potius 1 Cor. 1, 27. 28. infirma mundi elegisti ut confunderes fortia; et ignobilia hujus mundi elegisti et contemptibilia, et ea quæ non sunt, tanquam quæ * sint, ut ea quæ sunt evacuares . Et tamen idem ipse Id. 15, 9. minimus Apostolorum tuorum, per cujus linguam tua ista verba sonuisti, cum Paulus proconsul, per ejus militiam debellata superbia, sub lene jugum Christi tui missus esset, regis magni provincialis effectus; Act. 13, 7. l2. ipse quoque ex priore Saulo Paulus vocari amavit, ob tam magnæ * insigne victoriæ [192] . Plus enim hostis vincitur in eo quem plus tenet, de quo plures tenet. Plus autem superbos tenet nomine nobilitatis, et de his plures nomine auctoritatis. Quanto igitur gratius cogitabatur * Victorini pectus, quod tanquam inexpugnabile receptaculum diabolus obtinuerat, Victorini lingua, quo telo grandi et acuto multos peremerat; tanto abundantius exsultare oportuit filios tuos, quia Rex noster Mat. 12, 29. alligavit fortem , et videbant vasa ejus erepta mundari , et aptari in honorem tuum, et fieri 2 Tim. 2, 21. utilia Domino ad omne opus bonum .

> V. Quæ remorabantur eum a conversione.

> 10. Sed ubi mihi homo tuus Simplicianus de Victorino ista narravit, exarsi ad imitandum: ad hoc enim et ille narraverat. Posteaquam vero et illud addidit, quod imperatoris Juliani Page 132 temporibus lege data prohibiti sunt Christiani docere litteraturam et oratoriam; quam legem ille amplexus, loquacem scholam deserere maluit, quam verbum tuum, quo Sap. 10, 21. linguas infantium facis disertas : non mihi fortior quam felicior visus est, quia invenit occasionem vacandi tibi. Cui rei ego suspirabam ligatus, non ferro alieno, sed mea ferrea voluntate. Velle meum tenebat inimicus, et inde mihi catenam fecerat, et constrinxerat me. Quippe ex voluntate perversa, facta est libido: et dum servitur libidini, facta est consuetudo; et dum consuetudini non resistitur, facta est necessitas. Quibus quasi ansulis sibimet innexis, unde catenam appellavi, tenebat me obstrictum dura servitus. Voluntas autem nova quæ mihi esse cœperat ut te gratis colerem, fruique te vellem, Deus, sola jucunditas certa, nondum erat idonea ad superandam priorem vetustate roboratam. Ita duæ voluntates meæ, una vetus, alia nova, illa carnalis, illa spiritualis, confligebant inter se, atque discordando dissipabant animam meam.

> 11. Sic intelligebam, meipso experimento * , id quod legeram, quomodo Gal. 5, 17. caro concupisceret adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem . Ego quidem in utroque [193] ; sed magis ego in eo quod in me approbabam, quam in eo quod in me improbabam. Ibi enim magis jam non ego; quia ex magna parte id patiebar invitus, quam faciebam volens * . Sed tamen consuetudo adversus me pugnacior ex me facta erat, quoniam volens, quo nollem, perveneram. Et quis jure contradiceret, cum peccantem justa pœna sequeretur? [194] Et non erat jam illa excusatio * , qua videri mihi solebam propterea me nondum contempto sæculo servire tibi, quia incerta mihi esset perceptio veritatis: jam enim et ipsa certa erat. Ego autem adhuc terra obligatus, militare tibi recusabam; et impedimentis omnibus sic timebam expediri, quemadmodum impediri timendum est.

> 12. Ita sarcina sæculi, velut somno assolet, dulciter premebar; et cogitationes quibus meditabar in te, similes erant conatibus expergisci volentium, qui tamen superati soporis Page 133 altitudine remerguntur. Et sicut nemo est qui dormire semper velit, omniumque sano judicio vigilare præstat; differt tamen plerumque homo somnum excutere, cum gravis torpor in membris est; eumque jam displicentem carpit libentius, quamvis surgendi tempus advenerit: ita certum habebam esse melius tuæ charitati me dedere, quam meæ cupiditati cedere; sed illud placebat, et vincebat * ; hoc libebat et vinciebat. Non enim erat quod tibi responderem dicenti mihi, Eph. 5, 14. Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis; et illuminabit te Christus : et undique ostendenti vera te dicere, non erat omnino quid responderem veritate convictus, nisi tantum verba lenta et somnolenta: Modo, ecce modo; sine paululum. Sed, Modo, et modo, non habebant modum; et, Sine paululum, in longum ibat. Frustra Rom. 7, 22-25. condelectabar legi tuæ secundum interiorem hominem, cum alia lex in membris meis repugnaret legi mentis meæ, et captivum me duceret in lege peccati, quæ in membris meis erat . Lex enim peccati est violentia consuetudinis, qua trahitur et tenetur etiam invitus animus, eo merito quo in eam volens illabitur. Miserum ergo me quis liberaret de corpore mortis hujus, nisi gratia tua per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum ?

> VI. Pontitianus narrat Antonii vitam.

> 13. Et de vinculo quidem desiderii concubitus quo arctissimo tenebar, et sæcularium negotiorum servitute, quemadmodum me exemeris, narrabo, et confitebor nomini tuo, Ps. 18, 15. Domine, adjutor meus et redemptor meus . Agebam solita, crescente anxietudine, et quotidie suspirabam tibi; frequentabam ecclesiam tuam, quantum vacabat ab eis negotiis sub quorum pondere gemebam * . Mecum erat Alypius otiosus ab opere jurisperitorum post assessionem tertiam, exspectans quibus iterum consilia venderet, sicut ego vendebam dicendi facultatem, si qua docendo præstari potest. Nebridius autem amicitiæ nostræ cesserat, ut omnium nostrum familiarissimo Verecundo, Mediolanensi et civi et grammatico subdoceret, et vehementer desideranti et familiaritatis jure flagitanti de numero nostro fidele adjutorium, quo indigebat nimis. Non itaque Nebridium cupiditas commodorum eo traxit: majora enim posset si vellet de litteris agere; sed officio benevolentiæ petitionem nostram contemnere noluit amicus dulcissimus et mitissimus. Agebat autem illud prudentissime, cavens innotescere personis secundum hoc sæculum majoribus, devitans Page 134 in eis omnem inquietudinem animi, quem volebat habere liberum et quam multis posset horis feriatum, ad quærendum aliquid, vel legendum vel audiendum de sapientia.

> 14. Quodam igitur die, non recolo causam qua erat absens Nebridius, cum ecce ad nos domum venit ad me et Alypium Pontitianus * quidam civis noster inquantum Afer, præclare in palatio militans [195] : nescio quid a nobis volebat. Et consedimus ut colloqueremur; et forte supra mensam lusoriam quæ ante nos erat, attendit codicem, tulit, aperuit, invenit apostolum Paulum, inopinate sane: putaverat enim aliquid de libris quorum professio me conterebat. Tum vero arridens, meque intuens, gratulatorie miratus est quod eas et solas præ oculis meis Litteras repente comperisset. Christianus quippe et fidelis erat, et sæpe tibi Deo nostro prosternebatur in ecclesia crebris et diuturnis orationibus. Cui ego cum indicassem illis me Scripturis curam maximam impendere, ortus est sermo, ipso narrante, de Antonio [196] Ægyptio monacho, cujus nomen excellenter clarebat apud servos tuos; nos autem usque in illam horam latebat. Quod ille ubi comperit, immoratus est in eo sermone, insinuans tantum virum ignorantibus, et admirans eamdem nostram ignorantiam. Stupebamus autem audientes tam recenti memoria, et prope nostris temporibus testatissima mirabilia [197] tua in fide recta et catholica Ecclesia. Omnes mirabamur, et nos quia tam magna erant, et ille quia inaudita nobis erant.

> 15. Inde sermo ejus devolutus est ad monasteriorum greges [198] , Page 135 et mores suaveolentiæ tuæ, et ubera deserta eremi, quorum nos nihil sciebamus. Et erat monasterium Mediolani [199] plenum bonis fratribus, extra urbis mœnia, sub Ambrosio nutritore; et non noveramus. Pertendebat ille et loquebatur adhuc, et nos intenti tacebamus. Unde et incidit ut diceret nescio quando se et tres alios contubernales suos, nimirum apud Treveros, cum Imperator pomeridiano Circensium spectaculo teneretur, exisse deambulatum in hortos muris contiguos; atque illic ut forte combinati spatiabantur, unum secum seorsum, et alios duos itidem seorsum pariterque digressos: sed illos vagabundos irruisse in quamdam casam, ubi habitabant quidam servi tui, Mat. 5, 3. spiritu pauperes, qualium est regnum cœlorum , et invenisse ibi codicem in quo scripta erat vita Antonii. Quam legere cœpit unus eorum, et mirari, et accendi, et inter legendum meditari arripere talem vitam, et relicta militia [200] sæculari servire tibi: erant * autem ex eis quos dicunt Agentes [201] in rebus. Tunc subito repletus amore sancto et sobrio pudore, iratus sibi conjecit oculos in amicum, et ait illi: "Dic, quæso te, omnibus istis laboribus nostris quo ambimus pervenire? quid quærimus? cujus rei causa militamus? Majorne esse poterit spes nostra in palatio, quam ut amici Imperatoris simus? Et ibi quid non fragile, plenumque periculis? Et per quot pericula pervenitur ad grandius periculum? Et quando * istud erit? Amicus autem Dei, si voluero, ecce nunc fio." Dixit hoc, et turbidus parturitione novæ vitæ, reddidit oculos paginis; et legebat, et mutabatur intus ubi tu videbas, et exuebatur mundo mens ejus, ut mox apparuit. Namque dum legit, et volvit fluctus cordis sui, Page 136 infremuit aliquando et discrevit, decrevitque meliora; jamque tuus, ait amico suo: "Ego jam abrupi me ab illa spe nostra, et Deo servire statui; et hoc ex hac hora, in hoc loco aggredior. Te si piget imitari, noli adversari." Respondit ille, adhærere se socium * tantæ mercedis tantæque militiæ. Et ambo jam tui, ædificabant turrim sumptu idoneo Luc. 14, 26-35. relinquendi omnia sua et sequendi te . Tum Pontitianus et qui cum eo per alias horti partes deambulabant, quærentes eos devenerunt in eumdem locum, et invenientes admonuerunt ut redirent, quod jam * declinasset dies. At illi narrato placito et proposito suo, quoque modo in eis talis voluntas orta esset atque firmata, petiverunt ne sibi molesti essent, si adjungi recusarent. Isti autem nihilo mutati a pristinis, fleverunt se tamen, ut dicebat * , atque illis pie congratulati sunt, et commendaverunt se orationibus eorum, et trahentes cor in terra abierunt in palatium; illi autem affigentes cor cœlo, manserunt in casa. Et habebant ambo sponsas: quæ posteaquam hoc audierunt, dicaverunt etiam ipsæ virginitatem tibi.

> VII. Rodebatur intus audito Pontitiano.

> 16. Narrabat hæc Pontitianus: tu autem, Domine, inter verba ejus retorquebas me ad meipsum, auferens me a dorso meo ubi me posueram, dum nollem me attendere; et constituebas me ante faciem meam, ut viderem quam turpis essem, quam distortus et sordidus, maculosus et ulcerosus. Et videbam, et horrebam; et quo a me fugerem non erat. Et si conabar avertere a me aspectum, narrabat ille quod narrabat, et tu me rursus opponebas mihi, et impingebas me in oculos meos, Ps. 35, 3. ut invenirem iniquitatem meam et odissem . Noveram eam, sed dissimulabam; et conhibebam [202] * , et obliviscebar.

> 17. Tunc vero, quanto ardentius amabam illos de quibus audiebam salubres affectus, quod se totos tibi sanandos dederant, tanto exsecrabilius me comparatum eis oderam [203] . Quoniam multi mei anni mecum effluxerant, forte duodecim anni, ex quo ab undevicesimo anno ætatis meæ, lecto [204] Ciceronis Hortensio, excitatus eram studio sapientiæ; et differebam contempta felicitate terrena ad eam investigandam vacare, Page 137 cujus non inventio, sed vel sola inquisitio jam præponenda erat etiam inventis thesauris regnisque gentium, et ad nutum circumfluentibus corporis voluptatibus. At ego adolescens miser, valde miser, in exordio ipsius adolescentiæ etiam petieram a te castitatem, et dixeram: Da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo. Timebam enim ne me cito exaudires, et cito sanares a morbo concupiscentiæ, quam malebam expleri quam exstingui.
