Non enim Joh. 1, 9. lumen nos sumus quod illuminat omnem hominem ; sed illuminamur a te, ut qui Eph. 5, 8.

fuimus aliquando tenebræ , simus lux in te . O si viderent internum æternum * , quod ego quia gustaveram, frendebam, quoniam non eis poteram ostendere, si afferrent ad me cor in oculis suis foris a te, et dicerent: Quis ostendet nobis bona? Ibi enim, ubi * mihi iratus eram intus in cubili, ut compunctus eram, ubi sacrificaveram mactans vetustatem meam, et inchoata meditatione renovationis meæ sperans in te, ibi mihi dulcescere cœperas, et Ps. 4, 7. dederas lætitiam in corde meo . Et exclamabam legens hæc foris, et agnoscens intus; nec volebam multiplicari [228] terrenis bonis, devorans tempora et devoratus temporibus * , cum haberem in æterna simplicitate [228] aliud Ver. 8. frumentum, et vinum, et oleum .

> 11. Et clamabam in consequenti versu clamore alto cordis mei: O in pace! o in idipsum! o quid dixit; Obdormiam et somnum capiam! Quoniam [229] quis resistet nobis cum fiet sermo qui scriptus est, 1 Cor. 15, 54. Absorpta est mors in victoriam? Et tu es Idipsum valde qui non mutaris ; et in te requies obliviscens Page 153 laborum omnium, quoniam nullus alius tecum, nec ad alia multa adipiscenda, quæ non sunt quod tu, sed tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me . Legebam, et ardebam; nec inveniebam quid facerem surdis mortuis, ex quibus fueram, pestis * , latrator amarus et cæcus adversus Litteras de melle cœli melleas, et de lumine tuo luminosas: et super inimicis * Scripturæ hujus tabescebam.
> Acerrimo dolore dentium subito liberatur.

> 12. Quando recordabor * omnia dierum illorum feriatorum? Sed nec oblitus sum nec silebo flagelli tui asperitatem, et misericordiæ tuæ mirabilem celeritatem. Dolore dentium tunc excruciabas me; et cum in tantum ingravesceret ut non valerem loqui [230] , ascendit in cor meum admonere omnes meos qui aderant, ut deprecarentur te pro me, Deum salutis omnimodæ. Et scripsi hoc in cera, et dedi ut eis legeretur. Mox ut genua supplici affectu fiximus, fugit dolor ille. Sed quis dolor? aut quomodo fugit? Expavi, fateor, Domine meus, Deus meus; nihil enim tale ab ineunte ætate expertus fueram. Et insinuati sunt mihi in profundo nutus tui; et gaudens in fide laudavi nomen tuum. Et ea fides me securum esse non sinebat de præteritis peccatis meis, quæ mihi per Baptismum tuum remissa nondum erant.
> V. Ambrosium consulit quid legendum.

> 13. Renuntiavi, peractis vindemialibus, ut scholasticis suis Mediolanenses venditorem verborum alium providerent; quod et tibi ego servire delegissem, et illi professioni, præ difficultate spirandi ac dolore pectoris, non sufficerem. Et insinuavi per litteras antistiti tuo viro sancto Ambrosio pristinos errores meos, et præsens votum meum, ut moneret quid mihi potissimum de Libris tuis legendum esset, quo percipiendæ tantæ gratiæ paratior aptiorque fierem. At ille jussit Isaiam prophetam; credo, quod præ cæteris Evangelii [231] vocationisque Gentium sit prænuntiator apertior. Verumtamen ego primam hujus lectionem non intelligens, totumque talem arbitrans, distuli repetendum exercitatior in dominico eloquio.
> Page 154
> VI. Mediolani baptizatur cum Alypin et Adeodato.

> 14. Inde ubi tempus advenit quo me nomen dare [232] oporteret relicto rure, Mediolanum remeavimus. Placuit et Alypio renasci in te mecum, jam induto humilitate Sacramentis tuis congrua, et fortissimo domitori corporis, usque ad Italicum solum glaciale nudo pede obterendum insolito ausu. Adjunximus etiam nobis puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter de peccato meo. Tu bene feceras eum. Annorum erat ferme quindecim [233] , et ingenio præveniebat multos graves et doctos viros. Munera tua tibi confiteor, Domine Deus meus, creator omnium, et multum potens formare * nostra deformia: nam ego in illo puero præter delictum non habebam. Quod enim enutriebatur a nobis in disciplina tua, tu inspiraveras nobis, nullus alius: munera tua tibi confiteor. Est liber noster qui inscribitur, de Magistro [234] : ipse ibi mecum loquitur.

Tu scis illius esse sensa omnia quæ inseruntur ibi ex persona collocutoris mei, cum esset in annis sexdecim. Multa ejus alia mirabiliora expertus sum. Horrori mihi erat illud ingenium; et quis præter te talium miraculorum opifex? Cito de terra abstulisti vitam ejus; et securior eum recordor, non timens quidquam pueritiæ, nec adolescentiæ; nec omnino homini illi. Sociavimus eum coævum nobis in gratia tua, educandum in disciplina tua; et baptizati sumus [235] et fugit a Page 155 nobis sollicitudo vitæ præteritæ. Nec satiabar illis diebus dulcedine mirabili, considerare altitudinem consilii tui super salutem generis humani. Quantum flevi in hymnis et canticis tuis, suave sonantis Ecclesiæ tuæ vocibus commotus acriter! Voces illæ influebant auribus meis, et eliquabatur veritas in cor meum; et exæstuabat inde affectus pietatis * , et currebant lacrymæ, et bene mihi erat cum eis.
> VII. Ecclesiastici cantus institutio Mediolani.

> 15. Non longe cœperat Mediolanensis Ecclesia genus hoc consolationis et exhortationis celebrare, magno studio fratrum concinentium vocibus et cordibus. Nimirum annus erat, aut non multo amplius, cum Justina Valentiniani regis pueri mater hominem tuum Ambrosium persequeretur [236] hæresis suæ causa, qua * fuerat seducta ab Arianis. Excubabat pia plebs in ecclesia mori parata cum episcopo suo, servo tuo. Ibi mea mater, ancilla tua, sollicitudinis et vigiliarum primas tenens, orationibus vivebat. Nos adhuc frigidi a calore Spiritus tui, excitabamur tamen civitate attonita atque turbata. Tunc hymni et psalmi ut canerentur secundum morem orientalium partium, ne populus mœroris tædio contabesceret, institutum est; et ex illo in hodiernum retentum, multis jam ac pene omnibus gregibus tuis et per cætera orbis imitantibus * .
> Inventio corporum SS. Protasii et Gervasii.

> 16. Tunc memorato antistiti tuo per visum aperuisti quo loco laterent martyrum corpora Protasii et Gervasii, quæ per tot annos incorrupta in thesauro secreti tui recondideras, unde opportune promeres ad coercendam rabiem femineam, sed regiam. [237] Cum enim propalata et effossa digno cum Page 156 honore transferrentur ad Ambrosianam basilicam, non solum quos immundi vexabant spiritus, confessis eisdem dæmonibus, sanabantur [238] , verum etiam quidam plures annos cæcus [239] , civis civitatique notissimus, cum populi tumultuante lætitia * causam quæsisset atque audisset, exsilivit, eoque se ut duceret, suum ducem rogavit. Quo perductus, impetravit admitti, ut sudario tangeret feretrum Ps. 115, 15. pretiosæ in conspectu tuo mortis sanctorum tuorum . Quod ubi fecit, atque admovit oculis, confestim aperti sunt.

Inde fama discurrens, inde laudes tuæ ferventes, lucentes * , inde illius inimicæ animus etsi ad credendi sanitatem non applicatus * , a persequendi tamen furore compressus est. Gratias tibi, Deus meus. Unde et quo duxisti recordationem meam, ut hæc etiam confiterer tibi, quæ magna oblitus præterieram? Et tamen tunc cum ita fragraret Cant 1, 3. odor unguentorum tuorum , non currebamus post te . Ideo plus flebam inter cantica hymnorum tuorum, olim suspirans tibi, et tandem respirans * , quantum patet aura in domo fenea.
> VIII. Evodii conversio. Ps. 67, 7.

> 17. Qui habitare facis unanimes in domo , consociasti nobis et Evodium juvenem ex nostro municipio. Qui cum agens in rebus [240] militaret; prior nobis ad te conversus est et Page 157 baptizatus, et relicta militia sæculari, accinctus in tua. Matris obitus, ejusque a teneris educatio. Simul eramus [241] , simul habitaturi * placito sancto. Quærebamus quisnam locus nos utilius haberet servientes tibi: pariter remeabamus in Africam. Et cum apud Ostia Tiberina essemus, mater defuncta est. Multa prætereo, quia multum festino. Accipe confessiones meas et gratiarum actiones, Deus meus, de rebus innumerabilibus etiam in silentio. Sed non præteribo quidquid mihi anima parturit de illa famula tua, quæ me parturivit; et carne, ut in hanc temporalem; et corde, ut in æternam lucem nascerer * [242] . Non ejus, sed tua dicam dona in ea; neque enim seipsam fecerat, aut educaverat seipsam.

Tu creasti eam, nec pater nec mater sciebat qualis ex eis fieret. Et erudivit eam in timore tuo virga Christi tui, regimen unici Filii tui in domo fideli, bono membro Ecclesiæ tuæ. Nec tantam erga suam disciplinam diligentiam matris prædicabat, quantam famulæ cujusdam decrepitæ, quæ patrem ejus infantem portaverat, sicut dorso grandiuscularum puellarum parvuli portari solent. Cujus rei gratia, et propter senectam ac mores optimos, in domo christiana satis a dominis honorabatur. Unde etiam curam filiarum dominicarum commissam * diligenter gerebat, et erat in eis coercendis, cum opus esset, sancta severitate vehemens, atque in docendis sobria prudentia.

Nam eas, præter illas horas quibus ad mensam parentum moderatissime alebantur, etiamsi exardescerent siti, nec aquam bibere sinebat, præcavens consuetudinem malam, et addens verbum sanum: "Modo aquam bibitis, quia in potestate vinum non habetis: cum autem ad maritos veneritis, factæ dominæ apothecarum et cellariorum, aqua sordebit; sed mos potandi permanebit * ." Hac ratione præcipiendi et auctoritate imperandi, frenabat Page 158 aviditatem tenerioris ætatis; et ipsam puellarum sitim formabat ad honestum modum, ut jam nec liberet quod non deceret.

> 18. Et surrepserat tamen, sicut mihi filio famula tua narrabat, surrepserat ei vinolentia. Nam cum de more, tanquam puella sobria, juberetur a parentibus de cuppa vinum depromere, submisso poculo qua desuper patet, priusquam in lagunculam funderet merum, primoribus labris sorbebat exiguum, quia non poterat amplius, sensu recusante. Non enim ulla temulenta * cupidine faciebat hoc, sed quibusdam superfluentibus ætatis excessibus, qui ludicris motibus ebulliunt, et in puerilibus animis majorum pondere premi solent. Itaque ad illud modicum quotidiana modica addendo, quoniam qui Eccli. 19, 1. modica spernit, paulatim decidit , in eam consuetudinem lapsa erat, ut prope jam plenos mero caliculos inhianter hauriret. Ubi tunc sagax anus, et vehemens illa prohibitio? Numquid valebat aliquid adversus latentem morbum, nisi tua medicina, Domine, vigilaret super nos?

Absente patre et matre et nutritoribus, tu præsens, qui creasti, qui vocas, qui etiam per præpositos * homines boni aliquid agis ad animarum salutem, quid tunc egisti, Deus meus? Unde curasti? unde sanasti? Nonne protulisti durum et acutum ex altera anima convicium, tanquam medicinale ferrum ex occultis provisionibus tuis, et uno ictu putredinem illam præcidisti? Ancilla enim cum qua solebat accedere ad cuppam, litigans cum domina minore, ut fit, sola cum sola, objecit hoc crimen, amarissima insultatione vocans meribibulam. Quo illa stimulo percussa respexit fœditatem suam, confestimque damnavit atque exuit. Sicut amici adulantes pervertunt, sic inimici litigantes plerumque corrigunt. Nec tu quod per eos agis, sed quod ipsi voluerunt, retribuis eis.

Illa enim irata exagitare appetivit minorem dominam, non sanare: et ideo clanculo, aut quia ita eas invenerat locus et tempus litis, aut ne forte et ipsa periclitaretur quod tam sero prodidisset. At tu, Domine, rector cœlitum * , et terrenorum, ad usus tuos contorquens profunda torrentis, fluxum sæculorum ordinate * turbulentum, etiam de alterius animæ insania [243] sanasti alteram; ne quisquam cum hoc adverterit, Page 159 potentiæ suæ tribuat, si verbo ejus alius corrigatur, quem vult corrigi.
> IX. Laudabiles matris suæ mores prosequitur.

> 19. Educata itaque pudice ac sobrie, potiusque a te subdita parentibus, quam a parentibus tibi, ubi plenis annis nubilis facta est, tradita viro servivit veluti domino; et sategit eum lucrari tibi, loquens te illi moribus suis, quibus eam pulchram faciebas, et reverenter amabilem atque mirabilem viro. Ita autem toleravit cubilis injurias, ut nullam de hac re cum marito haberet unquam simultatem. Exspectabat enim misericordiam tuam super eum, ut in te credens castificaretur. Erat vero ille præterea, sicut benevolentia præcipuus, ita ira fervidus. Sed noverat hæc non resistere irato viro, non tantum facto, sed ne verbo quidem. Jam vero refractum et quietum cum opportunum videret, rationem facti sui reddebat, si forte ille inconsideratius commotus fuerat.

Denique, cum matronæ multæ quarum viri mansuetiores erant, plagarum vestigia etiam dehonestata facie gererent, inter amica colloquia illæ arguebant maritorum vitam, hæc earum linguam, veluti per jocum graviter admonens, ex quo illas tabulas quæ matrimoniales vocantur, recitari audissent, tanquam instrumenta quibus ancillæ factæ essent, deputare debuisse; proinde memores conditionis superbire adversus dominos non oportere. Cumque mirarentur illæ, scientes quam ferocem conjugem sustineret, nunquam fuisse auditum, aut aliquo indicio claruisse, quod Patricius ceciderit uxorem, aut quod a se invicem vel unum diem domestica lite dissenserint, et causam familiariter quærerent; docebat illa institutum suum, quod supra memoravi. Quæ observabant, expertæ gratulabantur; quæ non observabant, subjectæ vexabantur.

> 20. Socrum etiam suam primo susurris malarum ancillarum adversum se irritatam sic evicit obsequiis, perseverans tolerantia et mansuetudine, ut illa ultro filio suo medias linguas famularum proderet, quibus inter se et nurum pax domestica turbabatur, expeteretque vindictam. Itaque posteaquam ille, et matri obtemperans, et curans familiæ disciplinam, et concordiæ suorum consulens, proditas ad prodentis arbitrium verberibus coercuit, promisit illa talia de se præmia sperare debere, quæcumque de sua nuru sibi, quo placeret, mali aliquid loqueretur: nullaque jam audente, memorabili inter se benevolentiæ suavitate vixerunt. Page 160

> 21. Hoc quoque illi bono mancipio tuo, in cujus utero me creasti, Deus meus, misericordia mea, munus grande donaveras, quod inter dissidentes atque discordes quaslibet animas, ubi poterat, tam se præbebat pacificam, ut cum ab utraque multa de invicem audiret amarissima, qualia solet eructare turgens atque indigesta discordia quando præsenti amicæ de absente inimica per acida colloquia cruditas * exhalatur odiorum; nihil tamen alteri de altera proderet, nisi quod ad eas reconciliandas valeret.

Parvum hoc bonum mihi videretur, nisi turbas innumerabiles tristis experirer, nescio qua horrenda pestilentia peccatorum latissime pervagante, non solum iratorum inimicorum iratis inimicis dicta prodere, sed etiam quæ non dicta sunt addere; cum contra homini * humano parum esse debeat inimicitias hominum nec excitare nec augere male loquendo, nisi eas etiam exstinguere bene loquendo studuerit; qualis illa erat, docente te magistro intimo in schola pectoris.

> 22. Denique etiam virum suum jam in extrema vita ejus temporali lucrata est tibi, nec in eo jam fideli planxit quod in nondum fideli toleraverat. Erat etiam serva servorum tuorum. Quisquis eorum noverat eam, multum in ea laudabat et honorabat et diligebat te; quia sentiebat præsentiam tuam in corde ejus, sanctæ conversationis fructibus testibus [244] . Fuerat enim 1 Tim. 5, 9, 4. 10. unius viri uxor, mutuam vicem parentibus reddiderat, domum suam pie tractaverat, in operibus bonis testimonium habebat . Gal. 4, 19. Nutrierat filios, toties eos parturiens , quoties abs te deviare cernebat. Postremo nobis, Domine, omnibus, quia ex munere tuo sinis loqui servis tuis, qui ante dormitionem ejus in te jam consociati vivebamus percepta gratia Baptismi tui, ita curam gessit quasi omnes genuisset, ita servivit quasi ab omnibus genita fuisset.
> X. Colloquium cum matre de regno cœlorum.

> 23. Impendente autem die quo ex hac vita erat exitura, quem diem tu noveras, ignorantibus nobis; provenerat, ut credo, procurante te occultis tuis modis, ut ego et ipsa soli Page 161 staremus incumbentes ad quamdam fenestram, unde hortus intra domum quæ nos habebat prospectabatur, illic apud Ostia Tiberina, ubi remoti a turbis post longi itineris laborem instaurabamus nos navigationi: colloquebamur ergo soli valde dulciter; et Phil. 3, 13. præterita obliviscentes, in ea quæ ante sunt extenti , quærebamus inter nos apud præsentem Veritatem, quod tu es, qualis futura esset vita æterna sanctorum, 1 Cor. 2, 9. quam nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit . Sed inhiabamus ore cordis in superna fluenta fontis tui, Ps. 35, 10. fontis vitæ qui est apud te ; ut inde pro captu nostro aspersi, quoquo modo rem tantam cogitaremus.

> 24. Cumque ad eum finem sermo perduceretur, ut carnalium sensuum delectatio quantalibet, in quantalibet luce corporea, præ illius vitæ jucunditate, non comparatione, sed ne commemoratione quidem digna videretur; erigentes nos ardentiore affectu in idipsum [245] , perambulavimus gradatim cuncta corporalia, et ipsum cœlum, unde sol et luna et stellæ lucent super terram. Et adhuc ascendebamus interius cogitando, et loquendo * , et mirando opera tua; et venimus in mentes nostras, et transcendimus [246] eas, ut attingeremus regionem ubertatis indeficientis, ubi Ps. 79, 2. pascis Israel in æternum veritatis pabulo, et ubi vita sapientia est, per quam fiunt omnia ista, et quæ fuerunt, et quæ futura sunt; et ipsa non fit, sed sic est ut fuit, et sic erit semper; quin potius fuisse, et futurum esse non est in ea, sed esse solum, quoniam æterna est: nam fuisse et futurum esse, non est æternum.

Et dum loquimur et inhiamus illi, attigimus eam modice toto ictu cordis; et suspiravimus * et relinquimus ibi religatas Rom. 8, 23. primitias spiritus [247] , et remeavimus ad strepitum oris nostri, ubi verbum et incipitur et finitur. Et quid simile Verbo tuo Domino nostro, Sap. 7, 27. in se permanenti sine vetustate, atque innovanti omnia ?

> 25. Dicebamus ergo: Si cui sileat tumultus carnis, sileant phantasiæ terræ et aquarum et aeris, sileant et poli, et ipsa sibi anima sileat, et transeat se non se cogitando, sileant Page 162 somnia et imaginariæ revelationes, omnis lingua et omne signum, et quidquid transeundo fit, si cui sileat omnino; quoniam si quis audiat * , dicunt hæc omnia, Ps. 99, 3. Non ipsa nos fecimus , sed fecit nos qui manet in æternum : his dictis si jam taceant quoniam erexerunt aurem in eum qui fecit ea, et loquatur ipse solus, non per ea, sed per seipsum, ut audiamus verbum ejus, non per linguam carnis, neque per vocem angeli, Ps. 76, 18. nec per sonitum nubis, nec 1 Cor. 13, 12.

per ænigma similitudinis; sed ipsum quem in his amamus, ipsum sine his audiamus, sicut nunc extendimus nos, et rapida cogitatione attingimus * æternam Sapientiam super omnia manentem; si continuetur hoc, et subtrahantur aliæ visiones longe imparis generis, et hæc una rapiat et absorbeat et recondat in interiora gaudia spectatorem suum, ut talis sit sempiterna vita, quale fuit hoc momentum intelligentiæ, cui suspiravimus; nonne hoc est, Mat. 25, 21. Intra in gaudium Domini tui? Et istud quando? An cum 1 Cor. 15, 51 omnes resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur ?

> 26. Dicebam talia * , et si non isto modo et his verbis, tamen, Domine, tu scis quod illo die, cum talia loqueremur, et mundus iste nobis inter verba vilesceret cum omnibus delectationibus suis, tunc ait illa: "Fili, quantum ad me attinet, nulla jam re delector in hac vita. Quid hic faciam adhuc, et cur hic sim nescio, jam consumpta spe hujus sæculi. Unum erat propter quod in hac vita aliquantum immorari cupiebam, ut te christianum catholicum viderem, priusquam morerer. Cumulatius hoc mihi Deus meus præstitit, ut te etiam, contempta felicitate terrena, servum ejus videam: quid hic facio?"
> XI. De ecstasi et morte matris.

> 27. Ad hæc ei quid responderim, non satis recolo. Cum interea vix intra quinque dies, aut non multo amplius decubuit febribus. Et cum ægrotaret, quodam die defectum animæ passa est, et paululum subtracta a præsentibus. Nos concurrimus, sed cito reddita est sensui, et aspexit astantes, me et fratrem [248] meum, et ait nobis quasi quærenti similis: "Ubi eram?" Deinde nos intuens mœrore attonitos: "Ponitis * hic, inquit, matrem vestram." Ego silebam, et fletum frenabam. Frater autem meus quiddam locutus est, quo eam non peregre, sed in patria defungi tanquam felicius optaret. Quo audito, illa vultu anxio reverberans eum oculis quod Page 163 talia saperet, atque inde me intuens: "Vide, ait, quid dicit." Et mox ambobus: "Ponite, inquit, hoc corpus ubicumque; nihil vos ejus cura conturbet: tantum illud vos rogo, ut ad Domini altare memineritis mei ubi ubi fueritis."
Cumque hanc sententiam verbis quibus poterat explicasset, conticuit; et ingravescente morbo exercebatur.

> 28. Ego vero cogitans dona tua, Deus invisibilis, quæ immittis in corda fidelium tuorum, et proveniunt inde fruges admirabiles; gaudebam et gratias tibi agebam, recolens quod noveram, quanta cura semper æstuasset de sepulcro quod sibi providerat et præparaverat juxta corpus viri sui. Quia enim valde concorditer vixerant, id etiam volebat, ut est animus humanus minus capax divinorum, adjungi ad illam felicitatem, et commemorari ab hominibus, concessum sibi esse post transmarinam peregrinationem, ut conjuncta terra amborum conjugum terra tegeretur. Quando autem ista inanitas plenitudine bonitatis tuæ cœperat in ejus corde non esse, nesciebam, et lætabar admirans quod sic mihi aperuisset * ; quanquam et in illo sermone nostro ad fenestram cum dixit, "Jam quid hic facio?" non apparuit desiderare in patria mori.

Audivi etiam postea, quod jam cum Ostiis essemus, cum quibusdam amicis meis materna fiducia colloquebatur quodam die de contemptu vitæ hujus et bono mortis, ubi ipse non aderam; illisque stupentibus virtutem feminæ, quam tu dederas ei, quærentibusque utrum non formidaret tam longe a sua civitate corpus relinquere: "Nihil, inquit, longe est Deo; neque timendum est ne ille non agnoscat in fine sæculi, unde me resuscitet." Ergo die nono ægritudinis suæ, quinquagesimo et sexto anno ætatis suæ, tricesimo et tertio ætatis meæ [249] , anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
> XII. Quomodo luxerit mortem matris.

> 29. Premebam oculos ejus, et confluebat in præcordia mea mœstitudo ingens, et transfluebat in lacrymas: ibidemque oculi mei violento animi imperio resorbebant fontem suum usque ad siccitatem, et in tali luctamine valde male mihi erat. Tum vero ubi efflavit extremum * , puer Adeodatus exclamavit in planctum, atque ab omnibus nobis coercitus tacuit. Hoc modo etiam meum quiddam puerile quod labebatur in fletus Page 164 juvenili voce cordis, coercebatur et tacebat. Neque enim decere arbitrabamur funus illud questibus lacrymosis gemitibusque celebrare * ; quia his plerumque solet deplorari quædam miseria morientium, aut quasi omnimoda exstinctio. At illa nec misere moriebatur, nec omnino moriebatur. Hoc et documentis morum ejus, et fide non ficta, rationibusque certis tenebamus.

> 30. Quid erat ergo quod intus mihi graviter dolebat, nisi ex consuetudine simul vivendi dulcissima et charissima repente disrupta vulnus recens? Gratulabar quidem testimonio ejus, quod in ea ipsa ultima ægritudine, obsequiis meis interblandiens, appellabat me pium, et commemorabat grandi dilectionis affectu nunquam se audisse ex ore meo jaculatum in se durum aut contumeliosum sonum * . Sed tamen quid tale, Deus meus, qui fecisti nos, quid comparabile habebat honor a me delatus illi, et servitus ab illa mihi? Quoniam itaque deserebar tam magno ejus solatio, sauciabatur anima * , et quasi dilaniabatur vita, quæ una facta erat ex mea et illius.

> 31. Cohibito ergo a fletu illo puero, Psalterium arripuit Evodius, et cantare cœpit psalmum [250] ; cui respondebamus omnis domus: Ps. 100, 1. Misericordiam et judicium cantabo tibi, Domine. Audito autem quid ageretur, convenerunt multi fratres ac religiosæ feminæ; et de more illis, quorum officium erat, funus curantibus, ego in parte ubi decenter poteram, cum eis qui me non deserendum esse censebant, quod erat tempori congruum disputabam; eoque fomento veritatis mitigabam cruciatum tibi notum, illis ignorantibus et intente audientibus, et sine sensu doloris me esse arbitrantibus. At ego in auribus tuis, ubi eorum nullus audiebat, increpabam mollitiem affectus mei, et constringebam fluxum mœroris: cedebatque mihi paululum; rursusque impetu suo ferebatur, non usque ad eruptionem lacrymarum, nec usque ad vultus mutationem, sed ego sciebam quid corde premerem.

Et quia mihi vehementer displicebat tantum in me posse hæc humana, quæ ordine debito et sorte conditionis nostræ accidere necesse est, alio dolore dolebam dolorem meum, et duplici tristitia macerabar.
> Page 165

> 32. Cum ecce corpus elatum est * , imus [251] , redimus sine lacrymis. Nam neque in eis precibus [252] quas tibi fudimus, cum offerretur pro ea sacrificium pretii nostri, jam juxta sepulcrum posito cadavere, priusquam deponeretur, sicut illic fieri solet, nec in eis ego precibus flevi: sed toto die graviter in occulto mœstus eram, et mente turbata rogabam te, ut poteram, quo sanares dolorem meum, nec faciebas; credo, commendans memoriæ meæ, vel hoc uno documento, omnis consuetudinis vinculum, etiam adversus mentem quæ jam non fallaci verbo pascitur * . Visum etiam mihi est ut irem lavatum; quod audieram inde balneis nomen inditum, quia Græci βαλανεῖον dixerint, quod anxietatem pellat ex animo. Ecce et hoc confiteor misericordiæ tuæ, Ps. 67, 6. Pater orphanorum , quoniam lavi, et talis eram qualis priusquam lavissem. Neque enim exsudavit de corde meo mœroris amaritudo.
Deinde dormivi et evigilavi, et non parva ex parte mitigatum inveni dolorem meum; atque ut eram in lecto meo solus, recordatus sum veridicos versus Ambrosii tui: tu es enim
> Deus creator omnium,
> Polique rector, vestiens
> Diem decoro lumine,
> Noctem sopore * gratiæ:
> Artus solutos ut quies
> Reddat laboris usui,
> Mentesque fessas allevet,
> Luctusque solvat anxios.

> 33. Atque inde paulatim reducebam in pristinum sensum ancillam tuam, conversationemque ejus piam in te, et sancte * in nos blandam atque morigeram, qua subito destitutus sum; et libuit flere in conspectu tuo de illa et pro illa, de me et pro me. Et dimisi lacrymas quas continebam, ut effluerent quantum vellent, substernens eas cordi meo; et requievi in eis * , quoniam ibi erant aures tuæ, non cujusquam hominis superbe interpretantis ploratum meum. Et nunc, Domine, confiteor tibi in litteris. Legat qui volet, et interpretetur ut volet; et si peccatum invenerit, flevisse me matrem exigua parte horæ, Page 166 matrem oculis meis interim mortuam, quæ me multos annos fleverat ut oculis tuis viverem, non irrideat; sed potius, si est grandi charitate, pro peccatis meis fleat ipse ad te Patrem omnium fratrum Christi tui.
> XIII. Orat pro matre defuncta.

> 34. Ego autem, jam sanato corde ab illo vulnere in quo poterat redargui carnalis affectus, fundo tibi, Deus noster, pro illa famula tua longe aliud lacrymarum genus, quod manat de concusso spiritu consideratione periculorum omnis animæ 1 Cor. 15, 22. quæ in Adam moritur . Quanquam illa in Christo vivificata , etiam nondum a carne resoluta, sic vixerit ut laudetur nomen tuum in fide moribusque ejus; non tamen audeo dicere, ex quo eam per Baptismum regenerasti, Mat. 12, 3. nullum verbum exisse ex ore ejus contra præceptum tuum. Et dictum est a Veritate Filio tuo: Ib. 5, 23. Si quis dixerit fratri suo, Fatue, reus erit gehennæ ignis. Et væ etiam laudabili vitæ hominum, si, remota misericordia, discutias eam. Quia vero non exquiris delicta vehementer, fiducialiter speramus aliquem apud te locum * . Quisquis autem tibi enumerat vera merita sua, quid tibi enumerat nisi munera tua [253] ?
O si cognoscant se homines homines; et 2 Cor. 10, 17. qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur * !

> 35. Ego itaque, laus mea et vita mea, Deus cordis mei, sepositis paulisper bonis ejus actibus, pro quibus tibi gaudens gratias ago, nunc pro peccatis matris meæ deprecor te; exaudi me per Medicinam vulnerum nostrorum quæ pependit in ligno, et sedens ad dexteram tuam Rom. 8, 34. interpellat te pro nobis . Scio misericorditer operatam, et Mat. 18, 36; 6, 12. ex corde dimisisse debita debitoribus suis ; dimitte illi et tu debita sua , si qua etiam contraxit per tot annos post aquam salutis. Dimitte, Domine, dimitte obsecro, Ps. 142, 2. ne intres cum ea in judicium . Jac. 2, 13. Superexaltet misericordia judicio , quoniam eloquia tua vera sunt, et promisisti Mat. 5, 7. misericordiam misericordibus : quod ut essent, tu dedisti eis, qui Ex. 33, 19; Ro. 9, 15. misereberis cui misertus eris, et misericordiam præstabis cui misericors fueris .

> 36. Et credo quod * jam feceris quod te rogo, sed Ps. 118, 108. voluntaria oris mei approba, Domine . Namque illa imminente die resolutionis suæ non cogitavit suum corpus sumptuose contegi, aut condiri aromatibus, aut monumentum electum concupivit aut curavit sepulcrum patrium; non ista mandavit Page 167 nobis: sed tantummodo memoriam sui ad altare tuum fieri desideravit, cui nullius diei prætermissione servierat; unde sciret dispensari victimam sanctam, qua Col. 2, 14. deletum est chirographum quod erat contrarium nobis , qua triumphatus est hostis computans delicta nostra, et quærens quid objiciat, et Joh. 14, 30. nihil inveniens in illo [254] in quo vincimus. Quis ei refundet innocentem sanguinem? Quis ei restituet pretium quo nos emit ut nos auferat ei * ? Ad cujus pretii nostri sacramentum ligavit ancilla tua animam suam vinculo fidei. Nemo a protectione tua disrumpat eam.

Non se interponat nec vi nec insidiis Ps. 90, 13. leo et draco : neque enim respondebit illa nihil se debere, ne convincatur et obtineatur ab accusatore callido; sed respondebit dimissa debita sua ab eo, cui nemo reddet quod pro nobis non debens reddidit.

> 37. Sit ergo in pace cum viro, ante quem nulli et post quem nulli nupta est; cui servivit Luc. 8, 15. fructum tibi afferens cum tolerantia , ut eum quoque lucraretur tibi. Et inspira, Domine Deus meus * , inspira servis tuis fratribus meis, filiis tuis dominis meis, quibus et corde et voce et litteris servio, ut quotquot hæc legerint, meminerint ad altare tuum Monnicæ famulæ tuæ [255] , cum Patricio quondam ejus conjuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam, quemadmodum, nescio. Meminerint cum affectu pio parentum meorum in hac luce transitoria, et fratrum meorum sub te patre in matre Catholica, et civium meorum in æterna Jerusalem, cui suspirat peregrinatio populi tui ab exitu usque ad reditum; ut quod a me illa poposcit extremum, uberius ei præstetur in multorum orationibus, per confessiones * , quam per orationes meas.
> Page 168

> Desiring to live for the one God, he resolved to abandon the profession of rhetoric, though not before the vintage holidays that were soon at hand had passed. Meanwhile, at the country estate of Cassiciacum, with his friend Verecundus, he prepared himself to receive the grace of Baptism; and at last he was baptized with Alypius and his son Adeodatus. Not long afterward, returning to Africa, he came to Ostia with his friends and his mother Monnica, whose life and holy character he presents in brief summary; and she died there, in the fifty-sixth year of her age, Augustine being thirty-three.
> I. He praises God's goodness, acknowledging his own wretchedness.

> 1. Ps. 115, 16. 17. O Lord, I am thy servant; I am thy servant, and the son of thy handmaid. Thou hast broken my bonds; unto thee will I sacrifice a victim * of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise thee, and Ps. 34, 10. 3. let all my bones say: Lord, who is like unto thee? Let them say it, and answer me, and say to my soul, I am thy salvation. Who was I, and what sort of man was I? What evil was there not in my deeds *; or, if not in my deeds, in my words; or, if not in my words, in my will? But thou, O Lord, art good and merciful, and thy right hand, looking upon the depth of my death, drained from the bottom of my heart the abyss of corruption. And this was the whole matter: no longer to will what I willed, and to will what thou willedst * . But where, through so many years, was my free will, and from what deep and hidden recess was it summoned forth in a moment, that I might submit my neck to Mat. 11, 30. thy gentle yoke, and my shoulders to thy light burden, O Christ Jesus, Ps. 18, 15. my helper and my redeemer?

How sweet it suddenly became to me to be without the delights of trifles! and what I had feared to lose was now a joy to let go. For thou didst cast them out from me, thou true and supreme sweetness [211]: thou didst cast them out and didst enter in their stead, sweeter than every sweetness * , yet not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light, yet more inward than every secret; higher than every honour, yet not to those who are high in themselves. Now my mind was free from the gnawing cares of ambition, acquisition, and wallowing in and scratching the itch of lusts; and I talked Page 146 with thee, my brightness, and my riches, and my salvation, O Lord my God.
> II. He postpones abandoning the profession of rhetoric until the vintage holidays.

> 2. And it pleased me in thy sight not to snatch away tumultuously, but gently to withdraw, the service of my tongue from the market-place of talkativeness *; lest boys, meditating not on thy law, not on thy peace, but on lying madnesses and forensic wars, should purchase from my mouth weapons for their frenzy. And there remained by then but very few days before the vintage holidays, and I resolved to endure them, so that I might depart solemnly and, now redeemed by thee, no longer return for sale. Therefore our plan was before thee; but before men, except our own, it was not. And it had been agreed among us that it should not be spread abroad indiscriminately to anyone; although thou, to us Ps. 83, 6. 7. ascending from the valley of weeping, and singing the song of degrees, Ps. 129, 3-5. hadst given sharp arrows and devastating coals against the deceitful tongue [212], which, as though giving counsel, opposed us, and, as is its custom with food, consumed us by loving us.

> 3. Thou hadst pierced our heart with thy charity, and we bore thy words [212] transfixed in our inmost parts; and the examples [212] of thy servants, whom thou hadst made bright from black, and living from dead, heaped together in the bosom of our thought, burned and consumed our heavy torpor, lest we should incline toward the depths *; and they kindled us so strongly that every blast of contradiction from the deceitful tongue might inflame us more keenly, not extinguish us. Nevertheless, because on account of thy name, which thou hast sanctified throughout the earth, our vow and purpose would certainly have its praisers also, it seemed like vainglory not to wait for so near a holiday season, but to depart beforehand from a public profession situated before the eyes of all *; so that all who watched, turning their mouths toward my action, might say much about my wishing to anticipate the approaching vintage day *—that I had, as it were, sought to seem great.
Page 147 And what good was that to me, that men should think and dispute concerning my mind, and Rom. 14, 16. our good should be blasphemed?

> 4. Moreover, because during that very summer my lungs [213] had begun to yield beneath excessive literary labour, to draw breath with difficulty, and by pains in my chest to testify that they were wounded, refusing a clearer or more prolonged utterance, this had at first troubled me, since it almost compelled me by necessity to lay aside the burden of that teaching office, or at least, if I could be cured and recover, certainly to interrupt it * . But when the full resolve Ps. 45, 11. to be still, and to see that thou art the Lord, arose and was confirmed in me, thou knowest, my God, that I even began to rejoice that this too furnished no false excuse, which might moderate the offence taken by men who, because of their children, never wished me to be free.

Filled, therefore, with such joy, I endured that interval of time until it should run out: I do not know whether it was even twenty [214] days, yet they were endured bravely; because the desire had departed which had been accustomed to bear that burdensome business with me, and I remained to be crushed unless patience came to my aid. Some servant of thine, one of my brethren, may say that I sinned in this, that, already with a full heart in thy service, I suffered myself to sit even for one hour in the chair of falsehood. But I do not contend. Yet thou, most merciful Lord, didst thou not forgive and remit this sin also to me, together with the other horrible and deadly sins, in holy water?
> III. Verecundus grants him his country estate.

> 5. Verecundus was worn by anxiety over this good of ours, because, on account of his bonds, by which he was held most tightly, he saw himself abandoned by our companionship. Not yet a Christian, though he had a believing wife, he was nevertheless delayed from the course upon which we had entered by that very bond, more constraining than the rest; nor did he say that he wished to be a Christian in any other way than that in which he could not be. Very kindly, he offered that, as long as we remained there, we should be on his property * . Thou wilt repay him * , O Lord, in Luc. 14, 14. the resurrection of the just, because thou hast already repaid him with the very Ps. 124, 3. lot. For though, in our absence, when we were already at Rome, he was seized by bodily sickness, and in it became a Christian and a believer, and departed from this life: thus thou didst have mercy not only on him but also on us, lest, remembering the outstanding kindness of a friend toward us, and not counting him among thy flock, we should be tortured with intolerable grief.

Thanks be to thee, our God; we are thine: thy exhortations and consolations show it. Faithful promiser, thou renderest * to Verecundus, in return for that estate of his at Cassiciacum, where we rested from the heat of the world in thee, the loveliness of thy ever-green paradise, because thou didst forgive him his sins on earth, Ps. 67, 16. upon the curdled mountain [215], thy mountain, a fertile mountain.

> 6. He therefore was then distressed; but Nebridius rejoiced with us. For although he too, not yet a Christian, had fallen into that pit of most pernicious error, so as to believe the flesh of the Son of thy Truth to be a phantom [216]; yet emerging from it, he was such as he was, not yet initiated into any sacraments of thy Church, but a most ardent seeker [217] of truth. Not long after our conversion and regeneration through thy Baptism, when he too had become a Catholic believer, serving thee in Africa among his own people with perfect chastity and continence, and when through him his whole household had been made Christian, thou didst loose him from the flesh; and now he lives Luc. 16, 22. in Abraham's bosom. Whatever that bosom [218] may be which is signified thereby, there Nebridius * lives, my sweet friend, but thy adopted son, O Lord, from a freedman; there he lives. For what other place could there be for such a soul?

There he lives, whence he used to ask many questions of me, a little man without experience. Now he no longer lays his ear to my mouth, but his spiritual mouth to thy fountain; and he drinks, as much as he can, wisdom according to his longing, happy without end. Yet I do not suppose that he is thus intoxicated by it as to forget me, since thou, O Lord, whom he drinks * , art mindful of us. Thus, then, we were: consoling the sorrowful Verecundus, our friendship being preserved, concerning such conversion of ours * , and exhorting him to the faith appropriate to his station, namely married life; but waiting for Nebridius, when he would follow, which, being so near, he could do, and was now, now about to do: when behold, those days at last rolled away. For they seemed long and many because of our love for leisure and freedom, to sing from all our marrow, Ps. 26, 8. My heart said unto thee, I have sought thy face; thy face, O Lord, will I seek.
> IV. Books written at Cassiciacum. Letters to Nebridius.

> 7. And the day came * on which I was actually released from the profession of rhetoric, from which I had already been released in thought. And so it came to pass. Thou didst rescue my tongue, from which thou hadst already rescued my heart; and rejoicing, I blessed thee as I departed for the country house with all my household [219]. What I did there in writing—now indeed serving thee, but still breathing, as in a pause, the school of pride *—is attested by the books of dialogues [220] held with those present, and with myself alone [221] Page 150 before thee; while what I did with Nebridius absent [222] is attested by the letters. And when will time suffice me to recount all thy great benefits toward us in that season, especially as I hasten on to greater matters? For my remembrance calls me back, and it becomes sweet to me, O Lord, to confess to thee by what inward goads thou didst subdue me, and how thou didst Is. 40, 4. Luc. 3, 45.

make me level, when the mountains and hills of my thoughts had been humbled, and make straight my crooked ways, and smooth my rough ones; and how thou didst also bring Alypius, the brother of my heart, under the name of thy only-begotten Son, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, which at first he disdained to have inserted in our writings. For he preferred that they should smell more of the gymnasiums' Ps. 28, 5. cedars, which the Lord hath now broken, than of the wholesome ecclesiastical herbs adverse to serpents.
> With what graces from heaven they were suffused, and with what lively feeling of piety, while he unfolds the Psalms.

> 8. What utterances did I give thee, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, faithful songs and sounds of piety excluding the swollen spirit; inexperienced in thy genuine love, a catechumen taking holiday in the country house with Alypius, a catechumen, while my mother was joined to us in woman's garb, with manly faith, the security of old age, motherly charity, Christian piety! What utterances did I give thee in those psalms, and how I was inflamed toward thee by them, and kindled to recite them, if I could, throughout the whole world against the pride of the human race! And yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and Ps. 18, 7. there is none that hideth himself from thy heat. With what vehement and keen pain was I indignant at the Manichaeans; and again I pitied them, because they did not know those sacraments, those remedies, and were mad against the antidote by which they might have been made sound!

I wished that they might then be somewhere close by * , and, without my knowing that they were there, might watch my face and hear my words when I read the fourth psalm in that leisure then, and see what that psalm did to me. When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation thou hast enlarged me. Have mercy on me, O Lord, and hear my prayer. Let them hear, without my knowing whether they heard, lest they should think that I said on their account what I said amid these words. For indeed I would neither say those things, nor say them thus, if I perceived that I was being heard and seen by them; nor, if I said them, would they receive them as I received them with myself and for myself before thee, from the familiar affection of my mind.

> 9. I shuddered in fear, and in that very place I glowed in hope and exultation in thy mercy, O Father. And all these things came forth through my eyes and my voice, when thy good Spirit, turned toward us, said to us: Ps. 4, 3. Sons of men, how long are ye heavy-hearted? Why do ye love vanity and seek falsehood? For I had loved vanity and sought falsehood. And thou, O Lord, hadst already Ver. 4. magnified thy Holy One, raising him from the dead, and Eph. 1, 20. setting him at thy right hand, whence Luc. 24, 49. Joh. 14, 16. 17. Act. 2, 1-4. he might send from on high his promise, the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth: and he had already sent him, but I did not know it. He had sent him, because he had already been magnified, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven. But before then Joh. 7, 39. the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. And the prophet * cries: How long are ye heavy-hearted?

Why do ye love vanity and seek falsehood? And know that the Lord hath magnified his Holy One. He cries, how long; he cries, know: and I, for so long not knowing, “loved vanity and sought falsehood”; and therefore I heard and trembled, because such things are said to those such as I remembered myself to have been. For in the phantasms * which I had held for truth, there was vanity and falsehood. And I uttered many things loudly and vehemently in the pain of my remembrance. Would that those who even now “love vanity and seek falsehood” had heard them. Perhaps they would have been troubled and vomited it forth; and thou wouldst hear them when they cried out to thee: because by a true death of the flesh Rom. 8, 34. he died for us, who intercedes with thee for us.

> 10. I read: Be angry, and do not sin. And how I was moved, O my God, who had now learned to be angry with myself for the past, that in the future I might not sin! And rightly to be angry, because it was not some other nature of a race of darkness that sinned from me [223], as those say who are not angry with themselves, and Rom. 2, 5. treasure up wrath for themselves in the day of wrath and revelation of thy righteous judgment. Nor were my goods now outside, nor were they sought with eyes of flesh in this sun [224]. For those who wish to rejoice outwardly easily vanish away, and are poured out into the things that are seen and temporal [225], and with hungry [226] thought they lick the images of them. And O that they might be wearied by hunger [227], and say: Who will show us good things? And let us say, and let them hear: The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us. For we are not Joh. 1, 9. the light that enlighteneth every man; but we are enlightened by thee, that we who Eph. 5, 8.

We were once darkness; let us be light in thee. O if they could see the inward eternal thing, which, because I had tasted it, I was gnashing my teeth because I could not show it to them—if they were to bring to me their heart in their eyes, outside from thee, and say: Who will show us good things? For there, where I was angry with myself inwardly in my chamber, where I had been pierced, where I had sacrificed, slaying my old self, and, having begun the meditation of my renewal, was hoping in thee—there thou hadst begun to grow sweet to me, and Ps. 4, 7. hadst given gladness in my heart. And I cried aloud, reading these things without and recognizing them within; nor did I wish to be multiplied [228] by earthly goods, devouring times and devoured by times, when in eternal simplicity I had another [228] Ver. 8. wheat, and wine, and oil.

> 11. And in the following verse I cried out with a loud cry of my heart: O in peace! O in the selfsame! O what did he say: I will lie down and take sleep! For [229] who shall resist us when the saying which is written comes to pass, 1 Cor. 15, 54. Death is swallowed up in victory? And thou art the Selfsame, exceedingly, who dost not change; and in thee is rest, forgetful of all labours, because no other is with thee, nor are there many other things to be attained which are not what thou art; but thou, O Lord, hast established me singularly in hope. I read, and burned; nor did I find what I should do for the deaf dead, from among whom I had been—a pest, a bitter and blind barker against the Letters, honeyed with the honey of heaven and luminous with thy light; and I wasted away over the enemies of this Scripture.
> He is suddenly freed from a most acute toothache.

> 12. When shall I recall all the things of those holiday days? But I have neither forgotten nor will I be silent about the harshness of thy scourge and the wonderful swiftness of thy mercy. At that time thou didst torture me with toothache; and when it grew so severe that I was unable to speak [230] , it came into my heart to urge all my own who were present to pray to thee for me, the God of every kind of salvation. And I wrote this upon wax and gave it to them to be read. As soon as we had bent our knees in suppliant affection, that pain fled. But what pain? Or how did it flee? I was terrified, I confess, O my Lord, my God; for from my earliest age I had experienced nothing of the kind. And the intimations of thy will were made known to me in their depth; and, rejoicing in faith, I praised thy name. Yet that faith did not allow me to be secure concerning my past sins, which had not yet been remitted to me through thy Baptism.
> V. He consults Ambrose concerning what should be read.

> 13. When the vintage vacation was over, I resigned, so that the Milanese might provide another seller of words for their students; both because I had chosen to serve thee, and because, owing to difficulty in breathing and pain in my chest, I was not equal to that profession. And by letter I disclosed to thy bishop, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and my present resolve, that he might advise me what of thy Books it was especially fitting for me to read, so that I might become more ready and better fitted to receive so great a grace. But he commanded Isaiah the prophet; I believe because, above the rest, he is a more manifest foreteller of the Gospel [231] and of the calling of the Gentiles. Nevertheless, not understanding the beginning of this reading, and supposing the whole to be such, I deferred it until I should be more practised in the Lord's utterance.
> Page 154
> VI. At Milan he is baptized with Alypius and Adeodatus.

> 14. Then, when the time came at which I had to give in my name [232] , having left the country, we returned to Milan. Alypius too was pleased to be born again in thee with me, already clothed with humility befitting thy Sacraments, and a most valiant tamer of the body, even to treading the icy Italian ground with bare foot in unwonted boldness. We also joined to ourselves the boy Adeodatus, carnally born of me out of my sin. Thou hadst made him well. He was almost fifteen years old [233] , and in talent surpassed many grave and learned men. I confess thy gifts to thee, O Lord my God, creator of all things, and mighty indeed to form our deformities: for, apart from sin, I had nothing in that boy. For that he was nurtured by us in thy discipline, thou hadst inspired in us—none other; I confess thy gifts to thee. There is a book of ours entitled, On the Teacher [234] : there he speaks with me.

Thou knowest that all the thoughts inserted there under the person of my interlocutor are his, when he was sixteen years old. I experienced many other things in him still more wonderful. That talent was a horror to me; and who besides thee is the maker of such miracles? Thou didst quickly take his life away from the earth; and I recall him more securely, fearing nothing for his boyhood, nor for his youth, nor indeed for that man at all. We joined him to ourselves, his coeval, in thy grace, to be brought up in thy discipline; and we were baptized [235] , and anxiety concerning our past life fled from us. Nor in those days was I sated with the wonderful sweetness of considering the depth of thy counsel concerning the salvation of the human race. How much I wept amid thy hymns and canticles, deeply moved by the sweetly sounding voices of thy Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and truth was distilled into my heart; from this the affection of piety overflowed, tears ran, and it was well with me in them.
> VII. The institution of ecclesiastical chant at Milan.

> 15. Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to celebrate this kind of consolation and exhortation, with great zeal of brethren singing together in voices and hearts. Surely it was a year, or not much more, since Justina, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, was persecuting thy man Ambrose on account of her heresy, by which she had been seduced by the Arians. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, thy servant. There my mother, thy handmaid, taking the foremost part in anxieties and vigils, lived in prayers. Though we were still cold from the warmth of thy Spirit, we were nevertheless stirred by the astonished and troubled city. Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung after the custom of the eastern regions, lest the people waste away through the weariness of sorrow; and from that time to this it has been retained, with many, now almost all, of thy flocks, and the rest of the world besides, imitating it.
> The discovery of the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius.

> 16. Then thou didst reveal by a vision to thy aforesaid bishop in what place the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius lay hidden, which for so many years thou hadst kept incorrupt in the treasure-house of thy secrecy, whence thou didst seasonably bring them forth to restrain a woman's, yet royal, fury. [237] For when, having been made known and dug up, they were being transferred with due honour to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were those tormented by unclean spirits healed [238] , the same demons confessing, but also a certain man blind for many years [239] , a citizen most well known to the city, when amid the people's tumultuous joy he had asked and heard the cause, leapt up and asked that his guide lead him there. Brought there, he obtained leave to touch with his handkerchief the bier of Ps. 115, 15. the precious in thy sight death of thy saints. When he had done this and applied it to his eyes, they were opened immediately.

Thence the fame ran abroad, thence thy praises, fervent and shining; thence the mind of that enemy, though not turned toward the soundness of belief, was yet restrained from the frenzy of persecution. Thanks to thee, my God. Whence and whither hast thou led my remembrance, that I might confess these things also to thee, which, though great, I had passed over in forgetfulness? And yet then, when Cant 1, 3. the odour of thy ointments thus was fragrant, we did not run after thee. Therefore I wept more amid the songs of thy hymns, formerly sighing after thee and at last breathing, as far as air extends in a house of hay.
> VIII. The conversion of Evodius. Ps. 67, 7.

> 17. Thou who makest those of one mind to dwell in a house, didst join to us Evodius also, a young man from our municipality. While serving as an agent in affairs [240] , he had been a soldier; he was converted to thee before us and baptized, and, leaving secular military service, girded himself for thine. We were together [241] , to dwell together by a holy resolve. We were seeking what place would be more useful for us in serving thee; together we were returning to Africa. And when we were at Ostia on the Tiber, my mother died. I pass over much, because I am in great haste. Receive my confessions and thanksgivings, O my God, concerning innumerable things, even in silence. Yet I shall not pass over whatever my soul brings to birth concerning that thy handmaid, who gave birth to me both in flesh, that I might be born into this temporal life, and in heart, that I might be born into eternal light [242] . I shall speak not of her gifts, but of thine in her; for she had not made herself, nor had she brought herself up.

Thou didst create her, nor did father or mother know what she would become from them. And the rod of thy Christ, the governance of thine only Son, instructed her in thy fear in a faithful household, a good member of thy Church. And she did not praise so much the diligence of a mother toward her discipline as that of a certain aged maidservant, who had carried her father when he was an infant, just as little children are customarily carried on the backs of somewhat grown girls. On account of this, and because of her old age and excellent character, she was sufficiently honoured by her masters in the Christian household. Hence also she diligently discharged the care of the daughters of her masters entrusted to her, and, when need arose, was vigorously severe with holy severity in restraining them, and soberly prudent in instructing them.

For, apart from those hours when they were fed at their parents' table with the greatest moderation, even if they burned with thirst, she would not allow them to drink water, guarding against a bad habit and adding a sound saying: “Now you drink water because you do not have wine in your power; but when you have come to husbands, having become mistresses of storerooms and cellars, water will seem vile, but the habit of drinking will remain.” By this manner of commanding and authority of ordering, she restrained the greed of their tender age; and she shaped the girls' very thirst to an honourable measure, so that they no longer even desired what was unfitting.

> 18. Yet drunkenness had crept upon her, as thy handmaid related to me her son—had crept upon her. For when, as was customary, she was ordered by her parents, as a sober girl, to draw wine from the cask, lowering the cup by the opening above, before she poured the pure wine into the little flask, she would sip a little with the tip of her lips, because she could not do more, her sense rejecting it. For she did this not from any drunken desire, but through certain superfluous excesses of age, which bubble forth in playful impulses and are customarily pressed down in childish minds by the weight of their elders. Thus, adding daily small amounts to that small amount, since he who Eccli. 19, 1. despises little things falls little by little , she had slipped into the habit of greedily draining cups almost full of pure wine. Where then were that shrewd old woman and that vigorous prohibition? Could they avail anything against the hidden disease, unless thy medicine, O Lord, watched over us?

With father and mother and guardians absent, thou present—thou who createst, who callest, who also through persons set over us workest some good for the salvation of souls—what then didst thou do, O my God? Whence didst thou cure? Whence didst thou heal? Didst thou not bring forth from another soul a harsh and sharp reproach, like medicinal iron from thy hidden provisions, and with one blow cut away that corruption? For the maidservant with whom she used to go to the cask, quarrelling, as happens, alone with her young mistress, cast this charge in her teeth, with most bitter insult calling her a wine-bibber. Struck by that sting, she looked upon her foulness and immediately condemned and put it off. As flattering friends corrupt, so quarrelling enemies often correct. Yet thou dost not repay them for what thou workest through them, but for what they themselves intended.

For in anger she desired to vex her young mistress, not to heal her; and therefore secretly, either because place and time had found them thus, or lest perhaps she herself should be endangered for having disclosed it so late. But thou, O Lord, ruler of things heavenly and earthly, bending to thy uses the depths of the torrent, the orderly turbulent flow of the ages, didst even through the madness of one soul [243] heal another; lest anyone, when he notices this, should ascribe it to his own power if another is corrected by his word whom he wishes to be corrected.
> IX. He recounts the praiseworthy character of his mother.

> 19. Brought up therefore chastely and soberly, and made subject to her parents by thee rather than to thee by her parents, when she had reached marriageable age, she was given to a husband and served him as though a lord; and she strove to win him for thee, speaking to him of thee by her conduct, through which thou didst make her beautiful and reverently lovable and admirable to her husband. And she so endured the wrongs of his marriage bed that she never had any quarrel with her husband on this account. For she awaited thy mercy upon him, that, believing in thee, he might become chaste. Moreover, as he was eminent in kindness, so he was fervent in anger. But she knew not to resist an angry husband, not merely in deed, but not even in word. Then indeed, when she saw him broken and quiet at a fitting time, she gave an account of her action, if perhaps he had been moved too inconsiderately.

Finally, when many married women whose husbands were more gentle bore the marks of blows even upon their disfigured faces, in conversations among friends those women would accuse their husbands’ manner of life; but she, gravely admonishing their tongues as if in jest, would say that, from the time when they had heard those tablets called matrimonial read aloud, they ought to have regarded them as instruments by which they had been made handmaids; and therefore, mindful of their condition, they ought not to be proud against their masters. And when they wondered, knowing what a fierce husband she endured, that it had never been heard or made clear by any indication that Patricius had struck his wife, or that they had disagreed with one another in a domestic quarrel even for one day, and when they asked familiarly for the reason, she taught them her practice, which I mentioned above. Those who observed it, having tried it, congratulated her; those who did not observe it, being subject, were vexed.

> 20. She also so won over by her services her mother-in-law, who at first had been irritated against her by the whisperings of wicked maidservants, persevering in patience and gentleness, that the latter of her own accord disclosed to her son the half-spoken tales of the servants by which domestic peace between herself and her daughter-in-law was disturbed, and demanded vengeance. Accordingly, after he, both obeying his mother and attending to the discipline of the household and providing for the concord of his own people, restrained with beatings those who had been exposed, at the discretion of the informer, she promised that such rewards from herself ought to be expected by anyone who, in order to please her, should say anything bad to her about her daughter-in-law; and, as no one now dared do so, they lived together in a memorable sweetness of mutual goodwill. Page 160

> 21. This too you had bestowed as a great gift upon that good handmaid of yours, in whose womb you created me, my God, my mercy: that among any souls at variance and discord, wherever she could, she showed herself so peaceable that, though she heard from both sides many most bitter things about one another—the sort that swollen and undigested discord is wont to belch forth when, in bitter conversations with a friend present, the rawness * of hatreds is exhaled against an enemy absent—she would nevertheless disclose nothing of one to the other, unless it might avail toward reconciling them.

This good would seem small to me, if I did not sadly experience countless crowds, with I know not what dreadful pestilence of sins spreading most widely, who not only reveal to angry enemies words spoken by angry enemies, but even add things that were not said; whereas, on the contrary, it ought to be too little for a human person * merely not to stir up or increase the enmities of men by speaking ill, unless he also strives to extinguish them by speaking well; such as she was, with you teaching her as inward master in the school of her heart.

> 22. Finally, she won even her husband for you, now at the end of his temporal life; and in him now faithful she did not mourn what she had endured in him while not yet faithful. She was also a servant of your servants. Whoever among them knew her greatly praised and honored and loved you in her; for he sensed your presence in her heart, the fruits of her holy manner of life bearing witness [244]. For she had been 1 Tim. 5, 9, 4. 10. the wife of one husband, had rendered reciprocal service to her parents, had managed her household piously, had testimony in good works. Gal. 4, 19. She had nourished her children, travailing in birth with them as often as she saw them departing from you. Lastly, for all of us, Lord, because by your gift you permit your servants to speak, who before her falling asleep were already living united in you, having received the grace of your Baptism, she cared as though she had borne us all, served as though she had been born of us all.
> X. Conversation with his mother concerning the kingdom of heaven.

> 23. But as the day was imminent on which she was to depart from this life—a day which you knew, while we did not—it came about, as I believe, through your hidden workings, that she and I stood alone, leaning at a certain window from which the garden within the house that contained us could be seen, there at Ostia on the Tiber, where, withdrawn from the crowds, after the labor of a long journey, we were restoring ourselves for a voyage. Therefore we conversed alone very sweetly; and Phil. 3, 13. forgetting the things behind, and stretching forth unto those things which are before, we were asking one another, in the presence of the Truth—which you are—what would be the eternal life of the saints, 1 Cor. 2, 9. which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man. But with the mouth of our heart we thirsted for the heavenly streams of your fountain, Ps. 35, 10. the fountain of life which is with you; that, sprinkled thence according to our capacity, we might somehow contemplate so great a matter.

> 24. And when our discourse had been brought to this point—that the delight of carnal senses, however great, in however great a bodily light, seemed unworthy, in comparison with the pleasantness of that life, not merely of comparison, but even of mention—we, raising ourselves with a more ardent affection toward that selfsame thing [245], passed step by step through all bodily things, and heaven itself, whence sun and moon and stars shine upon the earth. And still we ascended inwardly by thinking, and speaking * , and wondering at your works; and we came to our own minds, and transcended [246] them, that we might attain the region of unfailing abundance, where Ps. 79, 2. you feed Israel forever with the pasture of truth, and where life is wisdom, through which all these things are made, both those that have been and those that are to be; and it itself is not made, but is as it was, and so shall be forever; indeed, rather, in it there is no having been and no being to come, but only being, because it is eternal: for to have been and to be to come is not eternal.

And while we speak and thirst after it, we touched it slightly with the whole thrust of the heart; and we sighed * and left bound there Rom. 8, 23. the firstfruits of the Spirit [247], and returned to the noise of our mouth, where a word both begins and ends. And what is like your Word, our Lord, Sap. 7, 27. abiding in himself without old age, and making all things new?

> 25. We were saying then: If for someone the tumult of the flesh should fall silent, the phantasies of earth and waters and air should fall silent, the very heavens should fall silent, and the soul itself should fall silent to itself and pass beyond itself by not thinking itself; if dreams and imaginary revelations should fall silent, every tongue and every sign, and whatever comes to be in passing, should altogether fall silent for someone; since, if anyone hears them * , all these things say, Ps. 99, 3. We did not make ourselves, but he who abides forever made us: if, having said this, they should now fall silent, since they have raised their ear toward him who made them, and he alone should speak, not through them but through himself, so that we may hear his word, not through the tongue of flesh nor through the voice of an angel, Ps. 76, 18. nor through the sound of a cloud, nor 1 Cor. 13, 12.

through the enigma of a likeness; but that we might hear himself whom we love in these things, himself without these things, just as now we stretch ourselves out and by swift thought touch * eternal Wisdom abiding above all things; if this should continue, and other visions of a far unequal kind should be withdrawn, and this one should seize and absorb and hide its beholder in inward joys, so that everlasting life might be such as was this moment of understanding for which we sighed—would not this be, Mat. 25, 21. Enter into the joy of thy Lord? And when shall this be? Is it when 1 Cor. 15, 51. we shall all rise again, but shall not all be changed?

> 26. I was saying such things * , and, even if not in this manner and with these words, nevertheless, Lord, you know that on that day, while we were speaking such things and this world with all its delights was becoming cheap to us amid our words, she then said: “My son, as far as I am concerned, I now delight in no thing in this life. What I am still doing here, and why I am here, I do not know, now that hope in this age has been exhausted. There was one thing for which I desired to remain somewhat longer in this life: that I might see you a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has granted me this more abundantly, in that I see you also, despising earthly happiness, as his servant. What am I doing here?”
> XI. Concerning the ecstasy and death of his mother.

> 27. What I replied to her, I do not sufficiently recall. Meanwhile, scarcely within five days, or not much more, she took to her bed with fevers. And while she was ill, one day she suffered a swoon, and was for a little while withdrawn from those present. We rushed together, but she was quickly restored to consciousness; and she looked at us standing by, myself and my brother [248], and said to us, as if like one asking, “Where was I?” Then, seeing us stunned with grief: “Here,” she said, “you shall lay your mother.” I was silent and held back my weeping. But my brother said something by which he wished, as something happier, that she might end her life not abroad but in her native land. Hearing this, she anxiously rebuked him with her eyes for thinking such things, and then looked at me: “See,” she said, “what he says.” And immediately to us both: “Lay this body anywhere,” she said; “let no concern about it trouble you. Only this I ask of you: remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you may be.”
And when she had explained this thought in such words as she could, she fell silent; and, as the sickness grew heavier, she was worn down.

> 28. But I, reflecting upon your gifts, invisible God, which you send into the hearts of your faithful and from which admirable fruits spring forth, rejoiced and gave thanks to you, recalling what I knew: how much concern she had always felt about the tomb that she had provided and prepared for herself beside the body of her husband. For because they had lived most harmoniously, she desired this also—such is the human mind, less capable of divine things—that it might be added to that happiness and remembered by people that after her pilgrimage across the sea it had been granted her that the earth covering the two spouses should cover them joined together. But when this vanity had begun not to be in her heart through the fullness of your goodness, I did not know; and I rejoiced in wonder that she had thus revealed it to me * ; although even in that conversation of ours at the window, when she said, “What am I doing here now?” she did not appear to desire to die in her native land.

I also heard later that, when we were already at Ostia, she was one day conversing with some of my friends, with maternal confidence, about contempt for this life and the good of death, where I myself was not present; and when they, astonished at the strength of the woman—which you had given her—asked whether she did not fear leaving her body so far from her own city, she said: “Nothing is far from God; nor need one fear that he will not recognize, at the end of the age, from where to raise me again.” Therefore, on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third of mine [249], that religious and pious soul was released from the body.
> XII. How he mourned his mother’s death.

> 29. I closed her eyes, and immense sorrow flowed together into my heart and overflowed into tears; and at the same time my eyes, by the violent command of my mind, drank back their own fountain unto dryness, and in such a struggle I was very ill. Then indeed, when she breathed her last * , the boy Adeodatus cried out in lamentation, and, restrained by us all, fell silent. In this way, too, something childish in me that was slipping into tears in the youthful voice of my heart was restrained and fell silent. For we did not think it fitting to celebrate that funeral with tearful wailings and groans * ; because by these there is usually lamented a certain misery of those dying, or as it were their complete extinction. But she neither died miserably nor died altogether. We held this by the testimonies of her character, by faith unfeigned, and by sure reasons.

> 30. What then was it that grievously pained me within, except the fresh wound from the suddenly broken habit of living together, so sweet and so dear? I indeed rejoiced at her testimony, that in that very last illness, flattering me with her services, she called me dutiful and recalled with great affection of love that she had never heard from my mouth a harsh or insulting sound hurled against her * . Yet what comparable thing, my God, who made us, was the honor rendered by me to her, and the service rendered by her to me? Therefore, because I was deprived of so great a consolation from her, my soul was wounded * , and my life, which had become one from hers and mine, was as it were torn apart.

> 31. When, then, that boy had been restrained from weeping, Evodius took up the Psalter and began to sing the psalm [250], to which the whole household responded: Ps. 100, 1. I will sing unto thee, O Lord, of mercy and judgment. But when they heard what was being done, many brethren and religious women assembled; and while those whose duty it was attended to the funeral in the customary way, I, in the place where I could suitably do so, discussed matters appropriate to the occasion with those who thought that I should not be left alone; and by that consolation of truth I softened a torment known to you, though unknown to them, who listened intently and thought me to be without feeling of grief. Yet in your ears, where none of them heard, I rebuked the softness of my feeling and constrained the flow of sorrow; and it yielded to me a little, but again was carried along by its own onset, though not so far as the bursting forth of tears or a change of countenance; but I knew what I was pressing down in my heart.

And because it greatly displeased me that these human things should have such power in me—things which must necessarily happen by the due order and lot of our condition—I grieved for my grief with another grief, and was worn away by a double sadness.
> Page 165

> 32. And behold, the body was carried out * ; we went, we returned, without tears. For neither in those prayers [252] which we poured out to you, when the sacrifice of our price was offered for her, with the corpse already placed beside the grave before it was lowered, as is customary there, nor in those prayers did I weep. But throughout the whole day I was grievously sad in secret, and with troubled mind I asked you, as I could, to heal my sorrow; and you did not do so, I believe, commending to my memory, even by this one proof, how strong is every bond of habit, even against a mind that now feeds upon no deceitful word * . It also seemed good to me to go and bathe, because I had heard that baths were given that name because the Greeks call them βαλανεῖον, since they drive anxiety from the mind. Behold, I confess this also to your mercy, Ps. 67, 6. Father of orphans, because I bathed, and I was such as I had been before I bathed. For the bitterness of sorrow did not sweat out from my heart.
Then I slept and awoke, and found my grief alleviated by no small degree; and, as I was alone in my bed, I recalled the truthful verses of your Ambrose: for you are
> God, Creator of all things,
> And ruler of the heavens, clothing
> The day with comely light,
> The night with the sleep * of grace:
> That rest may restore loosened limbs
> To the use of labour,
> And relieve weary minds,
> And unbind anxious griefs.

> 33. And thence, little by little, I brought back your handmaid to my former feeling, and her devout fellowship toward you, and her holy * tenderness and compliance toward us, of which I was suddenly bereft; and I wished to weep in your sight concerning her and for her, concerning myself and for myself. And I let loose the tears that I had restrained, that they might flow forth as much as they wished, laying them beneath my heart; and I rested in them * , because there were your ears, not those of some man who would proudly interpret my weeping. And now, Lord, I confess to you in writing. Let whoever wishes read, and interpret as he wishes; and if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for a small part of an hour—Page 166 a mother meanwhile dead to my eyes, who had wept for me for many years that I might live in your eyes—let him not mock; but rather, if he has great charity, let him himself weep to you, Father of all the brethren of your Christ, for my sins.
> XIII. He prays for his deceased mother.

> 34. But I, now that my heart has been healed from that wound in which carnal affection could be reproved, pour out to you, our God, for that your handmaid a far different kind of tears, which flows from a spirit shaken by consideration of the perils of every soul 1 Cor. 15, 22. that dies in Adam . Although she was made alive in Christ , and, even before being released from the flesh, lived in such a way that your name is praised in her faith and conduct; yet I do not dare to say that, from the time when you regenerated her through Baptism, Mat. 12, 3. no word went forth from her mouth against your commandment. And it was said by Truth, your Son: Ib. 5, 23. Whoever shall say to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the hell of fire. And woe even to the praiseworthy lives of human beings, if, mercy being set aside, you examine them. But because you do not rigorously investigate transgressions, we confidently hope for some place with you * . But whoever recounts to you his true merits, what does he recount to you but your gifts [253] ?
O that human beings might know themselves to be human beings; and 2 Cor. 10, 17. let him who glories, glory in the Lord * !

> 35. Therefore I, my praise and my life, God of my heart, setting aside for a little while her good deeds, for which I joyfully give you thanks, now pray to you for the sins of my mother; hear me through the Medicine of our wounds, who hung upon the wood and, seated at your right hand, Rom. 8, 34. intercedes with you for us . I know that she acted mercifully, and Mat. 18, 36; 6, 12. forgave from her heart the debts of her debtors ; do you also forgive her her debts , if she also contracted any through so many years after the water of salvation. Forgive, Lord, forgive, I beseech you; Ps. 142, 2. do not enter into judgment with her . Jac. 2, 13. Let mercy exalt itself over judgment , since your utterances are true, and you promised Mat. 5, 7. mercy to the merciful : and that they might be so, you gave it to them—you who Ex. 33, 19; Ro. 9, 15. will have mercy on whom you have had mercy, and will bestow mercy on whom you have been merciful .

> 36. And I believe that * you have already done what I ask of you, but Ps. 118, 108. approve the free-will offerings of my mouth, O Lord .
