> 67. Quem invenirem qui me reconciliaret tibi? Ambiendum * mihi fuit ad Angelos? Qua prece? quibus sacramentis? Multi conantes ad te redire, neque per seipsos valentes, sicut audio, tentaverunt hæc, et inciderunt in desiderium
> Page 202

> curiosarum visionum, et digni habiti sunt illusionibus. Elati enim te quærebant doctrinæ fastu, exerentes potius quam tundentes pectora, et adduxerunt sibi per similitudinem cordis sui conspirantes et socias superbiæ suæ Eph. 2, 2. potestates aeris hujus , a quibus per potentias magicas deciperentur, quærentes mediatorem per quem purgarentur, et non erat. 2 Cor. 11, 14. Diabolus enim erat transfigurans se in Angelum lucis . Et * multum illexit superbam carnem, quod carneo corpore ipse non esset. Erant enim illi mortales et peccatores; tu autem, Domine, cui reconciliari superbe quærebant, immortalis et sine peccato. 1 Tim. 2, 5. Mediator autem inter Deum et homines , oportebat ut haberet aliquid simile Deo, aliquid simile hominibus: ne in utroque hominibus similis, longe esset a Deo; aut in utroque Deo similis, longe esset ab hominibus, atque ita mediator non esset.

Fallax itaque ille mediator, quo per secreta judicia tua, superbia mereretur illudi, unum cum hominibus habet, id est peccatum; aliud videri vult habere cum Deo, ut quia carnis mortalitate [290] non tegitur, pro immortali se ostentet. Sed quia Rom. 6, 20. stipendium peccati mors est , hoc habet commune cum hominibus, unde simul damnetur in mortem.
> XLIII. Christus verus mediator.

> 68. Verax autem mediator quem secreta tua misericordia demonstrasti humilibus, et misisti ut ejus exemplo etiam ipsam discerent humilitatem, mediator ille Dei et hominum homo Christus Jesus , inter mortales peccatores et immortalem justum apparuit; mortalis cum hominibus, justus cum Deo. Ut quoniam stipendium justitiæ vita et pax est, per justitiam conjunctam Deo evacuaret mortem justificatorum impiorum * , quam cum illis voluit habere communem. Hinc * demonstratus est antiquis sanctis, ut ita ipsi per fidem futuræ passionis ejus, sicut nos per fidem præteritiæ, salvi fierent. Inquantum enim homo, intantum mediator [291] ; inquantum autem Verbum, non medius, quia æqualis Deo, et Deus apud Deum, et simul * unus Deus.

> 69. Quomodo [292] nos amasti, Pater bone, qui Rom. 8, 32. Filio tuo unico non pepercisti, sed pro nobis impiis tradidisti eum ! Phil. 2, 6. Quomodo nos amasti pro quibus ille, non rapinam arbitratus esse æqualis tibi, factus est subditus usque ad mortem crucis ; unus ille Ps. 87, 6-8. in mortuis liber, Joh. 10, 18. potestatem habens ponendi animam suam, et potestatem habens iterum sumendi eam [293] ; pro nobis tibi victor et victima, et ideo victor quia victima; pro nobis tibi sacerdos et sacrificium, et ideo sacerdos quia sacrificium; faciens tibi nos de servis filios, de te nascendo, nobis serviendo! Merito mihi spes valida in illo est, quod Rom. 8, 34. sanabis omnes languores meos , per eum qui sedet ad dexteram tuam et te interpellat pro nobis ; alioquin desperarem. Multi enim et magni sunt iidem languores mei, multi sunt et magni; sed amplior est medicina tua.
Potuimus putare Verbum tuum remotum esse a conjunctione hominis, et desperare de nobis, nisi Joh. 1, 14. caro fieret et habitaret in nobis .

> 70. Conterritus peccatis meis et mole miseriæ meæ, agitaveram * corde meditatusque fueram fugam in solitudinem; sed prohibuisti me, et confirmasti me, dicens: 2 Cor. 5, 15. Ideo Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui vivunt, jam non sibi vivant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est . Ecce, Domine, jacto in te curam meam ut vivam, et Ps. 118, 18. considerabo mirabilia de lege tua . Tu scis imperitiam meam et infirmitatem meam: doce me, et sana me. Ille tuus Unicus Col. 2, 3. in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi , redemit me sanguine suo. Non calumnientur mihi superbi: quoniam cogito pretium meum, et manduco, et bibo, et erogo; et pauper cupio saturari ex eo, inter illos qui Ps. 21, 27. edunt et saturantur , et laudant Deum qui requirunt eum .

> Hic ubi vitæ præteritæ enarrationem abrumpit Aug., haud inutile erit adponere, quid hæreticis responderit, auctoritatem ejus in fidei defensione elevantibus, propter ea, quæ nondum fidelis commiserit. Ii vero præcipue fuerunt Page 204 Donatistæ. His præclare coram populo respondit. (Serm. 3. in Ps. 36. §. 19) "Loquantur ergo adversus nos quidquid volunt: nos diligemus illos et nolentes. Novimus enim, Fratres, novimus linguas eorum; propter quas eis non irascamur, patienter ferte nobiscum. Vident enim in caussa se nihil habere, et linguas convertunt in nos; et incipiunt de nobis dicere mala, multa quæ sciunt, multa quæ nesciunt. Quæ sciunt, præterita nostra sunt. Fuimus enim aliquando, sicut dicit Apostolus, "stulti et increduli, et ad omne opus bonum reprobi."

In errore perverso desipientes et insanientes fuimus, non negamus; et quantum præteritum nostrum non negamus, tanto magis Deum qui nobis ignovit, laudamus. Quid ergo hæretice dimittis caussam, et is ad hominem? Quid enim ego sum? Quid sum? Numquid Catholica ego sum? Numquid hereditas Christi diffusa per gentes ego sum? Sufficit mihi ut in ea sim. Vituperas mala mea præterita, quid magnum facis? Severior sum ego in mala mea quam tu: quod tu vituperasti, ego damnavi . Utinam velles imitari, ut et error tuus fieret aliquando præteritus. Ista sunt mala præterita, quæ noverunt, maxime in ista civitate. Hic enim male viximus, quod ego confiteor: et quantum gaudeo de gratia Dei, tantum de meis præteritis quid dicam—Doleo? Dolorem, si adhuc essem. Sed quid dicam? Gaudeo? Nec hoc possum dicere: utinam enim numquam fuissem. Quidquid tamen fui, in nomine Christi præteritum est.

Quod autem modo reprehendunt, non norunt. Sunt quæ adhuc in me reprehendant: sed tamen multum est ad illos ut hæc noverint. Multa enim ago in cogitationibus meis, pugnans adversus malas suggestiones meas, et habens conflictationem diuturnam, et prope continuam cum tentationibus inimici subvertere me volentis. Gemo ad Deum in infirmitate mea; et novit quid parturit cor meum, ille qui novit partum meum. "Mihi autem minimum est, ut a vobis dijudicer, aut ab humano die," ait Apostolus; "sed neque ego meipsum judico." Melius enim me ego novi quam illi, sed melius Deus quam ego. Non ergo vobis insultent de nobis, non, faciat Christus. Dicunt enim, Et qui sunt? et unde sunt? malos hic illos novimus, ubi baptizati sunt? Si nos bene noverunt, sciunt quia et navigavimus aliquando; sciunt quia et peregrinati sumus; sciunt quia alii ivimus, et alii redivimus.

Non hic baptizati sumus; sed ubi baptizati sumus, Ecclesia est nota universo orbi terrarum. Et multi fratres nostri sunt, qui et norunt quia baptizati sumus, et nobiscum baptizati sunt. Facile est ergo hoc nosse, si quis fratrum est inde sollicitus.
> Page 205

> As he disclosed in the preceding Books what he had been before receiving the grace of baptism, so in this one he investigates what he was like at the time when he wrote these things. And first he professes that he loves God. Then, inquiring what path must be entered upon for knowing Him, he surveys all the powers of his soul; but above all memory, whose altogether astonishing power he displays, and shows that God deigns to dwell within it. Next he examines his actions, senses, and affections, in relation to the threefold temptation of pleasure, curiosity, and pride; and clearly teaches what Christian temperance prescribes concerning each. Then he discusses Christ the Mediator, by whose aid he trusts that all the languors of his soul will be healed.
> I. Hope and joy in God alone.

> 1. Let me know Thee, O my Knower, 1 Cor. 13, 12. let me know as I also am known. O strength of my soul, enter into it, and fit it to Thyself, that Thou mayest have and possess Eph. 5, 27. it without spot or wrinkle. This is my hope, Ps. 115, 10. therefore I speak; and in this hope I rejoice, when I rejoice soundly. But the other things of this life are the less to be wept for, the more they are wept for; and the more to be wept for, the less they are wept for in them. For behold, Ps. 50, 8. Thou hast loved truth, since Joh. 3, 21. he that does it comes to the light. I desire to do it in my heart before Thee in confession; but with my pen before many witnesses.
> II. Since the secrets of men are known to God, what it is to confess to Him.

> 2. And to Thee indeed, O Lord, Heb. 4, 13. to whose eyes the Ecclus. 42, 18. abyss of human conscience is naked, what could be hidden in me, even if I did not wish to confess to Thee? For I should hide Thee from myself, not myself from Thee. But now, since my groaning bears witness that I displease myself, Thou shinest forth and dost please, and art loved and desired; so that I may be ashamed of myself, and cast myself away and choose Thee, and please neither Thee nor myself except through Thee. Therefore, O Lord, I am manifest to Thee, whoever I may be; and I have said to what end I confess to Thee. For I do not do this * with words of flesh and sounds, but with words of the soul and the cry of thought, which Thine ear knows. For when I am evil, to confess to Thee is nothing else than to displease myself; but when I am pious, to confess to Thee is nothing else than not to attribute this to myself: Ps. 5, 13. for Thou, O Lord, blessest the righteous, but first Rom. 4, 5. Thou justifiest the ungodly.

My confession, therefore, O my God, is made before Thee to Thee silently, and not silently. Page 169 For it is silent in noise, it cries aloud in affection. Nor do I * say anything right to men which Thou hast not first heard from me; nor dost Thou hear anything such from me which Thou hast not first said to me.
> III. To what end he will henceforth confess what he is, not what he was.

> 3. What then have I to do with men, that they should hear my confessions, as though they themselves Ps. 102, 3. were going to heal all my languors? A curious race for knowing another's life, slothful for correcting their own. Why do they seek to hear from me what I am, when they are unwilling to hear from Thee what they are? And whence do they know, when they hear from myself concerning myself, whether I speak the truth, since 1 Cor. 2, 11. no man knows what is done in a man, save the spirit of the man which is in him? But if they hear from Thee concerning themselves, they cannot say, The Lord lies. For what is it to hear from Thee concerning oneself, but to know oneself? Moreover, who knows and says, It is false, unless he himself lies? But because Ibid. 13, 7. charity believes all things, at any rate among those whom, being joined together, it makes one with itself, I too, O Lord, thus confess to Thee, that men may hear, to whom I cannot demonstrate whether I confess truly; but those whose ears charity opens to me believe me.

> 4. Nevertheless, Thou, my inmost physician, make clear to me to what end I do these things. For confessions of my past evils, which Ps. 31, 1. Thou hast forgiven and covered, that Thou mightest make me blessed in Thee, changing my soul by Thy faith and Sacrament, when they are read and heard, stir up the heart not to sleep in despair and say, I cannot; but to wake in the love of Thy mercy and the sweetness of Thy grace, by which every weak person is mighty, who through it is made conscious of his own weakness. And good men delight to hear of the past evils of those who now lack them; nor do they delight because they are evils, but because they were and are not. To what end then, O Lord my God, to whom my conscience daily confesses, being more secure in the hope of Thy mercy than in its own innocence; to what end, I pray, do I also confess before men in Thy presence through these writings what I still am, not what I was? For I have seen and mentioned that fruit.

But what I still am, behold, at the very time of my confessions, many desire to know—those who have known me and have not known me, who have heard something from me or about me; but their ear is not at my heart, where I am, whatever I am. Therefore they wish to hear me confessing what I myself am within, where they cannot direct Page 170 eye or ear or mind; yet they are willing to believe: are they perhaps willing to know? For charity, by which they are good, tells them that I do not lie in confessing concerning myself, and it itself in them believes me.
> IV. That the fruits of such confession are great.

> 5. But to what end do they wish this? Do they desire to rejoice with me when they hear how far I advance * by Thy gift, and to pray for me when they hear how much I am delayed by my own weight? To such persons I shall make myself known. For it is no small fruit, O Lord my God, that 2 Cor. 1, 11. thanks may be given to Thee for us by many, and that Thou mayest be entreated for us by many. Let a brotherly mind love in me what Thou teachest to be loved, and grieve in me at what Thou teachest to be grieved. Let that mind do this as brotherly, not as alien, not Ps. 143, 8. of strange sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity; but as brotherly—that which, when it approves me, rejoices over me, but when it disapproves me, grieves for me: because whether it approves or disapproves me, it loves me. To such persons I shall make myself known; let them breathe again in my goods, let them sigh over my evils. My goods are Thy institutions and Thy gifts; my evils are my offences and Thy judgments [256].

Let them breathe again in the former and sigh in the latter; and let hymn and weeping ascend before Thee from brotherly hearts, Apoc. 8, 3. in Thy censers. But Thou, O Lord, delighted by the odour of Thy holy temple, Ps. 50, 1. have mercy upon me according to Thy great mercy, for Thy name's sake; and never forsaking what Thou hast begun, bring my imperfections to completion.

> 6. This is the fruit of my confessions: not what I was like, but what I am like, that I may confess this * not only before Thee in secret Ps. 2, 11. exultation with trembling and secret sorrow with hope; but also in the ears of believing sons of men, companions of my joy and sharers of my mortality, my fellow-citizens and pilgrims with me, those preceding and following, and companions of my way. These are Thy servants, my brothers, whom Thou hast willed to be Thy sons, my masters, whom Thou hast commanded me to serve, if I would live with Thee from Thee. And this Thy Word would have been too little for me, if it commanded by speaking, unless it also went before by doing. And I do this in deeds and words, I do it under Thy wings, with exceedingly great danger, unless because under Thy wings my soul is subjected to Thee, and my weakness is known to Thee.

I am little, but my Father ever lives, and my guardian is sufficient for me; for He Himself is the same who begot me and protects me: and Thou Thyself art all my goods, Thou Almighty One who art with me, and before I am with Thee. Therefore I shall make myself known to such persons as those whom Thou commandest me to serve—not what I was, but what I now am, and what I still am; 1 Cor. 4, 3. but neither do I judge myself: thus then may I be heard.
> V. A man does not know himself wholly.

> 7. 1 Cor. 4, 3. For Thou, O Lord, judgest me; for although no man knows the things of a man, save the spirit of the man which is in him; yet there is something in man which not even the spirit of the man that is in him knows; but Thou, O Lord, knowest all things of him whom Thou hast made. But I, although before Thy sight I despise myself, and reckon myself earth and ashes, yet know something of Thee which I do not know of myself. And certainly Id. 13, 12. we now see through a glass in an enigma, not yet face to face: and therefore, as long as 2 Cor. 5, 6. I journey away from Thee, I am more present to myself than to Thee, and yet I know that Thou canst in no way be violated; but by what temptations I am able to stand firm, and by which I am not able, I do not know. And there is hope, 1 Cor. 10, 13. because Thou art faithful, who dost not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation dost also make the way out, that we may be able to endure it.

Therefore let me confess what I know of myself; let me confess also what I do not know of myself. For even what I know of myself, I know by Thy shining upon me; and what I do not know of myself, I do not know until Is. 58, 10. my darkness becomes as noonday in Thy countenance.
> VI. What he loves when he loves God; and how God is known from creatures.

> 8. With a conscience not doubtful but certain, O Lord, I love Thee. Thou hast struck my heart with Thy word, and I loved Thee. But also Rom. 1, 20. heaven and earth and all things that are in them, behold, on every side say to me that I should love Thee, nor do they cease to say this to all Ib. 9, 15. that they may be without excuse. But more deeply wilt Thou have mercy on whom Thou hast mercy, and wilt show mercy to whom Thou wilt be merciful: otherwise heaven and earth speak Thy praises to the deaf. But what do I love when I love Thee? Not bodily beauty, nor the splendour of time, not the brightness of light, behold * friendly to these eyes, not the sweet melodies of every kind of song, not the sweet fragrance of flowers and ointments and spices, not manna and honey, not limbs welcome to the embraces of the flesh.

I do not love these things when I love my God; and yet I love a certain light, and a certain voice, and a certain fragrance, and a certain food, and a certain embrace, when I love my God: the light, voice, fragrance, food, and embrace of my inner man; where that shines for my soul which no place contains, and where that sounds which time does not carry away, and where that smells which no breeze disperses, and where that tastes which eating does not diminish, and where that clings which satiety does not tear away. This is what I love when I love my God.

> 9. And what is this? I questioned the earth [257], and it said, I am not; and whatever things are in it made the same confession. I questioned the sea and the abysses, and creeping things with living souls, and they answered: We are not thy God; seek above us. I questioned the blowing breezes, and the whole air with its inhabitants said: Anaximenes is mistaken; I am not God. I questioned heaven, sun, moon, and stars; Neither are we the God whom thou seekest, they say. And I said to all these things which surround the doors of my flesh: Ye have told * me concerning my God that ye are not He; tell me something concerning Him. And they cried out with a loud voice: Ps. 99, 3. He made us. My question was my attention; and their response was their appearance [258]. And I turned to myself and said to myself, Who art thou? And I answered, A man. And behold, body and soul are present to me in me; the one outward, the other inward. By which of these ought I to have sought my God *?

Already I had sought through the body from earth even to heaven, so far as I could send forth my messengers, the rays of my eyes. But the inward is better. For all the bodily messengers reported to it, as it presided and judged concerning the * responses of heaven and earth and all things that are in them, saying: We are not God, and He made us. The inner man knew these things through the ministry of the outer: I, the inner man, knew these things; I, I the soul, through the sense of my body. I questioned the mass of the world concerning my God, and it answered me: I am not He, but He made me.

> 10. Does not this appearance manifest itself to all whose sense is sound? Why does it not speak the same thing to all? Small and great animals see it, but they cannot question: for in them reason, the judge, is not set over the reporting senses. But men can question, so that Rom. 1, 20. the invisible things of God may be seen, being understood through the things which are made *; but they are subjected to those things by love, and, being subjected, cannot judge. Nor do these things answer those who question unless they judge; nor do they change their voice, that is, their appearance, if one merely sees, while another, seeing, questions, so that it appears in one way to the former and in another to the latter; but appearing in the same way to both, it is mute to the former and speaks to the latter: indeed, it speaks to all, but those understand who compare its voice received outside with truth within. For truth says to me: Thy God is not heaven and earth, nor any body.

This says [so] to one beholding their nature *: It is a mass; the mass is less in the part than in the whole. But now you are better; to you I speak, O soul, since you give life to the mass of your body, bestowing life upon it, which no body supplies to a body. But your God is even to you the life of life *.
> VII. God is not found by a bodily or sensitive power.

> 11. What, then, do I love when I love my God? Who is that one above the head of my soul? Through my very soul I shall ascend to him. I shall pass beyond my power by which I cling to the body and vitally fill out its frame. By that power I do not find my God: for Ps. 31, 9. the horse and mule, which have no understanding, would find him; because * it is the same power by which their bodies too live. There is another power, not only by which I enliven, but also by which I endow with sensation my flesh, which the Lord made for me; commanding the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but the former [to be that] through which I see, the latter [to be that] through which I hear; and likewise, severally, the other senses in their proper seats and offices—different things which I, one mind, perform through them * . I shall pass beyond this power of mine too: for the horse and mule have this also; for they too perceive through the body.
> VIII. The power of memory.

> 12. Therefore I shall pass beyond this power too of my nature, ascending by steps to him who made me; and I come to the fields and spacious courts of memory, where are the treasures of innumerable images, brought in from things perceived of whatever kind * . There is stored up whatever we think, whether by increasing or diminishing, or in whatever way varying, those things which sense has touched; and whatever else has been entrusted and deposited there, which forgetfulness has not yet swallowed up and buried. When I am there, I demand that whatever I will be brought forth, and some things come forth at once; others are sought for longer, and are, as it were, dug out of certain more hidden receptacles; others rush forth in crowds, and while something else is sought and asked for, leap into the midst, as though saying, “Perhaps we are it?” And I drive them away with the hand of my heart from the face of my recollection, until that which * I will is cleared of clouds and comes forth to view from its hiding places.

Other things are readily suggested in an undisturbed sequence, as they are called for; and those which precede give way to those which follow, and in giving way are stored away, to come forth again when I will. This whole thing happens when I narrate something from memory. Page 174

> 13. There all things are preserved distinctly and according to their kinds, each as it entered by its own avenue: as light and all colours and forms of bodies through the eyes; but through the ears, all kinds of sounds; all odours through the avenue of the nostrils; all tastes through the avenue of the mouth; and from the sense of the whole body, what is hard, what soft, what hot or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light, whether external or internal to the body. The vast recess of memory receives all these things, when they must be recalled and reconsidered, and I know not what secret and ineffable folds thereof; each of them enters it through its own doors and is laid away in it. Yet the things themselves do not enter; rather, the images of sensed things are there at hand for thought when it recollects them. But who can say how these images were fashioned, when it is apparent by which senses they were snatched up and stored within?

For even while I dwell in darkness and silence, I bring forth colours in my memory *, if I will, and distinguish between white and black, and among whatever other colours I will; nor do sounds intrude and disturb what I contemplate, having been drawn in through the eyes, although those sounds too are there, lying hidden as though stored separately. For I call for them also, if it pleases me, and they are present at once. And while tongue and throat are at rest and silent, I sing as much as I will; and those images of colours, which nonetheless are there, do not interpose or interrupt when another treasure, which flowed in through the ears, is being reviewed. Thus I recall, as I please, the other things which have been brought in and amassed through the other senses; and, smelling nothing, I distinguish the fragrance of lilies from violets; and, then neither tasting nor touching, but remembering, I prefer honey to must, smooth to rough.

> 14. These things I do within, in the vast hall of my memory. For there heaven and earth and sea are at hand to me, with all things that I was able to perceive in them, except those which I have forgotten. There too I meet myself and recollect myself: what I have done, when and where I have done it, and how I was affected when I did it. There are all the things that I remember either as experienced by me or as believed. From the same store I myself weave together, in one way or another, likenesses of things either experienced, or believed on the basis of things which I have experienced, with past things; and from these too I meditate, as though present, future actions and events and hopes. “I shall do this or* that,” I say to myself in that vast recess of my mind, full of images of so many and such great things; “and this Page 175 or that will follow.” “Oh, if only this or that were [so]!” “May God avert this or that!”
I say these things to myself; and when I say them, the images of all that I say are at hand from the same treasure of memory, nor could I say any of them at all if they were absent.

> 15. Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, my God—a vast and boundless inner place. Who has reached its bottom? Yet this is a power of my mind and belongs to my nature; nor do I myself grasp all that I am. Therefore the mind is too narrow to contain itself. And where is that which it does not contain of itself *? Is it outside itself and not within it? How then does it not contain it? Great wonder at this arises in me; stupefaction takes hold of me.

And men go to wonder at the heights of mountains, the mighty waves of the sea, the broad courses of rivers, the circuit of the Ocean, and the revolutions of the stars, and they abandon themselves; nor do they wonder that, when I was saying all these things, I did not see them with my eyes, and yet I could not say them unless I saw within my memory, in spaces so vast as though I saw them outside, the mountains and waves and rivers and stars which I have seen, and the Ocean which I have believed. Yet I did not swallow them up by seeing when I saw them with my eyes; nor are the things themselves with me, but their images. And I know what was impressed upon me from which bodily sense.
> IX. Memory of the disciplines.

> 16. But this immeasurable capacity of my memory does not bear only those things. Here are also all those things perceived from the liberal disciplines which have not yet slipped away, as though set apart in a more inward place—not in a place *; and I bear not their images, but the things themselves. For what literature is, what skill in disputation is, how many kinds of questions there are—whatever of these things I know is so * in my memory, that I have not retained an image and left the thing outside; nor has it sounded and passed away, like a voice impressed through the ears with a trace by which it might be recalled *, as though it were sounding when it no longer sounded; or like an odour which, as it passes and vanishes into the winds, affects the sense of smell, whence it conveys an image of itself into memory for us to recover in remembering; or like food, which certainly no longer tastes in the stomach, and yet in memory as it were tastes; or like something perceived by touching with the body, which memory imagines even when it is separated from us.
For these things are not admitted into memory, but only their images are seized with wondrous swiftness, stored away in wondrous cells as it were, and wonderfully brought forth by remembering.
> X. The disciplines are not introduced into memory through the senses, but are drawn out from its more hidden recess.

> 17. But indeed, when I hear that there are three kinds of questions—whether a thing is, what it is, and of what kind it is—I retain the images of the sounds of which these words are made, and I know that they have passed through the air * with noise and now no longer are. But the things themselves which are signified by those sounds, I have touched with no bodily sense and seen nowhere except in my mind; and I have stored in memory, not images of them, but themselves. Let them say, if they can *, whence they entered into me. For I run through all the gates of my flesh and do not find through which of them they entered. The eyes indeed say: “If they are coloured, we reported them.” The ears say: “If they sounded, they were made known by us.” The nostrils say: “If they smelled, they passed through us.” The sense of taste also says: “If there is no flavour, ask me nothing.” Touch says: “If it is not bodily, I did not touch it; if I did not touch it, I did not report it.” Whence and by what way did these things enter into my memory?

I do not know how; for when I learned them, I did not believe [them] on another's heart, but recognized [them] in my own, and approved that they were true, and entrusted [them] to it, as though laying them up whence I might bring them forth when I wished. Therefore they were there even before I learned them, but they were not in memory. Where then, or why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, “It is so; it is true,” unless because they were already in memory, though so remote and withdrawn, as though in more hidden caves, that unless they were dug out by someone's prompting, perhaps I could not think them?
> XI. What learning is.

> 18. Accordingly, we find that to learn these things, whose images we do not draw in through the senses, but which we behold inwardly without images just as they are in themselves, is nothing other than to gather together by thinking, as it were, those things which memory held scattered and indiscriminately, and to take care by attending that, as though placed at hand in memory itself—where they had previously lain hidden, dispersed and neglected—they may now readily present themselves to familiar attention. And how many things of this kind my memory bears which have already been found and, as I have said, are as though placed at hand, which we are said to have learned and to know! If I cease to recall them at moderate intervals of time, they again sink down and slip away as though into more remote inner places, so that they must again be thought out anew from there * as though new (for there is no other region of them), and must again be gathered together in order that they may be known—that is, collected as though from a certain dispersion—whence the word cogitare, “to think,” is derived.

For cogo and cogito stand as ago and agito, facio and factito. Yet the mind has claimed this word as properly its own, so that not what is gathered elsewhere, but what is gathered in the mind—that is, brought together—is now properly said to be thought. Page 177
> XII. Memory of mathematical things.

> 19. Likewise, memory contains innumerable principles and laws of numbers and dimensions, none of which any bodily sense impressed, because they are neither coloured, nor sound, nor smell, nor have been tasted or touched. I have heard the sounds of the words by which they are signified when these matters are discussed; but those sounds are one thing, these [principles] another: for the former sound differently in Greek and in Latin, whereas the latter are neither Greek nor Latin, nor of any other kind of speech. I have seen the lines made by craftsmen, even exceedingly fine ones like a spider's thread; but those are different: they are not images of those [lines] which the eye of my flesh reported to me. Whoever has inwardly recognized them without any thought of any sort of body knows them. I have also perceived by all the bodily senses the numbers which we number; but they are different from those by which we number, nor are they images of these, and therefore they truly are. Let him who does not see them laugh at me for saying these things, and let me pity him for laughing at me.
> XIII. By memory we remember that we remember.

> 20. I retain all these things in memory, and I retain in memory how I learned them. I have also heard many things argued, most falsely, against these, and I retain them in memory: although they are false, nevertheless it is not false that I remember them; and I remember that I have distinguished between those true things and these false things which are alleged in opposition; and I now see that I distinguish these things in one way, but remember that I have often distinguished them in another way, when I often thought about them. Therefore I remember also that I have understood these things more than once; and what I now discern and understand, I store away in memory, so that later I may remember that I now understood it. Therefore I also remember that I remember; just as later, if I shall recollect that I was now able to recall these things, I shall certainly recollect it through the power of memory.
> XIV. How memory contains the affections of the mind. How we recall joyful things without being joyful.

> 21. The same memory also contains the affections of my mind: not in the manner in which the mind itself has them when it suffers them, but in another manner very different, according as the power of memory is constituted. For I recall that I have been joyful without being joyful, and I remember my past sorrow without being sorrowful, and I recollect that I was once afraid without fear, and I am mindful of a former desire without desire; and sometimes, conversely, I joyfully recall my sorrow now past, and sorrowfully my joy. This is not surprising in the case of the body: for the mind is one thing, the body another. Thus, if I joyfully remember a past bodily pain, it is not so surprising.

But here, since the mind is also memory itself—for when we entrust something to be held in memory, we say, “See that you keep that in mind”; and when we forget, we say, “It was not Page 178 in mind,” and, “It slipped from the mind,” calling memory itself mind—since this is so, what is this: when I joyfully remember my past sorrow, the mind has joy and memory sorrow; and the mind is joyful because joy is in it, yet memory is not sorrowful because sorrow is in it? Is memory perhaps not part of the mind? Who would say this? Surely, then, memory is as it were the stomach of the mind, while joy and sorrow are like sweet and bitter food: when they are committed to memory, as though transferred into the stomach, they can be stored there but cannot taste. It is ridiculous to suppose these things similar to those, yet they are not altogether dissimilar.

> 22. But behold, I bring forth from memory, when I say that there are four disturbances of the mind: desire, joy, fear, sorrow; and whatever I may be able to discuss concerning these, dividing each into the species of its own genus and defining it, I find there what I may say, and bring it forth from there. Yet I am disturbed by none of these disturbances when I mention them in recollecting; and before they were recalled and reconsidered by me, they were there; and for that reason they could be drawn forth from there by recollection. Perhaps, then, as food from the stomach by rumination, so these things are brought forth from memory by recollection. Why then is not the sweetness of joy or the bitterness of sadness felt in the mouth of thought by one disputing, that is, recollecting? Or is it dissimilar in this respect, because it is not similar in every respect? For who would willingly speak of such things if, as often as we named sorrow or fear, we were compelled to grieve or be afraid?

And yet we would not speak of these things unless in our memory we found not only the sounds of names according to images impressed by bodily senses *; but also notions of the things themselves, which we have received through no gate of the flesh, but which the mind itself, feeling them through experience of its own passions, has committed to memory, or has itself retained even without committing them to itself.
> XV. We remember even things that are absent.

> 23. But whether through images or not, who could easily say? For I name a stone, I name the sun, when the things themselves are not present to my senses; certainly their images are at hand in my memory. I name bodily pain, and it is not present to me while nothing hurts; yet unless its image were present in my memory, I would not know what I was saying, nor in disputation would I distinguish it from pleasure. I name bodily health when I am sound in body: the thing itself is indeed present to me; nevertheless, unless its image too were in my memory, I could by no means recall what the sound of this name signified. Nor would the sick, when health was named, recognize what had been said, unless the same image were held by the power of memory, although the thing itself were absent from the body. I name the numbers by which we count: behold, not their images but the numbers themselves are present in my memory.

I name the image of the sun, and this is present in my memory; for I do not recall the image of its image, but the image itself; it is at hand for me as I recollect. I name memory, and I recognize what I name. And where do I recognize it, if not in memory itself? Is it itself also present to itself through its own image, and not through itself?
> XVI. There is also memory of forgetfulness.

> 24. What then, when I name forgetfulness and likewise recognize what I name? Whence would I recognize it unless I remembered? I do not speak of the same sound of the name, but the thing which it signifies; if I had forgotten it, I certainly would not be able to recognize what that sound availed. Therefore, when I remember memory, memory itself is at hand to itself through itself; but when I remember forgetfulness, both memory and forgetfulness are at hand: memory by which I remember, forgetfulness which I remember. But what is forgetfulness except a privation of memory? How then is it present, so that I may remember it, when, if it is present, I cannot remember? But if we retain in memory what we remember, and unless we remembered forgetfulness we could by no means, on hearing this name, recognize the thing signified by it, forgetfulness is retained in memory. Is it present, then, lest we forget, though when it is present we forget? Or is it understood from this that, when we remember it, it is in memory not through itself but through its image?
because, if forgetfulness were at hand through itself, it would bring about not our remembering but our forgetting. And who, after all, will investigate this? Who will comprehend how it is?

> 25. Gen. 3, 7. I certainly, O Lord, labor here, and labor in myself: I have become for myself a land of difficulty and of excessive sweat. For we are not now investigating the regions of heaven, or measuring the intervals of the stars *, or seeking the balances of the earth: it is I who remember, I the mind. It is not so surprising if whatever I am not is far from me. But what is nearer to me than myself? And behold, the power of my memory is not comprehended by me, though I do not call myself apart from it. For what shall I say when it is certain to me that I remember forgetfulness? Shall I say that what I remember is not in my memory? Or shall I say that forgetfulness is in my memory for the purpose that I may not forget? Both are utterly absurd. What of that third possibility? In what way shall I say that the image of forgetfulness, not forgetfulness itself, is held by my memory when I remember it?

How shall I say this too, when, whenever the image of any thing is impressed on memory, it is first necessary that the thing itself be present, from which that image may be impressed? For thus I remember Carthage, thus all places where I have been, thus the faces of people whom I have seen, and the reports of the other senses, thus the health or pain of the body itself. When these things were at hand, memory received images from them, which I might behold when present and reconsider in mind when recalling them even in their absence. If, therefore, forgetfulness is held in memory through its image and not through itself, it surely was itself present so that its image might be received. But when it was present, how did it inscribe its image upon memory, when forgetfulness by its presence erases even that which it finds already marked? And yet, in whatever way it may be—though this manner is incomprehensible and inexplicable—I am certain that I remember forgetfulness itself, by which that which we remember is overwhelmed.
> XVII. Great is the power of memory, but one must proceed beyond it in order to attain God.

> 26. Great is the power of memory, something awe-inspiring, my God, a profound and infinite multiplicity; and this is the mind, and this is I myself. What, then, am I, my God? What nature am I? A varied life, manifold, and exceedingly immense. Behold, in the fields and caverns and caves of my memory, innumerable and innumerably full with innumerable kinds of things, whether through images, as of all bodies; or through presence, as of the arts; or through I know not what notions or markings, as of affections of the mind, which memory retains even when the mind does not suffer them, although whatever is in memory is in the mind: through all these I run and fly about; here and there I penetrate, as far as I can, and nowhere is there an end. So great is the power of memory, so great the power of life in a human being living mortally! What then shall I do, you who are my true life, my God? I shall pass beyond even this power of mine which is called memory; I shall pass beyond it, that I may reach you, sweet light.

What do you say to me? Behold, I, ascending through my mind to you who remain above me, shall pass beyond even this power of mine, which is called memory, wishing to attain you where you can be attained, and to cleave to you where you can be cleaved to *. For beasts and birds too have memory; otherwise they would not return to their lairs or nests, nor do many other things to which they grow accustomed; indeed, they could not grow accustomed to anything except through memory. I shall therefore pass beyond memory, that I may attain him who separated me from the four-footed beasts and made me wiser than the birds of heaven. I shall pass beyond memory; and where shall I find you, truly good and secure sweetness? And where shall I find you? If I find you beyond my memory, I am forgetful of you. And how shall I now find you, if I am not mindful of you?
> XVIII. A thing that has slipped away would not be found unless it were held in memory.

> 27. Luc. 15, 8. For the woman had lost a drachma, and sought it with a lamp; and unless she remembered it, she would not find it. For when it had been found, how would she know whether it was the very one, if she did not remember it? I remember having sought and found many lost things. From this I know the following: when I sought any one of them and was told, “Perhaps this is it; perhaps that,” I kept saying, “It is not,” until that which I was seeking was offered. Unless I remembered it, whatever it was, even if it were offered to me I would not find it, because I would not recognize it. And this is always so when we seek and find something lost. Nevertheless, if something passes from the eyes, but not from memory—for example, any visible body—its image is held within, and it is sought until it is restored to sight *. When it has been found, it is recognized from the image that is within.
Nor do we say that we have found what was lost unless we recognize it; nor can we recognize it unless we remember it: but it had indeed been lost to the eyes, while memory held it.
> XIX. What it is to recollect.

> 28. What if memory itself loses something, as happens when we forget, and we seek to recollect it? Where, then, do we seek except in memory itself? And there, if perhaps one thing is offered in place of another, we reject it until that which we seek occurs; and when it occurs, we say, “This is it”; which we would not say unless we recognized it, nor would we recognize it unless we remembered it. Certainly, then, we had forgotten it. Or had it not wholly slipped away, but from the part by which another part was retained it was sought, because memory felt that it was not unrolling all at once what it was accustomed to unroll all at once, and, as though limping with its habit mutilated, demanded that what was lacking be restored? As when a familiar person is either seen with the eyes or thought of, and, having forgotten his name, we seek it: whatever else occurs does not fit, because it was not accustomed to be thought of together with him, and therefore is rejected until that is present in which the familiarity, accustomed to them together, may rest without inequality. And whence is it present, except from memory itself?

For even when reminded by another, we recognize it, and it is present from there. For we do not believe it as though it were new, but, remembering, we approve that this is what was said. But if it be wholly effaced from the mind, we do not recollect even when reminded. For we have not yet altogether forgotten that which we remember ourselves to have forgotten. Therefore we cannot seek as lost that which we have wholly forgotten.
> XX. In order that all may seek blessedness, they must have known it.

> 29. How then do I seek you, Lord? For when I seek you, my God, I seek the blessed life. I will seek you, that my soul may live. For my body lives from my soul, and * my soul lives from you. How then do I seek the blessed life, since it is not mine until I say, “It is enough,” there where I ought to say it? How do I seek it? Is it through recollection, as though I had forgotten it and yet still retained that I have forgotten it; or through a desire to learn, as something unknown, whether something I have never known, or something I have so forgotten that I do not even remember having forgotten it? Is not this the blessed life which all desire [259], and is there absolutely no one who does not wish it? Where did they know it, that they desire it thus? Where did they see it, in order that they might love it? Assuredly we have it somehow. And there is another certain way in which each person, when he has it, is then blessed; and there are those who are blessed in hope.

These have it in an inferior way to those who are already blessed in reality; yet they are better off than those who are blessed neither in reality nor in hope. Yet unless even these themselves had it in some way, they would not so desire to be blessed—which it is most certain that they do desire. Somehow they know it, and therefore have it in some kind of knowledge; and I am concerned whether this is in memory: because, if it is there, we were once blessed already—whether all individually, or in that man who first sinned, 1 Cor. 15, 22, in whom we all also died, and from whom we were all born with misery, I do not now inquire; but I inquire whether the blessed life is in memory. For we would not love it unless we knew it. We hear this name, and all confess that we desire the thing itself; for we are not delighted by the sound.

For when a Greek hears this in Latin, he is not delighted, because he does not know what has been said; but we are delighted, just as he too would be if he heard this in Greek; since the thing itself is neither Greek nor Latin, and Greeks and Latins, and men of other languages, yearn to attain it. It is therefore known to all, who, if they could be questioned with one voice, Page 183 whether they wished to be blessed, would answer without any hesitation that they did wish it. This would not happen unless the thing itself of which this is the name were held in their memory.
> XXI. How memory contains the blessed life.

> 30. Is it as * one remembers Carthage who has seen it? No: for the blessed life is not seen with the eyes, because it is not a body. Is it as we remember numbers? No: for one who has these in knowledge does not still seek to attain them; but we have the blessed life in knowledge, and therefore love * it, and yet we wish to attain it so that we may be blessed. Is it as we remember eloquence? No: although * those who are not yet eloquent, upon hearing this name, remember the thing itself, and many wish to be so, whence it appears that it is in their knowledge; yet through bodily senses they have observed others who are eloquent and have been delighted, and they desire to be this (although, unless from an interior knowledge * they would not be delighted, nor would they wish to be this unless they were delighted); but we do not experience the blessed life in others through any bodily sense. Is it as we remember joy? Perhaps so.

For I remember my joy even when sad, just as, being miserable, I remember the blessed life; and I have never seen, or heard, or smelled, or tasted, or touched my joy by a bodily sense; but I experienced it in my mind when I rejoiced, and its knowledge clung to my memory, so that I am able sometimes to recall it with disdain, sometimes with longing, according to the diversity of the things over which I remember that I rejoiced. For I was also flooded with a certain joy over shameful things, which now, recalling it, I detest and abhor; at other times over good and honorable things, which I recall with longing, although perhaps they are not present, and therefore, being sad, I recall my former joy.

> 31. Where then and when did I experience my blessed life, so that I recall it, and love and desire it? Nor do I alone, or with a few others, but we altogether all wish to be blessed. Unless we knew this by certain knowledge, we would not will it with such certain will. But what is this—that if two persons are asked whether they wish to serve as soldiers, it may happen that one answers that he does wish to, the other that he does not; but if they are asked whether they wish to be blessed, each immediately declares without any hesitation that he desires it; and the one wishes to serve as a soldier for no other reason, and the other refuses for no other reason, than in order that they may be blessed? Or * perhaps, because one rejoices in one thing, another in another, do all thus agree in wishing to be blessed, just as they would agree, if asked this, that they wish to rejoice, and call joy itself the blessed life? Although one attains it in one way, another in another, it is nevertheless one thing toward which all strive, that they may rejoice.
Since this is a thing of which no one can say that he has not experienced it, it is therefore found recognized in memory when the name of the blessed life is heard.
> XXII. What and where the blessed life is.

> 32. Far be it, Lord, far be it from the heart of your servant who confesses to you, that, whatever joy I may rejoice in, I should consider myself blessed. For there is Is. 48, 22. a joy which is not given to the wicked, but to those who worship you freely, whose joy you yourself are. And the blessed life itself is to rejoice toward you, in you, because of you; it is this, and there is no other [260]. But those who think it to be another pursue another joy, and not joy itself, the true one. Yet their will is not turned away from some image of joy.
> XXIII. He likewise continues what and where the blessed life is.

> 33. Therefore it is not certain that all wish to be blessed, since those who do not wish to rejoice in you—which alone is the blessed life—do not certainly wish for the blessed life. Do all wish this? But Gal. 5, 17. because the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that they do not do what they wish, they fall into what they are able to do, and are content with that; because what they are unable to do, they do not will so much as is enough for them to be able [261]. For I ask everyone whether they would rather rejoice in truth than in falsehood: they do not hesitate to say that they would rather rejoice in truth, any more than they hesitate to say that they wish to be blessed. For the blessed life is joy in truth. For this is joy in you, who Joh. 14, 6. are truth, God Ps. 26, 1; 41, 11. my illumination, the salvation of my countenance, my God. All wish this blessed life, all wish this life which alone is blessed, all wish joy in truth [262].

I have encountered many who wished to deceive; but none who wished to be deceived. Where then did they know this blessed life, unless where they also knew truth? For they love truth itself, because * they do not wish to be deceived. And when they love the blessed life—which is nothing other than joy in truth—they certainly also love truth; nor would they love it unless there were some knowledge of it in their memory. Why then do they not rejoice in it? Why are they not blessed? Because they are more strongly occupied with other things which make them more miserable than that makes them blessed which they remember faintly [263]. For there is still a little light Page 185 *in human beings; let them walk, Joh. 12, 35. let them walk, lest the darkness overtake them.

> 34. But why does “truth give birth to hatred [264],” and why has your man who preaches truth become their enemy, Joh. 8, 40, when the blessed life is loved, which is nothing but joy in truth? Unless it is because truth is loved in such a way that whoever love something else want what they love to be truth; and because they do not wish to be deceived, they do not wish to be convicted that they are false? Thus, on account of that thing, they hate truth, which they love in place of truth. Joh. 5, 35. They love it when it shines, they hate it when it rebukes. For because they do not wish to be deceived and wish to deceive, they love it when it discloses itself, and hate it when it discloses them themselves * . From this it will repay them: those who do not wish to be made manifest by it, it will make manifest against their will, and it itself will not be manifest to them. Thus, yes thus, even thus the human mind, even thus blind and feeble, base and unseemly, wishes to lie hidden; but it does not wish that anything should lie hidden from itself. The contrary is rendered to it: that it itself should not be hidden from truth, but that truth should be hidden from it.

Yet even thus, while it is miserable, it prefers to rejoice in things true * rather than in things false. Therefore it will be blessed if, with no annoyance interrupting, it rejoices in truth alone itself, through which all things are true.
> XXIV. He rejoices that God has a place in his memory.

> 35. Behold how far I have ranged through my memory, seeking you, Lord, and I did not find you outside it. For I found nothing concerning you which I did not remember from the time when I learned you. For from the time when I learned you, I have not forgotten you. For where I found truth, there I found my God, truth itself [265], which, from the time when I learned it, I have not forgotten. And so, from the time when I learned you, you remain in my memory, and there I find you when I recall you and delight in you. These are my holy delights, which you have given me, your mercy looking upon my poverty.
> XXV. At what level of memory God is found.

> 36. But where do you remain in my memory, Lord; where do you remain there? What sort of resting-place have you fashioned * for yourself? What sort of sanctuary have you built * for yourself? You have granted this dignity to my memory, that you remain in it; but in what part of it you remain, this I consider. For I passed beyond [266] those parts of it which beasts also possess, when I recalled you, because I did not find you there among images of bodily things; and I came to those parts where I had entrusted the Page 186 affections of my mind, and * I did not find you there.

And I entered into the seat of my mind itself, which it has in my memory, since the mind also remembers itself; nor were you there: because, just as you are not a bodily image, nor an affection of a living being, such as when we rejoice, are saddened * , desire, fear, remember, forget, and whatever else is of this kind; so neither are you the mind itself, because you are the Lord God of the mind, and all these things are changed, while you remain unchangeable above all things, and you have deigned to dwell in my memory from the time when I learned you. And why do I ask in what place of it you dwell, as though there were places there? You certainly dwell in it, because I remember you from the time when I learned you, and in it I find you when I recall you.
> XXVI. Where God is found.

> 37. Where then did I find you, so that I might learn you? For you were not yet in my memory before I learned you. Where then did I find you, so that I might learn you, unless in you above me? And nowhere is there a place; and we withdraw, and we draw near [267], and nowhere is there a place. Truth, everywhere you preside over all who consult you, and at the same time you answer all who consult you even about different things. You answer clearly, but not all hear clearly. All consult you concerning what they wish, but they do not always hear what they wish. Your best servant is the one who does not so much look to hear from you what he himself has wished, but rather to wish what he has heard from you.
> XXVII. How the beauty of God ravishes a human being.

> 38. Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new! Late have I loved you! And behold, you were within, and I outside, and there I sought you; and, misshapen, I rushed upon those beautiful things which you made [268]. You were with me, and I was not with you. Those things held me far from you which, if they were not in you, would not be [269]. You called, and cried out, and shattered my deafness. You flashed, you shone, and dispelled my blindness. You gave forth fragrance * , and I drew breath, and I pant for you. I tasted, and I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I burned for your peace.
> XXVIII. The miseries of this life.

> 39. When I shall cleave to you with all of myself, there will nowhere be for me pain and toil; and my life will be living, wholly full of you. But now, since you relieve him whom you fill, because I am not full of you, I am a burden to myself. My lamentable joys contend with joys that are to be rejoiced in; and on which side victory stands I do not know. Alas for me! Lord, have mercy on me. My evil sorrows contend Page 187 with good joys, and on which side victory stands I do not know. Alas for me! Lord, have mercy on me. Alas for me! behold, I do not hide my wounds: you are the physician, I am the sick man; you are merciful, I am miserable. Is not Job 7, 1. human life upon earth a temptation? Who would wish for troubles and difficulties? You command that they be endured * , not loved. No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it. For although he rejoices to endure it, he would nevertheless prefer that there be nothing for him to endure. In adversities I desire prosperities; in prosperities I fear adversities.

What middle place is there among these, where human life may not be a temptation * ? Woe to the prosperities of the age, once and again, from fear of adversity and from the corruption of joy! Woe to the adversities of the age, once and again and a third time, from the desire for prosperity, and because adversity itself is hard, and lest it break endurance * ! Is not human life upon earth a temptation without any interval?
> XXIX. In God is all hope.

> 40. And all my hope is only in your exceedingly great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will [270] . You command us continence. Sap. 8, 21. And when I knew, says someone, that no one can be continent unless God gives it: and this very thing was wisdom, to know whose gift this was. For by continence [271] we are gathered together and brought back into one, from which we flowed away into many things. For he loves you less who loves something together with you which he does not love for your sake [272] . O love, who always burn and are never extinguished! Charity, my God, kindle me. You command continence; give what you command, and command what you will.
> XXX. He confesses how he stands with respect to the temptations of carnal lust.

> 41. You certainly command that I refrain from 1 Joh. 2, 16. the concupiscence of the flesh, and Page 188 the concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the age [273] . You commanded abstinence from intercourse; and concerning marriage itself you advised something better than you permitted. And because you gave it, it came to pass, even before I became a dispenser of your sacrament. But there still live in my memory, of which I have spoken much, images of such things, which my habit fixed there * ; and they meet me when awake indeed lacking strength, but in dreams not only even to delight, but also even to consent and an act most like the real one. And so great is the power of the illusion of an image in my soul and in my flesh, that false visions persuade me while asleep of what true ones cannot while awake. Am I not then myself, O Lord my God? And yet there is so great a difference between myself and myself, within the moment in which I pass hence into sleep, or pass back from there hither!

Where then is reason, which while awake resists such suggestions? And if the things themselves are presented, it remains unshaken * . Is it shut with the eyes? Is it put to sleep with the senses of the body? And whence is it that we often resist even in dreams, and mindful of our purpose, remaining most chastely in it, grant no assent to such allurements? And yet there is so great a difference that, when it happens otherwise, on waking we return to the repose of conscience; and by that very difference we find that we have not done what nevertheless we grieve to have been done in us in some manner.

> 42. Are you not able * , God almighty, to heal all the languors of my soul, and by your more abundant grace to extinguish the wanton motions even of my sleep? You will increase, Lord, more and more in me your gifts, so that my soul may follow me to you, freed from the birdlime of concupiscence, that it may not be rebellious against itself, and that even in dreams it may not only not perpetrate these shameful corruptions through animal images unto the emission of the flesh, but may not even consent to them. For that nothing of this kind, however slight * , may please it, however little may be restrained by a nod, Page 189 even in the chaste affection of one asleep—not only in this life, but even at this age—is no great thing for the Almighty, who Eph. 3, 20. are able to do above what we ask and understand . Yet now, in what * state I still am in this kind of my evil, I have told the Lord my good Ps. 2, 11.

rejoicing with trembling in that which you have bestowed upon me, and mourning in that in which I am unfinished, hoping * that you will perfect your mercies in me unto full peace, which my inward and outward parts will have with you, when 1 Cor. 15, 54. death shall have been swallowed up in victory .
> XXXI. How he conducts himself with regard to the temptations of gluttony.

> 43. There is another Mat. 6, 34. evil of the day , which would that it might suffice for it. For we repair the daily ruins of the body by eating and drinking, before you 1 Cor. 6, 13. destroy food and the belly , when you shall have slain my need * by wondrous satiety, and Ib. 15, 54. clothed this corruptible thing with everlasting incorruption. But now necessity is sweet to me, and I fight against this sweetness lest I be captured; and I wage daily war in fasts, often Ib. 9, 27. reducing my body to servitude; and my pains are driven away by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are certain pains; they burn, and, like a fever, kill, unless the remedy of food comes to aid. Since this is at hand, from the consolation of your gifts, in which earth and water and heaven serve our infirmity, calamities are called delights * .

> 44. You have taught me this: that I should approach to take food as I would medicines. But while I pass from the trouble of need into the repose of satiety, in the very passage the snare of concupiscence lies in wait for me. For the passage itself is pleasure, and there is no other by which one may pass where * necessity compels one to pass. And since health is the cause of eating and drinking, dangerous enjoyment attaches itself as though a handmaid; and often it tries to go before, so that what I say, or will, that I do for the sake of health may be done for its sake. Nor is the measure of each the same: for what is enough for health is too little for delight. And often it becomes uncertain whether the still necessary care of the body seeks the assistance, or the pleasurable deceit of desire supplies the service.

At this uncertainty the unhappy soul becomes cheerful, and in it prepares the defence of an excuse, rejoicing that it does not appear what is enough for the moderation of health, so that under the pretext of health it may overshadow the business of pleasure. Against these temptations I try daily to resist, and I call upon your right hand * and refer my agitations to you, because my judgment concerning this matter is not yet settled.

> 45. I hear the voice of my commanding God: Luc. 21, 34. Let not your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness . Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, lest it come near me. But surfeiting [274] sometimes creeps upon your servant; you will have mercy, that it may be far from me. Sap. 8, 21. For no one can be continent unless you give it. You grant many things to us when we pray; and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from you; and that we might afterwards know this, we received it beforehand * . I have never been drunken, but I have known drunkards made sober by you. Therefore it was done by you that those who never were such should not be such, by whom it was done that those who were such should not always be such, by whom also it was done that both might know by whom it was done. I heard another voice of yours: Ecc. 18, 30. Do not go after your concupiscences, and turn away from your own will. And I heard also that from your gift which I loved greatly: 1 Cor. 8, 8.

Neither if we eat shall we abound; nor if we do not eat shall we lack. This is to say: Neither will that thing make me wealthy, nor will that make me wretched. I heard another also: Phil. 4, 11-13. For I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be sufficient; I know both how to abound and how to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Behold a soldier of the heavenly camp, not the dust that we * are. But remember, Lord, that we are dust, and that you made man from Ps. 102, 14; and Gen. 3, 19. dust ; and Luc. 15, 24. 32. he had perished, and was found . Nor could he in himself, because he too was the same dust—him who said such things I loved by the breath of your inspiration: I can do all things, he says, in him who strengthens me. Strengthen me, that I may be able. Give what you command, and command what you will [275] . This man confesses that he has received, and 1 Cor. 1, 30. 31. he who glories, glories in the Lord * . I heard another asking that he might receive: Ecc. 23, 6.
Take away from me, he says, the concupiscences of the belly. From which it is apparent, my holy God, that you give it when what you command to be done is done.

> 46. You have taught me, good Father, Rom. 14, 20. All things are clean to the clean ; but that it is evil for 1 Tim. 4, 4. the man who eats through offence ; and that every creature of yours is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving ; and that 1 Cor. 8, 8. food does not commend us to God ; and that Col. 2, 16. no one should judge us in food or in drink ; and that Rom. 14, 3. he who eats should not despise him who does not eat; and he who does not eat should not judge him who eats . I have learned these things; thanks to you, praises to you, my God, my teacher, striker of my ears, illuminator of my heart: deliver me from every temptation. I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire. Gen. 9, 2. 3. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh [276] that might be useful for food; 3 Reg. 17, 6. that Elijah was refreshed with flesh as food; Mat. 3, 4. that John, endowed with wondrous abstinence, was not defiled when animals—that is, locusts—became food for him.

Gen. 25, 34. And I know that Esau was deceived by desire for lentils; and 2 Reg. 23, 15-17. that David rebuked himself because of a desire for water; and Mat. 4, 3. that our King was tempted not by flesh, but by bread. Num. 11. And therefore the people in the wilderness deserved to be reproved, not because it desired flesh, but because through desire for food it murmured against the Lord.

> 47. Therefore, placed amid these temptations, I daily strive assuredly against the concupiscence of eating and drinking: for it is not something that I may resolve to cut off once and not touch thereafter, as I was able concerning intercourse. Thus the reins of the throat must be held with measured relaxation and constriction. And who is there, Lord, who is not carried a little beyond the bounds of necessity? Whoever he is, he is great; let him magnify your name. But I am not, because I am a sinful man. Yet I too magnify your name; and Rom. 8, 34. he intercedes with you for my sins who Joh. 16, 33. conquered the age , counting me among 1 Cor. 12, 22. the weak members of his body, Ps. 138, 16. because your eyes saw even his unfinished thing [277] * , and in your book all shall be written .
> XXXII. How he conducts himself with regard to the allurements of odors.

> 48. I do not trouble myself much about the allurement of odors. When they are absent, I do not seek them; when present, I do not reject them, being prepared always even to lack them. So it seems to me; perhaps * I am mistaken. For these too are Page 192 lamentable darknesses, in which the capacity that is in me lies hidden from me: so that my mind, questioning itself about its own powers, judges that it ought not readily to be believed, since what is within is for the most part hidden, unless experience reveals it [278] . And no one ought to be secure in this life, which Job 7, 1. is called wholly a temptation, whether one who could become better from worse may not also become worse from better. One hope, one confidence, one firm promise: your mercy.
> XXXIII. How he conducts himself with regard to the pleasures of the ears.

> 49. The pleasures of the ears had entangled and subdued me more tenaciously; but you have loosed and freed me. Now in sounds which give life to your utterances, when they are sung with a sweet and artful voice, I confess that I rest somewhat; not indeed so as to cling, but so as to rise when I will. Yet, together with the very sayings by which they live, when they seek admission to me, they seek in my heart a place of no small dignity, and I scarcely grant them a fitting one. For sometimes I seem to myself to pay them more honor than is fitting, while I feel that our minds are moved more religiously and ardently into the flame of piety by those very holy words when they are sung thus than if they were not sung thus; and that all the affections of our spirit, according to their sweet diversity * , have their proper modes in voice and song, by some hidden kinship of which I know not how they are aroused.

But the delight of my flesh, to which the mind ought not to be given over for enervation, often deceives me, while sense does not so follow reason as patiently to be behind it; but, merely because it has deserved to be admitted on reason's account, it even tries to run ahead and to lead. Thus in these things I sin without perceiving it, and afterward I perceive it.

> 50. But sometimes, guarding against this very deception too immoderately, I err by excessive severity: indeed, sometimes to such an extent that I would have every melody of sweet songs with which the Davidic Psalter is frequented removed from my ears, and from those of the Church itself; and safer seems to me what I remember often being told about Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: that he made the reader of the psalm sound it with so slight an inflection of voice that he was nearer to one speaking than to one singing. Nevertheless, when I recall my tears, which I shed at the songs of thy Church in the beginnings of my recovered faith, and now that I am moved by the very things that are sung, not by the singing, when they are sung with a clear voice and most fitting modulation, I again acknowledge the great usefulness of this institution * , Page 193.

Thus I fluctuate between the peril of pleasure and the experience of healthfulness; and I am more inclined—though not pronouncing an irrevocable judgment—to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the delights of the ears a weaker mind may rise into an affection of piety. Yet when it happens to me that the singing moves me more than the thing which is sung, I confess that I sin in a punishable manner, and then I would rather not hear the singer. Behold where I am; weep with me, and weep for me, you who inwardly work some good together with me, whence deeds proceed. For those who do not work do not have these things move them. But thou, O Lord my God, hear; look, and see * , and Ps. 6, 3. have mercy, and heal me , in whose eyes Ps. 77, 10. I have become a question to myself , and that itself is my sickness .
> XXXIV. How he bears himself toward the enticements of the eyes.

> 51. There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, concerning which I speak * confessions for the ears of thy temple to hear, for the brotherly and pious ears, that we may conclude the temptations of the lust of the flesh, which still assail me as I groan and 2 Cor. 5, 2. desire to be clothed upon with my habitation which is from heaven . Fair and varied forms, bright and pleasant colors, the eyes love. Let not these hold my soul; let God Gen. 1, 31. who made these hold it, things indeed very good ; but he is my good, not these. And they touch me while I am awake throughout all the days, nor is rest from them granted me, as it is granted from musical sounds, sometimes from them all, in silence. For this light itself, queen of colors, suffusing all things that we see, wherever I may be by day, flatters me by its manifold approach while I am doing something else and do not attend to it.
Yet it insinuates itself so forcefully that, if it is suddenly withdrawn, it is sought with longing; and if it is absent for long, it saddens the mind * .

> 52. Tob. 4. O light which Tobit saw, when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life, and went before him with the foot of charity, nowhere straying. Or what light Isaac saw when the eyes of his flesh were weighed down and covered by old age, when, by not recognizing his sons, he deserved to recognize them by blessing them. Gen. 27. Or what light Jacob saw, when he too, his eyes overcome by great age, shone with a luminous heart upon the kinds of the people prefigured in his sons; and upon his grandsons by Joseph he laid his hands, mystically spread apart, not as their father corrected them outwardly, Gen. 48. 49. but as he himself discerned inwardly. This is the light; it is one * , and all who see and love it are one. But this bodily light of which I was speaking seasons the life of the age for its blind lovers with an enticing Page 194 and dangerous sweetness.

But those who know how to praise thee even from it, “God [279] creator of all things,” take it up into thy hymn; they are not consumed by it in their sleep: such I desire to be. I resist the seductions of the eyes, lest my feet, by which I walk in thy way, be entangled; and I raise invisible eyes to thee, that thou Ps. 24, 15. mayst pluck my feet from the snare . Thou dost repeatedly pluck them out, for they become entangled. Thou dost not cease to pluck them out, but I often stick fast in snares scattered everywhere: Ps. 120, 4. for thou who keepest Israel shalt neither sleep nor slumber .

> 53. How countless things, by various arts and crafts—in garments, footwear, vessels, and every kind of manufacture * , in paintings also, and in diverse representations, and in things that far exceed necessary and moderate use and pious signification—have men added for the enticement of the eyes; pursuing outwardly what they make, abandoning inwardly him by whom they were made, and destroying what they have been made! But I, my God and my glory, even from this sing a hymn to thee, and sacrifice praise to my sacrificer * ; because beautiful things, passing through souls into skillful hands [280] , come from that beauty which is above souls, for which my soul sighs day and night. But the makers and followers of exterior beauties draw from it the measure of approval, but do not draw from it the measure of use [281] . And it is there, and they do not see it [282] , lest they go further away, and Ps. 58, 10.

may keep their strength for thee , and not scatter it in luxurious weariness. But I, speaking and discerning these things, also fasten my step upon these beautiful things; but thou pluckest it free, Lord, thou pluckest it free, Ps. 25, 3. because thy mercy is before my eyes . For * I am pitiably taken captive, and thou mercifully pluckest me free: sometimes when I do not feel it, because I had fallen in more lightly; sometimes with pain, because I had already clung fast.
> XXXV. How he bears himself toward the second kind of temptation, which is that of curiosity.

> 54. To this is added another form of temptation, more dangerously manifold. For besides * the lust of the flesh, which lies in the delight of all senses and pleasures, in service to which those who make themselves far from thee perish, there is in the soul, through these same bodily senses, a certain vain and curious desire, not to take delight in the flesh, but to make trial through the flesh, cloaked under the name of knowledge and science. And since this is in the appetite for knowing, while the eyes are the chief senses for knowing * , 1 Joh. 2, 16. it is called in divine speech the lust of the eyes. For seeing belongs properly to the eyes. Yet we use this word also of the other senses when we direct them toward knowing. For we do not say, Hear how it gleams; or, Smell how it shines; or, Taste how it glistens; or, Feel how it flashes: for all these things are said to be seen.

But we say not only, See what shines, which the eyes alone can perceive; but also, See what sounds; see what smells; see what tastes; see how hard it is.
