> XV. Quæ de Deo deque Angelis et informi materia sentit Augustinus, non possunt oblucutores negare.

> 18. "Num dicetis falsa esse, quæ mihi Veritas voce forti in aurem interiorem dicit de vera æternitate Creatoris, quod nequaquam ejus substantia per tempora varietur, nec ejus voluntas extra ejus substantiam sit? Unde non eum modo velle hoc, modo velle illud; sed semel et simul et semper velle omnia quæ vult; non iterum et iterum, neque nunc ista nunc illa, nec velle postea quod nolebat, aut nolle quod volebat prius: quia talis voluntas mutabilis est, et omne mutabile æternum non est; Deus autem noster æternus est. Item quod mihi dicit * in aurem interiorem, exspectatio rerum venturarum fit contuitus cum venerint; idemque contuitus fit memoria cum præterierint: omnis porro intentio quæ ita variatur, mutabilis est; et omne mutabile æternum non est: Deus autem noster æternus est."
Hæc colligo atque conjungo et invenio Deum meum, Deum æternum, non aliqua nova voluntate condidisse creaturam, nec scientiam ejus transitorium aliquid pati.

> 19. "Quid ergo dicetis, contradictores? An falsa sunt ista?" "Non," inquiunt. "Quid illud? num falsum est omnem naturam formatam materiamve formabilem non esse, nisi ab illo qui summe bonus est, quia summe est?" "Neque hoc negamus," inquiunt. "Quid igitur? an illud negatis, sublimem quamdam esse creaturam tam casto amore cohærentem Deo vero et vere æterno, ut quamvis ei coæterna non sit, in nullam tamen temporum varietatem et vicissitudinem ab illo se resolvat et defluat, sed in ejus solius veracissima Page 234 contemplatione requiescat?" Quoniam tu, Deus, diligenti te quantum præcipis, ostendis ei te et sufficis ei; et ideo non declinat a te, nec ad se [322] . Hæc est domus [323] Dei non terrena, neque ulla cœlesti mole corporea, sed spiritualis et particeps æternitatis tuæ, quia sine labe in æternum * . Ps. 148, 6.
Statuisti enim eam in sæculum et in sæculum sæculi; præceptum posuisti et non præteribit . Nec tamen tibi Deo coæterna, quoniam non sine initio; facta est enim.

> 20. Nam etsi non invenimus tempus ante illam, Eccli. 1, 4. prior quippe omnium creata est sapientia ; nec utique illa Sapientia tibi, Deus noster, Patri suo plane coæterna et æqualis et per quam creata sunt omnia , et in quo Principio fecisti cœlum et terram ; sed profecto sapientia quæ creata est, intellectualis natura scilicet, quæ contemplatione luminis lumen est: dicitur enim et ipsa, quamvis creata, sapientia. Sed quantum interest inter lumen quod illuminat et quod illuminatur [324] , tantum inter sapientiam quæ creat et istam quæ creata est; sicut inter justitiam justificantem et justitiam quæ justificatione facta est. Nam et nos dicti sumus justitia tua. Ait enim quidam servus tuus, 2 Cor. 5, 21. ut nos simus justitia Dei in ipso . Ergo quia prior omnium creata est quædam sapientia quæ creata est, mens rationalis et intellectualis castæ civitatis tuæ, Gal. 4, 26.

matris nostræ quæ sursum est, et libera est , et æterna in cœlis ; (quibus cœlis, nisi qui Ps. 148, 4. te laudant cœli cœlorum ; quia hoc est et cœlum cœli Domino?) etsi non invenimus tempus ante illam, quia et creaturam temporis antecedit, quæ prior omnium creata est; ante illam tamen est ipsius Creatoris æternitas, a quo facta sumpsit exordium, (quamvis non temporis quoniam * nondum erat tempus,) ipsius tamen conditionis suæ.

> 21. Unde ita est abs te Deo nostro, ut aliud sit plane quam tu, et non idipsum [325] . Quoniam etsi non solum ante illam , sed nec in illa invenimus tempus, quia est idonea faciem tuam Page 235 semper videre nec uspiam deflectitur ab ea, quo fit ut nulla mutatione varietur; inest ei tamen ipsa mutabilitas unde tenebresceret et frigesceret, nisi amore grandi tibi cohærens, tanquam semper meridies luceret et ferveret ex te. O Ps. 25, 8. domus luminosa et speciosa, dilexi decorem tuum, et locum habitationis gloriæ Domini mei fabricatoris et possessoris tui! Tibi suspiret * peregrinatio mea; et dico ei qui fecit te, ut possideat et me in te, quia fecit et me. Ps. 118, 176. Erravi sicut ovis perdita ; sed Luc. 15, 5. in humeris pastoris mei , structoris tui, spero me reportari tibi.

> 22. Quid dicitis mihi quos alloquebar contradictores, qui tamen et Moysen pium famulum Dei, et libros ejus oracula sancti Spiritus creditis? Estne ista domus Dei, non quidem Deo coæterna, sed tamen secundum modum suum æterna in cœlis , ubi vices temporum frustra quæritis, quia non invenietis? supergreditur enim omnem distentionem, et omne spatium ætatis volubile, cui semper Ps. 62, 28. inhærere Deo bonum est . "Est," inquiunt. Quid igitur ex iis quæ clamavit cor meum ad Deum meum, cum audiret interius vocem laudis ejus , quid tandem falsum esse contenditis? An quia erat informis materies, ubi propter nullam formam nullus ordo erat; ubi autem nullus ordo erat, nulla esse vicissitudo temporum poterat; et tamen hoc pene nihil, inquantum non omnino nihil erat, ab illo utique erat a quo est quidquid est, quod utcumque aliquid est? "Hoc quoque," aiunt, "non negamus."
> XVI. Rem habere non vult cum iis qui contradicunt veritati divinæ.

> 23. Cum his enim volo coram te aliquid colloqui, Deus meus, qui hæc omnia, quæ intus in mente mea non tacet veritas tua, vera esse concedunt * . Nam qui hæc negant, latrent quantum volunt et obstrepant sibi; persuadere conabor ut quiescant, et viam præbeant ad se verbo tuo: quod 1. si noluerint et repulerint me; obsecro, Deus meus, Ps. 27, 1. ne tu sileas a me .

Tu loquere in corde meo veraciter; solus enim sic loqueris; et dimittam eos foris sufflantes in pulverem, et excitantes terram in oculos suos; et intrem in cubile meum , et cantem tibi amatoria, gemens inenarrabiles gemitus in peregrinatione mea, et recordans Jerusalem, extento in eam sursum corde, Jerusalem patriam meam, Jerusalem matrem meam, teque super eam regnatorem, illustratorem, patrem, tutorem, maritum, castas et fortes delicias, et solidum gaudium, et omnia bona ineffabilia simul omnia; quia unum Page 236 summum et verum bonum: et non avertar, donec in ejus pacem matris charissimæ, ubi sunt primitiæ spiritus [326] mei, unde mihi ista certa sunt, colligas totum quod sum, a dispersione [327] et deformitate hac, et conformes atque confirmes in æternum, Deus meus, misericordia mea.

Cum his autem qui cuncta illa quæ vera sunt, falsa esse non dicunt, honorantes et in culmine sequendæ auctoritatis nobiscum constituentes illam per sanctum Moysen editam sanctam Scripturam tuam, et tamen nobis aliquid contradicunt, ita loquor: Tu esto, Deus noster, arbiter inter confessiones meas et contradictiones eorum.
> XVII. Ut cœli et terræ nominibus aliud et aliud intelligi potest.

> 24. Dicunt enim: "Quamvis vera sint hæc, non ea tamen duo Moyses intuebatur, cum revelante spiritu diceret: Gen. 1. 1. In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram. Non cœli nomine spiritualem vel intellectualem illam creaturam, semper faciem Dei contemplantem significavit; nec terræ nomine informem materiam." "Quid igitur?" "Quod nos dicimus," inquiunt, "hoc ille vir sensit, hoc verbis istis elocutus est." "Quid est illud?" "Nomine," aiunt, "cœli et terræ, totum istum visibilem mundum prius universaliter et breviter significare voluit, ut postea digereret dierum enumeratione, quasi articulatim, universa quæ sancto Spiritui placuit sic enuntiare. Tales quippe homines erant rudis ille atque carnalis populus cui loquebatur, ut eis opera Dei non nisi sola visibilia commendanda judicaret.

Terram vero invisibilem et incompositam , tenebrosamque abyssum, unde consequenter ostenditur per illos dies facta atque disposita esse cuncta ista visibilia quæ nota sunt omnibus, non incongruenter informem istam materiam intelligendam esse consentiunt."

> 25. Quid si dicat alius, "eamdem informitatem, confusionemque materiæ, cœli et terræ nomine prius insinuatam, quod ex ea mundus iste visibilis cum omnibus naturis quæ in eo manifestissime apparent, qui cœli et terræ nomine sæpe appellari solet, conditus atque perfectus est?"

Quid si dicat et alius, " cœlum et terram quidem invisibilem visibilemque naturam non indecenter appellatam; ac per hoc universam creaturam quam fecit in Sapientia, id est in Principio, Deus , hujuscemodi duobus vocabulis esse comprehensam: Page 237 verumtamen quia non de ipsa substantia Dei, sed ex nihilo cuncta facta sunt, quia non sunt idipsum quod Deus, et inest quædam mutabilitas omnibus, sive maneant, sicut æterna domus Dei; sive mutentur, sicut anima hominis et corpus; communem omnium rerum invisibilium visibiliumque materiem adhuc informem, sed certe formabilem, unde fieret cœlum et terra, id est invisibilis atque visibilis jam utraque formata creatura, his nominibus enuntiatam, quibus appellaretur Terra invisibilis et incomposita , et, Tenebræ super abyssum : ea distinctione, ut terra invisibilis et incomposita intelligatur materies corporalis ante qualitatem formæ; tenebræ
autem super abyssum , spiritualis materies ante cohibitionem quasi fluentis immoderationis et ante illuminationem Sapientiæ?"

> 26. Est adhuc quod dicat si quis alius velit, "non scilicet jam perfectas atque formatas invisibiles visibilesque naturas, cœli et terræ nomine significari cum legitur, In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram ; sed ipsam adhuc informem inchoationem rerum formabilem creabilemque materiam his nominibus appellatam, quod in ea jam essent ista confusa, nondum qualitatibus formisque distincta, quæ nunc jam digesta suis ordinibus vocantur cœlum et terra ; illa spiritualis, hæc corporalis creatura."
> XVIII. Quis error innoxius in Scripturis.

> 27. Quibus omnibus auditis et consideratis, nolo verbis contendere; 2 Tim. 2, 14. ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium . Ad ædificationem autem 1 Tim. 1, 8. 5. bona est lex, si quis ea legitime utatur; quia finis ejus est charitas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta . Et novit magister noster in quibus Matt. 22, 40. duobus præceptis totam Legem Prophetasque suspenderit . Quæ mihi ardenter confitenti, Deus meus, lumen oculorum meorum in occulto, quid mihi obest, cum diversa in his verbis intelligi possint, quæ tamen vera sint, quid, inquam, mihi, obest, si aliud ego sensero, quam sensit alius eum sensisse qui scripsit? Omnes quidem qui legimus, nitimur hoc indagare atque comprehendere, quod voluit ille quem legimus. Et cum eum veridicum credimus, nihil quod falsum esse vel novimus vel putamus, audemus eum existimare dixisse.

Dum ergo quisque conatur id sentire in Scripturis sanctis, quod in eis sensit ille qui scripsit; quid mali est si hoc sentiat, quod tu, lux omnium veridicarum Page 238 mentium, ostendis verum esse, etiamsi non hoc sensit ille quem legit; cum et ille verum, nec tamen hoc senserit?
> XIX. Quæ liquido vera.

> 28. Verum est enim, Domine, fecisse te cœlum et terram; et verum est esse Principium Ps. 103, 24. Sapientiam tuam in qua fecisti omnia . Item verum est, quod mundus iste visibilis habet magnas partes suas cœlum et terram, brevi complexione factarum omnium conditarumque naturarum. Et verum est, quod omne mutabile insinuat notitiæ nostræ quamdam informitatem, qua formam capit, vel qua mutatur et vertitur. Verum est, nulla tempora perpeti quod ita cohæret formæ incommutabili, ut quamvis sit mutabile, non mutetur. Verum est, informitatem, quæ prope * nihil est, vices temporum habere non posse. Verum est, quod unde fit aliquid, potest quodam genere locutionis habere jam nomen ejus rei quæ inde fit; unde potuit vocari cœlum et terra quælibet informitas unde factum est cœlum et terra. Verum est, omnium formatorum nihil esse informi vicinius quam terram et abyssum.

Verum est, quod non solum creatum atque formatum, sed etiam quidquid creabile atque formabile est, tu fecisti ex quo sunt omnia. Verum est, omne quod ex informi formatur, prius esse informe, deinde formatum.
> XX. In principio creavit &c. varie intellectum.

> 29. Ex his omnibus veris, de quibus non dubitant quorum interiori oculo talia videre donasti, et qui Moysen famulum tuum in Spiritu veritatis locutum esse immobiliter credunt; ex his ergo omnibus aliud sibi tollit qui dicit: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram , id est, "In Verbo suo sibi coæterno fecit Deus intelligibilem atque sensibilem, vel spiritualem corporalemque creaturam." Aliud qui dicit: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram , id est, "In Verbo suo sibi coæterno fecit Deus universam istam molem corporei mundi hujus, cum omnibus quas continet manifestis notisque naturis." Aliud qui dicit: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram , id est, "In Verbo suo sibi coæterno fecit Deus informem materiam [328] creaturæ spiritualis et corporalis."

Aliud qui dicit: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram , id est, "In Verbo suo sibi coæterno fecit Deus informem materiam creaturæ corporalis ubi confusum adhuc erat cœlum et terra, quæ nunc jam distincta atque formata in istius mundi mole sentimus." Aliud qui dicit: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram , id est, "In ipso exordio faciendi atque operandi, fecit Deus informem materiam confuse habentem cœlum et terram; unde formata nunc eminent et apparent, cum omnibus quæ in eis sunt."
> XXI. Terra erat invisibilis &c. varie intellectum.

> 30. Item quod attinet ad intellectum verborum sequentium, ex illis omnibus veris, aliud sibi tollit qui dicit: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebræ erant super abyssum , id est, "Corporale * illud quod fecit Deus, adhuc materies erat corporearum rerum informis, sine ordine, sine luce." Aliud qui dicit: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebræ erant super abyssum , id est, "Hoc totum quod cœlum et terra appellatum est, adhuc informis et tenebrosa materies erat, unde fieret cœlum corporeum et terra corporea, cum omnibus quæ in eis sunt corporeis sensibus nota." Aliud qui dicit: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebræ erant super abyssum , id est, "Hoc totum quod cœlum et terra appellatum est, adhuc informis et tenebrosa materies erat, unde fieret cœlum intelligibile quod alibi dicitur cœlum cœli; Ps. 113, 16.

et terra, scilicet omnis natura corporea, sub quo nomine intelligatur etiam hoc cœlum corporeum; id est unde fieret omnis invisibilis visibilisque creatura." Aliud qui dicit: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebræ erant super abyssum ; "non illam informitatem nomine cœli et terræ Scriptura appellavit; sed jam erat, inquit, ipsa informitas quam terram invisibilem et incompositam tenebrosamque abyssum nominavit, de qua cœlum et terram Deum fecisse prædixerat, spiritualem scilicet, corporalemque creaturam." Aliud qui dicit: Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebræ erant super abyssum , id est, "Informitas quædam jam materies erat, unde cœlum et terram Deum fecisse Scriptura prædixit; totam scilicet corpoream mundi molem, in duas maximas partes, superiorem atque inferiorem Page 240 distributam, cum omnibus, quæ in eis sunt, usitatis notisque creaturis."
> XXII. Aliquid esse a Deo conditum, de quo sileat liber Genesis, nihil repugnat.

> 31. Cum enim duabus istis extremis sententiis resistere quisquam ita tentaverit: "Si non vultis * hanc informitatem materiæ cœli et terræ nomine appellatam videri; erat ergo aliquid quod non fecerat Deus, unde cœlum et terram faceret; neque enim Scriptura narravit quod istam materiem Deus fecerit, nisi intelligamus * eam cœli et terræ, aut solius terræ vocabulo significatam cum diceretur, In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram ; ut id quod sequitur, Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita , quamvis informem materiam sic placuerit appellare, non tamen intelligamus nisi eam quam fecit Deus in eo quod præscriptum * est, fecit Deus cœlum et terram ."

Respondebunt assertores duarum istarum sententiarum quas extremas posuimus, aut illius, aut illius, cum hæc audierint, et dicent: "Informem quidem istam materiam non negamus a Deo * factam, Deo a quo sunt omnia bona valde: quia sicut dicimus amplius bonum esse quod creatum atque formatum est, ita fatemur minus bonum esse quod factum est creabile atque formabile, sed tamen bonum: non autem commemorasse Scripturam, quod hanc informitatem fecerit Deus, sicut alia multa non commemoravit, Isa. 6, 2; et 37, 16. ut Cherubim et Seraphim, et quæ Apostolus distincte ait, Col. 1, 16. Sedes, Dominationes, Principatus, Potestates , quæ tamen omnia Deum fecisse manifestum est. Aut si * eo quod dictum est, fecit cœlum et terram , comprehensa sunt omnia; quid de aquis dicimus, super quas ferebatur Spiritus Dei?

Si enim, terra nominata, simul intelliguntur; quomodo jam terræ nomine materies informis accipitur, quando tam speciosas aquas videmus? Aut si ita accipitur; cur ex eadem informitate scriptum est, factum firmamentum et vocatum cœlum, neque scriptum est factas esse aquas? Non enim adhuc informes sunt et invisæ, quas ita decora specie fluere cernimus. Aut si tunc acceperunt istam speciem cum dixit Deus, Gen. 1, 9. Congregetur aqua quæ est sub firmamento , ut congregatio sit ipsa formatio; quid respondebitur de aquis quæ super firmamentum sunt? quia neque informes tam honorabilem sedem accipere meruissent, nec scriptum est qua voce formatæ sint.

Unde si aliquid Genesis tacuit Deum fecisse, quod tamen Deum fecisse nec sana fides, nec certus ambigit intellectus; nec ideo ulla sobria doctrina dicere Page 241 audebit istas aquas coæternas Deo, quia in libro Geneseos commemoratas quidem audimus * , ubi autem factæ sint non invenimus: cur non informem quoque illam materiem, quam Scriptura hæc terram invisibilem et incompositam, tenebrosamque abyssum appellat, docente veritate intelligamus ex * Deo factam esse de nihilo, ideoque illi non esse coæternam, quamvis ubi facta sit, omiserit enuntiare ista narratio?"
> XXIII. Duo dissensionum genera in Scripturis interpretandis.

> 32. His ergo auditis atque perspectis pro captu infirmitatis meæ, quam tibi confiteor scienti Deo meo, duo video dissensionum genera oboriri posse, cum aliquid a nuntiis veracibus per signa enuntiatur: unum si de veritate rerum, alterum si de ipsius qui enuntiat voluntate dissensio est. Aliter enim quærimus de creaturæ conditione quid verum sit; aliter autem quid in his verbis Moyses, egregius domesticus fidei tuæ, intelligere lectorem auditoremque voluerit. In illo primo genere discedant a me omnes, qui ea quæ falsa sunt, se scire arbitrantur. In hoc item altero discedant a me omnes qui ea quæ falsa sunt, Moysen dixisse arbitrantur. Conjungar autem illis, Domine, in te, et delecter cum eis in te, qui veritate tua pascuntur in latitudine charitatis; et accedamus simul ad verba Libri tui, et quæramus in eis voluntatem tuam per voluntatem famuli tui, cujus calamo dispensasti ea.
> XXIV. Ex multis veris non debet fidenter asseri hoc aut illud sensisse Moysen.

> 33. Sed quis nostrum sic inveniet eam inter tam multa vera * , quæ in illis verbis aliter atque aliter intellectis occurrunt quærentibus; ut tam fidenter dicat hoc sensisse Moysen, atque hoc in illa narratione voluisse intelligi, quam fidenter dicit hoc verum esse, sive ille hoc senserit sive aliud? Ecce enim, Deus meus, ego servus tuus qui vovi tibi sacrificium confessionis in his litteris, et oro ut ex misericordia tua reddam tibi vota mea ; ecce ego quam fidenter dico in tuo Verbo incommutabili omnia te fecisse, invisibilia et visibilia, numquid tam fidenter dico non aliud quam hoc attendisse Moysen cum scriberet: In principio fecit Deus cœlum et terram? Quia non sicut in tua veritate hoc certum video, ita in ejus mente video id eum cogitasse cum hæc scriberet.

Potuit enim cogitare in ipso faciendi exordio, cum diceret, In principio : potuit et cœlum et terram hoc loco, nullam jam formatam perfectamque naturam sive spiritualem sive corporalem, sed utramque inchoatam et adhuc informem velle intelligi. Video quippe vere potuisse dici, quidquid horum Page 242 diceretur; sed quid horum in his verbis ille cogitaverit, non ita video: quamvis sive aliquid * horum, sive quid aliud quod a me commemoratum non est, tantus vir ille mente conspexerit, cum hæc verba promeret, verum eum vidisse apteque id enuntiasse non dubitem.
> XXV. Adversus eos qui aliorum interpretandi rationem temere rejiciunt.

> 34. Nemo jam mihi molestus sit dicendo mihi: Non hoc sensit Moyses quod tu dicis, sed hoc sensit quod ego dico. Si enim mihi diceret: "Unde scis hoc sensisse Moysen quod de his verbis ejus eloqueris?" æquo animo ferre deberem et responderem fortasse quæ superius respondi, vel aliquanto uberius, si esset durior. Cum vero dicit: "Non hoc ille sensit quod tu dicis, sed quod ego dico;" neque tamen negat, quod uterque nostrum dicit, utrumque verum esse; o vita pauperum Deus meus, in cujus sinu non est contradictio, plue mihi mitigationes in cor, ut patienter [329] tales feram qui non mihi hoc dicunt, quia divini sunt, et in corde famuli tui viderunt quod dicunt; sed quia superbi sunt: nec noverunt Moysi sententiam, sed amant suam; non quia vera est, sed quia sua est.

Alioquin [330] et aliam veram pariter amarent, sicut ego amo quod dicunt, quando verum dicunt; non quia ipsorum est, sed quia verum est; et ideo jam nec ipsorum est, quia verum est. Si autem ideo ament illud quia verum est, jam et ipsorum est, et meum est; quoniam in commune omnium est veritatis * amatorum. Illud autem quod contendunt non hoc sensisse Moysen quod ego dico, sed quod ipsi dicunt; nolo, non amo: quia etsi ita est, tamen ista temeritas non scientiæ sed audaciæ est; nec visus, sed typhus eam peperit. Ideoque, Domine, tremenda sunt judicia tua; quoniam veritas tua nec mea est, nec illius aut illius, sed omnium nostrum quos ad ejus communionem publice vocas, terribiliter admonens nos, ut eam nolimus habere privatam, ne privemur ea.

Nam quisquis id quod tu omnibus ad fruendum proponis, sibi proprie vindicat, Page 243 et suum vult esse quod omnium est; a communi propellitur ad sua, hoc est, a veritate ad mendacium. Joh. 8, 44. Qui enim loquitur mendacium, de suo loquitur.

> 35. Attende, judex optime, Deus ipsa veritas, attende quid dicam contradictori huic, attende; coram te enim dico, et coram fratribus meis, qui 1 Tim. 1, 8. legitime utuntur Lege usque ad finem charitatis ; attende, et vide quid ei dicam, si placet tibi. Hanc enim vocem huic refero fraternam et pacificam: "Si ambo videmus verum esse quod dicis, et ambo videmus verum esse quod dico; ubi, quæso, id videmus? Nec ego utique in te, nec tu in me; sed ambo in ipsa, quæ supra mentes nostras est, incommutabili Veritate. Cum ergo de ipsa Domini Dei nostri luce non contendamus; cur de proximi cogitatione contendimus, quam sic videre non possumus ut videtur incommutabilis Veritas; quando si ipse Moyses apparuisset nobis atque dixisset, 'Hoc cogitavi;' nec sic eam videremus, sed crederemus? Non itaque 1 Cor. 4, 6. supra quam scriptum est, unus pro altero infletur adversus alterum. Deut. 6, 5; Mat.

22, 37. Diligamus Dominum Deum nostrum ex toto corde, et ex tota anima, et ex tota mente nostra, et proximum nostrum sicut nosmetipsos . Propter quæ duo præcepta charitatis sensisse Moysen, quidquid in illis Libris sensit, nisi crediderimus, mendacem faciemus Deum, cum de animo conservi, aliter quam ille docuit opinamur. Jam vide quam stultum sit in tanta copia verissimarum sententiarum, quæ de illis verbis erui possunt temere affirmare, quam earum Moyses, potissimum senserit; et perniciosis contentionibus ipsam offendere charitatem, propter quam dixit omnia, cujus dicta conamur exponere."
> XXVI. Qui sermo deceat Scripturam.

> 36. Et tamen ego, Deus meus, celsitudo humilitatis meæ, et requies laboris mei, qui audis confessiones meas, et dimittis peccata mea ; quoniam tu mihi præcipis ut diligam proximum meum sicut meipsum , non possum minus credere de Moyse fidelissimo famulo tuo, quam mihi optarem ac desiderarem abs te dari muneris, si tempore illo natus essem quo ille, eoque loco me constituisses, ut per servitutem cordis ac linguæ meæ, Litteræ illæ dispensarentur, quæ tanto post essent omnibus gentibus profuturæ, et per universum orbem tanto auctoritatis culmine omnium falsarum superbarumque doctrinarum verba superaturæ. Vellem quippe, si tunc ego Page 244 essem Moyses, (ex eadem namque massa omnes venimus; et Ps. 8, 5. quid est homo, nisi quia memor es ejus ?)

vellem ergo, si tunc ego essem quod ille, et mihi abs te Geneseos liber scribendus injungeretur, talem mihi eloquendi facultatem dari, et eum texendi sermonis modum, ut neque illi qui nondum queunt intelligere quemadmodum creat Deus, tanquam excedentia vires suas dicta recusarent; et illi qui hoc jam possunt, in quamlibet veram sententiam cogitando venissent, eam non prætermissam in paucis verbis tui famuli reperirent; et si alius aliam vidisset in luce veritatis, nec ipsa in eisdem verbis intelligenda deesset.
> XXVII. Scripturam decet humile simplexque verborum genus.

> 37. Sicut enim fons in parvo loco uberior est, pluribusque rivis in ampliora spatia fluxum ministrat, quam quilibet eorum rivorum, qui per multa locorum ab eodem fonte deducitur; ita narratio dispensatoris tui sermocinaturis pluribus profutura, parvo sermonis modulo scatet fluenta liquidæ veritatis: unde sibi quisque verum quod de his rebus potest, hic illud, ille illud, per longiores loquelarum anfractus trahat. Alii enim cum hæc verba legunt vel audiunt, cogitant Deum quasi hominem, aut quasi aliquam molem immensa præditam potestate, novo quodam et repentino placito, extra seipsam tanquam locis distantibus fecisse cœlum et terram , duo magna corpora supra et infra, quibus omnia continerentur.

Et cum audiunt, Dixit Deus, Fiat illud, et factum est illud; cogitant verba cœpta et finita, sonantia temporibus atque transeuntia, post quorum transitum statim existere * quod jussum est ut existeret: et si quid forte aliud hoc modo ex familiaritate carnis opinantur. In quibus adhuc parvulis animalibus, dum isto humillimo genere verborum, tanquam materno sinu, eorum gestatur infirmitas, salubriter ædificatur fides, qua certum habeant et teneant Deum fecisse omnes naturas, quas eorum sensus mirabili varietate circumspicit. Quorum si quispiam quasi vilitatem dictorum aspernatus, extra nutritorias cunas superba imbecillitate se extenderit, heu! cadet miser. * Domine Deus, miserere, ne implumem pullum conculcent qui transeunt viam; et mitte angelum tuum, qui eum reponat in nido, ut vivat donec volet.
> XXVIII. Ut varie intelligitur ab eruditis Scriptura.

> 38. Alii vero quibus hæc verba non jam nidus, sed opaca fruteta sunt, vident in eis latentes fructus, et volitant lætantes, et garriunt scrutantes, et carpunt eos. Vident enim, cum hæc Page 245 verba legunt vel audiunt, tua, Deus, æterna et stabili permansione cuncta præterita et futura tempora superari; nec tamen quidquam esse temporalis creaturæ, quod tu non feceris: cujus voluntas quia id est quod tu, nullo modo mutata, vel, quæ antea non fuisset, exorta voluntate fecisti omnia: non de te similitudinem tuam formam omnium, sed de nihilo dissimilitudinem informem, quæ formaretur per similitudinem tuam, recurrens in te unum pro captu ordinato, quantum cuique rerum in suo genere datum est: et * fierent omnia bona valde, sive maneant circa te, sive gradatim remotiori distantia per tempora et locos pulchras variationes * faciant aut patiantur.
Vident hæc, et gaudent in luce veritatis tuæ, quantulum hic valent.

> 39. Et alius eorum intendit in id quod dictum est, In principio fecit Deus , et respicit Sapientiam Principium, quia et loquitur ipsa nobis . Alius itidem intendit in eadem verba, et principium intelligit exordium rerum conditarum; et sic accipit, In principio fecit , ac si diceretur, Primo fecit. Atque in eis qui intelligunt, In principio , quod in Sapientia fecisti cœlum et terram; alius eorum ipsum cœlum et terram, creabilem materiam cœli et terræ sic esse credit cognominatam; alius jam formatas distinctasque naturas; alius unam formatam, eamdemque spiritualem cœli nomine, aliam informem corporalis materiæ, terræ nomine.

Qui autem intelligunt in nominibus cœli et terræ, adhuc informem materiem, de qua formaretur cœlum et terra, nec ipsi uno modo id intelligunt: sed alius unde consummaretur intelligibilis sensibilisqne creatura; alius tantum unde sensibilis moles ista corporea, sinu grandi continens perspicuas promptasque naturas. Nec illi uno modo qui jam dispositas digestasque creaturas cœlum et terram vocari hoc loco credunt; sed alius invisibilem atque visibilem: alius solam visibilem in qua luminosum cœlum suspicimus, et terram caliginosam, quæque in eis sunt.
> XXIX. Quot modis dicitur aliquid prius.

> 40. At ille qui non aliter accipit, In principio fecit , quam si diceretur, "Primo fecit;" non habet quomodo veraciter intelligat cœlum et terram, nisi materiem cœli et terræ intelligat, videlicet universæ, id est intelligibilis corporalisque creaturæ * . Si enim jam formatam velit universam, recte ab eo quæri poterit, "Si hoc primo fecit Deus, quid fecerit deinceps:" et post universitatem non inveniet: ac per hoc Page 246 audiet invitus, "Quomodo illud primo, si postea nihil?" Cum vero dicit primo informem, deinde formatam, non est absurdus; si modo est idoneus discernere, quid præcedat æternitate, quid tempore, quid electione, quid origine. Æternitate, sicut Deus omnia; tempore, sicut flos fructum; electione, sicut fructus florem; origine, sicut sonus cantum. In his quatuor primum et ultimum quæ commemoravi, difficillime intelliguntur; duo media facillime.

Namque rara visio est et nimis ardua conspicere, Domine, æternitatem tuam incommutabiliter mutabilia facientem, ac per hoc priorem. Quis deinde sic acutum * cernat animo, ut sine labore magno dignoscere valeat, quomodo sit prior sonus quam cantus, ideo quia cantus est formatus sonus, et esse utique aliquid non formatum potest, formari autem quod non est, non potest? Sic est prior materies, quam id quod ex ea fit [331] : non ideo prior quia ipsa efficit, cum potius fiat; nec prior intervallo temporis. Neque enim priore tempore sonos edimus informes sine cantu, et eos posteriore tempore in formam cantici coaptamus aut fingimus; sicut ligna quibus arca, vel argentum quo vasculum fabricatur. Tales quippe materiæ, tempore etiam præcedunt formas rerum quæ fiunt ex eis: at in cantu non ita est. Cum enim cantatur, auditur sonus ejus; non prius informiter sonat, et deinde formatur in cantum.

Quod enim primo utrumque sonuerit, præterit; nec ex eo quidquam reperies quod resumptum arte componas: et ideo cantus in sono suo vertitur; qui sonus ejus, materies ejus est. Idem quippe formatur ut cantus sit; et ideo, sicut dicebam, prior materies sonandi quam forma cantandi: non per faciendi potentiam prior * ; neque enim sonus est cantandi artifex, sed cantanti animæ subjacet ex corpore, de quo cantum faciat. Nec tempore prior; simul enim cum cantu editur. Nec prior electione; non enim potior sonus quam cantus, quandoquidem cantus est non tantum sonus, verum etiam speciosus sonus. Sed prior est origine; quia non cantus formatur ut sonus sit, Page 247 sed sonus formatur ut cantus sit.

Hoc exemplo, qui potest intelligat materiam rerum primo factam, et appellatam cœlum et terram , quia inde facta sunt cœlum et terra: nec tempore primo factam; quia formæ rerum exserunt tempora [332] , illa autem erat informis; jamque in temporibus simul animadvertitur. nec tamen de illa narrari * aliquid potest, nisi velut tempore prior sit; cum pendatur extremior, quia profecto meliora sunt formata quam informia, et præcedatur * æternitate Creatoris, ut esset de nihilo, unde aliquid fieret.
> XXX. Tractatores Scripturæ diversa sentientes concordent invicem charitate et studio veritatis.

> 41. In hac diversitate sententiarum verarum concordiam pariat ipsa Veritas; et Deus noster misereatur nostri, ut legitime Lege utamur, præcepti fine, pura charitate : ac per hoc si quis quærit ex me, quid horum Moyses tuus ille famulus senserit, non sunt hi sermones confessionum mearum. Si tibi non confiteor, nescio; et scio tamen illas veras esse sententias, exceptis carnalibus de quibus quantum existimavi locutus sum: quos tamen bonæ spei parvulos hæc verba Libri tui non territant, alta humiliter, et pauca copiose.

Sed omnes quos in eis verbis vera cernere ac dicere fateor, diligamus nos invicem, pariterque diligamus te Deum nostrum fontem veritatis, si non vana, sed ipsam sitimus; eumdemque famulum tuum Scripturæ hujus dispensatorem, Spiritu tuo plenum, ita honoremus, ut hoc eum te revelante cum hæc scriberet attendisse credamus, quod in eis maxime et luce veritatis, et fruge utilitatis excellit.
> XXXI. Sensisse putandus est Moyses quidquid veri potest in ipsius verbis inveniri.

> 42. Ita cum alius dixerit, "Hoc sensit quod ego;" et alius, "Imo illud quod ego;" religiosius me arbitror dicere, "Cur non utrumque potius, si utrumque verum est?" Et si quid tertium, et si quid quartum, et si quid omnino aliud verum quispiam in his verbis videt; cur non illa omnia vidisse credatur, per quem Deus unus sacras Litteras vera et diversa visuris multorum sensibus temperavit? Ego certe, quod intrepidus de meo corde pronuntio, si ad culmen auctoritatis aliquid scriberem; sic mallem scribere, ut quod veri quisque de his rebus capere posset, mea verba resonarent, quam ut Page 248 veram sententiam ad hoc apertius ponerem, ut excluderem cæteras, quarum falsitas me non posset offendere. Nolo itaque, Deus meus, tam præceps esse, ut hoc illum virum de te meruisse non credam.
Sensit ille omnino in his verbis, atque cogitavit cum ea scriberet, quidquid hic veri potuimus invenire, et quidquid nos non potuimus, aut nondum possumus, et tamen in eis inveniri potest.
> XXXII. Veri Scripturæ sensus a Spiritu Sancto revelantur.

> 43. Postremo, Domine qui Deus es, et non caro et sanguis; si quid homo minus vidit * , numquid et Ps. 142, 10. Spiritum tuum bonum qui deducet me in terram rectam , latere potuit, quidquid eras in eis verbis tu ipse revelaturus legentibus posteris, etsiamsi ille per quem dicta sunt, unam fortassis ex multis veris sententiam cogitavit? Quod si ita est, sit igitur illa quam cogitavit cæteris excelsior * . Nobis autem, Domine, aut ipsam demonstra, aut quam placet alteram veram; ut sive nobis hoc quod etiam illi homini tuo, sive aliud ex eorumdem verborum occasione patefacias, tu tamen pascas nos, non error illudat [333] . Ecce, Domine Deus meus, quam multa de paucis verbis, quam multa, oro te, scripsimus! Quæ nostræ vires, quæ tempora omnibus Libris tuis ad istum modum sufficient * ?

Sine me itaque brevius in eis confiteri tibi, et eligere unum aliquid quod tu inspiraveris verum, certum et bonum, etiamsi multa occurrerint, ubi multa occurrere poterunt; ea fide confessionis meæ, ut si hoc dixero quod sensit minister tuus, recte atque optime; id enim conari me oportet: quod si assecutus non fuero, id tamen dicam quod mihi per ejus verba tua Veritas dicere voluerit, quæ illi quoque dixit quod voluit.
> Page 249

> He continues the interpretation of the first verses of Genesis, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; in which he teaches that by the name of heaven is signified that spiritual or intellectual creature which always contemplates the face of God; but by the term earth, the unformed matter from which the forms of bodily things were afterwards fashioned. Yet he acknowledges that other modes of interpretation are by no means to be disapproved; indeed, that from the profundity of divine Scripture a multiple sense can and ought to be elicited, nay rather, that whatever truth at all can be found in its words is truly contained in them.
> I. The difficult inquiry of truth.

> 1. My heart labours much, O Lord, in this poverty of my life, assailed by the words of thy holy Scripture: and therefore the poverty of human understanding is for the most part abundant in speech; because inquiry says more than discovery, and asking is longer than obtaining, and the hand that knocks is more laborious than the hand that receives. We hold thy promise; who shall corrupt it? Rom. 8, 31. If God be for us, who against us? Mat. 7, 7. 8. Ask, and ye shall receive; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. For every one that asketh receiveth, and he that seeketh findeth, and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. Thy promises are these; and who should fear to be deceived when Truth promises?
> II. Concerning the twofold heaven and earth.

> 2. The humility of my tongue confesses to thy height, since thou hast made heaven and earth; this heaven which I see, and the earth which I tread, whence comes this earth which I bear, thou hast made. But where is the heaven of heaven, O Lord, of which we have heard in the voice of the Psalm: Ps. 113, 16. The heaven of heaven is the Lord's; but the earth hath he given to the children of men? Where is that heaven which we do not discern, to which all this that we discern is earth? For this entire corporeal whole did not everywhere receive * its beautiful form in its lowest parts, whose * foundation is our earth; but in relation to that heaven of heaven, even the heaven of our earth is earth. And neither of these two great bodies is absurdly earth in relation to some heaven, I know not what kind, which belongs to the Lord, not to the children of men.
> III. What the darkness over the face of the abyss is.

> 3. And surely this earth was invisible and unformed, and there was some depth of abyss, I know not what, over which there was no light; because it had no form: whence thou didst command it to be written that Page 227 Gen. 1, 2. darkness was over the abyss; what else is this than the absence of light? For where would light be, if it were there, unless it were above, standing out and illuminating? Therefore, where light was not yet, what was it for darkness to be present except for light to be absent? Darkness, therefore, was above, because light was absent above; just as where sound is not, there is silence. And what is it for silence to be there except that sound is not there? Hast not thou, O Lord, taught this * soul which confesses to thee? Hast not thou, O Lord, taught me that, before thou didst form and distinguish this unformed matter, there was not anything: no colour, no figure, no body, no spirit? Yet it was not altogether nothing: there was a certain formlessness without any form.
> IV. What invisible and unformed earth is.

> 4. By what, then, could it be called, so that it might somehow be intimated even to slower minds, unless by some customary term? And what can be found in all the parts of the world closer to utter formlessness than earth and abyss? For, in accordance with their lowest rank, they are less beautiful than all the other higher things, clear and bright. Why, then, should I not understand the formlessness of matter, which thou hadst made without form, out of which thou wouldst make the beautiful world, to have been thus conveniently conveyed to men, so that it was called invisible and unformed earth?
> V. Why unformed matter seems to have been so called.

> 5. So that, when thought inquiring in it * what sense may attain says to itself, “It is not an intelligible form, like life, like justice, because it is the matter of bodies; nor is it sensible, because in the invisible and unformed there is nothing * to be seen or perceived:” while human thought says these things to itself, it strives either to know it by not knowing, or not to know it by knowing.
> VI. What he formerly thought with the Manichaeans concerning unformed matter, and what he thinks now.

> 6. But I, O Lord, if I confess the whole * to thee with my mouth and my pen, whatever thou hast taught me concerning this matter, whose name I had formerly heard and had not understood, those [309] relating it to me who did not understand it, I thought of it with innumerable and varied forms; and therefore I did not think of it. My mind rolled about foul and horrible forms in confused orders, but forms nonetheless; and I called it formless, not because it lacked form, but because it had such a form that, if it appeared, my sense would recoil from its strangeness and incongruity, and the weakness of man would be disturbed. But that which I thought was formless, not by deprivation of every form, but by comparison with more beautiful things: and true reason persuaded me that I must wholly remove all remnants whatsoever of form, if I wished to think of what was utterly formless; and I could not.

For I judged more readily that that which was deprived of every form did not exist than I thought of something between the formed and nothing, neither formed nor nothing, formless, almost nothing * . And my mind ceased to question my spirit on this matter, full of images of formed bodies and changing and varying them at will; and I directed my attention to bodies themselves, and looked more deeply into their mutability, by which they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not; and I suspected that this very passage from form to form takes place through something formless, not through utter nothing: but I desired to know, not to suspect. And if my voice and pen confess to thee the whole, whatever thou hast unraveled for me concerning this question, which of my readers will persist in grasping it? Yet my heart will not therefore cease to give thee honour and a song of praise for things which it is not sufficient to dictate. For the very mutability of mutable things is capable of all the forms into which mutable things are changed.

And what is this? Is it mind? Is it body? Is it a form of mind or body? If it could be said, “A nothing something,” and, “It is not is * ,” I would call it this; and yet it already in some way was, so as to receive those visible and composite forms.
> VII. God made heaven, that is, the angels, from nothing; and earth, that is, unformed matter.

> 7. And whence was it in any way, unless it were from thee, from whom are all things insofar as they are at all? But it was so much farther from thee as it was more unlike thee; for this is not a matter of places. Therefore thou, O Lord, who art not at one time one thing * and at another otherwise, but the selfsame [310] and the selfsame and the selfsame, Isa. 6, 3. Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty; in the Beginning which is from [311] thee, in thy Wisdom which was born from thy substance, thou didst make something also from nothing. For thou didst make heaven and earth; not from thyself, for then they would be equal to thy Only-begotten, and thereby to thee; and it would in no way be just that what was not from thee should be equal to thee. And besides thee there was nothing from which thou mightest make them, O God, one Trinity and triune Unity: and therefore from nothing * thou didst make heaven and earth, a great something and a small something; because thou art almighty and good for making all good things, a great heaven and a small earth.

Thou wast, and there was nothing else from which thou didst make heaven and earth, two somethings: one near thee, the other near nothing; one, than which thou shouldst be higher; the other, than which nothing should be lower.
> Page 229
> VIII. Unformed matter from nothing: from this, all visible things.

> 8. But that heaven of heaven is thine, O Lord; Ps. 113, 15. whereas the earth which thou gavest to the children of men to be seen and touched was not such * as we now see and touch. For it was invisible and unformed, and there was an abyss over which there was no light; or * , Gen. 1, 2. Darkness was over the abyss, that is, more than in the abyss. For this abyss of now visible waters, even in its depths, has in some way the light of its own form perceptible to fishes and to living creatures that creep upon its bottom: but that whole was almost nothing, since it was not yet altogether formed; yet it already was something that could be formed. For thou, O Lord, didst make the world from unformed matter, which thou didst make from no thing, an almost nothing thing, from which thou mightest make the great things at which we children of men marvel. For very marvelous is this corporeal heaven, which on the second day, after the creation of light, thou didst call the firmament between water and water, saying, Gen. 1, 6. 7. Let it be; and so it was made.

This firmament thou didst call heaven; but it is the heaven of this earth and sea, which thou didst make on the third day, giving visible form to the unformed matter which thou hadst made before every day. For thou hadst already made heaven before every day, but the heaven of the heaven of this world; because in the beginning thou hadst made heaven and earth. But the earth itself which thou hadst made was unformed matter, because it was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss * : from this invisible and unformed earth, from this formlessness, from this almost nothing, thou wouldst make all these things of which this mutable world consists, and does not consist, in which mutability itself appears, whereby times can be perceived and numbered; for times come to be through the changes of things, while forms, whose matter has been called the aforesaid invisible earth, are varied and turned.
> IX. Why it is written, without mention of days, that God made heaven and earth in the beginning.

> 9. And therefore the Spirit, the teacher of thy servant, when he recounts that thou didst make heaven and earth in the beginning, says nothing of times, is silent about days. For plainly the heaven of heaven which thou didst make in the beginning is some intellectual creature; although by no means coeternal with thee, the Trinity, yet a partaker of thy eternity, it greatly restrains its mutability through the sweetness of thy most blessed contemplation, and, clinging to thee without any lapse from the time it was made, transcends every changeable succession of times. But this formlessness, invisible and unformed earth, was not itself counted in days. For where there is no form, no order, nothing comes, nothing passes away: and where this does not occur, there assuredly are no days, nor any succession of temporal intervals. Page 230
> X. He desires to be taught by God.

> 10. O Light, Truth, Light of my heart, let not my darknesses speak to me. I flowed away into these things and was darkened; yet even from here, from here I loved thee. I went astray and remembered thee. I heard thy voice behind me, that I might return, and scarcely heard it because of the tumult of the unpeaceful [312] * . And now behold, I return, burning and panting, to thy fountain. Let no one hinder me; I shall drink from it, and then I shall live. Let me not be my own life; I lived badly from myself, I was death to myself; and in thee I come to life again * . Do thou address me, do thou speak to me. I have believed thy Books, and their words are exceedingly mysterious.
> XI. What he has learned from God.

> 11. Thou hast already said to me, Lord, with a mighty voice in my inner ear * , that thou art eternal, 1 Tim. 6, 16. and alone hast immortality [313] ; because thou art changed by no form or motion, nor is thy will varied by times; for a will that is one thing and another is not immortal. This is clear to me in thy sight, and may it become clearer and clearer, I pray thee; and may I remain sober in that manifestation beneath thy wings. Likewise thou hast said to me, Lord, with a mighty voice in my inner ear, that thou hast made all natures and substances which are not what thou art and yet are; and that this alone is not from thee, which is not; and the movement of the will from thee, who art, toward that which is less, because such a movement is transgression and sin [314] ; and that no one's sin either harms thee or disturbs the order of thy rule, whether in what is highest or in what is lowest [315] .
This is clear to me in thy sight, and may it become clearer and clearer, I pray thee; and may I remain sober in that manifestation beneath thy wings.

> 12. Likewise thou hast said to me with a mighty voice in my inner ear, that not even that creature is coeternal with thee, whose delight * thou alone art, and which, drinking thee in with most steadfast chastity [316] , nowhere and never displays its mutability [317] ; and, with thee ever present to it, to whom it clings with its whole affection, having no future to await Page 231 nor passing over into the past [318] to remember, is varied by no alternation, nor stretched out into any times. O blessed creature, if any such there be, by cleaving to thy blessedness; blessed in thee, its everlasting indweller and its illuminator! Nor do I find what I should judge more fittingly called the Heaven of heaven unto the Lord, than thy house, contemplating thy delight without any failing away into another thing; a pure mind, most harmoniously one in the steadfastness of the peace of holy spirits [319] , citizens of thy city in the heavens above these heavens.

> 13. Hence let the soul whose pilgrimage * has become distant understand, if now Ps. 41, 3. 4. 11. it thirsts for thee; if now its tears have become its bread, while it is said to it each day, Where is thy God? if now Ps. 26, 4. it asks one thing of thee and seeks this, that it may dwell in thy house all the days of its life: (And what is its life but thou? and what are thy days but thy eternity, as Ps. 101, 28. thy years that do not fail , because thou art the same?)—hence, then, let the soul that can understand how far thou, eternal, art above all times; since thy house, which has not gone on pilgrimage, though it is not coeternal with thee, yet by cleaving to thee without ceasing and without failing suffers no vicissitude of times. This is clear to me in thy sight, and may it become clearer and clearer, I pray thee; and may I remain sober in this manifestation beneath thy wings.

> 14. Behold, I know not what formless thing there is in these changes of the outermost and lowest things. And who will tell me—unless it be one who wanders and tosses about through the emptinesses of his own heart with his phantasms—who but such a one will tell me that, when every form has been diminished and consumed, if formlessness alone remains, through which a thing was changed and turned from form to form, it can exhibit the vicissitudes of times? For it absolutely cannot; because without variety of motions there are no times; and there is no variety where there is no form.
> XII. A twofold creature lacking time.

> 15. Considering these things, by how much thou grantest, my God, by how much thou stirrest me to knock, and by how much thou openest to one who knocks, I find two things that thou hast made which lack times, though neither is coeternal with thee. One is so formed that, without any defect of contemplation, without any interval of change, though mutable yet not changed, it enjoys thy eternity and immutability: the other was so formless that it had no form from which, or into which, it might be changed, whether by motion or by rest, so as to be subjected to time. But thou didst not leave it formless, since thou didst make, before every day, in the beginning heaven and earth, these two of which I was speaking. But the earth was invisible and unorganized, and darkness was upon the abyss.

By these words formlessness is indicated, so that those may be gradually received who cannot conceive a deprivation of all form and yet not an arrival at nothingness; from which would come the other heaven, and the visible and organized earth, and the beautiful water, and whatever thereafter is recalled as made in the establishment of this world not without days; because such things are of a kind in which vicissitudes of times take place, on account of ordered changes of motions and forms [320] .
> XIII. Why Scripture says, without mention of days, that in the beginning God made heaven and earth.

> 16. For the present, this is what I perceive, my God, when I hear thy Scripture speaking, Gen. 1, 1. In the beginning God made heaven and earth: but the earth was invisible and unorganized, and darkness was upon the abyss , and it does not mention on what * day thou didst make these things. For the present, I so perceive this because of that Heaven of heaven, the intellectual heaven, where understanding is to know simultaneously, not in part, nor 1 Cor. 13, 12. in an enigma , nor through a mirror ; but wholly, in manifestation * , face to face: not now this, now that; but, as has been said, to know simultaneously without any vicissitude of times: and because of the invisible and unorganized earth, without any vicissitude of times, which is wont to have now this and now that; for where there is no form, there is nowhere this and that.

Because of these two, the one formed in the first place and the other utterly formless—namely, that one, heaven, but the Heaven of heaven; this one, earth, but invisible and unorganized earth—because of these two, for the present I perceive that thy Scripture says without mention of days, In the beginning God made heaven and earth . For it immediately added what earth it had called. And when on the second day it is recalled that the firmament was made and called heaven, it indicates of what heaven the discourse had previously spoken without days.
> XIV. The profundity of Scripture.

> 17. Wondrous is the profundity of thy utterances, whose surface, behold, lies before us, gently alluring little ones; yet wondrous is their profundity, my God, wondrous profundity! It is fearful to direct one's attention into it: fearful with the fear of honour, and trembling with love. Ps. 138, 22. I hate its enemies [321] exceedingly. O that thou wouldst slay them with * the two-edged sword, and that they might not be its enemies! For thus I love them to be slain to themselves, that they may live to thee. But behold, others, not reprovers but praisers of the book of Genesis, say: “The Spirit of God, who through Moses his servant wrote these things, did not will this to be understood in these words; he did not will what thou sayest to be understood, but something else which we say.” To them I, with thee as arbiter, God of us all * , answer thus.
> XV. What Augustine thinks concerning God, the Angels, and formless matter, cannot be denied by objectors.

> 18. “Will you say false to be the things which Truth says to me with a mighty voice in my inner ear concerning the true eternity of the Creator: namely, that his substance is in no way varied through times, nor is his will outside his substance? Whence he does not now will this, now will that; but once and simultaneously and always wills all that he wills; not again and again, nor now these things, now those; nor does he later will what he did not will, or not will what he formerly willed: because such a will is mutable, and everything mutable is not eternal; but our God is eternal. Likewise, what it says * to me in my inner ear: expectation of things to come becomes sight when they have come; and that same sight becomes memory when they have passed: moreover, every attention that is so varied is mutable; and everything mutable is not eternal: but our God is eternal.”
I gather and join these things together, and find that my God, the eternal God, did not create the creature by some new will, nor does his knowledge suffer anything transitory.

> 19. “What then will you say, gainsayers? Are these things false?” “No,” they say. “What of this? Is it false that every formed nature or formable matter is not except from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is?” “Neither do we deny this,” they say. “What then? Do you deny that there is a certain sublime creature cleaving to the true and truly eternal God with so chaste a love that, although it is not coeternal with him, yet does not dissolve and flow away from him into any variety and vicissitude of times, but rests in the most true contemplation of him alone?” For thou, O God, showest thyself to it and sufficest for it, when it loves thee as much as thou commandest; and therefore it does not turn aside from thee, nor toward itself [322] . This is the house [323] of God, not earthly nor constituted of any heavenly bodily mass, but spiritual and a participant in thy eternity, because without stain for ever * . Ps. 148, 6.

For thou hast established it for age and for age of age; thou hast set a commandment, and it shall not pass away . Yet it is not coeternal with thee, God, because it is not without a beginning; for it was made.

> 20. For even if we find no time before it—for Eccli. 1, 4. wisdom was created before all things —yet certainly it is not that Wisdom coeternal and equal to thee, our God, its Father, through whom all things were made , and in which Beginning thou didst make heaven and earth; but assuredly the wisdom that was created, namely the intellectual nature, which by contemplation of the Light is light: for it too, though created, is called wisdom. But as great as is the difference between the light which illuminates and that which is illuminated [324] , so great is the difference between the wisdom which creates and this wisdom which was created; just as between the justice which justifies and the justice which has been made by justification. For we too have been called thy justice. For a certain servant of thine says, 2 Cor. 5, 21. that we might be the justice of God in him . Therefore, because a certain created wisdom was created before all things, the rational and intellectual mind of thy chaste city, Gal. 4, 26.

our mother which is above, and is free , and eternal in the heavens; (in what heavens, unless those Ps. 148, 4. heavens of heavens which praise thee ; because this too is the Heaven of heaven unto the Lord?)—even if we find no time before it, because it precedes the creature of time, being created before all things; yet before it is the eternity of its Creator himself, from whom, when it was made, it received the beginning of its existence (though not a beginning of time, since * time did not yet exist), yet a beginning of its condition.

> 21. Hence it is so from thee, our God, that it is plainly something other than thou, and not the selfsame [325] . For although we find time not only not before it, but not even in it, because it is capable always of seeing thy face and nowhere turns aside from it—whereby it is varied by no change—yet mutability itself is in it, by which it might be darkened and grow cold, unless, cleaving to thee in great love, it should as from an everlasting midday shine and glow from thee. O Ps. 25, 8. luminous and beautiful house, I have loved thy beauty, and the place of the habitation of the glory of my Lord, thy maker and possessor! Let my pilgrimage sigh for thee; and I say to him who made thee, that he may possess me also in thee, because he made me also. Ps. 118, 176. I have gone astray like a lost sheep ; but Luc. 15, 5. upon the shoulders of my shepherd , thy builder, I hope to be carried back to thee.

> 22. What do you say to me, you opponents whom I was addressing, who nevertheless believe both that Moses was a pious servant of God and that his books are oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is this that house of God, not indeed coeternal with God, yet eternal in its own mode in the heavens, where you seek in vain the alternations of times, because you will not find them? For it transcends every extension and every changing span of age, to which it is always Ps. 62, 28. good to cling to God. “It is,” they say. What then, of those things which my heart cried out to my God when it heard inwardly the voice of His praise, what, finally, do you contend to be false? Is it because there was formless matter, where, owing to the absence of all form, there was no order; but where there was no order, there could be no succession of times; and yet this almost-nothing, insofar as it was not altogether nothing, was surely from Him from whom is whatever is, insofar as it is in any way something? “This also,” they say, “we do not deny.”
> XVI. He does not wish to contend with those who contradict divine truth.

> 23. For with those who grant before You, my God, that all these things which Your truth does not cease to speak within my mind are true, I wish to converse somewhat. But as for those who deny these things, let them bark as much as they please and make a din against themselves; I shall try to persuade them to be quiet and to make way for Your word to reach them. But 1. if they are unwilling and repel me, I beseech You, my God, Ps. 27, 1. do not be silent to me.

Speak truly in my heart; for You alone speak thus. And I shall leave them outside, blowing dust about and stirring up the earth into their own eyes; and I shall enter into my chamber, and sing to You songs of love, groaning with unutterable groanings in my pilgrimage, and remembering Jerusalem, with my heart stretched upward toward her—Jerusalem, my homeland, Jerusalem, my mother—and You, reigning over her, illuminating her, her Father, guardian, husband, chaste and mighty delights, and solid joy, and all ineffable goods, all together; because You are the one Page 236 highest and true good. And I shall not turn away until You gather into the peace of that dearest mother, where are the firstfruits of my spirit [326], from which these things are certain to me, all that I am, from this dispersion [327] and deformity, and conform and establish it forever, my God, my mercy.

But with those who do not call false all those things that are true, honoring Your holy Scripture, published through holy Moses, and setting it with us at the summit of authority to be followed, yet who nevertheless contradict us in some point, I speak thus: Be You, our God, arbiter between my confessions and their contradictions.
> XVII. That one thing or another may be understood by the names heaven and earth.

> 24. For they say: “Although these things are true, Moses nevertheless did not have those two things in view when, with the Spirit revealing, he said: Gen. 1. 1. In the beginning God made heaven and earth. By the name heaven he did not signify that spiritual or intellectual creature which always contemplates the face of God; nor by the name earth, formless matter.” “What then?” “What we say,” they reply, “that man understood, and he expressed it in these words.” “What is that?” “By the name,” they say, “of heaven and earth, he first intended universally and briefly to signify this whole visible world, so that afterward he might set forth in the enumeration of the days, as though member by member, all those things which it pleased the Holy Spirit to declare thus. For such were the people, rude and carnal, to whom he spoke, that he judged that only the visible works of God should be commended to them.”

But they agree that by the invisible and unformed earth, and the dark abyss, from which it is subsequently shown that throughout those days all these visible things known to everyone were made and arranged, this formless matter is not incongruously to be understood.”

> 25. What if another should say, “The same formlessness and confusion of matter was first indicated by the name of heaven and earth, because from it this visible world was created and perfected, with all the natures that most clearly appear in it, which is often called by the name of heaven and earth?”

What if another should also say, “Heaven and earth are indeed not improperly called the invisible and visible nature; and therefore the whole creation which God made in Wisdom, that is, in the Beginning, is comprehended in these two terms: Page 237 nevertheless, because all things were made not from the substance of God himself, but from nothing, because they are not that very thing which God is, and because a certain mutability is present in all things, whether they remain, as the eternal house of God, or change, as the soul and body of man: the common matter of all invisible and visible things, still formless but certainly formable, from which heaven and earth would be made—that is, each creature, invisible and visible, now formed—was declared by these names by which Invisible and Unformed Earth and Darkness upon the Abyss would be called: with this distinction, that invisible and unformed earth is understood as corporeal matter before the quality of form; darkness
upon the abyss, however, as spiritual matter before the restraint, as it were, of flowing immoderation and before the illumination of Wisdom?”

> 26. There is still something else that another may say, if he wishes: “Not, to be sure, the invisible and visible natures already perfected and formed are signified by the name of heaven and earth when one reads, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the very as-yet formless beginning of things, formable and creatable matter, was called by these names, because in it these things were already confused, not yet distinguished by qualities and forms, which now, arranged in their own orders, are called heaven and earth—the former the spiritual creature, the latter the corporeal.”
> XVIII. What error in the Scriptures is harmless.

> 27. Having heard and considered all these things, I do not wish to contend about words; 2 Tim. 2, 14. for it is useful for nothing, except for the overthrow of the hearers. But for edification 1 Tim. 1, 8. 5. the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully; for its end is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. And our Master knows on which Matt. 22, 40. two commandments He has suspended the whole Law and the Prophets. What harm is it to me, who ardently confess You, my God, light of my eyes in secret, if different meanings may be understood in these words and yet be true? What harm, I say, is it to me if I understand something other than what another thinks the writer understood? Certainly, all of us who read endeavor to seek out and comprehend what he whom we read intended. And since we believe him truthful, we dare not think that he said anything which we either know or suppose to be false.

Therefore, while each person strives to understand in the holy Scriptures what he who wrote them understood in them, what evil is there if he understands that which You, light of all minds that speak truth, show to be true, even if he whom he reads did not understand this—when that writer too understood what was true, though not this?
> XIX. Things plainly true.

> 28. For it is true, Lord, that You made heaven and earth; and it is true that Your Wisdom is the Beginning Ps. 103, 24. in which You made all things. Likewise, it is true that this visible world has as its great parts heaven and earth, a brief comprehending of all made and created natures. And it is true that everything mutable suggests to our knowledge a certain formlessness, by which it receives form, or by which it is changed and turned. It is true that what so clings to the immutable form that, though mutable, it is not changed, suffers no times. It is true that formlessness, which is close to * nothing, cannot have successions of time. It is true that that from which something is made can, by a certain kind of expression, already bear the name of the thing made from it; whence any formlessness from which heaven and earth were made could be called heaven and earth. It is true that, of all formed things, nothing is nearer to the unformed than earth and abyss.

It is true that not only what has been created and formed, but also whatever is creatable and formable, You made, from whom are all things. It is true that everything which is formed from the unformed is first unformed and then formed.
> XX. “In the beginning He created,” etc., understood in various ways.

> 29. From among all these truths, concerning which those do not doubt to whom You have granted to see such things with the inward eye, and who unwaveringly believe that Moses Your servant spoke in the Spirit of truth—from all these, then, one person takes for himself one meaning when he says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, “In His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made the intelligible and sensible, or spiritual and corporeal, creature.” Another takes another who says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, “In His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made this whole mass of the corporeal world, with all the manifest and known natures which it contains.” Another takes another who says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, “In His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made formless matter [328] of spiritual and corporeal creation.”

Another takes another who says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, “In His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made the formless matter of corporeal creation, in which heaven and earth were still confused, which we now perceive as already distinct and formed in the mass of this world.” Another takes another who says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, that is, “In the very outset of making and working, God made formless matter, confusedly containing heaven and earth, from which, now formed, they stand forth and appear, together with all that is in them.”
> XXI. “And the earth was invisible,” etc., understood in various ways.

> 30. Likewise, regarding the understanding of the following words, from among all those truths one person takes one meaning who says: But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the abyss, that is, “That corporeal * thing which God made was still the formless matter of corporeal things, without order, without light.” Another takes another who says: But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the abyss, that is, “This whole thing which was called heaven and earth was still formless and dark matter, from which corporeal heaven and corporeal earth would be made, with all the things in them known to bodily senses.” Another takes another who says: But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the abyss, that is, “This whole thing which was called heaven and earth was still formless and dark matter, from which the intelligible heaven would be made, which elsewhere is called the heaven of heaven; Ps. 113, 16.

and earth, namely every corporeal nature, under which name this corporeal heaven also is understood; that is, from which every invisible and visible creature would be made.” Another takes another who says: But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the abyss: “Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth; rather, that very formlessness already existed,” he says, “which it called invisible and unformed earth and dark abyss, from which it had foretold that God made heaven and earth, namely the spiritual and corporeal creature.” Another takes another who says: But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the abyss, that is, “A certain formlessness was already matter, from which Scripture had foretold that God made heaven and earth, namely the whole corporeal mass of the world, divided into its two greatest parts, upper and lower Page 240, with all the familiar and known creatures that are in them.”
> XXII. That something was created by God, concerning which the book of Genesis is silent, is in no way objectionable.

> 31. For when someone has attempted to oppose these two extreme opinions in this manner: “If you do not wish * this formlessness of matter to be considered designated by the name of heaven and earth, then there was something which God had not made, from which he might make heaven and earth; for Scripture has not narrated that God made that matter, unless we understand * it to have been signified by the term heaven and earth, or earth alone, when it was said, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; so that what follows, But the earth was invisible and unformed, although it has pleased [you] thus to call formless matter, we nevertheless understand it to be none other than that which God made in what is written above *: God made heaven and earth.”

The defenders of those two opinions which we have set forth as extreme—of one or the other—when they hear this, will answer and say: “Indeed, we do not deny that this formless matter was * made by God, by the God from whom are all things very good: for just as we say that what has been created and formed is a greater good, so we confess that what has been made capable of being created and formed is a lesser good, yet still a good. But Scripture has not mentioned that God made this formlessness, just as it has not mentioned many other things, Isa. 6, 2; and 37, 16. such as the Cherubim and Seraphim, and those which the Apostle distinctly calls, Col. 1, 16. Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, all of which nevertheless it is manifest that God made. Or if * all things are comprehended in that which was said, he made heaven and earth, what shall we say of the waters over which the Spirit of God was borne?”

For if, when earth is named, they are understood together, how is formless matter now taken under the name of earth, when we see waters so beautiful? Or if it is taken thus, why is it written that the firmament was made from the same formlessness and called heaven, while it is not written that the waters were made? For they are not yet formless and unseen, which we discern flowing in so fair an appearance. Or if they received that appearance when God said, Gen. 1, 9. Let the water which is under the firmament be gathered together, so that the gathering itself is the formation, what answer will be given concerning the waters which are above the firmament? For neither, if formless, would they have deserved to receive so honorable a dwelling-place, nor is it written by what word they were formed.”

Hence, if Genesis has been silent about something which God made, though neither sound faith nor assured understanding doubts that God made it, and for that reason no sober doctrine will dare to say Page 241 that those waters are coeternal with God, because indeed we hear them mentioned * in the book of Genesis, but do not find where they were made: why should we not likewise understand, as truth teaches, that that formless matter, which this Scripture calls invisible and unformed earth and the dark abyss, was * made by God out of nothing, and therefore is not coeternal with him, although this narrative has omitted to declare where it was made?”
> XXIII. Two kinds of disagreement in interpreting the Scriptures.

> 32. Therefore, having heard and considered these things according to the capacity of my weakness—which I confess to you, my God who know me—I see that two kinds of disagreement can arise when something is declared through signs by truthful messengers: one, if the disagreement concerns the truth of things; the other, if it concerns the intention of the one who declares. For we inquire differently what is true concerning the condition of the creature, and differently what Moses, the eminent member of your household of faith, wished the reader and hearer to understand in these words. In the first kind, let all who suppose that they know things which are false depart from me. Likewise, in this second kind, let all who suppose that Moses said things which are false depart from me. But let me be joined to those, O Lord, in you, and delight with them in you, who are fed by your truth in the breadth of charity; and let us approach together the words of your Book, and seek in them your will through the will of your servant, by whose pen you dispensed them.
> XXIV. Among many truths one ought not confidently to assert that Moses meant this or that.

> 33. But which of us will so find, among so many truths * that present themselves to seekers when those words are understood in different ways, the one which is there, that he may say with as much confidence that Moses meant this and wished this to be understood in that narrative, as he says with confidence that this is true, whether Moses meant this or something else? For behold, my God, I your servant, who have vowed to you in these writings a sacrifice of confession, and pray that through your mercy I may render my vows to you: behold, how confidently I say that in your unchangeable Word you made all things, invisible and visible; do I say with equal confidence that Moses, when he wrote, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, had in view nothing other than this? For I do not see in his mind that he thought this when he wrote these things, as I see this as certain in your truth.

For he could have thought, at the very beginning of making, when he said, In the beginning; he could also have wished heaven and earth in this place to be understood as no already formed and perfected nature, whether spiritual or corporeal, but both as begun and still formless. For I see that whatever of these Page 242 might be said could truly have been said; but which of them he thought in these words I do not see in the same way. Although, whether that great man beheld in his mind any * of these things, or something else not mentioned by me, when he uttered these words, I do not doubt that he saw what was true and aptly declared it.
> XXV. Against those who rashly reject others’ manner of interpretation.

> 34. Let no one now trouble me by saying to me: Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say. For if he were to say to me, “How do you know that Moses meant what you declare concerning these words of his?” I should have to bear it with equanimity and perhaps answer what I answered above, or somewhat more fully, if he were more obstinate. But when he says, “He did not mean what you say, but what I say,” while nevertheless not denying that what each of us says is true—O God, life of the poor, in whose bosom there is no contradiction—rain consolations into my heart, so that I may patiently [329] bear such people, who say this to me not because they are divine and have seen in the heart of your servant what they say, but because they are proud: and they do not know Moses’ meaning, but love their own—not because it is true, but because it is their own.

Otherwise [330] they would equally love another true interpretation, just as I love what they say when they say what is true—not because it is theirs, but because it is true; and therefore it is no longer theirs, because it is true. But if they love it because it is true, then it is both theirs and mine, because it is held in common by all lovers * of truth. But I do not want, I do not love, what they contend: that Moses did not mean what I say, but what they say; because, even if it is so, such rashness is not of knowledge but of audacity; and not sight, but arrogance has begotten it. Therefore, O Lord, your judgments are dreadful, because your truth is neither mine nor this man’s nor that man’s, but belongs to all of us whom you publicly call to communion in it, warning us terribly that we should not wish to hold it as private, lest we be deprived of it.

For whoever claims for himself as private that which you offer to all for enjoyment, and wishes that to be his own which belongs to all, is driven from what is common to what is his own—that is, from truth to falsehood. Page 243 Joh. 8, 44. For he who speaks a lie speaks from his own.

> 35. Attend, O best Judge, God himself, Truth; attend to what I say to this opponent, attend: for I speak before you and before my brethren, who 1 Tim. 1, 8. use the Law lawfully unto the end of charity; attend, and see what I say to him, if it pleases you. For I return to him this brotherly and peaceable reply: “If we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true, where, I ask, do we see it? Surely neither I in you nor you in me, but both in that unchangeable Truth itself which is above our minds.
