Be not conformed to this age, but be reformed in the newness of your mind ; and, 1 Cor. 14, 20.

Do not become children in understanding * , but be little children in malice, that in understanding you may be perfect ; and, Gal. 3, 1. O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? But now not in his own voice; Act. 2, 2. rather in thine, who didst send thy Spirit from on high, through him who Ps. 67, 19. ascended on high, Mal. 3, 10. and opened the cataracts of his gifts, so that Ps. 45, 5. the rush of the river might make glad thy city. For the Rom. 8, 23. Joh. 3, 29. friend of the bridegroom sighs for him, having already the firstfruits of the Spirit with him, but still groaning in himself, awaiting adoption, the redemption of his body : he sighs for him, for he is a member of the bride; and he is zealous for him, for he is the friend of the bridegroom ; he is zealous for him, not for himself, because in the voice of thy cataracts , not in his own voice Ps. 41, 8. he calls upon the other deep , for whom, being zealous, 2 Cor. 11, 3.

he fears lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so also their minds should be corrupted from the chastity which is in our bridegroom, thine Only One. What is that light of sight? When 1 Joh. 3, 2. we shall see him as he is , and Ps. 41, 4. the tears which have become my bread day and night shall have passed away, while it is said to me daily, Where is thy God?
> XIV. We are strengthened by faith and hope.

> 15. And I say: My God, where art thou? Behold where thou art * . I breathe a little in thee, when Ps. 41, 5. I pour out my soul upon myself in the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one keeping festival . And it is still sorrowful , because it falls back and becomes a deep; or rather, still feels itself to be a deep . My faith, which thou hast kindled in the night before my feet, says to it: Why art thou sorrowful, O my soul, and why dost thou trouble me? Ps. 42, 5. 6. Hope in the Lord; Ps. 118, 105. his word is a lamp to thy feet. Rom. 8, 10. Hope and persevere, until the night, mother of the wicked, pass away; until the Cant. 2, 17. wrath of the Lord pass away, whose Ps. 29, 13. children we too were, when we were once darkness , the remnants of which we draw in a Ps. 5, 5. body dead because of sin, until the day breathe and the shadows be removed. Ps. 42, 5. Hope in the Lord: in the morning [354] I shall stand * , and contemplate; I shall always confess to him. In the morning I shall stand, and see the salvation of my countenance, Rom.

8, 11. my God, who will quicken even our mortal bodies, because of the Spirit who dwells in us ; because he was mercifully borne over our inner darkness and fluidity . Whence also in this pilgrimage 2 Cor. 1, 22. we have received a pledge, that Eph. 5, 8. we may already be light , while still Rom. 8, 24. we have been saved by hope, 1 Thess. 5, 5. and are sons of light and sons of day, not sons of night nor of darkness , though this is what we were . Among whom, even in this still uncertain state of human knowledge, thou alone dost divide us , who triest our hearts, and Gen. 1, 5. callest the light day, and the darkness night . For who distinguishes us, unless thou? 1 Cor. 4, 7. And what have we that we have not received from thee, Rom. 9, 21. from the same lump vessels unto honor, from which others also have been made unto dishonor?
> XV. He explains verse 6 of chapter 1 of Genesis: Let there be a firmament, etc. What the firmament is, what the upper waters are.

> 16. Or who, save thou, our God, hast made for us Is. 24, 4. the firmament of authority over us in thy divine Scripture? Ps. 103, 2. For heaven shall be folded up like a book , and now it is stretched out over us like a skin. For thy divine Scripture is of more sublime authority, now that those mortals have died this death through whom thou didst dispense it to us. And thou knowest, Lord, thou knowest how thou didst clothe men with skins, when they became mortal through sin [355] . Whence Gen. 3, 21. like a skin thou hast stretched out the firmament of thy Book, namely thy harmonious words, which thou hast placed over us through the ministry of mortals. For by their very death, the support [356] of authority in thy utterances published through them is sublimely stretched out over all things beneath; whereas, while they lived here, it was not stretched out so sublimely. Thou hadst not yet stretched out heaven like a skin , thou hadst not yet spread abroad everywhere the fame of their death [357] .

> 17. Let us behold , Lord, the heavens, the works of thy fingers ; clear away from our eyes the cloudiness with which thou hast covered them. There is Ps. 18, 8. thy testimony, giving wisdom to little ones. Ps. 8, 4. Perfect , O my God, thy praise out of the mouth of infants and sucklings . For we know no other books so destroying pride, so Ver. 3. destroying the enemy and defender , who resists thy reconciliation by defending his sins [358] . I know not, Lord, I know not other utterances so chaste, which would thus persuade me to confession, and soften my neck under thy yoke, and invite me to worship thee freely. May I understand them, good Father; grant this to me who am placed beneath, because thou hast made them firm for those who are placed beneath.

> 18. There are other waters above this firmament , I believe, immortal and set apart from earthly corruption. Let them praise thy name, let the heavenly peoples of thy Angels praise thee, who have no need to look up * to this firmament and, by reading, come to know thy word [359] . Mat. 18, 10. For they always see thy face , and there, without the syllables of times, they read what thy eternal will wills. They read, choose, and love; they always read, and what they read never passes away. For in choosing and loving they read the very immutability of thy counsel. Their codex is not closed, nor is their book folded up; because thou thyself art this to them, and art for ever: because above this firmament thou hast ordered them, which * thou hast made firm above the weakness of the lower peoples, where they might look up and know thy mercy, temporally proclaiming thee, who hast made the times. Ps. 35, 6.

For in heaven, O Lord, is thy mercy, and thy truth unto the clouds . The clouds pass away, but heaven remains. The preachers of thy word pass from this life into another life; but thy Scripture is stretched out over the peoples unto the end of the age. Yet Mat. 24, 35. heaven and earth shall pass away; but thy words shall not pass away : for the skin too shall be folded up , and the grass upon which it was stretched out shall pass away with its glory; Isa. 40, 6. but thy word remains for ever ; which now 1 Cor. 13, 12. in the riddle of clouds and through the mirror of heaven, not 1 Joh. 3, 2. as it is , appears to us; for although we are beloved by thy Son, Cant. 2, 9. Vers. Vet. it has not yet appeared what we shall be. He has looked through the nets of flesh, and caressed us, and kindled us, and Cant. 1, 6. we have run after his fragrance. But 1 Joh. 3, 2.
when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is : as he is, O Lord—our seeing, which is not yet ours * .
> XVI. God alone knows Himself altogether as He is.

> 19. For as altogether as you are, you alone know, who are unchangeably, and know unchangeably, and will unchangeably. And your essence knows and wills unchangeably, and your knowledge is and wills unchangeably, and your will is and knows unchangeably. Nor does it seem just before you that, as unchangeable light knows itself, so it should be known by mutable light. And therefore Ps. 142, 6. my soul is to you as land without water; because, just as it cannot illuminate itself from itself, so it cannot satisfy itself from itself. For thus Ps. 35, 10. with you is the fountain of life, how in your light shall we see light.
> XVII. On v. 9: Let the waters be gathered together, etc. What the sea is, what the dry land. Explained in v. 11: Let the earth bring forth, etc.

> 20. Who gathered together the bitter ones [360] into one society? Page 261 For their end is the same, that of temporal and earthly happiness, on account of which they do all things; although they surge with an innumerable variety of cares. Who, O Lord, unless you, who said that Ps. 94, 5. the waters should be gathered together into one gathering, and dry land should appear, thirsting for you? For yours is the sea, and Ps. 62, 2. you made it, and your hands formed the dry land; for it is not the bitterness of wills, but the gathering of waters, that is called sea. For you also restrain the evil desires of souls, and set bounds as far as they are permitted to proceed, Job 38, 10. 11. and * that their waves may break themselves upon themselves; and thus you make the sea by the order of your dominion over all things [361].

> 21. But souls thirsting for you, and appearing to you, distinguished by another end from the society of the sea, you water with a hidden and sweet spring, so that the earth too may yield its fruit [362]: and it yields its fruit * and, at your command, O Lord its God, our soul brings forth works of mercy according to their kind; loving its neighbour in supplying bodily needs, having seed in itself according to likeness; for out of our own infirmity we sympathize so as to aid the needy, helping in like manner as we would wish help to be brought to ourselves if we were in need in the same way; not only in easy matters, as in seed-bearing herb, but also in the protection of aid, with strong vigour, as a fruit-bearing tree; that is, beneficent * in rescuing one who suffers injury from the hand of the mighty, and in affording the sheltering shade of protection by the strong vigour of just judgment.
> XVIII. On v. 14: Let there be lights, etc. What lights divide between day and night.

> 22. Thus, O Lord, thus, I pray you, let it arise, as you make it arise, as you give cheerfulness and ability: Ps. 84, 12. let truth arise from the earth, and righteousness look down from heaven, and let lights be made in the firmament. Let us break our bread for the hungry, and bring the needy without shelter into our house; let us clothe the naked, and not despise those of our own seed. When these fruits have been born upon earth, see that it is good; and Isa. 58, 7. 8. let our temporal light break forth, and, from this lower fruit of action attaining above to the delights of contemplation, to the word of life, let us appear Phil. 2, 15. as lights in the world, clinging to the firmament of your Scripture.

For there you discourse with us, that we may divide between intelligible and sensible things, as between day and night, or between souls, some devoted to intelligible things, others to sensible things; so that now not you alone, in the hiddenness of your judgment, as before the firmament was made, divide between light and darkness, but also your spiritual ones, set and distinguished in that same firmament, may shine upon the earth through your grace manifested throughout the world, and divide between day and night, and signify times: because Rom. 13, 1. old things have passed away, and * behold, new things have been made; and 2 Cor. 5, 17. because our salvation is nearer than when we believed; and because the night has gone before, but the day has drawn near; and because Ps. 64, 2. you bless the crown of your year, Mat. 9, 38. sending * labourers of kindness into your harvest, in the sowing of which others laboured, sending also into another sowing, whose Joh. 4, 38. harvest is at the end.

Thus you grant vows to him who desires * and bless the years of the righteous; Mat. 13, 39. but you are the same, and in Ps. 101, 28. for your years which do not fail, you prepare a granary for passing years. For by eternal counsel you give heavenly good things upon earth in their proper times.

> 23. For 1 Cor. 12, 7-11. to one indeed is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom [363], as the greater light, for those who delight in the light of perspicuous truth, as at the beginning of day; but to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, as the lesser light; to another faith, to another gifts of healings, to another workings of powers, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues; and all these are as stars. For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing proper gifts to each as he wills, and causing stars to appear in manifestation for usefulness. 1 Cor. 13, 2. But the word of knowledge, by which are contained all the sacraments that vary with times [364], as the moon, and the other knowledges of gifts which were afterwards mentioned as stars, insofar as they differ from that brightness of wisdom in which the aforesaid day rejoices, so far are they in the beginnings * of night [365].

For these are necessary for those to whom that most prudent servant of yours 1 Cor. 3, 1. could not speak as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal, he who 1 Cor. 2, 6. speaks wisdom among the perfect. v. 14. But the natural man, like a little child in Christ, Id. 3, 2. and a drinker of milk, until he is strengthened for solid food and fixes his sight for looking upon the sun, should not have his night deserted, but should be content with the light of moon and stars. These things you discourse with us, O our most wise God, in your Book, your firmament; that we may discern all things by wondrous contemplation, although still in signs, and in times, and in days, and in years.
> XIX. He treats the same verse, Let there be lights, etc.

> 24. But first, Is. 1, 16. wash yourselves, be clean; put away evil from your souls, and from before my eyes, that dry land may appear. Learn to do good, judge for the orphan, and justify the widow; that the earth may bring forth fodder-herb and fruit-bearing tree; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord, that lights may be made in the firmament of heaven and shine upon the earth. That rich man asked the good master what he should do to obtain eternal life: let the good master say to him—whom he thought to be a man and nothing more; yet he is good because he is God—let him say to him that, if he wishes to come to life, he should keep the commandments; let him separate from himself the bitterness of malice and wickedness; let him not kill, not commit adultery, not steal, not bear false witness; that dry land may appear, and bring forth honour for father and mother, and love of neighbour. I have done, he says, all these things. Page 264 Whence then are so many thorns, if the land is fruitful?

Go, uproot the woody thickets of avarice; sell what you possess, and fill with fruits by giving to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven, and follow the Lord if you wish to be perfect, joined to those among whom he speaks wisdom who knows what to distribute to day and night; that you too may know, that lights may also be made for you in the firmament of heaven. This will not happen unless Mat. 6, 21. your heart is there; nor likewise will this happen unless your treasure is there, as you heard from the good master. But Mat. 19, 16-22. the barren land was saddened [366], and the thorns choked the word.

> 25. 1 Pet. 2, 9. But you, a chosen generation, weak things of the world, who have left all things in order to follow the Lord: go after him, and Mat. 10, 28. confound the strong: go after him, 1 Cor. 1, 7. 8. beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament; that Isa. 52, 7. the heavens may declare his glory, dividing between the light of the perfect, though not yet as of the Angels, and the darkness of little ones, though not despised *: shine over all the earth; and Ps. 18, 2. let day, glowing with the sun, utter to day the word of wisdom, and night, shining with the moon, announce to night the word of knowledge. Moon and stars shine for the night; but the night does not darken them, because they themselves illuminate it according to its measure. For behold, as if God were saying, Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven, there came suddenly a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty spirit, and there were seen divided tongues as of fire, Act. 2, 2. 3. which also sat upon each one of them; and Mat. 5, 14.

lights were made in the firmament of heaven, having the word of life. Run everywhere, holy fires, beautiful fires. 1 John 1, 1. For you are the light of the world, nor are you under a bushel. He to whom you have clung has been exalted, and has exalted you. Run, and make yourselves known to all nations.
> XX. On v. 20: Let the waters bring forth, etc. What creeping things are, what flying things.

> 26. Let the sea also conceive and give birth to your works, and let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls. Jer. 15, 19. For by separating the precious from the vile, you have become the mouth of God, through whom * he might say: Let the waters bring forth, not the living soul which the earth brings forth, but creeping things of living souls, and birds flying over the earth. For your sacraments, O God, have crept through the works of your saints amid the waves of the temptations of this age, to imbue nations in * your name, in your baptism. And among these were performed great wonders, as great sea-monsters, and the voices of your messengers flying over the earth beside the firmament of your Book, Page 265 set over them as an authority under which they might fly wherever they went. For Ps. 18, 4. 5.

there are no utterances nor speeches whose voices are not heard, when their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world; because you, O Lord, by blessing have multiplied these.

> 27. Am I lying, or mingling together by mixture, and not distinguishing the clear cognitions of these things in the firmament of heaven, and bodily works in the wave-tossed sea and beneath the firmament of heaven? For those things whose cognitions are solid and determinate, without the increases of generations, as lights of wisdom and knowledge, have bodily operations that are many and various; and, growing one from another, they are multiplied in your blessing, O God, who have consoled the weariness of mortal senses, so that in the cognition of the mind one thing may be figured and said in many ways through bodily movements [367]. The waters brought forth these things, but in your word. The needs of peoples alienated from the eternity of your truth brought forth these things, but in your Gospel; for the waters themselves cast forth these things, whose bitter languor was the cause why these things proceeded in your word.

> 28. And all things are beautiful because you make them, and behold, you are ineffably more beautiful, who made all things: from whom * if Adam had not fallen away, the briny sea would not be poured forth from his womb—the human race, profoundly curious, stormily swollen, and fluid with instability—and thus there would be no need for your stewards to work bodily and sensibly in many waters by mystical deeds and words. For thus creeping things and flying things have now occurred to me: men imbued and initiated by bodily sacraments, being subjected to them, would not advance further unless the soul were quickened spiritually at another stage and, after the word of initiation, looked toward consummation.
> XXI. On v. 24: Let the earth bring forth the living soul, etc.

> 29. And therefore, in your word, it was not the depth of the sea, but earth separated from the bitterness of waters, that brought forth * not creeping things of living souls and flying things, but the living soul. For it now has no need of the Baptism which the nations need, as it had need when it was covered by waters; for Joh. 3, 5. there is no other entrance into the kingdom of heaven than that which you instituted for entering thus; nor does it seek the great things of wonders by which faith may be made; for Joh. 4, 48. unless it sees signs and prodigies, it does not believe, when the faithful earth has already been distinguished from the waters of the sea bitter with unbelief; and 1 Cor. 14, 22. tongues are for a sign * not to believers but to unbelievers. Therefore Ps. 135, 6. the earth which you founded upon the waters [368] has no need of this flying kind either, which the waters brought forth by your word. Send into it your word through your messengers. For we recount their works, but you are he who works in them, that * they may work the living soul.

The earth brings it forth, because the earth is the cause that they do these things in it; just as the sea was the cause that they performed creeping things of living souls and flying things beneath the firmament of heaven, of which the earth now has no need; Luc. 24, 43. although it eats fish [369], raised from the deep, upon that Ps. 22, 5. table which you have prepared in the sight of believers; for it was raised from the deep in order that it might feed the dry land. And birds, offspring of the sea, nevertheless multiply over the earth. For the unbelief of men was the cause of the first utterances of those proclaiming the Gospel; but the faithful too are exhorted, and are blessed by them * manifoldly from day to day. But the living soul takes * its beginning from the earth, because it avails only for those already faithful to restrain themselves from love of this age, so that their soul, which 1 Tim. 5, 6. was dead while living in pleasures, may live for you—pleasures, O Lord, deadly pleasures; for you are the vital pleasures of the pure heart.

> 30. Therefore now let thy ministers work upon the earth, not as in the waters of unbelief, proclaiming and speaking through miracles and sacraments and mystical utterances, where ignorance, intent * upon the fear of hidden signs, is the mother of wonder; for such is the entrance into faith for the sons of Adam forgetful of thee, while Gen. 3, 8. they hide themselves from thy face and become an abyss: but let them work also as in the dry land separated from the whirlpools of the abyss; and let them be an example to the faithful, living before them and stirring them to imitation. For thus they hear not only in order to hear, but also in order to do: Ps. 68, 33. Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live, that the earth may bring forth the living soul. Rom. 12, 2. Be not conformed to this world, Page 267 restrain yourselves from it. By avoiding, the soul lives which by desiring dies. Restrain yourselves from the monstrous fierceness of pride, from the sluggish pleasure of luxury, and from the 1 Tim. 6, 20.

deceitful name of knowledge; that there may be gentle beasts, tamed cattle, and harmless serpents. For these are movements of the soul in allegory: but the arrogance of exaltation, and the delight of lust, and the poison of curiosity, are movements of the dead soul; because it does not so die as to be without all movement, since Jer. 2, 13. by departing from the fountain of life it dies [370], and is thus received by the passing world, and Rom. 12, 2. conformed to it.

> 31. But thy Word, O God, is the fountain of eternal life, and does not pass away: therefore that departure is restrained in thy word, when it is said to us, Be not conformed to this world; that the earth, in the fountain of life, may bring forth a living soul, in thy word through 1 Cor. 11, 1. thy Evangelists, a self-restrained soul, by imitating the imitators of thy Christ. For this is according to its kind, since emulation of a man comes from a friend: Gal. 4, 12. Be ye, he says, as I am; because I also am as ye are. Thus there will be in the living soul * good beasts in gentleness of action. For thou hast commanded, saying: Eccl. 3, 19. In gentleness accomplish thy works, and thou shalt be loved by every man. And 1 Cor. 8, 8. good cattle, neither, if they have eaten, abundance; nor, if they have not eaten, want: and good serpents, not harmful for hurting, but Mat. 10, 16. shrewd for guarding against; and exploring temporal nature only so far as suffices, that Rom. 1, 20.
through the things which have been made, eternity may be beheld as understood. For these animals [371] serve reason, when, restrained from deadly progress, they live and are good.

> XXII. On verse 26: Let us make man after the image, etc. The renewal of the mind.

> 32. For behold, O Lord our God, our Creator, when the affections have been restrained from love of the world, by which we were dying through living badly, and the soul has begun to be living through living well, and thy word has been fulfilled which thou didst speak through thine Apostle, Be not conformed to this world; that also follows which thou didst immediately add and say, But be reformed in the newness of your mind: no longer according to its kind, as though imitating a preceding neighbour, and * living by the authority of a better man (for thou didst not say, “Let man be made according to his kind”; but, Gen. 1, 26. Let us make man after our image and likeness); that we may prove what is thy will. For to this end 1 Cor. 4, 15. that steward of thine, begetting sons through the Gospel, that he might not always have little children to nourish with milk and cherish as a nurse: 1 Thess. 2, 7. Be reformed, he says, in the newness of your mind Rom. 12, 2.

that ye may prove * what is the will of God, what is good and well-pleasing and perfect. And therefore thou dost not say, Let man be made; but, Let us make man. Nor dost thou say, According to its kind; but, After our image and likeness. For, renewed in mind and beholding thy understood truth, he has no need of a man Jer. 31, 34. Heb. 8, 11. to show him, that he may imitate his kind; but with thee showing him, he himself proves what is thy will, what is good and well-pleasing and perfect: and thou teachest him * now capable of seeing the Trinity of unity, and the unity of Trinity [372]. And therefore, though it is said in the plural, Let us make man, yet it is added in the singular, Gen. 1, 27. And God made man; and though it is said in the plural, After our image, it is added in the singular, after the image of God. Thus man Col. 3, 10. is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of him who created him: and 1 Cor. 2, 15.
having become spiritual, judges all things, which assuredly are to be judged; but he himself is judged by no one.
> XXIII. On the same verse: And let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, etc. Concerning whom the Christian may judge.

> 33. But that he judges all things is this: that he has power over the fishes of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and all cattle and beasts, and all the earth, and all creeping things which creep upon the earth. For he does this through the understanding of the mind, through which 1 Cor. 2, 14. he perceives the things which are of the Spirit of God. Otherwise, man being placed in honour did not understand; Ps. 48, 13. he was compared to senseless beasts, and was made like unto them. Therefore in thy Church, O our God, according to thy grace which thou hast given it, because Eph. 2, 10. we are thy workmanship, created in good works, not only those who spiritually preside, but also those* who are spiritually subject to those who preside (for Gen. 1, 27. thou didst make man male and female in this manner in thy spiritual grace, where according to bodily sex Gal. 3, 28.

there is neither male nor female; because neither Jew nor Greek, neither bond nor free): therefore spiritual persons, whether those who preside or those who obey, spiritually 1 Cor. 2, 15. judge: not concerning spiritual knowledges, which shine in the firmament (for it is not fitting to judge concerning such sublime authority); nor indeed * concerning thy Book itself, even if anything there does not shine forth; because we submit our understanding to it, and hold it certain that even what is closed to our sight has been spoken rightly and truly. For thus a man, though already Col. 3, 10. spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of him who created him, nevertheless Jac. 4, 11. ought to be a doer of the law, not a judge. Nor does he judge concerning that distinction, namely of spiritual and carnal men, who are known to thy eyes, O our God, and have not yet appeared to us by any works, so that Mat. 7, 20.

we may know them by their fruits: but thou, O Lord, already knowest them and hast divided them and Ps. 49, 2. called them in secret, before the firmament was made. Nor does the spiritual man judge concerning the turbulent peoples of this world, although * 1 Cor. 5, 12. What have I to do with judging those who are without? For he does not know who from there will come into the sweetness of thy grace, and who will remain in the perpetual bitterness of ungodliness.

> 34. Therefore man, whom thou hast made after thine image, has not received power over the lights of heaven, nor over heaven itself in its hiddenness, nor over day and night, which thou didst call before the establishment of heaven, nor over the gathering of waters which is the sea; but he has received power over the fishes of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and all cattle, and all the earth, and all creeping things which creep upon the earth.

For he judges, and approves what he finds rightly done, but disapproves what he finds wrongly done; whether in that solemnity of the sacraments by which those are initiated whom thy mercy searches out in many waters; or in that in which that fish [373] is set forth, which, raised from the depth, the pious earth eats; or in the signs of words and utterances subject to the authority of thy Book, Page 270 flying as it were beneath the firmament, by interpreting, expounding, discoursing, disputing, blessing and invoking thee—signs bursting forth and sounding from the mouth, that the people may answer, Amen. For all these utterances to be bodily pronounced, the cause is the abyss of the world and the blindness of the flesh, by which * thoughts cannot be seen, so that it is necessary to make a sound in the ears: thus, although birds multiply above the earth, they nevertheless derive their origin from the waters.

The spiritual man also judges, approving what is right, but disapproving what he finds wrongly done in the works and manners of the faithful: in alms, as in fruitful earth; and in affections tamed from the living soul, in chastity, in fastings, in pious thoughts, concerning those things which are perceived through the bodily sense. For he is now said to judge concerning those things in which he also has the power of correcting.
> XXIV. On verse 28: And God blessed them, saying, Increase, etc.

> 35. But what is this, and what manner of mystery is it? Behold, thou blessest men, O Lord, that they may increase and multiply and fill the earth. Dost thou not thereby indicate to us that we should understand something? Why didst thou not so bless the light which thou calledst day, nor the firmament of heaven, nor the lights, nor the stars, nor the earth, nor the sea? I would say, O our God, who hast created us after thine image, I would say that thou didst will to bestow this gift of blessing particularly upon man; hadst thou not in this manner blessed fishes and whales, that they should increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and that birds should multiply above the earth. Again, I would say that this blessing belongs to those kinds of things which are propagated by generating from themselves, if I found it in shrubs and bushes and cattle of the earth.

But now it was said neither to herbs and trees, nor to beasts and serpents, Increase and multiply; although all these likewise, as fishes and birds and men, increase by generating and preserve their kind.

> 36. What then shall I say, O Truth, my light? “That this is idle, that it was thus said vainly?” By no means, Father of piety; far be it that a servant of thy Word should say this. And if I do not understand what thou dost signify by this utterance, let better men make better use of it—that is, men more intelligent than I am—each according to how much understanding thou hast given him, my God. Yet may my confession be pleasing before thine eyes, by which I confess to thee, O Lord, that I believe thou hast not spoken thus in vain; nor shall I be silent concerning what the occasion of this reading suggests to me. For it is true, nor do I see what prevents me from thus understanding the figurative sayings of thy books. For I know that what is understood in one way by the mind is signified in many ways through the body; and what is signified in one way through the body is understood in many ways by the mind.

Behold the simple love of God and neighbour, which is bodily uttered by manifold sacraments, and innumerable languages, and in each language by innumerable modes of expression! Thus the offspring of the waters increase and multiply. Attend again, whoever reads these things: behold what Scripture sets forth in one way *, and the voice sounds, Gen. 1, 1. In the beginning God made heaven and earth; is it not understood in many ways—not through the deceitfulness of errors, but by kinds of true understandings? Thus the offspring of men increase and multiply.

> 37. And so, if we consider the very natures of things not allegorically but properly, the saying, Increase and multiply, applies to all things which are generated from seeds. But if we treat these things as set forth figuratively—which I think Scripture rather intended, since it surely does not without purpose attribute this blessing only to the offspring of aquatic creatures and of men—we indeed find multitudes also among spiritual and bodily creatures, as in heaven and earth; and in righteous and unrighteous souls, as in light and darkness; and in the holy authors through whom the law was administered, as in the firmament which was made solid between water and water; and in the society of bitter peoples, as in the sea; and in the zeal of pious souls, as in the dry land; and in works of mercy according to the present life, as in seed-bearing herbs and fruit-bearing trees; and in spiritual gifts manifested for usefulness,

as in the lights of heaven; and in affections * formed unto temperance, as in the living soul. In all these we find multitudes, abundances, and increases: but that something may thus increase and multiply, so that one thing may be expressed in many ways, and one expression understood in many ways, we do not find, except in signs bodily produced and things intelligibly conceived. We understand the signs bodily produced to be generations of waters, because of the necessary causes of carnal depth; but the things intelligibly conceived, generations of men, because of the fruitfulness of reason. And therefore we believe that to each of these * kinds it was said by thee, O Lord, Increase and multiply.

For in this blessing I receive a power and capacity granted us by thee: to express in many ways what we have held as understood in one way, and to understand in many ways what we have read as obscurely expressed in one way. Thus the waters of the sea are filled, which are not moved except by various * significations: thus also the earth is filled with human offspring; its dryness appears in zeal, and reason has dominion over it.
> XXV. On verse 29: Behold, I have given you every herb ... for food, etc.

> 38. I also desire to say, O Lord my God, what your Scripture, following upon this, admonishes me; and I shall say it, nor shall I fear. For I shall speak truth, you inspiring me, since from those words you willed that I should speak. Nor do I believe that I speak truth with any other inspiring me than you, since you, Rom. 3, 4. are truth, while every man is a liar. And therefore he who, Joh. 8, 44. speaks a lie, speaks from his own. Therefore, that I may speak truth, let me speak from what is yours *. Behold, you have given us for food every sowing grass, bearing seed, which is upon all the earth, and every tree which has in itself the fruit of sowing seed. And not to us alone, but also to all the birds of heaven, and beasts of the earth, and creeping things *; but to fishes and great whales you have not given these things. For we said that in those fruits of the earth are signified, and in allegory figured, works of mercy, which are bestowed upon the necessities of this life from the fruitful earth. Such an earth was the pious 2 Tim. 1, 16.

Onesiphorus, to whose household you gave mercy, because he often refreshed your Paul, and was not ashamed of his chain. The brethren also did this, and bore fruit by such produce, who 2 Cor. 11, 9. supplied from Macedonia what he lacked. But how he grieves over certain trees which did not yield him the fruit due, when he says: 2 Tim. 4, 16. At my first defence no one stood by me, but all forsook me: may it not be laid to their charge! For these things are due to those who minister rational doctrine through understandings of divine mysteries; and thus they are due to them, as to men. But they are due to them as living souls, offering themselves for imitation in all continence. Likewise they are due to them as flying creatures, because of their blessings which are multiplied upon the earth, since Ps. 18, 5. their sound has gone out into all the earth.
> XXVI. Pleasure and profit from a benefit bestowed upon one's neighbour.

> 39. Now those are fed by these foods who rejoice in them; nor do those rejoice in them Phil. 3, 19. whose god is their belly. For the fruit is not in those who furnish these things, in the things which they give, but in the disposition with which they give. And so, concerning him who served God, not Rom. 16, 18. his own belly, I see clearly whence he rejoices; I see it, and greatly congratulate him. For he had received what the Philippians had sent through Epaphroditus; yet I see whence he rejoices. But whence he rejoices, thence he is fed, because, speaking in truth, he says, I rejoiced, Page 273 greatly in the Lord, because at last you have at some time flourished again in your concern for me, wherein you were also concerned; but you had weariness. Therefore these people had withered through long weariness, and had as it were dried up from this fruit of good work; and he rejoices in them because they have flourished again, not for himself because they had relieved his need. Therefore he goes on to say: Phil. 4, 10-13. Not that I speak as though I lacked anything; for I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be sufficient.

I know both how to have little and how to abound; in all things and unto all things I have been instructed; both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want: I can do all things in him who strengthens me.

> 40. Whence then * do you rejoice, O great Paul? Whence do you rejoice, whence are you fed, O man renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created you, and living soul of such great continence, and flying tongue, 1 Cor. 14, 2. speaking mysteries? For to such living creatures this food is due. What is it that feeds you? Joy. Let us hear what follows. Nevertheless, he says, you have done well, communicating with my tribulation. Herein he rejoices, herein he is fed, because they did him good, not because his distress was relieved—he who says to you, In tribulation you enlarged me: for he knows both Ps. 4, 2. how to abound and to suffer want in you who strengthen him. For, he says, you also know, Philippians, Phil. 4, 14, 16. that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me in the matter of giving and receiving, except you alone; because even to Thessalonica you sent for my needs once and again.
He now rejoices that they have returned to these good works, and delights that they have flourished again, as though the fertility of a field were becoming green again.

> 41. Is it for his own needs, because he said, You sent for my needs? Is it for that reason that he rejoices? Not for that reason. And how do we know this? Because he himself goes on, saying: Phil. 4, 17. Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit *. He has learned from you, my God, to distinguish between gift and fruit. The gift is the very thing which he gives who imparts these necessities: such as money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, assistance. But the fruit is the good and right will of the giver. For the good Master did not say only, He who receives a prophet, but added, in the name of a prophet; nor did he say only, He who receives a righteous man, but added, in the name of a righteous man. For so the one shall receive a prophet's reward, the other a righteous man's reward. Nor did he say only, Mat. 10, 41. 42. He who gives a cup of cold water to drink to one of my least ones; but added, only in the name of a disciple. And so he appended: Amen, I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.

The gift is to receive a prophet, to receive a righteous man, to offer a cup of cold water to a disciple; but the fruit is to do this in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous man, in the name of a disciple. 3 Reg. 17. Elijah is fed by fruit from the widow who knew that she was feeding a man of God, and fed him for that reason; but he was fed by a gift through the raven. Nor was the inner Elijah fed, but the outer, which could even be destroyed by lack of such food.
> XXVII. What is signified by fishes and whales.

> 42. And therefore I shall say what is true before you, O Lord: when unlearned and unbelieving men, for whose initiation and winning-over the sacraments of initiation and the greatnesses of miracles are necessary—which we believe to be signified by the name of fishes and whales *—receive your children in order that they may be bodily refreshed or helped in some use of the present life, while they do not know why this ought to be done or to what it pertains: neither do those feed these, nor are these fed by those; because neither do the former perform these things with a holy and right will, nor do the latter rejoice in their gifts, where they do not yet see fruit. For the mind is fed by that wherein it rejoices. And therefore fishes and whales do not feed upon foods which the earth does not bring forth unless it has already been separated and distinguished from the bitterness of the sea's waves.
> XXVIII. On verse 31: And God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good, etc.

> 43. And you saw, O God, all things which you made, and behold, they were very good; for we too see them *, and behold, all are very good. In the individual kinds of your works, when you had said that they should be made and they were made, you saw this and that * to be good. Seven times I have counted it written that you saw that what you made was good; and this is the eighth, that you saw all things which you made; and behold, not only good, but also very good, as all things together. For individually they were only good; but all together they were both good and very good. This is also said by all beautiful bodies; because far more beautiful is a body composed of all beautiful members than the individual members themselves, by whose most orderly union the whole is completed, although those too are beautiful individually [375].

> XXIX. How it is to be understood that God eight times saw his works to be good.

> 44. And I considered in order to discover whether you saw seven times or eight times that your works are good when they pleased you; and in your seeing I found no times by which I might understand that you saw so often the things which you made, and I said: “O Lord, is not this your Scripture true, since you who are true and truth brought it forth *? Why then do you tell me that there are no times in your seeing; while this your Scripture tells me that on each several day you saw the things which you made to be good; and when I counted them, how often did I find it?” To this you say to me, because you are my God, and you say in a strong voice in the inner ear of your servant, breaking through my deafness and crying: “O man, assuredly what my Scripture says, I say. Yet it speaks temporally, whereas time does not happen to my Word, because it abides with me in coequal eternity. Thus the things which you see through my Spirit, I see; just as the things which you say through my Spirit, I say.”
And thus, although you see them temporally, I do not see temporally; just as, although you say them temporally, I do not say temporally.”
> XXX. The ravings of the Manichaeans.

> 45. And I heard, O Lord my God, and licked up a drop of sweetness from your truth, and understood that there are some [376] to whom your works are displeasing; and they say that you made many of them under the compulsion of necessity, such as the structures of the heavens and the arrangements of the stars; and that these were not from what is yours [377], but had already been created elsewhere and from elsewhere, which you might draw together and fit and weave together, when from conquered enemies [378] you were constructing the ramparts of the world, so that, bound fast by that Page 276 construction *, they might not be able to rebel against you again. Yet they say that you made no others, nor indeed put them together at all, such as all flesh and every tiniest living creature, and whatever holds the earth by roots; but that a hostile mind and another nature, not created by you and contrary to you, produces and forms these things in the lower regions of the world. Madmen say these things, because they do not see your works through your Spirit, nor know you in them.
> XXXI. What pleases God is approved by the devout likewise.

> 46. But those who see them through your Spirit—you see in them. Therefore, when they see that they are good, you see that they are good; and whatever things please because of you, you please in them *; and whatever things please us through your Spirit please you in us. 1 Cor. 2, 11. 12. For who knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So too no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we, he says, have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things which have been given to us by God. And I am admonished to say: “Certainly no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. How then do we also know the things which have been given to us by God?” I am answered that the things we know through his Spirit, even thus no one knows except the Spirit of God. For just as it was rightly said, Mat. 10, 20.

For it is not you who speak, to those who were speaking in the Spirit of God; so it is rightly said, ‘It is not you who know,’ to those who know in the Spirit of God. Accordingly it is no less rightly said, ‘It is not you who see,’ to those who see in the Spirit of God: thus whatever they see in the Spirit of God to be good, it is not they but God who sees to be good. Therefore it is one thing for someone to think that what is good is evil, as are those mentioned above; another thing for a man to see that what is good is good (as your creation pleases many because it is good, yet you do not please them in it, whence they wish rather to enjoy it than you); but another thing when a man sees something to be good, for God to see in him that it is good; namely, that he may be loved in that which he made [379], who would not be loved Page 277 except through the Spirit * whom he gave; Rom. 5, 5.

because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, through whom we see that whatever in any manner is, is good: for it is from him who is not in some manner, but who is, is *.
> XXXII. He recounts the works of God briefly.

> 47. Thanks be to you, O Lord. We see heaven and earth, whether the higher and lower corporeal part, or the spiritual and corporeal creature; and in the adornment * of these parts, of which either the whole bulk of the world, or indeed the whole creation, consists, we see light made and divided from darkness. We see the firmament of heaven: whether the primary body of the world, between the higher spiritual waters and the lower corporeal [380] waters; or this expanse of air, since this too is called heaven, through which the birds of heaven wander among the waters that are borne above them in vapour, and that also distil dew on clear nights, and those which flow heavily upon the earth. We see the appearance of the gathered waters over the expanses of the sea; and the dry land, whether laid bare or formed so as to be visible and ordered; and likewise the material of herbs and trees.

We see the luminaries shining from above; the sun sufficient for the day, the moon and stars to solace the night, and times marked and signified by all these. We see the moist nature everywhere made fruitful with fishes, beasts, and birds, because the density of the air, which bears the flights of birds, is condensed by the exhalation of the waters [381]. We see the face of the earth adorned with terrestrial animals; and man, made in your image and likeness, set above all irrational living creatures by that very image and likeness of yours, that is, by the power of reason and understanding.

And just as in his soul one thing is that rules by counsel, another that is subjected in order to obey; so also woman was made for man even bodily: she indeed had in her mind an equal nature of rational understanding; yet in the sex of her body she was so subjected to the male sex, just as the appetite for action is subjected to the ingenuity of the mind's reason for conceiving [382] * right action. We see these things, both each one good and all very good.
> Page 278
> XXXIII. All things are from nothing, or from matter created together.

> 48. Let your works praise you, that we may love you; and let us love you * , that your works may praise you—works which have beginning and end from time, rising and setting, advance and decline, form and privation. Therefore they have, in succession, morning and evening, partly hidden, partly manifest. For they were made by you from nothing, not from you, not from anything not yours * , nor from anything that existed beforehand, but from matter created together, that is, created by you at the same time; because you formed its formlessness without any interval of time. For whereas the matter of heaven and earth is one thing, and the form of heaven and earth another: you made the matter indeed from absolute nothing, but the form of the world from unformed matter; yet you made both together, so that form followed matter with no intervening delay.
> XXXIV. An allegorical exposition of the whole creation of the world.

> 49. We have also considered for the signification of what things you willed these things to be made in such an order, or to be written in such an order; and we saw that each is good, and all are very good, in your Word, in your Only-Begotten: heaven and earth, the head and body of the Church, in predestination before all times, without morning and evening.

But when you began to carry out in time what had been predestined, in order to make manifest what was hidden and to order our disorder; since our sins were above us, and we had gone away from you into the dark deep, and your good Spirit was borne above to help us at the fitting time: you justified the ungodly and distinguished them from the wicked; and you established the authority of your Book between those above, who should be teachable to you, and those below, who should be subject to them; and you gathered the fellowship of unbelievers into one concord, so that the zeal of the faithful might appear, and works of mercy might be brought forth for you, as they distributed even earthly possessions to the poor in order to acquire heavenly ones.

And then you kindled certain luminaries in the firmament, your holy ones holding the word of life and shining with lofty authority, set before others by spiritual gifts: and then, for instructing unbelieving nations, you brought forth from corporeal matter visible Sacraments and miracles, and utterances of words according to the firmament of your Book, by which the faithful also might be blessed: and thereafter you formed the living soul of the faithful by the ordered affections of the strength of continence *; and then you renewed, after your image and likeness, the mind subject to you alone and needing no human Page 279 authority for imitation: and you subjected rational action to the higher understanding, as woman to man; and you willed that, for all your ministries necessary for the faithful to be perfected in this life, works fruitful for the future should be supplied by those same faithful for temporal uses [383].
We see all these things, and they are very good, because you see them in us—you who gave us the Spirit by whom we might see them and love you in them.
> XXXV. He desires peace.

> 50. Lord God, give us peace [384] (for you have supplied us with all things); the peace of rest, the peace of the sabbath, a sabbath without evening * . For this whole most beautiful order of very good things, when its modes have been completed, will pass away; and in them there was made morning, and evening.
> XXXVI. Why evening does not follow the seventh day.

> 51. But the seventh day is without evening, nor does it have a setting, because you sanctified it for everlasting continuance; so that this, that after your works, which were very good, although you made them in repose, you rested on the seventh day, may foretell to us in the voice of your Book that we too, after our works—therefore very good because you gave them to us—shall rest in you in the sabbath of eternal life.
> XXXVII. When God will rest in us.

> 52. For even then you will rest in us as you now work in us; and so that rest of yours will be through us, just as these works of yours are through us [385]. But you, O Lord, always work and always rest. You do not see in time * , nor are you moved in time, nor rest in time; and yet you make temporal visions, and the times themselves, and rest from time.
> XXXVIII. God sees created things differently from man.

> 53. Therefore we see these things which you have made, because they are; but they are because you see them. And we see outwardly that they are, and inwardly that they are good: but you saw them made there where you saw them to be made. At another time we were moved to do good, after our heart had conceived from your Spirit; but at an earlier Page 280 time we were moved to do evil, forsaking you: but you, O God, the one good, never ceased to do good. And some good works of ours exist by your gift indeed, but they are not everlasting; after them we hope to rest in your great sanctification: but you, the good needing no good, are always at rest, since your rest is yourself. And what man shall grant this understanding to a man? What angel to an angel? What angel to a man? Let it be asked from you, sought in you, knocked for at you: Mat. 7, 8. thus, thus shall it be received, thus found, thus opened. Amen.

items.text: Textus quaerit quomodo homo mortalis, peccator et memoria suorum principiorum carens Deum invocare, cognoscere atque laudare possit simulque vitam suam veraciter confiteri.
Assertio regens est omne esse et bonum a Deo dari, peccatum autem ex usu inordinato bonorum oriri, donec cor ad Deum redeat et in eo requiescat.
Argumentatio est simul metaphysica, confessionalis, diagnostica, polemica et reconstructiva.
Motus initialis procedit ab appetitu laudis per circulum fidei, invocationis et cognitionis ad distinctionem inter praesentiam divinam et continentiam spatialem.
Motus autobiographicus procedit ab absentia memoriae per testimonium et analogiam ad detectionem peccati in infantia atque continuationem eius in vita adulta.
Motus criticus procedit a disciplina puerili ad structuram moris humani, deinde ad distinctionem inter dona bona, usus perversos et providentiam quae etiam errores ad bonum ordinat.
Omne esse, vivere atque bonum creatum a Deo est.
Deus omnia continendo implet, ubique totus est, neque ab ulla re totus capitur.
Deus immutabili praesentia omne tempus transitivum continet.
Homo ad Deum factus est et inquietus manet donec in Deo requiescat.
Invocatio quae ad cognitionem et laudem ducit fide a Deo data, per Filium et praedicationem mediata, incipit.
Homo mortalitatem et peccatum circumferens non iudicio cum Deo contendit, sed sub misericordia se accusat.
Deus rerum naturalium creator est, peccatorum autem ordinator, non auctor.
Peccatum consistit in quaerendis voluptate, sublimitate et veritate in creaturis relicto Deo.
Animus inordinatus poena sua sibi est.
Deus erroribus et pravis intentionibus hominum ad utilitatem alterius uti potest sine approbatione eorum actuum.
Vita memoriae anterior per testimonium, analogiam et coniecturam cognoscitur.
Imbecillitas corporis infantilis innocentiam animi infantilis non constituit.
Signa linguistica pacto humano constant et ex usu contextualiter repetito discuntur.
Verba et facultates creatae bona instrumenta manent, quorum ratio moralis ex materia et usu pendet.
Libera curiositas ad discendum efficacior est quam meticulosa necessitas, quamvis necessitas fluxum eius sub lege cohibere possit.
Institutio scholastica ordinem valorum constituit in quo honor, divitiae et rectitudo sermonis praeceptis divinis anteponuntur.
Baptismus in narratione ut mundatio salutaris et remissio peccatorum accipitur.
Consilium relatum baptismum differebat quia delicta post lavacrum graviora et periculosiora putabantur.
Creatura sui esse, vitae vel facultatum artifex non est.
Deus in animam vel mundum tamquam in locum vacuum non introducitur.
Deus in partes maiores et minores inter creaturas non distribuitur.
Deus tempore non innovatur, non veterascit, non eget neque mutatione operum mutat consilium.
Sermo humanus Deum comprehendere non potest, sed silentium de Deo propterea non iustificatur.
Infantia propter infirmitatem membrorum innocens non est.
Vitium toleratum quia aetate periturum est eo ipso bonum vel parvum non fit.
Actus invitus moraliter bonus non fit ex sola bonitate rei quae per eum efficitur.
Utilitas disciplinae pravitatem intentionis docentium non absolvit.
Verba non accusantur quasi erroris causa, neque fabulae turpes ad verba discenda necessariae sunt.
Rectitudo grammatica rectitudinem animi non constituit.
Recessus a Deo et reditus ad eum motus localis non est.
Dilatio baptismi ex sola intentione prudentiae beneficium certum non efficitur.
Circulus inter cognitionem et invocationem non cognitione perfecta, sed fide antecedenter data aperitur.
Creatura Deum non recipit velut vas, sed ipsa existit quia a Deo sustentatur et in eo continetur.
Longinquitas a Deo est ordinatio affectus ad creaturas, non distantia spatii.
Laus Dei et accusatio sui unum actum confessionis constituunt, quia bonitas ad creatorem, defectus autem ad voluntatem inordinatam referuntur.
Identitas autobiographica ultra memoriam extenditur, quia idem subiectum ex Deo vivebat etiam in tempore quod recordari non potest.
Appetitus infantilis eandem formam inordinationis exhibet quae postea in cupiditate, invidia et dominatione explicatur.
Differentia inter vitia puerorum et adultorum principaliter est differentia instrumentorum, praemiorum et poenarum, non formae affectivae.
Coactio scholastica potest scientiam utilem producere, quamvis neque discens invitus neque cogentes eo ipso bene agant.
Institutio litteraria corrumpitur non per signa ipsa, sed cum instrumenta bona figmenta, libidinem et gloriam ministrant.
Pacta sonorum socialiter exacta cum neglectu pacti divini consistere possunt; scientia sermonis igitur conscientiam non implicat.
Facultates memoriae, sermonis, lectionis et numerationis ad Deum redirigi possunt, quia earum bonitas ab usu perverso non destruitur.
Dilatio baptismi moralem licentiam ante lavacrum generare potest, quamvis consilium maternum periculum futurorum peccatorum vitare intendat.
Communicatio signorum voluntatem interiorem exprimibilem facit atque simul puerum auctoritati parentum et maiorum inserit.
Confessio ipsa est effectus providentiae, quia subiectum Deum quaerit et errores suos enuntiat per fidem, memoriam et linguam quae omnia accepit.
Malum non est substantia creata, sed deordinatio bonorum, cuius effectus Deus ordinat sine eiusdem deordinationis auctoritate.
Persona autobiographica non fundatur in memoria sola, sed in continuitate ontologica, testimonio sociali et ordine temporis sub aeternitate divina.
Infantia microstructuram societatis adultae continet: appetitus dominationis, aemulatio et iniustitia permanent, dum obiecta et potestates augentur.
Institutio culturalis peccatum reproducit cum excellentiam formalem in gloriam convertit et vitium ornate expressum tolerat vel remuneratur.
Correctio institutionis non abolitionem litterarum, sed conversionem facultatum linguisticarum a vanitate ad veritatem et laudem requirit.
Consilium sacramentum differendi potest structuram permissionis peccandi instituere, quamvis ex providentia materna et metu futuri reatus oriatur.
Responsabilitas humana ex fine affectus iudicatur, dum utilitas effectuum ad providentiam refertur; intentio et effectus igitur diversis rationibus imputantur.
Systema falsitatem mali tamquam rei a Deo creatae requirit.
Systema subiectum sui ipsius principium, possessorem aut salvatorem esse non admittit.
Bonitas effectus bonitatem intentionis vel agentis probare non potest.
Laus socialis index veritatis aut rectitudinis moralis esse non potest.
Aetas infantilis spatium moraliter exemptum constituere non potest.
Memoria exhaustiva conditio identitatis personalis vel confessionis non est.
Lingua per se neque corrumpit neque salvat; ordinatio usus iudicium fert.
Coactio ex sola utilitate rei imperatae moraliter bona fieri non potest.
Educatio neutralis non est, quia semper facultates ad aliquem ordinem amoris, honoris et veritatis dirigit.
Sermo Deo adaequatus indisponibilis est, sed silentium absolutum pariter inadmissibile manet.
Nullum extra Deum spatium datur unde Deus vocetur aut quo homo recedat; omnis alienatio intra dependentiam ontologicam fit.
Nulla origo personalis innocens memoria recuperari potest; quaestio de principio iam sub peccato et oblivione constituitur.
Consuetudo humana auctoritatem ultimam sibi vindicare non potest, quia eius pacta linguistica sub pacto salutis iudicantur.
Reditus autonomus excluditur: excitatio, fides, invocatio, facultates et sanatio ab eo veniunt ad quem homo redit.
Medium causale neutrum, in quo providentia divina et culpa humana exhaustive concilientur, non praebetur; distinctio operatur sine mechanismo completo.
Series epistemica est: praedicatio et donum fidei → invocatio → quaesitio → inventio et cognitio → laus → requies.
Schema ontologicum est: Deus dat esse → creatura in Deo continetur → Deus non recipitur spatialiter → praesentia divina cum incomprehensibilitate cohaeret.
Schema autobiographicum est: defectus memoriae → testimonium et analogia → reconstructio infantiae → detectio inordinationis → continuatio eius in aetates posteriores.
Schema peccati est: facultas bona → amor creaturae relicto creatore → actus inordinatus → poena immanens → confessio sub misericordia.
Schema institutionale est: signa utilia → coactio et praemium sociale → eloquentia ad gloriam ordinata → vitium formaliter ornatum → neglectus conscientiae.
Schema providentiae est: intentio humana prava → effectus mixtus → appropriatio divina ad utilitatem → distinctio doni et abusus → facultatum conversio ad Deum.
Schema baptismale est: periculum mortis → petitio mundationis → recuperatio corporis → dilatio ob futurum reatum → permissio implicita peccandi → quaestio prudentiae insoluta.
Desiderium laudis → circulus invocationis et cognitionis → fides antecedens → praesentia Dei non spatialis → confessio sub misericordia → diagnosis amoris inordinati → reorientatio ad requiem.
Oblivio originis → testimonium de infantia → negatio innocentiae → pueritia scholastica → inversio valorum culturalium → continuatio vitiorum in vita adulta → recuperatio donorum ad usum divinum.
Baptismus petitus → mundatio dilata → ratio futuri periculi → analogia vulneris corporis → detectio licentiae ante sacramentum → iudicium finale suspensum.
Relatio Dei et mundi e tabula spatiali continentis et contenti in tabulam dependentiae ontologicae et distantiae affectivae transfertur.
Laus Dei et confessio peccati ex actibus separatis in unum actum attributionis rectae rediguntur.
Historia personalis ultra memoriam dilatatur, quia testimonium, analogia et dependentia ontologica partes identitatis fiunt.
Infantia ex regione innocentiae in formam initialem earumdem inordinationum quae societatem adultam regunt reclassificatur.
Educatio ex simplici transmissione scientiae in machinam mixtam facultatum utilium, coercitionis, gloriae et reproductionis moralis redescribitur.
Lingua in instrumentum bonum et materiam variabiliter ordinatam dividitur; medium a turpitudine contenti separatur.
Aestimatio actionis bifurcatur inter intentionem agentis et effectum a providentia ad utilitatem ordinatum.
Dilatio baptismi ex prudentia pastorali in structuram possibilis licentiae peccandi denuo describitur.
Surface — Precatio, confessio originum, infantiae et pueritiae atque iudicium de studiis constituunt obiectum immediatum.
Structural — Familia, schola, conventiones linguae, disciplina, praemia socialia et praxis baptismalis appetitus atque facultates ordinant.
Metastrategic — Textus normas aestimationis ab honore, eloquentia et consuetudine ad conscientiam, ordinem amoris et usum donorum transfert.
Ontological/Temporal — Subiectum creatum, in Deo contentum et per tempus mutabile sub aeterno Dei hodie persistit, quamvis sui principia memoria non teneat.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad motum a theologia invocationis ad confessionem autobiographicam, criticam institutionis et conversionem facultatum restituendum.
Cohaerentia systematis innititur distinctionibus inter creatorem et ordinatorem peccati, donum et abusum, intentionem et effectum, signum et materiam.
Structura firmissima est ubi omnia bona ad Deum referuntur, peccatum autem ut ordinatio affectus ad creaturas definitur.
Relatio exacta inter cognitionem, invocationem et fidem interrogationibus aperitur et mediatione fidei solvitur operationaliter, non demonstratione epistemica completa.
Iudicium de peccato infantili testimonio doctrinali, observatione aliorum infantium et analogia cum vita adulta nititur, non memoria directa.
Commissura inter providentiam et culpam fragilis manet, quia Deus ex actibus pravis bonum elicit sine explicatione completa causalitatis concurrentis.
Critica scholae ab exemplis grammaticae et litterarum ad totum flumen moris humani transit, antithesi morali magis quam analysi institutionali exhaustiva sustentata.
Aestimatio dilationis baptismi insoluta manet inter prudentiam matris de futuris tentationibus et analogiam sanitatis quae celerem mundationem postulat.
Restitutio verum motum servat: a Deo ut principio per reconstructionem sui peccatoris ad dona recuperanda et in Deum finaliter ordinanda.
The text asks how a mortal human being, a sinner lacking memory of his own beginnings, can invoke, know, and praise God, while also truthfully confessing his life.
The governing assertion is that all being and good are given by God, whereas sin arises from the disordered use of goods, until the heart returns to God and rests in him.
The argumentation is at once metaphysical, confessional, diagnostic, polemical, and reconstructive.
The initial movement proceeds from the desire for praise through the circle of faith, invocation, and knowledge to the distinction between divine presence and spatial containment.
The autobiographical movement proceeds from the absence of memory through testimony and analogy to the detection of sin in infancy and its continuation in adult life.

The critical movement proceeds from childhood discipline to the structure of human custom, then to the distinction between good gifts, perverse uses, and providence, which orders even errors toward good.
All created being, life, and good are from God.
God fills all things by containing them, is wholly everywhere, and is not wholly contained by any thing.
God, by immutable presence, contains all transitory time.
The human being is made for God and remains restless until he rests in God.
Invocation, which leads to knowledge and praise, begins from faith given by God, mediated through the Son and preaching.
The human being, bearing mortality and sin, does not contend with God in judgment, but accuses himself under mercy.
God is the creator of natural things, but the orderer, not the author, of sins.
Sin consists in seeking pleasure, sublimity, and truth in creatures while abandoning God.
The disordered mind is its own punishment.
God can use human errors and wicked intentions for the benefit of another without approving those acts.
Life prior to memory is known through testimony, analogy, and conjecture.
The weakness of an infant body does not establish the innocence of an infant mind.
Linguistic signs rest upon human convention and are learned from contextually repeated use.
Created words and faculties remain good instruments, whose moral character depends on matter and use.
Free curiosity for learning is more efficacious than fearful necessity, although necessity can restrain its course under law.
Schooling establishes an order of values in which honor, wealth, and correctness of speech are preferred to divine commands.
In the narrative, baptism is understood as salvific cleansing and remission of sins.
The reported counsel delayed baptism because offenses after the washing were thought more serious and dangerous.
A creature is not the maker of its own being, life, or faculties.
God is not introduced into the soul or the world as into an empty place.
God is not distributed among creatures into greater and lesser parts.
God is not renewed by time, does not grow old, does not lack, nor does he change his counsel through changes in works.
Human speech cannot comprehend God, but silence about God is not thereby justified.
Infancy is not innocent because of the weakness of its limbs.
A vice tolerated because it will perish with age does not thereby become good or slight.
An involuntary act does not become morally good merely from the goodness of the thing effected through it.
The usefulness of discipline does not absolve the perversity of the teachers' intention.
Words are not accused as though they were the cause of error, nor are shameful tales necessary for learning words.
Grammatical correctness does not constitute rectitude of mind.
Departure from God and return to him are not local motion.
The delay of baptism does not, from the intention of prudence alone, produce a certain benefit.
The circle between knowledge and invocation is opened not by perfect knowledge, but by antecedently given faith.
A creature does not receive God as a vessel does, but itself exists because it is sustained by God and contained in him.
Distance from God is the ordering of affection toward creatures, not spatial distance.
Praise of God and self-accusation constitute one act of confession, because goodness is referred to the creator, while defect is referred to disordered will.
Autobiographical identity extends beyond memory, because the same subject lived from God even in the time it cannot recall.
Infantile desire displays the same form of disorder later unfolded in cupidity, envy, and domination.
The difference between the vices of children and adults is principally a difference of instruments, rewards, and punishments, not of affective form.
Scholastic coercion can produce useful knowledge, although neither the unwilling learner nor those compelling him thereby act well.
Literary education is corrupted not through the signs themselves, but when good instruments serve fictions, lust, and glory.
Socially enforced compacts of sounds can coexist with neglect of the divine covenant; knowledge of speech therefore does not entail conscience.
The faculties of memory, speech, reading, and counting can be redirected toward God, because their goodness is not destroyed by perverse use.
The delay of baptism can generate moral license before the washing, although maternal counsel intends to avoid the danger of future sins.
The communication of signs makes inner will expressible and at the same time inserts the child into the authority of parents and elders.
Confession itself is an effect of providence, because the subject seeks God and states his errors through faith, memory, and language, all of which he has received.
Evil is not a created substance, but a disordering of goods, whose effects God orders without being the author of that same disordering.
The autobiographical person is founded not on memory alone, but on ontological continuity, social testimony, and the order of time under divine eternity.
Infancy contains the microstructure of adult society: the desire for domination, rivalry, and injustice remain, while objects and powers increase.
Cultural education reproduces sin when it turns formal excellence into glory and tolerates or rewards ornately expressed vice.
The correction of education requires not the abolition of letters, but the conversion of linguistic faculties from vanity to truth and praise.
The counsel to defer the sacrament can establish a structure of permission to sin, although it arises from maternal providence and fear of future guilt.
Human responsibility is judged from the end of affection, while the usefulness of effects is referred to providence; intention and effect are therefore imputed on different grounds.
The system requires the falsity of evil as a thing created by God.
The system does not admit that the subject is its own principle, possessor, or savior.
The goodness of an effect cannot prove the goodness of the intention or agent.
Social praise cannot be an index of truth or moral rectitude.
Infancy cannot constitute a morally exempt space.
Exhaustive memory is not a condition of personal identity or confession.
Language in itself neither corrupts nor saves; the ordering of use renders judgment.
Coercion cannot become morally good from the usefulness alone of the thing commanded.
Education is not neutral, because it always directs faculties toward some order of love, honor, and truth.
Speech adequate to God is unavailable, but absolute silence remains equally inadmissible.
No space outside God is given from which God may be called or to which the human being may depart; all alienation occurs within ontological dependence.
No innocent personal origin can be recovered by memory; the question of the beginning is already constituted under sin and forgetfulness.
Human custom cannot claim ultimate authority for itself, because its linguistic compacts are judged under the covenant of salvation.
Autonomous return is excluded: awakening, faith, invocation, faculties, and healing come from him to whom the human being returns.
No neutral causal medium is provided in which divine providence and human guilt are exhaustively reconciled; the distinction operates without a complete mechanism.
The epistemic series is: preaching and the gift of faith → invocation → seeking → finding and knowledge → praise → rest.
The ontological schema is: God gives being → the creature is contained in God → God is not received spatially → divine presence coheres with incomprehensibility.
The autobiographical schema is: lack of memory → testimony and analogy → reconstruction of infancy → detection of disorder → its continuation into later ages.
The schema of sin is: good faculty → love of creature with abandonment of creator → disordered act → immanent punishment → confession under mercy.
The institutional schema is: useful signs → coercion and social reward → eloquence ordered toward glory → formally adorned vice → neglect of conscience.
The schema of providence is: wicked human intention → mixed effect → divine appropriation for benefit → distinction between gift and abuse → conversion of faculties toward God.
The baptismal schema is: danger of death → request for cleansing → recovery of the body → delay owing to future guilt → implicit permission to sin → unresolved question of prudence.
Desire for praise → circle of invocation and knowledge → antecedent faith → non-spatial presence of God → confession under mercy → diagnosis of disordered love → reorientation toward rest.
Forgetfulness of origin → testimony about infancy → denial of innocence → schoolboyhood → inversion of cultural values → continuation of vices in adult life → recovery of gifts for divine use.
Baptism requested → cleansing delayed → reason of future danger → analogy of bodily wound → detection of license before the sacrament → final judgment suspended.
The relation of God and world is transferred from a spatial map of container and contained to a map of ontological dependence and affective distance.
Praise of God and confession of sin are reduced from separate acts to one act of right attribution.
Personal history is extended beyond memory, because testimony, analogy, and ontological dependence become parts of identity.
Infancy is reclassified from a region of innocence into an initial form of the same disorders governing adult society.
Education is redescribed from mere transmission of knowledge into a mixed machine of useful faculties, coercion, glory, and moral reproduction.
Language is divided into a good instrument and variably ordered matter; the medium is separated from the baseness of content.
The assessment of action bifurcates between the agent's intention and the effect ordered to benefit by providence.
The delay of baptism is redescribed from pastoral prudence into a structure of possible permission to sin.
Surface — Prayer, confession of origins, infancy and childhood, and judgment concerning studies constitute the immediate object.
Structural — Family, school, conventions of language, discipline, social rewards, and baptismal practice order desires and faculties.
Metastrategic — The text transfers norms of assessment from honor, eloquence, and custom to conscience, the order of love, and the use of gifts.
Ontological/Temporal — The created subject, contained in God and mutable through time, persists under God's eternal today, although memory does not retain its own beginnings.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from the theology of invocation to autobiographical confession, critique of education, and conversion of faculties.
The coherence of the system rests on distinctions between creator and orderer of sin, gift and abuse, intention and effect, sign and matter.
The structure is strongest where all goods are referred to God, while sin is defined as the ordering of affection toward creatures.
The precise relation between knowledge, invocation, and faith is opened by questions and resolved operationally through the mediation of faith, not by complete epistemic demonstration.
Judgment concerning infantile sin rests on doctrinal testimony, observation of other infants, and analogy with adult life, not on direct memory.
The juncture between providence and guilt remains fragile, because God elicits good from wicked acts without a complete explanation of concurrent causality.
The critique of school passes from examples of grammar and literature to the whole current of human custom, supported more by moral antithesis than by exhaustive institutional analysis.
The assessment of delaying baptism remains unresolved between a mother's prudence concerning future temptations and the analogy of health, which demands prompt cleansing.
