The reconstruction preserves the true movement: from God as principle, through reconstruction of the sinful self, toward gifts to be recovered and finally ordered to God.
Textus quaerit cur furtum perpetratum delectaverit, cum neque necessitas neque fructus neque ipsa res furtiva causam delectationis praebeat.
Adolescentia non ut series actuum discretorum, sed ut dispersio animi ab uno bono in multitudinem concupiscentiarum constituitur.
Argumentatio a causis ordinariis peccati per bona inferiora appetitis procedit ad furtum, quod causam utilitariam eludit et malitiam ipsam quaestionem facit.
Furtum explicatur ut imitatio perversa libertatis divinae, intensificata consortio simul peccantium et pudore ne minus impudens videatur.
Recordatio criminis in confessionem convertitur, qua culpa et abstinentia aequaliter misericordiae divinae attribuuntur.
Deus est summum, verum et stabile bonum, extra quod nulla delectatio pura aut secura invenitur.
Peccatum oritur cum anima bona inferiora immoderate appetit et bona superiora deserit.
Omne vitium speciem alicuius boni, potestatis, pulchritudinis, quietis, scientiae vel societatis imitatur.
Imitatio vitiosa bonum non creat, sed perfectionem divinam in formam imminutam et perversam convertit.
Anima a Deo aversa in multa diffluit et sibi ipsa fit regio egestatis.
Furtum piri nec egestate nec suavitate fructus nec utilitate rei causatum fuit.
In furto quaesita est transgressio legis, quia transgressio ipsa illicitam libertatis speciem praebuit.
Malitia gratuita non est bonum positivum, sed amor defectus, ruinae et aversionis a firmamento divino.
Consortio peccantium cupiditas accenditur, quia communis impudentia damnum alienum in ludum et laudem mutat.
Disciplina litteraria et eloquentia, si cultura cordis et castitatis non comitantur, adolescentem a dispersione non servant.
Deus etiam per correptionem amarumque eventum agit, ut delectationes illicitae ad se ipsum referantur.
Non solum peccata commissa, sed etiam peccata non commissa, gratiae et misericordiae divinae imputanda sunt.
Furtum non definitur appetitu pomorum, quia poma abundabant, meliora aderant, et rapina ad usum non ordinabatur.
Peccatum non est creatio boni autonomi, sed defectus boni et perversio boni creati.
Libertatem non efficit licentia faciendi quod non licet, quia talis licentia est captiva umbra omnipotentiae.
Amicitia non est vera unitas, si societas eius in laetitia nocendi et in contagione turpitudinis consistit.
Castitas et innocentia non sunt possessiones quas homo suis viribus sibi tribuere potest.
Silentium divinum non est absentia divina, cum monitus matris et flagella vitae eandem vocem divinam mediantur.
Studium, honor domesticus et spes socialis non sufficiunt ad rectam formationem, si ad Deum et veritatem non referuntur.
Cum bona inferiora sint realiter bona sed non suprema, peccatum non res pulchras destruit, sed ordinem amoris dissolvit.
Furtum piri fit probatio extrema, quia ostendit voluntatem posse non rem appetere, sed statum contra legem se ponendi.
Illicita voluptas libertatis ex eo nascitur quod anima, Deo subiecta, dominum suum fugere et potentiam sine potestate imitari conatur.
Consortium non est tantum circumstantia exterior actus, sed causa formalis delectationis, quando solitarius actus idem non placeret.
Pudor socialis invertitur: innocentia dedecus videtur, turpitudo gloria, et mendacium ad imitationem pravitatis adiungitur.
Correctio divina non peccatum approbat, sed voluptatem illicitam amaritudine vulnerat, ut desiderium suum falsum agnoscat.
Recordatio peccati recte ordinata non ad amorem turpitudinis, sed ad amorem Dei et ad recollectionem animi dispersi tendit.
Qui minus graviter peccavit non minus misericordiae debitor est, quia etiam imminutio morbi a medico divino procedit.
Ordo moralis non dividitur inter res bonas et res malas, sed inter amorem ordinate relatum ad summum bonum et amorem inferiorum bonorum absolutum.
Malum radicale non describitur ut substantia rivalis Deo, sed ut imminutio ontologica quae tamen voluntatem, societatem et memoriam efficaciter deformat.
Societas prava potest mechanismum conversionis valorum efficere, quo damnum alienum, legis transgressio et simulatio turpitudinis in fontes honoris mutantur.
Confessio reordinat causalitatem moralem: agens culpam actuum propriorum retinet, sed liberationem et abstinentiam gratiae attribuit.
Nulla aversio a Deo est absoluta, quia ipsa imitatio perversa bonorum divinorum persistentem dependentiam creaturae a creatore indicat.
Falsum esse debet exemplar quod peccatum ad ignorantiam rerum, ad necessitatem materialem vel ad calculum utilitatis redigit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar libertatis quod transgressionem legis pro actu sui-fundante accipit.
Falsum esse debet exemplar societatis quod consortium per se bonum putat, sine discrimine finis quo socii uniuntur.
Falsum esse debet exemplar virtutis quod innocentiam humanam a gratia separabilem et sibi sufficientem habet.
Falsum esse debet exemplar educationis quod eloquentiam, studium et ascensum socialem pro cultura interiori substituit.
Systema non admittit locum extra Deum unde anima bonum stabile, quietem certam aut libertatem veram sibi comparare possit.
Systema non admittit malitiam tamquam principium autonomum, quia etiam deformitas vitiorum formas bonorum divinorum parasitice supponit.
Systema non admittit memoriam moralem neutralem, quia recordatio aut in delectationem criminis recidit aut in confessionem et conversionem ordinatur.
Aversio ab uno bono → dispersio in bona multa → imminutio facultatis discernendi dilectionem a libidine.
Apparens bonum inferius → appetitus immoderatus → desertio boni superioris → peccatum.
Furtum sine utilitate → exclusio causae materialis → inquisitio delectationis ipsius transgressionis.
Transgressio → imitatio perversa potentiae → libertas mutila → servitus et defectus.
Consortium peccantium → mutua inflammatio cupiditatis → pudor innocentiae → consolidatio actus et simulatio turpitudinis.
Recordatio criminis → confessio infirmitatis → agnitio gratiae in peccatis commissis et evitatis → amor Dei recollectus.
Adolescentiae libido et dispersio animi → defectus disciplinae spiritualis et moderaminis.
Defectus moderaminis → furtum quod nullum commodum externum explicat.
Furtum inexplicabile per rem furtivam → distinctio inter bona quae vitia imitari conantur et malitiam quae defectum amat.
Malitia ut imitatio perversa libertatis → inventio consortii peccantium ut motoris affectivi actus.
Consortium et culpa recognita → confessio misericordiae quae culpam non delet ex memoria sed eius sensum transformat.
Peccatum reclassificatur non ut amor rei intrinsece malae, sed ut amor inferioris boni extra ordinem summi boni positus.
Furtum reclassificatur ex delicto proprietatis in experimentum perversae libertatis et in affectum socialiter productum.
Amicitia bifurcatur in unitatem animorum ordinatam ad bonum et consortium contagiosum ordinatum ad nocendum.
Educatio bifurcatur in acquisitionem eloquentiae externa et culturam cordis, quarum prima sine altera insufficienter formativa est.
Abstinentia reclassificatur ex merito privato in beneficium gratiae, sicut remissio actuum commissorum.
Surface — Textus examinatur adolescentiam libidinosam, furtum piri, monita parentum et consortium sodalium.
Structural — Mechanismus peccati consistit in aversione a bono supremo, appetitu inferiorum bonorum et deformatione sociali pudoris atque laudis.
Metastrategic — Quaestio de actu singulari transferitur ad investigationem generis desiderii quod transgressionem, imitationem et consortium producit.
Ontological/Temporal — Creatura a Deo aversa non ad alteram stabilitatem transit, sed in defectum, dispersionem et egestatem temporalem decidit.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam necessitatem qua peccatum ex inordinato amore bonorum inferiorum oritur et ad Deum reditus exigitur.
Explicatio furti sustinetur solum si transgressio, imitatio perversae libertatis et consortium peccantium simul retinentur.
Firmissimum systematis nexum constituit distinctio inter bonum creatum, cuius species vera manet, et usum eius inordinatum.
Tensionem relinquit enuntiatio malitiae gratuita, quia textus simul omne peccatum aliquo bono apparenti moveri et furtum malitiam ipsam appetere affirmat.
Tensionem relinquit relatio inter culpam voluntatis et gratiam divinam, quia agens proprie peccat, sed etiam imminutio peccati beneficio divino tribuitur.
Tensionem relinquit usus matrimonii tamquam remedii libidinis, cum idem matrimonium in ordine familiae etiam impedimentum spei litterariae describatur.
Restitutio motum textus servat, si recordatio non pro mera narratione praeteriti, sed pro operatione qua dispersio in confessionem et amor Dei convertitur accipitur.
The text asks why the committed theft delighted, when neither necessity nor gain nor the stolen thing itself supplied a cause of delight.
Adolescence is constituted not as a series of discrete acts, but as a dispersal of the soul from the one good into a multitude of desires.
The argument proceeds from the ordinary causes of sin through desired lower goods to theft, which evades a utilitarian cause and makes malice itself the question.
Theft is explained as a perverse imitation of divine freedom, intensified by the fellowship of those sinning together and by shame at appearing less shameless.
The recollection of the crime is converted into confession, by which guilt and abstinence alike are attributed to divine mercy.
God is the highest, true, and stable good, apart from whom no pure or secure delight is found.
Sin arises when the soul immoderately desires lower goods and abandons higher goods.
Every vice imitates the appearance of some good, power, beauty, rest, knowledge, or fellowship.
Vicious imitation does not create good, but converts divine perfection into a diminished and perverse form.
The soul turned away from God flows out into many things and becomes for itself a region of want.
The theft of the pear was caused neither by want, nor by the sweetness of the fruit, nor by the usefulness of the thing.
In theft, transgression of the law was sought, because transgression itself offered an illicit appearance of freedom.
Gratuitous malice is not a positive good, but love of deficiency, ruin, and turning away from the divine foundation.
In the fellowship of sinners, desire is inflamed, because shared shamelessness turns another's loss into sport and praise.
Literary training and eloquence, if they are not accompanied by cultivation of the heart and chastity, do not preserve the adolescent from dispersal.
God acts even through correction and bitter outcome, so that illicit delights may be referred back to Himself.
Not only sins committed, but also sins not committed, must be attributed to divine grace and mercy.
Theft is not defined by desire for the apples, because apples were abundant, better ones were present, and the robbery was not ordered to use.
Sin is not the creation of an autonomous good, but the privation of good and the perversion of created good.
Freedom is not effected by the license to do what is not permitted, because such license is a captive shadow of omnipotence.
Friendship is not true unity if its fellowship consists in the joy of harming and in the contagion of shamefulness.
Chastity and innocence are not possessions that a human being can ascribe to himself by his own powers.
Divine silence is not divine absence, since a mother's warnings and the scourges of life mediate the same divine voice.
Study, domestic honor, and social hope do not suffice for right formation if they are not referred to God and truth.
Since lower goods are truly goods but not supreme, sin does not destroy beautiful things, but dissolves the order of love.
The theft of the pear becomes an extreme test, because it shows that the will may desire not a thing, but the state of setting itself against the law.
The illicit pleasure of freedom arises from this: that the soul, subject to God, attempts to flee its lord and to imitate power without authority.
Fellowship is not merely an external circumstance of the act, but a formal cause of delight, when the same act would not please one acting alone.
Social shame is inverted: innocence seems disgraceful, shamefulness glorious, and lying is added for the imitation of depravity.
Divine correction does not approve sin, but wounds illicit pleasure with bitterness, so that it may recognize its false desire.
The rightly ordered recollection of sin tends not toward love of shamefulness, but toward love of God and the recollection of the dispersed soul.
One who has sinned less gravely is no less a debtor to mercy, because even the diminution of sickness proceeds from the divine physician.
The moral order is not divided between good things and bad things, but between love ordered in relation to the highest good and absolute love of lower goods.
Radical evil is not described as a substance rival to God, but as an ontological diminution that nevertheless effectively deforms will, fellowship, and memory.
A depraved fellowship can effect a mechanism of value-conversion, by which another's loss, transgression of the law, and feigning of shamefulness are changed into sources of honor.
Confession reorders moral causality: the agent retains the guilt of his own acts, but attributes liberation and abstinence to grace.
No turning away from God is absolute, because even the perverse imitation of divine goods indicates the creature's enduring dependence upon the Creator.
Any model that reduces sin to ignorance of things, material necessity, or a calculation of utility must be false.
Any model of freedom that takes transgression of the law as a self-founding act must be false.
Any model of fellowship that considers association good in itself, without distinguishing the end by which companions are united, must be false.
Any model of virtue that regards human innocence as separable from grace and self-sufficient must be false.
Any model of education that substitutes eloquence, study, and social ascent for inner cultivation must be false.
The system admits no place outside God from which the soul could procure for itself stable good, certain rest, or true freedom.
The system admits no malice as an autonomous principle, because even the deformity of vices parasitically presupposes forms of divine goods.
The system admits no neutral moral memory, because recollection either falls back into delight in crime or is ordered toward confession and conversion.
Turning away from the one good → dispersal into many goods → diminution of the capacity to distinguish love from lust.
Apparent lower good → immoderate desire → abandonment of higher good → sin.
Theft without utility → exclusion of material cause → inquiry into the delight of transgression itself.
Transgression → perverse imitation of power → mutilated freedom → servitude and deficiency.
Fellowship of sinners → mutual inflaming of desire → shame at innocence → consolidation of the act and feigning of shamefulness.
Recollection of crime → confession of weakness → recognition of grace in sins committed and avoided → recollected love of God.
Adolescent lust and dispersal of soul → lack of spiritual discipline and restraint.
Lack of restraint → theft that no external advantage explains.
Theft inexplicable through the stolen thing → distinction between goods that vices attempt to imitate and malice that loves deficiency.
Malice as a perverse imitation of freedom → discovery of the fellowship of sinners as the affective motor of the act.
Fellowship and recognized guilt → confession of mercy that does not erase guilt from memory but transforms its meaning.
Sin is reclassified not as love of a thing intrinsically evil, but as love of a lower good placed outside the order of the highest good.
Theft is reclassified from an offense against property into an experiment in perverse freedom and a socially produced affect.
Friendship bifurcates into a unity of souls ordered to the good and a contagious fellowship ordered to doing harm.
Education bifurcates into the acquisition of external eloquence and cultivation of the heart, the former of which is insufficiently formative without the latter.
Abstinence is reclassified from private merit into a benefit of grace, just as is the remission of acts committed.
Surface — The text examines lustful adolescence, the theft of the pear, parental warnings, and the fellowship of companions.
Structural — The mechanism of sin consists in turning away from the highest good, the desire for lower goods, and the social deformation of shame and praise.
Metastrategic — The question concerning a single act is transferred to an investigation of the kind of desire that produces transgression, imitation, and fellowship.
Ontological/Temporal — The creature turned away from God does not pass into another stability, but falls into deficiency, dispersal, and temporal want.
The axioms suffice to restore the necessity by which sin arises from the disordered love of lower goods and a return to God is required.
The explanation of the theft is sustained only if transgression, imitation of perverse freedom, and the fellowship of sinners are retained together.
The firmest link of the system is constituted by the distinction between created good, whose appearance remains true, and its disordered use.
The assertion of gratuitous malice leaves a tension, because the text simultaneously affirms that every sin is moved by some apparent good and that theft desires malice itself.
The relation between the guilt of the will and divine grace leaves a tension, because the agent properly sins, yet even the diminution of sin is attributed to divine benefit.
The use of marriage as a remedy for lust leaves a tension, since the same marriage is also described, in the order of the family, as an impediment to literary hope.

The reconstruction preserves the movement of the text if recollection is understood not as mere narration of the past, but as the operation by which dispersal is converted into confession and love of God.
Textus inquirit quomodo anima Deum nesciens appetat, appetitum in voluptates et errores convertat, atque ex ipsa aberratione ad veritatem praeparari possit.
Fames interior Dei, si non agnoscitur, amorem a creatore ad sensibilia, dolorem fictum, gloriam rhetoricam et doctrinam corpoream deflectit, quae animam non satiant sed exhauriunt.
Veritas affectu, consuetudine, specie facti aut nominibus sacris non mensuratur, sed Deo immutabili, ordine naturae et lege iustitiae.
Hortensius desiderium ab eloquentia ad sapientiam transfert, sed absentia nominis Christi et superbia adversus humilem Scripturam conversionem imperfectam relinquunt.
Reconstructio retrospectiva errores Manichaeorum dissolvit per Deum incorporeum, malum ut privationem boni, et iustitiam immutabilem quae diversa temporibus diversis distribuit.
Misericordia divina ante confessionem operatur per poenas, excitationes intellectuales, preces Monnicae, somnium et correctionem prudenter dilatam.
Argumentatio genealogica, diagnostica, polemica et reconstructiva ab effectibus amoris perversi ad causas ontologicas progreditur, deinde ad ordinem moralem et providentiam conversionis.
Deus est Veritas immutabilis, vita animarum et creator rectorque universi.
Anima, etiam sine desiderio conscio, Deo tamquam cibo incorruptibili indiget.
Bona creata amari possunt quia bona sunt, sed creatorem supplere nequeunt.
Peccatum est conversio amoris a bono universali ad partem privatam immoderate possessam vel adhibitam.
Misericordia vera miseriam auferri vult, non dolorem tamquam voluptatem retineri.
Malum non est substantia, sed privatio boni usque ad defectum essendi.
Deus est spiritus sine mole vel dimensionibus, totus ubique et nulli corpori aut animae creaturali idem.
Cognitio sensu corporis et phantasmate terminata Deum apprehendere nequit atque falsa infinita fabricatur.
Iustitia vera est lex Dei rectissima, ubique et semper eadem.
Iustitia immutabilis diversa praecepta distribuit secundum tempora, regiones, officia et personas.
Flagitia contra naturam semper damnanda sunt, violationes autem consuetudinum humanarum ex pacto civitatis vel gentis aestimantur.
Moralitas facti ex animo agentis, usu, tempore occulto et testimonio divino iudicatur, non ex sola specie externa.
Praeceptum Dei, ut supremi rectoris, consuetudini et pacto humano praevalet.
Superbia intellectum a forma humili veritatis avertit et ad novitatem, eloquentiam atque apparentiam sapientiae inclinat.
Frequentia vocum veritatis et nominum divinorum praesentiam veritatis non praestat.
Misericordia divina confessionem antecedit atque etiam poena, mediatione et dilatione conversionem ordinat.
Intensitas amoris vel mutua fruitio corporalis bonitatem amoris non constituit.
Dolor scenicis imaginibus excitatus misericordia non est, ubi nullum auxilium intenditur et dolor ipse delectat.
Dolor aliquando approbari potest, sed numquam propter se amandus est.
Humilitas stili Scripturae humilitatem vel indignitatem veritatis non significat.
Nomen philosophiae, veritatis, Christi aut Spiritus doctrinam veram per se non efficit.
Deus nec corpus, nec moles infinita, nec phantasma corporis, nec anima corporum est.
Malum principium substantiale vel Deo coaeternum non est.
Iustitia neque consuetudini locali reducitur neque uniformitatem praeceptorum per omnia tempora requirit.
Similitudo externa facti peccatum aut iustitiam sine consideratione animi et temporis non probat.
Peccatum Deum corrumpere non potest, nec fuga a Deo libertatem efficit; peccator se ipsum et societatem vulnerat.
Fames Dei non agnita sensibilia tamquam alimenta quaerit; quia ea Deum supplere nequeunt, delectatio in maiorem inanitatem et dolorem transit.
Theatrum misericordiam simulat, sed affectum in voluptatem doloris claudit quia spectatorem ad subveniendum non movet.
Hortensius desiderium ab arte dicendi ad sapientiam transfert, sed sapientia sine Christo Augustinum totum rapere non potest.
Superbia Scripturam ex dignitate Ciceroniana metitur atque formam humilem respuit antequam eius interiora penetret.
Coniunctio superbiae, imaginationis corporeae et nominum sacrorum Manichaeismum efficit apparentem satisfactionem desiderii veritatis.
Fabula agnita ut ficta minus fallit quam doctrina ficta ut vera credita, quia distinctio inter imaginationem et assertionem servatur.
Quaestio Manichaea de origine mali dissolvitur, si malum privatio est et Deus incorporeus atque immutabilis intelligitur.
Diversitas praeceptorum divinorum patriarchis et praesentibus data mutationem iustitiae non probat, sed applicationem unius ordinis ad tempora diversa.
Facta specie similia moraliter differre possunt, si alius est animus, usus, articulus temporis vel mandatum divinum.
Peccatum contra Deum non est laesio divinae substantiae, sed deformatio naturae agentis et disruptio ordinis quo pars universo congruit.
Monnicae emendatio interpretationis somnii directionem conversionis statuit: filius ad regulam matris accedet, non mater ad errorem filii.
Episcopi recusatio disputationis errorem non tolerat, sed inflationem praesentem indocilem iudicat atque lectioni, tempori et precibus correctionem committit.
Conversio requirit simul ordinationem amoris et mutationem modi cognoscendi, quia idem motus ad sensibilia et desiderium corrumpit et Deum in phantasma transformat.
Error Manichaeus parasitatur bona quae corrumpit: desiderium veritatis, nomina divina, pulchritudinem creatam et misericordiae speciem.
Universalitas moralis non uniformitatem materialem, sed constantiam ordinis per applicationes temporaliter distinctas significat.
Genealogia lapsus duas causalitates coniungit: voluntas culpabiliter se ad exteriora convertit, dum misericordia antecedens eandem historiam ad reditum ordinat.
Mora conversionis absentiam Dei non indicat, quia Deus interior manet dum subiectum relationaliter peregrinatur, et ipsa dilatio instrumentum correctionis fit.
Systema falsitatem dualismi requirit: malum non potest esse natura positiva contra bonum constituta.
Systema falsitatem reductionis ontologicae ad corpus requirit: realitas mensurabili mole non exhauritur.
Systema falsitatem identitatis inter veritatem et splendorem sermonis requirit: stilus sublimis, copia librorum et nomina sacra possunt errorem tegere.
Systema simul conventionalismum moralem et uniformitatem sine temporum discrimine excludit.
Systema falsitatem iudicii ex solo effectu visibili requirit, quia intentio et articulus temporis moralem speciem facti mutare possunt.
Systema falsitatem correctionis semper immediatae requirit: disputatio non prodest ubi superbia nondum capacitatem discendi admittit.
Nulla desiderii neutralitas admittitur: appetitus aut ad fontem vitae ordinatur aut bonum creatum in substitutum falsum convertit.
Creaturae exterioritas sibi sufficiens impossibilis est, quia recessus a Deo independentiam non parit sed defectum vitae.
Nullum principium mali Deo coaevum, comparabile aut ipsum laedere capax admittitur.
Iudicium morale totale ex brevi praesentia humana praecluditur, quia ordo iustitiae nexus temporum et causarum excedit quos homo experitur.
Reditus per eandem superbiam quae errorem genuit impossibilis est; accessus ad veritatem inclinationem, confessionem et patientiam requirit.
In hac narratione particulari finalis Augustini perditio per somnium et dictum episcopi praecluditur, quamvis haec praeclusio in legem universalem de omnibus filiis lacrimarum non convertatur.
Fames Dei non agnita → amor amoris → proiectio ad sensibilia → voluptas mixta dolore → exinanitio → renovata fuga ad exteriora.
Excitatio ad sapientiam → retentio criterii christiani → recusatio Scripturae humilis → quaestus corporeus veritatis → captatio per nomina sacra et phantasmata Manichaea.
Quaestiones Manichaeae → correctio modi cognoscendi → Deus incorporeus → malum ut privatio → iustitia immutabilis cum distributione temporali → reclassificatio factorum moralium.
Misericordia antecedens → poena et inquietudo → preces Monnicae → somnium directionis → dilatio disputationis → cognitio erroris per lectionem et tempus → reditus praenuntiatus.
Amor amoris → nexus libidinosus → voluptas doloris scenici → gloria rhetorica et societas perversa → Hortensiana conversio ad sapientiam → fastidium Scripturae → captatio Manichaea.

Quaestiones de malo, Deo et patriarchis → restitutio ontologiae et iustitiae → distinctio flagitiorum, facinorum et factorum apparentium → detectio absurditatis Manichaeae → intercessio Monnicae → promissio conversionis dilatae.
Amor ex intensitate affectus ad ordinem obiecti reclassificatur: quaestio decisiva non est quantum ametur, sed quid et quo ordine ametur.
Misericordia a delectatione doloris separatur et per voluntatem subveniendi definitur.
Ordo cognitionis distinguit corpora vera, imaginationes corporum, phantasmata rerum nullarum et Deum qui omnes has classes transcendit.
Oppositio inter legem universalem et varietatem historicam corruit; varietas praeceptorum fit modus applicationis legis immutabilis.
Factum visibile ab actu morali separatur, quia intentio, officium, tempus et auctoritas possunt eandem speciem externam aliter constituere.
Haeresis non ut pura absentia veritatis, sed ut captatio parasitica per signa vera, desideria bona et phantasmata falsa describitur.
Mora conversionis ex signo desertionis in instrumentum providentiae et maturitatis epistemicae convertitur.
Gradus superficiei continet amores Carthaginienses, spectacula, studia rhetorica, lectionem Hortensii, Manichaeismum et sollicitudinem Monnicae.
Gradus structuralis coniungit famem interiorem, conversionem ad sensibilia, superbiam, cognitionem phantasmaticam et captationem per nomina.
Gradus metastrategicus criteria iudicii transfert ab affectu, eloquentia, consuetudine et specie facti ad ordinem amoris, intentionem, tempora et auctoritatem divinam.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis Deum immutabilem atque incorporeum, malum privativum, creaturam dependentem et providentiam per moras agentem praesupponit.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem ab appetitu perverso per errorem ontologicum ad correctionem moralem et providentiam conversionis.
Systema principaliter cohaeret, sed relatio causalis inter culpabilem voluntatis conversionem et misericordiam divinam decisive antecedentem non plene determinatur.
Firmissima commissura est nexus inter superbiam, cognitionem corpoream, recusationem Scripturae et captationem Manichaeam.
Criterium quo mandatum divinum authenticum, somnium providentiale aut testimonium Dei certo agnoscatur intra capitulum nondum formaliter explicatur.
Iustitia immutabilis cum mandatis inusitatis cohaerere potest, sed occultatio causae mandati iudicium humanum dependentem ab auctoritate facit.
Reiectio phantasmatum corporeorum et acceptio somnii divini tensionem epistemicam relinquunt, quia discretio utriusque ex effectu providentiali potius quam ex criterio generali pendet.
Doctrina mali privativi cum activa seductione daemonum et flagellatione divina componitur, sed mediatio inter privationem, agentiam spiritualem et poenam rhetorice potius quam analytice exhibetur.
Dictum episcopi de filio lacrimarum intra historiam Augustini vim propheticam accipit, sed ex eo propositio universalis sine excessu deduci non potest.
Restitutio servat verum motum textus: experientia miseriae → diagnosis desiderii → falsa sapientiae solutio → correctio ontologica et moralis → providentia reditus dilati.
The text investigates how the soul, not knowing God, desires Him, turns desire into pleasures and errors, and can be prepared for truth from that very wandering.

The soul's inner hunger for God, if unrecognized, diverts love from the creator toward sensible things, fictive sorrow, rhetorical glory, and corporeal doctrine, which do not satisfy the soul but exhaust it.
Truth is not measured by feeling, custom, the appearance of a deed, or sacred names, but by immutable God, the order of nature, and the law of justice.
Hortensius transfers desire from eloquence to wisdom, but the absence of Christ's name and pride against humble Scripture leave conversion incomplete.
Retrospective reconstruction dissolves the errors of the Manichaeans through incorporeal God, evil as the privation of good, and immutable justice that assigns different things at different times.
Divine mercy operates before confession through punishments, intellectual awakenings, Monnica's prayers, a dream, and correction prudently delayed.
Genealogical, diagnostic, polemical, and reconstructive argumentation advances from the effects of perverse love to ontological causes, then to moral order and the providence of conversion.
God is immutable Truth, the life of souls, and the creator and governor of the universe.
The soul, even without conscious desire, needs God as incorruptible food.
Created goods can be loved because they are good, but they cannot replace the creator.
Sin is the turning of love from the universal good to a private part possessed or used immoderately.
True mercy wishes misery to be removed, not sorrow to be retained as pleasure.
Evil is not a substance, but the privation of good even unto a deficiency of being.
God is spirit without bulk or dimensions, wholly everywhere and identical with no body or created soul.
Cognition bounded by bodily sense and phantasm cannot apprehend God and fabricates false infinities.
True justice is God's most right law, the same everywhere and always.
Immutable justice distributes different precepts according to times, regions, offices, and persons.
Shameful acts against nature are always to be condemned, whereas violations of human customs are assessed according to the compact of city or nation.
The morality of a deed is judged by the agent's intention, usage, hidden time, and divine testimony, not by external appearance alone.
God's command, as that of the highest ruler, prevails over human custom and compact.
Pride turns the intellect away from the humble form of truth and inclines it toward novelty, eloquence, and the appearance of wisdom.
The frequency of words of truth and divine names does not ensure the presence of truth.
Divine mercy precedes confession and orders conversion even through punishment, mediation, and delay.
The intensity of love or mutual bodily enjoyment does not constitute the goodness of love.
Sorrow aroused by theatrical images is not mercy where no assistance is intended and sorrow itself delights.
Sorrow can sometimes be approved, but it must never be loved for its own sake.
The humility of Scripture's style does not signify the humility or unworthiness of truth.
The name of philosophy, truth, Christ, or Spirit does not in itself make doctrine true.
God is neither body, nor infinite bulk, nor phantasm of a body, nor the soul of bodies.
Evil is not a substantial principle or one coeternal with God.
Justice is neither reduced to local custom nor does it require uniformity of precepts through all times.
The external similarity of a deed does not establish sin or justice without consideration of intention and time.
Sin cannot corrupt God, nor does flight from God produce freedom; the sinner wounds himself and society.
Unrecognized hunger for God seeks sensible things as food; because they cannot replace God, delight passes into greater emptiness and sorrow.
The theater simulates mercy, but encloses feeling within pleasure in sorrow because it does not move the spectator to render aid.
Hortensius transfers desire from the art of speaking to wisdom, but wisdom without Christ cannot wholly carry Augustine away.
Pride measures Scripture by Ciceronian dignity and rejects its humble form before penetrating its interior.
The conjunction of pride, corporeal imagination, and sacred names makes Manichaeism an apparent satisfaction of the desire for truth.
A fable recognized as fictitious deceives less than fictitious doctrine believed true, because the distinction between imagination and assertion is preserved.
The Manichaean question concerning the origin of evil is dissolved if evil is understood as privation and God as incorporeal and immutable.
The diversity of divine precepts given to the patriarchs and to the present does not prove a change in justice, but the application of one order to different times.
Deeds similar in appearance can differ morally if the intention, use, juncture of time, or divine command is different.
Sin against God is not injury to the divine substance, but deformation of the agent's nature and disruption of the order by which a part accords with the universe.
The correction of Monnica's interpretation of the dream establishes the direction of conversion: the son will come to the mother's rule, not the mother to the son's error.
The bishop's refusal of disputation does not tolerate error, but judges present inflation unteachable and entrusts correction to reading, time, and prayers.
Conversion requires at once the ordering of love and a change in the mode of knowing, because the same motion toward sensible things both corrupts desire and transforms God into a phantasm.
Manichaean error parasitizes the goods it corrupts: desire for truth, divine names, created beauty, and the appearance of mercy.
Moral universality signifies not material uniformity, but constancy of order through temporally distinct applications.
The genealogy of the fall joins two causalities: the will culpably turns itself toward externals, while prevenient mercy orders the same history toward return.
The delay of conversion does not indicate God's absence, because God remains within while the subject journeys relationally, and the delay itself becomes an instrument of correction.
The system requires the falsity of dualism: evil cannot be a positive nature constituted against good.
The system requires the falsity of ontological reduction to body: reality is not exhausted by measurable bulk.
The system requires the falsity of the identity between truth and splendor of speech: lofty style, an abundance of books, and sacred names can conceal error.
The system excludes both moral conventionalism and uniformity without distinction of times.
The system requires the falsity of judgment from visible effect alone, because intention and the juncture of time can alter the moral character of a deed.
The system requires the falsity of correction that is always immediate: disputation does not profit where pride does not yet admit the capacity for learning.
No neutrality of desire is admitted: appetite is either ordered toward the source of life or converts a created good into a false substitute.
The self-sufficient exteriority of the creature is impossible, because withdrawal from God produces not independence but deficiency of life.
No principle of evil coeval with God, comparable to Him, or capable of injuring Him is admitted.
Total moral judgment from brief human presence is precluded, because the order of justice exceeds the connections of times and causes that a human being experiences.
Return through the same pride that generated error is impossible; access to truth requires humility, confession, and patience.

In this particular narrative, Augustine's final perdition is precluded by the dream and the bishop's saying, although this preclusion is not converted into a universal law concerning all sons of tears.
Unrecognized hunger for God → love of love → projection toward sensible things → pleasure mixed with sorrow → emptying → renewed flight toward externals.
Awakening to wisdom → retention of the Christian criterion → rejection of humble Scripture → corporeal pursuit of truth → enticement by sacred names and Manichaean phantasms.
Manichaean questions → correction of the mode of knowing → incorporeal God → evil as privation → immutable justice with temporal distribution → reclassification of moral deeds.
Prevenient mercy → punishment and unrest → Monnica's prayers → dream of direction → delay of disputation → knowledge of error through reading and time → return foretold.
Love of love → lustful attachment → pleasure in theatrical sorrow → rhetorical glory and perverse society → Hortensian conversion to wisdom → distaste for Scripture → Manichaean enticement.

Questions concerning evil, God, and the patriarchs → restoration of ontology and justice → distinction of shameful acts, criminal acts, and apparent deeds → detection of Manichaean absurdity → Monnica's intercession → promise of delayed conversion.
Love is reclassified from intensity of feeling to the order of its object: the decisive question is not how much one loves, but what one loves and in what order.
Mercy is separated from delight in sorrow and defined through the will to render aid.
The order of cognition distinguishes true bodies, imaginations of bodies, phantasms of non-existent things, and God, who transcends all these classes.
The opposition between universal law and historical variety collapses; diversity of precepts becomes a mode of application of immutable law.
The visible deed is separated from the moral act, because intention, office, time, and authority can constitute the same external appearance differently.
Heresy is described not as a pure absence of truth, but as parasitic enticement through true signs, good desires, and false phantasms.
The delay of conversion is transformed from a sign of abandonment into an instrument of providence and epistemic maturity.
The surface level contains Carthaginian loves, spectacles, rhetorical studies, the reading of Hortensius, Manichaeism, and Monnica's concern.
The structural level joins inner hunger, conversion toward sensible things, pride, phantasmal cognition, and enticement through names.
The metastrategic level transfers the criteria of judgment from feeling, eloquence, custom, and the appearance of a deed to the order of love, intention, times, and divine authority.
The ontological and temporal level presupposes immutable and incorporeal God, privative evil, the dependent creature, and providence acting through delays.
The extracted axioms suffice to restore the sequence from perverse appetite through ontological error to moral correction and the providence of conversion.
The system principally coheres, but the causal relation between the culpable conversion of the will and decisively prevenient divine mercy is not fully determined.
The strongest joint is the nexus between pride, corporeal cognition, rejection of Scripture, and Manichaean enticement.
The criterion by which an authentic divine command, a providential dream, or God's testimony may be certainly recognized is not yet formally explained within the chapter.
Immutable justice can cohere with unusual commands, but concealment of the reason for the command makes human judgment dependent on authority.

The rejection of corporeal phantasms and acceptance of the divine dream leave an epistemic tension, because the distinction between them depends on providential effect rather than on a general criterion.

The doctrine of privative evil is combined with the active seduction of demons and divine scourging, but the mediation between privation, spiritual agency, and punishment is presented rhetorically rather than analytically.
The bishop's saying concerning the son of tears acquires prophetic force within Augustine's history, but no universal proposition can be deduced from it without excess.
The reconstruction preserves the text's true movement: experience of misery → diagnosis of desire → false solution of wisdom → ontological and moral correction → providence of delayed return.
Textus quaerit quomodo ingenium acre, amicitia intensa et rectitudines particulares cum diuturno errore ac miseria cohaerere potuerint.
Bona creata perniciosa fiunt non natura sua, sed cum anima aversa a Deo ea tamquam fines stabiles amat vel interpretatur.
Distinctio generatrix opponit Deum incommutabilem creaturis mutabilibus, veritatem illuminantem menti participanti et amorem ordinatum fixationi in rebus caducis.
Argumentatio confessionalis simul diagnostica, genealogica, polemica et reconstructiva est.
Motus procedit ab errore culpabili ad mortem amici, a luctu ad ontologiam mutabilitatis, inde ad genealogiam erroris intellectualis et ad ordinem reditus.
Restitutio animi non abolendo creaturas vel facultates, sed referendo amorem, cognitionem et dona ad Deum efficitur.
Deus est veritas et bonum incommutabile, cui proprietates non quasi accidentia subiecto insunt.
Omne bonum creatum, omne verum cognitum et omnis facultas intellectualis a Deo creatore procedit.
Creatura temporalis per successionem partium constat, mutatur atque interit.
Mens humana mutabilis est et veritatis per illuminationem particeps, non ipsa natura veritatis.
Sensus corporeus partes transeuntes capit, non totum simul neque rem incorpoream.
Amor animam rei dilectae alligat et in ea requiem quaerit.
Diligere moriturum quasi non moriturum miseriam iam ante iacturam constituit.
Vera amicitia exsistit tantum ubi Deus amantes sibi invicem caritate coniungit.
Bonum creatum recte amatur in Deo et ad Creatorem refertur, non tamquam finis ab eo separatus.
Aversio superba a Deo est radix perversitatis affectivae et intellectualis.
Imaginatio corporea ad spiritualia translata phantasmata pro rebus constituit.
Malum non est substantia, sed vitium motus, affectionis vel mentis mutabilis.
Error et peccatum ex voluntaria deviatione creaturae oriuntur, non ex necessitate siderum, materiae vel substantiae divinae.
Consonantiae astrologicae possunt, secundum rationem senis medici ab Augustino receptam, sorte potius quam arte siderum oriri.
Laus socialis affectum audientis accendere potest, etiamsi res laudata ipsa non mutetur.
Celeritas intelligendi donum est cuius utilitas ex recto usu et fine, non ex sola possessione, pendet.
Deus animam per media curare potest quae ipsa nondum plene intellegit vel voluntarie eligit.
Vita divina incarnata mortem assumit atque vincit, ut homo ab exterioribus ad Deum redeat.
Rectitudo particularis conversionem integram non constituit, si finis actionis adhuc cupiditate vel superstitione regitur.
Astrologia non fit licita eo quod sacrificiis et precibus spirituum carere videatur.
Necessitas caelestis peccatorem a culpa non absolvit.
Sacramentum non redditur inefficax sola absentia cognitionis consciae recipientis.
Studia communia, mutua benevolentia et delectatio consortii ad veram amicitiam per se non sufficiunt.
Mutatio loci, voluptas sensibilis et occupatio litteraria animam a se ipsa fugere neque dolorem radicaliter sanare possunt.
Nulla creatura mutabilis est locus quietis imperturbabilis.
Deus non est corpus lucidum neque spatium lucis immensum.
Deus decem praedicamentis quasi subiectum accidentium non continetur.
Malum non est substantia adversa Deo neque vita sui iuris.
Mens humana non est pars substantiae divinae neque summum bonum incommutabile.
Acumen dialecticum et scientia artium salutem aut sapientiam per se non efficiunt.
Amor corporum, animarum et amicorum non abolendus, sed ordinandus est.
Rectitudines locales cum perversitate totius vitae coexistere possunt, quia bonitas actus particularis ordinem finis universalis non necessario mutat.
Astrologia, peccatum in necessitatem siderum transferens, hominem exculpat et Creatorem iustum implicite accusat.
Praedictio vera artem astrologicam non probat, quia observatio particularis causalitatem artis a consonantia fortuita distinguere non potest.
Narratio conversionis amici effectum baptismi tamquam operationem divinam cognitionem explicitam praecedentem interpretatur.
Mors amici non tantum gaudium aufert, sed miseriam iam inclusam in amore mortalis tamquam immortalis manifestat.
Fuga localis dolorem radicalem non removet, quia anima secum fert ordinem amoris quo ipsa sibi locus infelix facta est.
Successio temporis memorias et delectationes substituendo dolorem minuit, sed amicitiae extra Deum ordinatae causam futurorum dolorum servant.
Qui amicos in Deo amat ultimam amissionem non patitur, quia nexus amoris in eo fundatur qui non transit.
Transitus partium defectus universi non est, sed condicio qua totum temporale per successionem constituitur.
Anima veritati nondum stabiliter inhaerens eundem hominem aliter amat secundum affectum laudantium, rebus ipsis immutatis.
Imaginatio corporea cum superbia coniuncta mutabilitatem propriam in Deum transfert et vitium voluntatis in dualismum substantiarum transformat.
Praedicamenta ad res creatas utilia falsitatem generant cum divina simplicitas quasi subiectum magnitudinis aut pulchritudinis tractatur.
Ingenium a fonte suo aversum veritates locales assequi potest, sed eas in superbiam, errorem metaphysicum et perniciem convertit.
Incarnatio motum reditus ordinat per descensum humilem, mortis victoriam et recessionem a visu exteriori ad praesentiam interiorem.
Error moralis, luctus immoderatus, superstitiones et falsa metaphysica sunt diversi effectus eiusdem aversionis quae bonum creatum a fonte suo separat.
Conversio non destruit amorem, sensum, amicitiam vel scientiam, sed eorum obiecta et fines secundum ordinem Creatoris et creaturae reconstituit.
Miseria temporalis oritur cum anima permanentiam appetitam a partibus successive transeuntibus exigere conatur.
Possessio veritatis localis sapientiam non importat, quia ars recte intellecta cum falsa imagine Dei et perverso ordine amoris coexistere potest.
Confessio errata et dona retrospecte in laudem divinae misericordiae convertit, quia etiam media imperfecte intellecta intra processum curationis reponuntur.
Reditus ad Deum non est ascensus autonomus, sed participatio motus Christi qui descendendo mortem vincit et hominem ad interiora revocat.
Providentia divina et culpa humana simul retinentur: Deus per eventus curat, sed anima voluntarie avertitur et erroris poenam fert.
Auctoritas socialis errorem recursive propagat, quia anima ab opinionibus alienis mota doctrinam receptam amicis et discipulis tradit.
Anima sibi ipsi principium veritatis, firmitatis aut salutis esse non potest.
Usus facultatis a fine amoris separatim aestimari non potest.
Nulla relatio ad rem finitam possessionem sine periculo amissionis praestat.
Nulla pars sensibilis aut categoria creata legitimam totalizationem realitatis divinae praebet.
Culpa in carnem, sidera, materiam vel divinam substantiam transferri non potest quin confessio et iustitia dissolvantur.
Nullum principium mali Deo coaeternum vel substantialiter oppositum admittitur.
Ascensus per superbam assimilationem ad Deum reditum efficere non potest.
Amicitia ut nexus mere dyadicus sufficientem firmitatis causam non habet.
Consensus laudantium criterium veritatis aut valoris intrinseci non constituit.
Nullus locus exterior praesto est quo anima a corde suo aut a praesentia Dei effugiat.
Possessio permanens boni temporalis intra ipsum ordinem temporis impossibilis est.
Nullum punctum epistemicum omnino extra participationem lucis divinae datur, etiam ubi cognoscens fontem cognitionis ignorat.
Sanatio non consistit in restitutione praeteriti amissi, sed in reformatione rerum fluxarum sub bono permanente.
Absentia Dei localis vel ontologica esse non potest; quod absentia videtur aversio cordis est, quae etiam fugiendo sub lege divina manet.
Firmitas autonoma subiecti excluditur: anima firma est tantum cum firmitas eius Deus est.
Aversio a Deo superbiam generat; superbia donum creatum in cupiditatem, phantasma et doctrinam fallacem convertit; error inde se ipsum et alios reproducit.
Amor boni temporalis ut finis stabilis fixationem parit; mutabilitas obiecti iacturam infert; iactura miseriam antecedentem manifestat; fuga exterior animam ad se vulneratam remittit.
Sensus partis phantasma totius producit; phantasma Deum corporeum vel categoricum constituit; falsa imago dualismum et translationem culpae sustentat.
Laus socialis affectum accendit; affectus auctoritatem rei substituit; auctoritas recepta doctrinam falsam corroborat; doctrina per docentem vel amicum propagatur.
Divina mediatio per admonitionem, sacramentum, eventum et successionem temporis falsam securitatem perturbat atque memoriam ad ulteriorem conversionem praeparat.
Incarnatio per descensum mortem assumit, per abundantiam vitae mortem vincit, per absentiam visibilem cor ad praesentiam interiorem revocat et per humilitatem ascensum restituit.
Confessio effectus praesentis curationis ad errores praeteritos refert, ex eis principia aversionis extrahit et dona male usa ad fontem suum restituit.
Textus a seductione mutua et rectitudinibus imperfectis ad astrologiam transit, cuius fatalismus moraliter et causaliter dissolvitur.
Amicitia ad baptismum amici, baptismus ad mortem, mors ad luctum, luctus ad fugam sui et successio temporis ad consolationem imperfectam ducunt.
Experientia luctus in doctrinam mutabilitatis creaturarum, ordinationis amoris et quietis in Deo convertitur.
Quaestio pulchri et apti ad dependentiam a laude, inde ad imaginationem corpoream, dualismum, abusum categoriarum et vanitatem ingenii autonomi progreditur.
Omnes lineae in necessitatem reditus humilis ad Deum tamquam bonum, veritatem et firmitatem animae conveniunt.
Rectitudo moralis non iam per actus singulos tantum, sed per ordinem finis totius vitae describitur.
Luctus ex accidente post amissionem in revelationem miseriae iam praesentis ante amissionem reclassificatur.
Amicitia e nexu duorum affectuum in relationem triadicam per Deum constituentem transfertur.
Mutabilitas creaturarum non ut mera defectio, sed ut successio ordinata partium universi fit visibilis.
Astrologia e disciplina praedictiva in machinam exculpationis moralis et confusionis causalis reclassificatur.
Malum e substantia adversa in corruptionem motuum et facultatum mutabilium transfertur.
Pulchritudo, amicitia et artes ex finibus autonomis in bona signantia atque ad Creatorem referenda convertuntur.
Oppositio inter ingenium excellens et fidem simplicem corruit, quia tarditas intellectus cum recta orientatione tutior esse potest quam acumen aversum.
Conversio ex motu spatiali vel ascensu superbo in reditum interiorem per humilitatem et mediationem divinam redescribitur.
Gradus superficiei confessiones erroris, astrologiae, mortis amici, luctus, scriptorum philosophicorum et artium intellectarum continet.
Gradus structuralis unum mechanismum detegit quo aversio, fixatio amoris, auctoritas socialis et imaginatio corporea affectum atque cognitionem corrumpunt.
Gradus metastrategicus criterium quaerendi mutat: non amplius quaeritur quantum anima intelligat vel amet, sed ad quid intellectus et amor ordinentur.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis distinctione inter Creatorem incommutabilem et creaturam successive existentem limites sensus, amoris et praedicationis constituit.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad motum ab experientia erroris et luctus ad doctrinam mutabilitatis, illuminationis et amoris ordinati restituendum.
Cohaerentia firmissima est ubi mors amici structuram latentem amoris mortalis manifestat et ubi imaginatio corporea falsam metaphysicam generat.
Dulcedo fletus explicite indeterminata manet; textus hypotheses proponit, sed quaestionem confessioni subordinat.
Refutatio empirica astrologiae analogia sortis nititur neque documentum certum, quod Augustinus eo tempore quaerebat, plene exhibet.
Efficacia baptismi amici ex mutatione narrativa et interpretatione providentiali infertur, non per mechanismum sacramentalem formaliter explicatur.
Concordia inter providentiam divinam, quae eventus disponit, et voluntariam deviationem animae affirmatur potius quam causaliter resolvitur.
Definitio amicitiae verae per Deum cum reali vi consolatoria et bonis internis amicitiarum nondum ordinatarum tensionem servat.
Possibilitas veritates artium cognoscendi dum cognoscens ipse a lumine aversus manet distinctionem inter cognitionem localem et illuminationem sapientialem postulat, sed non plene formalizat.
Restitutio ordinem verum textus servat: confessio biographica in diagnosin amoris, ontologiae et cognitionis transit atque in reditum ad bonum incommutabile clauditur.
The text asks how keen intellect, intense friendship, and particular rectitudes could cohere with prolonged error and misery.
Created goods become pernicious not by their nature, but when the soul turned away from God loves or interprets them as stable ends.
The generative distinction opposes the immutable God to mutable creatures, truth illuminating the participating mind to love ordered to fixation upon perishable things.
The confessional argumentation is at once diagnostic, genealogical, polemical, and reconstructive.
The movement proceeds from culpable error to the death of a friend, from grief to the ontology of mutability, thence to the genealogy of intellectual error and to the order of return.
The restoration of the soul is effected not by abolishing creatures or faculties, but by referring love, knowledge, and gifts to God.
God is immutable truth and good, in whom properties do not inhere as though accidents in a subject.
Every created good, every known truth, and every intellectual faculty proceeds from God the creator.
A temporal creature consists through the succession of parts, changes, and perishes.
The human mind is mutable and shares in truth through illumination, not itself the nature of truth.
Bodily sense apprehends passing parts, not the whole at once nor an incorporeal thing.
Love binds the soul to the thing loved and seeks rest in it.
To love what will die as though it would not die establishes misery even before the loss.
True friendship exists only where God joins those who love one another in charity.
A created good is rightly loved in God and referred to the Creator, not as an end separate from him.
Proud turning away from God is the root of affective and intellectual perversity.
Bodily imagination, transferred to spiritual things, constitutes phantasms as realities.
Evil is not a substance, but a defect of movement, affection, or mutable mind.
Error and sin arise from the voluntary deviation of the creature, not from the necessity of the stars, matter, or divine substance.
Astrological correspondences can, according to the reasoning of the old physician accepted by Augustine, arise from chance rather than from the art of the stars.
Social praise can kindle the affection of the hearer, even if the thing praised itself does not change.
Quickness of understanding is a gift whose usefulness depends on right use and end, not on possession alone.
God can heal the soul through means that it itself does not yet fully understand or voluntarily choose.
Divine life incarnate assumes and conquers death, so that the human being may return from external things to God.
Particular rectitude does not constitute complete conversion if the end of action is still governed by cupidity or superstition.
Astrology does not become permissible because it seems to lack sacrifices and prayers to spirits.
Celestial necessity does not absolve the sinner from guilt.
A sacrament is not rendered ineffective by the mere absence of the recipient's conscious knowledge.
Shared studies, mutual goodwill, and delight in companionship do not by themselves suffice for true friendship.
Change of place, sensible pleasure, and literary occupation cannot enable the soul to flee from itself or radically heal pain.
No mutable creature is a place of undisturbed rest.
God is neither a luminous body nor an immense space of light.
God is not contained within the ten categories as though a subject of accidents.
Evil is neither a substance opposed to God nor a life existing in its own right.
The human mind is neither a part of the divine substance nor the immutable highest good.
Dialectical acumen and knowledge of the arts do not by themselves produce salvation or wisdom.
Love of bodies, souls, and friends is not to be abolished, but ordered.
Local rectitudes can coexist with the perversity of an entire life, because the goodness of a particular act does not necessarily alter the order of the universal end.
Astrology, transferring sin into the necessity of the stars, exculpates the human being and implicitly accuses the just Creator.
A true prediction does not prove astrological art, because a particular observation cannot distinguish the causality of the art from fortuitous correspondence.
The narrative of the friend's conversion interprets the effect of baptism as a divine operation preceding explicit knowledge.
The death of a friend does not merely remove joy, but manifests the misery already enclosed in love of the mortal as immortal.
Local flight does not remove radical pain, because the soul carries with it the order of love by which it has made itself an unhappy place for itself.
The succession of time lessens pain by replacing memories and pleasures, but friendships ordered outside God preserve the cause of future pains.
One who loves friends in God does not suffer ultimate loss, because the bond of love is founded in him who does not pass away.
The passing of parts is not a defect of the universe, but the condition by which the temporal whole is constituted through succession.
A soul not yet stably adhering to truth loves the same person differently according to the affection of those who praise, while the things themselves remain unchanged.
Bodily imagination joined with pride transfers its own mutability to God and transforms a defect of the will into a dualism of substances.
Categories useful for created things generate falsehood when divine simplicity is treated as though it were a subject of magnitude or beauty.
Intellect turned away from its source can attain local truths, but turns them into pride, metaphysical error, and ruin.
The Incarnation orders the movement of return through humble descent, victory over death, and withdrawal from exterior sight to interior presence.
Moral error, immoderate grief, superstitions, and false metaphysics are diverse effects of the same turning away that separates a created good from its source.
Conversion does not destroy love, sense, friendship, or knowledge, but reconstitutes their objects and ends according to the order of Creator and creature.
Temporal misery arises when the soul attempts to demand desired permanence from parts that pass away successively.
Possession of local truth does not entail wisdom, because rightly understood art can coexist with a false image of God and a perverse order of love.
Confession retrospectively converts errors and gifts into praise of divine mercy, because even imperfectly understood means are situated within the process of healing.
Return to God is not an autonomous ascent, but participation in the movement of Christ, who by descending conquers death and recalls the human being to interior things.
Divine providence and human guilt are retained together: God heals through events, but the soul voluntarily turns away and bears the penalty of error.
Social authority propagates error recursively, because a soul moved by the opinions of others hands down received doctrine to friends and pupils.
The soul cannot be for itself the principle of truth, stability, or salvation.
The use of a faculty cannot be assessed separately from the end of love.
No relation to a finite thing affords possession without the danger of loss.
No sensible part or created category provides a legitimate totalization of divine reality.
Guilt cannot be transferred to flesh, stars, matter, or divine substance without confession and justice being dissolved.
No principle of evil coeternal with God or substantially opposed to him is admitted.
Ascent through proud assimilation to God cannot effect return.
Friendship as a merely dyadic bond has no sufficient cause of stability.
The consensus of those who praise does not constitute a criterion of truth or intrinsic value.
No external place is available to which the soul may escape from its own heart or from the presence of God.
Permanent possession of a temporal good within the order of time itself is impossible.
No epistemic point wholly outside participation in divine light is given, even where the knower is ignorant of the source of knowledge.
Healing does not consist in the restoration of the lost past, but in the reformation of transient things under the permanent good.
The absence of God cannot be local or ontological; what appears to be absence is the turning away of the heart, which even in fleeing remains under divine law.
The autonomous stability of the subject is excluded: the soul is stable only when God is its stability.
Turning away from God generates pride; pride converts a created gift into cupidity, phantasm, and false doctrine; error thereafter reproduces itself and others.
Love of a temporal good as a stable end produces fixation; the mutability of the object brings loss; loss manifests antecedent misery; external flight sends the soul back to itself wounded.
Sense of a part produces a phantasm of the whole; the phantasm constitutes a corporeal or categorical God; the false image sustains dualism and the transfer of guilt.
Social praise kindles affection; affection substitutes for the authority of the thing; received authority reinforces false doctrine; doctrine is propagated through teacher or friend.
Divine mediation through admonition, sacrament, event, and the succession of time unsettles false security and prepares memory for further conversion.
The Incarnation through descent assumes death, through abundance of life conquers death, through visible absence recalls the heart to interior presence, and through humility restores ascent.
Confession refers the effects of present healing to past errors, extracts from them the principles of turning away, and restores misused gifts to their source.
The text moves from mutual seduction and imperfect rectitudes to astrology, whose fatalism is dissolved morally and causally.
Friendship leads to the baptism of the friend, baptism to death, death to grief, grief to flight from oneself, and the succession of time to imperfect consolation.
The experience of grief is converted into a doctrine of the mutability of creatures, the ordering of love, and rest in God.
The question of the beautiful and the fitting proceeds to dependence on praise, thence to bodily imagination, dualism, abuse of categories, and the vanity of autonomous intellect.
All lines converge upon the necessity of humble return to God as the good, truth, and stability of the soul.
Moral rectitude is described no longer through individual acts alone, but through the order of the end of the whole life.
Grief is reclassified from an accident after loss into the revelation of misery already present before loss.
Friendship is transferred from a bond of two affections into a triadic relation constituted through God.
The mutability of creatures becomes visible not as mere deficiency, but as the ordered succession of the parts of the universe.
Astrology is reclassified from a predictive discipline into a mechanism of moral exculpation and causal confusion.
Evil is transferred from an opposing substance into the corruption of mutable movements and faculties.
Beauty, friendship, and the arts are converted from autonomous ends into signifying goods to be referred to the Creator.
The opposition between outstanding intellect and simple faith collapses, because slowness of understanding with right orientation can be safer than turned-away acumen.
Conversion is redescribed from spatial movement or proud ascent into interior return through humility and divine mediation.
The surface level contains confessions of error, astrology, the death of a friend, grief, philosophical writings, and understood arts.
The structural level uncovers a single mechanism by which turning away, fixation of love, social authority, and bodily imagination corrupt affection and knowledge.
The metastrategic level changes the criterion of inquiry: no longer is it asked how much the soul understands or loves, but to what intellect and love are ordered.
The ontological and temporal level, through the distinction between immutable Creator and successively existing creature, establishes the limits of sense, love, and predication.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from the experience of error and grief to the doctrine of mutability, illumination, and ordered love.
The coherence is strongest where the death of the friend manifests the hidden structure of mortal love and where bodily imagination generates false metaphysics.
The sweetness of weeping remains explicitly indeterminate; the text proposes hypotheses, but subordinates the question to confession.
The empirical refutation of astrology relies upon the analogy of chance and does not fully furnish the certain proof that Augustine sought at that time.
The efficacy of the friend's baptism is inferred from narrative change and providential interpretation, not formally explained through a sacramental mechanism.
The concord between divine providence, which disposes events, and the voluntary deviation of the soul is affirmed rather than causally resolved.
The definition of true friendship through God retains tension with the real consolatory force and internal goods of friendships not yet ordered.

The possibility of knowing the truths of the arts while the knower himself remains turned away from light requires a distinction between local knowledge and sapiential illumination, but does not fully formalize it.
The restoration preserves the true order of the text: biographical confession passes into a diagnosis of love, ontology, and knowledge, and concludes in return to the immutable good.
Argumentatio quaerit quomodo auctoritas Manichaeorum dissolvatur et inquisitio veri ad Ecclesiam Catholicam nondum plene creditam transferatur.
Comparatio doctrinae cum ratione, experientia et exegesi ostendit Manichaeismum falsum, Catholicam autem fidem saltem defensibilem esse.
Argumentatio confessionalis, diagnostica, genealogica et reconstructiva est, quia errorem ex condicionibus epistemicis, moralibus et providentialibus resolvit.
Motus primus procedit a scientia creaturarum ad examen magistri, ab examine ad ruinam auctoritatis, a ruina ad remissionem vinculi sectarii.
Motus secundus procedit ab imaginatione corporea et excusatione culpae ad impassam doctrinalem, deinde per migrationes causis mixtis effectas ad auditionem Ambrosii.
Terminus non est plena conversio, sed desertio Manichaeorum, defensibilitas Catholica, dubitatio Academica et status catechumeni donec certius criterium elucescat.
A Deo averti non est eius praesentiam effugere, sed a se ipso discedere sub Deo semper praesente.
Confessio subiectum iam cognitum ad agnitionem culpae, laudem et sanationem convertit.
Vera de creatura per numeros, ordinem temporum et visibiles attestationes cognosci possunt.
Beatitudo non ex scientia creaturarum, sed ex cognitione, glorificatione et gratiarum actione erga Deum oritur.
Veritas et falsitas a cultu vel ruditate sermonis independent.
Confessio ignorantiae epistemice melior est quam pertinax assertio rei ignoratae.
Auctoritas plenariam praesentiam divinam sibi vindicans rationem etiam falsarum assertionum examinabilium reddere debet.
Doctrina Manichaeorum cosmologiam rationibus et observationibus adversam cum religiosis suis fabulis coniungit.
Impossibilitas substantiam spiritalem cogitandi imaginationem ad moles corporeas, dualismum et falsam fidei Catholicae effigiem cogit.
Totum ego agit et peccat; natura aliena intra hominem posita culpam eius suscipere non potest.
Reconciliatio per crucem veram incarnationem et mortem Christi, non phantasma carnis, praesupponit.
Expositio spiritalis Scripturarum objectiones ex sola litterali acceptione ortas dissolvere potest.
Possibilitas doctrinam defendendi nondum eius veritatem aut victoriam demonstrat.
Augustinus tunc censet modum verum quaerendi ab auctoritate divina petendum esse neque philosophiam sine Christo curationi animae sufficere.
Narratio retrospectiva providentiam causas externas, cupiditates perversas et actiones nescientium ad salutarem directionem ordinare affirmat.
Deus petitionem immediatam negare potest ut cardinem profundioris desiderii ordine temporali impleat.
Confessio Deum de statu confitentis non informat.
Iniquus praesentiam Dei mutatione loci effugere non potest.
Praedictio siderum et cognitio mundi neque pietatem neque beatitudinem constituunt.
Eloquium ornatum veritatem non efficit, sicut sermo incompositus falsitatem non efficit.
Ignorantia rerum naturalium per se fidem non destruit, nisi ad doctrinam pietatis referatur et pertinaciter affirmetur.
Falsitas astronomica religionis iudicium non effugit ubi tamquam auctoritate divina traditur.
Modestia Fausti circa propriam imperitiam doctrinam sectae non verificat.
Malum non est natura aliena cui peccator propriam actionem imputare possit.
Fides Catholica non est doctrina Dei figura humana corporaliter terminati.
Refutatio objectionum Manichaearum non constituit adhuc probationem plenam Catholicismi.
Dubitatio Academica permanentiam in doctrina iam infirmata non iustificat.
Negatio petitionis Monicae non significat eius orationem contemptam esse.
Comparatio cosmologiae Manichaeae cum rationibus numerorum et testimoniis visibilibus discrepantiam doctrinalem facit examinabilem.
Falsitas in rebus examinabilibus fit crisis auctoritatis, quia eadem doctrina plenitudinem divinae auctoritatis sibi vindicat.
Faustus suavitate sermonis delectare potest, sed munus magistri promissi implere nequit, cum quaestiones structurales sectae explicare non possit.
Philosophi possunt Manichaeis veriora de mundo dicere et tamen Creatorem non invenire neque ex scientia sua beati fieri.
Imaginatio omnis realitatis ut molis corporeae generat duas substantias oppositas, Christologiam phantasticam et repulsam fidei Catholicae male intellectae.
Externalizatio peccati sanationem impedit, quia subiectum quod culpam negat confessionem necessariam recusat.
Exegesis Ambrosii destruit persuasionem Scripturas omnino indefensibiles esse, sed nondum cogit Augustinum Catholicam doctrinam veram iudicare.
Manichaeismus relinquendus est, dum Ecclesia Catholica tamquam locus provisionalis inquisitionis retinetur sine assensu definitivo.
Attentio ad formam sermonis potest praeter intentionem auditorem materiae verae aperire, quia verba et res separari causaliter non semper possunt.
Licentia scholasticorum, ambitio, cupiditas lucri et auxilia Manichaeorum fiunt instrumenta migrationis quae Augustinum ad Ambrosium perducit.
Recuperatio corporis a febre non est salus perfecta, sed conservatio temporalis subiecti cui salus spiritualis postea danda est.
Petitio Monicae ne filius naviget negatur, ut desiderium eius profundius de salute filii per ipsam navigationem promoveatur.
Conversio epistemica incipit non a probatione positiva novi systematis, sed a degradatione certitudinis veteris per discrepantiam, defectum magistri et exegesim aemulam.
Rhetorica est medium causaliter efficax sed epistemice neutrum: apud Faustum errorem vestit, apud Ambrosium veritatem praeter intentionem auditoris transmittit.
Providentia non ponitur ut causa concurrens inter alias, sed ut ordinatio superior quae causas moraliter mixtas ad finem ab agentibus ignoratum dirigit.
Plena conversio requirit simul mutationem criterii epistemici, ontologiae corporis et spiritus, doctrinae responsabilitatis atque interpretationis Scripturae.
Dubitatio fit intervallum productivum inter sectam iam falsam et Ecclesiam nondum demonstratam, non autem terminus sufficiens inquisitionis.
Reditus ad Deum implicat reditum subiecti ad unitatem sui, quia alienatio a Deo, divisio culpae et recusatio confessionis eundem nexum constituunt.
Falsum esse debet doctrinam occultam ab erroribus examinabilibus immunem manere, ubi utraque eidem auctoritati divinae attribuitur.
Falsum esse debet defectum systematis sola eloquentia vel adventu magistri perfectioris sanari posse.
Falsum esse debet scientiam naturalem aut nullius valoris aut per se salutarem esse; ea vera et refutatoria esse potest sine beatitudine.
Falsum esse debet corporeitatem totum ambitum entis exhaurire.
Falsum esse debet divisionem agentis in ego innocens et naturam peccantem responsabilitatem conservare posse.
Falsum esse debet suspensionem iudicii modum quaerendi et auctoritatem veram per se praebere.
Falsum esse debet providentiam tantum per intentiones rectas, causas perspicuas et petitiones statim impletas operari.
Systema exigit ut malum neque substantia sui iuris neque pars Dei sit, quamquam huius exclusionis ontologia positiva nondum praebetur.
Conversio autonoma et sibi perfecte perspicua excluditur, quia subiectum neque causas veras itineris neque finem earum dum movetur cognoscit.
Accessus immediatus ad veritatem excluditur; creaturae, magistri, Scriptura, exegesis, Ecclesia et oratio omnes functionem mediationis exercent.
Certitudo totalis non est condicio primi motus conversionis, quia argumentatio procedit per refutationem asymmetricam et habitationem provisionalem.
Probatio positiva verae auctoritatis divinae adhuc abest, atque haec absentia statum catechumeni et continuationem quaestionis ordinat.
Aversio a Deo → caecitas → discessio a se → impossibilitas se vel Deum inveniendi, praesentia Dei tamen permanente.
Separatio eloquentiae a veritate → comparatio assertionum cum ratione et visibilibus testimoniis → detectio discrepantiae.
Discrepantia examinabilis + praetensio divina + defectus magistri promissi → ruina fidei in auctoritatem Manichaeam.
Ruina auctoritatis + imaginatio corporea + externalizatio culpae → desertio interna sectae sine possessione alternativa positiva.
Motiva perversa + pressiones externae + ordinatio providentialis → Roma → Mediolanum → accessus ad Ambrosium.
Auditio propter formam → ingressus inseparabilis rerum → exegesis spiritalis → defensibilitas Scripturae et Catholicismi.
Falsitas Manichaeorum + nondum probata victoria Catholica + insufficientia philosophiae sine Christo → dubitatio ordinata.
Dubitatio ordinata → desertio sectae → catechumenatus provisionalis → exspectatio criterii certioris.
Omnipraesentia Dei → distinctio scientiae a beatitudine → distinctio eloquentiae a veritate → examen auctoritatis Manichaeae.
Exspectatio Fausti → confessio eius imperitiae → defectus solutionis → remissio vinculi sectarii → migratio causis mixtis effecta.
Impassa imaginationis corporeae → auditio Ambrosii → dissolutio objectionum litteralium → defensibilitas Catholica → dubitatio Academica → catechumenatus.
Auctoritas religiosa denuo describitur ut examinabilis, ubi assertiones suas in agrum rationis et observationis extendit.
Veritas propositionis, forma sermonis, pietas loquentis et beatitudo cognoscentis in axes distinctos distribuuntur.
Ignorantia non amplius solo obiecto iudicatur, sed modo quo agnoscitur, occultatur aut auctoritate divina affirmatur.
Malum ab externa substantia ad divisionem et responsabilitatem subiecti reclassificatur.
Catholicismus ex caricatura corporea et scripturaliter indefensibili in candidatum rationaliter defensibilem transit.
Scepticismus ex doctrina finali in instrumentum dissolutionis et spatium transitionis convertitur.
Providentia ex interventu manifesto in ordinationem latentem causarum mixtarum et responsionum dilatarum transfertur.
Conversio ex actu singulari in seriem dissolutionis auctoritatis, mutationis ontologicae, recognitionis culpae et relocationis ecclesialis reconfiguratur.
Surface — Fausti imperitia, migratio Romam et Mediolanum, morbus, auditio Ambrosii et desertio Manichaeorum constituunt obiecta immediata.
Structural — Relatio inter auctoritatem, probationem, rhetoricam, exegesim, responsabilitatem et institutionem ecclesialem conversionem generat.
Metastrategic — Quaestio mutatur ab electione inter doctrinas ad inventionem criterii, modi quaerendi et loci provisionalis inquisitionis.
Ontological/Temporal — Argumentatio praesupponit realitatem spiritalem non spatialem, unitatem agentis moralis, providentiam supra intentiones particulares et impletionem finis per moram.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam ruinam auctoritatis Manichaeae, impassam materialisticam et transitum ad catechumenatum provisionalem.
Ontologia positiva substantiae spiritalis nondum determinatur; tantum necessitas eius et defectus imaginationis corporeae apparent.
Criterium quo vera auctoritas divina inter auctoritates aemulas agnoscatur nondum plene constituitur.
Structura firmissima est in distinctionibus inter veritatem et eloquentiam, scientiam et beatitudinem, ignorantiam confessam et falsitatem auctoritative assertam.
Commissura fragilis inter errores cosmologicos et falsitatem religionis tantum tenet quia secta utrumque sub eadem praetensione divina coniungit.
Modestia Fausti extrapolationem ab eius imperitia ad falsitatem totius sectae temperat; vis rupturae potius ex munere promisso non impleto provenit.
Eloquium tamquam criterium repudiatur, sed tamquam causa ingressus veritatis retinetur; distinctio inter valorem epistemicum et efficaciam causalem tensionem tantum partialiter solvit.
Providentia perversis causis utitur sine explicatione plena relationis inter ordinationem divinam et culpabilitatem humanam.
Restitutio verum motum servat, quia capitulum non ad conversionem completam, sed ad desertionem sectae, suspensionem iudicii et repositionem ecclesialem pervenit.
The argument seeks how the authority of the Manichaeans is dismantled and the inquiry into truth transferred to the Catholic Church, not yet fully believed.
Comparison of doctrine with reason, experience, and exegesis shows Manichaeism to be false, while the Catholic faith is at least defensible.
The argument is confessional, diagnostic, genealogical, and reconstructive, because it resolves error from epistemic, moral, and providential conditions.
