The first movement proceeds from knowledge of creatures to examination of the teacher, from examination to the collapse of authority, and from collapse to the loosening of the sectarian bond.
The second movement proceeds from bodily imagination and the excuse of guilt to a doctrinal impasse, then through migrations brought about by mixed causes to the hearing of Ambrose.

The terminus is not full conversion, but the abandonment of the Manichaeans, the defensibility of Catholicism, Academic doubt, and the status of catechumen until a more certain criterion becomes clear.
To turn away from God is not to escape His presence, but to depart from oneself beneath God ever present.
Confession turns a subject already known toward acknowledgment of guilt, praise, and healing.
Truths concerning creatures can be known through numbers, the order of times, and visible attestations.
Blessedness arises not from knowledge of creatures, but from knowledge, glorification, and thanksgiving toward God.
Truth and falsehood are independent of the refinement or roughness of speech.
Confession of ignorance is epistemically better than the stubborn assertion of an unknown matter.
An authority claiming for itself the full presence of the divine must also render its false assertions examinable by reason.
The doctrine of the Manichaeans joins a cosmology contrary to rational arguments and observations with its religious fables.
The inability to think spiritual substance compels imagination toward bodily masses, dualism, and a false image of the Catholic faith.
The whole self acts and sins; an alien nature placed within a human being cannot assume that person's guilt.
Reconciliation through the cross presupposes the true incarnation and death of Christ, not a phantom of flesh.
The spiritual exposition of the Scriptures can dissolve objections arising from a merely literal understanding.
The possibility of defending a doctrine does not yet demonstrate its truth or victory.
Augustine then judges that the true way of seeking must be obtained from divine authority and that philosophy without Christ does not suffice for the healing of the soul.
The retrospective narrative affirms that providence orders external causes, perverse desires, and the actions of the unaware toward a salvific direction.
God can deny an immediate petition in order to fulfill, in temporal order, the hinge of a deeper desire.
Confession does not inform God about the state of the one confessing.
The wicked person cannot escape God's presence by a change of place.
Prediction of the stars and knowledge of the world constitute neither piety nor blessedness.
Ornate speech does not produce truth, just as unpolished speech does not produce falsehood.
Ignorance of natural matters does not in itself destroy faith, unless it is referred to a doctrine of piety and stubbornly asserted.
Astronomical falsehood does not escape religious judgment where it is handed down as by divine authority.
Faustus's modesty concerning his own incompetence does not verify the doctrine of the sect.
Evil is not an alien nature to which the sinner can impute his own action.
The Catholic faith is not a doctrine of God as a human figure bounded bodily.
The refutation of Manichaean objections does not yet constitute a full proof of Catholicism.
Academic doubt does not justify remaining in a doctrine already weakened.
The denial of Monica's petition does not signify that her prayer was despised.
Comparison of Manichaean cosmology with numerical calculations and visible testimonies makes doctrinal discrepancy examinable.
Falsehood in examinable matters becomes a crisis of authority, because the same doctrine claims for itself the fullness of divine authority.
Faustus may delight by the sweetness of his speech, but he cannot fulfill the office of the promised teacher, since he cannot explain the structural questions of the sect.
Philosophers can say truer things about the world than the Manichaeans and yet fail to find the Creator or become blessed from their knowledge.
The imagination of all reality as bodily mass generates two opposed substances, a phantasmal Christology, and rejection of a misunderstood Catholic faith.
The externalization of sin impedes healing, because the subject who denies guilt refuses the necessary confession.
Ambrose's exegesis destroys the conviction that the Scriptures are altogether indefensible, but does not yet compel Augustine to judge Catholic doctrine true.
Manichaeism must be abandoned, while the Catholic Church is retained as a provisional place of inquiry without definitive assent.
Attention to the form of speech can, beyond intention, open the hearer to true matter, because words and things cannot always be causally separated.
The licentiousness of students, ambition, desire for gain, and Manichaean assistance become instruments of migration that bring Augustine to Ambrose.
Recovery of the body from fever is not perfect salvation, but the temporal preservation of a subject to whom spiritual salvation is later to be given.
Monica's petition that her son not sail is denied, so that her deeper desire for her son's salvation may be advanced through the very voyage.
Epistemic conversion begins not from the positive proof of a new system, but from the degradation of certainty in the old through discrepancy, the failure of the teacher, and rival exegesis.
Rhetoric is a causally effective but epistemically neutral medium: in Faustus it clothes error; in Ambrose it transmits truth beyond the hearer's intention.
Providence is not posited as one concurrent cause among others, but as a higher ordering that directs morally mixed causes toward an end unknown to the agents.
Full conversion requires at once a change of epistemic criterion, of the ontology of body and spirit, of the doctrine of responsibility, and of the interpretation of Scripture.
Doubt becomes a productive interval between a sect already false and a Church not yet demonstrated, but not a sufficient terminus of inquiry.
Return to God entails the subject's return to the unity of itself, because alienation from God, division of guilt, and refusal of confession constitute the same nexus.
It must be false that hidden doctrine remains immune from examinable errors, where both are attributed to the same divine authority.
It must be false that the defect of a system can be healed by eloquence alone or by the arrival of a more perfect teacher.
It must be false that natural knowledge is either of no value or salutary in itself; it can be true and refutatory without conferring blessedness.
It must be false that corporeality exhausts the whole scope of being.
It must be false that the division of the agent into an innocent self and a sinning nature can preserve responsibility.
It must be false that suspension of judgment can of itself provide a mode of seeking and true authority.
It must be false that providence operates only through right intentions, evident causes, and petitions fulfilled at once.
The system requires that evil be neither a self-subsisting substance nor a part of God, although the positive ontology of this exclusion is not yet provided.
Autonomous conversion, perfectly transparent to itself, is excluded, because the subject knows neither the true causes of the journey nor their end while it is moving.
Immediate access to truth is excluded; creatures, teachers, Scripture, exegesis, the Church, and prayer all perform a mediating function.
Total certainty is not the condition of the first movement of conversion, because the argument proceeds through asymmetric refutation and provisional dwelling.
Positive proof of true divine authority is still absent, and this absence orders the status of catechumen and the continuation of inquiry.
Turning away from God → blindness → departure from oneself → inability to find oneself or God, while God's presence nevertheless remains.
Separation of eloquence from truth → comparison of assertions with reason and visible testimonies → detection of discrepancy.
Examinable discrepancy + divine claim + failure of the promised teacher → collapse of faith in Manichaean authority.
Collapse of authority + bodily imagination + externalization of guilt → internal abandonment of the sect without possession of a positive alternative.
Perverse motives + external pressures + providential ordering → Rome → Milan → access to Ambrose.
Hearing because of form → inseparable entry of things → spiritual exegesis → defensibility of Scripture and Catholicism.
Falsehood of the Manichaeans + Catholic victory not yet proven + insufficiency of philosophy without Christ → ordered doubt.
Ordered doubt → abandonment of the sect → provisional catechumenate → expectation of a more certain criterion.
God's omnipresence → distinction of knowledge from blessedness → distinction of eloquence from truth → examination of Manichaean authority.
Expectation of Faustus → confession of his incompetence → failure of solution → loosening of the sectarian bond → migration produced by mixed causes.
Impasse of bodily imagination → hearing of Ambrose → dissolution of literal objections → defensibility of Catholicism → Academic doubt → catechumenate.
Religious authority is redescribed as examinable where it extends its assertions into the field of reason and observation.
The truth of a proposition, the form of speech, the piety of the speaker, and the blessedness of the knower are distributed across distinct axes.
Ignorance is no longer judged by its object alone, but by the manner in which it is acknowledged, concealed, or affirmed by divine authority.
Evil is reclassified from an external substance to the division and responsibility of the subject.
Catholicism passes from a bodily caricature and scripturally indefensible position into a rationally defensible candidate.
Skepticism is transformed from a final doctrine into an instrument of dissolution and a space of transition.
Providence is transferred from manifest intervention into a hidden ordering of mixed causes and delayed responses.
Conversion is reconfigured from a singular act into a series of the dissolution of authority, ontological change, acknowledgment of guilt, and ecclesial relocation.
Surface — Faustus's incompetence, migration to Rome and Milan, illness, the hearing of Ambrose, and abandonment of the Manichaeans constitute the immediate objects.
Structural — The relation among authority, proof, rhetoric, exegesis, responsibility, and ecclesial institution generates conversion.
Metastrategic — The question changes from choosing among doctrines to discovering a criterion, a mode of seeking, and a provisional place of inquiry.
Ontological/Temporal — The argument presupposes a non-spatial spiritual reality, the unity of the moral agent, providence above particular intentions, and fulfillment of an end through delay.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the collapse of Manichaean authority, the materialist impasse, and the transition to provisional catechumenate.
The positive ontology of spiritual substance is not yet determined; only its necessity and the defect of bodily imagination appear.
The criterion by which true divine authority is recognized among rival authorities is not yet fully established.
The firmest structure lies in the distinctions between truth and eloquence, knowledge and blessedness, confessed ignorance and falsehood authoritatively asserted.
The fragile joint between cosmological errors and the falsehood of religion holds only because the sect joins both under the same divine claim.
Faustus's modesty tempers extrapolation from his incompetence to the falsehood of the whole sect; the force of the rupture arises rather from the promised office left unfulfilled.
Eloquence is rejected as a criterion, but retained as a cause of truth's entry; the distinction between epistemic value and causal efficacy only partially resolves the tension.
Providence uses perverse causes without a full explanation of the relation between divine ordering and human culpability.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement, because the chapter reaches not complete conversion but abandonment of the sect, suspension of judgment, and ecclesial repositioning.
Textus quaerit quomodo animus, falsitate Manichaeorum liberatus sed veritati nondum assensus, ad fidem et conversionem adduci possit.
Impedimenta doctrinalia per doctrinam Ambrosii et auctoritatem Scripturae solvuntur, sed conversio differtur quia voluntas consuetudine, ambitione et concupiscentia ligatur.
Argumentatio confessionalis, diagnostica, reconstructiva et theologica eventus praeteritos tamquam operationes providentiae interpretatur.
Motus epistemicus procedit a desperatione veritatis ad dissolutionem falsae imaginis fidei catholicae, deinde ad legitimam necessitatem credendi.
Motus moralis procedit a detectione falsi gaudii ad agnitionem servitutis voluntatis et insufficientiae virium propriarum.
Casus Alypii demonstrant correctionem, captivitatem et disciplinam iudicii per mediationes ab agentibus non intentas produci posse.
Clausura non est conversio perfecta, sed constitutio condicionum quibus dilatio intolerabilis et gratia necessaria fiunt.
Deus ordinem creaturarum et eventuum providentia regit, etiam agentibus ignaris.
Anima extra Deum stabilem requiem et sanitatem invenire non potest.
Mens a Deo aversa veritatem extra se et sub imaginibus corporeis quaerit.
Doctrina catholica Deum forma humana aut spatio locali non terminat.
Apparentia litteralis Scripturae sensum spiritualem et sacramentalem non exhaurit.
Actio humana cotidiana necessario fide testium de rebus non visis innititur.
Ratio infirma ad veritatem liquidam sola pervenire non potest.
Fides auctoritate sustentata mentem ad veritatem cognoscendam purgat.
Auctoritas Scripturae per gentes diffusa voluntati divinae ut per eam Deus credatur et quaeratur attribuitur.
Bona saecularia neque verum gaudium neque securitatem stabilem praestant.
Correctio intellectus habitum cupiditatis per se non dissolvit.
Postulatio certitudinis demonstrativae ante omnem fidem impedit medicinam qua facultas cognoscendi sanatur.
Providentia verba non intenta et casus adversos in instrumenta correctionis convertere potest.
Animus propriae firmitati confidens sub impulsu sensuum et multitudinis facile capitur.
Continentia stabilisque virtus dono divino, non solis viribus propriis, constant.
Iudicium ex solis apparentiis ad damnationem innocentis labi potest.
Amicitia et honestas propter se dilectae ordinem bonorum voluptati corporali non reducibilem manifestant.
Mors et iudicium futurum dilationem conversionis in periculum practicum vertunt.
Relictus Manichaeismus non est iam adepta fides catholica.
Deus neque corpus humanum neque imago corporea in loco circumscripta est.
Littera Scripturae non est tota Scripturae significatio.
Fides catholica non definitur temeraria promissione scientiae quae postea fabulas credendas imponat.
Suspensio assensus falsitatem vitat, sed veritatem neque possidet neque sanitatem constituit.
Pietas neque voluptati rituali neque consuetudini hereditariae immobiliter adhaeret.
Hilaritas mendici non est verum gaudium, sed sollicitudo ambitiosi est etiam ab illa hilaritate remotior.
Eruditio ad placendum hominibus ordinata non est sapientia neque ministerium doctrinae.
Desiderium matrimonii Augustini non est principaliter amor ordinis coniugalis, sed continuatio concupiscentiae.
Consortium philosophicum sine renuntiatione domesticis cupiditatibus non est vita sapientiae stabilis.
Praesentia corporis clausis oculis non efficit libertatem animi a spectaculo.
Continentia non est facultas quam voluntas ex se certo possidet.
Impetus animae somniantis non est eo ipso revelatio divina.
Mors corporis non accipitur ut certa consumptio vitae animae.
Prior accusatio fidei catholicae obiectum suum non attigerat, quia figmentum corporeum pro doctrina catholica oppugnabat.

Apparens absurditas Scripturae desinit esse directa probatio falsitatis ubi interpretatio litteralis non habetur exhaustiva; interpretatio spiritualis tamen possibilitatem veritatis aperit, nondum veritatem demonstrat.
Obiectio universalis contra credere sibi contradicit, quia vita ordinaria innumeris testimoniis non inspectis necessario credit.
Fides medicinalis non cognitionem abolet, sed condicionem efficit qua intellectus infirmus ad cognitionem perduci possit.
Defectus colloquii privati cum Ambrosio correctionem non impedit, quia praedicatio publica sufficit ad dissolvendas calumnias doctrinales.
Post dissolutionem anthropomorphismi et literalismi, principale impedimentum conversionis ab intellectu ad voluntatem consuetudine ligatam transfertur.
Ambitio miseriam auget quia requiem quaerit per bona transitoria quae finem appetitus praestare non possunt.
Correctio Alypii per exemplum Circensium et captivitas eius in amphitheatro ostendunt receptionem moralem plus ab habitu et fiducia animi quam ab intentione exterioris agentis pendere.
Falsa comprehensio Alypii disciplinam iudicialem efficit, quia evidentia circumstantialis culpam manifestam simulare potest.
Propositum matrimonii et consilium vitae communis conversionem non efficiunt, quia ordinem novum instituere conantur sine radice concupiscentiae amputata.
Substitutio alterius concubinae demonstrat dolorem separationis non sanari, sed consuetudinem sub forma transitoria conservari.
Hypothesis beatitudinis ex perpetua voluptate corporali deficit, quia ipsa vita voluptuosa amicitiam gratuitam et bonum honestatis adhuc requirit.
Dilatio conversionis non est mora neutra, sed continuatio servitutis sub tempore mortis incertae.
Processus cognitionis est recursivus: aliqua fides requiritur ut mens sanetur ad iudicandum id cui ante sanationem assentiri dubitat.
Conversio epistemica conversionem moralem antecedit: falsae accusationes corruunt antequam voluntas ab obiectis suis avelli possit.
Mediatio moralis est non linearis: idem subiectum verbo fortuito corrigi, spectaculo sociali capi et adversitate ad prudentiam erudiri potest.
Honores, matrimonium et otium commune fiunt mechanismi dilationis quando appetitus saecularis sub nova dispositione servatur.
Retrospectus confessionalis casum, impedimentum, errorem et frustratum consilium intra unam ordinationem providentialem totalizat.
Incertitudo mortis interrogationem speculativam in necessitatem decisionis sub cognitione incompleta convertit.
Ratio a fide et auctoritate prorsus autonoma sufficiens esse non potest.
Recta doctrina sola voluntatem convertitam efficere non potest.
Desiderium sibi ipsi perfecte perspicuum non est, quia libido se matrimonium, ambitio se felicitatem et dilatio se prudentiam nominare potest.
Ambitus socialis moraliter neutralis non est; multitudo, amicitia et auctoritas habitum animi formant.
Auctoritas et libertas simpliciter adversae non sunt, quia auctoritas medicinalis a falsa imagine liberare potest.
Casus tamquam eventus sine ordine finali intra interpretationem confessionalem excluditur.
Tempus dilationis vacuum non est, quia consuetudinem corroborat et morti subiacet.
Bona divina et saecularia tamquam fines aequales componi non possunt.
Vera absentia Dei excluditur; absentia experta constituitur ut caecitas animae coram praesentia occulta.
Positio stabilis inter falsitatem relictam et conversionem recusatam non datur.
Subiectum se ipsum per scientiam aut voluntatem sui iuris redimere non potest.
Beatitudo intra totalitatem bonorum finitorum, etiam sine metu amissionis imaginatam, impossibilis habetur.
Certitudo transformationem antecedens indisponibilis est; postulatio eius ipsum iter transformationis claudit.
Prima operatio procedit: aversio a Deo → inquisitio exterior → imaginatio corporea → simulacrum doctrinae catholicae → accusatio falsa.
Secunda operatio procedit: praedicatio Ambrosii → remotio anthropomorphismi → exegesis spiritualis → dissolutio absurditatum apparentium → veritas possibilis sed nondum assensa.
Tertia operatio procedit: necessitas cotidiana testimonii → legitimatio credendi → auctoritas Scripturae → fides medicinalis → intellectus purgabilis.
Quarta operatio procedit: appetitus beatitudinis → honor, lucrum et connubium → anxietas → comparatio falsorum gaudiorum → detectio miseriae.
Quinta operatio procedit: clarificatio intellectus + consuetudo concupiscentiae → voluntas divisa → consilia compromissoria → procrastinatio → servitus aucta.
Sexta operatio procedit: verbum aut eventus non intentus + dispositio recipientis → correctio aut captivitas → memoria medicinalis → humilitas iudicii et fiducia Dei.
Ultima operatio procedit: mors et iudicium + insufficientia virium propriarum → clausura dilationis → necessitas gratiae → conversio imminens sed nondum effecta.
Desperatio veritatis → Manichaeismus relictus sine fide catholica → calumniae doctrinales dissolutae → credere rehabilitatum → impedimentum ad voluntatem translatum → gratia necessaria.
Appetitus beatitudinis → cursus saecularis → anxietas et falsum gaudium → consilia media → ruptura consiliorum → procrastinatio → metus mortis et iudicii.
Indoles moralis Alypii → captivitas socialis → correctio involuntaria → fiducia sui → nova captivitas → liberatio et disciplina iudicii → aptatio ad munus futurum.
Fides catholica ab obiecto quasi refutato in doctrinam nondum intellectam reclassificatur.
Oppositio inter fidem et cognitionem solvitur, quia fides fit condicio medicinalis cognitionis.
Distinctio litterae et spiritus apparentem absurditatem in quaestionem gradus interpretationis transfert.
Problema conversionis ab errore doctrinali ad habitum voluntatis et concupiscentiae relocatur.
Gaudium non amplius sola affectione mensuratur, sed fonte, obiecto et modo acquisitionis distinguitur.
Casus et influentia socialis ex circumstantiis exterioribus in mechanismos formationis moralis et providentiae convertuntur.
Honor, matrimonium et otium commune ex solutionibus possibilibus in formas dilationis sub desiderio non sanato reclassificantur.
Tempus inquisitionis ex spatio neutro deliberationis in medium servitutis crescentis sub morte incerta mutatur.
In gradu superficiei, Augustinus Manichaeismum relinquit, Ambrosium audit, fidem catholicam minus absurdum iudicat et conversionem tamen differt.
In gradu structurali, auctoritas, interpretatio, consuetudo, multitudo et disciplina providentiae intellectum atque voluntatem diversis modis formant.
In gradu metastrategico, quaestio mutatur ab exigentia demonstrationis antecedentis ad electionem auctoritatis quae mentem sanare et vitam ordinare possit.
In gradu ontologico et temporali, Deus non localis et semper praesens opponitur animae dispersae, temporali, mortali et tamen ad vitam post mortem ordinatae.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad restitutionem nexus inter correctionem doctrinalem, necessitatem fidei, servitutem voluntatis et operationem gratiae.
Restitutio verum motum servat: falsitas prius solvitur, auctoritas deinde rehabilitatur, impedimentum postremo in voluntate deprehenditur.
Pars firmissima est demonstratio quod prior polemica anthropomorphismum fictum, non doctrinam catholicam, oppugnaverat.
Nexus inter testimonium cotidianum et legitimam necessitatem credendi firmus est, sed non per se determinat cui auctoritati credendum sit.
Transitus ab auctoritate Scripturae late diffusa ad eius institutionem divinam criterio independente non plene explicatur et vi confessionali comprimitur.
Fides proponitur ut medicina rationis, sed divina auctoritas medicinae partim ex fide antecedenti in providentiam recognoscitur; circulus ut therapeuticus exhibetur, non formaliter solvitur.
Providentia eventus ordinat et tamen agentibus culpam vel meritum relinquit, sed relatio inter causalitatem divinam et responsabilitatem humanam nondum formaliter explicatur.
Obedientia Monnicae auctoritatem ecclesiasticam confirmat, sed effectus prohibitionis ex amore personali erga Ambrosium saltem partim pendet.
Matrimonium ut bonum legitimum admittitur et simul ut tegumentum libidinis fungitur; criterium utriusque usus implicite, non complete, determinatur.
Machina ad necessitatem conversionis et gratiae pervenit, non ad conversionem ipsam; haec incompletio est terminus structuralis libri, non defectus restitutionis.
The text asks how the mind, freed from Manichaean falsehood yet not having assented to truth, may be led to faith and conversion.
Doctrinal impediments are resolved through Ambrose's teaching and the authority of Scripture, but conversion is delayed because the will is bound by habit, ambition, and concupiscence.
Confessional, diagnostic, reconstructive, and theological argumentation interprets past events as operations of providence.
The epistemic movement proceeds from despair of truth to the dissolution of a false image of the Catholic faith, then to the legitimate necessity of believing.
The moral movement proceeds from the detection of false joy to recognition of the bondage of the will and the insufficiency of one's own powers.
Alypius's cases demonstrate that correction, captivity, and the discipline of judgment can be produced through mediations unintended by their agents.
The conclusion is not perfect conversion, but the establishment of conditions under which delay becomes intolerable and grace necessary.
God governs the order of creatures and events by providence, even when agents are unaware.
The soul cannot find stable rest and health outside God.
The mind turned away from God seeks truth outside itself and beneath bodily images.
Catholic doctrine does not delimit God by human form or local space.
The literal appearance of Scripture does not exhaust its spiritual and sacramental meaning.
Everyday human action necessarily rests on faith in witnesses concerning unseen things.
Weak reason cannot by itself attain clear truth.
Faith supported by authority purifies the mind for knowing truth.
The authority of Scripture, spread among the nations, is attributed to the divine will, so that through it God may be believed and sought.
Secular goods provide neither true joy nor stable security.
Correction of the intellect does not by itself dissolve the habit of desire.
The demand for demonstrative certainty before all faith obstructs the medicine by which the capacity for knowing is healed.
Providence can turn unintended words and adverse events into instruments of correction.
A mind trusting in its own firmness is easily captured under the impulse of the senses and the multitude.
Continence and steadfast virtue consist in divine gift, not in one's own powers alone.
Judgment from appearances alone can fall into the condemnation of the innocent.
Friendship and honesty loved for their own sake disclose an order of goods irreducible to bodily pleasure.
Death and future judgment turn delay in conversion into a practical danger.
Manichaeism having been abandoned is not yet Catholic faith attained.
God is neither a human body nor a bodily image circumscribed in a place.
The letter of Scripture is not the whole meaning of Scripture.
Catholic faith is not defined by a rash promise of knowledge that later imposes fables to be believed.
Suspension of assent avoids falsehood, but neither possesses truth nor establishes health.
Piety adheres immovably neither to ritual pleasure nor to hereditary custom.
The cheerfulness of the beggar is not true joy, but the anxiety of the ambitious man is still further removed even from that cheerfulness.
Learning ordered toward pleasing men is neither wisdom nor a ministry of teaching.
Augustine's desire for marriage is not principally love of the order of marriage, but the continuation of concupiscence.
A philosophical fellowship without renouncing domestic desires is not a stable life of wisdom.
The presence of the body with closed eyes does not effect the mind's freedom from the spectacle.
Continence is not a capacity that the will certainly possesses of itself.
The impulse of the dreaming soul is not thereby a divine revelation.
The death of the body is not received as the certain extinction of the soul's life.
The earlier accusation against the Catholic faith had not reached its object, because it attacked a bodily fabrication in place of Catholic doctrine.

The apparent absurdity of Scripture ceases to be direct proof of falsehood when literal interpretation is not held exhaustive; spiritual interpretation nevertheless opens the possibility of truth, not yet demonstrating truth.
The universal objection against believing contradicts itself, because ordinary life necessarily trusts countless unexamined testimonies.
Medicinal faith does not abolish knowledge, but makes possible the condition in which weak intellect can be led to knowledge.
The lack of private conversation with Ambrose does not impede correction, because public preaching suffices to dissolve doctrinal calumnies.
After the dissolution of anthropomorphism and literalism, the principal impediment to conversion is transferred from the intellect to the will bound by habit.
Ambition increases misery because it seeks rest through transitory goods that cannot provide the end of desire.

Alypius's correction through the example of the Circus Games and his captivity in the amphitheater show that moral reception depends more on habit and confidence of mind than on the intention of the external agent.
Alypius's false apprehension produces judicial discipline, because circumstantial evidence can simulate manifest guilt.
The intention of marriage and the plan of common life do not effect conversion, because they attempt to establish a new order without the root of concupiscence having been cut off.
The substitution of another concubine demonstrates that the pain of separation is not healed, but that habit is preserved under a transitory form.
The hypothesis of happiness from perpetual bodily pleasure fails, because even the pleasurable life itself still requires gratuitous friendship and the good of honesty.
Delay in conversion is not neutral postponement, but continuation of bondage under the time of uncertain death.
The process of knowledge is recursive: some faith is required for the mind to be healed so as to judge that to which it doubts whether to assent before healing.
Epistemic conversion precedes moral conversion: false accusations collapse before the will can be torn away from its objects.
Moral mediation is non-linear: the same subject can be corrected by a chance word, captured by a social spectacle, and instructed in prudence by adversity.
Honors, marriage, and common leisure become mechanisms of delay when secular desire is preserved under a new arrangement.
Confessional retrospection totalizes chance, impediment, error, and frustrated plan within a single providential ordering.
The uncertainty of death transforms speculative inquiry into the necessity of decision under incomplete knowledge.
Reason wholly autonomous from faith and authority cannot be sufficient.
Right doctrine alone cannot bring about a converted will.
Desire is not perfectly transparent to itself, because lust can call itself marriage, ambition can call itself happiness, and delay can call itself prudence.
The social environment is not morally neutral; the multitude, friendship, and authority shape the habit of the mind.
Authority and freedom are not simply opposed, because medicinal authority can liberate from a false image.
Chance as an event without final order is excluded within confessional interpretation.
The time of delay is not empty, because it reinforces habit and is subject to death.
Divine and secular goods cannot be composed as equal ends.
The true absence of God is excluded; experienced absence is constituted as the soul's blindness before hidden presence.
No stable position is given between abandoned falsehood and refused conversion.
The subject cannot redeem itself through knowledge or self-governing will.
Happiness within the totality of finite goods, even imagined without fear of loss, is held impossible.
Certainty preceding transformation is unavailable; its demand closes the very path of transformation.
The first operation proceeds: turning away from God → external inquiry → bodily imagination → simulacrum of Catholic doctrine → false accusation.
The second operation proceeds: Ambrose's preaching → removal of anthropomorphism → spiritual exegesis → dissolution of apparent absurdities → truth possible but not yet assented to.
The third operation proceeds: everyday necessity of testimony → legitimation of believing → authority of Scripture → medicinal faith → intellect capable of purification.
The fourth operation proceeds: desire for happiness → honor, profit, and marriage → anxiety → comparison of false joys → detection of misery.
The fifth operation proceeds: clarification of intellect + habit of concupiscence → divided will → compromising plans → procrastination → increased bondage.
The sixth operation proceeds: unintended word or event + disposition of the recipient → correction or captivity → medicinal memory → humility of judgment and trust in God.
The final operation proceeds: death and judgment + insufficiency of one's own powers → closure of delay → necessity of grace → conversion imminent but not yet effected.
Despair of truth → Manichaeism abandoned without Catholic faith → doctrinal calumnies dissolved → believing rehabilitated → impediment transferred to the will → grace necessary.
Desire for happiness → secular career → anxiety and false joy → intermediate plans → collapse of plans → procrastination → fear of death and judgment.
Alypius's moral character → social captivity → involuntary correction → self-confidence → new captivity → liberation and discipline of judgment → adaptation to a future office.
Catholic faith is reclassified from an object seemingly refuted into a doctrine not yet understood.
The opposition between faith and knowledge is dissolved, because faith becomes a medicinal condition of knowledge.
The distinction between letter and spirit transfers apparent absurdity into a question of the level of interpretation.
The problem of conversion is relocated from doctrinal error to the habit of will and concupiscence.
Joy is no longer measured by affection alone, but distinguished by source, object, and mode of acquisition.
Chance and social influence are transformed from external circumstances into mechanisms of moral formation and providence.
Honor, marriage, and common leisure are reclassified from possible solutions into forms of delay under unhealed desire.
The time of inquiry is transformed from a neutral space of deliberation into a medium of growing bondage under uncertain death.
At the surface level, Augustine abandons Manichaeism, listens to Ambrose, judges the Catholic faith less absurd, and nevertheless delays conversion.
At the structural level, authority, interpretation, habit, the multitude, and the discipline of providence form intellect and will in different ways.
At the metastrategic level, the question changes from the demand for prior demonstration to the choice of an authority able to heal the mind and order life.
At the ontological and temporal level, the non-local and ever-present God is opposed to the scattered, temporal, mortal soul, yet one ordered toward life after death.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the connection between doctrinal correction, the necessity of faith, the bondage of the will, and the operation of grace.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement: falsehood is first dissolved, authority is then rehabilitated, and the impediment is finally discovered in the will.
The strongest part is the demonstration that the earlier polemic had attacked a fictitious anthropomorphism, not Catholic doctrine.
The connection between everyday testimony and the legitimate necessity of believing is firm, but does not by itself determine which authority should be believed.
The transition from the widely diffused authority of Scripture to its divine institution is not fully explained by an independent criterion and is compressed by confessional force.

Faith is proposed as the medicine of reason, but the divine authority of the medicine is recognized partly from prior faith in providence; the circle is presented as therapeutic, not formally resolved.
Providence orders events and yet leaves agents blame or merit, but the relation between divine causality and human responsibility is not yet formally explained.
Monnica's obedience confirms ecclesiastical authority, but the effect of the prohibition depends at least in part on her personal love for Ambrose.
Marriage is admitted as a legitimate good and at the same time functions as a covering for lust; the criterion of either use is determined implicitly, not completely.
The mechanism arrives at the necessity of conversion and grace, not at conversion itself; this incompleteness is the structural terminus of the book, not a defect of reconstruction.
Textus solvere conatur quomodo malum esse possit, si Deus est incommutabile summum bonum et omnium naturarum creator.
Malum constituitur non substantia, sed privatio boni et perversio voluntatis a bono superiore ad inferiora.
Argumentatio diagnostica, reductiva et reconstructiva exemplaria corporea, dualistica, astrologica et intellectualistica successive excludit.
Motus primus a contradictionibus incorruptibilitatis Dei ad reiectionem substantiae malae et causalitatis astralis procedit.
Motus secundus ab interiori ascensu ad veritatem incorpoream transit, deinde ex infirmitate adhesionis necessitatem mediationis elicit.
Clausura Platonicam cognitionem patriae a Christiana via humilitatis, gratiae et liberationis distinguit.
Deus summum et optimum bonum est.
Incorruptibile ac incommutabile corruptibili ac mutabili verissime praeferuntur.
Voluntas et potentia Dei idem sunt.
Nulla natura est nisi a Deo creata.
Quidquid est, inquantum est, bonum est.
Corruptio non nocet nisi bonum minuendo.
Omnimoda privatio boni rei esse aufert.
Creaturae finitae, mutabiles et inaequales unum ordinem constituunt.
Res parti non conveniens potest in se bona et alteri parti congrua esse.
Voluntas propria eadem certitudine cognoscitur qua vita propria.
Culpa actui voluntario, poena passioni involuntariae competit.
Iudicium de mutabilibus normam incommutabilem supra mentem mutabilem requirit.
Veritas incommutabilis neque spatiis continetur neque a mente creata efficitur.
Conspectus veritatis non sufficit ad stabilem veritatis fruitionem.
Superbia et consuetudo carnalis mentem a viso bono retrahunt.
Libri Platonicorum aeternitatem Verbi ostendunt, incarnationis autem humilitatem et redemptionem non tradunt.
Incarnatio Christi et gratia Scripturarum intellectum humiliant, sanant et ad fruitionem ducunt.
Eadem astrorum configuratio cum contrariis vitae eventibus componi potest.
Deus neque figura humana neque corpus per infinita spatia diffusum est.
Spatiis carere non idem est ac nihil esse.
Natura tenebrarum Deo coaeterna aut nociva constitui non potest.
Malum ex materia increata quam Deus corrigere non potuerit oriri non potest.
Divinatio astrologica ars causaliter certa non est.
Inconvenientia localis creaturam malam secundum substantiam non facit.
Cognitio Platonicorum neque salutem neque stabilem Dei fruitionem per se confert.
Christus non est tantum homo sapientissimus perfectiore participatione praeditus.
Christus non est Deus carne indutus sine anima et mente humana.
Falsitas non est res creata, sed aestimatio qua aliquid putatur esse quod non est.
Deus corrumpi, violari aut mutari nullo modo potest; alioquin aliquid eo melius cogitari posset.
Certamen Manichaeum aut Deum corruptibilem facit aut causam certaminis tollit.
Malum substantia esse non potest, quia omnis substantia aliquod bonum habet.
Creaturae esse participant: sunt quia a Deo sunt, sed non sunt ipsum esse quia mutabiles sunt.
Iniquitas est voluntatis aversio a summo bono et conversio ad inferiora.
Mala particularia bonitatem universi non destruunt, quia eadem res alibi congrua et in se bona esse potest.
Ascensus a sensibilibus ad mentem iudicantem veritatem incommutabilem demonstrat, sed infirmitatem contemplantis non sanat.
Platonici terminum itineris ostendunt, Christus autem et gratia viam, robur et adhesionem praebent.
Vera astrologorum praedictio arti attribui non potest, ubi eadem signa eventus contrarios patiuntur.
Theoria mali tres gradus componit: malum ontologice est privatio, moraliter voluntatis perversio, poenaliter passio iusto iudicio ordinata.
Reiectio dualismi et determinismi simul bonitatem creatoris et responsabilitatem creaturae tuetur.
Cognitio salutaris duplicem operationem requirit: veritatem conspicere et subiectum sanari ut visae veritati adhaereat.
Incarnatio veritatem ontologice superiorem in viam anthropologice congruam convertit, quia humilitas superbiam sanat et infirmum ad superiora levat.
Ordo universalis omnem discordiam creatam intra bonitatem totius includit et exterioritatem ontologicam mali excludit.
Creatio non succedit otio divino intra tempus, quia ipsa temporum spatia ab operatione manentis Dei dependent.
Falsum esse oportet esse et spatialiter extendi converti.
Falsum esse oportet praesentiam Dei corporibus secundum magnitudinem dividi.
Falsum esse oportet creaturam inferiorem posse summum bonum invito Deo mutare.
Falsum esse oportet malum rationem positivam sui in aliqua natura habere.
Falsum esse oportet mentem mutabilem autonomam mensuram veritatis esse.
Falsum esse oportet cognitionem termini facultatem perveniendi et permanendi secum ferre.
Falsum esse oportet causas astrales culpam a voluntate ad ordinem externum transferre posse.
Falsum esse oportet displicentiam partis iudicium sufficiens de bonitate totius praebere.
Systema nullum ontologicum extra ordinem a Deo creatum admittit unde malum irruere possit.
Systema transitum a ratione superba ad stabilem Dei possessionem sine humiliatione et mediatione praecludit.
Systema causam positivam primae voluntatis malae admittere non potest, quia talis causa aut natura bona esset aut dualismum restitueret.
Ante tempus et extra creaturam nulla regio substantialis relinquitur in qua Deus, materia et malum quasi res coordinatae collocentur.
Machina invariantes statuit: Deus est summum bonum, incorruptibilis, omnipotens et creator omnis naturae.
Exemplaria corporea, dualistica et astrologica contra invariantes probantur atque contradictione eliminantur.
Iter cognitionis a sensibilibus per animam et rationem ad normam incommutabilem supra mentem ascendit.
Esse a Deo derivatum bonitatem implicat; corruptio bonum minuit; privatio totalis esse tollit; igitur malum substantia non est.
Malum morale localizatur in motu voluntatis quo subiectum a superiore ordine ad inferiora detorquetur.
Inconvenientiae particulares in ordinem totius referuntur, quo bonitas creaturarum sine aequalitate earum servatur.
Visio veritatis infirmitatem contemplantis detegit; infirmitas superbiam et consuetudinem indicat; haec diagnosis mediationem humilem requirit.
Veritas Platonica a Scriptura recipitur, sed per incarnationem, confessionem et gratiam in viam liberationis convertitur.

Motus principalis procedit: imaginatio corporea → contradictio incorruptibilitatis → reiectio dualismi → quaestio voluntatis → ascensus ad veritatem incorpoream → definitio mali ut privationis → insufficientia visionis → Christus mediator → gratia Paulina.
Submotus astrologicus procedit: eadem signa → eventus contrarii → defectus artis → restitutio causalitatis voluntariae et providentiae occultae.
Infinitas Dei a magnitudine spatiali ad eminentiam incorpoream et causalitatem omnitenentem transfertur.
Malum ex genere substantiarum in genus privationum et motuum voluntatis reclassificatur.
Interrogatio unde malum ab origine materialis rei ad defectionem agentis voluntarii convertitur.
Oppositio bonum–malum ut conflictus duarum naturarum corruit et ordine graduum boni substituitur.
Philosophia et revelatio non ut duae cosmologiae aequales, sed ut visio termini et via sanans distinguuntur.
Cognitio dividitur in demonstrationem obiecti, capacitatem videndi et facultatem permanendi in viso.
Astrologia a causa rerum ad coniecturam sine potestate explicativa reclassificatur.
Haeresis fit instrumentum differentiale quo limites doctrinae de Christo manifestantur.
Gradus superficiei continet quaestionem originis mali, dissolutionem opinionum priorum et transitum a Platonicis ad Paulum.
Gradus structuralis componit participationem essendi, corruptionem ut privationem, ordinem universi et voluntatem ut locum culpae.
Gradus metastrategicus discernit inter doctrinam quae obiectum ostendit et mediationem quae subiectum ad obiectum idoneum efficit.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis verum esse in immutabilitate collocat, creaturas participatione subsistere statuit et tempora operationi Dei subordinat.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad reicienda exemplaria corporea et dualistica, ad malum privative definiendum et ad mediationem Christi introducendam.
Structura interne cohaeret dum gradus ontologicus, moralis et poenalis mali distincti manent.
Firmissimae commissurae sunt reductio Manichaeorum et deductio qua substantia mali ex logica corruptionis excluditur.
Origo primae voluntatis malae nondum plene determinatur: perversio voluntatis describitur, sed causa primae defectionis positiva non redditur.
Bonitas universi praesupponit omnes inconvenientias particulares in ordine totali congruentiam habere, quam textus exemplis confirmat sed universaliter non demonstrat.
Tractatio astrologiae inter sortem et occultam providentiam tensionem servat, nisi sors ad solum defectum artis humanae restringatur.
Transitus a visione intellectuali ad necessitatem mediatoris experientia infirmitatis firmatur potius quam deductione ontologica completa.
Distinctio inter Verbum immutabile et totum hominem in Christo limites errorum constituit, sed modum unionis nondum formaliter explicat.
Restitutio motum verum servat: exclusio falsarum ontologiarum praecedit theoriam privationis, quam sequitur correctio soteriologica intellectus.
The text endeavors to resolve how evil can exist if God is the immutable highest good and creator of all natures.
Evil is constituted not as a substance, but as a privation of good and a perversion of the will from the higher good toward lower things.
The diagnostic, reductive, and reconstructive argument successively excludes corporeal, dualistic, astrological, and intellectualist models.
The first movement proceeds from the contradictions of God's incorruptibility to the rejection of evil substance and astral causality.
The second movement passes from an inward ascent to incorporeal truth, then infers from the weakness of adhesion the necessity of mediation.
The conclusion distinguishes Platonic knowledge of the homeland from the Christian way of humility, grace, and liberation.
God is the highest and best good.
The incorruptible and immutable are most truly preferred to the corruptible and mutable.
God's will and power are the same.
No nature exists unless created by God.
Whatever is, insofar as it is, is good.
Corruption harms only by diminishing good.
The complete privation of good removes a thing's being.
Finite, mutable, and unequal creatures constitute one order.
A thing unsuitable to one part can be good in itself and fitting to another part.
One's own will is known with the same certainty as one's own life.
Fault belongs to voluntary action, punishment to involuntary suffering.
Judgment concerning mutable things requires an immutable norm above the mutable mind.
Immutable truth is neither contained by spaces nor produced by a created mind.
The sight of truth does not suffice for stable enjoyment of truth.
Pride and carnal habit draw the mind back from the good it has seen.
The books of the Platonists show the eternity of the Word, but do not convey the humility of the incarnation and redemption.
The incarnation of Christ and the grace of the Scriptures humble, heal, and lead the understanding to enjoyment.
The same configuration of the stars can coincide with contrary events of life.
God is neither a human figure nor a body diffused through infinite spaces.
To lack spatial extension is not the same as to be nothing.
A nature of darkness coeternal with God or harmful to God cannot be posited.
Evil cannot arise from uncreated matter that God could not correct.
Astrological divination is not a causally certain art.
Local unsuitability does not make a creature evil according to substance.
Knowledge of the Platonists confers neither salvation nor stable enjoyment of God by itself.
Christ is not merely a most wise man endowed with more perfect participation.
Christ is not God clothed in flesh without a human soul and mind.
Falsehood is not a created thing, but an estimation by which something is thought to be that is not.
God can in no way be corrupted, violated, or changed; otherwise something better than him could be conceived.
The Manichaean conflict either makes God corruptible or removes the cause of the conflict.
Evil cannot be a substance, because every substance has some good.
Creatures participate in being: they are because they are from God, but they are not being itself because they are mutable.
Iniquity is the will's turning away from the highest good and turning toward lower things.
Particular evils do not destroy the goodness of the universe, because the same thing can be fitting elsewhere and good in itself.
The ascent from sensible things to the mind judging demonstrates immutable truth, but does not heal the weakness of the contemplator.
The Platonists show the destination of the journey, but Christ and grace provide the way, strength, and adhesion.
A true prediction by astrologers cannot be attributed to their art where the same signs admit contrary events.
The theory of evil combines three levels: ontologically, evil is privation; morally, a perversion of the will; penally, suffering ordered by just judgment.
The rejection of dualism and determinism simultaneously preserves the goodness of the creator and the responsibility of the creature.
Salvific knowledge requires a twofold operation: to behold truth and for the subject to be healed so as to adhere to the truth beheld.
The incarnation converts ontologically higher truth into an anthropologically fitting way, because humility heals pride and raises the weak toward higher things.
The universal order includes every created discord within the goodness of the whole and excludes the ontological exteriority of evil.
Creation does not succeed divine repose within time, because the very intervals of times depend upon the operation of the abiding God.
It must be false that to be is convertible with being spatially extended.
It must be false that God's presence in bodies is divided according to magnitude.
It must be false that a lower creature can change the highest good against God's will.
It must be false that evil has a positive rationale of itself in any nature.
It must be false that the mutable mind is an autonomous measure of truth.
It must be false that knowledge of the destination carries with it the capacity to arrive and remain there.
It must be false that astral causes can transfer fault from the will to an external order.
It must be false that the displeasure of a part provides a sufficient judgment concerning the goodness of the whole.
The system admits no ontological outside beyond the order created by God from which evil could break in.
The system precludes passage from proud reason to stable possession of God without humbling and mediation.
The system cannot admit a positive cause of the first evil will, because such a cause would either be a good nature or restore dualism.
Before time and outside creation, no substantial region remains in which God, matter, and evil might be placed as though coordinated things.
The engine establishes invariants: God is the highest good, incorruptible, omnipotent, and creator of every nature.
Corporeal, dualistic, and astrological models are tested against the invariants and eliminated by contradiction.
The path of knowledge ascends from sensible things through soul and reason to an immutable norm above the mind.
Being derived from God entails goodness; corruption diminishes good; total privation removes being; therefore evil is not a substance.
Moral evil is localized in the movement of the will by which the subject is twisted from the higher order toward lower things.
Particular unsuitabilities are referred to the order of the whole, through which the goodness of creatures is preserved without their equality.
The vision of truth reveals the weakness of the contemplator; weakness indicates pride and habit; this diagnosis requires humble mediation.
Platonic truth is received from Scripture, but through incarnation, confession, and grace is converted into a way of liberation.

The principal movement proceeds: corporeal imagination → contradiction of incorruptibility → rejection of dualism → question of the will → ascent to incorporeal truth → definition of evil as privation → insufficiency of vision → Christ the mediator → Pauline grace.
The astrological submovement proceeds: same signs → contrary events → failure of the art → restoration of voluntary causality and hidden providence.
God's infinity is transferred from spatial magnitude to incorporeal eminence and all-sustaining causality.
Evil is reclassified from the genus of substances into the genus of privations and movements of the will.
The question whence evil is converted from the origin of a material thing to the falling away of a voluntary agent.
The opposition good–evil as a conflict of two natures collapses and is replaced by an order of degrees of good.
Philosophy and revelation are distinguished not as two equal cosmologies, but as a vision of the destination and a healing way.
Knowledge is divided into demonstration of the object, capacity to see, and ability to remain in what is seen.
Astrology is reclassified from a cause of things to conjecture without explanatory power.
Heresy becomes a differential instrument through which the boundaries of doctrine concerning Christ are made manifest.
The surface level contains the question of the origin of evil, the dissolution of prior opinions, and the transition from the Platonists to Paul.
The structural level combines participation in being, corruption as privation, the order of the universe, and the will as the locus of fault.
The metastrategic level discerns between doctrine that shows the object and mediation that renders the subject suited to the object.
The ontological and temporal level locates true being in immutability, establishes that creatures subsist by participation, and subordinates times to God's operation.
The axioms suffice to reject corporeal and dualistic models, to define evil privatively, and to introduce the mediation of Christ.
The structure coheres internally so long as the ontological, moral, and penal levels of evil remain distinct.
The strongest joints are the reduction of the Manichaeans and the deduction by which the substance of evil is excluded from the logic of corruption.
The origin of the first evil will is not yet fully determined: the perversion of the will is described, but no positive cause of the first falling away is given.
The goodness of the universe presupposes that all particular unsuitabilities have fittingness in the total order, which the text confirms by examples but does not demonstrate universally.
The treatment of astrology retains a tension between chance and hidden providence, unless chance is restricted to the mere failure of human art.
The transition from intellectual vision to the necessity of a mediator is strengthened by the experience of weakness rather than by a complete ontological deduction.
The distinction between the immutable Word and the whole human being in Christ establishes the limits of errors, but does not yet formally explain the mode of union.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement: the exclusion of false ontologies precedes the theory of privation, which is followed by the soteriological correction of the understanding.
Textus quaerit quomodo homo de Deo iam certus vitam temporalem mutare nequeat et qua operatione voluntas divisa ad conversionem integram perducatur.
Conversio non ut acquisitio novae doctrinae, sed ut sanatio et liberatio voluntatis consuetudine divisae per gratiam constituitur.
Argumentatio confessionalis simul est reconstructiva, genealogica, diagnostica, polemica adversus dualismum Manichaeum et strategica circa exemplorum vim.
Motus procedit a certitudine metaphysica ad impotentiam practicam, ab exemplis alienarum conversionum ad sui accusationem, atque a genealogia consuetudinis ad discrimen voluntatis.
Conflictus interior in unius animae voluntates partiales resolvitur, ne in duas naturas vel substantias contrarias transferatur.
Crisis consummatur cum admonitio exterior per Scripturam in praeceptum personale recipitur, dubitatio solvitur et voluntas ad renuntiationem temporalium integratur.
Augustino iam certum est omnem substantiam a Deo incorruptibili per Verbum provenire.
Certitudo de Deo per se nec stabilitatem in Deo nec rectam institutionem vitae temporalis efficit.
Eadem anima potest bonum aeternum veritate praeponere et bonum temporale familiaritate retinere.
Voluntas perversa generat libidinem, libido consuetudinem, consuetudo non repugnata necessitatem servitutis.
Vis consuetudinis praesens ex voluntariis actibus orta est atque involuntariam passionem cum imputabilitate coniungit.
Contrariae voluntates sunt partes incompletae unius voluntatis aegrotantis, non operationes duarum naturarum.
In actu qui sola voluntate perficitur, integre velle est iam facere.
Gratia Dei per Iesum Christum sola catenam consuetudinis rumpit et voluntatem sanat.
Narrationes conversionum alienarum sunt media quibus Deus imitationem accendit, excusationes dissolvit et subiectum sibi ipsi opponit.
Conversio Victorini per publicam professionem ecclesialem timorem auctoritatis paganae vincit et fidem socialiter agnoscibilem facit.
Plena Augustini conversio secum fert abdicationem spei saecularis et consilii coniugalis, non solam mutationem opinionis.
Gaudium creaturae de re perdita ac reddita augetur secundum magnitudinem praecedentis periculi vel molestiae, Deo tamen invariabili.
Conversio hominis late noti maiorem effectum communem producit quia plures movet et pluribus exemplum praebet.
Admonitio Scripturae, cum ut sibi divinitus directa recipitur, potest voluntati praeceptum determinatum et securitatem finalem praebere.
Mora conversionis non amplius ex incertitudine veritatis explicatur.
Duae voluntates adversantes duas animas vel naturas contrarias non probant.
Omnis deliberatio non est certamen inter principium bonum et principium malum, quia voluntates plures omnes bonae vel omnes malae esse possunt.
Consuetudo non est vis ab agente origine aliena.
Involuntaria consuetudinis violentia agentem ab antecedenti responsabilitate non eximit.
Conversio non est motus localis aut opus corporis, sed integratio voluntatis.
Eruditio, eloquentia et dignitas socialis conversionem neque efficiunt neque eius mensuram constituunt.
Sola praesentia intra parietes ecclesiae Christianum non constituit.
Fides secreta quae confessionem metu hominum recusat formam publicae conversionis nondum implet.
Maius gaudium de nobili converso non oritur ex maiori dignitate personae coram Deo.
Coniugium universaliter prohibitum non est, quamquam continentia Augustino ut via melior proponitur.
Continentia propria subiecti virtute effici non potest.
Formulae morae, velut promissum conversionis futurae, non sunt decisionis initium determinatum, sed continuatio servitutis.
Sublata dubitatione metaphysica, impedimentum conversionis ex ordine cognitionis ad ordinem voluntatis transfertur.
Subiectum catenam patitur quam ipse per actus antecedentes fabricavit; servitus igitur simul est passio praesens et effectus culpae praeteritae.
Conflictus carnis et spiritus exprimit inaequalem unius animae adhaesionem bonis contrariis, non divisionem substantiae.
Exempla Victorini, Antonii et aulicorum demonstrant conversionem statim possibilem esse atque vetustatem excusationum Augustini in accusationem sui convertunt.
Gratia voluntatem non substituit, sed eam ab incomplete volendo ad actum integralem perducit.
Publica conversio personae auctoritate praeditae instrumenta pristinae dominationis in instrumenta confessionis et imitationis convertit.
Maius gaudium de Victorino ex magnitudine liberationis et multiplicatione effectuum nascitur, non ex favore divitibus aut nobilibus concesso.
Liberatio gratiae veritatem cognitam in novum ordinem vitae temporalis traducit.
Exemplum Antonii praebet formam interpretativam qua vox fortuita et lectio occurrens in admonitionem divinam personalem convertuntur.
Psychologia moralis textus temporaliter construitur: idem subiectum per actus suos sedimentatur, dividitur et sanatur, sine mutatione in duas substantias.
Responsabilitas et dependentia a gratia non excluduntur: homo causam servitutis participat, sed principium liberationis sibi solus praebere nequit.
Conversio est eventus punctiformis ex longa accumulatione mediationum ortus: exempla, pudor, autoaccusatio et Scriptura ad unum actum integrum comprimuntur.
Conversio efficit circuitum exemplaritatis: conversus publice visibilis alios accendit, quorum conversio gaudium et vim imitativam ulterius multiplicat.
Scriptura vim decisivam non tantum ex significatione generali, sed ex receptione temporali ut verbum nunc subiecto directum acquirit.
Dilatio non conservat statum neutrum, sed consuetudinem veterem roborat; momentum conversionis ideo oppositionem inter nunc et indefinitum postea instituit.
Ratio doctrinaliter illuminata non est causa sufficiens actionis rectae.
Malum morale non requirit substantiam malam, alteram mentem aut principium ontologice contrarium.
Necessitas consuetudinis non est necessitas naturalis ab initio data.
Gratia non est coactio externa quae voluntatem supervacaneam reddit.
Conversio mere privata et socialiter invisibilis non complet formam confessionis quam exempla textus postulant.
Mora deliberativa non est innocentia, quia ipsa retentio veteris vitae effectum electionis habet.
Continentia non est mera sterilitas vel subtractio voluptatis, sed forma fecundae vitae in Deo.
Variatio gaudii in creaturis mutationem scientiae aut essentiae divinae non implicat.
Nullum ego neutrum extra voluntates contendentes stat; subiectum in utraque adest, quamquam se magis cum voluntate approbata identificat.
Nullus terminus stabilis inter conversionem et non-conversionem datur, quia voluntas semiplena actum qui integrum velle requirit perficere nequit.
Voluntas non possidet fundamentum autonomum ex quo se ipsam a propria divisione extrahat.
Futurum indefinitum non praebet spatium conversioni reservatum, sed praesentem recusationem abscondit.
Salus non clauditur intra conscientiam singularem, quia confessio, exemplum, auctoritas et gaudium ecclesiale ad ipsam operationem conversionis pertinent.
Prima operatio dissonantiam constituit: certitudo de Deo → instabilitas vitae → translatio quaestionis a cognitione ad voluntatem.
Secunda operatio servitutem genealogice generat: voluntas perversa → libido → consuetudo → necessitas → voluntas divisa.
Tertia operatio exempla in iudicium sui convertit: narratio alienae conversionis → possibilitas praesentis mutationis → ruina excusationum → pudor.
Quarta operatio conflictum ontologice restringit: voluntates adversantes → partialitas utriusque → una anima aegrotans → exclusio dualismi.
Quinta operatio limen decisionis producit: autoaccusatio → exhaustio argumentorum → horror amissionis consuetudinis → incapax voluntas semiplena → imploratio liberationis.
Sexta operatio voluntatem claudit: vox admonens → exemplar Antonii → lectio apostolica → praeceptum personale → securitas → actus integer.
Ultima operatio eventum socialiter stabilit: renuntiatio temporalium → communicatio Alypio et Monicae → gaudium commune → incorporatio ecclesialis.

Motus principalis est: certitudo metaphysica → displicentia vitae temporalis → exempla conversionis → autoaccusatio → diagnosis voluntatis divisae → gratia mediata per Scripturam → voluntas integra → renuntiatio et gaudium ecclesiale.
Ramus polemicus est: experientia voluntatum contrariarum → experimenta plurium voluntatum bonarum vel malarum → impossibilitas binarii dualismi → una anima variis desideriis distenta.
Ramus socialis est: fides secreta → confessio publica → victoria super timorem auctoritatis → gaudium multitudinis → auctoritas conversa in exemplum salutis.
Quaestio conversionis ex oppositione inter fidem et incredulitatem ad oppositionem inter veritatem cognitam et voluntatem non integram transfertur.
Consuetudo denuo describitur ut necessitas historice a subiecto producta, non ut natura fixa aut vis omnino externa.
Conflictus interior ex argumento pro dualismo in indicium partialitatis unius animae reclassificatur.
Professio publica non ut ornamentum fidei privatae, sed ut ruptura timoris socialis et effectus conversionis visibilis apparet.
Nobilitas convertitur ex privilegio spirituali in facultatem multiplicandi exemplum, testimonium et gaudium commune.
Scriptura ex deposito propositionum in eventum allocutionis temporalis et personalis reordinatur.
Tempus deliberationis ex spatio neutro in mechanismum servitutis mutatur, dum nunc decisivum indefinito postea opponitur.
Gradus superficiei conversionem Augustini ex conflictibus, narrationibus, lacrimis, lectione apostolica et renuntiatione saeculari exhibet.
Gradus structuralis mechanismum quo voluntas consuetudinem gignit, consuetudo voluntatem dividit et exempla divisionem intolerabilem faciunt explicat.
Gradus metastrategicus confessionem publicam, auctoritatem socialem et narrationem exemplarem in instrumenta propagationis conversionis transformat.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis unam animam creatam, malum non substantializatum, Deum invariabilem, habitum sedimentatum et conversionem ut transitum decisivum inter vetus et novum constituit.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad motum a certitudine sine conversione ad voluntatem per gratiam integratam restituendum.
Structura firmissima est genealogia voluntatis perversae, libidinis, consuetudinis et necessitatis, cum analysi voluntatum partialium coniuncta.
Systema interne cohaeret quatenus epistemicam certitudinem, moralem responsabilitatem, impotentiam praesentem et necessitatem gratiae distinguit.
Relatio causalis inter actionem gratiae et actum voluntatis non plene formalizatur: gratia voluntatem sanat, sed modus huius efficientiae narratione potius quam analysi definitur.
Interpretatio vocis ut mandati divini analogia Antonii et praeparatione interiori nititur, sine criterio generali quo admonitio divina a casu distinguatur.
Refutatio Manichaeorum valide infirmat illationem a pluralitate voluntatum ad pluralitatem substantiarum, sed doctrinam poenae ex peccato liberiori et Adamica origine amplius probatam non reddit.
Incrementum gaudii et invariabilitas divina per gaudium in creaturis componuntur, sed relatio inter locutionem affectivam de Deo et immutabilitatem eius compressa manet.
Relatio inter fidem interiorem, praesentiam ecclesialem et confessionem publicam per Victorinum ostenditur, non tamen in regulam universalem omnino determinatur.
Praestantia continentiae in casu Augustini cum licitudine coniugii componitur, sed limes inter vocationem personalem et ordinem universalem imperfecte explicitur.
Restitutio servat verum motum textus: cognitio iam acquisita → servitus voluntatis → exempla et pudor → diagnosis anti-dualistica → interventus gratiae → actus conversionis → stabilizatio communis.
The text asks how a man already certain of God is unable to change his temporal life and by what operation a divided will is brought to complete conversion.
Conversion is constituted not as the acquisition of a new doctrine, but as the healing and liberation by grace of a will divided by habit.
The confessional argument is at once reconstructive, genealogical, diagnostic, polemical against Manichaean dualism, and strategic concerning the force of examples.
The movement proceeds from metaphysical certainty to practical impotence, from examples of others' conversions to self-accusation, and from the genealogy of habit to the crisis of the will.
The inner conflict is resolved into partial wills of one soul, lest it be transferred into two contrary natures or substances.
The crisis is consummated when an external admonition through Scripture is received as a personal command, doubt is dissolved, and the will is integrated toward the renunciation of temporal things.
For Augustine it is already certain that every substance proceeds from the incorruptible God through the Word.
Certainty about God does not of itself produce either stability in God or the right ordering of temporal life.
The same soul can prefer the eternal good in truth and retain the temporal good through familiarity.
A perverse will generates lust, lust habit, and habit, when not resisted, the necessity of bondage.
The present force of habit arose from voluntary acts and joins involuntary suffering with imputability.
Contrary wills are incomplete parts of one diseased will, not operations of two natures.
In an act accomplished by the will alone, to will wholly is already to do.
The grace of God through Jesus Christ alone breaks the chain of habit and heals the will.
Narratives of others' conversions are means by which God kindles imitation, dissolves excuses, and sets the subject against himself.
Victorinus's conversion, through public ecclesial profession, overcomes fear of pagan authority and makes faith socially recognizable.
Augustine's full conversion entails the renunciation of secular hope and of the plan for marriage, not a mere change of opinion.
The joy of a creature over what was lost and restored increases according to the magnitude of the preceding danger or distress, while God nevertheless remains unchangeable.
The conversion of a widely known man produces a greater common effect because it moves more people and provides an example to more people.
The admonition of Scripture, when received as divinely directed to oneself, can provide the will with a determinate command and final assurance.
The delay of conversion is no longer explained by uncertainty of truth.
Two opposing wills do not prove two souls or contrary natures.
Not every deliberation is a contest between a good principle and an evil principle, since multiple wills can all be good or all be evil.
Habit is not a force alien in origin to the agent.
The involuntary violence of habit does not exempt the agent from antecedent responsibility.
Conversion is not a local movement or a work of the body, but the integration of the will.
Learning, eloquence, and social rank neither effect conversion nor constitute its measure.
Mere presence within the walls of a church does not make one a Christian.
Secret faith that refuses confession from fear of men does not yet fulfill the form of public conversion.
Greater joy over a converted nobleman does not arise from the person's greater dignity before God.
Marriage is not universally forbidden, although continence is proposed to Augustine as a better way.
Continence cannot be effected by the subject's own strength.
Formulas of delay, such as a promise of future conversion, are not a determinate beginning of decision but a continuation of bondage.
Once metaphysical doubt has been removed, the obstacle to conversion is transferred from the order of knowledge to the order of the will.
The subject suffers the chain that he himself fashioned through antecedent acts; bondage is therefore at once present suffering and the effect of past guilt.
The conflict of flesh and spirit expresses the unequal adherence of one soul to contrary goods, not a division of substance.
The examples of Victorinus, Antony, and the courtiers demonstrate that conversion is immediately possible and turn the antiquity of Augustine's excuses into self-accusation.
Grace does not substitute for the will, but brings it from willing incompletely to integral action.
The public conversion of a person endowed with authority turns the instruments of former domination into instruments of confession and imitation.
Greater joy over Victorinus arises from the magnitude of his liberation and the multiplication of its effects, not from favor granted to the rich or noble.
The liberation of grace translates known truth into a new ordering of temporal life.
The example of Antony provides an interpretive form by which a chance voice and an encountered reading are transformed into a personal divine admonition.
The moral psychology of the text is temporally constructed: the same subject is sedimented, divided, and healed through his acts, without changing into two substances.
Responsibility and dependence on grace are not mutually exclusive: man participates in the cause of his bondage, but cannot by himself provide the principle of liberation.
Conversion is a punctiform event arising from a long accumulation of mediations: examples, shame, self-accusation, and Scripture are compressed into one integral act.
Conversion produces a circuit of exemplarity: the publicly visible convert kindles others, whose conversion further multiplies joy and imitative force.
Scripture acquires decisive force not only from its general meaning, but from temporal reception as a word now directed to the subject.
Delay does not preserve a neutral state, but strengthens the old habit; the moment of conversion therefore establishes an opposition between now and an indefinite later.
Doctrinally enlightened reason is not a sufficient cause of right action.
Moral evil does not require an evil substance, another mind, or an ontologically contrary principle.
The necessity of habit is not a natural necessity given from the beginning.
Grace is not an external compulsion that renders the will superfluous.
A merely private and socially invisible conversion does not complete the form of confession demanded by the text's examples.
Deliberative delay is not innocence, because the very retention of the old life has the effect of a choice.
Continence is not mere sterility or the subtraction of pleasure, but a form of fruitful life in God.
Variation of joy in creatures does not imply a change in divine knowledge or essence.
No neutral self stands outside the contending wills; the subject is present in both, although he identifies himself more with the approved will.
No stable boundary between conversion and non-conversion is given, because a half-full will cannot perform an act requiring whole willing.
The will does not possess an autonomous foundation from which it may draw itself out of its own division.
The indefinite future does not provide a space reserved for conversion, but conceals present refusal.
Salvation is not enclosed within individual consciousness, because confession, example, authority, and ecclesial joy belong to the very operation of conversion.
The first operation establishes dissonance: certainty about God → instability of life → transfer of the question from knowledge to will.
The second operation genealogically generates bondage: perverse will → lust → habit → necessity → divided will.
The third operation turns examples into self-judgment: narrative of another's conversion → possibility of present change → collapse of excuses → shame.
The fourth operation ontologically restricts conflict: opposing wills → partiality of each → one diseased soul → exclusion of dualism.
The fifth operation produces the threshold of decision: self-accusation → exhaustion of arguments → horror at the loss of habit → incapable half-full will → imploration of liberation.
The sixth operation closes the will: admonishing voice → example of Antony → apostolic reading → personal command → assurance → integral act.
The final operation socially stabilizes the event: renunciation of temporal things → communication to Alypius and Monica → common joy → ecclesial incorporation.

The principal movement is: metaphysical certainty → dissatisfaction with temporal life → examples of conversion → self-accusation → diagnosis of the divided will → grace mediated through Scripture → integral will → renunciation and ecclesial joy.
The polemical branch is: experience of contrary wills → experiences of multiple good or evil wills → impossibility of binary dualism → one soul stretched by various desires.
The social branch is: secret faith → public confession → victory over fear of authority → joy of the multitude → authority converted into an example of salvation.
The question of conversion is transferred from the opposition between faith and unbelief to the opposition between known truth and an unintegrated will.
Habit is redescribed as a necessity historically produced by the subject, not as a fixed nature or an entirely external force.
Inner conflict is reclassified from an argument for dualism into an indication of the partiality of one soul.
Public profession appears not as an ornament of private faith, but as a rupture with social fear and a visible effect of conversion.
Nobility is converted from a spiritual privilege into the capacity to multiply example, testimony, and common joy.
Scripture is reordered from a repository of propositions into an event of temporal and personal address.
The time of deliberation is changed from a neutral space into a mechanism of bondage, while the decisive now is opposed to an indefinite later.
The surface level presents Augustine's conversion through conflicts, narratives, tears, apostolic reading, and secular renunciation.
The structural level explains the mechanism by which the will generates habit, habit divides the will, and examples make the division intolerable.
The metastrategic level transforms public confession, social authority, and exemplary narrative into instruments for the propagation of conversion.
The ontological and temporal level establishes one created soul, unsubstantialized evil, an unchangeable God, sedimented habit, and conversion as a decisive passage between old and new.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the movement from certainty without conversion to a will integrated through grace.
The most robust structure is the genealogy of perverse will, lust, habit, and necessity, joined with the analysis of partial wills.
The system coheres internally insofar as it distinguishes epistemic certainty, moral responsibility, present impotence, and the necessity of grace.
The causal relation between the action of grace and the act of the will is not fully formalized: grace heals the will, but the mode of this efficacy is defined by narrative rather than analysis.
The interpretation of a voice as a divine command rests on the analogy of Antony and inner preparation, without a general criterion by which divine admonition may be distinguished from chance.

The refutation of the Manichaeans powerfully weakens the inference from a plurality of wills to a plurality of substances, but does not render the doctrine of punishment from freer sin and Adamic origin more fully proven.
The increase of joy and divine invariability are reconciled through joy in creatures, but the relation between affective speech about God and his immutability remains compressed.
The relation between inner faith, ecclesial presence, and public confession is shown through Victorinus, yet is not wholly determined as a universal rule.
The superiority of continence in Augustine's case is reconciled with the lawfulness of marriage, but the boundary between personal vocation and universal order is imperfectly explicated.
