The reconstruction preserves the true movement of the text: knowledge already acquired → bondage of the will → examples and shame → anti-dualistic diagnosis → intervention of grace → act of conversion → common stabilization.
Quaestio centralis est quomodo liberatio interior a voluntate divisa in renuntiationem, baptismum, communionem ecclesialem et mortis intelligentiam traducatur.
Liberatio efficitur cum Deus voluntatem ligatam excitat, falsas delectationes vera suavitate expellit et bona humana sibi tamquam fonti restituit.
Argumentatio confessionalis, reconstructiva, polemica et eschatologica effectus conversionis ad gratiam, providentiam et misericordiam tamquam principia refert.
Motus procedit a vinculis ruptis ad professionem depositam, deinde ad formationem, baptismum, vitam ecclesialem, contemplationem aeternitatis et mortem Monicae.
Narratio Monicae eandem structuram probat: disciplina, correctio, virtus et reconciliatio non merita autonoma, sed dona providentiae sunt.
Argumentatio in precem terminatur, quia nec conversio nec vita laudabilis necessitatem misericordiae, sacrificii Christi et intercessionis ecclesialis tollit.
Deus solus est bonum immutabile, summa suavitas et lux interior qua homo illuminatur.
Voluntas peccato et consuetudine ligata se ipsa liberare non potest.
Misericordia Dei vincula rumpit et liberum arbitrium ad consensum excitat.
Conversio consistit in recusatione voluntatis perversae et consensu voluntati divinae.
Bona sensibilia et temporalia desiderium dispergunt neque bono aeterno comparari possunt.
Liberatio cordis separationem externam antecedere atque eius tempus et modum regere potest.
Scriptura, sacramenta, cantus et communio Ecclesiae instrumenta divinae illuminationis et sanationis sunt.
Providentia etiam morbum, conflictum, contumeliam et perturbationem ad effectus salutares convertere potest.
Retributio moralis voluntatem agentis respicit, non solum effectum quem providentia ex actu producit.
Omne bonum humanum et omne meritum laudabile donum Dei est.
Baptismus peccata antecedentia remittit et hominem in vitam ecclesialem regenerat.
Regeneratio sacramentalis possibilitatem culpae posterioris neque necessitatem misericordiae aufert.
Sapientia aeterna facta non est, non mutatur et solo praesenti aeterno subsistit.
Mens temporalis Sapientiam aeternam breviter attingere potest, sed ad verba et successionem revertitur.
Consuetudo affectiva post correctionem intellectus et voluntatis permanere potest.
Mors fidelis non est annihilatio; resurrectio locum sepulturae et distantiam corporalem relativam facit.
Sacrificium et intercessio Christi fundamentum remissionis, spei et memoriae liturgicae defunctorum sunt.
Libertas non est possessio delectationum veterum, sed gaudium quod earum amissionem iam non timet.
Renuntiatio professionis non debet fieri ut ruptura publica qua magnitudo convertentis spectetur.
Professio rhetorica non est ministerium legis et pacis, sed mercatus verborum quibus furor forensis instruitur.
Infirmitas corporis conversionem non efficit, quamvis legitimam discessus excusationem praebeat.
Peccatum non procedit ex natura aliena gentis tenebrarum, sed ad voluntatem peccantis refertur.
Bonum verum neque extra hominem in rebus visibilibus quaeritur neque ab homine tamquam fonte luminis producitur.
Christi caro et mors non sunt phantasma Manichaeum.
In exemplari vitae aeternae Deus non auditur per linguam, angelum, sonitum, imaginem aut similitudinem, sed per se ipsum.
Virtutes Monicae non exponuntur ut opera quibus ipsa se formaverit.
Mors fidelis neque misera exstinctio est neque sepultura patria ad resurrectionem necessaria est.
Fides luctum tamquam desperationem vetat, non autem lacrimas coram Deo emissas.
Vita laudabilis neque innocentiam absolutam neque ius ad salutem sine misericordia constituit.
Vera suavitas veteres voluptates non sola prohibitione, sed delectationis ordine inverso expellit; inde amissio ante timenda fit gaudium.
Discessus usque ad ferias dilatus cum conversione congruit, quia libertas interior iam perfecta modum externae separationis sine iactantia ordinat.
Morbus pulmonis causa primaria renuntiationis non est, sed eventus contingens quem providentia in excusationem veracem assumit.
Repudiato dualismo Manichaeo, memoria peccati in iram adversus propriam voluntatem et in responsabilitatem moralem convertitur.
Lectio Psalmorum verba externa in recognitionem interiorem transfert atque desiderium a temporalibus ad lumen aeternum dirigit.
Conversio voluntatis maturitatem intellectualem statim non confert, quia scripta Cassiciacensia vestigia superbiae servant et lectio Isaiae adhuc differtur.
Baptismus conversionem privatam in regenerationem communem Augustini, Alypii et Adeodati traducit atque sollicitudinem vitae praeteritae removet.
Cantus communis veritatem per sensum et affectum infundit atque Ecclesiam sub pressione politica et haeretica sustinet.
Sanationes quas narratio precibus aut reliquiis coniungit functionem signorum obtinent: fidem confirmant et persecutionis impetum comprimunt.
Contumelia ancillae Monicam corrigit sine merito corrigentis, quia effectus salutaris a providentia, culpa autem ab intentione inimica aestimatur.
Patientia, castitas, prudentia domestica et opus pacis in Monica praesentiam Dei manifestant, non sufficientiam moralem sui ipsius.
Ascensus Ostiensis sensibilia, caelum et ipsam mentem transcendit, Sapientiam breviter attingit ac deinde necessario ad sonum finitum revertitur.
Contemplatio aeternitatis et impleta spes conversionis filii desiderium Monicae vitae terrestris, patriae sepulturae et ulterioris morae dissolvunt.
Dolor Augustini non procedit ex opinione annihilationis, sed ex abruptione consuetudinis qua duae vitae affective cohaeserant.
Laudatio Monicae in orationem pro peccatis transit, quia dona bona ius contra iudicium non efficiunt et spes in Christo ac misericordia ponitur.
Confessio totam narrationem in redistributionem causalitatis convertit: homo actus patitur et consentit, sed initium, medicina, fructus et consummatio Deo attribuuntur.
Conversio est processus multistratus, quia liberatio voluntatis professionem, intellectum, affectum, sacramentum et consuetudinem diversis temporibus transformat.
Oppositio inter successionem temporalem et praesentiam aeternam ordinat simul renuntiationem, contemplationem, mortem et memoriam.
Providentia asymmetricam causalitatem instituit: malus affectus vel adversus eventus bonum producere potest, quin voluntas mala propter effectum absolvatur.
Mediatio ecclesialis et exemplar apophaticum non sunt alternativa aequalia: signa sunt necessaria viatori, sed in visione desiderata ab immediata Dei praesentia superantur.
Vincula familiaria non destruuntur, sed ex possessione temporali in communionem ecclesialem, memoriam liturgicam et spem resurrectionis transferuntur.
Narratio sanctitatis necessario in intercessionem desinit, quia quo plura bona apparent, eo planius eorum ratio doni, non debiti, constituitur.
Systema falsam requirit doctrinam secundum quam subiectum autonomum conversionis suae initium et causam sufficientem praebet.
Systema excludit conversionem uno decreto consummatam, cuius intellectus, habitus et affectus nullam ulteriorem formationem requirant.
Systema excludit dualismum quo culpa in substantiam alienam transfertur et voluntas propria absolvitur.
Systema excludit aequationem inter effectum bonum et intentionem bonam.
Neque mediatio ecclesialis sine transformatione interiori neque interioritas privata sine sacramento et communione sufficit.
Recta doctrina dolorem et consuetudinem affectivam automatice non dissolvit.
Virtus humana nullum debitum efficit quo Deus misericordiam ex iustitia meriti praestare cogatur.
Nulla creatura, delectatio, professio, imago, vox aut institutum potest ultimus terminus desiderii esse.
Immediata possessio stabilis Sapientiae aeternae intra vitam temporalem indisponibilis manet.
Plena transparentia sui, memoriae et providentiae negatur; narratio causam ultimam confitetur sine omnibus mediis occultis cognitis.
Nulla ratio meritorum humanorum iudicium claudit aut misericordiam supervacaneam facit.
Patria terrestris, successus saecularis, propinquitas corporalis et sepultura familiaris formam patriae ultimae praebere non possunt.
Peregrinatio ad pacem aeternam immunitatem praesentem a vulnerabilitate, separatione et luctu non concedit.
Prima operatio hanc seriem habet: miseria recognita → misericordia irrumpens → vincula rupta → voluntas concordans → delectationes veteres expulsae.
Transitus vocationalis sic generatur: liberatio cordis → remotio cupiditatis → mora prudentialis → excusatio providentialiter data → professio deposita.
Formatio conversionis sequitur: otium Cassiciacense → Scriptura et disputatio → reliquiae superbiae detectae → instructio ecclesialis → Baptismus.
Incorporatio ecclesialis sequitur: sacramentum et cantus → veritas per sensus infusa → affectus pietatis → communitas sub adversitate corroborata.
Lectura providentiae sequitur: eventus ambiguus → effectus salutaris → distinctio effectus ab intentione → culpa agenti, bonum Deo tributum.
Ascensus contemplativus sequitur: sensibilia transcensa → mens ingressa → mens transcensa → Sapientia breviter tacta → reditus ad verba temporalia.
Processus luctus sequitur: mors non annihilans + consuetudo abrupta → dolor coercitus → dolor de dolore → lacrimae coram Deo → mitigatio.
Clausura soteriologica sequitur: vita laudabilis → bona tamquam dona → debitum possibile → sacrificium Christi → misericordia → memoria ad altare et oratio legentium.
Vincula voluntatis → gratia liberans → renuntiatio professionis → formatio Cassiciacensis → Baptismus → communio ecclesialis → reditus in Africam → mors Monicae → intercessio.
Bona exteriora → lumen interius → mens transcendens se → tactus praesentiae aeternae → defectus signorum desideratus → reditus ad sermonem temporalem.
Virtutes Monicae → attributio donorum Deo → negatio innocentiae absolutae → confessio debiti → misericordia Christi → memoria liturgica communis.
Conversio ex actu autonomo subiecti in libertatem a gratia excitatam denuo describitur.
Professio rhetorica ex arte neutra in mechanismum mercatus, ambitionis et armationis forensis reclassificatur.
Oppositio exterioris et interioris distinguit bona temporalia dispersiva a lumine quod intus a Deo recipitur.
Conversio ex momento clauso in processum temporale voluntatis, intellectus, sacramenti, habitus et affectus expanditur.
Causalitas moralis dividitur inter intentionem agentis et effectum quem providentia ex actu producit.
Ecclesia fit simul apparatus cognitionis, formationis affectivae, solidarietatis et resistentiae sub coercitione.
Mors ex annihilatione locali in separationem temporalem intra spem resurrectionis et communionem liturgicam transfertur.
Vita sancta ex argumento meriti in materiam gratiarum actionis et intercessionis reordinatur.
Altitude 1 — Surface — Professionis depositio, otium Cassiciacense, Baptismus, reditus, vita Monicae, colloquium Ostiense, mors, luctus et oratio seriem manifestam constituunt.
Altitude 2 — Structural — Gratia per voluntatem, consuetudinem, institutionem ecclesialem, sacramentum, Scripturam, affectum et providentiam operatur.
Altitude 3 — Metastrategic — Confessio memoriam ita ordinat ut causalitas ab ego ad Deum transferatur et lectores ex spectatoribus in intercessores mutentur.
Altitude 4 — Ontological/Temporal — Realitas dividitur inter creaturas mutabiles in successione et Sapientiam aeternam praesentem, cuius tactus nunc brevis, possessio autem eschatologica est.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem a liberatione voluntatis ad intercessionem pro defuncta.
Structura interne cohaeret quia conversionem, providentiam, virtutem, contemplationem et mortem eadem ratione doni ordinat.
Firmissima commissura est relatio inter attributum bonum humanum et gratiarum actionem Deo debitam.
Relatio causalis inter gratiam determinantem et liberum arbitrium consentientem affirmatur, sed non plene formaliter explicatur.
Distinctio inter providentiam bonum producentem et voluntatem malam culpabilem servatur, quamvis modus concursus nondum solvatur.
Remissio baptismalis et debitum post baptismum cohaerere possunt, sed limes exactus culpae posterioris non elaboratur.
Immediatio contemplativa desideratur, dum tota vita temporalis mediationibus ecclesialibus nititur; relatio utriusque per statum viatoris tantum componitur.
Luctus primum quasi mollities coercetur, deinde lacrimis coram Deo sanatur; discrimen inter affectum carnalem et dolorem recte ordinatum manet mobile.
Sanationes, status defunctorum et effectus eschatologici auctoritate testimonii, Scripturae et fidei nituntur potius quam probatione interna completa.
Restitutio verum motum servat: liberatio → mediatio ecclesialis → reinterpretatio providentiae → transcensus temporalis → luctus → misericordia et communio.
The central question is how interior liberation from a divided will is translated into renunciation, baptism, ecclesial communion, and an understanding of death.
Liberation is effected when God awakens the bound will, expels false delights through true sweetness, and restores human goods to himself as their source.
The confessional, reconstructive, polemical, and eschatological argument refers the effects of conversion to grace, providence, and mercy as principles.
The movement proceeds from broken bonds to the relinquished profession, then to formation, baptism, ecclesial life, contemplation of eternity, and Monica's death.
The narrative of Monica proves the same structure: discipline, correction, virtue, and reconciliation are not autonomous merits, but gifts of providence.
The argument ends in prayer, because neither conversion nor a praiseworthy life removes the need for mercy, Christ's sacrifice, and ecclesial intercession.
God alone is the immutable good, supreme sweetness, and interior light by which man is illuminated.
The will bound by sin and habit cannot liberate itself.
God's mercy breaks bonds and awakens free will to consent.
Conversion consists in rejecting the perverse will and consenting to the divine will.
Sensible and temporal goods scatter desire and cannot be compared with the eternal good.
Liberation of the heart can precede external separation and govern its time and manner.
Scripture, sacraments, chants, and the communion of the Church are instruments of divine illumination and healing.
Providence can turn even illness, conflict, insult, and disturbance toward salutary effects.
Moral retribution regards the will of the agent, not only the effect that providence produces from the act.
Every human good and every praiseworthy merit is a gift of God.
Baptism remits preceding sins and regenerates man into ecclesial life.
Sacramental regeneration removes neither the possibility of subsequent guilt nor the necessity of mercy.
Eternal Wisdom was not made, does not change, and subsists in the eternal present alone.
The temporal mind can briefly touch eternal Wisdom, but returns to words and succession.
Affective habit can remain after the correction of intellect and will.
The death of the faithful is not annihilation; resurrection renders the place of burial and bodily distance relative.
Christ's sacrifice and intercession are the foundation of remission, hope, and the liturgical remembrance of the dead.
Freedom is not possession of former delights, but joy that no longer fears their loss.
The renunciation of one's profession ought not to occur as a public rupture by which the convert's greatness is displayed.
The rhetorical profession is not a ministry of law and peace, but a marketplace of words by which forensic fury is equipped.
Bodily infirmity does not effect conversion, although it provides a legitimate excuse for departure.
Sin does not proceed from an alien nature of a race of darkness, but is referred to the will of the sinner.
True good is sought neither outside man in visible things nor produced by man as a source of light.
Christ's flesh and death are not a Manichaean phantom.
In the exemplar of eternal life, God is heard not through language, angel, sound, image, or likeness, but through himself.
Monica's virtues are not set forth as works by which she formed herself.
The death of the faithful is neither a miserable extinction nor is burial in one's homeland necessary for resurrection.
Faith forbids grief as despair, but not tears shed before God.
A praiseworthy life establishes neither absolute innocence nor a right to salvation without mercy.
True sweetness expels former pleasures not by prohibition alone, but by an inverted order of delight; hence what was formerly to be feared as loss becomes joy.
Departure delayed until the holidays accords with conversion, because interior freedom already perfected orders the manner of external separation without boasting.
Illness of the lungs is not the primary cause of renunciation, but a contingent event that providence assumes as a truthful excuse.
Once Manichaean dualism has been repudiated, memory of sin is transformed into anger against one's own will and into moral responsibility.
The reading of the Psalms transfers external words into interior recognition and directs desire from temporal things toward eternal light.
Conversion of the will does not immediately confer intellectual maturity, because the Cassiciacum writings retain traces of pride and the reading of Isaiah is still deferred.
Baptism translates the private conversion into the shared regeneration of Augustine, Alypius, and Adeodatus, and removes anxiety concerning past life.
Common chant instills truth through sense and affection and sustains the Church under political and heretical pressure.
The healings that the narrative connects with prayers or relics have the function of signs: they confirm faith and check the onslaught of persecution.
The insult of a maidservant corrects Monica without merit on the corrector's part, because the salutary effect is assessed as from providence, but guilt as from hostile intention.
Patience, chastity, domestic prudence, and the work of peace in Monica manifest God's presence, not her own moral self-sufficiency.
The Ostian ascent transcends sensible things, heaven, and the mind itself, briefly touches Wisdom, and then necessarily returns to finite sound.
Contemplation of eternity and the fulfilled hope of her son's conversion dissolve Monica's desire for earthly life, burial in her homeland, and further delay.
Augustine's sorrow does not proceed from the opinion of annihilation, but from the breaking of the habit by which two lives had affectively adhered together.
The praise of Monica passes into prayer for sins, because good gifts do not effect a right against judgment, and hope is placed in Christ and mercy.
Confession transforms the whole narrative into a redistribution of causality: man undergoes and consents to acts, but beginning, remedy, fruit, and consummation are attributed to God.
Conversion is a multilayered process, because liberation of the will transforms profession, intellect, affection, sacrament, and habit at different times.
The opposition between temporal succession and eternal presence orders together renunciation, contemplation, death, and memory.
Providence establishes asymmetric causality: an evil affection or adverse event can produce good, without the evil will being absolved on account of the effect.
Ecclesial mediation and the apophatic exemplar are not equal alternatives: signs are necessary for the wayfarer, but in the desired vision they are surpassed by God's immediate presence.
Familial bonds are not destroyed, but are transferred from temporal possession into ecclesial communion, liturgical remembrance, and hope of resurrection.
The narrative of holiness necessarily ends in intercession, because the more goods appear, the more clearly their character as gift, not debt, is established.
The system rejects the false doctrine according to which the autonomous subject provides the beginning and sufficient cause of its own conversion.
The system excludes a conversion consummated by a single decree, whose intellect, habit, and affection require no further formation.
The system excludes a dualism by which guilt is transferred to an alien substance and one's own will is absolved.
The system excludes the equation of a good effect with a good intention.
Neither ecclesial mediation without interior transformation nor private interiority without sacrament and communion suffices.
Right doctrine does not automatically dissolve sorrow and affective habit.
Human virtue creates no debt by which God may be compelled to bestow mercy according to the justice of merit.
No creature, delight, profession, image, voice, or institution can be the ultimate end of desire.
Immediate stable possession of eternal Wisdom remains unavailable within temporal life.
Full transparency of self, memory, and providence is denied; the narrative confesses the ultimate cause without knowing all the hidden means.
No reckoning of human merits closes judgment or renders mercy superfluous.
An earthly homeland, secular success, bodily proximity, and family burial cannot provide the form of the ultimate homeland.
Pilgrimage toward eternal peace does not grant present immunity from vulnerability, separation, and grief.
The first operation has this sequence: recognized misery → irrupting mercy → broken bonds → concordant will → former delights expelled.
The vocational transition is generated thus: liberation of the heart → removal of desire → prudential delay → providentially given excuse → profession relinquished.
The formation of conversion follows: Cassiciacum leisure → Scripture and disputation → remnants of pride detected → ecclesial instruction → Baptism.
Ecclesial incorporation follows: sacrament and chant → truth infused through the senses → affection of piety → community strengthened under adversity.
The reading of providence follows: ambiguous event → salutary effect → distinction of effect from intention → guilt attributed to the agent, good to God.
The contemplative ascent follows: sensible things transcended → mind entered → mind transcended → Wisdom briefly touched → return to temporal words.
The process of mourning follows: non-annihilating death + broken habit → restrained sorrow → sorrow over sorrow → tears before God → mitigation.
The soteriological closure follows: praiseworthy life → goods as gifts → possible debt → Christ's sacrifice → mercy → remembrance at the altar and prayer of readers.
Bonds of the will → liberating grace → renunciation of profession → Cassiciacum formation → Baptism → ecclesial communion → return to Africa → Monica's death → intercession.
External goods → interior light → mind transcending itself → touch of eternal presence → desired failure of signs → return to temporal speech.
Monica's virtues → attribution of gifts to God → denial of absolute innocence → confession of debt → Christ's mercy → common liturgical remembrance.
Conversion is redescribed from an autonomous act of the subject into freedom awakened by grace.
The rhetorical profession is reclassified from a neutral art into a mechanism of marketplace, ambition, and forensic armament.
The opposition of exterior and interior distinguishes dispersive temporal goods from the light received inwardly from God.
Conversion is expanded from a closed moment into a temporal process of will, intellect, sacrament, habit, and affection.
Moral causality is divided between the agent's intention and the effect that providence produces from the act.
The Church becomes at once an apparatus of knowledge, affective formation, solidarity, and resistance under coercion.
Death is transferred from local annihilation into temporal separation within the hope of resurrection and liturgical communion.
Holy life is reordered from an argument of merit into matter for thanksgiving and intercession.
Altitude 1 — Surface — The relinquishment of profession, Cassiciacum leisure, Baptism, return, Monica's life, the Ostian conversation, death, mourning, and prayer constitute the manifest sequence.
Altitude 2 — Structural — Grace works through will, habit, ecclesial institution, sacrament, Scripture, affection, and providence.
Altitude 3 — Metastrategic — Confession orders memory so that causality is transferred from ego to God and readers are changed from spectators into intercessors.
Altitude 4 — Ontological/Temporal — Reality is divided between mutable creatures in succession and present eternal Wisdom, whose touch is now brief, but whose possession is eschatological.
The axioms suffice to restore the sequence from liberation of the will to intercession for the deceased woman.
The structure coheres internally because it orders conversion, providence, virtue, contemplation, and death according to the same logic of gift.
The strongest joint is the relation between attributed human good and thanksgiving owed to God.
The causal relation between determining grace and consenting free will is affirmed, but not fully formally explained.
The distinction between providence producing good and culpable evil will is preserved, although the mode of concurrence is not yet resolved.
Baptismal remission and debt after baptism can cohere, but the exact limit of subsequent guilt is not elaborated.
Contemplative immediacy is desired, while the whole temporal life rests upon ecclesial mediations; the relation of the two is reconciled only through the state of the wayfarer.
Mourning is first restrained as though it were weakness, then healed by tears before God; the distinction between carnal affection and rightly ordered sorrow remains mobile.
Healings, the state of the dead, and eschatological effects rest upon the authority of testimony, Scripture, and faith rather than upon complete internal proof.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement: liberation → ecclesial mediation → reinterpretation of providence → temporal transcendence → mourning → mercy and communion.
Textus quaerit quo fructu homo, Deo iam omnia cognoscente et sibi ipsi non plene noto, praesentem statum suum Deo et hominibus confiteatur.
Confessio veritatem in corde efficit, bona Deo tribuit, vulnera manifestat et auditores caritate coniunctos ad gratiarum actionem atque intercessionem convertit.
Quaestio quid homo amet cum Deum amat cognitionem constituit ut ascensum per signa creata et facultates interiores ad veritatem supra mentem.
Scrutinium memoriae simul condicionem quaerendi et agnoscendi aperit atque ostendit animam nec se comprehendere nec Deum velut obiectum intra se collocare posse.
Appetitus universalis vitae beatae ad gaudium, deinde ad gaudium de veritate reducitur, sed amor veritatis divisione voluntatis corrumpitur.
Examen praesentis status per triplicem cupiditatem ostendit vitam continuam esse tentationem, cuius vires, fines et intentiones subiecto saepe latent.
Impotentia continentiae autonomae et defectus mediatorum falsorum ad misericordiam divinam et Christum verum mediatorem ducunt.
Argumentatio est confessiva, apophatica, introspectiva, diagnostica et soteriologica; additamentum editoriale eandem structuram ad polemicam adversus iudicium ad hominem transfert.
Deus totam conscientiam hominis cognoscit et iudicat, homo autem nec se ipsum totum cognoscit.
Confessio veritatem coram Deo facit, cum malum sibi displicere et bonum non sibi sed Deo tribuere significat.
Confessio publica apud auditores caritate coniunctos gratiarum actionem pro bonis et intercessionem pro malis generat.
Ratio interior sensuum nuntios iudicat et creaturas tamquam effectus Conditoris interpretatur.
Deus est veritas incommutabilis et vita animae, supra mentem mutabilem praesidens.
Memoria imagines sensibilium, res intelligibiles, notiones affectionum et proprias operationes diversis modis continet.
Vis memoriae et animi propriam comprehensionem excedit.
Quaestio et agnitio rei aliquam eius notitiam retentam praesupponunt; quod omnino deletum est quaeri non potest.
Appetitus universalis vitae beatae communem aliquam eius notitiam implicat.
Vita beata est gaudium ad Deum, de Deo et propter Deum, id est gaudium de veritate.
Homo veritatem amat cum rem amatam confirmat, sed eam odit cum propriam falsitatem manifestat.
Creaturae bonae sunt, sed in laqueos vertuntur cum pro fine habentur aut usum necessarium et pium excedunt.
Vita praesens continua tentatio est, in qua vires, motiva et perseverantia hominis sibi incerta manent.
Concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum et ambitio saeculi animam a Deo in voluptatem, vanam cognitionem et propriam excellentiam dispergunt.
Continentia animam ex multiplici dispersione in unitatem recti amoris colligit et donum Dei est.
Misericordia divina facultatem ad imperata praebet, languores sanat et imperfecta perficit.
Mediator reconciliationis mortalitatem cum hominibus et iustitiam cum Deo coniungere debet.
Christus, mortalis cum hominibus et iustus cum Deo, morte voluntaria sacerdos et sacrificium factus reconciliationem atque spem sanationis efficit.
Confessio non est informatio Deo antea ignota neque solus strepitus vocis.
Auditores humani nec cor confitentis immediate cognoscunt nec eius languores sanant.
Homo non est iudex ultimus sui ipsius.
Creaturae Deum indicant, sed nulla creatura est Deus.
Deus non est corpus, qualitas sensibilis, vis vegetativa aut facultas sensitiva.
Deus non est imago corporalis, affectio, memoria, animus mutabilis aut res in loco memoriae inclusa.
Res disciplinarum et rationes mathematicae non sunt imagines per sensus corporales invectae.
Discere intelligibilia non est simpliciter aliena verba recipere, sed dispersa intus colligere et agnoscere.
Vita beata non est quodlibet gaudium neque sola delectatio nominis eius.
Immunditia moralis non in cibo vel creatura ipsa, sed in cupiditate inordinata consistit.
Curiositas non fit scientia vera eo solo quod appetitum experiendi nomine cognitionis tegit.
Laus humana non est mensura bonitatis nec finis operis boni.
Status conversus non tollit tentationem neque certitudinem de futura perseverantia praestat.
Angeli, daemones, visiones curiosae et artes magicae reconciliationem cum Deo non efficiunt.
Verbum, qua Deo aequale est, non est medius; Christus qua homo mediator est.
Fuga in solitudinem non constituit solutionem vocationis, conflictus aut infirmitatis.
Confessio non cognitionem Dei auget, sed subiectum intra veritatem divinae cognitionis ordinat.
Publicatio confessionis tantum per caritatem et fructum communem iustificatur, non per curiositatem de vita aliena.
Examen sui necessario provisionale manet, quia is qui examinat proprias vires et motiva non plene videt.
Creaturae theologice loquuntur tantum rationi quae earum speciem cum veritate interiore confert; amor subiciens iudicium impedit.
Memoria est via necessaria quaerendi Deum, sed non terminus neque essentia eius.
Animus sibi praesens est sine plena sui comprehensione; proximitas subiecti non efficit transparantiam.
Deus in memoria invenitur quatenus veritas agnoscitur, sed principium huius agnitionis supra memoriam et supra subiectum manet.
Consensus universalis circa beatitudinem non efficit consensum circa veram eius rationem neque voluntatem sufficientem ad eam adipiscendam.
Falsitas persistit quia homo veritatem vult ut electiones suas confirmet, sed eam recusat ut ipsum corrigat.
Triplex tentatio tres modos exhibet quibus bonum creatum ex medio in finem illicitum mutatur.
Delectatio sensibilis legitima manet dum rationem sequitur et ad pietatem servit; peccaminosa fit cum rem significatam antecedit aut excludit.
Incertitudo virium et perpetuitas tentationis mandatum continentiae in orationem pro dono convertunt.
Continentia non est mera privatio voluptatis, sed reintegratio amorum dispersorum sub uno fine.
Amor laudis difficillime probatur per absentiam, quia laus bonae vitae comes esse potest nec sine corruptione vitae deliberate removetur.
Vana gloria recursive se instaurat, quia homo etiam de contemptu laudis gloriari potest.
Christus solus condiciones mediationis implet et ideo desperationem quam distantia inter peccatorem et Deum generat removet.

Additamentum editoriale ex sermone Augustini structuram confessionis ad polemicam transfert: vitia ministri praeterita gratiam extollunt, causam catholicam non destruunt, et iudicium ad hominem scientiam cordis non praebet.
Epistemologia interior et soteriologia eandem formam habent: descensus in se non autonomiam, sed dependentiam a veritate supra se detegit.
Memoria limen est inter praesentiam et transcendentiam: sine ea Deus agnosci non potest, sed in ea Deus essentialiter aut spatialiter contineri non potest.
Appetitus beatitudinis simul vestigium veritatis et locus aberrationis est, quia finis communiter notus per gaudia falsa substitui potest.
Triplex cupiditas structuram captationis complet: sensus ab usu ad voluptatem, cognitio a sapientia ad experimentum, societas a caritate ad excellentiam privatam traducuntur.
Confessio machina therapeutica recursiva est: eandem opacitatem quam manifestat numquam exhaurit, sed eam in orationem, correctionem et communionem convertit.
Gratia actionem humanam non substituit, sed resistendi facultatem dat; ipsa resistentia simul donum receptum et vulnus residuum manifestat.
Ascensus ad veritatem distantiam cognoscendam facit, sed eam non superat; mediatio Christi solvit discontinuum quod introspectio tantum detegere potuit.
Subiectum christianum temporaliter inter sanationem iam incohatam et pacem nondum consummatam constituitur.
Ut confessionis necessitas constet, falsa esse debet plena sui transparentia et facultas hominis se ipsum definitive iudicandi.
Ut ascensus interior constet, falsa esse debet sufficientia sensus ad Deum vel veritatem ultimam cognoscendam.
Ut memoriae analysis constet, falsa esse debet memoria tamquam archivum mere passivum imaginum sensibilium.
Ut miseria voluntatis explicetur, falsum esse debet desiderium boni semper efficere rectam cognitionem, electionem et possessionem eius.
Ut doctrina moderationis constet, falsa esse debet intrinseca malitia corporis, sensuum et creaturarum.
Ut ratio gratiae constet, falsum esse debet mandatum divinum autonomam facultatem oboediendi praesupponere.
Ut diagnosis superbiae constet, falsum esse debet laudem humanam statum moralem laudati fideliter manifestare.
Ut incarnatio necessaria sit, falsa esse debet quaelibet superioritas spiritualis ad veram mediationem sufficere.
Ut confessio praesentis status permaneat, falsa esse debet perfectio stabilis hominis intra vitam mortalem.
Systema subiectum autonomum excludit: homo nec mensura, nec unitas, nec iudex, nec medicus sufficiens sui est.
Possessio Dei ut obiecti localis, sensibilis aut mentaliter inclusi structuraliter praecluditur.
In vita praesenti nullus medius locus securus datur, quia prosperitas, adversitas, sensus, cognitio et relatio socialis materiam tentationis praebent.
Innocentia praesens tamquam fundamentum spei indisponibilis est; sola misericordia spem sustinet.
Veritas et mendacium ut bona aeque possidenda simul consistere non possunt; conatus utrumque retinendi Deum amittit.
Ascensus superbus ad Deum impossibilis est, quia superbia mediatores sibi similes eligit et separationem quam superare vult reproducit.
Confessio praesentis hominis clausuram definitivam non admittit, quia subiectum inter cognitionem partialem, tentationem futuram et sanationem nondum completam manet.
Machina confessionis procedit: omniscientia divina plus opacitas sui → confessio ut effectio veritatis → auditio caritatis → gratiarum actio et intercessio.
Machina ascensus procedit: signa sensibilia → iudex interior → exclusio corporis et potentiarum communium animalibus → memoria → excessus memoriae supra comprehensionem sui → veritas supra mentem.

Machina beatitudinis procedit: quaestio requirit notitiam retentam → omnes beatitudinem quaerunt → beatitudo ad gaudium reducitur → gaudia discernuntur → verum gaudium est gaudium de veritate → veritas est Deus.
Machina tentationis procedit: bonum creatum → usus necessarius aut pius → voluptas, experimentum vel laus finem usurpat → anima dispergitur → intentio sibi obscuratur → infirmitas confitetur.
Machina continentiae procedit: mandatum → impotentia detecta → petitio doni → facultas divinitus data → recollectio partialis → nova tentatio → renovata petitio misericordiae.

Machina mediationis procedit: distantia peccatoris a Deo → defectus mediationis propriae et daemonicae → coniunctio mortalitatis et iustitiae requisita → Christus homo mediator → mors voluntaria → reconciliatio et sanatio.
Circuitus totius libri est: gratia elevat → consuetudo et cupiditas deprimunt → confessio discrimen aperit → misericordia iterum colligit → pax plenaria in futurum differtur.
Deus iam cognoscit → utilitas confessionis problematizatur → caritas distinguit auditorem a curioso → confessio praesentis status fit actus communis.
Amor Dei interrogatur → creaturae ut Deus excluduntur → facultates corporis transcenduntur → memoria exploratur → veritas supra memoriam invenitur.
Quaestio de inventione requirit memoriam → appetitus universalis beatitudinis detegitur → beatitudo a gaudio falso distinguitur → gaudium de veritate cum Deo identificatur.
Praesentia Dei agnoscitur → distantia per consuetudinem explicatur → vita tota tentatio constituitur → triplex cupiditas per actus cotidianos examinatur → fiducia sui dissolvitur.

Dispersio requirit continentiam → continentia requirit donum → superbia producit mediatores falsos → Christus humilis mediator demonstratur → desperatio in spem sanationis et vitam pro Christo mutatur.
Confessio ex relatione rerum occultarum in operationem veritatis coram Deo et communitate caritatis reclassificatur.
Memoria ex archivo imaginum in campum ontologice multiplicem mutatur, qui cognitionem, identitatem et temporalitatem sustinet sed subiectum excedit.
Interiorem sequi non significat in immanentia claudi, quia intimum subiecti ad veritatem supra subiectum aperitur.
Oppositio simplicis corporis mali et spiritus boni corruit; quaestio primaria fit ordo usus, fruitionis et amoris.
Quaestio beatitudinis a consensu circa nomen ad distinctionem gaudii veri, gaudii falsi et voluntatis divisae transfertur.
Voluptas, curiositas et ambitio sub una forma cupiditatis ordinantur tamquam modi quibus attentionem bonum creatum captivam facit.
Continentia ex suppressionis autonomae exemplari in recollectionem gratia effectam convertitur.
Mediatio ex mera superioritate spirituali in coniunctionem structuralem mortalitatis humanae et iustitiae divinae reconstituitur.
Identitas christiana non ut status perfectus, sed ut compositio donorum receptorum, vulnerum persistentium et consummationis futurae describitur.
**Altitude 1 — Surface:** Confessio praesentis status, exploratio memoriae et examen tentationum constituunt obiecta immediata.
**Altitude 2 — Structural:** Relationes inter sensum, memoriam, rationem, veritatem, cupiditatem et gratiam mechanismum internum constituunt.
**Altitude 3 — Metastrategic:** Textus introspectionem privatam in orationem, iudicium intentionum, communionem caritatis et resistentiam gratia sustentatam convertit.

**Altitude 4 — Ontological/Temporal:** Subiectum creatum et mutabile a veritate incommutabili dependet atque inter conversionem praeteritam, tentationem praesentem et pacem futuram temporaliter suspenditur.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad restituendos confessionis, ascensus interioris, memoriae, beatitudinis, tentationis, gratiae et mediationis nexus.
Systema firmissime cohaeret ubi omniscientiam Dei cum opacitate sui, triplicem cupiditatem cum dispersione et continentiam cum dono coniungit.

Transitus inter notitiam universalem veritatis vel beatitudinis et primam cognitionem personalem Dei nondum plene determinatur: Deus antequam discatur in memoria non est, sed sine notitia retenta quaeri non potest.
Paradoxum memoriae oblivionis explicite insolutum manet; certitudo actus retinetur sine sufficienti ratione mechanismi repraesentationis.
Ascensus a corpore ad animam et ab anima ad Deum hierarchiam valoris praesupponit quam capitulum adhibet potius quam integre demonstrat.
Assertio omnes beatitudinem et veritatem velle cum odio veritatis componitur per voluntatem divisam, sed diversa significatio verbi velle onus solutionis sustinet.
Responsabilitas mali et totalis dependentia boni a gratia simul affirmantur, sed modus exactus cooperationis inter voluntatem et donum non formaliter explicatur.
Terminus inter necessitatem et voluptatem, utilitatem cantus et captationem sensus, curam proximi et amorem laudis intentione discernitur, quae ipsa subiecto incerta est.
Clausura christologica interne congruit condicionibus mediatoris, sed incarnationis et redemptionis praemissis revelatis nititur quae ex analysi memoriae sola non derivantur.
Restitutio motum verum servat; additamentum editoriale anti-Donatisticum applicationem polemicam praebet, non novam praemissam generatricem libri.
The text asks to what end a man, though God already knows all things and he himself is not fully known to himself, confesses his present condition to God and to men.
Confession effects truth in the heart, attributes goods to God, makes wounds manifest, and turns hearers joined by charity toward thanksgiving and intercession.
The question of what a man loves when he loves God establishes knowledge as an ascent through created signs and interior faculties to truth above the mind.
The investigation of memory at once discloses the condition of seeking and recognizing and shows that the soul can neither comprehend itself nor place God within itself as an object.
The universal desire for the blessed life is reduced to joy, then to joy in truth, but love of truth is corrupted by the division of the will.
Examination of the present condition through the threefold desire shows that life is a continuous temptation, whose powers, limits, and intentions often remain hidden from the subject.
The impotence of autonomous continence and the failure of false mediators lead to divine mercy and Christ the true mediator.
The argumentation is confessional, apophatic, introspective, diagnostic, and soteriological; the editorial addition transfers the same structure to polemic against ad hominem judgment.
God knows and judges the whole consciousness of man, but man does not know even himself in his entirety.
Confession makes truth before God, insofar as it signifies that evil displeases one and that good is attributed not to oneself but to God.
Public confession among hearers joined by charity generates thanksgiving for goods and intercession for evils.
The inner reason judges the messages of the senses and interprets creatures as effects of the Creator.
God is immutable truth and the life of the soul, presiding above the mutable mind.
Memory contains, in different ways, images of sensible things, intelligible things, notions of affections, and its own operations.
The power of memory and of mind exceeds its own comprehension.
The seeking and recognition of a thing presuppose some retained knowledge of it; what has been wholly erased cannot be sought.
The universal desire for the blessed life implies some common knowledge of it.
The blessed life is joy toward God, in God, and because of God, that is, joy in truth.
Man loves truth when it confirms a thing loved, but hates it when it reveals his own falsity.
Creatures are good, but turn into snares when they are held as an end or exceed necessary and pious use.
Present life is a continuous temptation, in which a man's powers, motives, and perseverance remain uncertain to himself.
The concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition scatter the soul from God into pleasure, vain knowledge, and self-exaltation.
Continence gathers the soul from manifold dispersion into the unity of right love and is a gift of God.
Divine mercy provides the capacity for what is commanded, heals infirmities, and perfects what is imperfect.
The mediator of reconciliation must join mortality with men and justice with God.
Christ, mortal with men and just with God, having become priest and sacrifice by voluntary death, effects reconciliation and hope of healing.
Confession is not information previously unknown to God, nor mere noise of voice.
Human hearers neither know the heart of the confessor immediately nor heal his infirmities.
Man is not the ultimate judge of himself.
Creatures indicate God, but no creature is God.
God is not a body, a sensible quality, a vegetative power, or a sensitive faculty.
God is not a bodily image, an affection, memory, a mutable mind, or a thing enclosed in a place of memory.
The objects of disciplines and mathematical relations are not images brought in through bodily senses.
To learn intelligible things is not simply to receive foreign words, but to gather together and recognize what is scattered within.
The blessed life is not any joy whatsoever, nor mere delight in its name.
Moral uncleanness consists not in food or the creature itself, but in disordered desire.
Curiosity does not become true knowledge merely because it covers the desire of experiencing with the name of knowledge.
Human praise is not the measure of goodness nor the end of a good work.
A converted state neither removes temptation nor guarantees certainty about future perseverance.
Angels, demons, curious visions, and magical arts do not effect reconciliation with God.
The Word, insofar as it is equal to God, is not a mediator; Christ, insofar as he is man, is mediator.
Flight into solitude does not constitute a solution to vocation, conflict, or infirmity.
Confession does not increase God's knowledge, but orders the subject within the truth of divine knowledge.
Publication of confession is justified only through charity and common benefit, not through curiosity about another's life.
Self-examination necessarily remains provisional, because the one who examines his own powers and motives does not fully see them.
Creatures speak theologically only to reason that compares their appearance with interior truth; a subjecting love impedes judgment.
Memory is a necessary path for seeking God, but not his terminus or essence.
The mind is present to itself without fully comprehending itself; the proximity of the subject does not produce transparency.
God is found in memory insofar as truth is recognized, but the principle of this recognition remains above memory and above the subject.
Universal consensus concerning blessedness does not produce consensus concerning its true account, nor a will sufficient to attain it.
Falsity persists because man wants truth to confirm his choices, but rejects it in order not to correct himself.
Threefold temptation exhibits three modes by which created good is changed from a means into an illicit end.
Sensible delight remains legitimate so long as it follows reason and serves piety; it becomes sinful when it precedes or excludes the thing signified.
Uncertainty about one's powers and the perpetuity of temptation turn the command of continence into prayer for a gift.
Continence is not mere deprivation of pleasure, but the reintegration of scattered loves under one end.
Love of praise is most difficultly tested by its absence, because praise can be a companion of a good life and is not deliberately removed without corruption of life.
Vain glory recursively reestablishes itself, because a man can glory even in contempt for praise.
Christ alone fulfills the conditions of mediation and therefore removes the despair generated by the distance between sinner and God.

The editorial addition transfers from Augustine's discourse the structure of confession to polemic: the past vices of a minister magnify grace, do not destroy the Catholic cause, and ad hominem judgment provides no knowledge of the heart.
Interior epistemology and soteriology have the same form: descent into oneself discloses not autonomy but dependence on truth above oneself.
Memory is the threshold between presence and transcendence: without it God cannot be recognized, but in it God cannot be contained essentially or spatially.
The desire for blessedness is at once a trace of truth and a site of error, because an end commonly known can be substituted by false joys.
Threefold desire completes the structure of capture: sense is led from use to pleasure, knowledge from wisdom to experience, and society from charity to private excellence.
Confession is a recursive therapeutic machine: it never exhausts the very opacity it discloses, but converts it into prayer, correction, and communion.
Grace does not replace human action, but gives the capacity to resist; resistance itself simultaneously manifests the gift received and the residual wound.
Ascent to truth makes the distance known, but does not overcome it; Christ's mediation resolves the discontinuity that introspection could only disclose.
The Christian subject is temporally constituted between healing already begun and peace not yet consummated.
For the necessity of confession to hold, complete self-transparency and man's capacity definitively to judge himself must be false.
For interior ascent to hold, the sufficiency of sense for knowing God or ultimate truth must be false.
For the analysis of memory to hold, memory as a merely passive archive of sensible images must be false.
For the misery of the will to be explained, the desire for good must not always effect right knowledge, choice, and possession of it.
For the doctrine of moderation to hold, the intrinsic evilness of body, senses, and creatures must be false.
For the account of grace to hold, it must be false that divine command presupposes an autonomous capacity to obey.
For the diagnosis of pride to hold, it must be false that human praise faithfully manifests the moral state of the praised person.
For the incarnation to be necessary, it must be false that any spiritual superiority suffices for true mediation.
For confession of the present state to remain, stable human perfection within mortal life must be false.
The system excludes the autonomous subject: man is neither the sufficient measure, nor unity, nor judge, nor physician of himself.
Possession of God as a local, sensible, or mentally enclosed object is structurally precluded.
In the present life no secure middle ground is given, because prosperity, adversity, sense, knowledge, and social relation provide material for temptation.
Present innocence is unavailable as a foundation of hope; mercy alone sustains hope.
Truth and falsehood cannot coexist as goods equally to be possessed; the attempt to retain both loses God.
Proud ascent to God is impossible, because pride chooses mediators like itself and reproduces the separation it seeks to overcome.
Confession of present man admits no definitive closure, because the subject remains between partial knowledge, future temptation, and healing not yet complete.
The machine of confession proceeds: divine omniscience plus self-opacity → confession as the effecting of truth → hearing of charity → thanksgiving and intercession.
The machine of ascent proceeds: sensible signs → inner judge → exclusion of body and powers shared with animals → memory → excess of memory beyond self-comprehension → truth above the mind.
The machine of blessedness proceeds: seeking requires retained knowledge → all seek blessedness → blessedness is reduced to joy → joys are discerned → true joy is joy in truth → truth is God.

The machine of temptation proceeds: created good → necessary or pious use → pleasure, experience, or praise usurps the end → the soul is scattered → intention is obscured to itself → infirmity is confessed.
The machine of continence proceeds: command → impotence disclosed → request for a gift → divinely given capacity → partial recollection → new temptation → renewed request for mercy.

The machine of mediation proceeds: sinner's distance from God → failure of self-mediated and demonic mediation → required conjunction of mortality and justice → Christ the man mediator → voluntary death → reconciliation and healing.
The circuit of the whole book is: grace raises up → habit and desire cast down → confession discloses the crisis → mercy gathers again → full peace is deferred to the future.
God already knows → the utility of confession is problematized → charity distinguishes the hearer from the curious person → confession of the present state becomes a communal act.
Love of God is questioned → creatures as God are excluded → bodily faculties are transcended → memory is explored → truth above memory is found.
The question of finding requires memory → the universal desire for blessedness is disclosed → blessedness is distinguished from false joy → joy in truth is identified with God.
God's presence is recognized → distance is explained through habit → the whole of life is constituted as temptation → threefold desire is examined through daily acts → self-confidence is dissolved.
Dispersion requires continence → continence requires gift → pride produces false mediators → Christ the humble mediator is demonstrated → despair is changed into hope of healing and life for Christ.
Confession is reclassified from a report of hidden things into an operation of truth before God and the community of charity.
Memory is changed from an archive of images into an ontologically multiple field that sustains knowledge, identity, and temporality but exceeds the subject.
To follow the inner does not mean to be enclosed in immanence, because the innermost of the subject is opened to truth above the subject.
The opposition of simply evil body and good spirit collapses; the primary question becomes the order of use, enjoyment, and love.
The question of blessedness is transferred from consensus about the name to the distinction of true joy, false joy, and divided will.
Pleasure, curiosity, and ambition are ordered under one form of desire as modes by which created good holds attention captive.
Continence is converted from a model of autonomous suppression into a recollection effected by grace.
Mediation is reconstituted from mere spiritual superiority into a structural conjunction of human mortality and divine justice.
Christian identity is described not as a perfect state, but as a composition of received gifts, persistent wounds, and future consummation.
**Altitude 1 — Surface:** Confession of the present state, exploration of memory, and examination of temptations constitute the immediate objects.
**Altitude 2 — Structural:** The relations among sense, memory, reason, truth, desire, and grace constitute the internal mechanism.
**Altitude 3 — Metastrategic:** The text converts private introspection into prayer, judgment of intentions, communion of charity, and resistance sustained by grace.
**Altitude 4 — Ontological/Temporal:** The created and mutable subject depends on immutable truth and is temporally suspended between past conversion, present temptation, and future peace.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the connections of confession, interior ascent, memory, blessedness, temptation, grace, and mediation.
The system coheres most firmly where it joins God's omniscience with self-opacity, threefold desire with dispersion, and continence with gift.

The transition between universal knowledge of truth or blessedness and the first personal knowledge of God is not yet fully determined: God is not in memory before he is learned, but cannot be sought without retained knowledge.
The paradox of memory and forgetfulness remains explicitly unresolved; certainty of the act is retained without a sufficient account of the mechanism of representation.
The ascent from body to soul and from soul to God presupposes a hierarchy of value that the chapter employs rather than fully demonstrates.
The assertion that all desire blessedness and truth is reconciled with hatred of truth through the divided will, but the different meaning of the word “to will” bears the burden of the solution.
Responsibility for evil and total dependence of good on grace are affirmed together, but the exact mode of cooperation between will and gift is not formally explained.

The boundary between necessity and pleasure, the usefulness of song and the capture of sense, care for one's neighbor and love of praise, is discerned by intention, which itself is uncertain to the subject.

The Christological closure is internally congruent with the conditions of the mediator, but rests on revealed premises of incarnation and redemption that are not derived from analysis of memory alone.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement; the anti-Donatist editorial addition provides a polemical application, not a new generative premise of the book.
Textus quaerit quomodo creatio temporalis cum aeternitate divina componatur et quid sit tempus quod mens experitur atque metitur.
Deus extra omnem successionem in Verbo coaeterno omnia, etiam tempora, creat; temporis autem mensurabilis ratio in praesentibus animae operationibus reperitur.
Argumentatio est exegetica, metaphysica, diagnostica, apophatica et reconstructiva.
Confessio non informativa in petitionem illuminationis transit, qua sensus Scripturae per interiorem veritatem quaeritur.
Mutabilitas creaturae ad causam increatam, haec ad Verbum aeternum, Verbum autem ad distinctionem inter aeternitatem et successionem ducit.
Obiectio de eo quod Deus ante creationem faciebat dissolvitur ostendendo ipsam notionem temporis ante tempora contradictionem continere.
Analysis praesentis, memoriae, attentionis et exspectationis tempus in distentionem animi transfert, quae deinde in quaestionem collectionis animae ad Deum convertitur.
Confessio Deo omniscienti scientiam non addit, sed affectum confitentis et legentis ad Deum excitat.
Certitudo de veritate dicti non a lingua vel sono loquentis, sed a veritate stabili intus iudicante et divinitus aperiente pendet.
Principium in quo caelum et terra facta sunt est Verbum, Filius, Sapientia et Veritas Dei.
Res mutabilis, quia facta est et antequam esset operari non potuit, sui ipsius causa esse nequit.
Deus causa est omnis creaturae atque omnium condicionum artis creatae, etiam materiae, corporis, animi, instrumenti, mundani loci et temporis.
Verbum Deo coaeternum omnia simul et sempiterne dicit, nullo eius elemento cedente vel succedente.
Initia et fines rerum temporalium secundum aeternam rationem fiunt, sine nova voluntate aut mutatione in Deo.
Aeternitas divina tota praesens manet, successione caret, et nullum tempus ei coaeternum est.
Quod omnino non est neque videri neque mensurari potest; praeteritum autem iam non est et futurum nondum est.
Praesens, si extenditur, in praeteritum et futurum dividitur; si indivisibile est, spatio caret.
Tempus non est motus corporis, quia tam motus quam quies tempore mensurantur.
Praeterito, praesenti et futuro respondent tres operationes praesentes animae: memoria, attentio sive contuitus, et exspectatio.
Mens, cum tempus metitur, praesentem affectionem sive vestigium a rebus transeuntibus relictum metitur, non ipsas res iam absentes.
In actione temporali attentio id quod exspectatur in id quod memoratur continuo transfert.
Deus futura et praeterita cognoscit atque creaturas efficit sine variatione cognitionis et sine distentione actionis.
Distentio vitae humanae terminum suum normativum habet in collectione ad unum Deum per Mediatorem.
Confessio non est narratio qua Deus aliquid prius ignotum cognoscat.
Veritas Scripturae non constituitur praesentia corporali Moysis, lingua Hebraea, translatione Latina aut sono exteriori.
Creatio divina non est artificium humanum quod formam materiae iam existenti imponat.
Verbum creatorium non est vox temporalis syllabis successive sonantibus.
Quaestio quid Deus ante tempora faceret non designat condicionem realem, quia ubi tempus non erat nullum erat «tunc».
Aeternitas non est tempus infinitum neque interminabilis annorum series.
Praeteritum et futurum, qua praeteritum et futurum, non sunt entia praesentia in occultis locis reposita.
Praesens temporale non potest esse longum, quia omnis extensio eius in partes non praesentes solvitur.
Tempus non est circuitus solis, lunae, siderum aut cuiuslibet corporis.
Tempora non mensurantur ut res iam peractae vel nondum existentes.
Cognitio divina non est memoria et praescientia creaturae ad infinitam amplitudinem aucta.
Aporia non solvitur responsione ioculari, falsitate utili aut simulatione scientiae ubi ignorantia manet.
Confessio simul exercitium affectus et modus cognitionis est, quia mentem ad fontem illuminationis dirigit potius quam Deum informat.
Genesis Christologice legitur: formula «in principio» actum creationis per Verbum aeternum constituit.
Creatio ex nihilo sequitur, quia nulla materia, regio vel potentia a Deo non facta ante actum creatorium praesupponi potest.
Novitas creaturae novam voluntatem in Deo non postulat, quia effectus temporalis secundum rationem aeternam ex Verbo immutabili procedit.
Quaestio «quid Deus ante creationem faciebat?» falso praesupponit tempus a creatione independens et ideo semanticam condicionem propriae responsionis destruit.
Aeternitas et tempus non differunt quantitate durationis, sed modo praesentiae: aeternitas stat, tempus successione transit.
Tria tempora proprie reformulantur ut praesens memoriae, praesens attentionis et praesens exspectationis.
Praedictio futura non videt rem nondum existentem, sed ex causis, signis vel conceptionibus iam praesentibus futurum enuntiat.
Mensuratio temporis fit per comparationem vestigiorum praesentium in animo, non per apprehensionem motus cum tempore identificati.
Longum futurum est longa exspectatio futuri, et longum praeteritum est longa memoria praeteriti.
Eadem conversio ex exspectatione per attentionem in memoriam syllabam, canticum, actionem, vitam et saeculum ordinat.
Scientia et actio divina tempore non mensurantur, quamvis effectus cogniti et producti temporaliter ordinentur.
Quia vita temporalis per multa in memoriam et exspectationem dispergitur, conversio ad Deum ut transitus a distentione ad intentionem describitur.
Exegesis primi versus in censuram condicionum temporalium transit, quia creatio recte cogitari nequit nisi vis praesupposita vocabulorum «ante», «tunc» et «incipere» examinetur.
Discrimen Creatoris et creaturae simul ontologicum, temporale, causale et epistemicum est: creatura mutatur et distenditur, Deus autem manet et sine distentione efficit atque cognoscit.
Usus communis trium temporum retineri potest, dummodo eius grammatica non convertatur in ontologiam praeteriti et futuri quasi praesentium rerum.
Tempus mensurabile neque res caelestis autonoma neque mera fictio est, sed relatio praesentis animi ad impressiones successionis creatae.
Structura temporalis est recursive inclusiva: minima transitio soni eandem formam habet ac actio, vita singularis et historia humana.
Analysis temporis fit anthropologia spiritualis, quia distentio non solum mensurationem explicat sed etiam dispersionem vitae in multa constituit.
Cognitio progreditur per exclusionem exemplarium impossibilium et in confessione residuae ignorantiae terminatur, non in comprehensione exhaustiva.
Praedicata temporalia de Deo et creatura univoce dici non possunt.
Creatio novitatem effectus admittit, sed deliberationem, mutationem consilii aut novam inclinationem in Deo excludit.
Causalitas non requirit semper tempus prius, materiam praevium aut locum externum in quo effectus producatur.
Auctoritas exterior locutoris, etiam Moysis, sine iudicio veritatis interioris certitudinem non constituit.
Familiaritas vocabuli «tempus» scientiam naturae temporis non praestat.
Tempus non est receptaculum independens in quo Deus, creatio et anima successive collocentur.
Memoria et exspectatio res absentes non restituunt ut praesentes; tantum praesentia vestigia et intentiones continent.
Ratio creata sine illuminatione et sine confessione limitis sui mysterium aeternitatis aut temporis dominari non potest.
Nullus datur prospectus temporalis extra creationem ex quo Deus ante mundum collocari possit.
Nullum tempus, nulla materia, nullus locus et nulla creatura stat iuxta Deum ut alterum coaeternum.
Creaturae non competit praesens quod simul durationem integram possideat et omni transitu careat.
Anima temporalis sibi ipsi perfecte praesens non est, quia inter memoriam, attentionem et exspectationem distrahitur.
Praeteritum et futurum nullum proprium repositorium habent; absentia eorum ipsam structuram memoriae et exspectationis ordinat.
Essentia temporis et modus quo aeternitas successionem efficit comprehensioni positivae plenae indisponibiles manent.
Machina hermeneutica sic procedit: omniscientia Dei → confessio non informativa → affectus excitatus → petitio illuminationis → iudicium veritatis interioris → intellectus Scripturae.
Machina creationis sic procedit: mutabilitas rei → facticitas → impossibilitas autocausationis → causa increata → exclusio materiae et loci praevii → creatio ex nihilo.
Machina Verbi sic procedit: vox temporalis excluditur → Verbum coaeternum statuitur → omnia simul dicuntur → effectus secundum rationem aeternam temporaliter fiunt → immutabilitas Dei servatur.
Obiectio de actione divina ante mundum sic dissolvitur: «ante» praesupponit tempus → tempus est creatum → tempus ante tempus est impossibile → quaestio caret referente reali.

Reductio temporum sic procedit: praeteritum iam non est + futurum nondum est + praesens extensum dividitur → tria tempora substantialia corruunt → memoria, attentio et exspectatio praesentia substituuntur.
Discrimen motus et temporis sic producitur: motus variari vel cessare potest → motus et quies mensurantur → mensura ab utroque differt → tempus non est motus corporis.
Mensuratio sic operatur: res transit → affectionem in animo relinquit → attentio vestigium praesens retinet et comparat → proportio durationis enuntiatur.
Clausura anthropologica sic procedit: exspectatio → attentio → memoria → multiplicatio huius circuitus in vita → distentio animi → conversio per Mediatorem → intentio et collectio ad unum.

Confessio non informativa → petitio intelligentiae → iudicium veritatis interioris → lectio Verbi ut Principii → creatio ex nihilo → distinctio Verbi aeterni a voce temporali → dissolutio temporis ante creationem → analysis trium temporum → exclusio motus ut temporis essentiae → mensuratio vestigiorum in animo → distentio vitae → desiderium collectionis in Deo.
Creatio non amplius collocatur in tempore praevio, sed ipsum tempus intra ordinem creatum redigitur.
Oppositio aeternitatis et temporis a differentia quantitatis ad differentiam inter praesentiam stabilem et successionem mutabilem transfertur.
«Principium» a solo termino chronologico ad Verbum aeternum, quod simul causa creationis et magister interior est, reclassificatur.
Praeteritum, praesens et futurum ex tribus regionibus rerum in tres modos praesentis animae convertuntur.
Motus caelestis ex essentia temporis in obiectum tempore mensuratum demovetur.
Mensuratio temporis ab apprehensione rei transeuntis ad comparationem affectionum praesentium in memoria transfertur.
Vita humana ut structura temporalis recursive dispersa describitur, non ut simplex series eventuum exteriorum.
Lingua communis de tribus temporibus retinetur pragmatice, sed eius ontologia litteralis revocatur.
Altitude 1 — Surface — Obiectum immediatum est intellectus sententiae «In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram» atque responsio quaestioni quid Deus ante creationem faceret.
Altitude 2 — Structural — Structura causalis distinguit Creatorem, Verbum coaeternum, ordinem creatum et operationes animae quibus successio apprehenditur.

Altitude 3 — Metastrategic — Textus controversiam non responsione intra grammaticam adversarii vincit, sed praesuppositionem temporalem quaestionis destruit et vocabula communia semanticis limitibus subicit.

Altitude 4 — Ontological/Temporal — Realitas divina ut praesens immutabile, creatura ut mutabilis dependentia, et vita temporalis ut distentio inter memoriam, attentionem et exspectationem constituuntur.
Axiomata proposita sufficiunt ad restituendam concatenationem a confessione et exegesi ad creationem, tempus, mensurationem et collectionem spiritualem.
Nondum plene determinatur utrum tempus ontologice ipsa affectio animi sit an tantum per affectionem animi mensurari possit.
Doctrina vestigii explicat quid post transitum mensuretur, sed non perfecte explicat unde proportionalitas communis et certitudo mensurae oriatur.
Tensio manet inter praesens omni spatio carens et attentionem praesentem quae perdurare atque translationem futuri in praeteritum efficere dicitur.
Ratio aeterna novitatem effectuum sine mutatione Dei servat, sed productionem successionis ex causa omnino non successiva positive non explicat.
Possibilitas creaturae «supra tempora» admittitur, sed modus quo talis creatura nec temporalis nec Deo coaeterna sit indeterminatus manet.
Firmissima pars systematis est dissolutio temporis ante tempora atque distinctio temporis a motu corporali.
Transitus a distentione descriptiva ad collectionem normativam per Mediatorem praemissis theologicis, precatione et auctoritate Scripturae nititur, non ex sola analysi temporis deducitur.
Restitutio verum motum textus servat: exemplaria falsa excluduntur, aporia temporis in animam transfertur, et solutio phenomenologica in confessionem limitis atque desiderium aeternitatis clauditur.
The text asks how temporal creation may be reconciled with divine eternity and what time is that the mind experiences and measures.
God, outside all succession, creates all things, including times, in the coeternal Word; but the basis of measurable time is found in the present operations of the soul.
The argument is exegetical, metaphysical, diagnostic, apophatic, and reconstructive.
Non-informative confession passes into a petition for illumination, by which the meaning of Scripture is sought through interior truth.
The mutability of the creature leads to the uncreated cause, this to the eternal Word, and the Word to the distinction between eternity and succession.
The objection concerning what God was doing before creation is dissolved by showing that the very notion of time before times contains a contradiction.
The analysis of the present, memory, attention, and expectation transfers time into the distention of the mind, which is then converted into the question of the soul's gathering to God.
Confession adds no knowledge to God, who knows all things, but stirs the affection of the one confessing and reading toward God.
Certainty concerning the truth of what is said depends not on the language or sound of the speaker, but on stable truth judging within and divinely disclosing.
The beginning in which heaven and earth were made is the Word, the Son, the Wisdom, and the Truth of God.
A mutable thing, because it was made and could not act before it existed, cannot be the cause of itself.
God is the cause of every creature and of all conditions of created art, including matter, body, soul, instrument, worldly place, and time.
The Word coeternal with God says all things simultaneously and everlastingly, with no element of it passing away or succeeding another.
The beginnings and ends of temporal things occur according to eternal reason, without new will or change in God.
Divine eternity remains wholly present, lacks succession, and no time is coeternal with it.
What is not at all cannot be either seen or measured; but the past is no longer, and the future is not yet.
The present, if extended, is divided into past and future; if indivisible, it lacks duration.
Time is not the motion of a body, because both motion and rest are measured by time.
To past, present, and future correspond three present operations of the soul: memory, attention or regard, and expectation.
When the mind measures time, it measures a present affection or trace left by passing things, not the things themselves now absent.
In temporal action, attention continuously transfers what is expected into what is remembered.
God knows future and past things and brings creatures about without variation of knowledge and without distention of action.
The distention of human life has its normative end in gathering to the one God through the Mediator.
Confession is not a narration by which God comes to know something previously unknown.
The truth of Scripture is not constituted by the bodily presence of Moses, the Hebrew language, a Latin translation, or an exterior sound.
Divine creation is not a human craft that imposes form upon already existing matter.
The creative Word is not a temporal voice sounding forth syllables successively.
The question of what God was doing before times does not designate a real condition, because where time was not, there was no «then».
Eternity is not infinite time nor an endless series of years.
Past and future, as past and future, are not beings present and stored away in hidden places.
The temporal present cannot be long, because all its extension is dissolved into non-present parts.
Time is not the circuit of the sun, moon, stars, or of any body whatever.
Times are not measured as things already completed or not yet existing.
Divine knowledge is not creaturely memory and foreknowledge increased to infinite magnitude.
The aporia is not resolved by a joking answer, a useful falsehood, or a pretense of knowledge where ignorance remains.
Confession is at once an exercise of affection and a mode of cognition, because it directs the mind to the source of illumination rather than informing God.
Genesis is read Christologically: the formula «in principio» establishes the act of creation through the eternal Word.
Creation ex nihilo follows, because no matter, region, or power not made by God can be presupposed before the creative act.
The novelty of the creature does not require a new will in God, because the temporal effect proceeds according to eternal reason from the immutable Word.
The question «what was God doing before creation?» falsely presupposes time independent of creation and therefore destroys the semantic condition of its own answer.
Eternity and time differ not in quantity of duration but in mode of presence: eternity stands still; time passes in succession.
The three times are properly reformulated as the present of memory, the present of attention, and the present of expectation.
Prediction of the future does not see a thing not yet existing, but announces the future from causes, signs, or conceptions already present.
The measurement of time occurs through comparison of present traces in the mind, not through apprehension of motion identified with time.
A long future is a long expectation of the future, and a long past is a long memory of the past.
The same conversion from expectation through attention into memory orders a syllable, a song, an action, a life, and an age.
Divine knowledge and action are not measured by time, although known and produced effects are temporally ordered.
Because temporal life is dispersed through many things into memory and expectation, conversion to God is described as passage from distention to intention.

The exegesis of the first verse passes into a critique of temporal conditions, because creation cannot be rightly thought unless the presupposed force of the words «ante», «tunc», and «incipere» is examined.
The distinction between Creator and creature is at once ontological, temporal, causal, and epistemic: the creature changes and is distended, whereas God remains and acts and knows without distention.
The common use of the three times may be retained, provided that its grammar is not converted into an ontology of past and future as though they were present things.
Measurable time is neither an autonomous celestial thing nor a mere fiction, but a relation of the present mind to impressions of created succession.
Temporal structure is recursively inclusive: the smallest transition of sound has the same form as an action, an individual life, and human history.
The analysis of time becomes spiritual anthropology, because distention not only explains measurement but also constitutes the dispersion of life into many things.
Knowledge progresses through the exclusion of impossible models and terminates in confession of residual ignorance, not in exhaustive comprehension.
Temporal predicates cannot be said univocally of God and creature.
Creation admits novelty of effects, but excludes deliberation, change of plan, or new inclination in God.
Causality does not always require prior time, pre-existing matter, or an external place in which an effect may be produced.
The external authority of a speaker, even Moses, does not establish certainty without the judgment of interior truth.
Familiarity with the word «time» does not furnish knowledge of the nature of time.
Time is not an independent receptacle in which God, creation, and the soul are successively placed.
Memory and expectation do not restore absent things as present; they contain only present traces and intentions.
Created reason, without illumination and without confession of its own limit, cannot master the mystery of eternity or time.
No temporal perspective outside creation is given from which God could be situated before the world.
No time, no matter, no place, and no creature stands alongside God as another coeternal being.
The creature cannot possess a present that simultaneously possesses an entire duration and lacks all passage.
The temporal soul is not perfectly present to itself, because it is distracted among memory, attention, and expectation.
Past and future have no proper repository; their absence orders the very structure of memory and expectation.
The essence of time and the manner in which eternity brings about succession remain unavailable to full positive comprehension.
The hermeneutical machine proceeds thus: God's omniscience → non-informative confession → stirred affection → petition for illumination → judgment of interior truth → understanding of Scripture.
The machine of creation proceeds thus: mutability of a thing → facticity → impossibility of self-causation → uncreated cause → exclusion of prior matter and place → creation ex nihilo.

The machine of the Word proceeds thus: temporal voice is excluded → the coeternal Word is established → all things are said simultaneously → effects occur temporally according to eternal reason → God's immutability is preserved.
The objection concerning divine action before the world is dissolved thus: «before» presupposes time → time is created → time before time is impossible → the question lacks a real referent.

The reduction of times proceeds thus: the past is no longer + the future is not yet + the extended present is divided → the three substantial times collapse → present memory, attention, and expectation are substituted.
The distinction of motion and time is produced thus: motion can vary or cease → motion and rest are measured → the measure differs from both → time is not the motion of a body.
Measurement operates thus: a thing passes → it leaves an affection in the mind → attention retains and compares the present trace → a proportion of duration is stated.

The anthropological closure proceeds thus: expectation → attention → memory → multiplication of this circuit in life → distention of the mind → conversion through the Mediator → intention and gathering to the one.

Non-informative confession → petition for understanding → judgment of interior truth → reading of the Word as Principle → creation ex nihilo → distinction of the eternal Word from temporal voice → dissolution of time before creation → analysis of the three times → exclusion of motion as the essence of time → measurement of traces in the mind → distention of life → desire for gathering in God.
