## Book One

Mother of the Aeneads, delight of men and gods,

nourishing Venus, beneath the gliding signs of heaven,

you who haunt the ship-bearing sea, who haunt the fruit-bearing lands,

since through you every race of living things

is conceived and, having arisen, sees the light of the sun:

before you, goddess, before you the winds flee, before you the clouds of heaven

and your coming; for you the artful earth

puts forth sweet flowers, for you the plains of the sea smile,

and the tranquil heaven shines with outpoured light.

For as soon as the vernal aspect of day has been revealed

and the fecund breeze of the west wind, unbarred, flourishes,

first the birds of the air, goddess, proclaim you and your

entrance, their hearts struck by your power.

Then wild beasts and herds bound over the joyful pastures

and swim across swift streams: thus, seized by delight,

each follows you eagerly wherever you proceed to lead it.

Finally, through seas and mountains and rapacious rivers,

and the leafy homes of birds and verdant fields,

instilling soothing love into the breasts of all,

you bring it about that they eagerly propagate their races, each after its kind.

Since you alone govern the nature of things,

and without you nothing arises into the divine shores of light,

nor does anything come to be joyful or lovely,

I strive to have you as a partner in writing verses,

which I attempt to compose concerning the nature of things

for our Memmius, whom you, goddess, at every time

have wished, adorned with all things, to excel.

Therefore all the more, goddess, grant everlasting charm to my words.

Cause meanwhile the savage works of war

to lie lulled to rest throughout all seas and lands;

for you alone can aid mortals with tranquil peace,

since Mavors, mighty in arms, governs the savage works of war,

and he often casts himself back into your lap,

conquered by the everlasting wound of love,

and thus, looking up, with his shapely neck thrown back,

he feeds his eager eyes with love, gazing hungrily upon you, goddess,

and, as he lies on his back, his breath hangs upon your lips.

As he reclines thus, goddess, upon your sacred body,

pour forth, bending over and enfolding him, sweet speech from your lips,

seeking, glorious one, gentle peace for the Romans;

for neither can we pursue this task with an untroubled mind in this troubled time of our country,

nor can the illustrious offspring of Memmius fail

the common safety in such circumstances.

For it is necessary that the whole nature of the gods

enjoy immortal life with the greatest peace,

removed and separated far from our affairs;

for, free from every pain, free from dangers,

herself powerful in her own resources, needing nothing of us,

neither won over by good services nor touched by anger.

For what remains, lend empty ears and an acute mind,

withdrawn from cares, to true reasoning,

lest my gifts, laid out for you with faithful zeal,

you should abandon in contempt before they are understood.

For I shall begin to discourse to you on the supreme ordering of heaven and of the gods,

and I shall disclose the first-beginnings of things,

from which all nature creates things, increases and nourishes them,

and into which that same nature in turn resolves them when destroyed,

which, in setting forth our account, we are accustomed to call matter and generative bodies for things,

and the seeds of things,

and likewise to employ these same terms

as first bodies, because all things are from those first things.

When human life lay foully before men's eyes

upon the earth, crushed beneath the heavy weight of religion,

which showed its head from the regions of heaven,

looming over mortals with a horrible aspect from above,

a Greek man was the first of mortals to dare to raise his eyes against it,

and the first to stand against it;

him neither the renown of the gods nor thunderbolts nor heaven with threatening

murmur restrained, but all the more they stirred up the keen

courage of his mind, so that he first desired to break apart the tight

bars of nature's gates.

Therefore the living force of his mind prevailed and

went forth far beyond the flaming ramparts of the world

and traversed the whole immeasurable expanse in thought and spirit,

whence, victorious, he reports to us what can come to be,

what cannot, and finally by what power a limit is fixed for each thing,

and by what principle there is a boundary deeply set.

Wherefore religion, in turn, is cast beneath our feet

and trampled down; victory makes us equal to heaven.

In these matters I fear this: perhaps you may think

that you are entering upon the elements of an impious doctrine and a path

of crime. Yet, on the contrary, more often that

religion has brought forth criminal and impious deeds.

How at Aulis they foully defiled the altar of the maiden Trivia

with the blood of Iphianassa,

the chosen leaders of the Danaans, foremost among men.

As soon as she perceived that the fillet, encircling her maidenly tresses,

had been poured forth equally down each cheek,

and that her sorrowful father stood before the altars,

and beside him his attendants concealed the steel,

while the citizens shed tears at the sight of her,

speechless with fear, she sank to the ground on bended knees.

Nor could it avail the wretched girl at such a time

that she had first bestowed upon the king a father's name;

for, lifted up by men's hands and trembling, to the altars

you led forth, not so that, in the solemn custom of the rites,

when it was completed, she might be attended by bright Hymenaeus,

but so that, chaste though unchastely, at the very time of marriage,

she might fall as a sorrowful victim beneath her sorrowing father's sacrifice,

so that a happy and favorable departure might be granted to the fleet.

To such great evils was religion able to persuade.

You yourself, at any time now, will seek, overcome by the terrifying

sayings of seers, to desert us.

For indeed how many dreams can they now invent for you,

which can overturn the principles of life

and disturb all your fortunes with fear!

And deservedly; for if men saw that there were a sure end

to their miseries, they would be strong enough by some means

to withstand the religions and threats of seers.

Now there is no reason for resisting, no power,

since eternal punishments in death must be feared.

For it is unknown what the nature of the soul may be,

whether it is born, or, on the contrary, is implanted in beings as they are born,

and at the same time perishes with us, severed by death,

or visits the darkness of Orcus and the vast hollows,

or by divine agency inserts itself into other beasts,

as our Ennius sang, who first from lovely

Helicon bore down a crown of ever-living foliage,

which might be renowned and illustrious among the Italian tribes of men;

although nevertheless there are Acherusian temples besides,

Ennius sets forth in everlasting verses, declaring

that neither souls nor our bodies endure there,

but certain images, wan in wondrous ways;

whence he relates that there arose before him the form of ever-flourishing Homer

and began to shed salt tears

and to unfold the nature of things in words.

Wherefore we must rightly hold an account also of things above,

of the courses of the sun and moon,

by what method they come about, and by what force each thing is done

on earth; then, above all, it must be seen by keen reasoning

of what nature soul and mind consist,

and what thing, confronting our minds while we are awake,

terrifies us when we are afflicted by disease and buried in sleep,

so that we seem to see them and hear them face to face,

whose bones the earth embraces after death has been undergone.

Nor does it escape my mind that the obscure discoveries of the Greeks

are difficult to illuminate in Latin verses,

especially since many matters must be treated in new words

because of the poverty of the language and the novelty of the things;

yet your merit and the hoped-for pleasure

of sweet friendship persuade me to undertake any toil

and induce me to keep watch through the tranquil nights,

seeking by what words and finally by what poem

that I may be able to spread clear lights before your mind,

whereby you may be able to behold things hidden deep within.

This terror of the mind, therefore, and these shadows must

be dispelled not by the sun’s rays or the bright shafts of day,

but by the aspect and reasoning of nature.

The first principle from which our account shall here take its beginning:

nothing is ever begotten from nothing by divine power.

For indeed fear holds all mortals in this way,

because they observe many things happening on earth and in heaven,

the causes of whose workings they are unable by any reasoning to see,

and suppose that they come to pass by divine will.

For which reasons, when we have seen that nothing can be created

from nothing, then from that point we shall more rightly discern what follows,

both whence each thing can be created

and in what way each work comes to pass without the gods.

For if things came to be from nothing, from all things

every kind could be born; nothing would need seed.

First men could arise from the sea, from the earth

the scaly race, and birds burst forth from the sky;

herds and other cattle, every race of wild beasts,

would occupy cultivated and deserted places by uncertain birth.

Nor would the same fruits be wont to remain constant on trees,

but they would change; all could bear all things.

Indeed, if there were not for each its generative bodies,

how could a fixed mother-substance subsist for things?

But now, because all things are created from fixed seeds,

from these each is born and comes forth to the borders of light,

wherein there is the matter and the first bodies of each;

and for this reason not all things can be begotten from all things,

because in fixed things there is a hidden capacity.

Moreover, why do we see the rose in spring, grain in heat,

and vines pour forth at the prompting of autumn,

if not because, when the fixed seeds of things

have flowed together in their own time, whatever is created is disclosed,

while the seasons are present and the quickened earth

safely bears tender things forth to the borders of light?

But if they came to be from nothing, they would arise suddenly

at an uncertain time and in alien parts of the year,

since there would be no first beginnings which, from a generative

union, could be held back by an unfavorable season.

Nor, further, would there be need of an interval for things to grow,

for seeds to come together, if they could grow from nothing;

for young men would suddenly become from little infants,

and shrubs, springing from the earth, would leap up all at once.

That none of these things happens is manifest, since all things

grow gradually, as is fitting, from a fixed seed,

and in growing preserve their kind; so that you may recognize

that each thing likewise grows great from its own matter.

To this is added that without the regular rains of the year

the earth cannot send forth gladdening offspring,

nor, moreover, can the nature of living creatures, set apart by food,

propagate its kind and preserve life;

so that you would rather suppose that bodies are common to many things,

that there are many such, as we see elements in words,

than that anything can exist without first-beginnings.

Finally, why was nature unable to produce men so great

that they could cross the sea on foot through its shallows

and tear apart great mountains with their hands

and, by living, overcome many living ages,

if not because a fixed matter has been assigned to things

to be generated, from which it is established what can arise?

Therefore it must be confessed that nothing can be made from nothing,

since seed is needed for things, by which each created thing

may be brought forth into the tender breezes of air.

Lastly, since we see cultivated places excel uncultivated ones

and, through hands, render better fruits,

there are evidently in the earth first-beginnings of things,

which we, turning the fertile clods with the plough

and subduing the soil of earth, summon forth to birth;

but if there were none, without any labour of ours

you would see each thing come about of its own accord much better.

To this is added that everything returns again into its own bodies

nature dissolve and utterly destroy things into nothing.

For if anything were mortal in all its parts,

each thing snatched suddenly from sight would perish;

there would be no need of force, indeed, which could from its parts

produce disruption and unbind its fastenings.

But now, because all things consist of eternal seed,

until a force comes which shatters things by a blow

or penetrates within through the voids and dissolves them,

nature suffers the destruction of nothing to be seen.

Moreover, whatever time removes through age,

if, consuming all its matter, it utterly destroyed it,

whence does Venus bring back into the light of life the race of living things

kind by kind, or, once brought back, whence does the ingenious earth

nourish and increase it, providing food kind by kind?

Whence do the native springs and the rivers flowing from afar abroad

supply the sea? Whence does the ether feed the stars?

For infinite age and the days gone by ought to have consumed

all things which are of mortal body.

But if, in that span and in the age gone before, there have existed

those things from which this sum of things, renewed, consists,

certainly they are endowed with an immortal nature.

Therefore things cannot all return to nothing.

Finally, the same force and cause would commonly destroy all things,

unless eternal matter held them together,

linked together among themselves more or less entangled;

for touch would surely be a sufficient cause of death,

seeing that there would be no bodies of eternal substance, whose

texture some force would have to dissolve.

But now, because the linkages of the first-beginnings

subsist dissimilar among themselves and matter is eternal,

things remain with their body unharmed, until a force sufficiently keen

comes upon them, found adequate to the texture of each.

Therefore no thing returns to nothing, but all

return by dissolution into the bodies of matter.

Moreover, rains perish when father Aether

has cast them down into the lap of mother Earth;

but shining crops spring up and the branches grow green

upon the trees; they themselves grow and are laden with fruit.

Hence in turn our race and that of the wild beasts is nourished;

hence we see glad cities flourish with children

and the leafy woods sing everywhere with new birds;

hence weary cattle over the glad rich pastures

lay down their fat bodies, and a gleaming milky fluid

flows from their distended udders; hence new offspring

with feeble limbs, frolicsome through the tender grass,

plays, its young minds struck by pure milk.

Therefore, whatever things are seen do not perish utterly,

since nature nourishes from one thing and restores, nor does she any...

allows a thing to be produced only with the aid of another's death.

Come now, since I have taught that things cannot be created

from nothing, nor likewise be recalled, once produced, to nothing,

lest perhaps you should nevertheless begin to distrust my words,

because the first-beginnings of things cannot be discerned by the eyes,

receive besides those bodies which you yourself must needs

acknowledge to exist in things and yet cannot be seen.

First, the impetuous force of the wind buffets the body,

rushes upon huge ships and scatters clouds,

meanwhile, racing over the plains in a swift whirlwind,

it lays low great trees and the loftiest mountains,

it ravages forests with tree-breaking blasts: thus it rages wildly with sharp

roaring, and the sea is fierce with threatening murmur.

Therefore winds are, plainly, unseen bodies,

which sweep sea, lands, and finally the clouds of heaven,

and, harrying them, snatch them away in a sudden whirlwind,

nor do they flow and spread destruction by any other method

than when the soft nature of water is borne onward suddenly

in an overflowing stream, which a great descent of water

from the high mountains, swollen by abundant rains,

increases, hurling down fragments of forests and whole trees;

nor can strong bridges endure the sudden force of the oncoming water:

thus, turbid with mighty rain, the river rushes against

the solid structures with strong force.

it makes a great crashing sound and rolls destruction beneath the waves

and huge rocks; wherever it rushes, it sweeps away whatever withstands the floods.

Thus, therefore, the blasts of winds too must be borne along,

which, just as when a mighty river has rushed down

in whatever direction, drive things before them and rush on

with repeated assaults, and sometimes, in a twisted whirl,

snatch them up and carry them away in a swiftly spinning vortex.

Wherefore, again and again, winds too are unseen bodies,

since they are found to rival great

rivers, which are of visible body, in deeds and ways.

Further, we perceive the various odors of things,

yet we never discern them as they come to the nostrils;

nor are we able to behold hot heat or cold

with the eyes, nor are we accustomed to discern voices;

yet all these things must necessarily consist of bodily

nature, since they can impel the senses;

for no thing can touch or be touched, except body.

Finally, garments hung upon a wave-breaking shore

grow wet, and the same garments, spread out in the sun, grow dry.

But neither in what manner the moisture of water has settled in

has been seen, nor again in what manner it has fled through heat.

Therefore the moisture is dispersed into small parts,

which the eyes can by no means see.

Indeed, even after many returning years of the sun

a ring on the finger is worn thin by being worn,

the fall of dripping water hollows a stone, the hook of the plough,

the iron ploughshare secretly diminishes in the fields,

and we see the paved stone roads, already worn away

by the feet of the common people; then beside the gates bronze

statues show their right hands becoming thinner

often through the touch of those who greet them and pass by.

Therefore we see that these things are diminished, since they have been worn away.

But what bodies depart at any particular time,

envious nature has shut off from view.

Finally, whatever days and nature

gradually bestow upon things, compelling them to grow in due measure,

no strain of the eyes can keep fixed upon;

nor, further, can it see whatever things grow old through age and wasting,

nor what the rocks that overhang the sea, eaten away by the biting salt,

likewise lose in time.

Nature therefore conducts things by bodies unseen.

Yet not all things are held packed tight on every side

by body in nature; for there is void in things.

For you, to have learned this will be useful in many matters

and will not allow you, wandering, always to doubt and inquire

about the sum of things and to distrust my words.

For this reason there is untouched place, empty and void.

and if this did not exist, things could in no way be moved

could [move]; for the function that belongs to body,

to hinder and obstruct, would be present at all times

to all things; therefore nothing could proceed,

since no thing would afford a beginning of yielding.

But as it is, through seas and lands and the heights of heaven

we discern many things moving in many ways by varied means

before our eyes—things which, if there were no void,

would not so much lack their restless motion

as would never have been generated in any way at all,

since matter would have lain packed close on every side.

Moreover, however solid things may be thought to be,

from these facts nevertheless you may see that they are of rare body.

In rocks and caverns the liquid moisture of waters

percolates, and all things weep with copious drops.

Food disperses itself through the whole body of living creatures;

shrubs grow and in due season put forth their fruit,

because food, from the deepest roots onward, through their whole extent

is diffused through trunks and through branches.

Voices pass through barriers and the closed walls of houses,

and stiffening cold percolates to the bones.

Unless there were voids through which each body could

pass, you would see that this could occur by no means.

Finally, why do we see some things surpass others

in weight, though their form is not at all greater?

for if there is as much in a ball of wool as

there is of body in lead, it is fitting that it weigh as much,

since it is the function of body to press all things downward,

whereas the nature of void remains without weight.

Therefore, what seems equally large yet lighter

plainly declares that there is, no doubt, more void in it;

but, contrariwise, what is heavier shows that there is more body

in it and that it contains much less empty space within.

Therefore, no doubt, that which we seek by keen reasoning

is mingled with things—the thing we call void.

Lest, in these matters, that which certain men imagine lead you away

from the truth, I am compelled to anticipate it.

They say that the glittering liquids yield to scaly creatures

and open up liquid paths, because behind them the fishes

leave places into which the yielding waters may flow together;

thus other things too can move among one another

and change place, although all things are full.

Clearly, this whole view is accepted on false reasoning.

For where, in the end, will the scaly creatures be able to advance,

unless the liquids yield them space? Moreover, where

will the waters be able to withdraw, when the fishes cannot go?

Therefore either every body must be deprived of motion,

or it must be said that void is mingled with things,

from which each thing first takes the beginning of moving.

Finally, if two broad bodies, by collision,

spring apart swiftly, necessarily all the air must

that comes to be between the bodies occupy the void.

Moreover, although it flows together with swift currents all around,

yet it will not be able in a single moment wholly

to fill the space; for it must first occupy each place,

and then all be possessed.

But if perhaps anyone, when bodies have sprung apart,

then thinks that this happens because the air condenses itself,

he is mistaken; for then a void comes to be which was not there before,

and likewise a void is filled which existed before,

nor can the air be made denser in such a manner;

nor, even if it now could, could it, I think, without void,

draw itself into itself and gather its parts into one.

Wherefore, although you may linger long in adducing many causes,

still you must confess that there is void in things.

And besides, by recounting them I could

marshal many arguments to win credence for my words.

But these slight traces are enough for a keen mind,

through which you may be able to discover the rest by yourself.

For just as dogs often find the leaf-covered lairs

of mountain-ranging wild beasts by their nostrils,

once they have set upon the sure tracks of the path,

so you yourself, by yourself, may see one thing from another

in such matters you will be able to make your way into all the blind hiding-places

and thence bring forth the truth.

But if you are sluggish or withdraw even a little from the matter,

this I can promise you plainly, Memmius:

so copious draughts from great fountains

will my sweet tongue pour forth from my rich breast,

that I fear lest slow old age first creep through my limbs

and loose in us the fastenings of life,

before, concerning any one thing, all the abundance

of arguments has been sent through your ears in verse.

But now, that I may return to continue in words what I began,

therefore all nature, as it is in itself, consists of two things;

for there are bodies and void,

in which these are situated and through which they move in different directions.

For common sensation declares that body exists in itself;

unless primary trust in this prevails as a firmly grounded principle,

there will be no point of reference by which, concerning hidden things,

we can establish anything by reasoning of the mind.

Then again, if place and space, which we call void,

did not exist, bodies could not be situated anywhere

nor at all move in different directions anywhere;

as we showed you a little earlier above.

Moreover, there is nothing that you can say is separate from every

body and set apart from void,

because a nature, as it were third in number, has been discovered.

For whatever shall be, must itself be something,

whether of great or small, indeed, bulk, provided that it is;

if it has touch, however light and slight,

it will increase the number of body, and follow its sum;

but if it is intangible, so that in no respect it can

prevent anything from passing through it of its own accord,

then clearly this will be that which we call empty void.

Moreover, whatever exists by itself will either do something

or itself must be acted upon by other things acting,

or it will be such that things can be and be done in it.

But no thing can act or be acted upon without body,

nor, further, provide a place except empty void.

Therefore, besides void and bodies, no third nature in itself

can be left among the number of things,

either one that may at any time fall beneath our senses

or one which anyone can attain by reason of mind.

For whatever things are spoken of as existing, you will find either joined to these two

things, or you will see them as events of these.

A conjunction is that which nowhere can be separated and sundered

without destructive dissolution,

as weight to stones, heat to fire, fluidity to water,

touch to all bodies, intangibility to void.

But slavery, poverty, and riches,

liberty, war, concord, and all the rest whose

nature remains unharmed by their coming and departure,

we are accustomed, as is fitting, to call events.

Likewise, time does not exist through itself, but from things themselves

there follows a sense of what has been done in the past,

then of what is present, and what subsequently follows;

nor must one admit that anyone feels time through itself,

separated from the motion of things and from tranquil rest.

Finally, when they say that the Tyndarid was carried off and that the Trojan-born

race was subdued in war, one must take care

lest perhaps they compel us to confess that these exist through themselves,

since the ages of men to whom these events belonged

have already been carried away by irrevocable bygone time;

for one thing may be called an event in relation to the lands, another in relation to the regions themselves,

whatever shall have been done.

Finally, if there had been no matter of things

nor place and space in which each thing is done,

never would the fire, kindled by love of the Tyndarid's beauty,

waxing beneath the Phrygian breast of Alexander,

have kindled the famous contests of cruel war,

nor would the hidden, wooden Horse have set Pergama aflame for the Trojans by its birth,

with the nightly Greeks' offspring; 

so that you may perceive that all deeds done, fundamentally,

do not subsist or exist through themselves as a body does.

nor to be designated by the same reasoning by which void is constituted,

but rather so that you may rightly be able to call them accidents

of body and of place, in which each thing is done.

Bodies, moreover, are in part the first-beginnings of things,

in part those which consist in the union of first principles.

But as for those which are the first-beginnings of things, no force can

extinguish them; for in the end they prevail by their solid body.

Although it seems difficult to believe that anything

can be found in things with a solid body.

For the lightning of heaven passes through the barriers of houses,

as do shout and voices; iron grows white-hot in fire,

and stones burst apart under fierce, burning vapour;

when the hardened stiffness of gold, weakened, is dissolved by heat,

then the ice of bronze, conquered by flame, melts;

heat and penetrating cold pass through silver,

since, holding cups in our hands as is proper,

we have felt both, when moisture from waters was poured in from above.

To such a degree does there seem to be nothing solid in things.

But since true reasoning and the nature of things nevertheless

compel it, attend, while in a few verses I set forth

that there are things which consist of solid and eternal body,

which we teach to be the seeds and first-beginnings of things,

from which the whole sum of things, now created, consists.

First, since the nature of the twofold [kind] of the two...

It has been found that things—the body and the place in which each thing is done—consist far apart, dissimilar in kind;

the body and the place in which each thing is done,

it is necessary that each be pure and exist by itself.

For wherever there is space empty, which we call void,

there is no body there; and, further, wherever a body maintains itself,

there the void empty is by no means found to be.

Therefore the first bodies are solid and without void.

Moreover, since there is void in things that have come into being,

it is necessary that solid matter stand around it;

nor can any thing be proved by true reasoning

to conceal void in its body and hold it within,

unless you grant that what contains it consists of solid.

Further, this can be nothing but a union

of matter, which can contain the void of things.

Matter, therefore, which consists of solid body,

can be eternal, though other things are dissolved.

Then again, if there were nothing which might be called void,

all would be solid; unless, conversely, certain bodies

existed which filled whatever places they occupied,

all space that exists would prove to be void and empty.

Therefore, without doubt, body is distinguished from void in alternation,

since neither the full exists entirely

nor, further, the void; therefore there are certain bodies

which can distinguish void space by fullness.

these cannot be dissolved by blows struck from without,

nor thereafter, penetrated through and through, be unwoven,

nor can they, assailed by any other means, be made to fail;

a fact which I showed you a little earlier above.

For nothing, it seems, can be crushed without void,

nor broken nor split by cutting into two,

nor admit moisture, nor likewise penetrating cold,

nor inward-reaching fire, by which all things are brought to an end.

And the more each thing contains void shut up within,

the more deeply, when assailed by these agencies, it gives way.

Therefore, if first bodies are solid and without void

as I have taught, they must of necessity be eternal.

Moreover, unless matter had been eternal,

long ago every thing would have utterly returned to nothing,

and whatever things we see would have been born again from nothing.

But since I have taught above that nothing can be created

from nothing, nor what has been begotten be recalled to nothing,

the first beginnings must be of immortal body,

so that, at the final time, each thing may be able to be dissolved,

in order that matter may furnish a supply for things to be renewed.

The first beginnings, therefore, are solid in their simplicity,

nor can they by any other means, preserved through the age,

restore things from time infinite to the present.

Finally, if nature had appointed no limit

in the breaking of things, the bodies of matter had already

been reduced away by the earlier time that breaks,

so that nothing from them could, from a fixed time,

reach through to the conceived utmost end of its age.

For we see that anything whatsoever can be dissolved more quickly

than remade; wherefore, through the long

infinite age of all time previously elapsed,

whatever had thus far broken, scattering and dissolving,

could never be repaired in the remaining time.

But as it is, evidently, a fixed limit of breaking has been assigned and remains,

since we see each thing remade,

and, at the same time, periods limited according to kinds are set

for things, by which they may attain the flower of life.

To this is added that, although the bodies of matter are

most solid, nevertheless all things can be rendered,

which become soft—air, water, earth, vapours—

in what manner they come to be and by what force each is produced,

because void has once been intermixed among things.

But conversely, if the first-beginnings of things are soft,

whence may hard flints and iron be created?

No account will be able to be given; for from the very foundation every

nature will lack a principle of foundation.

Therefore there are solid bodies, powerful in their simplicity,

by whose denser union all things

can be compressed and display vigorous powers.

Furthermore, if no limit has been assigned to the breaking

of bodies, nevertheless from eternal time whatever

bodies must even now survive from things,

which have not yet become known as tried by any peril.

But since they are constituted endowed with a frail nature,

it is inconsistent that they could have remained through eternal time,

buffeted by innumerable blows throughout the age.

Finally, since it is now established that a limit has been assigned by kinds

to things in growing and in holding fast to life,

and what each can do according to the covenants of nature,

and furthermore what they cannot do, since indeed it stands decreed,

nor is anything changed, so that all things remain

to such an extent that all the various birds in their order

display the marks of their kind as being in their body,

they must also have a body of unchangeable matter,

unless, of course; for if the first beginnings of things

could be changed, having been overcome in some manner,

it would likewise be uncertain what could arise,

what could not, and finally what limited power belongs to each,

by what principle, and what deeply fixed boundary there is;

nor could generations so often reproduce by kind

the nature, habits, manner of life, and movements of their parents.

Then further, since every extremity is the utmost summit

of that body, which our senses discern

are now no longer able to discern, it exists, not surprisingly, without parts

and consists of a least nature, nor has it ever been

separate by itself, nor will it be able to be so hereafter,

since it is itself a part, and the first and single part, of another thing,

then other and other similar parts in succession

in a close-packed host fill out the nature of the body;

and since these cannot subsist by themselves, they must

cling to that from which they can by no means be torn away.

Therefore there are solid first-beginnings in their simplicity,

which, closely packed with least parts, cohere tightly.

not held together by the union of those parts,

but rather powerful through everlasting simplicity,

from which nature permits nothing now to be torn away or diminished,

preserving them as seeds for things.

Moreover, unless there be a least thing, every smallest

body will consist of infinite parts,

since indeed a part of a half will always have

a half-part, nor will any thing set a limit to this.

Therefore, between the sum of things and the least thing that exists,

there will be no difference; for however infinite in its entirety the whole

may be, nevertheless the things that are smallest

will likewise consist of infinite parts.

Since true reason protests and denies this

that the mind can exist, you must confess, once overcome,

that there are things which now exist endowed with no parts,

and consist of a minimal nature. Since these things exist,

you must also confess that they are solid and eternal.

Finally, if creative nature had been accustomed to compel all things to be dissolved

into their smallest parts,

she would now be unable to restore anything from them again,

because things that are augmented by no parts

cannot possess those things which generative

matter ought to possess: varied connections, weights, impacts,

collisions, motions, through which each thing is brought about.

Wherefore those who have supposed that the matter of things is

fire, and that the universe consists of fire alone,

appear to have fallen far from true reasoning.

Heraclitus, first leader in this battle-line,

famous for his obscure language rather among the empty-headed

than weighty among the Greeks, who seek the truth;

for fools especially admire and love all things

which they discern lurking beneath twisted words,

and regard as true those things which can pleasantly strike

the ears and are painted over with charming sound.

For why, I ask, could things be so varied,

if they were created from one pure fire?

For it would avail nothing for hot fire to become denser

nor would it rarely happen, if the parts of fire had the same

nature which the whole fire has above.

For the heat would be more keen when the parts were brought together,

but more languid when they were scattered and dispersed.

Moreover, there is nothing that you could suppose to be possible

in causes of such a kind, much less that the variation of things

could be so great from dense and rarefied fires.

This too: if they make void mixed in with things,

the fires will be able to become dense and to be left rarefied;

but because they discern many things that are contrary to them

and shrink from leaving pure void in things,

while they fear difficulties, they lose the true path

and, again, do not discern that, with void removed from things,

all things become dense and from all things one

body is made, having nothing of itself that it can swiftly send forth,

as heat-bearing fire casts forth light and vapour,

so that you may see that it is not from crowded parts.

But if perhaps they believe that in some other way it can be done

that fires in a mass are extinguished and change their substance,

clearly, if they refrain from making this out of any part,

all their heat will utterly perish into nothing, without doubt,

and whatever things are created will come to be from nothing;

for whatever, changed, passes beyond its own boundaries,

immediately this is the death of that which was before.

therefore something must remain over, unharmed, for them,

lest all things return for you utterly to nothing

and, reborn from nothing, the abundance of things grow strong.

Now therefore, since there are certain most steadfast bodies

which always preserve the same nature,

by whose departure or arrival and altered order things change

their nature and bodies transform themselves,

one may know that these are not fiery bodies of things.

For it would matter nothing that certain ones should withdraw, depart,

and that others be added, and certain ones changed in order,

if nevertheless all retained the nature of heat;

for whatever they created would in every way be fire.

But, as I think, it is thus: there are certain bodies whose

meetings, movements, order, position, and shapes

produce fires, and, when their order is changed, change

their nature; nor are they fashioned like fire, nor like any other

thing besides which can send bodies

to the senses and, by their impact, touch our touch.

Furthermore, to say that fire is all things, and that no

true thing in the number of things exists except fire,

as this same man does, seems to be sheer madness.

For he himself contends against the senses by means of the senses

and undermines them, on which all things believed depend,

by which fire itself, which he names, has become known to him;

for he believes that the senses truly recognize fire;

he does not believe the other things, which are no less clear.

which seems to me both vain and delirious;

for to what shall we refer? What can be more certain for us than the senses themselves,

by which we distinguish true things and false?

Moreover, why should anyone rather abolish all things

and wish to leave the nature of heat alone,

than deny that fires exist, yet leave another nature to exist?

For it seems an equal madness to say either.

Wherefore those who have thought that fire is the matter of things

and that the whole can consist from fire,

and those who have established air as the first principle for generating things,

or whoever have thought that moisture

fashions things by itself, or that earth creates them,

all things, and is changed into every nature of things,

seem to have wandered far, vastly far, from the truth.

Add also those who double the first beginnings of things,

joining air with fire and earth with liquid,

and those who suppose that all things can grow

from four things—from fire, earth, and breath and rain.

Foremost among these is Empedocles of Acragas,

whom the island bore upon the three-cornered coasts of its lands,

around which the flowing sea, in great windings,

the Ionian, sprinkles its brine from its grey-green waves.

and with a narrow strait divides with its waves the rushing sea

the shores of Aeolian land from the boundaries of this land.

here is vast Charybdis, and here the Aetnean roarings

of flames threaten anew to gather their wrath,

so that the force may again vomit forth from its jaws the fires burst out,

and again bear to heaven the flashes of flame.

Although this region seems in many ways greatly wondrous

to human nations and is said to be worth seeing,

rich in good things, fortified by the great strength of many men,

yet it seems to have possessed in itself nothing more illustrious than this man,

nor anything more sacred and wondrous and dear.

Indeed, the poems of his divine breast

cry aloud and set forth his splendid discoveries,

so that he scarcely seems to have been created of human stock.

Yet he, and those whom we have said above to be inferior,

outstandingly inferior in many respects and much lesser,

although discovering many things well and divinely,

gave forth responses from the shrine, as it were, of the heart,

more sacredly and with a far more certain reason than

the Pythia who speaks from the tripod and the laurel of Phoebus,

nevertheless brought ruin upon the first principles of things

and, great men, fell there by a great fall.

First, because they establish motion when void has been removed from things

and leave things soft and rarefied

bronze, sun, fire, earths, living creatures, crops

and yet they do not admit void into their body;

then, because they will make absolutely no end to the cutting

of bodies, nor let there be any halt to the breaking,

nor, moreover, allow anything least to stand in things,

since we see that the ultimate point of each thing

is what seems least to our senses,

so that from this you may infer that the things which you cannot discern

have as their ultimate point a least thing, standing firm.

To this is added likewise that, since they posit the first beginnings of things

as soft, which we see to be by nature

and endowed with a mortal body, it follows utterly that

the sum of things ought now to return to nothing,

and that, reborn from nothing, an abundance of things should flourish;

how far each of these is from the truth you will now understand.

Then, in many ways they are hostile and poisonous

to one another themselves; wherefore, either, having met, they will perish,

or they will flee apart as, when compelled by a storm,

we see lightning, rains, and winds flee apart.

Finally, if all things are created from four things

and all things are in turn dissolved back into those things,

why can those more rightly be called the first beginnings

of things than, conversely, things be thought theirs in return?

For they are generated in alternation and change their colour

and all nature among themselves from all time.

but if perhaps you think that fire and earth unite

in body, and the airy breezes and the moisture of liquid,

so that nothing in their assemblage changes its nature,

no thing will be able to be created for you out of them,

neither animate nor with an inanimate body, as a tree;

for each, in a shifting mass, will display its own

nature, and air, mixed, will be seen to remain

together with earth and with some moisture.

But in generating things the first-beginnings must

employ a hidden and blind nature,

lest anything stand out that might fight against and hinder

whatever is created from being able to exist in its own proper way.

Indeed, they also trace things back from the sky and its fires,

and first they make fire turn into the breezes

of air; thence rain be generated and earth be created

from rain, and, back again, all things return from earth,

first moisture, then air, then heat,

nor do these cease to change among themselves, to pass

from sky to earth, from earth to the stars of the world.

The first-beginnings ought by no means to do this.

For something immutable must remain over,

lest all things be reduced utterly to nothing;

for whatever, changed, passes beyond its own boundaries,

at once this is the death of that which was before.

Wherefore, since the things which we said a little before

come into change, it must needs be that they consist

of others which cannot be changed in any way,

lest all things wholly return to nothing for you;

nay rather, posit certain bodies endowed with such a nature

that, if perchance they have created fire,

the same bodies, with a few taken away and a few added,

their order and motion changed, can make the breezes of air,

and thus all things be changed into other things from others.

“But,” you say, “plainly manifest fact shows that all things grow into the breezes

of air from the earth; and unless the weather grants

rain at a favorable season,

so that the trees quiver beneath the soaking of the clouds,

and the sun, for its part, cherishes them and bestows heat,

crops, trees, and living creatures cannot grow.”

And indeed, unless dry food and tender moisture

aid us, once the body has been lost, all life likewise

would be released from all the sinews and bones;

for without doubt we are aided and nourished

by certain things, and different things by certain other things.

No wonder, since many first-beginnings, common in many ways,

of many things, are mingled in things;

therefore different things are nourished by different things in various ways.

and likewise it often greatly matters what first-beginnings

are held together with which others and in what arrangement,

and what motions they impart to and receive from one another;

for the same ones constitute heaven, sea, lands, rivers, and sun,

the same ones crops, shrubs, and living creatures,

but, mixed with others and in another manner, they are moved.

Indeed, even everywhere in our own verses themselves

you see many elements common to many words,

although you must nevertheless admit that verses and words among themselves

differ both in meaning and in their sounding sound.

So much can elements accomplish by a change of order alone;

but the first-beginnings of things that are can employ more means,

whereby each of the various things can be created.

Now let us also examine Anaxagoras' homoeomeria,

which the Greeks call thus, nor does the poverty of our native speech

allow us to express it in our language,

yet it is easy to set forth the thing itself in words.

First, by the homoeomeria of things, as he calls it,

he means, plainly, that bones [are formed] from tiny and minute

bones, and that flesh is produced from tiny and minute

pieces of flesh, and blood comes into being

from many drops of blood coming together among themselves;

and he thinks that gold can consist of particles of gold,

and earth grow together from small particles of earth,

fires from fires, moisture from moistures,

he fashions and supposes the rest by a similar reasoning.

Yet he grants that there is no void in things in any part,

nor that there is an end to bodies to be divided.

Wherefore, in each respect alike, it seems to me

that he too is mistaken, along with those whom we mentioned above before.

Add that he imagines first-beginnings far too feeble;

if the first-beginnings are constituted as endowed with a similar

nature, and are like the things themselves and likewise suffer

and perish, and nothing restrains them from destruction.

For what of these will endure under a mighty crushing,

so as to escape death, beneath the very teeth of destruction?

Fire, or moisture, or air? Which of these? Blood or bones?

None, as I think, when every thing alike utterly

will be as mortal as those things which we plainly see

perishing before our eyes, overcome by some force.

But that things can neither fall back into nothing nor indeed

grow from nothing, I maintain has previously been proved.

Moreover, since food increases and nourishes the body,

we may know that veins and blood and bones

* * *

or they will say that all foods, with their substance mingled,

exist and contain within themselves small bodies of sinews,

and bones, and in general veins and portions of blood,

it will come about that all food, both dry and liquid itself,

is thought to consist of things of another kind,

of bones and sinews and mixed pus and blood.

Moreover, whatever bodies grow from the earth,

if they are in the earth, the earth must consist

of things of another kind, which arise from the earth.

Transfer the argument likewise: you may use the same words:

if flame and smoke and ash lie hidden in woods,

the woods must consist of things of another kind,

of things of another kind, which arise from woods.

Here there remains a certain slender opportunity for hiding,

which Anaxagoras takes for himself: that he thinks all things

lie hidden, mingled with all things, but that that one thing

appears of which the greatest number are mixed

and are more at hand and placed in the foremost front.

Yet this is far removed from true reasoning;

for it would then be fitting that crops too, often, when shattered by the threatening

strength of a rock, should give forth a sign

of blood or something nourished in our body,

when we grind stone against stone, that gore should flow;

by like reasoning it was fitting that grasses too should often

send forth sweet liquids, drops of a similar taste,

such as milk is from the udder of the wool-bearing beast,

and indeed that often from crumbled clods of earth

that kinds of herbs, and crops and leaves, are seen

to lie hidden, minutely distributed throughout the earth;

finally, that ash and smoke are seen in logs,

when they have been broken apart, and tiny fires to lie hidden.

Since manifest reality teaches that none of these things happens,

you may know that things are not so mixed in things,

but that seeds, mixed in many ways, lie hidden

common to many things in things.

“But it often happens on great mountains,” you say, “that the lofty

topmost crowns of neighboring trees are rubbed

against one another, strong south winds compelling them to do this,

until they have flashed forth, the blossom of flame having arisen.”

To be sure, fire is nevertheless not implanted in the logs;

rather, there are many seeds of heat which, through rubbing,

when they have flowed together, create conflagrations in the woods.

But if flame had been hidden, already formed, in the woods,

the fires could not remain concealed for any length of time;

they would generally consume the woods, burn up the trees.

Do you now see, therefore, what we said a little before,

that it matters exceedingly much that the same first-beginnings

are held together with which others and in what arrangement,

and what motions they give and receive among themselves,

and that the same ones, slightly altered among themselves, create

fires and wood? In what way also the words themselves

the elements having been slightly altered among themselves,

although we designate woods and fires by distinct names.

Finally, whatever things you now discern in plain view,

if you think that they cannot come to pass unless you imagine

that the bodies of matter are endowed with a like nature,

by this reasoning the first-beginnings of things are lost to you:

it will come about that, shaken by trembling laughter, they guffaw

and moisten face and cheeks with salty tears.

Come now, learn what remains, and hear more clearly.

Nor does it escape my mind how obscure these things are; but a great hope

of praise has struck my heart with its sharp thyrsus

and at the same time has driven into my breast a sweet love

of the Muses, by which now, inspired and with vigorous mind,

I range through the pathless places of the Pierides, trodden before

by no one's foot.

It delights me to approach untouched springs,

and it delights me to draw from them and to pluck new flowers,

and thence to seek a distinguished crown for my head,

from where the Muses have veiled no one's temples before;

first because I teach concerning great things and proceed to free the mind

from the tight knots of religions,

then because, concerning so obscure a matter, I compose such lucid

verses, touching everything with the Muses' charm.

For this too seems not without reason;

but just as physicians, when they endeavor to give foul wormwood to children,

first touch the rims of the cup all around

with the sweet, golden liquid of honey,

so that the unguarded age of children may be deceived

to the very lips, while meanwhile it drinks deeply the bitter

fluid of wormwood, and, deceived, is not harmed,

but rather, restored by such means, grows strong,

so I now, since this doctrine for the most part seems

too grim to those by whom it has not been handled, and the common crowd

shrinks back from it, have wished to set forth to you our doctrine in sweet-speaking

Pierian song and, as it were, to touch it with the sweet honey

of the Muses,

if perhaps by such a method I might be able to hold your mind

in our verses, while you discern the whole

nature of things, with what formed shape it is endowed.

But since I have taught that the most solid bodies of matter

fly about forever, unconquered, through time,

come now, let us unfold whether there is any limit to their totality

or not; likewise, whether that void which has been found,

or place and space in which each thing is done,

is seen to be wholly finite at its foundation

or to lie open immeasurable and profoundly vast.

Therefore all that exists is limited in no direction of its paths;

for it would have to possess an extremity.

Moreover, an extremity seems unable to exist for anything.

to be, unless there be something beyond that sets a limit, so that it may be seen

beyond which this nature of sensation does not pursue farther.

Now, since it must be admitted that there is nothing outside the whole,

it has no extremity; therefore it lacks limit and measure.

Nor does it matter in what regions of it you stand;

so completely does whatever place each person has occupied leave in every

direction the whole infinite equally great.

Moreover, if all space that exists

be now supposed finite, if someone should run forth to its

furthest borders and, standing last, cast a flying missile,

do you prefer that it, hurled with mighty force, should go

where it has been sent and fly far on,

or do you think that something can prevent and obstruct it?

For you must confess and adopt one or the other.

Either of these alternatives bars every escape for you and

compels you to grant that it extends, removed from any limit.

For whether there is something that checks and brings it about

that it does not reach where it was sent and set itself at the boundary,

or it is borne outside, it did not set out from the boundary.

In this way I shall pursue the argument, and wherever you place

the outermost borders, I shall ask: what then will become of the missile?

It will come about that a limit can be established nowhere,

and the opportunity for flight will always extend the escape.

Moreover, all the space of the whole sum

if, enclosed on every side, it stood within fixed boundaries

and were finite, by now the abundance of matter

would have flowed together from every side by its solid weights to the bottom,

nor could any thing be done beneath the canopy of heaven,

nor would there be heaven at all, nor the lights of the sun,

since all matter, heaped together, would lie

settling down from infinite time already.

But now, evidently, no rest has been granted to the bodies

of the first-beginnings, because there is no lowest bottom at all,

whither they might, as it were, flow together and where they might establish their seats.

All things are ever carried on in unceasing motion

in every quarter, and bodies of matter are supplied from below,

swiftly, from the infinite.

Finally, before our eyes one thing seems to bound another:

air separates hills, and mountains the air,

land bounds sea, and conversely sea bounds all lands;

yet in truth there is nothing outside that sets a limit to the whole.

Therefore the nature of place and the expanse of the deep is such

that not even bright thunderbolts, running their course,

as they glide on through the everlasting stretch of time,

could traverse it, or bring it about that less remained to be gone over in their passage;

so vastly does an immense abundance lie open everywhere for things,

with boundaries removed in every direction on all sides.

Moreover, the sum of things itself to set a limit for itself

cannot be, nature holds, which [is] body [and] void;

and that which is void compels [it] to be bounded by body,

so that in this way it renders all things infinite in alternation,

or else one or the other, unless the other of them bounds it,

though of simple nature, may yet lie open unbounded,

nor sea nor earth nor the bright precincts of heaven

nor the race of mortals nor the sacred bodies of the gods

could endure for a scant moment of time;

for, dispersed from its assemblage, the abundance of matter

would be borne, loosened, through the great void,

or rather indeed would never have created any concrete thing,

since, scattered, it would not have been able to be gathered together.

For certainly not by design did the first-beginnings of things

each settle themselves in their place by keen intelligence and according to their own order,

nor indeed did they covenant what motions each should give;

but because, changed in many ways through all time by many means,

they are driven and agitated by blows from the infinite,

trying every kind of motion and combination,

at last they arrive at such arrangements,

as those by which this sum of things, having been created, endures,

and, preserved also through many great years,

once it has been cast into harmonious motions,

brings it about that rivers replenish the hungry sea with their abundant waves of water,

and that the earth, by the sun's heat—

cherished, may renew its offspring, and may the race of living things,

flourish, and the fires of the gliding ether may live.

which they could do in no way, unless a supply of matter

could arise from the infinite,

whence all things are wont in due time to repair what has been lost.

For just as the nature of living creatures, deprived of food,

wastes away, losing its body, so all things must

be dissolved, as soon as matter has failed to furnish

itself, having been turned aside by some means from its course.

Nor can blows from without on every side preserve the whole

entirety, whatever has been brought together.

For they can often strike and delay a part,

until others arrive and the whole can be made full;

yet meanwhile they are compelled to rebound, and at the same time

to grant to the first-beginnings of things space and time for flight,

so that they may be borne free from the assemblage.

Wherefore again and again many things must arise,

and yet, in order that the blows themselves also may be able to be supplied,

an infinite force of matter is needed on every side.

In these matters, Memmius, flee far from believing that

which they say: that all things lean toward the middle of the whole,

and that therefore the nature of the world stands without any

external blows and cannot anywhere be dissolved,

at top or bottom, because all things have leaned toward the middle.

if you believe that it itself can stand firm in itself at all,

and that all weights which are beneath the earth strive

upward, and rest, turned back, upon the earth,

as through waters we now see images of things;

and that by like reasoning animals wander upside down

and cannot fall away from the earth into the regions of heaven

downward any more than our bodies

can of their own accord fly into the temples of heaven;

that, when they see the sun, we behold the stars of night,

and that they divide with us in alternation the seasons of heaven

and pass nights equal to our days.

but vain [error] has * * * for fools

having embraced what they have, through * * *

for there can be no middle * * *

infinity; nor indeed, even if there should now be a middle,

could anything stand there * * *

than by any other far-off reasoning * * *

for every place and space, which we call void,

whether through the middle or not through the middle, must yield

equally to weights, in whatever direction they are borne by motion.

Nor is there any place where bodies, when they have arrived,

can stand in the void, having lost the force of weight;

nor, moreover, ought that which is void to support anything,

but, as its own nature demands, it must continue to yield.

Therefore things cannot be held by such a principle

conquered by a desire for the middle into a council.

Moreover, since they do not suppose that all bodies

strive toward the middle, but [only] those of lands and of liquid

the moisture of the sea and the great waves from the mountains,

and the things which, as it were, are held together in an earthly body;

but, on the contrary, they set forth that the thin breezes of air

and likewise hot fires are borne away from the middle,

and therefore that the whole ether trembles round about with constellations

and that the flame of the sun is fed through the blue regions of heaven,

because all heat, fleeing from the middle, gathers itself there,

nor at all can the topmost branches grow leafy on trees

unless nourishment comes gradually to each from the earth

lest, in the swift manner of flames, the walls of the world

suddenly fly apart, released through the great void,

and lest the rest follow by a similar principle

lest the thunderous temples of heaven crash down from above,

and the earth swiftly withdraw itself from beneath our feet, and all things,

amid the mingled ruins of things and heaven,

dissolving their bodies, depart into the deep void,

so that in an instant of time no remnant may remain

save deserted space and blind first-beginnings.

For from whatever part you first determine bodies to be absent,

this will be for things the gate of death,

by this way the whole throng of matter will give itself forth.

Thus you will discern these things, led on by a slight effort;

for one thing after another will grow clear, nor will blind

night snatch away your path, but you will see through to the utmost things of nature:

so will things kindle lights for things.
