so as to see by what principle each thing is done.

But certain men, on the contrary, ignorant of matter,

maintain that nature cannot, without the divinity of the gods,

in so great a work, suitably to human concerns,

change the seasons of the years and create crops,

and do besides all the rest which divine pleasure, the guide of life,

persuades mortals to seek and itself leads them to,

and, through the allurements of Venus, causes the generations to propagate,

lest the human race perish.

When they pretend that the gods established all these things

for that cause, they seem in all matters

to have fallen far away from true reasoning.

For although I do not know what the first-elements of things are,

yet from the very constitution of the sky I would dare

to affirm this, and to demonstrate it from many other things as well:

that the nature of the world was by no means created for us by divine power—so great a faultiness does it stand endowed with.

What these are, Memmius, we shall make clear to you later;

now we shall set forth what remains concerning motions.

Now is the place, I think, to establish for you this point also in these matters:

that no bodily thing can by its own force

be borne upward or move upward.

Let not bodies of flame deceive you in this regard;

for flames arise directed upward and take their increase,

and shining crops and trees grow upward,

although all weights, so far as lies in themselves, are borne downward.

nor when fires leap up to the roofs of houses

and with swift flame taste the beams and timbers,

must it be thought that they do this of their own accord, without force applied.

Thus blood, discharged from our body,

leaps forth, bounding high and scattering gore.

Do you not see also with how great a force the water

repels beams and timbers? For the more we have forced them down deep

straight down, and with great force have pressed many of them down with difficulty,

the more eagerly it thrusts them upward and sends them back,

so that more than half emerges and springs out above.

And yet, so far as lies in themselves, we do not doubt, I think,

that all these things are borne downward through the empty void.

Thus, therefore, flames too must be able, pressed out through the breezes

of air, to rise upward, although

their weights, so far as lies in them, struggle to draw them downward.

And the nocturnal torches of heaven flying on high—

do you not see them draw out long trails of flame

in whatever directions nature has granted them a path?

Do you not see stars and constellations fall to earth?

The sun too, from the summit of heaven, scatters all

its heat in every direction and sows the fields with light;

therefore the sun's heat too is directed toward the earth.

And you see thunderbolts fly crosswise through the rains,

now from this side, now from that, fires burst from the clouds

they clash together; fiery force falls everywhere upon the earth.

This too we desire that you should recognize in these matters:

when bodies are borne straight downward through the void

by their own weights, at times more or less uncertain

and at uncertain places, they swerve a little from their course,

only so much that you could say their motion has been altered.

For unless they were accustomed to swerve, all things downward

would fall like drops of rain through the deep void,

nor would collision arise, nor a blow be produced

among the first-beginnings; thus nature would never have created anything.

But if perhaps anyone believes that heavier

bodies, because they are borne more swiftly straight through the void,

fall from above upon lighter ones and thus generate blows

which can yield generative motions,

he strays far away from true reasoning.

For whatever things fall through water and thin air,

must accelerate their falls in proportion to their weights,

because the body of water and the thin nature

of air cannot equally delay every thing,

but, overcome, yield more quickly to heavier things;

but, on the contrary, the void can at no point, from no quarter, nor at any

time, offer resistance to any thing,

without continuing to give way, as its own nature demands;

wherefore all things ought through the untroubled void

to be driven with unequal weights equally.

Therefore the heavier will never be able to fall upon the lighter

from above, nor by themselves to produce blows

that vary their motions, through which nature conducts things.

Wherefore, again and again, it is necessary that bodies swerve a little;

and no more than the least, lest we seem to invent

oblique motions and the true fact refute this.

For we see that this is plain and manifest:

weights, so far as lies in themselves, cannot move obliquely

when they plunge down from above, as you may discern;

but that they swerve at all from the straight course of their path—

who is there that can discern it?

Finally, if every motion is always connected

and a new motion arises from the old in a fixed order,

and if the first-beginnings do not, by swerving, make

some beginning of motion that may break the bonds of fate,

so that cause does not follow cause from infinity,

whence comes this freedom in living creatures throughout the lands,

whence comes this will, I say, torn away from the fates,

by which we proceed wherever pleasure leads each one,

and likewise swerve in our motions neither at a fixed time

nor in a fixed region of place, but where the mind itself has borne us?

For beyond doubt in these matters each person’s own will

gives the beginning, and from it motions are spread through the limbs.

do you not see also, when the barriers have been opened in a point of time,

that nevertheless the eager force of the horses cannot burst forth

so suddenly as the mind itself desires?

For the whole supply of matter throughout the entire body

must be stirred up, stirred up through all the limbs,

so that it may follow, straining, the mind's impulse;

so that you may see that the beginning of motion is created from the heart

and proceeds first from the will of the mind,

then thereafter is imparted through the whole body and limbs.

Nor is it the same as when we move forward, impelled by a blow

through the great force and great compulsion of another;

for then the whole matter of the entire body,

as is clear to us, goes and is dragged on against our will,

until the will has checked it through the limbs.

Do you not now see, therefore, that although an external force may drive many men

and often compel them to move forward against their will

and to be swept headlong along, yet there is in our breast

something that can fight against and resist it?

At whose discretion also the supply of matter

is compelled sometimes to bend through the limbs and members,

and, when thrown forward, is checked and settles back again.

Wherefore you must admit that in the seeds too there is the same thing,

that there is another cause of motions besides blows and weights,

whence this inborn power is ours,

since we see that nothing can be made from nothing.

For weight prevents everything from occurring through blows

as though by an external force; but lest necessity itself

have mastery within in all things that are done,

and, as though conquered, be compelled to yield and suffer,

this is effected by the slight swerve of the first-beginnings,

neither at a fixed region of place nor at a fixed time.

Nor has the store of matter ever been more closely packed

nor, again, at greater intervals;

for nothing is increased, nor does anything perish from it.

Therefore, in whatever motion the bodies of the first-beginnings

now are, in the same they were borne in ages past,

and thereafter they will always be borne in like manner,

and the same things which have been wont to be begotten will be begotten

under the same condition, and will be and will grow and prevail by strength,

so far as is granted to each through the covenants of nature.

Nor can any force change the sum of things;

for there is no place to which any kind of matter

can escape from the whole, nor into the whole is there any place whence

a new force, having arisen, can break in and change the whole

nature of things and alter its motions.

In these matters it is not wonderful why,

although all the first-beginnings of things are in motion,

the totality nonetheless appears to stand in complete repose,

except insofar as it imparts motion from its own body.

For the nature of the first elements lies wholly far below

our senses; wherefore, when you can no longer

discern them themselves, their motions too must escape you;

especially since the things that we can discern conceal

their motions nevertheless, often when separated by a space of places.

For often on a hill, cropping the luxuriant pastures,

the fleecy flocks creep along, wherever the grasses, calling each one,

invite them, budding with fresh dew,

and the lambs, when sated, play and flash about gently;

all of which appear to us confused from afar

and as though a whiteness were standing still on the green hill.

Moreover, when great legions fill the places

of the plains in their course, stirring up the likenesses of war,

when their gleam rises to the sky and all around

the earth glitters with bronze, and beneath, by the force of men,

a sound is raised by their feet, and the mountains, struck by shouting,

throw back their voices to the stars of the world,

and horsemen fly about all around and suddenly through the midst

traverse the plains, shaking them with mighty onset;

and yet there is some place among the high mountains, from which

they seem to stand still and the gleam to remain fixed upon the plains.

Come now, next learn what kind the beginnings of all things are

and how far they differ in their shapes,

perceive how varied they are in their manifold shapes;

not because many are endowed with a form too little alike,

but because not all things universally consist alike for all.

Nor is this surprising; for since their abundance is so great

that there is neither an end, as I have taught, nor any sum,

they must, unsurprisingly, not all altogether

be affected with equal texture and similar shape.

Moreover, the human race, and the dumb swimming creatures,

the scaly herds, the glad cattle, and the wild beasts,

and the various birds, which the gladdening places of waters

throng around the banks, springs, and lakes,

and those which, flying about, haunt the pathless groves—

go on, take any one of these kinds;

yet you will find that they differ among themselves in shape.

Nor could offspring recognize their mother by any other means,

nor a mother her offspring; yet we see that they can do this

no less than humans are known among themselves.

For often before the splendid shrines of the gods a calf,

slain beside the incense-burning altars, falls down,

breathing out from its breast a warm stream of blood;

but its bereft mother, wandering through the green glades,

knows the tracks pressed on the ground by cloven hooves,

surveying every place with her eyes, if anywhere she may be able

to catch sight of her lost young, and fills [the place] with lamentations

standing by the leafy grove and repeatedly revisits it,

pierced by longing for the stallion's stall;

nor can the tender willows and the grasses thriving with dew,

nor any streams gliding down from their lofty banks,

delight her mind and turn away her sudden care,

nor can other forms of calves amid the happy pastures

divert her mind and lighten her care;

so greatly does she require something her own and familiar.

Moreover, tender kids, with trembling voices,

recognize their horned mothers, and wanton lambs the sheep

that bleat; thus, as nature demands,

nearly each runs down to its own udder of milk.

Finally, any grain, yet not every grain

of whatever kind, you will see to be like one another in its own kind,

without some difference in forms occurring among them.

And by a like principle we see the race of shells

paint the bosom of the earth, where with soft waves

the sea has fed the thirsty sand of the curving shore.

Wherefore, again and again, by a similar principle it is necessary,

since they endure by nature and are not made by hand,

that the first-beginnings of things are not fashioned

to one fixed form, but fly about, some unlike one another in shape.

It is very easy for us to resolve by the reasoning of the mind

why lightning's fire is far more penetrating

how our [fire] flows from earthly torches;

for you might say that the heavenly fire of lightning

consists of subtler and smaller shapes,

and therefore passes through openings through which the fire

of ours, arisen here from logs and created from torch-pine, cannot pass.

Moreover, light passes through horn, but rain

is repelled. Why, unless those [bodies] of light are smaller

than those of which the nourishing liquid of waters consists?

And although we see wines suddenly flow

through a strainer, olive oil, on the contrary, lingers slowly,

either because, doubtless, it consists of larger elements

or of elements more hooked and interwoven with one another,

and thus it comes about that the first-beginnings are not so suddenly drawn apart

from one another, each individual one

seeping singly through the openings of each [strainer].

To this is added the fact that the liquids of honey and milk

affect the tongue in the mouth with a pleasant sensation;

but, on the contrary, the foul nature of wormwood and of fierce

centaury wracks the mouth with a loathsome taste;

so that you may readily recognize that those things which can touch the senses

pleasantly are composed of smooth and round [particles],

whereas, on the contrary, whatever things seem bitter and rough,

these are held together more by hooked [particles] linked with one another

and for that reason are accustomed to cut through our passages

to break through the body by their senses and their entrance.

Finally, all good things and bad things in their effect upon the senses

contend among themselves, being formed in unlike shapes;

lest perhaps you should suppose that the bitter

harshness of the grating saw consists equally of smooth elements

and the music of the Muses, which through the strings of an instrument

they fashion, awakened by the moving fingers;

nor suppose that first-beginnings of similar shape penetrate

into men's nostrils when foul corpses are burning,

and when the stage is freshly drenched with Cilician saffron

and the altar nearby breathes out Panchaean scents;

nor should you establish that the good colours of things consist of similar

seed, colours which can feed the eyes,

and those which prick the sight and compel it to weep,

or which appear foul and hideous in their ugly appearance.

For every thing whatsoever that soothes the senses for you

has not been created without some primary smoothness;

but, on the contrary, whatever is constituted troublesome and rough

has not been found without some harshness of matter.

There are also things which are now rightly judged neither smooth

nor at all hooked with curved points,

but rather with angles projecting slightly, so that they can

tickle the senses rather than wound them;

of this kind are, now, dregs and the flavours of elecampane.

Finally, that hot fires and icy frost

by unlike means prick the senses of the body

is an indication to us of each kind of touch.

For touch—touch, by the holy divinities of the gods—

is the body's sense, whether an external thing

makes its way in, or whether that which has arisen within the body harms it

or gives pleasure as it issues forth in the generative acts of Venus,

or when, from a blow, within the body itself

the stirred seeds disturb and confound the sense among themselves;

as, for instance, if you yourself should happen with your hand

to strike any part of your own body and test it.

Wherefore it must needs be that the shapes differ greatly

in the first-beginnings, which can produce diverse sensations.

Finally, those things which seem to us hard and dense

must needs consist more of hooked atoms interlinked among themselves

and be held together, as it were, closely compacted by branching forms.

In this class, now, foremost are adamantine rocks,

which stand firm in the first rank, accustomed to scorn blows,

and strong flints and the hard strength of iron

and bronzes that cry out in resistance to bolts.

Those things, indeed, ought to consist more of smooth and round atoms

which are liquid, made up of a flowing body.

For a draught of poppy-seed is likewise easy to drink as water is;

for the particles of each are not held together among themselves

and, when struck, likewise stands out inclined to roll.

Finally, all things which you discern in a moment of time

to scatter abroad, like smoke, clouds, and flames, must,

if they are not all composed of smooth and round [elements],

yet not be entangled and intertwined in such a way

that they can prick bodies and penetrate rocks,

and yet not cling together among themselves; whatever we see

to be jagged to the senses, so that you may easily recognize

that it consists not of entangled, but of sharp, elements.

But that the same things which are fluid you see to be bitter

—as is the brine of the sea—ought by no means to be wonderful;

* * *

for, in so far as it is fluid, it is composed of smooth and round [elements],

but hooked bodies, productive of pain, are mixed with the smooth.

Yet these hooked [bodies] need not be held back:

to be sure, they are nevertheless spherical, since they are composed rough,

so that they may at once roll onward and injure the senses.

And that you may think that rougher [elements] are mixed with the smooth

first beginnings, whence comes the bitter substance of Neptune,

there is a means of separating and seeing them apart,

where the same fresh moisture, more abundantly through the lands,

is filtered, so that it flows into a pit and grows mild;

for it leaves above the first beginnings of foul savor,

the rougher to be able the more to cling in the earth.

Since I have shown this, I shall go on to link a matter

which may suitably derive credence from this: that the first-beginnings of things

are limited in the variety of their shapes.

But if this were not so, then certain seeds would have to be

be of infinite increase in body.

For within the same single smallness of any body,

the shapes cannot differ much among themselves. Suppose, indeed, that the first

bodies consist of three smallest parts, or increase them by a few more;

surely, when you have placed all those parts of one body,

the highest and the lowest, changing right and left,

and have tried every manner, you will see what appearance of form

each arrangement gives to the shape of that whole body;

if thereafter by chance you wish to vary the shapes,

you will have to add other parts.

It will then follow,

by like reasoning, that the arrangement will demand others,

if by chance you wish also to vary the shapes.

Therefore an increase of body follows upon the novelty

of shapes. Wherefore you cannot believe that seeds

are distinct in infinitely many shapes,

unless you compel some to be of monstrous vastness—

a thing which, as I have already shown, cannot be proved.

Already barbarian garments and the gleaming Meliboean

purple, touched by the Thessalian colour of shells,

the golden generations of peacocks, steeped in smiling beauty,

would lie surpassed by the novel colour of things;

and the scent of myrrh and the flavours of honey, held in contempt,

and the swan's melodies and Phoebean songs wrought upon strings

would in like manner be overwhelmed and fall silent;

for something else, more excellent than each, would arise.

Likewise all things could thus recede backward into worse things

by parts, as we said into better;

for something else too would be more foul for nostrils,

ears, and eyes, and for the taste of the mouth.

Since these things are not so, but a fixed limit assigned to things

holds the whole on either side, you must admit that matter also

differs in limited shapes.

Finally, from fires up to the cold frosts of winter

there is a limit, and the distance back is measured by equal reasoning.

For every heat and cold and the temperate warmths between

lie in order, filling out the whole between the two.

Therefore created things differ by a limited ratio,

since they are marked on either side by a two-edged point,

here assailed by flames, there by stiff frosts.

Since I have shown this, I shall go on to link a matter which

may suitably derive credence from this: that the first-beginnings of things,

which are made perfect in a shape similar among themselves,

are known to be infinite.

For, since the difference

of shapes is limited, it is necessary that those which are alike

be infinite, or that the sum of matter

consist of a finite amount—which I have proved not to be so.

* * *

In verses I shall show that the particles of matter

from infinity maintain the sum of things continually

on every side by an unbroken succession of blows.

For although you see certain living creatures to be more rare

and discern nature to be more fertile in those,

yet in another region and place, and in lands remote,

there may be many of that kind and the number be filled up;

just as among quadrupeds we see, before all else,

the elephant, with snaky hands, in whose kind India

is fortified by a barrier of many thousands of ivory,

so that it cannot be penetrated within: so great is the host

of wild beasts, of which we see exceedingly few examples.

But yet let me grant this also; let there be, if you please,

some single thing alone, unique in its native body,

such that nothing like it exists in the whole circle of lands;

nevertheless, unless the force of matter is infinite,

from which it may be produced after being conceived, it will not be able

to be created, nor, what remains, to grow and be nourished.

For suppose that the generative particles of one single thing, finite in number, are throughout

cast about among all bodies by others,

whence, when they have come together, by what force and in what manner will they unite

in so great a sea and in a strange throng of matter?

They do not, I think, possess a principle of bringing together;

but just as, when great and many shipwrecks have occurred,

the great sea is wont to scatter benches and hollow hulls,

yardarms, prows, masts, and swimming oars,

floating decorations over all the shores of the lands,

so that they may be seen and give warning to mortals

of the snares, the force, and the treachery of the faithless sea,

so that they may wish to avoid them and never trust it at any time,

when the deceptive guile of the calm sea smiles;

thus, if once you posit certain first beginnings as finite,

they must, scattered throughout all time,

be dispersed by the differing tides of matter,

so that, driven together, they can never assemble into a union,

nor remain in union, nor grow by addition;

yet manifest reality plainly teaches that both occur:

that things are produced and, once produced, can increase.

Therefore it is plainly the case that in every kind there are

infinite first beginnings of things, whence all things are supplied.

Thus destructive motions cannot prevail

continually, nor bury well-being for eternity;

nor, further, can the generative and augmentative

motions of things continually preserve what has been created.

Thus is the contest of the first-beginnings waged on equal terms,

a war drawn out from infinite time.

now here, now there, the vital elements of things prevail

and likewise are overcome. Wailing is mingled with the funeral cry,

which infants raise when they behold the shores of light;

nor has any night followed day, nor dawn night,

that has not heard lamentations mingled with sickly wailings,

companions of death and of the black funeral.

This also is fitting to have sealed up in these matters

and to keep committed to mindful memory:

that there is nothing, among things whose nature appears manifest,

which consists of one single kind of first-beginnings,

nor anything that does not consist of mingled seed.

And whatever possesses more powers and many forces in itself,

shows thereby that very many kinds of first-beginnings

and various shapes exist within it.

First, the earth has within itself the primary bodies,

whence fountains, rolling their coldness, may continually renew the vast sea;

it has whence fires may arise;

for in many places the soils of the earth, set ablaze, burn,

but from its depths the force of Aetna rages with fires.

Then moreover it has whence it may raise up shining crops and luxuriant trees

for the peoples of humankind,

whence also rivers, foliage, and luxuriant pastures

may furnish [food] for the mountain-roaming race of wild beasts.

wherefore she is called the great mother of the gods and mother of wild beasts

and, she alone, the begetter of our body.

Her the learned poets of the Greeks of old have sung

as driving a pair of yoked lions in a chariot from her seat,

teaching that the great earth hangs in the expanse of air

and that earth cannot rest upon earth.

They yoked wild beasts [to her], because however wild the offspring,

conquered, ought to be softened by the duties of parents.

They encircled her lofty head with a mural crown,

because, fortified in choice places, she supports cities.

Now adorned with this emblem throughout great lands,

the image of the divine mother is borne in awe-inspiring fashion.

By the ancient rite of sacred observances, diverse peoples

call her the Idaean Mother and assign Phrygian bands

as companions, because from those regions first, they say,

crops began to be produced throughout the circles of the earth.

They assign Galli [to her], because those who have violated the divinity

of the Mother and have been found ungrateful to their parents,

they wish to signify, ought to be thought unworthy

to bring forth living offspring into the realms of light.

Taut drums thunder beneath palms, and hollow cymbals round about;

horns threaten with their hoarse-sounding song,

and the hollow pipe goads minds with its Phrygian rhythm,

and bear weapons before her, signs of violent frenzy,

so as to terrify the ungrateful minds and impious breasts of the populace

with fear, which are able to be [terrified] by the goddess's divine power.

Therefore, as soon as she has been borne into the great cities,

she bestows a mute salvation upon mortals in silentness,

they carpet every course of the roads with bronze and silver

enriching [her] with lavish tribute, and shower [her] with roses,

overshadowing the mother and the troop of her attendants with flowers.

Here an armed band—the Greeks call them Curetes—

whom they relate, if perhaps they are among the Phrygian companies,

play and leap in rhythm, glad in blood,

shaking the terrible crests of their heads in divine frenzy;

they represent the Dictaean Curetes, who, they say,

once concealed that crying of Jupiter in Crete,

when boys around the boy, in swift dance,

armed, beat bronze against bronze in rhythm,

lest Saturn, having got hold of him, should consign him to evil

and give his mother an eternal wound beneath her breast.

For this reason armed men accompany the great mother,

or because they signify that the goddess declares that they should wish, by arms

and valour, to defend their native land

and to be a protection and an honour to their parents.

Although these things are handed down as well and excellently arranged,

yet they have been driven far away from true reason.

for it is necessary that the whole nature of the gods, in itself,

enjoy eternal life with the utmost peace,

removed and far separated from our affairs;

for, free from every pain, free from dangers,

itself strong in its own resources, needing nothing from us,

it is neither won by good services nor touched by anger.

The earth indeed is at all times devoid of sensation,

and because it possesses the first-beginnings of many things,

it brings many things forth into the light of the sun in many ways.

Here, if anyone shall resolve to call the sea Neptune and Ceres grain,

and to make use of the name of Bacchus

rather than to utter the proper name of liquid,

let us concede that he may also declare this orb of lands

to be the mother of the gods, provided only that he himself

refrains from tainting his mind with foul religion in truth.

Thus often, feeding on grass from one field,

the wool-bearing flocks and the warlike offspring of horses

and the herds of horned cattle, beneath the same canopy of heaven

and slaking their thirst from one stream of water,

live with unlike appearance and retain that of their parents,

and each imitates, according to its kind, its nature and habits.

So great is the dissimilarity of matter in every kind of plant,

so great is it likewise in every stream.

Hence furthermore, however much one living creature [be formed] from all [these].

bones, blood, veins, heat, moisture, entrails, nerves

constitute—which, moreover, are far different,

being made perfect by the dissimilar shape of their first-beginnings.

Then, moreover, whatever things, kindled, burn with fire,

even if nothing else, yet contain these things in their body,

whence they can cast forth fire and send out light

and drive forth sparks and scatter ashes far and wide.

Surveying the rest by a like reasoning of the mind,

you will therefore find that they conceal in their body

the seeds of many things and hold in check various shapes.

Lastly, you see many things to which colour and taste alike

have been imparted together with smell—most especially many fruits.

These, therefore, must consist of various shapes;

for smell penetrates where colour does not enter into the limbs,

and colour likewise separately, taste separately, makes its way

into the senses; so that you may know that they differ in their first shapes.

Dissimilar forms, therefore, come together into one mass,

and things consist of mingled seed.

Indeed, even everywhere in these verses of mine themselves

you see many elements common to many words,

although you must nevertheless admit that verses and words among themselves

consist of different elements from one another;

not because many letters do not occur in common,

or because no two things among all are the same with one another,

But because not all things are universally alike for all.

Thus likewise in other things, although many are common

to many things, the first-beginnings of things

can nevertheless subsist in a sum differing among themselves; so that rightly it may be said that

the human race, and crops and flourishing trees, consist of different [elements].

the human race and crops and flourishing trees.

Yet it must not be thought that all things can be connected in every way;

for you would see prodigies commonly come to pass,

half-wild races of men arise, and tall [trees]

be generated at times from living body,

and many land-limbs be joined to sea-[limbs],

then Chimaeras breathing flame from their foul mouth

be fed by nature, mother of all, over the earth.

That none of these things comes to pass is manifest, since all things,

created from fixed seeds and a fixed mother,

we see are able, as they grow, to preserve their kind.

Clearly, it necessarily happens by a fixed principle.

For, from all foods, bodies pass within into their own limbs for each thing,

and, joined together, produce suitable motions; but, conversely, we see

nature cast alien things back upon the earth, and many things, driven by blind

blows, flee from bodies out of the body,

driven by blind blows, flee from bodies out of the body,

which could neither be joined anywhere nor within

accord with and imitate the vital motions.

But lest perhaps you think that living creatures alone are held

by these laws, a certain principle sets bounds to all things.

For just as all things born are dissimilar

from one another in their whole nature, so each one must necessarily

consist of a dissimilar shape of first-beginnings;

not because many things are not endowed with a rather similar form,

but because all things do not universally consist alike for all.

Moreover, since the seeds differ, necessarily there differ

their intervals, paths, connections, weights, blows,

encounters, motions; and these not only separate living creatures

in their bodies, but also distinguish lands and the whole sea

and keep all the sky apart from the lands.

Come now, receive what has been sought out by my sweet labor,

lest perhaps you should suppose that these things which you discern white before your eyes

are from white first-beginnings,

or that those which are black are born from black seed;

or that things imbued with any other color whatsoever

bear this color for the reason that the bodies

of matter are tinged with a color similar to it;

for there is no color at all in the bodies

of matter, neither like to things nor, indeed, unlike.

If perhaps it seems to you that no casting of the mind can be made upon these bodies,

you wander far from the path.

Moreover, if no nature of color has been assigned to the first-beginnings,

and they are endowed with various shapes,

from which they produce and vary every kind of colors,

because it greatly matters which seeds

are held together with which others and in what arrangement,

and what motions they impart to and receive from one another,

you can very readily at once give an account

why those things which a little before were of black color

can suddenly become of marble whiteness,

as the sea, when the great winds have stirred its plains,

is turned into grey waves with gleaming marble whiteness;

for you might say that what we often see as black,

when its material is mixed together and its arrangement

among its first-beginnings altered, with certain elements added and removed,

thereupon comes to pass that it seems gleaming and white.

But if the sea's plains consisted of azure

seeds, they could by no means grow white;

for however you might disturb things that are blue,

they could never pass over into a marble colour.

But if the seeds that produce the sea's

single, pure sheen are dyed with one colour and another,

then, just as often from other forms and varied shapes

something square and of a single shape is produced,

it was fitting that, as we discern that in a square there are

unlike shapes, so in the sea's expanse we should discern

or in any other single and pure sheen

colours far unlike one another and various.

Moreover, unlike shapes do nothing to hinder or obstruct

the whole from being no less square outwardly;

but the various colours of things impede and prevent

the whole thing from being able to possess a single sheen.

Then furthermore, that which leads and allures us to ascribe

colours sometimes to the first-beginnings of things—the reason—

perishes, since white things are not created from white,

nor are those called black from black, but from varied things.

for indeed they will arise much more readily,

white things born from no colour than from black colour

or from any other whatsoever, which might fight and oppose.

Moreover, since colours cannot exist without light

nor do the first-beginnings of things come forth into the light,

you may know that they are veiled in no colour;

for what colour can there be in blind darkness?

Indeed, colour itself is changed by light, because it

shines when struck by direct or slanting light;

as the plumage of doves is seen in the sun,

which, placed about the nape, crowns the neck;

for at one time it happens to be red with bright ruby,

at times, in some manner, it happens that it seems

to mingle green emeralds amid blue.

And the peacock's tail, when it is filled with abundant light,

changes its colours in a similar manner when turned about;

and since these are produced by a certain stroke of light,

you may know that it must be thought impossible for them to occur without it.

And since the pupil receives into itself a certain kind of blow

when it is said to perceive a white colour,

and then another when it perceives black and the rest,

nor does it matter of what colour those things which you touch may happen to be

are endowed, but with what sort of figure they are more fitted,

you may know that the first beginnings have no need of colour,

but, varying by diverse shapes, produce varying touches.

Moreover, since the nature of colour is not fixed by fixed

figures, and all the formations of the first beginnings

can exist in any brightness,

why are those things which consist of them not likewise

steeped in every kind of colour in every kind?

For it would be fitting that ravens too, often flying,

should cast forth a white colour from white feathers,

and that black swans should arise from black seed,

or from any other single and varied colour.

Indeed, the more each thing is drawn apart into minute

parts, the more you can discern

that colour gradually vanishes and is extinguished;

as happens when purple cloth is torn into small parts:

purple and the bright scarlet colour in great measure,

when it has been drawn apart thread by thread, is wholly lost;

so that from this you may know that the particles breathe out all their colour

before they depart to the first beginnings of things.

Finally, since you grant that not all bodies

give forth sound or smell, it follows

that you do not attribute sounds and smells to all things:

thus, since we cannot see all things with our eyes,

One may know that certain things subsist wholly without colour

just as certain things are without any smell and removed from sound,

nor is a keen mind any less able to perceive these

than to discern things deprived of other properties.

But lest perhaps you should think that bodies first principles remain stripped of colour alone,

they are also wholly devoid of heat,

and cold and hot vapour,

and are said to be barren of sound and empty of taste,

nor do they emit from their body any smell of their own.

Just as, when you set about making the pleasant liquid of marjoram and stacte

and the flower of nard, nectar that breathes fragrance into the nostrils,

it is especially proper to seek out,

if you can and are able to find it, the nature of scentless olive oil,

which sends no breath at all into the nostrils,

so that as little as possible it may be able to destroy the odours mixed in the compound

and blended, by assailing them with its own strength;

for the same reason the first-beginnings of things ought

not to contribute their own smell to things being produced,

nor sound, since they can emit nothing from themselves,

nor, by like reasoning, any taste at all,

nor cold, nor likewise hot or tepid vapour,

nor the other things which are nevertheless such as to consist of mortal nature:

soft, pliant, brittle, rotten, hollow, and of sparse body—

all these must be separate from the first principles.

if we wish to assign to things immortal

foundations, upon which the sum of salvation may rest;

lest all things utterly return to nothing for you.

Now, whatever things we see to possess sensation, you must needs

nevertheless admit that all consist of insentient

principles. Nor do manifest facts refute this

or contend against it—facts which are known and ready to hand—

but rather themselves lead us by the hand and compel us to believe

that living creatures are generated from insentient things, as I say.

For indeed one may see living worms come into being

from foul dung, when the earth, having acquired rottenness for itself,

has become moist from unseasonable rains.

Moreover, in like manner all things transform themselves.

Rivers transform themselves into foliage and luxuriant fodder,

into cattle; cattle transform their nature into our bodies,

and often from our body the strength and bodies of wild beasts

and of winged creatures are increased.

Therefore nature transforms all foods into living bodies

and from these produces all the senses of living creatures,

by no far different method than she

unfolds dry logs into flames and transforms everything into fires.

Do you not see, then, that the first-beginnings of great things

matter greatly in what order each is placed

and with which things, when mixed, they impart and receive motions?

Then furthermore, what is it that strikes the mind itself,

that moves it and compels it to utter varied sensations—

do you not believe that the sentient is produced from the insentient?

Unless, indeed, stones and wood and earth, though mingled together,

are nevertheless unable to render vital sensation.

Therefore, in these matters it will be fitting to remember this:

not that from absolutely all things whatsoever that create

sentient things I say sensations are forthwith produced,

but that it matters greatly, first, of what smallness they consist—

the things that make the sentient—and with what shape they are endowed,

what motions, arrangements, and positions, finally, they possess.

Of these things we see nothing in wood and clods of earth;

and yet these, when they have been, as it were, rotted by rains,

produce little worms, because the bodies of matter,

moved from their ancient arrangements by a new circumstance,

are so brought together as they ought to be for animals to be produced.

Next, those who maintain that the sentient can be created from sentient things,

and, further, from others accustomed to sensation

* * *

make them soft; for every sensation is joined

to viscera, nerves, and veins, all of which we see

to be composed soft in a mortal body.

But let it now be granted that these can remain eternal;

yet surely they must either have the sensation of parts

or be thought similar to whole animals.

But it is necessary that the parts should be unable to feel by themselves:

for the mind rejects every sensation of the limbs,

nor can a hand, separated from us, nor any

part of the body whatsoever, by itself retain sensation.

It remains that they be likened to whole living creatures,

so that they may be able to share everywhere in vital sensation.

How then will they be able to be called the first-beginnings of things,

and to avoid the paths of death, when they are living creatures,

and living creatures of one and the same kind as mortal things?

Yet, though they could do this, by gathering and assembly

they will effect nothing beyond a populace and a throng of living creatures,

namely, so that neither men nor herds nor wild beasts

can produce anything among themselves by coming together.

Thus likewise the things that we perceive must necessarily perceive.

But if perhaps they abandon their own sensation with their body

and take on another, what need was there for that which

is taken away to be assigned? Then besides, as we set forth before,

inasmuch as we see the eggs of birds changed into living chicks

and the earth teem with worms,

when stench has seized it because of unseasonable rains,

one may know that sensations can be produced from things without sensation.

But if perhaps someone will say that sensation can arise only

from non-sensation through change,

or by some offspring, as it were, which is brought forth outside,

for him it will be enough to make that plain and prove,

that no offspring comes to be except after a union has first been brought together,

nor is anything changed without union.

First, there cannot be sensations of any body

before the very nature of a living creature has been born,

unless, indeed, because matter is held dispersed

in air, rivers, lands, and things created from earth,

nor, having assembled in a manner suited to life,

has it brought together among themselves motions by which, surveying all things,

kindled senses preserve each living creature.

Moreover, a blow greater than the nature of any living creature can endure

suddenly strikes it and proceeds to confound every

sensation of body and mind.

For the arrangements of the first-beginnings are dissolved,

and the vital motions are thoroughly impeded,

until all matter, shaken through the limbs,

loosens the knots of the vital soul from the body

and casts it, dispersed, entirely outside through all the passages;

for what else do we suppose an encountered blow can do

except scatter and dissolve everything?

It also happens that, when a less severe blow is encountered,

the remaining vital motions are often wont to prevail,

to prevail and to calm the great tumult of the blow.

and to recall whatever back again into its own courses,

and to dispel the motion of death, as it were already ruling in the body,

and to kindle the senses almost lost;

for by what means rather, from the very threshold of death now,

can they return to life, their mind gathered together,

than by that toward which they have almost already run down, to go and depart?

Moreover, since pain occurs when the bodies of matter,

stirred by some force through the living entrails, through the limbs,

tremble within in their own seats,

and when they migrate back to their place, pleasant pleasure comes about,

one may know that the first-beginnings can be assailed by no pain

and receive no pleasure from themselves;

since they are not composed of any bodies of first-beginnings,

by whose novelty of motion they might suffer

or gain some fruit of fostering sweetness.

Therefore they must not be endowed with any sensation.

Finally, in order that all animals may be able to feel,

if sensation must now be attributed to their first-beginnings,

what of those from which the human race in particular has been increased?

Surely they too, shaken by quivering laughter, guffaw,

and sprinkle face and cheeks with dripping tears,

and are skilled in speaking much about the mixture of things,

and moreover inquire for themselves what their first-beginnings are;

since indeed, made like all mortals,

must themselves also consist of other elements,

then others from others, never to come to a stop, if you dare?

Indeed, I shall follow you, whatever you say can speak and laugh

and understand, so that this same thing may arise from others doing these things.

But if we perceive these things to be mad and frenzied,

and [a thing] can laugh though not increased from laughing things,

and understand and render an account in learned speech

though not from seeds that are understanding and eloquent,

how can those things which we see to have sensation be any less able

to be mingled with seeds wholly lacking sensation?

Finally, we all arise from heavenly seed;

that same one is father to all, from whom, when nurturing Earth has received the flowing

drops of moisture as mother,

pregnant, she bears bright crops and luxuriant trees

and the human race; she bears every breed of wild beasts,

when she provides the food by which all nourish their bodies

and lead a sweet life and propagate offspring;

wherefore she has deservedly acquired the name of mother.

Likewise, what was formerly from earth returns back

into the earth, and what was sent from the regions of ether,

that in turn the precincts of heaven receive back.

Nor does death so destroy things as to bring the bodies of matter

to an end, but disperses their assemblage;

then it joins one thing to others and brings it about that all—

so that they may change their shapes and alter their colours,

and seize the senses and give them back in a moment of time;

so that you may know with what [elements] the first-beginnings of these things are connected,

and in what arrangement they are held together,

and what motions they give and receive among themselves,

and lest you suppose that the eternal first bodies can reside in themselves,

because we see them floating on the surfaces of things

and at times coming to birth and suddenly perishing.

Indeed, it matters even in our verses themselves

with which [letters], and in what order, each is placed;

for the same [letters] signify heaven, sea, lands, rivers, sun;

the same [letters], crops, shrubs, living creatures;

if they are not all the same, yet by far the greatest part is

similar; but things differ by their arrangement.

Thus likewise in things themselves, now, the [elements] of matter—

their collisions, motions, order, arrangement, shapes—

when these are changed, the things too must be changed.

Now apply your mind to true reasoning.

For a very new thing strives to reach your ears

and a new aspect of things to reveal itself.

But no matter is so easy that at first it does not appear

rather difficult to believe; and likewise

there is nothing so great nor anything so wonderful

that all do not gradually cease to marvel at it,

first, the bright and pure color of heaven,

and all that it contains within itself—the stars wandering everywhere,

and the moon, and the splendor shining with the sun’s brilliant light;

all these things, if now for the first time they existed for mortals,

if they had suddenly been presented unexpectedly,

what could be called more marvelous than these things,

or what would nations have dared less to believe could come to pass?

Nothing, I think; so wondrous would this spectacle have been.

Yet now no one, wearied and sated with seeing,

deigns to look up at the bright temples of heaven.

Therefore cease, terrified by novelty itself,

to spit out the argument from your mind, but rather with keen

judgment weigh it; and if it seems true to you,

yield assent, or, if it is false, gird yourself against it.

For the mind seeks an account, since the totality of space is

infinite outside these walls of the world,

what, further, is there there, whither the mind desires to look onward,

and whither the free flight of the spirit itself may wing its way.

First, for us in every direction on all sides,

and on either flank, above and below, throughout the whole,

there is no end; as I have taught, and the thing itself

proclaims aloud, and the nature of the deep makes clear.

By no means now must it be thought likely,

since empty space lies open infinitely in every direction

and seeds in numberless quantity and in a deep sum

fly about in manifold ways, stirred by everlasting motion,

that this one world of lands and heaven has been created,

while all those bodies of matter do nothing outside it;

especially since this nature here has been made, and of itself

by chance, through the seeds of things clashing together

in manifold ways, rashly, vainly, and to no purpose, when forced together,

at last those particles came together which, suddenly cast together,

would always become the beginnings of great things—

of earth, sea, and heaven, and of the race of living creatures.

Therefore again and again you must confess that there are

other assemblages of matter elsewhere,

such as this one which the ether holds in its greedy embrace.

Moreover, when much matter is ready,

when place is at hand and no thing or cause delays,

things must, assuredly, be done and come into being.

Now, if there is so great an abundance of seeds as

the whole age of living creatures cannot avail to enumerate,

and if the same nature remains which can cast the seeds

of things into each place by a like method

to that by which they have been cast hither, you must confess

that there are other worlds in other regions of the earths,

and diverse races of men and generations of wild beasts.

To this is added that in the whole sum there is no single thing,

solely one that is begotten and solely one that grows,

without belonging to some kind, and without very many being

of the same kind.

Foremost among living creatures, with mind as guide,

you will find that thus there is a mountain-roaming race of wild beasts,

thus a twofold offspring of men, thus finally the dumb

flocks of scaled creatures and every body of birds.

For which reason it must be confessed by like reasoning that heaven,

earth, and sun, moon, sea, and the rest that are,

are not single, but rather innumerable in number;

since indeed the deeply fixed boundary of life

abides for these just as much, and they consist of a body born by nature,

as does every kind which abounds in these things by kinds.

If you hold these things well understood, nature is seen at once

as free, deprived of haughty masters,

herself doing all things of her own accord, through herself, free from the gods.

For, by the holy peace of the gods' tranquil breasts,

which pass a placid age and a serene life,

who is able to govern the sum of the immeasurable, who to hold

in his strong hand the mighty reins with control,

who at once to turn all the heavens and all

to fumigate the fruitful lands with ethereal fires,

and to be present in all places at every time,

so that he makes darkness with clouds and shakes the clear skies

with sound, then sends thunderbolts and [overturns] temples

often throws its own affairs into disorder and, withdrawing into deserted places,

rages, wielding the weapon which often passes by the guilty

and strikes lifeless the undeserving and the deserving?

And long after the world's generative time and the first day

of sea and earth and sun had arisen,

bodies were added from without, seeds were added all around,

which the great whole contributed by casting them about,

whence sea and lands might grow, and whence

the expanse of heaven might appear and the lofty house of the sky

might raise its roof far from the earth, and air might rise.

For, from all places and regions, all bodies are distributed to each their own,

and return to their own kinds:

moisture to moisture; with earthly body earth

grows; fires forge fire, and ether ether,

until at last, to the final perfected limit of growth,

the creative nature of things has brought all things;

as happens when there is now no more given within

the veins of life than flows away and departs.

Here the age of all things must come to a standstill;

here nature checks their increase by her own powers.

For whatever things you see grow great with joyous increase

and gradually climb the steps of mature age,

take to themselves more bodies than they send forth from themselves,

so long as all nourishment is easily introduced into the veins and so long as

are not so widely dispersed that they give off much,

and cause more loss than age consumes.

For indeed, that many bodies flow away and withdraw from things

must certainly be granted; but more must be added,

until they have reached the highest summit of growth.

Thereafter, little by little, age breaks

strength and mature vigor, and melts away into a worse condition.

For indeed, the larger a thing is, once growth has been taken away,

and the broader it is, in every direction on all sides

the more bodies it now scatters and sends forth from itself;

nor is all nourishment easily distributed into its veins,

nor, in proportion to the abundant tides it seethes forth,

is there enough from which so much can arise and be supplied.

Rightly, therefore, they perish, when, being rarefied by flowing away,

they are, and when all things succumb to external blows,

since indeed nourishment at last fails in great age,

nor do bodies striking from without cease to wear down every thing

and to subdue it with hostile blows.

Thus, therefore, the walls also of the great world all around,

when stormed, will yield collapse and crumbling ruins;

for nourishment must renew and make whole all things,

and nourishment support all things and sustain all things—

to no avail, since neither do the veins endure

what is enough, nor does nature supply as much as is needed.

And now indeed the age is broken and the earth exhausted;

it scarcely creates small animals, though it created all

generations and gave forth the huge bodies of wild beasts in birth.

For not, I think, did a golden rope from above

lower mortal generations from heaven into the fields,

nor did the sea or waves breaking upon rocks create them,

but the same earth that now nourishes them from itself begot them.

Moreover, shining crops and joyful vineyards

it first itself created spontaneously for mortals;

it itself gave sweet fruits and joyful fodder;

which now scarcely grow large even when increased by our labor,

and we wear out oxen and the strength of farmers,

we exhaust iron, scarcely supplied for the fields:

so greatly do they stint their produce and increase toil.

And now, shaking his head, the aged ploughman sighs

more often that his great labors have fallen in vain,

and, when he compares present times with

times past, often praises the fortunes of his father.

Likewise the sad planter of an old and withered vine

blames the course of time and rails at the age,

and chatters that the ancient race, filled with piety,

most easily endured life within narrow bounds,

when formerly the measure of land for each man was much smaller;

nor does he grasp that all things gradually waste away and go

wearied unto the grave by the length of a long lifetime.

## Liber Tertius

  

E tenebris tantis tam clarum extollere lumen

 

qui primus potuisti inlustrans commoda vitae,

 

te sequor, o Graiae gentis decus, inque tuis nunc

 

ficta pedum pono pressis vestigia signis,

 

non ita certandi cupidus quam propter amorem

 

quod te imitari aveo; quid enim contendat hirundo

 

cycnis, aut quid nam tremulis facere artubus haedi

 

consimile in cursu possint et fortis equi vis?

 

tu, pater, es rerum inventor, tu patria nobis

 

suppeditas praecepta, tuisque ex, inclute, chartis,

 

floriferis ut apes in saltibus omnia libant,

 

omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta,

 

aurea, perpetua semper dignissima vita.

 

nam simul ac ratio tua coepit vociferari

 

naturam rerum divina mente coorta

 

diffugiunt animi terrores, moenia mundi

 

discedunt. totum video per inane geri res.

 

apparet divum numen sedesque quietae,

 

quas neque concutiunt venti nec nubila nimbis

 

aspergunt neque nix acri concreta pruina

 

cana cadens violat semper innubilus aether

 

integit et large diffuso lumine ridet:

 

omnia suppeditat porro natura neque ulla

 

res animi pacem delibat tempore in ullo.

 

at contra nusquam apparent Acherusia templa,

 

nec tellus obstat quin omnia dispiciantur,

 

sub pedibus quae cumque infra per inane geruntur.

 

his ibi me rebus quaedam divina voluptas

 

percipit atque horror, quod sic natura tua vi

 

tam manifesta patens ex omni parte retecta est.

 

Et quoniam docui, cunctarum exordia rerum

 

qualia sint et quam variis distantia formis

 

sponte sua volitent aeterno percita motu,

 

quove modo possint res ex his quaeque creari,

 

hasce secundum res animi natura videtur

 

atque animae claranda meis iam versibus esse

 

et metus ille foras praeceps Acheruntis agendus,

 

funditus humanam qui vitam turbat ab imo

 

omnia suffundens mortis nigrore neque ullam

 

esse voluptatem liquidam puramque relinquit.

  

nam quod saepe homines morbos magis esse timendos

 

infamemque ferunt vitam quam Tartara leti

 

et se scire animi naturam sanguinis esse,

 

aut etiam venti, si fert ita forte voluntas,

 

nec prosum quicquam nostrae rationis egere,

 

hinc licet advertas animum magis omnia laudis

 

iactari causa quam quod res ipsa probetur.

 

extorres idem patria longeque fugati

 

conspectu ex hominum, foedati crimine turpi,

 

omnibus aerumnis adfecti denique vivunt,

 

et quo cumque tamen miseri venere parentant

 

et nigras mactant pecudes et manibus divis

 

inferias mittunt multoque in rebus acerbis

 

 acrius advertunt animos ad religionem.

 

quo magis in dubiis hominem spectare periclis

 

convenit adversisque in rebus noscere qui sit;

Denique saepe hominem paulatim cernimus ire

 

et membratim vitalem deperdere sensum;

 

in pedibus primum digitos livescere et unguis,

 

inde pedes et crura mori, post inde per artus

 

ire alios tractim gelidi vestigia leti.

 

scinditur atque animae haec quoniam natura nec uno

quod si forte putas ipsam se posse per artus

atque ideo cunctis sensum diducere membris,

 

at locus ille tamen, quo copia tanta animai

 

cogitur, in sensu debet maiore videri;

 

qui quoniam nusquamst, ni mirum, ut diximus ,

 

dilaniata foras dispargitur, interit ergo.

 

quin etiam si iam libeat concedere falsum

lumina qui lincunt moribundi particulatim,

 

mortalem tamen esse animam fateare necesse

 

nec refert utrum pereat dispersa per auras

quando hominem totum magis ac magis undique sensus

 

deficit et vitae minus et minus undique restat.

  

 Et quoniam mens est hominis pars una locoque

secreta ab nobis nequeunt sentire neque esse,

 

sed tamen in parvo lincuntur tempore tali,

 

sic animus per se non quit sine corpore et ipso

 

esse homine, illius quasi quod vas esse videtur,

 

sive aliud quid vis potius coniunctius ei

Denique corporis atque animi vivata potestas

 

inter se coniuncta valent vitaque fruuntur;

 

nec sine corpore enim vitalis edere motus

scilicet avolsus radicibus ut nequit ullam

sic anima atque animus per se nil posse videtur.

 

ni mirum quia  venas et viscera mixtim,

 

per nervos atque ossa tenentur corpore ab omni

 

nec magnis intervallis primordia possunt

quare etiam atque etiam resoluto corporis omni

 

tegmine et eiectis extra vitalibus auris

 

dissolui sensus animi fateare necessest

Denique cum corpus nequeat perferre animai

quid dubitas quin ex imo penitusque coorta

 

emanarit uti fumus diffusa animae vis,

 

atque ideo tanta mutatum putre ruina

 

conciderit corpus, penitus quia mota loco sunt

 

fundamenta foras manant animaeque per artus

 

perque viarum omnis flexus, in corpore qui sunt,

 

atque foramina? multimodis ut noscere possis

 

dispertitam animae naturam exisse per artus

 

et prius esse sibi distractam corpore in ipso,

 

quam prolapsa foras enaret in aëris auras.

  

Quin etiam finis dum vitae vertitur intra,

molliaque exsangui cadere omnia  membra.

 

quod genus est, animo male factum cum perhibetur

 

aut animam liquisse; ubi iam trepidatur et omnes

conquassatur enim tum mens animaeque potestas

ut gravior paulo possit dissolvere causa.

 

 Quid dubitas tandem quin extra prodita corpus

sed minimum quodvis nequeat consistere tempus?

 

nec sibi enim quisquam moriens sentire videtur

 

ire foras animam incolumem de corpore toto,

 

nec prius ad iugulum et supera succedere fauces,

 

verum deficere in certa regione locatam;

 

ut sensus alios in parti quemque sua scit

non tam se moriens dissolvi conquereretur,

 

sed magis ire foras vestemque relinquere, ut anguis.

 

Denique cur animi numquam mens consiliumque

sunt, et ubi quicquid possit durare creatum

 

atque ita multimodis partitis artubus esse,

 

membrorum ut numquam existat praeposterus ordo?

 

usque adeo sequitur res rem, neque flamma creari

 

fluminibus solitast neque in igni gignier algor.

  

Praeterea si inmortalis natura animaist

pictores itaque et scriptorum saecla priora

at neque sorsum oculi neque nares nec manus ipsa

haud igitur per se possunt sentire neque esse.

 

Et quoniam toto sentimus corpore inesse

si subito medium celeri praeciderit ictu

et discissa simul cum corpore dissicietur.

 

at quod scinditur et partis discedit in ullas,

falciferos memorant currus abscidere membra

 

saepe ita de subito permixta caede calentis,

 

ut tremere in terra videatur ab artubus id quod

et simul in pugnae studio quod dedita mens est,

 

corpore relicuo pugnam caedesque petessit,

 

nec tenet amissam laevam cum tegmine saepe

nec cecidisse alius dextram, cum scandit et instat.

 

inde alius conatur adempto surgere crure,

 

cum digitos agitat propter moribundus humi pes.

 

et caput abscisum calido viventeque trunco

 

servat humi voltum vitalem oculosque patentis,

 

donec reliquias animai reddidit omnes.

 

quin etiam tibi si, lingua vibrante, minanti

 

 serpentis cauda, procero corpore, utrumque

omnia iam sorsum cernes ancisa recenti

 

volnere tortari et terram conspargere tabo,

 

ipsam seque retro partem petere ore priorem,

 

volneris ardenti ut morsu premat icta dolore.

 

omnibus esse igitur totas dicemus in illis

ergo divisast ea quae fuit una simul cum

 

corpore; quapropter mortale utrumque putandumst,

 

in multas quoniam partis disciditur aeque.

  

Praeterea si inmortalis natura animai

cur super ante actam aetatem meminisse nequimus

 

nec vestigia gestarum rerum ulla tenemus?

 

nam si tanto operest animi mutata potestas,

 

omnis ut actarum exciderit retinentia rerum,

 

non, ut opinor, id ab leto iam longius errat;

 

qua propter fateare necessest quae fuit ante

 

interiisse, et quae nunc est nunc esse creatam.

 

Praeterea si iam perfecto corpore nobis

 

inferri solitast animi vivata potestas

 

tum cum gignimur et vitae cum limen inimus,

 

haud ita conveniebat uti cum corpore et una

 

cum membris videatur in ipso sanguine cresse,

 

sed vel ut in cavea per se sibi vivere solam

 

convenit, ut sensu corpus tamen affluat omne.

 

quare etiam atque etiam neque originis esse putandumst

 

expertis animas nec leti lege solutas;

 

nam neque tanto opere adnecti potuisse putandumst

 

corporibus nostris extrinsecus insinuatas,

 

quod fieri totum contra manifesta docet res

 

ænamque ita conexa est per venas viscera nervos

 

ossaque, uti dentes quoque sensu participentur;

 

morbus ut indicat et gelidai stringor aquai

 

et lapis oppressus subitis e frugibus asperæ

 

nec, tam contextae cum sint, exire videntur

 

incolumes posse et salvas exsolvere sese

 

omnibus e nervis atque ossibus articulisque,

 

quod si forte putas extrinsecus insinuatam

 

permanare animam nobis per membra solere,

 

tanto quique magis cum corpore fusa peribit;

 

quod permanat enim, dissolvitur, interit ergo;

 

dispertitur enim per caulas corporis omnis.

 

ut cibus, in membra atque artus cum diditur omnis,

 

disperit atque aliam naturam sufficit ex se,

 

sic anima atque animus quamvis  integra recens 

 

corpus eunt, tamen in manando dissoluuntur,

 

dum quasi per caulas omnis diduntur in artus

 

particulae quibus haec animi natura creatur,

 

quae nunc in nostro dominatur corpore nata

 

ex illa quae tunc periit partita per artus.

  

quapropter neque natali privata videtur

 

 esse die natura animae nec funeris expers.

 

Semina praeterea linquontur necne animai

 

corpore in exanimo? quod si lincuntur et insunt,

 

haut erit ut merito inmortalis possit haberi,

 

partibus amissis quoniam libata recessit.

 

sin ita sinceris membris ablata profugit,

 

ut nullas partis in corpore liquerit ex se,

 

unde cadavera rancenti iam viscere vermes

 

expirant atque unde animantum copia tanta

 

exos et exanguis tumidos perfluctuat artus?

 

quod si forte animas extrinsecus insinuari?

 

vermibus et privas in corpora posse venire

 

credis nec reputas cur milia multa animarum

quaerendum videatur et in discrimen agendum,

 

utrum tandem animae venentur semina quaeque

an quasi corporibus perfectis insinuentur.

 

at neque cur faciant ipsae quareve laborent

corpus enim magis his vitiis adfine laborat,

 

et mala multa animus contage fungitur eius.

 

sed tamen his esto quamvis facere utile corpus,

 

cum subeant; at qua possint via nulla videtur.

 

haut igitur faciunt animae sibi corpora et artus.

 

nec tamen est ut qui  perfectis insinuentur

 

corporibus; neque enim poterunt suptiliter esse

 

conexae neque consensu contagia fient.

  

Denique cur acris violentia triste leonum

numquid ibi horribile apparet, num triste videtur

 

quicquam, non omni somno securius exstat?

  

Atque ea ni mirum quae cumque Acherunte profundo

 

prodita sunt esse, in vita sunt omnia nobis.

 

nec miser inpendens magnum timet aëre saxum

 

Tantalus, ut famast, cassa formidine torpens;

 

sed magis in vita divom metus urget inanis

 

mortalis casumque timent quem cuique ferat fors.

 

nec Tityon volucres ineunt Acherunte iacentem

 

nec quod sub magno scrutentur pectore quicquam

 

 perpetuam aetatem possunt reperire profecto.

 

quam libet immani proiectu corporis exstet,

 

qui non sola novem dispessis iugera membris

 

optineat, sed qui terrai totius orbem,

 

non tamen aeternum poterit perferre dolorem

 

nec praebere cibum proprio de corpore semper.

 

sed Tityos nobis hic est, in amore iacentem

 

quem volucres lacerant atque exest anxius angor

 

aut alia quavis scindunt cuppedine curae.

 

Sisyphus in vita quoque nobis ante oculos est,

 

qui petere a populo fasces saevasque secures

 

imbibit et semper victus tristisque recedit.

 

nam petere imperium, quod inanest nec datur umquam,

 

atque in eo semper durum sufferre laborem,

 

hoc est adverso nixantem trudere monte

 

saxum, quod tamen  summo iam vertice rusum

 

volvitur et plani raptim petit aequora campi.

 

deinde animi ingratam naturam pascere semper

 

atque explere bonis rebus satiareque numquam,

 

quod faciunt nobis annorum tempora, circum

 

cum redeunt fetusque ferunt variosque lepores,

 

nec tamen explemur vitai fructibus umquam,

 

hoc, ut opinor, id est, aevo florente puellas

 

quod memorant laticem pertusum congerere in vas,

 

quod tamen expleri nulla ratione potestur.

 

Cerberus et Furiae iam vero et lucis egestas,

 

Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus!

 

qui neque sunt usquam nec possunt esse profecto;

 

sed metus in vita poenarum pro male factis

 

est insignibus insignis scelerisque luela,

 

carcer et horribilis de saxo iactus deorsum,

 

verbera carnifices robur pix lammina taedae;

 

quae tamen etsi absunt, at mens sibi conscia factis

 

praemetuens adhibet stimulos torretque flagellis,

 

nec videt interea qui terminus esse malorum

 

possit nec quae sit poenarum denique finis,

 

atque eadem metuit magis haec ne in morte gravescant.

 

hic Acherusia fit stultorum denique vita.

  

Hoc etiam tibi tute interdum dicere possis.

 

'lumina sis oculis etiam bonus Ancus reliquit,

 

qui melior multis quam tu fuit, improbe, rebus.

 

inde alii multi reges rerumque potentes

 

occiderunt, magnis qui gentibus imperitarunt.

 

ille quoque ipse, viam qui quondam per mare magnum

 

stravit iterque dedit legionibus ire per altum

 

ac pedibus salsas docuit super ire lucunas

 

et contempsit equis insultans murmura ponti,

 

lumine adempto animam moribundo corpore fudit.

 

Scipiadas, belli fulmen, Carthaginis horror,

 

ossa dedit terrae proinde ac famul infimus esset.

 

adde repertores doctrinarum atque leporum,

 

adde Heliconiadum comites; quorum unus Homerus

 

sceptra potitus eadem aliis sopitus quietest.

 

denique Democritum post quam matura vetustas

 

admonuit memores motus languescere mentis,

 

 sponte sua leto caput obvius optulit ipse.

 

ipse Epicurus obit decurso lumine vitae,

 

qui genus humanum ingenio superavit et omnis

 

restinxit stellas exortus ut aetherius sol.

 

tu vero dubitabis et indignabere obire?

 

mortua cui vita est prope iam vivo atque videnti,

 

qui somno partem maiorem conteris aevi,

 

et viligans stertis nec somnia cernere cessas

 

sollicitamque geris cassa formidine mentem

 

nec reperire potes tibi quid sit saepe mali, cum

 

ebrius urgeris multis miser undique curis

 

atque animo incerto fluitans errore vagaris.'

  

Si possent homines, proinde ac sentire videntur

 

pondus inesse animo, quod se gravitate fatiget,

 

e quibus id fiat causis quoque noscere et unde

 

tanta mali tam quam moles in pectore constet,

 

haut ita vitam agerent, ut nunc plerumque videmus

 

quid sibi quisque velit nescire et quaerere semper,

 

commutare locum, quasi onus deponere possit.

 

exit saepe foras magnis ex aedibus ille,

 

esse domi quem pertaesumst, subitoque ,

 

quippe foris nihilo melius qui sentiat esse.

 

currit agens mannos ad villam praecipitanter

 

auxilium tectis quasi ferre ardentibus instans;

 

oscitat extemplo, tetigit cum limina villae,

 

aut abit in somnum gravis atque oblivia quaerit,

 

aut etiam properans urbem petit atque revisit.

 

hoc se quisque modo fugit, at quem scilicet, ut fit,

 

effugere haut potis est: ingratius haeret et odit

 

propterea, morbi quia causam non tenet aeger;

 

quam bene si videat, iam rebus quisque relictis

 

naturam primum studeat cognoscere rerum,

 

temporis aeterni quoniam, non unius horae,

 

ambigitur status, in quo sit mortalibus omnis

 

aetas, post mortem quae restat cumque manendo.

  

Denique tanto opere in dubiis trepidare periclis

 

quae mala nos subigit vitai tanta cupido?

 

certe equidem finis vitae mortalibus adstat

 

nec devitari letum pote, quin obeamus.

 

praeterea versamur ibidem atque insumus usque

 

nec nova vivendo procuditur ulla voluptas;

 

sed dum abest quod avemus, id exsuperare videtur

 

cetera; post aliud, cum contigit illud, avemus

 

et sitis aequa tenet vitai semper hiantis.

 

posteraque in dubiost fortunam quam vehat aetas,

 

quidve ferat nobis casus quive exitus instet.

 

nec prorsum vitam ducendo demimus hilum

 

tempore de mortis nec delibare valemus,

 

quo minus esse diu possimus forte perempti.

 

proinde licet quod vis vivendo condere saecla,

 

mors aeterna tamen nihilo minus illa manebit,

 

nec minus ille diu iam non erit, ex hodierno

 

lumine qui finem vitai fecit, et ille,

 

mensibus atque annis qui multis occidit ante.
