of how fine a texture it consists and how small a place

it occupies, if it can be compacted together,

because, as soon as the care-free repose of death has

come upon a man and the nature of mind and soul has departed,

you can discern nothing taken away from the whole body

in appearance, nothing in weight: death leaves all things intact,

life apart from sensation and warm vapor.

therefore it must be that the whole soul is bound

by exceedingly small seeds throughout veins, entrails, and sinews,

to such an extent that, when it has now wholly departed from the entire body,

the outer contour of the limbs nevertheless presents itself

unimpaired, nor is a jot of weight lacking.

Such is the case when the bloom of Bacchus has vanished, or when

the sweet breath of perfume has fled away into the air,

or when juice has now departed from some body;

yet the thing itself seems no smaller to the eyes,

and for that reason nothing whatever has been subtracted from its weight,

because, indeed, many tiny seeds produce

the juices and odor throughout the whole body of things.

wherefore again and again one may know that the nature of mind and soul

has been created from exceedingly few seeds,

since in fleeing it carries away no weight.

Yet we must not suppose that this nature is simple.

For a certain subtle breath, mingled with vapor, leaves the dying;

and vapor in turn draws air along with itself;

nor is there any heat to which air too is not mingled;

because its nature is rare, it must be that

many first-beginnings of air move among it.

Nor can pain penetrate hither without cause, nor can sharp

evil pervade, without all things being disturbed

to such an extent that room for life is lacking and the parts of the soul

scatter abroad through all the passages of the body.

But for the most part a limit to the motions occurs, as it were, on the surface of the body:

for this reason we are able to retain life.

Now, desiring to give an account in what way these things, mixed among themselves and in what

arrangement, flourish,

the poverty of my native speech draws me back against my will;

yet, as I shall be able, I shall touch upon it briefly.

For the first-beginnings of the principles run among one another

in their motions among themselves, so that no one thing

can be separated, nor can a divided power come to be through space,

but they exist as though the many forces were of one body.

Of this sort, in any living creature's flesh, commonly

there are smell and a certain color and taste, and yet from all these

there is one complete growth of body;

thus heat and air and the blind power of wind

mingled create one nature, and that mobile

force which, having begun motion from itself, imparts it to them,

whence feeling first arises, motion through the limbs.

For this nature lies hidden deep within and underlies them;

nor is there anything in our body further beneath than this,

and it is itself, moreover, the soul of the whole soul.

As in our limbs and throughout the whole body

the hidden force of mind and the power of soul are mingled,

because they have been created from small and few bodies,

so this force, devoid of a name, made from minute

bodies, lies hidden and is, as it were, itself the soul

of the whole soul, and rules the whole body.

By a like reasoning it is necessary that wind and air

and heat should be strong, mingled among themselves through the limbs,

and that one thing should underlie another more, and stand out more,

so that one something may seem to be made from all of them,

lest heat and wind, and each separate power,

destroy the sensation of air and dissolve it when drawn apart.

There is also that heat in the mind which it takes on in anger

when it grows hot and the blaze flashes more fiercely from the eyes;

there is also much cold air, companion of fear,

which rouses shuddering in the limbs and stirs the body;

there is likewise that air of a calm condition,

which comes about with a tranquil breast and a serene countenance.

But there is more of the hot in those whose hearts are fierce

and whose angry mind easily boils up in wrath,

of which kind pre-eminently is the violent force of lions,

who for the most part burst their breasts with roaring groans

and cannot contain the waves of anger in their breast.

But the cold mind of deer is more windy,

and more quickly stirs icy airs through their entrails,

which make a trembling motion arise in their limbs.

But the nature of oxen lives by a calmer air

and never is too much stirred by the smoky torch of anger,

pouring in the shadow of blind darkness,

nor does it grow numb, pierced by the icy darts of fear;

it is situated between the two, deer and savage lions.

So it is with the race of men: although training may equally refine

some, nevertheless it leaves behind those first traces

of the nature of each one's mind.

Nor must it be thought that evils can be plucked out by the roots,

or why this man should run down more readily into sharp anger,

that one be assailed somewhat more quickly by fear, while that other

third should take certain things more mildly than is fair.

And in many other matters it must needs be that there differ

the diverse natures of men and the habits that follow upon them;

the hidden causes of which I am now unable to set forth,

nor to discover names for so many shapes as there are

among the first-beginnings from which this variety of things arises.

This I see can be maintained concerning these matters:

that traces of natures are left so slight

that reason cannot drive them out of us,

as to hinder nothing from living a life worthy of the gods.

Therefore this nature is held fast by the whole body,

and is itself the body's guardian and cause of preservation;

for they cling together by roots shared between them,

nor do they seem able to be torn apart without destruction.

Just as it is not easy to tear scent from lumps of frankincense

without its nature also perishing,

so it is not easy to draw the nature of mind and soul from the whole body

without all things being dissolved.

Thus, from their first origin, with first-beginnings intertwined,

they come to be endowed with a life shared in common,

nor does the power of each seem able, without the force of the other,

to possess sensation separately, that of body and that of mind.

but by motions common to both, kindled on either side,

sensation is kindled within our entrails.

Moreover, the body is never generated by itself,

nor does it grow, nor does it seem to endure after death.

For it is not as water's moisture often gives off the vapour

which has been imparted to it, nor for that reason is itself torn apart,

but remains unharmed: not so, I say, can the parts of the soul,

when left behind, endure separation from the limbs,

but, violently wrenched away, perish utterly and rot together.

Thus from their earliest beginning, body and soul

learn the mutually shared contagions of vital motion,

even while placed back in the mother's limbs and womb,

so that their separation cannot occur without destructive bane and evil;

so that you may see that, since the cause of their preservation is joined,

their nature too is joined in its subsistence.

For the rest, if anyone denies that the body feels

and believes that the soul, intermingled with the whole body,

undergoes this motion which we call sensation,

he opposes manifest and true facts.

For who will ever set forth what it is for the body to feel,

if not that which the thing itself openly has given and taught us?

“But when the soul has departed, the body is altogether without sensation.”

For in life it loses what was not its own,

and loses many other things besides when it is driven out of life.

Moreover, to say that the eyes are unable to discern anything,

but that through them the mind looks out as through opened doors,

is difficult, since their sensation leads us to the contrary;

for sensation draws and thrusts the gaze forward to the things themselves,

especially since we are often unable to see bright

lights, because our eyes are hindered by lights.

But this does not happen with doors; for the gateways through which we ourselves see

do not, when opened, undergo any strain.

Furthermore, if our eyes are in place of doors,

then it seems that, once the eyes have been removed, the mind ought all the more

to discern things when the doorposts themselves have been taken away.

In these matters you can by no means adopt

what the holy opinion of the man Democritus maintains:

that the first-beginnings of body and soul, each set beside the first-beginnings

of the other in alternation, vary and bind together the limbs.

For since the elements of the soul are much smaller

than those of which our body and viscera consist,

they also yield in number and are sparsely dispersed

through the limbs, so that at most you can assert this:

how small first bodies, when cast in, can arouse in us

sentient motions in the body—so great

are the intervals maintained by the first beginnings of the soul.

For we do not at times feel dust clinging

to the body, nor chalk struck upon the limbs by a star,

nor a cloud by night, nor the slender threads of a spider,

do we perceive when they meet us as we go, when we are caught in them,

nor [do we perceive] that a vine has fallen upon the head of the same [person] from above,

nor a garment, nor birds’ feathers and the flying down,

which, through excessive lightness, generally fall slowly,

nor do we perceive the course of any creeping creature whatsoever,

nor each separate trace of feet

which gnats and other things set upon our body.

so greatly must many things first be set in motion within us

before the first-beginnings of the soul perceive that they have been shaken,

the seeds intermixed through the limbs with our bodies,

and before, in these intervals, they can, striking,

run together, unite, and in turn spring apart.

And the mind is more potent in holding fast the barriers of life

and has greater mastery over life than the force of the soul.

For without mind and soul, no part of the soul can remain

through the limbs for even a small portion of time;

but as a companion it readily follows, departs into the air,

and leaves the cold limbs in death’s chill.

But he remains alive in whom mind and soul have remained,

although he is mangled all around, with his limbs cut away;

the trunk, its soul taken away all around and its limbs removed,

lives and takes in the life-giving airs of heaven;

if not in every respect, yet with a great part of the soul.

though impaired, yet it lingers and clings to life;

as, when the eye is mangled, if the pupil remains

unharmed, the living power of seeing remains standing,

provided only that you do not destroy the whole orb of light

and cut away around it, leaving the pupil alone;

for this too will not happen without their destruction.

But if that tiny middle part of the eye is eaten away,

the light dies forthwith and darkness follows,

however unharmed and bright the rest of the orb may be.

By such a bond soul and mind are always held fast.

Now come, that you may be able to know that minds and souls are born

with living creatures and are mortal,

I shall proceed to set forth verses long sought out

and discovered by sweet labor, worthy of your life.

Do you make both of them subject to one name,

and when, for example, I go on to speak of the soul,

teaching that it is mortal, believe that I speak of the mind also,

insofar as it is one thing, joined together among itself.

First, since I have shown that it consists, thin as it is, of tiny

bodies, and is made of elements much smaller

than the liquid moisture of water,

or mist or smoke—for it far surpasses them in mobility

and is moved more by a slight cause,

indeed, since it is moved by images of smoke and mist;

such as, when asleep in dreams, we behold altars

exhaling vapor high aloft and bearing smoke;

for beyond doubt these images are produced for us at the same time.

Now therefore, since you see that, when vessels are shattered on every side,

moisture flows away and liquid departs,

and since mist and smoke depart into the air,

believe that the soul too is dispersed and perishes much

more swiftly and quickly, being dissolved into its first bodies,

once it has withdrawn, removed from a man's limbs;

since indeed the body, which stood as though its vessel,

when shattered by some cause, cannot contain it

and made porous by blood being drawn from the veins,

by what air would you believe that it can be contained,

when it is more rarefied, less capable of being contained, than our body?

Moreover, we perceive that the mind is begotten equally with the body and

grows equally with it and grows old equally.

For just as children move about with a weak and tender

body, so a slender judgment of mind follows.

Then, when age has grown up in vigorous strength,

counsel too is greater, and the power of the mind increased.

Afterward, when the body has been shaken by the strong powers of age

and the limbs have fallen with blunted powers,

the intellect falters, the tongue raves, the mind [raves];

all things fail and are wanting at one and the same time.

therefore it is fitting that the whole nature of the soul also be dissolved

like smoke, into the lofty breezes of the air;

since indeed we see it likewise come to birth and likewise

grow and, as I have shown, at the same time, worn out by age, decay.

To this is added that we see, just as the body itself

takes on dreadful diseases and harsh pain,

so the mind takes on sharp cares, grief, and fear;

wherefore it is fitting that it too be a sharer in death.

Nay more, in bodily diseases the mind often wanders astray;

for it raves and speaks deliriously,

and at times is borne into the deep by heavy lethargy,

into eternal sleep, with eyes and nodding head sinking;

whence it neither hears voices nor is able to recognize the faces

of those who, calling it back to life,

stand around, wetting cheeks and face with tears.

wherefore you must confess that the mind also is dissolved,

since the infections of disease penetrate into it;

for pain and disease are each the maker of death,

as we have learned before through the destruction of many.

Lastly, when the potent force of wine has penetrated a man

and its diffused burning has spread into his veins,

heaviness of the limbs follows; his legs are hampered as he staggers,

his tongue grows slow, his mind is sodden,

his eyes swim; shouting, hiccups, and quarrels grow apace,

and now all the other things of this kind, whatever follow,

why are they so, unless because the vehement violence of wine

is wont to throw the mind into confusion in the very body?

But whatever things can be thrown into confusion and impeded

indicate that, if a somewhat harsher cause has insinuated itself,

they will perish, deprived of future age.

Nay indeed, often someone, suddenly compelled by the force of disease,

before our eyes, as by a thunderbolt's stroke,

falls down and foams, groans and trembles in his limbs,

raves, stretches out his sinews, is twisted, gasps

irregularly, and in tossing about wears out his limbs,

clearly because the force of disease, dispersed through the limbs,

drives and disorders the mind, as in the salty sea

the waves boil under the mighty forces of winds.

Moreover, a groan is forced out because the limbs

are affected by pain, and altogether because the seeds of voice

are drawn forth and, gathered together, are borne outward through the mouth

by the way by which, as it were, they have grown accustomed and been provided with a passage.

Madness comes about because the force of mind and soul

is disturbed and, as I have taught, divided apart,

is scattered, torn asunder by that same poison.

Then, when now the cause of the disease has recoiled and returns

into the recesses, the sharp humour of the corrupted body,

then, as though staggering, he first rises, and all

little by little returns to the senses and recovers the soul.

Therefore, when these things amid such great diseases in the body itself

are tossed about and, racked in miserable ways, suffer,

why do you believe that the same things, without the body, in the open air,

can pass their lifetime amid strong winds?

And since we perceive that the mind is healed, like a sick body,

and we see that it can be altered by medicine,

this too foretells that the mind lives mortally.

For it is right either to add parts or to transpose them in order,

or to take away from the whole some tiny jot,

for whoever sets about and begins to change the mind,

or seeks to alter any other nature whatsoever.

But that which is immortal does not wish parts to be transferred to itself or bestowed upon it,

nor for anything at all to flow away from it, even by a tiny jot;

for whatever, changed, passes beyond its own boundaries,

is at once the death of that which it was before.

Therefore, whether the mind falls sick, it gives forth mortal signs,

as I have taught, or whether it is altered by medicine.

So greatly does the true thing seem to confront false reasoning

and to block escape for one proceeding,

and, by a two-edged refutation, to convict falsehood.

Finally, we often see a man gradually passing away

and losing life-sustaining sensation limb by limb;

first, in his feet, the toes and nails growing blue.

then the feet and legs die, thereafter from there through the limbs

the traces of chill death pass gradually to the rest.

And since this nature of the soul is divided and does not remain whole at one

time, it must be held to be mortal.

But if perhaps you think that it can draw itself inward through the limbs

and gather its parts into one

and thereby withdraw sensation from all the members,

yet that place into which so great an abundance of soul

is gathered ought to be seen to possess greater sensation;

and since it is nowhere, assuredly, as we have said,

being torn apart, it is scattered abroad and therefore perishes.

Nay even if now it pleased you to concede what is false

and grant that the soul can be massed together in the body of those

who, dying little by little, leave the light,

nevertheless you must admit that the soul is mortal,

nor does it matter whether it perishes dispersed through the air

or, contracted from its own parts, grows torpid,

since sensation fails the whole man more and more on every side

and less and less of life remains on every side.

And since the mind is one part of a human being and remains fixed in a definite

place, just as the ears and eyes are

and the other senses that govern life together,

and just as hand and eye or nostrils, separately

severed from us, can neither feel nor exist,

but nevertheless they are left behind in so brief a time of this kind,

thus the mind cannot by itself exist without the body and the man himself,

which seems to be, as it were, its vessel,

or whatever else you prefer to imagine as more closely joined to it,

since the body clings to it in connection.

Finally, the living power of body and mind,

joined together, are strong among themselves and enjoy life;

for without the body the nature of the mind alone cannot produce

vital motions by itself, nor, on the other hand,

can the body, bereft of soul, endure and make use of the senses.

Clearly, just as an eye torn from its roots cannot

itself discern any thing apart from the whole body,

so soul and mind appear able to do nothing by themselves.

No doubt because, mingled through veins and viscera,

they are held through nerves and bones by the whole body,

and their first-beginnings cannot, with great intervals,

spring apart freely; therefore, confined, they produce

sense-bearing motions, which, when cast out beyond the body into the breezes

of air after death, they cannot produce,

because they are not held together in a like manner;

for the air will be both body and living, if it can restrain

itself, the soul, and confine itself into those motions

which it formerly carried on in the nerves and in the body itself.

wherefore again and again, when the whole body has been dissolved

from its covering and with the vital airs cast out beyond,

you must confess that the senses of the mind are dissolved

and the soul, since the cause is conjoined for the two.

Finally, since the body cannot endure the soul's

severance, without wasting away in a foul stench,

why do you doubt that, having arisen from the bottom and utterly,

the force of the soul has flowed out, diffused like smoke,

and that therefore, altered by so great a ruin,

the body has fallen apart, because its foundations have been moved wholly from their place

and stream outward—the foundations of the soul—through the limbs

and through all the bendings of the passages that are in the body,

and the openings? So that in many ways you may be able to know

that the divided nature of the soul has gone forth through the limbs

and has first been torn apart within the body itself,

before, slipping forth, it swam out into the breezes of air.

Indeed, even while the end of life is being turned within,

the soul nevertheless often seems, shaken by some cause,

to depart and be dissolved from the whole body,

and the face, as if at the final moment, to grow languid,

and all the limbs to fall slack and bloodless.

Such is the case when one is said to have been stricken in spirit

or to have left one's soul; when now there is panic, and all

desire to seize hold of life's final bond;

for then the mind and the power of the soul are shaken.

whole. And these collapse together with the body itself,

so that a somewhat weightier cause can dissolve them.

Why, then, do you doubt that, brought forth outside the body,

feeble, out into the open, its covering removed,

it can not only not endure through all eternity,

but cannot even stand firm for any, however brief, time?

For no one, as he dies, seems to himself to feel

that his soul goes forth unharmed from his whole body,

nor that it first approaches the throat and the upper jaws;

rather, it fails, situated in a definite region;

just as he knows that each of the other senses is dissolved

in its own part. But if our mind were immortal,

in dying it would not complain so much that it is being dissolved,

but rather that it is going forth and leaving its garment behind, like a snake.

Finally, why is the mind and counsel of the spirit never

produced in the head or feet or hands, but clings

in one seat and in definite regions in all men,

unless definite places have been assigned to each for being born,

and places where whatever is created can endure,

and thus be in limbs divided in many ways,

so that the order of the members may never be inverted?

So strictly does thing follow thing: nor is flame accustomed to be created

in rivers, nor cold to be born in fire.

Moreover, if the nature of the soul is immortal

and can perceive things hidden from our body,

it must, I think, be made endowed with five senses.

nor by any other reasoning can we set before ourselves

souls wandering in the lower world by Acheron.

Thus painters and the generations of earlier writers

have introduced souls endowed with senses.

But neither eyes apart, nor nostrils, nor the hand itself

can belong to the soul, nor separately tongue or ears;

therefore they cannot perceive or exist by themselves.

And since we perceive that vital sensation is present throughout the whole body

and see that the whole is animate,

if suddenly some force should cut it through the middle with a swift blow,

so as to separate each part apart,

the force of the soul too, beyond doubt divided,

will be cut apart and rent at the same time as the body.

But what is cut and departs into any parts,

plainly denies that it has an eternal nature.

They tell how scythe-bearing chariots often cut off limbs

so suddenly amid the mingled warm slaughter,

that what has fallen, severed from the limbs, may be seen to tremble on the ground,

while nevertheless the mind and force of the man

cannot, because of the swiftness of the injury, feel the pain;

and at the same time, since the mind is given over to the ardor of battle,

with the rest of the body it seeks battle and slaughter,

nor is he often aware that his left hand, together with its shield, has been lost

among the horses, torn away by the wheels and ravening scythes,

nor does another notice that his right hand has fallen off, as he climbs and presses on.

Then another tries to rise with his leg taken away,

while nearby on the ground his dying foot moves its toes.

And a severed head from a warm and living trunk

keeps on the ground its vital expression and its open eyes,

until it has yielded up all the remnants of the soul.

Indeed, if you should wish, while the serpent's tail threatens with vibrating tongue,

to cut with steel both the tail and the tall body

into many parts,

you would see all the parts separately, cut by the fresh

wound, writhing and sprinkling the ground with gore,

and each part seeking backwards with its mouth the part before it,

so that, struck by the burning pain of the wound, it may press it with a bite.

Shall we say, then, that whole souls are in all those

particles? But by that reasoning it will follow

that one living creature has had many souls in its body.

Therefore that which was one has been divided together with

the body; wherefore each must be thought mortal,

since it is likewise cut into many parts.

Moreover, if the nature of the soul is immortal

and insinuates itself into bodies as they are born,

why are we unable to remember the age lived before?

nor do we retain any traces of things done?

For if the altered power of the mind is of such great force,

that all retention of things done has fallen away,

then, I think, it does not wander far from death already;

wherefore you must confess that that which existed before

has perished, and that what now exists has now been created.

Moreover, if, when the body has already been completed, the living power of the mind is wont to be brought into us

when the body has already been completed,

then when we are born and when we enter upon the threshold of life,

it would not be fitting that it should seem to grow together with the body and at the same time

with the limbs, in the very blood,

but rather, as in a cage, to live by itself and alone;

yet it is fitting that the whole body should abound in sensation.

Wherefore again and again souls must not be thought to be without origin

nor released from the law of death;

for neither must they be thought able to have been attached so closely

to our bodies, insinuated from without,

since the manifest fact teaches that this is altogether contrary to what happens:

for it is so connected through veins, entrails, and sinews,

and bones, that even the teeth too partake of sensation;

as disease shows, and the constriction of icy water,

and the harsh stone, pressed out from sudden fruits;

nor, since they are so interwoven, do they seem able to depart

unharmed and to disentangle themselves safe and sound.

from all the sinews and bones and joints,

but if perhaps you think that, insinuated from without,

the soul is wont to permeate through our limbs,

by so much the more, diffused with the body, it will perish;

for what permeates is dissolved, and therefore perishes;

for it is distributed through all the passages of the body.

as food, when it is distributed into all the limbs and members,

perishes and from itself supplies another nature,

so soul and mind, although fresh and whole,

enter the body, yet in permeating they are dissolved,

while, as it were, through all the passages they are distributed into the limbs—

the particles by which this nature of mind is created,

which now, having arisen, rules in our body,

divided from that which then perished through the limbs.

Wherefore the nature of the soul plainly seems neither to be deprived of

a day of birth nor exempt from death.

Moreover, are seeds of the soul left or not

in the lifeless body? If they are left and remain within,

it will not rightly be able to be held immortal,

since, with parts lost, it has departed diminished.

But if, taken away, it has fled forth with its limbs so intact

as to have left no parts of itself in the body,

whence do worms, in corpses with their flesh now putrefying,

come forth, and whence so great a multitude of living creatures

or, bloodless and drained of blood, does it surge through the swollen limbs?

But if perhaps you believe that souls are insinuated from without

into worms and can come into their separate bodies,

and do not reflect why many thousands of souls

should gather where one has departed, yet this would seem

to require inquiry and to be brought into question:

whether at last the souls hunt out the seeds of each

little worm and themselves fashion them where they are,

or are, as it were, insinuated into bodies already complete.

if they say that the souls of human beings always

enter into human bodies, nevertheless I shall ask why from a wise man

a foolish one can come to be, nor is any boy prudent,

nor is the foal of a mare as learned as the strength of a vigorous horse.

They will no doubt have recourse to the notion that the mind grows tender in a tender body.

But if this happens, you must admit

that the soul is mortal, since, altered throughout the limbs

by so great a change, it loses its former life and sense.

Or in what way will the power of mind, likewise strengthened together with the body,

be able to attain the desired flower of age,

unless it shall be a partner from the first origin?

Or what does it mean by wishing to go forth from aged limbs?

Does it fear to remain enclosed in a rotting body,

and lest its house, wearied by the space of old age,

collapse upon it?

But there are no dangers at all for an immortal being.

Finally, that souls should be at hand for the unions of Venus and the births of beasts

seems ridiculous:

that immortals should await mortal limbs,

contend with one another in countless number,

and in excessive haste, as to which shall first and most preferably make its way in;

unless perhaps the compacts of souls are so agreed,

that whichever, flying, arrives first shall enter

first, and they shall not contend at all with one another in strength.

Finally, in the sky there cannot be a tree, nor clouds in the deep sea, nor can fishes live in fields,

nor blood be in wood, nor sap reside in stones.

It is fixed and ordered where each thing may grow and exist.

Thus the nature of mind cannot arise alone without a body,

nor exist at any distance from sinews and blood.

For if it could, the very force of mind much sooner

could be in the head or shoulders or the soles of the feet,

and, being born in any part whatsoever, would be accustomed

nevertheless to remain in the same man and in the same vessel.

Since it is also established that our body has a definite...

...and seems so arranged that there it can be and grow...

...the more must it be denied that soul and mind separately...

...can endure and be generated wholly outside the body.

Wherefore, when the body has perished, you must confess...

...that the soul too has perished, scattered throughout the whole body.

For indeed, to join the mortal with the eternal and to suppose that they...

...are in harmony as one and can perform mutual offices...

...is madness. For what is to be thought more different...

...or more sundered and discordant among themselves...

...than that which is mortal, joined with the immortal and everlasting...

...should endure savage storms in an alliance?

Moreover, whatever things necessarily remain eternal...

...either, because they are things with solid body, repel blows...

...and suffer nothing to penetrate them that can...

...disunite their close-packed inner parts, as the bodies...

...of matter do, whose nature we showed before;

...or are able for this reason to endure through all time,

...because they are exempt from blows, as is the void,

...which remains untouched and is not affected in the least by a blow;

...or else because there is no available space around them...

...into which things might, as it were, depart and be dissolved,

...as the sum of sums is eternal; nor is there any place outside...

...to which they might flee away, nor are there bodies which...

may fall upon it and dissolve it with a mighty blow.

But if perhaps for this reason it must the more be held immortal,

because it is kept fortified against things vital,

or because things alien to its safety do not come at all,

or because those which come withdraw in some way

having first been driven away before we can perceive what harm they do,

[Gap in source]

for, besides the fact that it is sick along with the body's diseases,

there comes that which often, concerning things to come,

torments it and keeps it ill in fear and wearies it with cares,

and the sins of things ill done in the past gnaw at it.

Add the madness proper to the mind and forgetfulness of things,

add that it is plunged into the black waves of lethargy.

Therefore death is nothing to us and does not concern us a whit,

since the nature of the mind is held to be mortal.

And even as in the time gone by we felt no pain,

when the Carthaginians came from every side to contend,

when all things, shaken by the tremulous tumult of war,

trembled horribly beneath the high regions of heaven,

and it was uncertain under whose rule it must fall

for all mankind on land and sea,

so, when we shall no longer be, when the separation of body and soul

shall have occurred, of which we are composed in united conjunction,

assuredly nothing at all will be able to happen to us, who then shall not be,

can at all occur and move sensation,

not even if earth were mingled with sea and sea with sky.

And if it now has sensation from our body after

the nature of the mind and the power of the soul have been torn apart,

yet it is nothing to us, who by the combination and union

of body and soul consist, fitted together as one.

Nor, if time should gather together our matter

after death and bring it back again as it is now placed,

and the lights of life should again be given to us,

would that event too concern us at all,

once the continuity of ourselves has been interrupted.

And now nothing concerning ourselves pertains to us, before

we were; nor does any anguish affect us concerning those former selves.

For when you look back upon the whole

past expanse of immeasurable time, and upon how manifold the motions of matter are,

you may easily believe this:

that the seeds have often before been set in the same order

as now, these same seeds of which we now are composed.

Yet we cannot grasp this again in memory;

for a pause of life has been interposed, and all the motions have wandered

far and wide, away from the senses.

For, if misery and grief are perhaps to befall one,

there must also then be a person himself to whom ill can

happen. Since death removes this person and prevents him from existing

him to whom misfortunes can be joined,

we may know that there is nothing to be feared in death,

and that one who does not exist cannot become miserable, nor does it differ a jot

whether he has now been born at no time,

when immortal death has taken away mortal life.

Accordingly, when you see a man himself grow indignant,

that after death he will either rot, his body having been laid aside,

or be destroyed by flames or the jaws of wild beasts,

you may know that he does not ring true, and that beneath there lies

some blind sting in his heart, although he himself denies

that he believes any sensation will be his in death;

for, I think, he does not grant what he promises, nor the point from which [he speaks],

nor does he utterly remove and cast himself out of life,

but unwittingly makes some part of himself remain.

For, while alive, when each man sets before himself what will be,

that birds and wild beasts will tear his body in death,

he pities himself; for he does not separate himself from it,

nor remove himself sufficiently from the cast-off body, and he

imagines that body to be himself and, standing by, contaminates it with his own sensation.

Hence he resents that he was created mortal

and does not see that in true death there will be no other self,

who, alive, can mourn himself as slain

and, standing, grieve that he lying there is torn apart or burned.

For if in death it is an evil thing, the jaws and bite of wild beasts

to be handled, I find no one for whom it is not bitter;

to be placed upon hot fires and scorched by flames,

or, placed in honey, to be suffocated and stiffen

with cold, when he lies upon the upper surface of an icy rock,

or to be crushed, buried beneath the weight of earth.

“Now, now, no glad home will receive you, nor your

excellent wife, nor will your sweet children run to meet you

to snatch kisses first and touch your breast with silent sweetness.

You will not be able to be a protection to your own flourishing deeds.

‘Wretch, wretchedly,’ they say, ‘one hostile day has taken away

from you all these many prizes of life.’

In these matters they do not add this: ‘nor does there now

besides sit upon you any longing for these things.’

If they clearly perceived this in their minds and followed it in their words,

they would release themselves from great anguish and fear of mind.

‘You indeed, as you are sunk in death, so will you be for all

the time that remains, deprived of every painful suffering;

but we, beside the dreadful pyre, with you turned to ash,

have wept insatiably, and forever

no day will remove grief from our breast.’

This, therefore, must be asked of him: what is so bitter

if the matter returns to sleep and rest,

that anyone can waste away in eternal mourning.

This too they do when they have reclined and hold

Men often crown their cups and shade their faces with garlands,

so that they may say from the heart: “Brief is this enjoyment for little men;

soon it will have been, nor thereafter will it ever be permitted to recall it.”

just as though this were foremost among their evils in death,

that thirst burns up the wretched and parching heat scorches them,

or that desire for some other thing settles upon them.

For then no one will seek himself and his life,

when mind and body alike rest in sleep;

for sleep may thus be eternal for us,

and yet no longing for ourselves affects us,

and nevertheless at that time the first-beginnings do not at all wander through our limbs

far away from their sense-bearing motions,

when a man, seized from sleep, gathers himself together.

Therefore death must be thought to be much less to us,

if anything can be less than what we see to be nothing;

for a greater scattering of the mass of matter

follows upon death, nor does anyone stand forth awakened,

whom once the cold pause of life has followed.

Finally, if the nature of things should suddenly send forth a voice

and herself thus rebuke some one of us:

“What need is so great for you, mortal, that you indulge too much

in grievous lamentations? Why do you groan and weep over death?

For if the life previously lived and gone before was pleasing to you,

and not all things heaped together, as if into a perforated vessel

the advantages flowed past and perished unacknowledged;

why do you not depart like a guest filled with life

and, foolish man, take secure rest with an even mind?

But if those things which, whatever their fruits, you have squandered have perished,

and life is an offense to you, why do you seek to add more,

again something that may perish badly and all die ungratefully,

rather than make an end of life and toil?

For besides, what I might contrive and discover for you

that would please, there is nothing; all things are always the same.

Even if your body were not now decaying with years and your limbs

worn out and languishing, yet all things remain the same,

even if by living you should go on to conquer all ages,

and even more so, if you should never be going to die—

what do we reply, except to bring a just charge against

nature and set forth the true case in words?

But if one greater in age and now an old man should complain

and, wretched, lament his death more than is fair,

would nature not deservedly cry out all the more and rebuke him in a sharp voice:

‘Away with tears from here, you wretch, and restrain your complaints.

Having gone through all the prizes of life, you wither;

but because you always crave what is absent and despise what is present,

your life has slipped away incomplete and ungrateful to you,

and death stood by your head before you expected it,

before, sated and full of things, you could depart.’

now cast off all that is alien to your age,

with an even mind; come now, yield to a great necessity?”

rightly, I think, he would act, rightly rebuke and urge on;

for, driven out by the newness of things, old age yields

always, and one thing must be renewed from others.

Nor is anyone given over to the abyss or to gloomy Tartarus;

there is need of matter, that generations to come may grow;

yet, when you have finished life, all these things will follow you;

and no less than you, these things have fallen before and will fall.

Thus one thing will never cease to arise from another,

and life is granted to no one as property, to all for use.

Consider likewise how the antiquity of time gone by before us

has been nothing to us before we were born.

Therefore nature sets forth this as a mirror for us of the future

time after at last our death.

Does anything there appear horrible, does anything seem sad,

that does not stand out as more secure than every sleep?

And indeed, no wonder: whatever things are said to exist in deep

Acheron are all in life among us.

Nor does wretched Tantalus fear a huge rock hanging in the air,

as the tale goes, benumbed by empty dread;

but rather in life an idle fear of the gods presses upon

mortals, and they fear whatever disaster chance may bring to each.

nor do birds assail Tityos as he lies in Acheron.

nor because, searching with mighty breast, they can discover anything

that is of perpetual duration, assuredly.

However vast he may stand in the projection of his body,

though he occupy not nine acres with his limbs alone, stretched apart,

but though he occupy the orb of the whole earth,

he will nevertheless not be able to endure eternal pain

nor to furnish food from his own body forever.

But Tityos for us is here: lying in love,

him birds tear apart, and anxious anguish devours;

or cares rend him in some other desire whatsoever.

Sisyphus too is before our eyes in life,

who thirsts to seek from the people the fasces and savage axes

and always, defeated and sorrowful, withdraws.

For to seek power, which is empty and is never granted,

and in its pursuit always to undergo harsh toil—

this is to push, straining, a stone up a mountain against its slope,

which nevertheless, now from the very summit,

rolls back and swiftly seeks the level plains of the flat field.

Then always to feed the ungrateful nature of the mind

and to fill it with good things and never satisfy it—

as the seasons of the years do for us, when in their cycle

they return and bring forth their fruits and varied delights—

and yet we are never filled with the fruits of life:

this, I suppose, is to pluck maidens in the flower of their age

because they tell how they heap pierced liquid into a vessel,

which nevertheless can by no means be filled.

Cerberus too, and the Furies, and indeed the want of light,

Tartarus belching forth dreadful heat from its jaws!

which neither are anywhere nor certainly can be;

but in life there is fear of penalties for evil deeds,

for conspicuous crimes a conspicuous requital of crime,

prison and the dreadful casting down from a rock,

scourgings, executioners, the rack, pitch, metal plate, torches;

and yet, even if these are absent, the mind conscious of its deeds,

foreboding, applies goads to itself and sears itself with whips,

nor meanwhile sees what limit of evils there can be,

nor what finally may be the end of punishments,

and fears, all the more, that these same things may become more grievous in death.

Here, in short, the life of fools becomes Acherusian.

This too you yourself may sometimes say to yourself:

‘Even good Ancus left the light to his eyes,

who was better than you, wicked man, in many respects.

Then many other kings and potentates

died, who ruled over great nations.

He too himself, who once made a road across the great sea

and gave his legions a passage to go over the deep

and taught them to tread with their feet upon the salt pools

and, riding over them on horseback, despised the murmurings of the sea,

with the light taken away, he breathed forth his soul from his dying body.

The Scipio-born, thunderbolt of war, terror of Carthage,

gave his bones to earth just as though he were the lowliest slave.

Add the discoverers of doctrines and of charms,

add the companions of the Heliconian Muses; of whom Homer alone,

having gained the same sceptre, rests in sleep with the others.

Finally, after ripe old age had

warned Democritus that the mindful motions of his mind were growing weak,

he himself of his own accord offered his head to death, confronting it.

Epicurus himself dies, when the light of life has run its course,

he who surpassed the human race in intellect and all

eclipsed the stars, as the ethereal sun rising does.

And will you hesitate and be indignant to die?

You, for whom life is almost dead though alive and seeing,

who waste the greater part of your age in sleep,

and, awake, snore, nor cease to behold dreams,

and bear a mind troubled by empty fear,

nor can often discover what evil there is for you, when

wretched, you are pressed, drunken, from every side by many cares

and wander, drifting in the uncertain error of your mind.'

If men could, just as they seem to perceive

that there is a weight in the mind which wearies it with its heaviness,

also know from what causes and whence this comes about,

that so great a mass, as it were, of evil stands in the breast,

or live their lives in such a way as we now for the most part see,

not knowing what each wishes for himself and always seeking

to change his place, as though he could lay down a burden.

Often that man goes out from his great house,

weary of being at home, and suddenly,

since he feels that outside is no better at all.

He rushes on, driving his nags headlong toward his country villa,

as though urgently bringing aid to a house on fire;

at once he yawns when he has touched the threshold of the villa,

or, heavy with sleep, he goes off into slumber and seeks forgetfulness,

or even hastens to the city and visits it again.

In this way each man flees himself; but him, of course, as happens,

he is unable to escape, he clings to unwillingly and hates

for this reason, because, being sick, he does not grasp the cause of his disease;

if he saw it clearly, each man, abandoning everything else,

would first strive to know the nature of things,

since it is the condition of eternal time, not of a single hour,

that is at issue, the condition in which every age must be for mortals

after death, whatever remains in waiting.

Finally, what great desire for life compels us to tremble so greatly amid doubtful dangers?

what great desire for life compels us to tremble so greatly amid doubtful dangers?

Certainly the end of life stands before mortals,

nor can death be avoided, so that we do not meet it.

Moreover, we are ever turning about in the same place and remain there.

nor is any new pleasure hammered out by living;

but while what we desire is absent, it seems to surpass

all else; afterward, when that has fallen to our lot, we desire another,

and an equal thirst always holds us, gaping for life.

and it is uncertain what fortune the following age will bring,

or what chance may bear to us, or what end hangs over us.

Nor, by prolonging life, do we remove one jot

from the time of death, nor are we able to take anything away from it,

so that we may perhaps be able to exist for long when dead.

Accordingly, though you may wish by living to heap up whatever ages,

that eternal death will nevertheless remain no whit the less;

nor will he who already no longer exists be any less long gone, from today's

light, who has made an end of life, than he

who died many months and years before.

## Liber Quartus

  

Avia Pieridum peragro loca nullius ante

 

trita solo. iuvat integros accedere fontis

 

atque haurire, iuvatque novos decerpere flores

 

insignemque meo capiti petere inde coronam,

 

unde prius nulli velarint tempora musae;

 

primum quod magnis doceo de rebus et artis

 

religionum animum nodis exsolvere pergo,

 

deinde quod obscura de re tam lucida pango

 

carmina musaeo contingens cuncta lepore.

 

id quoque enim non ab nulla ratione videtur;

 

nam vel uti pueris absinthia taetra medentes

 

cum dare conantur, prius oras pocula circum

 

contingunt mellis dulci flavoque liquore,

 

ut puerorum aetas inprovida ludificetur

 

labrorum tenus, interea perpotet amarum

 

absinthi laticem deceptaque non capiatur,

 

sed potius tali facto recreata valescat,

 

sic ego nunc, quoniam haec ratio plerumque videtur

 

tristior esse quibus non est tractata, retroque

 

volgus abhorret ab hac, volui tibi suaviloquenti

 

carmine Pierio rationem exponere nostram

 

et quasi musaeo dulci contingere melle;

 

si tibi forte animum tali ratione tenere

 

versibus in nostris possem, dum percipis omnem

 

naturam rerum ac persentis utilitatem.

  

Sed quoniam docui cunctarum exordia rerum

 

qualia sint et quam variis distantia formis

 

sponte sua volitent aeterno percita motu

 

quoque modo possit res ex his quaeque creari,

 



 



 



 

atque animi quoniam docui natura quid esset

 

et quibus e rebus cum corpore compta vigeret

 

quove modo distracta rediret in ordia prima,

 

nunc agere incipiam tibi, quod vehementer ad has res

 

attinet esse ea quae rerum simulacra vocamus,

 

quod speciem ac formam similem gerit eius imago,

 

cuius cumque cluet de corpore fusa vagari;

 

quae quasi membranae summo de corpore rerum

 

dereptae volitant ultroque citroque per auras,

 

atque eadem nobis vigilantibus obvia mentes

 

terrificant atque in somnis, cum saepe figuras

 

contuimur miras simulacraque luce carentum,

 

quae nos horrifice languentis saepe sopore

 

excierunt ne forte animas Acherunte reamur

 

effugere aut umbras inter vivos volitare

 

neve aliquid nostri post mortem posse relinqui,

 

cum corpus simul atque animi natura perempta

 

in sua discessum dederint primordia quaeque.

 

dico igitur rerum effigias tenuisque figuras

 

mittier ab rebus summo de cortice eorum;

 

id licet hinc quamvis hebeti cognoscere corde.

  

 Principio quoniam mittunt in rebus apertis

 

corpora res multae, partim diffusa solute,

 

robora ceu fumum mittunt ignesque vaporem,

 

et partim contexta magis condensaque, ut olim

 

cum teretis ponunt tunicas aestate cicadae,

 

et vituli cum membranas de corpore summo

 

nascentes mittunt, et item cum lubrica serpens

 

exuit in spinis vestem; nam saepe videmus

 

illorum spoliis vepres volitantibus auctas.

 

quae quoniam fiunt, tenuis quoque debet imago

 

ab rebus mitti summo de corpore rerum.

 

nam cur illa cadant magis ab rebusque recedant

 

quam quae tenvia sunt, hiscendist nulla potestas;

 

praesertim cum sint in summis corpora rebus

 

multa minuta, iaci quae possint ordine eodem

 

quo fuerint et formai servare figuram,

 

et multo citius, quanto minus indupediri

 

pauca queunt et  sunt prima fronte locata.

 

nam certe iacere ac largiri multa videmus,

 

non solum ex alto penitusque, ut diximus ante,

 

verum de summis ipsum quoque saepe colorem.

 

et volgo faciunt id lutea russaque vela

 

et ferrugina, cum magnis intenta theatris

 

per malos volgata trabesque trementia flutant;

 

namque ibi consessum caveai supter et omnem

 

scaenai speciem patrum matrumque deorsum

 

inficiunt coguntque suo fluitare colore.

 

et quanto circum mage sunt inclusa theatri

 

moenia, tam magis haec intus perfusa lepore

 

omnia conrident correpta luce diei.

 

ergo lintea de summo cum corpore fucum

 

mittunt, effigias quoque debent mittere tenvis

 

res quaeque, ex summo quoniam iaculantur utraque.

 

sunt igitur iam formarum vestigia certa,

 

quae volgo volitant subtili praedita filo

 

nec singillatim possunt secreta videri.

  

Praeterea omnis odor fumus vapor atque aliae res

 

consimiles ideo diffusae rebus abundant,

 

ex alto quia dum veniunt extrinsecus ortae

 

scinduntur per iter flexum, nec recta viarum

 

ostia sunt, qua contendant exire coortae.

 

at contra tenuis summi membrana coloris

 

cum iacitur, nihil est quod eam discerpere possit,

 

in promptu quoniam est in prima fronte locata.

 

Postremo speculis in aqua splendoreque in omni

 

quae cumque apparent nobis simulacra, necessest,

 

quandoquidem simili specie sunt praedita rerum,

 

exin imaginibus missis consistere eorum.

 



 



 

sunt igitur tenues formarum illis similesque

 

effigiae, singillatim quas cernere nemo

 

cum possit, tamen adsiduo crebroque repulsu

 

reiectae reddunt speculorum ex aequore visum,

 

nec ratione alia servari posse videntur,

 

 tanto opere ut similes reddantur cuique figurae.

  

Nunc age, quam tenui natura constet imago

 

percipe. et in primis, quoniam primordia tantum

 

sunt infra nostros sensus tantoque minora

 

quam quae primum oculi coeptant non posse tueri,

 

nunc tamen id quoque uti confirmem, exordia rerum

 

cunctarum quam sint subtilia percipe paucis.

 

primum animalia sunt iam partim tantula, corum

 

tertia pars nulla possit ratione videri.

 

horum intestinum quodvis quale esse putandumst!

 

quid cordis globus aut oculi? quid membra? quid artus?

 

quantula sunt! quid praeterea primordia quaeque,

 

unde anima atque animi constet natura necessumst,

 

nonne vides quam sint subtilia quamque minuta?

 

praeterea quaecumque suo de corpore odorem

 

expirant acrem, panaces absinthia taetra

 

habrotonique graves et tristia centaurea,

 

quorum unum quidvis leviter si forte duobus

 

[Gap in source]

 

quin potius noscas rerum simulacra vagari

 

multa modis multis, nulla vi cassaque sensu?

 

Sed ne forte putes ea demum sola vagari,

 

quae cumque ab rebus rerum simulacra recedunt,

 

sunt etiam quae sponte sua gignuntur et ipsa

 

constituuntur in hoc caelo, qui dicitur aer,

 

quae multis formata modis sublime feruntur,

 

ut nubes facile inter dum concrescere in alto

 

cernimus et mundi speciem violare serenam

 

aëra mulcentes motu; nam saepe Gigantum

 

ora volare videntur et umbram ducere late,

 

inter dum magni montes avolsaque saxa

 

montibus ante ire et solem succedere praeter,

 

inde alios trahere atque inducere belua nimbos.

 

nec speciem mutare suam liquentia cessant

 

et cuiusque modi formarum vertere in oras.

  

Nunc ea quam facili et celeri ratione genantur

 

perpetuoque fluant ab rebus lapsaque cedant

 

[Gap in source]

 

semper enim summum quicquid de rebus abundat,

 

quod iaculentur. et hoc alias cum pervenit in res,

 

transit, ut in primis vestem; sed ubi aspera saxa

 

aut in materiam ligni pervenit, ibi iam

 

scinditur, ut nullum simulacrum reddere possit.

 

at cum splendida quae constant opposta fuerunt

 

densaque, ut in primis speculum est, nihil accidit horum;

 

nam neque, uti vestem, possunt transire, neque autem

 

scindi; quam meminit levor praestare salutem.

 

qua propter fit ut hinc nobis simulacra redundent.

 

et quamvis subito quovis in tempore quamque

 

rem contra speculum ponas, apparet imago;

 

perpetuo fluere ut noscas e corpore summo

 

texturas rerum tenuis tenuisque figuras.

 

ergo multa brevi spatio simulacra genuntur,

 

ut merito celer his rebus dicatur origo.

 

et quasi multa brevi spatio summittere debet

 

 lumina sol, ut perpetuo sint omnia plena,

 

sic ab rebus item simili ratione necessest

 

temporis in puncto rerum simulacra ferantur

 

multa modis multis in cunctas undique partis;

 

quandoquidem speculum quo cumque obvertimus oris,

 

res ibi respondent simili forma atque colore.

 

Praeterea modo cum fuerit liquidissima caeli

 

tempestas, perquam subito fit turbida foede,

 

undique uti tenebras omnis Acherunta rearis

 

liquisse et magnas caeli complesse cavernas.

 

usque adeo taetra nimborum nocte coorta

 

inpendent atrae Formidinis ora superne;

 

quorum quantula pars sit imago dicere nemost

 

qui possit neque eam rationem reddere dictis.

  

Nunc age, quam celeri motu simulacra ferantur,

 

et quae mobilitas ollis tranantibus auras

 

reddita sit, longo spatio ut brevis hora teratur,

 

in quem quaeque locum diverso numine tendunt,

 

suavidicis potius quam multis versibus edam;

 

parvus ut est cycni melior canor, ille gruum quam

 

clamor in aetheriis dispersus nubibus austri.

 

Principio persaepe levis res atque minutis

 

corporibus factas celeris licet esse videre.

 

in quo iam genere est solis lux et vapor eius,

 

propterea quia sunt e primis facta minutis,

 

quae quasi cuduntur perque aëris intervallum

 

non dubitant transire sequenti concita plaga;

 

suppeditatur enim confestim lumine lumen

 

et quasi protelo stimulatur fulgere fulgur.

 

qua propter simulacra pari ratione necessest

 

inmemorabile per spatium transcurrere posse

 

temporis in puncto, primum quod parvola causa

 

est procul a tergo quae provehat atque propellat,

 

quod super est, ubi tam volucri levitate ferantur,

 

deinde quod usque adeo textura praedita rara

 

mittuntur, facile ut quasvis penetrare queant res

 

et quasi permanare per aëris intervallum.

  

Praeterea si quae penitus corpuscula rerum

 

ex altoque foras mittuntur, solis uti lux

 

ac vapor, haec puncto cernuntur lapsa diei

 

per totum caeli spatium diffundere sese

 

perque volare mare ac terras caelumque rigare.

 

quid quae sunt igitur iam prima fronte parata,

 

cum iaciuntur et emissum res nulla moratur?

 

quone vides citius debere et longius ire

 

multiplexque loci spatium transcurrere eodem

 

tempore quo solis pervolgant lumina caelum?

 

Hoc etiam in primis specimen verum esse videtur,

 

quam celeri motu rerum simulacra ferantur,

 

quod simul ac primum sub diu splendor aquai

 

ponitur, extemplo caelo stellante serena

 

sidera respondent in aqua radiantia mundi.

 

iamne vides igitur quam puncto tempore imago

 

aetheris ex oris in terrarum accidat oras?

 

quare etiam atque etiam mitti fateare necessest

  

 corpora quae feriant oculos visumque lacessant.

 

perpetuoque fluunt certis ab rebus odores,

 

frigus ut a fluviis, calor ab sole, aestus ab undis

 

aequoris, exesor moerorum litora circum,

 

nec variae cessant voces volitare per auras.

 

denique in os salsi venit umor saepe saporis,

 

cum mare versamur propter, dilutaque contra

 

cum tuimur misceri absinthia, tangit amaror.

 

usque adeo omnibus ab rebus res quaeque fluenter

 

fertur et in cunctas dimittitur undique partis

 

nec mora nec requies interdatur ulla fluendi,

 

perpetuo quoniam sentimus et omnia semper

 

cernere odorari licet et sentire sonare.

  

Praeterea quoniam manibus tractata figura

 

in tenebris quaedam cognoscitur esse eadem quae

 

cernitur in luce et claro candore, necessest
