at those things which render vision from the smooth surface of mirrors, since each result is accomplished by two airs.

Now that which is the right-hand side of our limbs comes about to be seen as left in mirrors because, when an image coming to the plane of a mirror strikes it, it is not turned back intact but is dashed straight backward, just as if someone were to strike a ball against a dry mask before it is of clay, or against a beam, and if it should immediately preserve a straight figure before it and, dashed back, reproduce itself backward.

The result will be that the eye which had been the right will now be the left, and the right will correspondingly come from the left.

It also comes about that an image is passed on from mirror to mirror,

so that five or even six likenesses may be produced at the same time.

For whatever things shall lie hidden at the back, in the inner part,

from there nevertheless, however distorted and wholly remote,

all may be brought out through winding passages,

so that they are seen to be in a house by means of many mirrors.

So completely does an image shine through from mirror to mirror,

and when a left hand has been presented, it comes about again that it becomes a right;

then it returns backward once more and changes back to the same.

Moreover, whatever little sides of mirrors

are furnished with a bending like the side of our body,

for that reason send back right-hand images to us,

either because the image is transferred from mirror to mirror

and then, reflected twice, flies toward us, or also because,

when it arrives, the image is turned around, for this reason that

the bent shape of the mirror teaches it to be turned toward us.

Furthermore, you would suppose that images walk along equally and

set down a foot with us and imitate our movement,

because, from whichever side of the mirror you withdraw,

straightway the images cannot return from there;

since nature compels all things to be reflected

and to rebound from objects, returned at equal angles.

Furthermore, the eyes shun and avoid looking at bright things.

The sun also blinds, if you persist in directing your gaze against it,

because its force is great, and high up

through the clear air images are borne

and strike the eyes, disturbing their structures.

Moreover, every sharp brightness often burns

the eyes because it possesses many seeds of fire,

which, insinuating themselves, produce pain in the eyes.

Moreover, whatever jaundiced persons look upon become pale,

because many seeds of paleness flow from their bodies

to meet the images of things,

and many, finally, are mingled in their eyes,

which by their contagion dye everything with pallors.

But we look from darkness upon things that are in light

because, when the nearer black air of darkness

first enters the eyes and occupies them when opened,

bright, shining air immediately follows,

which, as it were, cleanses them and scatters the black shadows

of that air; for in many respects this air is

more mobile, more subtle, and more potent.

As soon as it has filled the passages of the eyes with light

and opened wide those which the black air

had previously besieged, immediately the images of things

which are situated in the light follow and stimulate us to see.

The reverse we cannot do, from light in darkness,

because the thicker air of darkness follows behind,

which fills all the openings

and besieges the passages of the eyes, so that the images

of any things, thrown in, cannot be moved.

And when we behold from afar the square towers of a city,

it comes about that they often appear round,

because every angle is seen as blunt from a distance,

or rather is not seen at all, and its blow

perishes and does not reach the vision of our eyes,

because, while the images are borne through much air,

the air compels it to grow dull by repeated impacts.

When every angle has at once escaped perception,

it comes about as though structures of stone were seen turned round;

yet not as things which are truly and actually round when seen close at hand,

but they appear somewhat as a shadowy imitation.

Likewise, a shadow seems to us to move in the sun

and to follow our footsteps and imitate our movement,

if you believe that air deprived of light can

walk along, following the movements and gestures of men;

for that which we are accustomed to call a shadow can be nothing else

than air devoid of light.

No doubt because the earth is deprived of the sun's light

in definite places in succession, wherever we pass along,

and likewise that which we have left is filled again,

therefore it comes about that what was the shadow

of the body seems to have continually followed us from the opposite side.

For ever new lights of rays pour themselves forth,

and the former perish, as though wool were drawn into fire.

Therefore the earth is easily stripped of light

and likewise filled again, and washes away its black shadows from itself.

Yet here we do not grant that the eyes are deceived by a jot.

For to see in whatever place light and shadow may be belongs to them;

but whether the lights are the same or not,

and whether the shadow which was here now passes there,

or rather whether what we said a little before comes to be,

this the reasoning of the mind alone ought to distinguish,

nor can the eyes know the nature of things.

Therefore do not fasten this fault of the mind upon the eyes.

The ship in which we are carried is borne along, though it seems to stand still;

that which remains at its station is believed to be passing by.

And hills and plains seem to flee toward the stern,

which we pass by in the ship and fly past under sail.

All the stars seem fixed in the ethereal vaults to stand still,

and yet all are in continual motion,

since, having risen, they revisit their long settings,

when they have measured the heaven with their bright body.

And by like reasoning the sun and moon seem to remain

in one place—things which reality itself shows to be carried along.

Mountains rising far off from the midst of the sea,

between which a great clear outlet lies open for fleets,

yet appear as one island joined from these.

It thus comes about that porticoes and columns seem to children

to turn about and run around,

when they themselves have ceased to turn,

so that they can scarcely now believe that all the roofs above them

are not threatening to fall down upon them.

And now, when nature begins to raise the red radiance high with trembling fires

and to lift it above the mountains,

which at that moment the sun seems to you to be above,

itself, burning, touching them close at hand with its own fire,

scarcely two thousand arrows' flights away from us,

scarcely even often five hundred casts of a javelin,

between them and the sun lie the vast level expanses

of sea, spread beneath the huge shores of heaven,

and many thousands of lands intervene,

which diverse nations and tribes of wild beasts occupy.

But a pool of water not one finger's breadth deep,

which stands between stones in the paved layers of roads,

offers a view downward beneath the earth with such an extent

as the deep chasm of heaven lies open from the earth,

so that you seem to look down upon clouds and to see heaven,

with bodies wondrously hidden beneath the earth in heaven.

Finally, when a spirited horse has halted for us in the middle

of a river and we have looked down into the swift waters of the stream,

the force of the standing horse's body seems to be carried sideways

and driven rapidly upstream against the current,

and wherever we cast our eyes, all things seem to be borne

and to flow in a manner similar to ourselves.

Although a portico is, finally, drawn in an even line

and stands out continuously, supported by equal columns,

yet, when its whole length is seen from the farthest end,

it gradually draws itself into the narrow point of a cone,

joining roof to floor and all the right sides to the left,

until it has led them together into the cone's obscure apex.

To sailors at sea, the sun rising from the waves seems

to set in the waves and conceal its light;

since they behold nothing but water and sky—

lest you lightly believe that the senses are everywhere shaken.

But to those ignorant of the sea, in harbor ships seem

to struggle with broken stern-ornaments against the waves.

For whatever part of the oars rises above the salt spray

is straight, and the rudders above are straight;

all that is submerged beneath the liquid seems broken,

to be turned back upward and to return lying on its back,

and, reflected, almost to float on the surface of the liquid.

And when winds bear scattered clouds through the sky

in the nighttime, then the bright constellations seem

to glide against the clouds and to go above

far away in another direction from that in which they are truly borne.

But if by chance a hand placed beneath one eye

presses it, by a certain effect it comes about that all things

which we behold then appear double to our sight:

the bright lights of lamps flowering with flames double,

and furniture throughout the whole house doubled,

and the faces of men twofold and their bodies double.

Finally, when sleep has bound our limbs in sweet slumber

and the whole body lies in deepest repose,

then nevertheless we seem to ourselves to be awake and to move

our limbs, and in the blind darkness of night

we judge that we see the sun and daylight,

and, shut in a place, we seem to change sky, sea, rivers, mountains,

and to cross plains with our feet,

and to hear sounds, though the stern silences of night

prevail everywhere, and to utter words while silent.

We see many other marvelous things of this kind,

which all, as it were, seek to violate confidence in the senses,

but in vain, since the greatest part of these things deceives

because of the opinions of the mind which we ourselves add,

so that things not seen by the senses are taken to be seen.

For nothing is harder than to distinguish clear things

from doubtful things, which the mind immediately adds of itself.

Finally, if anyone thinks that nothing can be known, he does not know even this,

whether it can be known, since he confesses that he knows nothing.

Against him, therefore, I shall refrain from contending the case,

who has set his own footprints upon his own head.

And yet, even if I grant that he knows this too, I would ask this very thing:

since he has never before seen anything true among things,

whence does he know what knowing and not knowing are in turn,

what thing has created the notion of truth and falsehood,

and what thing has proved the distinction of the doubtful from the certain?

You will find that the notion of truth has been created from the senses first,

and that the senses cannot be refuted.

For that must be discovered with greater trust,

which of its own accord can prevail over false things by true ones.

What, then, ought to be held in greater trust than the senses?

Will reason, arisen from false sense, be strong enough

to speak against them, when it has arisen wholly from the senses?

Unless they are true, all reason too becomes false.

Can the eyes reprove the ears, or the ears the touch? Or again,

will taste of the mouth convict this touch, or will the nostrils refute it,

or will the eyes prevail?

No, I think, it is not so. For to each separately a power

has been allotted; each has its own force, and therefore it is necessary

to see separately what is soft and cold or hot,

and separately to perceive the various colors of things

and whatever things are necessarily joined with colors.

Likewise taste in the mouth has its power separately, odors

arise separately, sounds separately. Therefore it is necessary

that one sense cannot convict the others.

Nor indeed will they be able to reprove themselves,

since equal trust must always be accorded them.

Therefore whatever has appeared to each of these at any time is true.

And if reason cannot explain the cause

why things which have been square close by are seen round at a distance,

yet it is better, for want of reasoning, to give faulty

causes for either shape,

than somewhere to let go things manifest to one's hands

and violate first confidence and tear away the whole

foundations upon which life and safety rest.

For not only would all reasoning collapse, but life itself also

would immediately fall, unless you dared to trust the senses

and to avoid precipitous places and other things

which are to be shunned in this kind, and to pursue their opposites.

Therefore all that abundance of words which has been prepared

and arrayed against the senses is empty.

Finally, just as in a building, if the first rule is crooked,

and if the square proves deceptive in its straight directions,

and if some level is even slightly faulty in one part,

all things must be made wrongly and askew,

crooked, leaning, sloping, inverted, and discordant—the roofs,

so that some seem already to wish to fall and do fall,

betrayed wholly by the deceptive first judgments—

so, therefore, your reasoning about things must be crooked

and false, whatever has arisen from false senses.

Now by what means each of the other senses perceives its own object

is by no means a difficult account left to give.

First, every sound and voice is heard when, insinuated into the ears,

they have struck the sense with their own body.

For it must be confessed that sound too

consists of body, since it can strike the senses.

Moreover, voice often scrapes the throat, and as it goes out

the cry makes the windpipe rougher,

since, when the first-beginnings of voices have arisen in a greater throng

and have begun to go out through a narrow passage,

of course the gateway of the mouth too is scraped when filled.

There is no doubt, therefore, that voices and words consist

of bodily first-beginnings, so that they can cause injury.

Nor does it escape you likewise how much of body continual speech

takes away and subtracts from men's sinews and strength itself,

when it is carried on from the shadow of black night

all the way to the rising brightness of dawn,

especially if it has been poured forth with the utmost shouting.

Therefore voice must consist of body,

since one who speaks much loses a part from his body.

But roughness of voice arises from roughness

of first-beginnings, and likewise smoothness is created by smoothness;

nor do first-beginnings of similar shape penetrate the ears,

when a trumpet bellows heavily with a deep murmur

and the lyre, struck back, resounds with its hoarse humming,

and when the daughters of Daulis in the gardens of Helicon

raise their clear lament in mournful voice.

Therefore, when we force these voices forth from deep within our body

and send them outward through the straight mouth,

the mobile, artful tongue of sinews articulates them,

and the shaping of the lips in part gives them shape.

When the distance from which each voice has set out is not long,

the words themselves too must necessarily be heard clearly

and distinguished articulation by articulation;

for it preserves its shaping and preserves its figure.

But if the intervening distance is longer than is fitting,

the words must necessarily be confused through much air

and the voice disordered while it flies through the breezes.

Therefore it comes about that you can perceive the sound but cannot

discern what the meaning of the words is;

so confused and impeded does the voice arrive.

Moreover, one word often strikes the ears

of all the people when sent from the mouth of a herald.

One voice, therefore, suddenly scatters into many voices,

since it divides itself among individual ears,

stamping upon the words their shape and clear sound.

But that part of the voices which does not strike the ears themselves

perishes beyond them, scattered in vain through the broad air.

A part, striking solid places, is thrown back

and returns a sound, and sometimes deceives by the semblance of a word.

When you see these things well, you can render the account

to yourself and others how, in lonely places,

rocks give back in succession sounds of words in like forms.

We seek companions wandering among shadowy mountains

and call aloud for those scattered abroad.

I have seen even six or seven places give back a voice

when you hurled out one; thus hills themselves, repelling words against hills,

repeated the utterances as they were returned.

The neighboring people imagine that goat-footed Satyrs and Nymphs possess

these places, and say that there are Fauns,

by whose night-wandering noise and jesting play

they commonly affirm that the silent silences are broken,

that sounds of strings and sweet complaints are made,

such as the pipe pours forth when struck by the fingers of players,

and that the race of farmers perceives far and wide, when Pan,

shaking the pine wreaths of his half-wild head,
often runs his hooked lip over the gaping reeds,

so that the pipe does not cease to pour forth its woodland music.

Moreover, voice is divided into all directions,

because some [voices] are generated from others, when one,

once dissolved, has arisen into many, just as fire

often is wont to scatter its spark into fires of its own.

Therefore hidden places in turn are filled with voices,

all places which boil around and are stirred by sound.

But images all proceed by straight paths,

as they have once been sent forth; wherefore no one is often

able to see beyond, but to receive voices from outside.

And yet even this voice itself, while it passes enclosed,

is blunted and enters the ear confused,

and we seem to hear a sound rather than words.

This too: the tongue and palate, by which we perceive flavour,

have in themselves somewhat more of contrivance, more labour.

First, we perceive flavour in the mouth, when we

squeeze out food by chewing, as if someone perhaps began

to press and dry a sponge full of water with his hand.

Then all that we squeeze out is distributed through the passages

of the palate and through the winding pores of the sparse tongue;

when the bodies of the flowing flavour are smooth,

they touch pleasantly and pleasantly affect all

the moist temples sweating around the tongue;

but, on the contrary, as they have arisen, they prick and tear sensation,

the more each is filled with roughness.

Then pleasure from the flavour extends as far as the palate;

but when it has rushed downward through the throat,

there is no pleasure, while it is all distributed among the limbs;

nor does it matter at all by what nourishment the body is fed,

provided only that you can distribute through the limbs what you take in,

once digested, and preserve the swollen condition of the stomach.

Now, that we may see what food is for one thing and what for another,

I shall explain why what is bitter and harsh to some

can nevertheless seem exceedingly sweet to others,

and why in these matters there is so great a difference and diversity,

that what is food to some may be sharp poison to others;

thus it happens that a serpent, touched by human saliva,

perishes and destroys itself by biting itself.

Moreover, hellebore is sharp poison to us,

but it fattens goats and quails.

That you may be able to know by what causes this comes about,

first it is fitting to remember what we said before,

that seeds are held mixed in things in many ways.

Furthermore, all living creatures that take food,

just as they are unlike externally and the encompassing

outline of their limbs restrains each kind,

so likewise consist of seeds differing in shape.

Moreover, since the seeds differ, the intervals and paths,

the pores, which we declare to exist,

must differ in all the limbs and in the mouth and palate itself.

Thus some must be smaller and others larger,

some necessarily three-cornered, others square,

many round, and certain many-angled in many ways.

For as the nature of their shapes and motions requires,

so the shapes must differ for the pores,

and the paths vary according as their texture restrains them.

Accordingly, when what is sweet to some becomes bitter to others,

for him to whom it is sweet the smoothest bodies must

enter flexibly into the passages of the palate;

but, on the contrary, for those to whom the same thing is bitter within,

rough and, plainly, hooked [bodies] penetrate the throat.

Now from these matters it is easy to know each thing.

Indeed, when fever has arisen in anyone through an excess of bile,

or some force of disease has been stirred up in another way,

then the whole body is already disturbed and all

the positions of the first-beginnings are changed;

it comes about that the bodies which formerly suited sensation

now do not suit it, and that others are more fitted,

which, penetrating, can produce bitter sensation;

for both are mixed in the flavour of honey—

a fact which I have often shown you before above.

Come now, I shall explain in what way the smell, applied to the nostrils,

touches [them]. First, there must necessarily be many things

from which a varied flood of odours, flowing, rolls itself forth,

and it must be thought that [odours] flow, are emitted, and scattered abroad;

but one [odour] is more suited to some living creatures, another to others,

on account of their differing shapes.

And therefore through the air

bees, however far away, are led by the smell of honey,

and vultures by corpses; then the promised power of dogs

leads their cloven paw whither the track of wild beasts has directed its step,

and the white goose, guardian of the citadel of Romulus' sons,

perceives from afar a human smell.

Thus one scent given to each leads it to its own

food and compels it to recoil from foul poison,

and in this way the races of wild creatures are preserved.

This smell itself, then, whatever it be that strikes the nostrils,

can be transmitted farther by one [thing] than by another;

but yet none of these is borne so far

as sound, as voice—not now to mention the things

which strike the eyes' sharpness and assault vision.

For it comes wandering slowly and perishes first,

gradually dispersed with ease into the breezes of air;

first because it is scarcely emitted from deep within a thing;

for that odours flow and withdraw from things deep within

is shown by the fact that all things seem to smell more strongly when broken,

when crushed, when weakened by fire.

Then you may see that it is produced from larger

first-beginnings than voice, since it does not penetrate

through stony barriers, where voice and sound are commonly borne.

Therefore you will also see that what smells is not so easy

to discover as to the region in which it is situated;

for its stroke cools by lingering through the air,

and the messengers of things do not run warmly to sensation.

Thus dogs often wander and seek the tracks.

Nor yet is this so only in the case of odours and kinds

of flavours; likewise the appearances and colours of things

do not all suit all senses so well

that some are not sharper to the sight of some [creatures].

Why, even the cock, accustomed with clear voice to call

the dawn when night is clapped away by its wings,

swift lions cannot withstand in turn

or look upon: so straightway they remember flight.

No doubt because there are certain seeds in the body of cocks

which, when sent into the eyes of lions,

pierce the pupils and inflict sharp pain,

so that the fierce creatures cannot endure them in return,

though these same [seeds] can do no harm to our eyes,

either because they do not penetrate, or because, when they penetrate,

a free exit is granted them from the eyes, so that by lingering

they cannot harm the lights from any quarter.

Come now, receive what things move the mind, and whence

the things that come into the mind come, in a few words.

First I say this: many images of things wander

in many ways, everywhere into all directions,

thin [images], which easily join together in the air

when they come in contact, like a spider's web and gold leaf.

For indeed these are much thinner in texture

than those which strike the eyes and assault vision,

since these penetrate through the body's rare spaces and stir

the thin nature of the mind within and assault sensation.

Thus we see Centaurs and limbs of Scyllas,

and the dog-like faces of Cerberus and images of those

whose bones, after death, the earth embraces;

because images of every kind are borne everywhere,

partly those which arise spontaneously in the air itself,

partly those which at any time withdraw from various things,

and those which are formed from the shapes made from these.

For certainly an image of a Centaur does not arise from a living [Centaur],

since no such animate nature has existed;

but when by chance an image of a horse and of a man comes together,

it immediately adheres easily, as we said before,

on account of its subtle nature and thin texture.

All other things of this kind are created by the same method.

And since they are borne about with mobile, utmost lightness,

as I showed before, any one thin image, with a single stroke,

easily moves the mind in us as it pleases;

for the mind is thin and itself wonderfully mobile.

That these things come about as I recount, you may easily learn from this:

insofar as what we see with the mind is like what [we see]

with the eyes, it must come about in a similar way.

Now therefore, since I have taught that, when I happen

to see lions through images which assault the eyes,

you may know that the mind is moved in a similar way

by images of lions and all other things which it sees equally,

and no less than the eyes, except that it sees thinner [images].

Nor for another reason, when sleep has poured over the limbs,

does the mind's consciousness remain awake, except because images

assault our minds, these same images which [assault them] when we are awake,

so much so that we certainly seem to see him whom,

his life relinquished, death and earth have already taken possession of.

Nature compels this to happen because all

the body's senses, disabled throughout the limbs, are at rest

and cannot refute false things by true realities.

Moreover, memory lies dormant and languishes in sleep,

nor does it protest that he has long since attained

death and destruction, whom the mind believes it sees alive.

As for the rest, it is not strange that images move

their arms and fling about their other limbs in rhythm;

for it happens that in dreams the image seems to do this.

Indeed, when the first [image] perishes and another has arisen

then in another position, the former seems to have changed its gesture.

Clearly this must be thought to occur with rapid process:

so great is the mobility and so great the abundance of things,

and so great, in any one perceptible instant, is the abundance

of particles, that it can furnish [them].

Many questions are asked concerning these matters, and much must be

made clear by us, if we desire to set forth the subject plainly.

First of all it is asked why, whatever desire has come to each person,

the mind straightway thinks of that very thing.

Do images watch for our will,

and as soon as we wish does the image meet us,

if the sea is in our heart, if earth, if finally heaven?

Assemblies of men, a procession, banquets, battles—

does nature create and prepare all things at a word?

Especially since in the same region and place

different minds think all things far differently.

What then? When we see images proceed in rhythm

and move their supple limbs in dreams,

when they nimbly stretch forth their supple arms alternately

and repeat the gesture before the eyes with corresponding foot?

Clearly the images are steeped in art and wander trained,

so that they may be able to perform their plays in the time of night.

Or will this rather be true? Because within a single time,

when we perceive—that is, when a single utterance is emitted—

many times lie hidden, which reason discovers to exist,

therefore it comes about that at every moment all images

are present, prepared in every place.

So great is the mobility and so great the abundance of things.

When the first [image] perishes and another has arisen

then in another position, the former seems to have changed its gesture.

And because they are thin, unless it strains, the mind

is unable to discern sharply; accordingly all the rest

perish, except those which it itself has prepared.

Moreover, it prepares itself and hopes that there will come about

the sight of what follows each thing: therefore it happens.

Do you not see that even the eyes, when they have begun

to discern thin things, strain and prepare themselves,

and that without this we cannot see sharply?

And yet even in things plainly visible you may recognize

that, if you do not direct your mind [to them], they are just as if

they had at every moment been set apart and removed far away.

Why then is it strange if the mind loses all other things

besides those matters to which it has itself applied?

Then we infer great things from small signs,

and ourselves enter into the deception of our own error.

It also happens sometimes that an image

of the same kind is not supplied, but that a woman who was before

seems to be present in the hands as a man,

or that one face and age follows upon another.

Sleep and forgetfulness ensure that we do not wonder at this.

In these matters there is a fault that must especially be avoided,

and error must be shunned with fearful care: do not suppose that

the bright lights of the eyes were created

so that we might be able to see, and that, in order that we might be able

to take long strides, the joints of shins and thighs, founded on the feet,

can bend; or again that arms were fitted to strong shoulders

and hands given as servants on either side,

so that we might be able to do in life what was useful.

All other explanations of this kind which they interpret together with these

are wholly perverse and backward in reasoning,

because nothing was born in the body in order that we might use it,

but what has been born itself creates its use.

Nor were the lights of the eyes born before seeing,

nor [was there] speaking with words before the tongue was created;

rather, the origin of the tongue far preceded

speech, and ears were created much earlier than sound was heard,

and finally all the limbs existed, as I think,

before there was any use of them; thus they could not have grown for the sake of use.

But, on the contrary, to join battle in hand-to-hand fighting,

and to tear limbs and stain the body with blood,

existed long before shining weapons flew;

and nature compelled [men] to avoid a wound before

the left hand, through art, was given the protection of a shield.

Clearly, too, to entrust the weary body to rest

is much more ancient than the soft spread coverings of a bed,

and to quench thirst is prior to the birth of cups.

These things, therefore, which have been discovered from use and life,

can be believed to have been recognized for the sake of use.

But all those things are separate which, first born themselves,

afterwards gave knowledge of their usefulness.

Among such things we see especially the senses and limbs;

therefore again and again it is far from possible for you to believe

that they could have been created for the service of usefulness.

Likewise, it is not surprising in these matters

that the nature of the body itself seeks food for each living creature.

For indeed I have taught that many bodies flow and withdraw

from things in many ways, but very many must [withdraw]

from animals, because they are exercised in motion:

many are breathed out through the mouth when they pant languidly,

and many, forced out from deep within, are carried away through sweat.

Thus by these things the body becomes rarefied and its whole

nature is undermined, a process followed by pain.

Therefore food is taken, that it may support the limbs

and, distributed among them, restore their strength, and stop up

the open craving for eating through the limbs and veins.

Moisture likewise goes into all whatever places

require moisture; and many gathered bodies of heat,

which supply fires to our stomach,

the liquid arriving disperses and extinguishes as though a fire,

so that dry heat can no longer burn the limbs.

Thus, then, the panting thirst is washed away from our body;

thus the hungry desire is filled.

Now how it comes about that we can put forth strides

when we wish, and why it has been granted to move the limbs,

and what cause has accustomed [them] to thrust forward this great weight

of our body, I shall say: take in my words.

I say that first images of walking

fall upon our mind and strike the mind, as we said before.

Then will arises; for no one begins to do

any action before the mind has first foreseen what it wishes.

What it foresees consists in an image of that thing;

therefore, when the mind so moves itself that it wishes to go

and step forward, it immediately strikes the force of spirit

dispersed through the whole body, throughout the limbs and joints;

and this is easy to do, since it is held in conjunction.

Then that force in turn strikes the body, and so the whole mass

is gradually thrust forward and moved.

Moreover, then the body too becomes rarefied, and air—

as indeed it must, since it is always mobile—

comes abundantly through the opened pores and penetrates,

and is thus dispersed through all the minute parts

of the body.

Here, therefore, it comes about in both cases,

that a body, like a ship, is borne by sails and wind.

Nor yet in these matters is it wonderful

that such tiny bodies can twist about so great a body

and turn our whole weight; 

for indeed wind, of subtle, thin body,

drives and impels with great force a great ship,

and one hand guides it, however great its speed,

and turns a single rudder wherever it pleases;

and by pulleys and drums many a machine moves great weights

and lifts them with a light exertion.

Now by what means sleep pours rest through the limbs

and releases from the breast the cares of the mind,

I shall set forth in pleasing speech rather than in many verses,

as the small song of the swan is better than the cry

of cranes scattered through the aetherial clouds of the south wind.

Do you grant me attentive ears and a discerning mind,

lest you deny that what I say can come to pass, and turn away

from truths with a resisting breast,

when you yourself are at fault and cannot discern it.

First, sleep occurs when the force of the soul has been dispersed

through the limbs, and in part has withdrawn, cast out abroad,

and in part, driven farther inward, has retired into the depths;

for only then are the limbs dissolved and grow slack.

For there is no doubt that this sensation in us

is the work of the soul; when sleep prevents it from existing,

then we must suppose that the soul is disturbed

and cast forth—not all of it; for the body would lie

steeped in the eternal cold of death.

Indeed, if no hidden part of the soul remained

in the limbs, as fire lies hidden buried beneath much ash,

whence could sensation suddenly be rekindled

through the limbs, as flame rises from hidden fire?

But by what causes this new condition is brought about, and whence

the soul can be disturbed and the body grow languid,

I shall explain: do you see to it that I do not pour words into the winds.

First, it is necessary that the body on its outer side,

since it is touched by the neighbouring blows of the air,

be struck and repeatedly beaten by its impact;

and therefore nearly all things are covered either with hide,

or even with shells, or with callus, or with bark.

This same air also beats the inner part in breathing,

when it is drawn in and breathed back out.

Therefore, since the body is struck from either side, and since

the blows reach us through the small openings

of the body to the primary parts and first elements,

there comes about, as it were, a gradual collapse through our limbs.

For the arrangements of the first-beginnings

of body and soul are thrown into confusion. Thus part of the soul

is drawn out, part hidden within recedes inward,

and part, dispersed through the limbs, cannot remain

joined with itself or perform reciprocal motion;

for nature blocks up its gatherings and pathways.

Therefore sensation departs, the motions being profoundly changed.

And since there is, as it were, nothing to support the limbs,

the body becomes weak and all the members languish;

the arms and eyelids droop, and the knees, in one lying down,

often give way and relax their strength.

Then sleep follows food, because what air does,

food too, while it is distributed through all the veins,

produces. And that sleep is by far the heaviest

which you take when sated or weary, because then very many

bodies are thrown into confusion, battered by great labour.

By the same reasoning, a deeper withdrawal of part of the soul occurs,

and a more abundant portion of it is cast outward,

and it is more divided within itself and more dispersed.

And whatever pursuit each person is generally bound to and clings to,

or whatever matters we have long dwelt upon before,

and in whatever occupation the mind has been more intent,

these same things we generally seem to pursue in dreams:

advocates to plead cases and compose laws,

commanders to fight and engage in battles,

sailors to wage their contracted war with the winds,

but I to pursue this work and always to inquire into the nature of things

and, once discovered, to set it forth in the writings of my fathers.

Thus other pursuits and arts too are generally seen

to hold men's minds deceived in dreams.

And all who for many days in succession

have given continuous attention to games, we generally see,

when they have now ceased to employ those things with their senses,

still to have open pathways remaining in the mind,

by which the same images of things may come in.

Thus for many days these same things present themselves

before their eyes, so that even while awake they seem

to see dancers and moving supple limbs,

and to receive in their ears the liquid song of the lyre and its speaking strings,

and to see the same assembly and the varied splendours

of the stage simultaneously shining.

So greatly do pursuit and inclination matter,

and the things in which they have been accustomed to be occupied—

not human beings alone, but indeed all animals.

Indeed, you will see strong horses, while their limbs lie at rest,

yet sweating and continually breathing in dreams,

and as though striving with all their strength for the prize,

or as though the barriers had been opened;

and hunting dogs, often in gentle repose,

yet suddenly toss their legs and all at once emit cries,

and repeatedly draw back breath through their nostrils,

as if they held the discovered tracks of wild beasts;

and, awakened, they often pursue the empty images

of deer, as though they saw them given over to flight,

until, their errors shaken off, they return to themselves.

But the gentle home-bred brood of pups strive

to shake themselves awake and lift their bodies from the ground,

just as though they were looking upon unknown faces and visages.

And the harsher the seeds of each kind are,

the more must they rage in dreams likewise.

But birds of various kinds take flight and suddenly with their wings

disturb the groves of the gods in the night-time,

if in gentle sleep they have seemed to engage in battles and combats,

pursuing and flying after hawks.

Moreover, the minds of men, which accomplish great things with great motions,

likewise often act and perform in dreams:

they storm kings, are captured, mingle battles,

raise a cry, as though they were being slaughtered there.

Many fight desperately and utter groans of pain,

and as though they were being bitten by a panther or fierce lion,

they fill everything with loud cries.

Many speak in sleep of great affairs

and have very often thereby betrayed their own deeds.

Many meet death. Many, as though they were falling

from high mountains to the ground with their whole body,

are terrified and, as though mentally distraught, scarcely

return to themselves from sleep, stirred by the agitation of the body.

Likewise, thirsty, one sits beside a river or a pleasant spring

and all but takes the whole stream into his throat.

Often, beside a pool or a vessel, pure boys,

bound in sleep, think that they are lifting up their garment,

and pour out the filtered moisture of their whole body,

when Babylonian coverings are drenched in magnificent splendour.

Then those into whose limbs the seed of age first insinuates itself,

when the day itself has made them mature in body,

are met from outside by images also, messengers

of a distinguished face and beautiful colour;

these stir and irritate places swollen with much seed,

so that, as though all things had often been accomplished, they pour forth

the waves of a mighty stream and stain the garment.

That seed of which we spoke before is set in motion in us

when mature age first strengthens the limbs.

Thus, then, one who receives a blow from Venus' weapons,

whether a boy with womanly limbs shoots him,

or a woman casting love from her whole body,

strains toward the source of the wound and longs to unite

and to cast moisture, drawn from body, into body;

for mute desire foresees pleasure.

This is Venus for us; hence too comes the name of Love,

hence first into the heart distilled that drop of Venus' sweetness,

and chilling care followed after;

for if that which you love is absent, nevertheless its images are at hand,

and its sweet name comes before your ears.

But it is fitting to flee images and drive away from oneself

the food of love, to turn the mind elsewhere,

and to cast the gathered moisture into whatever bodies,

not, once turned toward the love of one person, to retain it

and store up for oneself care and certain pain.

For the ulcer lives again and grows inveterate by being fed,

and day by day the madness increases and the misery grows heavier,

unless you disturb the first wounds with new blows

and, wandering, heal them while fresh by roaming Venus,

or can transfer the motions of your mind elsewhere.

Nor is he who avoids love deprived of Venus' fruit,

but rather takes those advantages which are without penalty;

for surely the pleasure thence is purer for the healthy than for the miserable.

For even at the very moment of possession

the passion of lovers wavers in uncertain wanderings,

nor is it settled what they should first enjoy with eyes and hands.

What they have sought, they press hard; they inflict pain on the body

and often drive their teeth into the lips

and fasten kisses there, because the pleasure is not pure,

and beneath lie stings that urge them to hurt that very thing,

whatever it is, whence those seeds of frenzy arise.

But Venus lightly breaks the penalties amid love,

and mingled pleasure restrains the biting.

For therein is the hope that, from the same body

whence the origin of the ardour comes, the flame can also be quenched.

That nature wholly resists being so.

And this is the one thing of which the more we have,

the more the breast burns with dreadful desire.

For food and moisture are taken into the limbs within;

and because they can occupy fixed places,

this desire for liquids and food is easily filled.

But from a human face and beautiful colour

nothing is given to the body but thin images to enjoy;

often wretched hope is snatched away by the wind.

As when, thirsty in dreams, a man seeks to drink, and no moisture

is given that can extinguish the burning in his limbs,

but he seeks images of liquid and labours in vain,

and, drinking in the midst of a rushing river, remains thirsty,

so in love Venus toys with lovers by images,

nor can they satisfy themselves by looking upon bodies face to face,

nor can their wandering hands rub off anything

from the tender limbs, uncertain over the whole body.

Finally, when with joined limbs they enjoy the flower

of youth, when now the body foresees joys

and Venus is on the point of sowing the woman's fields,

they eagerly fasten body to body and mingle their saliva

from their mouths, and breathe in, pressing mouths with teeth—

yet to no purpose, since they cannot rub anything off from there,

nor penetrate and pass with their whole body into body;

for sometimes they seem to wish and strive to do this.

So eagerly do they cling in Venus' bonds,

until the limbs, weakened by the force of pleasure, melt away.

At last, when the desire launched from the sinews has burst forth,

there comes for a little while a brief pause in the violent ardour.

Then the same frenzy returns and that madness revisits them,

when they seek to attain what they themselves desire,

and cannot discover what device may conquer that evil.

So uncertainly do they waste away with a hidden wound.

Add that they consume their strength and perish through labour;

add that life is lived at another's nod;

duties languish and reputation, sick and wavering, fails.

Meanwhile substance slips away; Babylonian

ointments are procured, and beautiful Sicyonian slippers smile upon the feet;

indeed large emeralds with green light

are set in gold, and sea-purple cloth is continually worn away

and, exercised, drinks in Venus' sweat.

And wealth well won by the fathers becomes diadems and turbans,

sometimes they turn it into a mantle and Alidensian and Cean garments.

Banquets with exquisite clothing and fare, games,

frequent cups, ointments, crowns, garlands are prepared—

to no purpose, since from the midst of the fountain of delights

something bitter rises that chokes even amid the flowers:

either when the conscious mind itself perhaps reproaches itself

for spending life idly and perishing in brothels,

or because she has left behind some word cast out ambiguously,

which, fixed in the desirous heart, lives again like fire;

or because he thinks that she casts her eyes about too freely or looks upon another,

and sees in her face traces of a smile.

And these evils are found in love at its height and greatest prosperity;

but in adverse and impoverished love there are innumerable evils,

which you may grasp with eyes unclosed.

Innumerable; so that it is better to be watchful beforehand,

in the manner I have taught, and take care not to be enticed.

For to avoid being struck by the darts of love

is not so difficult as, once caught in the nets themselves,

to get out and break through Venus' stout knots.

And yet, even entangled and caught in the noose, you can

escape the hostile thing, unless you yourself stand in your own way

and first overlook all the faults of mind,

or of body, of her whom you seek and desire.

For men, commonly blinded by desire,

do this and attribute to them advantages which are not truly theirs.

Thus we see in many ways women who are misshapen and ugly

held dear and flourishing in the highest honour.

And one mocks another and advises him to propitiate Venus,

since he is afflicted by foul love,

while the wretches often do not look back upon their own greatest evils.

The black woman is “honey-coloured”; the filthy and foul-smelling one, “unadorned”;

the grey-eyed one, “Pallas”; the sinewy and wooden one, “a gazelle.”

The tiny, dwarfish girl is “one little Grace,” all sheer salt;

the huge and monstrous one is “a cataplexy,” and full of dignity.

The stammerer cannot speak: she is “lisping”; the mute woman is modest.

But the fiery, hateful, talkative woman becomes a “Lampadium.”

Then she becomes a “slender darling” when she cannot live

for emaciation; and she who is already dead with a cough is truly “delicate.”

But the excessively fat and big-breasted woman is Ceres herself from Iacchus;

the snub-nosed is Silenus and Satyr, the thick-lipped woman a “kiss.”

It would take too long, if I tried to mention the rest of this kind.

But let her now be of however great distinction of face,

from whose limbs the power of Venus rises in all its force;

surely there are other women too; surely we lived without this one before;

surely she does, and we know that she does, everything that an ugly woman does,

and poor wretch fumigates herself with foul odours,

while her maidservants flee far away and secretly laugh.

But the lover, weeping, shut out, often covers the threshold

with flowers and garlands, anoints the proud doorposts

with marjoram-oil, and wretchedly plants kisses upon the doors.

If, once admitted, he should encounter but a single breath of odour as he comes in,

he would seek honourable reasons for departing,

and his complaint, long meditated and drawn from deep within, would fall;

and there he would condemn himself for folly,

when he saw that he had granted her more

than is right to concede to a mortal.

Nor does this escape our Venuses; therefore all the more carefully

they conceal all the backstage of life from those

whom they wish to hold fast and bound in love—

to no purpose, since you can nevertheless draw everything

forth into the light with your mind and investigate every cause of laughter,

and, if she is kindly disposed and not disagreeable, in turn

overlook it and make allowance for human things.

Nor does a woman always sigh with feigned love,

when, embracing, she joins her body to a man's body

and holds him, moistening kisses with lips drawn in;

for she often does it from the heart and, seeking mutual

joys, urges love's course to run its full length.

Nor by any other reason could birds, herds, wild beasts,

and flocks and mares submit to males,

if the abundant nature of the females did not itself grow hot

and gladly receive again the Venus of those that leap upon them.

Do you not see also how those whom mutual pleasure has often bound are tortured, as though in common chains, when at crossroads dogs, often eager to depart in different directions, strain greedily with all their utmost strength, while meanwhile they cling fast in the strong bonds of Venus? This they would never do unless they knew mutual joys which could cast them into a snare and hold them bound. Therefore, again and again, as I say, the pleasure is shared.

And when, by the mingling of seed, the woman has by chance overcome the man's force and seized it by sudden force, then offspring become like their mothers through the maternal seed, or like their fathers through the paternal. But those whom you see to be of the form of both, blending together the features of their parents, grow from the father's body and the mother's blood, when, stirred through the limbs by the goads of Venus, the seeds have clashed in encounter, the mutual ardor breathing together; and neither of the two has prevailed nor has been prevailed over.

It also happens sometimes that they may be born resembling their grandfathers and often reproduce the forms of their great-grandfathers, because the parents often conceal in their bodies many first-beginnings mingled in many ways, which fathers, sprung from their stock, hand down from fathers. From these Venus produces forms in varied allotment, and restores the faces, voices, and hair of ancestors; since these arise from no more determinate a seed than do our faces and bodies and limbs.

And a female offspring arises from the father's seed, and males come into being formed from the mother's body; for offspring always consists of a twofold seed, and whatever is created is more like that parent of whose share it has more than an equal part. This you may discern, whether the offspring is male or whether it has a female origin.

Nor do divine powers deprive anyone of generative capacity, so that he is never called father by sweet children and passes his life in barren Venus; though people generally think this, and sadly sprinkle the altars with much blood and load the shrines with offerings, that they may render their wives pregnant with abundant seed. Yet in vain do they weary the divine power and the lots. For some are sterile through seed that is too thick, and others, conversely, through seed that is fluid and thinner than is right.

Because the thin seed cannot adhere and fasten in the proper places, it at once flows away and, recalled, yields in miscarriage. But because the thicker seed is emitted more congealed than is fitting, either it does not fly forth in so extended a stroke, or it cannot penetrate the places equally, or, having penetrated, the seed is with difficulty mingled with the woman's seed. For the harmonies of Venus seem to differ greatly.

And some men impregnate some women more readily, and some women receive the burden more readily from some men and grow heavy. And many women were sterile in several marriages before, yet afterward found husbands by whom they could conceive children and become rich in sweet offspring.

And for those whose fertile wives had often previously been unable to bear at home, a nature suited to them too has been found, so that they might fortify their old age with children. So greatly does it matter that seeds be able to mingle with seeds in a generatively fitting way, and that thick ones meet with fluid and fluid with thick. And in this matter it is important by what diet life is sustained; for by some things the seeds are made thick in the limbs, and by others they are thinned and wasted in turn; and it matters in what ways the delightful pleasure itself is pursued.

This too matters very greatly; for wives are generally thought to conceive more in the manner of beasts and four-footed creatures, because in this way they can take in the seeds, with their breasts placed down and their loins raised. Nor do wives need soft movements at all. For a woman prevents herself from conceiving and resists if, joyfully, she draws back Venus from the man with her buttocks and sets all the waves in motion from her unboned breast; for she ejects the furrow from the straight line and course of the plowshare and turns aside the blow of the seed from its places. And courtesans have accustomed themselves to move for this reason: lest they be frequently filled and lie pregnant, and at the same time that Venus itself might be more pleasing to men; which seems to be of no use to our wives.

Nor is it by divine intervention and Venus' arrows that sometimes a little woman of inferior beauty is loved; for sometimes the woman herself, by her own deeds and accommodating ways and by a body kept neatly groomed, causes a man easily to grow accustomed to spending his life with her. Besides, habit makes love harmonious; for whatever, however lightly, is struck by frequent blows is nevertheless overcome and gives way over a long stretch of time. Do you not see too how drops of water falling upon rocks pierce the rocks over a long stretch of time?
