Since any fires whatever that we see upon earth,

while their bright flickering, while their heat is seen,

sometimes seem to alter their size by something very small,

toward one side or the other, the farther away they are.

Likewise it is not to be wondered by what means

that little sun can send forth so great a light,

which, watering seas and all lands and heaven,

fills them and bathes all things in warm vapour.

For it may be that from here one open fountain of the whole world,

bountifully flowing, wells up and bursts forth in light,

because thus elements of vapour from the whole world

come together from every side, and thus their gathering

flows together, so that this heat streams forth from one source.

Do you not see also how widely a small spring of water

waters the meadows at times and overflows the fields?

There is also this: that from no great fire of the sun

the air may receive heat with warm burnings,

if the air be by chance suitable and apt,

so that, struck by small burnings, it can be kindled;

as at times we see fires arise everywhere among crops

and stubble from a single spark.

Perhaps too the sun, shining with rosy-bright lamp,

possesses much fire about itself in unseen burnings,

which is marked by no radiance,

so that it may only increase the heat of the rays' stroke.

Nor does a single straightforward account of the sun stand revealed,

how from the summer regions of Capricorn

it approaches the wintry turning and then, returning,

turns its course toward the solstitial limits of Cancer,

and how the moon seems to traverse that space in months

which the sun consumes in its yearly course.

No, I say, a single cause has not been rendered for these matters.

For this seems especially able to happen,

which the revered opinion of Democritus lays down:

that the nearer each of the stars is to the earth,

the less it can be carried along with the revolution of heaven;

for the swift and keen force of that revolution

wanes and is diminished below, and therefore

the sun is gradually left behind with the signs that follow,

because it is far lower than the fiery signs.

And this is still more so for the moon: the more its

course, descending, lies far from heaven and draws near to earth,

the less it can strain onward with the signs.

And the more slackly it is now borne by the revolution,

being lower than the sun, the more all the signs

overtake it in their circuit and are borne past it.

Therefore it comes about that it seems to return

more quickly to each sign, because the signs return to it.

It also comes about that from the transverse parts of the world air

can flow alternately at a fixed time,

which can drive the sun from its summer signs

all the way to its wintry turnings and icy cold,

and which can cast it back from the cold shadows of frost

all the way into the summer regions and fiery signs.

And by like reasoning one must think that the moon and stars,

which roll their great years in great orbits,

can move by alternating airs from different regions.

Do you not see too clouds, driven by different winds,

go in different directions, the lower from the upper?

Why should those stars be less able to be borne among themselves

by differing tides through the great orbits of ether?

But night overwhelms the lands in mighty darkness,

either when the sun, from its long course, has reached the farthest part

of heaven and, languid, has breathed out its fires,

shaken by their journey and weakened by much air,

or because the same force which bore its orb above the lands

compels it to turn its course beneath the earth.

Likewise at a fixed time rosy Matuta spreads dawn

through the regions of ether and unveils the light,

either because that same sun, returning beneath the earth,

anticipates the sky, essaying to kindle it with rays,

or because fires gather and many seeds

of heat have been accustomed to flow together at a fixed time,

which cause ever-new lights of the sun to be born;

as report has it that from the high Idaean mountains

scattered fires are seen in the eastern light,

then gather, as it were, into one globe and make up an orb.

Yet in these matters it ought not to be thought wonderful

that these seeds of fire can so exactly at a fixed time

come together and restore the sun's brightness.

For we see many things that happen at a fixed time

in all matters. At a fixed time trees bloom,

and at a fixed time they shed their blossom.

Nor less does age command teeth to fall at a fixed

time, and the beardless youth to grow hairy in soft down

and likewise let a soft beard descend from his cheeks.

Lastly lightning, snow, rains, clouds, winds,

arise in not too uncertain seasons of the year.

For since the first beginnings of causes were so,

and the things of the world thus fell out from their first origin,

in consequence they now also return in fixed order.

Likewise, the days may grow and the nights waste away,

and the daylight diminish, as the nights take their increase,

either because that same sun, running beneath the earth and above it

through unequal windings, divides the regions of ether

and apportions its orb into unequal parts;

and what it has taken away from one of the two regions, it restores,

having travelled, by so much more in the opposite region,

until it reaches that sign of heaven where the knot of the year

makes the night-shadows equal to the daylight;

for midway in its course, the sky holds its boundaries

at equal division between the breath of the north wind and south wind,

on account of the position of the whole zodiacal circle,

in which the sun, gliding, completes the yearly seasons,

surveying lands and heaven with slanting light,

as the reasoning of those declares who have marked all

the regions of heaven adorned with arranged signs.

Or because the air is thicker in certain regions,

therefore beneath the earth the trembling radiance of fire lingers

and cannot easily penetrate and emerge at its rising;

therefore, in winter time, long nights

delay until the radiant badge of day arrives.

Or again, because in the alternating regions of the year

fires have been accustomed to gather more slowly and more swiftly,

which cause the sun to rise from a certain region,

therefore it comes about that they seem to speak truth.

The moon may shine when struck by the sun's rays

and turn toward us day by day more light

in appearance, by as much as it withdraws from the sun's orb,

until opposite it it shines brightly in full light

and, rising, has seen its setting from above;

then little by little it must in like manner hide its light backward,

by as much as it now glides nearer to the sun's fire

through another region of the circle of signs;

as those do who imagine the moon to be like a ball

and to hold its course beneath the sun.

There is also a reason why it may roll with its own light

and display varying forms of brightness;

for there may be another body, which is borne along and at the same time

glides in every way, confronting and obstructing it,

and it cannot be seen, because it is borne devoid of light.

And it can revolve, as, for example, a globe like a ball,

tinged on one half with shining light,

and, by revolving the globe, produce changing forms,

until it turns whatever part is increased by fires

toward our sight and open eyes;

then little by little it twists back and takes away

the light-bearing part of the rounded mass and ball;

as the Babylonian doctrine of the Chaldaeans, refuting

the art of the astrologers, strives to establish against it,

as though what each side contends could not happen,

or as though this had less cause to be embraced than that.

Finally, why a new moon cannot always be created

in a fixed order of forms and fixed figures,

and each thing created vanish into its private days,

while another be restored in that part and place of it,

is difficult to demonstrate by reasoning and establish by words,

when so many things are created in so fixed an order.

Spring goes, and Venus, and before Venus her winged herald

steps forth; and in the tracks of Zephyr,

mother Flora, scattering before them along the way,

fills all things with splendid colours and scents.

Then follows parched Heat, and with it dusty Ceres

and the Etesian blasts of the north winds.

Then Autumn approaches, and at the same time Euhius Euan advances.

Then other storms and winds follow,

loud-thundering Volturnus and the South Wind, mighty with lightning.

At last Winter brings snows and restores

sluggish cold.

Winter follows, clattering with cold in its teeth.

Thus it is less wonderful if at a fixed time the moon

is born and at a fixed time is again destroyed,

when so many things can happen at so fixed a time.

Likewise you must think that eclipses of the sun and obscurations of the moon

can occur from several causes.

For why, when the moon can shut out the earth from the sun's

light and bar from the earth its lofty head,

casting its dark orb before the burning rays,

should it be thought that at the same time another body cannot do this,

which always glides devoid of light?

And why can the sun not, languid, send forth its fires

at a fixed time and renew its light,

when it has passed through regions hostile to flames in the air,

which cause fires to be quenched and perish?

And why can the earth in turn strip the moon

of light and keep the sun oppressed above itself,

while the moon passes through the rigid shadows of the cone,

but at the same time another body cannot come to the moon's aid,

or glide above the sun's orb,

so as to break off its rays and outpoured light?

And yet, if the moon itself shines by its own radiance,

why can it not grow faint in a certain region of the world,

while it passes through places hostile to its own lights?

.

For the rest, since through the blue of the great world

I have explained by what reasoning whatever might happen,

so that we might know what force and cause stirred

the sun's various courses and the moon's wanderings,

and in what way, their light being extinguished, they are eclipsed

and shroud the unsuspecting lands in darkness,

when as though they wink, and again with open light

behold all clear places with bright radiance,

now I return to the newness of the world and the soft fields

of earth: what they first resolved, in new birth, to raise

into the regions of light and entrust to uncertain winds.

First the earth gave forth the race of grasses and green brightness

all around the hills and across all the plains;

the flowery meadows gleamed with verdant colour,

and thereafter to the diverse trees there was given through the air

a great contest of growing, with reins let loose.

As down and hair and bristles are first created

on the limbs of four-footed creatures and the bodies of winged ones,

so then the new earth first brought forth grasses and shrubs;

then in turn it created many mortal races,

arisen in many ways by diverse means.

For animals cannot have fallen from the sky,

nor can terrestrial creatures have come forth from the salt pools.

It remains that earth has deservedly gained

the name of mother, since all things have been created from earth.

And even now many animals arise from the earth,

formed by rains and the warm vapour of the sun;

so it is less wonderful that then more and greater ones arose,

nourished by the new earth and ether.

First the race of birds and varied flying creatures

left eggs, hatched in the season of spring,

as now in summer cicadas of rounded form

of their own accord leave their skins, seeking food and life.

Then the earth first gave you mortal races.

For much heat and moisture abounded in the fields.

Whenever, therefore, any region of ground offered a suitable place,

wombs grew, fastened to the earth by roots;

when at the ripe time age had opened these,

for the infants, fleeing moisture and seeking air,

nature there turned the pores of the earth,

and compelled it to pour out from open veins a juice

like milk, just as now every woman,

after she has borne, is filled with sweet milk, because all

that current of nourishment is turned toward the breasts.

The earth provided food for the children, heat clothing, and grass a bed,

abounding in much soft down.

But the newness of the world brought forth neither harsh colds

nor excessive heats nor winds of great strength.

For all things grow and gain strength alike.

Wherefore, again and again, the earth deservedly retains

the name of mother, since it itself created the human race

and at almost a fixed time poured forth every animal

which ranges wildly everywhere upon great mountains,

and likewise aerial birds of varying forms.

But because it must have some end of bearing,

it ceased, like a woman wearied by the long passage of time.

For age changes the nature of the whole world,

and one state must take up all things from another;

no thing remains like itself: all things migrate,

nature changes all things and compels them to be transformed.

For one thing decays and, weakened by age, languishes;

then another grows and emerges from contempt.

Thus age changes the nature of the whole world,

and one state of the earth takes up another,

so that what could do is unable, and what could not bear before is able.

Then too the earth tried to create many monsters,

arisen with wondrous face and limbs:

the androgyne, between the two sexes and removed from either;

some bereft of feet, in turn deprived of hands,

also mute without a mouth, found blind without a face,

and bound through the whole body by limbs adhering together,

so that they could neither do anything nor move anywhere

nor avoid harm nor take what need would desire.

It created other monsters and prodigies of this kind,

in vain, because nature barred their growth,

and they could not attain the desired flower of age,

nor find food, nor unite in the works of Venus.

For we see that many things must concur in creatures,

so that they can forge forth races by propagation:

first, that food may exist; then, that generative seeds

can flow through the limbs from relaxed members;

and that the female can be joined with the male, and that each may possess

mutual pleasures which they exchange between themselves.

And many races of living creatures must then have perished

and been unable by propagation to forge forth offspring.

For every kind that you see feeding on the vital breezes,

either craft or strength or finally swiftness

has preserved that race from its earliest age.

And there are many kinds which, commended to us by their usefulness,

remain entrusted to our protection.

First, strength has protected the fierce race of lions and savage breeds,

craft foxes, and flight deer.

But the lightly sleeping hearts of dogs with faithful breast,

and every race sprung from the seed of beasts of burden,

as well as wool-bearing flocks and horned herds,

all have been entrusted to the protection of men, Memmius;

for eagerly they fled wild beasts and followed peace,

and sought abundant food procured without their own labour,

which we give as rewards for their usefulness.

But those to which nature granted none of these things—neither

the power to live of their own accord, nor to render us

some usefulness for which we should allow their race

to feed and remain safe beneath our protection—

these plainly lay as prey and gain for others,

all entangled in their own fateful bonds,

until nature led that race to destruction.

But Centaurs neither existed nor can at any time

there exist a being of double nature and twofold body,

compacted from limbs of alien kinds, such that its power

from this side and that might be sufficiently equal.

This you may understand from this, however dull your mind.

First, when three years have passed in active course, the horse

is in its prime—not at all the boy; for even now he will often

seek in dreams the milk-filled breasts.

Later, when in old age the horse's strong powers

and limbs fail, with life languidly fleeing,

only then does flowering youth come upon boyish age

and clothe the cheeks with soft down;

lest by chance you should believe that Centaurs can be made and exist

from a man and the seed of a beast of burden, horses,

or Scyllas, girded with the bodies of swift half-marine dogs,

and the rest of this kind, whose limbs we see discordant

among themselves:

for they neither flower together nor gain strength

in their bodies nor waste away in old age,

nor burn with like love nor agree in one character,

nor are the same things pleasing through their limbs.

for one may often see bearded flocks grow fat on hemlock,

which is a sharp poison to man.

Indeed, since flame is wont to scorch and burn the tawny bodies of lions

just as much as every kind

of creature and blood that exists upon the earth,

how could it have come about that, with a triple body, one

first part a lion, last a dragon, and the middle part itself, the Chimera,

should breathe forth from its body fierce flame out of its mouth?

Therefore he also who imagines that in the new-made earth and fresh heaven

such animals could have been produced,

relying upon this one empty name of newness,

may with like reasoning utter many things from his mouth:

he may say that then streams of gold flowed everywhere over the earth

and that trees were wont to bloom with gems,

or that man was born with such mighty force of limbs

as to be able to plant his steps across the deep seas

and to turn the whole heaven about himself with his hands.

For although there were many seeds of things in the earth

at the time when the earth first brought forth animals,

yet there is no indication that mixed creatures could have been created

among themselves, and the limbs of living beings compounded together,

because the kinds of herbs and crops and luxuriant trees

which even now abound from the earth

cannot nevertheless be created interwoven with one another,

but each thing proceeds according to its own manner, and all

preserve their distinctions by a fixed covenant of nature.

And that race of men in the fields was much

harder, as was fitting, since the hard earth had created it,

founded inwardly on larger and more solid bones,

suited with strong sinews throughout its flesh,

not easily overcome by heat or cold,

or by novelty of food or any failing of the body.

And through many revolutions of the sun rolling through the sky

they led their lives after the wandering fashion of wild beasts.

Nor was anyone a sturdy guide of the curved plough,

nor did anyone know how to work the fields with iron

or to sink new saplings into the earth or cut down with high

sickles the old branches from tall trees.

What the sun and rains had given, what the earth had created

of its own accord, that gift was enough to delight their hearts.

Among acorn-bearing oaks they commonly tended their bodies;

and the arbutus fruits which now in winter time you see

ripen into a ruddy color,

the earth then bore in greater abundance, and larger too.

And besides, the flowering newness of the world then produced

many hard foods, ample for wretched mortals.

But rivers and springs summoned them to quench their thirst,

as now the downward rush of water from great mountains

cries aloud far and wide to the thirsty tribes of wild beasts.

Finally, wanderers occupied the woodland sanctuaries of nymphs, well known to them,

from which they knew that streams of water washed the slippery rocks

with abundant flowing flood—damp rocks,

damp rocks dripping above with green moss—

and in part bubbled up and burst forth upon the level plain.

Not yet did they know how to handle things with fire, nor to use

skins and spoils of beasts to clothe their bodies,

but they inhabited groves and hollow mountains and woods,

and hid their squalid limbs amid the thickets,

forced to avoid the blows of winds and rains.

Nor could they look to the common good, nor did they know how to use

any customs or laws among themselves.

Whatever prey fortune had offered to each, he carried off;

each one taught by himself to be strong and live for himself.

And Venus joined the bodies of lovers in the woods;

for each union was brought about either by mutual desire,

or by the man's violent force and vehement lust,

or by a price—acorns and arbutus fruits or picked pears.

And, trusting in the wondrous strength of hands and feet,

they pursued the woodland tribes of wild beasts

with hurled stones and the heavy weight of a club.

They conquered many, avoided a few by hiding places;

and, like bristle-bearing swine, they gave their woodland bodies

naked to the earth when overtaken by night,

wrapping themselves round with leaves and boughs.

Nor did they seek the day and sun through the fields

with loud lament, wandering fearful in the shadows of night;

but silently they waited, buried in sleep,

until the sun should bring light into heaven with his rosy torch.

For since from childhood they had always been accustomed to see

darkness and light arise in alternating time,

there was no way it could ever happen that they should wonder,

or despair lest everlasting night should hold the lands

forever, the sun's light having been withdrawn.

But this was more their concern: that tribes of wild beasts

often made repose hostile to the wretched.

Driven from their homes, they fled their rocky shelters

at the coming of a foam-flecked boar or mighty lion,

and in the dead of night, frightened, yielded up

their leaf-strewn beds to savage guests.

Nor then did mortal races leave behind the sweet light of life

with much more lamentation than they do now.

For then each one, more often seized among them,

provided living food for wild beasts, snatched by teeth,

and filled groves and mountains and woods with groaning,

seeing his living flesh buried in a living tomb.

But those whom flight had saved, though their bodies were devoured,

afterward, holding trembling palms over foul wounds,

called upon Orcus with dreadful cries,

until savage worms deprived them of life,

bereft of help, ignorant what their wounds required.

But not many thousands of men, led beneath standards,

did one day then give to destruction, nor did the troubled

waters of the sea dash ships and men against the rocks.

For the sea, having often risen rashly, vainly, to no purpose,

raged and lightly laid aside its empty threats;

nor could the treacherous blandishment of the calm sea

entice anyone into disaster with its smiling waves.

The wicked craft of navigation then lay neglected.

Then want of food gave their languishing limbs over to death;

whereas now abundance of things overwhelms them.

They themselves, unwitting, often poured out poison for themselves;

now they give it themselves more cunningly.

Thereafter, when they had prepared huts and skins and fire,

and woman joined to man had yielded herself into one

[Gap in source]

were known, and they saw offspring created from themselves,

then the human race first began to grow soft.

For fire brought it about that bodies chilled by cold

could no longer endure it so well beneath the canopy of heaven,

and Venus diminished their strength, and children easily broke

the proud temper of their parents by caresses.

Then neighboring men, desiring it, began to join friendship among themselves,

neither to harm nor be harmed,

and they commended children and the female sex,

signifying with voices and gesture, though inarticulately,

that it was right for all to pity the weak.

Yet concord could not arise in every respect,

but a great and good part faithfully kept the covenants;

otherwise the whole human race would already then have perished,

nor could propagation have prolonged the generations until now.

But nature compelled them to utter the various sounds of speech,

and use brought forth the names of things,

by no very different reasoning than infancy itself seems

to lead children on to gesture with the tongue,

when it makes them point with the finger to things present.

For each one perceives what use he can make of his own power.

Before horns born upon a calf stand out from its forehead,

angered, it attacks and presses with them in hostility.

But the cubs of panthers and the whelps of lions

already fight back with claws and feet and bite,

when teeth and claws have scarcely even been created.

Moreover, we see every race of birds

trusting to wings and seeking trembling aid from feathers.

Accordingly, to suppose that some one person then distributed names

to things, and that men thereafter learned their first words,

is madness.

For why should it be thought that this man could mark all things

with sounds and emit the various noises of speech,

while others at the same time could not do this?

Besides, if others too had not used speech

among themselves, whence was implanted in him knowledge

of its usefulness, and whence was first given to him the power

to know and see in his mind what he wished to do?

Nor could one man compel many and subdue them when conquered,

so that they would wish to learn thoroughly the names of things.

Nor is it easy by any reasoning to teach and persuade the deaf

what must be done; for they would not endure it,

nor would they any longer suffer their ears to be battered in vain

by unheard sounds of voice, by any reasoning.

Finally, what is so wondrous in this matter,

if the human race, in which voice and tongue were strong,

marked different things with different sound according to its various feeling?

When dumb cattle, when indeed the tribes of wild beasts,

are wont to utter unlike and various cries,

when there is fear or pain and when joys now increase.

For indeed one may learn this from clear instances.

When first the great soft muzzles of angered Molossian dogs growl,

baring their hard teeth,

their restrained rage threatens with a far different sound,

than when they are already barking and filling everything with cries.

But when they try gently to lick their pups with their tongues,

or when they suckle them, or, mighty in feet and bite,

imitate tender bites with suspended teeth,

they fawn with a far different fashion of voice and whimpering;

and so too when, deserted, they bay in a house, or when

they flee whimpering blows with crouching body.

Finally, does not neighing likewise seem to differ,

when among mares a youthful horse in flowering age,

struck by the spurs of winged Love, rages,

and gives forth a snort for battle from his open nostrils,

and when he neighs otherwise with limbs thus shaken?

Lastly, the race of birds and the various fowl,

hawks and sea-eagles and gulls seeking food and life

in the salty sea-waves,

send forth far different cries at one time than at another,

and when they contend over food and struggle over prey.

And some alter their hoarse-sounding songs along with the weather,

as the ancient tribes of crows

and the flock of ravens, when they are said to ask for water and rains,

and sometimes to call forth winds and breezes.

Therefore, if various feelings compel animals,

though they are dumb, to emit various sounds,

how much more fitting was it that mortals then should be able

to mark different things with one sound and another!

Lest perhaps in these matters you silently ask this:

lightning first brought fire down to earth for mortals,

and from it all the heat of flames spread abroad;

for we see many things flashing, kindled by heavenly flames,

when the blow of heaven has bestowed heat.

And yet when a branching tree, shaken by winds and swaying,

surges, leaning its boughs upon the boughs of another tree,

fire is squeezed out, worn away by mighty force,

and at times the hot heat of flame darts forth,

while branches and trunks rub against one another.

Either of these may have given fire to mortals.

Thereafter the sun taught them to cook food and soften it with the vapor of flame,

because they saw many things grow mild,

conquered in the fields by blows of rays and heat.

And day by day those who excelled in talent and were strong in mind

showed them how to change their former sustenance and life

by new things and fire.

Kings themselves began to found cities and establish a citadel,

a defense and refuge for themselves,

and divided and assigned cattle and fields

according to each man's appearance and strength and talent;

for appearance counted greatly, and strength was vigorous.

Later wealth was discovered and gold found,

which easily stripped even the strong and beautiful of honor;

for men generally prefer to follow the party of the richer man

rather than of the strong and those endowed with a handsome body.

But if anyone should govern life by true reasoning,

great riches for a man are to live sparingly

with an even mind; for there is never want in little.

But men wished themselves to be famous and powerful,

so that their fortune might remain on a firm foundation

and that, rich, they might be able to pass a tranquil life—

in vain, since in striving to attain the highest honor

they made the path of life a dangerous road,

and yet envy, like lightning, sometimes hurls them down from the height,

scornfully, into grim Tartarus.

For envy, as if with lightning, usually scorches the highest things

and whatever things stand out more than others;

so that it is now far better to obey in peace

than to wish to rule things by command and hold kingdoms.

Therefore let them, worn out, sweat blood in vain,

struggling along the narrow path of ambition;

since they take their wisdom from another's mouth and seek

things from hearsay rather than from their own senses,

and this is no more so now, nor will it be hereafter, than it was before.

Therefore, when kings had been slain, there lay overthrown

the former majesty of thrones and proud scepters,

and the splendid, blood-stained emblem of the highest head

beneath the feet of the mob mourned its great honor;

for what was too much feared before is eagerly trampled down.

Thus things returned to the utter dregs and confusion,

when each man sought dominion and sovereignty for himself.

Then some taught the creation of magistracies

and the establishment of laws, that they might wish to use laws.

For the human race, wearied with living an age by force,

languished from hostilities; and therefore more readily it itself

of its own accord fell under laws and binding statutes.

For each man made himself ready to avenge himself more fiercely in anger

than is now permitted by equitable laws;

for this reason men grew utterly weary of living an age by force.

Thereafter fear of punishments stains the prizes of life.

For violence and wrong entangle each man in a net,

and for the most part return to him from whom they arose;

nor is it easy to lead a calm and peaceful life

for one who violates by deeds the common covenants of peace.

For even if he deceives the race of gods and humankind,

yet he must distrust that this will remain hidden forever;

since many are often reported to have betrayed themselves while speaking in dreams

or raving in sickness,

and to have brought hidden things and sins into the open.

Now what cause has spread abroad the divinities of the gods among great nations

and filled cities with altars,

and brought it about that solemn sacred rites should be undertaken,

rites which now flourish in great affairs and places,

whence even now a terror is implanted in mortals,

which raises new shrines of gods throughout the whole circle

of lands and compels their celebration on festal days—

it is not so difficult to render an account of this in words.

For even then mortal races saw the gods' outstanding forms

in their waking mind,

and still more in sleep, of marvelous increase of body.

They attributed feeling to these, therefore, because

they seemed to move their limbs and utter proud voices,

in accordance with their splendid appearance and vast strength.

And they gave them eternal life, because their appearance

was always at hand and their form remained,

and moreover because they thought that those endowed with such great powers

could not lightly be overcome by any force.

And they thought them far superior in fortunes for this reason,

because fear of death troubled none of them,

and at the same time because in dreams they saw them accomplish

many marvelous things and suffer no toil thereby.

Besides, they perceived that the courses of heaven in fixed order

and the various seasons of the years revolved,

and could not discover by what causes this came about.

Therefore they had this refuge: to hand over all things to the gods

and make all things bend by their nod.

And they placed the dwellings and temples of the gods in heaven,

because through heaven night and moon are seen to roll,

the moon, day and night, and the stern signs of night,

night-wandering torches and the flying fires of heaven,

clouds, sun, rains, snow, winds, lightning, hail,
and swift rumblings and mighty murmurs of threats.

O unhappy race of men, when it attributed such deeds to the gods

and joined to them bitter angers!

What groans did they then beget for themselves, what wounds for us,

what tears for our descendants!

Nor is piety at all to be seen often veiled, turning toward a stone,

and approaching every altar,

nor to fall prostrate upon the ground and spread one's palms

before the shrines of the gods, nor to sprinkle altars

with much blood of four-footed beasts, nor to link vow upon vow,

but rather to be able to behold all things with a mind at peace.

For when we behold the great

temple-structures of the heavenly world above, and the aether fixed with gleaming stars,

and there comes to mind the courses of sun and moon,

then, oppressed by other evils, that care too

begins to raise its awakened head in our breasts:

whether perhaps there is for us some immeasurable power of the gods

which turns the bright stars in their various motion.

For poverty of reasoning assails the doubting mind,

both what was the generative origin of the world,

and likewise what its end may be, how long the walls of the world

can endure this strain of restless motion,

or whether, endowed by the gods with everlasting preservation,

they can, rolling on through the perpetual course of time,

despise the mighty forces of immeasurable age.

Moreover, whose mind is not contracted by fear of the gods,

whose limbs do not shudder with dread,

when the parched earth trembles beneath the dreadful blow

of lightning and great rumblings run through the sky?

Do not peoples and nations tremble, and proud kings

shrink in body, smitten by fear of the gods,

lest, because of some foul deed done or arrogant word spoken,

the heavy time for paying penalties has been increased?

Again, when the utmost force of a violent wind over the sea

sweeps the commander of a fleet across the waters

together with mighty legions and elephants,

does he not seek the peace of the gods by vows and prayers,

fearfully begging peaceful winds and favorable breaths?

Yet in vain, since, often caught in the violent whirlwind,

he is borne no less onward to the shoals of death.

So utterly does some hidden force trample upon human affairs

and seem to tread underfoot the splendid fasces and cruel axes

and hold them in mockery for itself.

Lastly, when the whole earth shakes beneath our feet

and shaken cities fall and others, tottering, threaten to fall,

what wonder if mortal races despise themselves

and leave to the gods great and marvelous powers

and forces in things, to govern the whole?

What remains: gold and iron alike were discovered,

and at the same time the weight of silver and the power of lead,

where the heat of a great fire had burned forests

on great mountains, whether by lightning sent from heaven,

or because, waging woodland warfare among themselves,

they had brought fire against their enemies for the sake of terror,

or because, induced by the goodness of the soil, they wished

to open rich fields and render the countryside pastureland,

or to kill wild beasts and grow rich by plunder.

For hunting by pit and fire arose earlier

than enclosing a woodland glade with nets and stirring it with dogs.

Whatever it was, from whatever cause the flaming heat

had consumed the woods with dreadful noise from their deep

roots and baked the earth with fire,

a stream of silver and gold, gathering from heated veins,

flowed down into hollow places of the ground,

and likewise of bronze and lead. When afterward they saw these

congealed and shining in the earth with bright color,

they lifted them up, captivated by their smooth and gleaming beauty,

and saw that they were fashioned in a shape

similar to the outlines of the hollows belonging to each.

Then it occurred to them that these, melted by heat,

could flow into any form and shape of things whatever,

and that, by hammering, they could be drawn out altogether into

the sharp and slender points of blades,

so that they might prepare weapons for themselves and be able to cut down woods,

hew timber and smooth light beams,

and even bore, pierce, and perforate through and through.

And they prepared to do these things with silver and gold

no less than at first with the strong might of violent bronze—

in vain, since their defeated strength gave way,

and they could not equally endure the hard labor.

For bronze was more highly valued, and gold lay neglected

because of its uselessness, blunted with its dull edge;

now bronze lies neglected, gold has risen to highest honor.

Thus the rolling age changes the seasons of things.

What was valued comes at last into no honor;

then another thing succeeds and emerges from contempt,

is sought more and more from day to day, and, once discovered, flourishes

in praise and is in marvelous honor among mortals.

Now, Memmius, in what manner the nature of iron

was discovered is easy for you yourself to learn by yourself.

The ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth,

and stones, and likewise broken branches from the woods,

and flame and fire, after these were first known.

Later the force of iron and bronze was discovered.

And the use of bronze was known before that of iron,

because its nature is more manageable and its abundance greater.

With bronze they worked the soil of the earth, and with bronze

they stirred up the waves of war and sowed vast wounds,

and took away flocks and fields; for all things unarmed and naked

easily yielded to those armed with it.

Thereupon the iron sword advanced little by little,

and the form of the bronze sickle was turned into reproach;

and with iron they began to cleave the soil of the earth,

and the doubtful contests of war were made equal.

And earlier was it to mount upon the armed back of a horse

and govern him with reins and display strength with the right hand,

than to try the perils of war in a two-horse chariot.

And earlier was the two-horse chariot than to yoke together two pairs,

and than to mount armed in scythe-bearing chariots.

Thereupon the Carthaginians taught Lucan oxen, with towered bodies,

dark, snake-handed, to endure the wounds of war

and to throw into confusion the great battalions of Mars.

Thus grim discord produced one thing from another,

something dreadful in arms for the races of men,

and day by day added increase to the terrors of war.

They also tried bulls in the business of war,

and experimented with sending savage boars against the enemy.

And some sent powerful lions before them,

with armed trainers and savage masters,

who might be able to govern them and hold them in bonds—

in vain, since, heated by indiscriminate slaughter,

the savage beasts threw the ranks into confusion without distinction,

shaking everywhere the dreadful crests of their heads;

nor could the horsemen soothe the breasts of their horses, terrified by the roaring,

and turn them with the reins against the enemy.

The enraged lionesses hurled their bodies in leaps

on every side and opened their mouths against those coming toward them,

and seized from behind those who did not expect them,

and, having thrown them down, gave them to the ground, conquered by wounds,

fastened upon them with strong bites and hooked claws.

And bulls tossed their own men and pierced them with their feet,

and tore open the flanks and bellies of horses from beneath

with their horns, and rushed upon the ground with threatening rage.

And boars savagely struck down allies with their strong teeth,

steeping in their own blood the weapons they had broken,

and spread mingled ruin among horsemen and foot-soldiers.

For the beasts, urged aside by the crosswise stroke of teeth,

would flee, or, rearing up, would strike at the winds with their feet—

in vain, since you would see them hamstrung

fall and cover the earth with a heavy crash.

If they thought some sufficiently tamed at home before,

they saw them grow wild in the business being done,

amid wounds, shouting, flight, terror, and tumult,

nor could they bring back any part of them;

for every varied kind of wild beast scattered in flight,

as now Lucan oxen, badly butchered by iron, often scatter,

after they have inflicted many savage deeds upon their own men.

But they wished to do this not so much in hope of victory

as to give the enemy cause to groan, while they themselves perished—

they who distrusted their numbers and lacked weapons—

if indeed it was so that they did this.

But I am scarcely persuaded that beforehand

they were unable in mind to foresee and see

what a common and foul evil would come to be.

And you could more plausibly maintain that this occurred in the whole

of the various worlds created in various ways,

than in any one fixed and single world of earth.

A sewn garment existed before a woven covering.

The woven covering is after iron, because the loom is prepared by iron,

nor can such light things otherwise be produced:

heddles and spindles, beams and sounding shuttles.

And nature compelled men to make wool before women;

for the whole male sex is far superior in skill

and much more ingenious—until stern farmers changed this by fault,

so that they wished to concede it to women's hands

and themselves equally to endure hard labor

and harden their limbs and hands in harsh work.

But the first model of sowing and grafting

was nature herself, the creatress of things;

for berries and fallen acorns beneath the trees

in their season gave forth swarms of young shoots.

Hence too came the desire to entrust grafts to branches

and to bury new slips in the earth through the fields.

Then they tried one cultivation after another of the pleasant little field,

and saw that wild fruits grew tame through yielding to the earth

and cultivating it gently.

And day by day they compelled the woods to retreat farther up the mountain

and below to yield their place to cultivation,

so that they might have meadows, pools, streams, grainfields, and joyful vineyards

on hills and plains, and so that a bluish band of olive trees,

distinguishing the space between, might run spread out

across mounds and valleys and plains—

as now you see all things distinguished by varied beauty,

which adorn them, interspersed with sweet fruits,

and hold them clothed round about with flourishing trees.

But to imitate with the mouth the clear voices of birds

was much earlier than men could celebrate smooth songs in singing

and delight the ears.

And the hollow whistles of the west wind through reeds first

taught countryfolk to blow into hollow hemlock pipes.

Then little by little they learned sweet plaints,

which the pipe, struck by the fingers of players, pours forth,

discovered through pathless groves and woods and glades,

through the deserted places of shepherds and their divine leisure.

These things soothed and delighted their minds

when they had their fill of food; for then all things are pleasing.

Thus often, stretched out together on soft grass

beside a stream of water, beneath the branches of a tall tree,

they disposed their bodies pleasantly, without great wealth,

especially when the weather smiled and the seasons of the year

painted the green grasses with flowers.

Then jests, then talk, then sweet laughter

had become customary; for then the rustic Muse was vigorous.

Then joyous wantonness moved them to crown head and shoulders

with intertwined garlands of flowers and leaves,

and to proceed moving their limbs out of measure

awkwardly and beat mother earth with hard foot;

whence arose laughter and sweet peals of laughter,

because all these things, then new and strange, flourished more greatly.

And for those awake there were henceforth consolations: to draw out sleep

with manifold sounds and bend songs,

and run over the reeds above with curved lip;

whence even now the wakeful preserve these practices received from them.

And they learned to keep measure, yet in the meantime they reap

not a whit greater fruit of sweetness

than the woodland race of earth-born men reaped.

For what is present and at hand, unless we have known something sweeter before,

pleases above all and seems to prevail;

and the later thing discovered, generally better,

destroys and changes our feeling toward every former thing.

Thus hatred of acorns began; thus were abandoned those beds

spread with grass and heaped with leaves.

Likewise the garment of animal skin fell into contempt;

and I think it was then discovered with such envy

that he who first wore it perished by treachery,

and yet that, torn apart among them with much blood,

it perished and could not be turned to use.

Then skins, now gold and purple,

torment the life of men with cares and weary it with war;

in which matter, I think, the greater fault rests with us.

For cold tortured the earth-born naked without skins;

but nothing harms us in lacking a garment

of purple, fitted with gold and great emblems,

provided there is nevertheless a common one able to protect us.

Therefore the race of men labors in vain and fruitlessly

always, and consumes its life in empty cares,

evidently because it has not known what is the limit

of possessing, or altogether how far true pleasure increases;

and this little by little drove life onward into the deep

and stirred up from its foundations the great billows of war.

But the watchmen of the world, the sun and moon,

surveying round about the great revolving temple with their own light,

thoroughly taught men that the seasons of the years turn

and that events are conducted by fixed method and fixed order.

Now, enclosed by strong towers, they were passing their life,

and the earth was cultivated, divided and apportioned;

then the sea was flourishing with sail-bearing ships upon the deep,

and they already had auxiliaries and allies by treaty compact,

when poets began to hand down deeds accomplished in song;

nor were letters discovered much earlier.

Therefore our age cannot look back to see what was done before,

except insofar as reason points out traces.

Ships and the cultivation of fields, walls, laws,

arms, roads, garments, and all else of this kind,

rewards, luxuries too, and every delight of life,

songs, paintings, and cunningly wrought polished statues—

use and the experience together of the vigorous mind,

advancing step by step, taught these things little by little.

Thus time gradually brings each thing whatsoever out into the open,

and reason raises it up to the borders of light;

for they saw one thing grow clear from another in the mind,

until they reached the highest summit by the arts.

## Liber Sextus

  

Primae frugiparos fetus mortalibus aegris

 

dididerunt quondam praeclaro nomine Athenae

 

et recreaverunt vitam legesque rogarunt

 

et primae dederunt solacia dulcia vitae,

 

cum genuere virum tali cum corde repertum,

 

omnia veridico qui quondam ex ore profudit;

 

cuius et extincti propter divina reperta

 

divolgata vetus iam ad caelum gloria fertur.

 

nam cum vidit hic ad victum quae flagitat usus

 

omnia iam ferme mortalibus esse parata

 

et, pro quam possent, vitam consistere tutam,

 

divitiis homines et honore et laude potentis

 

affluere atque bona gnatorum excellere fama,

 

nec minus esse domi cuiquam tamen anxia cordi,

 

atque animi ingratis vitam vexare sine ulla

 

pausa atque infestis cogi saevire querellis,

 

intellegit ibi vitium vas efficere ipsum

 

omniaque illius vitio corrumpier intus,

 

quae conlata foris et commoda cumque venirent;

 

partim quod fluxum pertusumque esse videbat,

 

ut nulla posset ratione explerier umquam,

 

partim quod taetro quasi conspurcare sapore

 

omnia cernebat, quae cumque receperat, intus.

 

veridicis igitur purgavit pectora dictis

 

et finem statuit cuppedinis atque timoris

 

exposuitque bonum summum, quo tendimus omnes,

 

quid foret, atque viam monstravit, tramite parvo

 

qua possemus ad id recto contendere cursu,

 

quidve mali foret in rebus mortalibus passim,

 

quod fieret naturali varieque volaret

 

seu casu seu vi, quod sic natura parasset,

 

et quibus e portis occurri cuique deceret,

 

et genus humanum frustra plerumque probavit

 

volvere curarum tristis in pectore fluctus.

 

nam vel uti pueri trepidant atque omnia caecis

 

in tenebris metuunt, sic nos in luce timemus

 

inter dum, nihilo quae sunt metuenda magis quam

 

quae pueri in tenebris pavitant finguntque futura.

 

hunc igitur terrorem animi tenebrasque necessest

 

non radii solis nec lucida tela diei

 

discutiant, sed naturae species ratioque.

 

quo magis inceptum pergam pertexere dictis.

  

Et quoniam docui mundi mortalia templa

 

esse  nativo consistere corpore caelum,

 

et quae cumque in eo fiunt fierique necessest

 

pleraque dissolui, qui restant percipe porro,

 

quandoquidem semel insignem conscendere currum

 

[Gap in source]

 

tu mihi supremae praescripta ad candida callis

 

currenti spatium praemonstra, callida musa

 

Calliope, requies hominum divomque voluptas,

 

te duce ut insigni capiam cum laude coronam.

 

[Gap in source]

 

 ventorum existant, placentur  omnia rursum

 

[Gap in source]

 

quae fuerint, sint placato conversa furore.

 

cetera quae fieri in terris caeloque tuentur

 

mortales, pavidis cum pendent mentibus saepe

 

et faciunt animos humilis formidine divom

 

depressosque premunt ad terram propterea quod

 

ignorantia causarum conferre deorum

 

cogit ad imperium res et concedere regnum.

 



 



 

nam bene qui didicere deos securum agere aevom,

 

si tamen interea mirantur qua ratione

 

quaeque geri possint, praesertim rebus in illis

 

quae supera caput aetheriis cernuntur in oris,

 

rursus in antiquas referuntur religionis

 

et dominos acris adsciscunt, omnia posse

 

quos miseri credunt, ignari quid queat esse,

 

quid nequeat, finita potestas denique cuique

 

qua nam sit ratione atque alte terminus haerens;

 

quo magis errantes caeca ratione feruntur.

 

quae nisi respuis ex animo longeque remittis

 

dis indigna putare alienaque pacis eorum,

 

delibata deum per te tibi numina sancta

 

saepe oberunt; non quo violari summa deum vis

 

possit, ut ex ira poenas petere inbibat acris,

 

sed quia tute tibi placida cum pace quietos

 

constitues magnos irarum volvere fluctus,

 

nec delubra deum placido cum pectore adibis,

 

nec de corpore quae sancto simulacra feruntur

 

in mentes hominum divinae nuntia formae,

 

suscipere haec animi tranquilla pace valebis.

 

inde videre licet qualis iam vita sequatur.

 

quam quidem ut a nobis ratio verissima longe

 

reiciat, quamquam sunt a me multa profecta,

 

multa tamen restant et sunt ornanda politis

 

versibus; est ratio caeliQUE ignisque tenenda,

 

sunt tempestates et fulmina clara canenda,

 

quid faciant et qua de causa cumque ferantur;

 

ne trepides caeli divisis partibus amens,

 

unde volans ignis pervenerit aut in utram se

 

verterit hinc partim, quo pacto per loca saepta

 

insinuarit, et hinc dominatus ut extulerit se.

 



 



  

Principio tonitru quatiuntur caerula caeli

 

propterea quia concurrunt sublime volantes

 

aetheriae nubes contra pugnantibus ventis.

 

nec fit enim sonitus caeli de parte serena,

 

verum ubi cumque magis denso sunt agmine nubes,

 

tam magis hinc magno fremitus fit murmure saepe.

 

praeterea neque tam condenso corpore nubes

 

esse queunt quam sunt lapides ac ligna, neque autem

 

tam tenues quam sunt nebulae fumique volantes;

 

nam cadere aut bruto deberent pondere pressae

 

 ut lapides, aut ut fumus constare nequirent

 

nec cohibere nives gelidas et grandinis imbris.

 

Dant etiam sonitum patuli super aequora mundi,

 

carbasus ut quondam magnis intenta theatris

 

dat crepitum malos inter iactata trabesque,

 

inter dum perscissa furit petulantibus auris

 

et fragilis  chartarum commeditatur;

 

id quoque enim genus in tonitru cognoscere possis,

 

aut ubi suspensam vestem chartasque volantis

 

verberibus venti versant planguntque per auras.

 

fit quoque enim inter dum  non tam concurrere nubes

 

frontibus adversis possint quam de latere ire

 

diverso motu radentes corpora tractim,

 

aridus unde auris terget sonus ille diuque

 

ducitur, exierunt donec regionibus artis.

  

Hoc etiam pacto tonitru concussa videntur

 

omnia saepe gravi tremere et divolsa repente

 

maxima dissiluisse capacis moenia mundi,

 

cum subito validi venti conlecta procella

 

nubibus intorsit sese conclusaque ibidem

 

turbine versanti magis ac magis undique nubem

 

cogit uti fiat spisso cava corpore circum,

 

post ubi conminuit vis eius et impetus acer,

 

tum perterricrepo sonitu dat scissa fragorem.

 

nec mirum, cum plena animae vensicula parva

 

saepe haud dat parvum sonitum displosa repente.

 

Est etiam ratio, cum venti nubila perflant,

 

ut sonitus faciant; etenim ramosa videmus

 

nubila saepe modis multis atque aspera ferri;

 

scilicet ut, crebram silvam cum flamina cauri

 

perflant, dant sonitum frondes ramique fragorem.

 

Fit quoque ut inter dum validi vis incita venti

 

perscindat nubem perfringens impete recto;

 

nam quid possit ibi flatus manifesta docet res,

 

hic, ubi lenior est, in terra cum tamen alta

 

arbusta evolvens radicibus haurit ab imis.

 

sunt etiam fluctus per nubila, qui quasi murmur

 

dant in frangendo graviter; quod item fit in altis

 

fluminibus magnoque mari, cum frangitur aestus.

 

Fit quoque, ubi e nubi in nubem vis incidit ardens

 

fulminis; haec multo si forte umore recepit

 

ignem, continuo magno clamore trucidat;

 

ut calidis candens ferrum e fornacibus olim

 

stridit, ubi in gelidum propter demersimus imbrem.

 

Aridior porro si nubes accipit ignem,

 

uritur ingenti sonitu succensa repente,

 

lauricomos ut si per montis flamma vagetur

 

turbine ventorum comburens impete magno;

 

nec res ulla magis quam Phoebi Delphica laurus

 

terribili sonitu flamma crepitante crematur.

 

Denique saepe geli multus fragor atque ruina

 

grandinis in magnis sonitum dat nubibus alte;

 

ventus enim cum confercit, franguntur in artum

 

concreti montes nimborum et grandine mixti.

  

Fulgit item, nubes ignis cum semina multa

 

 excussere suo concursu, ceu lapidem si

 

percutiat lapis aut ferrum; nam tum quoque lumen

 

exilit et claras scintillas dissipat ignis.

 

sed tonitrum fit uti post auribus accipiamus,

 

fulgere quam cernant oculi, quia semper ad auris

 

tardius adveniunt quam visum quae moveant res.

 

id licet hinc etiam cognoscere: caedere si quem

 

ancipiti videas ferro procul arboris auctum,

 

ante fit ut cernas ictum quam plaga per auris

 

det sonitum; sic fulgorem quoque cernimus ante

 

quam tonitrum accipimus, pariter qui mittitur igni

 

e simili causa, concursu natus eodem.

  

Hoc etiam pacto volucri loca lumine tingunt

 

nubes et tremulo tempestas impete fulgit.

 

ventus ubi invasit nubem et versatus ibidem

 

fecit ut ante cavam docui spissescere nubem,

 

mobilitate sua fervescit; ut omnia motu

 

percalefacta vides ardescere, plumbea vero

 

glans etiam longo cursu volvenda liquescit.

 

ergo fervidus hic nubem cum perscidit atram,

 

dissipat ardoris quasi per vim expressa repente

 

semina, quae faciunt nictantia fulgura flammae;

 

inde sonus sequitur, qui tardius adlicit auris

 

quam quae perveniunt oculorum ad lumina nostra.

 

scilicet hoc densis fit nubibus et simul alte

 

extructis aliis alias super impete miro.

 

ne tibi sit frudi quod nos inferne videmus

 

quam sint lata magis quam sursum extructa quid extent.

 

contemplator enim, cum montibus adsimulata

 

nubila portabunt venti transversa per auras,

 

aut ubi per magnos montis cumulata videbis

 

insuper esse aliis alia atque urguere superna

 

in statione locata sepultis undique ventis;

 

tum poteris magnas moles cognoscere eorum

 

speluncasque vel ut saxis pendentibus structas

 

cernere, quas venti cum tempestate coorta

 

conplerunt, magno indignantur murmure clausi

 

nubibus in caveisque ferarum more minantur,

 

nunc hinc nunc illinc fremitus per nubila mittunt,

 

quaerentesque viam circum versantur et ignis

 

semina convolvunt  nubibus atque ita cogunt

 

multa rotantque cavis flammam fornacibus intus,

 

donec divolsa fulserunt nube corusci.

  

Hac etiam fit uti de causa mobilis ille

 

devolet in terram liquidi color aureus ignis,

 

semina quod nubes ipsas permulta necessust

 

ignis habere; etenim cum sunt umore sine ullo,

 

flammeus  plerumque colos et splendidus ollis.

 

quippe etenim solis de lumine multa necessest

 

concipere, ut merito rubeant ignesque profundant.

 

hasce igitur cum ventus agens contrusit in unum

 

compressitque locum cogens, expressa profundunt

 

semina, quae faciunt flammae fulgere colores.

 

Fulgit item, cum rarescunt quoque nubila caeli;

 

nam cum ventus eas leviter diducit euntis

 

 dissoluitque, cadant ingratius illa necessest

 

semina quae faciunt fulgorem. tum sine taetro

 

terrore atque sonis fulgit nulloque tumultu.

  

Quod superest,  natura praedita constent

 

fulmina, declarant ictus et inusta vaporis

 

signa notaeque gravis halantis sulpuris auras;

 

ignis enim sunt haec non venti signa neque imbris.

 

praeterea saepe accendunt quoque tecta domorum

 

et celeri flamma dominantur in aedibus ipsis.

 

hunc tibi subtilem cum primis ignibus ignem

 

constituit natura minutis mobilibusque

 

corporibus, cui nil omnino obsistere possit.

 

transit enim validum fulmen per saepta domorum

 

clamor ut ac voces, transit per saxa, per aera

 

et liquidum puncto facit aes in tempore et aurum.

 

curat item vasis integris vina repente

 

diffugiant, quia ni mirum facile omnia circum

 

conlaxat rareque facit lateramina vasis

 

adveniens calor eius et insinuatus in ipsum

 

mobiliter soluens differt primordia vini.

 

quod solis vapor aetatem non posse videtur

 

efficere usque adeo pollens fervore corusco.

 

tanto mobilior vis et dominantior haec est.

 

Nunc ea quo pacto gignantur et impete tanto

 

fiant ut possint ictu discludere turris,

 

disturbare domos, avellere tigna trabesque

 

et monimenta virum commoliri atque ciere,

 

exanimare homines, pecudes prosternere passim,

 

cetera de genere hoc qua vi facere omnia possint,

 

expediam neque  in promissis plura morabor.

  

Fulmina gignier e crassis alteque putandumst

 

nubibus extructis; nam caelo nulla sereno

 

nec leviter densis mittuntur nubibus umquam.

 

nam dubio procul hoc fieri manifesta docet res;

 

quod tunc per totum concrescunt aeëra nubes,

 

undique uti tenebras omnis Acherunta reamur

 

liquisse et magnas caeli complesse cavernas,

 

æusque adeo tetra nimborum nocte coorta

 

inpendent atrae formidinis ora superne,æ

 

cum commoliri tempestas fulmina coeptat.

 

praeterea persaepe niger quoque per mare nimbus,

 

ut picis e caelo demissum flumen, in undas

 

sic cadit effertus tenebris procul et trahit atram

 

fulminibus gravidam tempestatem atque procellis,

 

ignibus ac ventis cum primis ipse repletus,

 

in terra quoque ut horrescant ac tecta requirant.

 

sic igitur supera nostrum caput esse putandumst

 

tempestatem altam; neque enim caligine tanta

 

obruerent terras, nisi inaedificata superne

 

multa forent multis exempto nubila sole;

 

nec tanto possent venientes opprimere imbri,

 

flumina abundare ut facerent camposque natare,

 

si non extructis foret alte nubibus aether.

 

hic igitur ventis atque ignibus omnia plena

 

sunt; ideo passim fremitus et fulgura fiunt.

 

 quippe etenim supra docui permulta vaporis

 

semina habere cavas nubes et multa necessest

 

concipere ex solis radiis ardoreque eorum.

 

hoc ubi ventus eas idem qui cogit in unum

 

forte locum quemvis, expressit multa vaporis

 

semina seque simul cum eo commiscuit igni,

 

insinuatus ibi vortex versatur in arto

 

et calidis acuit fulmen fornacibus intus;

 

nam duplici ratione accenditur: ipse sua cum

 

mobilitate calescit et e contagibus ignis.

 

inde ubi percaluit venti vis  gravis ignis

 

impetus incessit, maturum tum quasi fulmen

 

perscindit subito nubem ferturque coruscis

 

omnia luminibus lustrans loca percitus ardor.

 

quem gravis insequitur sonitus, displosa repente

 

opprimere ut caeli videantur templa superne.

 

inde tremor terras graviter pertemptat et altum

 

murmura percurrunt caelum; nam tota fere tum

 

tempestas concussa tremit fremitusque moventur.

 

quo de concussu sequitur gravis imber et uber,

 

omnis uti videatur in imbrem vertier aether

 

atque ita praecipitans ad diluviem revocare;

 

tantus discidio nubis ventique procella

 

mittitur, ardenti sonitus cum provolat ictu.

  

Est etiam cum vis extrinsecus incita venti

 

incidit in validam maturo culmine nubem;

 

quam cum perscidit, extemplo cadit igneus ille

 

vertex, quem patrio vocitamus nomine fulmen.

 

hoc fit idem in partis alias, quo cumque tulit vis.

 

Fit quoque ut inter dum venti vis missa sine igni

 

igniscat tamen in spatio longoque meatu,

 

dum venit amittens in cursu corpora quaedam

 

grandia, quae nequeunt pariter penetrare per auras,

 

atque alia ex ipso conradens aeëre portat

 

parvola, quae faciunt ignem commixta volando;

 

non alia longe ratione ac plumbea saepe

 

fervida fit glans in cursu, cum multa rigoris

 

corpora dimittens ignem concepit in auris.

 

Fit quoque ut ipsius plagae vis excitet ignem,

 

frigida cum venti pepulit vis missa sine igni,

 

ni mirum quia, cum vehementi perculit ictu,

 

confluere ex ipso possunt elementa vaporis

 

et simul ex illa quae tum res excipit ictum;

 

ut, lapidem ferro cum caedimus, evolat ignis,

 

nec, quod frigida vis ferrist, hoc setius illi

 

semina concurrunt calidi fulgoris ad ictum.

 

sic igitur quoque res accendi fulmine debet,

 

opportuna fuit si forte et idonea flammis.

 

nec temere omnino plane vis frigida venti

 

esse potest, ea quae tanta vi missa supernest,

 

quin, prius in cursu si non accenditur igni,

 

at tepefacta tamen veniat commixta calore.

  

Mobilitas autem fit fulminis et gravis ictus

 

et celeri ferme percurrunt fulmina lapsu,

 

nubibus ipsa quod omnino prius incita se vis

 

 colligit et magnum conamen sumit eundi,

 

inde ubi non potuit nubes capere inpetis auctum,

 

exprimitur vis atque ideo volat impete miro,

 

ut validis quae de tormentis missa feruntur.

 

Adde quod e parvis et levibus est elementis,

 

nec facilest tali naturae obsistere quicquam;

 

inter enim fugit ac penetrat per rara viarum,

 

non igitur multis offensibus in remorando

 

haesitat, hanc ob rem celeri volat impete labens.

 

Deinde, quod omnino natura pondera deorsum

 

omnia nituntur, cum plagast addita vero,

 

mobilitas duplicatur et impetus ille gravescit,

 

ut vehementius et citius quae cumque morantur

 

obvia discutiat plagis itinerque sequatur.

 

Denique quod longo venit impete, sumere debet

 

mobilitatem etiam atque etiam, quae crescit eundo

 

et validas auget viris et roborat ictum;

 

nam facit ut quae sint illius semina cumque

 

e regione locum quasi in unum cuncta ferantur,

 

omnia coniciens in eum volventia cursum.

 

Forsitan ex ipso veniens trahat aeëre quaedam

 

corpora, quae plagis incendunt mobilitatem.

 

incolumisque venit per res atque integra transit

 

multa, foraminibus liquidus quia transviat ignis.

 

multaque perfringit, cum corpora fulminis ipsa

 

corporibus rerum inciderunt, qua texta tenentur.

 

dissoluit porro facile aes aurumque repente

 

conferve facit, e parvis quia facta minute

 

corporibus vis est et levibus ex elementis,

 

quae facile insinuantur et insinuata repente

 

dissoluont nodos omnis et vincla relaxant.

  

Autumnoque magis stellis fulgentibus alta

 

concutitur caeli domus undique totaque tellus,

 

et cum tempora se veris florentia pandunt.

 

frigore enim desunt ignes ventique calore

 

deficiunt neque sunt tam denso corpore nubes.

 

interutrasque igitur cum caeli tempora constant,

 

tum variae causae concurrunt fulminis omnes.

 

nam fretus ipse anni permiscet frigus  aestum.

 

quorum utrumque opus est fabricanda ad fulmina nubi,

 

ut discordia  rerum magnoque tumultu

 

ignibus et ventis furibundus fluctuet aeër.

 

prima caloris enim pars est postrema rigoris;

 

tempus id est vernum; quare pugnare necessest

 

dissimilis  inter se turbareque mixtas.

 

et calor extremus primo cum frigore mixtus

 

volvitur, autumni quod fertur nomine tempus,

 

hic quoque confligunt hiemes aestatibus acres.

 

propterea  sunt haec anni nominitanda,

 

nec mirumst, in eo si tempore plurima fiunt

 

fulmina tempestasque cietur turbida caelo,

 

 ancipiti quoniam bello turbatur utrimque,

 

hinc flammis, illinc ventis umoreque mixto.

  

Hoc est igniferi naturam fulminis ipsam

 

perspicere et qua vi faciat rem quamque videre,

 

non Tyrrhena retro volventem carmina frustra

 

indicia occultae divum perquirere mentis,

 

unde volans ignis pervenerit aut in utram se

 

verterit hinc partim, quo pacto per loca saepta

 

insinuarit, et hinc dominatus ut extulerit se,

 

quidve nocere queat de caelo fulminis ictus.

 

quod si Iuppiter atque alii fulgentia divi

 

terrifico quatiunt sonitu caelestia templa

 

et iaciunt ignem quo cuiquest cumque voluntas,

 

cur quibus incautum scelus aversabile cumquest

 

non faciunt icti flammas ut fulguris halent

 

pectore perfixo, documen mortalibus acre,

 

et potius nulla sibi turpi conscius in re

 

volvitur in flammis innoxius inque peditur

 

turbine caelesti subito correptus et igni?

 

cur etiam loca sola petunt frustraque laborant?

 

an tum bracchia consuescunt firmantque lacertos?

 

in terraque patris cur telum perpetiuntur

 

optundi? cur ipse sinit neque parcit in hostis?

 

denique cur numquam caelo iacit undique puro

 

Iuppiter in terras fulmen sonitusque profundit?

 

an simul ac nubes successere, ipse in eas tum

 

descendit, prope ut hinc teli determinet ictus?

 

in mare qua porro mittit ratione? quid undas

 

arguit et liquidam molem camposque natantis?

 

praeterea si vult caveamus fulminis ictum,

 

cur dubitat facere ut possimus cernere missum?

 

si nec opinantis autem volt opprimere igni,

 

cur tonat ex illa parte, ut vitare queamus,

 

cur tenebras ante et fremitus et murmura concit?

 

et simul in multas partis qui credere possis

 

mittere? an hoc ausis numquam contendere factum,

 

ut fierent ictus uno sub tempore plures?

 

at saepest numero factum fierique necessest,

 

ut pluere in multis regionibus et cadere imbris,

 

fulmina sic uno fieri sub tempore multa.

 

postremo cur sancta deum delubra suasque

 

discutit infesto praeclaras fulmine sedes

 

et bene facta deum frangit simulacra suisque

 

demit imaginibus violento volnere honorem?

 

altaque cur plerumque petit loca plurimaque eius

 

montibus in summis vestigia cernimus ignis?

  

Quod super est, facilest ex his cognoscere rebus,

 

presteras Graii quos ab re nominitarunt,

 

in mare qua missi veniant ratione superne.

 

nam fit ut inter dum tam quam demissa columna

 

in mare de caelo descendat, quam freta circum

 

fervescunt graviter spirantibus incita flabris,

 

et quae cumque in eo tum sint deprensa tumultu

 

navigia in summum veniant vexata periclum.

 

hoc fit ubi inter dum non quit vis incita venti

 

 rumpere quam coepit nubem, sed deprimit, ut sit

 

in mare de caelo tam quam demissa columna,

 

paulatim, quasi quid pugno bracchique superne

 

coniectu trudatur et extendatur in undas;

 

quam cum discidit, hinc prorumpitur in mare venti

 

vis et fervorem mirum concinnat in undis;

 

versabundus enim turbo descendit et illam

 

deducit pariter lento cum corpore nubem;

 

quam simul ac gravidam detrusit ad aequora ponti,

 

ille in aquam subito totum se inmittit et omne

 

excitat ingenti sonitu mare fervere cogens.

  

Fit quoque ut involvat venti se nubibus ipse

 

vertex conradens ex aeëre semina nubis

 

et quasi demissum caelo prestera imitetur;

 

hic ubi se in terras demisit dissoluitque,

 

turbinis immanem vim provomit atque procellae.

 

sed quia fit raro omnino montisque necessest

 

officere in terris, apparet crebrius idem

 

prospectu maris in magno caeloque patenti.

 

Nubila concrescunt, ubi corpora multa volando

 

hoc super in caeli spatio coiere repente

 

asperiora, modis quae possint indupedita

 

exiguis tamen inter se compressa teneri.

 

haec faciunt primum parvas consistere nubes;

 

inde ea comprendunt inter se conque gregantur

 

et coniungendo crescunt ventisque feruntur

 

usque adeo donec tempestas saeva coortast.

 

Fit quoque uti montis vicina cacumina caelo

 

quam sint quoque magis, tanto magis edita fument

 

adsidue fulvae nubis caligine crassa

 

propterea quia, cum consistunt nubila primum,

 

ante videre oculi quam possint tenvia, venti

 

portantes cogunt ad summa cacumina montis;

 

hic demum fit uti turba maiore coorta

 

et condensa queant apparere et simul ipso

 

vertice de montis videantur surgere in aethram.

 

nam loca declarat sursum ventosa patere

 

res ipsa et sensus, montis cum ascendimus altos.

  

Praeterea permulta mari quoque tollere toto

 

corpora naturam declarant litore vestis

 

suspensae, cum concipiunt umoris adhaesum.

 

quo magis ad nubis augendas multa videntur

 

posse quoque e salso consurgere momine ponti;

 

nam ratio consanguineast umoribus omnis.

 

Praeterea fluviis ex omnibus et simul ipsa

 

surgere de terra nebulas aestumque videmus,

 

quae vel ut halitus hinc ita sursum expressa feruntur

 

suffunduntque sua caelum caligine et altas

 

sufficiunt nubis paulatim conveniundo;

 

urget enim quoque signiferi super aetheris aestus

 

et quasi densendo subtexit caerula nimbis.

 

Fit quoque ut hunc veniant in caelum extrinsecus illa

 

corpora quae faciunt nubis nimbosque volantis;

 

innumerabilem enim numerum summamque profundi

 

esse infinitam docui, quantaque volarent

 

 corpora mobilitate ostendi quamque repente

 

immemorabile  spatium transire solerent.

 

haut igitur mirumst, si parvo tempore saepe

 

tam magnis ventis tempestas atque tenebrae

 

coperiant maria ac terras inpensa superne,

 

undique quandoquidem per caulas aetheris omnis

 

et quasi per magni circum spiracula mundi

 

exitus introitusque elementis redditus extat.

  

Nunc age, quo pacto pluvius concrescat in altis

 

nubibus umor et in terras demissus ut imber

 

decidat, expediam. primum iam semina aquai

 

multa simul vincam consurgere nubibus ipsis

 

omnibus ex rebus pariterque ita crescere utrumque

 

et nubis et aquam, quae cumque in nubibus extat,

 

ut pariter nobis corpus cum sanguine crescit,

 

sudor item atque umor qui cumque est denique membris.

 

concipiunt etiam multum quoque saepe marinum

 

umorem, vel uti pendentia vellera lanae,

 

cum supera magnum mare venti nubila portant.

 

consimili ratione ex omnibus amnibus umor

 

tollitur in nubis. quo cum bene semina aquarum

 

multa modis multis convenere undique adaucta,

 

confertae nubes umorem mittere certant

 

dupliciter; nam vis venti contrudit et ipsa

 

copia nimborum turba maiore coacta

 

urget et e supero premit ac facit effluere imbris.

 

praeterea cum rarescunt quoque nubila ventis

 

aut dissolvuntur solis super icta calore,

 

mittunt umorem pluvium stillantque, quasi igni

 

cera super calido tabescens multa liquescat.

 

sed vehemens imber fit, ubi vehementer utraque

 

nubila vi cumulata premuntur et impete venti.

 

at retinere diu pluviae longumque morari

 

consuerunt, ubi multa cientur semina aquarum

 

atque aliis aliae nubes nimbique rigantes

 

insuper atque omni vulgo de parte feruntur,

 

terraque cum fumans umorem tota redhalat.

 

hic ubi sol radiis tempestatem inter opacam

 

adversa fulsit nimborum aspargine contra,

 

tum color in nigris existit nubibus arqui.

 

Cetera quae sursum crescunt sursumque creantur,

 

et quae concrescunt in nubibus, omnia, prorsum

 

omnia, nix venti grando gelidaeque pruinae

 

et vis magna geli, magnum duramen aquarum,

 

et mora quae fluvios passim refrenat aventis,

 

perfacilest tamen haec reperire animoque videre,

 

omnia quo pacto fiant quareve creentur,

 

cum bene cognoris elementis reddita quae sint.

  

Nunc age, quae ratio terrai motibus extet

 

percipe. et in primis terram fac ut esse rearis

 

supter item ut supera ventosis undique plenam

 

speluncis multosque lacus multasque lucunas

 

in gremio gerere et rupes deruptaque saxa;

 

multaque sub tergo terrai flumina tecta

 

volvere vi fluctus summersos ca putandumst;

 

 undique enim similem esse sui res postulat ipsa.

 

his igitur rebus subiunctis suppositisque

 

terra superne tremit magnis concussa ruinis,

 

subter ubi ingentis speluncas subruit aetas;

 

quippe cadunt toti montes magnoque repente

 

concussu late disserpunt inde tremores.
