in medio locus, extemplo primordia ferri

 

in vacuum prolapsa cadunt coniuncta, fit utque

 

anulus ipse sequatur eatque ita corpore toto.

 

nec res ulla magis primoribus ex elementis

 

indupedita suis arte conexa cohaeret

 

quam validi ferri natura et frigidus horror.

 

quo minus est mirum, quod dicitur esse alienum,

 

corpora si nequeunt e ferro plura coorta

 

in vacuum ferri, quin anulus ipse sequatur;

 

quod facit et sequitur, donec pervenit ad ipsum

 

iam lapidem caecisque in eo compagibus haesit.

 

hoc fit idem cunctas in partis; unde vace fit

 

cumque locus, sive e transverso sive superne,

 

corpora continuo in vacuum vicina feruntur;

 

quippe agitantur enim plagis aliunde nec ipsa

 

sponte sua sursum possunt consurgere in auras.

 

huc accedit item, quare queat id magis esse,

 

haec quoque res adiumento motuque iuvatur,

 

quod, simul a fronte est anelli rarior aeër

 

factus inanitusque locus magis ac vacuatus,

 

continuo fit uti qui post est cumque locatus

 

aeër a tergo quasi provehat atque propellat.

 

semper enim circum positus res verberat aeër;

 

sed tali fit uti propellat tempore ferrum,

 

parte quod ex una spatium vacat et capit in se.

 

hic, tibi quem memoro, per crebra foramina ferri

 

parvas ad partis subtiliter insinuatus

 

trudit et inpellit, quasi navem velaque ventus.

 

 denique res omnes debent in corpore habere

 

aeëra, quandoquidem raro sunt corpore et aeër

 

omnibus est rebus circum datus adpositusque.

 

hic igitur, penitus qui in ferrost abditus aeër,

 

sollicito motu semper iactatur eoque

 

verberat anellum dubio procul et ciet intus,

 

scilicet illo eodem fertur, quo praecipitavit

 

iam semel et partem in vacuam conamina sumpsit.

  

Fit quoque ut a lapide hoc ferri natura recedat

 

inter dum, fugere atque sequi consueta vicissim.

 

exultare etiam Samothracia ferrea vidi

 

et ramenta simul ferri furere intus ahenis

 

in scaphiis, lapis hic Magnes cum subditus esset;

 

usque adeo fugere a saxo gestire videtur.

 

aere interposito discordia tanta creatur

 

propterea quia ni mirum prius aestus ubi aeris

 

praecepit ferrique vias possedit apertas,

 

posterior lapidis venit aestus et omnia plena

 

invenit in ferro neque habet qua tranet ut ante;

 

cogitur offensare igitur pulsareque fluctu

 

ferrea texta suo; quo pacto respuit ab se

 

atque per aes agitat, sine eo quod saepe resorbet.

 

Illud in his rebus mirari mitte, quod aestus

 

non valet e lapide hoc alias impellere item res.

 

pondere enim fretae partim stant, quod genus aurum;

 

at partim raro quia sunt cum corpore, ut aestus

 

pervolet intactus, nequeunt inpellier usquam,

 

lignea materies in quo genere esse videtur.

 

interutrasque igitur ferri natura locata

 

aeris ubi accepit quaedam corpuscula, tum fit,

 

inpellant ut eo Magnesia flumine saxa.

  

nec tamen haec ita sunt aliarum rerum aliena,

 

ut mihi multa parum genere ex hoc suppeditentur,

 

quae memorare queam inter se singlariter apta.

 

saxa vides primum sola colescere calce.

 

glutine materies taurino iungitur una,

 

ut vitio venae tabularum saepius hiscant

 

quam laxare queant compages taurea vincla.

 

vitigeni latices aquai fontibus audent

 

misceri, cum pix nequeat gravis et leve olivom.

 

purpureusque colos conchyli iungitur uno

 

corpore cum lanae, dirimi qui non queat usquam,

 

non si Neptuni fluctu renovare operam des,

 

non mare si totum velit eluere omnibus undis.

 

denique res auro non aurum copulat una,

 

aerique  plumbo fit uti iungatur ab albo?

 

cetera iam quam multa licet reperire! quid ergo?

 

nec tibi tam longis opus est ambagibus usquam

 

nec me tam multam hic operam consumere par est,

 

sed breviter paucis praestat comprendere multa.

 

quorum ita texturae ceciderunt mutua contra,

 

ut cava conveniant plenis haec illius illa

 

huiusque inter se, iunctura haec optima constat.

 

est etiam, quasi ut anellis hamisque plicata

 

inter se quaedam possint coplata teneri;

 

 quod magis in lapide hoc fieri ferroque videtur.

  

Nunc ratio quae sit morbis aut unde repente

 

mortiferam possit cladem conflare coorta

 

morbida vis hominum generi pecudumque catervis,

 

expediam, primum multarum semina rerum

 

esse supra docui quae sint vitalia nobis,

 

et contra quae sint morbo mortique necessest

 

multa volare; ea cum casu sunt forte coorta

 

et perturbarunt caelum, fit morbidus aeër.

 

atque ea vis omnis morborum pestilitasque

 

aut extrinsecus ut nubes nebulaeque superne

 

per caelum veniunt aut ipsa saepe coorta

 

de terra surgunt, ubi putorem umida nactast

 

intempestivis pluviisque et solibus icta.

 

nonne vides etiam caeli novitate et aquarum

 

temptari procul a patria qui cumque domoque

 

adveniunt ideo quia longe discrepitant res?

 

nam quid Brittannis caelum differre putamus,

 

et quod in Aegypto est, qua mundi claudicat axis,

 

quidve quod in Ponto est differre et Gadibus atque

 

usque ad nigra virum percocto saecla colore?

 

quae cum quattuor inter se diversa videmus

 

quattuor a ventis et caeli partibus esse,

 

tum color et facies hominum distare videntur

 

largiter et morbi generatim saecla tenere.

 

est elephas morbus qui propter flumina Nili

 

gignitur Aegypto in media neque praeterea usquam.

 

Atthide temptantur gressus oculique in Achaeis

 

finibus. inde aliis alius locus est inimicus

 

partibus ac membris; varius concinnat id aeër.

 

proinde ubi se caelum, quod nobis forte alienum,

 

commovet atque aeër inimicus serpere coepit,

 

ut nebula ac nubes paulatim repit et omne

 

qua graditur conturbat et immutare coactat,

 

fit quoque ut, in nostrum cum venit denique caelum,

 

corrumpat reddatque sui simile atque alienum.

 

haec igitur subito clades nova pestilitasque

 

aut in aquas cadit aut fruges persidit in ipsas

 

aut alios hominum pastus pecudumque cibatus,

 

aut etiam suspensa manet vis aeëre in ipso

 

et, cum spirantes mixtas hinc ducimus auras,

 

illa quoque in corpus pariter sorbere necessest.

 

consimili ratione venit bubus quoque saepe

 

pestilitas et iam pigris balantibus aegror.

 

nec refert utrum nos in loca deveniamus

 

nobis adversa et caeli mutemus amictum,

 

an caelum nobis ultro natura corumptum

 

deferat aut aliquid quo non consuevimus uti,

 

quod nos adventu possit temptare recenti.

  

Haec ratio quondam morborum et mortifer aestus

 

finibus in Cecropis funestos reddidit agros

 

vastavitque vias, exhausit civibus urbem.

 

nam penitus veniens Aegypti finibus ortus,

 

aeëra permensus multum camposque natantis,

 

incubuit tandem populo Pandionis omni.

 

 inde catervatim morbo mortique dabantur.

 

principio caput incensum fervore gerebant

 

et duplicis oculos suffusa luce rubentes.

 

sudabant etiam fauces intrinsecus atrae

 

sanguine et ulceribus vocis via saepta coibat

 

atque animi interpres manabat lingua cruore

 

debilitata malis, motu gravis, aspera tactu.

 

inde ubi per fauces pectus complerat et ipsum

 

morbida vis in cor maestum confluxerat aegris,

 

omnia tum vero vitai claustra lababant.

 

spiritus ore foras taetrum volvebat odorem,

 

rancida quo perolent proiecta cadavera ritu.

 

atque animi prorsum  vires totius, omne

 

languebat corpus leti iam limine in ipso.

 

intolerabilibusque malis erat anxius angor

 

adsidue comes et gemitu commixta querella,

 

singultusque frequens noctem per saepe diemque

 

corripere adsidue nervos et membra coactans

 

dissoluebat eos, defessos ante, fatigans.

 

nec nimio cuiquam posses ardore tueri

 

corporis in summo summam fervescere partem,

 

sed potius tepidum manibus proponere tactum

 

et simul ulceribus quasi inustis omne rubere

 

corpus, ut est per membra sacer dum diditur ignis.

 

intima pars hominum vero flagrabat ad ossa,

 

flagrabat stomacho flamma ut fornacibus intus.

 

nil adeo posses cuiquam leve tenveque membris

 

vertere in utilitatem, at ventum et frigora semper.

 

in fluvios partim gelidos ardentia morbo

 

membra dabant nudum iacientes corpus in undas.

  

multi praecipites nymphis putealibus alte

 

inciderunt ipso venientes ore patente:

 

insedabiliter sitis arida corpora mersans

 

aequabat multum parvis umoribus imbrem.

 

nec requies erat ulla mali: defessa iacebant

 

corpora. mussabat tacito medicina timore,

 

quippe patentia cum totiens ardentia morbis

 

lumina versarent oculorum expertia somno.

 

multaque praeterea mortis tum signa dabantur:

 

perturbata animi mens in maerore metuque,

 

triste supercilium, furiosus voltus et acer,

 

sollicitae porro plenaeque sonoribus aures,

 

creber spiritus aut ingens raroque coortus,

 

sudorisque madens per collum splendidus umor,

 

tenvia sputa minuta, croci contacta colore

 

salsaque per fauces rauca vix edita tussi.

 

in manibus vero nervi trahere et tremere artus

 

a pedibusque minutatim succedere frigus

 

non dubitabat. item ad supremum denique tempus

 

conpressae nares, nasi primoris acumen

 

tenve, cavati oculi, cava tempora, frigida pellis

 

duraque in ore, iacens rictu, frons tenta manebat.

 

nec nimio rigida post artus morte iacebant.

 

octavoque fere candenti lumine solis

 

aut etiam nona reddebant lampade vitam.

 

 quorum siquis, ut est, vitarat funera leti,

 

ulceribus taetris et nigra proluvie alvi

 

posterius tamen hunc tabes letumque manebat,

 

aut etiam multus capitis cum saepe dolore

 

corruptus sanguis expletis naribus ibat.

 

huc hominis totae vires corpusque fluebat.

  

profluvium porro qui taetri sanguinis acre

 

exierat, tamen in nervos huic morbus et artus

 

ibat et in partis genitalis corporis ipsas.

 

et graviter partim metuentes limina leti

 

vivebant ferro privati parte virili,

 

et manibus sine non nulli pedibusque manebant

 

in vita tamen et perdebant lumina partim.

 

usque adeo mortis metus iis incesserat acer.

 

atque etiam quosdam cepere oblivia rerum

 

cunctarum, neque se possent cognoscere ut ipsi.

 

multaque humi cum inhumata iacerent corpora supra

 

corporibus, tamen alituum genus atque ferarum

 

aut procul absiliebat, ut acrem exiret odorem,

 

aut, ubi gustarat, languebat morte propinqua.

 

nec tamen omnino temere illis solibus ulla

 

comparebat avis, nec tristia saecla ferarum

 

exibant silvis. languebant pleraque morbo

 

et moriebantur. cum primis fida canum vis

 

strata viis animam ponebat in omnibus aegre;

 

extorquebat enim vitam vis morbida membris.

 

incomitata rapi certabant funera vasta

 

nec ratio remedii communis certa dabatur;

 

nam quod ali dederat vitalis aeëris auras

 

volvere in ore licere et caeli templa tueri,

 

hoc aliis erat exitio letumque parabat.

  

Illud in his rebus miserandum magnopere unum

 

aerumnabile erat, quod ubi se quisque videbat

 

implicitum morbo, morti damnatus ut esset,

 

deficiens animo maesto cum corde iacebat,

 

funera respectans animam amittebat ibidem.

 

quippe etenim nullo cessabant tempore apisci

 

ex aliis alios avidi contagia morbi,

 

lanigeras tam quam pecudes et bucera saecla,

 

idque vel in primis cumulabat funere funus

 

nam qui cumque suos fugitabant visere ad aegros,

 

vitai nimium cupidos mortisque timentis

 

poenibat paulo post turpi morte malaque,

 

desertos, opis expertis, incuria mactans.

 

qui fuerant autem praesto, contagibus ibant

 

atque labore, pudor quem tum cogebat obire

 

blandaque lassorum vox mixta voce querellae.

 

optimus hoc leti genus ergo quisque subibat.

  

Praeterea iam pastor et armentarius omnis

 

et robustus item curvi moderator aratri

 

languebat, penitusque casa contrusa iacebant

 

corpora paupertate et morbo dedita morti.

 

exanimis pueris super exanimata parentum

 

corpora non numquam posses retroque videre

 

matribus et patribus natos super edere vitam.

 

 nec minimam partem ex agris maeror is in urbem

 

confluxit, languens quem contulit agricolarum

 

copia conveniens ex omni morbida parte.

 

omnia conplebant loca tectaque quo magis aestu,

 

confertos ita acervatim mors accumulabat.

 

multa siti prostrata viam per proque voluta

 

corpora silanos ad aquarum strata iacebant

 

interclusa anima nimia ab dulcedine aquarum,

 

multaque per populi passim loca prompta viasque

 

languida semanimo cum corpore membra videres

 

horrida paedore et pannis cooperta perire,

 

corporis inluvie, pelli super ossibus una,

 

ulceribus taetris prope iam sordeque sepulta.

 

omnia denique sancta deum delubra replerat

 

corporibus mors exanimis onerataque passim

 

cuncta cadaveribus caelestum templa manebant,

 

hospitibus loca quae complerant aedituentes.

 

nec iam religio divom nec numina magni

 

pendebantur enim: praesens dolor exsuperabat.

 

nec mos ille sepulturae remanebat in urbe,

 

quo prius hic populus semper consuerat humari;

 

perturbatus enim totus trepidabat et unus

 

quisque suum pro re  maestus humabat.

 

multaque  subita et paupertas horrida suasit;

 

namque suos consanguineos aliena rogorum

 

insuper extructa ingenti clamore locabant

 

subdebantque faces, multo cum sanguine saepe

 

rixantes, potius quam corpora desererentur,

 

inque aliis alium populum sepelire suorum

 

certantes; lacrimis lassi luctuque redibant;

 

inde bonam partem in lectum maerore dabantur;

 

nec poterat quisquam reperiri, quem neque morbus

 

nec mors nec luctus temptaret tempore tali.

## Liber Sextus

  

Primae frugiparos fetus mortalibus aegris

 

dididerunt quondam praeclaro nomine Athenae

 

et recreaverunt vitam legesque rogarunt

 

et primae dederunt solacia dulcia vitae,

 

cum genuere virum tali cum corde repertum,

 

omnia veridico qui quondam ex ore profudit;

 

cuius et extincti propter divina reperta

 

divolgata vetus iam ad caelum gloria fertur.

 

nam cum vidit hic ad victum quae flagitat usus

 

omnia iam ferme mortalibus esse parata

 

et, pro quam possent, vitam consistere tutam,

 

divitiis homines et honore et laude potentis

 

affluere atque bona gnatorum excellere fama,

 

nec minus esse domi cuiquam tamen anxia cordi,

 

atque animi ingratis vitam vexare sine ulla

 

pausa atque infestis cogi saevire querellis,

 

intellegit ibi vitium vas efficere ipsum

 

omniaque illius vitio corrumpier intus,

 

quae conlata foris et commoda cumque venirent;

 

partim quod fluxum pertusumque esse videbat,

 

ut nulla posset ratione explerier umquam,

 

partim quod taetro quasi conspurcare sapore

 

omnia cernebat, quae cumque receperat, intus.

veridicis igitur purgavit pectora dictis

 

et finem statuit cuppedinis atque timoris

 

exposuitque bonum summum, quo tendimus omnes,

 

quid foret, atque viam monstravit, tramite parvo

 

qua possemus ad id recto contendere cursu,

 

quidve mali foret in rebus mortalibus passim,

 

quod fieret naturali varieque volaret

 

seu casu seu vi, quod sic natura parasset,

 

et quibus e portis occurri cuique deceret,

 

et genus humanum frustra plerumque probavit

 

volvere curarum tristis in pectore fluctus.

 

nam vel uti pueri trepidant atque omnia caecis

 

in tenebris metuunt, sic nos in luce timemus

 

inter dum, nihilo quae sunt metuenda magis quam

 

quae pueri in tenebris pavitant finguntque futura.

hunc igitur terrorem animi tenebrasque necessest

 

non radii solis nec lucida tela diei

 

discutiant, sed naturae species ratioque.

 

quo magis inceptum pergam pertexere dictis.

  

Et quoniam docui mundi mortalia templa

 

esse  nativo consistere corpore caelum,

 

et quae cumque in eo fiunt fierique necessest

 

pleraque dissolui, qui restant percipe porro,

 

quandoquidem semel insignem conscendere currum

 

[Gap in source]

 

tu mihi supremae praescripta ad candida callis

 

currenti spatium praemonstra, callida musa

 

Calliope, requies hominum divomque voluptas,

 

te duce ut insigni capiam cum laude coronam.

 

[Gap in source]

 

 ventorum existant, placentur  omnia rursum

 

[Gap in source]

 

quae fuerint, sint placato conversa furore.

cetera quae fieri in terris caeloque tuentur

 

mortales, pavidis cum pendent mentibus saepe

 

et faciunt animos humilis formidine divom

 

depressosque premunt ad terram propterea quod

 

ignorantia causarum conferre deorum

 

cogit ad imperium res et concedere regnum.

 



 



 

nam bene qui didicere deos securum agere aevom,

 

si tamen interea mirantur qua ratione

 

quaeque geri possint, praesertim rebus in illis

 

quae supera caput aetheriis cernuntur in oris,

 

rursus in antiquas referuntur religionis

 

et dominos acris adsciscunt, omnia posse

 

quos miseri credunt, ignari quid queat esse,

 

quid nequeat, finita potestas denique cuique

 

qua nam sit ratione atque alte terminus haerens;

 

quo magis errantes caeca ratione feruntur.

quae nisi respuis ex animo longeque remittis

 

dis indigna putare alienaque pacis eorum,

 

delibata deum per te tibi numina sancta

 

saepe oberunt; non quo violari summa deum vis

 

possit, ut ex ira poenas petere inbibat acris,

 

sed quia tute tibi placida cum pace quietos

 

constitues magnos irarum volvere fluctus,

 

nec delubra deum placido cum pectore adibis,

 

nec de corpore quae sancto simulacra feruntur

 

in mentes hominum divinae nuntia formae,

 

suscipere haec animi tranquilla pace valebis.

 

inde videre licet qualis iam vita sequatur.

quam quidem ut a nobis ratio verissima longe

 

reiciat, quamquam sunt a me multa profecta,

 

multa tamen restant et sunt ornanda politis

 

versibus; est ratio caeliQUE ignisque tenenda,

 

sunt tempestates et fulmina clara canenda,

 

quid faciant et qua de causa cumque ferantur;

 

ne trepides caeli divisis partibus amens,

 

unde volans ignis pervenerit aut in utram se

 

verterit hinc partim, quo pacto per loca saepta

 

insinuarit, et hinc dominatus ut extulerit se.

 



 



  

Principio tonitru quatiuntur caerula caeli

 

propterea quia concurrunt sublime volantes

 

aetheriae nubes contra pugnantibus ventis.

 

nec fit enim sonitus caeli de parte serena,

 

verum ubi cumque magis denso sunt agmine nubes,

 

tam magis hinc magno fremitus fit murmure saepe.

praeterea neque tam condenso corpore nubes

 

esse queunt quam sunt lapides ac ligna, neque autem

 

tam tenues quam sunt nebulae fumique volantes;

 

nam cadere aut bruto deberent pondere pressae

 

 ut lapides, aut ut fumus constare nequirent

 

nec cohibere nives gelidas et grandinis imbris.

 

Dant etiam sonitum patuli super aequora mundi,

 

carbasus ut quondam magnis intenta theatris

 

dat crepitum malos inter iactata trabesque,

 

inter dum perscissa furit petulantibus auris

 

et fragilis  chartarum commeditatur;

 

id quoque enim genus in tonitru cognoscere possis,

 

aut ubi suspensam vestem chartasque volantis

 

verberibus venti versant planguntque per auras.

fit quoque enim inter dum  non tam concurrere nubes

 

frontibus adversis possint quam de latere ire

 

diverso motu radentes corpora tractim,

 

aridus unde auris terget sonus ille diuque

 

ducitur, exierunt donec regionibus artis.

  

Hoc etiam pacto tonitru concussa videntur

 

omnia saepe gravi tremere et divolsa repente

 

maxima dissiluisse capacis moenia mundi,

 

cum subito validi venti conlecta procella

 

nubibus intorsit sese conclusaque ibidem

 

turbine versanti magis ac magis undique nubem

 

cogit uti fiat spisso cava corpore circum,

 

post ubi conminuit vis eius et impetus acer,

 

tum perterricrepo sonitu dat scissa fragorem.

 

nec mirum, cum plena animae vensicula parva

 

saepe haud dat parvum sonitum displosa repente.

Est etiam ratio, cum venti nubila perflant,

 

ut sonitus faciant; etenim ramosa videmus

 

nubila saepe modis multis atque aspera ferri;

 

scilicet ut, crebram silvam cum flamina cauri

 

perflant, dant sonitum frondes ramique fragorem.

 

Fit quoque ut inter dum validi vis incita venti

 

perscindat nubem perfringens impete recto;

 

nam quid possit ibi flatus manifesta docet res,

 

hic, ubi lenior est, in terra cum tamen alta

 

arbusta evolvens radicibus haurit ab imis.

 

sunt etiam fluctus per nubila, qui quasi murmur

 

dant in frangendo graviter; quod item fit in altis

 

fluminibus magnoque mari, cum frangitur aestus.

Fit quoque, ubi e nubi in nubem vis incidit ardens

 

fulminis; haec multo si forte umore recepit

 

ignem, continuo magno clamore trucidat;

 

ut calidis candens ferrum e fornacibus olim

 

stridit, ubi in gelidum propter demersimus imbrem.

 

Aridior porro si nubes accipit ignem,

 

uritur ingenti sonitu succensa repente,

 

lauricomos ut si per montis flamma vagetur

 

turbine ventorum comburens impete magno;

 

nec res ulla magis quam Phoebi Delphica laurus

 

terribili sonitu flamma crepitante crematur.

 

Denique saepe geli multus fragor atque ruina

 

grandinis in magnis sonitum dat nubibus alte;

 

ventus enim cum confercit, franguntur in artum

 

concreti montes nimborum et grandine mixti.

Fulgit item, nubes ignis cum semina multa

 

 excussere suo concursu, ceu lapidem si

 

percutiat lapis aut ferrum; nam tum quoque lumen

 

exilit et claras scintillas dissipat ignis.

 

sed tonitrum fit uti post auribus accipiamus,

 

fulgere quam cernant oculi, quia semper ad auris

 

tardius adveniunt quam visum quae moveant res.

 

id licet hinc etiam cognoscere: caedere si quem

 

ancipiti videas ferro procul arboris auctum,

 

ante fit ut cernas ictum quam plaga per auris

 

det sonitum; sic fulgorem quoque cernimus ante

 

quam tonitrum accipimus, pariter qui mittitur igni

 

e simili causa, concursu natus eodem.

  

Hoc etiam pacto volucri loca lumine tingunt

 

nubes et tremulo tempestas impete fulgit.

ventus ubi invasit nubem et versatus ibidem

 

fecit ut ante cavam docui spissescere nubem,

 

mobilitate sua fervescit; ut omnia motu

 

percalefacta vides ardescere, plumbea vero

 

glans etiam longo cursu volvenda liquescit.

 

ergo fervidus hic nubem cum perscidit atram,

 

dissipat ardoris quasi per vim expressa repente

 

semina, quae faciunt nictantia fulgura flammae;

 

inde sonus sequitur, qui tardius adlicit auris

## Book Six

First fruit-bearing crops for sickly mortals

once distributed renowned Athens by her illustrious name,

and renewed life and proposed laws,

and first gave sweet consolations to life,

when she bore the man found with such a heart,

who once poured forth all things from a truthful mouth;

and because of whose discoveries, divine and spread abroad,

the ancient glory even now is borne to heaven, though he is dead.

For when this man saw that all things which need demands for sustenance

were now almost prepared for mortals,

and that, so far as they could, life was established in safety,

that men abounded in wealth and honour and power of praise,

and excelled in the good repute of their children,

and yet that no one was any the less anxious at heart at home,

and that they tormented life with an ungrateful mind without

any respite and were compelled to rage with hostile complaints,

he understood then that the vessel itself produced the fault,

and that through its fault all things were corrupted within

which, brought together from without, came in however advantageous;

partly because he saw it was leaky and pierced through,

so that by no means could it ever be filled,

partly because he perceived that it, as it were, befouled with a foul taste

all things whatsoever it had received within.

Therefore he purified hearts with truthful sayings,

and set a limit to desire and fear,

and expounded what the highest good was, at which we all aim,

and showed the road by which, along a narrow path,

we might strive straight towards it in a direct course,

and what evil there might be everywhere in mortal affairs,

which came to pass by nature and flew about in various ways,

whether by chance or by force, as nature had so ordained,

and through what gates it was fitting to meet each thing;

and he proved that the human race for the most part rolls in vain

the sad waves of cares within its breast.

For just as children tremble and fear all things

in blind darkness, so we sometimes fear in the light

things no more to be feared than those which children in darkness

dread and imagine to be about to happen.

This terror of the mind, therefore, and these shadows must

be dispelled not by the rays of the sun nor the bright shafts of day,

but by the aspect and reason of nature.

All the more shall I proceed to weave out my undertaking in words.

And since I have taught that the mortal structures of the world—heaven—

consist of a native body,

and that whatever things occur in it and must occur

for the most part are dissolved, next receive what remains,

since once I have mounted the distinguished chariot

The other things which mortals behold coming to pass in earth and heaven,

when they often hang in fearful minds,

make their spirits lowly through fear of the gods

and press them down to earth, because

ignorance of causes compels them to refer things

to the dominion of gods and concede sovereignty.

For those who have well learned that the gods pass an untroubled age,

if nevertheless meanwhile they wonder by what means

each thing can be done, especially in those matters

which are seen above their heads in the ethereal regions,

they are carried back again into the old religions

and take unto themselves harsh masters, whom, miserable as they are, they believe

to be able to do all things, ignorant what can be,

what cannot be, and finally what limited power belongs to each,

by what principle and with what deeply fixed boundary;

all the more are they borne astray by blind reasoning.

Unless you reject these things from your mind and cast far away

the thought that they are unworthy of the gods and alien to their peace,

the sacred divinities of the gods, wronged by you, will often harm you—

not because the supreme power of the gods can be violated,

so that it may drink in cruel penalties from anger,

but because you yourself will establish that the great gods, tranquil in peaceful repose,

roll the waves of angers;

nor will you approach the shrines of the gods with a peaceful breast,

nor will you be able, in the tranquil peace of your mind,

to receive those images which are borne from their sacred bodies

into the minds of men, messengers of divine form.

From this one may see what manner of life now follows.

Although the truest reasoning casts that life far away from us,

although many things have been set forth by me,

many nevertheless remain and must be adorned in polished

verse; the nature of heaven AND fire must be grasped,

storms and bright thunderbolts must be sung,

what they do and for what cause they are borne in every case,

lest, mad with fear at the divided quarters of heaven,

you tremble whence flying fire has come or towards which quarter

it has turned itself, how it has slipped through enclosed places,

and how, having emerged from them, it has raised itself to mastery.

First, the blue regions of heaven are shaken by thunder

because ethereal clouds, flying on high, clash together

with winds fighting against one another.

For no sound is produced from the clear part of heaven;

but wherever clouds are in a denser mass,

there from this cause a rumbling often arises with great roar.

Moreover, clouds cannot consist of a body so dense

as stones and wood, nor indeed so thin

as mists and flying smokes;

for they would either have to fall, pressed down by their dull weight,

like stones, or, like smoke, could not hold together

nor retain chill snows and showers of hail.

They also give a sound over the plains of the open world,

as canvas once stretched in great theatres

gives a crackling, tossed among masts and beams,

and sometimes, torn through, rages under wanton winds

and imitates the brittle rustling of sheets;

for you may recognize this kind too in thunder,

or when suspended cloth and flying sheets

the blows of winds toss and beat through the air.

It also happens sometimes that clouds are able not so much to clash

with opposing fronts as to move sideways

with divergent motion, grazing their bodies continuously,

whence the dry sound rubs the air for a long time

and is prolonged until they have left the narrow regions.

In this fashion too all things often seem, shaken by thunder,

to tremble with a heavy motion, and suddenly the mighty walls

of the vast world to have been burst apart,

when the gathered storm of strong winds has hurled itself

into the clouds and, enclosed there,

with a whirling eddy compels the cloud more and more on every side

to become hollow around with a thick body;

afterward, when its force and fierce onset have worn it thin,

then, split apart, it gives forth a crash with terrifying sound.

Nor is it surprising, since a little bladder full of air

often, suddenly burst, makes no little sound.

There is also a means by which, when winds blow through clouds,

they make sounds; for we often see

branching and rough clouds borne along in many ways;

just as, plainly, when the blasts of the northwesterly wind blow

through a thick forest, the leaves give a sound and the branches a crash.

It also happens that sometimes the impetuous force of a strong wind

tears a cloud apart, breaking it with a direct onset;

for what a blast can do there the manifest fact teaches,

here, where it is gentler, when nevertheless on the deep earth

it overturns trees and draws them up from their lowest roots.

There are also waves through the clouds which give, as it were, a murmur

as they break heavily; and the same happens in deep

rivers and in the great sea, when the surge is broken.

It also happens when the burning force of thunderbolt falls

from cloud into cloud; if the latter by chance has received much

moisture, it immediately kills the fire with a great cry,

as glowing iron from hot furnaces once

hisses when we plunge it near at hand into cold water.

Further, if a drier cloud receives fire,

it is burned, suddenly kindled, with a huge sound,

as if flame should wander through laurel-covered mountains

in a whirlwind of winds, burning with great onset;

nor is anything burned with a more terrible sound than

the Delphic laurel of Phoebus, with crackling flame.

Finally, often the great crash and fall of ice

makes a sound high in great clouds;

for when wind packs them tightly, the compacted mountains

of storm-clouds, mingled with hail, are broken into a narrow space.

Likewise it flashes when clouds have shaken out many seeds of fire

by their collision, as if one stone

should strike another stone or iron; for then too light

leaps out and fire scatters bright sparks.

But thunder comes to be received by our ears after

the eyes perceive the flashing, because things which move sight

always arrive more slowly at the ears.

This too you may learn from the following: if from afar you see someone

cutting down a tall tree with a two-edged axe,

it comes about that you see the stroke before the blow

gives its sound to the ears; so too we see lightning before

we receive thunder, which is sent forth together with fire,

born from the same cause, from the same collision.

In this way too clouds dye places with swift light,

and the storm flashes with trembling onset.

When wind has entered a cloud and, whirling there,

has caused the cloud, as I taught before, to grow dense and hollow,

it grows hot by its own motion; just as you see all things

heated thoroughly by motion grow incandescent, while even a leaden

bullet, rolled by a long course, melts.

Therefore, when this hot wind has torn through the black cloud,

it scatters suddenly, as though forced out by violence, seeds

of heat, which make the flashing gleams of flame;

then sound follows, which reaches the ears more slowly

than those things which reach the light of our eyes.

Plainly this happens in dense clouds, and when at the same time they are piled

high, one above another, with marvellous force.

Let it not deceive you that we see from below

how much broader they are than how far upward they extend.

For observe, when winds carry clouds, made like mountains,

sideways through the air,

or when you see them heaped over great mountains,

one above another and pressing down from above,

set in their stations, with winds buried on every side;

then you will be able to recognize their great masses

and to discern their caverns, as it were, built of hanging rocks,

which, when a storm has arisen, winds

fill and, shut in, rage with a great murmur

within the clouds and, in the manner of wild beasts, threaten in their caves;

now from this side, now from that, they send roarings through the clouds,

and, seeking a way, wheel about and roll up seeds

of fire within the clouds, and so compel many together

and whirl flame inside the hollow furnaces,

until, with the cloud burst apart, they have flashed forth brightly.

For this cause also that mobile golden colour

of liquid fire flies down to earth,

because it is necessary that the clouds themselves have very many

seeds of fire; indeed, when they are without any moisture,

their colour for the most part is fiery and bright.

For it is necessary that they receive many things from the sun's light,

so that deservedly they grow red and pour forth fires.

Therefore when driving wind has thrust these together into one place

and, forcing them, compressed them into one spot, they pour forth the squeezed-out

seeds which make the colours of flame flash.

It flashes likewise when the clouds of heaven also grow thin;

for when wind lightly draws them apart as they move

and dissolves them, those seeds which make the lightning must necessarily

fall out without welcome. Then it flashes without foul

terror and sounds, and with no tumult.

As for the rest, that thunderbolts consist of endowed nature

their strokes declare, and the burnt marks of heat

and traces of heavy-smelling sulphur breathing out fumes;

for these are signs of fire, not of wind nor rain.

Moreover, they often set the roofs of houses ablaze,

and with swift flame hold sway in the very buildings.

Nature has composed for you this subtle fire, with the first fires,

of minute and mobile

bodies, to which nothing at all can offer resistance.

For the strong thunderbolt passes through the enclosures of houses,

like a cry and voices; it passes through stones, through bronze,

and in an instant makes bronze and gold liquid.

It also causes wine suddenly to escape from unbroken vessels,

because, plainly, its heat coming upon them easily

loosens all the surroundings and makes the sides of the vessel porous,

and, slipping into the wine itself,

by its motion loosens and disperses the first-beginnings of the wine.

This the heat of the sun does not seem able to accomplish,

although it is so powerful in brilliant heat.

So much more mobile and masterful is this force.

Now in what way these things are produced, and by so great an onset

come to be such that they can split open towers with a blow,

destroy houses, tear away timbers and beams,

break down and overthrow monuments of men,

kill men, lay cattle low everywhere,

and by what force they can do all the other things of this kind,

I shall explain, nor shall I linger longer over my promises.

Thunderbolts must be thought to be produced from thick clouds,

built up high; for they are never sent from a clear sky

nor from clouds lightly dense.

For manifest fact teaches beyond doubt that this happens:

because then clouds thicken throughout the whole air,

so that we may think that all darkness has left Acheron

and filled the great caverns of heaven,

æto such a degree, when the foul night of storm-clouds has arisen,

the faces of black dread hang over us from above,æ

when the storm begins to forge thunderbolts.

Moreover, very often a black cloud too over the sea,

like a river of pitch sent down from heaven, thus falls,

laden with darkness, upon the waves from afar and draws with it a black

storm, heavy with thunderbolts and squalls,

itself filled especially with fires and winds,

so that on land too men shudder and seek shelter.

Thus, therefore, we must think that a high storm is above

our head; for the lands would not be overwhelmed by so great

darkness, unless many clouds had been built above,

with the sun shut out by many others;

nor could they, as they came, oppress us with such rain

as to make rivers overflow and plains swim,

unless the air were built high with clouds.

Here, therefore, all things are full of winds and fires;

for this reason roars and flashes happen everywhere.

For indeed I have taught above that hollow clouds have very many

seeds of heat, and that they must necessarily

take in many things from the rays of the sun and their heat.

When the same wind which drives them into one place,

whatever place it may be, has squeezed out many

seeds of heat and mingled itself at the same time with that fire,

the vortex, having slipped in there, whirls in a narrow space

and sharpens the thunderbolt within hot furnaces;

for it is kindled in two ways: it grows hot both through its own

mobility and through contacts with fire.

Then, when the force of the wind has grown hot, the heavy onset

of fire begins; then, as though ripe, the thunderbolt

suddenly tears through the cloud and, a flashing heat, is borne on,

illuminating every place with brilliant lights.

A heavy sound follows it, so that the structures of heaven above

seem to be suddenly burst apart and to crush us.

Then a trembling violently assails the lands, and murmurs run through

the deep heaven; for then almost the whole

storm, shaken, trembles and roarings are set in motion.

From this concussion follows a heavy and abundant rain,

so that all the air seems to be turned into rain

and, rushing downward, to return to a deluge;

so great is the shower sent by the bursting cloud and storm of wind,

when the sound flies forth with the burning stroke.

There is also a time when the impetuous force of wind from without

falls upon a strong cloud at its ripened height;

when it tears this apart, immediately that fiery

whirl falls, which by our ancestral name we call thunderbolt.

The same occurs in other directions, wherever the force has borne it.

It also happens sometimes that a force of wind sent without fire

nevertheless catches fire in its course and long passage,

while it comes, shedding in its flight certain large bodies

which cannot penetrate through the air equally,

and carrying along other small ones scraped from the air itself,

which, mingled in flight, make fire;

by a reason not at all different from that by which a leaden

bullet often becomes hot in its course, when, giving off many

bodies of coldness, it has caught fire in the air.

It also comes about that the force of the very blow kindles fire,

when the cold force of wind, sent without fire, has struck;

unless perhaps because, when it has struck with a violent blow,

elements of heat can flow together from the thing itself

and at the same time from that which then receives the blow;

as, when we strike a stone with iron, fire flies out,

nor, because the force of iron is cold, do for that reason

the seeds of hot brightness fail to meet at the blow.

Thus therefore a thing too must be set alight by lightning,

if by chance it has been suitable and fit for flames.

Nor indeed can the force of wind altogether plainly be cold,

that force which is sent with so great violence,

without either being first kindled by fire on its course,

or at least arriving warmed and mingled with heat.

Moreover, the swiftness of lightning comes about, and its heavy blows,

and lightning for the most part runs through with rapid fall,

because its force first gathers itself wholly in the clouds

and takes up a great effort of going;

then, when the cloud has been unable to contain the increase of its onset,

the force is squeezed out, and therefore flies with wondrous impetus,

like things discharged from powerful engines of war.

Add that it consists of small and light elements,

nor is anything easily able to resist such a nature;

for it flees and penetrates through the sparse spaces of paths,

therefore it does not linger through many obstacles in delaying,

and for this reason flies, falling with swift impetus.

Then, because by their whole nature all weights strive downward,

when a blow is added, moreover,

its swiftness is doubled and that impetus becomes more weighty,

so that it more violently and swiftly scatters by its blows

whatever obstacles delay it, and follows its course.

Finally, because it comes with a long-continued impetus, it must

take on swiftness again and again, which increases as it goes

and augments its strong powers and strengthens its blow;

for it causes whatever seeds belong to it

to be borne, as it were, all together into one place from the opposite direction,

casting all things into that rolling course.

Perhaps, coming from itself, it draws along some bodies

from the air, which kindle its swiftness by blows.

And it comes unharmed through things and passes intact through many,

because liquid fire makes its way through their openings.

And it breaks through many things, when the bodies of lightning itself

fall upon the bodies of things by which they are woven together.

Moreover, it easily dissolves bronze and suddenly makes gold

boil, because its force is made of small, minute

bodies and of light elements,

which easily insinuate themselves and, once insinuated, suddenly

dissolve every knot and loosen the bonds.

And more in autumn, when the stars shine, the high

abode of heaven is shaken on every side, and the whole earth,

and when the flowering seasons of spring unfold themselves.

For fires are lacking in cold, and winds fail in heat,

nor are clouds of such dense body.

Therefore, when the intermediate seasons of heaven prevail,

then all the diverse causes of lightning meet together.

For the very turning of the year mingles cold and heat.

Both of these are needed for a cloud that must fashion lightnings,

so that, in the discord of things and in great tumult,

the air may surge madly with fires and winds.

For the first part of heat is the last of cold:

that is the season of spring; wherefore it is necessary that things unlike

one another should fight and disturb the mixture.

And the last heat, mingled with the first cold,

rolls on in the season which bears the name of autumn;

there too fierce winters contend with summers.

Therefore these are to be called the seasons of the year,

nor is it surprising if at that time very many

lightnings occur and a troubled storm is stirred in the sky,

because it is disturbed by a double war on either side,

on this side by flames, on that by winds mingled with moisture.

This is to discern the nature itself of fire-bearing lightning

and to see by what force it does each thing,

not uselessly to unroll backward Tyrrhenian verses,

seeking indications of the hidden mind of the gods—

whence the flying fire has come or toward which quarter

it has turned itself from here, in what way through enclosed places

it has insinuated itself, and how, having mastered them, it has emerged from them,

or what harm the stroke of lightning can do from heaven.

But if Jupiter and the other shining gods

shake the heavenly halls with terrifying sound

and hurl fire wherever each has the will,

why do they not cause those whose abominable crime is unguarded

to breathe out flames of lightning, pierced through the breast,

a keen warning for mortals,

and why rather does one conscious to himself of no shameful deed

roll in flames, innocent, and is caught in the fiery

whirlwind of heaven, suddenly?

Why too do they strike deserted places and labour in vain?

Or do they then accustom their arms and strengthen their muscles?

And why do they allow their weapon to be blunted upon the earth of their father?

Why does he himself permit it and not spare his enemies?

Finally, why does Jupiter never, from a sky wholly clear,

hurl lightning down to earth and send forth its sound?

Or, as soon as clouds have come up, does he then descend into them,

so as from there nearby to direct the blows of his weapon?

Moreover, for what reason does he cast it into the sea? What does he accuse—

the waves and the liquid mass and the swimming plains?

Furthermore, if he wishes us to beware the stroke of lightning,

why does he hesitate to make it possible for us to see it when launched?

But if he wishes to crush us with fire while we expect nothing,

why does he thunder from that quarter, so that we can avoid it?

Why does he first stir up darkness, rumblings, and murmurs?

And how can you believe that he sends it at once into many quarters?

Or would you never dare to maintain that this has happened,

that several strokes should be made at one time?

Yet it has often happened many times, and must happen,

that, just as rain falls in many regions and showers descend,

so many lightnings should occur at one time.

Finally, why does he shatter the holy shrines of the gods and their

splendid abodes with hostile lightning,

and break the well-made images of the gods and by a violent wound

take away honour from their own figures?

And why does he generally seek high places, and why do we see very many traces

of his fire upon mountain summits?

What remains is easy to learn from these things:

by what means the Greeks’ presters, so named from the thing,

when sent down from above, come into the sea.

For it happens that sometimes, like a column let down

from heaven into the sea, there descends something around which the straits

boil violently, stirred by blowing gusts,

and whatever ships are then caught in that tumult

come, harried, into the utmost danger.

This happens when sometimes the aroused force of wind cannot

break the cloud which it has begun upon, but presses it down, so that,

like a column let down from heaven, it reaches the sea,

gradually, as though something were pushed down from above

by the thrust of fist and arm and extended into the waters;

when it splits this cloud, the force of wind bursts out from it into the sea

and creates a wondrous boiling in the waves;

for the whirling vortex descends and at the same time

draws down that cloud with a slow body;

as soon as it has thrust it, heavy, down to the levels of the sea,

it suddenly casts itself wholly into the water and compels

the entire sea to boil, stirred with a mighty sound.

It also happens that the vortex of wind itself wraps itself in clouds,

scraping together from the air the seeds of cloud,

and as it were imitates a prester let down from heaven;

when it has cast itself down upon the lands and dissolved,

it vomits forth the immense force of whirlwind and storm.

But because this happens altogether rarely and mountains must

stand in the way on land, the same thing appears more often

in the wide prospect of the sea and in the open sky.

Clouds gather when many bodies, flying,

have suddenly come together above in this region of heaven—

rather rough bodies, which can, though impeded in slight ways,

be held compressed among themselves.

These first cause small clouds to stand together;

then they grasp one another and flock together,

and by joining grow and are carried by winds,

until a savage storm has arisen.

It also happens that mountain summits, the nearer they are to heaven,

so much the more continually smoke, rising aloft,

with the thick darkness of a tawny cloud,

because, when clouds first gather,

before the eyes can see them while they are thin, winds

carrying them compel them to the highest mountain tops;

there at last it comes about that, when a greater throng has arisen

and become dense, they can appear and at the same time be seen

to rise into the upper air from the very mountain peak.

For the fact itself and sense declare that windy places lie open above,

when we climb high mountains.

Moreover, suspended garments, when they take on clinging moisture,

declare that nature raises very many bodies also from the whole sea-shore.

Wherefore many things seem able also to rise

from the salty movement of the sea for increasing clouds;

for every nature is akin to moistures.

Moreover, from all rivers and from the earth itself

we see mists and vapour rise,

which, like breaths, pressed out from here, are borne upward

and cover the sky with their darkness and gradually,

by coming together, furnish up high clouds.

For the heat too of the upper star-bearing ether presses upon them

and, as though by thickening, weaves the blue sky beneath the rain-clouds.

It also happens that there come into this heaven from outside those

bodies which make clouds and flying rain-clouds;

for I have shown that their number is innumerable and the sum of the deep

is infinite, and I have shown with what swiftness

bodies fly and how suddenly they are accustomed to cross

unutterable space.

Therefore it is not surprising if, in a short time, storms and darkness

so often cover seas and lands from above with such great winds,

since through all the passages of ether

and, as it were, through the breathing-holes round about the great world,

an outlet and entrance has been granted to the elements.

Come now, I shall explain in what manner rainy moisture gathers

in the high clouds and, sent down, falls upon the lands as rain. First,

I shall establish that many seeds of water rise into the clouds themselves

at once from all things, and that both grow alike—

both the clouds and whatever water is in the clouds—

just as body grows in us together with blood,

and likewise sweat and whatever moisture there is finally in the limbs.

They also often take up much sea moisture,

as hanging fleeces of wool do,

when winds carry clouds above the great sea.

By a similar principle moisture is raised into clouds from all rivers.

When many seeds of waters,

grown in many ways, have well come together there from every side,

the dense clouds strive to send out moisture in two ways: for the force

of wind drives it onward, and the very abundance of rain-clouds, gathered in a greater throng,

presses and weighs down from above and makes the rains flow out.

Furthermore, when clouds too are made thin by winds

or are dissolved, struck from above by the sun’s heat,

they send out rainy moisture and drip, as wax,

melting upon a hot fire, liquefies abundantly.

But heavy rain comes when clouds are violently pressed together

by both force and the onset of wind.

Yet rains are accustomed to continue long and linger for a long time,

when many seeds of water are stirred,

and clouds and watering rain-clouds, one above another,

are borne from every quarter in abundance,

while the whole steaming earth exhales moisture.

Here, when the sun has shone with its rays amid the dark storm,

opposite the sprinkled rain-clouds,

then the colour of the rainbow appears in the black clouds.

All the other things which grow and are produced above,

and which gather in the clouds—all things, absolutely

all things: snow, winds, hail, cold hoar-frost,

and the great force of freezing, the great hardening of waters,

and the delay which everywhere restrains the eager rivers—

it is nevertheless very easy to discover and see in the mind

in what way all these things happen and why they are produced,

when you have well learned what has been assigned to the elements.

Come now, learn what principle exists for the motions of the earth.

And first of all, make yourself believe that the earth, below

just as above, is everywhere full of windy

caverns and bears in its breast many lakes and many pools,

and rocks and sheer stones;

and you must suppose that many hidden rivers beneath the earth’s back

roll along submerged waves by force;

for the nature of the thing itself requires it to be like itself everywhere.

With these things then joined beneath and laid below,

the earth above trembles, shaken by great collapses,

when time has caused huge caverns beneath to fall in;

for whole mountains collapse, and suddenly great tremors

spread widely from there by the concussion.

And rightly so, since houses tremble along the road, shaken by carts

of no great weight at all,

nor do they leap any less if anything whatever on the road

jolts the iron-shod rims of wheels on both sides.

It also happens, when a great mass of earth through age rolls down from land

into great and vast pools of water,

that the earth too, wavering, is shaken by the wave of water;

just as a vessel cannot stand firm, unless the moisture

has ceased to be tossed about in uncertain movement within.

Moreover, when wind gathered through the hollow places beneath the earth

leans from one side and, straining with great powers,

presses upon the deep caverns,

the earth inclines where the force of wind presses downward.

Then all structures standing upon the earth above,

and each one in proportion as it rises more high toward heaven,

threaten to incline, thrust forth in the same direction,

and their projecting beams hang, ready to fall.

And men fear to believe that some deadly time and disaster

await the nature of the great world,

when they see so great a mass of lands leaning over!

Unless the winds breathed out, no thing could check them

or restrain them from going to destruction;

but now, because they breathe out in turns, grow heavy,

and return as though gathered together, then yield back when repelled,

for this reason the earth more often threatens ruin

than brings it about; for it inclines and then draws back

and, having slipped down by its weight, receives back its own position.

For this reason all buildings sway,

the uppermost more than the middle, the middle than the lowest, the lowest very little.

This also is a cause of that same great earthquake.

When a certain very great force of wind and breath,

arising suddenly either from outside or from the earth itself,

has cast itself into the hollow places of the earth, and there

roars amid great caverns, borne about in tumult,

then, after the agitated force has burst forth, driven on,

and at once, splitting the deep earth, creates a great chasm.

This happened at Sidon in Syria and at Aegium

in the Peloponnese: this issuing forth of breath

destroyed these cities, together with the earthquake that arose.

Moreover, many walls have fallen in lands through great

movements, and many cities together with their inhabitants

have sunk beneath the sea.

But if it does not break forth, still the very impetus of breath

and the wild force of wind is distributed like a shiver

through the frequent openings of the earth and from there causes trembling;

just as when cold comes deep into our limbs,

it shakes us against our will, compelling us to tremble and move.

Therefore men quake in cities with double terror:

above, they fear their houses; below, they fear the caverns

of earth, lest nature suddenly dissolve them,

or, torn apart, spread wide its own chasm

and, in confusion, wish to fill it with its own ruins.

Accordingly, though they may think heaven and earth

incorruptible, consigned to eternal safety,

yet sometimes the present force of danger itself

instils this spur of fear in some degree:

that the earth, suddenly withdrawn from beneath their feet, may be carried

into the abyss, and the exposed sum of things may follow

utterly, and there may come to be the world’s confused ruin.

At the outset they wonder that the nature of the sea does not become greater,

into which there is so great a flow of waters,

into which all rivers come from every quarter.

Add wandering rains and flying storms,

all of which scatter and water seas and lands;

add its own springs: yet all this, compared with the whole sea,

will scarcely be the increase of a single drop;

wherefore it is less surprising that the great sea does not increase.

Moreover, the sun withdraws a great part of the moisture by its heat.

For we see the sun dry garments wet with moisture by its burning rays;

but we see the sea spread out wide and vast.

Therefore, although from each single place the sun may sip a small portion of moisture from the surface of the sea,

yet over so great a space it will take much away from the waves.

Then besides, winds too can carry off a great part of the moisture as they sweep over the sea; for we very often see in a single night paths dried by winds and the crusts of soft mud harden.

Moreover, I have shown that clouds also take up much moisture, drawn from the great surface of the sea, and scatter it everywhere throughout the whole circle of lands, when it rains upon the earth and winds bear the clouds along.

Lastly, since the earth is porous in body and, joined to the shores of the sea, surrounds it on every side, moisture ought, just as it comes into the sea from the lands, likewise to seep from the salt sea into the lands;

for the saltness is strained away, and the substance of the moisture flows back and gathers at the heads of all rivers; thence it returns over the lands in a sweet stream, wherever the channel once cut has carried down its waters with liquid foot.

Now I shall explain by what process fires sometimes breathe forth through the jaws of Mount Etna with so great a whirlwind; for no moderate disaster having arisen, the tempest of flame, reigning over the Sicilian fields, turned toward itself the faces of neighbouring peoples,

when, seeing all the smoky temples of heaven glittering, they filled their fearful breasts with anxiety as to what new thing the nature of things might be devising.

In these matters you must look deeply and far, and survey all directions from afar, so that you may remember that the sum of things is profound, and may see how very small a part of the whole sum is the heaven, and what a minute fraction it constitutes—not even a whole part—of the entire earth, one man.

If you contemplate this proposition well and see it clearly, you will cease to wonder at many things.

For does any one of us wonder if someone has taken into his limbs a fever arising with hot burning, or any other pain of disease through his members?

For suddenly a foot swells, sharp pain often seizes the teeth, attacks the very eyes; sacred fire arises and, creeping over the body, burns whatever part it has seized and makes its way through the limbs—no wonder, since there are seeds of many things, and this earth and heaven bear enough of evil disease from which the force of an immense malady may grow.

Thus, then, we must suppose that from the infinite all things are supplied in sufficient abundance to the entire heaven and earth, whence the earth, suddenly shaken, may be moved, and a swift whirlwind may run through sea and lands, Etnean fire may abound, and heaven blaze;

for this too happens, and the heavenly regions burn, and storms of rain arise with a more violent outbreak, when by chance the seeds of waters have so borne themselves.

“But the troubled burning heat is exceedingly great.”

To be sure, any river that seems greatest to one who has not before seen a greater is great; and a tree and a man seem great, and everything of every kind which each person has seen greatest he imagines immense, though all things together with heaven, earth, and sea are nothing in comparison with the entire sum of the whole.

Yet now I shall explain in what ways the flame, suddenly stirred, blows forth from the vast furnaces of Etna. First, the nature of the whole mountain is for the most part hollow beneath, supported by caverns of rock.

Moreover, in all caverns there is wind and air.

For wind comes into being when air is set in motion and stirred up.

When this has grown thoroughly hot and, raging, has heated all the rocks and earth around it wherever it touches them, and has struck hot fire from them with swift flames,

it lifts itself and thus casts itself high up through the straight jaws.

Thus it carries its heat far, scatters ashes far and wide, rolls forth smoke in thick darkness, and at the same time drives out rocks of wondrous weight; so that you need not doubt that this is the stormy force of air.

Moreover, for a great part of its extent the sea breaks its waves at the mountain’s roots and loosens the surge.

From this sea caverns reach beneath to the high jaws of the mountain. It must be admitted that by this way

things are compelled to go and penetrate deeply from the open sea, and therefore to blow forth outside and raise up flame, hurl up rocks, and lift clouds of sand.

For on the highest summit are craters, as they themselves name them, which we call jaws and mouths.

There are also some things of which it is not enough to state one cause, but several, though one alone may be the actual cause; as if you yourself should see from afar the lifeless body of a man lying there, it would be fitting to state all causes of death, so that one might be named as his;

for you could not establish that he had died by the sword, or by cold, or by disease, or perhaps by poison; but we know that something of this kind has befallen him.

Likewise, in many matters we must speak in this way.

The Nile rises in summer and overflows its fields, the single river throughout the earth of all Egypt.

It waters Egypt often in the midst of heat, either because in summer the north winds blow against its mouths at that season of the year which they say is the time of the Etesian winds, and, blowing against the river, delay it and, forcing its waters upstream, fill it and make them remain.

For without doubt these blasts are borne against the stream, driven from the icy stars of the pole;

that river comes from the southward, from the heat-bearing region, rising deep among the black races of men, scorched in complexion, from the middle region of day.

It may also be that a great accumulation of sand blocks the mouths from the opposing waves, when the sea, stirred by winds, rushes sand inward;

by which means the river has a less free outlet, and likewise the downward rush of its waters becomes less.

It may also be that perhaps rains occur more abundantly at its source at the season when the Etesian blasts of the north cast all clouds toward those regions.

For surely, when they have gathered, cast toward the middle region of day, the clouds, driven together there, are at last forced and pressed upon the high mountains.

Perhaps it rises deep in the high mountains of the Ethiopians, where the sun that surveys all things compels white snows to descend into the plains by his melting rays.

Come now, I shall explain to you what manner of places and lakes Avernian places are, and with what nature they are endowed.

First, that they are called by the name of Avernian is due to this: they are hostile to all birds, because, when flying creatures have come opposite those places, forgetting the oarage of their wings they slacken the sails and fall headlong, their necks drooping, to the ground, if by chance the nature of the places so brings it about, or into water, if a lake of Avernus lies beneath.

Such a place is by Cumae, filled with the sharp sulphur of a mountain, where it smokes, increased by hot springs.

There is one also within the walls of Athens, on the very summit of the citadel, beside the temple of kindly Tritonian Pallas, where hoarse crows never set down their winged bodies, not even when the altars smoke with offerings;

so greatly do they flee—not because of the keen wrath of Pallas, on account of the watchful cause, as the poets of the Greeks have sung—but the nature of the place itself accomplishes the work by its own power.

In Syria too, likewise, there is said to be a place to be seen where, as soon as four-footed beasts have set their first steps, a force itself compels them to fall heavily, as though they had suddenly been sacrificed to the divine powers.

All these things occur by natural process, and the origin from which they arise is evident;

lest it be believed that this is a gate into the regions of Orcus, and lest afterwards we suppose that the gods of the shades draw souls hence to the shores of Acheron below, just as winged stags are often thought to draw the creeping tribes of wild beasts from their lairs with their nostrils.

Learn how far this has been driven from true reason; for I now endeavour to speak of the matter itself.

First I say this, which I have also said often before: that in the earth there are figures of things of every kind;

many which are vital for food, and many which can inflict diseases and hasten death.

And we have shown before that different things are more suited to the mode of life of different living creatures, because of their dissimilar nature, their different textures among themselves, and their primary figures.

Many hostile things pass through the ears; many things, noxious and harsh to the touch, make their way in through the nostrils themselves; nor are there few things which must be avoided by touch, or shunned by sight, or are bitter in taste.

Next, you may see how many things are foul and grievous to a human being by their sharply hostile sensation; first, a heavy shade has been allotted to certain trees, so much so that they often cause headaches if anyone lies stretched out beneath them on the grass.

There is also a tree in the great mountains of Helicon, accustomed to kill a man by the foul smell of its blossom.

Surely all these things arise from the earth because the earth bears, mixed together and yet separately distributed, many seeds of many things in many ways.

And when the keen smell of a newly extinguished night-lamp strikes the nostrils, it immediately puts to sleep one who is accustomed to collapse and foam at the mouth from disease.

And a woman, overcome by the heavy smell of castor, lies back; and bright work slips from her tender hands at the time when she has smelt it while discharging her menses.

And many other things relax the languishing limbs throughout the body and unsettle the soul in its inner seats.

Finally, if you linger even in hot baths when full and wash yourself in a basin of burning water, how easily does it happen that you often fall down in the midst of it!

And how easily the heavy force and smell of charcoal make their way into the brain, unless we have first taken water!

But when a burning fever has taken hold, subduing the limbs, then the smell of wine becomes like a blow fit for slaughter.

Do you not see, too, that sulphur is generated in the earth itself and bitumen congeals with a foul smell; and finally, where men follow veins of silver and gold, searching out with iron the hidden recesses of the earth, what odours does Scaptensula breathe out below?

Or what evil smell do gilded metals exhale!

What faces and what complexions do they give men!

Do you not see or hear how in a short time they are wont to perish, and how greatly they lack the means of life, whom the mighty force of necessity confines in such work?

Thus the whole earth seethes with these heats and breathes them forth outside into the open and ready space of heaven.

Thus Avernian places too must send up from the earth into the air a death-dealing force for birds, so that it poisons some portion of the space of heaven.

As soon as a bird has first been borne into it on wings, it is hampered there, seized by unseen poison, so that it falls straight down in the direction toward which the vapour is directed.

When it has fallen, this same force of the vapour takes from all its limbs the remaining remnants of life.

For indeed at first it stirs up, as it were, a certain disturbance; afterwards it happens that, when the things of poison have already fallen into the springs themselves, life too must there be vomited forth, because a great abundance of evil arises around it.

It also happens sometimes that this force and vapour of Avernus disperses the air which lies between the bird and the earth.

Thus this place is left nearly empty.

When flying creatures have come opposite this place, the vain effort of their wings immediately fails, and every exertion of both wings is betrayed.

When they cannot struggle or keep themselves aloft on their wings, nature, plainly, compels them to glide down to earth by their weight; and, lying now almost in a void through the empty space, they scatter their souls through all the channels of the body.

Moreover, water in wells becomes colder in summer, because the earth dries up with heat and, if it happens to contain seeds of vapour of its own, sends them forth into the air.

Therefore, the more exhausted the earth is by heat, the colder becomes the moisture hidden in the earth.

Moreover, when all the earth is pressed by cold, it contracts and, as it were, congeals; and in contracting it naturally presses out into wells whatever heat it itself contains.

By the shrine of Hammon there is said to be a spring cold in daylight and hot in the time of night.

Men marvel excessively at this spring and suppose that, when night covers the earth in dreadful darkness, it is heated beneath the ground in part by the keen sun.

But this is far removed from true reason.

For when the sun, touching the bare body of the water, cannot render it hot from above, though the light above enjoys so great a heat, how can it here beneath, through so thick a body of earth, boil the moisture through and warm it with hot vapour?

Especially since it can scarcely make its heat penetrate with burning rays through the walls of houses.

What, then, is the explanation? Surely it is because the earth about the spring is more porous than the rest of the earth, and there are many seeds of fire close to the body of the water.

When night has overwhelmed the earth with dew-bearing waters, the earth immediately grows cold deep within and contracts.

By this process it happens that, as though compressed by a hand, it presses into the spring whatever seeds of fire it has, which make the touch and vapour of the water hot.

Then, when the risen sun has disturbed the earth with his rays and made it porous by mingling hot vapour, the first-beginnings of fire return again to their former seats, and all the heat of the water retreats into the earth.

For this reason the spring becomes cold in daylight.

Moreover, the moisture of the water is agitated by the sun’s rays and grows porous in the light under the trembling heat; therefore it happens that it releases whatever seeds of fire it has—just as frost often sends forth what it contains within itself, melts the ice, and loosens its knots.

There is also a cold spring above which tow often at once catches fire when flame has been taken up, and a torch, kindled in a like manner, shines over the waters wherever, floating, it is driven by the breeze.

Surely this is because there are very many seeds of heat in the water, and it is necessary that bodies of fire rise from the earth itself throughout the entire spring and at the same time breathe out and pass forth into the air—not, however, so many that the spring can become hot;

moreover, a force compels them suddenly to burst forth dispersed through the water and to be gathered upward.

Of this kind is the spring in the sea near Aradus, which bubbles with sweet water and drives away the salt waves around itself;

and in many other regions the sea affords timely aid to thirsty sailors, because it pours forth sweet water amid the salt waves.

Thus those seeds can burst out and bubble forth through that spring; when they gather in tow or cling to the body of a torch, they immediately catch fire easily, because tow and torches too contain within themselves many seeds of fire.

Do you not see also that, when you bring newly extinguished flax to a night-lamp, it catches fire before it has touched the flame, and a torch in like manner?

And many other things, touched beforehand by the very vapour, catch fire from a distance before fire wets them at close range.

Thus we must suppose that this too occurs in that spring.

For what remains, I shall begin to explain by what covenant of nature it comes about that this stone can draw iron, which the Greeks call Magnet from its native name, because it arose in the native territory of the Magnetes.

Men marvel at this stone; for it often makes a chain of rings hanging from itself.

Indeed, one may sometimes see five or more suspended in descending order, tossed by light breezes, when one hangs beneath another, clinging to it, and each from another learns the force and bonds of the stone;

so unfailingly does its force prevail.

In matters of this kind many points must first be established before you can give an account of the thing itself, and one must proceed by exceedingly long windings; therefore I ask for the more attentive ears and mind.

First, from all things whatsoever that we see,

bodies must continually flow and be sent forth and scattered, 

which strike the eyes and provoke sight.

And continually odours flow from certain things;

as cold from rivers, heat from the sun, spray from the waves

of the sea, the eater-away of walls, beside the shores;

nor do varied sounds cease to stream through the air;

finally, moisture of a salty taste often comes into the mouth,

when we wander beside the sea; and, conversely,

when we see wormwood being diluted, bitterness touches us.

So greatly from all things each thing flows

and is borne and emitted everywhere into all directions,

nor is any delay or rest granted to its flowing,

since we continually perceive, and are always able

to see, to smell, and to hear sounds.

Now I shall set forth how sparse in body things are,

as I mentioned; this is clear in each first poem.

For indeed, although it pertains to many matters to know this,

above all it is necessary for this very matter at once,

concerning which I undertake to discourse, to establish

that nothing is manifest except body mixed with void.

First, it comes about that in caverns the rocks above

sweat with moisture and drip with falling drops.

Likewise sweat streams from our whole body,

the beard and hairs grow over all the limbs, over the members.

All food is distributed into the veins, and increases and nourishes

even the furthest parts of the body and the nails.

Likewise we perceive cold passing through bronze and hot vapour;

we perceive it likewise passing through gold

and through silver, when we hold full cups.

Finally, through the stone partitions of houses voices

fly through, odour and cold and the vapours

of fire penetrate, which is accustomed even to penetrate the force of iron;

finally, wherever the armour of heaven constrains things round about,

disease and force alike, when they steal in from outside,

and, when a storm has arisen on earth and in heaven,

they duly depart, carried off to heaven and earth;

since nothing exists save what is bound together with sparse body.

To this is added that not all bodies which are thrown off

from whatever things are endowed with the same sensation

and in the same manner are suited to all things.

First, the sun bakes the earth and makes it dry,

but melts ice and compels the deep snows

piled high on lofty mountains to waste away beneath its rays;

finally, wax becomes liquid placed near its vapour.

Likewise fire makes bronze liquid and melts gold,

but draws together and congeals hides and flesh into one.

Moreover, the moisture of water hardens iron from fire,

but softens hides and flesh hardened by heat.

The wild olive delights the bearded goats so greatly,

as though it flowed with ambrosia and were steeped in nectar;

while nothing stands out more bitter to man than its leaf.

Finally, the sow shuns marjoram and fears every

ointment; for to bristly swine it is sharp poison;

though to us at times it seems, as it were, to refresh us.

But, conversely, though mud is the foulest filth to us,

the same seems pleasant to swine,

so that they roll there wholly, insatiably.

This also remains, concerning the very matter which I undertake to discuss,

which seems necessary to be said first.

Since many openings have been allotted to diverse things,

they must be endowed with natures unlike one another

and each have its own nature and paths.

For indeed various senses dwell in living creatures,

and each of them properly perceives its own object within itself;

for we see sound penetrate by one way, taste from juices by another,

and odours of scent by another.

Moreover, one thing seems to stream through rocks,

another through wood, another to pass through gold,

another to make its way out through silver and glass;

for form seems to flow by this route, heat to go by that,

and the same things to pass more swiftly through some than through others.

Clearly the nature of paths, varying in many ways,

compels this to occur, as we showed a little before,

because of the unlike nature and textures of things.

Therefore, when all these things have been well established and set in place,

and have stood before us prepared and ready,

what remains will readily from this point have its account rendered, and every

cause will become clear which draws the force of iron.

First, it is necessary that from this stone very many

seeds, or an effluence, flow which by its blows disperses the air

that is situated between the stone and the iron.

When this space is emptied and a large void

is made in the middle, at once the first-beginnings of iron,

falling together into the void, drop down; and it comes about

that the ring itself follows and thus goes with its whole body.

Nor does any thing cohere more, entangled from its first elements

by a closely connected structure,

than the nature and cold horror of strong iron.

Wherefore it is less strange, what is said to be alien,

if more bodies born from the iron cannot be borne

into the void without the ring itself following;

and it does follow, until it reaches

the stone itself and clings there in unseen fastenings.

The same occurs in every direction: wherever a void place

comes to be, whether sideways or above,

the neighbouring bodies are immediately carried into the void;

for they are driven by blows from elsewhere, nor can they themselves

of their own accord rise upward into the air.

To this is likewise added, whereby it may be still more able to occur:

this matter too is assisted and aided by motion,

because, as soon as the air before the ring has been made thinner,

and the place more emptied and evacuated,

it immediately comes about that whatever air is situated behind

as it were drives and pushes it forward from the rear.

For air placed all around always beats upon things;

but it comes about that at such a time it drives the iron,

because space is vacant on one side and receives it into itself.

This air, of which I speak to you, having subtly crept

through the close openings of the iron

into its small parts, thrusts and impels it, as wind does

a ship and sails.

Finally, all things must have air within their body,

since they are of sparse body, and air

is given and placed around all things.

Therefore this air, which is hidden deep within the iron,

is always tossed by restless motion, and thereby

without doubt beats and stirs the ring within;

clearly it is borne in that same direction whither it once rushed headlong

and took up its endeavour toward the vacant part.

It also happens that the nature of iron withdraws from this stone

at times, accustomed alternately to flee and to follow.

I have also seen Samothracian iron leap
