and iron filings at the same time rage inside bronze

bowls, when this magnet-stone had been placed beneath;

so greatly does it seem eager to flee from the stone.

Such great discord is produced when bronze is interposed,

because, naturally, when first the effluence of bronze

has rushed in and occupied the open paths of the iron,

the later effluence from the stone comes and finds all things full

in the iron, nor has it a way to pass through as before;

therefore it is forced to dash against and beat with its wave

the iron textures by its own force; in this way it repels them from itself

and drives them through the bronze, though without it it often draws them back.

In these matters cease to wonder that the effluence

from this stone cannot in the same way impel other things.

For some stand supported by weight, as gold does;

others, because they are of sparse body, so that the effluence

flies through untouched, cannot be impelled anywhere,

among which kinds woody material appears to be.

Thus, the nature of iron being placed between the two,

when it has received certain corpuscles of bronze,

then it comes about that Magnesian stones impel it by that stream.

Yet these things are not so alien from other things

that many examples of this kind, severally suited among themselves,

are not abundantly supplied to me,

which I might recount. First you see stones alone adhere to lime.

Wood is joined together by bull's glue,

so that the veins of planks more often gape because of it

than the bull's bonds of their structure can be loosened.

Wine-born liquids dare to mingle with springs of water,

where heavy pitch cannot, nor light olive oil.

And the purple dye of the shellfish is joined in one

body with wool, and cannot be separated anywhere,

not if you should renew the task with Neptune's wave,

nor if the whole sea should wish to wash it out with all its waters.

Finally, does not one thing join gold to gold,

and cause bronze to be joined with white lead?

How many other things may now be found! What then?

You have no need anywhere of such long digressions,

nor is it fitting for me to spend so much labour here,

but it is better briefly to comprehend many things in a few words.

Those whose textures have thus fallen mutually opposite,

so that these hollows fit the solids of that thing and those

of this thing among themselves—this is the best junction.

There are also some things which, as though folded with rings and hooks,

can be held joined together;

which seems to occur especially in this stone and in iron.

Now I shall explain what is the account of diseases, or whence a baneful force,

arising suddenly, can produce

a deadly destruction for the race of men and herds of beasts.

First, I have shown above that there are seeds of many things

which are vital to us,

and, conversely, that many must fly about which are necessary

for disease and death; when these by chance have arisen

and disturbed the sky, the air becomes diseased.

And all this force of diseases and pestilence

either comes from outside through the sky above, like clouds and mists,

or often, arising from the earth itself, rises up

where it has gained putrefaction, being moist

and struck by untimely rains and suns.

Do you not see also that those who come from far from country and home

are affected by a change of sky and waters,

because things differ widely?

For how different do we think the sky is in Britain,

and that which is in Egypt, where the axis of the world slopes,

or that in Pontus and at Gades, and onward

to the black races of men, their colour baked through?

Since we see these four things to be different among themselves

according to the four winds and regions of the sky,

then the colour and appearance of men seem to differ greatly,

and diseases to hold races according to their kinds.

There is an elephant disease that arises beside the river Nile

in mid Egypt, and nowhere else.

In Attica the feet are affected, and the eyes in the Achaean

lands. Hence one place is hostile to some parts,

another to others and to the limbs; the varying air causes this.

Accordingly, when a sky foreign to us by chance

moves itself, and hostile air begins to creep along,

as mist and cloud gradually creep and disturb everything

wherever they proceed and compel it to change,

it likewise comes about that, when it finally enters our sky,

it corrupts it and renders it like itself and foreign.

Thus this sudden disaster and new pestilence

either falls into the waters, or settles upon the crops themselves,

or upon other fodder of men and food of cattle,

or else its force remains suspended in the very air,

and, when breathing we draw in the mingled airs from there,

it is necessary that we also at the same time absorb it into the body.

By a like account pestilence often comes also to cattle,

and sickness now to sluggish bleating creatures.

Nor does it matter whether we arrive in places

hostile to us and change the covering of the sky,

or whether nature itself brings to us a corrupted sky,

or something that we are unaccustomed to use,

which by its new arrival can assail us.

This account of diseases and deadly effluence once

made the fields within Cecrops' borders deadly

and laid waste the roads, emptied the city of citizens.

For, having come deep from the borders of Egypt,

having traversed much air and floating plains,

it settled at last upon all the people of Pandion.

Then they were given over in crowds to disease and death.

First they bore a head inflamed with heat

and glowing eyes suffused with double light.

Their black throats too sweated within with blood, and the passage of voice,

blocked by ulcers, closed up;

and the tongue, interpreter of the mind, streamed with gore,

weakened by evils, heavy in motion, rough to the touch.

Then, when through the throat the diseased force had filled the chest

and had flowed together into the very sorrowful heart of the sick,

all the barriers of life then indeed gave way.

The breath from the mouth rolled forth a foul odour,

as corpses cast out reek with their rancid fashion.

And utterly the powers of the whole mind, the whole

body, languished, already on death's very threshold.

And anxious anguish was a constant companion to intolerable evils,

with complaint mingled with groaning,

and a frequent hiccup by night and often by day,

continually compelling the sinews and limbs to contract,

broke them down, exhausting those already wearied.

Nor could you observe in anyone, by excessive heat,

the outermost part of the body burning exceedingly,

but rather a lukewarm touch presented to the hands,

while the whole body at once reddened with ulcers as though burned,

as when the sacred fire spreads through the limbs.

But the innermost part of men burned to the very bones,

there burned a flame within the stomach as in furnaces.

Nothing so light or thin could you put upon anyone's limbs

to advantage, but always wind and cold.

Some gave their limbs burning with disease to chill streams,

casting their naked body into the waters.

Many headlong fell deep into the water-nymphs of wells,

coming upon them with mouth itself agape:

an unquenchable dry thirst, plunging their bodies,

made much water equal to scant moisture.

Nor was there any rest from the evil: the bodies lay exhausted.

Medicine muttered in silent fear,

as their burning eyes, so often open in sickness,

rolled about, deprived of sleep.

And besides, many signs of death then appeared:

the mind's disturbed thought in sorrow and fear,

a grim brow, a frantic and fierce expression,

ears moreover troubled and full of sounds,

breathing frequent or great and arising at rare intervals,

and bright moisture of sweat wetting the neck,

thin scant spittle, touched with saffron colour,

and salt, scarcely emitted through the throat by a hoarse cough.

Indeed in the hands the sinews began to contract and the limbs to tremble,

and cold did not hesitate gradually to advance from the feet.

Likewise, finally at the last time,

the nostrils were compressed, the tip of the nose thin,

the eyes sunken, the temples hollow, the skin cold,

and hard upon the face; it lay with the mouth agape, the brow stretched, and remained so.

Nor after death did their limbs lie excessively stiff.

And at about the eighth bright light of the sun,

or even the ninth torch, they gave up life.

If any one of them, as sometimes happened, had escaped the funeral rites of death,

yet afterward wasting and death awaited him,

with foul ulcers and black flux of the belly;

or else, often with great pain of the head,

corrupted blood flowed from his full nostrils.

Into this all the powers and body of the man flowed away.

Moreover, when the sharp flux of foul blood had gone out,

the disease nonetheless passed into the sinews and limbs

and into the very genital parts of the body.

And some, grievously fearing the thresholds of death,

lived deprived by the knife of their manly part;

and some remained in life without hands and feet,

and some lost their eyes.

So keenly had the fear of death assailed them.

And some were even seized by forgetfulness of all things,

so that they could not recognize themselves.

And though many bodies lay unburied on the ground, piled over

other bodies, yet the race of birds and beasts

either leapt away far off, that the sharp smell might escape them,

or, when it had tasted, languished in death nearby.

Nor indeed did any bird at all readily appear in those days,

nor did the gloomy tribes of beasts come forth from the woods. Most languished

with disease and died. Above all the faithful force of dogs,

strewn in every road, laid down its life in distress;

for the diseased force wrenched life from their limbs.

Unattended vast funerals strove to be carried off,

nor was any sure common plan of remedy given;

for what had granted to one to draw the vital breezes

of air in his mouth and to behold the regions of heaven,

was destruction to others and prepared death.

One thing in these circumstances was especially pitiable

and grievous: when each man saw himself

entangled in disease, as though condemned to death,

failing in spirit, he lay with a sorrowful heart,

looking upon funerals and thereupon gave up his life.

For indeed, at no time did the greedy contagions of disease cease

to seize one from another,

as wool-bearing flocks and horned herds;

and this, above all, heaped funeral upon funeral.

For all who avoided visiting their sick relations,

too desirous of life and fearful of death,

soon afterward paid the penalty by a shameful and evil death,

deserted and bereft of aid, slaughtered by neglect.

But those who had been present went to their deaths through contagion

and labor, which shame then compelled them to undertake,

and through the winning voice of the exhausted, mingled with the voice of complaint.

Thus each best man underwent this kind of death.

Moreover, now every shepherd and herdsman,

and likewise the sturdy driver of the curved plough,

grew weak; and bodies, huddled deep within their huts,

lay delivered over to death by poverty and disease.

Over the lifeless bodies of parents, lifeless children,

and again, over mothers and fathers, their offspring,

you might sometimes see them yield up life.

Nor did a smallest part of that affliction flow from the fields into the city,

brought there by the gathering multitude of sickly farmers

converging from every quarter.

They filled all places and dwellings; the more densely packed they were in the heat,

the more death piled them up in heaps.

Many bodies, struck down by thirst and rolled along the road and everywhere,

lay stretched beside the water-basins,

their breath cut off by an excessive sweetness of the waters;

and in many public places and open streets, here and there,

you could see limbs with languid, half-living bodies

perishing, hideous with filth and covered with rags,

with the body's uncleanness, skin alone over bones,

almost already buried beneath loathsome ulcers and dirt.

Finally death had filled all the sacred shrines of the gods

with lifeless bodies, and everywhere

the temples of the heavenly gods remained burdened with corpses—

places which the temple-keepers had filled with guests.

Nor now were the religion of the gods or their divinities

held in great account: present suffering prevailed.

Nor did that custom of burial remain in the city

by which this people had formerly always been accustomed to be buried;

for, utterly disordered, it was all in a state of panic, and each man,

sorrowful according to his means, buried his own.

items.text: Quaeritur quibus principiis rerum natura constet et quomodo eorum cognitio terrorem religiosum dissolvat.
Natura ex corporibus primis et inani constat; generationes, mutationes et interitus sunt compositiones aut dissolutiones materiae permanentis.
Argumentatio diagnostica, demonstrativa, polemica et reconstructiva est: causam terroris detegit, principia naturae probat, exemplaria aemula excludit et campum cosmologicum restituit.
Motus diagnosticus ab ignorantia causarum et animi ad timorem, a timore ad religionis dominationem, inde ad necessitatem rationis naturalis procedit.
Motus probativus ab effectibus sensibilibus ad corpora invisibilia, ab existentia motus ad inane, ab utroque ad ontologiam bipartitam procedit.
Motus reconstructivus a conservatione materiae ad primordia solida, a stabilitate generum ad immutabilitatem principiorum, inde ad variationem per ordinem, figuram et motum transit.
Motus cosmologicus exemplaria finita, centralia et providentialia removet atque ordinem mundanum ex infinitis concursibus sine consilio producit.
Natura deorum a rebus humanis semota est neque meritis aut ira movetur.
Terror religiosus ex ignorantia causarum naturalium atque naturae animi nascitur et naturae ratione dissolvitur.
Sensus prima fides est qua ratiocinatio de rebus occultis confirmatur.
Nulla res e nihilo gignitur.
Nulla res ad nihilum interit.
Genera ex seminibus certis intra finitas potestates naturae oriuntur.
Omnis natura per se aut corpus aut inane est.
Corpus tangendo agit et obstat, inane autem corporibus locum motuique cessionem praebet.
Qualitates, coniunctiones, eventa et tempus non sunt naturae per se, sed a corporibus, loco et motu dependent.
Res genitae sunt concilia principiorum.
Primordia sunt solida et inanis expertia.
Primordia sunt aeterna.
Primordia naturam immutabilem servant.
Divisio corporis terminatur in minimis inseparabilibus.
Diversitas rerum ex concursu, motu, ordine, positura et figura primordiorum efficitur.
Summa corporis et inanis infinita est neque terminum externum aut medium universale habet.
Primordia perpetuo moventur et plagis inter se concurrunt.
Dispositiones stabiles ex innumeris concursibus per infinitum tempus sine consilio proveniunt.
Via rationis naturalis non est via impietatis aut sceleris.
Religio non est necessarium pietatis praesidium, quia ipsa scelerosa facta suadere potest.
Terror animi non radiis solis neque luce diei dissolvitur.
Generatio non est productio ex nihilo.
Interitus non est reductio ad nihilum.
Inobservabilitas corporis non probat eius inexist­entiam.
Natura non est plenum continuum sine intervallis.
Tertia natura per se praeter corpus et inane non datur.
Tempus non est substantia separata a motu et quiete rerum.
Ignis, aer, aqua aut terra sensibilis non sunt soli neque sufficientes rerum principia.
Primordia non sunt particulae homoeomericae eiusdem naturae ac res mortales quas constituunt.
Divisio corporum non procedit in infinitum.
Summa rerum non continetur finibus externis.
Medium universale ad quod omnia corpora naturaliter nitantur non datur.
Primordia neque consilio ordinem elegerunt neque motus inter se pepigerunt.
Regularitas originum, temporum et incrementorum requirit materiam generativam determinatam.
Mors et corruptio nexus corporum solvunt, sed materiam constituentem non abolent.
Effectus tactiles et mutationes sensibiles corpora caeca inferre permittunt, quamvis ipsa corpora oculis non cernantur.
Motus corporum impossibilis esset nisi inane corporibus cederet.
Quidquid per se agit aut tangitur corpus est; quidquid transitum sine obstaculo praebet inane est; reliqua dependentia sunt.
Praeteritum, praesens et futurum ex ordine eventuum sentiuntur neque sine rerum motu subsistunt.
Dissolutio compositorum requirit principia quae dissolutioni supersint et materiam novis compositionibus suppeditent.
Minima inseparabilia infinitam divisionem impediunt atque simplicitatem primordiorum conservant.
Stabilitas generum et finita potestas cuiusque rei immutabile substratum compositivum requirunt.
Mutatio rei non est conversio principiorum in alias substantias, sed aditus, abitus aut ordinatio diversa principiorum permanentium.
Exemplaria ex elementis sensibilibus aut partibus homoeomericis composita motum, conservationem, diversitatem et stabilitatem generum simul explicare nequeunt.
Quicumque terminus summae ponitur aliquid ultra se requirit; ideo terminus ultimus constitui nequit.
Mundus ordinatus est dispositio localis et temporarie stabilis intra infinitam copiam materiae et inanis.
Divinae minae auctoritatem coercitivam amittunt ubi eventus naturales ex causis naturalibus et dii ex humana administratione semoti intelleguntur.
Natura causaliter clauditur: defectus cognitionis causae non constituit locum interventionis divinae.
Generatio et interitus constituunt circuitum conservationis in quo materia ex aliis formis solvitur et alias formas alit.
Qualitates macroscopiae ex relationibus principiorum immutabilium oriuntur neque in singulis principiis eiusdem formae inesse debent.
Cognitio naturae est empirica origine sed inferentialis extensione: sensus effectus praebet, ratio structuram invisibilem restituit.
Possibilitas naturalis lege finitur: quid oriri possit ex natura principiorum et eorum compositionibus, non ex arbitrio externo, determinatur.
Ordo mundanus neque necessitatem consilii neque privilegium centri requirit, sed ex selectione dispositionum durabilium intra infinitos concursus emergit.
Liberatio a religione non est mera negatio cultus, sed effectus epistemicus translationis terroris in quaestionem de natura.
Eventus cuius causa nondum cognoscitur non potest propter solam ignorantiam pro signo numinis haberi.
Causa efficiens incorporea intra naturam excluditur, quia actio et passio tactum corporeum requirunt.
Qualitates sensibiles non possunt simul esse principia ultima et formae mortales compositorum.
Conversio absoluta unius naturae in aliam excluditur, quia sine substrato invarianti creationem ex nihilo et annihilationem restitueret.
Apparentia sensibilis non est inventarium completum realitatis, quamvis sensus fundamentum probationis maneat.
Homo, terra et mundus visibilis nullum privilegium centri cosmici possident.
Stabilitas ordinis non requirit intentionem, finem praestitutum aut consensum principiorum.
Initium absolutum et interitus absolutus e campo naturae excluduntur; solae compositiones et dissolutiones admittuntur.
Providentia divina mundum administrans tacite removetur, quia dii remoti sunt et natura per leges materiales sufficit.
Poenae aeternae post mortem non possunt manere fundamentum rationalis actionis, cum earum vis ab ignorantia animi, non a natura demonstrata, pendeat.
Creator aut terminator extra summam rerum locari nequit, quia nihil extra infinitam summam conceditur.
Gubernatio Veneris ad litteram accepta cum remotione deorum componi nequit; vis invocationis tacite ad generationem naturalem, voluptatem poeticam et pacis desiderium transfertur.
Conditio enuntiandi sic constituitur: vis generatrix Veneris et pax postulata → animus ad doctrinam dispositus → investigatio naturae.
Mechanismus expositionis sic operatur: doctrina obscura et ingrata → carmen suaviloquens → attentio retenta → ratio percepta.
Catena diagnostica est: ignorantia causarum et animi → timor indefinitus → minae vatum et religio → subiectio animi.
Catena epistemica est: effectus sensibilis → vestigium causae invisibilis → ratiocinatio → corpus caecum confirmatum.
Catena conservationis est: nihil ex nihilo et nihil ad nihilum → substratum permanens → primordia aeterna → dissolutio sine annihilatione.
Catena ontologica est: tactus et actio → corpus; cessio et locus → inane; reliqua → coniuncta aut eventa.
Catena compositionis est: primordia solida et immutabilia → ordines, figurae et motus diversi → qualitates et genera diversa.
Examinatio exemplarium procedit per incompatibilitatem cum motu, conservatione, minimis et diversitate atque monismum, elementarismum et homoeomeriam excludit.
Catena cosmologica est: nulla ora ultima → infinitum spatium et materia infinita → concursus perpetui → dispositiones stabiles sine consilio → mundus contingens.

Venus et pax → dispositio lectoris → diagnosis terroris religiosi → constitutio rationis naturalis → principia conservationis → corpora et inane → primordia immutabilia → infinitas summae → cosmogenesis sine consilio.
Regularitas sensibilis → semina certa → corpora invisibilia → inane necessarium → ontologia bipartita → compositio configurativa → exclusio principiorum sensibilium → naturalis causalitas clausa.
Quod antea tamquam indicium numinis apparebat denuo describitur ut effectus naturalis cuius causa adhuc quaerenda est.
Oppositio inter visibile et reale corruit; corpora invisibilia per effectus suos cognoscibilia fiunt.
Ager ontologicus in corpus, inane et dependentias eorum reordinatur, tertia natura exclusa.
Generatio et mors a creatione et abolitione ad compositionem et dissolutionem materiae transferuntur.
Qualitates, historia et tempus a substantiis ad eventa corporum et loci reclas­sificantur.
Genera naturalia definiuntur per semina, compositiones et fines potestatum, non per conversionem arbitrariam elementorum.
Elementa sensibilia ex principiis ultimorum graduum ad effectus compositorum demoventur.
Mundus visibilis ex totalitate finita et centrata in dispositionem localem intra infinitam summam convertitur.
Oppositio inter carmen et rationem dissolvitur: carmen fit instrumentum transmissionis, ratio autem manet norma probationis.
Surface — Exponuntur principia rerum ut lector a religione et metu mortis ad cognitionem naturae traducatur.
Structural — Generatio, motus, mutatio et interitus per corpora, inane, primordia et leges compositionis explicantur.
Metastrategic — Auctoritas religionis debilitatur, sensus cum ratione componitur et voluptas poetica ad doctrinam difficilem recipiendam adhibetur.
Ontological/Temporal — Realitas primaria est corpus in inani; qualitates et tempus dependent, materia manet, summa caret termino, ordo autem ex processu infinito nascitur.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad restituendam catenam centralem a conservatione materiae ad corpora prima, inane, compositionem et infinitatem.
Structura firmissima est nexus inter impossibilitatem creationis aut annihilationis et necessitatem substrati aeterni.
Probatio inanis et corporum invisibilium cohaeret quatenus effectus sensibiles ad causas corporeas inferendas admittuntur.
Natura animi, status post mortem et plena dissolutio terroris adhuc programmatice proponuntur, non hoc libro perfecte demonstrantur.
Causa prima motus, genera atomorum et mechanica plena concursuum nondum satis determinantur.
Commissura epistemica manet inter fidem sensuum et necessitatem rationis quae apparentiam corrigit; regula correctionis non omnino formalizatur.
Notio minimi inseparabilis atomum partibus constare concedit, sed eandem atomum simplicem et indivisibilem retinet; relatio inter partem et divisionem tensionem servat.
Invocatio Veneris cum deorum remotione cohaeret tantum si vis deae non tamquam interventio physica, sed tamquam figura generationis et pacis accipitur.
Lacunae finales plenam restitutionem argumenti contra medium cosmicum impediunt, sed motum ab infinitate ad cosmologiam non centralem non evertunt.
It is asked by what principles the nature of things consists and how knowledge of them dissolves religious terror.
Nature consists of primary bodies and void; generations, changes, and destructions are compositions or dissolutions of permanent matter.
The argument is diagnostic, demonstrative, polemical, and reconstructive: it uncovers the cause of terror, proves the principles of nature, excludes rival models, and restores the cosmological field.
The diagnostic movement proceeds from ignorance of causes and of the mind's nature to fear, from fear to the domination of religion, and thence to the necessity of natural reason.
The probative movement proceeds from sensible effects to invisible bodies, from the existence of motion to void, and from both to a bipartite ontology.

The reconstructive movement passes from the conservation of matter to solid first-beginnings, from the stability of kinds to the immutability of principles, and thence to variation through order, shape, and motion.
The cosmological movement removes finite, central, and providential models and produces cosmic order from infinite collisions without design.
The nature of the gods is removed from human affairs and is moved neither by merits nor by anger.
Religious terror arises from ignorance of natural causes and of the nature of the mind, and is dissolved by the account of nature.
Sensation is the first trust by which reasoning about hidden things is confirmed.
Nothing is generated from nothing.
Nothing perishes into nothing.
Kinds arise from determinate seeds within the finite powers of nature.
Every nature is, in itself, either body or void.
Body acts and resists by touching, whereas void affords bodies room and yielding for motion.
Qualities, conjunctions, events, and time are not natures in themselves, but depend on bodies, place, and motion.
Generated things are combinations of principles.
First-beginnings are solid and devoid of void.
First-beginnings are eternal.
First-beginnings preserve an immutable nature.
The division of body terminates in inseparable minima.
The diversity of things is brought about by the collision, motion, order, position, and shape of first-beginnings.
The totality of body and void is infinite and has neither an external boundary nor a universal center.
First-beginnings move perpetually and collide with one another by blows.
Stable arrangements arise from innumerable collisions over infinite time without design.
The way of natural reason is not a way of impiety or crime.
Religion is not a necessary safeguard of piety, because it itself can recommend criminal deeds.
Terror of the mind is not dissolved by the rays of the sun or the light of day.
Generation is not production from nothing.
Destruction is not reduction to nothing.
The unobservability of a body does not prove its nonexistence.
Nature is not a full continuum without intervals.
No third nature in itself besides body and void is given.
Time is not a substance separate from the motion and rest of things.
Perceptible fire, air, water, or earth are neither the sole nor sufficient principles of things.
First-beginnings are not homoeomeric particles of the same nature as the mortal things they constitute.
The division of bodies does not proceed to infinity.
The totality of things is not contained by external boundaries.
No universal center toward which all bodies naturally strive is given.
First-beginnings neither chose order by design nor made a compact concerning motions with one another.
The regularity of origins, seasons, and growths requires determinate generative matter.
Death and decay dissolve the connections of bodies, but do not abolish the constituting matter.
Tactile effects and perceptible changes permit the inference of unseen bodies, although the bodies themselves are not discerned by the eyes.
The motion of bodies would be impossible unless void yielded to bodies.
Whatever acts or is touched in itself is body; whatever affords passage without obstacle is void; the rest are dependencies.
Past, present, and future are perceived from the order of events and do not subsist without the motion of things.
The dissolution of composites requires principles that survive dissolution and furnish matter for new compositions.
Inseparable minima prevent infinite division and preserve the simplicity of first-beginnings.
The stability of kinds and the finite power of each thing require an immutable compositional substrate.
The change of a thing is not the conversion of principles into other substances, but the accession, departure, or different arrangement of permanent principles.
Models composed of perceptible elements or homoeomeric parts cannot simultaneously explain motion, conservation, diversity, and the stability of kinds.
Any boundary posited for the totality requires something beyond itself; therefore an ultimate boundary cannot be established.
An ordered world is a local and temporarily stable arrangement within an infinite abundance of matter and void.
Divine threats lose coercive authority when natural events are understood from natural causes and the gods as removed from human administration.
Nature is causally closed: a deficiency in knowledge of a cause does not establish a place for divine intervention.
Generation and destruction constitute a circuit of conservation in which matter is dissolved from some forms and nourishes other forms.
Macroscopic qualities arise from relations among immutable principles and need not inhere in the individual principles in the same form.
Knowledge of nature is empirical in origin but inferential in extension: sensation provides effects, reason reconstructs invisible structure.
Natural possibility is bounded by law: what can arise from the nature of principles and their compositions, not from external will, is determined.
Cosmic order requires neither the necessity of design nor the privilege of a center, but emerges from the selection of durable arrangements amid infinite collisions.
Liberation from religion is not a mere negation of worship, but an epistemic effect of translating terror into a question concerning nature.
An event whose cause is not yet known cannot, solely on account of ignorance, be considered a sign of divinity.
An incorporeal efficient cause within nature is excluded, because action and passion require bodily touch.
Perceptible qualities cannot simultaneously be ultimate principles and the mortal forms of composites.
The absolute conversion of one nature into another is excluded, because without an invariant substrate it would restore creation from nothing and annihilation.
Perceptible appearance is not a complete inventory of reality, although sensation remains the foundation of proof.
Human being, earth, and the visible world possess no privilege of a cosmic center.
The stability of order requires neither intention, a predetermined end, nor the agreement of principles.
Absolute beginning and absolute destruction are excluded from the domain of nature; only compositions and dissolutions are admitted.
Divine providence governing the world is tacitly removed, because the gods are remote and nature suffices through material laws.
Eternal punishments after death cannot remain the foundation of rational action, since their force depends on ignorance of the mind, not on demonstrated nature.
A creator or terminator cannot be situated outside the totality of things, because nothing outside the infinite totality is granted.

The governance of Venus taken literally cannot be reconciled with the removal of the gods; the force of the invocation is tacitly transferred to natural generation, poetic pleasure, and the desire for peace.
The condition of enunciation is constituted thus: Venus's generative force and the peace sought → a mind disposed toward doctrine → investigation of nature.
The mechanism of exposition operates thus: obscure and ungrateful doctrine → sweet-speaking poem → attention retained → reason apprehended.
The diagnostic chain is: ignorance of causes and of the mind → indefinite fear → threats of seers and religion → subjection of the mind.
The epistemic chain is: perceptible effect → trace of invisible cause → reasoning → unseen body confirmed.
The conservation chain is: nothing from nothing and nothing into nothing → permanent substrate → eternal first-beginnings → dissolution without annihilation.
The ontological chain is: touch and action → body; yielding and place → void; the rest → conjunctions or events.
The composition chain is: solid and immutable first-beginnings → different orders, shapes, and motions → different qualities and kinds.
The examination of models proceeds through incompatibility with motion, conservation, minima, and diversity, and excludes monism, elementarism, and homoeomery.
The cosmological chain is: no ultimate shore → infinite space and infinite matter → perpetual collisions → stable arrangements without design → contingent world.

Venus and peace → disposition of the reader → diagnosis of religious terror → establishment of natural reason → principles of conservation → bodies and void → immutable first-beginnings → infinity of the totality → cosmogenesis without design.
Perceptible regularity → determinate seeds → invisible bodies → necessary void → bipartite ontology → configurative composition → exclusion of perceptible principles → closed natural causality.
What previously appeared as an indication of divinity is redescribed as a natural effect whose cause is still to be sought.
The opposition between visible and real collapses; invisible bodies become knowable through their effects.
The ontological field is reordered into body, void, and their dependencies, with a third nature excluded.
Generation and death are transferred from creation and abolition to the composition and dissolution of matter.
Qualities, history, and time are reclassified from substances to events of bodies and place.
Natural kinds are defined by seeds, compositions, and limits of powers, not by the arbitrary conversion of elements.
Perceptible elements are demoted from principles of ultimate rank to effects of composites.
The visible world is converted from a finite and centered totality into a local arrangement within an infinite totality.
The opposition between poem and reason is dissolved: poem becomes an instrument of transmission, while reason remains the norm of proof.
Surface — The principles of things are set forth so that the reader may be led from religion and fear of death to knowledge of nature.
Structural — Generation, motion, change, and destruction are explained through bodies, void, first-beginnings, and laws of composition.
Metastrategic — The authority of religion is weakened, sensation is combined with reason, and poetic pleasure is employed for receiving difficult doctrine.
Ontological/Temporal — Primary reality is body in void; qualities and time are dependent, matter remains, the totality lacks a boundary, and order arises from infinite process.
The axioms suffice to reconstruct the central chain from the conservation of matter to primary bodies, void, composition, and infinity.
The most secure structure is the connection between the impossibility of creation or annihilation and the necessity of an eternal substrate.
The proof of void and invisible bodies coheres insofar as perceptible effects are admitted for inferring bodily causes.
The nature of the mind, the state after death, and the full dissolution of terror are still proposed programmatically, not perfectly demonstrated in this book.
The first cause of motion, the kinds of atoms, and the full mechanics of collisions are not yet sufficiently determined.
An epistemic juncture remains between trust in the senses and the necessity of reason that corrects appearance; the rule of correction is not fully formalized.
The notion of the inseparable minimum allows the atom to consist of parts, yet retains that same atom as simple and indivisible; the relation between part and division preserves a tension.
The invocation of Venus coheres with the removal of the gods only if the goddess's force is understood not as physical intervention, but as a figure of generation and peace.
Final gaps hinder a full reconstruction of the argument against a cosmic center, but do not overturn the movement from infinity to non-central cosmology.
Textus quaerit quomodo motus, differentiae et concilia principiorum qualitates, animantia, mundos atque mutationes mundanas producant.
Rerum natura ex corporibus primis aeternis in infinito inani motis constat, quorum figurae, ordines, positurae, concursus et motus omnia composita sine administratione divina efficiunt.
Argumentatio simul reconstructiva, diagnostica, antiteleologica et therapeutica est: ex effectibus conspicuis causas occultas restituit atque cognitionem earum contra metum adhibet.
Motus progreditur ab insufficientia bonorum externorum ad mechanicam principiorum, inde ad formas et mixturas, tum ad emergentiam sensus, pluralitatem mundorum et mortalitatem mundi.
Probatio alternat inter necessitatem deductam, analogiam ex rebus conspicuis, exclusionem exemplarium aemulorum et reductionem qualitatum ad dispositiones materiales.
Finis strategicus est naturam a providentia et fato clauso liberare, ut metus religiosus, mortis timor et falsa bonorum aestimatio ratione naturali dissolvantur.
Rerum summa corporibus primis et inani infinito constat.
Corpora prima solida, simplicia, magnitudine finita, aeterna atque immutabilia sunt.
Summa materiae neque augetur neque deperit.
Corpora prima per inane numquam quiescunt.
Pondus, plagae et minimum clinamen causas motuum principiorum constituunt.
Corpora in vacuo, quamvis ponderibus imparia, aequa celeritate feruntur.
Clinamen loco temporeque incertum seriem causarum necessariam rumpit.
Figurae principiorum numero finitae sunt, sed principia cuiusque figurae numero infinita sunt.
Proprietates compositorum pendent a figuris, ordinibus, posituris, concursibus et motibus principiorum.
Omnis res conspicua pluribus generibus principiorum permixtis constat.
Non omnia principia omnibus modis inter se conecti possunt.
Principia colore, odore, sapore, calore, frigore, sono et sensu carent.
Vita et sensus ex apto concilio principiorum insensilium oriuntur.
Mors coetum principiorum dissolvit, non principia ipsa.
Materiae corpora numero infinito per spatium infinitum distribuuntur.
Dei in pace a rebus humanis semoti naturam mundi neque propter homines creant neque administrant.
Res mundanae crescunt dum acceptio materiae iacturam superat, consistunt dum aequantur, atque decrescunt dum iactura superat.
Metus animi ratione naturae, non divitiis, nobilitate, imperio aut luce sensibili, depellitur.
Suavitas spectandi laborem alienum non ex aliena vexatione, sed ex conscientia propriae immunitatis nascitur.
Natura corporis aurum, purpuram, splendorem aedium et copias magnas non requirit.
Divitiae, nobilitas, gloria et vis militaris curas, religionem et mortis timorem non expellunt.
Tenebrae animi radiis solis aut luce diei non dissolvuntur.
Principia rerum cessando novos motus producere non possunt.
Motus flammarum sursum non est motus spontaneus contra pondus, sed effectus vis subiectae.
Corpora graviora in vacuo leviora non assequuntur neque hoc modo plagas genitales efficiunt.
Clinamen non est motus obliquus sensibilis, sed declinatio minima.
Mundus propter homines divinitus creatus non est.
Terra neque dea sentiens neque mater divina proprie est; appellatio mythica tantum conceditur, si vera causalitas retinetur.
Quies rerum conspicuarum quietem principiorum non probat.
Omnia principia promiscue omnibus rebus conecti non possunt.
Colores rerum ex principiis coloratis non oriuntur.
Sensus animantium ex principiis iam sentientibus non componitur.
Hic mundus neque unicus neque cosmicum exemplar privilegio singulari praeditum est.
Defectus fecunditatis et labor crescente aetate non ex sola corruptione morali aut pietatis diminutione explicantur.
Generatio est accessio et ordinatio principiorum, interitus autem eorum discessio et redistributio.
Aequalis casus per inane congressus non produceret, nisi plagae et minimum clinamen parallelismum motuum interrumperent.
Clinamen principium motus non fataliter praefixi praebet, quo voluntas animantium intra naturam materialem collocatur.
Durities, fluiditas, penetrabilitas et effectus tactiles ex figuris atomorum et modis conexionis oriuntur.
Color mutari potest sine mutatione principiorum, quia ex ordine, positura, motu et lumine resultat.
Sensus, dolor et voluptas sunt effectus motuum vitalium in composito, non affectiones principiorum singulorum.
Infinitas principiorum similium reproductionem generum sustinet, dum leges conexionis eorum discrimina conservant.
In infinito spatio eadem vis materialis alios congressus mundo nostro similes atque alios mundos efficere debet.
Ordo naturalis ex motibus et limitibus materiae constat neque rectorem divinum requirit.
Mundus, quia compositum materiale est, generationi, incremento, maturitati et ruinae subiacet.
Motus principiorum sub limine sensuum positus quietis speciem in summa conspicua producere potest.
Cognitio causarum materialium religionem timidam et aestimationem falsam bonorum externorum infirmat.
Ontologia compositorum relationalis est: proprietas rei non in semine singulari, sed in modo compositionis residet.
Systema plures ordines temporis distinguit: principia immutabilia, summam materiae sempiternam, concilia temporaria et mundos mortales.
Natura neque fato perfecte clauso neque arbitrio extra naturam posito regitur; necessitas conexionum et clinamen indeterminatum simul operantur.
Mundus noster est concilium locale intra summam infinitam, non terminus aut centrum rerum.
Vita et mors in gradu materiae non sunt potestates absolutae, sed vicissitudines compositionis et dispersionis.
Regularitas generum ex compatibilitate selectiva principiorum nascitur, non ex exemplari divino aut materia homogenea.
Therapia animi a cosmologia pendet, quia securitas efficitur mutando tabulam causalitatis, non augendo potestatem externam.
Falsum esse oportet qualitates conspicuas essentiam intrinsecam principiorum immediate manifestare.
Falsum esse oportet omnem motum novo motui ordine antecedenti necessario necti.
Falsum esse oportet ordinem rerum consilium, usum humanum aut administratorem divinum praesupponere.
Falsum esse oportet singularitatem mundi aut hominis ex ipsa natura inferri.
Falsum esse oportet summam rerum terminum externum, fundum aut receptaculum extra se habere.
Falsum esse oportet identitatem rei ex materia uniformi constitui; identitas ex mixtura ordinata et selectiva pendet.
Falsum esse oportet effectum sensilem tantum ex causis eiusdem qualitatis produci posse.
Falsum esse oportet mutationem naturalem aut senescentiam cosmicam ad historiam moralem hominum reduci.
Falsum esse oportet quietem, colorem, sensum aut stabilitatem in gradu conspicuo observata ad principia eodem modo pertinere.
Summa rerum circa absentiam omnis exterioris ordinatur: nihil est extra quod materiam augeat, minuat aut cursum universum convertat.
Creatio absoluta et annihilatio absoluta excluduntur; novitas tantum ex novo concilio immutabilium oritur.
Natura caret centro, fine providentiae et destinatario privilegiato.
Fundamentum rerum per privationes constituitur: principia stabilia sunt quatenus qualitatibus mortalibus, sensu et mutatione carent.
Nullus status finalis generationis aut interitus admittitur; neutra vis certamen principiorum perpetuo vincit.
Origo particularis voluntatis causaliter indisponibilis manet: clinamen seriem fatalem aperit, sed transitum ab indeterminatione atomica ad arbitrium non complet.
Egestas naturalis minima → falsa amplificatio desideriorum → impotentia bonorum externorum contra metum → necessitas rationis naturae.
Effectus conspicuus → vestigium analogicum → causa materialis occulta → exclusio causae divinae vel qualitatis intrinsecae → confirmatio per consequentias.
Corpora aeterna + inane infinitum → motus perpetuus per pondus, plagas et clinamen → concilia et discidia → generatio et interitus compositorum → summa materiae invariata.
Figurae finitae × exemplaria infinita → compatibilitas selectiva → ordines et positurae variae → genera stabilia et proprietates diversae.
Principia qualitatibus et sensu privata → ordinatio vitalis → sensus et qualitates emergentes → perturbatio ordinis → dolor, mors et dispersio.
Spatium infinitum + materia infinita + eadem causalitas → congressus multiplicati → mundi innumerabiles → remotio privilegii cosmici et providentiae.
Accessio maior quam iactura → incrementum → aequalitas → maturitas → iactura maior quam accessio → senectus et ruina mundi.
Tabula causalitatis materialis → remotio terroris religiosi et fatalis → imminutio cupiditatum falsarum → securitas mentis.
Securitas doctrinae → diagnosis metus et cupiditatis → motus principiorum → clinamen et voluntas → figurae et mixturae → qualitates et sensus emergentes → pluralitas mundorum → senectus mundi.
Apparentia mutabilis → principium immutabile → dispositio materialis → lex conexionis → effectus compositus → exclusio providentiae → applicatio cosmologica et therapeutica.
Bona externa ex remediis animi in adiumenta corporalia limitata reclassificantur.
Qualitates sensibiles ex proprietatibus primariis materiae in effectus dispositionis et relationis convertuntur.
Quies et stabilitas conspicuae ut effectus distantiae et gradus perceptionis denuo describuntur.
Nativitas et mors ex creatione et annihilatione in compositionem et dispersionem transferuntur.
Libertas ex exemptione supernaturali in interruptionem naturalem seriei fatalis reponitur.
Differentia specierum et constantia generum ex legibus compatibilitatis materialis, non ex formis exemplaribus, explicantur.
Mundus ex creatione unica in concilium locale, multiplicabile et mortale reclassificatur.
Dei ex rectoribus causalibus in naturas remotas et causaliter otiosas transferuntur.
Defectus terrae ex signo corruptionis moralis in momentum cycli materialis mundi mutatur.
Gradus superficiei complectitur metus humanos, cupiditates, qualitates sensibiles, motus conspicuos atque indicia incrementi et senectutis.
Gradus structuralis complectitur corpora prima, inane, pondus, plagas, clinamen, figuras, mixturas et leges conexionis.
Gradus metastrategicus apparentias in vestigia causarum convertit atque certamen inter providentiam, fatum et naturalismum materialem aliter constituit.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis distinguit principia immutabilia, compositiones mortales, summam sempiternam et mundos plurales generationi atque ruinae subiectos.
Axiomata proposita sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem a mechanica principiorum ad emergentiam, cosmologiam et therapiam animi.
Firmissima pars systematis est coniunctio conservationis materiae cum explicatione configurationali generationis, qualitatum et mortis.
Nexus inter minimum clinamen et voluntatem conscientem non mechanice demonstratur, sed ex necessitate rumpendi fatum infertur.
Explicationes qualitatum ex figuris et motibus saepe analogia sensibili nituntur, nec exactam correspondentiam inter figuram et effectum determinant.
Deductio mundorum innumerabilium principium plenitudinis adhibet: materia, locus et causa sufficientes ex possibilitate ad necessitatem productionis ducuntur.
Senectus universi ex lege generali compositorum et indiciis terrestribus infertur; transitus ab defectu locali ad ruinam cosmicam breviter munitur.
Immortalitas deorum cum dissolutione compositorum hoc libro non mechanice conciliatur, quia dei causaliter semoti potius quam atomice restituti sunt.
Probationes de magnitudine principiorum, infinitate spatii aliisque fundamentis prioribus libris pendent, iarumque nonnullae commissurae lacunis textus comprimuntur.
Structura interne cohaeret quatenus immutabilitatem principiorum a mutabilitate ordinum constanter distinguit; maxima tensio inter leges certas naturae et clinamen incertum manet.
Restitutio verum motum textus servat: ab effectu ethico ad causam physicam, ab ea ad structuram ontologicam, deinde ad consequentiam cosmologicam et therapeuticam.
The text asks how the motions, differences, and assemblages of principles produce qualities, living beings, worlds, and worldly changes.
The nature of things consists of eternal primary bodies moving in infinite void, whose shapes, orders, positions, collisions, and motions produce all compounds without divine governance.
The argument is simultaneously reconstructive, diagnostic, anti-teleological, and therapeutic: it restores hidden causes from visible effects and employs knowledge of them against fear.

The movement proceeds from the insufficiency of external goods to the mechanics of principles, thence to forms and mixtures, then to the emergence of sensation, the plurality of worlds, and the mortality of the world.
The demonstration alternates between deduced necessity, analogy from visible things, exclusion of rival models, and reduction of qualities to material arrangements.
The strategic aim is to free nature from providence and closed fate, so that religious fear, fear of death, and false valuation of goods may be dissolved by natural reason.
The totality of things consists of primary bodies and infinite void.
Primary bodies are solid, simple, finite in magnitude, eternal, and immutable.
The total quantity of matter neither increases nor perishes.
Primary bodies never rest in the void.
Weight, blows, and the slightest clinamen constitute the causes of the motions of principles.
Bodies in a vacuum, although unequal in weight, are borne at equal speed.
The clinamen, uncertain in place and time, breaks the necessary sequence of causes.
The shapes of principles are finite in number, but the principles of each shape are infinite in number.
The properties of compounds depend on the shapes, orders, positions, collisions, and motions of principles.
Every visible thing consists of several kinds of principles intermixed.
Not all principles can be connected to one another in every way.
Principles lack color, smell, taste, heat, cold, sound, and sensation.
Life and sensation arise from a fitting assemblage of insentient principles.
Death dissolves the aggregate of principles, not the principles themselves.
The bodies of matter are distributed in infinite number through infinite space.
Gods, remote from human affairs in peace, neither create nor govern the nature of the world for the sake of human beings.
Worldly things grow while the intake of matter exceeds loss, remain steady while they are equal, and decline while loss exceeds intake.
Fear of mind is dispelled by the reason of nature, not by riches, nobility, power, or sensible light.
The pleasure of observing another's labor arises not from another's distress, but from awareness of one's own immunity.
The nature of the body does not require gold, purple, the splendor of buildings, or great wealth.
Riches, nobility, glory, and military force do not banish cares, religion, and fear of death.
The darkness of the mind is not dissolved by the rays of the sun or daylight.
The principles of things cannot produce new motions by ceasing.
The upward motion of flames is not spontaneous motion against weight, but the effect of an underlying force.
Heavier bodies do not overtake lighter ones in a vacuum, nor thus produce generative blows.
The clinamen is not a sensible oblique motion, but the slightest deviation.
The world was not divinely created for the sake of human beings.
The earth is properly neither a sentient goddess nor a divine mother; the mythical appellation is granted only if true causality is retained.
The rest of visible things does not prove the rest of principles.
All principles cannot indiscriminately be connected to all things.
The colors of things do not arise from colored principles.
The sensation of living beings is not composed from principles already sentient.
This world is neither unique nor endowed with singular privilege as a cosmic model.
Decline in fertility and toil with advancing age are not explained by moral corruption alone or by a diminution of piety.
Generation is the accession and ordering of principles, whereas destruction is their departure and redistribution.
Equal falling through the void would not produce encounters unless blows and the slightest clinamen interrupted the parallelism of motions.
The clinamen provides the principle of motion not fatally predetermined, whereby the will of living beings is situated within material nature.
Hardness, fluidity, penetrability, and tactile effects arise from the shapes of atoms and modes of connection.
Color can change without a change of principles, because it results from order, position, motion, and light.
Sensation, pain, and pleasure are effects of vital motions in the compound, not affections of individual principles.
The infinity of similar principles sustains the reproduction of kinds, while their laws of connection preserve distinctions.
In infinite space, the same material force must produce other encounters similar to our world and other worlds.
Natural order consists of the motions and limits of matter and requires no divine ruler.
The world, because it is a material compound, is subject to generation, growth, maturity, and ruin.
The motion of principles placed below the threshold of the senses can produce an appearance of rest in the visible totality.
Knowledge of material causes weakens fearful religion and the false valuation of external goods.
The ontology of compounds is relational: the property of a thing resides not in a singular seed, but in the mode of composition.
The system distinguishes several orders of time: immutable principles, the everlasting totality of matter, temporary assemblages, and mortal worlds.
Nature is governed neither by a fate perfectly closed nor by a will situated outside nature; the necessity of connections and indeterminate clinamen operate together.
Our world is a local assemblage within the infinite totality, not the boundary or center of things.
Life and death at the level of matter are not absolute powers, but alternations of composition and dispersion.
The regularity of kinds arises from the selective compatibility of principles, not from a divine model or homogeneous matter.
Therapy of the mind depends on cosmology, because security is achieved by changing the map of causality, not by increasing external power.
It must be false that visible qualities immediately manifest the intrinsic essence of principles.
It must be false that every motion is necessarily connected to a new motion in a preceding order.
It must be false that the order of things presupposes a plan, human use, or a divine governor.
It must be false that the singularity of the world or of the human being is inferred from nature itself.
It must be false that the totality of things has an external boundary, bottom, or receptacle outside itself.
It must be false that the identity of a thing is constituted by uniform matter; identity depends on ordered and selective mixture.
It must be false that a sensible effect can be produced only from causes of the same quality.
It must be false that natural change or cosmic aging is reduced to the moral history of human beings.
It must be false that rest, color, sensation, or stability observed at the visible level belong to principles in the same way.
The totality of things is ordered around the absence of every exterior: there is nothing outside that increases or diminishes matter or redirects the universal course.
Absolute creation and absolute annihilation are excluded; novelty arises only from a new assemblage of immutable things.
Nature lacks a center, an end of providence, and a privileged recipient.
The foundation of things is constituted through privations: principles are stable insofar as they lack mortal qualities, sensation, and change.
No final state of generation or destruction is admitted; neither force perpetually wins the struggle of principles.
The particular origin of will remains causally unavailable: the clinamen opens the fated sequence, but does not complete the transition from atomic indeterminacy to choice.
Minimal natural need → false amplification of desires → impotence of external goods against fear → necessity of the reason of nature.
Visible effect → analogical trace → hidden material cause → exclusion of divine cause or intrinsic quality → confirmation through consequences.
Eternal bodies + infinite void → perpetual motion through weight, blows, and clinamen → assemblages and disintegrations → generation and destruction of compounds → unchanged total quantity of matter.
Finite shapes × infinite instances → selective compatibility → diverse orders and positions → stable kinds and diverse properties.
Principles deprived of qualities and sensation → vital ordering → emergent sensation and qualities → disturbance of order → pain, death, and dispersion.
Infinite space + infinite matter + the same causality → multiplied encounters → innumerable worlds → removal of cosmic privilege and providence.
Intake greater than loss → growth → equality → maturity → loss greater than intake → old age and ruin of the world.
Material map of causality → removal of religious and fatal terror → diminution of false desires → security of mind.

Security through doctrine → diagnosis of fear and desire → motion of principles → clinamen and will → shapes and mixtures → emergent qualities and sensation → plurality of worlds → aging of the world.
Changeable appearance → immutable principle → material arrangement → law of connection → compound effect → exclusion of providence → cosmological and therapeutic application.
External goods are reclassified from remedies of the mind into aids limited to the body.
Sensible qualities are converted from primary properties of matter into effects of arrangement and relation.
Visible rest and stability are redescribed as effects of distance and degree of perception.
Birth and death are transferred from creation and annihilation to composition and dispersion.
Freedom is relocated from supernatural exemption into a natural interruption of the fated sequence.
The difference of species and the constancy of kinds are explained by laws of material compatibility, not by exemplary forms.
The world is reclassified from a unique creation into a local, replicable, and mortal assemblage.
Gods are transferred from causal rulers into remote and causally idle natures.
The decline of the earth is changed from a sign of moral corruption into a phase of the world's material cycle.
The surface level comprises human fears, desires, sensible qualities, visible motions, and signs of growth and old age.
The structural level comprises primary bodies, void, weight, blows, clinamen, shapes, mixtures, and laws of connection.
The metastrategic level converts appearances into traces of causes and reconstitutes the contest between providence, fate, and material naturalism.
The ontological and temporal level distinguishes immutable principles, mortal compositions, the everlasting totality, and plural worlds subject to generation and ruin.
The proposed axioms suffice to reconstruct the sequence from the mechanics of principles to emergence, cosmology, and therapy of the mind.
The firmest part of the system is the conjunction of the conservation of matter with a configurational explanation of generation, qualities, and death.
The connection between the slightest clinamen and conscious will is not mechanically demonstrated, but inferred from the necessity of breaking fate.
Explanations of qualities from shapes and motions often rely on sensible analogy and do not determine an exact correspondence between shape and effect.
The deduction of innumerable worlds employs a principle of plenitude: sufficient matter, place, and cause lead from possibility to the necessity of production.
The aging of the universe is inferred from the general law of compounds and terrestrial indications; the transition from local decline to cosmic ruin is briefly supported.
The immortality of the gods is not mechanically reconciled in this book with the dissolution of compounds, because the gods are reconstructed as causally remote rather than atomically.
Demonstrations concerning the magnitude of principles, the infinity of space, and other foundations depend on earlier books, and some of their joints are compressed by gaps in the text.

The structure coheres internally insofar as it consistently distinguishes the immutability of principles from the mutability of orders; the greatest tension remains between the fixed laws of nature and uncertain clinamen.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement of the text: from ethical effect to physical cause, from this to ontological structure, then to cosmological and therapeutic consequence.
Quaeritur quomodo cognitio naturae animi et animae metum mortis, radicem perturbationis humanae, auferre possit.
Thesis principalis est naturam animi animaeque corpoream, coniunctam, nativam ac mortalem esse, unde mors ad eum qui iam non est nihil pertineat.
Argumentatio diagnostica, physice reconstructiva, polemica et therapeutica est.
Doctrina primordiorum et inanis fundamentum praebet quo terrores divini, Acheruntis opiniones et immortalitas animae dissolvantur.

Motus argumenti procedit ab effectibus timoris ad structuram corporis et animae, deinde a coniunctione, alteratione ac divisione ad mortalitatem, postremo a mortalitate ad nullitatem mali post mortem.
Conclusio physica in conversionem ethicam transit: qui causam perturbationis novit nec mortem fugit nec vitam indefinita possessione, potentia aut mutatione loci explere conatur.
Res naturales ex primordiis corporeis motu aeterno per inane componuntur et dissolvuntur.
Metus mortis et Acheruntis praecipua radix est avaritiae, ambitionis, invidiae, proditionis atque odii vitae.
Terror animi non radiis diei, religione aut professione verbali, sed naturae specie rationeque dissolvitur.
Animus et anima sunt partes constitutivae hominis, non habitus corporis sine sede aut substantia propria.
Animus et anima coniuncti unam naturam efficiunt.
Animus in pectore situs consilium ac regimen tenet, anima autem per corpus dissita motibus eius consentit.
Actio physica fit per tactum, tactus autem sine corpore esse non potest.
Natura animi animaeque corporea est.
Natura animi animaeque ex subtilissimis seminibus caloris, venti, aeris et quartae potestatis nomine carentis componitur.
Sensus ex communibus corporis, animi atque animae motibus oritur.
Animus et anima una cum corpore gignuntur, crescunt, senescunt, aegrescunt et labefactantur.
Quod mutari, dividi, dissipari aut ordine partium transferri potest aeternum esse non potest.
Animus et anima certis corporis sedibus, organis et complexionibus indigent ut nascantur, permaneant et sentiant.
Aeternum manet aut quia ictus soliditate respuit, aut quia ictibus caret, aut quia nullum locum externum habet in quem dissolvatur.
Persona humana ex coniunctione corporis, animi et animae atque ex continuitate motuum sensiferorum constituitur.
Incommodum alicui accidere non potest nisi idem subiectum tempore incommodi existat et sentiat.
Vita nulli mancipio datur, sed omnibus ad tempus usu conceditur, dum materia ad formas posteriores transit.
Poenae Acheruntis sunt figurae timoris, cupiditatis, ambitionis, insatiabilitatis et conscientiae scelerum quae in vita operantur.
Animus non est harmonia neque habitus vitalis corporis nulla in parte situs.
Anima neque incorporea neque simplex est.
Animus non per oculos quasi per fores separatus spectat.
Corpus vivum non est instrumentum prorsus expers sensus, quia sentit ex coniunctione cum anima.
Primordia animae non singulis corporis primordiis alternatim adposita sunt, contra Democriti sententiam relatam.
Animus et anima non possunt extra corpus integre vivere, sentire aut motus vitales continuare.
Anima non est substantia immortalis extrinsecus insinuata, ante corpus perfecta aut inter corpora transmigrans.
Sensus post mortem sine oculis, auribus, naribus, lingua, manibus ceterisque organis consistere non potest.
Acheron, Tartarus, Cerberus, Furiae et poenae infernae non sunt loca aut res post mortem existentes.
Mors non est malum quod mortuus pati, desiderare aut deplorare possit.
Lumen diei, religio intensior et professio audaciae metum occultum non tollunt.
Mutatio loci, divitiarum, honoris aut occupationis causam perturbationis interioris non removet.
Contemptus, egestas et obscuritas, quia mortis quasi limina aestimantur, cupiditatem opum atque honorum acuunt.
Metus mortis, dum mortem evitare conatur, ad proditionem, caedem, dissolutionem amicitiae et mortem voluntariam impellere potest.
Reciproca efficacia animi et corporis, qua metus membra concutit et vulnera mentem afficiunt, coniunctionem corporalem demonstrat.
Quia calor, ventus et aer soli sensum explicare non possunt, quarta vis subtilior ponitur quae motum sensiferum prima initiet.
Quia minima externa corpus tangunt antequam sentiantur, primordia animae rarius quam primordia corporis per membra distributa sunt.
Communis ortus, incrementum, senectus, morbus, ebrietas et curatio animi cum corpore mortalitatem animi indicant.
Gradualis sensus amissio et divisio animae cum membris ostendunt animam partibilem atque ideo mortalem esse.
Quia sensus a certa dispositione corporis et animae pendet, anima e corpore eiecta neque contineri neque sentire potest.
Dissoluta coniunctione constitutiva, nullum idem subiectum superest cui mors nocere possit.
Etiam perfecta eiusdem materiae futura recompositio ad nos non pertineret, si continuitas vitae et memoriae semel interrupta esset.
Insensibilitas temporis ante ortum exemplar praebet insensibilitatis temporis post mortem.
Dolor de propria putrefactione aut laceratione post mortem nascitur ex tacita fictione qua vivus se corpori mortuo adhuc sentientem adstat.
Fabulae infernae futurum locum non describunt, sed passiones, poenas civiles et conscientiae cruciatus praesentis vitae figurant.
Qui causam perturbationis ignorat se ipsum per mutationem loci fugit, sed causam secum transfert.
Productio vitae non minuit futurum tempus non-exsistentiae, quia nullus mortuus diutius aut brevius mortem sentit.
Successio formarum requirit ut vetustas novitati cedat et materia post vitam ad postera saecla redeat.
Physica fit therapeutica, quia correcta ontologia animi tollit subiectum imaginarium cui supplicia post mortem tribuebantur.
Mortalitas animae multipliciter firmatur per compositionem, dependentiam organicam, alterationem, divisibilitatem, localizationem et dissolutionem.
Etiam concessa per hypothesim aliqua sensatione animae separatae, illa ad nos non pertineret sine continuitate coniunctionis qua persona constituitur.
Avaritia, ambitio, invidia et violentia politica denuo intelliguntur ut artes fallaces quibus homo mortem symbolicam per opes, potentiam aut nomen vitare conatur.
Persona non est substantia simplex inter corpora migrans, sed temporaria ordinatio corporis, animi, animae et motuum sensiferorum.
Tempus ante ortum et tempus post mortem ontologice respondent, quamquam imaginatio posterius falso quasi experientiam futuram repraesentat.
Sufficientia vitae non ex indefinita duratione aut novitate rerum, sed ex termino cupiditatis et aequa cessationis acceptione oritur.
Mythologia inferorum in cartam affectuum praesentium convertitur, qua terror divinus, libido, ambitio, insatiabilitas et culpa diversis figuris ordinantur.
Falsum esse debet dualismum secundum quem mens integra corpori extrinsecus advenit et ab eo separata easdem operationes retinet.
Falsum esse debet subiectum propriae non-exsistentiae testem, victimam aut possessorem esse posse.
Falsum esse debet identitatem personalem ex sola identitate materiae sine continuitate sensus et memoriae restitui.
Falsum esse debet naturam immortalem substantialiter mutari, aegrescere, sanari, dividi aut ordinem partium commutare posse.
Falsum esse debet infinitam vitae productionem novitatem qualitativam aut ultimam satietatem necessario parere.
Falsum esse debet opes, honores, nomen aut potentiam metum mortis abolere posse.
Falsum esse debet ordinem moralem post mortem per loca, iudices et tormenta externa compleri.
Falsum esse debet perturbationem interiorem mutatione domicilii, itineris aut occupationis curari posse.
Falsum esse debet professionem doctrinalem firmam convictionem probare, quia adversitas opiniones tacitas aperit.
Nulla res transcendens personam integram post dissolutionem corporis reservat.
Nullus prospectus personalis trans mortis terminum continuatur ex quo mors ut status proprius experiatur.
Nulla exceptio individualis hominem a communi compositionis, dissolutionis et restitutionis materiae lege eximit.
Nullum obiectum futurum cupiditatem per se claudit, quia desiderium absentis post adeptam rem in aliud transfertur.
Nullum theatrum posthumum requiritur ut culpa puniatur, quia mens sibi conscia poenam praesentem anticipando constituit.
Vita neque perpetua possessio neque debitum naturae est, sed usus temporarius materiae communis.
Mors non est experientia extrema vitae, sed terminus quo ipsa possibilitas experientiae aufertur.
Machina epistemica initium capit hac serie: primordia et inane → natura sine interventu divino explicabilis → moenia mundi aperta → terror religiosus imminutio.
Machina diagnostica hac serie operatur: metus mortis → egestas et contemptus quasi mortis imagines → opes, honores et violentia ut fugae → maior perturbatio.
Machina reconstructiva procedit per distinctionem: animus centralis et regens / anima diffusa et consentiens / corpus commune / motus sensifer ex coniunctione.
Machina mortalitatis hac serie concludit: compositio corporea → dependentia organica → communis alteratio → divisibilitas → dissipatio → impossibilitas immortalitatis.
Machina identitatis hac serie clauditur: dissolutio coniunctionis → interruptio continuitatis → absentia eiusdem subiecti → impossibilitas mali post mortem.
Machina temporalis utitur symmetria: nulla experientia ante ortum → nulla experientia post dissolutionem → posteritas non magis timenda quam praeterita vetustas.
Machina mythologica convertit inferos futuros in figuras passionum, poenarum et conscientiae iam praesentium.
Machina therapeutica concludit: cognitio causae → cessatio fugae exterioris → limitatio cupiditatis → acceptio mortalitatis → tranquillitas vitae finitae.
Epicuri ratio naturae → diagnosis timoris Acheruntis → constitutio corporea animi et animae → probatio mortalitatis → remotio subiecti post mortem → mors nihil ad nos → conversio vitae praesentis.
Motus probatorius est: efficacia tactilis → corporeitas → compositio subtilis → coniunctio organica → alteratio et divisio → dissolutio.
Motus therapeuticus est: terror occultus → cupiditas compensatoria → frustratio recursiva → cognitio causae → terminus desiderii → aequa cessatio.
Mens et anima ex substantiis separabilibus in organizationem materialem localem et mortalem transferuntur.
Sensus ex proprietate animae solitariae in effectum communium motuum corporis, animi et animae reclassificatur.
Mors ex statu futuro ab homine patiendo in absentiam subiecti patientis convertitur.
Avaritia, ambitio, invidia et violentia ex vitiis discretis in effectus secundarios timoris mortis rediguntur.
Identitas personalis non amplius ex materia eadem, sed ex coniunctione et continuitate motuum sensiferorum describitur.
Inferi ex geographia posthuma in cartam passionum, poenarum civilium et conscientiae praesentis transferuntur.
Ager therapeuticus a religione, mutatione loci et amplificatione vitae ad cognitionem naturae et limitationem cupiditatis transfertur.
Gradus superficiei tractat metum mortis, naturam animi animaeque et quaestionem num aliquid post mortem sentiri possit.
Gradus structuralis exponit compositionem atomicam, localizationem, hierarchiam animi et animae, coniunctionem organicam atque productionem sensus.
Gradus metastrategicus mutat certamen contra mortem in certamen contra errorem quo vivus se post mortem adhuc sentientem fingit.
Gradus ontologicus et temporalis personam definit ut coniunctionem materialem finitam, identitatem ut continuitatem, mortem ut interruptionem et materiam ut successionis communis fundamentum.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad restituendam seriem a physica animi per probationem mortalitatis ad conclusionem mortem nihil ad nos esse.
Minus determinatus manet transitus a figuris et mobilitate primordiorum ad qualitatem sensus, quam quarta natura nomine carens explere debet.
Lacunae fontis nexus locales circa refutationem harmoniae et condiciones immortalitatis minuunt, sed motum principalem non interrumpunt.
Systema maxime cohaeret ubi dependentiam organicam, alterationem, divisionem et absentiam subiecti in probationem cumulativam coniungit.
Firmissima clausura est quod malum sine subiecto sentiente consistere non potest, etiam si hypothesis aliqua posthuma ad tempus concedatur.
Commissura fragilis est principium secundum quod omnis mutatio substantialis morti rei prioris aequiparatur, quia hoc principium potius assumitur quam plene demonstratur.
Tensio manet inter unitatem animi et animae atque hierarchiam qua animus dominatur, anima paret et quarta vis sensum initiare dicitur.
Restitutio verum motum textus servat: indicia perturbationis → physica coniunctionis → mortalitas → nulla experientia mortis → reordinatio vitae praesentis.
It is asked how knowledge of the nature of the mind and soul can remove the fear of death, the root of human disturbance.
The principal thesis is that the nature of the mind and soul is corporeal, conjoined, born, and mortal, whence death pertains in no way to one who no longer exists.
The argumentation is diagnostic, physically reconstructive, polemical, and therapeutic.
The doctrine of first-beginnings and void provides the foundation by which divine terrors, beliefs about Acheron, and the immortality of the soul are dissolved.

The movement of the argument proceeds from the effects of fear to the structure of body and soul, then from conjunction, alteration, and division to mortality, and finally from mortality to the nullity of evil after death.
The physical conclusion passes into an ethical conversion: one who knows the cause of disturbance neither flees death nor tries to fill life through indefinite possession, power, or change of place.
Natural things are compounded and dissolved from corporeal first-beginnings in eternal motion through the void.
Fear of death and of Acheron is the chief root of greed, ambition, envy, treachery, and hatred of life.
Terror of mind is dissolved not by the rays of day, religion, or verbal profession, but by the aspect and reason of nature.
Mind and soul are constitutive parts of the human being, not a condition of the body without a seat or substance of their own.
Mind and soul conjoined produce one nature.
The mind, situated in the breast, holds deliberation and governance, while the soul, dispersed through the body, accords with its motions.
Physical action occurs through touch, and touch cannot exist without body.
The nature of mind and soul is corporeal.
The nature of mind and soul is composed of the most subtle seeds of heat, wind, air, and a fourth power lacking a name.
Sensation arises from the shared motions of body, mind, and soul.
Mind and soul are generated, grow old, become diseased, and are weakened together with the body.
What can be changed, divided, dissipated, or transferred by an ordering of parts cannot be eternal.
Mind and soul require definite seats, organs, and constitutions of the body in order to be born, persist, and sense.
What is eternal remains so either because it repels blows by solidity, or because it lacks blows, or because it has no external place into which it may dissolve.
The human person is constituted from the conjunction of body, mind, and soul, and from the continuity of sentient motions.
A harm cannot happen to anyone unless that same subject exists and senses at the time of the harm.
Life is given to no one as property, but granted to all for temporary use, while matter passes into later forms.
The punishments of Acheron are figures of fear, desire, ambition, insatiability, and consciousness of crimes operating in life.
The mind is neither harmony nor a vital condition of the body situated in no part.
The soul is neither incorporeal nor simple.
The mind does not see separately through the eyes as though through doors.
The living body is not an instrument wholly devoid of sensation, because it senses through conjunction with the soul.
The first-beginnings of the soul are not placed alternately alongside the individual first-beginnings of the body, contrary to the reported view of Democritus.
Mind and soul cannot live, sense, or continue vital motions intact outside the body.
The soul is not an immortal substance introduced from without, complete before the body, or transmigrating among bodies.
Sensation after death cannot subsist without eyes, ears, nostrils, tongue, hands, and the other organs.
Acheron, Tartarus, Cerberus, the Furies, and infernal punishments are not places or things existing after death.
Death is not an evil that the dead person can suffer, desire, or lament.
The light of day, more intense religion, and a profession of boldness do not remove hidden fear.
A change of place, wealth, honor, or occupation does not remove the cause of inner disturbance.
Contempt, poverty, and obscurity, because they are judged to be as it were thresholds of death, sharpen the desire for wealth and honors.
Fear of death, while attempting to avoid death, can impel one toward treachery, slaughter, the dissolution of friendship, and voluntary death.
The reciprocal efficacy of mind and body, whereby fear shakes the limbs and wounds affect the mind, demonstrates corporeal conjunction.
Because heat, wind, and air alone cannot explain sensation, a subtler fourth force is posited that first initiates sentient motion.
Because the smallest external things touch the body before they are sensed, the first-beginnings of the soul are distributed through the limbs more sparsely than the first-beginnings of the body.
The shared origin, growth, old age, disease, drunkenness, and treatment of mind with body indicate the mortality of mind.
The gradual loss of sensation and the division of the soul with the limbs show that the soul is divisible and therefore mortal.
Because sensation depends on a definite disposition of body and soul, the soul expelled from the body can neither be contained nor sense.
Once the constitutive conjunction is dissolved, no same subject remains to which death can do harm.
Even a future perfect recomposition of the same matter would not pertain to us if the continuity of life and memory had once been interrupted.
The insensibility of time before birth provides a model for the insensibility of time after death.
Pain concerning one's own putrefaction or mutilation after death arises from the tacit fiction by which, living, one imagines oneself still present to the dead body as sensing.
Infernal tales do not describe a future place, but figure the passions, civil punishments, and torments of conscience of present life.
One who does not know the cause of disturbance flees oneself through a change of place, but carries the cause along.
The prolongation of life does not diminish future time of non-existence, because no dead person senses death for longer or shorter.
The succession of forms requires that oldness yield to newness and that matter return after life to later ages.
Physics becomes therapeutic because a corrected ontology of mind removes the imaginary subject to which punishments after death were attributed.
