The mortality of the soul is established in multiple ways through composition, organic dependence, alteration, divisibility, localization, and dissolution.
Even if some sensation of the separated soul were granted by hypothesis, it would not pertain to us without the continuity of conjunction by which the person is constituted.
Greed, ambition, envy, and political violence are understood anew as deceptive arts by which a human being attempts to avoid symbolic death through wealth, power, or name.
The person is not a simple substance migrating among bodies, but a temporary ordering of body, mind, soul, and sentient motions.
Time before birth and time after death correspond ontologically, although imagination falsely represents the latter as though it were a future experience.
The sufficiency of life arises not from indefinite duration or novelty of things, but from the limit of desire and an equitable acceptance of cessation.
The mythology of the underworld is converted into a map of present affects, in which divine terror, desire, ambition, insatiability, and guilt are arranged under diverse figures.
It must be false that dualism according to which an intact mind comes to the body from without and, separated from it, retains the same operations.
It must be false that a subject can be witness, victim, or possessor of its own non-existence.
It must be false that personal identity is restored from identity of matter alone without continuity of sensation and memory.
It must be false that an immortal nature can be substantially changed, become diseased, be healed, divided, or alter the order of its parts.
It must be false that an infinite prolongation of life necessarily produces qualitative novelty or ultimate satiety.
It must be false that wealth, honors, name, or power can abolish the fear of death.
It must be false that the moral order is fulfilled after death through places, judges, and external torments.
It must be false that inner disturbance can be cured by a change of dwelling, journey, or occupation.
It must be false that doctrinal profession proves firm conviction, because adversity reveals tacit beliefs.
No transcendent thing preserves the intact person after the dissolution of the body.
No personal perspective continues beyond the boundary of death from which death might be experienced as one's own state.
No individual exception exempts a human being from the common law of composition, dissolution, and restoration of matter.
No future object closes desire by itself, because desire for what is absent transfers to another thing once the thing has been attained.
No posthumous theater is required for guilt to be punished, because the self-conscious mind constitutes present punishment by anticipating it.
Life is neither perpetual possession nor a debt owed to nature, but the temporary use of common matter.
Death is not the ultimate experience of life, but the boundary at which the very possibility of experience is removed.
The epistemic machine begins with this sequence: first-beginnings and void → nature explicable without divine intervention → walls of the world opened → diminution of religious terror.
The diagnostic machine operates through this sequence: fear of death → poverty and contempt as images of death → wealth, honors, and violence as escapes → greater disturbance.
The reconstructive machine proceeds through a distinction: central and governing mind / diffuse and accordant soul / common body / sentient motion from conjunction.
The mortality machine concludes through this sequence: corporeal composition → organic dependence → shared alteration → divisibility → dissipation → impossibility of immortality.
The identity machine closes through this sequence: dissolution of conjunction → interruption of continuity → absence of the same subject → impossibility of evil after death.
The temporal machine employs symmetry: no experience before birth → no experience after dissolution → posterity no more to be feared than past antiquity.
The mythological machine converts the future underworld into figures of passions, punishments, and conscience already present.
The therapeutic machine concludes: knowledge of the cause → cessation of external flight → limitation of desire → acceptance of mortality → tranquility of finite life.

Epicurus' account of nature → diagnosis of fear of Acheron → corporeal constitution of mind and soul → proof of mortality → removal of the subject after death → death is nothing to us → conversion of present life.
The probative movement is: tactile efficacy → corporeality → subtle composition → organic conjunction → alteration and division → dissolution.
The therapeutic movement is: hidden terror → compensatory desire → recurrent frustration → knowledge of the cause → limit of desire → equitable cessation.
Mind and soul are transferred from separable substances into a local and mortal material organization.
Sensation is reclassified from a property of the solitary soul into an effect of the shared motions of body, mind, and soul.
Death is converted from a future state to be undergone by a human being into the absence of a subject undergoing it.
Greed, ambition, envy, and violence are reduced from distinct vices to secondary effects of fear of death.
Personal identity is no longer described from the same matter, but from conjunction and the continuity of sentient motions.
The underworld is transferred from posthumous geography into a map of passions, civil punishments, and present conscience.
The therapeutic field is transferred from religion, change of place, and enlargement of life to knowledge of nature and limitation of desire.
The surface level treats fear of death, the nature of mind and soul, and the question whether anything can be sensed after death.
The structural level expounds atomic composition, localization, the hierarchy of mind and soul, organic conjunction, and the production of sensation.
The metastrategic level changes the struggle against death into a struggle against the error by which the living person imagines oneself still sensing after death.
The ontological and temporal level defines the person as a finite material conjunction, identity as continuity, death as interruption, and matter as the foundation of common succession.
The extracted axioms suffice to reconstruct the sequence from the physics of mind through proof of mortality to the conclusion that death is nothing to us.
Less determinate remains the transition from the shapes and mobility of first-beginnings to the quality of sensation, which the nameless fourth nature must fulfill.
Gaps in the source lessen local connections around the refutation of harmony and the conditions of immortality, but do not interrupt the principal movement.
The system is most coherent where it joins organic dependence, alteration, division, and absence of the subject into a cumulative proof.
The strongest closure is that evil cannot subsist without a sensing subject, even if some posthumous hypothesis is conceded temporarily.
A fragile joint is the principle according to which every substantial change is equated with the death of the prior thing, because this principle is assumed rather than fully demonstrated.
A tension remains between the unity of mind and soul and the hierarchy by which mind rules, soul obeys, and the fourth force is said to initiate sensation.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement of the text: signs of disturbance → physics of conjunction → mortality → no experience of death → reordering of present life.
Quaeritur quomodo perceptio, cogitatio, somnus, actio, cupiditas et generatio ex principiis corporeis explicari possint sine animis immortalibus, providentia aut causis finalibus.
Omnes hae operationes ex emissione, transmissione, congruentia et ictu corporum tenuissimorum oriuntur.
Argumentatio est materialiter reconstructiva, adversus superstitionem, scepticismum et finalitatem polemica, atque doctrinae asperae lepore poetico tradendae strategice accommodata.
Ex doctrina primordiorum proceditur ad necessitatem simulacrorum, inde ad mechanismum visionis et ad apparentium errorum dissolutionem.
Defensio sensuum errorem ab affectione sensibili ad opiniones animi transfert atque sensus fundamentum rationis constituit.
Eadem grammatica corporei contactus ad auditum, saporem, odorem, cogitationem, somnum, voluntatem et motum extenditur.
Analysis denique ad usum membrorum, cupiditatem Veneream, captivitatem amoris et generationem transfertur, ut causalitas naturalis simul cognitionem et regimen affectuum ordinet.
Omnes res, animus atque anima inclusi, ex primordiis corporeis componuntur.
Primordia figura, magnitudine, motu, ordine et textura differunt.
Ex rebus corpora perpetuo fluunt et in omnes partes emittuntur.
Simulacra sunt texturae tenuissimae quae a superficie rerum emissae formam coloremque originis servant.
Omnis sensus corporeo ictu proprii nuntii movetur.
Cuique sensui potestas propria et ab aliis sensibus distincta est.
Qualitas sensibilis ex congruentia figurarum incidentium cum viis et textura recipientis oritur.
Tenuitas, medium, spatium, obstacula et rectitudo itineris transmissionem corporum determinant.
Simulacra possunt in aere constitui vel ex imaginibus diversarum rerum coalescere.
Animus simulacris tenuioribus quam quae oculos movent corpore penetrantibus lacessitur.
Animus ex copia imaginum eas potissimum recipit ad quas attentione, habitu aut statu corporis praeparatus est.
Quod cuique sensui suo tempore apparet verum est quatenus affectio illius sensus est.
Falsitas oritur ex opinionibus quas animus rebus sensu datis adiungit.
Notitia veri a sensibus initium capit, atque ratio sensuum fide nititur.
Structura membrorum usum antecedit, et quod natum est facultatem utendi postea gignit.
Vita animalis a distributione, coniunctione et motibus animae corporeae per membra pendet.
Voluntas agendi oritur postquam animus imaginem actionis futurae concepit.
Cupiditas Venerea est perturbatio materialis seminis a simulacro vel corpore congruo excitata.
Partus ex concursu et congruentia seminum maternorum atque paternorum constat.
Simulacra mortuorum non probant animas ab Acherunte redire neque aliquid personale post corporis et animi dissolutionem superesse.
Simulacra singillatim videri non possunt, quamvis creber eorum concursus rem visibilem efficiat.
Fallaciae perspectivae non demonstrant oculos ipsos mentiri.
Sententia nihil sciri posse se ipsam sine contradictione affirmare non potest.
Ratio a sensibus orta sensus tamquam universaliter falsos refellere non potest.
Unus sensus potestatem propriam alterius sensus iudicare aut convincere non potest.
Centauri, Scyllae et imagines mortuorum non requirunt naturas animatas sibi correspondentes.
Echoes et soni repercussi Satyrorum, Nympharum, Faunorum aut Panis praesentiam non requirunt.
Simulacra voluntatem humanam non perspiciunt neque arte instructa motus somniorum componunt.
Oculi, lingua, aures et membra non sunt ad futuros usus creata.
Somnus non est plena animae e corpore expulsio.
Sterilitas et fecunditas non a numinibus divinis distribuuntur.
Voluptas Venerea amorem exclusivum non requirit, neque amor possessione corporis amati satiatur.
Repentina imago specularis ex adsiduo simulacrorum fluxu et repercussu oritur.
Simulacra ob tenuitatem, levitatem et positionem superficialem figuram servant atque velocissime feruntur.
Visio fit cum simulacrum oculos ferit, distantia autem ex aere interposito ante imaginem moto percipitur.
Situs, inversio et multiplicatio imaginum specularium ex ordine aerum, repercussionum et flexuum superficiei oriuntur.
Figurae remotae, lumina, umbrae et corpora refracta aliter apparent cum transmissio ictibus, intervallis aut mediis mutatur.
Apparentia sensibilis recte praesentem affectionem indicat, dum error ex iudicio de causa, identitate aut motu rei nascitur.
Vox corpus est quod a loquente emissum aures ferit, per spatium confunditur, in plures partes dividitur et a solidis repercutitur.
Sapores et odores secundum figuram particularum, magnitudinem viarum et texturam animalis diversa vel contraria efficiunt.
Monstra imaginata ex concursu imaginum verarum partium componuntur, non ex existentia monstrorum correspondentium.
In somno simulacra mentem movent dum sensus externi quiescunt et memoria correctionem praesentis rei non suppeditat.
Cogitatio voluntaria non imagines ad nutum creat, sed ex copia iam praesenti imagines attentioni congruentes seligit.
Motus voluntarius procedit ab imagine motus ad voluntatem, a voluntate ad animam per membra diffusam, atque inde ad corpus aere adiutum.
Somnus oritur cum ictus externi et interiores dispositionem animae perturbant, partem expellunt et partem in interiora contrudunt.
Fames et sitis sunt effectus amissionis corporum, rarefactionis membrorum et necessitatis materiam congruentem restituendi.
Utilitas membrorum est effectus posterior structurae iam natae, non causa originis eius.
Voluptas Venerea utrique sexui communis esse potest quia utriusque corpus congruo ictu et mutuo ardore movetur.
Amor exclusivus crescit cum simulacra, memoria et opinio idem obiectum continenter repetunt, quamvis corpus ex imaginibus satiari non possit.
Similitudo, varietas hereditaria et fecunditas ex proportione, mixtura et compatibilitate duplicis seminis oriuntur.
Visio, auditus, odoratus, gustus, cogitatio et cupiditas unam grammaticam materialem emissionis, itineris, ictus et congruentiae variant.
Veritas sensibilis et falsitas iudicialis ad diversos gradus pertinent, unde apparentia servari potest dum interpretatio corrigitur.
Apparitiones mortuorum, monstra, deos locorum et motus somniorum explicatio materialis ex indicibus alterius mundi in effectus transmissionis reclasificat.
Agens humanum non est principium motus a materia separatum, sed nexus imaginum, attentionis, voluntatis, animae et corporis.
Facultates biologicae et usus historice emergunt ex structuris, congruentiis et consuetudinibus iam constitutis.
Amor est circuitus recursivus in quo imago cupiditatem excitat, cupiditas opinionem auget, opinio attentionem figit, et attentio imaginem perpetuat.
Continuitas apparentis rei vel motus ex successione celerrima formarum pereuntium et substitutarum construitur.
Correctio affectuum fit non sensibus repudiatis, sed opinionibus retractatis, attentione conversa et imaginum pabulo interrupto.
Qualitates sensibiles non sunt valores absoluti in obiecto clausi, sed relationes inter figuras incidentes et structuram recipientis.
Nulla perceptio fit per accessum incorporeum aut sine medio ad essentiam rei.
Stabilitas imaginis non requirit formam permanentem, quia successio formarum discretarum effectum continuitatis praestat.
Voluntas non incipit ex nihilo, sed ab imagine praevia et dispositione materiali dependet.
Futurus usus non potest esse causa temporalis organi iam ante usum constituti.
Pulchritudo amata non continet necessario perfectiones quas cupiditas ei attribuit.
Mens non stat extra naturam ut imaginum fluxum absolute regat aut sensuum testimonium ex fundamento extrinseco iudicet.
Causa divina admitti non debet ubi differentia figurarum, motuum et congruentiarum effectum sufficit producere.
Systema nullo ordinatore providentiali indiget qui sensus, membra, cupiditates aut generationem ad fines praestitutos dirigat.
Nullum tribunal cognitionis extra sensus et ab eis independens praesto est.
Nullum subiectum personale permanens dissolutionem corporis et animi integrum superat.
Possessio totalis corporis amati impossibilis est, quia amanti simulacra tantum incorporantur, non ipsum corpus alterius.
Praesentia immobilis rerum excluditur, quoniam perceptio et vita ex fluxu, ictu, substitutione et recompositione constant.
Primordia figurata → compositio rerum → effluxus corporeus → transmissio → ictus recipientis → affectio sensibilis.
Superficies rei → simulacrum formam retinens → motus per aerem → oculus percussus → species rei → distantia ex aere propulso.
Affectio sensibilis vera → opinio animi addita → falsa causalitatis vel identitatis assignatio → ratio sensibus innixa → distinctio dati ab addito.
Differentia figurarum et viarum → diversa penetratio vel repercussio → distinctio visus, vocis, odoris et saporis → varietas secundum recipientem.
Copia simulacrorum → compositio vel successio → praeparatio attentionis aut habitus → imago mentalis → cogitatio, somnium vel apparitio.
Ictus aut amissio corporum → mutatio dispositionis animae et corporis → somnus, fames, sitis vel cupiditas → restitutio aut motus compensatorius.
Structura nata → actio possibilis → repetitio → usus agnitus → ars vel consuetudo; futurus usus causam originis non constituit.
Simulacrum amati → commotio seminis → cupiditas → opinio idealizans → attentio fixa → insatiabilitas → dolor; conversio attentionis circuitum frangit.
Semen duplex → concursus → proportio et congruentia → conceptio → mixtura primordiorum parentum atque maiorum → figura prolis.
Atomismus iam constitutus → quaestio de apparitionibus → positio simulacrorum → probatio per emissiones et specula → explicatio visionis.
Varietas apparentiarum → analysis mediorum et ictuum → distinctio sensus ab opinione → refutatio scepticismi → sensus ut fundamentum rationis.
Communis causalitas corporea → auditus, gustus et odoratus → imagines mentales et somnia → voluntas, motus et somnus → repudiatio finalitatis.
Physiologia seminis → cupiditas Venerea → diagnosis amoris captivi → regimen attentionis → generatio et consuetudo materialiter explicatae.
Perceptio ex receptione passiva speciei incorporeae in commercium materiale emittere, transire et ferire reordinatur.
Oppositio simplicis apparentiae et veritatis solvitur per distinctionem inter affectionem sensus et opinionem animi.
Diversi sensus tamquam canales distincti unius causalitatis corporeae, non tamquam iudices mutuo substituendi, disponuntur.
Somnia, monstra, umbrae mortuorum et voces locorum ex ordine supernaturali in ordinem imaginum compositarum et repercussarum transferuntur.
Utilitas membrorum ex causa originis in effectum posterioris usus convertitur.
Actio voluntaria ex imperio immateriali in seriem materialem imaginationis, voluntatis, animae et corporis transfertur.
Amor a valore absoluto obiecti separatur et tamquam captatio per simulacra, opinionem, habitum et attentionem describitur.
Fecunditas, hereditas et differentia prolis ex dominio divino in agrum compatibilitatis materialis seminum reponuntur.
Surface — Imagines speculares, errores perspectivi, voces, sapores, odores, somnia, motus, cupiditates et generationes sunt obiecta immediata explicanda.
Structural — Omnia obiecta per emissionem corporum, vias mediorum, congruentiam texturarum et ictus organorum conectuntur.
Metastrategic — Textus certamen a repudiatione sensuum ad separationem affectionis ab opinione transfert atque superstitionem, scepticismum et finalitatem eodem motu debilitare conatur.
Ontological/Temporal — Realitas est compositio corporum in fluxu, subiectum est nexus corporeus mobilis, et continuitas ex successione celerrima effectuum nascitur.
Axiomata extracta sufficiunt ad motum principalem a simulacris ad sensus, mentem, physiologiam, amorem et generationem restituendum.
Lacunae fontis demonstrationes de subtilitate imaginum, earum generatione, speculis et quibusdam somniorum exemplis incompletas relinquunt.
Cohaerentia firmissima est ubi unum exemplar emissionis, itineris et ictus plures sensus et processus corporales explicat.
Defensio sensuum stabilitur per distinctionem inter id quod sensus patitur et id quod animus de causa affectionis conicit.
Probatio simulacrorum invisibilium analogiis emissionum visibilium et exclusione causarum aemularum nititur, non inspectione directa.
Assertio omne sensibile apparens esse verum cum apparentibus distortionibus conciliatur tantum si veritas ad affectionem, non ad omne iudicium de obiecto, restringitur.
Ratio tota a sensibus pendere dicitur, quamvis primordia, simulacra singula et tempora minima sensum excedant; transitus inferentialis non plene formalizatur.
Origo imaginum sponte in aere factarum et exacta selectio simulacrorum ab attentione causata minus determinate explicantur quam transmissio sensibilis.
Pars erotica a mechanismo materiali ad praeceptum evitandi vel avertendi amorem per aestimationem poenae transit, non per deductionem physicam omnino necessariam.
Restitutio verum textus motum servat: a fluxu corporeo ad cognitionem, ab errore ad opinionem, a functione ad emergentiam, atque a cupiditate ad captationem et regimen.
It is asked how perception, thought, sleep, action, desire, and generation can be explained from bodily principles without immortal souls, providence, or final causes.
All these operations arise from the emission, transmission, congruence, and impact of the most subtle bodies.
The argument is materially reconstructive, polemical against superstition, scepticism, and finality, and strategically adapted for conveying a harsh doctrine with poetic charm.
From the doctrine of first beginnings one proceeds to the necessity of simulacra, thence to the mechanism of vision and the dissolution of apparent errors.
The defence of the senses transfers error from sensible affection to the opinions of the mind and establishes the senses as the foundation of reason.
The same grammar of bodily contact is extended to hearing, taste, smell, thought, sleep, will, and motion.
Finally, the analysis is transferred to the use of limbs, Venusian desire, the captivity of love, and generation, so that natural causality may order both knowledge and the governance of the affects.
All things, including mind and soul, are composed of bodily first beginnings.
First beginnings differ in shape, size, motion, order, and texture.
Bodies continually flow from things and are emitted in all directions.
Simulacra are the most subtle textures which, emitted from the surface of things, preserve the form and color of their source.
Every sense is moved by the bodily impact of its proper messenger.
Each sense has a power proper to itself and distinct from the other senses.
Sensible quality arises from the congruence of impacting shapes with the passages and texture of the recipient.
Subtlety, medium, space, obstacles, and straightness of path determine the transmission of bodies.
Simulacra can be formed in the air or coalesce from images of different things.
The mind is struck by simulacra subtler than those which move the eyes and which penetrate the body.
From an abundance of images, the mind chiefly receives those for which it has been prepared by attention, habit, or bodily state.
What appears to each sense at its own time is true insofar as it is an affection of that sense.
Falsity arises from the opinions which the mind adds to things given by sense.
Knowledge of truth takes its beginning from the senses, and reason depends upon the trustworthiness of the senses.
The structure of limbs precedes use, and what has been born afterwards produces the capacity for use.
Animal life depends upon the distribution, conjunction, and motions of the bodily soul through the limbs.
The will to act arises after the mind has conceived an image of the future action.
Venusian desire is a material disturbance of seed excited by a congruent simulacrum or body.
Offspring consists in the encounter and congruence of maternal and paternal seeds.
Simulacra of the dead do not prove that souls return from Acheron or that anything personal survives after the dissolution of body and mind.
Simulacra cannot be seen individually, although their frequent concurrence produces a visible thing.
Perspective illusions do not demonstrate that the eyes themselves lie.
The proposition that nothing can be known cannot affirm itself without contradiction.
Reason arising from the senses cannot refute the senses as universally false.
One sense cannot judge or convict the proper power of another sense.
Centaurs, Scyllas, and images of the dead do not require corresponding animate natures.
Echoes and reflected sounds do not require the presence of Satyrs, Nymphs, Fauns, or Pan.
Simulacra do not discern human will, nor do they artfully compose the motions of dreams.
Eyes, tongue, ears, and limbs were not created for future uses.
Sleep is not the complete expulsion of the soul from the body.
Sterility and fertility are not distributed by divine powers.
Venusian pleasure does not require exclusive love, nor is love sated by possession of the beloved body.
A sudden mirror image arises from the continual flow and reflection of simulacra.
By reason of their subtlety, lightness, and superficial position, simulacra preserve their shape and move most swiftly.
Vision occurs when a simulacrum strikes the eyes, while distance is perceived from the air set in motion before the image.
The placement, inversion, and multiplication of mirror images arise from the arrangement of airs, reflections, and bends of the surface.
Distant shapes, lights, shadows, and refracted bodies appear otherwise when transmission changes through impacts, intervals, or media.
Sensible appearance correctly indicates the present affection, while error arises from judgment about the cause, identity, or motion of the thing.
Voice is a body emitted by the speaker which strikes the ears, is confused through space, divided into many parts, and reflected by solids.
Tastes and odors produce different or contrary effects according to the shape of particles, the size of passages, and the texture of the animal.
Imagined monsters are composed from the concurrence of images of real parts, not from the existence of corresponding monsters.
In sleep, simulacra move the mind while the external senses rest and memory does not supply correction from the present thing.
Voluntary thought does not create images at will, but selects from the abundance already present images congruent with attention.
Voluntary motion proceeds from the image of motion to will, from will to the soul diffused through the limbs, and thence to the body aided by air.
Sleep arises when external and internal impacts disturb the disposition of the soul, expel one part, and drive another part inward.
Hunger and thirst are effects of the loss of bodies, the rarefaction of limbs, and the necessity of restoring congruent matter.
The utility of limbs is a subsequent effect of an already-born structure, not the cause of its origin.
Venusian pleasure can be common to both sexes because the body of each is moved by a congruent impact and mutual ardor.
Exclusive love grows when simulacra, memory, and opinion continually repeat the same object, although the body cannot be sated by images.
Resemblance, hereditary variation, and fertility arise from the proportion, mixture, and compatibility of the double seed.
Vision, hearing, smell, taste, thought, and desire vary a single material grammar of emission, passage, impact, and congruence.
Sensible truth and judicial falsity belong to different levels, whence appearance can be preserved while interpretation is corrected.
Material explanation reclassifies apparitions of the dead, monsters, gods of places, and dream motions from signs of another world into effects of transmission.
The human agent is not a principle of motion separate from matter, but a nexus of images, attention, will, soul, and body.
Biological capacities and uses emerge historically from structures, congruences, and habits already established.
Love is a recursive circuit in which image excites desire, desire increases opinion, opinion fixes attention, and attention perpetuates image.
The continuity of an apparent thing or motion is constructed from the most swift succession of perishing and substituted forms.
The correction of affects occurs not by repudiating the senses, but by retracting opinions, redirecting attention, and interrupting the fodder of images.
Sensible qualities are not absolute values enclosed in the object, but relations between impacting shapes and the structure of the recipient.
No perception occurs through incorporeal access, or without a medium, to the essence of the thing.
The stability of an image does not require a permanent form, because the succession of discrete forms supplies the effect of continuity.
Will does not begin from nothing, but depends on a prior image and material disposition.
A future use cannot be the temporal cause of an organ already constituted before use.
Beloved beauty does not necessarily contain the perfections which desire attributes to it.
The mind does not stand outside nature so as absolutely to govern the flow of images or judge the testimony of the senses from an extrinsic foundation.
A divine cause must not be admitted where the difference of shapes, motions, and congruences suffices to produce the effect.
The system requires no providential organizer to direct senses, limbs, desires, or generation toward pre-established ends.
No tribunal of knowledge external to and independent of the senses is available.
No enduring personal subject survives intact the dissolution of body and mind.
Total possession of the beloved body is impossible, because only simulacra, not the very body of the other, are incorporated by the lover.
The immobile presence of things is excluded, since perception and life consist in flow, impact, substitution, and recomposition.
Shaped first beginnings → composition of things → bodily efflux → transmission → impact upon recipient → sensible affection.
Surface of a thing → simulacrum retaining form → motion through air → eye struck → appearance of the thing → distance from air driven forth.
True sensible affection → added opinion of the mind → false attribution of causality or identity → reason grounded in the senses → distinction of the given from the added.
Difference of shapes and passages → different penetration or reflection → distinction of sight, voice, smell, and taste → variation according to recipient.
Abundance of simulacra → composition or succession → preparation of attention or habit → mental image → thought, dream, or apparition.
Impact or loss of bodies → change in the disposition of soul and body → sleep, hunger, thirst, or desire → restoration or compensatory motion.
Born structure → possible action → repetition → recognized use → art or habit; future use does not constitute the cause of origin.
Simulacrum of the beloved → disturbance of seed → desire → idealizing opinion → fixed attention → insatiability → pain; redirection of attention breaks the circuit.
Double seed → encounter → proportion and congruence → conception → mixture of the first beginnings of parents and ancestors → form of offspring.
Atomism already established → question concerning apparitions → posit of simulacra → proof through emissions and mirrors → explanation of vision.
Variety of appearances → analysis of media and impacts → distinction of sense from opinion → refutation of scepticism → senses as foundation of reason.
Common bodily causality → hearing, taste, and smell → mental images and dreams → will, motion, and sleep → rejection of finality.
Physiology of seed → Venusian desire → diagnosis of captive love → governance of attention → generation and habit materially explained.
Perception is reordered from the passive reception of an incorporeal species into a material commerce of emitting, passing, and striking.
The opposition of simple appearance and truth is dissolved through the distinction between the affection of sense and the opinion of mind.
The different senses are arranged as distinct channels of one bodily causality, not as judges to be mutually substituted.
Dreams, monsters, shades of the dead, and voices of places are transferred from a supernatural order into an order of composite and reflected images.
The utility of limbs is converted from a cause of origin into an effect of subsequent use.
Voluntary action is transferred from an immaterial command into a material series of imagination, will, soul, and body.
Love is separated from the absolute value of the object and described as captivation through simulacra, opinion, habit, and attention.
Fertility, inheritance, and difference of offspring are relocated from divine dominion into the field of the material compatibility of seeds.
Surface — Mirror images, perspective errors, voices, tastes, odors, dreams, motions, desires, and generations are the immediate objects to be explained.
Structural — All objects are connected through the emission of bodies, pathways of media, congruence of textures, and impacts upon organs.

Metastrategic — The text transfers the contest from repudiation of the senses to the separation of affection from opinion and seeks to weaken superstition, scepticism, and finality in the same movement.
Ontological/Temporal — Reality is a composition of bodies in flux, the subject is a mobile bodily nexus, and continuity arises from the most swift succession of effects.
The extracted axioms suffice to restore the principal movement from simulacra to the senses, mind, physiology, love, and generation.
Gaps in the source leave incomplete the demonstrations concerning the subtlety of images, their generation, mirrors, and certain examples of dreams.
The strongest coherence is where one model of emission, passage, and impact explains multiple senses and bodily processes.
The defence of the senses is stabilized by the distinction between what the sense undergoes and what the mind conjectures about the cause of the affection.
The proof of invisible simulacra relies on analogies with visible emissions and the exclusion of rival causes, not on direct inspection.
The assertion that every sensible appearance is true is reconciled with apparent distortions only if truth is restricted to affection, not to every judgment about the object.
The whole of reason is said to depend upon the senses, although first beginnings, individual simulacra, and minimal times exceed sense; the inferential transition is not fully formalized.
The origin of images spontaneously formed in the air and the exact selection of simulacra caused by attention are explained less determinately than sensible transmission.
The erotic part passes from material mechanism to the precept of avoiding or turning away from love through the estimation of punishment, not through an entirely necessary physical deduction.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement of the text: from bodily flux to cognition, from error to opinion, from function to emergence, and from desire to captivation and governance.
Quaestio est quomodo mundus, sidera, vita et instituta humana sine providentia divina oriri, ordinari et interire possint, ita ut religiosus timor tollatur.
Mundus est compositum nativum et mortale, ex primordiorum concursibus sine consilio ortum, cuius ordines naturales vitam, societatem et religionem generant.
Argumentatio est simul reconstructiva, polemica, genealogica et therapeutica: causas naturales restituit, exemplaria providentialia excludit et animum a metu purgat.
Demonstratio ab universis naturae finibus, mortalitate partium, defectibus mundi, analogiis sensibilibus et causarum naturalium possibilitate procedit.
Motus argumenti transit a sapientia purgatrice ad mortalitatem mundi, inde ad cosmogoniam, astronomiam, biogenesim, historiam humanam et originem religionis atque artium.
Cuique naturae potestas finita terminusque operationis certus inest.
Animus et sensus tantum in corpore animali apte disposito consistere possunt.
Natura deorum tenuis, beata et a rebus humanis remota neque utilitate neque novitatis desiderio ad mundum administrandum movetur.
Primordia rerum sine consilio sagaci ponderibus, plagis et motibus propriis feruntur.
Concursus primordiorum per tempus infinitum innumeras compositiones pertemptat, donec configurationes stabiles emergant.
Mundi membra sunt nativa, mortalia et per generationem consumptionemque mutabilia.
Totum ex partibus nativis mortalibusque constitutum eandem generationis et dissolutionis condicionem participat.
Mundus neque solidus neque clausus est, sed inane continet, ictibus externis patet et spatium habet in quod partes dissolutae discedant.
Natura mundi necessitatibus humanis non est apte ordinata, sed regiones inhabitabiles, labores, morbos, feras et mortem immaturam continet.
Ordines recurrentes ex primis condicionibus causalibus et stabilita rerum consecutione, non ex gubernatione divina, oriuntur.
Ubi effectus pluribus modis naturalibus fieri potest, plures causae physice possibiles disponendae sunt, quamquam una tantum actu viget.
Terra recens, calore et umore abundans, formas viventes naturaliter producere potuit.
Propagatio vitae cibum, organa congruentia, semina genitalia et mutuam corporum compatibilitatem requirit.
Genera viventium permanent si dolo, virtute, mobilitate aut utilitate hominibus praestita tutantur; deficientia pereunt.
Facultates, vocabula, pacta, instituta et artes humanae ex natura, utilitate, necessitate et experientia paulatim oriuntur.
Religio ex imaginibus deorum, ignoratione causarum caelestium et timore virium naturalium generatur.
Ignoratio finis habendi et verae voluptatis curas inanes, ambitionem, invidiam atque bellum generat.
Cognitio causarum naturalium timorem divinum et perturbationes animi dissolvere potest.
Mundus neque aeternus neque divino sensu praeditus est.
Natura rerum hominum causa non est creata.
Sol, luna et sidera neque libera voluntate neque divino imperio cursus suos agunt.
Animus neque sine corpore neque in quolibet corpore consistere potest.
Sedes deorum intra mundum non sunt, nec cultus humanus deos ad gubernationem rerum movet.
Ordo mundi non est dispositio primordiorum a mente sagaci instituta.
Pietas non consistit in ritibus, victimis, votis aut corporis humiliatione.
Summum beneficium humanum neque frugibus neque vino neque armata monstrorum victoria continetur.
Monstra ex membris naturarum incompatibilium compacta neque fuerunt neque generari possunt.
Vocabula rerum ab uno nominum auctore ceteris hominibus imposita non sunt.
Regna, proprietas, magistratus et leges neque prima neque immutabilia societatis humanae fundamenta sunt.
Incrementum opum et artium non constituit necessarium incrementum felicitatis.
Phenomenis caelestibus causa singularis certo definita non semper assignari potest.
Terra, mare, caelum et sidera sensu divino carent, quia dispositionem corporis animalis non habent.
Defectus et hostilitas mundi cum natura deorum beata componi non possunt si mundus opus providentiale hominum causa factum ponitur.
Mundus, quia ex partibus mortalibus constat et dissolutioni patet, ortum habuit et exitium habiturus est.
Mundus mortalis ab infinito tempore integer permanere non potuit; mortalitas eius nativitatem implicat.
Cosmogonia non requirit exemplar antecedens, quia innumeri concursus primordiorum configurationes mundi experiendo producunt.
Discretio terrae, maris, aeris et aetheris ex differentiis ponderum, figurarum, nexuum et motuum, non ex consilio, oritur.
Regularitas motuum caelestium cum causalitate naturali congruit neque voluntatem siderum aut imperium deorum probat.
Expositio plurium causarum naturalium sufficientium reditum ab admiratione caelesti ad religionem impedit, etiam si causa actualis nondum discernitur.
Terra formas multas producit, sed tantum genera condicionibus victus, propagationis et tutelae congruentia permanent.
Formae hybridae mythicae excluduntur quia membra discordantia neque eodem tempore crescunt neque iisdem victus et generationis legibus parent.
Lingua ex facultate vocis, sensuum varietate et utilitate communi emergit, non ex institutione unius legislatoris.
Familia, amicitia, pacta et leges ex vulnerabilitate mutua atque taedio violentiae paulatim constituuntur.
Ordo caelestis, ubi causae ignorantur, in imaginem potestatis divinae convertitur et timorem religiosum nutrit.
Progressus technicus per se ad quietem non convergit, quia novas opes, distinctiones, arma et certamina desiderii producit.
Doctrina quae cupiditates et timores expellit utilior est armis quae pericula externa tantum removent.
Pietas vera est rerum naturam mente pacata intueri, non potestates invisibiles ritibus placare.
Cosmogonia, biologia et historia humana unam continuitatem materialem constituunt: eadem natura compositiones cosmicas, formas viventes et instituta socialia sine ruptura supernaturali generat.
Ordo est stabilitas temporaria configurationum inter innumeras coniunctiones, non finis antecedenter praescriptus.
Mortalitas non est casus mundo extrinsecus accidens, sed effectus necessarius compositionis, permeabilitatis et conflictus partium.
Ad providentiam excludendam sufficit ostendere effectum naturaliter possibilem esse, quamquam ad historiam physicam completam causa actualis discernenda manet.
Civilizatio pericula naturae minuit, sed per opes, dominationem et artem bellicam pericula collectiva maiora generare potest.
Religio circuitum sui conservationis efficit: ignorantia causae timorem parit, timor attributionem divinam, attributio divina maiorem observationis anxietatem.
Dignitas divina a creatione mundi ad liberationem animi transfertur: creator providentialis excluditur, inventor autem sapientiae propter vim purgatricem honorifice deus appellatur.
Tempus naturalis historiae est successio statuum irreversibilium, in qua quod ante potuit postea nequit et novae facultates ex condicionibus mutatis oriuntur.
Ignorantia causae naturalis testimonium causae divinae esse non potest.
Regularitas effectuum intentionem ordinatricem tacite non implicat.
Homo neque finis cosmici processus neque mensura aptitudinis mundi est.
Stabilitas foederum naturalium aeternitatem mundorum, specierum aut institutionum non implicat.
Lingua, lex, proprietas et valor auctoritatem transcendentem ad suam validitatem non requirunt.
Potentia politica, divitiae et ars technica securitatem stabilem praestare non possunt.
Permanentia generis perfectionem non probat, sed tantum sufficientem congruentiam cum condicionibus conservationis.
Fama poetica et figura mythica limites physicae possibilitatis superare non possunt.
Indeterminatio causae particularis eventum neque supernaturalem neque omnino inexplicabilem reddit.
Concursus fortuitus primordiorum ab foederibus naturae solutus non est.
Systema nullum custodem cosmicum, iudicem providentem aut rectorem historiae admittit.
Nulla mundi aeternitas humanis operibus, civitatibus aut speciei permanentiam spondet.
Historia humana neque ad perfectionem necessariam neque ad ultimum artium et imperii statum ordinatur.
Nulla dignitas politica, oeconomica aut technica naturali ordine semel constituto immobilis manet.
Salus animi neque a cultu divino neque ab abundantia materiali neque ab externa victoria provenit.
Certitudo singularis de omni causa caelesti indisponibilis esse potest neque tamen naturalem explicationem impedit.

Machina principalis ita procedit: foedera finita naturae → exclusio animi cosmici et providentiae → generatio mundi ex concursibus → mortalitas compositi → naturalis genealogia vitae et societatis → purgatio timoris.
Circuitus cosmologicus est: primordia mota → concursus innumeri → coetus stabilis → discretio elementorum → fluxus et conflictus membrorum → dissolutio mundi.
Exemplar biologicum est: terra recens → multiplicitas formarum → probatio per victum et generationem → tutela aut defectus → propagatio aut interitus.
Genealogia humana est: vita dispersa → ignis, habitatio et coniunctio familiaris → pacta et voces → proprietas et regnum → ambitio et eversio → leges → artes, opes et bellum.
Circuitus religiosus et eius solutio sunt: spectaculum caeleste → egestas rationis → attributio divina → timor et ritus → causae naturales possibiles → mens pacata.

Motus textualis transit a divinizatione sapientiae purgatricis ad propositum doctrinae, inde ad mortalitatem mundi, cosmogoniam, causas astrorum, ortum viventium, historiam societatis, religionis, metallorum, belli et artium.

Motus inferentialis recurrens transit ab effectu observato ad fines naturae, a finibus ad causam naturalem possibilem, a causa possibili ad exclusionem gubernationis divinae, atque ab exclusione ad tranquillitatem animi.
Sapientia denuo describitur ut ars liberationis interioris, cuius utilitas dona materialia et victoriam armatam superat.
Mundus ex sede vel corpore divino in compositum materiale nativum et dissolubile transfertur.
Ordo naturalis a consilio antecedente separatur et ut effectus stabilitatis post innumeros concursus intelligitur.
Astronomia ab interpretatione religiosorum signorum ad agrum causarum naturalium plurium transfertur.
Genera viventium non ut formae perfecte datae, sed ut effectus productionis, congruentiae, tutelae et extinctionis ordinantur.
Religio ex veritate de rebus divinis in effectum imaginum, ignorantiae causalis et timoris reclassificatur.
Lingua, lex, regnum et ars ex institutionibus originariis in eventus genealogicos utilitatis et experientiae mutantur.
Progressus technicus ab incremento necessario boni separatur et ut amplificator simul commodorum, desideriorum et belli ponitur.
Pietas ab obsequio rituali ad contemplationem naturae mente pacata transfertur.
Surface — Mundus mortalis esse demonstratur, motus caelestes naturaliter explicantur, atque origines vitae et cultus humani exponuntur.
Structural — Concursus primordiorum, mortalitas partium, selectio formarum viabilium, utilitas et conflictus mechanismos cosmicos, biologicos et sociales constituunt.
Metastrategic — Explanatio naturalis quaestionem ab imperio deorum ad limites possibilitatis materialis transfert et religionem in genealogiam timoris convertit.
Ontological/Temporal — Realitas ex compositis temporalibus, potestatibus finitis et statuum successione constat; permanentia localis sine aeternitate vel fine providentiali emergit.
Axiomata sufficiunt ad mortalitatem mundi, generationem naturalem ordinis, genealogiam vitae et societatis atque finem therapeuticum restituenda.
Structura firmissima est ubi causalitas naturalis, limites potestatum et mortalitas compositionis contra providentiam coniunguntur.
Systema cohaeret si foedera naturae stabilia a configurationibus et statibus temporaliter mutabilibus distinguuntur.
Pluralitas causarum astronomicarum supernaturalem necessitatem infirmat, sed causam actualem saepe indeterminatam relinquit.
Transitus a mortalitate partium ad mortalitatem totius vi regulae compositionis nititur, cuius ambitus potius affirmatur quam separatim demonstratur.
Argumentum a recentia monumentorum et artium ad recentiam mundi fragile manet, quia priora excidia admitti possunt; ea tamen mortalitatem mundi confirmant.
Generatio viventium e terra recenti analogiis praesentibus et congruentiae principiis nititur, non observatione directa originis.
Lacuna fontis transitum inter coniunctionem domesticam et primam mollitiem socialem incompletum relinquit, quamquam posterior pactarum relationum series servatur.
Appellatio inventoris sapientiae ut dei et remotio deorum ontologicorum a rebus humanis distinctionem honorificam requirunt quam textus non plene formalizat.
Restitutio verum motum servat: a purificatione animi per cosmologiam naturalem ad genealogiam vitae, religionis et civilis ambivalentiae procedit.
The question is how the world, stars, life, and human institutions can arise, be ordered, and perish without divine providence, such that religious fear is removed.
The world is a native and mortal composite, arisen from collisions of first-beginnings without design, whose natural orders generate life, society, and religion.
The argumentation is at once reconstructive, polemical, genealogical, and therapeutic: it restores natural causes, excludes providential models, and purges the mind of fear.
The demonstration proceeds from the universal limits of nature, the mortality of parts, the defects of the world, sensible analogies, and the possibility of natural causes.
The movement of the argument passes from purgative wisdom to the mortality of the world, thence to cosmogony, astronomy, biogenesis, human history, and the origin of religion and the arts.
In every nature there inheres a finite power and a determinate limit of operation.
Mind and sensation can subsist only in an animal body suitably arranged.
The nature of the gods, subtle, blessed, and removed from human affairs, is moved to administer the world neither by utility nor by desire for novelty.
The first-beginnings of things are borne without intelligent design by their own weights, blows, and motions.
The collisions of first-beginnings, through infinite time, try innumerable compositions until stable configurations emerge.
The members of the world are native, mortal, and mutable through generation and consumption.
A whole constituted from native and mortal parts shares the same condition of generation and dissolution.
The world is neither solid nor closed, but contains void, lies open to external blows, and has space into which its dissolved parts may depart.
The nature of the world is not suitably ordered for human needs, but contains uninhabitable regions, labors, diseases, wild beasts, and premature death.
Recurrent orders arise from initial causal conditions and the established succession of things, not from divine governance.
Where an effect can occur in several natural ways, several physically possible causes must be set forth, although only one is actually operative.
The young earth, abounding in heat and moisture, could naturally produce living forms.
The propagation of life requires food, suitable organs, generative seeds, and the mutual compatibility of bodies.
Kinds of living beings persist if they are protected by cunning, strength, mobility, or utility afforded to human beings; through deficiency they perish.
Human faculties, words, compacts, institutions, and arts gradually arise from nature, utility, necessity, and experience.
Religion is generated from images of gods, ignorance of celestial causes, and fear of natural forces.
Ignorance of the end to be attained and of true pleasure generates vain anxieties, ambition, envy, and war.
Knowledge of natural causes can dissolve divine fear and disturbances of mind.
The world is neither eternal nor endowed with divine sensation.
The nature of things was not created for the sake of human beings.
The sun, moon, and stars do not pursue their courses either by free will or by divine command.
Mind can subsist neither without a body nor in any body whatsoever.
The abodes of the gods are not within the world, nor does human worship move the gods to govern affairs.
The order of the world is not an arrangement of first-beginnings established by an intelligent mind.
Piety does not consist in rites, sacrifices, vows, or humiliation of the body.
The highest human benefit is contained neither in crops, nor wine, nor the armed defeat of monsters.
Monsters compounded from the members of incompatible natures neither existed nor can be generated.
The names of things were not imposed upon other human beings by a single originator of names.
Kingdoms, property, magistracies, and laws are neither the first nor immutable foundations of human society.
The increase of wealth and arts does not constitute a necessary increase in happiness.
A singular, certainly determined cause cannot always be assigned to celestial phenomena.
Earth, sea, heaven, and stars lack divine sensation because they do not possess the arrangement of an animal body.
The defects and hostility of the world cannot be reconciled with the blessed nature of the gods if the world is posited as a providential work made for the sake of human beings.
The world, because it consists of mortal parts and is open to dissolution, had an origin and will have destruction.
The mortal world could not have remained whole from infinite time; its mortality entails its birth.
Cosmogony does not require a prior model, because innumerable collisions of first-beginnings produce configurations of the world by trial.
The differentiation of earth, sea, air, and ether arises from differences of weights, shapes, connections, and motions, not from design.
The regularity of celestial motions accords with natural causality and proves neither the will of the stars nor the command of the gods.
The exposition of several sufficient natural causes prevents a return from celestial wonder to religion, even if the actual cause is not yet discerned.
The earth produces many forms, but only kinds suited to the conditions of sustenance, propagation, and protection endure.
Mythical hybrid forms are excluded because discordant members neither grow at the same time nor obey the same laws of sustenance and generation.
Language emerges from the faculty of voice, the variety of perceptions, and common utility, not from the institution of one lawgiver.
Family, friendship, compacts, and laws are gradually constituted from mutual vulnerability and weariness of violence.
Celestial order, where causes are unknown, is transformed into an image of divine power and nourishes religious fear.
Technical progress does not of itself tend toward tranquility, because it produces new resources, distinctions, weapons, and contests of desire.
A doctrine that expels desires and fears is more useful than arms that remove only external dangers.
True piety is to behold the nature of things with a tranquil mind, not to propitiate invisible powers with rites.
Cosmogony, biology, and human history constitute one material continuity: the same nature generates cosmic compositions, living forms, and social institutions without supernatural rupture.
Order is the temporary stability of configurations among innumerable conjunctions, not an end prescribed in advance.
Mortality is not an accident befalling the world from outside, but a necessary effect of the composition, permeability, and conflict of its parts.
To exclude providence, it is sufficient to show that an effect is naturally possible, although for a complete physical history the actual cause remains to be discerned.
Civilization diminishes the dangers of nature, but through wealth, domination, and the art of war it can generate greater collective dangers.
Religion produces a circuit of self-preservation: ignorance of a cause begets fear, fear divine attribution, divine attribution greater anxiety of observation.

Divine dignity is transferred from the creation of the world to the liberation of the mind: the providential creator is excluded, but the discoverer of wisdom is honorifically called a god on account of his purgative power.
The time of natural history is a succession of irreversible states, in which what could be before cannot be afterward, and new faculties arise from altered conditions.
Ignorance of a natural cause cannot be evidence of a divine cause.
The regularity of effects does not tacitly entail an ordering intention.
The human being is neither the end of the cosmic process nor the measure of the world's fitness.
The stability of natural compacts does not entail the eternity of worlds, species, or institutions.
Language, law, property, and value do not require transcendent authority for their validity.
Political power, riches, and technical art cannot provide stable security.
The persistence of a kind does not prove perfection, but only sufficient suitability to conditions of preservation.
Poetic fame and mythical form cannot surpass the limits of physical possibility.
The indeterminacy of a particular cause does not render an event either supernatural or wholly inexplicable.
The fortuitous collision of first-beginnings is not free from the compacts of nature.
The system admits no cosmic guardian, provident judge, or ruler of history.
No eternity of the world guarantees permanence to human works, cities, or the species.
Human history is ordered neither toward necessary perfection nor toward an ultimate state of the arts and empire.
No political, economic, or technical dignity remains immovable once established by natural order.
The salvation of the mind proceeds neither from divine worship, nor material abundance, nor external victory.
Singular certainty concerning every celestial cause may be unavailable and yet does not impede natural explanation.

The principal mechanism proceeds thus: finite compacts of nature → exclusion of cosmic mind and providence → generation of the world from collisions → mortality of the composite → natural genealogy of life and society → purgation of fear.
The cosmological circuit is: moving first-beginnings → innumerable collisions → stable aggregate → differentiation of elements → flux and conflict of members → dissolution of the world.
The biological model is: young earth → multiplicity of forms → testing through sustenance and generation → protection or deficiency → propagation or destruction.
The human genealogy is: dispersed life → fire, habitation, and family union → compacts and voices → property and kingship → ambition and overthrow → laws → arts, wealth, and war.
The religious circuit and its dissolution are: celestial spectacle → poverty of reason → divine attribution → fear and rites → possible natural causes → tranquil mind.

The textual movement passes from the divinization of purgative wisdom to the purpose of doctrine, thence to the mortality of the world, cosmogony, the causes of the stars, the origin of living beings, the history of society, religion, metals, war, and the arts.

The recurrent inferential movement passes from an observed effect to the limits of nature, from limits to a possible natural cause, from possible cause to the exclusion of divine governance, and from exclusion to tranquility of mind.
Wisdom is again described as an art of inner liberation, whose utility surpasses material gifts and armed victory.
The world is transferred from a divine abode or body into a native and dissoluble material composite.
Natural order is separated from prior design and understood as the effect of stability after innumerable collisions.
Astronomy is transferred from the interpretation of religious signs to the field of multiple natural causes.
Kinds of living beings are ordered not as perfectly given forms, but as effects of production, suitability, protection, and extinction.
Religion is reclassified from truth concerning divine things into an effect of images, causal ignorance, and fear.
Language, law, kingship, and art are transformed from original institutions into genealogical events of utility and experience.
Technical progress is separated from the necessary increase of good and posited as an amplifier at once of conveniences, desires, and war.
Piety is transferred from ritual obedience to the contemplation of nature with a tranquil mind.
Surface — The world is demonstrated to be mortal, celestial motions are naturally explained, and the origins of life and human culture are set forth.
Structural — Collisions of first-beginnings, mortality of parts, selection of viable forms, utility, and conflict constitute cosmic, biological, and social mechanisms.
Metastrategic — Natural explanation transfers the question from the rule of the gods to the limits of material possibility and converts religion into a genealogy of fear.
Ontological/Temporal — Reality consists of temporal composites, finite powers, and a succession of states; local permanence emerges without eternity or providential end.
The axioms suffice for reconstructing the mortality of the world, the natural generation of order, the genealogy of life and society, and the therapeutic end.
The structure is strongest where natural causality, limits of powers, and mortality of composition are joined against providence.
The system coheres if stable compacts of nature are distinguished from temporally mutable configurations and states.
The plurality of astronomical causes weakens supernatural necessity, but often leaves the actual cause indeterminate.
The transition from the mortality of parts to the mortality of the whole rests on the force of the rule of composition, whose scope is asserted rather than separately demonstrated.

The argument from the recentness of monuments and arts to the recentness of the world remains fragile, because earlier destructions can be admitted; nevertheless, these confirm the mortality of the world.
The generation of living beings from the young earth rests on present analogies and principles of suitability, not on direct observation of origin.
A gap in the source leaves incomplete the transition between domestic union and the first social softening, although the subsequent series of contractual relations is preserved.
The appellation of the discoverer of wisdom as a god and the removal of ontological gods from human affairs require an honorific distinction that the text does not fully formalize.
The reconstruction preserves the true movement: it proceeds from purification of the mind through natural cosmology to the genealogy of life, religion, and civil ambivalence.
Quaeritur quomodo metus caelestium, terrestrium morborumque tolli possit, cum commoda externa anxietatem animi non tollant.
Ratio naturae animum purgat, quia eventus intra fines potestatum materialium explicat et regimen divinum a causalitate mundi excludit.
Argumentatio diagnostica, polemica, reconstructiva atque therapeutica est: timorem ad ignorantiam, ignorantiam ad falsam religionem, utramque ad cognitionem causarum refert.
Motus argumenti ab animi receptaculo vitioso ad corpora, inane, motus et texturas tamquam grammaticam communem eventuum progreditur.
Unumquodque phaenomenon ex signis sensibilibus ad causas naturales possibiles reducitur, dum explicationes divinae per limites potestatum et distributionem effectuum refutantur.
Pestilentia argumentum a physicis causis ad mortalitatem biologicam et dissolutionem socialem producit, ostendens intellegentiam naturae non idem esse ac remedium vel imperium.
Exteriorum bonorum copia anxietatem non tollit, si animi receptaculum fluxum, inexplebile vel corruptivum manet.
Animi sanatio fines cupidinis ac timoris et rationem summi boni determinari postulat.
Terror animi non lumine sensibili, sed conspectu naturae et ratione dissolvitur.
Ignorantia causarum eventus naturales ad deorum imperium refert.
Dei aevum securum et placidum agunt nec eventus mundi ira aut arbitrio administrant.
Mundus caelumque corporea, nata, mortalia et dissolubilia sunt.
Nullum corpus manifestum omnino plenum est; omne ex corpore et inani contextum est.
Potestas cuiusque naturae finita est et certo termino continetur.
Ab omnibus rebus corpora perpetuo fluunt et in circumiecta spatia sparguntur.
Texturae primordiorum et formae viarum determinant quae corpora inter se recipiant, penetrent, iungantur vel repellantur.
Motus materialis per concursum, ictum, pressionem, pondus et loci inanitionem mutationes naturales efficit.
Causae occultae ex effectibus manifestis et analogiis rerum sensibilium inferuntur.
Quorundam effectuum causa singularis determinari nequit; plures causae naturales possibiles enumerandae sunt, quarum una reapse operatur.
Summa rerum infinita et mobilitas primordiorum materiam sufficientem eventibus localibus suppeditant.
Regiones propter diversam corporum compositionem diversos effectus in animantes producunt.
Semina morbida ex externo caelo vel terra corrupta coire, aerem, aquas cibosque inficere, corpora intrare et ab aliis ad alios propagari possunt.
In clade contagiosa propinquitas ad aegros contagionem auget, absentia autem eos auxilio privat.
Divitiae, honores, laus et fama domesticam anxietatem per se non sanant.
Radii solis et lux diei tenebras animi non discutiunt.
Tonitrua, fulmina, terrae motus, eruptiones et pestilentiae non sunt actus irae vel arbitrii divini.
Falsa opinio de deis deos non violat, sed tranquillitatem opinantis corrumpit.
Fulmen poenam moralem non distribuit, quia innocentes, loca deserta, montes, templa et simulacra indiscrete ferit.
Carmina divinatoria occultam deorum mentem non aperiunt nec naturam fulminis explicant.
Loca Averna non sunt ianuae Orci nec casus animantium transitum animarum ad inferos probat.
Fons noctu calidus non a sole per crassam terram penetrante calefit.
Magnitudo insolita eventus supernaturalitatem eius non probat.
Unica causa certa non est condicio necessaria omnis explicationis naturalis.
Mundus incorruptae et aeternae saluti non est mandatus.
In pestilentia certa communisque ratio remedii non necessario praesto est.
Nec religio nec mos sepulturae sub vi praesentis doloris inviolabilis manet.
Therapia ad formam animi corrigendam, non ad infinitam bonorum externorum accumulationem dirigitur.
Etiam cognita deorum tranquillitate, admiratio sine cognitione causarum ad veterem religionem relabitur.
Eventus caelestes et terrestres eadem grammatica corporum, inanis et motuum explicantur.
Penetratio, attractio et actio inter corpora distantia per effluvia, foramina et displacementem medii effici possunt.
Diversitas effectuum ex aptitudine selectiva texturarum et viarum, non ex qualitate occulta indeterminata, deducitur.
Pluralitas causarum legitima manet, si unaquaeque causa effectui, signis et finibus naturae congruit.
Exemplar gubernationis divinae deficit, quia eventuum distributio nec voluntatem constantem nec discrimen morale exhibet.
Eventus localiter ingens pars exigua summae rerum esse potest atque ideo ordinem naturalem non excedit.
Morborum regionalium diversitas ex compositione locali caeli, aquarum, terrae et corporum explicatur.
Organismus ambitu suo materialiter continuus est, quia corpora externa per aerem, cibum, aquam et foramina corporis recipit.
Contagio officium curandi in structuram duplicis periculi convertit, qua praesentia curantem, fuga aegrotum perdit.
Materialis pestilentia, ubi remedium commune deest, ordines curae, religionis et sepulturae dissolvere potest.
Physica munus ethicum gerit, quia emendatio opinionum causalium fines timori cupidinique imponit.
Eadem ontologia materialis caelum, terram, corpora animantia et pestilentiam complectitur, quamvis mechanismi particulares varientur.
Pluralismus causalis non in relativismum abit, quia possibilia per signa, texturas et potestatum fines restringuntur.
Recta pietas deos a gubernatione mundi removet, quoniam pax divina cum administratione irata rerum componi nequit.
Meritium, innocentia et sanctitas nullam vim causaliter determinantem in distributione calamitatum habent.
Subiectum humanum non est unitas clausa, sed nodus permeabilis intra circulationem corporum ambientalium.
Contingentia concursus intra necessitates potestatum materialium operatur; casus eventum eligit, non rationem naturae tollit.
Intelligibilitas naturalis neque remedium certum neque imperium practicum neque conservationem ordinis socialis praestat.
Quod causa nondum cognita est, inde gubernator divinus inferri non potest.
Admiratio et magnitudo percepta auctoritatem epistemicam per se non habent.
Ordo physicus non continet legem qua eventus secundum meritum morale distribuuntur.
Explicatio naturalis non semper cognitionem unius causae actualis requirit.
Mensura humana magnitudinis non est mensura summae rerum.
Terminus inter corpus et ambitum neque clausus neque causaliter absolutus est.
Regularitas naturae providentiam, propositum morale vel ordinationem ad usum humanum non implicat.
Naturalitas causae neque benignitatem effectus neque facultatem eius coercendi implicat.
Providentia divina ex systemate tamquam principium supervacuum et cum pace deorum incompatibile excluditur.
Humanitas neque centrum summae rerum neque mensura magnitudinis aut finalitatis cosmicae est.
Nulla immunitas ontologica hominibus, innocentibus, templis aut ipsi mundo conceditur.
Clausura epistemica totalis et dominium practicum naturae indisponibilia manent, quamvis fines causarum cognoscantur.
Calamitas causam materialem habet, sed nullum destinatarium moralem vel auctorem iratum requirit.
Geographia naturae nullam aperturam ad regnum poenale post mortem admittere cogitur.
Machina therapeutica hunc ordinem sequitur: copia externa sine receptaculo sano → inexpletio et corruptio → cupiditas ac timor → definitio finium → tranquillitas.
Machina diagnostica hunc ordinem sequitur: phaenomenon terribile → ignorantia causae → attributio divina → timor religiosus → inquisitio materialis → remotio gubernationis divinae.
Machina explicativa hunc ordinem sequitur: effectus sensibilis → signa et analogiae → fines potestatum → mechanismi possibiles → selectio causae vel pluralitas conclusa.
Machina interactionis hunc ordinem sequitur: corpus cum inani → emanatio corporum → viae selectivae → pressio, penetratio, coniunctio vel repulsio → effectus manifestus.
Machina pestilentiae hunc ordinem sequitur: semina morbida → corruptio aeris vel alimentorum → ingressus in corpora → contagio → dilemmata curae → dissolutio remedii, ritus et ordinis socialis.
Clausura systematis hunc ordinem sequitur: cognitio causarum → cognitio finium → imminutio admirationis → remotio timoris divini → pax animi et rectior deorum conceptio.

Inventio therapeutica → diagnosis animi vitiosi → necessitas rationis naturae → mortalitas mundi → explicatio caelestium → explicatio terrestrium → interactiones singulares → pestilentia → dissolutio socialis.
In singulis tractationibus motus recurrit: admiratio vel terror → effectus observatus → mechanismus materialis unus vel multiplex → refutatio causae divinae → reductio timoris.
Securitas ab possessione rerum externarum ad capacitatem animi eas recipiendi transfertur.
Religio terrifica ex cognitione deorum in effectum ignorantiae causarum reclassificatur.
Oppositio inter pietatem et naturalismum corruit, quia pax deorum per exclusionem interventus divini servatur.
Pluralitas causarum ex defectu rationis in formam disciplinae causaliter restrictae convertitur.
Caelum, terra, corpus et morbus in unum continuum mechanismorum materialium rediguntur.
Miraculum ex genere separato rerum in effectum magnitudinis, raritatis et ignorantiae transfertur.
Corpus animatum ex unitate clausa in structuram permeabilem et ambientaliter dependentem reclassificatur.
Calamitas ex iudicio morali in processum materialem cum effectibus biologicis, socialibus et ritualibus reordinatur.
Cognitio naturae a promissione remedii, tutelae vel imperii practici distinguitur.
In gradu superficiei explicantur eventus caelestes, terrestres, magnetici, morbidi et pestilentiales qui admirationem vel timorem movent.
In gradu structurali eventus ex corporibus, inani, effluviis, texturis, viis, motibus et compositionibus localibus generantur.
In gradu metastrategico certamen a placandis potestatibus divinis ad corrigendas opiniones et definiendos fines causalium potentiarum transfertur.
In gradu ontologico et temporali realitas ex corporibus mortalibus, compositione, dissolutione, contingentibus concursibus et summa infinita constat.
Corpus axiomatum sufficit ad motum ab anxietate animi per naturalem causalitatem ad pestilentiae consequentias restituendum.
Summi boni materia et plena doctrina cupidinis ac timoris praesupponuntur potius quam hoc libro determinate explicantur.
Multorum eventuum mechanismus actualis indeterminatus manet, quia textus saepe possibilitatem naturalem demonstrat sine causa singulari eligenda.
Systema interne cohaeret, quia pluralitatem mechanismorum cum unitate ontologiae et finibus potestatum componit; contradictio directa non emergit.
Firmissima commissura est nexus inter ignorantiam causarum, attributionem divinam, timorem et disciplinam finium naturalium.
Fragilitas principalis in analogiis consistit, quae mechanismi possibilitatem firmant sed eius actualitatem non semper probant.
Affirmatio rationis verissimae cum frequenti pluralitate causarum tensionem gignit inter certitudinem therapeuticam et modestiam epistemicam.
Promissio purificationis animi a pestilentiae clausura comprimitur, quia cognitio naturalis nec remedium commune nec stabilitatem socialem praestat.
Dei tamquam entia pacata servantur, sed eorum status ontologicus et relatio ad simulacra divina intra hanc machinam non plene derivantur.
Lacunae fontis nexus quosdam locales relinquunt, sed restitutio servat motum principalem a therapia animi ad physicam causarum et inde ad vulnerabilitatem mortalem.
It is asked how fear of celestial, terrestrial, and diseased things may be removed, since external advantages do not remove anxiety of mind.
The account of nature purifies the mind, because it explains events within the limits of material powers and excludes divine governance from the causality of the world.
The argumentation is diagnostic, polemical, reconstructive, and therapeutic: it refers fear to ignorance, ignorance to false religion, and both to knowledge of causes.
The movement of the argument proceeds from the defective receptacle of the mind to bodies, void, motions, and textures as the common grammar of events.
Each phenomenon is reduced from sensible signs to possible natural causes, while divine explanations are refuted through the limits of powers and the distribution of effects.
Plague carries the argument from physical causes to biological mortality and social dissolution, showing that understanding nature is not the same as remedy or control.
An abundance of external goods does not remove anxiety if the receptacle of the mind remains fluid, insatiable, or corruptive.
The healing of the mind requires the limits of desire and fear, and the account of the highest good, to be determined.
Terror of mind is dissolved not by sensible light, but by the sight of nature and by reason.
Ignorance of causes refers natural events to the rule of the gods.
The gods live a secure and tranquil eternity and do not administer the events of the world by anger or will.
The world and heaven are bodily, born, mortal, and dissoluble.
No manifest body is wholly full; every one is woven together from body and void.
The power of every nature is finite and contained by a fixed limit.
From all things bodies continually flow and are scattered into the surrounding spaces.
The textures of first-beginnings and the forms of passages determine which bodies receive, penetrate, join with, or repel one another.
Material motion produces natural changes through collision, impact, pressure, weight, and the evacuation of place.
Hidden causes are inferred from manifest effects and analogies of sensible things.
The single cause of certain effects cannot be determined; several possible natural causes must be enumerated, one of which actually operates.
The infinite totality of things and the mobility of first-beginnings supply sufficient matter for local events.
Regions, on account of the diverse composition of bodies, produce diverse effects in living beings.
Disease-bearing seeds may gather from an external heaven or corrupted earth, infect air, waters, and foods, enter bodies, and spread from some to others.
In a contagious calamity, proximity to the sick increases contagion, whereas absence deprives them of aid.
Riches, honors, praise, and fame do not of themselves heal domestic anxiety.
The rays of the sun and the light of day do not dispel the darkness of the mind.
Thunder, lightning, earthquakes, eruptions, and plagues are not acts of divine anger or will.
A false opinion about the gods does not violate the gods, but corrupts the tranquility of the one holding the opinion.
Lightning does not distribute moral punishment, because it strikes indiscriminately the innocent, deserted places, mountains, temples, and images.
Divinatory songs do not disclose the hidden mind of the gods, nor do they explain the nature of lightning.
Avernian places are not gates of Orcus, nor does the falling of living beings prove the passage of souls to the underworld.
A spring warm by night is not heated by the sun penetrating through thick earth.
The unusual magnitude of an event does not prove its supernatural character.
One certain cause is not a necessary condition of every natural explanation.
The world has not been entrusted with incorruptible and eternal preservation.
In plague, a certain and common means of remedy is not necessarily at hand.
Neither religion nor the custom of burial remains inviolate under the force of present suffering.
Therapy is directed toward correcting the form of the mind, not toward the infinite accumulation of external goods.
Even when the tranquility of the gods is known, wonder without knowledge of causes falls back into the old religion.
Celestial and terrestrial events are explained by the same grammar of bodies, void, and motions.
Penetration, attraction, and action between distant bodies may be effected through effluvia, openings, and displacement of the medium.
The diversity of effects is deduced from the selective suitability of textures and passages, not from an indeterminate hidden quality.
A plurality of causes remains legitimate if each cause accords with the effect, the signs, and the limits of nature.
The model of divine governance fails, because the distribution of events displays neither constant will nor moral discrimination.
An event immense locally may be a small part of the totality of things and therefore does not exceed natural order.
The diversity of regional diseases is explained by the local composition of the sky, waters, earth, and bodies.
The organism is materially continuous with its environment, because it receives external bodies through air, food, water, and bodily openings.
Contagion transforms the duty of care into a structure of double danger, in which presence destroys the caregiver and flight destroys the sick person.
Material plague, where a common remedy is lacking, can dissolve the orders of care, religion, and burial.
Physics performs an ethical function, because the correction of causal opinions imposes limits upon fear and desire.
The same material ontology encompasses heaven, earth, living bodies, and plague, although particular mechanisms vary.
Causal pluralism does not lapse into relativism, because possibilities are constrained by signs, textures, and limits of powers.
Right piety removes the gods from governance of the world, since divine peace cannot be reconciled with an angry administration of things.
Merit, innocence, and sanctity have no causally determining force in the distribution of calamities.
The human subject is not a closed unity, but a permeable node within the circulation of environmental bodies.
The contingency of encounters operates within the necessities of material powers; chance selects the event, but does not remove the account of nature.
Natural intelligibility guarantees neither a certain remedy, nor practical control, nor preservation of social order.
From the fact that a cause is not yet known, a divine governor cannot be inferred.
Wonder and perceived magnitude have no epistemic authority in themselves.
Physical order does not contain a law by which events are distributed according to moral merit.
Natural explanation does not always require knowledge of one actual cause.
The human measure of magnitude is not the measure of the totality of things.
The boundary between body and environment is neither closed nor causally absolute.
The regularity of nature does not imply providence, moral purpose, or an ordering for human use.
The naturalness of a cause implies neither the beneficence of its effect nor the capacity to restrain it.
Divine providence is excluded from the system as a superfluous principle and one incompatible with the peace of the gods.
Humanity is neither the center of the totality of things nor the measure of cosmic magnitude or finality.
No ontological immunity is granted to human beings, the innocent, temples, or the world itself.
Total epistemic closure and practical mastery of nature remain unavailable, even though the limits of causes are known.
Calamity has a material cause, but requires no moral recipient or angry author.
